## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library**, entire, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully corrected by comparison with one another and with certain manuscript codices; continually illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and every author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched by two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is easy for the reader to discover which Fathers commented on the individual texts of the several books of Scripture, and in which places in their works they did so.

A most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others if the following are taken into consideration: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the extremely convenient format of the volumes and its consistent uniformity throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection itself—unique, systematic, and chronological—which for the first time gathers together in our library six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, assembled from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

**Second Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the universal library of the clergy, or complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition is sold for 1,200 francs per thousand volumes; the Greek-Latin for 1,300 francs per thousand. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are supplied in it only in Latin translation.

# In the Year of Our Lord 960  
## Atto, Bishop of Vercelli

# Preliminary Matter

*(From the Vercelli edition of 1768, prepared by Don Carlo Burontius del Signore.)*

[Col. 0009]

## Dedication

**To the most excellent prince Victor Amadeus, Duke of Savoy, Carlo Burontius del Signore.**

Why I have dared to raise my eyes even to you, and have hoped that you would receive this work of mine, whatever its quality, with a grateful spirit, most illustrious Prince, the matter itself will say better than I can.

The works of Atto, bishop of our Church eight centuries ago, partly already published by Don Luca d’Achery in the *Spicilegium*, though weakened by numerous gaps and lacunae, and partly hitherto lying obscurely in our chapter archive, are now at last being brought into public view complete and everywhere conformed to the authority of the autograph. They could neither seek nor have another patron than one who, by hereditary example and by reason of intellect and dignity, must rightly be regarded as a supporter, guardian, and defender of religion, morals, ecclesiastical discipline, and letters.

Receive, therefore, with your customary kindness, most humane Prince, these works which are now brought to light both by the zeal and confidence of my colleagues toward me and by my own care. Continue to preserve this Church, myself, and all my associates under your patronage, while we daily pray God to grant every prosperity to you and to the royal family; and be pleased to commend us most earnestly to our excellent father, our most august king.

---

[Col. 0009]

## Carlo Burontius del Signore to the Benevolent Reader

[Col. 0009A]

As we were planning to make Atto’s works public, it seemed worthwhile briefly to preface them with some remarks about the author, the works themselves, and our edition of them.

## On the Author

### I

That two men named Atto held the episcopal see of Vercelli, and that our Atto was the later in age, has been reported in writing by Rossotto in his *Syllabus* and by d’Achery in the *Spicilegium*. Yet among us there survives the memory of only one Atto, celebrated for his writings and deeds; of any other who either preceded or followed him by some years, we possess nothing in the monuments.

### II

We infer that Atto came here from a distant region from what he says at the conclusion of his *Exposition of the Epistles of Saint Paul*:

“You granted that, because of the taste and sweetness of this life, I should leave my nation and fatherland.”

For the rest, the writers who mention him do not agree with certainty under what sky he was born or from what people he came to us. For Rossotto, cited immediately above, asserts that he was descended from the marquises of Ivrea, calling as witnesses authors of the highest authority; yet he has concealed their names, as well as the grounds by which confidence might be placed in their testimony.

Moreover, in the passage mentioned, d’Achery says, following Ferdinando Ughelli, that Atto was the son of Aldegarius; but neither of them explains who this Aldegarius was or to what people he should be assigned.

[Note: [Col. 0009B] It is scarcely necessary to mention that authors of lesser reputation who wrote about the affairs of the Church of Vercelli—such as Modena, Corbellinus, and Cusanus—asserted that Atto was descended from the family of advocates or viscounts, since this is derived from no serious monument.]

If we may offer our own judgment, someone might reasonably suppose that Atto belonged in some way to the Lombards. For from his testament, which we shall cite under number 10, it is clear that he had a brother named Aupertus, and that, by nationality, he lived according to the laws of the Lombards. The names Atto and Aupertus, and similar names, have the character of that people; and the laws and customs by which a person lives generally offer some indication of the people to which he belongs.

### III

It is certain that Atto was made bishop of Vercelli in the year 924, after Ragembert, who immediately preceded him, had been carried off by the fire set by the Hungarians at Pavia on the fourth day before the Ides of March of that same year.

[Note: [Col. 0011C] See Frodoard, *Chronicle*, and Liutprand, *History*, book III, chapter 1 and following.]

The strongest proof that Atto was adorned with the sacred episcopal insignia in that year and ascended the chair of our Church is supplied by the original instruments of a donation, [Note: [Col. 0011D] These are preserved in our archive, and we shall reproduce a copy of them under number 8.] by which he enriched this same Church and which are dated to the year 945 from the Lord’s incarnation, but to the twenty-first year of Atto’s pontificate.

For if, from the 945 years since the Lord’s incarnation, you subtract the twenty-one years of his pontificate, you are brought back to the year 924.

From this you will gather that Ughelli departed from the truth [Note: [Col. 0011D] In the *Italia sacra*.] when he asserted that Norgandus presided over the Church of Vercelli in the year 925.

### IV

That Atto immediately succeeded this Norgandus, after Ragembert had been sent into the twelfth century, is stated by Giovanni Stefano Ferreri, himself also bishop of Vercelli, [Note: [Col. 0011D] In *Saint Eusebius and His Successor*. The *Life* was published at Rome in 1602.] who continued the *Table* of his predecessor Bonomius, [Note: [Col. 0011D] An addition to the *Collectanea* published on Saint Eusebius.] and was most recently joined by the distinguished Iricus in his *History of Trent*.

Against these authorities we set our most ancient Necrology, where we read concerning Norgandus:

“On the fifth day before the Kalends of March died Norgandus, of venerable memory, bishop of this Church, who arranged the canons and instituted the orders of nobility of this Church.”

For, apart from the fact that it is unlikely that the writer of the Necrology would have omitted the manner of a lamentable death if Norgandus had perished in the fire at Pavia, the date recorded in the Necrology does not agree with the date to which Liutprand, a contemporary writer, assigns the fire—namely, the fourth day before the Ides of March in the year 924.

Therefore you may rightly conclude that Norgandus was neither killed in the aforesaid fire [Col. 0012A] nor, consequently, succeeded by Atto, who was invested with the sacred insignia in that same year of the fire.

### V

Two monuments are much more weighty in this matter, and clearly establish that Ragembert governed the Church of Vercelli during the years immediately preceding Atto. We undertake to bring them forward all the more willingly because they deserve, in our judgment, to be desired by every learned person.

The first is a *formata* letter, which we copied from an ancient codex of our archive, shelfmark 53, containing a collection of canons together with several minor works of Atto. Its form of letters, characteristic of the tenth century, and entirely identical with the script of Atto’s works, suggests both that it was written in that century and that it was entered into the codex at Atto’s command.

[Note: [Col. 0011D] At the end of this codex these verses are also found:

> Atto, to you, bishop, I offer three books;  
> Eusebius the martyr, receive, I beg, my vows.  
>   
> The first contains glosses; the other treats of psalms;  
> The third discusses the entire office of the Fathers.  
>   
> Nor should those who are accustomed to despoil churches think that I am giving you this gift alone.  
>   
> And if, dying intestate, I should perhaps leave something behind,  
> I wish it to belong to the Church.  
>   
> So may the estates remain; so may everything else remain as well;  
> May no opportunity be given to wicked men.  
>   
> If some predatory person should perhaps carry off any part,  
> May he feel the punishments and the place of Tartarus.  
>   
> Let one be another Judas, another Dathan, another Abiron,  
> If anyone despoils the divine temples of their goods.]

Here is a splendid copy of the document, transcribed with exactness from the autograph:

> “Here begins the letter which Latin custom calls a *formata*, established by the holy Fathers at the Council of Nicaea.
>
> “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.
>
> “ΠΦϹΠΡΝΛΚ [Note: [Col. 0012D] This number is read as one thousand thirty-one, written in darker ink and in somewhat different characters, on paper that has also been somewhat more heavily scraped away; perhaps the more correct calculation originally read 1067. For since in the letter the number expressed by the letters is indicated by the total sum and by the same letters subsequently attached, we rightly suspect that 1067 should first have been read there, since both the place where it stood appears and the number is in fact formed from these letters with the addition of the letter Z, or the number of the seventh indiction. Or, at least, after removing the indiction number, it should be read as 1050; that is, two numbers XX were scraped away. For in these codices the number fifty is not always expressed by the sign L, but is also represented by five X.] One thousand thirty-one [I].

> “To the most reverend and most sacredly venerated Father Andrew, archbishop of the holy Church of Milan, Ragembert, humble bishop of the holy Church of Vercelli, sends present and eternal happiness in the Lord.
>
> “Since by your sacred letters you have requested Walfred, a subdeacon of our Church, to be consecrated by you and, at the request of the clergy and people, to be desired as bishop of the Church of Ivrea, we consider it wrong to deny anything to your holy petitions. In accordance with the love and reverence owed to canonical definition, we grant to your Paternity, for advancement to the episcopal chair, this man who, through the diligence of our predecessors, has been promoted as far as the rank of subdeacon, with the Lord’s assistance.
>
> “So that it may not be necessary for your Holiness to have any doubt concerning either his past conduct or this present grant, we have sent him to you with these letters of our humility. In them we testify that, as far as we have heard and learned, and as human frailty is capable of judging, he has until now conducted himself in sacred religion; and we declare him sufficiently suitable to perform that ministry.
>
> “Furthermore, in order to remove every ambiguity concerning his commendation, we have thought it fitting to insert Greek letters together with the numerical value belonging to each. These are: the first letters of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; the first letter of the apostle Peter; the first letter of our own name; the second of yours; the third of the departing brother; and the fourth of our city. When these are added together, their number is subsequently attached to the letters themselves.
>
> “We have also thought it right to add the number of the present indiction to the same calculation, as reason dictates. In addition we have added the ninety-ninth number [Note: [Col. 0013B] We have decided that this is how it should be read, where the autograph allowed only a lesser reading. The number ninety-nine was customarily added and was signified by the Hebrew word *amen*, expressed in Greek letters: α indicated 1, μ 40, η 8, and ν 50; together these form the number 99. See Cabassutius on these letters and his *History of the Councils*, under Nicaea. See *Acts of the Councils*, vol. V, on these letters.], by which the figure of the divine oath is unmistakably and openly expressed: ΛC-ϹΗΝ. XCVIIII. Given on the day of the giving. In the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 904, indiction VII.”

[Col. 0013]

[Col. 0013B]

Now it appears that this Andrew, archbishop of Milan, lived around the end of the tenth century, from a charter in Muratori [Note: [Col. 0014B] In *Italian Antiquities*, dissertation 14.], in which we read:

“In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 996, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of the aforesaid lord Andrew the archbishop, in the month of July, indiction VIII.”

But we must listen to Muratori himself in his *Italian Annals* under this year:

> “But without doubt,” he says, “one must write 905, because in that year it was the sixth year of Andrew, who had been elected archbishop in the year 900; and in July of that same year the eighth indiction was running. More correct is the other record, consisting of a placitum held by the same archbishop at Bellano on Lake Como and by Ragifredus, judge of the sacred palace, both envoys of the lord emperor, and written as follows: ‘In the fifth year of the reign of Lord Louis the emperor, in the month of July, indiction VIII.’”

Add to this, from Ughelli [Note: [Col. 0014B] In the *Italia sacra*.], that at the same time the bishop of Ivrea was the aforesaid Walfrid, or Walfred.

Thus you have learned that in the first five years of the tenth century Andrew presided over the Church of Milan, Walfred over that of Ivrea, and Ragembert over that of Vercelli.

### VI

Let a second and very weighty monument concerning the same matter now be brought forward. We take it from a codex of the Church of Verona, shelfmark 62, and it reads as follows:

**Copy of the privilege which Pope Anastasius granted to Ragembert, bishop of the holy Church of Vercelli.**

**Anastasius, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and most holy Ragembert, bishop of the holy Church of Vercelli, for the days of his life only.**

“If shepherds of sheep endure sun and frost, etc. For the remainder, see Pope Anastasius III.”

Although the year is not written in these papal letters, and although they are attributed to Anastasius without specifying which of the four supreme pontiffs bearing this name is meant, we can easily infer from the fifteenth indiction that they belong to Anastasius III and should be assigned to the year 912.

To pass over Anastasius I, who, according to the distinguished Muratori [Note: [Col. 0015D] In the *Italian Annals*.], was made pope in the year 398, indiction XI, and died in the year 401, in December, indiction XIV; and to say nothing also of Anastasius II, who presided over the Church from 496, indiction IV, through the year 498, when the sixth indiction was running; Anastasius IV was certainly raised to the supreme pontificate in 1153, indiction I, and reached only the second indiction. At that time, numerous and very weighty arguments confirm that there was no other bishop of Vercelli than Ugutio.

The aforementioned Giovanni Stefano Ferreri states that Ugutio, formerly archdeacon of Bergamo, became bishop of Vercelli and succeeded Gisulf in the episcopate. From Ughelli we learn that this occurred in the year 1150, although Ughelli is mistaken in saying that Ugutio did not immediately succeed Gisulf.

That Ugutio presided over this Church from 1152 to 1170 is proved by a judgment issued by him among the canons of Saint Eusebius and Saint Mary on the ninth day before the Kalends of August 1152, recorded by Gandulfus; by a diploma of the Emperor Frederick, dated in the same year and the fifteenth indiction, of which we present part here from our chapter register:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Frederick, by the grace of God august king of the Romans.
>
> “Since we have undertaken the government and power of the Roman Empire, it is fitting that we should prudently care for the Churches elevated by the great generosity of our predecessors, and provide sufficient assistance lest their possessions perish through any diminution.
>
> “Therefore we wish it to be known to all present and future Christian believers that, at the petition of Lord Pope Eugene III, and through the intervention of our most beloved chancellor Arnold, together with the other leading princes of the kingdom, we have taken the venerable Ugutio, bishop of Vercelli, and the Church of Saint Eusebius under royal protection, and have strengthened them by the charter of this privilege.
>
> “Whatever, therefore, is known to have been conferred upon the aforesaid Church by the generosity of the kingdom, by the grant of pontiffs, or by the offering of any of the faithful, and whatever shall hereafter, by the Lord’s generosity, be conferred, we confirm, etc.
>
> “Furthermore, we annul and by royal authority revoke the grants, exchanges, alienations, and dispossessions made by the invaders of Saint Eusebius who had not obtained pontifical blessing—namely, by Gregory of Verucha, Liprandus, Evaradus, and Ardicio.
>
> “Likewise, our patron and predecessor Conrad, king of the Romans, annulled the investiture and his own grant made by Anselm, bishop of Vercelli, against the will of his Church, secretly and irrationally, concerning Clavasiolo; and the investiture made by Gisulf, bishop of that same Church, concerning the toll and ferry of Saluggia, which Gisulf himself confessed that he had not made, against the oath he had sworn and against the prohibition of Lord Pope Eugene III; and any others that they may have been able to establish; and all other investitures secretly and stealthily made by bishops in the Church of Saint Eusebius we entirely annul. By royal authority we prohibit that they be made in the future, under penalty of one hundred pounds of gold, etc.
>
> “Thus we also grant in perpetuity a prescription of one hundred years both to the bishops of Vercelli and to the Church of Saint Eusebius and Saint Mary.
>
> “The following witnesses were also present, whose names are seen subscribed: Hartunicus, archbishop of Bremen; Ghebaardus, bishop of Würzburg; Henselmus, bishop of Altenburg; Duke Welfo; Henry, duke of Saxony; Conrad and Albert, margraves of Saxony; Guido, count of Blandrata.
>
> “Sign of the lord Frederick, most invincible king of the Romans. I, Arnold, chancellor, in the place of Henry, archbishop of Mainz and archchancellor, have examined and subscribed.
>
> “Given at Würzburg, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1152, indiction XV, while the most glorious lord Frederick was reigning as king of the Romans, in the first year of his reign. Happily.”

That Ugutio remained in the episcopate until 1170 is also proved by his donation to the canons of Saint Eusebius of both Montanario and the tithes of Roasio and Roaxenda in 1155, from our registers; by the cession, made in the name of his Church, of the rights belonging to it over the castle and territory of Trent, granted in the same year to William, marquis of Montferrat, which the distinguished Iricus gives in his *History of Trent*, folio 28; by the transfer from Biella in the valley to the mountain called Platium, concerning which a diploma dated 1160 exists in the Biella registers; and finally by the cession of the episcopate made to Lord Wala, provost and canon of Saint Eusebius, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September in the year 1170, drawn up by Otto, notary of the sacred palace, from our register.

But enough has already been said, and more than is appropriate. It remains, therefore, to vindicate the papal letters under discussion for Anastasius III and conclude that in the year 912 Ragembert was bishop of Vercelli.

### VII

How, in those extremely dark times, the all-good and all-great God sent Atto to us like a most brilliant star is known to all who have examined the history of that age.

Barbarians were ravaging Italy in every direction, driving one another by force from the settlements they had occupied, and often being driven out again themselves. They had overturned everything human and divine; the liberal arts had been ruined, religion disturbed, and the greatest calamity had been inflicted upon all things. The people of Vercelli experienced these evils above all others, being particularly exposed to the path of the barbarians as they came and went and fought among themselves over plunder.

What sort of bishops were usually placed over Churches in that age, to pass over other examples, Muratori reports [Note: [Col. 0017D] In the *Italian Annals* under the year 958.]:

> “The worthy candidates who had been elected—that is, the shepherds—were rejected, and it was necessary to accept those preferred by them—that is, by the princes—even when they were unworthy. They did not consider merit in learning or goodness of character, but only wealth, family connection, and services. And although they did not sell the Churches for money, they nevertheless gave them in payment for the servitude which those men or their relatives had rendered at court. Thus children were seen raised to the episcopate, and the people were compelled to give favorable testimony to these beardless boys, who had scarcely memorized some article of the faith so that they might answer, albeit trembling, when examined. The examination, however, was still conducted more as a formality than to establish their learning. Such was the miserable condition of the Churches of Italy in those times.”

Add to this Atto’s own testimony concerning that calamity in his treatise *On Ecclesiastical Distresses*.

[Col. 0017C]

Indeed, Christ the Lord, who had promised that he would never abandon the Church, now raised up Atto, as it were along with the collapse of everything else, as an outstanding restorer of religion. From the episcopal chair, like a man standing in an elevated place, he shone first upon the people of Vercelli, then upon neighboring peoples and the universal Church, with the most radiant light of piety and ecclesiastical learning. Wherever the gravest evils could be remedied, he brought relief with the utmost vigilance and tireless strength.

To this belong his care in visiting his diocese every year; the outstanding *Capitulary* issued by him for the reform of clergy and people and for restoring ecclesiastical discipline as though by a return from exile; the sacred sermons frequently delivered to his flock, by which they were instructed according to the norm of the Gospel; the numerous letters addressed either to other bishops, ecclesiastics, his clergy, or his own people; and all his other writings and deeds, which everywhere reveal him as a prelate distinguished by learning and zeal for religion.

### VIII

At this point one must not omit the splendid example of Christian generosity by which this outstanding bishop, not when dying—when, namely, we give away with affected munificence what we can no longer retain—but while still relying on the hope of living for a long time, enriched his canons with a splendid donation.

For they had been reduced by the frequent incursions of enemies to such straits that, since they had nothing available even for the most meager sustenance, they were compelled to abandon their office.

Understanding this, Atto most generously transferred estates and possessions to them, so that, once necessity had been driven away, they might turn all their thought to divine things.

Here is a copy of the donation charter:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Atto, by the gift of divine mercy humble bishop of the holy Church of Vercelli.
>
> “Whenever we provide for the needy and for those who serve God, who cry out because of their distress, we have no doubt that they will serve God more freely and pray more readily for us and for our benefactors. Therefore let the diligence of all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, know that the canons of holy Mary, the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin, and of the blessed martyr Eusebius, living under our government, have sought our favor.
>
> “For although, by God’s permission, they numbered thirty, they had no sufficient means by which they could subsist and duly perform the divine office in the churches already mentioned. They therefore asked us either to reduce their number or to grant them such assistance.
>
> “Moved, therefore, by such cries, we have granted them one small estate situated in Montanario, belonging to a former royal estate that was at Vercelli, which our lords and most serene kings Hugh and Lothair granted to us and to our Church by a charter of command, together with all its appurtenances and families of both sexes. We grant it so that they may have food from its crops or from the other revenue belonging to us.
>
> “The condition, however, is that they are not to divide the crops of the aforesaid small estate individually, but are to prepare their annual meal from them together, for themselves, in the appointed place of their canonry.
>
> “For since the Lord says: ‘Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them,’ we are even less doubtful that he is present among so many brothers who together offer praises to God for these benefits of his and together meditate upon the divine mystery and the welfare of both their own bodies and souls and those of their benefactors.
>
> “When these arrangements had thus been completed, lest any ambiguity should arise in the future concerning this charter of our grant, and so that they might more freely praise God and diligently pray for the salvation of our senior lords and kings, Hugh and Lothair, and for our own, we ordered all these matters to be committed to writing by Vercellinus the priest, acting in place of Eistulfus, chancellor of our Church. We confirmed them below with our own hand.
>
> “In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 945, in the twenty-first year of our pontificate, indiction III. In the name of God. Done successfully at Vercelli.
>
> “I, Atto, bishop by the grace of God, have subscribed to what I have done.
>
> “Peter, judge and notary of the lords the kings, subscribed.
>
> “Cunibertus, judge and notary of the lords the kings, subscribed.
>
> “Odelricus, judge and notary, subscribed as my witness.
>
> [Col. 0019A]
>
> “Avaericus, notary, having been requested, subscribed.
>
> “Judge and notary of the lords the kings, subscribed.
>
> “Giselbertus, royal notary, subscribed.
>
> “Ragembertus, requested as above, subscribed.
>
> “Vercellinus the priest: I wrote and subscribed as above.”

### IX

Since Atto enjoyed great favor with princes and their officials, he used it not to enlarge his own dignity or increase his authority over his subjects, as sometimes happens, but above all for the protection of the clergy and the Church. For this reason we have learned from reliable documents that our Church was enlarged by splendid donations in those times.

Here is one containing a donation by Kings Hugh and Lothair.

[Col. 0019B]

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Hugh and Lothair, kings by the providential clemency of God.
>
> “If, according to the custom of good Christians, we most devoutly bestow the support of our office upon holy and venerable places dedicated to divine worship, we firmly believe that we and our kingdom will always be raised up by the intercessions of the saints through heavenly assistance and exalted by divine benefits.
>
> “Therefore let the devotion of all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, know that Berengar, our faithful, beloved, and illustrious margrave, has urged our clemency to grant, for the love of almighty God and of Saint Eusebius, who most worthily obtained the palm of martyrdom by preaching the Catholic faith, the riverbeds of the Sicida and the Sarvo to the canons of the Church of Vercelli, over which the venerable Atto is seen to preside as bishop.
>
> “Accepting this petition as approved by nearly all the princes of this kingdom, by a charter of our authority we presently grant the beds of the aforesaid rivers to the dominion of the canons of Vercelli, insofar as we can do so justly and legally, as the boundaries of the *briula* have been laid out, up to the bank beside the chapel of Saint Columbanus. The rivers flowing within these boundaries, together with the islands and their banks belonging to us, we grant, as stated, to the aforesaid canons of Saint Eusebius, so that the fisheries and the dues from boats and banks may serve their use.
>
> “Moreover, by this charter we confirm the ports of Vercelli, just as our predecessors ordained for the love of the lighting of the Church of Saint Eusebius, in which his most sacred body rests, and for the clothing of the clerics who continually serve there.
>
> “Therefore, if anyone should at any time attempt in any way, at the devil’s instigation, to violate the statute of this charter, let him know that he shall pay one thousand pounds of the finest gold, half to our treasury and half to the Church of Saint Eusebius and its clerics who shall at that time be serving there.
>
> [Col. 0019D] “And so that it may be believed more truly and observed more diligently by all, we have strengthened it with our own hands and ordered it to be marked with our ring.
>
> “The signs of the most serene Kings Hugh and Lothair. I, Geseprandus, bishop and chancellor, acting in place of Boso, bishop and archchancellor, have examined and subscribed.
>
> “Given on the Ides of August, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 945; in the twentieth year of the reign of Lord Hugh, the fifteenth of Lothair; indiction III. Given successfully at Pavia. Amen.”

### X

Muratori, in *Italian Antiquities*, dissertation 66, proves that Lothair also bestowed many gifts upon the canons of Parma through Atto’s influence, from a diploma given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July [Col. 0020A] in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 948, and in the eighteenth year of Lothair, the most pious king, indiction VII. The distinguished Muratori rightly observes that “sixth” should be read instead.

### XI

The same care with which Atto had provided for his own clergy and Churches, and for the Church of Parma, he also exercised toward the people of Milan when drawing up his testament. Here is a copy of it:

“In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ. Lotharius, by the grace of God king, in the eighteenth year of his reign, in the month of August, in the sixth indiction [Note: [Col. 0019D] Therefore, the year 948.]. While the course of human life is being lived out in a state of health, and the reasoning faculty of the mind is vigorous with unimpaired spirit, a person ought always to think and make arrangements concerning his own possessions for the sake of the reward of his soul, which things are to come and will endure, so that when the Lord commands him to be called from this world [Col. 0020B], he may not be judged for negligence but may rejoice in what has been rightly arranged, as a pious man.

Therefore I, Atto, bishop in the name of God of the holy Church of Vercelli, who have professed that, by my nation, I live according to the law of the Lombards, being present and speaking before those present, have declared: Life and death are in the hand of God. It is better for a man to live in fear of death than, trusting in the hope of living, to be overtaken by sudden death. Considering the mercy of almighty God, and the reward and remedy of my soul, I have determined not to leave certain possessions and dependents of mine disordered after my departure, but that everything should remain so firm and established as I have arranged and judged below in individual clauses.

Therefore I wish, judge, and establish—and by this my testament, for the reward of my soul, I confirm—that those valleys, Bellenica and Lebentina, which I appear to possess and hold in my own right, immediately after my death and that of my brother Aupertus, shall pass into the right and power of the holy Church of Milan, and of the cardinal presbyters and deacons, as well as the decuman presbyters, who at that time shall be in that city, together with all their appurtenances: courts, houses, cultivated plots, castles, chapels, mills, fisheries with lands, vineyards, meadows, pastures, woods and stablareia, banks, ravines, and marshes, cultivated and uncultivated lands, mountains, Alps, plains; aldiones or aldion women, male slaves and female slaves—in short, everything, and from everything whatever I am seen to possess in the aforesaid valleys of Bellenica and Lebentina, or whatever legally belongs to me there, to be held wholly and intact.

The arrangement shall be this: whatever census or income the Lord shall annually grant from the aforesaid valleys, or whatever shall come from them each year, shall be divided among those priests and levites on the first Monday, at the beginning of Lent. Each ordinary priest shall receive twice as much from it as one of the decumans. Moreover, the cardinal archpriest and cardinal archdeacon of that city shall each receive twice as much as one of the other ordinary priests [Col. 0021A]. Likewise, the chief priest of the decumans shall receive twice as much as one of the other decumans—that is, as much as one ordinary priest—so that all those priests and deacons may hasten to implore the mercy of almighty God for the remedy of my soul, so that they may have God as their rewarder for this.

For at no time shall they have the power to alienate or exchange anything from the aforesaid possessions and dependents, or to enter into a contract under the name of a liberarius or a tintheocharius; rather, they must and shall possess and hold them for their own use, as written above. From the produce of those possessions they shall provide the census or income as written above, and from the service of those dependents, and from whatever shall come from me, they shall at all times do whatever they wish according to what I have established above, without any opposition from me or from my heirs.

Nevertheless, so long as anything of us, these two brothers, remains alive in this world, I reserve in my power the usufruct alone of those possessions—either for myself or for my aforesaid brother, if he survives me—on the condition that, in return for that usufruct, I, or my aforesaid brother if he survives me, must each year pay to the aforesaid priests and levites, according to the arrangement established here, namely on the first Monday of Lent, forty solidi of good silver denarii, to be divided among them as stated above.

If we delay fulfilling this, then the aforesaid priests and deacons shall have the power to enter the possessions themselves, take possession of them, and hold them [Col. 0021C], just as I have established above that this shall be done after our death, so that it may benefit me and my parents toward the salvation of the soul and everlasting joy.

And this is what I wish: that at no time shall the pontiff of that holy Church of Milan have the power to inflict any opposition or violence upon those priests and levites concerning those possessions and dependents. Rather, they shall be permitted to possess and hold those possessions and dependents quietly and peacefully, according to the arrangement I have established and judged above, for the reward and remedy of my soul and for the honor of my episcopate.

Nor shall it be permitted to me at any time to reject what I have willed; rather, whatever has once been done or written by me, I promise to preserve inviolably under oath [Col. 0021D], with the stipulation appended below. For I have delivered this document of judgment and disposition to Anselm, notary and judge of the lord king, and have asked him to write it; below I have confirmed it and offered it for strengthening by witnesses. Done in the city of Milan.

I, Atto, bishop by the grace of God, have subscribed to what I myself have done. Aupertus, brother of the same lord Atto, have subscribed.

Angelbertus, judge of the lord king, having been asked, subscribed.

The marks made by the hands of Natalis and Aufredus, who professed that they lived according to Roman law, witnesses.

Bertericus, judge of the lord king, having been asked by this bishop Atto, subscribed as witness.

[Col. 0022A] Gumbertus, judge of the lord king, having been asked, subscribed as witness.

Rodulphus, judge of the lord king, having been asked, subscribed.

Joannes, judge of the lord king, having been asked, subscribed.

Anselmus, judge of the lord king, having been asked, subscribed as witness.

Arialdus, having been asked, subscribed.

Luitprandus, having been asked, subscribed.

Daibertus, judge of the lord king, having been asked, subscribed.

Henricus, having been asked, subscribed.

I, Anselmus, notary and judge of the lord king, wrote this after it had been delivered, completed it, and handed it over.”

[Col. 0022B] XII. We infer from the very placitum held at Pavia by King Hugh, which Muratori reports (*Antiquitates Italicae*, dissertation 31), that Atto attended it together with Ratherius, bishop of Verona. It is recorded as having been issued: “In the reign of our lord Hugh and his son Lotharius, kings by the grace of God, by God’s favor, in the tenth year of the lord Hugh and the fifth of Lotharius, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the ninth indiction—that is, in the year 935.”

We also rightly suspect that Hugh and Lotharius honored him with the title and office of royal archchancellor, since, as we have shown above, he enjoyed their very great favor. For in a charter reported by Ughellus among the bishops of Asti, recording a donation made by the said kings to the Church of Asti, we read: “Issued on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 938, in the thirteenth year of the most pious king Hugh and the eighth of Lotharius, in the eleventh indiction. Done happily at Pavia. Amen. Gisprandus, chancellor, recognized it in place of Atto, bishop and archchancellor.” Who could this be other than our Atto?

XIII. Some writers have reported that Atto lived as far as the year 960. Yet there is reason not to place certain reliance upon them, since they have supported the claim with no documentary evidence. For us, this one fact is certain: Ingon, Atto’s immediate successor in the episcopate, was already presiding over our Church in the year 964. For the following fragment, copied from an ancient codex of our archives, shows that in that year Ingon convened a synod.

[Col. 0022D] “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 964, in the seventh indiction, on the Nones of November, the lord Ingo, bishop, took his seat—as it is known to have been the custom of the ancient Fathers, his predecessors—at Vercelli before the altar of the most blessed Eusebius, martyr of Christ, for the purpose of a synodal council. In it, compelled by divine love, he most suitably instructed almost all the clergy subject to his governance, especially concerning the observance of faith and charity, as the canonical institution holds throughout the world.

Moreover, he sought with the greatest zeal that ecclesiastical property should be governed piously and that what had fallen into ruin should be restored. In addition, at the urging of his clergy, he decreed—as ancient custom requires, though it had been devastated by the disastrous incursion of the Hungarians—that the cardinal clergy of the Church should render due and proper service to the baptistery celebrated in this city. Thus, from those churches established in the villages—namely Petiana, Petroriolum, Quinto, Calviniascum, Casale, and Auzeningum—the presbyters should come, equipped with their vestments, who would be able here at Vercelli to baptize the children [Col. 0023A] with water.

And lest a dispute [the reading should perhaps be *contentio*, ‘dispute’, rather than *intentio*, ‘intention’] arise from this, he added: ‘It pleases us and seems right that only two presbyters from the aforesaid churches should diligently come to perform this mystery: namely, two together from Petiana and Petroriolum [Col. 0024A]; and from Quinto and Calviniascum, and from Casale and Auzeningum, we establish the same arrangement, until they in turn fulfill their duties and begin again to fulfill them annually.’”

## ON ATTO’S WORKS

[Col. 0023]

[Col. 0023A] XIV. So much for Atto; now for his works. How highly all learned men who knew them have always valued these works, with what prayers they have desired that they be brought forth from their archives into public light, and with what applause they were received when, through the efforts of the distinguished d’Achery, they appeared—although neither all of them nor complete—can scarcely be expressed. Let what Natalis Alexander says be read (*Ecclesiastical History*, vol. II, fol. 338, Paris edition of 1743). See also Pagi under the year 960; Fleury, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. XII, book LV, § 54; William Cave, *Literary History*, vol. II, p. 99, Basel edition; Dupin, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. VIII, p. 26; Racine, vol. IV, p. 109, Utrecht edition, article 6, § 4; and Muratori under the years 958 and 959 in the *Italian Annals*.

XV. When Joannes Stephanus Ferrerius, cited above [Note: [Col. 0023D] Number 4.], undertook to catalogue Atto’s works, he placed the sermons first, then the letters, next the *Polypticus*, or *Perpendiculum*, then the *Canons*, or *Capitulare*, and finally the treatise *On Ecclesiastical Pressures*. Nearly all who have so far undertaken to compose a history of ecclesiastical affairs likewise mention these works everywhere with great praise.

It is nevertheless appropriate to place before the eyes of readers here what the author of the supplement to Bellarmine reports concerning their number and fate:

“‘The works of Atto,’ says the most distinguished Joannes Bona, general abbot of the reformed congregation of Saint Bernard, or the Feuillants in Italy (a Piedmontese, that is, who later became a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church), ‘he extracted from a manuscript Vatican codex, no. 4322, had copied at Rome in the year 1664, and sent to Luca d’Achery, the Benedictine monk, who inserted them in volume VIII of his *Spicilegium*, from page 1 to page 138. They are: the *Capitulare*, or *Chapters of Atto, bishop*; the *Book on Ecclesiastical Pressures*; and various letters.

In those same codices, both the Vatican and the Vercelli codex, there were also seventeen sermons [Col. 0023D] on various subjects, and the *Polypticus*, which he calls the *Perpendiculum*, by which harmful things are to be rebuked and honorable things sanctioned, together with scholia. But because they can scarcely be read, they were not transcribed.

It is regrettable that the Vatican manuscript codex is riddled with many lacunae in its folios, so that it could not be considered wholly complete and sound, nor could it be repaired by comparison with the Vercelli manuscript codex, which the canons refused to provide. Atto flourished until the year 960 and beyond,’ and so forth.”

These statements agree with what d’Achery himself continues in a somewhat fuller account: “Atto, second of that name,” and so forth. See below d’Achery’s Preface to his edition of Atto’s works.

XVI. Although this is so, another outstanding work of Atto has until now escaped the notice of scholars: namely, a commentary on all the Epistles of Saint Paul. Those who read it will surely be unable to refrain from marveling greatly that, in an age shrouded in the dark night of ignorance, there existed a man who wrote with such wisdom and such keen judgment on the most important subjects, and in an elegant style [Col. 0024B]. What knowledge of the Scriptures they will observe there! What purity of doctrine! What, finally, a selection of ideas!

And what of the fact that the most holy doctrines of religion later attacked by innovators—such as the presence of Christ in the sacrament of the Eucharist, such as the fire of purgatory, and many other doctrines—are confirmed by invincible arguments and transmitted to posterity through these commentaries in an unbroken tradition? Nor will those devoted to sounder doctrine regard as insignificant the fact that they will find the Augustinian position concerning divine grace consistently asserted in these commentaries as a dogma held in the highest esteem in those times, with all positions tending in any degree toward Pelagianism rejected.

[Col. 0024C] XVII. By what fate this precious treasure remained hidden for so many centuries, I do not know well enough. But that it proceeded from Atto’s most fertile storehouse, I regard as no less certain than anything can be. For when I compare the style of these commentaries with Atto’s other works, I find it everywhere extremely similar. I also often find in the commentaries the same ideas that occur in the letters, expressed in almost the same words. Compare the letter on the obedience owed to princes, sent to Bishop Waldo, with the exposition of chapter 13 of the Epistle to the Romans.

Moreover, at the end of the commentaries we read: “Vercellinus the deacon and Tetbertus the subdeacon wrote [this] at the command of the lord Atto.” The complete codex of Atto’s works, marked with number 40 among many others in our archive [Col. 0024D], was written by these two scribes.

In the year 945, Vercellinus, already ordained a priest, wrote the original document of a donation. If you inspect the characters of that charter, you will rightly say that they are identical with the characters of the commentaries in the part written by Vercellinus the deacon. Thus, just as you will correctly infer from this that the commentaries were written before the year 945 by Vercellinus while still a deacon, with Tetbertus assisting him, so by the same reasoning you may conclude that Atto was the author both of the donation and of the commentaries.

XVIII. Before I bring this to an end, I wish to reproduce a letter of Joseph Blanchini, formerly [Col. 0025A] a priest of the Roman Oratory and a most distinguished defender of the canonical Scriptures, which he sent from here to an eminent man after, while passing through the city, he had visited the archive of the cathedral church.

“‘I would have stayed in Vercelli as long as necessary if I had been able to copy the entire codex marked 40 (that is, the codex which we are publishing), which is of great interest to that illustrious Church and to Atto. It contains a commentary by Atto on the Epistles of Saint Paul. I transcribed this note, which stands at the end of the codex:

*The treatise on the Epistle of Paul to the Hebrews is complete. Vercellinus the deacon and Tetbertus the subdeacon wrote it at the command of the lord Atto, bishop. Pray for us, brothers.*

After the aforesaid commentary [Col. 0026A] come various letters and statutes of the Church of Vercelli, which are interesting, and then a small collection of canons with this exact title, which I copied word for word:

*Chapters of canons drawn from various councils, decretal letters, statutes, and letters, suitable for a secular court in the time of the lord Atto, bishop . . .*

Canon Fileppi tells me that he intended to publish an edition of Atto’s works. But if he delays any longer in copying the codices, since he is old, I fear that he will die before accomplishing anything [Note: [Col. 0025A] The prediction proved all too true, for before he could begin this work, he died.]. He ought, however, to be urged on for the benefit of the republic of letters, and especially for the glory of that most ancient Church.

[Col. 0025]

## D’ACHERY’S PREFACE

Atto, second of that name, son of Aldegarius (says Ferdinand Ughellus in *Italia Sacra*), was bishop of Vercelli in the year 945, a most learned theologian and canonist. He left several monuments of his intellect and learning, which are contained in an ancient manuscript codex in the Vatican Library and in the archive of Vercelli,” and so forth.

“Again, canons and statutes of the Church of Vercelli, extracted from councils and decretal letters, a work which he suitably divided into one hundred chapters. Likewise, a work *On Ecclesiastical Pressures*, divided into three parts: the first concerning the judgments of bishops, the second concerning their ordinations, and the third concerning the resources of Churches. In his time the kings Hugh and Lotharius adorned the Church of Vercelli,” and so forth.

The distinguished Joannes Bona, general abbot of the reformed congregation of Saint Bernard, extracted Atto’s works from Vatican manuscript codex no. 4322, had them copied at Rome in the year 1664, and sent them to me. But it is especially regrettable that the codex itself was found disfigured by numerous lacunae, particularly throughout its entire upper portion, either damaged by rain or eaten away by decay, so that one line is missing on every page.

Nevertheless, in his letters the most learned abbot gave me hope of obtaining a complete codex, stating that one existed in the archive of the Church of Vercelli—as I had already read in the learned Ughellus, in *Italia sacra* (vol. IV, col. 2, p. 1060)—and asking the bishop of Vercelli to deal with the canons on the matter, so that they might permit those works to be copied. But the bishop met with a refusal.

When I had reported this affair to the most illustrious Signor Caroccio, then the ambassador in France of the most serene Duke of Savoy, a man outstanding in religion, prudence, and learning, he immediately applied every care and effort—both personally and through friends residing at Vercelli—to obtain a copy of this monument, or at least to fill the lacunae in the Roman codex. At first the canons made extraordinary promises; but after letters had passed back and forth, they finally confessed—whether honestly or deceptively, let others judge—that there was no one in their Church skilled in antiquarian matters.

The most illustrious Caroccio’s diligence and kindness did not stop there. For when he had successfully completed his embassy and returned to Savoy, he urged the matter again and requested that those canons send the original manuscript to him at Turin, promising in good faith to return it after having arranged, at his own expense, for it to be copied.

What should I do, having abandoned every hope of possessing so great a treasure in complete form? Should I publish the works, weakened by gaps that often interrupt the sense, or devote my efforts to publishing other works? Friends distinguished for their learning came to me in my anxiety. They said that it was better to bring into the light these excellent little works on ecclesiastical matters, even though disfigured by some lacunae, than to leave them perhaps forever buried in darkness; and better to publish them lest they perish in a fire, the fate that many monuments of earlier ages have suffered in numerous places. Finally, they added that even fragments of antiquarian material are valued. Moved by these considerations, I arranged for them to be committed to print.

And since Atto, most skilled in divine and ecclesiastical matters, adorned his scholarly labors with testimonies drawn like pearls from Holy Scripture, from councils, and from the Fathers of the Church, while generally failing to indicate the passages, we expended no little effort—especially in the collection of canons which we have entitled the *Capitulare*—in adding to the margins the references that had not been supplied, and by this labor we filled many lacunae.

Besides the works we are publishing, so that you may know, reader, Atto’s shorter works are found both in the Vercelli and in the Vatican codex: namely, seventeen sermons to the people, and the *Polyptych*, which he calls the *Perpendiculum*, by which he teaches that harmful things should be rebuked and honorable things sanctioned, together with scholia.

Furthermore, the custodians of the library arranged for the Vatican codex to be transcribed, lest it perish entirely. It contains first the sermons, which can scarcely be read and therefore were not transcribed, and so forth. Thus wrote the distinguished Joannes Bona in a letter to me in the year 1664.

The following points should be noted in Atto’s *Capitulare*:

1. The words “the catholic faith” signify the Athanasian Creed. The author uses them twice in this sense, in chapter 4, and by Ratherius of Verona—or, as others prefer, by Udalricus, though incorrectly—in a synodal letter to priests: “The sermon, as I said above, of Athanasius, bishop, concerning faith in the Trinity, whose beginning is: *Whoever wishes*,” and so forth. Riculfus likewise has almost the same words in chapter 5 of his *Constitutions*: “Let each one of you know the psalms and the sermon of the catholic faith, whose beginning is: *Whoever*,” and so forth.

2. The gatherings or conferences of priests mentioned as having been established in chapter 29 appear to belong to approximately the ninth century, on the basis of chapter 10 of Riculfus of Soissons:

“Moreover, we have decreed that it is close to reason that in each month, on a fixed day—that is, on the Kalends of every month—the priests of each deanery should meet together. They should not devote themselves to feasts or drinking, but should discuss their ministry, their religious conduct, and the matters that occur in their parish; and they should consider how they ought to pray for the king, for the rulers of the Church, and for their own dependents, both living and dead.”

The fifteenth chapter of Hincmar’s *Admonitions to Priests* is relevant here (at the end of volume I of his works):

“When the priests have met together on the Kalends, after completing the divine office and the necessary conference, they should not sit there at table as though for a meal,” and so forth.

3. Chapter 90 may be elucidated by Bede in the preface to his *Remedies for Sins*, or penitential book:

“Let us carefully admonish every learned priest of Christ that, in all the matters noted here, he should diligently discern the sex, age, condition, status, and person of each individual wishing to do penance, as well as the penitent’s own heart, and judge each matter according to what seems appropriate to him. For some should abstain from food; others should bend their knees more frequently, or stand in the form of a cross, or do something else of this kind that pertains to the purification of sins.”

Heriveus of Reims repeats these very words in his letter to Witon of Rouen, chapter 23. This is what d’Achery says. We will add only that we repaired a considerable number of lacunae in the book *On Ecclesiastical Pressures* with the aid of a manuscript codex from the monastery of Reimsbach, which the Reverend Father Dom Edmond Martène once consulted and from which he most courteously shared with us whatever he had excerpted.

[Col. 0027]

## THE CAPITULARY OF ATTO, BISHOP OF VERCELLI

### CHAPTER I.—The bishop’s admonition to priests concerning how they should act toward their subjects

[Col. 0027A]

(Theodulf, chapter 1 of the *Capitulary*.) I beseech you, dearly beloved brothers, to labor with the most vigilant care for the progress and correction of the peoples entrusted to you, so that, showing them the way of salvation and instructing them by word and example, we may, with the help of the Lord Jesus Christ, bring back to him fruitful sheaves—you because of their progress, and we because of yours.

I also beseech your fraternity to read these chapters, which I have briefly arranged for the correction of life, continually, to commit them to memory, and to shape your conduct and amend your life through reading them and the other Holy Scriptures, so that, with the Lord’s help, you may strive to proceed with the peoples entrusted to you toward the heavenly kingdoms.

### CHAPTER II.—A repetition of the same matter, with an exhortation concerning distinction of rank and a good life

[Col. 0027B]

(The same.) You must truly know and always remember [Col. 0028A] that we, to whom the care of governing souls has been entrusted, shall have to render an account for those who perish through our negligence. But for those whom we shall have won through words and examples, we shall receive the reward of eternal life.

If the faithful people are God’s food, then we are the seasoning of that food. Know that your rank is second to, and almost joined with, our rank. For just as bishops hold the place of the apostles in the Church, so priests plainly hold the place of the Lord’s other disciples. The bishops hold the rank of the high priest Aaron, while you hold that of his sons.

Therefore you must always remember so great a dignity, remember your consecration, remember the sacred anointing that you received into your hands, so that you neither degenerate from that dignity, nor make your consecration void, nor pollute by sinning hands stained with sacred blood. Rather, preserving purity of heart and body, offering the peoples an example of good living [Col. 0029A], provide those over whom you preside with guidance toward the heavenly kingdoms.

### CHAPTER III.—The avoidance of ignorance and the preservation of learning

(Council of Toledo IV, canon 24.) Ignorance is the mother of all errors. It must be avoided above all by the priests of God, who have undertaken the duty of teaching the peoples. For the Apostle frequently admonishes priests to read the Holy Scriptures, saying to Timothy: “Attend to reading, exhortation, and teaching. Remain constantly in these things” (1 Timothy 4:13). Priests must therefore know the Scriptures and the canons, and their entire work must consist in preaching and teaching; they must edify everyone alike through knowledge of the faith and discipline of works.

### CHAPTER IV.—That all should retain the catholic faith by heart

[Col. 0029B]

First of all, all priests, deacons, and subdeacons must retain the catholic faith [Note: [Col. 0029D] “The catholic faith.” d’Achery has already noted that the Athanasian Creed is meant here. At the end, I read *sciat* (“let him know”) as the sense requires.] by heart. If anyone neglects to do this, let him abstain from wine for forty days. If, after this abstinence, he neglects it, the sentence against him is to be doubled.

### CHAPTER V.—The avoidance of negligence, the embrace of justice, and the amendment of life

Let no cleric disregard anything beyond what has been commanded, or dare in any way to neglect it; rather, let him willingly fulfill it and handle the divine sacraments with no negligence whatsoever.

Therefore both young and old must be very concerned about these matters, about their entire conversion, conduct, and penance, and must act diligently, so that they may perform these things worthily. For the rest, both clerics and laypeople should adorn their souls with the most fitting ornaments: namely, the doctrines of truth, the beauty of chastity, the splendor of justice, the brightness of piety, and all the other qualities with which a rational mind ought to be adorned.

They must also avoid associations with dishonorable and unbelieving people, associate with the faithful, and frequent those gatherings at which chastity, justice, and piety are discussed. They must always pray to God with their whole heart, ask him for what is fitting, give him thanks, and show genuine repentance for past deeds. If possible, they should also assist their penance to some extent through mercy toward the poor.

### CHAPTER VI.—By what weapons the devil and vices are to be overcome

[Col. 0029D]

(Theodulf, chapter 2.) You must be constant in reading and assiduous in prayer. For the life of a just man is instructed by reading and adorned by prayer; and through continual reading a person is fortified against sin, according to the one who said: “I have hidden your words in my heart, so that I may not sin against you” (Psalm 118:11).

For these are the weapons—namely, reading and prayer—by which the devil is overcome. These are the instruments by which eternal [Col. 0030A] blessedness is acquired. By these weapons vices are suppressed. By this nourishment virtues are sustained.

### CHAPTER VII.—That a priest should by no means celebrate Mass alone

(The same Theodulf, chapter 7.) A priest should by no means celebrate Mass alone. For just as it cannot be celebrated without the priest’s greeting, the people’s response, the priest’s admonition, and likewise the people’s response, so it certainly ought not to be celebrated by one person alone.

There must be people standing around him, whom he may greet and from whom he may receive a response; and this saying of the Lord must be recalled to him: “Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst” (Matthew 18:20).

### CHAPTER VIII.—That a priest should not presume to celebrate Mass except in places consecrated by a bishop

[Note: [Col. 0029D] Council of Rome under Sylvester, in the epilogue. It is reported in Anselm, book VII, chapters 137 and 138, and in Gratian [Col. 0030D], chapter “No priest,” *On Consecration*, distinction 1.]

[Col. 0030B]

It was established here in the Roman synod, with the agreement of the entire synod, that no priest should presume to celebrate Mass except in places consecrated by a bishop, if he wishes thereafter to remain a participant in that bishop’s priesthood.

### CHAPTER IX.—That the divine mysteries should be celebrated diligently

(Theodulf, chapter 5.) In the sacrifices, dearly beloved, let this above all be carefully observed: that the bread, wine, and water, without which Masses cannot be celebrated, be handled with the utmost cleanliness and care. Let nothing cheap, nothing unapproved, be found among them, according to what Scripture says: “Let the fear of the Lord be with you; act with care in everything” (2 Chronicles 19:7).

### CHAPTER X.—Likewise from the same source

The Lord’s Body must in no way be consecrated except from an entire offering. For the Lord suffered no diminution of his body, as it is written: “Nor will you permit your holy one to see corruption” (Psalm XV, 21 [the printed citation is erroneous]). And elsewhere: “You shall not break a bone of it” (John 19:36). Masses, moreover, must not be celebrated except by priests who are fasting.

### CHAPTER XI.—That women should not approach the altar

(Theodulf, chapter 6.) While a priest is celebrating Mass, women should by no means approach the altar; rather, they should stand in their own places, and there the priest should receive their offerings in order to offer them to God.

Women must remember their weakness and the frailty of their sex. Therefore each of them should fear touching anything sacred in the divine ministry. Laymen also should fear this, lest they suffer the punishment of Uzzah, who, when he tried to touch the Ark of the Lord in an unauthorized manner, perished when the Lord struck him (2 Samuel 6).

### CHAPTER XII.—That women should not touch sacred vessels or cloths

[Note: [Col. 0030D] From the letter said to be by Soter, letter 2 to the bishops of Italy. It appears in *On Consecration*, distinction 23, chapter “Sacred”; and in Ivo of Chartres, *Decretum*, part II, chapter 72, and part III, chapter 265.]

It has been reported to the apostolic see that women or nuns dedicated to God among us touch sacred vessels or sacred cloths and carry incense around the altars. No rightly minded person can doubt that all these practices are full of reproach and blame.

Therefore, by the authority of this holy see, we decree that you cut all these practices out completely as soon as possible; and, lest this plague spread more widely, we order that it be removed with the utmost speed throughout all the provinces.

### CHAPTER XIII.—That no one should presume unlawfully to appropriate anything sacred for another use

(Theodulf, chapter 18.) No one should presume to turn either a chalice, a paten, or any sacred vessel dedicated to divine service to other uses. No one should drink from the sacred chalice anything except the blood of Christ, which is received in the sacrament; nor should anyone dare to use the paten for any function other than the ministry of the altar.

Altars should be covered only with clean and new cloths; and the bodies of the dead must in no way be wrapped in those cloths.

### CHAPTER XIV.—That ecclesiastical vestments should be sacred and honorable

[Note: [Col. 0031D] Pope Stephen to Hilary, letter 1, chapter 3. It is reported in *On Consecration*, distinction 1, chapter “Vestments”; and in Ivo of Chartres, part II, chapter 74.]

The ecclesiastical vestments in which the Lord is served must therefore be sacred and honorable. No one should use them for purposes other than ecclesiastical and worthy divine offices. Nor should they be touched or carried by anyone except consecrated persons, lest divine vengeance—which struck King Belshazzar—come upon those who transgress these rules and presume other uses. For when he took the vessels of the Lord for common uses, he lost both his life and his kingdom.

### CHAPTER XV.—That clerics should not use secular clothing

[Col. 0031C]

(Pope Zacharias, reported in *Question 21*, question 4, chapter “Bishops.”) Priests and deacons should not use secular clothing at all, except, as is fitting, a priestly tunic. Nor, when they walk in the city, on the road, or through the streets, should they presume to walk without a covering, except when they are traveling on a long journey.

For just as a woman praying in churches with an uncovered head dishonors her head (1 Corinthians 11:5), according to the apostolic word, so a priest without a covering dishonors his priesthood. If anyone rashly presumes to act against the statutes, let him be deprived of communion until he hastens to fulfill what has been established.

### CHAPTER XVI.—When the Creed should be handed over to the candidates for baptism

[Col. 0031D]

(Council of Agde, canon 13.) It was also decreed that by all the Churches, on one day—namely, eight days before the Sunday of the Resurrection—the Creed should be publicly handed over in the church to the candidates for baptism.

### CHAPTER XVII.—The time of baptism

(Gelasius, letter to the bishops of Lucania, chapter 12.) No one who is to be baptized should imagine that he may confidently receive baptism indiscriminately at any time, except at the Paschal feast and the venerable sacrament of Pentecost, with the sole exception of an attack of the gravest illness, when there is fear that, as the danger of the disease increases, the sick person may perhaps depart, overtaken by death without the saving remedy.

### CHAPTER XVIII.—How the sacrament of baptism ought to be celebrated
Catechumens, before they are baptized, are to be instructed how they should believe, so that when they are baptized they may answer the priests. They are not to be baptized in any way unless they have confessed their faith—if they have the ability to speak. But if, when danger suddenly threatens, they become speechless, their faith is to be examined through thoroughly Christian witnesses who had been present with them before they became speechless. If they are found worthy on the testimony of these witnesses, they are to be baptized. Those who have been mute from infancy, however, if by some gestures or indications they appear to wish to become Christians or to request baptism, are not to be denied it. As for infants whose age does not yet permit them to speak, we do not refuse that others answer on their behalf, provided that they are Catholics. But those who make profession of faith for them must take care and show concern that the children fulfill what they themselves promised on their behalf. If, however, their parents are religious and learned, such children are to be entrusted to them with this stipulation. If these parents are lacking, others are to instruct the children more frequently and strive more diligently to strengthen them by their benefits.

[Note: “If they are lacking.” This has been restored conjecturally, and the conjecture is by no means implausible. Previously it read, “if they have been in faith,” which Acherius, not understanding it, observed to require the omission of some word, such as “weak.”]

## CHAPTER XIX. Likewise, concerning sick infants

[Col. 0032C]

(Theodulf, chapter 17.) If a sick infant is brought from any parish to any priest for the sake of baptism, the sacrament of baptism must in no way be refused. If anyone, possessing the power to grant this benefit, refuses to do so, and the infant dies without the grace of baptism, let the one who did not baptize the child know that he will have to render an account for its soul.

## CHAPTER XX. That priests should not celebrate baptism without deacons

In no church of any diocese where baptism is celebrated should a priest be found without a deacon.

[Note: “In no church.” I supplied the missing preposition.]

Therefore every priest who does not have a deacon should choose someone and make him known to his people. Then, presenting him to his bishop, he should bring him forward—someone whose life he has found to be approved—and he is to be ordained deacon. But if the priest delays, saying that he does not have such a cleric, his bishop is to provide a good person from his own church or from wherever he wishes. The only requirement is that he not be without a deacon.

## CHAPTER XXI. What may be stored in churches

(Theodulf, chapter 8.) We frequently see harvests and hay being piled up in churches. Therefore we wish the following to be strictly observed: nothing is to be stored in a church except ecclesiastical vestments, sacred vessels, and books. If, however, during a time of persecution, because of the violence of robbers, poor people place their food there for safekeeping, it is not to be thrown out—provided, of course, that once peace has been restored, it is immediately removed from the church. No permission is to be given there for buying or selling. Otherwise, if other business is conducted there than what is proper, we may hear the Lord say: “My house is a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves” (Luke 19:46).

[Note: From “But if” through “lest” these words are not found in Theodulf.]

## CHAPTER XXII. That banquets and reclining feasts should not take place in a church

(Laodicea, canon 27; Trullo, canon 72; Aachen, canon 80.) It is not proper that banquets called *agapae* be held in the churches of the Lord, nor that people eat within the house of God or spread couches there.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That burials should not take place in churches

(Theodulf, chapter 9.) In these regions there was formerly a custom of burying the dead in churches, and many places dedicated to divine worship and prepared for offering sacrifices to God were made into cemeteries or burial grounds (*polyandria*). Therefore we wish this practice to cease from now on, and no one is to be buried in a church unless perhaps the person is a priest or some just man who, through the merit of his life, acquired such a place for his dead body by the manner in which he lived. Bodies that were buried in churches in ancient times are not, however, to be cast out. Rather, the tombs that are visible are to be sunk deeper into the earth, and a pavement is to be laid over them so that no trace of the tombs remains visible and the reverence due to the church may be preserved. But where there is such a great multitude of corpses that this is difficult to do, let that place be regarded as a cemetery. The altar is to be removed from it and set up in a place where sacrifice may be offered to God reverently and in purity.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That burials are not to be sold

(Gregory, book VII, letter 55.) The most distinguished woman Nereida has complained to us that your fraternity wishes to demand from her one hundred solidi for the burial of her daughter and, on top of the lamentation caused by her grief, seeks to inflict upon her the additional distress of this expense. If the matter is indeed as reported, since it is exceedingly grave and exceedingly far removed from the duty of a priest to seek payment for earth granted to corruption and to wish to profit from another’s grief, let your fraternity refrain from this practice and do not trouble her any further. We too, after by God’s authority attaining the honor of the episcopate, completely prohibited this vice in our church and did not permit the depraved custom to be resumed, remembering that when Abraham requested from the sons of Emor—that is, from Ephron, the son of Segor—the land of a tomb in which to bury his wife’s body, he refused to accept payment, lest he appear to have gained an advantage from a corpse.

If, therefore, a pagan man showed such consideration, how much more ought we, who are called priests, not to do this? Therefore, so that this vice of avarice may not again be attempted even against others, I admonish you: whenever you permit someone to be buried in your church, if his parents or nearest heirs wish voluntarily to offer something for the lights, we do not forbid you to accept it; but we entirely prohibit you from asking for or demanding anything. This is highly irreligious, lest the church perhaps—God forbid—be called venal, or lest you appear to rejoice in human deaths if you seek in any way to profit from their corpses.

## CHAPTER XXV. That dioceses are to be visited every year

(Council of Tarragona under Hormisdas, canon 8.) Guided by experience of many circumstances, we have discovered that some dioceses are without churches. For this reason we have decreed by this constitution that the order of ancient custom be maintained and that dioceses be visited by bishops every year. If any basilica is found to be abandoned, it is to be repaired by the bishop’s arrangement.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Which priests are to request chrism

(Council of Carthage IV, canon 36.) Priests who govern churches throughout the dioceses are to request chrism before the solemnity of Easter—not from just any bishops, but from their own bishop; and not through a junior cleric, but in person or through the one who has charge of the sacristy.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That a synod is to be held every year

(Toledo IV, canon 3.) Almost nothing has driven discipline and good conduct farther from the Church of Christ than the negligence of priests who, disregarding the canons, neglect to hold a synod for the correction of ecclesiastical morals. For this reason it has been universally defined by us that, since the difficulty of the season does not permit a council to be held twice a year, in accordance with the ancient decrees of the Fathers, it should at least be celebrated once a year by us.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How senior priests are to come to the synod

(Theodulf, chapter 4.) When you assemble for the synod in the customary manner, bring with you the vestments, books, and sacred vessels with which you will perform your ministry and the office entrusted to you. Also bring two or three clerics or laymen with whom you celebrate the solemnities of Mass, so that it may be demonstrated how diligently and zealously you perform the service of God.

## CHAPTER XXIX. That a conference is to be held in the parishes on every Kalends

[Col. 0034D]

We have learned by experience that good conference is no less beneficial than reading. Therefore we now decree that in every parish, on each Kalends, all the priests or clerics are to assemble together in order to discuss collectively the faith and the divine sacraments, as well as life and conduct and each of the duties belonging to them. If anyone among them is found to be negligent or blameworthy, let the others correct him. If he makes no effort at all to be corrected, let them immediately report him to his bishop, so that the bishop may strive to correct these matters more rigorously and as quickly as possible. Otherwise, when the same diocese is visited by the bishop or when the priests themselves come to the synod, all might alike be marked with the disgrace of some individuals. If the Kalends fall on a feast day, they are not to delay fulfilling this on the following day.

## CHAPTER XXX. That no cleric is to be ordained without a specific appointment

(Council of Chalcedon, canon 6.) No one is to be ordained absolutely as a priest, deacon, or anyone else in an ecclesiastical rank unless the church of the city, estate, martyr-shrine, or monastery to which the person being ordained is assigned is specifically declared. Whoever is ordained without such an assignment—the holy synod has decreed that this kind of laying on of hands is invalid and that the person may nowhere minister, to the injury of the ordaining bishop.

## CHAPTER XXXI. That priests are to be ordained for each church

[Col. 0035B]

(Attributed to Clement’s second letter to James.) Establish churches in suitable and useful places, which ought to be consecrated for divine prayers, and place in each of them priests devoted to God through divine prayers. Everyone ought to venerate these priests, and no one ought to burden them.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning clerics who leave the places in which they were ordained

(Council of Arles I, canon 21.)
