Concerning priests or deacons who are accustomed to leave the places in which they were ordained and transfer themselves to other places: it has been decided that they are to minister in the same places to which they were assigned. If, however, after abandoning their own places, they wish to transfer themselves elsewhere, they are to be deposed.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning priests who promise gifts in favor of another church

(Theodulf, chapter 16.) If any priest or anyone found among the clergy is henceforth discovered to give or promise gifts to a cleric or layman in order to seize the church of another priest, let him know that for this robbery and savage greed he will either lose his rank or be confined for a long time in the misery of prison, doing penance. Let him also be compelled to restore to the person whom he has presumed to harass every loss that has resulted from this dispute, as well as the expenses of the legal action.

[Note: “Let him also.” The earlier edition corruptly read “But he.” The words from here through “No priest” are not found in Theodulf.]

No priest is to urge the faithful of the holy Church of God from another priest’s parish to abandon their own church, come to his church, and give their tithes to him. Let each priest be content with his own church and people, and never do to another what he does not want done to himself, in accordance with the Gospel: “Whatever you wish that people would do to you, do the same to them” (Matthew 7:12).

## CHAPTER XXXIV. That no one should give or receive the offerings of a church without the bishop’s knowledge and consent

(Council of Gangra, canon 7.) If anyone wishes to receive or give the offerings of a church outside the church, without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person to whom such duties have been entrusted, and without wishing to act with his counsel, let him be anathema.

## CHAPTER XXXV. That no priest should do anything in a bishop’s parish without his permission

[Col. 0036A]

(First letter circulated under the name of Clement of Rome.) It taught that no priest ought to do anything in the parish of another bishop without permission, and it also taught that all priests ought, by the Lord’s institution, to obey their own bishops in everything without delay. It likewise taught that no one should covet or presume upon what belonged to another, but that each person should be content with what was his own and with what had been entrusted to him. It also instructed no one to do anything to another unless he wished it done to himself.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. That no cleric should keep a woman in a relationship of familiarity

(Council of Toledo II, canon 3.) We further decree by a special ordinance what the ancient councils have also not been silent about in almost all their canons: no cleric from the rank of subdeacon and above is to keep in a relationship of familiarity any woman, whether freeborn, freed, or enslaved. If he has women performing such services for him, he is to assign them to his mother, sister, or another relative of any kind, and whatever they earn with their hands is to be delivered to their proper master. If the relatives mentioned are lacking, another house far away is to be sought as their dwelling, in such a way that women are not permitted, under any pretext, to enter the clerics’ house, lest the cleric incur a snare or the reputation of an innocent person perhaps be stained by a harmful accusation.

From now on, after this admonition has been given, whoever wishes to enjoy the company of such women is to know that he will not only be removed from clerical office or driven from the doors of the church, but also deprived of the communion of all Catholics, clerics and laymen alike, with no consolation of conversation left to him at all.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. That a cleric is to have no dealings with a woman after an accusation

(See Riculfus, chapter 15.) If an accusation concerning any woman is brought against a priest, so that suspicion of a bad reputation arises, he is to have no dealings with her, either secretly or openly. If he is subsequently found to have done so, after a second and third warning he is to bear the penalty of contempt for his rank.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. What profession priests and deacons are to make when they are ordained

[Col. 0036D]

(Council of Toledo IV, chapter 26.) When priests and deacons are appointed throughout the parishes, they ought first to make a profession before their bishop that they will live chastely and purely in the fear of God, so that such a profession may keep them bound to holy discipline.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Likewise, what sort of deacon a bishop is to make

From this day forward let all bishops be instructed not to presume to make anyone a deacon unless he has promised that he will live chastely.

## CHAPTER XL. That clerics are to obey their bishops

[Col. 0037A]

(Council of Carthage, canon 31.) It has likewise been decided that any clerics or deacons who, for the sake of the needs of ecclesiastical affairs, do not obey their bishops when the bishops wish to promote them to greater honor in their church, they are not to minister there in the rank from which they refused to withdraw.

## CHAPTER XLI. That no cleric should presume to take up secular business on Sunday

(Council of Tarragona, canon 4.) No priest or cleric is to presume on Sunday to take up the business of any case, except only what is required for carrying out the solemn rites established for God. On the other days, with suitable persons restraining them, they may have permission to judge matters that are appropriate, except criminal cases.

## CHAPTER XLII. That clerics should not attend theatrical entertainments

(Council of Laodicea, canon 54.) Ministers of the altar, or any clerics, ought not to attend entertainments presented either at weddings or on the stage. They are to rise from the banquet and leave before the theatrical performers enter.

## CHAPTER XLIII. That clerics should not walk through streets, covered passageways, or markets

(Council of Carthage IV, canons 47–48; Carthage III, canon 27.) Clerics are not to walk through streets, covered passageways, or markets, and they are not to go to the forum or taverns except because of a definite necessity concerning their body or office, or because they have been compelled to travel. Nor are they to presume to eat or drink there.

## CHAPTER XLIV. Likewise, that a buffoonish cleric is to be punished

(Council of Carthage IV, canon 60.) We decree that a cleric who behaves like a buffoon and jokes with disgraceful words is to be removed from office.

## CHAPTER XLV. Likewise, that a flattering and treacherous cleric is to be degraded

(The same, canon 56.) A cleric who is discovered to engage in flattery and treachery is to be degraded from office.

## CHAPTER XLVI. Likewise, a cleric who sings during meals

(The same, canon 61.) A cleric who sings during meals is to be restrained with the severity of the sentence stated above.

## CHAPTER XLVII. In what business clerics should engage

[Col. 0037D]

(Quoted as Melchiades, Distinction 88, chapter “He decreed.”) The Council of Nicaea decreed that no cleric should lease estates or involve himself in secular business, unless perhaps the bishop of the city orders him to attend to ecclesiastical affairs, or to the affairs of wards, orphans, or widows. Here it is plainly evident that secular business is one thing and ecclesiastical business another.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. That clerics should not believe in omens or seek divinations

(Council of Toledo IV, canon 29.) If any bishop, priest, or deacon, or anyone from the clerical order, is discovered to have consulted magicians, diviners, *haruspices*, *arioli*, augurs, or *sortilegi*, or those who profess the art of magic, or anyone practicing similar activities, he is to be deposed from the honor of his dignity, enter a monastery, and there undergo the penalty, devoting himself to perpetual penance and making atonement for the sacrilege he has committed.

[Note: “Make atonement.” The words that follow are not taken from the Council of Toledo.]

Likewise, if anyone after this warning, despising ecclesiastical teaching, goes to those whom they falsely call prophets, angels, or certain deceased saints—calling them “equivocals”—and clings to their wicked teachings, let him be anathema, and let him not participate in any ecclesiastical mysteries until he comes to the bishop for satisfaction.

[Note: Burchard, book X, chapter 48; Ivo, part II, chapters 5 and 73; see the Council of Laodicea, canons 34–35.]

For the Lord himself teaches in the Gospel: “For false Christs and false prophets will arise and will lead many astray” (Matthew 24:24). And the apostle Paul says: “Do not be led away by various and strange doctrines” (Hebrews 13:9).

We have likewise taken care to deliberate concerning those who venerate trees or approach such springs in a religious manner. Moreover, no one is to presume to associate with such people.

## CHAPTER XLIX. That clerics should not accept interest, nor laymen either

(Council of Carthage III, canon 16.) It has likewise been decided that if a cleric lends money, he is to receive money; if he lends goods, he is to receive the same kind of goods in the amount that he gave. Likewise, laymen are also to abstain from interest. If they do not, they are to be excommunicated.

## CHAPTER L. That clerics should not engage in buying cheaply and selling dearly

[Col. 0038C]

(Council of Tarragona, canon 2.) As has been established by the statutes of the canons, whoever wishes to belong to the clergy is not to engage in the pursuit of buying cheaply or selling more dearly. If he wishes to practice this, he is to be restrained from the clergy.

## CHAPTER LI. That clerics should not seek secular protection against ecclesiastical discipline

(Council of Agde, canon 8.) It has also been decided that if a cleric, abandoning his office because of discipline, should perhaps turn to secular protection, and the person to whom he has fled provides him the support of protection, both he and the person who received him are to be expelled from the communion of the Church.

## CHAPTER LII. That clerics should be content with ecclesiastical judgment

[Col. 0038D]

(Pseudo-Clement, first letter to James.) If any of the brothers have disputes among themselves, they are not to be judged before secular judges, but whatever the matter may be is to be settled before the priests of the Church.

## CHAPTER LIII. That clerics should not be absent from vigils

(Council of Carthage IV, canon 49.) A cleric who is absent from the vigils without bodily weakness is to be deprived of his stipend.

## CHAPTER LIV. That a priest should not dine at the wedding of a digamist

(Council of Neocaesarea, canon 7.) It is not appropriate for a priest to dine at the wedding of a digamist, because, since a digamist requires penance, what priest could, for the sake of a banquet, give approval to such a marriage?

## CHAPTER LV. That banquets should not be celebrated from collected contributions

(Council of Laodicea, canon 55.) It is not proper for priests or clerics to hold banquets from collected contributions or common meals. This is likewise not fitting for laymen.

## CHAPTER LVI. That those invited to an *agape* should not take portions of food

(Council of Laodicea, canon 27.) It is not proper for clerics devoted to the sacred ministry, when invited to an *agape*, to accept portions of food, because this causes injury to the ecclesiastical order.

## CHAPTER LVII. That clerics ought diligently to pray, read, and work with their hands

[Col. 0039B]

(Council of Carthage IV, canons 50–53; from chapter 3 of Theodulf of Orléans’ Capitula.) A cleric is to provide himself with food and clothing by craftsmanship or agriculture, provided that this does not impair his office. Whenever he ceases from reading, the work of his hands ought to follow, because idleness is hostile to the soul, and the ancient enemy, when he finds someone free from reading or prayer, easily drags him into vices. Through the practice of reading you will learn how both to live yourselves and to teach others. Through the practice of prayer you will be able to benefit both yourselves and those joined to you in charity. Through work with your hands and mortification of the body, you will both deny nourishment to vices and provide for your needs; and you will have something to extend to those suffering want.

## CHAPTER LVIII. Which psalms should be sung in church and which books should be read

(Martin of Braga, Eastern Collection of Canons, canon 67; Carthage III, canon 47.) It is not proper for popular or non-scriptural psalms to be sung in church, nor for books other than the canonical books to be read—only the sacred volumes of the New or Old Testament. It is also permitted to read the passions of the martyrs when their anniversaries are celebrated.

## CHAPTER LIX. That the Lord’s Prayer should be recited daily

(From chapter 10 of the Council of Toledo IV.) The prayer called the Lord’s Prayer, which the Lord composed with his own mouth and by which he taught his disciples to pray, is to be used frequently not only on Sundays but every day, in every undertaking. Nevertheless, each person should examine his conscience, because if he does not forgive from a pure heart everyone by whom he has been wronged, this prayer appears to him to serve more as an occasion for condemnation than as a means of forgiveness.

## CHAPTER LX. That deeper questions should not be asserted at all

(Celestine I to the bishops of Gaul, chapter 13.) As for the deeper and more difficult aspects of the questions that arise, which those who resisted heretics have treated at greater length: just as we do not dare to despise them, so we do not need to assert them. For the confession of God’s grace—which must not in any way be diminished in its work and favor—we believe that whatever Scripture has taught us according to the rules stated above by the apostolic see is sufficient, so that we may in no way consider Catholic what appears contrary to the propositions set forth.

## CHAPTER LXI. Where and how schools are to be maintained

(Theodulf, chapter 20.) Priests are also to maintain schools in villages and hamlets. If any of the faithful wishes to entrust his little children to them to learn letters, they are not to refuse to receive and teach them, but are to instruct them with the greatest charity. “Those who are wise will shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness will shine like stars for everlasting ages” (Daniel 12:3). When they teach them, they are not to demand any payment from them for this, nor accept anything from them except what their parents voluntarily offer out of love.

## CHAPTER LXII. To which freedmen manumission is to be granted

(Council of Toledo IV, chapter 72.) Whoever receives freedom from his masters in such a way that the patron retains no service from him—if such people are without crime, they are to be freely admitted to the clerical order, because they are known to have been released by direct manumission. Those, however, who were manumitted while retaining an obligation of service are not at all to be promoted to ecclesiastical rank, because they remain subject to their patron in servitude; otherwise, whenever their masters wish, they could turn clerics into slaves.

## CHAPTER LXIII. What kind of men are to be chosen for clerical ministry

(Attributed to Clement’s second letter.) Clerics are to be chosen for the ministry who are worthy to handle the Lord’s sacraments. It is better for the Lord’s priest to have a few ministers who can worthily perform the work of God than many useless ones who bring a heavy burden upon the one who ordains them.

## CHAPTER LXIV. Concerning the Lenten fast of clerics

(Attributed to a letter of Telesphorus.) Know that it has been established by us and by all the bishops assembled in this holy and apostolic see that, for seven full weeks before holy Easter, all clerics called to the Lord’s portion are to abstain from meat. For just as the life of clerics ought to be distinct from the conduct of laymen, so there ought also to be a distinction in fasting. Therefore, throughout these seven weeks, let all clerics fast from meat and delicacies, and strive day and night to cling to the Lord through hymns, vigils, and prayers.

## CHAPTER LXV. That no priest is permitted to be ignorant of the canons

(Celestine, third letter to the bishops established throughout Calabria.) No priest is permitted to be ignorant of his canons, nor to do anything that could oppose the rules of the Fathers. For what order can be worthily preserved by us if the standard of the decrees is broken at the whim of some people, with permission granted to the populace?

## CHAPTER LXVI. How adversity should patiently be endured for Christ

(Attributed to Anacletus’ first letter.) Beloved, do not be surprised, you who suffer persecutions, as though something new were happening to you. Rather, sharing in Christ’s sufferings, rejoice, so that at the revelation of his glory you may rejoice and exult. If you are reproached in the name of Christ, you will be blessed. Do not, because of any desire, sloth, or fear, omit the things that ought to be done or said by you. Do not in any way cease rebuking the people if they have gone astray.

Let none of you suffer as a murderer, thief, slanderer, or coveter of what belongs to others. But if he suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed; rather, let him glorify God in this name, because it is written: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:16). Take care, because he said “for righteousness’ sake.” For whoever suffers on account of some crime will not be blessed for that reason.

## CHAPTER LXVII. That one must not pray with an excommunicated person

[Col. 0041B]

(Apostolic canon 11.) If anyone prays together with an excommunicated person, even in a house, let him be deprived of communion.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. That the offerings of those who are quarrelsome or oppress the poor are to be rejected

(Council of Carthage IV, canons 93–94.) The offerings of brothers who are at odds with one another are not to be received either in the sacristy or in the treasury. The gifts of those who oppress the poor are likewise to be rejected by priests.

## CHAPTER LXIX. That drunkenness is to be prohibited

(Council of Agde, canon 41.) Above all, drunkenness is to be prohibited to clerics, since it is the source and nurse of every vice. Accordingly, concerning anyone proved to have been drunk, we decree, as the order requires, either that he be removed from wine for three days or subjected to corporal punishment. If he makes a habit of this, the excommunication is to be prolonged; but if he cannot be corrected, he is to be expelled from the priestly order.

## CHAPTER LXX. How each weekday should be observed

(Council of Carthage IV, canon 74.) Anyone who deliberately fasts on Sunday is not to be considered a Catholic. No business and no servile work is to be done on that day. On Thursday no one is to be required to fast, so that there may be a distinction between the fasting of Christians and that of pagans, Catholics, and heretics.

[Note: Melchiades, as it is said, in his letter to the bishops of Spain, cited in *On Consecration*, distinction 14, “Fasting.”]

For Sunday and Thursday are rightly considered more solemn than the other days: on Sunday the Lord Jesus Christ, having overcome the instrument of death, rose from the dead; and on that day, after his ascension into heaven, the grace of the Holy Spirit inflamed the disciples, sending and imparting to them the gifts of the charisms. On Thursday he celebrated the mysteries of the Last Supper with those same disciples. Not long afterward, as the day came around again, he ascended into heaven while they were alive. On that same day chrism is also prepared, and on that day penitents are reconciled.

(Innocent I, letter 1, chapter 4.) Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday are to be observed as fast days above the others, because on Wednesday Judas arranged with the Jews to betray the Savior; on Friday Christ was crucified; and on Saturday the apostles spent the day in sadness, between fear and hope, remaining somewhat uncertain about the glory of the Resurrection. Whoever, therefore, on these three days is found in drunkenness or at banquets, without a major intervening feast or necessity, appears either to betray along with the betrayer, to crucify along with those who crucified him, or to mock the sufferings of the apostles. For whoever wishes to rejoice with them in the Lord’s resurrection ought in some way to grieve with them over his passion.

## CHAPTER LXXI. That we should pray standing on Sunday

(Council of Nicaea I, canon 20.) Since there are some who kneel for prayer on Sunday and during the days of Pentecost, it has pleased the holy council, so that everything may be observed harmoniously in all places, that on these days we should pay our vows to the Lord standing.

## CHAPTER LXXII. That priests should instruct the people how to conduct themselves on feast days

Priests are to instruct the people not to devote themselves on feast days to harmful banquets and disgraceful amusements, but to prayers.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. On which feasts the people should receive communion

(Council of Agde, canon 18.) Laypeople who do not receive communion at the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and Pentecost are not to be considered Catholics or counted among Catholics.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. If the sacrifice falls through negligence

[Col. 0042C]

If the sacrifice falls through someone’s negligence, let him either lick it with his tongue so that nothing remains of it, or fast for forty days.

[Note: From a decree circulated under the name of Pope Pius and cited in *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter “If through negligence,” with some words altered.]

But if this happened through the negligence of another, let the person whose negligence it was do penance. The place where it fell is either to be burned with fire or thoroughly wiped clean, and whatever has been wiped up is to be burned.

## CHAPTER LXXV. If vomiting occurs negligently within three days after communion

If anyone, after receiving the most holy mysteries, vomits through negligence within three days—

[Note: “Three days”: perhaps rather “three hours,” as Acherius thought?]

—if he is a priest, let him do penance for forty days; the others are to be judged according to their own rank. Whatever has been expelled is to be burned.

## CHAPTER LXXVI. That the possessed should not receive communion and should not bathe in consecrated water

No one is permitted to give the body or blood of our Lord Jesus Christ to persons possessed by an evil spirit (*energumeni*) while they remain in that condition, unless perhaps they are in danger of death. For if such sacraments are forbidden to criminals, how much more to those whom the author of crime himself attacks? But if they are freed by divine mercy, let them remain for a long time in abstinence and prayer, according to the judgment of the priests, and only then receive communion among the other Christians. If they have not been baptized or confirmed, however, they may be baptized or confirmed at any time.

No one is to presume to bathe in consecrated water on account of any illness or necessity. Such water is permitted only to be sprinkled. We find no such baths among sacred practices, have heard of none performed by the Fathers, and do not consider them useful.

## CHAPTER LXXVII. How the mysteries of baptism and chrism are to be observed

Those who have received the mystery of holy baptism or the gift of the Holy Spirit in chrism are in no way to have intercourse with women before the ninth day. Likewise, women in this condition are entirely to abstain from men and are in no way to engage in any shameful game or business. They are to abstain for a long time from eating meat, until the bishop of the place, according to the character of the persons or the circumstances of the time, has made provision.

No one is to presume to lift a person from the sacred font or hold someone before the bishop for confirmation. Nor is a cleric to presume to assume any sacred order unless these same sacraments mentioned above have first been celebrated for him. If anyone is found to have violated any of the matters stated above, he is to do penance according to the judgment of the bishop.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. That theatrical and other games are not to be held on feast days

(Council of Africa, canon 61.) We must also request that theatrical entertainments and other games be removed from Sunday and from the other most solemn days of the Christian religion. This is especially necessary because on the eighth day of holy Easter the people gather at the circus rather than at the church. When the appointed days of these entertainments occur, they ought to be transferred, and no Christian should be compelled to attend them.

## CHAPTER LXXIX. That no one should observe the Kalends of January or lead dances

(Zacharias, in the Roman council, canon 9, also cited in *Question* 27, canon 7, chapter “If anyone.”) No one is to presume to observe the Kalends of January or the winter festivals according to pagan custom. If anyone presumes to observe the Kalends of January or the winter festivals, or to prepare tables with lamps in houses, or to lead songs and dances through villages and streets—which is a great iniquity—let him be anathema before God.

## CHAPTER LXXX. That people are to assemble at the church
(Theodulf, ch. 10.) You ought not to assemble in church for any other reason than to praise God and perform his service. Disputes, disturbances, idle talk, and other such activities must be entirely prohibited from that holy place. For where God’s name is invoked, a sacrifice is offered to God [Col. 0044A], and the presence of angels is beyond doubt, it is dangerous to say or do anything unsuitable to the place. If the Lord drove from the temple those who bought or sold the victims offered to him, how much more angrily will he drive out those who defile a place dedicated to divine worship with lies, idle talk, laughter, and such trifles?

### CHAPTER LXXXI — On the instruction of men and women

(Council of Carthage IV, ch. 98; likewise, ch. 99.) A layman must not presume to teach in the presence of clergy unless they approve. Nor may a woman, however learned and holy, teach or presume to teach men in an assembly.

### CHAPTER LXXXII — Likewise, on their clothing

[Col. 0044B]

(Council of Gangra, ch. 12; likewise, ch. 13.) If any man, on account of a supposed continence, wears a cloak, believing that by this he possesses righteousness, and despises those who reverently wear the birrus and other ordinary customary garments, let him be anathema. Likewise, if a woman, on account of a supposed continence, changes her dress and adopts a man’s clothing instead of the customary clothing of women, let her be anathema.

### CHAPTER LXXXIII — That anniversaries or weddings not take place during Lent

(Council of Braga, ch. 48.) It is not appropriate to celebrate the anniversaries of martyrs during Lent; rather, their memory is to be observed only on Saturday and Sunday. Weddings or anniversaries are in no way to be celebrated on those same days.

### CHAPTER LXXXIV — On the Lenten fast

(Council of Agde, ch. 12.) It was also decided that all the churches, except on Sundays, must fast during Lent, even on Saturday, according to priestly ordinance and the discretion of communion [Note: [Col. 0043D] “And the discretion.” In the published councils one reads, “and by a change in strictness”].

### CHAPTER LXXXV — Likewise, on the observance of the same

(Council of Laodicea, ch. 50.) It is not appropriate during Lent, in the final week, to break the fast on Thursday and to pass through the whole of Lent without reverence. Rather, it is more fitting to observe the whole of Lent with a strict fast.

### CHAPTER LXXXVI — Likewise, concerning the foregoing

(Council of Toledo IV, ch. 4.) Some break the fast at the ninth hour on the day of the Lord’s Passion [Col. 0044D] and abstain from banquets [Note: [Col. 0043D] “Abstain.” Here everyone can easily see that something is missing; but the council’s meaning is so clear that it does not seem necessary to dwell on the wording.]. While on that day the sun itself, shrouded in darkness, withdrew its light, and the elements themselves were disturbed and displayed the sorrow of the whole world, they profane the fast of so great a day and devote themselves to feasting. Since the universal Church spends that entire day in mourning and abstinence because of the Lord’s Passion, anyone who breaks the fast on it—apart from children, the elderly, and the sick—before the prayers of absolution have been completed is to be excluded from paschal joy and is not to receive on that day the sacrament of the Lord’s body [Col. 0045A] and blood, since he does not honor the day of his Passion through abstinence.

### CHAPTER LXXXVII — On the fast of the Four Seasons

(The so-called first letter of Pope Calixtus.) The fast which you have learned to celebrate among us three times a year we now say should more appropriately be held four times, during the four seasons: just as the year revolves through four seasons, so we should observe four solemn fasts, one in each season, according to the words of the prophet Zechariah, who says:

> Thus says the Lord of hosts: The fast of the fourth month, and the fast of the fifth month, and the fast of the seventh month, and the fast of the tenth month shall become for the house of Judah joy and gladness and splendid festivals. Nevertheless, love truth and peace, says the Lord of hosts. (Zechariah 8:19)

Therefore, we must all be of one mind in this, so that, in accordance with apostolic teaching, “we may all say the same thing, and there may be no divisions among us” (1 Corinthians 1:10).

### CHAPTER LXXXVIII — That the ecclesiastical fast is not to be dissolved

(Council of Gangra, ch. 19.) If anyone among those devoted to continence, without bodily necessity, arrogantly dissolves the fasts handed down in common and observed by the Church, driven on by the impulse of his own thought, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER LXXXIX — That consecrated oil not be administered to the sick who are doing penance

(Innocent I, letter to Decentius, ch. 8.) This cannot be administered to penitents, because it is a kind of sacrament. For when the other sacraments are denied to them, how can it be thought that one kind may be granted?

### CHAPTER XC — How priests are to deal with penitents

[Col. 0045C]

A priest must not impose the laws of penance without regard to the person or the cause. Rather, he should grant the periods of penance or reconciliation according to the judgment of the bishop. A priest must not reconcile a penitent without consulting the bishop, unless the bishop permits it. Instead, priests appointed in parishes should exercise great vigilance lest their parishioners fall into criminal offenses.

If this should occur, they must carefully inquire from the offenders themselves and from all their neighbors how the matter happened, and must not delay recording it in writing. They should frequently admonish them to hasten as quickly as possible to the satisfaction of peace and penance. The first priest of that parish, or the one who is its teacher after him, must come with them and bring with him what he has written [Col. 0045D].

If those penitents delay coming, the priest himself must in no way fail to appear, at the beginning of the fast, at the principal seat of that bishop, bringing the written account with him, and he must inform his bishop so that he may consider what should thereafter be done. If the penitents also appear, he must again write down the rules of penance imposed upon them and exercise the greatest care and concern for them, so that he may become fully acquainted with their conduct.

If he sees someone earnestly undertaking penance, or fears that he may be endangered by weakness, or if illness should overwhelm anyone [Col. 0046A], he must have recourse to his own priest, the bishop, so that remedies may be granted to him through the bishop. If the bishop is absent, the matter should meanwhile be brought to the attention of the cardinal bishops of the principal see. On the day of reconciliation—that is, the Lord’s Supper—the priest himself should hasten to be present with them, so that he may again learn and record what has been commanded them.

### CHAPTER XCI — That penitents kneel daily

(Council of Carthage, ch. 8.) Penitents are also to kneel on days of remission.

### CHAPTER XCII — That penitents who have died be buried

(Ibid., ch. 83.) They are to present deceased penitents to the church and bury them.

### CHAPTER XCIII — That penitents abstain from secular business

[Col. 0046B]

(Leo the Great, letter 91, ch. 9.) The character of profit either excuses or condemns the person engaged in trade, since there is both honest and shameful gain. Nevertheless, for a penitent it is more beneficial to suffer loss than to be entangled in the dangers of commerce, because it is difficult for sin not to intervene in the transactions of buyer and seller. Therefore we admonish [Note: [Col. 0045] “Therefore we admonish.” These words, through “But neither,” are not found in Leo’s letters.] that a penitent not bind himself to any business or hunting, but, under the supervision of the priest in charge of the place, devote himself to prayer and fasting.

If he is poor, he should seek his livelihood by such a craft as has no stain of sin attached to it, so that, supported in this way by the priest’s testimony, he may more securely have recourse to the judgment of his bishop (of the same letter, ch. 10).

But neither after completing his penance should he enter secular military service, since the Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Timothy 2:4). Therefore, the person who wishes to entangle himself in worldly military service is not free from the snares of the devil. Accordingly, one who asks pardon for unlawful acts ought also to abstain from many lawful ones, as the Apostle says: “Everything is lawful, but not everything is expedient” (1 Corinthians 6:12). Thus, if a penitent has a case which he perhaps ought not to neglect, he should seek an ecclesiastical judgment rather than a civil one.

### CHAPTER XCIV — How the bridegroom and bride are to be blessed by the priest

(Carthage IV, ch. 13.) When the bridegroom and bride are to be blessed by the priest, they are to be presented by their parents or by the bridal attendants. After receiving the blessing, they are to remain virginal that night out of reverence for the blessing itself [Col. 0046D].

### CHAPTER XCV — Which marriages are to be avoided

(Council of Rome I under Gregory II; Rome under Eugenius II and Leo III.) No one may presume to take in marriage a woman consecrated to God, or his own godmother, stepmother, mother, sister, spiritual daughter, a woman related to him by blood, or one whom a relative has had. No one may presume to abduct or steal a virgin or widow as a wife unless he has received her in betrothal from her own parents or guardians, even if she herself wished it.

If any man or woman should enter into one of the aforesaid wicked marriages and remain in it, let that person know that, by canonical authority, he or she is bound by the sentence of anathema. Those who consent or give counsel are likewise to be bound by anathema. If, however, those who have been joined together, after being admonished, withdraw and separate from one another, they are to be subjected to penance, as the bishop of the place shall determine. The same applies to those who gave counsel in the matter or had any share in it.

Whatever priest or cleric gives his consent in such matters, or associates himself with their fellowship, is to be condemned and deprived of the honor of his priesthood or ministry.

### CHAPTER XCVI — How each person is to be instructed

(Theodulf, ch. 21.) Since the pages of all Holy Scripture are filled with instruments of good works, and throughout the fields of the Holy Scriptures weapons can be found by which vices may be restrained and virtues nourished, we have been permitted to insert into this Capitular a saying of a certain Father—Saint Benedict, Rule, ch. 4—concerning the instruments of good works. It sets forth, with great brevity, what should be done and what should be avoided.

First, to love the Lord God with all one’s heart, all one’s soul, and all one’s strength; then, one’s neighbor as oneself. Next: not to kill; not to commit adultery; not to steal; not to covet; not to bear false witness; to honor all people; and not to do to another what one does not wish to be done to oneself.

To deny oneself in order to follow Christ; to chastise the body; not to embrace pleasures. To love fasting and refresh the poor; to clothe the naked; to visit the sick; to bury the dead; to console the sorrowful. To make oneself a stranger to the works of the world; to prefer nothing to the love of Christ.

Not to carry anger through to action; not to reserve time for wrath. Not to harbor deceit in the heart. Not to offer false peace; not to abandon charity. Not to swear, lest one perhaps perjure oneself. To speak the truth from the heart and mouth. Not to repay evil for evil; not to inflict injury, but patiently to endure injury inflicted. To love enemies; not to curse those who curse, but rather to bless them. To endure persecution for the sake of justice.

Not to be proud, not to be addicted to wine, not to eat excessively, not to be sleepy, not to be lazy, not to grumble, not to be a detractor. To entrust one’s hope to God. When one sees something good in oneself, to attribute it to God [Col. 0047D], not to oneself; but to recognize that evil is always one’s own doing and to reckon it as one’s own.

To fear the day of judgment; to dread hell; to desire eternal life with all spiritual longing; to regard death as ever before one’s eyes each day; to guard the actions of one’s life at every hour. To see God in every place. When evil thoughts arise in one’s heart, immediately to dash them against Christ and reveal them to one’s spiritual elder.

To guard one’s mouth from evil or corrupt speech. To see God in every place. Not to love much speaking; not to speak empty words or words suited to laughter; not to love excessive or uncontrolled laughter; willingly to hear holy readings; frequently to devote oneself to prayer.

Daily in prayer to confess one’s past evils to God with tears or groaning [Col. 0048A] and to amend those evils. Not to fulfill the desires of the flesh. To hate one’s own will. To obey in everything the commands of the priest and teacher, even if he himself, God forbid, acts otherwise, remembering that command of the Lord: “Do what they say; but do not do what they do” (Matthew 23:3).

Not to wish to be called holy before one is holy, but first to be what one is more truthfully called. To strive daily to fulfill God’s commands in deeds. To love chastity. To hate no one. Not to harbor jealousy or envy. Not to love contention. To avoid tale-bearing. To honor elders. To love the younger. In the love of Christ, to pray for enemies. To make peace with those with whom one is at odds before sunset. Never to despair of God’s mercy.

[Col. 0048B]

Behold, these are the instruments of the spiritual craft. When we have fulfilled them continually, day and night, and they have been returned to us on the day of judgment, the Lord will recompense us with those things he himself promised:

> What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—what God has prepared for those who love him. (1 Corinthians 2:9)

### CHAPTER XCVII — That they should know the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed by heart

(Theodulf, ch. 22.) All the faithful, from the least to the greatest, are to be admonished to know the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed by heart. They are to be told that the whole foundation of the Christian faith rests upon these two statements, and that no one who has not memorized these two statements, believed them with all his heart, and very frequently repeated them in prayer can be a Catholic.

It has therefore been established that no one may be chrismated or baptized, receive another from the baptismal font, or stand before the bishop as sponsor for anyone at confirmation, unless he knows the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer by heart—except those whom age has not yet sufficiently enabled to speak.

### CHAPTER XCVIII — That no one presume to reject these canons

(Gelasius I, letter 9.) Since we wish to permit ourselves no rash act contrary to the reverence due to salutary rules, and since the Apostolic See, superior to all these matters, by the Lord’s favor strives with pious and devoted purpose to preserve what has been established by the canons of the Fathers [Col. 0048D], it is altogether unworthy for any bishop or member of the subordinate orders to reject this observance, which he sees the See of blessed Peter both following and teaching (Gelasius borrowed this from Julius I, letter 1, ch. 4). It is also entirely fitting that the whole body of the Church should agree among itself in this observance, which it sees prevailing where the Lord has established the primacy of the whole Church.

### CHAPTER XCIX — That what has been established must in no way be altered

These decrees must not be overthrown by any wickedness or changed by any novelty, because the order of secular matters is one thing and that of divine matters another.

### CHAPTER C — That we ought also to know which writings are to be received in Holy Scripture and which rejected

[Col. 0049A]

(Gelasius I, at the First Council of Rome.) Although no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, namely Christ Jesus (1 Corinthians 3:11), nevertheless, for the building up of the holy Church, after those books of the Old and New Testament which we regularly receive, it is not forbidden to receive these writings also:

The holy Council of Nicaea of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers, held under the auspices of the great Constantine Augustus; the holy Council of Ephesus, at which Nestorius was condemned, with the agreement of the most blessed Pope Celestine, through Cyril, bishop of the holy see of Alexandria, and Arcadius, sent from Italy; [Col. 0049B] and the holy Council of Chalcedon, held under the auspices of the Emperor Marcian and Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, at which the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies, together with Dioscorus and his accomplices, were condemned.

Likewise, the works of blessed Caecilius Cyprian, martyr and bishop of Carthage; the works of blessed Gregory Nazianzen, bishop; the works of blessed Basil, bishop of Cappadocia; the works of blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria; the works of blessed John, bishop of Constantinople; the works of blessed Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria; the works of blessed Proterius, bishop of Alexandria; the works of blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers; the works of blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan; the works of blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo; the works of blessed Jerome, priest; the works of blessed Prosper, a religious man; and the letter of blessed Pope Leo to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople. If anyone disputes its text down to a single iota and does not reverently receive it in all respects, let him be anathema.

Likewise, we decree that all the works and treatises of the various orthodox Fathers who in no way departed from the fellowship of the holy Church or separated themselves from the proclamation of its faith, but by the grace of God remained participants in that communion until the last day of their lives, are to be read. Likewise, the decretal letters which the most blessed popes issued from the city of Rome at various times in response to consultations from various Fathers are to be received with reverence.

Likewise, the acts of the holy martyrs, which shine with manifold torments and the triumphant splendor of their confessions [Col. 0049D]. Who among Catholics could doubt that these things happened, that the martyrs endured greater sufferings in their contests, and that they bore everything not by their own strength but by the grace and help of God?

Nevertheless, according to ancient custom, they are not read in the holy Roman Church with particular caution, because the names of those who wrote them are entirely unknown, and because they are thought to have been written by unbelievers or ignorant people with additions that were superfluous or less suitable than the proper order required. Such are the passions of Cyricus and Julitta, and of George and others of this kind, which are said to have been composed by heretics. For this reason, as has been said, they are not read in the holy Church, lest even a slight opportunity for mockery arise. Nevertheless, together with the aforesaid Church, we venerate with complete devotion all the martyrs and their glorious contests, who are known more to God than to men.

Likewise, we receive with all honor the lives of the Fathers Paul, Antony, and Hilarion, and of all the hermits, which the most blessed man Jerome wrote. Likewise, although the name of the person who wrote them is unknown, we have learned that the acts of blessed Sylvester, bishop of the Apostolic See, are read by many Catholics in the city of Rome, and that many churches imitate this practice because of its antiquity.

Likewise, the writings concerning the discovery of the holy cross and another concerning the head of John the Baptist are certain recent accounts, and some Catholics accept them. But when these writings come into the hands of Catholics, the saying of blessed Paul should prevail: “Test everything; hold fast to what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21).

Likewise, Rufinus, a religious man, published many books of ecclesiastical works and interpreted several writings. But because blessed Jerome censured him in certain matters concerning freedom of choice, we hold those views which we know the aforesaid blessed Jerome held. This applies not only to Rufinus but also to all those whom that frequently mentioned man reproved out of zeal for God [Col. 0050C] and reverence for the faith.

Likewise, we accept for reading some works of Origen which the most blessed man Jerome does not reject. All the rest, however, are to be rejected together with their author.

Likewise, although Eusebius of Caesarea, in the first book of his Chronicle and of his Ecclesiastical History, became lukewarm [Note: [Col. 0049D] “Became lukewarm.” Here Gelasius treats Eusebius rather leniently; for one would have to be blind not to see that, in the first book of the Ecclesiastical History, his discussion of the Word is framed not merely so that the Son is nowhere acknowledged as equal to the Father, but so that he is called inferior to the Father and almost denied to be God. When this offended Rufinus, who had undertaken the labor of translating his History into Latin, he altered many passages, and indeed with such success that the very sources from which Eusebius had drawn arguments for loudly denying that Christ is God were used by his translator to prove Christ’s divinity. Eusebius is also blamed for having praised Origen; everyone can see what kind of praise this was.], and later wrote a book in praise and defense of the schismatic Origen, we nevertheless do not say that they are to be rejected in every respect because of the exceptional knowledge relevant to instruction that they contain.

We highly praise Orosius, a most learned man, because he composed for us a history very necessary against the calumnies of the pagans and woven together with remarkable brevity. We proclaim with distinguished praise the Paschal work of the venerable Sedulius, which he composed in heroic verse [Col. 0050D]. Nor do we reject the laborious work of Juvencus; rather, we marvel at it.

All the other writings composed or proclaimed by heretics or schismatics are in no way received by the Catholic and Apostolic Church. Of these, we believe that a few which have come to memory, and which Catholics must avoid, should be listed.

First, we confess that the synod of Rimini, convened by Constantius Caesar, son of Constantine Augustus, under the auspices of the prefect Taurus, was then and remains condemned forever. We know that the book entitled *The Itinerary of the Apostle Peter*, called *of Saint Clement*, in eight books, is apocryphal; the *Acts in the Name of the Apostle Andrew*, apocryphal; the *Acts in the Name of the Apostle Thomas*, in ten books, apocryphal; the *Acts in the Name of the Apostle Peter*, apocryphal; the *Acts in the Name of the Apostle Philip*, apocryphal; those of Thaddeus, apocryphal; the *Gospel in the Name of the Apostle Matthew*, apocryphal; the *Gospel in the Name of Barnabas*, apocryphal; the *Gospel in the Name of James the Less*, apocryphal; the *Gospel in the Name of the Apostle Peter*, apocryphal; the *Gospel in the Name of the Apostle Bartholomew*, apocryphal; the *Gospel in the Name of the Apostle Andrew* [Col. 0051B], apocryphal; the *Gospel in the Name of Thomas*, used by the Manichaeans, apocryphal; the Gospels falsified by Lucian, apocryphal; the book concerning the infancy of the Savior, apocryphal; the book concerning the birth of the Savior, and concerning Mary and the midwife, apocryphal; the book called *The Shepherd*, apocryphal; all the books written by Seleucus, the disciple of the devil, apocryphal; the book called *The Foundation*, apocryphal; the book called *The Treasure*, apocryphal; the book concerning the daughters of Adam’s genealogy, apocryphal; the *Centimeter* concerning Christ, composed in Virgilian verses, apocryphal; the book called *of Thecla and Paul*, apocryphal; the book called *of Nepos*, apocryphal; the book of *Proverbs* written by heretics and bearing the name of Saint Xystus, apocryphal; the revelation called that of the Apostle Paul [Col. 0051C], apocryphal; the revelation called that of the Apostle Thomas, apocryphal; the revelation called that of Stephen, apocryphal; the revelation called *The Passing*, that is, *The Assumption of Saint Mary*, apocryphal; the book called *The Penance of Adam*, apocryphal; the book concerning the giant named Ogias, whom heretics claim fought with a dragon after the Flood, apocryphal; the book called *The Testament of Job*, apocryphal; the book called *The Penance of Origen*, apocryphal; the book called *The Penance of Saint Cyprian*, apocryphal; the book called *The Penance of Jannes and Jambres*, apocryphal; the book called *The Lots of the Apostles*, apocryphal; the book called *The Praise of the Apostles*, apocryphal; [Col. 0052A] the book called *The Canons of the Apostles*, apocryphal; the book *Physiologus*, written by heretics and marked with the name of blessed Ambrose, apocryphal; the history of Eusebius Pamphilus, apocryphal; the works of Tertullian, apocryphal; the works of Lactantius, apocryphal; the works of Africanus, apocryphal; the works of Postumianus and Gallus, apocryphal; the works of Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla, apocryphal; all the works of Faustus the Manichaean, apocryphal; the works of Commodianus, apocryphal; the works of another Clement of Alexandria, apocryphal; the works of Tatius Cyprian, apocryphal; the works of Arnobius, apocryphal; the works of Tyconius, apocryphal; the works of Cassian, priest of Gaul, apocryphal; the works of Victorinus of Poitiers, apocryphal; the works of Faustus of Riez, of Gaul, apocryphal; [Col. 0052B] the works of Frumentius the blind, apocryphal; the letter of Jesus to Abgar, apocryphal; the letter of Abgar to Jesus, apocryphal; the passion of Quiricus and Julitta, apocryphal; the passion of George, apocryphal; the writing called *The Contradiction of Solomon*, apocryphal; all phylacteries, which, contrary to their claim, were written not by the art of angels but rather by the art of demons, apocryphal.

These and similar works, which Simon Magus, Nicholas, Cerinthus, Marcion, Basilides, Ebion, Paul of Samosata, Photinus and Bonosus, who fell away through a similar error, Montanus with his most obscene followers, Apollinaris, Valentinus or Manichaeus, Faustus the African, Arius, Sabellius, Macedonius, Eunomius, Novatus, Sabbatius, Caelestius, Donatus, Eustathius, Jovinian, [Col. 0052C] Pelagius, Julian of Celanum, Caelestinus, Maximinus, Priscillian of Spain, Nestorius of Constantinople, Maximus the Cynic, Lampetius, Dioscorus, Eutyches, Peter, and another Peter—one of whom disgraced Alexandria and the other Antioch—Acacius of Constantinople with his associates, and all other heretics and their disciples, whether schismatics, taught or wrote, whose names are not retained, are not merely rejected but also expelled from the entire holy Catholic and Apostolic Church. Together with their authors and the followers of those authors, we confess them to be condemned forever under the unbreakable bond of anathema.

# Atto, Bishop of Vercelli: A Short Work on Ecclesiastical Pressures

(Apud Acherium, *Spicilegium*, vol. I, p. 414.)

## PART ONE — On the judgments of bishops

[Col. 0051D]

The Gospel history tells us that when the Lord, intending to teach his disciples, had left the crowd and gone up the mountain, and after he had instructed them most perfectly concerning all the commandments by which the Christian religion ought to be formed, he said at the end of that sermon:

> Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house upon rock. The rain fell, the rivers came, the winds blew, and they struck that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded upon rock. (Matthew 7:24)

That wise man is undoubtedly the one of whom blessed Paul the Apostle also says: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). He rightly built his house—that is, the holy Church, of which he says elsewhere, “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Luke 19:46)—upon rock, namely upon himself, just as the same Apostle says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:1). And elsewhere: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Corinthians 3:11).

Foretelling the pressures that would come upon this house, the same Lord immediately added:

> The rain fell, the rivers came, the winds blew, and they struck that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded upon rock. (Matthew 7:25)

He graciously foretold its coming evils so that, when they occurred, the holy Church would bear them more lightly because it had known them beforehand. He armed it with the shield of patience, since foreseen evils can be borne more lightly than those which occur suddenly and unexpectedly. Hence the Lord says elsewhere: “I have told you this so that, when the hour comes, you may remember that I told you” (John 16:4).

This house, therefore, consists not of walls made by human hands but most beautifully of living and chosen stones, that is, of assemblies of the saints. Its structure consists of the faithful, each of whom shines with various [lacuna] virtues. The builders themselves are the teachers [lacuna], whose faith and works [lacuna]—the beginning of whose instruction we believe to have been founded upon the faithful confession of the most blessed Peter, when he said to the Lord: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

For this he also deserved to hear, among other things, as a reward:

> And I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. (Matthew 16:16–18)

The holy Church, therefore, has been built upon rock [Col. 0053D], upon the solidity of apostolic faith, through faith in and love of Christ, reception of the sacraments, and observance of his commandments.

Blessed is the house which is not harmed when rains strike, is not swept away when rivers overflow, and is not thrown down when winds beat upon it. Against it the gates of hell do not prevail, although they continually assail it with various struggles. It yields in no way either to hidden temptations, open persecutions, the attacks of evil spirits themselves, or the weight of vices and crimes.

Let those who persecute the holy Church therefore lay aside their obstinacy; let the faithful take up steadfastness in persecution. Let the former hear that they will not prevail; let the latter prepare themselves, because they truly will be persecuted, and those who persevere to the end will be crowned with happiness.

At no time, therefore, will the foundation of the holy Church fail. Every day, thanks be to God, it receives increase. Nor will it lack persecutors—those most savage lacerators of the faithful—who, after many tribulations, cause them to reach an eternally blessed reward.

The Lord also seems to explain such words when he says to the apostles: “Behold, I send you like sheep among wolves; therefore be wise as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matthew 10:16), and so forth, up to: “But whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 14:13).

These were undoubtedly that house, namely the Church, which, shaken by various disturbances yet built upon rock [Col. 0054B], was not cast down but persevered in steadfastness of faith. The holy apostles themselves, and the other teachers of the holy churches, keeping the Lord’s command in mind, prepared themselves to endure sufferings and constantly invited others to do the same. They also reproved their persecutors with moderation, taught the foolish, and vehemently rebuked the hardness of their hearts. Thus, at times they miraculously corrected some of them from their perversities, while at other times they provoked others even more against themselves.

The same thing is done today in the holy Church: when the conduct of wicked people is rebuked by its rulers, those people themselves persecute their teachers and, in order to escape ecclesiastical discipline, do not fear to defame the lives of pastors. [Col. 0054C] But the holy Fathers, considering this most carefully [lacuna], therefore decreed that the privilege of pastors should remain inviolable [lacuna], so that the proud and senseless would in no way dare to despise them or scorn their commands.

For how can bishops rebuke the faults of others if others dare to attack them? Therefore, the statutes of the holy Fathers entirely forbid their being lightly accused or slandered. Nor do the holy canons admit anyone to accuse them unless he is found, after faithful examination, to be comparable in life and conduct to priests worthy of such an inquiry.

Nor did they decree that accusers should go unpunished if they could not prove the crimes which they did not fear to charge against priests. Rather, they imposed upon rejected accusers the same penalty which convicted accused persons ought to have suffered. They most wisely decreed that no accusation brought against them should be accepted or defended unless security had been given mutually, and that they should be judged only on the basis of written documents [Col. 0054D]. They also declare that such security has no force if it arose through violence, fear, or deceit.

They likewise excluded entirely, in one and the same case, the authority of anyone—whatever his rank—to judge and accuse at the same time. They most carefully prescribed the place and time in which these matters should be examined, as well as the person whose hearing they belonged to. They assert that the judgment of judges has no validity unless those judges were chosen by the accused themselves.

They also granted a considerable period for considering a response, on account of the simplicity of the innocent and the elaborate schemes of the wicked [Col. 0055A]. They altogether forbade anyone’s being condemned without the authority of the holy Roman See, although metropolitan bishops were granted permission to hear and examine cases with the consent of all the bishops of their province.

But lest we appear to say anything immoderate, let us for the present confirm what we have already said by the ordinances of the holy Fathers. For the most holy martyr Alexander, bishop of Rome, says (Epistle 1):

> If anyone believes that he has any just complaint against a bishop or the officials of a church, he should not first approach the primates or other judges, but should meet privately with the very persons by whom he considers himself injured—not [Col. 0055B] merely once, but very often—so that he may receive from them either the justice due him or a just explanation.

Likewise Anacletus (Epistle 2):

> For if it is commanded that a priest be chosen free from crime, he is by no means permitted to be accused or slandered by people entangled in crimes. Nor may he be accused by any except those who are themselves free from crime and who, in accordance with the rules for election, could—if necessity arose, or if they themselves chose willingly to serve the Lord—be made and ordained priests without crime, and who are in every respect such persons as priests are commanded to be when chosen.

Eutychianus (Epistle 2):

> Whoever brings the charge must come into court, state the defendant’s name, undertake the obligation imposed by his written accusation, and submit to a corresponding custody, due regard nevertheless being had for his rank. Otherwise he might suppose that he had been granted [Col. 0055C] license to lie, whereas the equivalence of the penalty calls slanderers to punishment.

Alexander again (Epistle 1):

> Likewise, if writings of any kind have been extorted from such persons by fear, fraud, or violence, or if, in order to free themselves, they have by any device written or confirmed anything whatsoever, we decree that it shall cause them no prejudice or injury.

Fabian (Epistle 2):

> Nor may anyone ever presume to be accuser, judge, and witness at the same time, since in every trial four classes of persons must always be present: chosen judges, accusers, defenders, and witnesses.

Felix says (Epistle 2):

> If any bishop has been accused by accusers who are admissible, and after they have approached him in charity [Col. 0055D] so that he ought to amend and correct the matter he has refused to correct it, then—not before, but at that point—his case is to be referred canonically to the highest primates. At a suitable place within that province and at a suitable time, namely autumn or summer, they must summon a council according to rule, so that he may be heard there by all the bishops of that province. Once he too has been summoned according to rule, he must attend unless illness or another grave necessity detains him; for there is no permission to bring an accusation beyond the boundaries of the province before a hearing has been requested.

Gaius likewise (sole Epistle):

> Let no one ever presume to accuse a bishop or other clerics before secular judges.

Zephyrinus (Epistle 1):

> Let none [Col. 0056A] of them be bound by a sentence pronounced by one who is not his own judge.

And the same author:

> If necessary, let every accused bishop choose twelve judges by whom his case may be judged justly; and let him neither be heard, excommunicated, nor judged before he himself has chosen them.

And Felix:

> Concerning the periods of delay for bishops about which you consulted us, we find various rules established by the Fathers. Some ordered that a year and six months be granted for repelling the contrivances of the unskilled, preparing their answers, confirming witnesses, and seeking the counsel of bishops and friends. Others granted a year, on which most agree. I find no period shorter than six months.

Zephyrinus again (in the same place):

> When patriarchs or primates examine [Col. 0056B] an accused bishop, they must not deliver a final sentence until they have the support of apostolic authority and either he confesses himself guilty or is convicted by innocent witnesses examined according to rule. These witnesses must be no fewer than the disciples whom the Lord commanded to be chosen as assistants to the apostles.

That is, seventy-two.

The decrees of the canons plainly show that many other teachers of the holy Church also agree in all these matters. Yet now—alas!—what we cannot say without injury to God’s holy Church has been so thoroughly abolished that even in a properly instituted accusation scarcely any place remains for a lawful defense. They do not consider that the allegations made unjustly must be proved; they seek only to punish whatever has been alleged. If a defense is sought [Col. 0056C] before them, they set aside every synodal decree and decide from their own inventions that it must be conducted in a way the accused cannot possibly fulfill, or in a way that wholly obstructs their exercise of the rights of their office, so that they may rage more freely against God’s priests. For although, according to the blessed apostle Paul, they are a law to themselves (Romans 2:14), they act [as the supplied text inserts, ‘simultaneously’] as accusers, judges, and witnesses, through force rather than reason.

They therefore say that the accused priest’s declaration of innocence [under oath is of no force unless he compels several other priests together with him] to swear. They unjustly claim as evidence something they boast of having read in the acts of the Roman pontiffs. For it is recorded of the venerable pontiffs Damasus, Sixtus, and Symmachus that, when certain wicked persons accused them of crimes, [Col. 0056D] councils of bishops were assembled and they were cleared synodically. They profess to understand these words in precisely this sense: that all those bishops swore concerning the alleged crimes together with the pontiffs, as though the pontiffs’ own declarations of innocence would not have absolved them unless the oaths of the aforesaid brethren had also confirmed them.

To us, however, it is by no means evident that the passage must be understood in this way. We plainly understand that the pontiffs were cleared by the aforesaid bishops if, on the bishops’ recommendation and with their support, it was established through the pontiffs’ own declarations alone that they were innocent of the crimes. But if anyone has chosen, for charity’s sake, to offer an oath in support of some just person’s innocence so that he might thereby free him from his persecutors, this is altogether [Col. 0057A] [acceptable. Nevertheless, although because of wicked men’s harassment in the primitive] Church this might have happened, [no precedent] ought to have been left for the future.

For we are wholly ignorant of any holy council or decree of any catholic and apostolic man establishing that God’s priests cannot be absolved from crimes except by the declarations of innocence of their brethren. Since oaths are forbidden to all Christians, it is very pernicious for priests to compel others to swear in matters from which they ought both to guard themselves and to restrain others. The Lord says in the Gospel: “But I say to you, do not swear at all” (Matthew 5:34). The apostle James, speaking of an oath, says: “Above all things, my brethren, do not swear” (James 5:12). And Pope Cornelius says (Epistle 2):

> We know of no instance [Col. 0057B] hitherto in which an oath was exacted from the highest priests except concerning the true faith, nor do we find that they swore voluntarily.

Besides, who can bring witnesses with him to a trial when the ruler is hostile and the judges too are unfriendly? Could Joseph oppose witnesses to his lying mistress so as not to suffer the wrong of imprisonment? Yet he was found just. He could indeed be committed to prison, but could in no way be made subject to the crime. Could witnesses come to Naboth’s aid when royal greed deceitfully charged that he had cursed God and the king? Or could the blessed Pope Silverius bring witnesses, when through the faction of the rulers—because he would not obey their wicked commands—he was falsely accused of betraying his fellow citizens and, moreover, of disloyalty to those very rulers, and was immediately condemned [Col. 0057C] to exile, though unjustly? He underwent the penalty of exile precisely because he did not turn aside from the line of justice. If this is unknown to anyone, a reading of his acts will be able to show it fully.

Many other holy Fathers of both the Old and New Testaments were also condemned through falsehood and endured various torments at the hands of unbelievers, though neither witnesses nor defenders were present to provide them any aid that might seem to defend them. But why say more? When danger pressed upon the holy apostles themselves, they abandoned the Lord and fled. Is Pilate or the Jewish people therefore to be excused because, when he was accused, witnesses by whom he might be absolved were entirely lacking? He was accused, judged, and condemned, yet was found just and without deceit.

[Col. 0057D] For very often, according to blessed Gregory (Morals, book XXXI, chapter 23), we are left quiet and unexamined if we take no care to oppose the wicked for the sake of justice. But if we begin to rebuke their wickedness, they immediately persecute and even defame us, so that by discrediting the teacher’s life they may thereby suppress his word of correction.

But to return to our subject: we never read that any of the holy Fathers [ever dragged or invited others to take an oath on his behalf. For our lord] Pope Pelagius, although accused not merely from envy but on suspicion [because of certain serious circumstances concerning the death] of his predecessor, that he had been involved in it, [Col. 0058A] satisfied everyone by an oath offered with his own hand alone. Likewise the venerable Pope Leo, when he too was harassed by certain liars with an accusation of crime, was cleared by his own oath alone.

Blessed Gregory, the universal shepherd of the Church and a most shrewd investigator in examining the crimes of priests, steadfastly taught that those accused of any crimes whatsoever were to be held in full honor after they had made their declaration of innocence. We have seen this most clearly in the pages of his register concerning the venerable bishop Leo, Menna, Maximus bishop of Salona—who was accused before him of many crimes—and many other priests. Nevertheless, if the priestly state were examined according to the will of the wicked [Note: [Col. 0057D] *Exquireretur*, “were examined.” Codex Resb. reads *exsequeretur*, “were to carry out/pursue” (a deponent form, syntactically difficult here).], [Col. 0058B] either scarcely one priest or none at all would be found.

They add, moreover, that if any soldier charges God’s priests with a crime, the matter must be decided by combat in a single duel [Note: [Col. 0058D] *Discernendum*, “to be decided.” The same codex reads *discutiendum*, “to be examined.”]. Yet that judgment belongs only to certain laymen, and is not altogether approved even for them. For in such a judgment the innocent are often seen to be defeated and the guilty victorious. Blessed Gregory says: “Who can understand what the reason for hidden judgments may be, such that often a just man returns from a trial not only without vindication [the supplied text reads *non solum vindicatus*, apparently lacking the second negative required by the contrast] but even punished, while his unjust adversary is not merely unpunished but departs victorious?”

And in the Gospel, when the Devil urged the Lord to show that he was the Son of God by throwing himself from the pinnacle of the temple, the Lord said: “It is written: You shall not tempt the Lord [Col. 0058C] your God” (Matthew 4:7). By both example and words he taught us not to choose for ourselves the danger of some peril. Yet even today the sons of that same Satan compel us to do this, though we are greatly afflicted by them, because they declare that they can believe what we say in no other way. Similarly, when he was on the cross the Jews said: “If he is the Son of God, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him. He trusted in God; let God deliver him if he wills” (Matthew 27:41 in the supplied citation). Although the Lord did not fulfill this, he never ceased to be the Son of God. For the Lord does not disclose everything by his judgment in the present; he reserves many things for the future, when he will illuminate the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts.

By God’s hidden judgment James was seized by Herod and immediately killed, while Peter, [Col. 0058D] who was to be brought out after Passover and was being kept in prison, was meanwhile miraculously freed, although both are known to have preached one teaching with the same steadfastness, under one ruler and at the same time. Likewise Uriah son of Shemaiah falls: prophesying in Jerusalem alongside Jeremiah, he is brought back from Egypt after fleeing and is killed, while Jeremiah remains there and is preserved [the supplied clause has the defective *simulque Jeremias ... prophetans*; the preceding Uriah is understood as the subject of being brought back and killed]. Blessed Lawrence was burned by fire and gave his spirit back to Christ, although we know that women and little children of the same confession and faith were cast into a much greater fire and not only remained unharmed by the conflagration but completely extinguished the violence of the flame.

[Col. 0059A] John the Baptist, the Lord’s forerunner, was immediately beheaded when the executioner was sent, although we have read of some who wished to strike saints whose arms stiffened so completely that they could no longer move them unless the saints themselves intervened. Thus we read in the books of the Dialogues (Gregory, Dialogues, book III, chapter 37) of a certain man named Sanctulus [or: ‘a certain holy man’; the transmitted form is ambiguous] who, after the Lombards had seized him to kill him, was finally led out to be beheaded. Because they had already known him very well, they gathered from every side to watch his death. The troops stood around; the man of God was led into their midst; and from all the strong men one was chosen about whom there was no doubt that he could cut off the holy man’s head with one blow.

The venerable man, led among armed men, immediately resorted to his own weapons: he asked to be given [Col. 0059B] a little time to pray. When this was granted, he prostrated himself on the ground and prayed. As he continued praying for rather a long time, his executioner kicked him and said: “Rise and, bending your knee, stretch out your neck.” The man of God rose, bent his knee, and extended his neck. But when he saw the drawn sword poised against him, he is reported to have said publicly this one thing: “Saint John the Baptist, receive it.”

Then the chosen executioner, holding the unsheathed sword, raised his arm high with a mighty effort to strike, but could not bring it down at all. It suddenly stiffened, and his arm remained inflexible with the sword raised toward heaven. Then the whole crowd of Lombards present at that spectacle of death changed from terror into wondering praise and began to venerate the man of God with fear, because [Col. 0059C] it had become manifest what holiness belonged to the man who had bound his executioner’s arm in the air.

When they asked him to rise, he rose. When they asked him to heal his executioner’s arm, he refused, saying: “I will by no means pray for him unless he first gives me an oath that with this hand he will not kill a Christian.” That same Lombard—who, so to speak, had lost his arm by stretching it out against God—was compelled by his punishment to swear that he would never kill a Christian with his own hand. Then the man of God said to him, “Lower your hand,” and he immediately lowered it. He at once added, “Return the drawn sword to its sheath,” and he immediately returned it.

Thus, in a marvelous manner, it came about that the blessed John himself unhesitatingly [Col. 0059D] lost his head to an executioner, while this blessed man, by invoking John’s name, not only preserved his own head but also so disabled in his limbs the man who wished to strike him.

In the same work (ibid., chapter 18) one also reads of a young man named Benedict. When the Goths could in no way burn his cell, they dragged him out of it and shut him in a heated oven. The next day they found him unharmed, and not even his clothes had been burned. Hence blessed Gregory says in the same book of Dialogues: “Peter walked with his feet upon the sea, while Paul suffered shipwreck; and in one and the same element, where Paul could not travel with a ship, Peter made his journey on foot.”

This happened although Peter was still wavering in faith, while Paul, already perfect in faith and deed, was hastening with the greatest constancy toward martyrdom for Christ [Col. 0060A] at that time. For the Lord miraculously snatches from approaching danger those whom he wills, while he permits some innocent people to suffer even here, who will be crowned by him much more worthily in the future. Therefore we must by no means judge the former holier or the latter inferior.

But care must also be taken that just people who suffer evils do not despair as though defeated, and that those who inflict punishments do not presume upon their apparent victory. For the Lord says to Job concerning Leviathan’s wicked power: “Deceit will be directed in his hand” (Job 8:25 in the supplied citation). Blessed Gregory, explaining this, says: “Deceit is in his hand, fraud in his strength, because whatever wicked thing he wills he is for a time also able forcefully to carry out. His deceit is said to be directed because the malice of his fraud is [Col. 0060B] obstructed by no difficulty.” For this Leviathan and his vessels repeatedly have this as their peculiar trait: to fill up the measure of their iniquity, they can most wickedly accomplish the things they wickedly desire.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, “do not judge according to appearance, but judge a just judgment” considering that the Gospel’s sentence addresses perverse—indeed, utterly unjust—judges when it says: “Why do you also transgress the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition?” (Matthew 15:3). For the Lord says: “If anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also; and if anyone wishes to contend with you in court and take your tunic, leave him your cloak as well” (Matthew 5:39). And: “If they have called the master of the household Beelzebub, how much more those of his household?” [The supplied text corruptly runs *patremfilias*, evidently for *patremfamilias*.] And in the Passion: “If they have done these things [Col. 0060C] in the green wood, what will be done in the dry?” And elsewhere: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21:19).

Yet they say: “If anything is alleged against God’s priests, it must be overcome by combat.” Hence the aforesaid Gospel sentence immediately continues: “Hypocrites, Isaiah prophesied well of you, saying: This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; in vain do they worship me, teaching the doctrines and commandments of men” (Matthew 15:7).
