Isaiah likewise says: “Woe to those who make unjust laws and, writing, have written injustice, so as to oppress the poor in judgment and do violence to the cause of the humble” (Isaiah 10:1).

Perhaps they have heard the apostle Paul say: “Take up the armor of God, that you may be able to resist in the evil day” (Ephesians 6:13). But if they have heard it, would that they understood what follows: “[Col. 0060D] Put on the breastplate of justice, take up the shield of faith, assume the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6:15). Solomon too, speaking of the just, says: “They shall put on justice as a breastplate, take sure judgment as a helmet, and take the invincible shield of equity” (Wisdom 5:19). Our standard-bearers instruct us to fight with weapons of this kind.

Paul himself forbids us to fight with secular weapons, saying: “Do not avenge yourselves, dearly beloved, but give place to wrath. For it is written: Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord” (Romans 12:12 in the supplied citation). And the apostle Peter says: “Do not return evil for evil or abuse for abuse, but on the contrary bless, because to this [Col. 0061A] you were called, that you might possess a blessing as an inheritance” (1 Peter 3:9).

Nevertheless, the wicked and depraved hold all these and the other teachings of holy Scripture in contempt and seek to drive priests into combat. They observe no further reverence toward them except that they judge [Note: [Col. 0061D] *Judicant*, “they judge.” We have restored this from codex Resb.; the editions read *indicant*, “they indicate.”] that the priests should fight, not with their own hands, but through agents substituted for them in such a trial. Those who are forbidden to attend formations of armed men or even public spectacles—alas!—are compelled to produce our representatives for combat, so that we may seem either defeated by the slaughter of our men or acquitted, as it were, by that of theirs, and so that we cannot be cleared of one crime without committing another.

For David was commanded not to build the visible temple because he was a man of blood through the frequency of war [Note: [Col. 0061D] *Frequentia*, “through frequency.” Thus the cited codex Resb.; the editions read *frequentis*, [Col. 0062D] “of frequent [war].”]. [Col. 0061B] How, then, can priests undertake war or combat, even for justice, when they ought to build the temple—that is, to teach the Church of God? Blessed Paul the Apostle says: “For the temple of God is what you are” (1 Corinthians 3:17). And elsewhere: “For you are the temple of the living God, as God says: I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people” (2 Corinthians 6:16).

Blessed Ambrose therefore says (On Duties, book I): “Concern with warfare now appears foreign to our office, because we attend to the duty of the soul rather than that of the body, and our practice no longer has regard to arms. For practice quickly bends nature.” And a little afterward: “Courage without justice is material for injustice. David too, when established in the kingdom, never [Col. 0061C] undertook war without consulting the Lord.” And elsewhere: “It seems to me that a just and wise Christian man ought not seek his own life through another’s death, since even if he falls among armed robbers he cannot strike back at the one striking him, lest while defending his safety he stain his piety.”

Concerning this there is a plain and evident sentence in the Gospels: “Put your sword back into its place, for everyone who strikes with the sword shall be struck by the sword” (Matthew 24:52 in the supplied citation). What robber is more detestable than the persecutor who had come to kill Christ? Yet Christ did not wish to be defended by wounding his persecutors, nor did he allow his apostle, even out of religious zeal, to proceed as far as homicide; hence he immediately deigned to heal the man whom the apostle had struck.

It is therefore fitting neither to fight [Col. 0061D] with secular arms for our innocence nor to compel others to do so for us. For if those who act and those who consent are bound by an equal penalty, how much more are those who urge combat or put others forward in their own place implicated in the danger of combat? Senseless and faithless men! Surely, if it were fitting for us to contend with weapons, we would believe it more fitting to fight freely for our brethren than to expose others for ourselves. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John 10:11). He does not say that the good shepherd lays down the sheep entrusted to him for his own life, but that he lays down [Col. 0062A] his life for the sheep.

Again: “The hired man, whose own the sheep are not, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees” (John 10:12). If those who merely abandon the sheep and flee are called hired men, by what name are those judged who expose them to death? Or how can we fight with weapons against those whom we are commanded by the Lord himself wholly to love and even to pray for? For the Lord says in the Gospel: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matthew 5:44). And: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Luke 23:34 in the supplied citation). He himself taught this while placed on the cross, saying: “Father, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:59 in the supplied citation).

By both command and example he deigned so to form his blessed deacon and protomartyr Stephen that [Col. 0062B] Stephen too knew how to pray for his killers. Blessed Paul the Apostle says to the Romans: “Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse.” And elsewhere: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink” (Romans 12:22 in the supplied citation). Ambrose likewise (On Duties, book I, chapter 48): “If I am perfect, I bless the one who curses me, just as Paul blessed when he said: We are cursed and we bless; we suffer persecution and endure” (1 Corinthians 4:12).

We can also show that holy David was not inferior to Paul in this kind of virtue. At first, when the son of Shimei [as the supplied text reads] cursed him and alleged crimes against him, David was silent, humbled himself, and kept silent concerning his good things—that is, the consciousness of his good works. Then he waited to be cursed, because through that curse he was obtaining divine mercy. [Col. 0062C] He also says in the Psalms: “Turn evils upon my enemies, and in your truth destroy them” (Psalm 53:7).

What benefit is there, then, if according to the judgment of certain people we wrongly free this mortal body from defamation or punishment but condemn the soul forever, when the Lord says: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matthew 16:16 in the supplied citation). Only that unhappy soul will obey in carrying this out [Note: [Col. 0062D] *Perficiendum*, “to be carried out.” Codex Resb. reads *proficiendum*, “to make progress.”] of which it is written: “God deprived her of wisdom and gave her no understanding” (Job 39:7 in the supplied citation).

But it is fitting for us continually to implore divine aid and strive by every means so that, because [Note: [Col. 0062D] *Ut quia*, “so that, because.” Thus the cited codex; the editions read *ut qui jam*, “so that those who now.”] we cannot be without sin, we may at least remain free from crimes, since according to blessed Paul [Col. 0062D] priests must be without crime. Although we cannot entirely stop the mouths of the perverse, let us rejoice inwardly and confidently in a pure conscience. For what wonder is it if ruined and subverted people do not fear to defame the lives of the good? Blessed Gregory says: “The envy of the ancient enemy has this peculiar trait: those whom, because God resists him, he cannot deceive into committing wicked deeds, he rends for the present by fabricating false reports about them.”

Although their malicious slanders seem to hinder us greatly, [Col. 0063A] we judge that we must answer them in no other way than as we are admonished by the most salutary ordinances of the holy Fathers, because it is written: “Do not cross the boundaries which your fathers have set” (Proverbs 22:28). If anyone refuses to be content in these matters with canonical judgment [Note: [Col. 0063D] *Canonico … contentus*, “content with canonical [judgment].” Thus corrected from codex Resb.; the earlier edition corruptly reads *canonice … contemptus*, “canonically … despised.”], but devises his own method to burden, harass, or despoil God’s priests—and even presumes to kill them—it is fitting that we suffer punishment while observing the decree of the saints rather than satisfy his wicked will, although doing this too is pernicious and such punishment or death appears sufficiently harsh. [The clauses describing imprisonment and exile that follow are supplied in bracketed reconstruction.]

For what death in this present age could be crueler than when the shepherds of the Church are separated from their sheep and are either confined in prison or driven into exile, [[Col. 0063B] their bodies worn down by want and their minds afflicted by grief]? They sigh over themselves and lament over those entrusted to them. They suffer present torments, while future ones are promised by the executioners. They fear still greater things; their comforters are taken from them; those who reproach or terrify them stand by continually. Would they not fall more easily if their necks were cut? Or perhaps those who do such things are not murderers simply because these men are killed without bloodshed.

Certainly Julian was called crueler than other tyrants because he did not allow the blood of Christ’s martyrs to be shed, but tortured them with various punishments and compelled them to end their lives after prolonged wasting. Hence Isaiah says: “Every head is faint and every heart grieving; from the sole of the foot to the crown there is no soundness in it” (Isaiah 1:3 in the supplied citation). [Col. 0063C] Nevertheless, although these things seem exceedingly hard, let us have the divine consolation which says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell” (Matthew 10:28). According to blessed Ambrose (On Duties, book III, chapter 9), holy Naboth showed himself perfect in that he defended the rights of his ancestors with his own blood and, from regard for honor, did not fear to incur death. When the king sought his vineyard from him and promised to give money, he refused a dishonorable price for his paternal inheritance and chose instead to avoid such disgrace through death: “May God forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers” (1 Kings 21:3). [Col. 0063D] That is: “May so great a reproach not befall me; may God not permit so great a disgrace to be extorted.”

He certainly does not say this for the sake of the vines, for God is concerned neither with vines nor with an earthly plot, but he speaks of the right of the Fathers. He could have received another vineyard from the king’s vineyards and become the king’s friend, in which no small advantage of this age is usually reckoned. But he judged that what was dishonorable could not be regarded as useful and chose to undergo danger with honor rather than advantage with reproach. We therefore observe that [Col. 0064A] what is dishonorable cannot be useful, nor again can what is honorable be useless, because advantage is always joined to honor and honor to advantage.

But if people despise the decrees of the holy Fathers, it is no great thing if they also reprove our works: those who do not fear to violate their statutes do not fear to disparage our life or even to burden our trial. Even if, departing from ecclesiastical discipline, with some of those very men supporting us, we could by their judgment find an opportunity among secular judges to clear ourselves in such a case, we consider it disadvantageous: lest it become a precedent for others wishing, or able, to do likewise, and what had in any way been extorted from us become a stumbling block to the brethren [the supplied source reconstructs the passage from *faventibus*, “supporting,” through *vel etiam*, “or even”] [Note: [Col. 0063D] *Produceretur*, “should be brought forward.” Thus codex Resb.; the earlier edition reads [Col. 0064D] *procuretur*, “should be procured.” Where we have arranged to print *extortum*, “extorted,” from the same codex, Acherius had printed *exortum*, “arisen.”].

[Col. 0064B] For one who harms is not wise. It is one thing to be wise in the common manner, another to be perfectly wise. One who is wise in the common manner is wise concerning temporal things; one who is perfectly wise does not seek merely what is useful to himself, but what is useful to everyone. Gregory says: “Weak fear is often called prudent management by men, and they claim to have prudently avoided the assault, when in their shameful flight [Note: [Col. 0064D] *Cum fugientes*, “when fleeing.” This reading has pleased us; the earlier edition had *asserunt. Confugientes*, “they claim. Fleeing for refuge.”] they are struck in the back.”

It is therefore more fitting that we choose to bear injury ourselves than to inflict slander upon others, and to suffer injustice from others rather than defend ourselves unjustly. For we are not condemned forever when we are judged unjustly, as the Psalmist says: “Nor shall he condemn him when judgment is given against him” (Psalm 36:33).

Finally, many [Col. 0064C] profess that they pursue the faults of priests out of zeal for God, but while they do this without discretion they incur the crime of sacrilege; and while they rush headlong, as though to correct something, they themselves fall much more grievously. Hence it is read in the book of Kings concerning the ark of the Lord that, after they came to the threshing floor of Nachor [as printed], Uzzah stretched out his hand to the ark of the Lord and took hold of it because the oxen kicked and caused it to lean; and the Lord was angry with indignation against Uzzah and struck him for his rashness, and he died there beside the ark of the Lord (2 Samuel 6:6). What is better signified by the ark than the holy Church? What by the oxen but dissenting priests? What do we understand by Uzzah except a rash person?

Saul too, chosen by the Lord himself for the kingdom, deserved to hear from the prophet—because he dared to usurp the priest’s ministry—[Col. 0064D] “You have acted foolishly and have not kept the commands of the Lord your God which he commanded you. Had you not done this, the Lord would now have established your kingdom over Israel forever; but your kingdom shall no longer arise. The Lord has sought for himself a man according to his own heart and commanded him to be leader over his people, because you have not kept what the Lord commanded” (1 Samuel 13:13).

King Uzziah likewise, after he had reigned prosperously over the people for some years with the favor of God, whom he appeared to serve devoutly, [Col. 0065A] finally wished by an impious presumption to seize the priesthood unlawfully as well. Struck with leprosy for that unlawful rashness, he lost both the kingdom which he could lawfully have exercised and his health.

Everyone must therefore walk along the royal road, just as [lacuna] the Lord’s way is also straight, lest [lacuna] he turned aside to the right who does more than is necessary; to the left [lacuna] The Psalmist says: “Lead me, Lord, in your way” (Psalm 35:11 in the supplied citation). Blessed Paul the Apostle likewise says: “Let each person remain in the calling in which he was called” (1 Corinthians 4:20 in the supplied citation), lest while he seeks unlawful things he justly lose what he has acquired, and while he rejoices to usurp the ministries of others [Col. 0065B] he rightly become sluggish in the duties owed to him. Hence it commonly happens that secular men who presume to invade ecclesiastical governance deserve neither to obtain peace through the prayers of the Church nor to gain victory through their own weapons.

But someone says: “Are all the evils committed by priests therefore to be endured?” The appropriate answer is that they are to be endured by many, but by certain persons, according to the stewardship entrusted to them, they must be reproved with the greatest caution. For those who have received from God the power to judge even angels must not be rashly examined by human beings. As blessed Augustine says (*On the Sermon on the Mount*, book II, chapter 18): “Often the person rashly judged suffers no harm from it; but the very rashness must necessarily harm the one who rashly judges.” [Col. 0065C] And again: “For the one who causes harm,” says the Apostle, “receives what he knows.” And the Lord says in the Gospel: “With the judgment you judge, you shall be judged; and with the measure you measure, it shall be measured back to you” (Matt. 7:2).

Those, therefore, to whom the power of judging others has been assigned ought to exercise it so moderately that they will have no fear of the retaliation returning upon themselves. They must also beware lest, through hatred or envy, or because of some hostility toward their neighbors, they bring charges exceeding what the present action requires. They must likewise take care not to be deceived in any way by the trickery or instructions of accusers; not to allow flattery or pleasure to gain a foothold; not to show favoritism toward persons, or consideration of kinship or any patronage; and not to flare up in anger, which must be driven altogether from the judgment seat.

For the Lord says in the Gospel: “Everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” (Matt. 5:22). And blessed James the Apostle says: “The anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (Jas. 1:20). And again: “A man keeps anger against another man, and from God he seeks healing” (Ecclus. 28:3). Solomon indeed says: “Anger rests in the bosom of a fool” (Ecclus. 7:10).

Therefore blessed Gregory, writing to Leontius, former consul, says (book VIII, letter 51): “Whenever anger invades the mind, subdue it; conquer yourself; postpone the time of fury. When the mind has become tranquil, judge what is pleasing.” And shortly afterward: “For when, in carrying out justice, we become angry with a composed mind, we neither follow our anger nor give it expression.”

How carefully, then, anger that disturbs justice must be avoided is shown by what is written: “Let every person be quick to hear and slow to anger; for the anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (Jas. 1:19–20). Again it is written: “Who can dwell with a man whose spirit is quick to anger?” (Prov. 18:14.) It is also said: “Do not be with an angry man, nor walk with a furious man, lest perhaps you learn his ways and take a snare for your soul” (Prov. 22:24).

Against this, in praise of patience, it is written: “The man who conquers anger is better than the one who captures a great city” (Prov. 16:32). Hence David, assuming in himself the condition of the weak, says: “My eye has been troubled because of anger.” And he adds what follows from that disturbance: “I have grown old among all my enemies” (Ps. 6:8). For when the eye of the heart has been troubled by anger, we are reduced to old age among our enemies, because among malignant spirits we are recalled to the likeness of the old man.

Since, therefore, the sacred writings condemn the anger that moves the heart with so many testimonies, let us consider with what determination we ought to flee this vice, which, with God as judge, is so often rejected in his testimony.

Likewise, to Godescalc, duke of Campania (the same Saint Gregory, book VIII, letter 12): “That concern of superiors is useful, and that caution is praiseworthy, in which reason governs everything and fury claims nothing for itself. Power must therefore be restrained beneath reason, and nothing should be done before the mind, once stirred, returns to tranquility. For in a time of agitation anger considers everything it has done to be just. But since we pray that the Lord may not rebuke us in anger, it is fitting that we should not judge others in anger. For it is written: ‘Remember the fear of the Lord, and do not be angry with your neighbor’” (Ecclus. 28:8).

And blessed Augustine says: “Whoever, by becoming angry, shows himself terrifying to his brother will endure the terror of divine judgment.”

We find that this was observed not only by Christians and Catholics but also, in many instances, by pagans: namely, that when they were angry they did not presume to examine or punish anyone. For the philosopher Terentianus said to his steward: “O unhappy man, whom I would afflict, if I were not angry.”

Moreover, we are taught by very many statements that we ought not to judge uncertain matters. Hence the most blessed Pope Julius says (*Letter against the Easterners on behalf of Athanasius*, chapter 19): “Let no pontiff ever presume to judge uncertain matters; for although they may be true, they are not to be believed unless they are confirmed by manifest indications, unless they are convicted by an open judgment, unless they are made public according to judicial procedure.”

Almighty God also, in order to restrain us from pronouncing a hasty sentence—although everything is naked and open before his eyes—did not wish to judge the evils of Sodom precipitately. He says: “I shall descend and see whether they have completed in action the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Gen. 18:27). Since the almighty Lord knows everything, why does he seem to doubt before testing [lacuna] than to prove?

Hence blessed the Apostle says to Timothy: “Do not receive an accusation against a presbyter.” And shortly afterward: “Those who are sinning, rebuke before all, so that the others may have fear” (1 Tim. 5:19). For one ought not readily to believe an accusation against a bishop or presbyter—whose order had not yet been divided—although a crime may be brought against them, unless it is proved; because no one may condemn a priest unless he has either confessed voluntarily or been canonically convicted by legitimate witnesses.

Nevertheless, if what has been alleged has been lawfully proved or is manifest, he must be rebuked publicly, so that the others may be terrified. When they see so great a man corrected because of error, the rest must necessarily take care for themselves.

That saying of the Lord in the Gospel must also be clearly heeded: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” (1 Cor. 4:5). For no one may be condemned by human examination whom God has reserved for his own judgment.

The most holy emperor Constantine, too, when he saw that the complaint of certain bishops had been brought before him at the Council of Nicaea, said: “You cannot be judged by anyone, because you are reserved for the judgment of God alone. You have been called gods; therefore you cannot be judged by human beings.” The Lord also demonstrates this in Exodus, saying: “You shall not revile the gods, nor curse the ruler of your people” (Exod. 22:28).

And blessed Gregory, praising the emperor Maurice in this matter, says (book II, letter 56): “Because we are not unaware of the mind of our most serene lord the emperor: he does not ordinarily involve himself in the cases of priests, lest he be burdened in any way by our sins.”

Likewise, to John the Defender: “Concerning the person of a presbyter, this must be observed: if he had any case, it ought not to have been held by another, but his own bishop should have been approached.”

The most blessed Sylvester, supreme pontiff, and the universal Apostle, in a synod gathered in the holy and venerable Roman Church, expressly prohibited the following in every respect: no layman should dare to bring an accusation against a cleric; nor should a presbyter bring one against a bishop, nor a deacon against a presbyter, nor a subdeacon against a deacon, nor an acolyte against a subdeacon, nor an exorcist against an acolyte, nor a lector against an exorcist, nor a doorkeeper against a lector. Nor should any prelate be condemned except by seventy-two [judges], nor should the supreme prelate be judged by anyone, because it is written: “The disciple is not above his teacher” (Matt. 10:24).

Blessed Paul the Apostle also says to Timothy: “Do not rebuke an older man, but entreat him as a father” (1 Tim. 5:1).

It is therefore no wonder [that what was said above concerning bishops, whose judgment has particular jurisdiction over all clerics, applies], since even with regard to the other priests of the Lord, levites and subdeacons, and clerics of the succeeding orders down to the lowest rank, the permission for laymen to accuse or judge has been entirely excluded—except if one of them, which God forbid, lifted up by the swelling of pride, abandons ecclesiastical discipline and turns to secular power, so that he may be defended against the authority of his own bishop contrary to law. Then, at the bishop’s urging, if necessary, such a person must be pursued with the assistance of the ruler or judge until he learns to obey ecclesiastical rules, even against his will.

Laymen must not presume to investigate or judge the accusations of such persons in any other way unless they are invited by the bishops, to whose parish these matters appear to belong. For blessed Paul the Apostle says: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master” (Rom. 14:4).

Secular power, however, by contrast—lamentably—sometimes suppresses ecclesiastical authority in many ways; and the power by whose support it ought to be raised is accustomed to afflict it by its adversities. Just as, in the election of prelates, rulers strive to establish their own votes rather than the institutions of the holy Fathers, so also, in hearing, judging, or even expelling both the bishops themselves and those entrusted to them, they seek in every respect to satisfy their own will against the law of the canons.

According to the sentence of perverse judges, neither does guilt restrain anyone from the summit of government, nor does any office excuse anyone from the accusation of a crime. Blessed Pope Anacletus vigorously opposed this, saying: “The Lord reserved the election of the chief priests to himself, although he granted their election to good priests and spiritual peoples. To whom, then, will the one who dares to seize what God reserved solely for himself be thought similar?” It remains, of course, that he who said: “I shall set my throne in the north, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:24).

## The First Part Concerning the Judgments of Bishops Ends

## The Second Part Begins: Concerning Their Ordinations

This must plainly be guarded against with careful attention: no one should dare to turn into a privilege for himself what God granted to good priests and spiritual peoples. Since, in the election of a bishop, general rather than personal advantage must be sought, and since an administrator of ecclesiastical affairs—not a public or private procurator—must be sought, who could ever find someone suitable for this except the one who knows hidden things? [lacuna] [Col. 0068D] [lacuna], [lacuna] custody?

He rightly also often grants this knowledge to good priests and spiritual peoples, because elsewhere he himself promised: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst” (Matt. 18:20). And in the Psalms: “The Lord stood in the assembly of gods; in their midst he judges” (Ps. 81:1).

He plainly does what those themselves do who gather in his name, because it is truly evident that they cannot be there without him. He himself, both in the Old and in the New Testament, deigned to choose priests personally.

For in the Old Testament he says concerning the Levites—that is, the sons of Levi, from whose stock alone it then pleased him that priests should be established in Israel: “Behold, I choose the Levites from among the sons of Israel in place of every firstborn who opens the womb among the sons of Israel; they shall be their ransom, and the Levites shall be mine. For I consecrated the firstborn to myself in the land of Egypt” (Num. 3:21).

Here Saint Ambrose says: “The office of the Levites is no insignificant one. We know, indeed, that the Levites are counted among the others, but they are preferred to all who are chosen from among human beings and sanctified, like the firstfruits of produce and the offerings of first produce assigned to the Lord, in which there is the fulfillment of vows and the redemption of sins.”

Hence it is added: “You shall not take them,” he says, “among the children of Israel, and you shall appoint the Levites over the tabernacle of the testimony, over all its vessels, and over everything that is in it. They shall carry the tabernacle and all its vessels; they shall minister in it; they shall pitch their camps around the tabernacle; and when the tabernacle is moved, they shall set it up. Any outsider who approaches shall be put to death” (Num. 1:49).

Similarly, in the Gospel he says to the Apostles—who are clearly the foundation of the Church and the firstfruits of the prelates: “You are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world” (John 15:19). What he said to them, it is evident that he also said to their successors.

And the Apostle Paul says: “Every high priest taken from among human beings is appointed on behalf of human beings” (Heb. 5:1).

From this it is evident that bishops can be worthily chosen and justly judged by no one except God. This, however, must be noted: when they are lawfully ordained or judged by those to whom this has been granted by him, it is unquestionably he who acts through them, as has already been said above.

It is therefore fitting that those should be chosen from the world for this office who, as he himself says, are already not of the world and do not walk according to the flesh. Those who also [lacuna] can be made; but may the prince of this world find nothing (John 8:13; Rom. 8:1; John 12:31).

Irreligious rulers, however, disregarding all these things, prepare only to make their own edict prevail in them. They are also accustomed to become extremely indignant if someone of whatever merit is chosen bishop by others, or if someone chosen by them, whatever his wickedness, is rejected by anyone.

The vices of those whom they themselves choose, however numerous and great they may be, are nevertheless regarded as though they were nothing. In their examination, charity, faith, and hope are not sought; rather, wealth, kinship, and service are considered. If these three—or, more precisely, what might seem the lesser—if two of them come together in one and the same person [Note: *Contra jus* (“contrary to law”). This is the excellent reading of the Resbach codex; the reading of the earlier edition, *contrarius* (“contrary”), is very poor.], that person will truly be counted among the citizens of heaven; and they believe that even one of these is sufficient for the dignity of the episcopal see.

But let us carefully inquire what the Lord says to such people. Let us see, therefore, beloved, how he threatens lovers of money in the Gospel: “You cannot serve God and Mammon” (Luke 16:23). And again: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God” (Matt. 19:24).

And again to the rich man: “Fool, this night they shall demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20.) And elsewhere: “Do not lay up treasures for yourselves on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves break in and steal. But lay up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal. For where your treasure is, there is your heart” (Matt. 6:19).

Blessed Ambrose says: “Wealth provides no assistance toward the blessed life.” The Lord clearly shows this in the Gospel, saying: “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God. Blessed are you who hunger now, for you shall be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh” (Luke 6:20).

And to the rich: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation. Woe to you who are filled, for you shall hunger; and to those who laugh, for they shall mourn” (ibid., 24).

And the Apostle Paul says: “Desire for money is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:10). James says: “The sun rose with its burning heat and dried up the grass, and its flower fell, and the beauty of its appearance perished; so also the rich man withers in his ways” (Jas. 1:11). And again: “Has not God chosen the poor in this world, rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom that he promised to those who love him?” (Jas. 2:5.) And shortly afterward: “Do not the rich oppress you by their power?” (ibid., 6.)

Ambrose also says: “Joachim, who kept gold during the siege and did not spend it to obtain food, saw the gold plundered and himself led into captivity.” And shortly afterward: “That [lacuna] which we use; but what [lacuna] does not have the fruit of possession, but the danger of custody.”

Isaiah also says concerning the people’s transgression [lacuna]: “Everyone loves gifts; they pursue rewards” (Isa. 1:23). And again: “Woe to those who justify the wicked for gifts and take away the righteousness of the just from him” (Isa. 5:23).

For if those who run in a race are instructed and trained by rules so that each person strives for speed, not deceit, and hastens by running as much as he can toward victory, while he must not trip another or throw him down by hand, how much more must we seek victory in the course of this life without deceiving another and with renewed vigilance.

Jeremiah says: “Woe to those who dwell upon the earth, because from the least to the greatest they pursue greed” (Jer. 6:13). And again: “The partridge broods over what it did not hatch, an insensible creature” (Jer. 17:11). And likewise: “Woe to you who join house to house and connect field to field, even to the limit of the place. Will you alone dwell upon the earth?” (Isa. 5:8.)

Solomon says: “Gifts blind the hearts of the powerful” (Ecclus. 20:31). For the service of God and profit from money cannot be acquired together.

And the Psalmist says: “Better is a little to the just man than the many riches of sinners” (Ps. 39:16). And elsewhere: “Because I have not known commerce, I shall enter into the powers of the Lord” (Ps. 70:15).

For what commerce could be worse than to sell the holy Church, the immaculate bride of Christ and mistress of all, whom the Lord redeemed with his precious blood, to unworthy priests for money? Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not make my Father’s house a house of commerce” (John 2:16).

Blessed Peter, the shepherd of the Church, also said to Simon Magus, when he promised him money so that he might receive the gift of the Holy Spirit: “May your money be with you for destruction, because you thought that the gift of the Holy Spirit could be obtained with money” (Acts 8:20).

Hence this heresy was called simoniacal; it is seen to be harmful both to the seller and to the buyer. Blessed Gregory also condemned it most steadfastly and fought against many on its account.

Writing to Brunhild, queen of the Franks, among other things he says (Saint Gregory, book VII, letter 113): “We do not pass over this either, but utterly detest it as abominable and most grievous: that sacred orders are conferred among you through the Simoniacal heresy, which first arose against the Church and was condemned by a strict curse. Thus it comes about that the dignity of the priesthood is held in contempt and holy honor becomes a crime. Reverence perishes and discipline is taken away, because the one who ought to correct faults commits them, and the authority of the honorable priesthood is dragged into corruption by wicked ambition.

“For who would again venerate what is sold, or who would not consider worthless what is bought? Therefore I am deeply distressed and grieve for that land, because, while they disdain to possess as a divine gift the Holy Spirit whom almighty God deigns to bestow upon human beings through the laying on of hands, they obtain him by payments. I do not think that the priesthood can be said to remain there. For where the gifts of heavenly grace are judged to be for sale, service to God is not sought through life, but rather money is worshiped against God.”

Likewise, to the kings Theuderic and Theudebert of the Franks, after some preceding remarks (the same, in the same book, letter 116): “It is reported and widely proclaimed among us that the Simoniacal heresy—which first crept against the Church of God through a planting of the devil, and which at its very origin was struck down and condemned by the weapon of apostolic vengeance—rules within the boundaries of your kingdom.

“For what works can belong to a priest who is convicted of possessing the honors of so great a sacrament through payment? Thus it comes about that those who desire sacred orders do not strive to correct their life or arrange their conduct, but to gather wealth with which sacred honor is bought.

“Hence also the innocent and poor are barred from sacred orders and turn away in contempt; and while the innocence of the poor is displeasing, there is no doubt that payment commends wrongdoing there, because gold is pleasing and vice is favored.

“Thus not only is a mortal wound inflicted upon the souls of the ordainer and the ordained, but your kingdom is also weighed down by the fault of bishops, whose intercessions ought rather to have helped it. For if the one who is believed worthy of the priesthood is the one supported not by merits of conduct but by abundance of payments, it follows that seriousness and industry defend nothing for anyone in ecclesiastical honors, but that profane love of gold obtains everything.

“What fruit will such a man produce from himself, whose root has been infected by so grave a disease? A greater calamity, therefore, must be feared in those places where such intercessors are brought to positions of government—men who provoke God’s anger against themselves more than they ought to have appeased him on behalf of the peoples.”

Likewise, to Syagrius, bishop of Autun (the same, in the same book, letter 110): “A report long ago circulated and became known among us: that in the regions of Gaul sacred orders are conferred through the Simoniacal heresy. We are afflicted with intense disgust and grief if money has any place in ecclesiastical offices and what is sacred is made secular.

“Therefore whoever strives to obtain this by the payment of a price desires not to be a priest but merely, vainly, to be called one. For what else is accomplished by this except that there is no examination of conduct, no concern for morals, and no investigation of life, but only the person who has been able to provide the price is judged worthy?

“If the matter is weighed according to a sound balance, when someone improperly hastens toward empty glory and seizes a position of usefulness, he is by that very fact unworthy because he seeks the honor. Just as the one who, when invited, refuses, and when sought, withdraws, ought to be brought to the sacred altars, so the one who eagerly seeks the office or thrusts himself forward importunately must certainly be rejected.

“For what does the one who struggles to climb to higher things accomplish except that, while rising, he declines, and while ascending outwardly, descends inwardly into the depths?

“Therefore, beloved brothers, let sincerity prevail in the ordination of priests; let consent be simple and free from venality; let pure election be preferred, so that advancement to the highest priesthood may be believed to result not from the support of those who sell but from the judgment of God.

“That it is altogether a grave crime to buy or sell the gift of God for a price is testified by the authority of the Gospel. For when the Lord and our Redeemer entered the Temple, he overturned the seats of those selling doves. What else is it to sell doves except to receive a price for the laying on of hands and to sell the Holy Spirit, whom almighty God mercifully wished to grant to human beings? Their priesthood’s fall before the eyes of God was clearly marked by the overthrow of the seats.

“And yet the perversity of wickedness still exerts its strength. For it compels those whom it deceived into buying to sell; and while no attention is paid to what the divine voice commands—‘You have received freely; give freely’ (Matt. 10:8)—the contagion of one and the same crime, namely that of buyer and seller, is made to grow and become doubled.

“Since it is clear that this heresy crept in before all others by a poisonous root and was condemned at its very origin by apostolic detestation, why is it not avoided? Why is it not considered that the blessing of the one who is promoted in order to become a heretic is turned into a curse?”

“Thus, often, when the adversary of souls cannot secretly introduce what is plainly perverse, he craftily tries to overthrow it by injecting the appearance, as it were, of piety. Perhaps he persuades people that something ought to be accepted from those who have it, so that it may be distributed to those who do not have it, provided that in this way he may pour deadly poisons through the concealed covering of almsgiving.

“For it must not be considered almsgiving if what is received from illicit things is distributed to the poor; for the one who accepts wrongly with the intention of distributing as though rightly is burdened rather than helped.

“For it is clear that those things are perpetual and solid which are true and which are gathered sincerely rather than deceitfully. The almsgiving that pleases the eyes of our Redeemer is that which is not gathered from illicit things and iniquity.

“Thus it is also certain that even if monasteries, or hospices, or anything else is built, it does not benefit the reward; for when the perverse purchaser of honor is transferred into office and establishes others in his own likeness under the pretext of deferred advantage, by appointing many badly he destroys more than the man who accepted money from him for the ordination can build.

“Therefore, lest under the pretext of almsgiving we strive to accept something together with sin, holy Scripture openly forbids us, saying: ‘The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable, those offered from crime’ (Prov. 21:27). For whatever is offered in God’s sacrifice from crime does not appease the anger of almighty God but provokes it.

“Again it is written: ‘Honor the Lord from your just labors’ (Prov. 3:9). Therefore whoever takes wrongly in order to give as though rightly plainly does not honor the Lord.

“Through Solomon it is also said: ‘Whoever offers sacrifice from the substance of the poor is as though he were sacrificing a son in the sight of his father’ (Ecclus. 34:24). Let us consider how great the father’s grief would be if his son were sacrificed in his presence. From this we readily understand how greatly almighty God is provoked to grief when a sacrifice from plunder is offered to him.

“Therefore, beloved brothers, we must turn far away from committing the sins of the Simoniacal heresy under the pretext of almsgiving. For it is one thing to give alms because of sins, and another to commit sins because of alms.”

These are the most salutary admonitions of Gregory, the most holy and learned pope, against simoniacal practices and illicit ordinations. Nor did he rest at all until he had obtained, through a general synod, the complete condemnation of these practices under an anathema.

But the crafty iniquity of the most shameful greed, unable to endure being constricted even in its most shameful—and indeed most dangerous—advantages, devised a sufficiently artful scheme: namely, to elevate to the priesthood those who, after consecration, ought to have been so much more subject to it as they would undoubtedly consider themselves promoted not by divine but by human judgment.

Therefore Gregory, the herald of almighty God, in his *Treatises on the Gospels* (Homily 4 on the Gospels), so that this might be read or heard more frequently, argues as follows:

“There are some who indeed do not accept monetary payments for ordination, yet confer sacred orders for the sake of human glory and seek from that very generosity only the repayment of praise. These people do not give freely what they received freely, because from the office of holiness they have bestowed they demand the coin of favor.

“Therefore, when the prophet described the just man, he rightly said: ‘He shakes his hands free from every gift’ (Isa. 33:15). For he did not say, ‘He shakes his hands free from a gift,’ but added ‘from every gift,’ because one kind of gift comes from service, another from the hand, and another from the tongue.

“A gift from service is subjection improperly rendered; a gift from the hand is money; a gift from the tongue is favor. Therefore the one who bestows sacred honors shakes his hands free from every gift when, in divine matters, he seeks not only no money but also no human favor.”

Hence the same Gregory, writing to John, bishop of Corinth, after much else, says (book IV, letter 55): “You must neither consent nor permit anyone to be brought to sacred orders through advantage, favor, or the supplication of certain persons. For, as we have said, the sin is grave, and we cannot allow this to remain without correction.”

Wherefore Gregory by no means wished [lacuna] “Therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John 3:47); and elsewhere: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John 14:23). And the Psalmist says of the unjust man: “He was unwilling to understand, so as to do good” (Ps. 35:4).

Although such men may appear, in the ordination of bishops, to withdraw their hand to some extent from avarice for money, ecclesiastical election will not thereby belong to legitimate liberality. Rather, affection for relatives, love of friends, or the services of household dependents will prevail.

And what does it profit to avoid one snare if we fall into a pit? Blessed Jerome says: “The election of priests must now be conferred not according to blood but according to merits and virtues.”

When a most worthy priest, having served in the Church for a long time, is rejected by rulers from the episcopal election of the very Church he had served, is not a son of God despised, in accordance with the words: “I said: You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High”? (Ps. 81:6.)

But when the son of some powerful man, unequal in merits, is unjustly preferred, what else is chosen than Barabbas, whose name is interpreted as “son of the father,” so that what is written may rightly come to pass: “I am God almighty, repaying the iniquity of the fathers upon the sons and grandchildren” (Exod. 34:7).

Some are so blinded in mind and body that they do not hesitate to promote even children to pastoral care, although it is clear that they are fit for neither mind nor body. They are not afraid to raise to the teaching office those who have not yet been able to learn even the rudiments of human nature, and to appoint as judges of souls those who are still utterly unable to understand what a soul is.

Those who ought urgently to teach the people about divine matters begin by being taught secular and even trivial subjects through the blows of their instructors. And those who ought to be feared by everyone fear even schoolboys.

Just as formerly the holy prelates, withdrawing from pagan rites, endured injuries and blows inflicted by unbelievers, so these men in turn suffer the same things in order that they may be instructed according to pagan rules. They do not fear raising the unlearned to the chair, and then, once raised, submitting them to the discipline of philosophers.

Blessed Gregory indeed restrained all bishops from reading the books of the Gentiles. Therefore, writing to Desiderius, bishop of Gaul, he says (Book IX, Letter 48):

> “It has come to our attention—something we cannot recall without embarrassment—that your Fraternity explains grammar to certain persons. We received this matter with such displeasure and rejected it so vehemently that the good things formerly reported to us about you were turned into groaning and sadness. For praises of Christ and praises of Jove cannot be contained in the same mouth; and you yourself should consider how grave and abominable it is for bishops to sing what is not fitting even for a religious layman.”

[Col. 0075B] [We also read of blessed Jerome that, when he was reading Cicero’s book, he was rebuked by an angel because a Christian man] was attending to [the fictions of pagans.]

Scholars still inexperienced devote themselves to studies, although no merits support them; they are praised solely and exclusively for their chastity. But how can one who is still unable to feel the incentives [Note: [Col. 0075] *Incentiva.* We chose to print this form, although Acherius had printed *incentina*.] be called chaste?

[Col. 0075C] A little boy is placed before the assembly, and the people are asked what sort of person he is who is to be ordained. Yet the people bear witness concerning him, not willingly but under compulsion. Why is anything superfluously sought in order to praise him, when he appears useless to everyone? The votes of all are solicited, though they are afraid even to display them publicly; nevertheless, the things they voice are extracted from them by fear, and those who conduct the inquiry do not themselves desire them.

Many laugh: some as though rejoicing in the child’s honor, while others mock the obvious and manifest charade. The boy himself, when questioned about certain passages which, if he has been able to prepare them, he will recite from memory—or, trembling, read from a written slip—fears not the loss of episcopal favor but the teacher’s rod. For he does not understand what he recites; his little heart is not sufficient even to learn it. He merely seeks to run through the words.

He is questioned, though those who question him do not doubt that he is ignorant of the subject; nevertheless, they trust that he has somehow learned to answer. They do not ask him to explain the meaning, but only to produce the words in some fashion. The inquiry is not conducted as an examination, but as though merely to preserve canonical order, and so that the lie and fraud may be stronger when shaded by the appearance of truth and confirmed by many people. But who can confirm what God makes invalid?

[Col. 0075D] What can we say when such a man is placed over the Church, except that an idol has been set up? He has eyes, but does not see, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Leave them; they are blind leaders of the blind” (Matt. 15:14). He has ears, but does not hear, as it says elsewhere: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. 11:15). And, speaking to the disciples: “But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear” (Matt. 13:16).

[Col. 0076A] Here we must greatly fear what the Psalmist says about idols: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Ps. 113:8). Blessed Jerome says indeed (Book VI on Jeremiah, chapter 12):

> “An idol is still set up today whenever a new doctrine is established in the Church.”

We have thought it appropriate to insert here also what we remember having read in the prophet Ezekiel:

> “And it came to pass in the thirtieth year of Ezekiel the prophet: the heavens were opened, and he saw visions of the Lord, and the hand of the Lord was upon him there” (Ezek. 1:1).

Blessed Gregory, a most prudent disputant in divine doctrines, expounded this as follows (Book I on Ezekiel, Homily 2):

> “Now the statement that he received the spirit of prophecy in his thirtieth year indicates that something requires our consideration: namely, that, according to the use of reason, the word of doctrine is not supplied except in mature age. Hence the Lord himself, in the twelfth year of his age, wished to be found sitting in the midst of the teachers in the temple—not teaching, but asking questions (Luke 2:46). Thus, so that men would not dare to preach in weakness, he who by his divinity always teaches the angels in heaven deigned, in the twelfth year of his age, to question men on earth. For he himself is the Wisdom of God; by seeing him the angels live, and by this they are satisfied with eternal blessedness.
>
> [Col. 0076B] “Moses also admonishes us through the mystery of allegory when he says: ‘You shall not plough with the firstborn of an ox’ (Deut. 22:10). By the firstborn of the ox we understand the good work of our earliest period, in the weakness of youth. Yet one must not plough in that condition. For while the first periods of our adolescence or youth are still with us, we must refrain from preaching, so that the ploughshare of our tongue may not dare to cleave the soil of another’s heart.
>
> [Col. 0076C] “For as long as we are weak, we must contain ourselves within ourselves, lest, by displaying tender virtues too quickly, we perish. Planted trees, if they have not first taken root in the earth, dry up quickly when touched by hand; but if they have once firmly rooted, a hand may touch them without harm, and winds may buffet them without injuring them. Walls that have been built collapse when shaken unless they have first been dried of their moisture.
>
> [Col. 0076D] “Therefore, until the mind has been completely dried of the moisture of its perversity, it must not be touched by the hand of another’s tongue, lest, before it fully receives strength, it lose its firmness; lest, when shaken, it fall; lest, like a plant without roots, it be disturbed beyond what it can bear and dry out under the blasts of wind.
>
> [Col. 0077A] “Accordingly, only what is firm should be displayed as an example. The mind must first grow strong and afterward be shown for the benefit of its neighbors, when it can no longer fall because it has been lifted up by praise, nor wither because it has been struck by reproach.
>
> “For although it is said to Timothy, ‘Command and teach these things; let no one despise your youth’ (1 Tim. 4:11), it must be understood that in sacred speech youth is sometimes called adolescence. Hence it is written: ‘Rejoice, young man, in your youth’ (Ecclus. 11:9). Clearly, therefore, in order to show how great authority solid age possesses in preaching, the text describes him in such a way that his life and spirit, together with all that is appropriate for preaching, appear to agree with it.
>
> “No one should be troubled by the fact that Jeremiah and Daniel received the spirit of prophecy as boys, because miracles must not be turned into examples for ordinary practice. The almighty Lord has made the tongues of infants eloquent and perfected praise from the mouths of infants; but what we say about the use of doctrine and discipline is one thing, and what we know about a miracle is another.
>
> [Col. 0077B] “If, however, one asks whether the very expression of that age also signifies something mystical, it is not absurd that the prophet should reveal by the time of his own age the Lord whom he announces in words, when it is said: ‘In the thirtieth year of Ezekiel the prophet, the heavens were opened, and he saw visions of the Lord, and the hand of the Lord was upon him there’ (Ezek. 1:1).”

Jesus Christ is never read to have preached to the people before the thirtieth year of his age [lacuna]. All the holy Fathers, following his example, likewise never wished the pastoral ministry to be granted to anyone before the age of thirty. With what audacity, then, can we believe that something may in any way be done in his members which we have shown was not presumed in the supreme Head himself?

[Col. 0077C] Therefore we must greatly fear that, while we rashly presume to attribute the grace of the Holy Spirit ineptly to others, we may drive it away from ourselves and be left naked while attempting improperly to clothe others. It is unworthy to neglect our own salvation when we cannot benefit others.

For blessed Peter the apostle said to Ananias and Sapphira: “Why have you agreed to tempt the Holy Spirit? You have not lied to men, but to God” (Acts 5:9). If those who merely lied about the price of their own field were punished with death, what remains for those who, by false assertions, falsely answer one another in such a matter, so that they may appear to grant lawfully to some fool the holy inheritance of Christ—the Church of God—and even the gift of the Holy Spirit? To some this may seem ridiculous; to us, however, it appears grievous.

“Fools! Does he who planted the ear not hear? Or does he who formed the eye not observe?” (Ps. 93:9). Solomon says: “For the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and it will withdraw from foolish thoughts” (Wis. 1:5).

[Col. 0077D] Blessed Ambrose says truly:

> “It is therefore clear that those things are lasting and solid which are true and gathered sincerely rather than deceitfully. But things prepared through pretense and flattery cannot endure for long. Who, then, would consider them faithful whom he has believed he must bind to himself either by money or by flattery?”

A little later he says:

> “Therefore I think that one should be sent to honor through good arts and sincere purpose, especially to ecclesiastical honor. Finally, if they have fraudulently bound themselves by an oath on his behalf, or obligated themselves by the bond of a written agreement through force, fear, or deceit, it ought to have no validity.”

Hence the same blessed Ambrose says:

> “It is sometimes also contrary to duty to break a promise in order to keep an oath, because it is clear that things prepared through pretense and flattery cannot endure for long.”

[Col. 0078A] And a little later:

> “The rule of justice, however, is clear: a good man ought not to depart from the truth, nor inflict injury upon anyone who is just, nor add any deceit to [lacuna]”

[lacuna] “not to fulfill a promise rather than to do what [lacuna]”; and although they themselves recognized that the promise ought never to have been made, they nevertheless, out of regard for their oaths, [lacuna] hung upon it, as we read of Herod, who shamefully promised a reward to the dancing girl and cruelly paid it.

[Col. 0078B] It is shameful that a kingdom was promised for a dance; cruel that the death of a prophet was granted under the pretext of reverence for an oath. How much more tolerable would such perjury have been—if what he swore while drunk amid wine, or what he promised after being adjured amid the choruses of dancers, could even be called perjury—than that the prophet’s head should be brought on a platter! This was judged to be fidelity, though it was madness.

Nor could I ever be persuaded that Jephthah the prince made his vow prudently, promising to sacrifice to God whatever should first meet him on his return within the threshold of his house, since he himself regretted his vow after his daughter came out to meet him. Finally, he tore his garments and said: “Alas, my daughter! You have hindered me; you have become a goad of sorrow to me” (Judg. 11:35). It would have been better to promise nothing of the kind than to fulfill a promise with the result of parricide.

[Col. 0078C] What, moreover, should be said about the deceit of the Gibeonites? Fearing the Israelites, they came with cunning, pretending that they were from a distant land and had traveled for a long time. They began asking Joshua to establish an alliance with them. Because he was still unfamiliar with the region and ignorant of its inhabitants, he did not recognize their deceit and did not inquire of the Lord. He quickly believed them, made a covenant, granted peace, and confirmed the alliance.

But when they entered their lands and the deceit was discovered—that although they were neighbors they had pretended to be foreigners—the people of the fathers began to resent having been deceived. Joshua, however, did not think that the peace he had granted should be revoked, because it had been confirmed by the sanctity of the oath: he did not wish, while accusing another’s faithlessness, to break his own faith. Yet he acted with such prudence that he neither violated the oath himself nor allowed them to enjoy entirely the freedom they had acquired by deceit. For this reason he punished them with the service of a lower station: a gentler sentence, but a more enduring one. The penalty for their ancient cunning remains assigned to them in hereditary service to this day.

[Col. 0078D] When one can fulfill a promise while preserving justice, it is best that what has been promised be carried out in every respect. Otherwise, it is better to violate a promise in some fashion than, out of regard for the promise, to fall into more serious sins.

For what should I say of the man who, regarding him [lacuna], falsely uses him as though he were guilty of a crime [lacuna]? Therefore, how terrible a judgment must remain against those who handle the priesthood by lies or deceit, when, as has been said, falsehood pursues even matters of such importance. What deceit, then, could be milder than to place over these people as a mirror someone who, when he comes, cannot perceive the danger? Or who would entrust himself to one whom he does not think wiser than himself, when he is seeking counsel?

[Col. 0079A] It is therefore necessary that the person from whom counsel is sought be more outstanding than the one who seeks it. For what advice would you seek from a man whom you did not think capable of discovering something better than what you yourself understand?

Even if someone appears poor in material possessions, if he is wise he can provide great comfort to those who trust him. There are many good men who are poor in wealth: content with little for their own use, they are nevertheless unable to relieve another’s poverty materially. Yet another kind of beneficence is available, by which they can help an inferior person.

[Col. 0079B] There are two kinds of generosity: one that assists through material support, that is, through the use of money; the other that is expended through the contribution of services, often much more splendid and much more noble. How much more illustriously Abraham recovered his nephew after defeating his captors by arms than if he had ransomed him! How much more usefully did holy Joseph help Pharaoh through provident counsel than if he had contributed money! Money is easily spent, but counsel cannot be exhausted.

We also say that graciousness in speech is of the greatest value for winning favor. From this it is apparent that wisdom is better than the commerce of silver and the finest, purest gold; and blessed is the one who holds fast to it.

[Col. 0079C] It must certainly be understood that unless the pastor of the Church has been seasoned with the salt of wisdom, he will be entirely unable to provide salutary nourishment to the Lord’s sheep, as the Lord says: “If the salt loses its savor, with what shall it be salted?” (Matt. 5:13).

The apostle Paul says to the Romans: “Because they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do things that are not fitting” (Rom. 1:28). He says also to Timothy: “If anyone does not know how to preside over his own household, how will he care for the Church of God?” (1 Tim. 3:5). Hence it is clear that a ruler can then be proved fit when he has first governed his own household rightly.

[Col. 0079D] And immediately it is added:

> “I testify before God and Christ Jesus and the elect angels that you observe these things without prejudice, doing nothing by partiality. Do not lay hands hastily on anyone, nor share in the sins of others” (1 Tim. 5:21–22).

[Under solemn attestation, he commands that those things] concerning the ordering of the Church [be observed, and] [that nothing be done without prejudice; and that no one easily] receive ecclesiastical dignity unless his life and conduct have first been examined, [so that, once approved as worthy,] he may be appointed minister or priest. Otherwise, if he later appears blameworthy, the ruler of the people may perhaps regret that he did not fully investigate him beforehand and may fear that he must answer for having appointed him unacceptably.

[Note: *Si eum.* We have boldly, but correctly, emended this; for the reading *civem* was so nonsensical that it could not be tolerated.]

[Col. 0080A] He sins if he does not test a man and nevertheless ordains him. For the one who is to be ordained ought to be proved better than the others. It is not enough for him to be free from crime; his merits must precede him along the path of good works, so that he may be considered worthy of ordination, as blessed Ambrose says.

A priest ought therefore to be hospitable, kind, and just; not covetous of what belongs to another, but rather willing to yield something of his own right if challenged, instead of attacking the rights of others, and so forth.

[Col. 0080B] Hence blessed Jerome says (Book XVI on Isaiah, chapter 58):

> “For it is no slight sin to cast pearls before swine, to give what is holy to dogs, and to assign clerical ordination not to holy men and those most learned in the law of God, but to one’s own followers, to ministers of base offices, and—what is more shameful—even at the entreaties of little women. Here one must consider the wisdom of Christ speaking through himself in the apostle, who, in order to demonstrate the danger of ordination, added the punishment of sinners. For when he had said, ‘Do not lay hands hastily on anyone,’ he immediately added: ‘Nor share in the sins of others’ (1 Tim. 5:22).”

Therefore, just as the one who appoints bad men becomes a participant in their sins, so in the ordination of holy men the one who chooses good men becomes a participant in their righteousness.

[Col. 0080C] But to ordain foolish and unworthy men—what is it other than to defile the priesthood, obstruct the Church, and corrupt the people? Hence the prophet says: “Everyone who has not learned righteousness upon the earth will not practice truth” (Isa. 26:10).

Isaiah also threatens Israel, saying:

> “Behold, the Lord, the ruler, will remove from Jerusalem the strong and mighty man, the honorable face, the counselor, the wise architect, and the prudent interpreter of mystical speech; and I will make boys their princes” (Isa. 3:1).

And a little later:

> “His watchmen are blind; all of them are ignorant. These are all silent dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. 56:10).

And again:

> “The shepherds themselves did not understand” (Isa. 56:11).

And elsewhere:

> “Learn to do good; seek justice” (Isa. 1:17).

And concerning the people:

> “They have become plunder, and there is no one to rescue them; booty, and there is no one to say, ‘Give them back’” (Isa. 42:22).

[lacuna] he himself afterward [lacuna] says of Israel’s foolishness [lacuna]:

> “The priests did not say, ‘Where is the Lord?’ Those who held my law did not know me” (Jer. 2:8).

And again:

> “Break up for yourselves uncultivated ground, and do not sow upon thorns” (Jer. 4:3).

[Col. 0080D] And again:

> “I looked upon the earth, and behold, it was empty and nothing; and upon the heavens, and there was no light in them” (Jer. 4:23).

And concerning the words of drought:

> “The doe gave birth in the field and abandoned it, and the wild asses failed, because there was no grass” (Jer. 14:5–6).

Hence blessed Jerome says (the same work, chapter 14):

> “This drought often occurs in the Churches when deer and wild asses are found among the peoples, who waste away from a lack of teachers. There are those who are able to learn, but there are none who are able to teach.”

[Col. 0081A] For how can a man be a shepherd if he does not know how to judge among pastures, does not distinguish between clean and unclean animals, between one form of leprosy and another, and has no understanding of a ripe grape as opposed to a sour one?

From this we can truly recognize that, when the Lord is angry, foolish shepherds are appointed in the Churches, and, when he is appeased, wise men are appointed through his favor. After inflicting scourges, he himself promises Israel forgiveness through the same Jeremiah, saying: “I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they will feed you with knowledge and doctrine” (Jer. 3:15).

[Note: *Post illata.* Here too we have indulged ourselves, and perhaps not excessively. For in this place the reading was *postulata*.]

Foolish bishops can be called not shepherds but incubuses, because they lie upon the holy Church. They do not seek out the wandering sheep, but even permit those gathered together to wander, so that each may walk along whatever path he wishes. In these circumstances what is written in the Book of Judges is truly fulfilled:

> “In those days there was no king in Israel, but each person did what seemed right to himself” (Judg. 21:24).

Of such men it is written in the Gospel:

> “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. 3:10).

[Col. 0081B] Gregory (Part I, Book I, *Pastoral Care*, chapter 1) says:

> “The ignorance of shepherds is rebuked by the voice of truth when it is said through the prophet: ‘The shepherds themselves did not understand’ (Isa. 56:11). The Lord also detests them again, saying: ‘Those who held the law did not know me’ (Jer. 2:8).
>
> “Truth therefore complains that it is not known by them, and it declares that it does not know the authority of those who do not know it. For certainly those who do not know the things that belong to the Lord are not known by the Lord, as Paul bears witness when he says: ‘If anyone is ignorant, he will be ignored’ (1 Cor. 14:38).
>
> “Often the ignorance of shepherds corresponds to the merits of their subjects. Although they do not possess the light of knowledge because their own fault demands it, nevertheless, by the strict judgment of God, it happens that through their ignorance even those who follow them stumble.
>
> “Hence Truth itself says in the Gospel: ‘If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into the pit’ (Matt. 15:14).
>
> [Col. 0081C] “For this reason the Psalmist announces—not in the spirit of one who wishes it, but in the ministry of prophecy—saying: ‘Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and continually bend their backs’ (Ps. 68:24).
>
> “The eyes are those who, placed in the very face of supreme honor, undertake the duty of watching over the road; those who cling to them as followers are rightly called their backs. The back is bent by the darkening of the eyes, because when those who lead lose the light of knowledge, all who follow are bent beneath the burden of carrying their sins.”

[Col. 0081D] Gregory also says (in the prologue to Part I):

> “There are many shepherds who, although they do not know how to lie, desire to teach what they have not learned. They consider the burden of teaching all the lighter because they are ignorant of its greatness. Thus, when unlearned and rash men desire to hold the citadel of doctrine, they are driven back from the rashness of their undertaking at the very gate of speech.
>
> “No art is presumed to be taught unless it has first been learned through attentive meditation. [Note: [Col. 0082D] *Intenta.* The printed editions read *in tanta*; since this was unsatisfactory, we emended it as you see.] With what audacity, then, is pastoral teaching undertaken by the inexperienced? For it is the art of arts, the governance of souls.
>
> [Col. 0082A] “Who does not know that the wounds of thoughts are deeper than wounds of the flesh? Yet often those who have never learned spiritual precepts do not fear to claim that they are physicians of the heart, while those who do not know the power of medicines are ashamed to appear physicians of the body.
>
> “There are also some who, within the holy Church, seek the glory of honor under the appearance of governance. They desire to be seen as teachers and long to rise above others. Truth bears witness that they seek the first greetings, the first couches at banquets, and the first chairs in assemblies (Matt. 23:2). The more they have come to the teaching of humility through pride alone, the less able they are to minister worthily to the pastoral office they have undertaken.
>
> “For the tongue itself is confounded in its teaching when one thing is said and another is taught.”

Hence James says:

> “Do not become many teachers, my brothers, knowing that you are taking upon yourselves a greater judgment” (Jas. 3:1).

Gregory likewise: “He who does not know how to obey the sacred canons is not worthy to administer at the sacred altars. He who does not know how to precede his subjects along the path of a better life ought not to assume the leadership of honor.”

And again: “Just as the wicked and sinners are forbidden to attain the priestly ministry, so the unlearned and inexperienced are kept from such an office. For the former corrupt the life of the good by their examples; the latter, through their negligence, do not know how to correct the wicked. What, indeed, will they be able to teach that they have not learned? Let him cease to assume the place of teaching who does not know how to teach. For the ignorance of rulers is not compatible with the life of their subjects.”

And elsewhere [Col. 0082C] (Part II, Book *Pastoral Care*, chapter 3): “Let the ruler be discerning in silence and humble in speech, so that he neither says what ought to be silent nor remains silent about what ought to be said. For just as careless speech leads into error, so indiscreet silence abandons in error those who could have been instructed. For often imprudent rulers lose human favor [lacuna]. The blind shepherd is he who, pressed by the darkness of the present life, does not perceive the light above [lacuna]. [He] says: ‘He has a small nose who is not suited to maintaining the measure of discernment.’ We distinguish smells and foul odors by the nose. Therefore discernment is rightly expressed by the nose, through which we choose virtues and reject faults.”

And again: “It is difficult when one who does not know how to hold the reins of his own life becomes judge of another’s life. Hence it is rightly said through the prophet: ‘They were killing souls that do not die, and making alive souls that do not live’ (Ezek. 13:19). He kills those who do not die who condemns the righteous, and he tries to give life to one who will not live who attempts to release the guilty from punishment.”

Isidore (*Sentences*, Book III, chapter 36): “An ecclesiastical teacher ought to shine in both doctrine and life; for doctrine without life makes one arrogant, while life without doctrine makes one useless.”

[Col. 0083A] The same author (in the same work, chapter 46): “Priests are condemned for the iniquity of the peoples if they either do not instruct the ignorant or do not rebuke sinners. As the Lord testifies to the prophet: ‘I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel. If you do not speak so that the wicked may guard himself from his way, he will die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand’ (Ezek. 33:7).”

Prosper (or Julianus Pomerius, Book I of *On the Contemplative Life*, chapter 20): “As the Apostle says that we ought to present ourselves as an example to the faithful, what value will this have if the man entrusted with the care either of exhorting the good or of chastising the wicked does not, by living well, present himself to the good as someone to imitate, and does not rebuke the wicked by remaining silent?”

I therefore wonder by what empty intention those are deceived who, disregarding the Lord’s judgment, seek to elect just anyone to episcopal dignity—men whom they suspect will be more useful to themselves than beneficial to the Church. Hence it often happens that they find them suitable neither for the Church nor advantageous to themselves; and while they do not fear offending God for the love of a man, they commonly suffer injury even at the hands of those whom, contrary to God’s will, they advance to the episcopal seat. They therefore rightly grieve that they have gone astray because they did not place God’s honor before their own.

Hence blessed Ambrose says (Book III of *Duties*, chapter 16): “He cannot be a friend to a human being who has been unfaithful to God.”

If, according to the blessed Apostle, “we do not know what we ought to pray for as we should” (Rom. 8:26), how can we know [lacuna] which would be evident, they were [lacuna] if we entrusted them solely to our own care? Hence it will very rarely happen that, on account of [lacuna], “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6:33). If anyone should attempt [lacuna] to seek what will benefit him without righteousness, he will destroy himself [lacuna] and will not be able to establish [lacuna].

For the Lord himself says concerning the rich man who promised himself many things in the future: “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20). And elsewhere: “Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted” (Matt. 15:13). And again: “He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters” (Matt. 12:30). John the Baptist also says: “No one can have anything unless it has been given to him from above” (John 19:11).

And blessed Peter the Apostle: “Humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you in the time of tribulation. Cast all your anxiety upon him, because he cares for you” (1 Pet. 5:6). The evangelist John likewise says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1:17).

And the Apostle James: “Come now, you who say: ‘Today or tomorrow we will go into that city, spend a year there, trade, and make a profit.’ What, after all, is your life? It is a vapor that appears for a little while and afterward will vanish” (James 4:13).

The Psalmist also says: “Cast your thought upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you” (Ps. 54:23). And again: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain” (Ps. 93:11). And elsewhere: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Ps. 126:1).

Isaiah says: “Woe to the rebellious children, says the Lord, who make a plan but not from me, and weave a web but not by my spirit” (Isa. 30:1). And again: “You have done evil in my sight, and you have chosen what I did not want” (Isa. 65:12). And again: “For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are my ways your ways, says the Lord” (Isa. 55:8). And elsewhere: “I did not send the prophets, yet they ran” (Jer. 23:21).

Jeremiah likewise says: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm” (Jer. 17:5). And: “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord will be his confidence” (ibid., 7). And again: “I know, Lord, that the ways of a man are not his own, nor is it given to a man to walk and direct his steps” (Jer. 10:23).
