And again: “Stand upon the ways, look, and inquire about the ancient paths, which is the good way; walk in it, and you will find refreshment” (Jer. 6:16).

It is the height of presumption to offer the grace of the Holy Spirit unjustly, when we know that the same Spirit does not at all confirm it [lacuna], and one who unworthily assumes such an office cannot be secure concerning the gift [lacuna], like Aaron. But lest anyone [lacuna], the Lord has granted us to seek his commandments [lacuna]. Let us question [lacuna] the testament, and also the Gospel; let us question the prophets, let us question the Apostles, let us question the decrees of the sacred canons and the statutes of the other holy Fathers; and whatever we have learned from them [lacuna], let us hold with complete certainty.

Let us not be deceived by novel counsels, so that we attempt in any way to violate what they themselves have decreed; for whoever strives to attack their rules will consequently prove unworthy of obtaining their fellowship. For the Lord himself says, as has been stated: “He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather scatters” (Luke 11:23). And again: “He who does not enter the sheepfold through the gate, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber” (John 10:1). Hence it immediately follows: “I am the gate; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (ibid., 9).

And against unworthy shepherds he himself complains through the prophet, saying: “They have reigned, but not from me; they have become princes, but I did not acknowledge them” (Hos. 8:4). Hence blessed Gregory says (Part I of *Pastoral Care*, chapter 4): “Those reign from themselves and not by the decision of the supreme ruler who, supported by no virtues and not called by God, but inflamed by their own desire, seize the summit of rule rather than attain it.”

The inner Judge both advances useless priests and does not acknowledge them, because those whom he tolerates by permitting them, he certainly does not recognize in them as approved by judgment. Hence he says to certain people who come to him with miracles: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know who you are” (Matt. 7:23).

[Col. 0085A] It must certainly be understood that episcopal reverence can remain sincere and unimpaired if the proper rights of ordination have been preserved in every respect. For we believe that one who has been regularly elected after careful examination will, through Christ’s mercy, scarcely ever be deposed while his faults remain unproven. But because men are irreligiously elected, vainly ordained, indiscriminately accused, unjustly oppressed, treacherously deposed, and sometimes even cruelly killed, it is clear that all the evils arising from such an illicit ordination belong to the danger of the one who ordained him.

Finally, the man who is to be advanced to pontifical dignity must be sought out and examined for as long as necessary, until one is found who, because of his merits, is deservedly revered by all and will not thereafter be accused by anyone; and whose holy conduct will not allow any shameful suspicion to arise.

[Note: [Col. 0085D] *Examinandus.* The Resb. manuscript correctly reads this way; the earlier edition has *excommunicandus*, corruptly.]

For blessed Augustine says: “He who wishes to hear the name ‘shepherd’ [lacuna]. [He who can legitimately be accused ought not to be ordained. But if—as in such cases, which is what most often happens for the worse—false rumor is afterward spread by the idle talk of certain people, they themselves] [lacuna] will suffer the fitting punishment for their iniquity. Yet concerning that man nothing dishonorable or sinister should thereafter be believed in any way.”

For how will a bishop be able freely to rebuke the errors of fools if he fears that he himself will be hindered [lacuna]? Therefore it is appropriate to use sounder counsel, and thus the will of the Almighty has not been followed [Note: [Col. 0085D] *Secuta non est.* This passage is certainly corrupt. I conjecture that it ought to read *sequenda nobis est*; and for *pia majestas* I read *pietas*.] so that his pious Majesty may direct all our actions [Col. 0085C]. If we rightly attain his service, he himself will also bring our salvation to its proper condition.

It is therefore fitting that neither the unworthy be ordained nor those who have been ordained be harassed. Such a man ought to be ordained who will not thereafter be harassed forever, but will be treated with great honor and watched over with the utmost diligence. Let favor be absent; let merits decide the matter. For whoever sees the man whom he loves unjustly made prelate must then necessarily mourn when he sees him deposed. Thus one who strives to raise someone unworthily is like one who drags a man toward a higher precipice so that he may plunge more disastrously from it.

Hence the Lord also speaks to Ezekiel, saying (Ezek. 34:2): “Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel; prophesy and say to the shepherds: Thus says the Lord God: Woe to the shepherds of Israel who were feeding themselves. Are not flocks fed by shepherds? You ate the milk, clothed yourselves with the wool, and slaughtered what was fat; but you did not feed the flock. You did not strengthen the weak, heal the sick, bind up the broken, bring back the castaway, or seek the lost; but you ruled them with harshness and with power. And my sheep were scattered because there was no shepherd, and they became food for all the wild beasts of the field, and they were scattered.

“My flocks wandered over all the mountains and every high hill; all my flocks were scattered over the whole face of the earth, and there was no one who sought them—there was, I say, no one who sought them. Therefore, shepherds, hear the word of the Lord. As I live, says the Lord God, because my flocks became prey and my sheep became food for every wild beast of the field, because there was no shepherd—for the shepherds did not seek my flock, but the shepherds fed themselves and did not feed my flocks—therefore, shepherds, hear the word of the Lord.

“Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I myself will require my flock from the shepherds’ hand; I will make them cease from feeding the flock, and the shepherds will no longer feed themselves. I will rescue my flock from their mouth, and it will no longer be food for them.

“For thus says the Lord God: Behold, I myself will seek my sheep and visit them. As a shepherd visits his flock on the day when he is among his scattered sheep, so I will visit my sheep and rescue them from all the places where they were scattered on the day of cloud and darkness. I will lead them out from the peoples, gather them from the lands, and bring them into their own land. I will feed them on the mountains of Israel, by the streams, and in all the inhabited places of the land. I will feed them in the richest pastures; on the high mountains of Israel their pastures shall be. There they will rest in green grass, and they will feed in rich pastures upon the mountains of Israel.

“I will feed my sheep, and I will make them lie down, says the Lord God. I will seek what was lost, bring back what was cast away, bind up what was broken, and strengthen what was weak; but I will guard what is fat and strong, and I will feed them with judgment.”

Why, I ask, do we dare to turn to our own uses the things that specially belong to him, and do not fear to assign to our own followers what he commands to be entrusted to his beloved? Can he not, whenever he wishes, involve us and them alike in everlasting ruin? We must not do what pleases us, but what God commands us to preserve.

Nor should we consider that these things are harsh; rather, we should attend to the fact that they must be observed in every respect. For when the Lord said to Abraham: “Go out from your land and from your kindred, and go into the land that I will show you” (Gen. 12:1), the sweetness of his own people was pleasing to Abraham, but the consideration of the heavenly command and eternal reward moved him more strongly.

Therefore it is fitting to change evil customs for the better, and for each person to guard his own ministry diligently, without attempting to usurp another’s. Clerics must not serve in the army, exact public taxes, or engage in usury in any way. Laypeople also, whatever their rank or dignity, must not presume to seize control or administration of ecclesiastical possessions; nor should they attempt to judge or harass anyone established in the clerical order, unless they are invited by the bishops, to whom—as has already been said—such matters belong, for some useful purpose.

Blessed Pope Cornelius says: “Although laypeople may be religious, no authority to dispose of ecclesiastical resources is ever recorded as having been granted to them.”

Blessed John the Baptist also said to publicans and soldiers who came to his baptism and asked what they should do: “Do nothing more than what has been appointed for you; extort no one, bring no false accusation, and be content with your pay” (Luke 3:13). They are content with their pay who add nothing illicit and covet nothing belonging to another.

In the election of pontiffs, the order of the sacred canons must be observed in every respect, and neither clergy nor people must suffer prejudice; rather, they must freely and peacefully have the opportunity, without anyone’s opposition, to elect the man whom they foresee to be the better one. The man elected must then be examined with the greatest care both by the metropolitan and by the other bishops of the province. If anyone can justly bring any objection against him, they must then have permission to air the matter fully; and if they can convict him of fault, he must be removed from the grace of the blessing. But if he is found worthy, then, with the consent and knowledge of the prince under whose authority the same diocese appears to fall, he must be solemnly and most devoutly consecrated.

After his ordination, the tongues of all his adversaries must be restrained, and they must no longer think themselves permitted to bring against the prelate what they were once permitted to bring against a colleague. No one should thereafter presume to accuse or judge him except in the manner prescribed by the decrees of the canons.

We have taken care to mention some of these decrees, although only a few, at the beginning of this present treatise, so that they would not appear to have been entirely omitted by us. But if they should perhaps not suffice for anyone, let him diligently seek out the statutes of the holy Fathers, so that he may thereby be more fully instructed.

*The second part concerning the ordinations of bishops ends here.*

## PART THREE. Concerning the Resources of the Churches

We cannot pass over the fact that ecclesiastical possessions, after the death or expulsion of a bishop, are handed over to secular people for plunder and robbery, whereas it is fitting that they remain in the bishop’s residence and be preserved inviolate by the steward and the other administrators of the church until the ordination of the future bishop, lest they be stolen in any way by others through some device.

For what difference does it make whether, while the bishop is alive or after his death, ecclesiastical possessions are plundered by outsiders? Or what benefit is there if similar things are preserved while the granaries and storerooms, the clergy and household, and the other things belonging to the Church are ravaged?

To such people the Lord says in the Gospel: “You say: ‘Whoever swears by the altar is not bound; but whoever swears by the gold that is upon the altar is bound.’ Fools and blind! Which is greater, the gold or the altar that sanctifies the gold?” (Matt. 23:17). And again: “Straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel” (ibid., 24).

Indeed, if necessity should require it, the whole treasure of the Church could laudably be spent on the matters mentioned above; nevertheless, none of these things should be exchanged for treasure. Rather, everything belonging to the uses of the Church is an ornament of the Church—especially the priests, clergy, and household—and these cannot be misused without danger.

Rebuking such persecutors of the holy churches, blessed Pius, Roman pontiff (Pope Pius I), says (Letter 2): “It has been reported to the Apostolic See that there are disputes and rivalries among you, and that some apply to human uses estates dedicated to divine purposes, taking them away from the Lord God to whom they were entrusted so that they may serve their own uses. Therefore the insult of that usurpation must be removed by everyone, lest estates dedicated to the uses of the heavenly mysteries be harassed by certain invading persons. If anyone should presume to do this, let him be regarded as a sacrilegious person and judged as such.

“We have heard that those who do these things also persecute clerics and the Lord’s priests and defame them, thereby adding evil to evil and becoming worse; they do not understand that the Lord’s Church consists in its priests and grows into the temple of God. And just as the person who devastates God’s Church, strips it of its estates and gifts, and seizes them becomes sacrilegious, so the person who persecutes its priests is guilty of sacrilege and is judged sacrilegious.

“If someone had stripped jewels from your brides, would you not complain that an injury had been done to them, and rather to you?”

For blessed Gregory says: “Everyone who takes away what belongs to us is an enemy. Since everything that the bride appears to possess is recognized as falling under the ownership of her bridegroom, and no Catholic denies that the holy Church is the bride of Christ, everything belonging to the Church is proved to belong to Christ; and whatever is taken away from her is unquestionably taken away from him.”

The one who attempts to usurp ecclesiastical possessions therefore truly becomes an enemy of Christ, and rightly falls under the same sentence that blessed David proclaimed: “The enemies of the Lord, once they have been honored and exalted, will fail; they will fail like smoke” (Ps. 36:20).

For whoever is proved to be an enemy of God his Creator and the giver of every benefit falsely claims to be faithful to the human being through whom these things can in some way be administered. What good, then, does it do them to be Christians while plundering Christ’s Church? Blessed Paul the Apostle rebukes this, saying: “You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege?” (Rom. 2:22).

Divine possessions are understood not to be the property of human beings, nor is it permitted for them to become an addition to secular dignities, since they have been prepared for the use of ecclesiastical persons and the poor. It is fitting that the holy Church be observed by all worshipers of Christ as unshaken and unharmed, and that it be dishonored by none of them in any respect.

For, as we have already said, she is the bride of Christ and the mistress of all who confess themselves to belong to the household of the Lord. What Christian, then, so foolish as to dare to call himself her master, or presumptuously enjoy her possessions?

For it is written: “A servant is not above his master” (Matt. 10:24). We can scarcely find for her among human beings a steward worthy of her; but we know absolutely no lord of hers except him of whom John the Baptist says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3:29).

Can the holy Church, the bride of Christ, [lacuna] therefore, with Solomon at the summit, [lacuna] let us once again devoutly beseech her to intercede for us with him [lacuna], not to take away [lacuna], but most devoutly to request what is necessary there [lacuna]. For even David, when hungry, did not presume by force to seize the bread of the Presence from the temple [lacuna]. And because he wished to take something from the temple of God, even though he had been sent by the king, he was struck by an angel [Col. 0089B].

But what wonder is it if a faithful prince, even when placed in the greatest necessity, feared to seize something dedicated to God, when we read that the same principle was observed even by pagans and barbarians, both in the Old Testament and in the New?

For Pompey, a pagan and warlike man, after he had conquered rebellious Jerusalem, had heard that an immeasurable quantity of treasure had been gathered in the temple of the Lord. When he approached it solely in order to see it, he ordered everything that was there to be displayed to him item by item. Astonished at its abundance, he presumed to touch nothing at all.

Likewise, Alaric, an unbelieving barbarian, after capturing the city of Rome in war, allowed all who had taken refuge in the Church to remain safe. And they did this though they were ignorant of the divine mysteries.

It is evident, however, that Catholic princes did not presume to dominate the Church of God, but chose diligently to serve it. Even those who served idols exempted the land of their priests and temples from public taxation. We read the same concerning Pharaoh, king of Egypt: when he had brought the whole land of Egypt under his authority, he made an exception for the priests’ land and allowed it to remain unharmed.

What, then, are we to say about those who plunder what they find at present and sell to a tax collector, under what is supposedly the name of a shepherd, what they believe can be gathered in the future—and the greater the estates were, the more extensively the episcopal ordination is publicized—so that nothing remains unexamined that appears useful for use? Thus the Church suffers at once the loss of souls and the loss of possessions.

Only then, at the very end, does the episcopal ordination follow, preceded by the election of misers; merits are not investigated, but gifts are chosen. Whose estates have ever been found so repeatedly plundered and afterward sold as those of the holy Church? Or by what sacrifices will such plunderers be able to make expiation?

For it is written: “If a man sins against another man, God can be entreated for him; but if a man sins against God, who will pray for him?” (1 Sam. 2:25).

Some also [lacuna] have been placed under firm security by the bishops themselves [lacuna]. “All the princes of those who said: ‘Let us take possession of the sanctuary of God as our inheritance.’ My God, make them like a wheel and like straw before the face of the wind” (Ps. 82:15).

And Jeremiah: “Thus says the Lord against all my worst neighbors who touch the inheritance that I gave to my people Israel: Behold, I will tear them out of their land” (Jer. 12:14). It is fitting that those who presume to defile ecclesiastical possessions, which are indeed God’s inheritance, be excluded from the possessions that they might otherwise justly enjoy.

This must be examined most carefully: although almighty God, because of our sins, may wish to scourge his Church through plunder or some affliction, he permits this to be done not by his beloved ones but by those to whom he will afterward repay it with a dreadful recompense.

As we read in Isaiah, the Lord says to Babylon concerning Jerusalem: “Sit silently in darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans, for you will no longer be called mistress of kingdoms. I was angry with my people, I profaned my inheritance, and I gave them into your hand; you showed them no mercy” (Isa. 47:5).

Although the Lord sent the Chaldeans to capture Israel, because they abused their power with their own cruelty and inflicted greater blows upon them than God’s vengeance demanded, he most clearly declares that he was angry with them.

A little later he says again to Jerusalem: “I will judge those who judged you” (Isa. 49:25), and “You will judge every tongue that resists you in judgment” (Isa. 54:17); and again: “I will not contend forever, nor will I be angry to the end” (Isa. 57:16); and again: “In my indignation I struck you, but in my reconciliation I had mercy on you” (Isa. 60:10).

And Jeremiah: “Israel was holy to the Lord, the firstfruits of his harvest; all who devour him will be guilty; evils will come upon them, says the Lord” (Jer. 2:3).

And David in the Psalms: “They were bound and fell, but we have risen and stood upright” (Ps. 19:9); and again: “Those who trouble me, my enemies, have themselves grown weak and fallen” (Ps. 26:2).

And the Lord says again concerning Israel: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with blows. But I will not withdraw my mercy from them, nor will I harm them in my faithfulness” (Ps. 88:33).

And Jeremiah says to the Lord: “For you handed us over so that we might be corrected, but they made their yoke heavier upon us.”

And the Lord in the Gospel: “If anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and he be drowned in the depths of the sea” (Matt. 18:6).

But someone may say: “Although ecclesiastical possessions are held by me, it is clear that more benefits are administered by me from them to the same Church than would be administered if they were held by ecclesiastical persons.” But they are mistaken [lacuna].

What works of mercy, then, can such people legitimately prepare from such produce? Can they give alms [lacuna]? Or perhaps rather cover the altars, light the lamps, and repair the buildings of the very church whose benefits they forcibly enjoy [lacuna]?

The Lord cries out through Hosea: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice, and knowledge of God more than holocausts” (Hos. 6:6). And again: “I am the Lord, loving judgment and hating robbery in a burnt offering” (Isa. 61:8).

God loves the poverty of the righteous rather than the gifts of the rich that come from plunder [lacuna]. God [lacuna] Cain’s gifts, because although he offered correctly, he did not divide correctly with his brother [lacuna].

Blessed Ambrose says (Book I of *Duties*, chapter 30): “Generosity is not approved if what one person gives to another one extorts from someone else, or if one acquires it unjustly and thinks it should be distributed justly.”

And again: “Let your generosity therefore have a foundation. This is sought first: that when you give in faith, you do not commit fraud in what is offered.”

And shortly afterward: “If one person cannot be helped unless another is harmed, it is more advantageous that neither be helped than that one be burdened. Although some, understanding perversely, take as testimony for themselves what the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings’ (Luke 16:9).

“*Mammon* means riches, which are rightly called ‘iniquities,’ because secular riches scarcely increase without plunder. Every act of plunder is iniquity, but not every iniquity is plunder. Iniquity is whatever is done either more or less than what is equitable; plunder, however, is booty, so called from *rapere*, that is, ‘to seize violently.’

“We are therefore not commanded to make friends from plunder, but from the mammon of iniquity. We can in no way give alms from plunder.

“Zacchaeus, that publican, wisely considering this, said to the Lord: ‘Behold, Lord, I give half of my possessions to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold’ (Luke 19:8).

“He would have given everything to the poor if he had known that he had lived innocently before his conversion. But because he had considered that he had taken something by fraud, he judged it right first to restore what had been taken according to the law, and afterward to distribute to the poor what remained. For the ancient law commanded that what had been taken be restored fourfold.

“And because he believed that half of his possessions was sufficient for this, he appropriately distributed half to the needy and reserved nothing for himself thereafter.

“Therefore, if it happens that those to whom what was unjustly taken should be returned, or their heirs cannot be found, it is better that it be distributed in alms in the name of those to whom it belonged than that it be seized by plunderers. But if it can be done, it should be returned rather than distributed in any other way” [lacuna].

[Lacuna] he did for the Lord [lacuna] an example, so that in the hope of giving alms [lacuna] he was praised, but for prudence. For if he had been praised for goodness [lacuna], he would not have been called [lacuna]; rather, his prudence is praised in him because he foresaw [lacuna]. This is what we must imitate.

We are all stewards, certainly, because we have all received the administration of the Lord’s possessions. For according to the blessed Apostle Paul: “What do we have that we have not received?” and “We brought nothing into the world, and we can take nothing out” (1 Tim. 6:8).

The time for administering our stewardship and rendering an account is near its appointed end. Therefore let us look ahead for our future, and while we have time, let us do good to all, especially to those who belong to the household of faith.

For, as blessed Ambrose says (Book I of *Duties*, chapter 30, midway through): “We owe mercy to everyone; but because many seek it through fraud and fabricate distress, when the case is revealed, the person is known, and time presses, mercy ought to pour itself forth more generously.”

Hence blessed John the Apostle says: “Do not believe every spirit, but test whether it is from God” (1 John 4:1).

Let us therefore not cease to bring aid to such people, so that through their merits and intercessions we may deserve to be admitted into eternal dwellings.

But since what we announce appears altogether harsh to those who wish to observe it, while the authors do not dare openly to blaspheme the holy Scriptures, they do not cease to persecute the reporters, so that they may excuse themselves more safely on the ground of ignorance, if they have not heard these things at all.

On the contrary, the Lord admonishes us through the prophet Ezekiel, saying:

> “Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel. Hearing a word from my mouth, you shall announce it to them from me. If, when I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ you do not announce it to him, nor speak to him so that he may turn from his wicked way and live, that wicked man shall indeed die in his iniquity; but I will require his blood at your hand. But if you announce it to the wicked, and he is not converted from his wickedness and his evil way, he himself shall die in his iniquity, but you will have delivered your own soul” (Ezek. III, 17).

And the apostle James says:

> “Whoever converts a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul and cover a multitude of sins” (James V, 20).

Isaiah likewise says:

> “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet and announce to my people their crimes, and to the house of Israel their sins. For they seek me day after day and desire to know my ways, like a nation that has practiced justice and has not abandoned the judgment of its God. They ask me for judgments of justice; they desire to draw near to God” (Isa. LVIII, 1).

[long lacuna]

And again:

> “But even if you suffer anything for the sake of righteousness, you will be blessed” (I Pet. III, 14);

and again:

> “Do not fear their fear, and do not be troubled” (ibid.).

For when he commanded us to be subject, he said, “for God’s sake,” because apart from him nothing is intended for us [lacuna] we are compelled by artifice. And again:

> “Fear God; honor the king” (I Pet. II, 17).

For the king must be honored in such a way that the fear of God is seen to precede it. Hence, promising a reward, he immediately added:

> “But even if you suffer anything for the sake of righteousness, you will be blessed” (ibid.);

and again:

> “Do not fear their fear, and do not be troubled” (ibid.).

And the blessed apostle Paul says to Titus:

> “Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities, to obey their command, to be ready for every good work” (Titus III, 1).

Hence the blessed Jerome says:

> “If what the emperor and governor commands is good, obey the will of the one giving the order; but if it is evil and contrary to God, answer him with the words from the Acts of the Apostles: ‘We must obey God rather than human beings’” (Acts V, 29).

The blessed Ambrose likewise says:

> “You may keep silent in a merely financial matter, although it is a mark of steadfastness to stand by justice. But in God’s cause, where there is a common danger, even to dissemble is no slight sin” (Book I of *The Duties*, chapter 47).

And again:

> “A bishop must neither present himself as a flatterer nor allow himself to be flattered by anyone. The one is a mark of cunning, the other of vanity” (Book I of *The Duties*, chapter 47).

Therefore we must greatly fear that, by seeking human favor, we may stir up divine anger against ourselves; and that, while we seek to guard ourselves against the momentary snares of our adversaries, we may be enslaved to eternal dangers, and what is read in Solomon may happen:

> “He who fears the frost will have snow fall upon him” (Job VI, 16).

For the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his majesty, and that of the Father and of the holy angels” (Luke IX, 26).

And the blessed Pope Sixtus says:

> “The matter rightly concerns us if we favor error by our silence.”

And Isidore says (*Sentences*, Book III, chapter 44):

> “Whoever can correct and dissimulates truly gives consent to another’s error.”

And the blessed Jerome says:

> “Every correction that contributes to salvation appears for the present to bring sadness, but afterward it produces peaceful fruits.”

But what cannot be said without a grave sigh is this: [some of our own people submit themselves so completely to wicked powers that they strive so to obscure, by false accusations, even the divine words and the decrees of the holy Fathers brought forth for the correction of vices, that they appear even to confirm by sacred teachings things that have long since been utterly destroyed in themselves. Such men are rightly called false prophets and false Christs.] [Col. 0093C]

[lacuna] or the glory of temporal life, by a lapse into flattery, they submit themselves to earthly powers [lacuna]. And certain people seem to do this precisely so that their offenses may be left unexamined under the authority of the powerful; and, conscious of their own wrongdoing, they fear being accused if they do not strive to defend the wickedness of those men.

The same authority fittingly admonishes them, saying:

> “Let a person consider against what adversary he is waging war, and let him fear that he may at least be dragged into the guilt of the evil which he recognizes himself to have committed.”

To such men the Lord also threatens through Isaiah, saying:

> “Woe to you who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness” (Isa. V, 20).

And above, concerning Jerusalem:

> “Your wine-sellers have mixed wine with water” (Isa. I, 22).

Jerome says (*Commentary on Jeremiah*, Book IV, chapter 13):

> “Falsehood often imitates truth, and unless it possesses some likeness of what is right, it cannot deceive the innocent.”

And again:

> “If at any time humility is necessary for us because of needs and hardships, let us adopt it in such a way that we do not abandon truth and steadfastness.”

For some, it is not enough merely to have gone astray themselves; they seek, to increase their own ruin, to lead everyone they can into their own error. They also rebuke those who resist them in such matters with the greater insolence the more confidently they trust in the power of the wicked.

For liars always oppose those who speak the truth, and the wicked do not cease persecuting the faithful, because, according to the blessed Ambrose:

> “Arrogance very often arises even from instruction.”

For this reason we read in Jeremiah that the false prophet Shemaiah became angry because Jeremiah had written the truth against his falsehood. Hence the Lord says:

> “Behold, I will visit Shemaiah” (Jer. XXIX, 32).

And Isaiah says:

> “Where shall I strike you further, as you continue to add transgressions?” (Isa. I, 5.)

Likewise in the Psalms:

> “But those who turn aside into obligation, the Lord will lead away with the workers of iniquity” (Ps. CXXIV, 5).

And the apostle Peter says:

> “No prophecy or Scripture is made by private interpretation” (I Pet. I, 20).

And John says:

> “Whoever goes ahead and does not remain in the teaching of Christ does not have God” (II John 9).

And James says:

> “If you have bitter jealousy and contention in your hearts, do not boast” (James III, 14).

For these men fear nothing about unjustly condemning their neighbor when they hope to gain the favor of princes. Concerning such men the blessed Pope Alexander also [lacuna]

[Note: The following material is added from Mansi in Baluz., *Miscellanea sacra*, Lucca edition.]

[lacuna] to accept the person of the powerful, so that, when requested by him for favor, they do not hesitate in the case of their neighbor [lacuna]. Who is the truth except the one who said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6)? [lacuna] is also increased [lacuna] by crime and by the miserable crushing of the oppressed, although it is our duty to be oppressed [lacuna] and to help most earnestly.

Hence the blessed Ambrose says:

> “Rebuke a friend who is going astray [lacuna] do not abandon him; for a friend is proved in adversity. In prosperity everyone appears to be a friend.”

And again:

> “Do not defend the wicked, and do not consider holy things to be entrusted to one who is unworthy; nor attack a crime too harshly when you have not detected it” (source reads *deprehendis*, sic).

And elsewhere:

> “Nothing burdens reputation—or rather faith—more than, in judgment, giving the case of the inferior to the more powerful, accusing the innocent poor man, and excusing the rich man guilty of wrongdoing.”

And again:

> “For we frequently favor those from whom we hope to receive a return of gratitude. But all the more ought we to support the weak and needy, because for the sake of one who has nothing we hope for a reward from the Lord Jesus. Under the guise of a banquet he set forth the universal rule of the virtues, so that we should confer our benefits especially upon those who cannot repay them, saying that the poor, not the rich, should be invited to the banquet and the feast.”

It also contributes to the advancement of a good reputation if you rescue the needy from the hands of the powerful. For if you free someone oppressed by the wealth and faction of the powerful, burdened more by conspiracy than by his own crime, you greatly strengthen the testimony to your reputation.

Job says:

> “I rescued the poor man from the hand of the powerful, and I helped the orphan who had no helper” (Job XXIX, 12).

And again:

> “May the blessing of the perishing come upon me” (ibid., 13).

And Isaiah says:

> “Strengthen the slack hands and make firm the weak knees; say to the fainthearted, ‘Do not fear’” (Isa. XXXV, 3).

Therefore, my most beloved brothers, let us in no way depart from the path of uprightness, because, according to that same blessed Ambrose, justice makes no exception for places, persons, or times. Rather, trusting unanimously in the Lord, let us say:

> “It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man. It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes” (Ps. CXVII, 8–9).

And without doubt let us patiently await that Gospel saying:

> “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 10).

May the merciful Lord deign to lead us there, he whose kingdom and dominion remain without end forever and ever. Amen.

(Mansi, in Baluz., *Miscellanea sacra*.)

[Col. 0095]

# LETTERS OF ATTO, BISHOP OF VERCELLI

(Apud Acherium, *Spicilegium*, volume I, p. 431.)

## FIRST LETTER TO BISHOP WALDO

[Col. 0095B]

Atto, by the grace of God a humble bishop, sends faithful service together with devoted prayers.

We return many thanks to your charity for the benevolent embassy undertaken through fraternal goodwill. As for your indication that you wished to have a conversation with us—or with our messenger—God knows that, if the proper unity between us had remained, we would gladly both have come to you and sent a representative to serve you.

But, what is worse, such disagreement has grown between our senior lord and you that it is now not fitting for us, without his permission, either to speak with you or to send our messenger into your service. Nevertheless, what we have recognized to be more necessary for the common good, bound as we are by the bond of due charity, we cannot conceal from you.

We humbly ask your highness to deign, laying aside all pride, to hear peacefully what must humbly be said to you by me, your faithful—and indeed most insignificant—brother. Let it not offend you, my lord, that I presume to suggest something to you as though I were your teacher, since, like a familiar servant, I desire to offer your magnificence an appropriate admonition.

How, then, my lord, could such rashness creep into your heart? From where could such an opportunity for action have been sought? How could your mind so quickly have been stirred that, forgetful of priestly reverence, you suddenly withdrew from your senior lord and from your well-disposed brothers, and did not fear to rise up against them without cause?

It is no small matter to attack royal majesty, even if it appears unjust in some respect. It is God’s ordinance; it is God’s administration. For it is sacrilegious to violate what God ordains.

The Lord says through Moses:

> “You shall not curse the prince of your people” (Exod. XXIII, 28).

For if it is not permitted even to curse him, it is plainly not permitted to persecute him either. And through the blessed David:

> “Do not touch my anointed ones” (Ps. CIV, 15).

How carefully David himself observed this is clear. Saul had already been rejected by God because of his insolence; David himself had already been anointed king by divine grace. Yet when Saul fell into David’s hands in a cave, David’s servants said to him:

> “Behold, the day of which the Lord spoke to you: ‘I will give your enemy into your hand, so that you may do to him as it seems good in your eyes.’”

David therefore rose and quietly cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak. After this, David’s heart struck him because he had cut off the edge. He said to his men:

> “May the Lord be gracious to me, that I should not do this thing to my lord, the Lord’s anointed, or lay my hand upon him, because he is the Lord’s anointed. As the Lord lives, unless the Lord strikes him, or his day comes that he dies, or he descends into battle and perishes, may the Lord be gracious to me, that I should not lay my hand upon the Lord’s anointed.”

And David restrained his men by these words and did not permit them to rise against Saul (I Sam. XXIV, 5).

Although he had no doubt about Saul’s rejection and his own election, and although Saul’s persecution had driven him into the innermost recesses of the cave, he nevertheless refused to extend his hand against him and awaited divine judgment. And afterward he repented even of cutting off only the edge of Saul’s cloak, because he had dishonored the garment of the ruler, however slightly.

Thus the chosen king spared the rejected king, although the latter was persecuting him, though David was innocent and was being grievously oppressed unjustly.

Samuel likewise, when he had anointed this man king over Israel at the Lord’s command, did not delay when summoned by Saul to go to him; indeed, he promised that he would pray for him, saying:

> “Far be it from me that I should cease to pray for you” (I Sam. XII, 23).

But now rebellious soldiers do not fear to resist their own lord with armed force, and they strive by every means to expel him from the throne of the kingdom. Of such men the Lord says:

> “Leave them; they are blind guides of the blind. And if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit” (Matt. XV, 14).

But the priests of God, who must examine the divine commandments, ought not only to guard themselves against such men but also to restrain from them as many others as they can.

Certainly the Lord himself in no way forbade the payment of tribute when Caesar commanded it, saying:

> “Give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s” (Matt. XXII, 21).

This is to be understood not only of the payment of tribute but also of reverence for every due honor. When he himself was pressed by the collectors to pay it, he did not disdain to do so; rather, he said to Peter:

> “Go to the sea and cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up. When you open its mouth, you will find a coin. Take it and give it to them for me and for you” (Matt. XVII, 26).

Thus, instructed by such teaching from his Master, Peter exhorts the Church to preserve obedience to kings in every way. He says:

> “Fear God; honor the king” (I Pet. III, 14).

For immediately after the fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom, he commanded that royal honor be preserved.

And again:

> “Be subject for God’s sake to every human institution, whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good.”

Thus he teaches us to be subject to the king as to one who is supreme, and to governors as to those sent by him. There is a great difference between the ruler and one sent by him. But this is what the prince teaches the Church.

Let us see what his associate also says:

> “There is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been ordained by God. Therefore whoever resists authority resists what God has appointed, and those who resist will incur judgment upon themselves. For rulers are not a terror to good conduct but to bad. Do you wish not to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will receive praise from it, for it is God’s servant for your good. But if you do evil, be afraid, for it does not bear the sword without cause. It is God’s servant, an avenger for wrath against the one who does evil. Therefore you must be subject, not only because of wrath but also because of conscience. For this reason you also pay taxes, since they are God’s ministers, serving precisely for this. Render to all what is due: tax to whom tax is due, revenue to whom revenue is due, fear to whom fear is due, honor to whom honor is due” (Rom. XIII, 2).

Likewise, to Timothy:

> “First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and for all who are in high positions” (I Tim. II, 1).

For the blessed David also, when confessing his sin to the Lord, says:

> “Against you alone have I sinned” (Ps. L, 6).

Explaining this statement most carefully, Cassiodorus says:

> “If anyone from the people goes astray, he sins both against God and against the king; but when the king sins, he is guilty before God alone, because he has no human being who can judge his actions. Therefore the king rightly says that he has sinned against God alone, because he alone was able to examine his offenses.”

But what should be said about all the other holy teachers who agree on this? Whoever wishes to kick against all of them clearly does not belong to the Lord’s sheep. He does not hear the Lord’s voice, does not recognize the good shepherd, does not understand the one who feeds the sheep, and despises the teacher. It remains that he is a thief and a robber, who kills and destroys. And if he sees himself in the Lord’s sheepfold, let him consider from where or how he entered.

The Lord says:

> “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Luke XI, 23).

It must certainly be understood that when almighty God deigns to grant the people a useful ruler, it is right that they should ascribe this to his goodness and render worthy thanks for it. But if the ruler is adverse, they should attribute this to their own sins and should not cease to beseech God to arrange the matter favorably according to the multitude of his mercy.

For a ruler who has already been established by God must in no way be overthrown or attacked by the people. Indeed, it is written in Daniel:

> “The Most High rules in the kingdom of men and gives it to whomever he wishes” (Dan. IV, 14).

Let no one take confidence for himself from the injury inflicted upon any deposed king. For although many [lacuna] suffered the miserable ruin of so great a crime, if anyone is permitted to enumerate these examples, let him investigate them most carefully from the beginning of that nation, and then he will be able to recognize that the destruction of this people occurred chiefly for this reason.

For as long as they sought to resist kings, they were oppressed on every side by pagans and for this reason were trampled by neighboring peoples. And while they presumed to do what was unlawful, they were likewise deprived of their rightful honors.

But let us hear what the blessed Gregory says concerning royal fidelity. Writing to the emperor Maurice, he says (Book II, Letter 61):

> “He is guilty before almighty God who is not pure in everything that he does and says to his most serene lords. But I, an unworthy servant of your piety, speak in this petition neither as a bishop nor as a servant by public law, but by private right; for, most serene lord, you have been my lord from the time when you were not yet lord of all.”

Although Maurice acted harshly in certain matters, especially against Gregory himself, as his own writings make clear, Gregory nevertheless entrusted the matter to the Lord, preserved his loyalty to him, and did not delay praying for him.

Finally, after listing the injuries inflicted upon him, he says again (Book II, Letter 31, at the end):

> “Amid all these uncertainties I return to tears alone, asking that the same almighty God both govern our most pious lord here with his own hand and find him free from all sins in that fearful judgment.”

That the Lord does not delay exacting vengeance entrusted to him was afterward openly demonstrated in the case of that same Maurice.

The blessed Ambrose likewise, when he was unjustly persecuted by a ruler, commended himself entirely to the Lord and did not seek to resist by defending himself. In this way the priests of God must arm themselves against wicked rulers.

As the blessed apostle Paul says:

> “Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath. It is written: ‘Vengeance is mine; I will repay,’ says the Lord” (Rom. XII, 17).

For to defend oneself by weapons, to take vengeance through plundering or devastation, to enrich oneself with spoil, or to inspire fear through murder or mutilation belongs not to priests but to demons.

The blessed David says:

> “Do not hope in iniquity, and do not desire plunder” (Ps. LXI, 11).

Those who perpetrate such acts may be called mercenaries, but they can in no way be shepherds.

Or how will they dare to offer sacrifice to God when they hear the Lord himself saying:

> “If you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matt. V, 23–24)?

[lacuna] if we sense that they hold something against us, we must in no way offer sacrifice to God.

Therefore, we have taken care to record what must thus far be said concerning the fidelity to be preserved toward wicked kings, so that from it we may understand with what diligence and caution we ought to obey good rulers, when we are advised that not even wicked rulers are to be harassed by their subjects.

But if the ruler’s anger should rage so fiercely, or if the offense should be so serious that no way of returning to his favor can be found—not through priestly intervention, nor through the pleas of the nobles, nor even through the advice or entreaties of his household, and his spirit cannot be appeased by any satisfaction—then we advise that one should flee, as the Lord says:

> “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. X, 23),

until the Lord sends help from his sanctuary and the Almighty has mercy from on high.

It can therefore be done more appropriately for one of the nobles to avoid the fury of his king by fleeing than for a king, within the boundaries of his own kingdom, to neglect pursuing a rebel who rises against him.

For we have heard that some who escaped in this way afterward returned most happily to their former honors, while others who entered obstinately proceeded even to a contemptible end.

There is a natural remedy: those who cannot remain together because of differences in character should have the greater expel the lesser, while the lesser should flee from the greater. For it is disgraceful for superiors to endure violence from their subjects for a long time.

The Lord says:

> “A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master” (ibid., 24).

The venerable John Chrysostom likewise says in a certain homily:

> “For we see in these worldly kingdoms how at first no one can make himself king, but the people choose for themselves whatever king they wish. But when that king has been made and established in the kingdom, he already has power over the people, and the people cannot throw off his yoke from their neck. At first it is in the power of the people to make whatever king they wish; but once he has been made king, it is no longer in their power to remove him from the kingdom. Thus the will of the people afterward becomes necessity.”

The holy Fathers also, when celebrating sacred councils, issued very astute decrees for the strength of kings and the stability of the kingdom.

From the Council of Toledo, chapter 75, after certain regulations of ecclesiastical order and decrees pertaining to the discipline of some people:

> “Our final judgment, made by all of us priests, is to issue, under God the judge, a final episcopal decree for the strength of our kings and the stability of the Gothic people. For, as is reported, there is among many nations such great treachery of mind that they disdain to preserve the faith promised by oath to their kings. They simulate the profession of an oath with their mouths while retaining the impiety of treachery in their minds. They swear to their kings and violate the faith they promise; nor do they fear that book of God’s judgment through which a curse is pronounced. Great is the threat of punishment against those who swear falsely in the name of God.

> “What hope, then, is there for such peoples when they labor against their enemies? Will there henceforth be faith to be trusted with other nations in peace? What treaty will remain inviolate among enemies when they do not preserve the sworn faith given to their own kings? Who is so mad as to cut off his own head with his own hand? Yet these men, forgetful of their own salvation, plainly kill themselves with their own hands by turning their strength against themselves and against their own kings.

> “And while the Lord says, ‘Do not touch my anointed ones’ (Ps. CIV, 15), and David says, ‘Who,’ he asks, ‘will stretch out his hand against the Lord’s anointed and be innocent?’ (I Sam. XXVI, 9), they do not fear to commit perjury or to bring destruction upon their kings. Faith to a pact is given to enemies and is not violated. If faith is valid in war, how much more must it be preserved among one’s own people?

> “It is sacrilege if the promised faith of peoples to their kings is violated, because the transgression of sin is committed not only against them but also against God, in whose name the promise itself is made. For this reason heavenly anger has changed many kingdoms of the earth, so that through the impiety of faith and morals one was separated from another.

> “Therefore we must beware of the downfall of such peoples, lest we likewise be struck by a sudden blow and punished with cruel punishment. For if God did not spare the angels who transgressed against him and who lost their heavenly dwelling through disobedience—hence through Isaiah he says, ‘My sword has become drunk in heaven’ (Isa. XXXIV, 5)—how much more must we fear the destruction of our salvation, lest through faithlessness we perish by the sword of the enraged God?

> “If we wish to avoid divine anger and desire to turn his severity toward clemency, [Note: *Cupimus*. Acherius indicates that much is omitted here.] lest the same punishment of destruction bind us together with those who strive by the same conspiracy, whom wicked fellowship unites in ruin: if this judgment, repeated now for the third time, pleases all of you who are present, confirm it by the agreement of your voices.”

The entire clergy and people replied:

> “Whoever presumes to act against this your definition, let him be anathema, maranatha—that is, let destruction come at the Lord’s advent—and let him, together with Judas Iscariot, have his portion, both he and his companions. Amen.”

And now [lacuna]

> “Although at the earlier council, held in the first year of our most glorious prince, a judgment concerning this matter was promulgated, nevertheless it is pleasing to repeat what must be observed” (Council of Toledo VI, chapter 17): “Therefore, while the king lives, no layman of any rank or dignity, nor anyone consecrated in the episcopal, presbyteral, or diaconal order, nor anyone devoted to the offices of the remaining clergy, shall in any action or deliberation provide a king for himself against the welfare of the living king. Let no one, by flattery or persuasion, draw another to himself through this hope, nor assent to another who seeks to do so. For it must be regarded by Christians as wicked and utterly detestable to anticipate unlawful things for future times and to arrange what is to come while unaware of one’s own life.”

And again:

[Note: *Confinitimi*. This material is absent from the published council.]

> “The priests of peoples bordering on the enemies, except those who have received permission from royal authority, must not secretly receive or send any message to a foreign people. Whoever is discovered and convicted shall be denounced to the rulers and punished at the council with a fitting penalty. Whoever attempts to oppose the commandments already mentioned of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of the other holy Fathers, should know without doubt that he has the devil as his guide; and because he did not wish to have Jesus, he will certainly have Barabbas.”

Therefore, most reverend lord, considering these and similar matters, do not disdain to return to the favor of our most serene king and lord, remembering the fidelity that you promised him by oath.

It is written, as the Lord says:

> “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain, for the Lord will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain” (Exod. X, 7).

Remember royal dignity; remember also your own order. We shall be supporters in these matters insofar as we are able, if you command it. We shall also be your most faithful helpers.

Do not doubt this, my father; it is not expedient. For, God as our witness, we love the good of peace and hasten to attain the fruit of charity.

Not every peace, however, is the same peace. There is a saving peace, and a harmful one. Saving peace is that of which the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “I leave you peace; my peace I give you” (John XIV, 27).

And because he recognized that it was unlike the other, he added:

> “I do not give to you as the world gives” (ibid.).

There is also the good peace that the angels announced to the shepherds, saying:

> “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II, 14).

And the blessed apostle Paul says of it:

> “Christ is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II, 14).

Again, there is an unjust peace, of which [lacuna]

> “When a strong armed man guards his courtyard, all that he possesses is in peace” (Luke XI, 21).

Was it not the devil himself, whom we understand by the armed strong man, who sought peace from the Lord when he fell before him, the stronger one, and said:

> “Jesus, Son of the Most High God, I adjure you by God, do not torment me” (Mark V, 7)?

But because he sought it unjustly, he did not deserve to obtain it from him.

The blessed David, considering the peace of the wicked harmful, says:

> “Because I was jealous of the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners” (Ps. LXXII, 3).

Just as the angels judged the peace of the good useful, so David judged the peace of the wicked useless.

Therefore peace must be sought with great discernment, so that we may labor in every way to strengthen what is saving and be able to avoid what is useless.

It is better for us, then, to endure adversaries in whatever way we can than to make an unjust agreement with them, as the Lord says:

> “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy” (Mark VIII, 15).

The blessed apostle Paul says:

> “If it is possible, so far as it depends on you” (Rom. XII, 18),

that is, “from your side,” as though he were saying: Whatever evil people may do, always seek their salvation; teach them what is appropriate; rebuke what is useless, even if they are ungrateful; and, if it is possible, strive to correct them.

This is useful peace. If they reject it, that is no reason for us to depart from uprightness. For it is clearly harmful to withdraw from what is good and become entangled in the errors of others.

It is written:

> “Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it, and whoever associates with the proud will be clothed with pride” (Ecclus. XIII, 1).

Let us therefore approach, with a sincere mind, the path of true peace—that is, our Lord Jesus Christ—and the examples and teachings of the holy Fathers. Let us firmly preserve royal fidelity, as we know that they themselves taught; let us prepare ourselves with complete readiness for the service of almighty God, for obedience to our senior lord, and for the support of our faithful brothers; and let us invite everyone we can by every means to these duties.

But those who prove rebellious toward such admonitions are no longer to be joined by the bond of peace. Rather, the counsel of separation must be sought, so that we may bring at least some of them into the grace of fellowship and prevent them all from perishing in guilt.

We are compelled to introduce this separation by the sacred example of the Savior himself, which we mentioned above. For it is entirely fitting that we take care to separate the one who wishes to be given to righteousness from those who do not wish this.

For if he remains with them in error and does not expose them, he too will perish together with them. Just as many advance through association with the good, so very many perish through the company of the wicked.

For the association of the wicked [lacuna] the wickedness of many people, like the weakness of one [lacuna] must be judged, as it is written:

> “All the nations are as nothing before him; they are regarded by him as nothing and emptiness” (Isa. XL, 17).

Nor should anyone place confidence in the protection of fortresses or any other defenses in such matters, because, as the prophet says:

> “If you are exalted like an eagle, and if you place your nest among the stars, from there I will bring you down, says the Lord” (Obad. 4).

If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them (Ps. LXI, 11), lest one day they look upon you and mock you, saying:

> “Behold the man who did not make God his helper, but trusted in the abundance of his riches and prevailed in his vanity” (Ps. LI, 9).

We do not consider it superfluous to acquire friends, to construct useful buildings, to guard what we possess, and to prosper in all things while preserving honorable moderation. But to rely upon these supports and become in any way arrogant we certainly judge harmful.

The Lord says in the Gospel:

> “A person’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” (Luke XII, 15).

And again:

> “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (ibid., 20.)

Therefore:

> “Hope in the Lord and do good; dwell in the land and you will be fed by its riches. Delight in the Lord, and he will grant you the desires of your heart. Commit your way to the Lord and hope in him, and he will act” (Ps. XXXVI, 3).

Let us exhort one another with these and similar words of the holy Scriptures, and let us not delay in advancing ourselves toward better things. Those whom we cannot draw along with us, let us at least fear to pursue toward worse things, as the Apostle says:

> “If the unbeliever departs, let him depart” (I Cor. XVII, 15).

For one person truly departs from another when he chooses the worse way—when he abandons the way of the Lord and proceeds wandering through byways.

To descend toward a precipice with a friend is not the act of a sound mind but of madness; nor can the grace of companionship exist where there is no hope of helping.

But lest we seem to be advising only ourselves, let us turn also to the others. We ought likewise to admonish the soldiers of the second rank, so that they continually observe the divine commandments, keep inviolate the loyalty to their king which they promised under oath, and in no way become transgressors of their law. This law, already at its very beginning, severely condemns the disloyalty of kings, indicates what punishment is owed to transgressors, and demonstrates how great is the excellence of kings; for if anyone proves an observer of these commandments, he will deserve both to acquire the greatest honor in the present age and to attain the gain of happiness for his soul in the age to come. But whoever, by resisting these commandments, incurs the judgment of death will doubtless bear the peril of his soul [lacuna] than what has been decreed for you [Col. 0103C] [lacuna].

Alas, alas! What punishment will be paid for the loss of the souls of those whom a bishop commands to resist the king—those entrusted and even committed to him—against the precept of divine speech, against the pledged oath, and even against secular law, in which the danger of death is also specified? It remains altogether that the souls endangered by his example or instruction must be required from his hands; moreover, the estates and resources of the churches, or the possessions of the poor, which have been laid waste as sins required, may avail toward his own destruction. For I confess before God that I desire to attain his loyalty more because of the divine commandments and the admonitions of the holy Fathers than because of any desire for earthly advantage or hostility toward a rebel [Col. 0103D]. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matt. XVI, 26). Hear blessed Susanna crying out: “It is better for me to fall without guilt into the hands of men than to sin in the sight of the Lord” (Dan. XIII, 23). And blessed David: “A little is better to the righteous man than the abundant riches of sinners” (Ps. XXXVI, 16). Solomon also says: “A dry morsel with joy is better than a whole house full of sacrifices with strife” (Prov. XVII, 1). Therefore let us humbly implore the Lord Jesus Christ, so that he who stretched out his hand to sinking blessed Peter in order to raise him [Col. 0104A] may rescue us from every evil and lead us to the path of righteousness. Amen.

*(The following letters are entitled: SENT CONCERNING CERTAIN ERRORS.)*

## EPISTLE II. TO ALL THE FAITHFUL OF HIS DIOCESE

ATTO, by the grace of God humble bishop, sends greeting and joy to all the faithful residing in our parish.

Recently, on the vigil of the Lord’s Octave, by God’s favor we delivered a sermon to those who were present, and we consider it necessary to send it to you. Alas! There are many in your regions who despise divine services and attend to omens, or signs of the sky, or vain incantations; nor do they fear what the Lord says concerning the Jews: “An evil and faithless generation seeks a sign” (Matt. XVI, 4), and so forth. Blessed Paul the Apostle also cries out: “See that no one deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human traditions, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ” (Col. II, 8). And elsewhere: “How are you turning again to the weak and impoverished elements, to which you desire to be enslaved anew? You observe days and months and seasons and years; I fear that I may have labored among you in vain” (Gal. IV, 9). The Psalmist indeed says: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. IV, 3); and again: “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, and who has not turned toward vanities and false insanities” (Ps. XXXIX, 5). [Col. 0104C] Farewell in the Lord.

## EPISTLE III. TO THE PEOPLE OF VERCELLI

ATTO, by the mercy of Christ humble bishop, sends to all the people of the diocese of the holy mother Church of Vercelli, our most beloved sons, peace, salvation, and joy in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Know, therefore, that through Christ the Lord himself and through the holy apostles and prophets, or through the other holy teachers, we have heard that many false prophets would come—who, what is most serious, would strive to turn many away from the way of truth, so that they would lead to destruction those who believed them. Therefore, since not only those who at that time perform miracles and various signs, or defend falsehoods with philosophical [Col. 0104D] doctrines [Note: [Col. 0103D] “Defend.” Some material is missing here.], but also since the heart is not so readily upright that you should hasten altogether to believe even those who merely report simple and foolish words, and since, alas, most wretched men, deceived by diabolical error, you call such persons prophets, abandoning your holy mother Church and the priests through whom you ought to attain eternal salvation: for this reason, when you have seen, heard, or learned of these letters, if any of you should henceforth, God forbid, perpetrate such wickedness, let him know that he will be condemned in every respect. He shall have no permission to eat anything cooked, except bread, nor [Col. 0105A] to drink wine, until he comes to his holy mother, namely the Church of Vercelli, and to our presence, to be judged for satisfaction and true humility of penitence. But if anyone, puffed up with pride, attempts to act against this, let him know that he must be driven from the thresholds of the Church and excluded from holy communion, and that all the faithful must abhor him, until he has received correction from the holy Church—both he himself and all who associate with him after they have recognized him as such. But if any priest, God forbid, should have been polluted by such an abomination, let him dare to usurp no divine mystery until, according to God and our judgment, he has rendered worthy satisfaction.

## EPISTLE IV. TO ALL THE FAITHFUL OF HIS DIOCESE

[Col. 0105B]

ATTO, by the grace of God humble bishop, sends peace and joy to all the faithful of our Church and to our most beloved sons.

If you preserve inviolate, with sincere hearts, what is known to have been handed down by the holy Fathers, you prepare great joy for us in this matter. But if, God forbid, we discover that you have been corrupted by various errors, great sorrow will thereby accumulate in our hearts. For if the rejection of a disciple is the teacher’s loss, how much more can the transgression of sons be a danger to their father? May the almighty Father grant us to live in such a way that each of us may receive a reward concerning the other, and that we may not be judged worthy of condemnation.

We have therefore heard that a certain new error has arisen among you [Col. 0105C]: that you say Friday should be given over to idleness and that food or banquets should be indulged in; and although the Redeemer of all regarded that same day as more sorrowful than all others, and endured such great insults for us, you strive to devote yourselves to games and pursue leisure. The apostles and all the other faithful likewise regarded that day as so sorrowful that, fleeing through various hiding places, scarcely two of them could be found together. There could be no thought of banquets, when despair had almost clung to life itself. On that same day the sun, clothed in darkness, withdrew its light, and the elements themselves, thrown into confusion, displayed the confusion of the whole world.

For if we celebrate the Lord’s Day because of the venerable Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ and the joy of the apostles and the other faithful—not only at Easter [Col. 0105D] but also by recurring weekly observance of the image of that day—he is mad who refuses to celebrate Friday, on which the Lord was crucified, throughout all the weeks, in its commemorative observance with abstinence and sorrowful contrition. Labor, finally, is called an impediment. On that day, therefore, Christ had been engaged in great labor, since he had endured such torments from the impious. Likewise, all his faithful, while they fled, were pressed by grief within and anguish without, and were granted no respite for rest when such an outrage was being prepared for them [Col. 0106A].

Flee, therefore, brothers, from this folly. It is enough for you to observe the Lord’s Day and the other most celebrated festivals approved by the priests. On those days you ought to rest so that, freed from secular business, you may more freely praise or proclaim the Lord and his saints, and serve them. For on Friday it is better to work for bread, by which you can refresh both your own hunger and that of another, than to sit with idle hands and cast forth empty tales with a chattering mouth.

## EPISTLE V. TO BISHOP AZO

To the most reverend and holy prelate, the lord AZO, worthy of the highest devotion, ATTO, by the grace of God humble [Col. 0106B] bishop and your most faithful servant, sends the persistence of prayers with devoted service.

May almighty God, who has deigned to place you upon the pastoral throne, himself deign to guard you with continual assistance, so that priestly honor may direct all your actions, and so that the priestly order may in turn shine forth through your sacred deeds.

As for the matter concerning which your prudence deigned to consult my dull insignificance—why we prevented a certain son of our Church from marrying the daughter of a woman who had received him from the sacred font—you additionally commanded us to send you any chapter we might find. You know, my lords, that in carnal marriages not only spiritual law but also secular law must be investigated.

Accordingly, Luitprand, the Catholic king of this country in which we live, promulgated the following chapter with the consent of the nobles and judges of that time (Longobard Law, book II, title 8, law 5) [Col. 0106C]:

> “We have judged and commanded this: no one shall presume to take his godmother as wife, nor the daughter whom he has lifted from the sacred font; nor shall his son presume to take as wife the daughter of the man who received him from the font, because they are known to be spiritual brothers. Whoever attempts to commit this evil shall lose all his property. The sons born from such an illicit marriage shall not be heirs, but the near relatives shall be. Wherever those who have contracted the illicit marriages written above are found, they shall be separated immediately and shall be subject to the penalty written above.”

The law called Salic also contains this [Col. 0106D]:

> “If anyone takes his father’s wife, let him incur the danger of death; and concerning former unions that appear to be incestuous, we have ordered that they be corrected through the prayers of the bishops. Whoever refuses to hear his bishop and is excommunicated shall endure perpetual condemnation [Note: [Col. 0106D] “Conditionem.” It is clear that “condemnation” (*condemnationem*) ought to be read here.] before God, shall be entirely excluded from our palace, and shall lose all his possessions to his legitimate relatives.”

The Roman emperors also, who ruled almost the whole monarchy and whose law it is fitting for us priests to observe in many matters, issued such enactments concerning marriages [Col. 0107A]:

> “But if, through adoption, someone has begun to be your sister, then, as long as the adoption remains established, marriage between you and her cannot lawfully take place.”

And likewise:

> “If anyone has intercourse contrary to what we have said, neither the man nor the woman, neither the nuptials nor the marriage nor the dowry, is recognized. Therefore those born from such intercourse are not under the father’s authority, but, so far as paternal authority is concerned, are like those whom their mother has conceived promiscuously. It follows that, once the intercourse has been dissolved, there is no place for demanding a dowry, and that they also suffer the other penalties contained in the sacred constitutions.”

No adoption can, finally, be like that by which human beings become sons of God. For this is an adoption that cannot be emancipated. Hence blessed Paul the Apostle says: “He predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace” (Eph. I, 5). No one doubts that the person who presents children to priests for baptism according to the order of the sacraments shares in this adoption; for, on their behalf and according to the rule of the Catholic faith, he responds in the first person—not as though speaking about another, but as about his own—because through sacred adoption his spirit has already been joined to theirs.

Again, after baptism they are entrusted by the priests themselves for instruction, as though from the sacred font, like a mother’s womb. For just as our carnal parents are ministers of our generation, as blessed Clement asserts in his Decretals, so these ministers are ministers of sacred regeneration. God is the author in both cases, as it is written: “To each one as the Lord has given. I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth” (I Cor. III, 6). Those who, as we said above, act on behalf of the children plant spiritually and are fathers. Those who water are ministers of the churches, conferring the sacrament of baptism. The Lord, however, gives growth in all things, whether in spiritual or in carnal progress.

It is also read in the Book of the Codices, which is the book of Roman law, as follows:

> “Nothing else can so introduce paternal affection and a just prohibition of marriage as this kind of bond, by which their souls have been joined to God.”

Likewise, from a Novella (Nov. 12, ch. 1) [Col. 0107D]:

> “If any persons contract a wicked and condemned marriage, and have no children from a previous marriage, let them immediately lose their property, and let the dowry be claimed for the rights of the treasury. After confiscation, let them also suffer the loss of their belt and be punished by exile. If the person is of lower status, let him undergo corporal torture, and let his wife, who has married contrary to the laws, suffer the same penalties. These provisions shall apply after two years; for a two-year indulgence has been granted to those who have already contracted marriages contrary to the laws, so that they may separate within two years. If they have not separated but have persisted throughout the whole two-year period, let them be subjected to the penalties stated in the first section.”

For it is exceedingly shameful that what secular people strive to preserve for the sake of religion, the priests of God should seek to violate [Col. 0108A]. Nor did the supreme pontiffs crush the secular laws by rejecting them so completely, since our Lord and their Lord and Master says: “I have not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it” (Matt. V, 17).

Likewise, the most holy Pope Calixtus (Epistle 2, to all the bishops of Gaul) says:

> “Nor ought we to receive those men whom the laws of the world reject. We cannot erase the disgrace with which they have been stained, but we desire to heal their souls through public penance and the satisfaction of the Church.”

Likewise Dionysius:

> “We judge all those to be infamous who transgress their Christian law.”

Likewise Eutychianus:

> “Similarly, we prohibit ecclesiastical judges from hearing cases that are not contained in the laws or that are known to be prohibited.”

Here the most holy Pope Julius also confirms this. [Col. 0108B] Blessed Gregory likewise, confirming many chapters of Roman law, inserted them into his register.

Therefore, my lord, it seems absurd that spiritual kinship should be compelled to serve carnal embraces. For blessed Paul the Apostle says: “You were called to freedom, brothers; only do not use freedom as an opportunity for the flesh” (Gal. V, 13); and again: “He who sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, but he who sows in the spirit will reap eternal life from the spirit” (Gal. VI, 8). And again: “Where the Spirit is, there is freedom” (II Cor. III, 17). And in Leviticus: “Every consecrated thing that is offered shall not be redeemed by man” (Lev. XXVII, 29), lest, by submitting to our uses, what has been consecrated become accursed.

But even if all those things which we have said above in condemning such a marriage [Col. 0108C] were lacking, enough would still remain to repress it. For this practice has by now been so thoroughly abolished for the sake of religion that it seems profane not only to the learned and prudent but even to the peasants themselves, as a matter of custom; wherever they hear of anything of this kind, demanded by sins, they are scandalized. Hence a grave sin arises for those who commit it.

The Lord says: “Woe to that man through whom scandal comes” (Matt. XVIII, 7); and blessed Paul: “We take care to do what is good not only before God but also before men” (II Cor. VIII, 21); and again: “Be without offense to Jews and Greeks and the Church of God” (I Cor. X, 32); and again: “If food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I cause my brother to stumble” (I Cor. VIII, 13); and again: “Let no one seek his own good, but that of the other” (I Cor. X, 24).

Indeed, the person who presumes to alter or erase ancient customs observed by the most religious and prudent gives offense to many, although blessed Isidore says (book II of the *Etymologies*, chapter 10):

> “Custom is a certain law established by practice, which is accepted through law when written law is lacking. It makes no difference whether it rests upon writing or reason, since reason also commends law. Moreover, if law is established by reason, then everything established by reason will already be law, provided only that it agrees with religion, accords with discipline, and advances salvation.”

Blessed Pope Gregory also, by whose institutions almost the whole world is governed, says in the first part of his register (book I, letter 75) [Col. 0109A]:
