> “We, following the tenor of your report, likewise permit the custom—which is nevertheless recognized as usurping nothing against the Catholic faith—to remain unchanged, whether concerning the establishment of primates or other chapters, except in the case of those who come to the episcopate from the Donatists.”

Blessed Augustine too, from whose garden’s herbs the whole Lord’s flock feeds, writes in response to an inquiry from Januarius (Epistle 118, to Januarius):

> “Even a change of custom that is beneficial in its usefulness disturbs by its novelty.”

Therefore what is not useful is consequently harmful through its unfruitful disturbance. It is apparent, then, that a custom which harms neither the Catholic faith nor secular laws must in every respect be preserved; this is confirmed by the Theodosian edict.

But the custom now under discussion is in no way opposed either to the Catholic faith or to any law of Christians. Although there are certain laws in which this matter is not specifically contained, there is none that appears to oppose it. For this reason, we believe that many of the ancients remained silent about it: because, in the new religion of baptism, no Christian attempted to presume such things; nor did they judge that something needed to be forbidden which they did not believe anyone would presume to do. For “the law is not laid down for the just, but for the unjust” (I Tim. I, 9).

Nevertheless, we, upon whom—though unworthy—the duty of discernment has been imposed, so that we may distinguish between clean and unclean, and diagnose leprosy, ought to proclaim such matters, lest, by keeping silent, we be accused by the Lord through the prophet, who says: “Dumb dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. LVI, 10), and lest we appear to consent to the people’s crimes and become blameworthy by concealing our failure to rebuke the wickedness of others. But in all things let us show ourselves as ministers of God (II Cor. VI, 4), because it is written: “Do not share in the sins of others” (I Tim. V, 22); and again: “Do not touch what is unclean” (II Cor. VI, 17).

As for what you say from the Lord’s judgment: “What God has joined, let no man separate” (Matt. XIX, 6), this religion appears in every way to be observed; but not all who are joined together have been joined by the Lord. The union of those whom he himself has joined is good, since it neither harms the laws nor disturbs Catholic practice. But “marriage is honorable and the marriage bed undefiled” (Heb. XIII, 4), as blessed Paul the Apostle says:

> “To those who are joined in marriage I give this command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband, and that a husband should not dismiss his wife” (I Cor. VII, 10).

Observe that he says “to those who are joined in marriage.” Marriage is the lawful agreement and condition of spouses. Those who mingle in wicked and detestable intercourse against the laws and customs must be separated altogether, since in such a union there can be neither husband nor wife.

The Lord says in the Gospel: “If your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you” (Matt. V, 30). What better can we understand by the right hand that causes scandal than a wrongly joined wife? And again: “Everyone who has left house or brothers or sisters or father or mother or wife for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (Matt. XIX, 29) [Col. 0110A]. And the Apostle Paul: “A brother or sister is not enslaved in such a matter; the Lord has called us to peace” (I Cor. VII, 15).

The Lord, moreover, while forbidding divorce, excepted the case of fornication, saying: “Except for the cause of fornication” (Matt. V, 32). As you know, there are two kinds of this, about which it is not necessary for us now to dispute in every detail.

Do not disdain, my lord, to counsel your faithful man—namely, our son—with kindly and honeyed words, as you know well, so that, abandoning his former ways, he may attain better things. For you know well that all discipline, in the present, seems not to be of joy but of sorrow; afterward, however, it yields the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those trained by it (Heb. XII, 11). And the Apostle James says: “He should know that whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way saves his soul from death and covers a multitude of sins” (Jas. V, 20).

Your Magnificence has also informed us that there are many, both great and small, in this kingdom who have such wives, and you have promised to inform us about them. With God as our witness, this remains unknown to us and seems very strange. But if there are some who do such things, either their rarity has kept the matter obscure to us, or it has been concealed through dissimulation. Nevertheless, in these regions we have never heard of anyone except this man. Yet even if there were many who did this, the Lord’s sentence ought to prevail: “You shall not follow the crowd to do evil, nor shall you give way in judgment to the opinion of the majority, so as to deviate from the truth” (Exod. XXIII, 2) [Col. 0110C]. And Paul says: “If I were still pleasing men, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. I, 10). The Apostle James says: “Whoever therefore wishes to be a friend of this world makes himself an enemy of God” (Jas. IV, 4).

Moses denied that he was the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing instead to be afflicted with the people of God rather than to possess the enjoyment of temporal sin, considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasure of Egypt (Hebr. IV, 24). According to the decree of Pope Celestine, the people are to be taught, not followed. But even if neither law prevails nor custom is effective, at least reason itself should proceed.

Everyone clearly testifies that marriages between godfathers and godmothers are forbidden, although the mystery of this sacrament is celebrated not specifically in them but in their children. For they themselves can also be separate from one another. Who, then, would dare say that this sacrament binds those who are absent, but does not concern those who are present, in whom it is celebrated? The force of the word itself also makes this clear. For what does *compater* or *commater* mean except “co-father” or “co-mother”? If, then, they are co-fathers or co-mothers, all their sons or daughters will be brothers or sisters of one another.

The Lord, rebuking the scribes and Pharisees, says: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, fools and blind, who say: Whoever swears by the altar, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gift that is upon it is obligated. Blind men, which is greater: the gift, or the altar that sanctifies the gift? Therefore whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything that is upon it. And whoever swears by the temple swears by it and by him who dwells in it” (Matt. III, 17) [Col. 0111A].

It therefore seems to us that if this adoption pertains to the parents, it pertains even more to the children; and if it does not pertain to the children, it plainly appears not to pertain to the parents either.

With these considerations in mind, we suspended the aforementioned Theoderic from such a marriage bed, but we did not altogether prohibit the marriage, nor did we otherwise excommunicate him, until we come before the hearing of the lord archbishop, yourself, and our other venerable brothers. This is not because we now doubt what is right, but so that the assertion of the majority may be confirmed by greater authority.

Often, when the wound of a crime is pressed upon delinquents, the judgment of the physician appears objectionable; and when the perverse stain of a crime is unwilling to be washed away, they rush to accuse the person who would wash it away. We deprive their slanders of force by meanwhile awaiting the judgment of the majority, as blessed Paul says to Timothy: “Show yourself irreproachable, so that the one who is opposed may be ashamed, having nothing evil to say about us” (Tit. II, 8).

For, my lord, when this matter is pursued against this man, the labor is undertaken not only for him but for all such people. The law does not admit personal distinction: if it is permitted to this man, it is plainly permitted to everyone; and if it is forbidden to this man, no one will afterward excuse himself on the grounds of ignorance.

You have also informed us that there are some entangled in such marriages [Col. 0111C] who will not abandon their unions because no one has excommunicated them. Would that, my lord, we might be able to fulfill the duty imposed upon us. Whatever they do, let us at least take care to free ourselves. For concerning such people the Apostle John cries out: “Whoever is not from God does not listen to us” (I John IV, 6). By this we recognize the spirit of truth and the spirit of error.

May the God of peace and charity so join you to himself that, as good stewards of the things that belong to him, you may not grow sluggish through the darkness of any obscurity; but, enlightened by the divine radiance, may you labor in the vineyard in the present in such a way that in the future you may deserve to hear the Lord’s “Well done.”

## EPISTLE VI. OF GUNZO, DEACON OF NOVARA, TO ATTO

[Col. 0111D]

To the lord ATTO, worthy of reverence as a bishop, GUNZO, the least of the deacons of the Church of Novara, sends the service of due veneration.

Concerning the matter on which your Highness deigned to consult my insignificance, I delayed responding until now so that prolonged reflection might provide firmer answers. Although the matter is entirely clear to your dignity, I thought it appropriate to bring forward a most authoritative rescript from the Apostolic See, addressed to Theodore, bishop of Ticinum.

Zacharias, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and holy brother Theodore, bishop of the Church of Ticinum.

Your venerable fraternity presented us with a written inquiry, by which you asked us whether it is permitted for a son whose father has received another man’s daughter from sacred baptism—that is, the spiritual daughter of that same father—to take her in marriage, a thing cruel to say, which you asserted had happened in an outrageous manner [Note: [Col. 0111D] “You asserted outrageously.” The same manuscript corrects the wording: the edition of Acherius has the corrupt reading “you discussed an outrage.” From the same manuscript I restored “he commanded,” where the reading had been “he may command.”].

But your holy fraternity knows well what the Lord commanded through Moses [Col. 0112B],* saying: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your mother. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister, or the nakedness of your father’s daughter. For it is your nakedness” (Lev. XVIII, 7).

One is said to uncover nakedness when we are commanded to abstain from our own blood relationship; much more, after every occasion or argument has been set aside, must we carefully guard ourselves from the spiritual daughter of our father, under the strictest discipline [Note: [Col. 0111D] “Set aside.” Here too I follow the royal manuscript: the earlier edition reads “replaced,” and shortly afterward “by crime.”], lest anyone involved in such a crime,* having failed altogether to restrain the reins of lust, fall into the wrath of the divine judgment.

Therefore everyone must entirely beware of participation in such a crime, lest they perish eternally. But those who, despising the salvation of their souls, have entered into this pernicious and presumptuous wicked marriage, your fraternity must strive in every way to separate and subject to worthy penance, so that, rescuing their souls from eternal condemnation, you may gain them, with the Lord and [Note: [Col. 0111D] “And God the Savior.” The royal manuscript reads “with the Lord.” Concerning the sons born from them, you reported [Col. 0112D] whether it is permitted for them to be joined in marriage. But why should these be prohibited from marriage or compelled to do penance for such a matter, when they are declared to be free from condemnation? For the father will not bear torment for the son, nor the son for the father, as the Lord says through the prophet: “The soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine; the soul that sins, it shall die.” But concerning these matters, dearest brother, it will be enough to have spoken. Take care, however, not to permit the subjects to act otherwise, lest you be found to have departed from the straight path. This is the other part of the letter, which Gunzo mentions at the end of this letter.] God our Savior Jesus Christ.

Your Prudence therefore is not unaware that not only those who have polluted themselves with a wicked marriage must be struck by ecclesiastical censure, but also those who were the authors of this crime: namely, the man who is known to be both the carnal father of one person and the spiritual father of another. He must be subjected to so much greater penance insofar as he is shown to have possessed greater authority in the matter. Concerning the sons of these people, the same venerable father writes back to the same Theodore, bishop, that they are not held by the crime of their parents.

## EPISTLE VII. OF AMBROSE, PRIEST OF MILAN, TO ATTO

[Col. 0112D]

To the unconquered athlete of the heavenly court and one joined to the assemblies of the citizens above, ATTO, thrice most blessed bishop, the humble servant of Christ and your most faithful [Col. 0113A] AMBROSE, a priest—though unworthy of the holy office in the holy Church of Milan—sends the continual service of due obedience with everlasting happiness.

The letter recently sent by your holiness, in which your holiness and our memory were marked in your sacred prayers, made us secure on every side with indescribable joy. We are, of course, rejected [Note: [Col. 0113] “Rejected.” The earlier edition reads “rejected and repudiated … we know clearly,” but this is plainly erroneous.] and repudiated,* and are not* worthy even to be compared with the shoes of your holy feet. How, then, are we worthy to be remembered in the prayers of so religious and powerful a lord and father? But we believe that you remember the saying: “God does not labor over great things, nor disdain small things.” Moreover, no one doubts that the divine Spirit dwelling in your breast makes you most ready for every holy work.

The marriage about which you consulted our feebleness is, as you should know, entirely forbidden by our teachers and priests, because they are called spiritual brothers, as you also asserted. Secular law likewise forbids this, as I have heard from a certain lawgiver. Moreover, chapter 3 of the decrees of Pope Zacharias contains the following:

> “No one shall take a priestess, or a deaconess, or a spiritual godmother into marriage.”

From this it is understood that no one is permitted to take the spiritual father’s daughter in marriage. But if it pleases your Lordship, explain to us in your reply whom we ought to understand by those whom the aforesaid chapter calls a priestess or a deaconess, since this is entirely unknown to us [Col. 0113C].

May Christ preserve you, commended to him by your continual prayers, for a long time.

## EPISTLE VIII. ATTO TO AMBROSE THE PRIEST

ATTO, by the grace of God humble bishop, sends to the lord AMBROSE, most reverend and holy priest, devoted prayers in Christ with the bond of charity.

To your Holiness, since, despite our weakness, we know how to entreat the Almighty, we beseech God for immense recompense. Prostrate at your sacred feet, we earnestly implore that the same be done hereafter. We too, although unequal in merits, nevertheless trusting in your virtues, do not fail in every way to do this also for you. For whenever we hear of the frequent illnesses of your body, they pierce us as though they were our own limbs. But we believe that you heed blessed Paul, when he says: “For when I am weak, then I am stronger” (II Cor. XII, 10). May God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, sustain and chastise you in such a way that neither adversity may cast you down nor prosperity make you arrogant.

Finally, we again offer many thanks, because you have taken care to instruct us abundantly concerning all the matters we entrusted to you. Moreover, we are altogether astonished that an immense spring, established among so many flowing streams, should seek the liquid of some neighboring vein that scarcely labors. For even if some moisture is found there, it is proven to have been distilled from a superior fluid.

Therefore, concerning what your prudence has judged necessary to consult—what we ought to understand by “presbyteress” and what by “deaconess”—it seems to us that in the primitive Church, because, according to the Lord’s saying, “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Luke X, 2), devout women as well as men were appointed as attendants in the holy Church, for the assistance of the men. Blessed Paul shows this in his Epistle to the Romans, when he says: “I commend to you Phoebe our sister, who is in the ministry of the Church at Cenchreae” (Rom. XVI, 1). Here it is understood that at that time not only men but also women presided over churches, evidently for a very useful purpose. For women long accustomed to pagan rites and also instructed in philosophical doctrines were more readily converted through these women, and were taught more freely about the practice of religion.

The Council of Laodicea later prohibited this in chapter 11, where it says: “Those who are called presbyteresses or presiding women ought not to be appointed in the churches.” We believe that deaconesses were the attendants of such women. For we call a *diaconus* a minister, and we see that *diacona* is derived from it. Finally, we read in the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 15 (canon 15), that a deaconess was not to be ordained before the age of forty, and that she was to be ordained only with the greatest deliberation.

We also believe that such women were entrusted with the duty of baptizing women, so that the bodies of others could be handled by them without any embarrassment whatsoever. For it is written in the statutes of the Easterners (Council of Carthage IV, canon 12):

> Widows or religious women who are chosen for the ministry of baptizing women must be so instructed for this office that they can teach uneducated and rustic women, in suitable and sound language, at the time when they are to be baptized, how they should answer the questions put to them and how they should live after receiving baptism.

For just as those who were called presbyteresses had undertaken the duty of preaching, commanding, or teaching, so deaconesses had undertaken the duty of ministering or baptizing. This, however, is now by no means necessary. For today infant girls are baptized at such an early age, because of their parents’ religious observance, that neither shame on their part nor any stimulus of pleasure on the part of those baptizing them can cause an impediment. Hence it has now been decreed that a woman must not presume to undertake the practice of baptizing.

There are also those who have asserted that in ancient times those whom we now call abbesses were called deaconesses. This seems to us wholly inappropriate. For *abbas* means “Father”; hence, according to the pattern of other nouns, *abbatissa* is derived in the feminine gender, with the same meaning retained. The force of this word expresses a quality combining fear and love, reverence and affection. By “deaconess,” however, we understand nothing other than “a female minister.” Therefore, if the name of this office somehow still survived today, we would consider those women deaconesses who, overcome by advanced age, preserving a religious life in chastity, faithfully prepare the offerings to be presented to priests, keep vigil at the entrances of churches, and sweep the floors.

We can also regard as presbyteresses or deaconesses those women who were joined in marriage to priests or deacons before their ordination and who afterward ought to govern them chastely, as has been promulgated in the canons attributed to the apostles, chapter 6:

> Let no bishop, priest, or deacon cast away his own wife under the pretext of religion; but if he casts her away, let him be excommunicated. If he persists, let him be deposed.

Likewise, from the Decrees of Pope Leo, chapter 17:

> The law of continence is the same for ministers of the altar as for bishops and priests. When they were laymen or readers, they could lawfully marry wives and beget children; but once they reached the aforementioned ranks, what had been lawful for them began to be unlawful.

Thus, so that a carnal marriage may become a spiritual one, they ought neither to dismiss their wives, but to have them as though they did not have them. In this way the affection of marriage remains preserved, while the activity of marriage ceases.

Nevertheless, dearest teacher, we gladly accept the matters explained according to the foregoing interpretation, until we may deserve to receive more certain instruction from you. In all these cases, as you commanded, marriages are denied, so that ecclesiastical honor may be preserved in every respect.

Furthermore, we humbly ask your sincere charity about the epistle found among the canons, which is also called canonical and is known to contain eleven chapters. They seem to us extremely useful. Its beginning is:

> First of all, let all priests, deacons, and subdeacons retain the Catholic faith by heart, so that if anyone neglects to do this, he shall abstain from wine for forty days; and if after the abstinence he neglects the instruction entrusted to him, the sentence against him shall be doubled.

We also ask about the ancient statutes of the Easterners, which are counted as one hundred chapters. Of these, the first is sought among us at every episcopal consecration; it begins:

> He who is to be a bishop must first be examined, etc.

May you deign to certify us concerning all these matters: when and where they were established, under which ruler and by which Fathers, how they ought to be treated, and whether they should be accepted in their entirety or rejected in some part. May the Almighty Lord deign to preserve your prudence for us, so that, guided by it, we may be able to proceed along the right path.

## EPISTLE IX. TO ALL THE PRIESTS OF THE DIOCESE OF VERCELLI

Atto, by the grace of God humble bishop, to all the priests and their ministers residing in our diocese of Vercelli: the crown of eternal happiness.

Dearest brothers, there are many forms of incontinence. Whenever we commit some crime, we fall into it through incontinence. Yet the particular form of incontinence is lust, which corrupts body and soul together. For although there are many vices which, while offending one part, nevertheless nourish the other, this is the vice by which the body is dissolved, the mind wearied, and the soul afflicted. This is what David desired and what prostrated Solomon. This is what attempts to take away the palm from martyrs and, beyond that, the crown of prolonged mortification from confessors.

Thus, while the other vices can also be carried out through ministers, this one can in no way be served without the pollution of one’s own body. There are also many acts of which it is uncertain with what intention they are performed; and although they condemn their accomplices through their own conscience, the perpetrators themselves can nevertheless excuse themselves in one way or another before others. Adultery, however, can neither be committed with a good intention nor find any avenue for excuse. As blessed Clement says, it holds second place among punishments.

Therefore all Christians, but especially priests who serve the ministry of preaching, and their ministers, must be extremely careful to avoid it. If they should fall into it, it will nevertheless be punishment for them, lamentation for the continent, scandal for the married, an example for fools, and harm to the holy Church of God. For, according to blessed Gregory, when someone’s life is despised, it remains that his preaching too will be despised.

Finally, the names of our offices themselves indicate that we must abstain from such things. A priest is so called as one who gives what is sacred; a minister, from ministering. With what wicked presumption, then, does someone who knows himself to persist in such filth dare to consecrate or give to others the sacred body or blood of the Lord Jesus Christ? Or how does one who continually serves lust at home presume to minister in the church?

Accordingly, priests ought to regulate the people by both word and example. They must therefore take care lest, when they preach to others, they themselves be found rejected and hear what the Lord said in rebuking hypocrisy: “Hypocrite, first cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to cast the splinter out of your brother’s eye” (Luke VI, 42). Worse still, there are those who neither cast the beam from their own eye nor presume to remove the splinter from their brother’s eye; instead, recognizing themselves as rejected, they fall silent in confusion. While these nourish the sins of others by their own sins, they will rightly bear the burden of both.

For the Lord says:

> If, when I say to the wicked, “You shall surely die,” you do not warn him, nor speak to turn him from his wicked way so that he may live, that wicked person shall die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood at your hand (Ezek. III, 18).

Moreover—something shameful to say but dangerous to keep silent—some become so enslaved to lust that they permit obscene prostitutes to live with them in their own houses, eat with them, and conduct themselves publicly. Ensnared by their allurements, they appoint them over their household, their entire family, and their possessions, establish their harlot as their heir after their death, and leave to such hands whatever they can acquire from the resources of the Church, from alms, or from any other source.

Thus, when they bring a prostitute upon the holy Church of God, its mother and bride, they deprive God the Father and the faithful husband of the soul and hand it over to the devil for adultery.

There are also those who come naked to the Church but grow rich from its benefits. At first they feign continence because of poverty, and afterward, once enriched, they take up prostitutes. When they were suffering from want, they were despised by these women and received into the bosom of the holy Church. From then on, they do not cease to distribute to them whatever they are later able to steal. Thus prostitutes are adorned, churches are devastated, and the poor are afflicted.

On this account, public officials [Note: [Col. 0117D] *Publicani*. Acherius rightly observed that Atto uses this word with a new meaning; it should be understood either as public judges or, rather, as their officials.] break into the houses of clerics, pretending that they are not extracting the clerics themselves but the women living with them, together with the illegitimate children they have borne, as though those people had been entrusted to them. The wretched men are terrified, promise every kind of gift, and those who could have been worshiped are compelled to worship everyone. Those who ought manfully to denounce the vices of all seek permission for their own vices from the judge.

Thus sacred buildings are made public property and mocked by the common people, and the name of the Lord is blasphemed, as it is written: “You are the ones through whom the name of the Lord is blasphemed among the nations” (Rom. II, 24).

They also commonly incur the hatred of their neighbors, men and women, on account of such crimes. Whenever such women or their illegitimate children quarrel with someone, the clerics themselves, casting aside all priestly reverence, intervene; they inflict whatever insults and injuries they can [Note: [Col. 0118D] *Inferre*. I read *inferunt*], and threaten worse things.

Moreover, in order to enrich such a household, they become greedy, rapacious, usurious, avaricious, envious, and deceitful. Hence the Church of Christ suffers no small harm. For when the people observe this, they despise returning tithes and first fruits to God when these men demand them, and they refuse to render any service to the holy Church of God from which the priests themselves might obtain some benefit. Thus the people become sacrilegious. The clerics themselves, however, often fall into such poverty that they can scarcely support themselves.

Again, there are those who, when their bishops accuse them of such a crime, reject paternal charity and disdain obedience. They do not fear to violate the fidelity they had promised under oath, but attack their bishops by appealing to worldly power, entrust themselves and their households to their opponents, and, relying finally on such assistance, make light of ecclesiastical discipline. At the command of their lords, in any place or at any time, they presume—against the law of the canons and without any discernment—to sing Masses, celebrate baptisms, loose those who are bound, and bind those who are free. Thus those who ought to have been principal members of the holy Church become weapons of its enemies; they lead themselves to destruction and the people into error.

From this there often arises a great scandal against the holy Church, because those whom it wishes to have as sons it sees as enemies, and those whom it wishes as counselors as harsh adversaries.

Again, there are those who seek to excuse themselves for keeping women as companions by presenting their supposed necessity. They say that unless they were supported by the hands of these women, they would already perish from hunger or nakedness. We know this to be false when we consider the women’s circumstances. Indicating the pressures of persecution, the Lord says: “But woe to those who are pregnant and to those who nurse in those days” (Matt. XIII, 17). We understand him to have said this because such women, encumbered and burdened, were less able than others to assist themselves in their needs. How, then, can someone lift up another who is unable to raise himself?

Certainly, unless others minister to such women, they themselves cannot subsist by their own labor. But a crime committed for pleasure is sought to be excused by utility; yet an advantage that reason does not commend ought not to be preserved. Even if, as is claimed, some profit could be found in such an arrangement, because it appears contrary to our ministry it must be rejected in every way.

For which of the apostles, or of the other teachers of the Church, ever went forth to preach with women? Indeed, after their calling, they withdrew from the company of those women whom they had lawfully married before their vocation. Blessed Clement likewise commands this in the Apostolic Decretals:

> Let ministers of the altar be chosen for the Lord’s offices from among those who have left their wives before ordination.

Likewise, the Council of Carthage, chapter 25 [2, or 4]:

> It has seemed good—and this has also been confirmed in various councils—that subdeacons who handle the sacred mysteries, deacons and priests, and also bishops, according to their own statutes, should likewise abstain from their wives.

Thus testify Innocent and Leo, Roman pontiffs, and likewise the other authorities. For the more we withdraw from carnal desires and worldly affairs, the more ready we become as servants of divine work, as the distinguished man Boethius testifies when he says:

> If you had entered this stage of the world naked, you would sing fearlessly before the robber.

Our robbers are demons and their ministers, who always attempt to plunder our possessions. Indeed, if we are naked and free from unlawful things, we shall sing fearlessly before them, either by freely exposing their perversities to the reprobate and preaching their future miseries, or by proclaiming to the demons, in David’s little songs:

> “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters. The snare has been broken, and we have been freed” (Ps. CXXIII, 7).

Therefore, dearest brothers, guard yourselves from the company of women, lest you make the members of Christ members of prostitutes (I Cor. VI, 15). You can scarcely escape this unless you withdraw from their companionship. For whom would carefully arranged hair, a beautiful face, the fluttering of the eyelids, the narrowing of the eyes, affable speech, a talkative melody, an unguarded gaze, seductive persuasion, splendid necklaces, elaborate clothing, the scent of perfumes, a soft gait, and the luxury of the entire body not loosen into depravity?

Seeing this, blessed Paul the apostle cries out: “Flee fornication” (I Cor. II, 18). For while we can avoid the other vices by resisting them, against this one we must flee with our feet, and, lest we fail, we must implore divine assistance.

Dearest brothers, search the pages of the Holy Scriptures and meditate on them more diligently, so that what we have said may not seem worthless as though it were our own, since we have explained to our brothers what we received from the holy Fathers. Because we cannot explain all their examples, we have presented a few of the many; others we have judged should be appended below.

First is the Council of Nicaea, consisting of three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers. In it the Catholic faith was strengthened by the divine Spirit and the perfidy of the Arians destroyed. It is preserved among men as the words of the Gospel are preserved, chapter 3 (Council of Nicaea, canon 2):

> The great council absolutely forbade any bishop, priest, deacon, or anyone at all belonging to the clergy to have a woman introduced into his household, unless perhaps she were his mother, sister, aunt, or only such persons as escaped suspicion.

Likewise, from the Decrees of Pope Clement:

> No one shall live with a woman who is not a relative, unless she is a sister or close relation; and even this must be done with great care. For we are not ignorant of Satan’s malice.

Likewise, from Siricius (Epistle 1, chapter 12):

> We do not permit any women other than those whom the Council of Nicaea allowed to live with clerics solely because of the necessities of relationship.

Many councils and the opinions of many teachers have not kept silent on this matter. In this the honor of the Church and the dignity of the clergy endure; from this charity grows and the rust of avarice is wiped away. Thus the holy Church is united, and no fissure of dissension or envy is seen.

May the triune and one God, who lives and reigns forever and ever, help you to observe this. Amen.

## EPISTLE X. TO THE SAME

Atto, by the grace of God humble bishop, to all the priests and their ministers residing in our diocese of Vercelli: the crown of eternal happiness.

Dearest brothers, what is practiced repeatedly must be repeatedly restrained with denunciation, until it is emptied out and utterly abolished. If, after being forbidden, such practices are neglected and remain covered over by silence, they appear to be strengthened rather than renounced. Woe to us, who have undertaken the burden of this ministry, if we neglect to preach the truth. Woe to us if we suppress in silence what we are commanded to distribute to the money-changers. What will we say at the future judgment if we are ashamed to preach the truth? For whoever can cast down the wicked but neglects to do so does nothing other than encourage them. Nor is he free from the suspicion of secret partnership who ceases openly to oppose a crime.

Concerning the good of chastity, my brothers, we communicated some things to you in words long ago; we also did not fail to offer certain matters in writing. In those writings we described some of its incentives and undertook to enumerate part of its disasters. We taught you to avoid prostitutes and utterly prohibited the companionship of foreign women. We also confirmed these prohibitions by the testimonies of the holy Fathers, lest you think that you could transgress them with impunity.

But since we know that this has benefited some, we first offer devoted praises to God the Father; through him we also give you immense thanks, praying that you may deserve to ascend from virtue to virtue and behold the God of gods in Zion.

Therefore, dearest brothers, if any are still entangled, submerged in the mire of such wickedness, let them not delay to entreat the Lord with tearful groans. Let them not cease to raise their hands, so that they may more quickly be freed from so great a chasm. For it is written: “Everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Matt. VII, 2).

Trusting, therefore, in so great a promise of the Lord, brothers, without any hesitation take up the path of chastity without delay. The one who gave the command of continence will certainly grant progress in perseverance. But if anyone, lifted up by the goads of pride or struck down by the decay of despair, neglects to rise, he will by no means pass through this stage without danger to himself. [Lacuna: the surviving, syntactically damaged text reads, “that of no teachers … may encounter the divine judgment with evil deeds.”]

May I, weighed down by my own iniquities, nevertheless deserve to rejoice with you over your good conduct and to be excused with you from innumerable offenses, as the apostle James says: “Whoever brings a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins” (James V, 20).

But you, brothers, whom the eye of the Lord has already mercifully regarded and rescued from such things, ought continually to entreat the Almighty for others and exhort them by salutary admonitions to better things, so that in whatever way you may be able to raise them up together with yourselves. The Lord says: “If a brother helps his brother, both will be exalted.” And the apostle Paul says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. VI, 2). James also says: “Pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James V, 16).

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and is glorified, God, forever and ever. Amen.

## EPISTLE XI. TO HIS SUFFRAGAN BISHOPS

To those most holy and beloved fellow brothers, the venerable bishops: Atto, by the grace of God humble bishop, offers faithful prayers in Christ with devoted service.

Your charity knows that our princes and lords, the most glorious kings, when they claim to suspect an enemy attack, seek our assistance—that is, the assistance of us bishops—against it. Not content with our promises and not relying on fidelity confirmed by oath, they are also, as you have recently heard, making every effort to receive hostages from us for this purpose.

Do not disdain to explain to us in your sacred letters what your Holiness has thought about this matter, since we cannot now speak together suitably. If the aforementioned hostages are to be given by us, or if those designated are to know that they are to bind themselves on our behalf, what should be done? If they consent, in what manner and with what security ought this to be carried out? Should this agreement be recorded in writing, or should it be entrusted only to common verbal assurances? Should a limit be imposed, and if so, to what extent? If something concerning us is secretly reported to the princes—that we have violated the pledge proposed for which the aforementioned hostages are ordered to be given—how should the matter be proved or defended? What law has force in such cases, ecclesiastical or also worldly? By which witnesses should the same agreement be approved? If the different parties should openly disagree, how should this be proclaimed, if it can be done? We humbly ask for instruction on all these points.

For it will be of very great importance, both now and in the future, if so great and unprecedented a matter is treated at its very beginning with the most salutary counsels and its definition committed to writing, so that it admits no further ambiguity. I confess that, so idle and inexperienced am I, I have so far found nothing of this kind established with authority or proposed by example by ecclesiastical teachers. But if some most diligent investigator should be able to discover such a precedent, I affirm inviolably that whatever has been established by the holy Fathers must be observed.

I also judge that the fidelity owed to our lords and kings must be fully observed in every respect. For we can in no way be found pure before the eyes of divine majesty if we are in any way unfaithful to them. The Lord says in the Gospel: “If you do not love the human being whom you see, how can you love God whom you do not see?” (I John IV, 7–8.) Therefore it is fitting that we labor for their fidelity, and for the stability and peace of the kingdom, just as we know that the most holy prelates, our predecessors, labored for the salvation of religious princes.

Otherwise, I judge that nothing new should be added unless the greatest utility or necessity compels it, and it has been deliberated by the judgment of the supreme pontiff or by the counsel of prudent bishops. For we know that, as the Lord says through the prophet:

> What is this proverb that you turn into a saying, “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge”? As I live, says the Lord, this proverb shall no longer be used in Israel: the soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine (Ezek. XVIII, 2).

The soul that sins shall itself die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, and the father shall not bear the iniquity of the son (ibid., 20). Who, then, being religious, would dare to speak against the Lord’s judgment and say that a faithful person should be condemned for the iniquity of his father or for that of his son, when he hears the Lord himself saying: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father that of the son”?

Although children draw from their parents the guilt of the first human being, to be cleansed by the baptism of the sacred font, who doubts that sins subsequently committed by parents, in which their children do not share, do not pertain to the children? Even if it could happen that fathers ate sour grapes and the children’s teeth were set on edge, nevertheless not among us, not in Israel. For the Lord says: “As I live, this proverb shall no longer be used in Israel” (Ezek. XVIII, 3). Whoever sets this judgment aside and condemns a son for the fault of his father or of any parent will be guilty and will not be counted among the people of Israel.

Perhaps someone says: “Whatever I do to such a person belongs to the one who handed him over to me.” Certainly, it truly does belong to him; but for that reason you will not be excused. You cannot cancel your own sin by his sin. If he handed the person over wickedly and you accepted him wickedly, iniquity will hold both of you. He places a Christian under your sword; but because you are a Christian, you are not thereby permitted to strike him. What did the person do to deserve being struck? What evil did he commit? Indeed, if he offered himself for the sake of charity in order to free another, he must be honored, not killed.

Blessed Peter the apostle says:

> Above all, maintain continual mutual charity among yourselves, because charity covers a multitude of sins (I Peter IV, 8).

And the Lord says in the Gospel:

> No one has greater charity than this: that someone should lay down his life for his friends (John XV, 17).

Moses, offering himself for the people of Israel, said to the Lord:

> Either forgive them this offense, Lord, or erase me from your book that you have written (Exod. XXXII, 31).

The Lord replied:

> Whoever has sinned against me, I will erase him from my book (ibid., 33).

It is as though he were saying: “You ask well, because you ask piously; but I will not act in this way. I will render a just judgment.”

But if someone offers himself in such a way for another’s benefit that the other thereby gains profit or glory, I do not approve this at all. In such a case, if it occurs, the homicide will truly be tripled. The guilt will not be absent from the one who committed the homicide, from the one who handed over the person under such an agreement, or from the person who allowed this to be done to him, if he has already reached an age capable of understanding.

For what else can be said about little children except that the innocent perish and remain guiltless?

Hear what happened to the Lord himself. The Jews handed him, bound, over to Pilate so that he might be crucified, saying: “Crucify him. We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die” (John XIX, 7). And again: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII, 23). Although Pilate himself said, “I am innocent of the blood of this man” (ibid., 24), and although he washed his hands, nevertheless, because he wickedly perpetrated the homicide, he could in no way be excused from the crime. For the shedding of the Lord’s blood stained them and condemned him forever.

The same must be thought concerning all innocent people handed over for punishment. Some, out of distress, place another in their stead so that they may free themselves from someone; others do so for advantage, appearing to wish to become rich through such flattery. Still others, trusting too much in themselves, promise things that are not within their power and, on the basis of such a promise, give hostages, although they are scarcely permitted to fulfill what they have promised.

Who would dare presume upon himself, or who could be secure concerning himself? Who could ever be more confident of someone’s fidelity than blessed Peter, who said to the Lord: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matt. XXVI, 35)? Yet, when the Lord foretold it, Peter denied him three times before the cock crowed.

Christ, as God, knew Peter’s weakness; Peter, however, considered the ardor of his own faith. What the Lord foretold, Peter denied out of love. Here we are morally instructed that, to the extent that we trust in the ardor of faith, we must fear the weakness of the flesh, since willing is ours, but accomplishing is God’s.

Nor, as blessed Augustine says (Treatise 66 on John), do we take pleasure in accusing the first of the apostles when we say these things. Rather, by looking upon him, we ought to be admonished so that no human being may place confidence in human strength. For what else did our Teacher and Savior intend except to demonstrate, in the example of the first of the apostles, that no one ought to presume upon himself?

Thus what Peter offered occurred in his soul. He offered bodily death, but incurred death of the soul; for just as confessing Christ is life, so denying him is death. We also know what blessed Thomas said: “Let us also go and die with him”; and likewise all the others said the same (John XI, 16). Yet all of them abandoned him and fled (Matt. XXVII, 59).

It is certain that at that time the apostles loved the Lord more than all of you love your relatives. Therefore, those who were not held back by love for him then would certainly not stand as hostages for anyone.

We have also heard and seen many people invalidate their pledge after hostages had been given, while some have preserved their fidelity until death even without giving hostages. Nevertheless, if such an obligation is to be sought, it should be demanded only from fools and perverse people who do not care about God. A prudent and Catholic man cannot preserve for the sake of any hostages what he does not keep out of fear of Almighty God and concern for the danger to his soul.

Therefore all Christians must beware of this, but I judge that bishops must presume upon it in no way. For just as apostates are called those who, after receiving Christ’s baptism, return to pagan rites and the worship of idols, so priests too are called apostates when, abandoning ecclesiastical discipline, they turn to military action. How could those who ought to offer themselves for others’ sake place others in danger for their own sake?

We read of blessed Paulinus, bishop, that when he had handed himself over to captivity, indeed even to slavery, for the sake of one widow’s son alone, he freed many captives by this act. For this deed he was praised both by blessed Gregory and by many other most holy Fathers.

There is nevertheless one thing I know beyond doubt, which will be said everywhere: if that bond of fidelity which once prevailed between our princes and our predecessors is not believed to be preserved among us, then either the princes are worse or we are more wicked. Either they are considered so hateful because of their savagery that they can no longer return to popular affection, or we are suspected of being so treacherous that no strength of fidelity remains in us—or both. Whichever side is proved to have deserved this, it ought to stand firm rather than allow itself to be prolonged for long in such disgrace, which God forbid.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us pray to Almighty God that he preserve our most glorious kings everywhere, deem it worthy to protect us who have been entrusted to them, and be gracious to us in all our adversities. May he grant them confidence in our fidelity and give us constancy in their service. May he make them peaceful toward us and make us devoted to them. If, through weakness, either they have committed some injustice against us or we against them, may his clemency erase it in such a way that no vengeance may thereafter be prepared on account of it.

Let us forgive debts so that we may be forgiven; let us not avenge everything, lest everything be avenged. Let the greatest offenses not be avenged for the smallest, but let moderation be preserved even in great matters. Let no one presume to desire what is owed to another, since quarrels usually grow from this. Let what belongs to each person be sufficient for each, and let no one take pleasure in invading what is not his. For whoever unjustly rejoices in acquiring something commonly comes to lose even what he holds justly. Although he may be able to corrupt the voices of judges, he will not be able to escape divine judgment.

May the Lord give us peace from outsiders and confer his charity among us. May there be one heart among all, so that we may love God and our neighbor. May we always praise the Lord worthily and bless his name forever. Amen.

[Col. 0125]

## ATTO, BISHOP OF VERCELLI, EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLES OF SAINT PAUL

This book contains the dictated sayings of the blessed [Atto] and treatises, composed together in eloquent language.

## EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

### Argument

[Col. 0125A]

First, it must be examined why the Epistle to the Romans is placed at the beginning, although the Apostle did not write it first, but after certain others. For they say that he first wrote to the Hebrews. Some resolve this question in the following manner: Rome was almost the capital of the whole empire, since at that time the Romans ruled almost all nations; and therefore it was fitting that, out of respect for them, the Epistle written to them should be placed first. Others, as Origen asserts, decided, when considering the faith and merits of the various nations that believed, and to which the Apostle addressed epistles, to arrange those epistles according to the faith and merits of those nations.

But the Romans were lesser in faith and merit. [Col. 0125B] For some of them were so unformed that they believed they had been saved not by the grace of God but by their own merits; and therefore they placed the Epistle written to them first. Then, ascending gradually according to the faith and merits of the Gentiles, as has been said, they arranged the Epistles.

This is why they placed the Epistle written to the Hebrews last, since they were greater in faith, merit, and knowledge; hence they are also preferred by the Apostle with every commendation. But since, when the Epistle is read, it is customarily pronounced, “The Epistle of the blessed apostle Paul,” the pronunciation itself must also be examined carefully and attentively. *Epistle* in Greek is said in Latin to mean “that which is sent over.” For *epi* in Greek means “over,” while *stola* means “sent”: [Col. 0125C] thus *epistle* is formed in the same way as *epitaph* and *epithalamium*. An *epitaph* is a poem written over the tombs of the dead; an *epithalamium* is what is sung over a wedding, at the bridal chamber. King Solomon of Israel first sang it in praise of the bridegroom and bride, that is, Christ and the Church. [Col. 0126A]

But it must be asked why the writings both of this apostle and of the other apostles are called *epistles* by a particular name. The name is indeed appropriate, since they were added and sent over the Law and the Prophets, and also over his grace, to cut away the vices that had newly arisen from transgressing the Gospel. For with what purpose were the prophets sent after the Law had been received? Clearly, so that by their prophecies the vices arising from transgression of the Law might be cut away. In the same way, after the grace of the Gospel had been received, the epistles were sent so that by their judgments and commands the vices born of transgression of the Law might be cleansed.

It should also be noted that the Apostle fittingly sent epistles to only ten Churches. For he sent four to disciples: just as the children of Israel, liberated from Egyptian slavery, crossed the Red Sea and, having been received into the desert, received the ten words of the Law by which they were instructed for salvation, so true Israelites—that is, the faithful—liberated from Egypt, that is, from the slavery of demons, and crossing the sea of baptism, which is therefore called Red because it has been reddened with the Lord’s blood, and received into the desert of the present Church, might be instructed by the judgments of ten Epistles for eternal life and perpetual salvation. [Col. 0126B]

He also wrote fourteen appropriately. For just as the Decalogue is signified by the number ten, so the teaching of the Gospel is signified by the number four. The Apostle therefore wrote fourteen Epistles, so that by this number he might demonstrate the concord of Law and grace, and also that he was the fulfiller, teacher, [Col. 0126C] and interpreter of that same Law and grace.

“Blessed” is said as if meaning “well-fitted” or “well-enriched”; and truly blessed is the one who is without every evil and abounds in every good. The Apostle, therefore, was truly blessed, because although he was afflicted by temporal adversities, he was nevertheless filled with spiritual [Col. 0127A] goods.

[Note: [Col. 0127D] In the margin of the autograph there it reads “chapter I.”]

*Paul*, in the Hebrew language, is said in Latin to mean “admirable” or “elect.” And he was aptly called “admirable” by a kind of presage, since, beginning at Jerusalem, he preached the Gospel wondrously through each of the surrounding regions as far as Illyricum; or because he performed many wonders—that is, signs and prodigies. He was called “elect” because he was chosen by the Lord for the ministry of preaching. Hence elsewhere he says: “As he chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4). For this reason also the Holy Spirit speaks in the Acts of the Apostles, saying: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have chosen them” (Acts 13:2).

But in Latin speech *Paul* is derived from “small”; for it is a word expressing humility. Hence blessed Augustine says: “Observe the usage of Latin speech; for *Paul* means ‘small.’ Thus we customarily say: ‘I will see you a little later,’ and ‘Wait here a little,’ that is, ‘I will see you after a short time, and wait here for a short while.’” He was therefore aptly called “small,” since he possessed great humility. Hence elsewhere he himself says: “For I am the least of the apostles, and am not worthy to be called an apostle” (1 Corinthians 15:9).

*Apostle* in Greek is said in Latin to mean “one sent.” He was aptly called “one sent,” because he did not come at the impulse of his own flesh, as the false apostles did, nor was he sent by the devil or by a human being, but by God, so that he might preach him to the Gentiles. Hence the Lord says to him in the Acts of the Apostles: “Behold, I shall send you to nations far away.”

[Note: [Col. 0127D] Acts 22:21: “For I shall send you to nations far away.” Thus the Vulgate.]

This name, when used by itself, is always understood positively.

It is clear that the Romans were Italians, since Rome is situated in a certain part of Italy. Their empire, as blessed Augustine says, was at its beginning all the shorter and narrower, and afterward all the greater and broader. For they grew so greatly that they subjected almost the entire world to themselves, partly by killing with swords and partly by reducing peoples to tribute. Hence the Romans were also aptly called Romans, which is interpreted as “exalted” or “thunderers,” because just as thunder terrifies people, so the fear of them had invaded the whole world. [Col. 0127C]

Moreover, it must be understood that the Apostle was not the first to announce the Gospel to the Romans or to lay the foundation of their faith. Some say that Peter did so; others, Barnabas or one of the seventy disciples. It could indeed have happened that, while Barnabas or one of the Lord’s disciples was preaching, they accepted the faith of Christ and were confirmed in that same faith by Peter, but were strengthened still more by Paul. However the word of the Gospel reached them, they accepted it; but afterward they were corrupted by false apostles and induced to understand the Law and the Prophets in a carnal manner. For very many of the Jews who had believed maintained to the Gentiles who likewise believed that it was of no benefit to accept the faith of Christ and pass over to the grace of the Gospel without carnal circumcision. Hence they also persistently disparaged the Apostle because he had accepted the Gentiles into the faith of Christ without observance of the carnal Law.

[Col. 0128A] And because both peoples—Jews and Gentiles—inhabited the aforesaid city, greatly divided among themselves and fighting almost as if in battle, they habitually hurled these accusations at one another by taunting and disputing. The Jews said:

“We are the chosen race, the people acquired by God, the holy nation descended from the stock of the patriarchs. The Lord liberated us from Egyptian slavery by many signs and wonders. We crossed the sea on dry feet while the most violent waves overwhelmed our enemies. He gave us the Law in the desert and rained manna from heaven; he caused water to flow from the rock. He promised us a land flowing with milk and honey and, as he had promised, brought us into it. From us came the prophets; from us he promised that he himself would come in the flesh; and when he came, he took flesh from us, lived among us, and performed many signs and wonders. In the Gospel he called us sons, but called you rather dogs. Therefore you are not worthy of our fellowship, because you have always worshiped empty and mute idols.”

To this the Gentiles replied:

“We believe that what you say is true. Nevertheless, the greater the benefits of God toward you that you recount, the worse you show yourselves to be. For with the very feet with which you crossed the sea on dry ground, you played by dancing before idols; with the very mouth with which you ate manna, you praised golden gods, saying, ‘These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.’ And, to pass over the rest, when he appeared through the mystery of the incarnation, you not only refused to receive him but, what is worse, condemned him to the most shameful death. We, however, seeing none of his signs, but hearing only the report of his name, immediately believed. Therefore you are not worthy of our fellowship, nor can you be compared with us.”

When the Apostle heard of this dissension among them, he acted as an ambassador for the Lord, Jesus Christ, the cornerstone—as he himself says: “We are ambassadors for Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:20; Ephesians 6:20). He placed himself between them and, in order to recall them to peaceful concord and unity of faith, sent them this Epistle. In it he shows that they are all sinners and need the grace of God. Hence a little farther on he says: “There is no distinction between Jew and Greek” (Romans 10:12). “All have sinned and lack the grace of God.”

[Note: [Col. 0128D] Romans 3:22–23: “And lack the glory of God,” according to the Vulgate.]

He also shows that they were saved not by their own merits but by the grace of God, and that therefore there ought to be no dissension. Hence near the end of this Epistle he exhorts them in the cities, saying: “Therefore receive one another, just as Christ also received you, to the honor of God” (Romans 15:7).

[BEGINNING OF THE TEXT.]

## (CHAPTER I)

Paul, servant of Jesus Christ, called apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God.

At the beginning of this Epistle a question arises: why was the one who was previously called Saul called Paul after his conversion? In the Old Testament we read that the names of certain persons were changed: Abram was afterward called Abraham, Sarai Sarah, and Jacob also Israel. This is found in the New Testament as well, for the one who was previously Simon was afterward called Peter; and the sons of Zebedee, John and James, were called Boanerges, [Col. 0129A] that is, “sons of thunder” (Mark 3:17).

But these changes were made by divine command, whereas nothing of this kind is read concerning Paul. Hence some say that he acquired this name from victory, because he defeated Paul, the proconsul of Cyprus—because he overcame him by preaching and subjected him to the yoke of faith (Acts 13:12)—after the manner of kings who, having conquered the Parthians, are called Parthian, and, having conquered the Goths, Gothic. This interpretation should not be rejected altogether. Nevertheless, since such names are found not in divine writings but in human literature, the solution to this question must be examined more deeply and appropriately.

Therefore it should be understood that it was customary in the Old Testament for one and the same person to be called by two or three names. Solomon, for example, was called Jedidiah and Ecclesiastes. Uzziah is the same person as Azariah; Jehoiakim is the same as Jeconiah.

[Note: [Col. 0129D] In the autograph it reads *idiola*, perhaps an excessively abbreviated form of *Jedidiah*, that is, “beloved by God,” as Solomon was called through the prophet Nathan. 2 Kings 12:25.]

[Col. 0129B] The New Testament also preserves this custom. Matthew is in fact the same person as Levi; Judas is the same as Thaddaeus, or, as certain copies have it, Lebbaeus. Thus it could have happened that the Apostle was known by two names, Saul and Paul. As long as he remained an administrator of his own people, he was called Saul; but after he began to minister the grace of the Gospel to the Gentiles, he was called Paul. That this is so is made clear by the book of the Acts of the Apostles, where we read: “Paul, who is also Saul” (Acts 13:9).

Saul, as some wish, was named after King Saul, from whose stock he descended.

Again, it must be asked why he called himself a servant, when the Lord says in the Gospel to those who love him: “I shall no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15:15). So that this may not seem contradictory, it should be understood that there is a servitude of slavish fear and one of chaste fear. For a son serves in one way and a slave in another: the latter through fear, the former through love. The Lord himself, who calls those who love him friends, elsewhere says to them: “When you have completed everything that has been commanded you, say: ‘We are useless servants’” (Luke 17:10).

The Lord therefore called his disciples servants, not with slavish fear but with chaste fear, of which the Prophet says: “The fear of the Lord is holy” (Psalm 18:10). Thus the Apostle also called himself a servant, not through slavish fear but through chaste fear, so that he might leave us an example of humility. For in this way the saints are called servants, as are the angels, who always serve the Lord—not through fear but through love.

Whose servant he was, he clearly shows by adding: “of Christ Jesus,” as if he were saying: “Although a servant, yet not of sin, not of iniquity, but of Christ Jesus.”

*Christ* in Greek, *Messiah* in Hebrew, is said in Latin to mean “anointed.” It is a general name applicable to all who are anointed, for all who were anointed with oil in the Old Testament were called “Christs.” But this one was specially anointed by God the Father above his companions (Psalm 44:8; Hebrews 1:9), with the fullness of the Holy Spirit.

*Jesus* in Hebrew, *Sotir* in Greek, is said in Latin to mean “Savior.” Although many in that region were then called by this name, it is clear that in this man the name was principal and essential. Thus *Christ* is the name of royal dignity, while *Jesus* is the name of the Savior. Explaining the etymology of this name in the Gospel, the angel says: “For he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21).

Again, it must be asked why the Apostle called himself “called,” when the Lord says in the Gospel: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 20:16). It must be understood that the Lord intended that saying to refer to the general calling by which all are called, whereas the Apostle calls divine calling predestination, according to which only the elect are called. Hence elsewhere he says: “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose as saints” (Romans 8:28); and again: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined; and those whom he predestined, he also called” (ibid., 29).

[Note: [Col. 0130D] In the autograph it reads *eite*.]

It must also be examined why he called himself “set apart,” since he knew that he was one of those who were preserved, for whom the Son pleads with the Father, saying: “Holy Father, preserve them in your name, whom you have given me” (John 17:11); and concerning whose unity he prays: “Father, I will that they be one, just as we are one.” This is especially puzzling since “set apart” means separated from the flock. Was he separated from the flock of the holy Church? Certainly not.

But he calls himself “set apart” because he was chosen from among many by the Lord to be directed to the ministry of preaching. Hence we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul” (Acts 13:2). And the Lord says to Ananias: “Go, for this man is a chosen vessel for me, to carry my name before the Gentiles” (Acts 9:15).

For what purpose he was set apart is disclosed when he adds: “for the Gospel of God.” He says “for the Gospel of God,” that is, for preaching the Gospel; “of God” in order to distinguish it from his own. Hence he says to the Corinthians: “Through my Gospel I begot you” (1 Corinthians 4:15).

And to show what that Gospel was, he added: “which he had promised beforehand through his prophets.” By these words the Apostle demonstrates the concord of the New and Old Testaments. He plainly shows that what the prophets foresaw and foretold, the apostles preached and witnessed. For the Gospel would not have been presented through the apostles unless it had first been promised through the prophets. Consequently, the prophets are in no way opposed to the Gospel, but agree with it.

By this statement the error of the Manichaeans is also destroyed, since they do not accept the prophets, as well as the error of those who assert that the God of the New Testament is different from the God of the Old Testament.

He says “his” prophets in order to distinguish them from false prophets. For there were many, not only among the Jewish people but also among the Gentiles, who prophesied falsely about him, such as the Sibyl and Virgil, who says:

> Now a new generation is sent down from high heaven.

How they prophesied falsely about him, blessed Augustine clearly demonstrates in his book *The City of God*. And lest the poets of the Gentiles be thought to be prophets [Col. 0131A] because they prophesied certain things about God, he immediately added: “in the Holy Scriptures.”

[Note: [Col. 0130D] In the autograph it reads *et noepere*.]

He calls those writings “Holy Scriptures” that were produced by holy men under the influence, overflow, and dictation of the Holy Spirit. Again, lest the fabrications of the Gentiles be thought to be Holy Scripture, he added: “concerning his Son.”

And since all the faithful are sons of God, to indicate which Son he meant, he added: “who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh.” He says that he was made according to the flesh from the seed of David because the blessed virgin Mary descended from the line of David, and in her virginal womb the Son of God assumed the reality of human substance.

It should be understood that David was king of that people from whom the Lord took flesh; [Col. 0131D] therefore it was fitting that prophets should be born from his line to proclaim that he would come. For this reason the Apostle mentioned David.

[Note: [Col. 0131D] The words “from … took flesh” are written in the upper margin of the autograph.]

It should also be noted that the Apostle, an expert instructed both in the divinity and humanity of the Savior [Note: [Col. 0131D] In the autograph: “an expert instructed”], says that he was made according to the flesh from the seed of David in order to make room for his divinity. For it was not the divinity that was made, but the humanity. The Word of God, that is, the only-begotten Son, was not made, but is the maker of all things. For insofar as the Lord Jesus Christ is God, all things were made through him. Hence John says: “All things were made through him” (John 1:3), and so forth.

For unless he were God, all things could by no means have been made through him; rather, he himself would be counted among the things that were made. He therefore who existed and was made—what was he, and what was he made? He was the Word; he was made flesh. He was the Son of God; he was made the Son of Man.

[Col. 0131C] It follows: “who was predestined to be the Son of God in power according to the spirit of sanctification.”

It should be noted that the one whom he earlier said was made from the seed of David according to the flesh, he now says was predestined to be the Son of God in power, in order to show that the one who was to be the son of David according to the flesh was the same, and not another, who was the Son of God in power.

He was predestined according to the spirit of sanctification. He says “according to the spirit of sanctification” because he was conceived and born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin. This is that singular, indescribable [Note: [Col. 0131D] In the autograph, instead of *indescribable*, it reads *inenarra*], and ineffably accomplished assumption by which the Son of God joined a true human being to himself in the unity of person, so that he was the same God and man—God because of the God who assumed, and man because of the man who was assumed—so that God would be not a Quaternity but a Trinity. [Col. 0131D]

But why does the Apostle call him “predestined,” when all the faithful have been predestined? If we are predestined and he is predestined, then he is not the proper Son but an adopted son. Far be it from us to think so.

Nevertheless, it must be understood that by the same grace by which each person becomes a Christian from the beginning of his faith, he too became Christ from the beginning of his incarnation; and by the same Spirit by which each person is reborn, he was born of the Virgin. By the same Spirit through whom forgiveness of sins comes to this person, it came about that he himself had absolutely no sin.

[Col. 0132A] The Lord both foreknew and predestined that he would do all these things. But what merit of any kind preceded him, so that he might attain such excellence? Certainly no preceding merits: rather, by the sole grace of God, a man was assumed into the unity of the person of the Word of God. Hence he is rightly said to have been predestined.

He predestined him, therefore, and he predestined us also, because neither in him, so that he might be our head, nor in us, so that we might be his members, did any merits precede; only the works of God did so.

And note that the Holy Spirit is aptly called the spirit of sanctification, because all sanctification consists in him, proceeds from him, and he bestows sanctification upon all.

It follows: “from the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord.”

Because the Apostle had said above that the Lord Jesus was predestined in power according to the spirit of sanctification, in order to show that he was also predestined from the resurrection of the dead, he added: “from the resurrection of the dead,” and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0132D] The words “predestined … from the dead” are written in the same script at the bottom of the margin.]

When he says “of the dead,” we should not understand those whom the Lord will condemn at the judgment, but those whom he will serve after passing through the judgment. By this statement, therefore, he wished to show that the Lord Jesus preceded the resurrection of all the dead. Hence he is called “the firstborn of the dead” (Revelation 1:5), and afterward “of the elect alone” (Romans 8:29), because he alone rose from the dead by his own power.

The Apostle therefore aptly did not say “Jesus Christ” but “of Jesus Christ,” as though he were saying, “of his own.” For if he were asked from whose resurrection he said that he had been predestined, he would certainly answer, “from the resurrection of his own.” This is what he says by “of Jesus Christ.”

There can also be another arrangement of the words, so that “from the resurrection of the dead” does not refer to “the Son of God in power,” but to what he previously said, “who was predestined.” The intervening words would then be “the Son of God in power according to the spirit of sanctification.” If these are removed, the order of the words would be:

“Who was predestined from the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord, to be the Son of God in power.”

The meaning would be this: He was predestined as the son of David in the weakness of the flesh; predestined as the Son of God in power. Thus the one who assumed flesh is referred to David, because of which he also died, whereas his resurrection is referred to the Son of God, because he rose by the power of his divinity.

Then, to show that the Apostle did not come on his own but was sent by Christ, he added: “Through whom we have received grace and apostleship.”

Here it should be noted that he did not say merely “grace,” lest he seem ungrateful for the grace he had received by failing to proclaim that same grace. Therefore he adds: “and apostleship.” For he received grace generally together with all, whereas he obtained apostleship in a special way, as though he alone had merited it.

Grace is that by which sins are released. And to make clear why he had received these things, he immediately added: “for obedience to the faith,” that is, so that all might obey the faith.

But for whose sake? “For his name,” he says, as though he were saying: “For this reason I received grace and apostleship, so that all might obey the faith and believe in him; and so that all who are predestined and to be saved might be marked with the sign of his name.”

And lest this grace seem to have been granted only to the Jews, he says: “among all the nations.” Again, lest the Romans appear to be excluded, he added [Note: [Col. 0133D] In the autograph, after the word *added*, which is written in abbreviated form, there is an added *he said*, perhaps erroneously inserted by the copyist]:

“among whom you also are called by Jesus Christ.”

This is plainly to say: “You too belong to the Savior of all nations, and you have been called by him, although you are found not among the number of the Jews but among that of the Gentiles.”

Since he had said who was writing—“Paul, servant of Christ Jesus,” and so forth—in order to show to whom he was writing, he added: “To all who are in Rome, beloved of God, called saints,” and the rest.

[Note: [Col. 0133D] Compare what follows with the interpretation given below of the words “those who are called saints according to his purpose,” and of what follows through chapter VIII. From this it will be possible to discover what the opinion of teachers and of the Church was in those times concerning matters that today provoke so much controversy.]

By these words he commends divine mercy and cancels human merit. For it should be noted that he does not say “those who love God,” but “beloved of God.” They were not beloved because they loved; rather, because they were beloved, they therefore loved. Hence John says: “Let us love God, because he first loved us” (1 John 4:10).

But what does he mean by “called saints”? Were they called saints? Certainly not; they were called, and were saints. This expression resembles that of Zechariah, who says: “He visited and made redemption for his people” (Luke 1:48)—not for a people that had been his, but one whom, by visiting, he had made his own.

John also says: “that he might gather into one the children of God who were scattered” (John 11:52). For they were not still children of God while scattered; rather, by gathering them into one, he made them children of God.

And Solomon says: “Who will find a strong woman?” (Proverbs 31:10). For this woman—that is, the holy Church—was not found strong by the Lord; rather, by finding her he made her strong.

Finally, after showing to whom he was writing, nothing remained except to set down the greeting. In place of this he put peace and grace, adding: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

What he says, “from God,” corresponds to grace and peace. He appropriately says that grace is from God, since he knew that there is also grace from human beings: judges, considering persons, or constrained by greed, enticed by it, or terrified by fear, commonly grant favors to people.

Similarly, he wishes peace from God, because he knew that there is also a peace from human beings, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Not the kind of peace that the world gives do I give you” (John 4:10).

And it should be noted that, in a principal and excellent order, he placed grace before peace. For grace is that by which sins are released, [Note: [Col. 0134D] In the autograph, instead of *by which*, it reads *because*. I regard this as a copyist’s error, and the author’s meaning is better represented by the reading translated here.] whereas peace is that by which we are reconciled to God.

Our sins separated us from God [Note: [Col. 0134D] The words “our sins … from God” are written in the lower margin.] and we had turned away from him.
