Since, therefore, through grace the forgiveness of sins takes place and we are reconciled to God, that reconciliation is called peace. Thus grace is rightly preferred to peace.

But someone may ask: Why did the Apostle mention only the Father and the Son, and not the Holy Spirit? The answer is that grace and peace are gifts of God; and the Holy Spirit is the gift of God, as the Lord makes clear when he says to the Samaritan woman: “If you knew the gift of God” (John 4:10), and so forth. If, therefore, grace and peace are gifts of God, it is unquestionably clear that the Apostle has mentioned the whole Trinity.

Thus, after completing the greeting, the Apostle fittingly began the opening of his account with thanksgiving, saying: “First, I give thanks to my God,” and so forth.

Thanksgivings are praises that we offer to God. Therefore, in the fact that the Apostle gives thanks to God for the faith of the Romans, we are admonished to strive to give thanks to God for all our circumstances, both prosperous and adverse, and for those of others, but only for their prosperity.

But why does the Apostle say not simply “God,” but, with an addition, “my God”? Clearly, to show that God is God by nature of all, but by will and merit of only a few, that is, of the elect alone.

This, therefore, is the voice of those alone of whom the Lord says: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” For in these three all the elect are included.

Through whom he gives thanks, he shows by saying: “Through Jesus Christ.” For he was offering the sacrifice of his praise to God; and therefore, wishing to offer it through the hand of the High Priest so that it might be acceptable, he said: “Through Jesus Christ.”

Hence we are admonished that whenever we wish to offer to God the sacrifice of our prayer or of any action, we should offer it through his hand.

[Note: [Col. 0134D] In the margin: “chapter II.”]

From this the custom of the Church has arisen, whereby priests add to each prayer: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

For whom he gives thanks, he makes clear: “For all of you.” Here it should be noted that he does not say “for the wise” or “for the rich,” lest he seem to be a respecter of persons, but generally “for you,” as if he were saying, “for those established in the unity of faith.”

Why he gives thanks is disclosed when he adds: “because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world.”

Faith is confession of the Trinity, the foundation of all piety and goodness, and religion. Faith concerns those things that are not seen. Hence the Apostle says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1).

Faith is so called because what is said or promised is made real.

When he says “throughout the whole world,” if we understand it simply, he intends the various regions of the world. And this could certainly have happened, since at that time the Romans ruled almost all nations, so that the reputation of their faith might have traveled throughout all the regions of the world.

We can also understand it as spoken by synecdoche, so that a part is understood from the whole.

It follows: “God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his Son,” and so forth.

Here it must be asked why the Apostle swore an oath, when the Lord commands in the Gospel: “Do not swear at all” (John 14:17). Did the Apostle act against the Lord’s command? Certainly not.

From the fact that the Lord commanded that one should not swear, while the Apostle swore, it may be understood that the Lord did not command that no one should use an oath in necessary matters, but that no one should desire an oath as though it were the highest good.

There are some things that are good in themselves and by themselves, and therefore ought to be desired, such as the virtues. There are others that are good neither in themselves nor by themselves, but are necessary for the sake of other things, such as food, drink, [Col. 0135B] and clothing. These are necessary for sustaining the present life, but they should not be desired as the highest good.

An oath is similar: it is good neither in itself nor by itself, but one may use it in necessary circumstances. For example, you wish to lead someone to faith, but he refuses to believe you unless you swear. If, therefore, you swear with the intention that the Apostle had, you do not sin.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Anything beyond this is from evil” (Matthew 5:37). Here it should be noted that he does not say “is evil,” but “is from evil,” as if he were saying: “The oath you swear proceeds from the evil of the one who compelled you to swear.”

The Lord therefore commanded that one should not swear so that no one might fall into perjury through constant swearing. For just as one who does not speak does not lie, so one who does not swear does not commit perjury.

But what does it mean that the Apostle asserts that he serves God in his spirit, when servitude is an activity of the body, whereas prayer belongs to the mind? It must nevertheless be understood that he wished to demonstrate something greater: the force of his devotion and affection. Someone may pray without devotion or affection, but no one can serve God in spirit without these.

Therefore, in order to show the devotion and affection of his mind, the Apostle added: “in the Gospel of his Son.” For no one can serve God without the Gospel.

Why he called God as his witness, he shows by adding: “that without ceasing I make mention of you always in my prayers,” and the rest.

What does he mean by saying that he always and without ceasing makes mention of the Romans in his prayers? Did he not eat or drink? So that this may not appear contradictory, it must be understood that by “without ceasing” he means without an interval of any day. For no day passed in which the Apostle did not pour out special prayers to God for the Romans.

By this statement he shows himself to be fulfilling the command that he taught elsewhere, saying: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17).

But why did he wish to inform the Romans that he always prayed for them? What necessity is there for us to tell our friends if we pray for them? The Apostle did this so that the Romans might love him more and obey his instructions. Those who love us listen to us more readily than those who hate us.

Nevertheless, the Apostle placed the intention and goal of his purpose not in himself but in the Lord, so that through his own love he might lead them to the love of God.

It follows: “Praying that, if somehow at last I may have a prosperous journey, by the will of God, to come to you.” As the Apostle was setting out for the ministry of preaching, he hoped to obtain through prayers and supplications that he might have a prosperous journey to come to the Romans. But why did he add, “by the will of God”? Evidently because he knew that there can be prosperity without the will of God: for, behold, the wicked prosper in temporal goods.

[Note: “Prosperity without the will of God” should not here be understood to mean that some prosperity comes to human beings against God’s will. Our author could not have spoken in that way, since later in this epistle he asserts that temporal goods—food, joy, fair weather, and fruitful seasons—are given by God even to wicked people. Rather, temporal prosperity is not to be understood as that which God wills us to desire and for which he created us, but rather our eternal happiness and sanctification. For this is the will of God, your sanctification (I Thess. IV, 3). Since God wills us to desire this, temporal happiness is rightly said, by comparison with it, not to be according to the will of God.]

But this prosperity is not according to the will of God. It follows: “For I long to see you, that I may impart something to you,” and so forth. Why did he desire to see them? Was it from a frivolous desire, like people who visit their relatives for the sake of feasting? No. He himself gives the reason, saying: “That I may impart to you some spiritual grace”—that is, that I may give you instruction and the working of miracles.

[Note: Perhaps this should read: “that I may impart to you the working of miracles.”]

For what purpose he wished these things to be imparted is made clear when he adds: “To strengthen you.” By these words he shows that they still needed confirmation in the faith, although above he had commended them with praise—doing so, of course, with the intention that whatever needed correction in them might more easily be corrected. In this action we are warned that whenever we wish to correct anything blameworthy in persons of distinction, we should first commend whatever good there may be in them with praise.

It follows: “That is, that we may be mutually comforted among you.” The Apostle certainly desired to be comforted in the Romans, and the Romans in him—not on one side only, but through their common faith and the illumination of the Holy Spirit. Hence he immediately adds: “Through the faith that is mutually yours and mine.”

[Note: The Vulgate text there reads: “through the faith that is mutually yours and mine.”]

The Apostle would then be comforted in the Romans if he saw the work of his preaching firmly established among them; and they would be comforted in the Apostle if they understood that they were to be participants in the same apostleship and dignity.

[Note: In the autograph this is perhaps to be understood as “participants,” which seemed to me alien to the genuine reading.]

[Note: In the autograph, on the margin: chapter III.]

It follows: “But I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that I have often resolved to come to you and have been hindered until now.” It is as though he were saying: “I do not want you to be unaware that I had the intention and desire to come to you, but I have been hindered until now by the preaching among the other nations. When they have believed and my preaching has been confirmed among them, I shall come to you.”

To show that he would not be coming from a frivolous impulse, he added: “That I may have some fruit among you also, as among the other nations.” It is as though he were saying: “The fruit that I believe I shall receive from the other nations—which, through my preaching, I have called to faith in Christ from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, which is the head of Europe—I shall also have among you, by the generosity of divine mercy.”

It follows: “I am a debtor both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish.” He calls the Greeks wise—that is, those who devoted themselves to philosophical learning, or who lived according to laws—but the barbarians uneducated people (*idiotae*). To make clear whom he meant by Greeks and barbarians, he therefore added: “I am a debtor to the wise and to the foolish.” He was their debtor through the virtue of patience; and truly no patience is greater than enduring the attacks of fools.

“Thus, as far as I am concerned, I am ready to preach the gospel to you also who are in Rome.” It is as though he were saying: “Just as I am a debtor to the wise and the foolish, so I am a debtor to preach the gospel to you also who are in Rome; as far as I am concerned, I am ready.”

And since someone might say, “Whom do you wish to evangelize? Surely the crucified Christ? Why are you not ashamed to preach him crucified?” he himself answers: “For I am not ashamed of the gospel.” This was said, of course, to the confusion of the nations, who worshiped Jupiter, Saturn, and the other gods but were ashamed to acknowledge their shameful deeds. The Apostle might be understood as saying: “I am not ashamed to preach Christ crucified and risen from the dead, because, although there is disgrace in one aspect, there is in the other a mark of outstanding power.”

There were indeed some who were ashamed of his birth, passion, and death. Against them the Apostle says: “I am not ashamed of the gospel.” He shows why he was not ashamed: “For it is the power of God,” and so forth. He calls the power of God the power of divinity by which Christ rose from the dead. And truly there can be no greater power than to restore life to one who has died; and for God nothing is more worthy than to die for the restoration of his image.

For what purpose this power exists he demonstrates: “For salvation to everyone who believes.” He says “everyone,” so that no one might seem to be excluded. And lest anyone suppose that there is a distinction between Jews and Greeks, he says: “To the Jew first, and to the Greek.”

The Greeks made two divisions, between themselves and the barbarians; but the Apostle made three: Jew, Greek, and barbarian. For if the Greeks were preferred to the barbarians because they devoted themselves to philosophy and lived according to laws, then the Jews are rightly preferred to the Greeks, since they lived according to laws promulgated by God. Therefore the Apostle says: “To the Jew first.”

It follows: “For the righteousness of God is revealed in it, from faith to faith.” Righteousness is so called as the state of right. Righteousness, therefore, exists when each person is granted his proper right; hence someone is called righteous because he preserves what is right.

The righteousness of God is Christ, and it is revealed in him—that is, through him, namely, through the gospel. What he means by “from faith to faith” is like what he says elsewhere: “But we, beholding the glory of God with unveiled face, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (II Cor. III, 18). By “from glory” he means from the glory of the gospel to the glory of eternal reward.

Similarly here, it is from the faith of the law to the faith of the gospel; or from the faith of words and works to faith in eternal recompense; or from faith in human beings to faith in God.

To confirm his account by prophetic testimony, he added: “As it is written: ‘But the righteous lives by faith.’” By “faith” he does not mean that which is held merely in words, but that which is completed in works, because “faith without works is dead in itself” (James II, 17, 20, 26).

It follows: “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of human beings.” Above he had said that the righteousness of God is revealed to the righteous through the gospel. It followed that he should show that the wrath of God is revealed to the ungodly; and he added “from heaven,” hence: “It is revealed,” and so forth.

Here one must carefully observe why he said either “the wrath of God is revealed” or “from heaven.” He says “is revealed” because what had previously been hidden was made open through the gospel, or because what had been less well known was made manifest through the gospel.

Wrath is spoken of God not properly but figuratively, for no passion falls within the nature of divinity. Whenever wrath is attributed to God, therefore, it must be understood as vengeance. And he fittingly says that it is received from heaven, since we receive from heaven both benefits and scourges, and every kind of adversity.

Mystically, heaven signifies evangelical teaching or the faith of the Church. Thus he appropriately says that the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against the ungodly, because through the trumpet of evangelical preaching and the faith of the Church it is made manifest how greatly the worshipers of idols are to be condemned.

Alternatively: The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against the ungodly because, from the very beginning of the world, the invisible Creator could be recognized through visible creatures. For when God created such bright heavenly bodies, it could easily be understood from them that he alone is God and alone is to be worshiped.

Against what, then, is the wrath of God revealed? This is explained when he adds: “Against all ungodliness and unrighteousness.” Here it should be noted that he mentioned two things: ungodliness and unrighteousness. For although all ungodliness is unrighteousness, not all unrighteousness is ungodliness. He calls unbelief ungodliness; unrighteousness he calls iniquity and wickedness.

Against whose ungodliness and unrighteousness the wrath of God is revealed, he shows when he says: “Of those who hold back the truth of God in unrighteousness.”

[Note: In the autograph, the preposition in is absent before the word “unrighteousness.”]

It is unrighteous that the honor owed to the Creator should be given to a creature. They therefore hold back the truth—that is, the divinity of God—in unrighteousness who, having abandoned the Creator, serve the creature.

[Note: Here too the preposition in is absent, contrary to the Vulgate, and the text reads: “They hold back the divinity of God in unrighteousness.”]

[Note: In the autograph, on the margin: chapter IV.]

“For what is known of God is manifest in them.” Here one must supply “to be,” so that the sense is: “The essence and knowledge of God are manifest to them.”

Why it is manifest he shows: “For God has manifested it to them.” But he does not clearly explain how he manifested it. One must therefore supply: “by making the work through which he himself could be recognized as Creator.” Every creature proclaims that it is not the Creator, especially since no creature surpasses all things in every respect.

For example, heaven excels in greatness, the sun, moon, and stars in brightness, and the earth in fertility. Through this it is clearly shown that all things have a Creator who made, rules, and governs them, and who precedes them all.

It follows: “For his invisible things are clearly seen, being understood through the things that have been made, from the creation of the world.”

His eternal power and divinity are likewise clearly seen, being understood by the creation of the world through the things that have been made. By “the creation of the world” is meant from the very beginning of the world: through visible creatures, the invisible Creator could be recognized.

For when the Lord had created such beautiful elements that human beings worshiped them as gods, it could easily be understood that the one who had made them was incomparably more beautiful. He therefore calls “power” the might of divinity that rules all things; “divinity,” however, he calls the very majesty of God, which fills the universe.

These things—that is, power and divinity—could be recognized through visible creatures. But because they were not recognized, they are therefore without excuse. Hence he adds: “So that they are without excuse.”

Why they are without excuse he makes clear: “Because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks,” and so forth.

They could recognize the power of invisible being through visible creatures, as has been said. For although the name of God was still unknown, his power was nevertheless manifest. Thus they are reproved not for ignorance,

[Note: The preposition de should probably be placed before “ignorance,” although that particle is absent in the autograph.]

but for their failure to glorify him, when it is said: “They did not glorify him as God”—that is, they did not offer him the honor due to him.

Since God had granted them not only knowledge of highly useful disciplines but also the ability to reflect upon the highest good, they attributed the good they possessed not to God but to themselves. They did not believe that they had received it from God’s gratuitous goodness, but from their own merits; and therefore “they became futile.” Hence he immediately adds: “But they became futile in their thoughts,” and so forth.

[Note: In the autograph, the preposition in incorrectly precedes the word “likeness”; it seemed to me that it should be deleted.]

Nothing is a greater becoming-futile than to attribute to oneself the good received from God. “And their foolish heart was darkened.” Behold, the Apostle says that their heart was darkened, but he does not show from what it was darkened. It must therefore be understood that it was darkened by the cloud of human praise. For they sought human praise for the good things they had received, and therefore their foolish heart came to be what it was.

A heart is rightly called foolish when it attributes the good it has received to itself and seeks its own glory rather than God’s.

It follows: “For, claiming to be wise, they became fools,” and so forth. They boasted that they were wise because of their knowledge of various arts, and therefore they became fools. How they became fools is made clear when he adds: “And they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible human beings, and of birds, and four-footed animals, and serpents.”

By these words the Apostle marks out the philosophers and rebukes the poets of the nations—Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Zeno, Virgil, Cato, Ovid Naso, and the others—who bestowed the honor of divinity upon dead human beings, thinking that these could benefit them more after death than while they were still alive. For while they lived, they did not offer them any honor of divinity.

Observe that he does not say “in the likeness of a human being,” but “in the likeness of the image of human beings.” They could not form the appearance of a human body itself, but they made a likeness of an image and bestowed divine honor upon it.

That the nations worshiped the likeness of a human image instead of God is shown by Daniel, who says that the Babylonians worshiped the likeness of Bel (Dan. XIV, 2). Bel was the father of Ninus, king of the Assyrians.

Again, that they worshiped serpents is demonstrated by the same Daniel, who says that the Babylonians mentioned above worshiped a dragon, which he himself killed.

They also worshiped images of four-footed animals, as the Egyptians worshiped Apis. Apis was a king of the Argives who was carried by ship from Greece to Egypt; there he died and was buried. And because they began to sacrifice to him before his temple had been built, he was called Serapis: for *seros* in Greek means “tomb.” They used to sacrifice a bull to him; hence the bull itself was called Apis, and the Egyptians worshiped it as a god.

This is why the children of Israel made the likeness of a calf in the desert.

They also worshiped birds, as the Egyptians worshiped the raven, which in Latin is called *nycticorax*, as though “the raven of the night,” and the Romans worshiped the goose.

They worshiped not only these but many other things. Hence Solomon says: “The wicked person fashions a dead thing with sinful hands” (Wis. XV, 17); and the Psalmist: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold” (Ps. CXIII, 1).

Moreover, one should know that even now human beings worship idols by loving the creature more than the Creator. For example, gluttons love their belly more than God; therefore the belly of a glutton is his god. Hence the Apostle says: “Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame.”

[Note: Philippians III, 19. In the autograph it reads “in confusion,” contrary to the Vulgate.]

If, then, the belly is the god of the glutton, and gold the god of the miser, the god of the impure and adulterer is the prostitute.

It follows: “Therefore God gave them over to the desires of their heart,” and so forth.

[Note: The autograph reads *eos* (“them”), whereas the Vulgate reads *illos* (“them”).]

What he says by “gave over” must be understood as “permitted to be given over,” just as God is said to have hardened Pharaoh’s heart because he did not soften what was hard.

But in this statement one must observe the greatness of divine compassion. God did not give them over to contrary things, but to things pleasant and delightful. This is what he means by “to the desires of their heart.”

Why he permitted them to be given over he shows: “So that they might dishonor their bodies among themselves.”

[Note: In the Vulgate, the word “bodies” is placed after “might dishonor.”]

Dishonors are reproaches. They therefore dishonor their bodies who heap sins upon sins and vices upon vices. For every sin that a person first commits, unless it is quickly corrected through repentance, becomes the cause of sin, since another sin arises from it. If that one is not corrected in turn, it becomes both the punishment of sin and the cause of sin—the punishment of the preceding sin and the cause of the following one.

It follows: “They exchanged the truth of God for a lie.” He calls the power of divinity “truth.” One therefore exchanges the truth of God for a lie when one gives the honor owed to the Creator to a creature.

And this is what follows: “They worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator.” In these words the Apostle does not condemn the creature. For whoever condemns the creature wrongs the Creator, because he uses his good things badly. Nevertheless, God himself knows how to dispose and order justly the army of those whom he sees using his goods unjustly.

It follows: “Who is God,”

[Note: In the autograph it reads “who is God,” but in the Vulgate the word “God” is not named; it reads: “who is blessed.”]

“blessed forever. Amen.”

He uses the same words elsewhere of the Son that he now uses of the Father, saying: “Whose fathers are theirs, and from whom is Christ, who is blessed forever and ever” (Rom. IX, 5). Accordingly, the Father and the Son are one God.

[Note: In the autograph, on the margin: chapter V.]

It follows: “Therefore God gave them over to dishonorable passions.”

[Note: The Vulgate reads *illos* (“them”) instead of the autograph’s *eos* (“them”).]

Above he had said: “They exchanged the truth of God for a lie.” By these words he showed that they had been abandoned because they had abandoned the Lord; therefore he says: “Therefore,” and so forth.

“Gave over” must be understood as has already been explained. He calls “dishonorable passions” the sins that are described below. A thing is called dishonorable because it is without a name, just as an infamous person is without fame and an ignoble person without nobility. Whoever is caught in sexual misconduct, fornication, or adultery is rightly called ignoble and dishonorable, because he lacks nobility.

Moreover, every sin is called dishonor because it lacks the name of nature: it was not created by God but devised by the devil.

How they were given over to dishonorable passions is made clear when he adds: “For their women exchanged the natural use for that which is against nature.”

Here the Apostle avoided the shameful matter through circumlocution. But one should know that this passage has been interpreted in different ways by teachers. Nevertheless, how the Apostle is to be understood he makes clear when he adds: “And likewise the males, abandoning the natural use,” and so forth.

When he says “likewise,” he clearly shows that just as males practiced shameful acts with males, so females also desired females with shameful desire.

It should therefore be noted that he does not say “they exchanged the conjugal use,” but “the natural use.” For whoever joins his members to those members that God created for the procreation of offspring—even if they are the members of a prostitute—is engaging in a natural use, although in an illicit intercourse. But whoever joins himself to those members that God did not create for the procreation of offspring—even if they are the members of a wife—is not engaging in a natural use.

And therefore the Apostle says: “Likewise the males, abandoning the natural use of the female, burned in their desires for one another, males committing shameful acts with males.”

“Burned,” he says—that is, they were inflamed with an incredible ardor of lust.

[Note: The autograph reads *accensis* (“having been inflamed”), which seemed to me to be an error.]

This accords with the prophet’s words: “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flames that you have kindled.”

[Note: Hosea VII, 4. The Vulgate reads: “All adulterers, like an oven kindled by the baker.”]

And likewise: “All are adulterers” (Isa. L, 11), “like an oven—their hearts.”

It follows: “And receiving in themselves the recompense that was fitting for their error.”

They received in themselves the recompense that was fitting,

[Note: The words “the recompense … they received” are indicated in the lower margin of the autograph by a note placed between the interlinear words “receiving” and “because.”]

because, having abandoned God, they were abandoned by him. For they abandoned him in order that they might be abandoned, and, having become entangled in the crimes that follow, they might recognize whom they had abandoned.

Since they were unwilling to correct by suitable satisfaction the sin they had first committed, they were therefore, by God’s just judgment, given over to those vices by which they would be punished more severely.

It follows: “And just as they did not approve of having God in their knowledge,”

[Note: The Vulgate reads “in knowledge.”]

“God gave them over to a reprobate mind.”

[Note: The Vulgate reads “gave them over” with the alternate pronoun.]

It should be noted here that he does not say “they did not know God,” but “they did not approve of having God in their knowledge.” To know God is to understand the Creator through creatures; but to approve of having God in one’s knowledge is to keep him always present before the eyes of the mind and, through fear of him, to avoid vices.

By “a reprobate mind” he means a perverse mind. Of this he immediately adds: “So that they might do what is not fitting”—that is, what the divine laws condemn.

For although all sins are detestable to God, those committed against nature are nevertheless more detestable than all the others. On account of these there was the cataclysm—that is, the flood. On account of these four cities—Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim—were overthrown and burned with fire and sulfur. On account of these, many plagues and disasters come upon human beings every day.

It follows: “Filled with all unrighteousness,” and so forth. Unrighteousness is the desire and pleasure of a malicious mind. It is called *iniquitas* as though “inequity,” that is, lack of fairness; and because it is the head and root of all evils, it is rightly placed first.

There is, however, a distinction between unrighteousness and sin. Unrighteousness is what has been described; sin is a falling away of the body.

It follows: “Malice.” Malice is the thought of a perverse mind. It differs from malignity, which is the work of that same perverse thought.

“Fornication.” A man or woman is called a fornicator when his or her body is publicly available. The term is derived from the arched or vaulted structures called *fornices*, where brothels were formerly built for the prostitution of harlots.

There is a particular and a general fornication. Particular fornication is the corruption of soul and body; general fornication is every corruption of the mind and every sin that separates a person from God. Hence the Psalmist says: “You will destroy all who fornicate away from you.”

[Note: The autograph reads *superat* (“surpasses”) instead of *separat* (“separates”).]

[Note: Psalm LXII, 27. The Vulgate reads: “You have destroyed all who fornicate away from you.”]

“Avarice.” Avarice properly means seizing what belongs to another and not giving away what belongs to oneself.

It is called avarice as though “desire for gold,” and it is appropriately placed after fornication, because these two pertain to the worship of idols. Hence the same Apostle says: “Neither the fornicator, nor the impure, nor the avaricious person, who is an idolater, has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Eph. V, 5).

[Note: The words “which pertains … to the worship of idols” were added in the lower margin, in the same hand.]

“Wickedness” is the cunning or craftiness of the mind. But by cunning in wickedness one must not understand the kind of cunning of which Solomon says: “The astute person acts in everything with deliberation” (Prov. XIII, 16); rather, it is the cunning of deception. It is called wickedness as though “inequity,” that is, lack of fairness.

It follows: “Full of envy.” Envy is so called from looking upon another person’s happiness. It has two forms under it: grief and fear. For every envious person, when seeing another’s happiness, either grieves or fears. He grieves that someone is greater than himself; he fears that someone inferior to him may become his equal.

Every envious person is small-minded and dies from his own envy. Every envious person is also his own destroyer. Hence a certain poet says: “Nothing is more just than envy, which immediately gnaws at its own author and torments his soul.”

“Murder.” Murder takes its name from the killing of a human being. It is both spiritual and bodily, but the spiritual is incomparably greater.

[Note: In the autograph, instead of *incomparabiliter* (“incomparably”), the reading is *incorporabiliter*. Let the reader judge which reading is better.]

For by bodily murder a body that will eventually die is killed; by spiritual murder, however, a soul that will live forever is killed. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel concerning the devil: “He was a murderer from the beginning” (John VIII, 44). The devil uttered words alone and killed our first parents.

From this it is understood that whoever destroys someone by an evil word or example is rightly called a murderer. And murder is appropriately placed after envy, because envy leads to murder. Through envy the devil killed our first parents, and likewise Cain killed his brother.

“Contention.” Contention occurs when the truth is not sought but contentiousness is exerted.

“Deceit.” Deceit is pretense or fraud of the mind. It differs from pain in this respect: pain is bodily discomfort.

There is also a distinction among ambushes, fraud, and deceit. Ambushes belong to a place; fraud is a violation of trust; deceit is pretense of the mind.

“Malignity.” What malignity is has already been explained above.

It follows: “Whisperers.” A whisperer is one who slanders not to someone’s face but in his ear. Hence the name comes from the sound made in the ears, because he makes a sound beneath the ear. This is why the Lord commanded: “You shall not be an accuser or a whisperer among the peoples” (Lev. XIX, 16).

“Slanderers.” A slanderer is one who calls another person’s good evil, or who says that another person’s great good is small. Whoever falsely speaks evil about another person’s evil is likewise a slanderer; but if he speaks the truth about another’s evil, he is not a slanderer but an advocate of truth.

For whoever praises good and censures evil with a simple intention joins his will to divine truth.

“Hateful to God.” Here it should be noted that he does not simply say “hateful,” but adds “to God,” distinguishing them from human beings. Many are hateful to God who are loved by the world, and conversely many are loved by God and hated by the world. Those who possess all these vices are rightly called hateful to God.

“Insulting.” Insulting people are prone to verbal injuries, for insults are reproaches and abusive words.

“Proud.” Pride is every unlawful and disordered desire. This vice is so serious that, although all other vices are overcome by their contrary virtues, it alone fights against all virtues. Hence it is rightly called the mother and nurse of all vices and the destroyer of good things.

This vice is born when people love themselves more than God, because they wish to appear to be their own origin.

It follows: “Arrogant.” Someone is called arrogant as though he were carried outside himself. Arrogance is an elevation of the mind. This vice is born when the mind, swollen with pride, believes itself to be what it is not.

Hence it is appropriately placed after pride, from which it arises.

[Note: The words “swollen … pride” are found in the upper margin of the page, in the same hand.]

“Inventors of evil.” By this statement the Apostle shows that not all sins are committed at the devil’s instigation. Human beings devise some sins for themselves. Thus they are shown to be worse than the devil, who confesses that he received power from God, saying according to Luke’s Gospel: “All these things have been delivered to me, and I give them to whomever I wish. I shall give all these to you if, falling down, you will worship me” (Luke IV, 6).

For this reason, when he wished to test Job, he asked God for power; and when expelled by the Lord from human beings, he did not dare to enter the swine except at his command.

“Disobedient to parents.” Those who are entangled in the preceding vices, by God’s just judgment, go so far as to be disobedient even to their parents. Hence they are worse than beasts, which love their own parents.

“Foolish.” Someone is called foolish because he is without taste. Whoever therefore departs from the taste of spiritual teaching is rightly called foolish.

[Note: The words “foolish … foolish” are found in the lower margin of the page, in the same hand.]

“Disorderly,” that is, unorganized. Whoever is devoted to these vices is rightly called disorderly and unorganized, because he lacks order.

“Without affection,” that is, without friendliness.

[Note: The words “whoever … among” are written in the lower margin. Since the page is found to be awkwardly divided lower down, I suspect that there is a lacuna here, although it is very small, both because of the sequence of the text and because of a defect in the place or paper, which should not be extensive. In my judgment the passage should read: “There is this difference between piety and friendliness: …”]

[Between …] piety is properly spoken of toward relatives, whereas friendliness extends also to strangers.

“Without a covenant,” that is, without an agreement. There is this distinction between a covenant and an agreement: a covenant is an earlier agreement, namely, reconciliation after hostility; an agreement is an association that follows reconciliation.

[Note: In the autograph, the reading is “peace” instead of “agreement.” This seemed to me an error requiring correction.]

“Without mercy.” Mercy takes its name from the misery of the heart. The person who truly is merciful is the one who mourns another’s misery as though it were his own.

Mercy is spoken of God not properly but figuratively, because no passion falls within the nature of divinity. And he fittingly concludes all the vices with this clause, because those corrupted by them go so far as to be without mercy both toward themselves and toward others. For whoever shows mercy in an orderly manner—

Hence Solomon says: “Son, have mercy on yourself while pleasing God.”

[Note: Not Solomon, but Ecclesiasticus, chapter 30, verse 24.]

It follows: “Although they knew the righteousness of God, they did not understand,” and so forth. They knew the righteousness of God through the law of nature. He calls the righteousness of God that by which he justly punishes the wicked and rewards the good.

“They did not understand”—that is, because they were blinded by their sins. What they did not understand he shows by adding: “That those who do such things are worthy of death.” Not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them.

By these words the Apostle shows that both the person who sins willingly and those who sin under compulsion will nevertheless suffer; and those who favor the perpetrators must be punished with eternal death.

There are, however, some who do not favor the perpetrators and openly persecute evil, yet commit it secretly. Therefore, lest these appear not to be condemned, he adds:

“Therefore you are without excuse, O man, every one who judges.”

[Note: In the autograph, on the margin: chapter VI. Here begins the second chapter of the Epistle according to the Vulgate division.]

It is as though he were saying: “You, whoever you are, who openly persecute evil but commit it secretly, do not suppose that you will not be condemned. For you will be punished all the more severely because, although you are evil, you desire through hypocrisy to appear good.”

Hence it is written in the Book of Job: “The crafty and hypocritical provoke the wrath of God” (Job XXXVI, 13).

Why he is without excuse he shows: “For in judging another, you condemn yourself,”

[Note: The Vulgate reads “another person.”]

“for you do the same things that you judge.”

And lest anyone flatter himself concerning impunity by saying, “God is merciful and will not allow his creature to perish forever,” he therefore added: “But we know that the judgment of God is according to truth against those who do such things.”

[Note: The Vulgate reads: “For we know.”]

It is as though he were saying: “If you, an unjust person, unjustly judge one who is just, how much more will God, who is just, justly judge you, an unjust person?”

By “judgment” he means condemnation. He added “according to truth” to distinguish it from human judgments, which are often deceived by compassion, desire, or fear. God’s judgments, however, are altogether true and just, because they are carried out without respect of persons.

It follows: “Do you suppose, O man, who judge those who do such things and do them yourself, that you will escape the judgment of God?”

[Note: The Vulgate reads “because” instead of “that.”]

It is as though he were saying: “Do not suppose that you will not be punished because God postpones his judgment; for at some time he will fulfill what he has promised.” He waits patiently for you to turn to him through repentance. He postpones judgment for this reason: he does not wish to find people whom he must condemn, but people whom he may crown.

It follows: “Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering?”

By the riches of God’s goodness, patience, and long-suffering he means the temporal goods that God bestows on both the good and the wicked. The wicked person despises these because he does not wish to turn to God through repentance.

God is called good because he gives good things; patient and long-suffering because he endures evil.

One should also know that some copies read “goodness and forbearance.” There is nevertheless a distinction between patience and forbearance. God’s forbearance is exercised toward those who sin more through weakness than through will; patience, however, toward those who rather through will—

[Note: The words “patience … will” are written in the side margin.]

It follows: “Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance?”

[Note: After the word “leads,” there is no question mark.]

The sense is: God grants you time for repentance, but you use it badly. Hence it is written in the Book of Job concerning the wicked person: “God gave him a place for repentance, and he abuses it in pride” (Job XXIV, 23).

Hence Solomon also says: “Son, do not delay turning to God, nor postpone it from day to day; for suddenly the wrath of God will come and remove you.”

[Note: Not Solomon, but Ecclesiasticus, chapter 5, verse 8.]

According to your hardness, however, and impenitent heart, you are storing up for yourself the wrath of God [Note: [Col. 0146D] In the Vulgate, the word “of God” is not found there.] on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment. A hard mind is one which, hardened by the coldness of its service, cannot receive within itself the image of its Creator [Col. 0146D]—just as hard wax cannot receive the form of any seal. An impenitent heart, moreover, is one that cannot be softened toward repentance; concerning it the prophet says: “I will take from you your stony heart and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. 36:26). “To store up” is used both in a good and in a bad sense, but here in the bad sense. Therefore, the one who heaps sin upon sin stores up wrath. “Wrath,” as has already been said, is understood as vengeance. The day of wrath is called the day of judgment, in accordance with the prophet’s words: “That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress” (Zeph. 1:15). It is also called the day of revelation, because what is now hidden will then be made manifest. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Nothing is covered that will not be revealed” (Matt. 10:26; Luke 12:2). And to make clear why he said “of God’s just judgment,” he immediately added: “Who will repay each according to his works” [Col. 0147B] [Note: [Col. 0147D] In the Vulgate, “his” is read.].

To show the equity of that same judgment, he immediately continued: “To those who, according to the perseverance of good work”—here one must understand, “live”—[he will give] glory, honor, and incorruption. He appropriately says, “to those who live according to the perseverance of good work,” since the reward of good work is awaited through perseverance and will be bestowed in the future. Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “We walk by faith, and not by sight” (2 Cor. 5:7). He calls “glory” the beauty of eternal blessedness, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13:43). “Honor,” however, is the dignity by which they will be made sons, like the Father; hence John says: “When he appears, we shall be like him” (1 John 3:2). By “incorruption” he means immortality; hence the same Apostle says: “This mortal must put on immortality, and this corruptible must put on incorruption” (1 Cor. 15:53).

He shows to whom he will grant these things when he continues: “To those who seek eternal life” [Note: [Col. 0147D] In the Vulgate, “who seek” is read.]—that is, to those who seek him who is eternal life. Since he had stated what good things are to be repaid to those who live according to the perseverance of good work, he immediately adds, to show what evils are to be repaid to the wicked: “But to those who are contentious”—here one must understand, “who are”—“and who do not obey the truth” (that is, the truth which they received through the grace of the Gospel), namely, the Lord Jesus Christ or his teaching, “but believe in iniquity” (that is, the iniquity which they have always loved), there will be wrath and indignation [Note: [Col. 0148D] That is, as was said above concerning the verse “the wrath of God is revealed.” In the autograph there is an error here: instead of “for vengeance,” as above in the cited verse, “providence” is read. I have thought it appropriate to correct it.].

“Wrath,” as has been said, must be understood as vengeance, concerning which the Psalmist says: “Who knows the power of your wrath?” (Ps. 89:11), and so forth [Col. 0147D]. And because wrath is often displayed without indignation, to indicate a more terrible wrath he added: “And indignation.” Indignation is the force of future chastisement and just punishment.

“Tribulation and distress.” Tribulation will be repaid on account of the guilt of conscience, but distress on account of delayed repentance, in accordance with the prophet’s words: “Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished” (Isa. 66:24). For he calls the worm the gnawing of one’s own conscience.

Upon whom these things will be inflicted is made clear when he continues: “Upon every soul of a person who does evil.” But what does he mean by saying “upon every soul of a person”? Will the soul alone suffer punishment? No, but soul and body together. There were indeed some who, because the Apostle says “upon every soul,” wanted to understand that, just as the soul is spiritual, so the future punishment is not bodily but spiritual. This is entirely false. The Apostle says “every soul” because the rational soul is a creature, and it is the first to sin; therefore it will be punished first.

Or, speaking figuratively, he wished the whole person to be understood from a part, that is, from the soul, as in the passage: “Jacob went down into Egypt with seventy souls” (Gen. 46:27). But when he says “those who do evil,” this is not to be referred to any particular action, but to perverse thought, because he is speaking about unbelief.

And to show that there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, he added: “Jew first, and Greek.” He says “first” to show that the Jews are preferred to the Greeks: they received the Law first, and they were also the first to transgress it. Therefore they are preferred to the Greeks both in good and in evil, both in punishment and in reward.

Since, then, he had said that three afflictions were to be repaid to the wicked, wishing to show that three splendid and honorable gifts are to be repaid to the righteous, he immediately continued: “But glory, honor, and peace to everyone who does good.” These three may be referred both to the present life and to the future life.

If they are referred to the present life, they should be understood as follows: the glory of resurrection and the renewal of the soul, which takes place through faith, is repaid; glory and honor—that is, the dignity by which each person, having received forgiveness of sins, passes into adoption as a son of God—are also bestowed; and peace—that is, reconciliation, by which those who were enemies become friends of God—is likewise bestowed.

If, however, they are referred to the future, they should be understood in this way: glory will be bestowed upon the righteous, that is, the splendor of eternal blessedness; honor will be bestowed, that is, the dignity by which they will be made sons like the Father [Note: [Col. 0148D] In the autograph, “they will be cast out” is read.]; and likewise peace, that is, perfect security. For there will be no struggle with vices there, but human beings will be joined to God and the angels.

“To the Jew first, and to the Greek.” If we consider the matter more carefully, the Jews are preferred to the Greeks not only in dignity [Col. 0148D] but also in time, for they came into existence earlier.

And because the Jews could say, “O Apostle, why do you equate the nations with us, who received the Law and possess knowledge of Christ?” he himself answers: “For there is no partiality with God.” His fellow Apostle Peter clearly explains the meaning of this passage in his Epistle, saying: “God is not a respecter of persons [Note: [Col. 0148D] I do not know how Peter’s Epistle is cited here, since this text is found in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 10, verses 34–35. It is indeed Peter’s statement, but it is not in his Epistles. In the First Epistle, only chapter 1, verse 17, contains a corresponding text: “And if you invoke as Father him who judges without partiality,” and so forth.], but in every nation whoever fears God and practices righteousness is acceptable to him” [Col. 0149A].

To demonstrate this more clearly, the Apostle continued: “For whoever sinned without the Law will perish without the Law, and whoever sinned under the Law will be judged by the Law.” By these words the Apostle shows that neither the Jews are excusable on account of ignorance, since they received the Law, nor the Gentiles, since through creation they were able to recognize the Creator.

The Lord makes the meaning of this passage clear in the Gospel, saying: “The servant who knows his lord’s will and does what deserves punishment will be beaten with many blows; but the one who does not know his lord’s will and does what deserves punishment will be beaten with few blows” (Luke 12:48).

But behold: these words of the Apostle seem to sound as though the Gentiles are to be punished more severely than the Jews. Of the Gentiles he says, “they will perish,” but of the Jews, “they will be judged.” Hence Origen says: “The Apostle does not seem to me to have meant this in that way; rather, in what he says, ‘they will be judged,’ one must understand, ‘so that they may perish,’ since the Law itself teaches how they are to be judged.” But of the Gentiles he says “they will perish” because “the ungodly will not rise in the judgment, nor sinners in the assembly [Note: [Col. 0149D] Psalm 1:6; in the autograph, “counsel.”] of the righteous.”

It follows: “For the hearers of the Law are not righteous before God, but the doers of the Law will be justified.” What does he mean by saying that the doers of the Law will be justified, when they are undoubtedly already righteous? Therefore, here “will be justified” must be understood as in the Gospel, where it is said of a certain Pharisee: “But he, wishing to justify himself”—that is, wishing to appear or be thought righteous—(Luke 10:29). Similarly, here the Apostle says “will be justified,” that is, the doers of the Law will be created so that they may be righteous, or they will be considered and thought righteous.

It follows: “For when the Gentiles, who do not have the Law, naturally do what belongs to the Law,” and so forth. By these words he shows that the Gentiles, by naturally doing the commandments of the Law, will not be deprived of that promise concerning which the Lord speaks through the prophet: “This is the covenant that I will establish with the house of Jacob: after those days, I will put my laws into their hearts, and I will inscribe them upon their inward parts” (Jer. 31:33; Heb. 8:10).

Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Although you were a wild olive tree, you were grafted into the good olive tree” (Rom. 11:17). The prophet’s words correspond closely to the Apostle’s statements. There it is said, “I will inscribe them upon their inward parts,” and here the Apostle says: “They show,” he says, “the work of the Law written in their hearts” [Col. 0149D].

Here the Apostle is speaking about the natural law, which God writes in each person’s heart with his own finger. This is the law that contains within itself the commandments of the written Law, namely, “You shall not kill,” and so forth. This is the law that contains knowledge of the one God, and that is close to the grace of the Gospel—namely, “Do not do to another what you do not want done to you.” The Lord also says in the Gospel: “Whatever you want people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. 7:12).

He therefore says: “When the Gentiles, who do not have the Law”—that is, the written Law—“naturally do what belongs to the Law,” that is, observe the commandments of the natural law, “although they do not have such a law”—that is, the kind that God gave through Moses—“they are a law to themselves. They show the work of the Law written in their hearts, while their conscience bears witness to them.”

Here one must ask about which thoughts the Apostle is speaking: whether those that exist now, or those that will exist in the future. In fact, he is speaking about those that exist now, because not only the things we do but also the things we think are written, like signs and characters in wax, upon the tablets of our hearts, and remain hidden until the day of judgment. Then all things will be made manifest and judged. Hence he immediately continues: “On the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings.”

How he will judge is made clear by the words “according to my Gospel,” that is, according to my teaching and preaching. Through whom he will judge he indicates by adding: “Through Jesus Christ our Lord” [Note: [Col. 0149D] These words, “our Lord,” are not found in the Vulgate.].

But why does he say that judgment will be carried out through him? Clearly because the Lord says in the Gospel: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22).

We must therefore examine carefully how thoughts will accuse or defend people on the day of judgment. It should be understood that whoever, having been stirred by divine inspiration, by his own thought, or by someone’s preaching, does not believe will be accused and [Note: [Col. 0150D] In the autograph, the particle “not” lies between “and” and “will condemn”; reader, consider whether it rightly stood there or was rightly deleted.] condemned by his thoughts [Col. 0150C]—not as one ignorant, but as a rebel. If, however, someone has not been stirred by these influences and does not believe, his thoughts will not defend him but condemn him, because through creation he ought to have recognized the Creator. Otherwise, whoever has believed and has fulfilled his faith through works will be saved, because his thoughts will defend him.

Since, then, he had said much about the crimes of the Gentiles, he now rebukes the Jews for their unbelief, continuing: “But if you are called a Jew,” and so forth. In saying “you are called,” he shows that “Jew” is not a name but a surname [Note: [Col. 0150D] It is worth noting in what sense “surname” was understood in the tenth century. Here it is not taken as an agnatic or family-distinguishing name, but as the common name of an entire nation or people.], that is, a common name.

And note that, just as he addressed portions of the Gentiles [Col. 0150D], so now he addresses portions of the Jews. In these words the Apostle shows that it is not a great good if a Jew believes, since he has been instructed by the Law and possesses knowledge of God’s will. He wants it to be understood that it is a great evil if he does not believe.

It follows: “And you rest in the Law.” Those rested in the Law of God who, by meditating on the Law, were free from earthly cares.

“And you glory in God.” The Jews gloried in God because they thought that they had been saved by their own merits, had received the Law on account of their own merits, and were able to fulfill it by their own strength, in accordance with the words: “He has not dealt so with every nation [Note: [Col. 0151D] Psalm 147:20. In the Vulgate the verse reads: “He has not dealt so with every nation, and he has not manifested his judgments to them.”], and he has not made known his judgments to them.”

“And you know God’s will.” They recognized God’s will through the commandments of the Law, in which what God wills is shown.

It follows: “And you approve what is more useful, instructed through the Law.” Here one must note that he does not say “what is useful,” but “what is more useful,” to show that many useful things are also contained in the law of nature, although it is weak because they cannot be fulfilled without the grace of the Gospel. In the written Law there are more useful things, but in the grace of the Gospel there are more perfect things.

“You are confident that you yourself are a guide to the blind,” and so forth. These duties also belong to a true worshiper of the Law. But [Note: [Col. 0151D] In the autograph, “as if” (*quasi*) is read in place of the adverb “because” (*quia*). Since this did not seem to me to express the author’s meaning at all well, I judged it should be corrected, especially because of the adverb “therefore” (*ideo*) which follows and has a grammatical relation to the preceding *quia*.] because they falsely boasted that these things applied to them, the Apostle rebuked them, saying: “You are confident that you yourself are a guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants,” and so forth [Col. 0151B].

It is as though he were saying: If you are a guide to the blind, as you falsely boast, why do you yourself not walk along the right path? If you are a light to those who are in darkness, why do you follow the darkness of unbelief? If you are an instructor of the foolish, why do you depart from the fear of the Lord, which, according to the prophet, is the beginning of wisdom? If you are a teacher of infants, why are you yourself a child in understanding?

And because they falsely boasted that these things belonged to them, they seemed to possess in the Law the form of knowledge and truth. Hence he immediately adds: “Having the form of knowledge and truth in the Law.”

[Col. 0151C] It follows: “You, therefore, who teach another, do you not teach yourself?” [Note: [Col. 0152D] The question mark is not found here in the Vulgate; there are two points.] It is as though he were saying: Why do you destroy your teaching and preaching by your works?

And to make this clearer, he added: “You who preach against stealing, do you steal?” The Jews stole because in the Law and the Prophets they concealed knowledge of Christ. No theft can be greater than this.

“You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?” The Jews committed adultery when, by wrongly interpreting the Law, they corrupted the word of God, because they did not speak sincerely, as from God, before God, in Christ. Moreover, whoever gives to human beings what is owed specifically to God commits adultery.

“You who abhor idols”—one must understand, the idols of the Gentiles—“do you commit sacrilege?” Sacrilege is called the transgression of the sacred Law, or the theft of the sacred Law [Note: [Col. 0152D] In the autograph, “sacrilegious persons” is read instead of “the sacred Law.” Certainly this is a copyist’s error, as can be seen slightly above.], or the theft of a sacred object. For, as blessed Augustine says: “To take (*legere*), or to steal secretly (*sublegere*), is to steal.” Hence a sacrilegious person is called a thief or transgressor of the sacred Law. The Jews, therefore, were sacrilegious because they both corrupted the Law and, as has been said, committed theft within it.

It follows: “You who glory in the Law, through transgression of the Law you dishonor God.” The Jews gloried in the Law because they believed that they had received it on account of their own merits and thought that they could fulfill it by their own strength. But through transgressing that same Law they dishonored God, because they refused to believe that he was God to whom the Father bears witness, saying: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 17:5), and to whom the prophet says: “You were God, and we did not know it.”

This must certainly be understood not of the Father but of the Son. The name of the Father had always been known to them; that of the Son, however, was unknown. Hence those who had refused to believe before the Passion, after recognizing the glory of his resurrection, said, believing and giving thanks: “You were God, and we did not know it.”

It follows: “For the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you, as it is written” [Col. 0152B]. Behold, the Apostle says that it is written, but he does not indicate where. Nevertheless, he leaves it to be understood that it is in the prophet Isaiah (Isa. 52:5).

For when the Lord was rebuking the Jews through the prophet, he said among other things: “You have profaned my holy name among the Gentiles” (Ezek. 36:22). But one must ask how the name of God was then profaned and blasphemed among the Gentiles through the Jews, or how this happened in the Apostle’s time.

It should be understood that the Jews, entangled in many vices and crushed by various afflictions, were handed over into captivity. While detained there, they gave the Gentiles an occasion to say: “Behold, the holy nation, once God’s special people, liberated from Egyptian slavery by many signs, is held in captivity and reduced to servitude. Truly our gods have overcome their God; and therefore they have been delivered into our hands.”

For they did not know that, if they had always served God and kept his commandments, they would have had him as their protector everywhere.

The name of God was also blasphemed through them in the time of the Apostles, because, filled with zeal and envy, they continually resisted the apostolic teaching. This is shown in the Acts of the Apostles, where we read: “The Jews, filled with zeal in the synagogue, contradicted what was being said by Paul” (Acts 13:45). Or because they gave those who believed less an occasion to say: “The promise made to Abraham has been emptied and annulled; God is deceitful: he was unable to fulfill what he promised.”

“Circumcision indeed is beneficial, if you keep the Law” [Note: [Col. 0152D] The Vulgate reads “observe.”]. It is as though he were saying: If you keep the commandments of the Law, circumcision is beneficial, because it causes you to remain under the Law. But while you remain under the Law, you understand that carnal circumcision must cease and that spiritual circumcision must take its place, which takes place through faith in Christ. Otherwise it is of no benefit to you.

But one must ask how the Apostle can say, “Circumcision is beneficial,” when elsewhere he says, “Circumcision is of no benefit”; for he seems to contradict himself. Yet, so that he would not appear contradictory, some people, by allegorizing, said that “circumcision” ought to be understood as the seed of Abraham, that is, a Jew, and “foreskin” as a Gentile. The meaning would then be: If you understand the commandments of the Law spiritually, recognize in them the knowledge of Christ, and trust that you can be saved through faith in him, then it benefits you that you are the seed of Abraham—that is, that you are a Jew. Otherwise it benefits you nothing, because you have degenerated from the nobility of Abraham’s seed and passed over to the unbelief of a Gentile.

And this is what follows: “But if you are a transgressor of the Law, your circumcision has become foreskin.”

It follows: “Therefore, if the foreskin keeps the righteousnesses of the Law, will not his foreskin be counted as circumcision?” [Note: [Col. 0153D] The Vulgate has “circumcision.”] As above, “foreskin” refers to some Gentile. It is right that those carnal commandments should be understood as spiritually fulfilled.

The meaning is this: If the foreskin—that is, some Gentile who by nature has a foreskin—understands the commandments of the Law spiritually, recognizes in them the knowledge of Christ, and trusts that he can be saved through faith in him, his foreskin will be counted as circumcision, because he will pass over into the nobility of Abraham’s race and become his son, in accordance with what the Apostle himself says elsewhere: “If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise” (Gal. 3:29).

It follows: “And the foreskin which is by nature, while fulfilling the Law, will judge you who, through the letter and circumcision, are a transgressor of the Law” [Note: [Col. 0153D] The Vulgate has the pronoun “that” between “will judge” and “which.”] [Note: [Col. 0153D] After “you are,” the Vulgate has a question mark, which is absent in our autograph.].

The meaning is this: The foreskin which is by nature—that is, some Gentile who by nature has a foreskin—will judge you who, through the letter and circumcision, are a transgressor of the Law. That is, he will condemn you, not by authority but by comparison with his better conduct, in accordance with what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Therefore they themselves will be your judges” (Matt. 12:27; Luke 11:19). And again: “The queen of the South will rise in judgment with this generation” (Matt. 12:42; Luke 11:31), and so forth.

“For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is that circumcision which is outward, in the flesh” [Note: [Col. 0153D] The word “is,” which precedes “circumcision” in the Vulgate, is missing there.], and so forth. A Jew outwardly is one who glories in carnal circumcision. Of such people the Apostle says: “Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame” (Phil. 3:19). Their glory is in their shame because they glory in their private parts.

And to show the true Jew and spiritual circumcision, he immediately continued: “But the one who is in secret is a Jew, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit” [Note: [Col. 0154D] In the autograph, not “the one who,” but “because” is read. This seems faulty not only against the Vulgate reading but also against the meaning.].

Here one must ask what circumcision is. Circumcision is the stripping away of the flesh, which bore the figure of true circumcision. True circumcision, however, is the abolition and purification of all carnal pleasures and delights [Note: [Col. 0154D] Consider whether “stripping away” might be preferable.]. Whoever renders his mind alien to these things circumcises himself truly.

Moses also spoke of this circumcision, saying: “Circumcise the hardness of your heart.” And again: “Be circumcised for the Lord your God” (Deut. 10:16). Jeremiah likewise says: “Circumcise the foreskins of your hearts” (Jer. 4:4).

The sign of circumcision was given to the Jews so that by it they might be distinguished from all the nations. This was almost prefigured at the very beginning of the world in Cain, to whom the Lord gave a sign of fear. And just as Cain persisted in that sign until death, so they will persist in the sign of circumcision until the day of judgment, so that what the same Apostle says may be fulfilled: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel may be saved” (Rom. 11:25).

This is especially confirmed by the fact that none of the rulers or kings under whom they lived attempted to take away from them the sign of circumcision.

“Whose praise is not from human beings but from God”: namely, the praise of the one who does not glory in carnal circumcision and recognizes that he has been saved not by his own merits but by the grace of God.

Above, he addressed unbelieving Jews. Then he had said that the true Jew is one whose good works are not outward but hidden, and that true circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit and not in the letter. And because he had said that there is no partiality with God, lest believing Jews should perhaps think that they were to be despised, he therefore continued by proposing a question to himself:

(CAP. III.) [Col. 0154C] [Note: [Col. 0154D] In the autograph, “chapter VII” is written in the margin. According to the Vulgate, the third chapter of the Epistle begins with these words.]

“What, then, is the Jew’s advantage? Or what is the benefit of circumcision?” And, speaking either from his own person or from that of others, he answered himself: “Much in every way.” To show how, he continued: “First, because the words of God were entrusted to them.”

Here one must note that he says “first,” but does not identify a second point, leaving it to be understood. By these words the Apostle shows that, among all the things bestowed from heaven upon the Jews, the chief and most distinguished was that not only the patriarchs but the entire Israelite people were deemed worthy to enjoy God’s address and to receive the Law promulgated by God.

The second was that they were liberated from Egyptian slavery by many signs and wonders and crossed the Red Sea on dry feet. Next, the other things divinely bestowed upon them should be considered, down to the time when they entered the promised land.

But because some might say, “What benefit did the entrusted utterances of God bring them, since they perished by murmuring in the wilderness?” the Apostle responds: “What if some of them did not believe”—the unstated question being, “What harm does that do?”—“did their unbelief nullify the faithfulness of God?” He calls the promise by which Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, “faithfulness.” The sense is: It is not as you claim. For although the promise made to Abraham was nullified in unbelievers, it was nevertheless fulfilled in those who believed. This is what he says: “By no means.” Hence he immediately adds: “For God is truthful, but every human being is a liar.”

God is truthful because, neither by being born nor by living [Note: [Col. 0155D] In the autograph, *videndo* (“by seeing”) is read; it seemed to me that *vivendo* (“by living”) should be read, since in this way the author appears to have referred to both original and actual sin: God contracted no sin either by being born or by living. But perhaps *videndo* may also be read correctly, namely in the sense in which the prophets are reported to have been called “seers” in 1 Kings 9:9: “Come, and let us go to the seer.” For one who is now called a prophet was formerly called a seer. In that case he may have wished to say: God, the truthful God in his prophecies and promises, contracted no sin—that is, no falsehood—by seeing, that is, by promising what was to come.], contracted any sin; but every human being is a liar, because he is human.

God is truthful because, although his promises were not fulfilled in those who perished by murmuring in the wilderness, they were fulfilled in those who, with God and faith cooperating, entered the promised land. God is truthful because, although his promise was nullified in unbelievers, it nevertheless remains fulfilled in believers. For all who believe in Christ and trust that they can be saved through his faith are counted within this promise and become children of Abraham. Thus the promise, nullified in the faithless, was fulfilled in the faithful, just as the dignity of the apostleship, although annulled in Judas the betrayer, was fulfilled in Peter, who believed and remained steadfast in faith.

And to confirm his account by prophetic testimony, he added: “As it is written: So that you may be justified in your words, and may prevail when you are judged.” But how does this testimony relate to what precedes? If we examine it carefully, it is certainly found to correspond. To whom was the prophet speaking? To God, certainly—not to the Father, however, but to the Son, because he was judged by the wicked as though he were wicked. Praying to him, he said: “Against you alone I have sinned, and I have done what is evil before you” (Psalm 56:6), as though he were saying: Because you alone are righteous, alone without sin, “so that you may be justified in your words, and may prevail when you are judged.” When he was judged by sinners, he prevailed, because he was proved righteous.

We must therefore ask with what intention the prophet used this expression in his own time, and with what intention the Apostle took it to confirm his account. It should be understood that God had promised to take vengeance upon sinners without respect of persons. David, however, because he had sinned while he was king, said: “Against you alone I have sinned,” and so forth. It was as though he were saying: You, Lord, promised that you would take vengeance upon sinners without respect of persons. When, therefore, you forgive my sin, people judge your patience [Note: [Col. 0156D] In the autograph, instead of *judicant* (“they judge”), *judicantem* (“judging”) is read. Let others decide which reading is more suitable.] to be false. Yet, because I confess and make satisfaction, you forgive my sin so that you may be justified and prevail over those who judge that you have lied, since you do not judge twice for the same matter. For the compassion of your mercy shows that you have not lied.

Alternatively: There were some, such as the Epicureans, who said that God had no concern for human beings, any more than for beasts. Therefore the prophet said: “Against you alone I have sinned,” and so forth. It was as though he were saying: O Lord, you rebuke my sin through your prophet so that you may be justified and prevail over those who judge that you do not have [Note: [Col. 0156D] Instead of *non habere*, the autograph has *inherem*.] concern for human beings.

More honorably, however, it may be understood in this way: God had promised that the Savior of the world would be born from David’s seed. Because David himself had committed both adultery and murder, he therefore said in repentance: “Against you alone I have sinned,” and so forth. It was as though he were saying: You, Lord, promised that the Savior of the world would be born from my seed. But because your people see me stained by a twofold crime, you cause the children of Israel to blaspheme. For when they see both adultery and murder in me, they judge that you have lied. Therefore receive the prayers of my satisfaction and, in your mercy, forgive what I condemn, so that, when you make me worthy of your promise by granting forgiveness of sins, you may both be justified and prevail over those who judge that you have lied.

The Apostle followed this line, this order, and this intention. For in his own time there were many who said: “Behold, a holy nation, a people acquired for God, liberated from Egyptian servitude by many signs and wonders! How does it remain in unbelief and become entangled in various crimes? The promise made to Abraham has been nullified” [Note: [Col. 0156D] Perhaps, through the copyist’s forgetfulness, the verb *est* (“is”) has been omitted; or, to continue the sense, *promissione* (“by the promise”) should have been written instead of *promissio* (“the promise”).]. The Apostle refutes them, saying: “God is truthful,” and so forth. It was as though he were saying: It is not as you say. For if the promise was nullified in unbelievers, it was fulfilled in believers.

And because he said, “God is truthful, and every human being is a liar,” and then, “As it is written: So that you may be justified in your words,” the perverse might say: If God is just because humanity is unjust, and if God is truthful because humanity is false, then our injustice establishes God’s justice, and our falsehood approves his truth. If that is so, then God is unjust when he inflicts wrath—that is, vengeance—if he takes vengeance upon those who sin for the very purpose that he himself may be proved just and truthful.

The Apostle is therefore pressed into a difficult position and compelled to assume two persons: one under the guise of an ignorant interpreter, and the other under that of an Apostle teaching and refuting. In the voice of the opposing party [Note: [Col. 0156D] In the autograph, *adversa patris* is read.] he says [Note: [Col. 0156D] In the autograph’s margin, “Chapter VIII” is written.]: “But if our unrighteousness demonstrates the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Is God unrighteous when he inflicts wrath?” It is as though the opposing party were saying: O Apostle, your words have given great consolation to our sins. For if God’s truth and justice are proved by our unrighteousness and falsehood, [Col. 0157A] we should not be condemned as sinners; rather, the more we sin, the greater benefits we ought to receive.

And as someone might say: If, then, I lie, I should not be judged as a sinner, because God’s truth abounds in my falsehood for his glory—for this reason he says a little later: “But if [Note: [Col. 0157D] The Vulgate has *enim* (“for”).] the truth of God abounds through my falsehood for his glory” [Note: [Col. 0157D] The Vulgate has *gloriam* (“glory”) instead of *gloria* (“for glory”).], “why am I still judged as a sinner?”

Against these, therefore, the Apostle says: “I speak according to human reasoning: By no means.” “According to human reasoning,” that is, according to reason and understanding. He says this in order to show that those who speak such things are not human beings. It was as though he were saying: It is not as you say. God’s truth and justice are not approved by your falsehood and unrighteousness, because our God delights not in evil works but in good works, and he glories not in evil deeds but in good ones. For by punishing the wicked he proves himself just.

Hence he immediately adds: “Otherwise, how will God judge the world?” It is as though he were saying: If he does not punish the wicked in order to prove himself just, how will the judgment take place that he himself promised would come?

There were also some who falsely claimed that the Apostle preached: “Let us do evil so that good may come”—which is nothing other than saying: If our unrighteousness commends God’s justice, then God is unjust when he inflicts wrath.
