Against them he immediately added: “And not as we are slanderously reported to say”—the unstated conclusion being, “it is so”—“and as some claim that we say: Let us do evil so that good may come; their condemnation is just.” The sense is: We do not preach as you say. Rather, because you flatter yourselves with impunity and abuse God’s patience, the one who is to come to judge the world and render to each according to his works will justly condemn you. Let us not therefore say, “Let us do evil so that good may come,” but rather: “Because we did evil, good came to us through God’s gratuitous goodness.”

Since, then, he had said, “What advantage has the Jew?” and immediately added, “Much in every way,” lest the Jews, puffed up with empty pride, should exalt themselves above believing Gentiles, he added [Note: [Col. 0157D] In the autograph’s margin, “Chapter IX” is written.]: “What then? Do we have precedence over them?” And he answers himself: “Not at all.” It was as though he were saying: I find no reason why we who are Jews by nature should place ourselves above believing Gentiles, for we are all sinners and have been redeemed solely by God’s grace.

Hence he immediately adds: “For we have already charged that all, Jews and Greeks alike, are under sin.” By “we have charged,” he means: We have demonstrated by manifest reasons that Jews and Gentiles, the wise and the foolish alike, are all under sin.

And to prove this by the testimony of the prophet, he added: “As it is written: There is no one who is righteous; there is no one who understands; there is no one who seeks God,” and so forth. As a certain wise man says: “The body that is corrupted [Note: [Col. 0157D] Wisdom 9:15. The Vulgate has *corrumpitur* (“is corrupted”) rather than *rumpitur* (“is broken”).] weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling burdens the mind occupied with many thoughts.” Whoever, therefore, entangles himself in worldly affairs and earthly cares cannot sincerely understand or sincerely seek God.

For this reason the Lord also says in the Gospel: “No one can serve two masters” [Note: [Col. 0157D] The words “to seek … masters,” written in the lower margin of the autograph in the same though smaller hand, have been found there.]. “All have turned aside” (Psalm 13:3), that is, they have withdrawn from God. By these words he wishes to show that, when the Lord came through the mystery of the Incarnation, he found the Jews like the Gentiles. Hence elsewhere he says: “Scripture confined all things under sin” (Galatians 3:22).

“They have all alike become useless,” that is, the Jews have become like the Gentiles. Some derive *inutilis* (“useless”) from *idolum* (“idol”). An idol is vanity; therefore what is useless is also vain.

“There is no one who does good; there is not even one.” The phrase “not even one” may be understood as “altogether, including that one,” that is, no one at all. It may also mean “apart from the One,” with reference to Christ. This is the kind of expression by which we customarily say: “This field extends as far as the sea,” where we do not include the sea itself. In truth, apart from Christ and without Christ, no one can do any good.

“Their throat is an open tomb.” It should be noted that he does not say merely “a tomb,” but adds “open,” wishing to show that one thing is a closed tomb and another an open one. The throat of the wicked—that is, the voraciousness of an eager appetite and the desire of the mind—is like a closed tomb when they perform evil without reverence [Note: [Col. 0158D] Perhaps *reverenter*, that is, “with fear”; let the reader decide.]; but it is open when they do not fear to commit evil. It should also be noted that an open tomb awaits the bones of the dead in order to receive them. Likewise, the wicked await not only their own ruin but also that of others, because they desire others to become like themselves.

“With their tongues they acted deceitfully.” “Their own,” that is, evil tongues. For the wicked act deceitfully with their own—that is, evil—tongues, because they devise one thing in their hearts and utter another with their mouths.

“The poison of asps is under their lips.” He calls deceit, fraud, and trickery “poison.” The asp is so called from scattering poison. The fraud of the wicked is aptly compared with the poison of asps, because, just as an asp kills the body by scattering its poison, so they destroy souls by uttering evil words and offering evil examples.

And just as an asp, so that it may not hear the voices of enchanters, presses one ear against the ground or a stone and sends its tail to the other, so the wicked close the ears of their hearts lest they hear the commandments of the law. Their mouth, filled with cursing and bitterness, is therefore the poison of asps under their lips. Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness if they are easily and readily inclined to verbal insults and blasphemies.

“Their feet are swift to shed blood.” Here it should be noted that he does not say “swift to run.” For he does not mean bodily feet but the feet of the heart, that is, the wicked desires of the evil. Those feet are swift to shed blood which draw others into sin both by admonition and by suggestion. “Blood” is to be understood here as sin.

“Destruction and misery are in their ways.” He calls their doctrine and examples of living “ways”; whoever walks in these ways is made broken and miserable.

“And they have not known the way of peace.” Likewise he calls doctrine a “way,” but “peace” means Christ, of whom the Apostle says: “Christ is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14). The sense is: They have disdained to receive the preaching of Christ.

“There is no fear of God before their eyes.” He fittingly concludes the testimony with such a clause. They are entangled in all the vices mentioned above because they have not possessed the fear of God. For when does a servant sin in the presence of his master? Whoever, therefore, keeps the fear of God before his eyes does not sin—indeed, cannot sin—because the grace of the one whom he fears goes before him and follows him, as the one who said: “Like swelling waves, I have always feared God” (Job 31:23).

The Jews could therefore say: “Apostle, the testimony you have produced has nothing to do with us. The prophet did not say this about Jews but about Gentiles, since nowhere is a Jew recorded as having said, ‘There is no God.’” Therefore he immediately added: “We know, however, that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law.” It was as though he were saying: If the prophet said this about the Gentiles, how much more did he say it about you, who glory in the law. For although you did not say this in words, you said it by your deeds. Hence elsewhere he says: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16).

Why he said this, he shows by adding: “So that every mouth may be stopped,” and so forth. By “every” he means that the mouth of both Jews and Gentiles—even of the righteous—may be stopped from praising themselves and opened only in praise of God. This occurs when no one acknowledges himself as saved by his own merits or strength, but all acknowledge that they have been saved by God’s grace.

“And the whole world may become subject to God.” “The whole world,” that is, every human being living in the world. The whole world becomes subject to God when all confess themselves to be sinners and acknowledge that they have been saved solely by God’s grace.

“For no flesh will be justified before him by works of the law.” “All flesh,” that is, every human being; the whole is designated by a part—or every person who lives and thinks according to the flesh. It is rightly said: “No flesh will be justified before him by works of the law,” because the law brought no one to perfection [Note: [Col. 0159D] That is, to perfect fulfillment.]. For when someone learns through the law what must be avoided, unless divine grace helps him to avoid it, the law produces wrath—that is, vengeance. Hence it is said a little later: “The law produces wrath.”

Therefore the person who is not justified by works of the law is the one who, while fulfilling the work of the law, attributes it not to the grace of the merciful God but to himself. And because someone may appear righteous before human beings while being rejected by God, he says: “Before him.” Hence it is said of Zechariah and Elizabeth: “Both were righteous before the Lord” (Luke 1:6).

But since someone might say in response: “How can you say, Apostle, that a person is not justified by works of the law, when the commandments of the law and of the Gospel are the same?” he therefore added: “For through the law comes knowledge of sin”—the unstated conclusion being, “knowledge comes about.” Here it should be noted that he does not say “destruction” but “knowledge.” For the law does not destroy sins, that is, forgive them; it merely reveals them. It can command, but it cannot help.

Hence elsewhere he says: “I did not know sin except through the law,” for I would not have known that sin lay in desire unless the law had said: “You shall not desire” [Note: [Col. 0159D] The autograph has *concupiscentiam* (“desire”) instead of *concupiscentiae* (“of desire”).].

A Jew might have answered: The Apostle rightly says that through the law there is only knowledge of sin, and that a person is not justified by works of the law, since the law reveals sins but does not forgive them. Nevertheless, when the will itself fulfills the work of the law, a person is justified before God.

Therefore he added: “But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law.” He calls the grace by which a person is clothed for justification “the righteousness of God,” not the righteousness by which God himself is justified. The law commands, and weakness succumbs to its command; grace helps, through which charity is poured forth. Faith obtains what the law commands.

“Attested by the law and the prophets.” The law and the prophets bear witness to grace. For the law, by perceiving [Note: [Col. 0160D] This is probably an error; *praecipiendo* (“by commanding”) fits the law better.] and threatening, but not justifying, shows that a human being cannot be justified except by God’s gift through the help of the Holy Spirit. The prophets also bear witness, because the coming of Christ fulfilled what they foretold.

And because the law and the prophets bear witness to the grace of the Gospel, the Lord is therefore said, when glorified on the mountain, to have sat between Moses and Elijah.

But what does he mean by saying “attested by the law,” when he had already said: “But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law”? It should not therefore be understood exactly as the words seem to sound. For the righteousness of God was not manifested apart from the law, since it was attested by the law. Rather, the righteousness that was apart from the law was manifested—that is, the righteousness that God bestowed upon human beings through the help of his grace, without any assistance from the law.

It should therefore be noted that the Apostle mentions many laws: the law of nature, the written law, the law of grace, the law of the mind, the law of the members, and the law of sin. For this reason, each passage must be examined carefully [Note: [Col. 0160D] The repetition of *sollicite* (“carefully”) appears erroneous.] to determine which law he is discussing. Thus he speaks of the law of nature when he says: “No flesh will be justified before him by works of the law”; and again: “Through the law comes knowledge of sin”; and once more: “But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law.”

It should further be noted that in this passage the Apostle seems to say many things to the detriment of the law. He also seems to nullify free will. This passage must therefore be read cautiously. For it should be understood that there are four stages.

The first is before the law was given, namely, under the law of nature. The second is after the law was given, under the law of Moses. The third is under grace, namely, in the Gospel. The fourth is under peace, which will be in the future.

In the first stage we are drawn by carnal desire and follow it, because we not only sin but also approve sin, being blinded by the darkness of ignorance and living entirely according to the flesh.

In the second stage we are indeed drawn and follow, but we recognize what we nevertheless cannot avoid. For when we wish to live according to the law, we succumb through weakness [Note: [Col. 0161D] In the autograph, *non* (“not”) is written; it seems to have fallen out by error, since the sense appears rather to require the particle *cum* (“when”).] [Note: [Col. 0161D] The autograph has *succumbimur* (“we are overcome”) instead of *succumbimus* (“we succumb”).]. And the more we recognize what must be avoided yet cannot avoid it, the more deeply we grieve.

In the third stage, that is, under the grace of the Gospel, we are neither drawn nor do we follow; instead, while fighting, we resist the desires of the flesh. Unless we willingly succumb, we overcome with the help of divine grace [Note: [Col. 0161D] The autograph has *superamur* (“we are overcome”) instead of *superamus* (“we overcome”).].

In the fourth stage there will be no struggle against vices, but human beings will be like God and the angels. Through these stages the people of God have passed at successive periods of time.

It should also be noted that the Apostle does not destroy free will, which was granted to the first human being so that, if he wished, he would not sin. But because free will was once weakened, it reached the point that a person sinned even unwillingly. Now, however, by God’s grace, it has been restored and strengthened so that, not only do we not sin, but, with his grace going before and following us, we can fulfill the good that we will.

Next: “But the righteousness of God is through the faith of Jesus Christ upon all [Note: [Col. 0161D] Before *super omnes*, the Vulgate has *in omnes* (“upon all”), and so forth.] who believe.” As stated, he calls grace “righteousness,” because it is not God himself but we who are justified. Likewise, he means by “the faith of Christ” not faith by which Christ believes, but faith by which human beings believe in Christ. Both, therefore, belong to us—that is, both righteousness and faith—yet they are said to belong to God because they are given to us by his generosity.

By “upon all” he means Jews and Greeks alike, the wise and the foolish alike. Hence he immediately adds: “For there is no distinction”—the unstated conclusion being, “between Jew and Greek.” He demonstrates why there is no distinction: “For all have sinned.” The grace of the Savior, when it came, found all as transgressors. Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “God confined all things under sin” (Galatians 3:12).

“And they lack the glory of God.” “Glory,” that is, grace, through which God is glorified.

“Justified freely by his grace.” “Freely,” that is, without any preceding merits.

“Through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus our Lord” [Note: [Col. 0161D] *Our Lord* is absent from the Vulgate.]. By saying “redemption,” he shows that we were captives; and in truth we were held under the captivity of the devil. Hence he says through the prophet: “You were sold because of your crimes, and I dismissed your mother because of your sins” (Isaiah 50:1); and again: “You were sold without payment, and you shall be redeemed without silver.” In certain copies, “without a price” is found, where the unstated meaning is “not your price, but mine.” [Col. 0161D]

The same Apostle speaks elsewhere of this price: “You were bought with a great price” (1 Corinthians 6:10). His fellow Apostle Peter shows what this price is when he says: “You were redeemed from your futile way of life inherited from your ancestors, not with perishable gold or silver, but with the precious blood” [Col. 0162A] [Note: [Col. 0161D] In the First Epistle of the blessed Apostle Peter, verse 19, the Vulgate reads: “but with the precious blood of Christ, as of an unblemished [Note: [Col. 0162D] In other versions, *tanquam* (“as”) is read instead of *quasi* (“as”).] and undefiled Lamb.”] “of the undefiled and immaculate Lamb, Jesus Christ our Lord.”

Next: “Whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood.” God the Father set forth the Son as a propitiation when, before the ages, he predestined him to send him into the world for the redemption of the human race. He made him a propitiation when he offered him to himself upon the altar of the cross for the redemption of human beings.

And he appropriately says: “In his blood.” For forgiveness of sins was accomplished through the shedding of his blood. Hence the same Apostle says: “Without blood there is no forgiveness” (Hebrews 11:22). For this reason the blood of all the animals that were sacrificed in the Temple was commanded to be offered for the expiation of the soul.

“To demonstrate his righteousness.” “Righteousness,” that is, grace.

“Because of the forgiveness of previous sins,” that is, original sins, which are forgiven us through God’s righteousness together with the *amissis* (reading uncertain) [Note: [Col. 0162D] Perhaps *commissis* or *admissis* (“committed,” “admitted”) should be read, meaning actual faults; or perhaps *amissis* (“lost”) is correct in the sense in which Plautus used *amittere*, namely, “to let go of a fault” or “to forgive an offense.”].

In the forbearance of God his righteousness was demonstrated [Note: [Col. 0162D] The autograph has *justitiam* (“righteousness”) instead of *justitia* (“his righteousness”).], because the more abundantly he bears with the weak so that they may be converted, the more clearly he shows himself to be just. For forbearance and patience differ in this respect: forbearance properly concerns those who sin through weakness, whereas patience concerns those who sin rather through will.

And he appropriately adds: “At the present time,” because God has granted this present time to repentance, while he has assigned the future to judgment. Otherwise he would seem to punish the wicked unjustly if he granted them no time for repentance.

“So that he himself may be just and the one who justifies.” He is just in himself and justifies others through himself. For unless he were just, he could not justify others.

And to show that he would not justify everyone, he added: “The one who is of the faith of Jesus Christ.” In this statement he clearly shows that no one can be justified except through the faith of Christ.

Since, therefore, the Jews gloried in the works of the law, he put the question to them, saying [Note: [Col. 0162D] In the autograph’s margin, “Chapter X” is written.]: “Where, then, is your boasting?” It was as though he were saying: If God’s grace found all to be sinners and justified them freely, you have no ground for boasting.

He speaks not of true and praiseworthy boasting but of detestable and false boasting, which arises from pride. And because he had put the question to the Jews, he answered in his own person, saying: “It has been excluded,” that is, cast away and driven out.

And lest they should think that it had been excluded by the law of Moses, he therefore added: “By what law? Of works? No, but by the law of faith.” By “the law of works” he means the law of deeds, that is, the law of Moses, which contains many carnal works, namely, circumcision, new moons, Sabbaths, and the other carnal rites, all of which were performed as figures.

That is the law of works of which he said above: “Through the law of sin,” and elsewhere: “The law entered so that transgression might abound” (Romans 5:20). It is the law of works that commands: “You shall not desire.”

But do not many works also belong to the law of faith? They certainly do, but they are not carnal works, as in the law of Moses. Does the law of faith not say: “You shall not desire”? It certainly does, as many commandments of the Gospel continually testify and proclaim.

What, then, is the difference? It is a great one. What the law of works commands by threatening, the law of faith obtains by believing. In the law of works, God says: “Do what I command.” In the law of faith, one says to God: “Grant what you command.” For the law of faith consists in our praying that God grant us to do what we cannot fulfill by our own power.

In the law of works, righteousness belongs to the God who commands; in the law of faith, it belongs to the mercy that comes to our aid.

And because the Jews could say that a person is justified without the works of the law, he himself responds: “We hold that a person is justified by faith apart from the works of the law” [Note: [Col. 0163D] Between *arbitramur* (“we hold”) and *justificari* (“to be justified”), the Vulgate reads *enim* (“for”).]. Here “we hold” should not be understood as spoken doubtfully but affirmatively. It was as though he were saying: We firmly believe that a person is justified by faith apart from the works of the law.

Great, therefore, is the merit of faith. For it releases past sins, absolves present sins, makes its possessor avoid future sins, and renders him stronger for accomplishing future good.

But what does he mean by saying that a person is justified by faith alone, when elsewhere he says: “It is faith that works through love” (Galatians 5:6)? And his fellow Apostle James says: “Faith without works is dead” (James 2:20).

These apostolic statements are not therefore contrary to one another. The Apostle does not say that a person is justified by faith alone so that, if he lives wickedly after receiving faith, he should be righteous. Rather, if it happens that someone dies immediately after receiving faith, he will be justified by faith alone, even if he was granted no time in which to act.

For the Apostle Paul is not speaking of the works that follow faith but, like James, of those that precede faith. No one can be justified by these, because “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11:6).

“Is God the God of Jews only?” It was as though he were saying: If God were the Creator of the Jews alone, you would rightly say that he sent his Son only for your salvation. But since he is the Creator of all, he sent him for the salvation of all.

And this is what follows: “Is he not also the God of the Gentiles? Yes, of the Gentiles also.” Although *imo* (“yes,” literally “rather”) is usually taken here to mean “also,” in this passage it signifies something stronger.

But why does he say that God is more the God of the Gentiles than of the Jews? Clearly because he foresaw that more of the Gentiles would believe; or because God was the Father of the Gentiles through faith, but of the Jews through circumcision. It is evident, however, that faith is greater than circumcision.

And lest one should think that the God of the Old Testament was different from the God of the New Testament, he added: “Since there is one God, who justifies the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith.” [Col. 0164A] It was as though he were saying: There is one God who justifies circumcised Jews and uncircumcised Gentiles.

When he says “the circumcised by faith” and “the uncircumcised through faith,” he does not do so because of any difference. For elsewhere, speaking of the Gentiles, he says: “Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith” (Galatians 3:8). And speaking of the Jews, from whom he himself came, he says: “We are Jews by nature and not sinners from the Gentiles; yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, and we too have believed in Christ Jesus so that we might be justified” (Galatians 2:15–16). He says “by faith” and “through faith” because of variation in expression.

Up to this point the Apostle seems to have said many things to the detriment of the law. And because a Jew might say: “O Paul, you are destroying the law and nullifying circumcision,” [Col. 0164B] he therefore added: “Do we then destroy the law through faith?” [Note: [Col. 0163D] The Vulgate has *ergo* (“therefore”) instead of *enim* (“for”).]

It was as though he were saying: Because we say that a person can be justified by faith without the works of the law, you say that we are destroying the law. It is not so. [Note: [Col. 0163D–0164D] I do not know how this word slipped from the copyist’s pen, since the author ought rather to have written *accusaremur* (“we would be accused”).] We would rightly be accused of destroying the law if we preached anything other than what the law teaches. For the law itself teaches the same spiritual circumcision that we proclaim is accomplished through faith and the grace of Christ.

Thus it says: “Circumcise the hardness of your heart.” And the prophet says: “Circumcise the foreskins of your hearts.” Since, therefore, we preach nothing other than what the law teaches, we are not destroyers of the law but rather its affirmers.

And this is what follows: “By no means! Rather, we uphold the law.” The law is not destroyed through faith but upheld, because faith obtains grace, through which the law can be fulfilled. Grace heals the will so that free righteousness may be directed.

The law says: “You shall not desire.” Faith, however, cries out: “Heal my soul, Lord, for I have sinned against you” (Psalm 40:5). Grace says: “See, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14).

(CAP. IV.) [Note: [Col. 0164D] Here begins chapter IV of the Epistle, according to the division of the Vulgate.]

And as though he were saying, “Then the Jew has gained nothing through bodily circumcision,” he immediately added: “For what [Note: [Col. 0164D] The Vulgate has *ergo* (“therefore”).] shall we say that Abraham our father found according to the flesh?” For Abraham could not have found anything that he might be said to have obtained “according to the flesh,” that is, through bodily circumcision, since neither did he receive the promise of the land of Canaan, nor the increase of his offspring, nor the blessing when he was circumcised.

He continues: “For if Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not before God.” As though he were saying: “If Abraham was justified by works, he certainly has glory before human beings, but not before God, because he does not possess that glory by which God is glorified: he was justified not by God’s grace, but by his own merits.” For someone may appear good before human beings through good works without faith, or through faith without good works, but not before God. For just as good works are worthless without faith, so faith, as time proceeds, is worthless unless good works follow.

And, in order to confirm his account by the testimony of Genesis, he added: “For what does Scripture say?” That is: “From what does Scripture say that Abraham was justified—from works or from faith?” Certainly from faith: “For Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness” (Gal. III, 6). Here it should be noted that he does not say, “He was circumcised,” but “He believed,” because he was justified by faith.

“But to the one who works, the reward is not counted according to grace, but according to debt.” The meaning is: To the one who works, that is, who presumes upon his works, the reward is not counted according to grace, but according to debt, because he is justified by his own merits. The Apostle is speaking here according to human practice: when someone gives another person something in order to receive something in return, the reward is not counted to him according to grace, because he has given nothing freely. But it is not so with God, because he has received nothing from a human being for which he should render something in return. Hence he says to Job: “Who has given to me first, that I should repay him?” (Job XLI, 2.) Likewise, elsewhere the same Apostle says: “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, so that no one may boast” (Eph. II, 8).

Hence it is immediately added: “But to the one who does not work, yet believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness.” To the one who does not work, that is, who does not presume upon works and does not believe that he has obtained grace through his own merits, his faith is counted as righteousness, just as Abraham’s was. But, lest the Apostle seem to have meant that faith was counted as righteousness for everyone, he prefaced the statement with “to the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly.”

Here it should be noted that he does not say, “to the one who believes him.” To believe God is to place one’s faith in his promises; to believe in God is to place all one’s hope in him.

And, in order to confirm his account by the testimony of the Psalmist, he added: “As David also speaks of the blessedness of the person to whom God counts righteousness without works,” that is, to whom God freely and willingly grants justification:

“Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven,  
and whose sins are covered.  
Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Ps. XXXI, 1–2).

Here it should be noted that the Psalmist seems to speak of three things: iniquities being forgiven, sins being covered, and sin not being imputed. Hence some say that iniquities are forgiven through repentance, whereas sin is not imputed in martyrdom. But it should be noted that he does not say, “in whom sins are not found,” but “whose sins are covered.” Hence blessed Gregory says: “When we wish to conceal something for which we are guilty, we place something over it so that it may not be seen; so too, by placing not only confession but also good works over our sins, we cover them, so that God may not notice them—that is, punish them.” Hence the same Psalmist says: “Turn your face away from my sins” (Ps. L, 11).

We therefore ought to believe without hesitation that all these things take place in baptism. Nor can there be any greater blessedness than to obtain forgiveness of all sins without any labor of repentance.

But, behold, he proposes the question to the Jew, adding: “Does this blessedness, then, remain in circumcision [Note: [Col. 0165D] The Vulgate has: ‘Does it remain in circumcision alone, or also…’], or also in uncircumcision?” While the question remained suspended, he continued: “For we say that faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness.” As though he were saying: “We are certain [Note: [Col. 0165D] The autograph has *certissimus* (“most certain”) in place of *certi sumus* (“we are certain”).] about the justification; but we are asking about the time.” This is what follows: “How, then, was it counted? In circumcision, [Note: [Col. 0166D] The words ‘when he was’ are not found in the Vulgate reading.] when he was circumcised, or in uncircumcision?”

And while the Jew remained suspended and dared not answer, lest he be caught by his own words, he answered himself, saying: “Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision.” If we observe these words carefully, the Apostle seems to say that Abraham was named at the time when he was called not Abraham but Abram. He did this because he knew that everything predestined by God remains fixed and immutable.

And as though some Jew were saying, “Why did Abraham receive circumcision if he obtained no blessedness through it?” he immediately added: “And he received the sign of circumcision, the seal of the righteousness of faith that he had while in uncircumcision.” As though he were saying: “He received circumcision not for blessedness or justification, but as a sign.”

Here it should be noted that he uses two terms, “sign” and “seal,” which may perhaps be identical; but, if we attend carefully, there is a great distinction. A sign is something that signifies something other than what it is. Thus, when the Jews asked the Lord for signs, he says: “An adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah” (Matt. XII, 39). Here he shows that nearly everything that happened in connection with Jonah pertains to himself.

For this reason Simeon also says of the Lord: “Behold, this child is set for the falling and for a sign” (Luke II, 34). The Son of God is rightly called a sign, because he appeared to be one thing—namely, a human being—but was believed to be another—namely, God.

Carnal circumcision, therefore, is rightly called a sign, because it signified the spiritual circumcision that takes place through the grace and faith of Christ. For it signified the author of regeneration himself, namely the Lord Jesus Christ, through whose grace hearts are cleansed and consciences purified.

A seal, however, is something placed temporarily upon an object that is to be kept, so that it may not be opened by anyone other than the one who placed it. That circumcision, therefore, is rightly called a seal, because it was given to the Jews as a seal, so that it might not be opened or removed by anyone other than the one who placed it.

Hence the same Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. IV, 4), because this would not take place before what he says elsewhere had been fulfilled: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved” (Rom. II, 25). It is rightly called a seal.

Why he received the seal of circumcision is disclosed when he adds: “That he might be the father of all who believe through uncircumcision [Note: [Col. 0167D] The Vulgate has ‘through,’ rather than ‘because of,’] so that righteousness might be counted to them also; and the father of circumcision.”

He appropriately says “of all who believe,” because Abraham, while uncircumcised, became the father of the uncircumcised through believing, whereas, once circumcised, he became the father of the Jews. For all who believe while uncircumcised pass into the dignity of Abraham’s offspring, and faith is counted to them as righteousness, just as it was to Abraham. This is what is meant by “so that faith might be counted to them also as righteousness.”

But, if we attend more carefully, the Apostle seems by these words to show that uncircumcision and circumcision are one and the same, since all who imitate Abraham’s footsteps of faith become his children and are circumcised in heart, not in body; and their uncircumcision is counted as circumcision. Thus Abraham is the father of circumcision, that is, of all believers.

Hence it is immediately added: “Not only to those who are of the circumcision, but also to those who follow the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had in uncircumcision.” [Note: [Col. 0167D] The Vulgate has *quae* where this text has *quod*; some other readings, instead of *quae est*, have *quae fuit*.]

Nevertheless, it must be asked why the Apostle placed uncircumcision before circumcision. The answer is that he foresaw that more people would first believe from the Gentiles than from the Jews. Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord has made known his salvation in the sight of the nations” (Ps. XCVII, 2). And shortly afterward: “He remembered his mercy toward Jacob” (ibid., 3). Simeon likewise says: “A light for revelation to the Gentiles, and the glory of your people Israel” (Luke II, 32).

The Apostle had earlier begun to speak about the law against those who thought that the promise made to Abraham had been fulfilled through the law. Continuing the argument he had begun, he says: “For the promise to Abraham or to his offspring, that he should be heir of the world, was not through the law, but through the righteousness of faith.” As though he were saying: “It is not as you say. The law, which was given after many cycles of years, could not fulfill the promise made to Abraham under oath, because that promise was neither made through the law nor fulfilled through the law.”

Hence, speaking to the Galatians, he says among other things: “The law, made four hundred and thirty years afterward, does not render the promise void so as to abolish it” (Gal. III, 17). [Note: [Col. 0167D] In the Vulgate, chapter III, verse 17, the wording is: “The law, which was made four hundred and thirty years afterward, does not render it void so as to abolish the promise.”]

But, in order to show through whom it was fulfilled, he added: “But through the righteousness of faith,” that is, because Abraham was justified by faith, as were the Gentiles.

He continues: “For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith has been emptied and the promise abolished.” The meaning is: If you alone are heirs who received circumcision through the law, then the faith of Christ has been annulled. But this is not so.

Hence he immediately gives the reason, adding: “For the law produces wrath.” As we have often said, he calls vengeance “wrath.” The law therefore produces wrath because it does not preach repentance, saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matt. III, 2), but rather, “If anyone does this or that, let him die.”

And because the Jews might say, “Does the law produce wrath only for us?” he therefore added: “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression.”

But is there no transgression among the Gentiles, who did not receive the law of Moses? Who would dare say this, when the same Apostle says elsewhere: “All who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law”? How, then, is this to be understood? It is as though he were saying in other words: “Where there is no commandment, the transgression is less.” Hence the word “so great” is appropriately understood, so that the order of the words is: “Where there is no law, there is not so great a transgression.”

And appropriately so, because the more knowingly someone sins, the more severely he will be punished. [Note: [Col. 0168D] The autograph has *puniretur* (“would be punished”).] Hence blessed Augustine says: “Everyone who passes beyond the law is unrighteous; yet not every unrighteous person passes beyond the law.” Those who sin without having received the law may therefore be called unrighteous, but they cannot be called transgressors.

But we must consider which law the Apostle is discussing here. Is it the written law? This interpretation is possible, but it is more appropriate to understand him as speaking of the law of nature. For human beings, while they are still in early childhood, scarcely recognize what ought or ought not to be done. Therefore, although there is some small [Note: [Col. 0168D] The autograph has *prava* (“wrong”) instead of *parva* (“small”).] fault, there is nevertheless guilt. But when they reach the years of rational maturity, the more clearly they understand what they ought to do, the more severely they will be punished if they sin [Note: [Col. 0168D] The autograph has *dereliquerint* (“if they abandon [it]”); perhaps correct, but less fitting.]. Hence the Psalmist says: “I have counted all the sinners of the earth as transgressors” (Ps. CXVIII, 119). For not all sinners were transgressors of the Mosaic law, since not all received it; rather, they were transgressors of the law of nature.

Therefore the promise was fulfilled through faith—this is understood—so that, according to grace, the promise might be firm for all the offspring, that is, for both Jew and Gentile. And it should be noted that he does not say “according to merit” or “according to observance of the law,” but “according to grace,” because the Gentiles were justified by God’s grace alone.

It was not for the one who is of the law alone, that is, for the one who passes from the Old Testament to the grace of the New, but also for the one who is of Abraham’s faith, that is, for the imitator of Abraham’s faith, who is the father of us all, both Jews and Gentiles.

And, in order to confirm this by the testimony of Genesis, he added: “As it is written: I have appointed you the father of many nations before God.” By “many,” not merely some, we should understand all. Accordingly, it is written in the same book: “In your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII, 18).

But what follows—“before God, whom you believed” [Note: [Col. 0168D] The autograph has *credidistis* (“you believed”).]—is not found in the book of Genesis. Rather, the Apostle added it on his own in explanation, wishing to show that Abraham was justified by faith. The meaning is: “Before God, whom you believed, you were appointed to be the father of many nations.”

“He gives life to the dead.” Here we must understand “the dead” not bodily but spiritually, in accordance with the saying: “The soul that sins shall die.” For just as a body is dead when it has eyes and the other senses but cannot exercise their functions, so the soul is dead when it lacks all these senses together with their functions: it has no eyes with which it can see God, no ears with which it can hear God’s commandments, no nostrils with which it can bring forth the fragrance of a good reputation, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying, “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (II Cor. II, 15); no mouth with which it can taste how sweet the Lord is; no hands with which, according to John’s words, it can handle the word of life; and no feet for which the word of God may be a lamp, enabling it to walk in the law of the Lord.

The Lord gives life to such people by inspiring them, so that, though dead in vices, they may live by virtues; and, by believing in him, may pass into the dignity of Abraham’s offspring, so that faith may be counted to them as righteousness.

He continues: “And he calls those things that are not as though they were.” Existence belongs properly to God alone, for in him existence cannot be otherwise or different. For him, to be is simply to be. But existence does not properly belong to creatures, because they can exist otherwise and differently.

The same Apostle makes this clear when, speaking to the Ephesians [Note: [Col. 0169D] These words are not found in the Epistle to the Ephesians, but in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter I, verse 19.], he says among other things: “The Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, who was preached among you through us, through me and Silvanus and Timothy, was not Yes and No, but Yes was in him.” Hence the Lord says to Moses: “I am who I am,” and, “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. III, 14).

Therefore all who merit to be joined to God through faith are themselves as those of whom the Lord bears witness, saying: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” He therefore calls those things that are not so that they may be, as though they were: by predestining and inspiring those who are not joined to him through faith, he calls them to believe in him and to be like those who are already joined to him through faith.

“Against hope”—that is, against the hope of human nature—“he believed in hope” [Note: [Col. 0169D] The Vulgate has *spem* (“hope,” accusative) in place of *spe* (“in hope,” ablative).], namely, in the hope of divine grace. For he believed in hope against hope because he held most firmly that what Sarah, while a young girl, had been unable to accomplish, she could now, as an old woman aided by divine grace, accomplish: namely, bear a son in whom all the nations would be blessed.

This is what follows: “So that he might become the father of many nations, according to what was said to him: So shall your offspring be” (Gen. XV, 5). Here it should be noted that the Apostle has stated concisely what is written at length in the book of Genesis. There we read that the Lord led Abraham outside and said: “Look up at the sky and count the stars, if you can; so shall your offspring be. I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the seashore.”

This was said hyperbolically. From the first human being to the last, there will not be so many human beings that they can be compared with the stars of heaven or the sand of the sea, especially since there have not been so many that they could equal the other nations in number. But because human beings were innumerable, like the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea, they were compared with them. To God, however, from whom neither the number of blades of grass nor of grains of sand is hidden, they were certainly countable.

“And he did not grow weak in faith,” as did Zechariah, who hesitated to believe the angelic promises. “And he did not consider his own body, already dead, since he was nearly a hundred years old, nor the dead womb of Sarah,” that is, he did not consider that he could beget a son.

“And concerning the renewed promise also, he did not waver in distrust.” [Note: [Col. 0169D] The Vulgate has *Dei* (“of God”) between *etiam* (“also”) and *non* (“not”).] Here it should be noted that the text does not say “in the promise,” but “in the renewed promise.” [Note: [Col. 0169D] The autograph has *repromissione* (“renewed promise”), but it seemed necessary to emend it. Some biblical copies nevertheless read *promissione* (“promise”) here.]

At first he hesitated when he said: “Lord God, what will you give me? For behold, the son of the steward of my house, this Damascus-born man, will be my heir” (Gen. XV, 3). But after the Lord said to him, “This man shall not be your heir, but one who will come from your own womb shall be your heir,” he did not hesitate; rather, he held most firmly that what nature had withheld from him could be fulfilled by divine favor.

This is what follows: “But he was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, fully convinced that whatever he had promised, he was able also to do.” Here it should be noted that he does not say, “Whatever he foreknew, he was able to promise,” or “Whatever he promised, he was able to foresee,” but “Whatever he promised, he was able to do,” showing that the one who makes people good is himself the one who makes them persevere in goodness.

“And because he believed most firmly in him, it was counted to him as righteousness”; that is, he was justified by faith.

“Now it was not written for his sake alone that it was counted to him.” He says this aptly, because many cycles of years passed between the time when this promise was made to Abraham and the time when the law was written; therefore Abraham could not have read it. And, in order to show for whose sake it was written, he added: “But also for our sake” [Note: [Col. 0170D] The Vulgate has “but also for the sake of.”], for whom it will be counted, who believe in him. By this statement he includes all believers, for whose sake it was written, so that by reading they might believe and faith might be counted to them as righteousness.

In what follows—“who raised our Lord Jesus Christ from the dead”—the person of the Father is intended. Yet the Father alone did not raise him; the Son and the Holy Spirit also did so, because the action of the whole Trinity is involved in the mention of one person.

Likewise, in what follows—“who was handed over for our offenses and rose for our justification”—he says that he was handed over by the Father. Nevertheless, the Son also handed himself over. Hence the same Apostle says: “He handed himself over for us as an offering.” The Holy Spirit did likewise, since the operation of the whole Trinity is inseparable.

In the fact that he handed himself over willingly, he is shown to be merciful; in the fact that he rose by his own power, he is shown to be almighty. In this deed he left us an example of dying to vices and rising to virtues, or so that in baptism we might die and be buried with him, and rise in newness of life.

Hence the same Apostle says: “For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. VI, 4).

He continues: [Note: [Col. 0171D] The Vulgate has chapter V.] [Note: [Col. 0171D] In the autograph margin: chapter XI.]

(CAP. V.) “Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace.” Because the Jews gloried in their knowledge of God or of the law, while the Gentiles gloried in their new and recent calling—and for this reason they were greatly at odds with one another—the Apostle, in order to show that they were all sinners, had earlier said: “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God.” He showed that they had all turned aside and become useless, and that there was no one who did good, not even one.

Having now completed this argument, he admonishes them what they ought to do and exhorts them to have peace with one another, saying: “Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace.” As though he were saying: “Since no one is saved by merits or observance of the law, but we have all been saved by God’s grace and justified by faith, we ought no longer to be at variance, but let us have peace.”

And because there is also a peace belonging to the wicked, he therefore added “with God,” that is, according to God. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “Not as the world gives do I give to you” (John XIV, 27).

“Through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have also obtained access by faith” [Note: [Col. 0172D] The Vulgate has “through faith.”]. He aptly says “access,” because just as someone enters a house or a church through a door, so through Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, we have access to the Father. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV, 6). And again: “I am the door” (John X, 9), and so forth.

What sort of access we have is disclosed when he adds: “Into this grace.” He calls the adoption of sons “grace,” by which the faithful, their sins released, become adopted children of God. He says “in which we stand” to show that previously we had lain in the mire of sins. For he stood upon the stronghold of faith and virtues who said: “The Lord lives, before whom I stand” (IV Kings V, 16).

“And we glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God.” It should be noted that he does not say “in glory,” but “in the hope of glory.” We do indeed now possess the glory of the children of God, but in hope; nevertheless, one day we shall possess it in reality. Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “We walk by faith, and not by sight” (II Cor. V, 7). And John says: “Beloved, we are now children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be” (I John III, 2).

“Not only so”—that is, not only do we glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God—“but we also glory in tribulations.” Why do the saints glory in tribulations? Because through light and momentary tribulations they understand that they are reaching joys that will endure without end. Hence James says: “Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various trials” (James I, 2). And again: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation” (ibid., 12), and so forth.

The saints also glory in inward tribulations, because they restrain lust, moderate gluttony, and repress the enticements of the flesh.

Why the saints glory in tribulations is disclosed when he adds: “Knowing that tribulation produces patience” (ibid., 3). *Patientia* (“patience”) is derived from *pati* (“to suffer”), or, as some maintain, from *pavere* (“to fear”); both etymologies are agreeable. For when the saints suffer, they are indeed afraid, but they endure patiently.

“Patience produces probation.” Probation is a perfect and noble state of mind. Hence a person is rightly called *probus* (“upright”) who brings an undertaking of good work properly to completion.

“Probation produces hope.” Hope is desire for future goods. Hence *spes* (“hope”) is said almost as though it were *est pes* (“it is a foot”): just as someone moves toward a definite place on foot, so the saints hasten toward eternal joys by the virtue of hope.

Conversely, among evils there is despair. For the person who despairs has no desire to proceed. “But hope does not disappoint,” because it does not fear. It does not instill fear but rather drives it away. Hence John says: “Perfect love casts out fear” (I John IV, 18).

Why hope does not disappoint is disclosed when he adds: “Because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts.” He speaks of love as poured out in order to indicate its breadth. Hence the Psalmist says: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. CXVIII, 96).

Love has indeed been poured out because we are commanded to love not only God but also our neighbor—not only our friends in God, but even our enemies for God’s sake.

But, lest anyone suppose that the love of God had been poured into him through his own merits or observance of the law, he added: “Through the Holy Spirit.” Again, lest he be thought to possess the same Holy Spirit from himself, he added: “Who has been given to us.” For the one who gave the Holy Spirit to human beings is the one who, by his power, took our captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings.

Therefore, in order to show the immeasurable force of love, he added: [Note: [Col. 0172D] In the autograph margin: chapter XII.] “For why, when we were still weak, did Christ, at the appointed time, die for the ungodly?” (The implied meaning is: “if not to show how greatly he loved the human race?”)

God the Father showed immense love and overflowing compassion toward the human race when he handed over his Son for it; and the Son himself showed the same when he was willing to die for the ungodly.

For when the Apostle adds: “Hardly will anyone die for a righteous person; perhaps someone might dare to die for a good person,” and Christ died for the ungodly, he shows an incredible and unheard-of love.

But it should be understood that when he speaks of “the righteous” and “the good,” this does not refer to particular persons, as certain heretics wished, interpreting “the good” as the Son and “the righteous” as the Father. Rather, as blessed Jerome says, it refers to something righteous or good.

Some have understood “the righteous” as the righteousness of the Old Testament, and “the good” as the grace of the New, so that the meaning is: “Hardly will anyone die for the righteous,” because scarcely anyone has been found willing to die for the righteousness of the Old Testament; “but perhaps someone might dare to die for the good,” because it was easier to find someone who would surrender himself to death for the grace of the Gospel.

[Note: [Col. 0173] It should be noted that the wording “but perhaps someone might dare to die for the good” is interrogative in the Vulgate, but is written and expounded positively here.]

And it should be noted that, although scarcely anyone dies for the righteous, and someone might dare to die for the good, the Lord was willing to die not only for the ungodly but also at the fitting time.

This is what the Apostle means by “at the appointed time,” that is, according to the appropriateness of the time. Hence the prophet himself says: “In an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you” (Isa. XLIX, 8). Explaining this, the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI, 2).

For he was willing to die at the time when all had turned aside, all together had become useless, and there was no one who did good, not even one.

Finally, it should be understood that, by saying “perhaps someone might dare to die for the good,” the Apostle, although modestly, wished his own person to be included in the statement; he showed that he and all the faithful were prepared to die for Christ.

He continues: “But God commends his love toward us.” God commends his love toward us because he grants us forgiveness of sins though it is not owed to us, and because he hands over his Son for the ungodly.

When the one who owed nothing paid the debt of death to the devil, in order to rescue us, who were held by the deserved obligation of death, he certainly commended his love toward us. Hence he says through the Prophet: “What I did not seize, I then repaid” (Ps. LXVIII, 5).

“For if, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, much more, having now been justified in his blood, shall we be saved from wrath through him.” He calls those justified who have been freed from the bonds of sins. And he aptly says “in his blood,” because no justification can take place without his blood. Hence in the Old Testament no purification was performed without the sprinkling of blood.

By “wrath” he means the vengeance of eternal condemnation.

“For if, while we were enemies…” We were enemies of God because of original sin, for it had separated us from God. But we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son. By saying “reconciled,” he shows that we were held captive by the devil.

Yet this must not be understood as though, just as human beings are first at odds with one another and afterward reconciled, so we had first been at odds with God and were afterward reconciled. For even before we were reconciled, we were loved by the Lord.

Hence the same Apostle says: “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph. I, 4); and elsewhere: “He loved us and washed us from our sins” (Rev. I, 5). John likewise says: “Let us love God, because he first loved us” (I John IV, 19).

But the question arises: How can the Apostle say that we were chosen and loved before reconciliation, when the Prophet says, “You hate all who work iniquity” (Ps. V, 7)? For if we were sinners, we worked iniquity; how, then, were we loved if God hates those who work iniquity?

There is no contradiction if we observe the matter carefully. God hates by loving, and loves by hating. In every person God has something to love and something to hate: he loves what he himself made, and he hates what the human being himself did at the devil’s prompting. In each sinner he loves the benefit of mercy and hates the judgment of condemnation.

Furthermore, it should be noted that these words seem to sound as though we had God the Father as angry and the Son as pacified. But the Apostle does not think this, for elsewhere he says: “He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Rom. VIII, 32).

Therefore God the Father did not hand over an unwilling Son, nor did the Son hand himself over against the Father’s will. Rather, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit of them both handed him over.

It should be noted, moreover, that he calls the same people sinners whom he calls enemies of God; those whom he calls justified in the blood of Christ, he calls reconciled through the death of his Son; and those whom he calls saved from wrath through him, he calls destined to be saved by his life. It should also be understood that he first mentioned two conditions, the ungodly and the weak, and called us by two names, one of which is very mild and the other extremely harsh. Weakness is something comparatively slight, but it is a kind of weakness designated by the term “ungodliness,” since, unless there were need, it would not require a physician. And because he first mentioned two conditions, he consequently supplied two corresponding terms, namely, sinners and enemies of God. For he calls the ungodly enemies of God, and in truth we were devoted to such sins that we deserved to be called God’s enemies.

But, having been reconciled to God, we shall be saved by his life. Beautifully he says “by his life,” since, if he died for the ungodly and enemies, he will much more give life to his friends. Not only that—we are to understand, “we shall be saved”—but “we also glory in God.” Beautifully he says “in God,” because it is written: “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord” (II Cor. X, 17). And because no one can glory in God except through the Lord Jesus Christ, he added: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.”

By “reconciliation” he means justification, which was accomplished in his blood. For it should be understood that, by a certain justice of God, the human race was handed over to the devil; yet God himself did not hand it over, but permitted it to be handed over. For as soon as Adam sinned, when the Creator withdrew from him, the author of sin invaded humanity. Yet God did not abandon him completely, because he always sustained him by his benefits. And because humanity was handed over by a certain justice, it was fitting that the devil should be defeated not by power but by justice. This was accomplished by our Lord and Redeemer.

For he came in the likeness of sinful flesh, while having no sin whatsoever. Therefore, believing him to be merely a man, the devil killed the innocent one. Since, then, he killed an innocent man, it was fitting that he should lose those who believe in Christ, whom he had previously held liable under the debt of death and sin. The Apostle therefore calls this justification reconciliation.

Accordingly, just as through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned—it is to be understood that, just as this happened, so life returned through one man. By “the world” he means the human race from the first man. For in truth matters stood as the Apostle says. The human race was lying prostrate and was being hurled from evil to evil; and because it had been joined to the angels when they sinned, it was consequently paying the penalties of its own abandonment and condemnation.

For this reason the Apostle is compelled to assume two persons in himself: one of the first Adam, through whom sin entered the world, and the other of the second Adam, through whom life returned. He speaks at length about them.

It should be understood, moreover, that by these words the Apostle destroys the error of the Pelagians, who are accustomed to say that human beings acquire original sin from Adam not by being born but by imitation, and therefore that the sacrament of baptism ought not to be given to infants, since there would be no original sin to be wiped away. For they say:

“Whenever people wish to sin, they take an example from the first man, and by imitating him they advance to many sins.”

The Apostle refutes such people, saying: “Therefore, and so forth” [Note: In the autograph, instead of “and so forth” there is clearly written “et Isrl,” that is, “and Israel.” Since I have been unable to make this fit either the citation or the sense in any way, I thought it preferable to emend it. Whether I have erred, let the reader judge. In the meantime, in justification of my decision, I add that these final words—“and so forth”—are always, or almost always, found abbreviated in the autograph, as is also *et coet.* (“and the rest”). Perhaps he also intended “and the rest,” which is almost always found written in this way [Col. 0176D] as “et r. l.” At that point, the words, or rather the letters, would evidently have been inserted incorrectly beforehand; the same thing can be found elsewhere above.]

For if human beings acquired original sin not by being born but by imitation, he would not say “through one man,” but “through the devil,” of whom it is written: “The devil sins from the beginning” (I John III, 8), and of whom we read in the Book of Wisdom: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wis. II, 24). And to show from Scripture that death did not come upon human beings from the devil as though they had been propagated from him, but because they imitate him, he added: “But those who belong to his side imitate him” (ibid., 25).

The Apostle, therefore, wishing to show that Adam was the author of original sin, says: “Just as through one man sin entered the world”—namely, original sin—“and through sin death,” because death became the punishment of original sin, “and so it passed into all human beings,” because no one lives who will not die, “in whom all sinned.”

If the phrase “in whom” is referred to sin, it plainly destroys the Pelagian heresy, since all offenses were committed in that one sin. But if it is referred to the person of Adam, it destroys that heresy even more clearly. For all sinned in that one man who sinned, because, as blessed Augustine says, all human beings were that one man. And when he was driven from paradise, so were we all, because we were in his loins—as we read of Levi, who was in Abraham’s loins when Abraham himself offered tithes to Melchizedek (Hebr. VII, 9–10).

“Until the law, sin was in the world.”

What does the Apostle wish to show by this statement? Does he mean that after the law there was no sin in the world? He therefore wishes to show that the law was of such a kind that it could not abolish sin. This is the meaning of the words “until the law, sin was in the world,” as though one were to say: “It was indeed there, but it was not recognized.” Thus he shows that through the law the knowledge of sin came about. By “sin” he means original sin, and by “the law” the written law.

It can also be referred to the law of nature. For as long as people are in early childhood, they scarcely recognize what ought or ought not to be done. Consequently, although sin exists in them, it is as though it did not, because they do not know that it is sin.

It follows:

“But sin was not counted when there was no law.”

It was not counted because it was not thought to be sin. It should be noted that he does not say “it did not exist,” but “it was not counted.” It existed among human beings, [Col. 0176B] but it was not recognized. [Note: The sense makes clear that the particle *non*, perhaps omitted from the autograph through inadvertence, ought to have been written.] Hence the Apostle says above: “All who sinned without the law will also perish without the law.”

“But death reigned from Adam to Moses” [Note: In the autograph, in the margin, chapter XIII is indicated.]

Here Moses figuratively signifies the law; for by the giver of the law the law itself is designated. Therefore death reigned from Adam to Moses, that is, from the first man to the law.

When he says “to the law,” we should not understand “up to the beginning of the law,” but “up to its end.” For it is as though someone were to say: “The Jews reigned until Jeconiah.” Here one should understand not the beginning of Jeconiah’s reign but its end, when they were transferred to Babylon.

He says beautifully “reigned,” because death had invaded every part of the world. But what does it mean that he says death reigned until Moses? Did it not reign afterward? Human beings die every day.

It should therefore be understood that here the Apostle wishes the reign of death to be understood. At first death reigned universally, because it barred everyone from access to the heavenly kingdom. It reigned, then, but only until the end of the law, that is, until Christ. For, as the Apostle says: “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X, 4). He is the end not in the sense of destruction, but of completion and fulfillment.

But after divine mercy poured itself from heaven upon the earth, and consented to die for us, by his death he destroyed the dominion of death. Rising again, he restored life to us; then, ascending into heaven, he opened for us the door of the heavenly kingdom. Consequently, death can no longer reign over everyone, because it cannot bar the elect from access to the heavenly kingdom.

For it is one thing for a plague to reign broadly and generally over all, and another for it to reign over only a few. Death therefore reigns, but only until baptism. For there we die and are buried with Christ, and rise with him, so that we may walk in newness of life.

But, lest anyone believe that he had been freed from death by his own merits, he added: “Even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” [Note: The Vulgate has *in eos*, “over them.” The particle *cum*, which, in my judgment, was incorrectly inserted before the verb in the autograph, is lying there and should be omitted.]

That is, they did not sin by their own will as Adam did, but through the weakness of the flesh, like the patriarchs, the prophets, and certain Gentiles in whom the natural power of wisdom was so strong that they added no criminal sins to original sin.

“Who is the form of those who were to come” [Note: The Vulgate has *futuri*, “of the one to come.”]

Some copies have *futuri*, so that the phrase may be referred to Christ. Adam was the form of the one to come, because, just as death entered through him, so life returned through Christ. Hence a little farther on the Apostle says: “Just as through the disobedience of one man the many were constituted sinners, so through the obedience of one the many will be constituted righteous.”

If it is read as *futuris*, “of those who were to come,” it should be understood as referring to descendants. Adam, therefore, was a form of those who were to come, because he was an example of sin and condemnation [Note: In the autograph, chapter XIV is indicated in the margin.]

“But not as the offense, so also the gift.”

These words seem elliptical. Yet one may supply: “Not as the offense corrupted us, so the gift of God restored us.” The following words make their meaning clear:

“For if, through the offense of one, the many died, much more the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abounded to the many.”

It is as though he were saying: That original sin was so great that it was sufficient to destroy everyone; but the gift of God not only freed them from that sin, but also forgives all their other sins.

But what does he mean by saying, “The grace of God abounded much more to the many,” when more are lost than saved? To prevent this from seeming contradictory, the phrase “much more” should not be referred to the persons—that is, to “more”—but to the verb “abounded.” For the grace of God abounded much more because it releases not only from original sin but also from offenses committed by one’s own will.

Alternatively, he says “much more to the many” because, although the wicked seem numerous, they are few, since they are nothing. The good, although they seem few, are nevertheless many, because God’s grace in them is great.

“And not as through one who sinned, so also the gift” [Note: Thus some editions read it; the Vulgate, however, has *attamen peccatum*, “yet the sin.”]

These words also seem elliptical. Yet one may supply: “Not as through one who sinned we were lost, so the gift of God redeems us.” The Apostle explains their meaning, adding:

“For the judgment indeed was from one offense unto condemnation.”

When he says “from one,” “offense” must be supplied. He explains this himself by adding:

“But the gift was from many offenses unto justification.”

By these words he destroys the error of the Pelagians. For he shows that people draw original sin not by imitation but by being born.

But Pelagius says: What he says, “from one,” should be referred to Adam. Human beings take an example of sinning from Adam, and by imitating him advance to many sins. Yet if the Apostle held this view, he would not say “the gift was from many offenses unto justification,” but “from one.”

It should also be understood that the Pelagians are accustomed to say to the faithful: “From where do human beings draw original sin—from marriage, from parents, or from the will?” There is nothing that should be answered to them in these questions. Hear the Apostle saying: “The judgment was from one unto condemnation.”

But what does he mean by saying, “The judgment was from one unto condemnation”? Does judgment lead to condemnation from only one sin, namely original sin, and not from the other sins? For if the grace of God releases not only from original sin but also from sins of one’s own will, then judgment likewise leads to condemnation not from original sin alone but also from the other sins that are added to it.

What, then, does he wish to show by these words? Clearly, that original sin was so great that it was sufficient for condemnation even if nothing were added to it, although the punishment of those who add sins of their own is more severe, and all the more severe the more gravely each person has sinned.

Therefore, from one—that is, from Adam—we draw not all our sins but original sin alone. From the one Christ, however, we receive remission not only of original sin but of all sins.

The Apostle had begun to distinguish original sin from the grace of God, and, continuing the intention he had begun, he says:

“For if, through the offense of one, death reigned through one, much more those who receive the abundance of grace, gift, and righteousness will reign in life through the one Jesus Christ” [Note: The particle *si enim* does not occur in the Vulgate.]

He calls the offense of one original sin, which Adam committed in paradise. But how did death reign through one in the offense of one? Clearly, because everyone was bound by the chain of death in that one offense alone, even if they added nothing by their own will.

The faithful therefore receive the abundance of grace and gift because they are forgiven not only that original sin but also the other sins they have added. They also receive an abundance of righteousness, because God bestows on them such righteousness that they may be justified, so that, whereas Adam in paradise consented to the devil when he persuaded him to sin, they yield or consent neither to one who persuades nor even to one who compels.

But what does he mean by saying, “They will reign much more,” when the kingdom of death draws more people into punishment than grace draws into eternal life? The phrase must therefore not be referred to persons or to their number, but to the increase of God’s grace.

For they will reign much more because all who pass from Adam to Christ—that is, from death to life—will reign with him forever in eternal life. Or he says “much more” because those whom death destroyed temporarily, the grace of God has made alive eternally. [Note: In the margin of the autograph, “D. V after Pentecost” is marked; perhaps these notes, or homilies, on this portion of St. Paul’s epistle were customarily read on the fifth Sunday after Pentecost.]

Therefore, just as through one offense condemnation came upon all human beings, so also through one righteousness justification of life came upon all human beings.

In these words, if we attend to imitation, as the Pelagians claim, the “offense of one” would belong to no one other than the devil. But because the Apostle is appropriately speaking of Adam, no imitation is to be understood here, but the propagation of sin.

He therefore says: “Just as through one offense”—we are to supply, “death reigned”—“condemnation came upon all human beings, so also through one righteousness”—we are to supply, “grace reigned”—“justification of life came upon all human beings.”

By “the righteousness of one man” he means the righteousness of Jesus Christ, by which he justifies the ungodly. He did not propose this righteousness for imitation; rather, he alone can accomplish it, for he is “free among the dead” (Ps. LXXXVII, 6). Neither Peter nor Paul possessed this power, because neither could justify the ungodly.

If, then, imitation alone makes sinners through Adam, why does imitation alone not make righteous through Christ? Far from it. Christ is rightly called one because it is not his imitation alone that makes people righteous, but grace, which regenerates through the Holy Spirit.

Adam likewise is called one because it is not his imitation alone that makes people sinners, but also the punishment of sin, which gives birth through death. Therefore he rightly says there, “upon all human beings unto condemnation,” but here, “upon all human beings unto justification.” For not all who are generated through Adam are themselves regenerated through Christ.

He therefore says “all” in the first case because no one’s carnal generation exists except through Adam; and “all” in the second because no one’s spiritual generation exists except through Christ.

Thus, by “all unto condemnation,” he means those born through Adam and belonging to carnal generation; by “all unto justification,” those born through Christ and belonging to spiritual generation.

Note that those whom he calls “all” here he calls “many” a little later. There is no contradiction. For “many” can be said of people in some respect even when they are few.

For example, if we say: “There is one midwife in the city who receives all, and one teacher of letters who teaches all,” we cannot understand that she receives all the inhabitants of the city or that he teaches them all. She is said to receive all because no one is born except through her hands; and he is said to teach all because no one learns except through his instruction.

Thus carnal generation has many, and spiritual generation also has many; but carnal generation has more than spiritual generation. Yet just as the former has all human beings, so the latter has all righteous human beings. And just as no human being exists apart from the former, so no righteous person exists apart from the latter [Note: These words, or similar ones, seem to be missing: “so likewise no righteous person exists apart from the latter,” so that the sense may attain completeness.]

Hence he immediately adds:

“For just as through the disobedience of one man the many were constituted sinners, so also through the obedience of one the many will be constituted righteous.”

By “many” he does not mean some with others excepted, but all. Obedience, both in human beings and in every rational creature, is the origin and perfection of all righteousness.

Therefore, wishing to show the difference between the two men—the first Adam, who is the head of our death, and the second, who is the head of our salvation—the Apostle says: “Just as through disobedience, and so forth.” By these words he wished to display, with great devotion, the grace by which we have been saved.

But what does it mean that, speaking of sinners, he says “they were constituted,” while of the righteous he says “they will be constituted”? If the righteous have not yet been constituted, what are we to say about the Fathers of the Old Testament? If they pleased God, they were certainly righteous, for they were saved by the same faith as we are. What we believe has already happened, they believed would happen.

Hence the Apostle says elsewhere: “Having the same spirit of faith” (II Cor. IV, 13). Blessed Peter the Apostle presents this even more clearly when he says: “But through the grace of God we believe that we are saved, just as they are” (Acts XV, 12).

If, then, they were righteous, why did the Apostle use the future tense, saying “they will be constituted”? Clearly, because he foresaw that more would believe in the New Testament than in the Old; or because, although the constitution of the righteous exists in the present life, it will be more perfect in the future.

Therefore, on account of the perfect constitution of the righteous, he used a verb in the future tense [futuri temporis] [Note: The words “of the future tense” occur several lines later, and an expunction mark—that is, a line drawn beneath them—indicates that they were written there incorrectly [Col. 0180D]. We have judged that they should be restored to their proper place.]

And, lest the Jews should glory in the law, he added:

“But the law entered alongside, so that the offense might abound.”
