“To enter alongside” means to succeed to the place of another or to occupy another’s place beforehand. The written law therefore entered alongside because it succeeded to the place of the law of nature. The Apostle shows by his words that the law of nature had already been annulled and that, once the written law had been given, it began to prevail.

By “offense” he does not mean original sin, but what human beings added after original sin. How, then, did the offense abound when the law entered alongside? Because, when the written law was given, knowledge of original sin arose, and the punishment of the offense increased.

The law therefore entered alongside so that the offense might abound—that is, so that knowledge and punishment of the offense might abound. For this reason alone the written law was given: so that knowledge of original sin might arise.

“But where sin abounded” [that is, the knowledge and punishment of sin] “grace superabounded” [Note: The Vulgate has *delictum*, “offense.” Some editions agree with the autograph.]

Because the law merely showed and condemned those whom it revealed to be transgressors, whereas divine grace justified and gave life to them, it is said to have superabounded. The law threatened but did not help; it commanded but did not heal; it revealed the illness but did not remove it.

The law, then, was given so that grace might be sought; grace was given so that the law might be fulfilled.

“So that, just as sin reigned unto death.”

It should be understood that there are certain sins besides Adam’s. Therefore the Apostle does not add here “through one” or “through a man,” because, as was said a little earlier, he is not speaking of original sin. Sin reigned unto death because the sin that human beings added to original sin increased death.

But because there can be no justification except through Christ, after saying, “So also grace may reign through righteousness unto eternal life,” he added, “through Jesus Christ our Lord” [Col. 0181A].

Through the flesh as it generates, we draw only original sin; but through the Holy Spirit as he regenerates, we obtain remission not only of that sin but also of all sins.

Therefore, because the Apostle had said, “Where sin abounded, grace superabounded” [Note: Here the Vulgate’s chapter VI begins.] (CHAP. VI), he foresaw that this statement would be perversely understood by perverse people, as though he were saying: “Because grace abounds, it is beneficial to sin.” For this reason he raised an objection against himself, saying:

“What then shall we say? Shall we remain in sin so that grace may abound?”

And, to dissolve and remove this objection, he added: “By no means!” It is as though he were saying: It is not as you have thought; for it is not the case that, because you commit greater sins, you will obtain greater benefits. For if you receive remission of your sins, your sins do not deserve this; rather, God’s grace works in you.

Again presenting the objection to himself, he adds:

“For if we have died to sin, how shall we still live in it?”

It is as though he were saying: Since the grace of God has granted us so great a benefit that we have died to sin, how shall we, having died to sin, live in it—that is, in sin? If we live in sin, we do nothing other than show ourselves ungrateful for the grace of God.

For one who praises the benefit of medicine does not commend the wounds and diseases from which it heals. Rather, the greater the praise given to the medicine, the more the diseases and wounds are abhorred. Thus praise and proclamation of the grace of God are condemnation and reproach of sins.

For the grace of God applied medicine to our wounds by which we might be healed. Therefore, where sin abounded, grace superabounded—not through the merit of the sinner, but through the help of God who comes to our aid.

And, to show that the medicine of God’s grace mystically consists in the Lord’s passion and resurrection, he added:

“Or do you not know, brothers” [Note: “Brothers” does not occur in the Vulgate. In the margin of the autograph, D. VII is marked here, that is, Sunday VII.], “that all of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?”

By these words he clearly shows that, in the Lord’s passion and resurrection, the destruction and passing away of our former life and the beginning of the new life, the abolition of iniquity and the renewal of righteousness, were prefigured.

But from where was this benefit conferred upon humanity? Clearly, through faith in Jesus Christ, because with him is the fountain of life, and in his light we shall see light.

We were therefore baptized into his death, because, just as he died, so also we, when we renounce the devil and his works, the world and its pomps, die in a certain manner while we are immersed in water.

And because he had said that his death signified our death, to show that his burial signified our burial, he added:

“For we were buried with him through baptism into death.”

For we are, as it were, buried with Christ when we lie beneath the waters [Note: This note concerns baptism by immersion, and speaks entirely and exclusively of the form used by the Church at that time.]. And as though rising with him, we are reborn from the waters, so that, dead to vices, we may begin to live to God through virtues.

It should be understood that the sacraments possess a certain likeness to the things of which they are sacraments. If they did not, they would not be sacraments. They therefore take their names from a certain likeness to the things of which they are sacraments.

Christ was offered once in himself for the salvation of humanity; but in the mystery he is sacrificed for the faithful not only throughout all the celebrations of Easter but also every day. Accordingly, in a certain manner, the sacrament of his body is his body itself; the sacrament of his blood is his blood itself. Likewise, the sacrament of his death is death itself; the sacrament of his burial is burial itself; and the sacrament of his resurrection is resurrection itself.

Hence the Apostle does not say: “All of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus have signified his death or burial,” but: “We were baptized into his death, and we were buried with him.”

“So that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so also we might walk in newness of life.”

By “through the glory of the Father” he means “on account of the glory” or “unto the glory of the Father.” For the resurrection of the Son was the glorification of the Father, because, when he rose by his own power, he glorified God the Father, whose Son he showed himself to be. [Note: In the autograph, between *quia* (“because”) and the second *dum* (“when”), the negative particle *non* occurs; I judged it erroneously present and deleted it. The immediately following words support its deletion.]

“So also we might walk in newness of life,” that is, because we have now died to vices and been renewed, we must in no way stain ourselves with the filth of our former life, but persevere in newness of life. For just as the resurrection of the Son is the glorification of the Father, so also the newness of our life is our glorification.

“For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be in the likeness of his resurrection.”

It should be understood that Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, became for us, in a wondrous and ineffable manner, the tree of life, so that we might be planted together with him in death and planted together with him in life. Therefore the Apostle says: “If we have been planted together,” and so forth.

It should be noted that he does not say: “We have been planted together with death,” but “in the likeness of death,” because he is speaking not of the death of the body but of the death of the spirit.

What he says about likeness pertains both to death and to resurrection. We have been planted together in the likeness of his death because, just as he died, so we also die in a certain likeness when we are immersed in water. We are also planted together in the likeness of his resurrection because, just as he rose, so we too rise in a certain manner when we are reborn from the waters.

“Knowing this, that our old man was crucified together with him.”

By “the old man” he means the conduct of the old man, or—and this is what should more properly be understood—the mortality of our flesh, which arose from the punishment of the curse and from the sin of the first man. The Lord assumed this mortality and bore our sins in his body upon the wood.

Death, therefore, is a curse, because it derives from a malediction (*male dictum*, literally “evil saying”). Thus the Lord’s death hung upon the cross so that, by dying, he might overcome death.

Sin likewise is a curse. Therefore the sin of the old man hung upon the wood, which the Lord assumed in the very mortality of the flesh. Hence the Apostle neither blushed nor feared to call it sin when, speaking of God the Father, he said:

“He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us” (II Cor. V, 21),

that is, he caused his Son to assume the likeness of sinful flesh and offered him as a sacrifice to himself for the salvation of humanity.

Hence he immediately gives the reason, adding:

“So that, from sin, he might condemn sin.”

Moses had previously prophesied many things about him, saying:

“Cursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree” (Deut. XXI, 23).

He called the Son of God cursed because he assumed the curse—that is, the mortality—of our flesh.

Our old man, therefore, was crucified because the mortality of our flesh, which Christ assumed, hung upon the wood in his very death, under the figure of our sin.

Why our old man was crucified is explained when he adds:

“So that the body of sin might be destroyed.”

For the body of sin is destroyed through the baptism of the one who came in the likeness of sinful flesh. Yet it is not destroyed in such a way that concupiscence is completely taken away while the flesh itself continues to live [Note: In the autograph: *asumatur*.], or that it ceases to exist; rather, it is destroyed so that, once a person has died, concupiscence—which previously existed while he was alive—may no longer harm him.

As long as a person lives, he always has concupiscence with which to struggle, and eventually, with God’s help, he will overcome it—unless, perhaps, he has received the grace of God in vain.

Note that he does not say “so that the member of sin might be destroyed,” but “the body.” For each individual vice is a member of sin, whereas he calls the mass of vices the body of sin.

By this statement he therefore shows that the Lord releases not only from original sin but from all sins.

“So that we may no longer serve sin.”

That is: having died to sins, we have been renewed; let us now serve not sin but God.

But what is the meaning of what follows?

“For whoever has died has been justified from sin.”

If all who have died have been justified, then all are saved. How, then, is it true that he says elsewhere: “Faith is not of all” (II Thess. III, 2)? If faith is not of all, neither are all saved, because, as he likewise says: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebr. II, 6).

It is therefore clear that the Apostle is speaking not of bodily death but of spiritual death, which is celebrated in the sacrament of baptism. Whoever dies this death is justified from sins, because all his sins are forgiven through the Holy Spirit.

Note that he uses the singular “sin” in place of the plural. For in baptism not only original sin but also committed sins are forgiven.

“But if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him.”

We have died with Christ in baptism because, immersed in the waters according to the likeness of his death, we have been put to death with respect to sins. Therefore we believe that we shall also live with him, since, in the words of the same Apostle: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (II Tim. II, 12), and “if we have become partners in his passion, we shall also be partners in his resurrection” (Rom. VI, 5).

“Knowing that Christ, rising from the dead” [Note: The autograph has *surgens*, “rising,” but the words that follow make it clear that *resurgens*, “rising again,” should be read, as in the Vulgate.] “dies no more.”

Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more because, rising by the power of his own divinity, he destroyed the dominion of death and restored life to us. According to the likeness of his death, therefore, having once died to sins, we must no longer live in them.

Alternatively: just as Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more, so we, once baptized, must not be baptized again. For those who are rebaptized crucify Christ for themselves and hold him up to contempt.

Hence he himself says in the Epistle to the Hebrews:

“It is impossible for those who have once been enlightened” [Note: The Vulgate has *eos*, “those,” between *est* and *qui*.], “who have tasted the heavenly gift, have become sharers in the Holy Spirit, have also tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and then have fallen away, to be renewed again unto repentance, crucifying Christ again for themselves and holding him up to contempt” (Hebr. II, 6) [Note: The Vulgate has *sibimetipsis Filium Dei*, “for themselves the Son of God.”]

It should be noted here that, when he forbids renewal, he does not deny repentance; rather, he prohibits a second baptism.

“Death will no longer rule over him.”

By this statement the error of those who say that the Lord had not a true body but a phantom body is destroyed. For death would not have ruled over him even once if he had not assumed a true body.

But what does the following mean?

“For the death that he died, he died to sin once.”

Yet the Apostle Peter says of him: “He committed no sin” (I Pet. II, 22). Lest this seem contradictory, it should be understood that by “sin” he means the frailty of the flesh, which arose because of sin.

Whatever the Lord did should not merely be expounded mystically but also followed by imitation. Because he was crucified, the Apostle teaches:

“Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and concupiscences” (Gal. V, 24).

Because he died, the same Apostle elsewhere exhorts:

“Put to death your members that are upon the earth,” that is, fornication, avarice, and so forth (Col. III, 5).

Because he was buried, he left us an example so that we might be buried with him in baptism. Hence above he himself says:

“For we were buried with him through baptism into death.”

Because he rose, the Apostle says elsewhere:

“You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (ibid., 3).

Because he ascended into heaven, he teaches elsewhere:

“If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above” (ibid., 1).

“But as for the life he lives, he lives to God.”

The Son of God, remaining in equality with the Father, emptied himself by assuming the form of a servant. In that form he died and rose again; then, ascending into heaven, he sits at the right hand of the Father.

This is what the Apostle says: “He lives to God.” For he lives to God because he remains in equality with the Father [Note: These words are written at the very bottom of the autograph’s margin, in the same handwriting.]

So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus.

By these words the Apostle admonishes us that, whenever the appearance of anything—that is, of a woman, gold, silver, or any other object—or the persuasion of an enemy has crept into us and generated a deadly thought, we should immediately consider ourselves dead to sins. For in this way, with God’s help, we shall be able to overcome the poisonous thought; it is utterly impossible for us to live both for God and for sin. Therefore, if we wish to live for God, we must die to sins. This is what he means when he says, “but alive to God in Christ Jesus.” “In Christ Jesus,” that is, through Christ Jesus, because, as he himself says, “No one knows [Note: In the autograph it reads, “No one knows the Father.” Perhaps it should read “No one comes,” in accordance with John 14:6: “No one comes to the Father except through me.”] the Father except through me.” [Note: In the autograph’s margin, “chapter 16” is written; chapter 15, however, is nowhere indicated.]

“Therefore, let not sin reign in your mortal body.” It should be noted that he does not say, “Let sin not exist,” but, “Let it not reign.” For as long as we are in this life, we cannot be without sin. Yet sin reigns only in those who, while experiencing desire, give their consent to their desires; hence he immediately adds, “so that you obey its desires.” According to some, the Apostle called it a mortal body not because of the common death, but because of eternal condemnation; nevertheless, there is no objection to understanding him as referring to either death.

Therefore, to show what it means for sin to reign, he added: “Nor present your members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin.” It must be understood that each of our members has its own function. Whoever therefore uses these functions perversely presents his members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin, because he supplies strength to the devil, by which he may be killed more easily.

“But present yourselves to God”—“alive” is understood—“as living from the dead,” that is, as rising from the dead. The meaning is this: once you have died to sin, you ought no longer wish to live in sins, like those who are going to rise again, for whom neither the desire nor the ability to sin will remain.

“And your members as weapons of righteousness for God.” Whoever uses the functions of his members in an orderly way presents his members as weapons of righteousness to God. For example, if our eyes are active for the purpose of desiring and snatching what belongs to others, they are weapons for the devil. Conversely, if they are active so that they neither desire nor snatch what belongs to others, but distribute their own possessions to others, we present our members as a sword to God, by which both sin may be killed and we may be justified. By doing this we avoid sin’s dominion. Hence it immediately follows: “For sin will not rule over you; for you are not under the law but under grace,” that is, you are not children but mature persons. Those are under the law who both fulfill and understand the law carnally; those are under grace who both understand and fulfill it spiritually. Accordingly, it is made clear that many are under the law who live under grace, and many are under grace who live under the law.

But simple and less perceptive people might answer: “If we are not under the law but under grace, because there is no law that terrifies us and punishes sin, we shall be able to sin freely and without fear.” Therefore the Apostle, proposing the question to himself, says: “What then”—“shall we say” is understood—“shall we sin because we are not under the law but under grace?” As if he were saying: You are not made subject to grace for the purpose of sinning freely. For how could grace, which has freed you, allow you to sin freely? This is what follows: “By no means.”

And because he was still speaking to those who understood little, he added: “Do you not know that to whomever you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one whom you obeyed?” [Note: The Vulgate reads, “whom you obey,” rather than “whom you obeyed.”] The meaning is: You know well that you will be slaves not of another, but of the one whom you serve. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24). Therefore, all who serve sin become slaves of sin; and those who obey righteousness become slaves of obedience. Hence it immediately follows: “Whether of sin unto death” [Note: The Vulgate reads, “unto death,” rather than “into death.”] “or of obedience unto righteousness.”

He appropriately says, “whether of sin unto death,” because completed sin plunges a person into death. He also beautifully adds, “or of obedience unto righteousness,” because all who obey the divine commandments acquire righteousness, since they are deemed worthy to be justified.

Next comes: “But thanks be to God that, although you were slaves of sin, you obeyed from the heart,” and so forth. Observe that the Apostle does not give thanks because they had been slaves of sin, but because afterward they obeyed. He says “from the heart” because of the dignity of sons. A slave acts from fear, a hired servant from desire for wages, but a son from love alone. [Col. 0186C] These people therefore obeyed from the heart because they had become children of God.

For God often accepts the offering of the outward person because of the affection of the inward person. This is shown in Genesis, where it is written: “God looked upon Abel and upon his offerings” (Genesis 4:4). “Upon Abel” means upon Abel’s intention.

What they obeyed is explained when he adds: “Into that form of teaching in which you were delivered” [Note: The Vulgate reads, “into which,” rather than “in which.”]—“to God” is understood. By “form of teaching” he means the pattern of the Gospel. By saying this, he shows that the Romans obeyed the Lord according to the Gospel’s pattern, in which they were delivered to God, since they had become his children.

“But having been freed from sin.” He uses the singular in place of the plural; therefore “every sin” must be understood.

“You have become slaves of righteousness.” By “righteousness” he means the Lord Jesus [Col. 0186D] Christ, who is the Father’s righteousness, and all the virtues that are interpreted in him.

“I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh.” [Note: In the autograph this passage is marked “Lord’s Day 8 after Pentecost.”] Here he instilled great shame in his hearers. What he means becomes clear when he adds: “Just as you presented your members,” and so forth. As if he were saying: What is more human, what is easier, than that, just as you were eager for evil, so you should be eager for good? I ought indeed to have demanded much greater things from you, and you ought to have been more eager for good than you had been for evil. But because of the weakness of your flesh, I ask for an equal measure: “Just as you presented your members to serve impurity” [Note: The Vulgate reads, “impurity and iniquity unto iniquity.”] “unto iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification.” For example, just as your eyes were eager to desire, so let them be eager to show mercy. The same applies to the other members.

“For when you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness.” By “free from righteousness” he means strangers to righteousness. Thus it is made clear that, just as servitude to righteousness is praiseworthy, so freedom from righteousness is detestable. To be free from righteousness is a detestable freedom; to be a slave of righteousness is a praiseworthy servitude, which surpasses [Note: In the autograph this word is written in abbreviation as *pcellit*. The sense may be indicated by either *praecellit*, “surpasses,” or *percellit*, “strikes down,” and both possibilities may be retained. Since the verb governs *libertatem* in the accusative, some may find it more plausible, and preferable, to understand *percellit*, which always requires the accusative, rather than *praecellit*, which takes the dative.] every freedom.

It should also be noted that free choice remains active even in evil people. Hence, as soon as they satisfy their own pleasures, they become free from righteousness. Otherwise the Apostle would not call them “free from righteousness.” For it must be understood that God created the first human being upright in such a way that, by his own will and in the state of his uprightness, he could not remain without God’s assistance, although by his own effort he could fall. Therefore, as soon as he satisfied his desires, he collapsed.

Thus God’s will, although it is not made by that person, is nevertheless daily accomplished in him. For the one who created him forms from him—that is, from the mass of his iniquity—different vessels every day, some for honor and others for dishonor. He makes the vessels for honor by his gratuitous goodness, but the vessels for dishonor by his just judgment, which is hidden from us.

“What fruit, then, did you have at that time in those things of which you are now ashamed?” The Apostle said this to people who were confounded by the recollection of their former evil deeds. As if he were saying: If at that time you had no fruit in those things of which you are now ashamed, why do you raise the waves of your life’s boasting high, when those waves are broken within you yourselves? For to the extent that those same things raise you up as proud and exalted, they make you humble and cast down. It should also be noted that “fruit” is used of both good and evil. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “A good tree cannot produce evil fruits,” and so forth (Matthew 7:18).

“For their end is death.” By “end” he means payment and recompense. Thus the end of evil works is death, because completed sins generate death. Alternatively, the end of evil works—that is, their termination—is death, but in baptism. For all who are immersed in the waters of baptism die and are reborn from the waters, and receive remission of their sins. Although this interpretation is fitting, the preceding one is more fitting, since it immediately follows: “But now” [Note: The Vulgate reads “but indeed,” rather than “but now.”] “having been freed from sin and having become servants of God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end eternal life.”

“You have your fruit unto sanctification,” that is, unto chastity, which the Apostle sometimes commends specifically and sometimes generally along with the other virtues. He appropriately says, “You have your fruit unto sanctification,” since those who become servants of God deserve to be sanctified.

A little earlier he said: “You were free from righteousness; now, however, freed from sin,” in order to preserve caution in his words. There he calls them “free,” that is, alienated; here “freed,” that is, delivered.

A little earlier he said “end,” that is, the recompense of evil works, is death; here, however, he says that the recompense of good works is life. And lest anyone think that this means temporal life, he added “eternal.” What eternal life is, the Lord makes clear in the Gospel when he says: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the true God,” and so forth (John 17:3).

“For the wages” [Note: The Vulgate reads the plural “wages,” rather than the singular.] “of sin is death.” “Wages” derives from *stipes*, “a stake” or “post.” Among the ancients, money was not counted out but hung on a stake. Soldiers therefore were those who received wages; they were not so much given money as paid a reward. Thus all who serve as soldiers of sin receive death as their wages.

“But the grace of God is eternal life.” Since he had said, “The wages of sin is death,” it would have followed for him to say, “The wages of righteousness is eternal life.” Yet he did not wish to do so, lest he provide an occasion for criticism. Why then does he say, “The grace of God is eternal life”? He says this to show that the good things of the saints do not belong to them but to God, from whom they are given. Whenever God rewards the elect, he rewards his own gifts in them, because he himself has given them the good things for which they are rewarded.

“In Christ Jesus our Lord.” It should be noted that the Apostle frequently adds this conclusion to his exposition, especially in this Epistle, wishing to show that through Christ both knowledge of the Father is given and salvation is administered to the human race.

### Chapter 7 [Note: The Vulgate has “chapter 7.”]

Therefore, since he had said that he and his assistants were not under the law, and had argued at considerable length on this point, he added, in order to make it clearer: “Or are you ignorant, brothers?” As if he were saying: You are not ignorant. [Note: In the autograph’s margin, “chapter 17” is written.]

He shows why they should not be ignorant when he adds: “For I am speaking to those who know the law.” Here it must be asked how he could say that he was speaking to people who knew the law, when he was speaking to the Romans. For it was not the Romans but the Jews who received the law from God. This is nevertheless not contradictory, because the Romans were already Greeks and had received a law from the Athenians.

What he was saying to them he shows by adding: “For the law rules over a person for as long as he lives.” Here it should be noted that when he said “lives,” he wished “in sin” to be understood. For the law rules over a person for as long as he lives in sin, because it rules over him only so long as it finds something in him to punish or penalize.

“For the woman who is under a husband is bound by the law while her husband lives; but if her husband has died, she is released from the law of her husband.” The Apostle adds an analogy to his exposition so that it may be understood more easily. Just as the Creator is recognized through creation, so something hidden is revealed through analogy.

He therefore says: “For the woman who is under a husband,” and so forth. As far as the historical sense is concerned, the meaning is clear. Allegorically, however, he calls the husband the commandment of the law, and the woman the soul of each individual or the people. Therefore, just as a woman is subject to the law of her husband while her husband lives, so whoever has the law alive in him—that is, whoever understands and fulfills it carnally, or whoever lives under sin—is bound by the bond of the law. Otherwise, he is released from the yoke of the law, just as the woman, when her husband has died, is released from his law.

“Therefore, while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she is with another man; but if her husband has died, she is freed from her husband’s law, so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another man.” Just as a woman is called an adulteress while her husband lives if she is with another man, so anyone in whom the law is alive is an adulterer if he passes over to the grace of the Gospel. He is an adulterer both of the law and of grace: of the law because he has passed over to grace; of grace because, while remaining in grace, he understands and fulfills the law carnally.

“Therefore, my brothers, you also have died to the law.” It appears that this exposition differs greatly from the analogy he previously offered. There he said that the husband must die for the woman to be released; here, however, he says that the woman has died to the husband—that is, that the Romans have been put to death in relation to the law.

It must be understood that this analogy was obscure, indeed difficult to grasp, for the Romans. Therefore, in order to clarify it, he did not wish to say that the law had been extinguished for the Romans, but that the Romans had been put to death in relation to the law. Although he did not say this explicitly, he left it to be understood, just as above, where he said: “First, that the oracles of God were entrusted to them”; he did not state the second point, but left it to be supplied.

How they have died to the law he makes clear: “through the body of Christ.” But how through the body of Christ? Because, in the passion of his cross, all who believe in him were crucified together with him. Hence the earlier statement: “All of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death.”

For it must be understood that the devil greatly offended and deceived himself when he killed the innocent Christ. When he handed over to an undeserved death the one who owed nothing to death, he lost all those whom he held under the debt of death.

“So that we may belong to another, who has risen from the dead.” Just as a woman, after her husband’s death, passes to another man without the guilt of fornication, so whoever has the law extinguished passes freely to the grace of the Gospel, so as to belong to another—namely, the Lord Jesus Christ, who rose from the dead.

“So that we may bear fruit for God.” A person bears fruit for God who not only gives examples of good works but also edifies others by them. [Note: Here I would think that *sed etiam*, “but also,” or an equivalent expression should be added, lest the sense remain incomplete.]

“When we were in the flesh,” and so forth. It must be asked why the Apostle says that he and his successors were in the flesh but are now no longer so. Was he not in the flesh when he was speaking these things to the Romans? He both was and was not. He was in the flesh because he still remained in the weakness of the flesh; he was not in the flesh because he did not place his confidence in carnal things.

Hence blessed Augustine says: “When we were in the flesh,” that is, when we were held bound by carnal desires, “the passions of sins that were through the law,” and so forth. “The passions of sins” are called the desires of the flesh, because, as long as we are in this life, they continually afflict us and incite us to sin. But why are they said to be through the law, when they are prohibited in the law? Because, by being prohibited in the law, they are made more ardent and more pleasurable.

“They were active in our members,” that is, they dragged us toward sin, “so that they might bear fruit for death.” They bear fruit for death because, by the example of evil speech or action, they destroy others.

“But we have not been released from the law of death in which we were held.” What does it mean that it is called the law of death, when it does not produce death? For if it produces death, it is evil. Yet the same Apostle says elsewhere (Romans 7:12): “The law is holy, and the commandment,” and so forth.

It is therefore not called the law of death because it produces death, but because it reveals death. For a thing is not always identical with what it reveals. Thus medicine is called deadly, not because it brings death, but because it reveals deadly poisons. Hence blessed Augustine says: “It is called the law of sin and death because it was set before those who sin and die.” Therefore the same Apostle says elsewhere (1 Timothy 1:9): “The law is not imposed for the righteous but for the unrighteous.”

“So that we may serve in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter.” Those serve in the oldness of the letter who understand and fulfill the law carnally. Those walk in the newness of the Spirit who deal with the divine commandments spiritually. Alternatively: They walk not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the Spirit who put off the old person with his deeds and put on the new person, who has been created according to God in the righteousness and holiness of truth.

Therefore, since he had called it “the law of death,” and seemed to be speaking many things against the dignity of the law, indeed toward its destruction, someone might say: “Then the law is sin.” Accordingly, he proposed the question to himself, saying: “What then shall we say? Is the law sin?” As if he were saying: It is not as you say. The law is not evil because it reveals evil, that is, sin, since a thing is not necessarily identical with what it reveals. This is what he means by “By no means.”

To show the law’s power and why it was given, he added: “But I did not know sin except through the law.” Here it must be asked whether he is speaking of the written law or of the law of nature. That he is speaking of the law of nature, no one doubts. It may also be understood of the written law, for the two are one: what this law and that law prohibit is the same, namely, “What you do not wish done to you, do not do to another.”

But if they are the same, why was the written law given? Because the law of nature had already failed, and free choice had almost been abolished. [Note: That is, because of ignorance regarding what was permitted and what was not.]

As long as people are in early childhood and do not know what should or should not be done, it is as though the law is lacking for them; and therefore sin is, as it were, lacking for them. Infancy does not know this law, and childhood is ignorant of it. Hence a child curses his father and mother and strikes his parents, yet this is not imputed to him, because the law is lacking for him.

But who discovered this? Wisdom. Is wisdom, then, evil because it discovered this? By no means. Yet wisdom itself often finds evil through knowledge of vices and virtues, when it follows evil.

“For I did not know covetous desire unless the law said, ‘You shall not covet.’” Observe that he does not say, “I coveted,” but, “I did not know covetous desire,” as if he were saying: Covetous desire certainly existed, and I coveted, but I thought it was a natural good. As soon as the law began to say to me, “You shall not covet,” I understood that it was not a natural good but an accidental evil.

The law is therefore a great good, since it commands that one should not covet; but I cannot fulfill this command by my own strength.

“But sin, finding an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me every covetous desire.” What opportunity is he referring to? The age of reason, certainly. As long as people are in early childhood and do not know what should or should not be done, sin is lacking for them. When they reach the years of rational age, however, they are punished more severely because they sin knowingly.

Therefore the Apostle says: “Finding an opportunity”—namely, the age of reason—as if he were saying: When I reached the years of rational age, I began to covet, but not everything. When the law said to me, “You shall not covet,” the sin of covetous desire that had previously existed in me, although I did not know it, produced in me every covetous desire through the commandment of the law, which prohibited covetousness, because it made me a transgressor of the law. Hence I was found to be coveting everything.

From this blessed Augustine says: “Your covetous desire was smaller when, before the law, you sinned securely; but now, when the barriers of the law have been placed before you, the river of covetous desire has been restrained, not dried up. It was carrying you along without any barriers; when the barriers were broken, it overwhelmed you. Your covetous desire was smaller when it stirred your lust; it is universal when it transgresses the law. Do you wish to know how great it is? See what it broke. ‘You shall not covet’: a human being did not say this; God said it,” and so forth.

“For without the law sin was dead.” What does “was dead” mean? It was hidden; it did not appear. It lay buried, as it were, in the darkness of ignorance.

“But I was once alive without the law.” What does it mean that he says he once lived without the law, when elsewhere he says: “I was an Israelite, a Hebrew of Hebrews, from the seed of Abraham and the tribe of Benjamin, circumcised on the eighth day”? [Note: Philippians 3:5: “Circumcised on the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews, according to the law a Pharisee.”]

There is no contradiction. As long as he was in early childhood and did not know what should or should not be done, the law of nature was, as it were, lacking for him; therefore he did not know sin. It may also be understood of the written law. For although he was circumcised on the eighth day and received certain other sacraments of the law, he did not understand what they signified. Hence he lived, as it were, without the law.

Nevertheless, it is more fittingly understood in this way: “But I was once alive without the law”—that is, established amid various covetous desires; or, I thought that I was alive. [Note: In the autograph this passage is written in abbreviated form as: “Ego aus. l. a.”]

“But when the commandment came, sin revived.” What does “revived” mean? It began to appear, to be felt, and to rebel. And because he does not say “lived” but “revived”: in the first human being sin lived through the transgression of the law of nature and first took him captive; afterward it revived in all transgressors.

“But I died.” Why does he say that he died? Was he not in the flesh? He certainly was, since he remained in the weakness of the flesh; but he says that he died because he had become a manifest transgressor. “I died,” he says—that is, I came to know that I was dead, because I sinned knowingly. For the more knowingly someone sins, the more severely he will be punished.

“And the commandment that was for life was found by me to be for death.” It should be noted that he does not say “was given,” because the commandment was given not for death but for life. He therefore says “was found,” as if he were saying: The commandment, which could have been for life if it had been observed, was found by me to be for death because it was not observed. For its transgression produces death.

Hence he adds appropriately: “For sin, finding an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me, and through it killed me.” What opportunity? The age of reason, certainly. He appropriately says “deceived,” as if he were saying: Sin, finding the opportunity of rational age, accepted the price of carnal pleasure, deceived me, and through it killed me by causing me to transgress the commandment of the law.

And because someone might say, “Then the law is evil, since by its commandment it kills a human being,” he immediately bursts into its praise, saying: “Therefore the law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good.” The law is holy because it makes those who observe it holy. The commandment is likewise holy, and by its holiness, justice, and goodness it makes those who observe it holy, just, and good; it also commands that one should not covet.

Again, someone might say: “Then the good commandment of the law became evil for you.” Anticipating this, he adds: “Did then what is good become death for me?” As if he were saying: It is not as you assert. I do not die because of the good commandment, but through my own fault, when I transgress the commandment of the law. The law is not death; rather, transgression of the law produces death. This is what he adds: “By no means.”

Next comes: “But sin, so that it might appear to be sin, worked death in me through what is good.” Here it must be observed that he does not say “so that it might be sin,” but “so that it might appear,” as if he were saying: Sin existed, but it did not appear. In order that sin might appear, it worked death in me through the good commandment of the law. For when I transgress the commandment, I incur death, and sin is made more manifest.

“So that sin might become sinning beyond measure through the commandment.” How does sin become sinning beyond measure through the commandment? Because the more something is prohibited in the law, the more ardently it is loved and the less the commandment is observed.

Blessed Augustine, however, says that sin becomes sinning beyond measure through the commandment because it is not merely sin but transgression. [Note: In the *Proposition on this Epistle*, the wording is: “where there is no law, neither is there transgression.”] Sin is less serious when someone sins without a commandment; but when it is committed against a commandment, it exceeds the measure. [Note: The word *per*, which lay improperly—or rather contrary to the sense—between the words “according to” and “commandment,” has been judged worthy of deletion.] [Note: In the autograph’s margin, “chapter 18” is written.]

“For we know that the law is spiritual.” The law is spiritual for spiritual people, but carnal for carnal people. It is spiritual for those who handle and observe it spiritually; it is carnal for those who understand and fulfill it carnally. When it is carnal for them, however, this is not the law’s fault but the fault of those who use it carnally.

“But I am carnal.” What does it mean that he calls himself carnal, when earlier he said that he and his assistants were not in the flesh but in the Spirit? Therefore it must be understood that he was not “in the flesh,” because he did not place his confidence in the hope of carnal things. But when he says, “I am carnal,” he means “mortal.” If he had said this explicitly, he would certainly have spoken correctly.

Alternatively, he calls himself carnal because he confidently hoped, without ambiguity, for the future resurrection of the flesh.

“Sold under sin.” What does it mean that he says he was sold under sin, when he had already been redeemed? He says that he was sold under sin because he remained in the weakness of the flesh, which the first human being incurred by transgressing God’s commandment. Having accepted the price of carnal pleasures, the first man subjected himself to the devil, and, being sold under sin, he begot all his descendants in a sold condition. Everyone remains in this condition even after Christ’s baptism.

For in baptism, although sins are forgiven, the weakness of the flesh nevertheless remains until the day of resurrection. Christ therefore redeemed us from both forms of bondage: that of the soul and that of the body. Hence he is beautifully called the Redeemer. He frees the soul from bondage when he remits sins in baptism; he will redeem the body when he causes us to rise from the dead. Concerning this redemption he says elsewhere: “Awaiting the adoption of the children of God, the redemption of our body” (Romans 8:23).

Blessed Augustine explains it as follows: “But I am carnal, sold under sin,” that is, sinning for the price of carnal pleasures. [Note: In the autograph this text, like several others above, is written in abbreviation: “ego autem c. s. u. s. p.” The first five letters, being the initials of the words in the cited text, were easy for me to interpret; but I do not know why the final *r* was written.]

“For what I do, I do not understand.” How does he not understand, if he does it? Or who can do what he does not understand? It must therefore be understood in this way: “What I do, I do not understand,” that is, I do not approve, desire, praise, or take pleasure in it. For the expression is used in the same way as when the Lord says in the Gospel: “I do not know you” (Matthew 25:12), that is, “I do not approve of you.”

Alternatively: “What I do, I do not understand,” that is, I desire to obey the precept of the law, but I cannot fulfill it by my own strength. [Note: This passage, like the preceding one, is written by means of initials: “quod enim o. n. o.”]

“For I do not do what I want.” That is, I do not want to covet, but I covet. This is what follows: “But what I hate, that I do.” That is, unwillingly I covet. [Note: The Vulgate reads: “For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, that I do.”]

Alternatively: “I do not do what I want, but what I hate, that I do,” that is, in the case of evil, which I desire to keep away, I am found to have been called [Note: This word, *vocatus*, “called,” is not entirely clear in the autograph. The first two letters appear to have been partially, and in my judgment deliberately, erased; between the following letters *c* and *a*, the letter *o* can be seen somewhat higher, thus: [unclear mark]. Perhaps it should be read *coactus*, “compelled,” which receives greater support from the later repetition of this text, where *coactus concupisco*, “I am compelled to covet,” is written very clearly.]

Some people could therefore suspect and say that the Apostle had gone as far as sinning and had actually sinned. Hence he adds: “But if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law that it is good.”

But how did he agree with the law if he did what he did not want? Evidently because the law is good and his will is good. The meaning is this: When the law commands, “You shall not covet,” and I do not want to covet, then, since I desire what the law desires, my will and the law’s will are shown to be one.

Alternatively: The law commands that one should not covet, but I covet. Yet because the law also says, “Do not follow your desires, and turn away from your pleasures,” when I resist my desires and do not follow my pleasures, my will and the law’s will are shown to be one.

“But now it is no longer I who do it.” It should be noted that he does not say, “But I do not do it,” but, “But now it is no longer I who do it.” By this he shows that, as long as he was under the law, he coveted willingly; but after he was redeemed, aided by divine grace, although he coveted, he resisted vigorously.

He therefore says, “But now”—that is, freed by divine grace—“it is no longer I who do it,” that is, I sin unwillingly. Someone might ask: “Who, then, does it?” He immediately adds: “But sin that dwells in me.”

By “sin” he means the weakness of the flesh, into which the first human being fell because of sin. Again it could be objected: “How do you know that it is not you who does it, but sin that dwells in you?” He therefore immediately adds: “For I know that good does not dwell in me.” And, lest there be any doubt about what he means by “in me,” he explains: “that is, in my flesh.”

“For to will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find.” It should be noted that he does not say “to do,” but “to accomplish,” as if he were saying: The will is present—that is, the will not to covet; the ability to do is present—that is, to resist desires; but the ability to accomplish is not present—that is, to be without desires.

Why, then, was this commandment given if it cannot be fulfilled? Because although in this life we cannot live without covetous desire—for “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation depresses the mind that thinks of many things” (Wisdom 9:15)—it will nevertheless be fulfilled in the future, when we are joined to God and the angels.

To show how he did not find the ability to accomplish it, he added: “For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, that I do.” But what was the evil he did unwillingly? Coveting. Likewise, the good that he wanted to do but could not was to be without covetous desire.

Hence blessed Augustine says: “‘The evil that I do not want, that I do,’ that is, I covet; but I am not overcome, because I do not consent to evil desire.” The same blessed Augustine says that the evil which he did not want to do but did was lust. Concerning this evil he says elsewhere: “A thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to strike me” (2 Corinthians 12:7).

For he wanted to overcome lust by his own strength; but because he could not, he cried out: “For I do not do the good that I want,” and so forth.

“But if I do what I do not want”—that is, if I am compelled to covet [Note: “Compelled” should perhaps also be read in the preceding note, where *vocatus*, “called,” is not entirely clear in reference to this same text.]—“it is no longer I who do it.” The word “now” must be understood in the sense given above. And because someone might ask, “Who, then, does it?” he adds: “But sin that dwells in me,” that is, the weakness of the flesh. For he wished this weakness to be designated by the name “sin.”

What, then, does the Apostle mean when he now says that he does not act, and now that he does act, except that he was acting by resisting desires? He acted through weakness; he did not act through the will. He acted through the flesh; he did not act through the mind.

“I find, therefore, a law, when I want to do good, that evil is present to me.” The meaning is: when I want to do good, I find the law good. For the law is good because it proclaims good things. But I cannot fulfill this good by my own strength, because evil is present to me—that is, the weakness of the flesh compels me toward evil desire. And because what he had said was obscure, he added, as though explaining it: “For I delight in the law of God,” and so forth. In these words it should be noted that the Apostle mentions four laws: the law of God, of the mind, of sin, and of the members. Yet these four are two, for the law of God and the law of the mind are one; likewise, the law of the members and the law of sin are one.

But when did these laws arise? Clearly, when the first man transgressed God’s law in paradise: that he should eat from every tree of paradise, but should not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Gen. II, 16–17). It was then that this conflict began. But why is that evil law—the law of the members and of sin—called a law? Because it was justly ordained that, for the man who had refused to obey his God, his flesh should not obey him. For it descended as the punishment of sin.

The meaning is: “For I delight in the law of God according to the inner man.” [Col. 0195D] In the autograph, these four words are written after the note in abbreviated form: “e. l. d. s. h.” I delight in the law of God according to the man, that is, I do not want to desire wrongly. “But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin, which is in my members”—that is, compelled, I desire wrongly. [Col. 0195D] Here again the same words are repeated, by which the interpretation of one of the notes above, concerning the words “I am found called,” is confirmed. He says “taking captive,” meaning “wanting to take captive”; or certainly this refers to the outer man, who is corrupted daily.

In the fact that the man, according to the inner man, delights in the law of God, great mercy on God’s part is shown. For the outer man is corrupted daily, whereas the inner man, inspired by divine mercy, advances and is renewed from day to day.

“Wretched man that I am!” Because the Apostle had seen that this battle existed within him, he could find no refuge in himself; therefore he cried out, “Wretched man that I am!” He calls himself wretched on account of the weakness of the flesh, in which, while remaining in it, he desired wrongly even against his will.

But since all die—the good as well as the wicked, the godly as well as the ungodly—as their final day makes clear, what does the Apostle mean when he adds: “Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” And they attribute this to a great [benefit or, rather, refuge] of God’s grace. [Col. 0196D] The epithet “great” seems to leave the sense incomplete. From what follows, one may infer that a substantive should perhaps be added, possibly “benefit,” or rather “refuge,” in accordance with what is found below: “Thus he found one and only one refuge in God’s grace.”

It should be noted that he does not say merely “from the body of death,” but adds “of this.” For although the wicked may be delivered from the body of this death, they will nevertheless return to the body of this death, since the dead will be led away to punishment. And when they have risen, although they will receive immortal bodies, they will nevertheless be corruptible bodies, with which they will be tormented without end.

Only the elect, therefore, are delivered from the body of this death. For when they die, they are freed from this conflict and pass into joy; and when they rise again, they will receive incorruptible and immortal bodies, with which they will rejoice without end.

Thus he found one and only one refuge in God’s grace. [Col. 0196D] Compare these words with the preceding note. Therefore he added, “the grace of God,” as if he were saying: “I shall be delivered not by my own strength or my own effort, but by God’s mercy.” And beautifully he adds, “through Jesus Christ our Lord,” because, just as through one came death, so also through one came the resurrection of the dead; for just as all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ.

Thus, as though someone had asked, “What is this death for which you so greatly desire to be freed from the body?” he immediately added: “Therefore I myself serve the law of God with the mind, but with the flesh the law of sin; this is death.” [Col. 0196D] These words are found in the lower margin of the autograph.

When he says “I myself,” this means “I and no other.” For through the Holy Spirit he foresaw future heretics who would say that the nature of the soul was from God, but that of the flesh from the prince of darkness. Therefore he said “I myself,” as if he were saying: “It is not as you assert. There are not two contrary natures in me, one from God and the other from the prince of darkness. Rather, I myself, one and the same man, serve the law of sin with the flesh—that is, by desiring wrongly—but with the mind I serve the law of God—that is, by resisting desires.”

Someone might say in response: “Because you serve the law of sin with the flesh, do you acquire some condemnation on account of this servitude, or not?” Therefore he added: [Col. 0197D] Here Vulgate chapter VIII begins.

**(CHAPTER VIII.)** “There is therefore now no condemnation” [Col. 0197D] In the autograph, the word *ergo* (“therefore”) in this passage is marked with the sign ordinarily placed beneath words to be deleted. Above it is written the word *nunc* (“now”). After the word *est*, before the next word, there is *nec* (“nor”), likewise marked with the same sign indicating deletion as the word *ergo*. It should nevertheless be noted that *ergo* is also read in the Vulgate and other texts, whereas *nec* is found nowhere. “for those who are in Christ Jesus,” and so forth.

As if he were saying: “There is no condemnation for me”—and not for me alone, but also for all who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh. They do not walk according to the flesh who, although they experience desire, nevertheless resist their desires with strength, and therefore are in Christ Jesus. Even if, before baptism, they had consented to desires or committed some disgraceful act, everything in them has nevertheless been erased through the sacrament of baptism and the washing of regeneration; therefore there is no condemnation for them.

And as though someone were asking how he had been freed from condemnation, he added: “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death.” Here the Apostle mentions a third law. But what is this law of the Spirit and of life? It is the law of faith and mercy; it is the law of the grace of the Gospel. It is called the law of life because it frees from death; the law of the Spirit because it gives life.

How, then, does this law free from the law of sin and death? Clearly, by granting through baptism the remission of all sins. It also frees from the law of bodily death, since the saints, although they remain in the body, have already been freed from the death of the flesh through hope, because they will eventually rise again. And because the law of the Gospel’s grace frees no one except through Christ Jesus, he therefore says, “the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus.”

To show how this had happened, he added: “For what was impossible for the law,” and so forth. Here the Apostle now mentions a fourth law. But what law is this? Is it the law of the mind, or of the members and sin? Certainly not, but the law of deeds and works. This is the law that was given to God’s people through Moses on Mount Sinai, concerning which he said above, “the law indeed is holy.” What, then, was impossible for this law? It could not make its hearer obedient and perfect, since this law brings no one to perfection. Hence blessed Augustine says that it was impossible for this law to free anyone from the law of sin and death.

[Col. 0198A] He shows why this was impossible when he adds: “in which it was weakened through the flesh.” For it commanded but did not assist; it gave weak commandments but did not heal. By “through the flesh” he means through the understanding of the flesh; for the law, when understood spiritually, is the same as the grace of the Gospel.

“God, sending his own Son in the likeness” [Note: [Col. 0198D] The Vulgate has *similitudinem* (“likeness,” accusative).] “of sinful flesh.” By saying “his own,” he shows that the Son existed even before he was sent. And note that he does not say “in sinful flesh,” but “in the likeness of sinful flesh.” For the Son of God, when he came, did not assume sinful flesh from the Virgin, but the likeness of sinful flesh. In sinful flesh there is both death and sin; in the likeness of sinful flesh there is only the death that the Lord endured for us, possessing no sin whatsoever. Hence the apostle Peter says: “He committed no sin” (I Pet. II, 22), and so forth.

“And on account of sin he condemned sin in the flesh.” What does he mean by saying “on account of sin,” when Peter says that he committed no sin? It should be understood that in the Old Testament it was customary for every sacrifice for sin to be called “sin.” The Lord became such a sacrifice when he offered himself for us on the altar of the cross. Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “He made him who [does] not know sin to be sin for us” [Note: [Col. 0198D] The particle *non* (“not”) is absent in the autograph.] (II Cor. V, 22), that is, a sacrifice for sin. Therefore, by the flesh which he took from the Virgin without sin, and in which he never sinned, he condemned all sin in us, when he made it a sacrifice for sin to the Father. [Col. 0198D] In the autograph it reads *ea* (“it”), but I judged that *eam*, namely “the flesh,” should be read.

The purpose for which he condemned sin is disclosed when he adds: [Col. 0198C] “so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us.” By “the justification of the law” he means the spiritual understanding within the law. The justification of the law, therefore, has been fulfilled in us when, understanding the law spiritually, we have been justified through the washing of baptism and the grace of the Holy Spirit. And lest, by saying “in us,” he seem to have included everyone, he added: “who do not walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit,” concerning whom he had spoken a little earlier.

“For those who are according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh.” Those are according to the flesh who repay an enemy in kind, seize what belongs to others, do not give away what belongs to themselves, and perform other similar acts. Therefore they perceive the things that belong to the flesh. Conversely, those are according to the Spirit who do not do these things, but, with the Holy Spirit’s help, despise earthly things and desire heavenly things. Of them he adds: “But those who are according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit.”

The flesh was made from earth; the Spirit was given from heaven. Therefore each seeks its proper place. Thus, if it happens that the flesh is overcome by the Spirit, the whole man is called spiritual; but if the Spirit is overcome by the flesh, the whole man is called carnal.

“For the wisdom of the flesh is death” [Col. 0199D] In the autograph margin: “chapter XIX.” The wisdom of the flesh consists in loving earthly things and despising heavenly things; therefore it is called death because it brings about death. But “the wisdom of the Spirit is life and peace.” The wisdom of the Spirit consists in despising temporal things and desiring eternal things. It is called life because it confers life; peace because it makes one rest in peace. For although many temporal losses are inflicted upon the saints, nevertheless, while they despise all temporal things, they rest in peace. Or it is called peace because it leads to knowledge of the true peace, which is Christ.

“For the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God.” The wisdom of the flesh is the same as its prudence. Because it does not obey God’s commandments but contradicts his orders, it is called hostile to God. For, as he himself says in the Gospel, “If anyone loves me, he will keep my commandments” (John XIV, 23). Therefore it is not subject to the law of God [Note: [Col. 0199D] The Vulgate has “is not subject,” rather than “is not subjected.”]

Charity, however, is subject to the law of God, because it is shown to be the law of God; desire, on the other hand, which is the wisdom of the flesh, is not subject to it. For if, on one side, it sees justice and equity and, on the other, earthly advantage, it desires to attain the latter more than to preserve justice and equity.

But what does he mean by adding, “for it cannot”? Is it not possible for a human being to be subject to the law of God? Certainly it is; but the wisdom of the flesh cannot. For it is a corruption and defect of the mind, not created by God but devised by the devil; whereas the human being can be healed of this defect.

But what does he mean by adding: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God”? Were not the Apostle and the Romans in the flesh? Did not all the holy martyrs, placed in the flesh, please God? It should be understood that they carried the flesh; they were not carried by the flesh. Those are “in the flesh” who perform the works of the flesh, who take pleasure in carnal delights, and therefore cannot please God.

Therefore, lest the Romans be scandalized, thinking that the Apostle had said that only those who had already died could please God, he added, wishing to urge them toward better things: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit.” Those are in the Spirit who trust that they can fulfill good works not by their own power, but with the help of the Holy Spirit. Therefore he added: “if indeed” [Note: [Col. 0199D] Some other texts have *si quidem* (“if indeed”) in place of *si tamen* (“provided that,” “if nevertheless”); this reading could certainly produce a substantial difference. For the adverb *tamen* indicates a condition without which he would assert that the Romans cannot be in the Spirit. But *si quidem*, if taken separately—that is, if *si* is separated from *quidem*—could signify the same thing, though less strictly. It would not have the same meaning, indeed it would have an entirely different sense, if *siquidem* were read as one word, producing an absolute statement: that the Romans truly are in the Spirit, since—that is, because—the Spirit of God dwells in them.] “the Spirit of God dwells in you”—that is, if you are led by the Spirit of God, if you are taught by the Spirit of God.

Therefore, lest the Romans regard possessing the Spirit of God as something insignificant, he added: “But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him.” As if he were saying: “Do not despise or consider it insignificant to have the Spirit of Christ, because otherwise you cannot belong to him.” The Spirit of Christ is the same as the Spirit of God, because the Father and the Son have one Spirit. Those, therefore, have the Spirit of Christ who love Christ and keep his commandments; and therefore they belong to Christ, because Christ remains in them.

For he himself says: “Whoever loves me” [Col. 0200D] The Vulgate has “my word,” rather than “my commandments.”] “will keep my commandments, and my Father will love him” [Note: [Col. 0200D] In the autograph: *diligit* (“loves”).] “and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (ibid.). Where the Father and the Son remain, there too is the Holy Spirit of both. But those who wickedly resist, curse the one who curses them, and do all such things do not have the Spirit of God; therefore they do not belong to him. It follows that they belong to another, namely the devil, because whoever performs someone’s works is called that person’s son.

[Col. 0200B] To show how great a gift it is to have Christ, the Apostle added: “But if Christ is in you, the body is indeed dead because of sin,” and so forth. Here it should be noted that he does not say “because of earthly weakness.” For the first man did not die because he had been made from the dust of the earth, but because he sinned. He had been fashioned by God in such a way that, if he did not sin, he would pass to the dignity of the angels even without death. For free will had been granted to him so that, if he wished, he would not sin—or rather, would not be able to sin.

For, when the number of the predestined had been completed, he would have passed, together with all who would be created from him, into the steadfast state of the angels [Note: [Col. 0200D] “Steadfastness,” that is, eternal, unfading life, and firm in this sense; others judge that *felicitatem* (“happiness”) or *soliditatem* (“steadfastness”) should perhaps be written, although *sodalitatem* (“fellowship”) is read very clearly.] But because he chose rather to sin [Note: [Col. 0200D] In the autograph, *peccare* (“to sin”) and *ruere* (“to fall”) are read.] [Col. 0200C] he died, and he begot all whom he begot as dead. Therefore the Apostle says: “The body is dead because of sin.” [Col. 0200D] The initial letters of this passage are wrongly repeated there in the form: “m. c. p. p.”

It should also be noted that he does not say “about to die,” but “dead,” because, although each person’s body appears to live, it is nevertheless already dead, since in it—being not yet renewed through the resurrection—the consequence of sin, namely the necessity of death, remains.

“But the Spirit is life” [Col. 0200D] The Vulgate reads *vivit* (“lives”) instead of *vita* (“life”); nevertheless, some other texts also read *vita est* (“is life”).] “because of justification.” He means the justification that is accomplished in baptism. In baptism, the soul of a believer, once sins have been forgiven, is given life through the grace of the Holy Spirit; therefore it is life.

But the Romans could have said in response: “Behold, we have the Spirit of Christ. This is shown by the complete and catholic faith that is in us and by our love of justice. What, then, will become of that mortal flesh and of the law that is in our members, warring against the law of our mind?” To show, therefore, that a great gift had been bestowed upon redeemed humanity, the Apostle answered: “But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies, because of his Spirit dwelling in you.”

As if he were saying: “Certainly a great gift has been bestowed upon redeemed humanity” [Note: [Col. 0201D] The autograph has *collocatum* (“placed,” “bestowed”).] “because not only does the soul live in the present after its sins have been forgiven, but the body too will be given life and will pass into the glory of immortality.”

In saying “he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead,” he wishes God the Father to be understood. Yet the Father alone did not raise him; the Son and the Holy Spirit did so as well, because the operation of the whole Trinity is one.

And note that he does not say “dead bodies,” but “mortal bodies.” Adam in paradise was mortal before sin because he could die if he sinned; and he did die when he sinned. Thus he was called mortal before he sinned in the same way that a body without illness is called “liable to illness,” not “ill.” If it happens to die without illness, it can rightly be called “liable to illness,” but not “ill.”

So too the saints, although they bear mortal bodies because of the necessity of death, nevertheless possess immortal bodies in hope, as Adam possessed such a hope before sin. For they have received hope from God and firmly believe that one day they will rise and pass to the dignity of the angels, to which the first man would have come without death if he had not sinned.

Then they will have bodies that are neither dead nor mortal, because they will possess neither the necessity of death nor the ability to sin. This will take place when what the prophet says has been fulfilled: “Death has been swallowed up in victory” (Hos. XIII, 14)—that is, when “this mortal has put on immortality, and this corruptible has put on incorruption” (II Cor. XV, 53–54).

Therefore, because he had shown that a great gift had been bestowed upon humanity, [Note: [Col. 0201D] Again, the autograph has *collocatum* (“bestowed”).] he added: [Note: [Col. 0201D] In the autograph’s margin is written “Lord’s Day X after Pentecost.”] “Therefore, brothers, we are debtors,” and so forth. Since he simply said “debtors,” lest anyone think that they were debtors to the flesh, he added “not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh.”

Those are debtors to the flesh who follow its desires. He shows how great an evil this is by adding: “For if you live according to the flesh, you will die”—that is, if you live according to yourselves. The first angel, because he lived according to himself, therefore fell. What he says, “you will die,” should be understood not of bodily death, but rather of the death of the soul or eternal condemnation.

Someone might say in response: “If we are not debtors to the flesh, then to what are we debtors?” The Apostle answers as though: “To the Spirit, because we are not debtors according to that by which we die, but according to that by which we live.”

This is what he means when he adds: “But if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live.” By “the deeds of the flesh” he means the works of the flesh, concerning which he says elsewhere: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth”—that is, fornication, and so forth (Col. III, 5).

Those put to death the deeds of the flesh by the Spirit who, through the operation of the Holy Spirit, extinguish vices and sins within themselves, and discipline their bodies and bring them into servitude (I Cor. IX, 27). Therefore they will live—not so much with the life of the body as with the life of the soul and eternal blessedness.

And as though they were saying, “How shall we prove that the Spirit of God is in us?” he adds: “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God.” The meaning is: this is the true proof that they are sons of God, if they are led by the Spirit of God.

They are led by the Spirit of God—that is, guided by him—who, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, are stirred to compunction of mind, to tears, and to other things of this kind. Therefore they are sons of God.

A great dignity has been bestowed upon humanity, [Col. 0202B] since those who were not worthy to be called servants of God received such power that they are and are called sons of God (I John III, 1).

Thus those who are led by the Spirit of God are led by love, because the same Apostle says: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit” (above, V, 3). Therefore he immediately adds: “For you did not receive again the spirit of servitude into fear” [Note: [Col. 0202D] The Vulgate has *timore* (“fear,” ablative), while some other texts agree with ours, *timorem* (“fear,” accusative).] For, as John says: “Perfect love casts out fear” (I John IV, 18).

But what does he mean by “again”? That is, as on Mount Sinai. By saying this, he shows that they had been under the law.

Someone may say: “One spirit was given to God’s people in the Old Testament, and another in the New.” If that were so, the Apostle would certainly not have said “again.” The spirit of servitude and the spirit of freedom are therefore the same; but the spirit of fear and servitude was given on tablets of stone, while the spirit of love and freedom was given on the tablets of the heart.

“But you received the Spirit of adoption as sons”—that is, the Holy Spirit, through whose grace the faithful, once their sins have been forgiven in baptism, become adopted sons of God.

“In whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’” Some copies have *clamantem* (“making [one] cry”), which means “causing one to cry out.” The explanation, therefore, is that found in our copies. This cry is not of the mouth or throat, but of the heart.

*Abba* is Syriac and Hebrew; *pater* (“father”) is Greek and Latin. We therefore cry in the Spirit, “Abba, Father,” when, while praying, we say, “Our Father,” and so forth.

But why did he use both expressions when they are one? Clearly, because he foresaw that many from both peoples would come to the one faith of Christ. Therefore, on account of the cornerstone, he used both, so that each nation might have a way of glorifying God in its own language.

“For the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are sons of God.” Note that he does not say merely “the Spirit,” but adds *himself*—that is, the Spirit in whom we cry, “Abba, Father.” The Holy Spirit is our earnest, because he has bestowed upon us the pledge of his grace as an earnest of what we are to receive. Therefore he says: “The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit.” He bears witness to our spirit that we are sons of God because he has bestowed upon us the pledge of his grace; and he certainly would not bestow it unless we were sons of God.

Therefore, because the inheritance of the father is owed to sons, he added: “But if sons, then heirs.” The father’s inheritance is owed to sons. Yet it is not so with the sons of human beings as it is with the sons of God. A human being leaves an inheritance to his sons, which he cannot possess together with them; God, however, gives his sons an inheritance that he will possess with them forever. Indeed, he himself is their inheritance, as the Psalmist says: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. XV, 5).

But lest anyone think it a small thing to be heirs of Christ, he added what should give us still greater joy: “heirs indeed of God, but fellow-heirs of Christ.” We are fellow-heirs of Christ because our bodies will be conformed to his glorious body (Phil. III, 21). For when they have risen, they will be led into the glory of immortality, to which Christ’s body came after the resurrection.

We are heirs of God. We shall be fellow-heirs of Christ when what we are has appeared. Hence John says: “Beloved, now we are sons of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. But when it has appeared, we shall be like him” (I John III, 2). He himself shows in what way we shall be like him by adding: “We shall see him as he is” (ibid.).

Therefore, to show how one must attain this dignity, he added: “provided that” [Note: [Col. 0203D] Other texts read *si quidem* (“if indeed”) instead of *si tamen* (“provided that”).] “we suffer with him” [Note: [Col. 0203D] The Vulgate has *sustinemus* (“we endure”). II Tim. II, 12.] “so that we may also be glorified with him.” By “we suffer with him” he means the same as “we die with him.” Hence elsewhere: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him; if we die with him, we shall also live with him” [Note: [Col. 0203D] The Vulgate has “if we have died with him, we shall also live with him,” ibid., 11.]

For it is necessary that we endure for his love sufferings like those that Christ endured for our salvation. If we do this, we shall reach the point at which we are glorified together with him, because we shall be led into that glory of immortality to which Christ came after the resurrection.

But someone may say: “How can we suffer for Christ what Christ suffered for us, when there are no bodily persecutors or outward torments?” Nevertheless, although bodily persecutors and persecutions are absent, spiritual persecutors and persecutions are present, against which we must always fight as long as we are in the flesh.
