For no one can overcome lack of restraint by restraint, or other vices [Note: [Col. 0203D] In place of *caetera* (“the others”), the autograph reads *contra* (“against”). Reader, judge whether I have read it correctly.] by the virtues opposed to them, except with great labor.

[Col. 0203D] Here is written “Lord’s Day XI after Pentecost.” And lest suffering for Christ seem harsh and difficult to anyone, he took care to make it lighter by adding: “For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy,” and so forth.

What he says, “I consider” [Note: [Col. 0203D] In the autograph margin: “chapter XX.”] is not spoken doubtfully, but affirmatively. Thus elsewhere: “But I think” [Note: [Col. 0203D] The words “but I think,” which appear in the Epistle but are absent from the autograph, and which supply both a similarity of phrasing and a logical force, I judged should be added.] “that I too have the Spirit of God” (I Cor. VII, 40) [Note: [Col. 0204D] The Vulgate has *habeam* (“that I may have”).] And again: “I think that God has appointed us apostles last, as men destined for death” (I Cor. IV, 9).

By saying “of this present time,” he shows that the persecutions of the present life are light and momentary. Hence he also prefaced it with “are not worthy”; for earthly things can in no way be equated with heavenly things, nor temporal things with eternal things. Hence Origen says: “Even if I should suffer throughout the whole time of my life such things as Job suffered, I would not consider myself worthy of the blessedness of eternal life.”

“Of the glory that is to come.” By saying “that is to come,” he shows that it is everlasting. Because it cannot be explained in words, he himself says elsewhere: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard—the things God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II, 9).

But in adding, “which will be revealed in us,” he shows that it is now hidden. Hence John says: “It has not yet appeared what we shall be.” When he says “in us,” he shows that the dignity of the apostles will differ greatly from the dignity of the other sons, since this glory will be revealed in them to a much greater degree.

But what does he mean by the following: “The expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God”? [Note: The Vulgate has: “For the expectation.”] For what is this creation? Or who are the sons of God? Creation consists of the angels, the sublime powers and heavenly virtues, heaven, earth, and everything that God the Father created through the Son. From this it is clear that he alone, and not creation, is the Creator, from whom all things were also brought to perfection. We must therefore not understand “creation” as one thing and “the sons of God” as another, since they are one. [Col. 0204C]

“The expectation awaits” is said in the same way as in John: “The friend of the bridegroom rejoices with joy” (John III, 29). Thus “the expectation of creation awaits” not the revelation of another nature that is not creation, but its own revelation. For he says: “The expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God,” as if he were saying: Our expectation awaits the revelation that will be in us who are the sons of God; it awaits the manifestation of what has been promised, since, according to John’s statement, it still lies hidden; it awaits the manifestation in us, who already are, of what we shall be (I John III, 2); it awaits the time when creation, such as it now is, will become what it is destined to be.

This was said, surely, as though one were saying to a painter who was prepared and possessed many colors: “The expectation of your colors awaits the manifestation of the image”—not because the colors will not exist, or because different colors will exist, but because they will possess greater dignity, that is, the beauty of the image. [Col. 0204D]

[Note: Observe this very beautiful comparison. Taking the opportunity, I would have the reader note that it could scarcely be hoped that the author of such an age would possess greater elegance of style, or a wiser and more beautiful choice of tropes, figures, and, indeed, thoughts. Jokes involving trivial and childish words with similar endings or sounds were then highly commended by their frequent use; how far removed they are from this!]

He continues: “For creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope.” [Col. 0205A] [Note: The Vulgate has: “subjected it in hope.”]

This statement has been explained in various ways by learned interpreters. It must therefore be carefully investigated what this vanity is, and what creation has been subjected to vanity.

As some understand it, “vanity” means man. Hence Solomon says: “Vanity of vanities, says Ecclesiastes; all is vanity” (Ecclesiastes I, 2). Likewise: “Everything under the sun is vanity” (ibid., 14). The Psalmist also says: “All is vanity; every living man” (Psalm XXXVIII, 6). If, then, all is vanity and every man is vanity, and everything under the sun is vanity, man is nevertheless the vanity of vanities. And truly there is nothing more vain than man—in the taking of food, in the stench of digestion, in the redness and filth involved in the begetting of offspring, and in other matters of this kind.

They understood “creation,” however, to mean the sun, moon, and the rest of the things that are said to have been subjected to vanity because they were made for human beings. For the sun rises and sets for human beings, and the other stars likewise. Why, then, does he add “not willingly,” since all these things are inanimate? Unless perhaps we accept the opinion of the philosophers, who assert that all these things are animate, and understand the statement to mean that they were subjected “because of him who subjected them in hope,” since they have hope of being liberated from this servitude. But because this interpretation comes close to error, it must be rejected altogether.

Others, such as Origen [Note: In the autograph it always reads “Origen’s.”], understand “creation” [Note: Perhaps “creation” should be read here in place of the present form.] to mean the angels, whom we read presided over wars. And truly nothing is more vain than war, in which man labors for the purpose of ceasing to be. [Col. 0205B] [Note: Here is a remarkable saying by this author, worthy of him and most appropriate to his times.] But if the angels are read to have presided over wars, as Origen endeavors to prove by many testimonies of the prophets, and especially of Daniel, then they are subject to human beings; hence they do not wish to be subjected: “Not willingly, but because of him who subjected them in hope.” [Col. 0205C] For they are compelled to withdraw from contemplation of their Creator in order to serve human beings, while retaining hope of being liberated from human servitude. [Col. 0206D] [Note: In the autograph, in place of *non* (“not”), *tum* (“then”) is read.]

It remains, therefore, that we understand human beings to be happier than the angels, especially those who now rest, such as Lazarus in Abraham’s bosom and that venerable robber who, on the day he believed, was placed with God in Paradise. But this interpretation too must be rejected. [Col. 0205D]

The statement must therefore be understood in an entirely different way. Each of the teachers contributed to God’s treasury what he possessed: one gold, another silver, another iron, and so forth. Not only in this matter, but also in every passage of sacred Scripture, one must seek an interpretation that does not injure the catholic faith or divide the unity of the Church.

Accordingly, it should be known that blessed Augustine investigated and resolved this question most profoundly. He says that “creation” signifies man—not only “creation,” but “every creature.” Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI, 15). The Apostle likewise says: “In the whole creation that is under heaven” (Colossians I, 23), that is, in man, who is called “every creature”—not because he contains every creature within himself, but because he is partly bodily, partly animate, and partly spiritual. The bodily extends through places; the animate gives life to the bodily; the spiritual governs the animate, and does so rightly when it subjects itself to God’s governance. Thus man perceives through the spirit, is given life through the soul, and moves locally through the body. [Col. 0206A]

Blessed Gregory says that man is called “every creature” because he possesses something of every creature: he has being with the stones, life with the trees and plants, sensation with the irrational animals, and discernment with the angels.

This creation, then, has been subjected to vanity—that is, to death, weakness, or some other misery to which man has been subjected because of sin. Hence he appropriately adds, “not willingly.” For since man sinned voluntarily, he was subjected to vanity unwillingly. Or he says “not willingly” because holy men desire to depart and be with Christ (Philippians I, 23), yet are compelled and unwillingly subjected to these miseries. [Col. 0206B]

“But because of him who subjected it in hope.” He says “because of him,” that is, because of the justice and mercy of the one who neither left sin unpunished nor permitted it to remain incurable. Or he says “because of him who subjected it in hope” because the elect have hope of being liberated from the servitude of corruption.

Therefore, since he had mentioned hope, in order to show what that hope was, he added: “For creation itself will be liberated from the servitude of corruption.” Here it should be noted that he does not say merely *ipsa* (“itself”), but *et ipsa* (“also itself”), on account of those who were going to believe and be liberated. “Ipsa creatura” means the human being himself. It is the creation that has not yet attained the perfect form of the sons of God, but is called merely creation. [Col. 0206C]

For when he says *et ipsa* (“also itself”), he wished the words “as we” to be understood, so that the sense is: We must not despair even of those who have not yet believed and are not yet called sons of God, since they too will believe and be liberated from this servitude, as we have been, who are already sons of God, although what we shall be has not yet appeared.

To what, then, will they pass when liberated? “Into the freedom,” he says, “of the glory of the sons of God.” The meaning is that they too, from slaves, will become free; from the dead, glorious in the eternal life that the sons of God will possess.

“For we know that all creation,” and so forth. Above he said “I consider”; now he says “we know.” Thus both this statement and the earlier one must be understood as affirmations. As has been said, “all creation” is counted in man. [Col. 0206D]

“It groans and labors in birth until now”; some copies read, “it groans and suffers.” Thus the statement is made as though he were saying: It groans and, like a woman in labor, suffers. Creation groans in those who have not yet been liberated. They groan because of the various difficulties and hardships that they endure in the present life. He rightly says “until now,” since, although there are some who are already resting, there are still many who suffer these miseries. [Col. 0207A]

Not only that creation—that is, all creation—but we ourselves [Note: The Vulgate has “but we ourselves also.”], as though he were saying plainly: They groan outwardly in the body, because the spirit, soul, and body suffer together. We, however, who have overcome the body’s afflictions and conquered the desires of the flesh, suffer in spirit alone, apart from bodily troubles. [Col. 0207B]

To show who these are, he added: “Having the firstfruits of the Spirit,” that is, those who have offered the sacrifice of our spirits to God, and in whom the spirits have been kindled and seized by the fire of charity. We are souls who have offered our minds as firstfruits to God. [Note: Here a distinction is made between spirit and soul.] For he had already offered the sacrifice of his spirit to God who said: “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin” (Romans I, 9); and again: “Whom I serve in my spirit” (Romans VII, 25).

Or he says “having the firstfruits of the Spirit” because the Holy Spirit was first manifestly given to them.

“And we ourselves groan within ourselves”—that is, they groan outwardly in the body, whereas we groan outwardly apart from the body. He shows the source of this groaning by adding: “Awaiting the adoption of sons” [Note: The Vulgate has “the adoption of the sons of God.”], “the redemption of our body.” [Col. 0207C]

But was it not already redeemed? Was he not already a son of God? Certainly he was, since Christ had already shed his blood for him; since, through the remission of sins in baptism, he had already passed by the grace of the Holy Spirit into the adoption of sons. How, then, was he still awaiting it? Clearly, because this redemption and adoption are not yet perfect. They will be completed when this mortal nature is swallowed up by life.

He therefore says: “Awaiting the adoption of sons, the redemption of our body,” as though he were plainly saying: We await the time when the body will receive the benefit of the adoption by which we were called sons of God, so that it may show us to be wholly liberated and manifest us as sons of God in every respect.

Nevertheless, someone might say: “O Apostle, why do you groan? Why do you suffer? What benefit has Christ brought you? How has your Savior saved you, if you still groan? For whoever groans is weak.” [Note: In the autograph, marginal chapter XXI.] [Col. 0207D]

He answers this as though saying: “For we have been saved in hope.” Here it should be noted that he does not say, “We are saved in hope,” but “We have been saved.” Christ saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal; but this salvation is not yet perfect, because we do not yet possess it in actuality, since what we shall be has not yet appeared.

The present, therefore, is the time of faith, since we are saved by believing in Christ through faith. For, as the same Apostle says: “We walk by faith and not by sight” (II Corinthians V, 7). The reward of faith is the salvation of our souls; but this salvation of souls and redemption of bodies is not yet perfect, because we possess it only in hope and not in actuality. “For the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wisdom IX, 15).

This salvation and redemption, however, went before us in our Head, namely, the Lord Jesus Christ, since the flesh that he took from us rose again and ascended into heaven; and thus it was saved. [Col. 0208A] Therefore we too have been saved in hope, because we hold with complete certainty the hope that one day we shall attain that glory of immortality.

Finally, wishing to show that hope concerns those things that are not seen, the Apostle added: “But hope that is seen is not hope.” Again, to show the difference between hope and actuality, he added: “For what does someone see and hope for?” [Note: The Vulgate has: “For what someone sees, why does he hope for it?” The following context sufficiently indicates that, instead of “what” at the first occurrence, “what he sees” should be read.] No one hopes for what he sees, because he holds it either with his eyes or with his hands. But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience.

The meaning is: If we hope for what we do not see, then we desire it; and if we desire it, we await it patiently, so that at last we may obtain it. [Col. 0208B]

The Apostle clearly wished to show by these words that the virtue of hope generates patience in us. Patience, however, does not exist in prosperous circumstances, which we enjoy, but in adverse circumstances, by which we are afflicted.

Therefore, because he had said above: “The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit,” he now added: “Likewise the Spirit also helps our weakness,” that is, just as he bears witness, so also he helps our weakness.

Accordingly, “Spirit” must be understood here not as our spirit but as the Holy Spirit. By “weakness” he means not bodily weakness but weakness of the mind. He plainly calls ignorance weakness. For our mind is burdened by ignorance, but the Holy Spirit helps our weakness: while pouring into us charity and the devout inclination of spiritual grace, he reveals what we do not know. [Col. 0208C]

Thus, to show what weakness he meant, the Apostle added: “For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought.” Prayer, which obtains what it asks, clearly shows itself to be a gift of God.

Therefore, to show that prayer too is to be counted among God’s gifts, the Apostle says: “For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought.” Since we do not see what has been promised [Note: The autograph has “what is promised.”], we do not know how to pray as we ought—that is, how to ask for what benefits us and reject what harms us.

No one has sound wisdom; no one has right understanding; no one acts with sound counsel and strength; no one is knowingly devout, nor devoutly knowledgeable; no one loves God with chaste fear unless he receives the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the fear of the Lord.

Likewise, no one possesses true virtue, sincere charity, or religious self-restraint unless he has received the spirit of virtue, charity, and self-restraint. In the same way, no one believes rightly unless he has the spirit of faith. So too no one prays rightly unless he receives the spirit of prayer—not because there are so many spirits, for the Holy Spirit is one, but because this one and the same Spirit accomplishes all these things, distributing to each as he wills (I Corinthians XII, 11). [Col. 0209A]

Therefore the Apostle says: “We do not know what we should pray for as we ought,” unless the grace of the Holy Spirit grants this to us.

In temporal matters, then, as blessed Augustine says, we should ask for nothing fixed [Note: Would that Christians seriously weighed this saying of Saint Augustine, fixed it deeply in their hearts, and prudently put it into practice. Prayer would then become worthier and more acceptable to him whom we pray, and far more useful to us and our affairs, if we used more often that part of prayer which our Lord Jesus Christ taught us: “Your will be done”; as also elsewhere: “Nevertheless, let not my will but yours be done.”], since we do not know what is expedient and what is not. Thus we often ask for things that we think will benefit us, yet they harm us; conversely, we do not wish to ask for things that we believe will harm us, yet they benefit us.

And what wonder is this, when the Apostle himself asked the Lord three times that the angel of Satan, who was striking him, might depart from him? Yet he was not heard; rather, he received the answer: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (II Corinthians XII, 8–9).

Therefore, as has already been said, we should ask for nothing fixed in temporal matters, but say to God: “Lord, command what you will, and yourself grant what you command, because without you we can do nothing.” [Note: Here is a most excellent manner of prayer.] [Col. 0209B]

“But the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings” [Note: The Vulgate has “pleads for us.”]. What he means by “intercedes” must not be understood as though the Holy Spirit needed anything or suffered any troubles or distresses. [Note: In the autograph, where the construction with *indigere* would apparently require *aliquo* or *alicujus*, it reads *aliquid* (“something”).] For he is equal to the Father and the Son [Note: “Is” is understood], since there is one person in the Trinity. [Col. 0209C]

Rather, it must be understood in the same way as the statement: “The Lord your God tests you, to know whether you love him” (Deuteronomy XIII, 3), that is, to make you know; and in the same way as the same Apostle speaks elsewhere of the same Spirit: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Galatians IV, 6).

Similarly, in this passage “he intercedes” means that he makes the saints intercede. For when he moves us, when he arouses us to compunction of heart, to tears, and to prayer, so that we ask with groanings, what we do under his prompting is said to be done by him—by that figure of speech by which we commonly speak of a joyful day because it makes us joyful.

Since the Holy Spirit says this invisibly and it cannot be expressed in words, the Apostle therefore added: “with inexpressible groanings.” [Col. 0209D]

Someone might ask: “From where does this come to us? Who can comprehend it?” The Apostle answers: “He who searches the hearts knows what the Spirit desires,” as though he were saying: He who looks into the secrets of all knows what his Spirit desires, namely, the salvation and redemption of the human race.

For when the charity of spiritual grace pours into us a devout inclination, it pleads for the saints—that is, it makes them plead for their own salvation and redemption. This is what follows: “For he pleads for the saints according to God,” that is, according to what pleases God; he makes them plead for it.

Someone among the faithful might ask: “If the Holy Spirit pleads for the saints, why then do they suffer so many adversities? Or what are we to say about those who go astray for a time?” [Col. 0210A]

The Apostle answers them: “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God.” Here it should be noted that he does not say “for those who love the world,” but “for those who love God.” By “all things” he means both adversity and prosperity.

The meaning is: For those who love God, all things work together for good, because even if they go astray for a time, God nevertheless turns everything toward their good.

And because there are some who love God for a time but do not persevere in the good they began, to show whom he meant he adds: “For those who are called saints according to the purpose.” Here “purpose” refers not to man’s purpose but to God’s—that is, divine predestination.

For those who have been called saints according to this purpose, all things work together for good. For even if they stray for a time, they return humbled and wiser; in their very falls they learn to work out their salvation with fear and trembling. [Col. 0210B]

When he says “they are called saints,” this should not be understood to mean that they were saints when they were called, but that they became saints by being called. [Note: This very excellent interpretation should be joined with the interpretation given at the beginning of this Epistle in the words: “To all who are in Rome, beloved of God, called saints”; and with what is said below in the interpretation of verses 11, 12, and 13, especially the words “so that, according to the election, the purpose of God might remain.”] [Col. 0210D]

And because he had said “according to the purpose,” to make this clearer he added: “For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed,” and so forth.

As Fulgentius says, foreknowledge differs from predestination in this respect: foreknowledge concerns both good and evil, whereas predestination concerns only good. Both the good and the evil are foreknown, but only the good are predestined, since God predestines no one to evil. [Col. 0210C]

Predestination, therefore, cannot exist without foreknowledge, because God foreknew through predestination only those things that he himself was going to do. Foreknowledge, however, can exist without predestination, because God also foreknew things that he was not going to do, such as sins.

Predestination is the preparation of God’s grace. [Note: Here is a definition of predestination.] Grace, however, is the effect of predestination. [Note: Here is the nature of gratuitous grace.]

Those, therefore, whom God foreknew he would make good and cause to persevere in goodness, he predestined—that is, he prepared them to be conformed to the image of his Son.

He says “conformed,” meaning of one form with him. For people are said to be conformed to the image of the Son of God in the same way that they are said to be conformed to the world. Hence the Apostle says elsewhere: “Do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed in the renewal of your mind” (Romans XII, 2). [Col. 0210D]

When he says, therefore, that we are to be conformed to the image of his Son, this must be understood according to the inner man. For when we are transformed in the renewal of our mind, putting off the old man with his deeds and putting on the new (Colossians III, 9–10), then we are conformed to the image of the Son of God. [Col. 0211A]

It may also be understood in this way: Just as he became a participant with us in mortality, so we are conformed to his image through immortality, when we pass into that glory of immortality to which he passed after the resurrection.

The faithful are therefore conformed to him both by action and by imitation, because they keep his commandments and follow his footsteps. Hence he says in the Gospel: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there my servant will be also” (John XII, 26).

“So that he himself might be the firstborn among many brothers.”

In these words it should be noted that the Apostle speaks carefully about the Son of God. Speaking of his humanity, he says: “so that he himself might be the firstborn among many brothers.” [Note: The verb “he said,” “he says,” or something similar may perhaps be understood there; or one might properly argue that the particle “for” should be removed, so that the text reads: “because the Apostle spoke carefully about the Son of God, speaking of his humanity.”]

He wished to show [Note: Instead of “to show,” the autograph reads “he might show,” and so forth] that by nature the Son of God was the only-begotten Son, but by his humanity he became the firstborn. [Col. 0211B]

For although he was the only one, he did not wish to remain alone; rather, he descended and became the firstborn in order to acquire many brothers for himself, with whom he would divide his Father’s kingdom.

He is therefore called “the firstborn among many brothers” because he first opened the womb of Mother Church for the begetting of sons for God. He is called the firstborn because, as John says: “To all who received him, he gave power to become sons of God” (John I, 12).

It should also be noted that, just as he is called the firstborn among many brothers according to the flesh, so too he is called “the firstborn of the dead” (Revelation I, 5; Colossians I, 18), because he first rose from the dead by his own power. [Col. 0211C]

Therefore, since he had previously said, “those whom he foreknew and predestined,” he now adds: “Those whom he predestined, he also called.” Here “according to the purpose” must be understood, since there is another kind of calling, about which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew XXII, 14).

“Those whom he called”—namely, according to the purpose—“he also justified,” through the washing of baptism and the grace of the Holy Spirit.

“Those whom he justified, he will also glorify” [Note: The Vulgate has “he glorified.”].

It should therefore be known [Note: The autograph has *quae* (“which”).] that predestination was not accomplished in us, but secretly with God, in his foreknowledge. What follows—that is, calling, justification, and glorification—is accomplished in us.

We are called by the preaching of repentance, according to the words: “Repent” and so forth (Matthew III, 2). We are justified in the renewal of mercy and in fear of judgment. Hence the Psalmist prays: “Save me, O God, by your name, and by your power free me” [Note: Psalm LIII, 3. The Vulgate has “judge me.”]. For the one who has first obtained liberation does not fear judgment. [Col. 0212A]

We shall be glorified when we pass into eternal life.

These apostolic words must therefore be distinguished with the greatest care, and we must diligently observe what we have received and what we are going to receive. Thus, when we understand what we have received, we may give thanks to the one from whom we received it. Conversely, when we recognize what we are going to receive, we may understand God as our debtor—not as a human being is his debtor. A human being is indebted to the one from whom he has received a benefit, but God has bestowed and will bestow gifts upon us out of his free goodness. Hence he says to Job: “Who has given to me first, that I should repay him?” (Job XLI, 2).

Accordingly, it should be known that the four things the Apostle mentioned have already been fulfilled. All the saints have already been foreknown and predestined; many of them have already been called and justified. One thing, however, has not yet been fulfilled: the final item, when he says, “he will glorify them.” This glory must be understood as none other than that of which the same Apostle says elsewhere: “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians III, 4). [Col. 0212B]

Nevertheless, the two things just mentioned—calling and justification—have not yet been fulfilled in everyone, since there will be people to be called and justified until the end of the age.

The Apostle therefore used verbs of the past tense even of future events, to show that with God all things have been accomplished that he determined from eternity to do. Hence Isaiah says of him [Note: See Isaiah chapter 41, although the exact words are not found there]: “He has done the things that are to come.” [Col. 0212C]

Therefore, all who have been foreknown and predestined in that most provident disposition of God, and who have been called and justified, are sons of God—not only those [Note: The sense seems to require reading: “not only those who have already been born, but also those who do not yet exist,” and so forth] who are not yet reborn [Note: In the autograph it reads “have been born”; immediately above, between the words “have been born,” the word “re” is written in the same script, but in ink that is not the same, being less black and somewhat reddish. Reader, consider whether “reborn,” “born,” or “re-born” should be read, so that the meaning concerns either ordinary birth properly so called or that birth by which a person is reborn through baptism], and can in no way perish. [The transmitted wording is syntactically defective; its intended continuation is uncertain.]

Finally, God foreknew and predestined us when we were unborn; he called us when we were hostile and enemies; he justified us when we were sinners; and he will glorify us when we have been raised. By these acts he demonstrates that he is almighty.

Thus he immediately added [Note: In the autograph, chapter XXII is written here]: “What, then, shall we say to these things?” The implied meaning is: “What shall we say, except that God is most powerful, and that while he protects us by his power no one can harm us?”

Hence he immediately adds: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” That is: If he protects us by his omnipotence, who will be able to harm us?

For whoever strives to harm us attempts to rebel against him; but who can conquer the Omnipotent? Whoever kicks against the goad rages against himself.

This, then, is the voice of all good people, especially of the martyrs.

How is it true, glorious martyrs, that what you say is: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” Behold, the whole world rages against you; punishments are devised; your bodies are afflicted by various tortures.

Therefore, to prove by the clearest evidence that what he had said was true, he added in the voice of the martyrs themselves: “He who did not spare even his own Son, but delivered him up for us all—how will he not also, with him, freely give us all things?” [Col. 0213A]

As though they were saying: “By this we prove that what we say is true: God loved us so greatly that he did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us. Therefore, although our bodies are tortured in the present, the Lord, our liberator and protector, brings our souls into rest and will one day glorify our resurrected bodies.”

Therefore, because all the faithful are adopted sons of God, he prefaced the phrase with “his own,” to distinguish them from him. By this expression he showed that he is the Son in one way, while they are sons in another.

But the Apostle says that God the Father delivered up the Son. Yet he did not do this alone: the Son and the Holy Spirit did so as well, since the operation of the whole Trinity is one. [Col. 0213B]

Judas also delivered him up. What, then, was his sin, if he did what the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit did? He sinned because he did not will or desire the good that was bestowed upon us through Christ’s Passion; rather, he delivered him up because of greed. Thus the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit deserved the praise of their grace, whereas Judas received the reward of his greed.

He continues: “How will he not also, with him, freely give us all things?”

The meaning is: If he did the greater thing, how will he not do the lesser? The greater thing was that he delivered up his Son for us; the lesser is that he gave us all things, since in giving us the Son himself he gave us the one in whom all things are. [Col. 0213C]

But what are these “all things”? Did he give us angels so that we might rule over them? No, for, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Human beings will be equal to the angels” (Luke XX, 36; Matthew XXII, 30).

He has already given and will give all things, because he grants forgiveness of sins and strength to resist adversities, and he will give the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom. When we have received it, we shall possess all things in him.

The things above will be ours for contemplation; the equal things, for fellowship; the lower things, for dominion. Each of these will belong to all, and all to each.

He continues: “Who will accuse God’s elect?” [Note: The Vulgate has: “Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect?” and so forth. In the autograph, chapter XXIII.] [Col. 0213D]

It is as though he were saying: Since God has predestined, called, and justified the elect, who will be able to accuse them? [Col. 0214A]

And because someone might answer, “A human being, an angel, or God,” he adds: “God, who justifies” [Note: In the autograph, a question mark follows the words “God, who justifies.” Thus the following words show that our interpreter understood this phrase interrogatively.]

As though he were saying: It is clear that an angel or a human being cannot. But what about God, who justifies? No; for the one who came to justify will in no way accuse.

Hence he adds: “Who is he that condemns?”

Again, because someone might answer, “An angel, a human being, or Christ,” he adds: “Christ Jesus,” and so forth.

As though he were saying: Not a human being or an angel—and not Christ either. For those whom he loved so greatly that he suffered such things for them, he neither condemns nor accuses. Certainly he does not condemn who came to save what had perished (Luke XIX, 10).

The ancients held that the difference between a *percontatio* and a question was this: many answers can be given to a *percontatio*, but to a question only one—either yes or no. [Col. 0214B]

Thus “Will he accuse the elect?” was spoken as a *percontatio*: “Who will accuse against God’s elect?” [Note: This text seems to receive the adverb “against” just as in the Vulgate. It is written in abbreviated form as “qs. a. a. e. di.” Of these initial letters, the second “a” can signify nothing other than “against.”]

But “God, who justifies?” was spoken as a question, with “no” understood.

Likewise, “Who is he that condemns?” is a *percontatio*, whereas “Christ Jesus, who died?” is a question. “Indeed, who also rose again? Who is at the right hand of God the Father? Who also intercedes for us?” [Note: None of these question marks appears in the Vulgate. After the word “God,” the Vulgate does not read “the Father.”] In all these cases “no” must be understood.

Christ, therefore, seated at the right hand of the Father—that is, remaining in equality with him—intercedes for the elect in two ways: either because he assumed the frailty of our flesh into the unity of his person, or because he displays to the Father the kind of suffering he endured.

For when he shows God the Father the scars of the wounds that he received on the cross, he manifests how greatly he loved us, for whom he endured these things.

Blessed Augustine says that our Head intercedes for us when he receives some of his members, scourges others, cleanses others, calls others, recalls others, creates others, corrects others, and restores others. [Col. 0214C]

Who, then, will separate us from the love of God [Note: [Col. 0214D] The Vulgate reads “of Christ.”]? That is, since God loved us so greatly that he did not even spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all, and in him granted us everything—so much so that we can neither be accused nor condemned—what, then, could separate us from his love? This was certainly said in the form of a question. What follows—“Tribulation? Or distress, etc.?”—is to be read with the intonation of someone asking questions.

Tribulation, therefore, cannot separate the elect from the love of Christ, because they produce in them the virtue of wisdom [Note: [Col. 0214D] From what follows, I think this is an error, and that “patience” should be read instead of “wisdom.” Nevertheless, “wisdom” could also be considered an excellent reading by way of argument, if it is compared with what was said somewhat earlier: for tribulations, as was very well observed above, make us learned, so that we may endure them with an increasingly even spirit, be perfected in imitation of Christ, and be made worthy to become participants in his glory.]. Hence the earlier statement: “Tribulation produces patience.” For the more they are afflicted, the more they are enlarged. Thus the Psalmist says: “In tribulation you enlarged me” (Ps. IV, 2); and again: “In tribulation I called upon the Lord, and he answered me in spaciousness” (Ps. CXVII, 5).

Distress cannot separate them, because the more severely they are distressed, the more greatly they rejoice. Hence it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “They went away from the presence of the council rejoicing, because they had been deemed worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus” (Acts V, 41). Hence James says: “Consider it all joy, my brothers, whenever you fall into various trials” (Jas. I, 2).

Persecution cannot separate them, because while they suffer persecutions they are made more blessed. Hence the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “You will be blessed when people persecute you and curse you” (Matt. V, 11; Luke VI, 22), and so forth.

Bodily hunger cannot separate them, because although the body outwardly feels deprivation of food, inwardly it is refreshed by that heavenly bread which says of itself: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John LI, 52).

Nakedness has no power to separate them, because although they feel the numbness of cold, they grow warm with the fire of love, concerning which the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke XII, 49); and they are already clothed in hope with the robe of immortality.

Danger cannot separate them, because, established upon the most solid rock of faith, whatever danger they suffer is endured through contemplation of that good which they are to receive. Hence the Psalmist says: “He established my feet upon a rock” (Ps. XXXIX, 3).

The material sword cannot separate them, because they possess the sword of the word of God, by which they overcome all the flaming weapons of the Evil One. Hence the Apostle says elsewhere: “The sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI, 17)—“receive” is understood.

[Col. 0215C] To confirm this with the testimony of the prophet, he added: “As it is written: Because of you we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter.” While the Apostle was laboring amid the persecution of the Gentiles, he took up the voice of all the martyrs and said: “Because of you, etc.” Here one must note that he did not merely say “we are put to death,” but added “all day long.” For, as Origen says, it is not enough for us to be put to death for a moment, an hour, a month, or a year, unless we are put to death throughout the whole day—that is, for the entire duration of our present life.

The saints are regarded as sheep for slaughter, because they were slaughtered like sheep. They are beautifully compared to a sheep [Note: [Col. 0215D] In the author’s manuscript, *assimulantur* is found; this too can correctly be read in the same sense, namely, that the holy martyrs are called sheep figuratively or by comparison.], because of their innocence and simplicity, or because they have been joined to the one of whom Isaiah says: “Like a sheep he will be led to the slaughter” (Isa. LVII, 7).

[Col. 0215D] But what do they accomplish in these things [Note: [Col. 0215D] “The following” is understood.]? We are not cast down, we do not perish, but we overcome in all things. Here one must note that he did not merely say “in these things,” but added “in all things.” Someone may overcome tribulation and distress; but unless he also conquers hunger, nakedness, and the other afflictions, that is not sufficient for perfection.

And he says beautifully, “we overcome”: for whoever conquers is superior. The saints therefore overcame, because they were not defeated by living, but gloriously conquered by dying. This is to be attributed not to their merits or their strength, but to the grace of God [Note: [Col. 0215D] Here is the consistent opinion of this most eminent man.]. Hence the Apostle added: “Because of him who loved us.”

Accordingly, since he had said above, “Who will separate us from the love of God?”, in order to affirm this more strongly he added: “For I am sure that neither death nor life, etc.” As if he were saying: I have no doubt whatever that neither death, nor life, nor anything else will be able to separate us from the love of God.

Death cannot separate the saints from this love, because no one can separate them by threatening death, since the one whom they love cannot die; nor can anyone separate them by promising life, since the one they love is himself true life, and he says of himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, [Col. 0216B] 6).

In this passage “angels” should be understood as good angels. Here too, similarly [Note: [Col. 0216D] The two words “similarly here” are written in this form: *si. h.*], it is said as he says elsewhere: “But even if an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to what was preached, let him be accursed” (Gal. I, 8). An angel therefore cannot separate us, because he is not more powerful than our mind while we cling to God.

He calls evil angels “principalities,” concerning whom he says elsewhere: “Having stripped principalities and powers, he led them forth boldly [Note: [Col. 0216D] Coloss. II, 15. The Vulgate reads “confidently.”], triumphing over them openly in himself.” These have no power to separate us, because they can neither promise nor give anything of the kind that God promises and gives.

“Nor things present, nor things future”—that is, neither the granting of present things nor the promise of future things; for the things granted with assurance are transitory, while those promised are uncertain. Nothing, however, is more eternal or more certain than what God gives.

Nor can “strength” separate us. Here this should be understood of evil spirits, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “When a strong man, fully armed, guards his courtyard” (Luke XI, 21), and so forth. The power of these cannot separate us, because God is incomparably stronger than they are.

He speaks of the height of heaven and the depth of the earth. Thus Isaiah says to Ahaz: “Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord God, whether in the heights above or in the earth below” [Note: [Col. 0216D] The Vulgate reads: “Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, in the depth of hell or in the height above.”]. The meaning is: Ask for the opening of heaven and the opening of the earth, so that, when you see what you have now seen, you may believe in the Lord God of Israel.

These things, therefore, cannot separate us, because even if the hidden place of heaven and the secret of the earth should be revealed, there is nevertheless nothing in them better than God himself [Note: [Col. 0216D] That is, nothing that can be compared with God.], who has promised that he will give himself to us.

He continues: “Nor will any other creature be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus.” He added this by way of amplification, as if he were saying: Even if there is some other creature, it will not be able to separate us from the love of God.

He says “which is in Christ Jesus” because it is in him by nature: for he himself is love. It is also in him as an activity, because he emptied himself and handed himself over for our salvation [Col. 0217A]; but in the saints it exists only as an activity through the grace of God [Note: [Col. 0217D] Observe this very beautiful distinction. Here the Vulgate begins chapter IX, whereas in the margin of the author’s manuscript chapter XXIII is read.].

To show that this love was also present in himself, he added: “For I myself was wishing to be accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers, etc.” To make himself more readily believed, he first introduced an oath, saying: “I speak the truth” (CHAP. IX); and, so that still greater credence might be given him, he added: “I do not lie in Christ.” He says “in Christ” beautifully: whoever speaks the truth speaks in Christ, because he himself is the truth.

He shows why he had said these things: “Because I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart.” Here the question must be asked why he asserts that sorrow is present in him, when Solomon says: “Whatever happens to the just man will not grieve him” (Prov. XII, 21). Was he not just? Since no one doubts his righteousness, let him himself resolve the question.

He says elsewhere: “The sorrow of the world produces death, but the sorrow that is according to God produces repentance leading to steadfast salvation” (II Cor. VII, 10). He was therefore sorrowful, but with that sorrow which is according to God, since he was sorrowful for the salvation of his brothers. Hence he says that pain is also present in him, and not just any pain, but continual pain: “For I myself was wishing to be accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers.”

This love is incredible. But one must note that he says “I was wishing,” not “I wish.” The following may be understood: “I was wishing then, when I was an imitator of my ancestral traditions, surpassing many of my contemporaries in my own race” (Gal. I, 14). The meaning is: “At that time I was wishing to be separated from Christ for the salvation of my brothers.”

Alternatively: Consider the intention with which Moses prayed, saying: “Lord, either forgive this offense of the people, or erase me from the book that your hand has written” (Exod. XXXII, 31); and Micah: “Would that I were not a man possessing the spirit, and that I spoke falsehood instead” (Mic. II, 11); and the Apostle was wishing to become accursed from Christ so that his brothers might come to faith.

Moses, inflamed by the fire of love, prayed this so that he might more easily obtain pardon for the people; Micah did likewise so that the destructions and blows which he had foreseen would come might not befall the people of God.

But one must know that *anathema* is Greek, while in Latin it means “alienation.” At times, however, it signifies death, as in the Old Testament: “If anyone does this or that, let him be accursed”—that is, “let him be condemned to death.” In the same way, therefore, it can be understood here as referring to death [Col. 0217D]. He was wishing to die bodily so that his brothers might be saved in soul, as if he were saying: “I was wishing to pour out my blood for them, so that they might live in spirit.”

He calls his brothers Jews; hence he immediately added: “Who are my kinsmen according to the flesh.” By saying this he shows that they are not his kinsmen according to the spirit. Concerning them he further adds: “Who are Israelites.” By these words he shows himself to be an Israelite, descended from the seed of Abraham: “Whose is the adoption [Col. 0218A] of sons.” [Note: [Col. 0217D] In the author’s manuscript it is not *adoptio est*, but *adoptionem*; I judged that it should be corrected in accordance with the Vulgate.]

The adoption of sons belongs to the Jews, because they were the first to be called to become adopted sons of God, in accordance with the statement: “Israel is my firstborn” (Exod. IV, 22). And the Lord says through Isaiah: “I have begotten and raised sons; but they despised and rejected me” (Isa. I, 2).

Alternatively, they are called adopted sons of God because, when the Lord came, many of them believed and became adopted sons of God. Hence he says elsewhere: “God sent his Son into this world, born of a woman, born under the law, so that he might redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive the adoption of the sons of God” (Gal. IV, 4).

“And the glory.” Here “glory” should be understood as that by which the Jews were specially taken from all the nations into God’s own people. Hence he said above: “What advantage has the Jew?” And immediately afterward: “Much, in every way, etc.”

“And the covenants” [Note: [Col. 0218D] The Vulgate reads the singular, “covenant”; other readings, however, agree with the author’s manuscript.]. We must understand the Old and the New Covenants. For while the Old was given to them, the New was prefigured in it.

“And the legislation.” Legislation—that is, the establishment of the law—belongs to them, because the law was established for them, so that they might know how to live and obey its commands.

“And the worship.” By “worship” he means the worship of that Old Covenant, by which the Jews served God in offering sacrifices and observing his commandments.

“And the promises.” By “promises” he means the promises made through the prophets and patriarchs concerning God, such as: “So shall your offspring be” (Gen. XV, 5); and again: “I will surely multiply your offspring” (Gen. XVI, 10), and so forth. [Col. 0218C] And again: “In your offspring all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII, 18). Hence the Apostle also grieves that the sons did not follow the promises made to their fathers.

“Their fathers,” namely, the patriarchs and prophets, “from whom Christ is according to the flesh.” He appropriately added “according to the flesh,” because according to his divinity he was begotten by God the Father before all ages; but according to the flesh he is from the Jews, since the blessed Virgin Mary, from whom he took flesh, descended from the stock of the Jews.

And to show that, according to the nature of his divinity, he did not take his beginning from the Virgin, he added: “Who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.” Christ, therefore, is God blessed above all—not, however, by virtue of having taken flesh from the Virgin, but because before all ages he was begotten by the Father.

Moreover, because he had said that continual pain was present in him over the destruction of his brothers, lest anyone should think that the promise made to Abraham had been nullified, the Apostle, wishing to show that God is powerful to do what he promised and to commend his grace, added: “But not”—the following is understood: “I say this because”—“that the word of God has failed” [Note: [Col. 0218D] In the margin of the author’s manuscript, chapter XXV is written here, while chapter XXIV is marked nowhere.]; that is, that the promise made to Abraham has been nullified [Col. 0219A]. For although the word of God failed among unbelievers, it was nevertheless fulfilled among believers.

To make this clear, he added almost as an explanation: “For not all who are from Israel are Israelites.” That is: Not all who descend according to the flesh from the stock of Jacob are men who see God, because not all believe in Christ. Whoever, therefore, from every nation believes in him—these are the Israelite men.

“Nor, because they are the seed of Abraham, are they all sons” [Note: [Col. 0219D] The Vulgate reads *qui*; other readings, however, also agree with ours.]. That is: Not all who descend from him according to the flesh are sons, but whoever from every nation imitates his footsteps—these are the sons of Abraham.

And this is what he intends in what follows: “But in Isaac your offspring shall be called” (Gen. XXI, 12). In these words he recalls the passage where it is written that the Lord commanded Abraham to obey the voice of his wife Sarah and cast out the slave woman and her son (ibid., 10), because the son of the slave woman would not be heir with the son of the free woman, but “in Isaac your offspring shall be called.”

Abraham, as the same Apostle says elsewhere, “had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. But the one by the slave woman was born according to the flesh” (Gal. IV, 22; Gen. XVI, 15)—that is, according to carnal custom—“while the one by the free woman was born according to the promise” [Note: [Col. 0219D] The Vulgate reads “through the promise.”], because he was promised to him before he was conceived or born.

Through these two men, therefore, both believers and unbelievers are represented: by Isaac, the faithful; by Ishmael, the unfaithful.

Accordingly, to show what “in Isaac your offspring shall be called” means, he added by way of explanation: “That is, it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but the children of the promise are counted [Note: [Col. 0219D] The Vulgate reads: “They are the children of the promise, they are counted,” etc.] as offspring.” This is plainly to say: Only those are counted as offspring who are represented in Isaac, the son of the promise. They are counted as offspring because, when divine grace calls them, they are gathered into Christ.

To show what this promise was, he added: “For the word of promise is this: At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son.” In these words he recalls the passage where it is written that, while Abraham was sitting at midday beneath the oak of Mamre (Gen. XVIII, 1), three angels appeared to him in the form of the Trinity. He received them as guests and washed their feet; after they had eaten, the Lord called Sarah and said: “At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son” [Note: [Col. 0219D] Gen. XVIII, 10; the Vulgate reads: “Returning, I will come to you at this time.”].

But lest anyone should believe that all who descended from Isaac are counted as offspring, since he had said, “In Isaac your offspring shall be called,” he therefore adds: “But not only so [Note: [Col. 0219D] The Vulgate reads “but not only she”], but Rebecca also, having conceived by one intercourse with Isaac our father.” It is as if he were saying: This distinction was made not only in the two sons of Abraham, but Rebecca also made this distinction, having conceived twins from a single intercourse with our father Isaac.

In these words he recalls the passage where it is written that, when the twins struggled in Rebecca’s womb (Gen. XXV, 22), she went to consult the Lord, and the Lord answered her: “Two nations and two peoples are in your womb, and one people shall surpass the other, and the elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. XXV, 23). These two sons of Rebecca also represent believers and unbelievers: the elder, Esau, represents unbelievers; the younger, Jacob, represents believers.

But why did the Apostle add “by one intercourse”? Clearly, so that it might not be said that Jacob was chosen on account of his own merits, or those of his parents or some relatives; or that his father was of greater merit and better character when he begot Jacob than when he begot his brother; or that his mother was of a different disposition when she conceived him than when she conceived his brother.

By this statement he shows that the father’s merit in begetting both was one and the same, and the mother’s merit in conceiving both was one and the same. For although afterward she could change her will, while carrying both in her womb, she did not change it for only one [Note: [Col. 0220D] The author’s manuscript reads: “not merely in unity.” I regard this as an error arising from what follows: “but equally toward both.”], but changed it equally toward both.

He said this, therefore, to commend the grace of God, wishing to show that both were born of one father, one mother, and one intercourse; but that one was chosen through undeserved mercy, while the other was rejected by the just judgment of God. Thus no one should presume to glory in himself, but “let the one who glories glory in the Lord” (I Cor. I, 31).

Accordingly, lest someone should say: “God foresaw good works in Jacob and therefore chose him, and likewise foresaw evil works in Esau and therefore rejected him,” he added: “For when they had not yet been born, and had done nothing good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain, it was said to her, not from works but from him who calls: The elder shall serve the younger.”

Before they were born, no faith or works could have preceded by which one of them would be chosen and the other rejected. These words clearly show that election does not depend upon purpose, but purpose upon election. For it is not purpose that precedes election, but election that precedes purpose; just as justification does not precede grace, but grace precedes justification. Likewise, calling does not precede election, but election precedes calling [Note: [Col. 0220D] Join this with what was said at the beginning of this Epistle concerning the words “to all who are in Rome, beloved of God, called as saints,” and with what was said in chapter VIII concerning the words “who are called as saints according to the purpose.”].

Nevertheless, not all who are called are chosen, because, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX, 16). The Apostle therefore plainly shows that just as Esau was rejected without any preceding merits of his own, so Jacob was chosen without any preceding merits of his own. For if there had been some merits preceding on account of which Jacob was chosen, there would certainly have been corresponding merits on account of which Esau was rejected.

But God’s purpose according to election remained, because, as the same Apostle testifies elsewhere, just as election is accomplished without any preceding merits, so also is predestination, which he calls “purpose”: “So also at the present time a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” [Note: [Col. 0221D] Romans XI, 5. In the author’s manuscript *sicut* is read instead of *sic*.].

It was therefore said to him, not on account of works—which had not preceded—but through the grace of him who calls: “The elder shall serve the younger.” In these words he recalls the passage where it is written that, when the twins struggled in Rebecca’s womb and she went to consult the Lord, the Lord answered her: “Two nations” (Gen. XXV, 22–23) “and two peoples are in the womb, and one people shall surpass the other, and the elder shall serve the younger.”

He calls Esau the elder; he was also called Edom, from whom the nation of the Idumeans arose. Jacob, however, was the younger.

This prophecy was therefore fulfilled according to its historical sense at the time when the Jewish people, which arose from the younger brother—that is, Jacob—overcame the people of Idumea through King David [Note: [Col. 0221D] The author’s manuscript reads “separated”], and made it tributary to itself, up to the king under whom they rebelled and cast the yoke of servitude from their neck.

Alternatively: Through the elder brother the Jewish people is represented, since it first came to knowledge of Christ; through the younger, the ecclesiastical people. This prophecy was therefore fulfilled because the Jewish people, scattered throughout the whole world, serves the ecclesiastical people.

Alternatively: Through the elder the carnal people is represented, and through the younger the spiritual people. For just as those two were enclosed in the womb, so these two are enclosed in the single womb of Mother Church and fight with one another; yet the carnal serves the spiritual, because the spiritual judges all things, while it itself is judged by no one (I Cor. II, 14–15).

To confirm his account by prophetic testimony, he added the testimony of a much later prophet, saying: “As it is written: Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. I, 2–3). For he shows that what had remained present before God from his ancient purpose through grace was disclosed through the prophet.

But one must ask what the Lord loved in Jacob, or what he hated in Esau. In Jacob, who had not yet been born and could do nothing, he loved nothing other than the gratuitous gift of his mercy. Similarly, in Esau he hated nothing other than original sin, by whose desert the entire mass of the human race was condemned.

[Note: [Col. 0221D] What immediately precedes and what follows are especially worthy of notice.] For the human race was so condemned in its very root that, even if no human being were saved, no one could find a just complaint against God; rather, by seeing others perish, each person would learn that he too would perish unless divine grace rescued him.

Someone might say in response: If what you say is true, then God is unjust, since from the condemned mass of the human race he chose one person and rejected another without any preceding merits of their own.

Therefore the Apostle raised this question against himself, adding: “What then shall we say?” [Note: [Col. 0221D] In the margin of the author’s manuscript, chapter XXVI is written here.] “Is there injustice with God?” As if he were saying: This was done not through any injustice of God, but through justice and mercy. For he chose one through undeserved grace and rejected the other by a most just judgment.

This is what he means by saying: “Certainly not.” Wishing to prove by reasoning what he had said, he added: “For he says to Moses: I will have mercy on whomever I have had mercy” [Note: [Col. 0222D] Exod. XXXIII, 19. The Vulgate reads: “I will have mercy on whomever I have mercy.”], “and I will show compassion to whomever I show compassion.”

But does he resolve the question by these words? Indeed, he seems rather to make it more difficult. Nevertheless, it can be understood in this way: “I will have mercy on whomever I have had mercy”—by choosing and predestining him; “I will have mercy on him”—by calling him through grace; and “on whomever I have mercy”—by calling him through grace—“I will show compassion,” by bringing him to faith and justifying him.

And because he had said that Jacob was chosen through the undeserved grace of God, he immediately drew a general conclusion in order to commend the same grace, saying: “So then it depends not on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who has mercy.”

It must certainly be understood that just as no one believes unless divine grace calls him, so no one believes unless he wills. Why, then, does the Apostle say, “It depends not on the one who wills or on the one who runs”? Clearly, because he wished to refer both—namely, the will and the running—to divine grace.

It does not depend on the human being who wills, because he cannot possess the will to do good from himself; it does not depend on the one who runs, because he cannot run by himself—that is, he cannot advance through good works. Rather, it depends on God who has mercy, whose grace anticipates him [Note: [Col. 0222D] Here is the doctrine of prevenient grace. Join this with what is said below in the interpretation of chapter XI, concerning the words: “I appeared openly to those who did not ask me.”], so that he receives the will to do good, and whose mercy assists him sufficiently to run well.

Nevertheless, just as our will and our running can accomplish no good unless divine grace precedes them, so the grace of God accomplishes no good in us unless we join our will to the divine will.

Therefore, just as we say, “It depends not on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who has mercy,” can we likewise say: “It depends not on God who has mercy, but on the human being who wills and runs”? But who would dare say this? Did the Apostle mean this? Certainly not. Rather, he wished everything to be referred to the one of whom it is written: “The will is prepared by the Lord.” For he himself both prepares it and assists it once prepared.

The text continues: “For Scripture says to Pharaoh, etc.” Above he had said, “Jacob I loved,” and therefore he introduced the testimony of Scripture that says: “I will have mercy on whomever I have had mercy, and I will show compassion to whomever I show compassion.” From this he also drew the general conclusion: “So then it depends not on the one who wills, etc.” This was said with reference to those who, liberated by divine grace, are justified.

Again, because he had said, “Esau I hated,” he therefore introduced this testimony: “For Scripture says to Pharaoh: For this very purpose I raised you up, etc.” This was said with reference to those upon whom wrath remains and who are condemned by his most just judgment.

It must therefore be understood that the completion of sins imposes an end and limit upon sinners. This happens not only to the dead but also to the living, as happened to the Sodomites, Jebusites, Perizzites, and all the nations of Canaan.

The sin of this Pharaoh had therefore already reached completion, and the time was at hand for him to be punished. For this reason God raised him up. After miracles had been performed in Egypt, God liberated the children of Israel so that they might believe in the God of Israel and learn not to fear their adversaries, and so that he might make them more cautious.

Pharaoh was evil, although this was hidden [Note: [Col. 0223D] Perhaps *occulte* or *occultim* should be read.]. But in order that what he was might be revealed and he might be punished, God raised him up for this reason.

Observe that he does not say, “I created you” or “I made you,” but “I raised you up.” Every creature of God is good; but this man became evil through his own wickedness.

This is not to deny original sin: rather, he became evil through original sin together with his own wickedness.

Thus the Lord said, “I raised you up,” as if someone were holding two small vessels in his hands, one full of balm and the other full of stench. If he shook them, no one could rightly say to him, “You made the fragrance” or “You made the stench,” but rather, “You shook this vessel full of stench” [Note: [Col. 0223D] Note this very beautiful example.].

The Lord therefore raised Pharaoh up by performing miracles, so that, when Pharaoh refused to believe, he might be punished. For he caused the children of Israel to cross the sea on dry feet, but drowned Pharaoh and his army in the sea.

Hence it follows: “So that I may show my power in you.” By this deed his name was proclaimed throughout the whole earth. Hence the further statement: “So that my name may be proclaimed throughout the whole earth.”

Finally, because he had shown that God chose Jacob through undeserved grace, while he rejected Esau and Pharaoh by the most just judgment, he immediately drew a general conclusion, saying: “Therefore, on whom he wills he has mercy, and whom he wills he hardens” [Note: [Col. 0223D] The Vulgate reads “makes hard.”].

“He has mercy on whom he wills,” according to the grace that is freely given; “he hardens whom he wills,” according to the most just judgment that repays each person according to his merits.

He is said to harden not because he makes a soft heart hard, but because he does not soften a hard heart. He is said to harden not because he compels or drives sinners to sin—for he compels no one to sin—but because he does not bestow the justification of his grace upon sinners; those whom he does not wish to have mercy on are therefore said to be hardened by him.

He hardens not by inflicting something that makes a person worse, but by not inflicting something that would make him better. He hardens not by imparting wickedness, but by not imparting righteousness. The hardening of God, therefore, is nothing other than his unwillingness to have mercy.

Someone might nevertheless say: If God hardens whom he wills, why do we sin if we fail to do good or perform some evil deed [Note: [Col. 0224D] The author’s manuscript reads *nisi*.], especially since human weakness is entirely unable to resist the divine will?

Seeing that this question could arise from his own words, he himself raised it against himself, saying: “You will say to me, then: Why does he still find fault?” That is: If God hardens whom he wills, what complaint can a human being bring against God while he does evil? And he introduces the apparent reason: “For who can resist his will?”

But he strongly suppressed the rashness of this question, adding: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” [Note: [Col. 0224D] In the author’s manuscript, chapter XXVII is written here.] He did not say this because of any lack of knowledge, but out of the abundance of his knowledge; and it must be read not lightly but with great seriousness. The meaning is: O man, since you are fragile, dust and ashes, who are you to bring a complaint against God about why he has mercy on some and hardens others?

Hence he introduced a most fitting comparison, saying: “Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why have you made me like this?’ Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?”

The meaning is this: Since you know that you are a thing formed, and that you arose from a condemned mass, and since you understand that a thing formed does not say to its maker, “Why have you made me like this?”, and that the potter has authority to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor, what just complaint could you bring against God if he saves some and hardens others?

For he is almighty and does whatever he wills. But to make a vessel for honor is a manifest act of clemency, whereas to make one for dishonor is his most just judgment. You ought therefore to rest in perpetual silence.

Someone might nevertheless say: Why does God make some vessels from the condemned mass for honor and others for dishonor? Why does he not make all of them for honor?

[Col. 0224C] The Apostle seems to answer this by saying that he is almighty and does whatever he wills. This is what he adds [Note: [Col. 0224D] In the author’s manuscript, chapter XXVIII is written here.]: “But if God, wishing to show his wrath and to make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction”—the following is understood: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?”

By “wrath” he does not mean the disturbance of mind that is usually found in human beings, but the just and fixed vengeance of God, which he exercises against sinners. By “power” he means the power by which he makes good use even of evil people.

“Vessels of wrath” means the reprobate, against whom God takes vengeance by a just judgment. A vessel is said to be the vessel of that thing with which it is full. He says “prepared,” however, not prepared by God, but prepared by original sin and by their own merits.

He therefore beautifully says: “He endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction,” because God waits with great patience for the reprobate to be converted. When they do not turn, his omnipotence makes one vessel for honor and another for dishonor.

Why does he do this? In order to show his wrath—that is, the wrath by which he justly condemns unconverted sinners—and his power, by which he makes good use of evil people, while bestowing many temporal blessings upon them, giving them calm and fruitful seasons and filling their hearts with food and gladness.

The holy Apostle shows why he does all this, adding: “So that he might make known the riches of his glory upon the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory.” For this reason he waits a long time for sinners: so that, when they do not turn, they may be justly punished; and by this the saints may understand that they are justified not by any merits of their own, but by the grace of God alone. They should not exalt themselves over good works as though these were their own possessions, but should recognize, when those others perish, that they too would perish with them unless divine grace rescued them.

He calls the elect “vessels of mercy,” whom God, by mercy alone, made vessels for honor and prepared for glory. For he chose them from the condemned mass and justified them, so that he himself might be glorified through them and might bring them into glory.

Hence he had already said: “So that he might make known the riches of his glory.” For he displays the riches of his glory by making vessels for honor from a condemned mass. His goodness is so powerful that it can change vessels of wrath and discord into vessels of mercy and peace.

And to show whom he had called vessels of mercy, he added: “Whom he also called—even us.” That is: “Us, whom he also called.” It is as if he were saying: He called us, whom he prepared—that is, predestined—for glory, and called through grace.

But lest it be thought that he intended to speak only of the Jews, since he himself arose from the Jews, he added: “Not only from the Jews, but also from the Gentiles.” By these words he shows that not only those who descend from Abraham’s stock are his sons, but that all who, from every nation, imitate the footsteps of Abraham’s faith are counted among Abraham’s sons. He also shows that, through Rebekah’s two sons, he intended us to understand not the Jewish and Gentile peoples, but the believing and the unbelieving; for Rebekah signifies the holy Church.

As for what is read about her, that she went to consult the Lord, it is not to be understood as though the wife of so great a patriarch believed God to be confined to a particular place and went to consult him by the movement of her feet. Rather, when Scripture says that she went, it means that she advanced in virtues. In the moral sense, every faithful soul is signified by Rebekah; by her two sons, the armies of vices and virtues. Hence it is aptly said: “The elder shall serve the younger,” because, although the army of vices may be greater, the army of virtues nevertheless often conquers it.

As he says in Hosea: “I will call ‘My people’ the one who was not my people, and ‘Beloved’ the one who was not beloved, and ‘Having obtained mercy’ the one who had not obtained mercy” (Hos. II, 24; 1 Pet. II, 10). The holy apostles understood this testimony as referring to the calling of the Gentiles. For the Gentile people were not God’s people, since they served idols; but they became God’s beloved people and obtained mercy, because through faith in Christ they were deemed worthy to be justified, and received such power that they became sons of God, according to John’s statement: “But as many as received him” (John I, 12), etc.

Hence the prophet immediately adds: “And it shall be that in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called sons of the living God” (Hos. I, 10). By “the place” he means the whole world, where the Gentiles lived, to whom it had been said: “You are not my people,” because they worshiped idols. But afterward they themselves were called sons of God, because believers from every nation became sons of God. He says “of the living God” to distinguish them from the dead.

The Lord explains the meaning of this passage according to another prophet, saying: “I will set Jerusalem throughout the whole world.” For Jerusalem, established throughout the whole world, is the holy Church spread throughout the entire world.

And because he had said, “Not only from the Jews, but also from the Gentiles,” wishing to show that only a few Jews would believe, he added: “But Isaiah cries out on behalf of Israel: If the number of the sons of Israel should be like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” [Note: Vulgate: “cries out” is “cries”; Col. 0225D.]. The prophet foresaw that few Jews would believe, and therefore said that only a remnant would be saved.

For this reason the Apostle, in order to show the sorrow of the prophetic heart, prefaced the quotation with: “Isaiah cries out.”

By the sand, therefore, the unbelievers are signified; by the remnant, the believers. Both were promised to Abraham, when the Lord said: “Multiplying, I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the shore of the sea” (Gen. XXVI, 4). Those who are represented there by the stars are represented here by the remnant.

How, then, the remnant was saved is disclosed when he adds: “For, completing and abbreviating the word in righteousness” (the implied sense is: “the Lord will save the remnant”). The Lord completed the word because he fulfilled all the precepts of the Law. Hence the same Apostle says: “Christ is the end of the Law” (Rom. X, 4). He abbreviated the word in righteousness because the commandments spread far and wide throughout the Law the Lord gathered into a few words, saying: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. XI, 29–30).

“For the Lord will make an abbreviated word upon the earth.” The abbreviated word is most appropriately understood as the teaching of the Gospel, because the commandments given to God’s people through innumerable observances the Lord showed to be contained in two commandments, saying: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your mind, and with all your strength, and your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. XXII, 37). Hence he immediately adds: “On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. XXII, 40).

Or by the abbreviated word he means the Creed of the Lord’s faith, in which the salvation and perfection of the whole Church consist. For it is, as it were, the Church’s sign: just as armies are distinguished from one another by a particular sign, so by this sign the faithful are distinguished from the unfaithful.

Alternatively, by the abbreviated word he means the Lord’s Prayer, which the Lord taught to be so brief because he knew that human frailty cannot remain for long in the same state of attention, so that during the time of prayer each person may gather his mind and, having driven away all the cares of earthly affairs, think only of what he is praying.

Accordingly, since the prophet’s testimony had shown that only a few Jews would believe, he added, to establish this more firmly, the testimony of that same prophet, saying: “And as Isaiah foretold: Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah” (Isa. I, 9).
