*Sabaoth* in the Hebrew language is rendered in Latin as “Almighty” or “of hosts.” The meaning is: Unless the Lord Almighty, or the Lord of hosts, had left us offspring—that is, unless by his grace he had saved a few—we would all likewise have perished as the Sodomites and Gomorrhites. And note that he beautifully says “offspring,” for this was sown throughout the whole world.

At this point someone might perhaps say: By what justice of God did it happen that only a few Jews were chosen, while more were chosen from the Gentiles, when the Jews had knowledge of God and had received the Law from God, whereas the Gentiles had always worshiped idols?

For this reason the Apostle questions himself, adding [Note: In the author’s autograph margin, chapter XXX is marked here.]: “What shall we say, then? That the Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, attained righteousness—the righteousness that is from faith. But Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, did not attain the law of righteousness.” It is as though he were saying: Did this happen through God’s injustice? Certainly not. What, then, shall we say except: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” Let us therefore cry out with the Psalmist: “The righteousness of the Lord is a great abyss” (Ps. XXXV, 7). Again: “How awesome he is in his counsels over the sons of men” (Ps. LXV, 5). For he is awesome in his counsels over the sons of men, because no one is sufficient to understand what has been determined for him in God’s counsel.

The Gentiles, therefore, who were not pursuing righteousness because they worshiped idols and for that reason were not worthy to be justified, attained righteousness because, when they recognized that they could not be saved by their own merits or powers, they were justified through faith in Christ. Hence the Apostle says: “But the righteousness that is from faith.”

Israel, however, pursued the law of righteousness—that is, the law of the Old Testament, in which it was prescribed how God’s people were to be purified by the offering of sacrifices. Because Israel believed that it could be saved by the works of that Law, it did not attain the law of righteousness. It must be understood that by “the law of righteousness” he means the grace of the Gospel, through which a person is justified.

And because someone might ask why this happened, he himself therefore asks, saying: “Why?” And he answers: “Because it was not from faith, but from the works” [Note: Vulgate: “but as though from the works.”] “of the Law” (the implied sense is: “they believed that they could be saved”). For because they believed that they had received the Law through their own merits, that they could fulfill it by their own powers, and that they could be saved by its works, they were not deemed worthy to be justified.

“For they stumbled over the stone of stumbling.” The stone of stumbling is Christ, who is called a stone because of the humility associated with human frailty. For when he appeared as a humble man among human beings, he lay like a stone. Yet Christ is a stone only to those who see; to the blind, that is, to unbelievers, he is a stone of stumbling, for the blind stumble against a stone.

This stone, initially small according to Daniel’s prophecy, grew and became a great mountain, because Christ, having become a humble man, was recognized as God and is worshiped by all nations. The Jews stumbled over this stone because, thinking him merely a man, they refused to believe in him.

As it is written: “Behold, I will place in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense” [Note: Isaiah VIII, 14, and XXVIII, 16; the Vulgate has “I place” rather than “I will place.”]. These are the words of God the Father to the prophet. Zion is the mountain on which Jerusalem stands. The Lord therefore placed a stone of stumbling in Zion because he caused his Son to take flesh from the Jews.

Christ is called a rock because of the firmness of faith. For he is the foundation of faith, and also because he is an unconquerable and unique refuge for all who flee to him. But he became a rock of offense to the Jews, because, seeing a dead man, they were scandalized and despised believing in him. Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “We preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to the Jews, but foolishness to the Gentiles” (1 Cor. I, 23).

“And everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.” The belief referred to here is belief that is fulfilled through works. The shame, however, is the shame that only the wicked will have on the day of judgment, when their sins will be manifest to all. Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes and brings to light the things hidden in darkness” (1 Cor. IV, 5), etc. And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Nothing is covered that will not be revealed” (Matt. X, 26).

Whoever, therefore, believes and fulfills his faith through works will not be put to shame, because he will not be found in sins for which he should be ashamed. Such shame belongs only to the reprobate, to whom it will be said: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire” (Matt. XXV, 41), etc.

Because he had preferred the Gentiles in praise, saying that they had attained righteousness, while the Jews had stumbled over the stone of stumbling, he added, lest the Gentiles should therefore become proud [Note: Here Vulgate chapter X begins; Col. 0228D.]:  

**(CHAPTER X)** “Brothers, indeed the desire of my heart and my supplication to God on their behalf is for their salvation.”

It is as though he were saying: Do not become proud because of this, since you were saved not by your own merits but by the grace of God alone; and although the Jews stumbled over Christ, nevertheless the desire of my heart and my supplication to God on their behalf are that they may be converted and believe, for otherwise they cannot be saved [Note: In the author’s autograph margin, chapter XXXI is marked here.].

The Apostle’s prayer, then, and the faith of believers who prayed for the unbelieving Jews—although it preceded the grace of God—did the faith of those who did not yet believe precede God’s grace? Certainly not. For the Apostle prayed for those who did not yet believe, so that faith might be given to them by God. He considered it insufficient that he preached the Gospel to them earnestly unless he also implored God for their faith.

He calls the Gentiles “brothers,” because by believing they became sons of God, and therefore were the Apostle’s brothers.

Accordingly, wishing to show that the Jews sinned in ignorance while persecuting the heralds of grace, he added: “For I bear them witness that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.” It is as though he were saying: I know, and I understand; I myself was once such a person among them, when I persecuted the Church of God.

The Lord explains the meaning of this passage according to John’s Gospel, saying: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God”; and again: “They will do these things because they have not known the Father, nor me” (John XVI, 2).

But it must be asked what sort of knowledge the Apostle is speaking of here. Is it the knowledge that puffs up without charity (1 Cor. VIII, 1)? No. Rather, it is that knowledge which is the companion of charity and the teacher of humility. For truly, and in its entirety, human knowledge consists in knowing that a person can do nothing by himself, and that whatever exists is from God and through God. The Jews did not possess this knowledge, because they gloried in the Law; therefore they persecuted the heralds of grace.

And as though someone were saying: “Show us, Apostle, what this knowledge is that you commend as useful and grieve over its absence among the Jews,” he therefore explained by adding: “For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted to God’s righteousness.”

The righteousness of God is not that by which he himself is justified, but that by which a human being is justified and which is given to a human being by God.

The righteousness of God, therefore, is Christ, or the faith of Christ, through which the one who believes in him is justified—he who justifies the ungodly. The Jews were ignorant of this righteousness of God, because, being sick, they did not seek the physician; and, glorying in the works of the Law, they disdained to confess that they were sinners. By glorying in the works of the Law, they drove the grace of God away from themselves.

He calls it “their righteousness” because they thought they could be justified by it, judging that they had received the Law through their own merits and could fulfill it by their own powers. They wished to establish this righteousness—that is, to place it above the grace of God—and therefore they did not submit to God’s righteousness.

Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “But if righteousness is through the Law, then Christ died for nothing” (Gal. II, 21). But if Christ did not die for nothing [Note: “A most beautiful statement.”], then in him alone the ungodly is justified.

Wishing to show what this righteousness of God was, the Apostle added: “For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes.” Christ is the end of the Law, not by bringing it to destruction, but by bringing it to completion, because he does not destroy the Law but perfects it, in accordance with what he says in the Gospel: “I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it” [Note: Matt. V, 17; Vulgate: “but to fulfill it completely.”].

Christ is the end. We believe in him when we begin to enter upon the good way, and we shall see him alone when we reach him. Christ is called the end because we refer everything we do to him; and when we reach him, we shall have nothing further to seek.

Our end, therefore, ought to be our perfection. Our perfection, however, is Christ, because in him we are perfected [Note: The autograph has *perficimus* (“we perfect”), or one may correctly read *perficimus* if “the Law” is understood], for we are members of his head. Christ is therefore rightly called the end, because no one perfects the Law without him.

Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes, because whoever is justified through faith in Christ is perfected in him.

Accordingly, to explain what he meant by the Jews’ righteousness, he added: “For Moses wrote that the person who does the righteousness that is from the Law will live by it” [Note: Lev. XVIII, 5; Ezek. XX, 11. The Vulgate has “in it” where this text has “in them,” although the same Apostle, in Galatians III, 12, uses nearly the same wording and context: “But the Law is not from faith; rather, the one who does these things will live in them”—that is, in the works mentioned above, to which the pronoun “them” refers. The passages cited above from Leviticus and Ezekiel, from which the Apostle appears to have drawn this statement, have “will live in them,” that is, in the commandments mentioned shortly before in those texts. In fact, other copies of this Epistle also have “in them.”].

Here it must be noted that he does not say “in it,” but “in them,” that is, in the precepts or works of the Law. Hence it is evident that Moses placed the righteousness that is from the Law in the works of the Law. Whoever does the righteousness that is from the Law—that is, the works of the Law—will live in them, because he will receive the reward of the present life.

For he fears that, if he does not perform the works of the Law [Note: The autograph reads “unless he does not” (*nisi* rather than *ne si*)], he will be crucified, stoned, or subjected to something of that sort. He therefore lives because he receives the reward of not being punished by bodily death.

Those who fulfill grace, however, do not receive the reward of the present life but of the eternal, according to the saying: “When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord” (Ps. CXXVI, 3). For when the elect fall into the sleep of death, then they attain the inheritance of eternal life.

But someone might say: If Moses says, “The person who does the righteousness that is from the Law will live by it” [Note: Here the autograph has “in it”], what does he say about the righteousness that is from faith? [Note: Understand: “about the righteousness that is from faith,” etc.] Therefore the Apostle added: “But the righteousness that is from faith speaks in this way: Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’” [Note: Deut. XXX, 12. The autograph nowhere has a question mark.]—that is, “to bring Christ down,” etc.

The Apostle took the preceding testimony from Leviticus; this one, however, from Deuteronomy, which is interpreted as “a recapitulation of the Law” [Note: Lev. XVIII, 5. From the Greek *deuteros*, “second,” and *nomos*, “law.”]. Hence it aptly signifies the grace of the Gospel.

It must be asked with what intention Moses said this, or with what intention the Apostle took it as a testimony. Moses said this in order to teach the children of Israel that they did not need to seek the divine commandment outside themselves—that is, from heaven or from the abyss—since they had the Law of the Lord before their eyes, provided only that they were willing to fulfill it.

He therefore says: “Do not say,” etc., as though he were saying: You, whoever you are, Israelite, do not say in your heart: “Who will ascend into heaven, to bring us the divine commandment from there, so that we may hear it, understand it, and fulfill it? Or who will descend into the abyss, to report to us what is happening in hell, so that we may know what we ought to do?” For you have God’s commandments before your eyes; only be their fulfiller. Hence he immediately adds: “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart.”

He calls the word God’s commandment, as though he were saying: The word is near you in your mouth because you read it, and in your heart because you meditate upon it.

The Apostle, however, took this testimony to show that Christ is true God and true man, and not confined to a place; that he reigns with the Father not only in heaven but everywhere—not spread out bodily, but extended in power. The meaning is therefore: You, whoever you are, a believer, do not say in your heart: “Who will ascend into heaven?”—that is, do not believe that Christ is God alone and was not made man, or that he dwells only in heaven and that the abyss is empty of his presence [Note: In the author’s autograph margin, chapter XXXII is marked here.].

Hence, in explaining the passage, he added words of his own: “That is, to bring Christ down,” for these words are not found in the Book of Deuteronomy.

He continues: “Or who will descend into the abyss?” That is, do not believe that he was merely a man who suffered, died, and descended to the regions below, where he is still detained and heaven is empty of his presence. Therefore, in explaining it, he adds: “That is, to bring Christ back from the dead.” For he is himself true God and man, wholly present everywhere.

Accordingly, as though someone were asking: If the law of faith forbids saying, “Who will ascend into heaven?” and so forth, what must be said? The Apostle adds this, wishing to show how he is wholly present everywhere. But what does Scripture say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (Deut. XXX, 14).

It is as though he were saying: Since Christ, the Word of God the Father, is wholly present everywhere, he is therefore in your mouth and in your heart. For he himself grants the grace both of thinking well and of speaking well. Christ is not only the Word of God the Father, but also charity, truth, and wisdom. Therefore, like all these, Christ too is contained not by place but by merits [Note: That is, by power, not by human nature, as stated somewhat earlier.].

To show of what word he was speaking, he added: “This is the word of faith that we preach.” He calls it the word of faith because through faith in it the ungodly is justified.

Again, to explain what his preaching was, he added: “For if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.”

The Apostle foresaw that there would be some who would confess Christ with their mouths but refuse to believe, and others who would believe him in their hearts but, because of torments and punishments, fear to confess him. Therefore he placed both together: belief of the heart and confession of the mouth, wishing to show that neither is sufficient for perfection without the other.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Everyone who confesses me before men, I also will confess before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. X, 32). And note that he does not say, “If you believe that he was born, suffered, and died,” but “that God raised him from the dead.”

For the pagans also believe that he died, and they reproach us with this as a crime. Our praise, therefore, does not consist in believing merely that he died, unless we also believe that he rose again and that we shall rise according to his example.

We too believe that he died, because otherwise we cannot believe that he rose again.

To reinforce still more strongly that neither belief of the heart without confession of the mouth, nor confession without belief, is sufficient for salvation, he added: “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.”

By these words he shows that whoever believes in his heart that Christ is true God and true man is deemed worthy to be justified, because he obtains forgiveness of his sins. But this is not sufficient for perfect salvation unless he also confesses with his mouth, since the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father” (Matt. X, 33).

For Scripture says: “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame” (Isa. XXVIII, 16). This statement was explained somewhat earlier. And lest it should perhaps appear to have been said only about the Jews, it is therefore added: “For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek.” His fellow apostle Peter explains the meaning of this passage, saying: “In every nation, whoever fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts X, 35).

Why there is no distinction between Jew and Greek the Apostle showed above, when, after setting forth this brief statement, he added: “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. III, 23).

Hence here too it is added: “For the same Lord is Lord of all”—namely, Christ, who rules over all, because through him all things were made—“rich toward all who call upon him,” because he bestows the gift of his grace upon all who call upon him.

For even if all people, from the first human being to the one who will be born last, were to believe, he would have something to give to them all; for the more he gives, the more abundantly he possesses.

Wishing to confirm what he had said by prophetic testimony (Joel II, 32; Acts II, 21), he added: “For everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.”

He says “everyone,” that is, both Jew and Gentile. But the invocation meant here is not an invocation held only in words and not in works, because the Lord says in the Gospel: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VII, 21).

Everyone, therefore, who calls upon the name of the Lord in both words and works will be saved.

The human race was pressed down by the great misery of original sin and needed divine mercy. Therefore, foreseeing the time of grace, the prophet said: “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Joel II, 32).

The Apostle applied this testimony to the commendation of God’s grace, wishing to show that it had been said not only about the Jews but also about the Gentiles. For this reason the Lord’s Prayer was composed, so that human beings might be saved by invoking and praying.

But it must be known that there were many who said that the Gospel ought to be preached only to the Jews. To destroy their error, the Apostle added: “How, then, will they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” [Note: Chapter XXXIII is marked in the autograph margin here.]

By these words he clearly shows that preachers were also sent to the Gentiles. Otherwise they would not believe, and by calling upon him they would not be saved [Note: The autograph reads “would be healed” (*sanarentur*), but it is certain that “would be saved” (*salvarentur*) must be read in light of what immediately follows.].

For this reason the Creed was composed, so that human beings might be saved by believing and calling upon him. In these two things the three virtues are contained: faith, hope, and charity. Faith believes; hope and charity pray truly, for hope and charity cannot exist without faith, and faith prays together with them.

To prove still more firmly that the apostles had also been sent to the Gentiles, after saying, “How will they believe in him whom they have not heard?” he added: “And how will they hear without a preacher? And how will they preach unless they are sent?”

For if preachers had not been sent to the Gentiles, they would not preach to them; if they did not preach to them, the Gentiles would not hear; if they did not hear, they certainly would not believe; if they did not believe, they would in no way call upon him or be saved. The fault, therefore, would not belong to the Gentiles but to the one who had not sent preachers.

Wishing to show that preachers had indeed been sent, and that the Gentiles had called upon him by believing and had been saved, he added Isaiah’s testimony: “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace!” (Isa. LII, 7; Nahum I, 15.)

The particle “how” is often used to express admiration, as in: “How lovely are your dwelling places, O Lord!” (Ps. LXXXIII, 2). Again: “O Israel, how great is the house of the Lord!” (Baruch III, 24).

So also here: Saint Isaiah foresaw with spiritual eyes preachers running throughout the Gentile nations, and in admiration he said: “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace!”

We must understand these feet not as bodily but as spiritual. The inner person has feet of his own, just as he has nostrils and eyes. The feet of the righteous are therefore spiritual affections and holy desires by which the preachers desired the salvation of the Gentiles.

But what road do these feet walk? The road of which he says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6). He speaks of that peace concerning which it is written: “Christ is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II, 14).

Accordingly, to show what the Gospel is, he added: “Those who announce good things.” In Latin, *evangelium* means “good news” [Note: The autograph has “those who announce” (*evangelizantium*)]; for it announces good things: life after death, rest after labor, and a homeland after exile.

But because faith does not belong to everyone, it is therefore added: “But not all obey the Gospel.” That is, not all believe. For Isaiah says: “Lord, who has believed our report?” (Isa. LIII, 1; John XII, 38.)

“Who” is sometimes used because of difficulty, as in: “Who among the clouds can be compared to the Lord?” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 7). Again: “Who is like God among the sons of God?” (Exod. XV, 11)—the implied answer being “no one.”

At other times it is used because of rarity, as here; likewise: “Who will ascend the mountain of the Lord?” (Ps. XXIII, 3), etc.

The holy prophet had foreseen that few would believe the preaching of the apostles. Therefore, speaking in their voice, he said: “Lord, who has believed our report?”—as though he were saying, “Very few.”

And because he had said, “He believed the report,” he therefore adds: “So faith comes from hearing.” For no one believes unless he hears.

Accordingly, because hearing does not arise from nothing but is the sound of something, it is therefore added: “But hearing comes through the word of God” [Note: The Vulgate has “of Christ,” but other readings agree with our autograph]—that is, through God’s teaching and preaching.

Someone might perhaps say: Those who do not believe do not believe because they have not heard. For this reason the Apostle adds: “But I ask: Have they not heard? Indeed, their sound has gone out through the whole earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII, 5).

It is as though he were saying openly: If their sound has gone out through the whole earth and their words have reached the ends of the world, then those who were in the midst of it certainly heard.

And note that, as we find here and in what follows, the prophets use words of the past tense for future events, because they foresaw that what they proclaimed as future was fixed and unchangeable.

Therefore, lest anyone say that the Jews did not believe because, although they had heard, they did not understand, the Apostle adds: “But I ask: Did Israel not know?”

Wishing to show that they had both heard and understood, but had refused to believe out of envy toward the Gentiles, he added: “Moses is the first to say: ‘I will provoke you to jealousy by a non-nation; by a foolish nation I will anger you’” (Deut. XXXII, 21; Rom. X, 19).

*Aemulatio* sometimes means imitation, as in: “Be zealous for the better gifts” (1 Cor. XII, 31). Sometimes it means jealous envy, as here. He calls the Gentile people “not a nation,” because, having departed from the worship of God, it lost the name of a nation and became foolish.

Moses, therefore, foreseeing that the Gentiles would come to faith while the Jews would remain in unbelief out of envy, spoke in the voice of the Lord: “I will provoke you to jealousy,” etc.

The meaning is: When you see that people which, having departed from God and sacrificed to idols, became foolish and lost the name of a nation [Note: The autograph reads “lost” (*amisit*)], believing in me, you will grow angry and indignant [Note: The autograph has the imperative “be indignant” (*indignamini*)]; you will waste away with envy and, as a result, remain in unbelief.

Alternatively: The people of the Gentiles was formerly God’s people; but, having departed from God and served demons, it received the wretched name of “nation.” Thus he calls the Gentile people “not a nation” because, by abandoning idols and believing in Christ, it became God’s people and lost the wretched name of “nation.”

Moreover, wishing to show that the Gentiles were preceded by God’s grace so that they might believe, he added Isaiah’s testimony, speaking in the person of the Lord: “I was found by those who did not seek me; I appeared openly to those who did not ask about me.”

Isaiah, disregarding all the threats and persecutions of the Jews and valuing the Gospel of Christ more highly than himself, boldly proclaimed to them that the Gentiles would be preceded by God’s grace so that they might believe. Therefore the Apostle prefaced the quotation by saying: “Isaiah is bold, and says.”

But when he says, “I was found,” this is not to be understood as meaning that the Gentiles found him first. Rather, because they were sought and found, they were therefore deemed worthy to seek and find. He himself makes clear how he was found when he says: “I appeared openly to those who did not ask about me” [Note: Chapter XXXIV is marked here in the autograph margin.]. He appeared openly to those who did not ask about him because, preceding them by his grace, he displayed many signs and wonders through which they might believe [Note: This should be joined with what is said above concerning the words: “It depends not on the one who wills or runs, but on God who shows mercy,” chapter X.].

But lest someone say that the Jews did not believe because they had not seen signs and miracles, he added: “But to Israel he says”—understand, Isaiah: “All day long I stretched out my hands,” etc. (Isa. LXV, 2).

Here it must be noted that he does not say “for a month” or “for a year,” but “all day long,” that is, at all times. By “hands” he means works. At all times he extended his hands to the Jews, not only by preaching but also by performing many signs and wonders: first through the patriarchs, then through the lawgiver, afterward through the prophets, finally through himself, and then through the apostles. But they never believed.

Hence it immediately adds: “To an unbelieving people.” And because they not only did not believe but also persecuted the heralds of grace, it soon adds: “And one who contradicted me.” It is a great evil not to believe, but incomparably greater to persecute the heralds of grace, for whoever resists them contradicts the Lord himself.

**(CHAPTER XI)** But lest the Gentiles should perhaps become proud and believe that the whole Jewish people had been condemned for the crime of unbelief and contradiction, the Apostle added: “I ask, then: Has God rejected his people?”

It is as though he were saying openly: Gentiles, do not become proud, and do not suppose that the entire people has been rejected, since, although not all believed, many nevertheless did.

This is what he says: “Certainly not.” Wishing to prove this more firmly, he offered himself as an example, saying: “For I too am an Israelite, from the offspring of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.”

The meaning is: It is proved by this that the Lord has not rejected his people [Note: The words “that the Lord has not rejected his people” are placed in the upper margin of the autograph], because I myself belong to that people and am a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.

The following is to be understood: Nor am I alone, but the other ministers and my fellow apostles also came from that people: Joseph the righteous; Mary the virgin, who bore Christ; John, the Lord’s forerunner; and his parents, Simeon and Anna; the other Joseph; and Nathanael, the one in whom there was no deceit (John I, 47); the crowd also that went before and followed his beast.

From that people likewise came the three thousand and the five thousand who believed after his resurrection.

To establish more clearly what he had said, he added: “God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.” Here it must be noted that he does not say merely “the people,” but adds “his.” The meaning is: He did not reject the people whom he foreknew he would make his own.

But it must be asked why he said “foreknew,” since foreknowledge is ordinarily used both in reference to good and to evil. We must understand, however, that “foreknowledge” is sometimes used for predestination. Thus in this passage he says, “foreknew,” that is, “predestined.” Hence above the Apostle says: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined” [Note: Rom. 8:29. The remarks made by our author on this and other similar passages should be examined and weighed carefully.]. Elsewhere he calls this foreknowledge, or predestination, “election,” saying: “Just as he chose us in him” (Eph. 1:4).

Finally, wishing to show that a remnant had been saved by the grace of God, he added: “Or do you not know what Scripture says in the passage about Elijah?” [Col. 0236D] As though he were saying: Surely you know, since you have read it. Or as though someone were asking: What does it say? He continued: “How” [Note: The Vulgate has *quemadmodum*, “how/as.”] “he pleads with God against Israel? ‘Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have torn down your altars, and I alone have been left, and they are seeking my life.’” And, as though speaking in the person of another, he asks himself, continuing: “But what does the divine reply say to him? ‘I have kept for myself seven thousand’” [Note: 3 Kings 19:18. Both here and in the cited passage from Kings, the Vulgate has *men* after “thousand.”] “who have not bent the knee before Baal.”

This example is plainly set forth in the Book of Kings (3 Kings 18:40). For we read that, after the prophet Elijah had killed four hundred prophets of Baal with his own hand, a violent persecution arose against the Lord’s prophets, so that Elijah, fleeing, hid among the mountain heights and in caves in the rocks, believing himself to be the only one of the Lord’s servants left. Then the word of the Lord came to him, saying: “What are you doing here, Elijah?” He replied: “I have been very zealous for the Lord God of Israel, because the children of Israel have killed your prophets, torn down your altars, and I alone have been left, and they are seeking my life.” [Col. 0237B] The Lord said to him: “I have kept” [Note: 3 Kings 19:9. The Vulgate has “I will leave” here.] “for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal.” It is as though he were saying: Do not think that you alone are a faithful servant who labors well, for I have others also, and not a few. There, where you think yourself alone, I have seven thousand who have not bent the knee before Baal.

Here it must be noted that he does not say, “They have been left,” or “They have left themselves for me,” but, “I have kept them.” It is as though he were saying plainly: I saved them; I guarded them; I caused them not to bend the knee before Baal. Therefore do not boast that you alone are engaged in the service, for I also have other fellow servants of yours, whose minds I found [Note: The autograph has *invidi*, but in my judgment this seems to require correction to *inveni*.], relying not on themselves, not on Baal, but on me.

And you who say, “I alone have been left”—if you were not filled with my grace, where would you be? You too would bend your knees before Baal. The bending of the knees signifies a certain submission of the mind, concerning which the same Apostle says elsewhere: “At the name of Jesus every knee should bend” (Phil. 2:10). There the bending of the knees signifies the humbling of the mind, by which all creatures are subjected to God [Note: In the autograph, “chapter 35” is written here in the margin.]. Those, therefore, bend their knees before Baal who, by a certain submission of the mind—that is, by consent—subject themselves to the devil.

Baal is also Beel; he is likewise Beelphegor and Belbrit. He was called Baal because he was worshiped on a high place, but Beelphegor because he was worshiped on Mount Phegor.

Why he has taken this testimony is made clear when he continues: “So therefore at the present time also a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace.” It is as though he were saying: The Lord Christ is now the same as he was then, and he has saved the remnant by the same grace by which he saved those others.

This is what he says [Note: A noteworthy passage, to be compared with the observations made by our author elsewhere in this Epistle on the same subject.]: “According to the election of grace,” that is, according to predestination. For predestination and election are the grace of God. Grace, moreover, is the gift itself by which each person is justified, without any preceding merits. Hence he immediately adds: “But if by grace, then it is no longer from works,” by which statement he argues against the Jews [Note: After “the Jews,” the autograph reads *aut*, perhaps *ait*.], who believed that they could be saved by the works of the Law.

It is called grace because it is given freely; therefore he continues: “Otherwise grace is no longer grace.” That is: If any merits preceded, then you were not saved by the grace of God, since a reward is granted not freely but according to merit.

Then, as though someone were asking why God had saved by his grace not everyone but only a remnant, the Apostle raised the question himself and asked: “What then?”—that is, What shall we say? Nothing, certainly, except that Israel did not obtain what it was seeking. By “Israel” he means that Jewish people which believed that it had received the Law because of its own merits, that it could fulfill it by its own strength, and that it could be justified by its works; therefore it did not deserve to obtain the salvation it was seeking. Spiritual Israel, however, relying solely upon the grace of God, attained salvation.

Hence what follows immediately: “But the elect obtained it.” For he calls those who were saved through election “the election.” Of carnal Israel, however, he adds: “But the rest were blinded” [Note: The autograph has *excusati*, “excused.”], as it is written: “God gave them a spirit of compunction” [Note: Observe these two kinds of compunction: toward evil and toward good.]. Compunction is used both in a good sanctification and in an evil one. People are pricked toward good when, pierced by the Spirit of God, they perform some good work; and they are pricked toward evil when, prompted by the devil, they carry out some evil deed.

[Col. 0238C] But if God gave them a spirit of compunction so that they would not believe, what fault was theirs, since they did not believe? Indeed, it seems to belong to the one who gave it. But far be it from us. For whatever God permits to happen by a just judgment, Scripture’s customary manner of speaking says that he himself does. He therefore “gave” them eyes so that they would not see, and ears so that they would not hear, because he permitted such eyes and ears to be given. Here we must understand “eyes” and “ears” not bodily ones but spiritual ones, that is, of the mind. God therefore gave them eyes so that they would not see—that is, would not understand spiritual realities. He gave them ears so that they would not hear—that is, would not obey the divine commandments.

And notice that he does not say “until eternity,” but “until the present day,” lest he seem to remove their hope of salvation. For the Church firmly believes that a remnant will be saved, according to the testimony the Apostle set forth above from Isaiah: “Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Isa. 10:22).

It follows: “And David says: ‘Let their table before them become a snare and a trap’” (Ps. 68:23). The prophet spoke this not as the wish of one uttering a curse, but as one proclaiming what was to come. It did not happen because the prophet said it; rather, because it was going to happen, the prophet foretold it.

Why, then, is the table cursed? Clearly, because many evils are committed at a table. Innocent people are invited to a table so that they may be deceived; at a table Absalom killed Amnon; Holofernes invited Judith to a table in order to deceive her; at Herod’s table his guests obtained the head of John.

Spiritually, however, the table signifies Holy Scripture, which is laden with spiritual food and drink by which souls are refreshed. This table is rightly said to belong to the Jews, because they thought they had received it on account of their own merits. Concerning this table the Church speaks in the Psalm: “You have prepared a table before me, against those who afflict me” (Ps. 22:5)—that is, against heretics.

This table, therefore, became for the Jews a snare and a trap, because by following the letter alone they were entangled, and deceived by a carnal understanding, so that they would not believe; and they themselves fell into the snare that they were preparing for the Gentiles. He rightly says “before them,” because they see their iniquity and do not wish to turn away from it.

What follows—“and as a recompense, and as a stumbling block”—is one and the same, as though he were saying: “As a recompense for the stumbling block.” Because they refused to believe, this was repaid to them by God, so that Holy Scripture became a stumbling block to them. Whenever they see something interpreted spiritually in it, they are scandalized, and thus they themselves become a stumbling block to themselves.

“Let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see, and keep their back always bent.” The Psalmist likewise said this not in wishing it but in prophesying it. Their eyes were therefore darkened by the cloud of carnal understanding, so that they did not see spiritual realities and did not believe that the prophecies previously uttered about Christ had been fulfilled [Note: The words “and did not believe … fulfilled” are placed in the side margin.]. The Jews, moreover, turned their back toward Christ, because they disdained to believe in him. Thus it is said: “Keep their back always bent,” as though it meant: Let them never be converted for the better, but always for the worse.

Their back is therefore bent because they always acquire not heavenly but earthly things. To bend one’s back is to look constantly toward what is below.

Accordingly, wishing to show that the fall of the unbelieving Jews was by no means without effect, he added [Note: In the autograph margin, “chapter 36” is written here.]: “I ask, then: Have they stumbled so as to fall?” The word “only” is to be understood. The meaning is: Gentiles, do not rise up against the Jews [Note: Perhaps “be elated” or “become angry”], because although they stumbled so as to fall, their fall is not without purpose: while they were falling, an opportunity for your rising was given to you.

Hence he continues: “But through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to provoke them to emulation.” Through the trespass of the Jews’ unbelief, salvation came to the Gentiles, because their unbelief gave the Gentiles an opportunity to believe, and they were saved.

What he says—“so as to provoke them to emulation”—must not be understood to mean that the Gentiles imitated the Jews as they persisted in unbelief. Rather, they received an example from them: if they did not believe, they too would perish as those others had perished.

For this reason he continues: “But if their trespass is the riches of the world, and their diminution the riches of the Gentiles, how much more their fullness?” Their trespass is the world’s riches because, while persisting in unbelief, they were devastated by the Romans and led captive through the various provinces, far and wide, carrying with them the books of the Law and the Prophets. Through these books the world—that is, the inhabitants of the world—were enriched. For everywhere the holy Church received from them the books of the Law and the Prophets, through which it demonstrated that the prophecies previously uttered about Christ had already been fulfilled.

Their diminution is likewise the world’s riches, because, when a few of the Jews believed and were expelled by the unbelievers, the Gentiles were enriched in faith and in every virtue through their preaching. The meaning, therefore, is this: If the Gentiles believed and were saved through the preaching of the few Jews who believed, how much more would they be saved if all, or many, of the Jews believed?

But the Gentiles could say: Since you are the Apostle of the Gentiles, why do you preach the Gospel to the Jews? Therefore he continues: “For I speak to you Gentiles” [Note: In the autograph margin, “chapter 37” is written here.]—“you who are saying these things” is understood—“inasmuch as I am the Apostle of the Gentiles, I will honor my ministry.”

By “his ministry” he means the office of preaching, which he specially undertook among the Gentiles, in accordance with what the Holy Spirit says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul” [Note: The Vulgate has “Saul”] “for the work to which I have chosen them.” And the Lord said to Ananias: “Go, for he is a vessel of election for me, to carry my name among the Gentiles” (Acts 9:15).

How, then, did he honor this ministry of his? Clearly, because he did not care only for those among whom he had specially received the office of preaching, but also preached the Gospel persistently to the Jews.

He himself makes clear why he did this when he adds: “If somehow I might provoke my flesh to emulation.” By “his flesh,” that is, the Jewish people from whom he derived his fleshly origin, he meant that he wished to provoke them to imitate him, so that, just as he believed, they too might believe and be saved. This is what follows: “That I might save some of them.”

And, to show nevertheless that their fall was not without effect, he added: “For if their loss is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be but life from the dead?” He calls the Jews’ loss their destruction, which came about through unbelief. It was the reconciliation of the world because, while they persisted in unbelief, the world—that is, the inhabitants of the world—believed through the preaching of the apostles who had been expelled, and were reconciled and recalled to the peace of God, becoming children of promise and grace.

He calls their “acceptance” that by which the Jews will be received into the faith. According to these words of the Apostle, this will occur when the resurrection is about to be celebrated—that is, when life will be given to the dead and perpetuity to what is perishable.

“Acceptance” can also be referred to the Gentiles, if by “life” we understand Christ, who says of himself: “I am the life” (John 11:25). The acceptance of the Gentiles was therefore life from the dead, because when Christ rose from the dead, then the Gentiles, received into the faith, were given life.

Or certainly he calls the apostles “life.” For they themselves, born from dead—that is, unbelieving—parents, ministered life to the Gentiles by preaching. Thus they were the cause of their being received into the faith.

But someone might say: Since the Jews arose from the patriarchs, why did they persist in unbelief? For this reason the Apostle continues: “And if the first portion is holy, so is the lump.” The first portion is properly that from which the lump is made and brought together. He therefore calls the patriarchs the first portion, from whom the lump—that is, the multitude of the Jews—proceeded. If, then, the first portion is holy, so is the lump, because, just as the patriarchs were sanctified through faith, so also were many of the Jews.

To show what he meant by the first portion and what by the lump, he added: “And if the root is holy, so are the branches.” The first portion refers to the root, while the lump refers to the branches. The holy root, however, is not to be understood as Adam, since from Adam there flowed not holiness but sin, bringing death upon all, in accordance with what the Apostle said above: “Just as through one man sin entered this world, and through sin death” (Rom. 5:12), and so forth.

He therefore calls the patriarchs—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—the holy root, from whom the holiness of faith proceeded into the branches. But notice that he does not say “all the branches,” but speaks without qualification. He wishes only those Jews who believed to be understood.

And, lest anyone think that the entire nation had perished, he added: “But if some of the branches were broken off, while you, though you were a wild olive, were grafted in among them and made a sharer in the root and the richness of the olive tree.” He calls the unbelieving Jews branches that were broken off.

It must be understood that the entire forest of the human race had been full of bitter wild olives, because it bore no fruit of good works. From this forest, however, a wild olive was cut off and grafted into a good olive tree. He therefore calls the Church gathered from the Gentiles a wild olive, which was grafted, as it were, into a good olive tree—that is, joined through faith to the primitive Church.

For the Gentile people, by imitating the footsteps of Abraham’s faith, became a child of the promise and of the grace of God, and a sharer in the root and richness of the olive tree, because it was deemed worthy to receive the faith and devotion that had existed in the patriarchs and to produce the fruit of good works.

[Col. 0242A] But why did the Apostle wish to introduce this comparison, which is contrary to nature? No one grafts a shoot of a wild olive into the trunk of an olive tree. If it is done, it is without benefit; for it is not the trunk but the shoot that will produce fruit. The Apostle therefore wished to show that what is impossible among human beings is possible with God.

By his omnipotence he does what he wishes. He cut off the bitter wild olive—that is, the Gentile people—from the forest of the human race and joined it to the good olive tree—that is, the primitive Church—so that it might now bear not bitter but sweet berries, that is, the fruit of good works.

It follows: “Do not boast against the branches”—“that were broken off” is understood. Why there should be no boasting is made clear when he continues: “But if you boast, you do not bear the root; the root bears you.”

Some have understood Abraham as the root, others Christ. Abraham is appropriately called the root because the beginning of faith came from him. Christ, however, is called the root because he is himself the beginning and foundation of all good things. Hence he is also called the firstborn of every creature. Elsewhere the same Apostle says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3:11).

Christ is appropriately called the root because, like the root of a tree, he gives to the branches clinging to him the sap of his sweetness—that is, the pleasantness of good works—and himself helps them to reach perfection.

If the passage is referred to Abraham, its meaning is: “You do not bear the root, but the root bears you,” because you are not yourself the beginning of faith, but you have taken Abraham as your example. If, however, it is referred to Christ, it should be understood thus: “You do not bear the root, but the root bears you” [Note: The words “but if it is referred to Christ … the root bears you” are written at the bottom of the margin.]; that is, you were saved not by your own merits but by the grace of God.

You say, then: “The branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in” [Note: The Vulgate has it thus, and treats this text very differently: “You will say, then: The branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in” [Col. 0242D]—namely, in verse 19. Then, once the sense is complete and a period has been inserted, verse 20 begins: “Well.”]. The Apostle was speaking to the Gentiles. Because he foresaw that they would become elated, thinking that they had been saved by their own merits and that the Jews had fallen, he himself raised the objection that he foresaw they would make, saying: “You will say,” and so forth.

The meaning is: Do not think, O Gentile people, that you were saved by your merits or that the Jews fell through theirs. It was not your merit but God’s favor. They fell through unbelief, whereas you were saved solely by the grace of God.

This is what follows: “They were broken off because of unbelief, but you stand by faith”—that is, aided by divine grace, you persevere in faith.

[Col. 0242D] Finally, lest he fall through pride, just as the Jews had fallen through pride together with unbelief, he admonished him by a command and terrified him by an example, adding: “Do not be high-minded, but fear.” To be high-minded is to be proud. Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Do not set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble” (Rom. 12:16).

But it must be asked why he commanded the Romans to fear, when above he says: “You did not receive a spirit of slavery again into fear” (Rom. 8:15). Therefore we must understand that he is urging them to possess a holy and chaste fear, namely, so that by fearing to turn away from Christ they might be made firmer in faith.

For this reason he also frightened them, adding: “For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps he will not spare you either.” He calls the Jews natural branches because they derived their fleshly origin from the patriarchs. The meaning is therefore: If God did not spare the Jews, who by the nature of the flesh arose from Abraham while persisting in unbelief, he will spare you much less, since by nature you were a bitter wild olive, cut off and grafted into a sweet olive.

But because the judgments of God are uncertain and incomprehensible, he prefaced this with “perhaps.” It follows: “See, therefore, the goodness and severity of God.”

Blessed Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth, was exhorting the Jews to remain firm and steadfast in faith. He admonished them by a command and terrified them by an example, saying: “Do not,” and so forth. Therefore he also adds: “See, therefore, the goodness and severity of God.” By the goodness of God he means the free mercy by which he justifies those who believe in him; by his severity, the justice of his righteous judgment by which he condemns the reprobate.

He makes clear in whom they should consider this severity, adding: “Severity indeed toward those who fell.” This is said of the Jews, who, like branches from that olive tree that bears fruit in the root of the patriarchs, were broken off and cut away. “But toward you, the goodness of God”—that is, you were saved by the goodness of God alone, without any merits demanding it.

But lest they perish either through pride or through idleness, he added: “If you remain in his goodness.” Otherwise they could not be saved. Hence it continues: “Otherwise you too will be cut off.” For this reason the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24:13).

Moreover, it must be understood that in these words the Apostle shows that human beings have been granted free choice. For just as people can do nothing good unless the grace of God goes before them, so this grace can accomplish nothing in them unless they themselves join their willingness to it [Note: Here is evidence of what opinion our author held concerning free choice and grace.].

And because some of the Jews were going to believe, he added: “But they also, if they do not remain in unbelief” [Note: The Vulgate has “if they do not remain” in place of “who do not remain.”] “will be grafted in.” But lest this be thought to happen through their merits, he wished to show that God, by his omnipotence, does what he wishes, and therefore added: “For God is able” [Col. 0243D] “to graft them in again.”

The meaning is: By the power with which he converted and saved you, he can also convert them to faith and save them. By saying “again,” he shows that they have already been grafted in—namely, because, by God’s permission, they arose from the seed of the patriarchs and imitated their footsteps of faith.

Notice also that great compassion is displayed in these words. The Apostle shows that God is so rich in mercy that even those who, after baptism, fall into some serious sin can be converted through repentance. Thus he says: “God is able to graft them in again,” that is, to restore them to their former standing.

For if you were cut from a natural wild olive and grafted, contrary to nature, into a good olive, how much more will these, according to nature, be grafted into their own olive tree? The meaning is this: If you, O Gentile people, were cut off from the wild and bitter olive of the human race—that is, separated by the grace of God—and grafted contrary to nature into the good olive—that is, the primitive Church—then much more will these, born according to the nature of the flesh from the olive tree—that is, from the patriarchs—if they are converted to the faith, be grafted into their own olive tree; that is, they will be joined to the patriarchs and to the primitive Church.

But what does he mean by “contrary to nature”? Is God, the Creator of all nature, doing something contrary to nature? Certainly not. “Contrary to nature,” therefore, means contrary to the usage and customary course of nature. No one grafts a wild olive into an olive tree. God therefore does nothing contrary to nature; rather, whatever he does is natural to all things, since from him come every measure, number, and order of nature.

Finally, because the Gentiles could say, “Why are you writing this comparison to us?” he added [Note: “Chapter 38” is written here in the autograph margin.]: “For I do not want you to be ignorant of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own estimation.” It is as though he were saying: I want you to know this mystery so that you may not become proud or exalted.

A mystery is something divine and sacred, yet hidden. Those are wise in their own estimation who think their foolishness wisdom, who boast that they are wise, and who glory in the rejection or contempt of others.

What he meant by “mystery” he shows by continuing: “Because a hardening has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness,” and so forth. He says that although hardening happened in Israel, it did not happen to the whole nation but only in part. Nor did Israel fall in such a way as to remain fallen forever, but only “until the fullness of the Gentiles enters.” “And thus all Israel will be saved.”

By these words the Apostle clearly shows that the one who will come to judge the world has already come into the world for judgment, as he says in the Gospel: “For judgment I have come into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39).

He came for a judgment of discrimination, so that those who did not see—that is, who confessed themselves blinded by sins—might be enlightened, while those who did see—that is, who thought that they saw and disdained to confess themselves sinners—might be hardened more cruelly and become blinder.

This, then, is the hardening that happened in Israel. By “the fullness of the Gentiles” he does not mean all the Gentiles, since not all believed, but as many as among the Gentiles have believed or will believe. For this is the true Israel.

Likewise, by “all Israel” he means those Jews who believed through the preaching of the apostles and who thereafter either have believed or will believe, especially around the day of judgment.

Blessed Augustine, however, in his book *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, explains it thus: “All Israel,” that is, from the remnant of Israel according to the flesh, and the fullness of the Gentiles, because in the faith of Christ according to the Holy Spirit, Israel [Note: Blessed Augustine, Letter to Paulinus 149, §19, says that “Israel” can be understood in two ways: either according to the flesh, that is, the fullness of the Gentiles, or according to the spirit, that is, the calling of the elect.].

As it is written: “He will come from Zion, who will deliver and turn ungodliness away from Jacob” (Isa. 59:20). Zion is the mountain of Jerusalem, which is sometimes used to designate the city itself. Concerning this Zion the prophet Micah, or Isaiah, says: “From Zion the law went forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2:3; Mic. 4:2).

Isaiah shows the manner of this going forth when he says: “Behold, a virgin will conceive in the womb and bear a son” (Isa. 7:14). The word of the Lord therefore went forth from Jerusalem, and the law came from Zion, because Christ, the Word of God the Father, assumed flesh from the Jewish people. By preaching the Gospel and performing miracles, he delivered Jacob and turned ungodliness away from him—that is, unbelief.

Although he converted many to the faith by his own teaching, he converted still more through the preaching of his apostles. But this turning away of ungodliness will be completed when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered [Note: The autograph reads *introiret*, “might enter,” but *introierit*, “will have entered,” is preferable.], that is, around the end of the age.

In Jacob, therefore, although believing Jews are understood according to the Apostle’s intention, all the faithful may nevertheless be understood in a general sense.

“And this will be my covenant with them”—“it will be given” is understood—“when I take away their sins”; that is, when by dying I justify them from their sins. This covenant will be given to them by me, by which they can be saved.

He calls it the covenant of which the prophet says: “I will make a new covenant with the house of Jacob and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers; but this is the covenant that I will establish with them, says the Lord: After those days I will put my law within them,” and so forth (Jer. 31:31).

This is the New Testament, that is, the grace of the Gospel. It is called “New” in distinction from the Old, and because it renews human beings.

The Jews, then, might say: If ungodliness has been turned away from them, why are they enemies of you? For this reason the Apostle continues: “According to the Gospel, indeed, they are enemies for your sake.”

He appropriately says “according to the Gospel,” because when the Jews hear it preached from the Gospel that they themselves killed Christ, that he died and rose again, and that he ascended into heaven, they are scandalized and become enemies of the preachers—especially on account of the Gentiles, whom they envy because they believe. This is what the Apostle means by “for your sake.”

[Col. 0245D] But what does the following mean: “According to the election, however, they are beloved for the sake of the fathers”? Are the same people both enemies and beloved? Certainly not. In both peoples there are those who belong to Jacob’s lameness, and there are those who belong to his blessing.

When we hear: “What Israel was seeking, it did not obtain; but the election obtained it; the rest were blinded” [Note: Rom. 11:7. In place of “the rest,” the autograph reads “all,” which I judged should be corrected as an error on the basis of the preceding reading of this passage.], we clearly understand that there are enemies, namely, those who have been blinded; and there are beloved, that is, the elect.

They were called not by that calling of which the Gospel says, “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16), but by that calling which is according to God’s purpose, which the Apostle calls election.

He says “for the sake of the fathers,” meaning the patriarchs, to whom the promises were made, and especially Abraham. They are therefore beloved for the sake of the fathers, because they followed the footsteps of the patriarchs’ faith.

“Without repentance,” so that the mercy of God might be declared above all, “are the gifts and the calling of God” [Note: The Vulgate has “for the gifts and calling of God are.”]. They are without repentance because they are unchangeable. Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:4).

“He has sworn and will not repent”—that is, this priesthood of the New Testament, sanctified in his Son, will by no means be changed. Wherever God is said to have repented, we must understand that he changed his sentence, as in: “It repents me that I made humankind” (Gen. 6:7), and again: “It repents me that I made Saul king over Israel” (1 Sam. 15:11).

This does not mean that there is mutability in God, since James says: “With whom there is no change” (Jas. 1:17). Rather, God’s sentence is changed in accordance with human merits.

Alternatively: Two things ordinarily belong to repentance: labor and affliction. The gifts and calling of God are therefore without repentance, because, when the grace of God goes before them, people are called to the faith without any bodily labor or distress, and through the washing of baptism they obtain the remission of sins. He calls it the calling that is according to God’s purpose.

[Col. 0246C] It follows: “Just as you once did not believe God, but now have obtained mercy because of their unbelief,” and so forth. The meaning is: You too were once unbelievers, but, converted to the faith, you obtained mercy—that is, the remission of your sins—because of their unbelief, from which you took an example of salvation, lest you perish as they did.

So also these others, namely, those who once believed, have now not believed in your mercy—that is, in Christ, by whose mercy you were saved—so that they too may obtain mercy, that is, the remission of their sins [Note: The Vulgate has “so that they too.”]. If they believed, they would certainly obtain it.

Thus, wishing to show that neither Jew nor Gentile could boast of his own merits, he added: “For God has enclosed all things in unbelief.”

From eternity God had determined to redeem the human race through the Passion of his Son. Nevertheless, he chose the time at which to send him, namely, the time when both the Gentile and Jewish peoples were alike. From the very beginning of the world the Gentile people had withdrawn from God by worshiping idols; the Jewish people, gradually departing from knowledge of God and from the commandments of the Law, had almost become Gentile.

Therefore the Apostle says: “God has enclosed all in unbelief” [Note: “Chapter 39” is written there in the autograph margin.]. But “enclosed” must not be understood to mean that God compelled or impelled anyone to sin. Rather, whatever he permits to happen by a just judgment, Scripture’s customary manner of speaking says that he himself does. He therefore “enclosed” them because he permitted them to be enclosed.

But whom does “all” mean? All classes of human beings, clearly. For he wishes those to whom he was speaking to be understood, as though he were saying: You and the Jews.

Why he enclosed all in unbelief he shows by continuing: “So that he might have mercy on all,” that is, so that no one might now boast of his own merits, but that all might boast in the Lord.

But what does he mean by “all”? If he will have mercy on all, then when he comes to judgment he will condemn no one. Therefore “all” refers to all the vessels of mercy, that is, all those whom he chose both from the Jews and from the Gentiles. Thus he will condemn no one of all these—not all human beings, but all of these.

Therefore, since he has uttered a statement of great profundity, and, overcome by its awe, has been unable to comprehend God’s hidden dispensation—why he saves some by undeserved grace, but rejects others by a just judgment—and especially terrified by the rejection of the Jews and the election of the Gentiles, he burst forth in wonder, adding:

“ O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!”

“Depth” pertains not only to riches but also to wisdom and knowledge. The depth of God’s riches is such that they cannot be grasped by the mind; among these riches are those which he has displayed in the vessels of mercy. There is also a depth of God’s wisdom and knowledge, because his wisdom and knowledge are so great that neither human nor angelic nature can penetrate them. Hence it is also added:

“How incomprehensible are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways!” [Note: [Col. 0247D] The autograph, in place of “and unsearchable” (*et investigabiles*), has *evestigabiles*—a variant spelling meaning “unsearchable.”] [Col. 0247C]

These are the judgments of which the Psalmist says: “The judgments of the Lord are a great abyss” (Psalm 35:7). Astonished at the depth of this abyss, he cried out: “How…” and so forth. The ways of the Lord, as the same Psalmist says, are “truth and mercy” (Psalm 24:10). They are “unsearchable” because he has mercy on those whom he wills, not on the basis of justice but by the gift of his mercy; and he hardens those whom he wills, not through iniquity but through the truth of retribution.

And because these things can neither be expressed in words nor even grasped by the mind, he added:

“For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” [Col. 0247D]

The implied answer is: no one.

Again, because no one can anticipate God’s grace so as to say to God, “You are my debtor,” he added:

“Or who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him?”

For this reason he himself says to Job: “Who has given to me first, and I will repay him?” (Job 41:2).

Wishing openly to show that all things are from God, he added:

“For from him, and through him, and in him are all things.”

The expression is one, because there is one God, from whom, through whom, and in whom all things exist. It should be understood that whatever is from him is through him, and whatever is of him is from him; yet not everything that is from him is also of him. Heaven and earth, and so forth, are from him, but not of him, because they are not of his substance. The Son alone is of him: he was begotten from him and is in all things equal to God the Father.

Therefore, all things that are from God are through him, because he created them; and they are governed and directed in him. By “all things” he means those things that subsist and are therefore creatures, and are good [Note: That is, they subsist and are good.], because they were created by the good God. Sin, however, does not subsist, since it is not a creature but a defect of the creature.

Others understand this as referring to the distinction of the persons who are in the Trinity: when we say “from him,” the Father is understood; “through him,” the Son; “in him,” the Holy Spirit, since all things that are from God were made through the Son and are governed in the Holy Spirit.

But it is better, following the authority of blessed Augustine, to understand that he wished to express the unity of the divine substance. Hence he continued in the singular number:

“To him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.”

That is, to that God from whom, through whom, and in whom all things exist. Moreover, by these words the Apostle warns us not to transfer the honor owed to God to anyone else.

Next follows: [Note: [Col. 0248D] Here, in the autograph margin, chapter XL is written.] [Col. 0248D]

“(CHAPTER XII.) Therefore I beseech you, brothers, by the mercy of God.”

Up to this point, throughout nearly the whole text of the Epistle, the Apostle has warned his assistants to withdraw from carnal sacrifices. Now, however, he proceeds to teach them the precepts of immortality and the sacrifices to which they should devote themselves. Since he had forbidden them carnal sacrifices, it was appropriate that he should teach them most clearly which sacrifices they ought to pursue.

A true sacrifice is some good thing, if it is undertaken so that we may cleave to God with a holy intention. A sacrifice is a divine thing. Hence the human being himself, who has been consecrated in God’s name and devoted to God, is a sacrifice insofar as he dies to the world and to vices. And when we afflict our bodies through continence and abstinence [Note: Perhaps “affligimus,” “we afflict.”], if this is done for God, it is a sacrifice.

Urging his hearers to this sacrifice, the Apostle said: “I beseech you,” and so forth. Here it should be noted that he does not say, “I command” or “I order,” as the law does, but “I beseech.” Commanding belongs to the law; assisting or beseeching belongs to grace.

Notice also that he does not say merely “you,” but adds: “By the mercy of God,” as if he were saying: “By that mercy I beseech you by which, without any merits demanding it, you have been saved, to present your bodies.”

He says “your” in distinction from the Old Testament. There the bodies of animals were offered to God:

“A living sacrifice.”

A “victim” is called a sacrifice made for the purpose of overcoming enemies. The Apostle therefore urges us to offer our bodies to God as a victim, so that we may be able to overcome our enemies, the demons.

He says “living” in distinction from the Old Testament, in which the bodies of animals were slaughtered and then offered to God.

“Holy,” that is, separated from sins.

“Pleasing to God”—the implied phrase is, “through his indwelling Spirit.” Hence elsewhere: “You are the temple of the living God” (2 Corinthians 6:16). Again: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16). [Col. 0249A]

“Your rational service.”

He says this likewise in distinction from that Testament in which the bodies of irrational animals were offered to God. By “rational service” he means the worship of the New Testament. For it would not have been fitting to offer the bodies of irrational animals to the wise and rational God rather than offering ourselves.

Therefore, because the sacrifice is not only of the body but also of the mind, he added:

“And do not be conformed to this age.”

Those who are conformed are uniform. By “the age” he means the people who dwell in the age and love the age. He therefore warns us not to be conformed to people who love the world—that is, not to associate with them or become like them by imitating their footsteps.

To whom we ought to be conformed [Note: [Col. 0249D] The autograph has *informari*, “to be formed,” in place of *conformari*, “to be conformed.”] he shows by adding:

“But be transformed in the newness of your mind.”

Those are transformed in the newness of their mind who make progress in the wisdom of God. Hence Origen says: “As many steps as we advance in the wisdom of God, so many times are we transformed in the newness of our mind.”

The soul, therefore, which, kindled by the fire of charity, drives away from itself all worldly desires and the desires of the world, is certainly a sacrifice. The Apostle warns us to offer such a sacrifice.

For it should be understood that not everything in the human being perished. If everything, or if nothing, had perished, there would be nothing to transform. Since the image of God has been corrupted by vices, the Apostle urges us to be transformed in the newness of our mind. We do this when, having driven away our vices, we renew God’s image within us, stripping off the old person with his deeds and putting on the new (Ephesians 4:22–24). [Col. 0249C]

“So that you may prove what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.”

Those who make progress in divine wisdom can prove what the will of God is; and the more each person advances, the more fully he recognizes what that will is.

The will of God was therefore “good” in Saul, “pleasing and perfect” in David. These three degrees must be distinguished. The will of God is good in the thirtyfold fruit, pleasing in the sixtyfold, and perfect in the hundredfold (Matthew 13:8): that is, good in married persons, pleasing in those who practice continence, and perfect in virgins or martyrs. [Col. 0249D]

Alternatively: it is good in holy thought, pleasing in holy speech, and perfect in action.

Next follows: [Note: Here, in the autograph margin, chapter XLI is written.]

“I say, through the grace that has been given to me.”

Above, he said that he was beseeching them by mercy, wishing to show that they had been saved not by any merits of their own but by the grace of God alone. Now he asserts that he speaks through grace, to show that what he was saying was not his own gift but God’s grace.

Grace was given to him because, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, he was chosen to preach the Gospel to the Gentiles.

To whom he is speaking he makes clear:

“To everyone who is among you.” [Col. 0250A]

Here it should be noted that he does not say “to all of you,” but “to everyone who is among you.” His words seem to sound as though he were not speaking or writing to those with whom he was conversing, but to those who were among them. He did this in order to identify only those who were blameworthy, namely, those who were boasting of their own merits and of the rejection of the Jews.

What he was saying to them is disclosed when he adds:

“Not to think more highly than one ought to think.”

Those think more highly than they ought who do not think rightly; who presume on their own works and glory in the contempt of others.

There were therefore some who thought more highly than they ought regarding marriage, loving marriage so greatly that they condemned continence; and others who loved continence so greatly that they condemned marriage. The same applies in other matters. [Col. 0250B]

But how one ought to think the Apostle shows by adding:

“But to think with sobriety,” that is, according to sobriety or temperance.

This is one of the four virtues about which it is written in the Book of Wisdom: “She”—that is, wisdom—“teaches prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance, than which nothing is more useful for human beings in life” (Wisdom 8:7).

Temperance is also called moderation, because it keeps measure in all things. Whoever therefore preserves measure in every matter is truly sober, moderate, and temperate, and consequently prudent, just, and courageous, since these four virtues are so closely joined that one cannot exist without the others.

“And to each person according to the measure of faith that God has distributed.” [Col. 0250C]

The order is this: “To each person I say: not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think according to the measure of faith that God has distributed.”

By these words he shows that faith is the measure of all gifts, since the gifts of the Holy Spirit are bestowed according to the merits of faith. Hence elsewhere: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good; to one the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge” (1 Corinthians 12:7), and so forth.

When he says “as God has distributed,” this must not be understood to mean that the Holy Spirit is divisible, since he is God; rather, this is said because his gifts are diverse. The Holy Spirit is not divided, but his gifts are. For this reason it is also added (1 Corinthians 8:12): [Note: Here, in the autograph margin, chapter XLII is written.]

“For just as in one body we have many members, but all the members do not have the same function” (1 Corinthians 13:14), and so forth. [Col. 0250D]

Here it should be noted that he beautifully says “in one body,” because there is one body with different members. The whole body is not an eye (1 Corinthians 14:17), nor is the whole body an ear. The members do not all have the same function: the eye sees, the ear hears, and the foot walks.

By “one function” he means the same office.

Thus, although many, we are one body in Christ. He calls the Church “one body”; hence he appropriately adds “in Christ,” because Christ is the head of this body.

If Christ is the head and the Church is the body, all the faithful are members of this body. Hence it is also added:

“And individually members of one another.” [Col. 0251A]

In this body there are eyes—that is, those who rightly discern; ears, namely, those who rightly hear; noses, which receive the fragrance of good works and offer it to others as an example; feet, which walk in the way of God’s commandments and show others the path by which to walk; and hands, which rightly serve others by distributing their possessions and handle the word of life well.

Therefore, just as none of the bodily members usurps another’s function—for example, when the eye is closed the ear does not see, and when the ears are stopped the eye does not hear [Note: The autograph has “the ears are stopped” in the feminine plural]—so no one in the Church ought to usurp another’s gift.

It should also be understood that each member receives the office assigned to it not for itself alone but for all. The eye does not see only for itself but for all the members. Thus each of the faithful ought to share with everyone the gift granted to him.

For it should be understood that each person in the Church makes another’s gift his own through charity.

Therefore, to show the difference among God’s gifts, he added:
