“But having gifts differing according to the grace that has been given to us.”

By “gifts” he means the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Wishing to show that the faithful receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit not because of any merits that demand them but by the grace of God alone, he added:

“According to grace.”

By “grace” he means faith. This grace was given to us because, without any merits demanding it, we were called and believed.

“Differing” means distinct. The gifts of the Holy Spirit differ from one another. Yet we must not believe that the Holy Spirit is divisible, since God cannot be divided; rather, his gifts are various and are distributed among the faithful. [Col. 0251C]

Wishing to show this difference, he added:

“Whether prophecy.”

He says “according to the proportion of faith,” because the gifts of the Holy Spirit are bestowed according to the measure of faith. Beautifully, he placed prophecy first, because, just as the eye is the most excellent member in the body, so this gift is preeminent above all others in the Church. He appropriately compares it to the eye, because, just as the eye sees things at a distance, so prophecy looks ahead to things that will happen in the distant future.

Whenever the following expressions occur, “according to the proportion of faith” is to be understood.

“Or ministry”—the implied phrase is, “having ministry according to the proportion of faith.”

“In ministering”—the implied phrase is, “say, ‘Do not think more highly than one ought to think.’”

By “ministry” he means the distribution of alms, which is the office of the hands; or he calls the office of preaching ministry.

To explain what ministry he meant, he added:

“Or the one who teaches, in teaching”—the implied phrase is, “I say, do not think more highly than one ought to think.”

This office is attributed to the mouth.

But it may be asked why the Apostle added:

“The one who exhorts, in exhortation,”

after having said:

“The one who teaches, in teaching,”

since they appear to be the same thing.

Nevertheless, it should be understood that some people can teach and bring many things together in an orderly way, but do not possess the power of exhortation. Others, by contrast, are able to say less but possess the power of exhortation. By bringing together testimonies from Scripture, they can offer great consolation to the sorrowful and to those grieving temporal losses or the deaths of relatives. Therefore, “the one who exhorts, in exhortation” implies: “Let him not think more highly than he ought to think.” [Col. 0252A]

“The one who gives, in simplicity”—the implied phrase is, “let him give, and not think more highly than he ought to think.”

There are some who do not give in simplicity—that is, who distribute their possessions while seeking human praise and earthly profit. Those give in simplicity who desire heavenly things in place of earthly things, lasting things in place of things that pass away, and eternal things in place of temporal things.

“The one who presides, with diligence” [Col. 0252B]—the implied phrase is, “let him preside, and not think more highly than he ought to think.”

But what sort of diligence does the Apostle urge upon those who preside? [Note: What follows bears the marks of a man who has been entrusted with the care of a flock and who knows very well everything that the divine Paul chiefly requires of a bishop in the Epistle to Titus. This is our Atto.] Is it carnal diligence, from which everyone ought to be estranged? No, but spiritual diligence: every person who presides ought to be diligent lest, through negligence, he lose any of the sheep entrusted to him.

Again, what does he mean when he adds:

“The one who shows mercy, with cheerfulness”?

A little earlier he had said:

“The one who gives, in simplicity,”

and the two seem to be the same. But it should be understood that some give what is theirs without showing mercy—namely, those who lend at interest, expecting to receive the same or an equivalent amount. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not turn away from the one who wishes to borrow from you” (Matthew 5:42).

Those show mercy who distribute their possessions to the needy without expecting to receive the same or an equal amount from them. [Col. 0252C] The Apostle urges that this be done not with weariness of mind or distress, but with sincerity of heart. Hence elsewhere: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

“Let love be without pretense”—the implied phrase is, “let it be so.”

Those love without pretense who love God with all their heart, with all their mind, and with all their strength, and their neighbors as themselves.

“Hating evil, clinging to good.”

Why does the Apostle commend hatred so insistently? Because there is an evil hatred by which someone hates his brothers, and there is a good hatred by which we hate evil. He therefore commends this hatred so that, by hating evil, we may be able to cling to good.

The person clings to good who performs a good work solely in order to receive the reward of eternal life.

“In brotherly charity, being kind to one another” [Col. 0252D] [Note: The Vulgate has: “loving one another with the charity of brotherhood.”]

Charity is love of God and neighbor. Therefore, in distinction from divine charity, the Apostle added: “of brotherhood.”

It should be understood that just as charity in general is superior to every virtue, so this particular charity is preferred to everything that pertains to brotherhood. And just as all virtues proceed from that charity, so everything pertaining to brotherly uprightness proceeds from this one.

By “kind” he means humane and generous.

To show what arises from this charity, he added:

“Outdoing one another in honor” [Col. 0253A]—the implied phrase here, as above, is “be.”

The Apostle therefore urges us to anticipate one another in the honor of love, so that the charity of brotherhood may be strengthened in us.

But what does the following mean?

“Not lagging in diligence,”

since above he had said:

“The one who presides, let him preside with diligence”?

It seems to have been said twice. Nevertheless, it should be understood that above he commanded a particular diligence, which only those who preside ought to possess; here he commands a general diligence, which all the faithful ought to have, namely, that they should diligently avoid the devil’s snares. [Note: The following words appear in the autograph in the lateral margin: “ille et Vercellinus diacon pi.” These words, insofar as they concern Vercellinus, will receive their interpretation at the end of the Epistles of Saint Paul.] [Col. 0253B]

Every faithful person is an animal of God; but God’s animal ought to be endowed with eyes, so that it may look around on every side and avoid being caught by the devil. Blessed Peter the Apostle teaches this diligence when he says:

“Be diligent and watchful” [Note: 1 Peter 4:7. There the Vulgate has “prudent” instead of “diligent.”], and so forth.

“Fervent in spirit, serving the Lord”—the implied phrase is, “be.”

We are urged to be fervent in spirit so that, kindled by the fire of charity, we may strive to do what pleases God, lest perhaps what the Lord says to the angel of the church of Laodicea in the Apocalypse be said to us: “Would that you were hot or cold! But because you are lukewarm, I am beginning to vomit you out of my mouth” (Revelation 3:15–16). [Note: The autograph has “Laudociae.”]

But what does it mean that he specifically admonishes us here to serve God? His words seem to sound as though the person who does what he said above does not serve God.

Nevertheless, it should be understood that although those who do the preceding things do serve God, the Apostle wished especially to commend and teach this: whatever we do must be done not for any earthly advantage but solely for the service of God—that is, so that we may be able to please him.

“Rejoicing in hope.”

Those rejoice in hope who possess the joy of eternal blessedness in hope as though they already possessed it in reality. Therefore, whatever adversity they suffer in this age, they bear patiently. For this reason the Apostle added:

“Patient in tribulation.”

Hence James says: “Consider it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various trials” (James 1:2).

Therefore, since no one can attain these things without continual prayer, he added:

“Devoting yourselves to prayer”—the implied phrase is, “be.”

Notice that he does not say merely “praying” [Note: The autograph has “prayers”], but “devoting yourselves to prayer.” It is not enough to pray only for a time unless we also pray continually. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Praying at all times, that you may be worthy” (Luke 21:36), and so forth. Elsewhere the same Apostle says: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17).

“Sharing in the needs of the saints.”

It may be asked why the Apostle commanded this, since above he had said:

“The one who gives, let him give in simplicity.”

The two appear to be the same. But it should be understood that above he commended the general work of mercy; here he commends the particular work that ought to be offered to the principal members of Christ. [Col. 0254A]

It should be observed what word the Apostle uses. He says:

“Sharing in the needs of the saints,”

that is, participating in them—as if he were openly saying: “Distribute what is yours to the principal members of Christ, not as though it were yours and private, but as though it were the Creator’s gifts, alien and common.” [Note: The implied phrase is “you ought,” or perhaps, instead of “distribute,” one should read “distribute yourselves.”]

“Pursuing hospitality.”

Notice that he does not command them merely to be hospitable, but to pursue hospitality. A hospitable person is one who receives guests who come to him; a person pursues hospitality who goes around the villages and streets of the city so that perhaps none of the poor may remain without shelter or suffer any hardship. [Col. 0254B]

“Bless those who persecute you.”

The meaning is: You have already been renewed; you have already tasted the new person. Therefore you must not be people who curse. For a curse ought not to proceed from the mouth from which blessing proceeds. As James says (James 3:11): “Sweet and bitter water cannot come forth from one spring.”

“Bless, and do not curse.”

But it may be asked why the Apostle then adds:

“Rejoice with those who rejoice.”

Should we rejoice with those who take pleasure in temporal goods or in the death of their enemies? Certainly not.

It should be understood that there is a carnal joy, of which the Lord says: “Woe to you who laugh” (Luke 6:25); and there is a spiritual joy, of which the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Rejoice in the Lord always” (Philippians 3:1). We ought therefore to rejoice with those who rejoice in spiritual goods and labor so that their names may be written in heaven. To them the Lord also says: “Rejoice and exult, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). [Col. 0254C]

“Weep with those who weep”—the implied phrase is, “you ought.”

But should one weep with those who mourn temporal losses or the death of relatives? No. Rather, one should weep with those who mourn their own sins or the sins of others, and the delay of their sojourn—that is, the fact that they are kept longer away from the sight of their Creator. Such was the one who said:

“Every night I wash my bed; I water my couch with tears” (Psalm 6:7).

“Having the same mind toward one another”—the implied phrase is, “be.”

As though he were saying openly: “Do not be dissident, but think the same about your brothers as you think about yourselves.”

“Not thinking lofty thoughts”—the implied phrase is, “do not be.”

To think loftily is to be proud. This statement refers spiritually to those who gloried in their own merits and in the rejection of the Jews.

“But associating with the humble.”

He calls humble those of whom the Lord says in the Gospel:

“Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matthew 5:3),

that is, the humble in heart.

The Apostle urges us to associate with these, meaning that we should concur with them in conversation, friendliness, agreement, and in every way by assisting them in their needs. [Col. 0255A]

Therefore, to show what it means to think lofty thoughts and how we ought to associate with the humble, he added:

“Do not be wise in your own estimation.”

By this statement he shows that those who think lofty thoughts are wise in their own estimation.

Notice that he does not say merely, “Do not be wise,” lest this appear contrary to the Lord’s command, who said: “Be wise.” Instead he added: “In your own estimation” (Matthew 10:16).

Those are wise in their own estimation who boast of their wisdom, who count their own foolishness as supreme wisdom, who presume upon their merits and glory in the rejection of others. These are the people who follow the wisdom of the flesh, about which the Apostle said above:

“The wisdom of the flesh is death” (Romans 8:6).

That is, they return evil to one who has harmed them and curse one who curses them. Therefore he added:

“Returning evil to no one for evil.”

For if it is evil to inflict evil upon someone, it is incomparably worse to return evil for evil. The former often happens through ignorance, but the latter always deliberately.

By these words the Apostle teaches what the Lord teaches in the Gospel:

“If anyone strikes you on one cheek, offer him the other also” (Matthew 5:39; Luke 6:29).

In this matter, as blessed Augustine says, there are six distinctions:

- returning good for evil;
- not returning evil for evil;
- returning good for good;
- returning evil for evil;
- not returning good for good;
- returning evil for good.

The first two belong to the righteous, and the first is the better. The last two belong to the reprobate, and the second of them is the worse. The middle two are intermediate: the first is closer to good, the second to evil.

Those who are moderately good return good for good, and those who are moderately evil return evil for evil.

The law itself also commands this, saying:

“You shall love your friend, and hate your enemy” (Leviticus 19:18; Matthew 5:43).

It commands that retaliation be returned for retaliation, along with other things of this kind. [Note: Exodus 21:23–24 and following; Leviticus 24:20; Deuteronomy 19:21; Matthew 5:38. See blessed Augustine, Against Faustus, book 22, chapter 25. The punishment of retaliation was inflicted not by any private individual but by a judge. This law was concerned more with avoiding hatred than with exercising vengeance. For God’s law commanded hatred of God’s enemies, not of private individuals, whom, on the contrary, it commanded people to love. Leviticus 19:17–18; Exodus 23:4–5; Deuteronomy 22:1–4.] [Col. 0255D]

The Lord, therefore, not wishing his disciples to remain at this level, but calling them to higher things, commanded:

“Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matthew 5:44; Luke 6:27).

To show who those are who do not return evil for evil, he added:

“Providing what is good not only before God but also before [Note: The Vulgate has: “before all people”] human beings.”

Those who arrange and order their ways and actions so that they cannot be reproached by anyone provide what is good before God. Those who arrange them so that they also appear worthy of imitation provide what is good before human beings.

Such were the parents of our Lord’s forerunner, Zechariah and Elizabeth, of whom it is written:

“They were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord” (Luke 1:6). [Col. 0256A]

Next follows:

“If it is possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people.”

Peace joins two people, and therefore peace cannot exist except between two. Hence the same Apostle says:

“Christ is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2:14).

Foreseeing, therefore, that peace could not be preserved unshaken on the part of enemies—namely, those who are reproved by the good—he moderated his statement by saying:

“If it is possible.”

He foresaw that it might not be possible; therefore he added:

“So far as it depends on you.”

As though he were saying openly: Since peace cannot remain unshaken on the part of enemies, let it remain unshaken insofar as it depends on you—that is, insofar as it concerns you, on your side—so that you may always desire their salvation.

By these words he does not at all abolish ecclesiastical discipline, as though, when we see a brother fallen, we should not correct him. We ought indeed to do so, if perhaps we can amend him.

But how we can have peace with all people he himself makes clear when he adds:

“Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath.”

Although “wrath” here may be understood as human wrath, it is more appropriately understood as the wrath of God, that is, vengeance.

When we do not defend ourselves, we give place to wrath in two ways: either because the anger of the enemy is calmed when he does not see vengeance returned to him, or because, patiently enduring adversity for the love of God, we leave room for God to avenge us.

Nevertheless, we must not refrain from doing evil with the intention that God may punish our enemy; rather, we must persevere so that he may be converted to peace and saved. [Note: [Col. 0256D] The autograph has *facere* without *non*; perhaps “endure,” “suffer,” or a similar word should be read.] [Col. 0256C]

But a question arises. Since the Lord says, “Love your enemies,” and the Apostle says, “Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath,” why do the saints cry out beneath God’s altar, as we read in the Apocalypse:

“How long, holy and true Lord, will you not judge and avenge our blood?” (Revelation 6:10).

Lest this appear contradictory, it should be understood that the saints do not desire the vengeance of their enemies for their damnation, but for their conversion. This is the vengeance for their blood. Or certainly they desire the day of judgment, when their number will be complete and the wicked will be punished, so that they will no longer be permitted to sin.

Therefore, wishing to confirm his account by an example, he added:

“As it is written,” namely, in the book of a certain wise man:

“Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord” (Deuteronomy 32:35). [Col. 0256D]

These are the Lord’s words, and therefore the implied sense is: “Leave vengeance to me; I will repay,” that is, “I will reward your patience, or I will exact vengeance on your behalf.” The statement can be understood in either way.

But because he had said, “Vengeance is mine,” and so forth, in order to show what we ought to do he added:

“If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink.” [Col. 0257A]

Here we should understand food and drink not only bodily but also spiritual—that is, the word of preaching. For just as the body is sustained by visible food and drink, so the soul is nourished by that spiritual food.

What reward the person who does this will receive he makes clear when he adds:

“For by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head.”

Every imperative statement, if it forbids a disgraceful or criminal act and commands usefulness and benevolence, is not figurative. But if it appears to command a disgraceful or criminal act and to forbid usefulness and benevolence, it is certainly figurative.

No one therefore doubts that in the words in which the Apostle says, “If your enemy is hungry,” and so forth, he commends the benefit of benevolence; consequently, the language is not figurative.

But in what he adds—“For by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head”—he seems to commend an act of ill will. Therefore the expression is figurative and must be understood spiritually.

By the head, then, the mind is signified, since it is the chief part of the inner person, just as the head is the chief part of the body. And just as all the members are directed by the head, so everything inward is ordered by the mind.

By fire, charity is signified; by the burning coals, the same ardor of charity [Note: The autograph has: “the same ardor of charity”], as blessed Augustine says: “The burning groans of repentance.”

Whoever therefore supplies food to his hungry enemy, drink to his thirsty enemy—that is, everything necessary—heaps such coals upon his enemy’s mind. When the enemy sees necessities being supplied by the person he hates, he burns with groans of remorse, asking why he is an enemy to one who comes to his misery’s aid:

“I persecute him; he loves me. I seize what belongs to him; he generously gives me what is his. What remains except that I should love the one who loves me?”

Thus the enemy is provoked to love.

Concerning these coals the Lord says to Jerusalem through the prophet:

“You have coals; sit upon them. They will be a help to you.”

Some, however, have understood the coals as the punishments of eternal damnation. But the person who supplies his enemy’s necessities with the intention of increasing his punishment of eternal damnation does not love him; rather, he hates him.

It must therefore be understood absolutely that this was not the Apostle’s intention. He commanded these things so that the enemy might be converted to peace. Hence he also added:

“Do not be overcome by evil,” namely, by impatience.

The person is overcome by evil who, troubled by the fury of impatience, either returns vengeance to his enemy or desires that vengeance be returned.

“But overcome evil with good”—he calls patience “good.” The person therefore overcomes evil with good who, through the virtue of patience, endures every adversity patiently and with an even spirit. [Col. 0258A]

Furthermore, lest anyone should say, “I have passed over to the grace of the Gospel; I am free; I ought to be subject to no one,” the Apostle, so that nothing might be lacking for his hearers, added the following for the sake of peace and concord:

## Chapter XIII

**Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities.**

[Note: [Col. 0257D] In the autograph margin, “Chapter XLIII” is written.]

From the superior part—namely, the soul—the whole human being is designated. By “higher authorities” he means the emperors, kings, and rulers of this world, to whom he urges people to be subject for the sake of peace and concord, lest the name of God or the teaching of Christ be blasphemed.

[Note: [Cols. 0257D–0258D] From what follows in the chapter, the reader may understand what this very serious man’s judgment was concerning the obedience and subjection owed to rulers, to whom authority over all their subjects has been given by God. A true follower of evangelical teaching—how far he was from teaching resistance to rulers, from opposing authority to authority, from attacking them, or even, as has been heard with horror from certain innovators, from plotting against their lives or kingdom, or from laying sacrilegious and impious hands upon them under any pretext—will become clear. Indeed, it will become clear how highly our truly evangelical author valued ecclesiastical jurisdiction, and how he judged that it ought to be placed below the spiritual profit of souls. He certainly would never have judged in favor of defending jurisdiction if the matter concerned, on the one side, the gain or loss of souls or churches and, on the other, the defense of that jurisdiction. Compare this passage and what follows with what Atto himself has in his letter to Bishop Waldo, beginning, “Many [things are due] to your charity.”]

Hence his fellow apostle Peter also says: “Be subject, for God’s sake, to every human institution, whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him” (1 Peter 2:13).

What Peter explicitly stated with the words “for God’s sake,” Paul wished to be understood implicitly.

[Note: The autograph reads “placed.”]

Why we ought to be subject he shows by adding: **For there is no authority except from God.**

But since it is written in the book of a certain wise man, “Kings have reigned, but not through me; princes have arisen, and I did not know them” (Hosea 8:4), how can there be no authority except from God? We must therefore understand that there are things which God, in his mercy, orders and arranges, and things which, in his anger, he permits to happen.

Of those things which he permits in anger it is said: “Kings have reigned, and not through me,” and so forth. And in the Book of Job: “God permits the hypocrite to reign because of the sins of the people.”

[Note: Job 34:30. The Vulgate reads: “who makes a hypocritical man reign.”]

But of those things which he himself orders, it is written in the Book of Proverbs: “Through me kings reign” (Proverbs 8:15), and so forth. Thus every authority is from God, whether ordered by him in mercy or permitted by him in anger.

It should also be noted that he does not say, “Desire is not from God,” but “authority,” because the wicked have from themselves the desire to harm others, whereas they cannot possess authority except from God. For the devil could not touch even one little sheep of Job unless the Lord permitted it; therefore he said: “Stretch out your hand a little” (Job 1:11), that is, “Grant me permission to test him.”

And beautifully he adds: **But the authorities that exist have been ordered by God**, for from a good disposer nothing disordered is left.

By these words the Apostle plainly shows that every authority, among pagans as well as among Christians, has been ordered by God, whether in mercy or in anger. The fear of God was lacking in humanity; therefore, lest people devour one another like fish, authorities were given even to the wicked, so that the good might be tested through the virtue of patience and the wicked might be restrained and punished by worldly laws.

Why we ought not to resist authority he shows by adding: **Therefore whoever resists authority resists the ordinance of God.**

It is as though he said plainly: He attempts to rebel against God who contradicts the authority ordered by God.

[Note: What follows is highly worthy of notice, since it reveals the judgment of the teachers of that Church in that period, removes all room for subtle interpretations, and lays open the evangelical teaching proclaimed and sealed by Saint Paul and his fellow apostle Peter, especially in the First Epistle, chapter 2, verses 13, 14, 15, and following. It persuades us that this teaching was recognized and followed in those times by learned men and ought to be followed by us.]

Yet because there were some who said, “In secular affairs we ought to be subject, but in matters of faith and in things belonging to God, in no way,” the Apostle, wishing to show that we ought to be subject in all things for God’s sake, added: **Those who resist will acquire condemnation for themselves.**

It is as though he said plainly: By supplying their persecutors with an occasion to persecute them, they make their persecutors excusable and themselves blameworthy; and therefore they have a worthy cause of death and receive a worthy reward of death.

[Note: The meaning here becomes somewhat obscure. Perhaps, instead of *ideoque* (“and therefore”), one should write *ideo quia* (“because”): “because they have a worthy cause of death and receive a worthy reward of death.” For *ideoque* has been written in an abbreviated form as *ideoque*, whereas the conjunction *quia* is always, or almost always, written in abbreviation in the form in which the final syllable of *ideoque* is written, namely *q.* Clearly, by commending martyrdom our author wished it to have a worthy and unique cause—namely, religion in doctrine and morals. Or perhaps one should read: “because they do not have a worthy cause of death, nor do they receive a worthy reward of death,” that is, the palm of martyrdom.]

Why rulers have been appointed he makes clear by adding: **For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad.** They were not appointed to terrify those who do good, but those who do evil.

Therefore, to show the power of authority and why authority was given, he added: **Do you wish not to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it.**

But perhaps someone will say: “Were the holy apostles subject to the authorities, when they resisted rulers even unto death so as not to lose the faith of Christ?” They truly were subject, because they gave an occasion for being persecuted not on account of evil deeds, but on account of good ones.

[Note: “Here is a worthy cause of death.”]

But how can he say, “You will have praise from it”? Did the holy apostles receive praise from the rulers by whom they were killed? Therefore it must be understood that he does not say *through it* but *from it*. He looked around and moderated his expression, as though he said: “From the authority itself, whether just or savage.”

If the authority is just, you will have praise from it, even as it praises you. But if it is impious, while you suffer persecution for the faith of Christ and for truth,

[Note: “Here the worthy cause of martyrdom is demonstrated still more clearly.”]

you will have praise, since it provides an occasion for praise even by raging against you; for you will attain the crown of martyrdom, from which you will obtain praise.

Therefore he adds: **For he is God’s minister to you for good.** The ruler of this world is God’s minister for the good of the saints, because in this way—whether the authority is just or unjust—he ministers to the saints for the good of praise.

Finally, because he had said beforehand, “Rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad,” to make this clearer he added: **But if you do evil, be afraid**, since the ruler received authority for this purpose: to punish those who do evil.

Hence it follows: **For he does not bear the sword without cause**—that is, he does not exercise authority without cause. By “the sword” he means authority.

And to show more clearly why the one who does evil should fear him, he added: **For he is God’s minister, an avenger in wrath against the one who does evil.** He calls the ruler a minister because he received authority from God to take vengeance on those who do evil.

But it may be asked why the Apostle so often mentions authority, God’s ministers, wrath, and vengeance. Clearly, it is to show that God does not wish these things to be carried out through his bishops, but through secular authorities.

[Note: The words “but through secular authorities” occur in the lower margin.]

For the administration of a province is to be conducted with severity, whereas gentleness is to be commended in the Church with mercy.

[Note: [Col. 0260D] In the margin, in the same hand but in somewhat redder ink, are written these words: “Concerning bishops: that they ought not to exercise judicial proceedings.”]

[Note: “Here is the evangelical custom consistently maintained.”]

The words of Irenaeus clearly demonstrate the meaning of this passage.

[Note: The autograph has “Hyrineus.”]

He reports that when the Lord had come to Capernaum, he asked Peter: “The kings of the earth—from whom do they collect tribute or the census tax, from their own sons or from strangers?” When Peter said, “From strangers,” the Lord said: “Then let us not scandalize them. Go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up; when you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater. Take it and give it to them for me and for you” (Matthew 17:24–25).

For with the same intention with which the Lord commanded Peter to pay the census tax,

[Note: The meaning might perhaps be clearer if one read: “He commanded Peter to pay the census tax.”]

the Apostle instructed his assistants to be subject to every higher authority—for the sake, namely, of peace and concord.

Therefore he adds here also: **For this reason, be subject out of necessity**, and so forth.

In the faith of Christ there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, master and servant, male and female; rather, insofar as they are believers, all are one. Nevertheless, because believers must travel through the course of this present life to the homeland of their eternal inheritance, they must in the order of this life be subject to higher authorities, lest we give an occasion for persecution and the name of God and the teaching of Christ be blasphemed.

And this is what the Apostle means by “necessity.” Since there were people who said that they ought to be subject for this reason alone—that they should not give an occasion for persecution and punishment—he therefore adds: **Not only because of wrath**, that is, vengeance, **but also because of conscience**, that is, for love of the one whose command you wish to fulfill. You ought to do this with a pure mind, “not serving for appearance, as people-pleasers” (Ephesians 6:6), but serving God, who tests your hearts.

[Note: “Here is a bishop truly imbued with evangelical morals and teaching.”]

And because he had said earlier, “He is God’s minister, an avenger in wrath against the one who does evil,” he therefore adds: **For this reason you also pay taxes**, that is, so that you may not give an occasion for persecution. **For they are God’s ministers, serving precisely for this purpose.** He calls rulers God’s ministers because God has granted them authority to demand tribute.

Therefore, exhorting everyone generally, he adds: **Pay everyone what is owed: tribute to whom tribute is owed, revenue to whom revenue is owed.**

[Note: In the autograph margin, “Chapter XLIV” is written here.]

Some maintain that *tributum* derives from *tribuere*, “to assign” or “to give.” It is a census or income that is exacted from colonists or territories; in truth, however, *tributum* derives from *tribus*, “tribes.” For the Romans divided the world into three parts—Asia, Africa, and Europe—and those who ruled them were called tribunes, while those who paid the census were called tributaries.

*Vectigal*, “revenue,” is derived from *vehere*, “to transport,” since it is a tax belonging to the treasury.

The meaning, then, is: Pay everyone what is owed according to his proper dignity. If he is an emperor, a king, a ruler, a teacher, a master, a father, or anything of this sort, then give emperors, kings, and rulers tribute and revenue; give a teacher and father honor; give a master fear.

And this is what follows: **Fear to whom fear is owed, honor to whom honor is owed.**

But because it would have been lengthy to enumerate each case individually, he therefore gathers everything together generally and adds: **Owe no one anything**, that is, render to everyone what is owed according to his dignity.

Yet because the good of charity must be rendered not once but continually, he adds: **Except that you love one another.** It is as though he said: “You must always pay this good of love to one another, because the more it is rendered, the more it increases.”

And to show how great a good love is, he adds: **For whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.**

But since the Lord, after commending love of God and neighbor, says in the Gospel, “On these two commandments depend the whole law” (Matthew 22:40), how can the Apostle say that the one who loves his neighbor fulfills the law?

Lest this appear contradictory, it should be observed that the Apostle does not say “the whole law,” but simply “the law,” intending the law that commands love of neighbor. If he did intend the whole law, even then there would be no contradiction. For whoever loves God certainly loves his neighbor, because God himself commands that one’s neighbor be loved; and whoever loves his neighbor certainly loves God, because he fulfills God’s command.

The Lord himself says in the Gospel: **Whoever loves me will keep my commandments** (John 14:15).

To show which law he meant, he adds: **For “You shall not kill”—the words “it is written” being understood—“you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not covet, you shall not bear false witness.”**

And because he did not mention every commandment that pertains to love of neighbor, he therefore adds generally: **And if there is any other commandment**, that is, any other commandment pertaining to love of neighbor, **it is summed up in this word**, that is, it is fulfilled in the word of love.

Hence he immediately introduces the word itself, saying: **You shall love your neighbor as yourself.**

To show how the one who loves his neighbor fulfills the law, he adds: **Love of neighbor does no evil.** Whoever loves his neighbor in a holy and devout manner as himself has no occasion for sinning. Since he does not want his own wife to be corrupted, he does not corrupt another’s wife; since he does not want to be killed, he himself does not seek to kill his neighbor. The same applies in other cases.

By “neighbor” he means every human being with whom we can sin.

The fullness of the law, therefore, is love. If charity, according to the Apostle’s words, is the fullness of the law, and if, as John says, “God is charity” (1 John 4:16), then the fullness of the law is God, who said: “I have not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5:17).

Perhaps someone could say in response: “Apostle, who, being established in a mortal body, can fulfill what you say—that by loving his neighbor he should do no evil?”

Therefore the Apostle adds: **And knowing the time**

[Note: “The suitable time” is written here in the autograph margin.]

—the phrase “to be suitable” being understood.

Appropriately, he says that this time is suitable for doing good, because after this life there will be a time when each person will receive from God what he has done.

Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you” (Isaiah 49:8; 2 Corinthians 6:2). Explaining this, the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (ibid.).

What he means by saying that this time is suitable is made clear when he adds: **For it is already the hour for us to rise from sleep.** It is as though he said: “For a long time you lay asleep in the sleep of unbelief, bodily sluggishness, and the other vices. It is now the hour to rise.”

Why it is now the hour he explains: **For now our salvation is nearer than when we believed.** The meaning is that, because the day of judgment has arrived and the end of our life is approaching, our salvation is now nearer than it was when we believed, because as the past increases, the future diminishes.

He speaks not of temporal salvation but of eternal salvation. The faithful receive it fully when they depart from their bodies, but they will receive it more fully when they rise from the dead.

Next comes: **The night has passed**, and so forth.

This holy Apostle, preaching the Gospel, traveled through nearly the whole world. When he saw it lying in the darkness of unbelief and the remaining vices, he exclaimed: **The night has passed**—namely, the night of ancient blindness, that is, unbelief—**but the day has drawn near**, the day of eternal salvation, that is, the day of faith and the other virtues. This day arrived when Christ appeared in the world through the mystery of the Incarnation; by the light of faith, the darkness of unbelief was driven away.

And because he had said, “The night has passed,” he therefore adds in exhortation: **Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness**, that is, unbelief and the other vices.

Again, because he had said, “The day has drawn near,” he adds here also: **Let us put on the weapons of light**, that is, faith, hope, charity, and the remaining virtues. They are rightly called weapons, because with these swords the weapons of the devil are overcome.

Hence the Apostle says elsewhere: “Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist the snares of the devil and stand perfect in all things” (Ephesians 6:11).

They are called the weapons of light because the life of believers, in comparison with that of unbelievers, is light and day. Yet this day has darkness mingled with it, because “the life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job 7:1). It will then be without any darkness, when the elect enjoy the light of eternity.

To show how we ought to put on the weapons of light, he adds: **Let us walk honorably as in the day.**

Here it must be asked why he added “as in the day.” Clearly, because those who walk at night commonly go about disheveled and disorderly; some even go naked, since they are not seen by others. Those who walk during the day, however, arrange themselves in every way so as not to offend the eyes of those who look upon them.

He therefore wished to show that we must adorn ourselves with good works and walk in the splendor of the virtues, so that we do not offend the eyes of God, our observer. That is, in good works we should seek neither the desire for human praise nor earthly profits, but only to please him.

Therefore, because he had urged us to cast off the works of darkness, to show what they were he adds: **Not in revelries**, and so forth.

*Comessatio*, “revelry,” is so called as though from *collatio mensae*, “the bringing together of the table,” which occurs when different things from different people, or many things from many people, are brought together so that they may feast together.

Among the many other vices, drunkenness arises from revelry; therefore he immediately adds: **And drunkenness.**

Then, because lust is generated from drunkenness, he adds: **Not in bedrooms.** *Cubile*, “bedroom,” derives from *cubare*, “to lie down,” that is, from shameful intercourse, something more fitting to wild animals and beasts than to human beings endowed with reason.

Therefore, because impurities and fornications are committed in bedrooms, he adds: **And impurities.**

[Note: The Vulgate reads “immodesties.”]

**Not in strife.** Strife is the vehemence of the mind, that is, the fury of the spirit. Since envy or deceit often arises from it, he therefore adds: **And rivalry**, or, as certain copies have it, **deceit**.

But it must be asked why the Apostle joined two spiritual vices—strife and envy—to four carnal vices. Clearly, he wished to show that these two also are practiced only by those who are carnal.

Nevertheless, it should be understood that blessed Augustine says that in this passage the Apostle mentioned only three vices: he takes revelry and drunkenness as one; likewise bedrooms and impurities; and likewise strife and rivalry. Therefore he says that the Apostle mentioned only these three, because from them, as from a root, the whole crop of vices sprouts.

Again, to show what the weapons of light are, or in what they consist, he adds: **But put on the Lord Jesus Christ.** This is to walk honorably in the day.

He urges us to put on the Lord Jesus, that is, faith, truth, and all the virtues that are interpreted in Christ.

But because one who is entangled in worldly cares cannot put on these weapons, he adds: **And do not make provision for your flesh in its desires.**

[Note: “Chapter XLVI” is written here in the autograph margin.]

The Apostle foresaw that a human being cannot exist without care for the flesh; therefore he added: **In its desires.**

It is as though he said: “It is impossible for you not to care for the flesh. If, then, you do care for it, do so not in its desires—that is, not in its lusts, or in order to satisfy your desires.”

By this statement he clearly indicates that care for the flesh must be provided in necessary matters but removed from superfluous ones.

And this is what the Lord says in the Gospel: **Do not be anxious about tomorrow** (Matthew 6:31). Blessed Jerome says concerning this: “Labor must be undertaken; anxiety must be removed.”

[Note: The autograph reads *excredendus*. I have corrected the error from the text of Saint Jerome on the cited passage of Matthew 6:24.]

Furthermore, it should be understood that the believing Gentiles were so strong and perfect in faith that they considered all things clean; therefore they also ate what was prohibited in the Law, knowing that such things had been prohibited symbolically.

The believing Jews, however, were weak and did not consider it lawful to eat anything except what had been commanded in the Law.

Seeing this disagreement, the Apostle, in order to bring them back to peace, added:

## Chapter XIV

**Receive the one who is weak in faith.**

He said this to the Gentiles, who were so firm in faith that they considered all things clean.

The meaning is: Receive into your fellowship the Jew who is weak in faith—that is, who does not consider all things clean—so that he may perhaps progress in faith; and do not judge him to be rejected and imperfect.

And this is what follows: **Not for disputes about thoughts**, that is, not so that you may judge his thoughts, concerning which God alone judges.

The Apostle chose that his weakness should be borne so that he might progress in faith, lest, having been scandalized, he should withdraw from the faith.

Hence he adds: **One person believes that he may eat all things.** He says this of the Gentile, who believed that all things were lawful and clean. The calling of God prohibits no foods, but the discipline of abstinence also teaches one to abstain from things that are lawful.

**But the one who is weak eats vegetables.** He says this of the Jew, who was weak in faith and believed that only those things were clean which had not been prohibited in the Law.

The meaning is: Let him eat only those things that he believes to be pleasant for him and permitted by the commandment of the Law, such as vegetables.

Hence it follows: **Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat.** That is, let the Gentile, who eats because he believes all things clean, not despise the Jew who does not eat—that is, who does not believe all things clean—but let him bear with him patiently so that he may progress in faith.

**And let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats.** That is, let the Jew, who does not believe all things clean and therefore does not eat all things, not judge the Gentile who believes all things clean and eats them; that is, let him not condemn him or think evil of him.

There are certain actions concerning which it is uncertain with what intention they are done, because they can be done with either a good or a bad intention. Therefore we ought not to pass judgment in such matters; judgment is permitted in those actions whose intention can be perceived, such as thefts, adulteries, blasphemies, and other things of this sort.

At that time, therefore, there were people who abstained from meat and wine, and there were others who consumed them; consequently they judged one another.

Since they were mortal human beings, they wished to pass judgment concerning uncertain matters—that is, matters which could be done with either a simple or an evil intention—in the hidden places of the heart, concerning which God alone judges. Therefore the Apostle says: **Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat, and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats.**

We ought not to judge uncertain matters, especially in order to condemn, lest we fall into rash judgment.

Hence he says elsewhere: **Do not judge before the time** (1 Corinthians 4:5).

And the Lord says in the Gospel: **Do not judge, so that you may not be judged** (Matthew 7:1).

Why neither the Jew should be despised nor the Gentile judged he shows by adding: **For God has accepted him**, that is, chosen him and called him to faith by his grace.

For this reason it also follows: **Who are you to judge another’s servant?**

It is as though he said: “Since God has accepted him, he is God’s servant. Who, then, are you—being weak and unable to know the hidden things of the heart—to judge God’s servant?”

Hence he adds: **He stands or falls before his own master.**

[Note: The Vulgate has no question mark but reads affirmatively: “He stands or falls before his own master.”]

He stands as one who is strong, because he perseveres in faith; he falls as one who is weak, but the strong person stands by the grace of the Lord, while the weak person falls through his own frailty.

And note that, although he was speaking generally about all the regenerate, he suddenly turned his attention to the predestined and added: **But he will stand**, namely, because each predestined person, aided by divine grace, will persevere in faith.

And lest the predestined person attribute his standing to himself, he adds: **For God is able to make him stand.**

It is as though he said: “The one by whose grace he stands is also able to grant perseverance, so that he may persevere most steadfastly.” By “make him stand” he means “strengthen him in faith.”

Alternatively: “Him”—that is, the weak person who has fallen—“God is able to make stand,” that is, to restore him to his former state.

And it should be understood that at that time there were some who taught that one should always devote oneself to abstinence, while others taught that it should be practiced only at intervals.

Seeing this variety among believers, the Apostle adds: **One person judges one day to be different from another; another judges every day alike.**

He judges one day to be different from another who assigns one period to fasting and another to the consumption of food; he judges every day alike who commands abstinence at all times.

For, as was said above, the calling of God prohibits no foods, whereas the discipline of abstinence always urges that one abstain from certain lawful things as well.

Some, however, have understood this passage more profoundly, so that it refers not only to the persons of human beings but also to the persons of God and human beings. Thus, the one who judges one day to be different from another is the human being; the one who judges every day alike is God.

A human being judges one day to be different from another because he judges only what he sees in the present. He sees what someone is like today, but he does not know what that person will be in the future. Thus he sees someone who is evil today and nevertheless does not doubt that tomorrow, through divine grace, he may become good.

But God judges every day alike because in his foreknowledge he knows everything, even before it happens: what each person is like today and what each person will be in the future.

[Note: The words “because he judges only what he sees” are written in the upper margin.]

Since the Apostle saw the variety among believers that we have mentioned, and since both alternatives are acceptable to God, he added: **Let each person abound in his own judgment.**

Some have understood this passage in the following way: Let each person abundantly do what he has decided is sufficient for himself.

But should a heretic, a schismatic, or a bad Catholic do whatever he believes is sufficient for himself? Certainly not.

It should therefore be understood in this way: Let each person act according to the sound judgment that has been granted to him by God.

It is as though he said more plainly: Let each person abundantly practice whatever he recognizes, according to the institutions and examples of the saints, as things to be believed, confessed, and done, so that by exercising himself in them he may attain greater things that he did not previously understand.

Next comes: **The one who observes the day observes it for the Lord.**

He observes the day who sees what someone is like today but does not know what he will be tomorrow—that is, the one who observes only what he sees in the present. And he observes it for the Lord because he understands this very thing through the Lord’s gift.

Alternatively: He observes the day and observes it for the Lord who fasts not for the sake of a human being but for the love of God.

**And the one who eats eats for the Lord.** This was said of the Gentiles.

The meaning is: The Gentile who eats everything eats for the Lord, because he gives praise to the Lord, by whose grace he was enabled to believe that all things are clean.

And this is what follows: **For he gives thanks to God.**

**And the one who does not eat does not eat for the Lord.** He says this of the Jews.

It is as though he said: “The Jew who does not believe that all things are clean and therefore does not eat everything fasts for the Lord, because he gives thanks to God, whose gift it is that he abstains from those things prohibited in the Law.”

And this is what follows: **And he gives thanks to God.**

The expression “he eats for the Lord” is used in the same way as in the Psalm: “The coming generation shall be announced to the Lord” (Psalm 21:31), that is, “for the praise of the Lord.”

It is as though he said plainly: Those who announce the coming generation will please the Lord, not themselves.

The Apostle shows that some good is done laudably when it is done for the praise of the one by whose grace the ability to do it has been granted.

[Note: “Chapter XLVII” is written here in the autograph margin.]

**For none of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself.**

No one lives for himself, because no one has life from himself. Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “For in him we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:28).

God created all things for human beings, but he created the human being to praise him. Therefore none of us dies for himself, because no faithful person who has died will cease from praising God.

How, then, is it written: **The dead shall not praise you, O Lord** (Psalm 113:17)?

Therefore it must be understood that those dead do not praise the Lord who are like the one of whom it is written: “From a dead person, as though he did not exist, confession perishes” (Sirach 17:26).

But those dead praise the Lord more who are like the one of whom the Lord says: “Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live; and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die” (John 11:25); and like those to whom the Apostle says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ” (Colossians 3:3).

Alternatively: None of us dies for himself because whoever dies to vices dies not for himself but for God, by whose grace he received the ability to die.

Hence he said above: “All of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death” (Romans 6:2–3).

Similarly, whoever lives by the virtues lives not for himself but for God, because he lives for the praise of the one by whose grace he was enabled to live.

Hence he said above: “Just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too should walk in newness of life” (ibid. 6:4).

Blessed Gregory, however, explains this passage in the following way: “None of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself,” because whoever is good and whoever is evil exists not only for himself but also for others, to whom he provides an example either of good or of evil living.

To demonstrate plainly why he had said this, he adds: **For whether we live, we live for the Lord; or whether we die, we die for the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or whether we die, we belong to the Lord.**

We belong to the Lord because we were redeemed by the price of his blood. Hence he immediately adds: **For to this end Christ died and rose again**, and so forth.

[Note: “Chapter XLVIII” is scarcely legible here in the autograph margin.]

It is as though he said: “For this reason Christ suffered, so that by the price of his blood he might redeem the faithful and rule over both the dead and the living.”

He rules over the living because he dwells in them by grace and governs and directs them. He also rules over the dead because they reign together with him in heaven, concerning whom it is written: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Revelation 14:13).

Finally, to frighten those who despised and condemned one another, he adds: **But you—why do you judge your brother?**

He says this specifically to the Jew.

**Or you—why do you despise your brother?**

He says this specifically to the Gentile.

But because judging is a greater evil than despising, he leaves aside the evil of contempt and emphasizes the rashness of judgment, adding: **For we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ.**

The meaning is: “With what rashness do you dare to anticipate God’s judgment and judge hidden things, when we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ?”

To show plainly what that judgment will be like, he therefore used the form of an earthly comparison, saying: **We shall stand before the tribunal.**

Earthly kings, when they are about to judge something, climb to a higher place from which they can observe everyone, so that those who are to be condemned cannot remain hidden, nor those who are to receive a reward. That place is properly called a tribunal because commands or judgments are issued from it.

The Apostle, therefore, to show that no one will be able to escape that judgment, called the judgment seat itself a tribunal. All sins will be manifest not only to the eyes of God but also to all human beings.

For the Judge himself will come not only with regard to deeds, according to the statement, “Each one will receive what is due for what he has done in the body” (2 Corinthians 5:10), but also with regard to thoughts, as the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes and brings to light the things hidden in darkness” (1 Corinthians 4:5), and so forth.

The Lord also says in the Gospel: “Nothing is covered that will not be revealed, nor hidden that will not be known” (Luke 12:2).

The judgment will likewise concern words, because, as he himself says in the Gospel: “For every idle word a person will give an account on the day of judgment” (Matthew 12:36).

And to confirm his account by an example, he adds: **As it is written**—namely, in the prophet Isaiah—**“As I live, says the Lord”** (Isaiah 45:24; Philippians 2:10), and so forth.

These are the words of the Son of God. The prophet foresaw the Lord coming to judgment; therefore, speaking in his voice, he said: **As I live.**

It is as though he said: “I live through immortality, because I died through the dispensation of the flesh.”

**For every knee shall bow to me.**

By the bending of the knee the humbling of the mind is signified, because every creature is subjected to God.

The prophet wished to show the Lord as superior to all creatures; therefore, speaking in his person, he says: “For every knee shall bow to me.” Hence elsewhere the same Apostle says: “At the name of Jesus every knee shall bend, and every tongue shall confess to God” (ibid.). Here the whole is indicated by a part: “every tongue,” that is, every creature—not merely human, but also angelic. This does not mean that the angelic creature possesses a corruptible body whose tongue confesses to God; rather, by “angelic tongues” we understand the hidden and secret praises that the angels offer to God. Since we praise with the mouth through the tongue, praise is rightly attributed to the tongue itself [Col. 0268D].

But because he had said, “We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ,” to show what we shall do there he added: “Therefore each of us shall give an account of himself to God.” The sense is: With what presumption do you dare to anticipate God’s judgment and judge one another, when each person will have to give an account of himself to God before Christ’s tribunal? Hence he immediately adds: “Therefore let us no longer judge one another”; as though he were saying: Until now, perhaps because you did not acknowledge the judge, you judged one another; but since you acknowledge the judge, do not rashly pass judgment on one another any longer [Col. 0269A]. And to bend them more readily toward what he was urging, he joined his own person to theirs, saying, “let us judge.”

“But judge this rather: not to place a stumbling-block or a scandal before your brother.” It should be noted that above “judgment” signifies condemnation, whereas here it signifies discernment. The sense is: Resolve and determine this: by eating what you believe to be clean and lawful, do not give your weak brother—that is, the Jew—an occasion for offense or scandal.

Since, therefore, some Gentile might say, “Apostle, since you forbid us to eat everything, you too must think that not everything is clean,” he therefore added: “I know” [Note: [Col. 0269D] In the author’s own manuscript, the heading “chap. XLIX” is written here in the margin.]. But this alone was not enough; he added: “And I am confident in the Lord Jesus.” To impress more firmly upon their hearts what he was saying, he added this [Col. 0269B]. He shows what he knew and trusted: “That nothing is common through him.” As though he were saying plainly: I do not forbid this because I consider it unclean, but so that you may not place a stumbling-block or a scandal before your brother. For the Jews understood the word “common,” that is, *common* or profane, as meaning unclean. Thus they called the animals permitted by the Law for eating “clean,” while they called the rest “common.” The vessels used by the priests in the Temple were also called holy; in comparison with them, everything else was unclean, that is, common.

Yet they did not understand the force of this expression. Although they called animals and vessels “common,” that is, unclean, they did not understand that they themselves were common. Just as the remaining vessels were called common in comparison with those used by the priests in the Temple [Col. 0269C], so a sinful soul is called common in comparison with a holy and devout soul, because it belongs not to one Lord but to many—that is, it is the servant of vices and demons.

“Through him” means through Christ. Nothing is common through him, because everything was created good and clean by the good God. Hence we read in Genesis: “God saw everything that he had made, and it was very good” (Gen. I, 10–12).

The Apostle therefore seems by these words to accuse the Law, which teaches that certain things are unclean. Far from it. Rather, he shows that the things prohibited were prohibited under a figure. It should also be known that a person’s conscience often makes something unclean for him that is clean, or conversely. For example, if meat sacrificed to idols is being sold in the market and someone buys and eats it unknowingly, it is clean for him according to his conscience; conversely, whatever someone judges to be unclean is unclean for him. This is what follows: “Except for him who considers anything to be common, for him it is common.”

To show why he had previously said, “Judge this rather: not to place a stumbling-block or a scandal” [Note: [Col. 0269D] The author’s own manuscript has “chap. L” in the margin here.], he added: “For if your brother is scandalized because of food” [Note: [Col. 0270D] The Vulgate reads *is saddened*.], “you are no longer walking according to charity”—that is, if you take what you believe to be lawful and clean for the purpose of scandalizing your brother, you are not walking according to charity, because [Col. 0270A] you are not imitating the one who descended from heaven to earth and shed his blood for him.

Hence he immediately adds: “Do not destroy by your food the one for whom Christ died.” He says plainly: By your food you destroy one whom you could have saved, had you not eaten it in his presence. By this statement he shows that whoever perishes, though he could have been saved, is destroyed by those through whom he could have been saved.

Finally, because the name of Christ is blasphemed when someone destroys his brother by food, he added an exhortation: “Therefore let not our good be blasphemed.” He calls “our good” the gift of faith and of all the virtues—or certainly the name of God, besides which there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved (Acts IV, 12). Or he calls the grace of the Gospel “the good.” This good is ours when we receive it, but God’s because it is given by him.

It follows: “For the kingdom of God is not food and drink.” Food and drink are not the kingdom of God, because they do not lead to the kingdom of God, nor will they remain in it. They are perishable, and scarcely suffice us for the present life. “But righteousness, peace, and joy.” These are the kingdom of God, because they are the chief gifts by which we can attain eternal life.

“Righteousness” is so called as though it were the condition of law or right. Righteousness, therefore, exists when each person is given his proper right. The righteousness of God is therefore Christ, who justified us from sins and redeemed us. Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Who was made for us by God righteousness and redemption” (I Cor. I, 30). He is also peace, as the same Apostle says: “Christ is our peace” (Eph. II, 14).

By “joy” he means the blessedness of eternity. For joy is applied improperly to temporal things, but properly to spiritual things; hence in spiritual matters it is used without qualification. Thus by “joy” he means the contemplation of the present face of God. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “This is eternal life, that they should know you, the true God,” etc. (John XVII, 3). And because no one can possess these gifts without the grace of the Holy Spirit, he added: “In the Holy Spirit.”

It follows: “For whoever serves Christ in this way is acceptable to God and approved by human beings.” By “in this way” he means in the Holy Spirit. Whoever serves in him serves through the word of wisdom and through charity; consequently he pleases God and is acceptable to human beings, because these gifts are so outstanding that no one can disparage them. Therefore he is shown to be perfect before God and before human beings [Col. 0270D].

Accordingly, to urge them toward the good of peace and concord, he added: “Therefore let us pursue the things that make for peace.” Here it should be noted that he does not say, “let us follow,” as above: “pursuing hospitality” (Rom. XII, 13). For the person who orders and governs his habits and actions so that no one can reproach him possesses and follows peace; but the person who orders and governs himself so that others may advance and be built up in goodness by his example pursues peace. Hence here too he adds: “[Col. 0271A] and the things that make for mutual edification” [Note: [Col. 0271D] The Vulgate adds *let us preserve* after the adverb *mutually*—that is, “let us pursue and preserve the things that make for mutual edification.”]

“Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food.” These words seem to imply that food is not the work of God. It should be understood, however, that it is God’s work, since it exists. Nevertheless, what God created for its own sake is very different from what he created for the sake of something else. Food was created not for its own sake but for the sake of human beings; the human being, however, was created for his own sake, because he was created to praise God.

Accordingly, among all earthly creatures the Apostle calls the human being in particular the work of God, or rather his salvation and redemption [Col. 0271B].

Therefore the work of God is destroyed for the sake of food when a weak person is scandalized by another’s food. And as though someone might say, “By forbidding us in this way to partake of everything, you too seem to judge these things unclean,” he added: “Everything indeed is clean”; as though he were saying: I do not forbid this because I judge it unclean, since things created by the clean and good God cannot be unclean, but so that, by eating in the presence of the weak, you may not give them an occasion for scandal.

This is what follows: “But it is evil for the person who eats through an offense.” “It is good not to eat meat, nor to drink wine, nor to do anything by which your brother is offended” [Note: [Col. 0271D] The Vulgate reads *is offended*, rather than *offends*.], “or scandalized, or made weak.”

Why does the Apostle commend abstinence as though it were the supreme good, when it is not the supreme good? For every good that evil people can also possess is not the supreme good but a moderate good. It should be understood, however, that although abstinence is not the supreme good, preserving charity toward one’s neighbor and not scandalizing him is the supreme good. To commend this, the Apostle says: “Nor to do anything”—that is understood—“by which your brother is offended,” that is, sins, “or is scandalized,” that is, departs from the faith, “or is made weak,” namely, in that same faith.

It should also be noted that he does not say, “It is good to eat meat,” lest he give the gluttonous an occasion to say to those who abstain: “Eat meat, because the Apostle commanded it,” and thus, once the reins of abstinence had been loosened, they might fall into the abyss of gluttony. Since the Apostle’s intention was to speak only about foods, why did he add, “nor to drink wine”? Clearly, lest he give drunkards an occasion to say: “Drink, because the Apostle only warned against abstaining from meat,” and thus they might indulge in the vice of drunkenness.

But does the Apostle condemn the creature [Col. 0271D]? Far from it. Rather, he shows that before a weak brother one must not consume what places a stumbling-block or a scandal before him.

Hence he adds: “You have faith; have it within yourself before God” [Note: [Col. 0271D] The Vulgate reads: “Do you have faith? Have it within yourself before God.”]—as though he were saying: It is enough for you to believe through faith that everything is clean; but you must also refrain, for the love of God, from consuming these things in the presence of your weak brother, lest you give him an occasion for scandal. This is what he means by “Have it before God.”

And this is what follows: “Blessed is the one who does not judge himself in what he approves” [Col. 0272A]. Blessed is the person who does not misuse what he approves as clean and lawful—that is, who does not consume it in the presence of a weak brother, lest he give him an occasion for scandal, for which he himself will be judged.

“But whoever distinguishes”—that is, judges one thing to be clean and another unclean—“if he eats”—namely, what he judges to be unclean—“is condemned”—by his own judgment—“because it is not from faith” [Note: [Col. 0271D] The Vulgate reads: “because it is not from faith.”]—that is, because he believes something unclean to be such.

“But whatever is not from faith is sin.” This is evidently because “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI, 6). The life of unbelievers, therefore, because it is not from faith, is sin [Note: [Col. 0272D] It is clear that our author is to be understood in the sense of Blessed Augustine, as is evident from the many passages he draws from him; readers cannot fail to recognize how devotedly he studied Augustine. See D. Prosper, *Against the Ungrateful*, part II, lines 405–410, on this interpretation.]. For where knowledge of eternal and unchangeable truth—that is, of divinity—is absent, even virtue in the best conduct is false [Col. 0272B].

**Chapter XV**

Since someone might say, “What is it to us if they are weak? Why should we refrain, on account of their weakness, from things we believe lawful?” the Apostle responds as though to this objection: “But we who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak,” etc. He says plainly: You must not partake of these things for the reason that you must not scandalize weak brothers.

To bend them more readily, he joined his own person to theirs. His calling himself and his hearers “stronger” was not arrogance but arose from the requirements of the divine dispensation. None of the weak would dare to associate himself with the strength of the greater unless the Apostle also called his hearers, together with himself, stronger [Col. 0272C]. Furthermore, by these words he urges those who in the Church can benefit weak brothers through some office not to withdraw from that office under the pretext of humility, and he urges us to bear patiently with the weak in the Church. Hence elsewhere: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. VI, 2), etc.

“And not to please ourselves,” that is, not to satisfy our own desires: not to seek what is ours, but what belongs to Jesus Christ. He shows whom we ought to please: “Let each of us please his neighbor.” But is this for doing evil? Far from it. Therefore he adds: “For good,” that is, in order to do good. To make this clearer, he adds: “For edification.”

Finally, to bend the minds of his hearers, he introduces the example of the Lord himself, saying: “For Christ did not please himself,” etc. Christ did not please himself, because, although in his divinity he was the only-begotten Son of God, he descended to earth to acquire many brothers for himself, to whom he would distribute his Father’s kingdom. “He emptied himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Phil. II, 7).

“But, as it is written”—with the sense understood, “so he acted”—“The reproaches of those who reproached you have fallen upon me” [Col. 0273A] (Ps. LXVIII, 10). The prophet foresaw that Christ would suffer many insults from the Jews; therefore he said this in Christ’s person. The sense is: The reproaches of the unbelieving Jews who reproached you, O Father, fell upon me, because they found in me one whom they could reproach.

He says “those who reproached you” because whoever reviles the Father also reviles the Son, and whoever does not receive the Son does not receive the Father. Hence in the Gospel: “Whoever receives me receives him who sent me” (Luke IX, 48).

To show the usefulness of divine reading, he added [Note: [Col. 0273] “Chapter LI” is written here in the author’s own margin.]: “Whatever things were written were written for our benefit.” Everything contained far and wide in Holy Scripture was written so that we might be formed and instructed by the example of those people. This is what follows: “So that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we may have hope.” When we hear from Holy Scripture that holy men patiently endured many adversities for God’s sake, we receive great consolation from it, so that we may hope eventually to possess in reality what we now possess in hope.

Accordingly, taking the opportunity from his own words, he added a prayer no less exalted than the blessing of the patriarchs. That blessing was carnal, as in: “May your blessing be in the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth” (Gen. XXVII, 28); this one, however, is spiritual.

He says: “May the God of patience and consolation grant you to think the same thing toward one another.” He is called the God of patience and consolation, as he is called the God of charity and peace, because he himself grants the virtue of consolation and patience.

“To think the same thing” means not to dissent. “Toward one another” means mutually, or concerning one another. He shows how he wished them to know one thing by adding: “So that with one mind and one mouth you may honor God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ”—that is, possessing one mind and glorifying with a harmonious voice not yourselves but God. Hence in the Gospel the Lord says: “That they may see your good works and glorify your Father” (Matt. V, 16). And because the Jews believed in God while denying that he had a Son, he says: “And the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Accordingly, to call them back to peace, he added: “Therefore”—that is, so that you may be able to think the same thing—“receive one another,” namely, in faith. And because evil people too can receive one another in evil, he explains how they ought to receive one another: “Just as Christ also received you.” It is as though he were saying: He descended from heaven to earth, and, in order to save everyone, did not disdain to assume our flesh; he did not abhor your crimes. Therefore you ought to do as he did, and no longer judge or despise one another.

Beautifully he adds: “For the honor of God,” because in everything the Son of God did or taught, he sought not his own glory but that of the Father.

Therefore, because the Gentiles especially despised the Jews on account of circumcision [Col. 0274A], he added: “For I say that Jesus Christ was a minister of circumcision.” He says plainly: Why do you despise the Jews because they are unwilling to depart from the carnal observance of the Law, in which they long remained, when Christ too was a minister of circumcision?

For, as the sacred history of the Gospel relates, he was circumcised by his parents on the eighth day (Luke II, 21). He wished this to be done so that he would not appear to dissent from the Fathers and thereby give the Jews an occasion not to receive him.

Hence it follows: “For the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers.” Insofar as the truth of God was manifested, the promises made concerning him to the fathers were confirmed.

It should be understood that Christ was the minister not only of carnal but also of spiritual circumcision. For he who was circumcised by his parents on the eighth day was baptized in the Jordan by John the Baptist in his thirtieth year; in this he provided us with an example of spiritual circumcision, that is, of baptism.

It should further be understood that by these words the Apostle shows how greatly the Lord loved the Jewish people: the Son of God took flesh from them and lived bodily among them. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “I was not sent except to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. XV, 24).

But the Gentiles, since they had no knowledge of him, he called to faith solely through gratuitous mercy. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold” (John X, 16), etc.

Therefore he now adds: “But the Gentiles, on account of mercy”—with the words understood, “which he showed toward them”—“to honor God” [Col. 0274C], with “I say” understood from what precedes. For “to whom more is forgiven, he loves more” (Luke VII, 47). How much more, therefore, did God make the Gentile people a debtor to praise his mercy, since he gave them so much, although they had withdrawn from knowledge of God almost from the beginning of the world and remained in the worship of idols?

To show that the salvation of both Jews and Gentiles had been foretold by the prophets, he brings four testimonies [Note: [Col. 0273] A verb such as *he brought forward* or something similar may perhaps be missing here.], corresponding to the four books of the Gospels, in which the teaching of the New Testament is chiefly contained.

He says: “As it is written: For this reason I will confess to you among the Gentiles” (II Sam. XXII, 50; Ps. XVII, 50). These are the words of the Son of God. The prophet foresaw that the Gentiles would believe; therefore he speaks this to the Father in the Son’s voice.

When he says “I will confess,” it should be understood as “I will cause them to confess.” Confession is not only of sins but also of praise. Hence in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Father” (Matt. XI, 25; Luke X, 21), that is, “I praise you.” So here too: “I will confess,” that is, “I will cause you to be praised among the Gentiles.” Likewise: “And I will sing to your name,” that is, “I will cause them to sing to your name.”

The prophet does not show here what he promises to sing, but elsewhere he declares it, saying: “Sing to the Lord a new song” (Ps. XXXII, 3)—that is, the salvation and redemption of the new people.
