Not all who sound with the mouth sing this song, but those who sing in the manner urged by the Apostle: “Singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord” (Eph. V, 19). Joy is within, where the voice of praise is heard and felt.

And again he says: “Rejoice, Gentiles.” This example is taken from Deuteronomy. Moses foresaw that the Gentiles would come to faith, and therefore exhorted them, saying: “Rejoice, Gentiles” [Note: [Col. 0275] Deut. XXXII, 43 reads *praise, Gentiles*; I have not been able to find the text in the form *rejoice, Gentiles*.].

But lest anyone think that only the Gentiles would believe, he added: “With his people.” By “his people” he means those who believed from among the Jews.

And again: “Praise God, all Gentiles” (Ps. CXVI, 1). Here too, lest anyone think that only Gentiles would come to faith, it adds: “And magnify him, all peoples.” The Jewish people too are understood among “all.”

And again Isaiah says: “There shall be the root of Jesse” (Isa. XI, [Col. 0275B] 10). By the root of Jesse is designated the one who arose from David’s stock. Jesse was the root; David was the tree of this root, from which there proceeded the branch (Isa. XI, 1), namely, blessed Mary, who produced fruit when she bore the Savior. Concerning this fruit the same Isaiah says: “The fruit of the earth shall be exalted” (Isa. IV, 2). This happened when the Lord, rising from the dead, ascended into heaven. David too says of this fruit: “Our earth shall give its fruit” (Ps. LXXXIV, 13).

“Jesse” is interpreted as “there is for me.” Therefore whoever rejoices at the coming of the Son of God can appropriately say: “There is for me”—with “a hearer” understood.

“And he who shall arise to rule the Gentiles.” He arose to rule the Gentiles because, rejected by the Jews on account of their unbelief, he called the Gentiles to faith, so that he might reign among them through grace. “In him the Gentiles will hope.” For all who believe from among the Gentiles place all their hope in him [Col. 0275C].

Since he had cited the prophet’s testimony, “In him the Gentiles will hope,” he took the opportunity from those very words to add a prayer: “May the God of hope fill you with all joy.” He is called the God of hope because he himself grants the virtue of hope.

By “all joy” he means the gladness of eternal blessedness. No one in this life can be filled with all joy; nevertheless, every believer, even if not filled with it in reality, is filled with it in hope. But because no one can be filled with this joy without peace, he added: “And peace.” True peace exists when a person wills what God wills, and when the body wills what the soul wills—the soul being a heavenly creature.

“In believing,” that is, so that you may believe, or while you believe.

[Col. 0275D] “So that you may abound in hope”—that is, so that what you now possess in hope you may eventually possess abundantly in reality. Since no one can attain this except through the grace of the Holy Spirit, he added: “In the power of the Holy Spirit.”

But lest the Romans suppose, because of this repeated admonition, that the Apostle believed them to be without love, he added: “I am confident, my brothers—and I myself concerning you—that you yourselves are full of love.” It is as though he were saying: Just as your conscience bears witness to you, so do I concerning your love.

But to whom was he speaking? To the Romans. Were all the Romans therefore full of love? Certainly not. Yet there were some perfect among them; for their sake, lest they be scandalized, he said: “I am confident,” etc. Those are full of love who stand perfectly in love of God and of their neighbor.

“Filled with all knowledge.” Knowledge is the understanding of divine and human matters. Who, therefore, can be filled with all knowledge in this life? To prevent the Apostle from being criticized, he shows what knowledge he means by adding: “So that you can admonish one another.” It should be noted that he does not say “teach” but “admonish.” Teaching belongs to the perfect, whereas admonition belongs to the weak. Admonition is necessary where knowledge is followed by forgetfulness, and where people see negligence but are sluggish in correcting it.

[Col. 0276B] Since he had said that they were full of all love, he immediately added: “But I have written to you more boldly, brothers, in part.” It is as though he were saying: Trusting in your love, I have written to you more boldly, in part. By this he shows that he knew much more than he had written. For this reason he wrote only in part and not everything, so that through what he had written and what he had not written they might understand.

This is what he adds: “As though reminding you.” He wrote for this purpose, so that not only they but also everyone to whom this Epistle was to come might, through what is written, be reminded of what he himself had taught.

He shows why he was recalling them to memory by adding: “Because of the grace given to me by God.” By “grace” we may understand the election by which he was chosen by God before the foundation of the world, or redemption. More appropriately, however, we understand it as the gift by which he was set apart to be the apostle of the Gentiles. Hence it follows: “So that I might be a minister of Jesus Christ among the Gentiles.”

Elsewhere he says: “He who worked in Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision worked also in me among the Gentiles” (Gal. II, 8). By “to be a minister of Jesus Christ” he means, as though saying: I who formerly was a minister of circumcision. Since he had entirely withdrawn from the carnal observance of the Law, he calls himself a minister of Jesus Christ.

But what does he mean when he adds: “Sanctifying the Gospel of God”? Is the Gospel not holy? Certainly it is. How, then, did he sanctify it? By showing through his own example that it was holy. He therefore says: “Sanctifying the Gospel of God,” as though saying: By my example I show the Gospel to be holy, preaching it with modesty and reverence, because I confirm by my deeds what I teach in words.

Why he sanctified the Gospel is made clear when he adds: “So that the offering of the Gentiles might become acceptable.” He desired that the Gentiles who had believed through his preaching might become an acceptable gift to God.

For just as in the Old Testament it was the priests’ task to examine the animals that were to be offered, lest anything be lame, spotted, or weak, so that the sacrifice might be acceptable to God, so in the New Testament it is the task of preachers to examine carefully lest their preaching have stain or wrinkle, and lest their hearers be corrupted by some vice that would prevent them from becoming an acceptable sacrifice to God [Col. 0277A].

And because no offering can be acceptable to God unless it has been sanctified, and because it cannot be sanctified except through the grace of the Holy Spirit, he added: “In the Holy Spirit.”

Someone might say: “You boast of sanctifying the Gospel because you seek human glory.” Wishing to show that he did not seek human glory but possessed divine glory, the Apostle added: “Therefore I have glory in Christ Jesus before God”—that is, according to God. Everything he did, he referred not to human praise but to the glory of God.

He appropriately placed “in Christ” first, because, as he himself shows in the Gospel, no one comes to the glory of the Father except through the Son (John XIV, 6).

He shows why he referred all glory to God by adding: “For I do not dare to speak of anything that Christ does not accomplish through me.” He says plainly: Whatever I speak, I speak not through myself but through Christ, because he himself accomplishes these things through me.

He clearly shows that he is not usurping another’s praise and that he preaches nothing besides what Christ preached. Hence in the Gospel the Lord says: “Go, teach them, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; teach them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Matt. XXVIII, 19–20). Elsewhere the same Apostle says: “Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (II Cor. XIII, 3).

[Col. 0277C] “For the obedience of the Gentiles.” He preached for this purpose: that the Gentiles might obey the teaching of the Gospel.

“By word and deed,” that is, by preaching and signs. Hence Mark the Evangelist says: “But they went out and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (Mark XVI, 20).

Hence it follows: “Through the power of signs and wonders” [Note: [Col. 0277D] The Vulgate reads: “In the power of signs,” etc.]. For whatever they said, they confirmed with signs. They are called “signs” because they signify something; “wonders” are so called as though from *porrodicia* [Note: [Col. 0277D] This word, said to be formed by joining the words *porro dicere* (“to declare further”), is found nowhere.], because they portend something. He shows by whose power he performed these things by adding: “In the power of the Holy Spirit.”

It follows: “So that from Jerusalem and the surrounding region as far as Illyricum I have filled the Gospel of Christ.” Illyricum is a province of the Greeks, near Italy and Venetia, adjoining the Adriatic Sea.

Note that the Apostle wished to show that he did not descend from Jerusalem to Illyricum by a direct route, but preached through the individual regions all around; therefore he first said, “and the surrounding region.” He “filled” the Gospel because he confirmed its truth by signs.

“Thus I preached this Gospel, not where Christ had been named,” etc. How can he say that he preached only where Christ had not been named, when he could not have descended from Jerusalem to Illyricum while preaching if he passed through Achaia or Asia, and it is established that blessed John converted Asia to the faith, while Andrew converted Achaia?

It should therefore be understood that by this statement the Apostle wished to show that, although those people had believed, they had nevertheless been deceived by false apostles. He therefore had more labor among them than among those where Christ had never been named. He found such people as though the fame of Christ’s name had never reached them.

“Lest I should preach upon another’s foundation” [Note: [Col. 0278D] The Vulgate reads *build upon another’s foundation*.]—that is, lest I build the gift of my preaching upon the beginning of another’s preaching and appear to usurp another’s work.

“But as it is written”—with the sense understood, “so I preached”—“Those to whom he was not announced will see” (Isa. [Col. 0278B] LVII, 15).

It must be asked why the Apostle says that this testimony was fulfilled spiritually in himself, since other apostles too preached to those to whom Christ had not been announced. It should be understood that he labored there more than all the others in preaching; therefore he says that this was fulfilled, as it were, particularly in himself.

Those to whom he was announced “saw,” with spiritual eyes, because they understood him to be God and in every respect equal to the Father. This is what follows: “And those who have not heard will understand.”

“For this reason I was greatly hindered from coming to you.” He was hindered not by Satan but by the labor of preaching.

It follows [Note: [Col. 0278D] The words found in the Vulgate, “and I have been prevented until now,” are missing here.]: “But now, having no further place in these regions,” etc.

How could he have no place in those regions if they had believed through his preaching? The statement must therefore be understood in this sense: He had no place in those regions because there was no city, town, village, or any place to which the fame of Christ’s name had not reached through his preaching.

“Having for many years desired to come to you.” Why did he wish to indicate this to the Romans? In order to draw them toward love for him.

“When I begin my journey to Spain, I hope to see you as I pass by.” Why does he say that he will see the Romans in passing? To show that he placed in their power how they would receive him and how long they would keep him with them. For it should be understood that we hold more carefully and more tightly what we think we shall soon lose. Therefore he said that he would see the Romans in passing, so that they might receive him with greater affection.

“And that I may be sent on my way there by you, if I have first enjoyed you in part.” The Apostle knew that he was loved by the Romans, and therefore he said, “if I have enjoyed you in part,” in order to nurture their affection for him; or certainly he said “in part” because nothing can ever be enough in love.

“But now I shall set out for Jerusalem to minister to the saints.” By “the saints” he means the apostles who were in Jerusalem [Col. 0279A], or those who had believed through the apostles’ preaching. We read that five thousand believed on one day (Acts IV, 4), and three thousand on another (Acts II, 41).

For Macedonia and Achaia were pleased to make a contribution, etc. Macedonia and Achaia are provinces of the Greeks. Corinth, in fact, is the metropolis of Achaia, which was the glory of all Greece. Achaia has Macedonia joined to it on its northern side. The meaning, therefore, is: Macedonia and Achaia—that is, the Macedonians and Achaeans—were pleased, that is, resolved, to make a contribution, that is, a collection for the poor of Christ. For *collatio* means not only an assembling of words but also a collection of any kind of thing.

By “the poor of the saints” he means those who became poor for the sake of the saints [Col. 0279B]—that is, those who, believing at the apostles’ preaching, sold all their possessions, brought the proceeds, and laid them at the apostles’ feet; and it was distributed to each according to his need (Acts 4:34–35). When their houses, vineyards, and money had consequently run out, and they had neither what they could cultivate nor the means by which they could subsist, the apostles decreed that throughout all the nations whom they converted to faith in Christ by their preaching, they should earnestly urge that a collection be made by which the poor of the saints in Jerusalem might be supported.

The apostle Paul labored especially in this matter. Throughout all the nations that had believed through his preaching he established churches. Since his hearers had only recently abandoned the worship of idols, they could not sell everything, distribute it to the poor, and serve the Lord [Col. 0279C]. He therefore urged them to make collections by which those in Jerusalem might be supported, so that through their prayer these converts might be strengthened in faith.

Why, then, did he wish to make this known to the Romans concerning the Macedonians and Achaeans? Clearly, so that by their example they too might be encouraged to make collections; for people are moved to do some good more by example than by words. But lest the Romans think that those people had been compelled to do this, he added: “For it pleased them,” as though he were saying: “What I urged, they accepted willingly.” When he says “it pleased them,” he shows their goodwill; but when he adds, “and they are their debtors,” he shows that the Gentiles believed through the preaching of those who had come down from Jerusalem and received the teaching of evangelical grace.

To demonstrate this more clearly, [Col. 0279D] he added: “For if the Gentiles have become partakers of their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in carnal things.” The Gentiles became partakers of their spiritual things—that is, of the Jews’ spiritual things—because through them they received the secrets of heavenly mysteries. He calls “carnal things” the necessities of the present life, which are transitory, like flesh.

When I have therefore completed this (the word “work” being understood) and delivered this fruit to them, I shall depart through you to Spain. He calls the collections “fruit,” appropriately, since those who made them were to be rewarded with the fruit of eternal blessedness.

It follows: “But I know that when I come to you, I shall come in the abundance of the blessing [Col. 0280A] of Christ.”

[Note: [Col. 0279D] The Vulgate reads, “of the blessing of the Gospel of Christ.”]

The Apostle foresaw that he would not only preach among the Romans but would also perform signs and miracles. Therefore he says that he would come in the abundance of blessing—that is, in an abundance of preaching and miracle-working.

Therefore I beseech you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Holy Spirit, to assist me in prayers for me to God. The Apostle knew that holy men had obtained many things through prayer: Elijah, for example, obtained that heaven should be closed and afterward opened; and through the prayer of the saints Peter was freed from prison. Therefore he asked the Romans to pray for him.

He did not ask simply, but with adjuration, saying “by [Col. 0280B] our Lord Jesus Christ,” as though he were saying: “By our Creator and Redeemer, and by the love of the Holy Spirit”—that is, by the Holy Spirit, who is the love of the Father and the Son, or who grants you the gift of love.

That I may be delivered from the unbelievers who are in Judea. Why did he desire to be delivered from the unbelievers? Was it because of fear of death? How, then, does he say in the Acts of the Apostles: “I know that tribulations await me in Jerusalem; but I do not make my life more precious than myself”? (Acts 20:23–24.) He did not desire this, therefore, out of fear of death, but lest he encounter some obstacle in his preaching, or suffer loss regarding the collections, or be delayed in returning to the Romans.

[Col. 0280C] And that the offering of my service may be acceptable to the saints in Jerusalem. By “the offering of his service” he means the collections. For he accepted the ministry of preaching among the Gentiles in such a way that he would remember the poor of Christ. He therefore desired this offering to be acceptable to the saints, because he knew that it would also be acceptable to God if it were acceptable to the saints. By this we are admonished to strive especially to please those whom we recognize as Christ’s pre-eminent members.

That I may come to you with joy. He does not mean bodily joy but spiritual joy—namely, the gladness with which he rejoiced over the progress and salvation of believers. Since he could not obtain this joy except through God, he added: “by the will of God,” that is, through Christ, who is the Father’s will.

And may I be refreshed with you. Likewise, he desires spiritual refreshment—that is, rest [Col. 0280D] in faith and good works. And because throughout almost the whole text of the Epistle he recalled Jews and Gentiles to peace, so that they might attain it he added a prayer at the end, saying: “Now may the God of peace be with you all. Amen.”

He is called the God of peace because he himself bestows the good of peace. “Amen,” however, is a Hebrew expression; in Latin it means “truly,” “faithfully,” or “may it be so.” The Apostle placed it at the end of this Epistle either to confirm his prayer by this word or to show that everything he had said previously was true, so that they might receive it more devoutly and fulfill it more diligently in their works.

[Col. 0281A] (CHAP. XVI.) Finally, after completing the text, he turns to salutations. He greets some people, while on his own behalf he commends others, such as Phoebe, saying: “I commend to you Phoebe, my sister.” When he adds, “who is in the ministry of the Church,” he shows that at that time not only men but also women presided over churches.

He identifies the church over which Phoebe presided by adding: “who is at Cenchrea.” Cenchrea is a place in Greece, specifically the harbor of Corinth, from which the Apostle sent this Epistle to the Romans through Phoebe. He also urges that she be received carefully, saying: “that you may receive her worthily in the Lord, as becomes the saints”—that is, with the reception by which saints ought to be received. By “in the Lord” he means “in the love of the Lord.”

A little later he shows why she should be received in this way, saying: [Col. 0281B] “For she herself also assisted many, and me,” as though he were saying in other words: “For as long as Phoebe remained in her own home, she supplied the needs of the other saints and of me. But now, because she has chosen voluntary poverty and has resolved to come to Rome for the sake of prayer, I command you to receive her worthily and assist her in whatever matter she may need from you”—that is, not only in spiritual matters but also in the necessities of the present life.

Greet Prisca and Aquila. By these words we must understand those of whom it is written in the Acts of the Apostles (chap. 18:2) that, when Paul had come from Athens to Antioch [Note: [Col. 0281D] In the Acts of the Apostles this is said of Paul’s coming to Corinth, not to Antioch.], he found there a Jewish man, a native of Pontus, named Aquila, with his wife Priscilla, and attached himself to them.

[Col. 0281C] Hence it is also added here: “My helpers in Christ Jesus”—that is, fellow workers in the preaching of Christ Jesus. He shows their extraordinary love for him when he adds: “Who for my life laid down their necks.” When the Apostle was about to be punished, they chose to die for him, lest so great a lamp of the Church should be extinguished. Hence they are praised by the whole Church because of their extraordinary love.

And therefore it is added: “To whom not only I give thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles.” But since the work of mercy is found not only among masters but also among servants, and not only among rulers but also among subjects, he rightly adds: “and their household church” (with “greet” understood).

Greet Epaenetus, beloved by me, who is the first-fruit of Asia [Col. 0281D] in the Lord. He was certainly the first of all the Asians to believe at the Apostle’s preaching. Since he merely believed simply and did not labor in preaching, the Apostle therefore called him only “beloved.”

Greet Mary, who labored greatly among you. By these words he shows that women too presided over churches. This Mary labored greatly among the Romans because she converted many of them to the faith; and therefore he judged her worthy of a special greeting.

[Col. 0282A] Greet Andronicus and Julia [Note: [Col. 0281D] The Vulgate reads “Junia.”]. We must understand them to have been a man and a woman, husband and wife. When he adds, “my kinsmen and fellow prisoners,” he shows that they were Jews and his fellow workers in preaching. For they too, voluntarily abandoning their own homeland, as the Apostle had done, preached among the Gentiles as though in captivity.

But what does the following mean: “who are noble among the apostles,” when among the twelve Apostles there are found not only no noble persons but not even any of the least? It must be understood that *apostle* in Greek means “one who is sent.” Hence it can be understood that those too may be called apostles of whom Luke the Evangelist says (10:1): “The Lord Jesus appointed also seventy-two other disciples and sent them” [Note: [Col. 0282D] The words of this passage that follow are written here in highly abbreviated form in the autograph manuscript.], “into every city and place [Col. 0282B] where he himself was about to come.”

Those two were among these. Since they were not the least among them, he therefore says that they were noble among the apostles. Of them it is also added: “who were in Christ before me”—that is, who believed in Christ Jesus before I did.

Greet Ampliatus, most beloved by me in the Lord. It must be asked why he called Epaenetus “beloved” but this man “most beloved.” Clearly, because the former simply believed, while this man labored in preaching.

Greet Urbanus, our helper in Christ, and Stachys, my beloved. Urbanus labored in preaching; Stachys simply believed. Therefore he called the former “helper” but the latter only “beloved.”

Greet Apelles, approved in Christ. This Apelles endured many adversities for Christ, but preserved the virtue of patience uncorrupted to the end, knowing what the Apostle teaches: “Tribulation produces patience, and patience produces approval” (above, 5:4–5). Therefore the Apostle called him “approved.”

If anyone carefully examines and remembers that God was speaking in him, he will surely find that no sentence in his words, no syllable at all, is empty. For he saw with spiritual eyes the merits of each person distinguished before God. Therefore he called one “beloved,” another “most beloved,” another “helper,” and another “approved.”

Greet those who are of Aristobulus—here “household” must be understood [Note: [Col. 0282D] The word “household” is explicitly found in the Vulgate.], so that Aristobulus may be understood as a man’s proper name; or certainly it may be taken as a place.

[Col. 0282D] Greet Herodion, my kinsman. When he calls him a kinsman, he shows that he was a Jew. Why, then, did he not join him to Andronicus and Julia, whom he had called his kinsmen? Because he did not labor in preaching as they did.

Greet those who are of Narcissus—“household” is understood [Note: [Col. 0282D] This word is likewise explicitly read in the Vulgate.]. Narcissus was a presbyter, but he did not have a church or people of his own. Rather, traveling here and there, he preached, and he distributed to the needy whatever he was able to receive from his hearers [Col. 0283A]. Therefore, because of his goodwill, the Apostle resolved to greet those who were with him as well.

But because Narcissus had many households and many unbelievers still adhered to him, lest the Apostle seem to greet them [Note: [Col. 0283D] These words are found in the lateral margin of the autograph manuscript.], he added: “who are in the Lord”—that is, who already believe.

Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who labor in the Lord. These women had labored to some extent in preaching and were still laboring; therefore the Apostle judged them worthy of his greeting.

Greet Persida [Note: [Col. 0283D] The Vulgate reads “Persis.”], most dear, who labored greatly in the Lord. Why did he not join her to the women mentioned above? Clearly, because she did not assist the Apostle merely to some extent, as those women did, but greatly in preaching. Hence it is also added: [Col. 0283B] “who labored greatly in the Lord”—and therefore he called her “most dear” [Note: [Col. 0283D] These words are found in the lateral margin.].

Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine. When he calls him “chosen in the Lord,” he also shows that he was beloved. He was chosen by that election of which the Lord says, “Few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16), and the same Apostle says, “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph. 1:4).

It must be understood that Rufus was a man of great merit; therefore the Apostle called his mother his own, just as the Lord, during his Passion, said that his mother belonged to the disciple (John 19:26).

Greet Asyncritus [Note: [Col. 0283D] The Vulgate reads “Asyncritus.”], Phlegon [Note: [Col. 0283D] The Vulgate reads “Phlegon.”], Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them. Since these people did not preach, he greeted them simply.

This Hermes [Note: [Col. 0283D] Or rather, Hermas.], as some maintain [Note: [Col. 0283D] Namely, Origen, Eusebius, and St. Jerome.], [Col. 0283C] wrote a book entitled *The Shepherd*.

Greet Philologus and Julia; we must understand them to have been a man and a woman, husband and wife. Since he immediately added, “Nereus and his sister, and Olympias,” and joined them to the persons previously mentioned, he perhaps wished to indicate that they were connected by some relationship.

And because many saints were with them, lest he pass over anyone, he added: “and the saints who are with them.” Finally, after the special greetings, he turned to a general one, saying: “Greet one another with a kiss.” And because some people’s kisses are deceitful, like Judas’s, to prohibit such kisses he added: “holy.”

To show how solicitously he cared for the Romans—namely, by commending them to the prayers of all the churches that had believed through him—he added: [Col. 0284A] “All the churches of Christ greet you.” (Here the following is to be understood: “which are in these provinces.”)

Since there were still among the Romans people who, through their preaching, produced dissensions and occasions of stumbling—for by heresies they sought to divide the unity of the Church, and some scandalized weak brothers—he therefore added: “I beseech you, brothers, to observe those who cause dissensions and occasions of stumbling contrary to the doctrine that you have learned, and avoid them.” And so that he might obtain more quickly what he desired, he did not say, “I command” or “I admonish,” but “I beseech.”

The Romans could have said: “How can we avoid them, since they are more powerful than we are and cannot be expelled from the Church?” Therefore he added: “and avoid them.” By these words he shows that great discernment must be exercised not only by rulers but also by subjects [Note: [Col. 0283D]

This statement agrees altogether with the doctrine and practice of the universal Church, both in those times and in earlier ones. Its chief testimony is furnished by that outstanding light of the Church, St. Augustine, *Against Parmenian* III, chap. 2, nos. 8, 12, 13, in the same place.

But someone may say: “How shall we be able to obey the Apostle’s command, when he forbids us to eat with such a person?” In this seeming difficulty of the question I shall say nothing new or unusual, but what the holy Church observes: when any one of the brothers, that is, of Christians established within the fellowship of the Church, is found guilty of some such sin and judged worthy of anathema, this may be done where there is no danger of schism . . . when a person’s crime is so well known that he has absolutely no defenders, or no defenders of such a kind through whom schism might arise . . . then this can be done without violating peace, unity, or injuring the wheat, when the multitude of the Church’s congregation is alien from the crime being anathematized. For then it assists the ruler who corrects rather than the criminal who resists.

Then also the offender is struck with fear and healed by shame, when, seeing himself anathematized by the whole Church, he cannot find a companion crowd with whom he may rejoice in his offense and insult the good . . . For correction by many cannot be salutary unless the person being corrected has no multitude as his companion. But when the same disease has seized many, nothing remains for the good except grief and lamentation.

[Col. 0285D] With St. Augustine’s teaching—indeed, with that of the whole primitive Church—there agrees wonderfully the teaching of the most weighty Tridentine Fathers, and in them of the whole Church, indeed of the Holy Spirit: Twenty-fifth Session, *On Reform*, chapter 3.]

For if those who cause dissensions and occasions of stumbling possess no authority or little authority, they must be expelled from the Church, so that, confounded, they may turn to repentance. But if they possess such great authority that they cannot be expelled entirely, they must be avoided, lest the good be corrupted by association with the wicked.

Why they must be avoided, he shows by adding: “For such persons do not serve Christ our Lord but their own belly”—that is, they seek not the gain of souls but earthly advantages. “And by smooth words and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent.” For they deceive the hearts of the innocent by smooth words and blessings: so that they may be regarded as holy by the innocent and their words be trusted, they sometimes preach gently and sometimes bestow certain blessings.

Therefore, to incline them toward what he was asking, he added: “For your obedience has been proclaimed in every place”—that is, it has been spread throughout the whole world that you are obedient to the teaching of the Gospel. For this reason he said much earlier: “Your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world” (above, 1:8).

To show that he rejoiced over their progress, he added: “I rejoice, therefore, in you.” Again, to make clear that they were not yet perfect in every respect, he added: [Col. 0285A] “But I want you to be wise in what is good and simple in what is evil.”

They are wise in what is good who avoid evil with every effort and wisdom. They are simple in what is evil who do not return evil for evil or abuse for abuse. Hence elsewhere: “Be children in malice, but mature in understanding” (1 Cor. 14:20).

To show that they could do this not by their own power but by God’s power, he added: “But the God of peace will crush Satan”—as though he were saying: “If you strive to be wise in what is good and simple in what is evil, the God of peace will crush every Satan before you and grant you perfect peace.”

“Satan” is interpreted as “adversary.” Therefore anyone who resists the divine commandments is rightly called Satan. To demonstrate complete crushing, he added: “under your feet.” Again, lest they think it would be delayed longer, and wishing to urge them to pursue wisdom in what is good and simplicity in what is evil, he added: “swiftly.”

Then he supplied the prayer through which his hearers might obtain what he desired, saying: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.” Here it must be noted that, although the work of the entire Trinity is one, grace is nevertheless called the Son’s, because every grace bestowed on human beings has been conferred through him. Nevertheless, whenever one person of the Trinity is mentioned, the whole Trinity is undoubtedly meant.

Moreover, wishing to show how solicitous even those who were staying with him were concerning the Romans, he also included their greetings, saying: “Timothy, my helper, and Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, my kinsmen, greet you.” Timothy was from Derbe, the son of a certain widow, with a Gentile father (Acts 16), a disciple of blessed Paul and his fellow worker in preaching. This is why he calls him “helper.”

Lucius is the same as Luke, who is also called Lucanus and Lucan. This is not surprising, since Greek and Hebrew names are declined one way in their own language and another way when transferred into another language.

Jason and Sosipater are those concerning whom it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “Jason and Sosipater accompanied him” [Note: [Col. 0285D] Not Sosipater but Sopater; and Jason is not mentioned. Here is the text of the verse: “Sopater of Pyrrhus, a Berean, accompanied him; of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe and [Col. 0286D] Timothy; and of Asia, Tychicus and Trophimus.”] (Acts 20:4).

How, then, does he call them his kinsmen, when Timothy was from Derbe, Luke was a Syrian [Note: [Col. 0286D] These words are written at the bottom of the margin of the autograph manuscript.], by nationality an Antiochene, and Sosipater was from Beroea, the son of Pyrrhus? This ought not to seem contradictory. For the Jews, after being conquered, were led away captive and scattered throughout the individual provinces, cities, [Col. 0285D] and towns. Therefore, although they came from different places, we can understand that they were related to the Apostle in some way.

More appropriately, however, we should understand that he called them kinsmen spiritually—that is, near relatives in the faith—thereby indicating that they were his fellow workers in preaching.

[Col. 0286A] I, Tertius, who wrote the Epistle in the Lord, greet you. What he says by “Tertius” does not refer to numerical order but to the proper name: the man who wrote this Epistle was so called.

Gaius, my host, greets you. This Gaius was a man of great hospitality, as John also confirms in his Epistle (3 John 1). Therefore, to show that he offered hospitality not only to the Apostle but also to everyone who came to him, he added: “and of the whole Church” [Note: [Col. 0286D] The Vulgate reads “the whole Church,” but other readings also agree with ours.] (with “host” understood).

Erastus, the city treasurer, greets you. By saying “treasurer,” he wished to indicate a chief official: *archos* [Note: [Col. 0286D] Greek: ἄρχος.] in Greek means “highest” or “chief.” He mentioned him, therefore, so that when the Romans heard that the chief official of Corinth had already believed, those who were chiefs among them might also believe.

And Quartus, a brother. “Quartus” refers not to rank but to the proper name. His merit can be inferred from this: after the hospitable Gaius he received a place among those giving greetings. Likewise, Tertius’s great merit is proved by the fact that he deserved to occupy the place of greeting after the Apostle’s kinsmen.

After the greetings were finished, he turned to giving glory to God, saying [Note: [Col. 0286D] The repetition found in the Vulgate is lacking here: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.”]:

“Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my Gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery kept silent through eternal times—which has now been made manifest through the Scriptures of the prophets, according to the command of the eternal God, for the obedience [Note: [Col. 0286D] The Vulgate reads “obedience” in another form.] of faith, made known among all the Gentiles—to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, [Col. 0286C] to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.”

The word “to him” must be referred to what he says, “to the only wise God.” But the phrase “through Jesus Christ” appears ambiguous: whether it refers to what precedes, so that the punctuation is “to the only wise God through Jesus Christ,” and we understand the Father to be wise through the Son—not by participation in wisdom, but by begetting Wisdom, who is Christ—or whether it refers to what follows, with the punctuation altered so that we say, “through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory.”

But who would dare to say that God the Father is wise through the Son, when he is wise according to his own substance? It seems more fitting to say that the one begotten is wise through the one who begets than that the one who begets is wise through the one begotten.

It is therefore more correct and more noble to punctuate the phrase with what follows. Although it is an unusual expression to say, “to him to whom there be,” nothing is lost from the meaning. The order of the words can be understood through ellipsis as follows: “To the only wise God be glory forever and ever, to whom there is glory through Jesus Christ.”

When he says “to the only wise God,” we must understand not the Father alone but the whole Trinity, which is one God. God is therefore appropriately called the only wise God, because he is wise not through an accidental or acquired participation in substance but according to his own substance. A human being is called good through participation in the highest good; yet God alone is good, because he is good in his own nature and through himself.

He who is able to strengthen you—that is, to fortify you in faith and good works.

According to my Gospel. By “his Gospel” he means his teaching; hence he also says to the Corinthians: “Through my Gospel I begot you in Christ” (1 Cor. 4:15). To show that his Gospel was the same as Christ’s preaching, he added: “and the preaching of Jesus Christ.” He calls it his Gospel because he himself taught it; Christ’s, because it was first given and preached by Christ.

[Col. 0287B] According to the revelation of the mystery kept silent through eternal times—that is, according to its manifestation. By “mystery” he means the sacrament of human redemption: namely, the Lord’s conception, incarnation, birth, passion, death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven.

This mystery is said to have been kept silent through eternal times because it was hidden from eternity from the rulers and powers of this age—that is, from the demons. For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2:8).

But because he had said that this mystery was kept silent, wishing to show that it had been revealed, a little [Col. 0288A] later he says “made known.” Again, to demonstrate how it was made known, he first stated: “which has now been made manifest through the Scriptures of the prophets.” For it is now openly demonstrated in the prophecies of the prophets that this mystery had been foretold long before—namely, that Christ was to be conceived.

He appropriately adds: “according to the command of the eternal God.” From eternity God commanded that this mystery should be made known to the Gentiles in the last times. He says “of the eternal God” to distinguish him from angels or human beings, for they too are called gods. It must be understood, however, that “eternal fire” is said in one way and “eternal God” in another: fire is eternal because it has no end, whereas God is eternal because he has no beginning.

He shows why this mystery was revealed by adding: “for the obedience of faith among all the Gentiles”—that is, so that people from all the nations might obey the faith.

Therefore, to the only wise God, through whom all these things have been accomplished, be glory—that is, knowledge made manifest with praise—because he shows that God is Trinity, and through Jesus Christ, who in many of his commandments showed that God is Trinity. To say nothing of everything else, he made this most clearly known when he commanded his disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

The end of the Epistle to the Romans.

# THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 0287]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0287C]

I remember that, when I was interpreting what is written to the Corinthians—“To the Church of God which is at Corinth, with all who invoke the name of the Lord” (2 Cor. 1:1)—I said that there was a distinction between the Church and those who invoke the name of the Lord.

For I think that the monogamous man, the virgin, and the person who perseveres in chastity belong to the Church of God; but that the man who has married twice, although he may have a good manner of life and abound in every virtue, nevertheless does not belong to the Church or to that number which has neither wrinkle nor spot nor anything of this kind (Eph. 5:27). Rather, he belongs to a second rank and to those who invoke the name of the Lord—those who are indeed saved in the name of Jesus Christ but are nevertheless not crowned by him, to whom belong glory and dominion [Col. 0287D] forever and ever. (Origen, in the homily on Anna and Simeon.)

In this Epistle the Apostle is shown to have possessed great devotion toward his hearers. Sometimes he admonishes them, sometimes exhorts them, at times rebukes them, and occasionally addresses them with the tenderness of a father speaking gently to his children, wishing to recall them to the state of their former faith.

He is also shown to have possessed great wisdom. This is not surprising, for Christ was speaking in him. In this Epistle, which scarcely extends to a thousand lines, he explained so many and such great statements that hardly anyone could explain as many in ten thousand [Col. 0288C].

It must also be noted that the Apostle knew that his name had been derived from Saul, the proud king, from whose stock he had descended. He did not wish to call himself Saul but Paul, a name which in Latin speech derives from humility, for we call something small *paulum*, “a little.” These matters must be stated below, before the interpretation of Paul’s name is given.

Blessed Paul, an outstanding preacher and teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles (18:1), came to Corinth after being admonished by the divine Spirit, and there preached the word of God for a year and a half.

Corinth is the metropolis of Achaia. Achaia is a province of Greece, named after King Achaeus, situated like an island, for it is surrounded on every side by the sea; only on its northern side is it joined to Macedonia. Corinth, therefore, was the glory of all Greece. In it the study of philosophy flourished especially, and it abounded greatly in secular disciplines.

The Corinthians, then, were Achaeans. Having received the word of God from the Apostle for a year and a half, they believed in Christ. After his departure, however, they were led astray by false apostles and entangled in various errors: some by followers of human wisdom, others by observers of the Mosaic law.

The Apostle recalls them to the true and catholic faith, writing [Col. 0289A] to them from Ephesus through Timothy, his most beloved disciple. [Note: [Col. 0289D] In the autograph manuscript, “chapter 1” is written here.]

## [HERE BEGINS THE TEXT]

(CHAP. I.) Paul, as was said in the preceding Epistle, is interpreted as “admirable.” He is admirable not only because he delivered the Gospel to the Roman city, which was the head of the whole world, but also because he instructed Corinth, which was the glory of all Greece, with saving commandments.

He was called in three ways: first, in God’s foreknowledge and predestination, as in the words: “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph. 1:4); second, in figure, as in: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf” (Gen. 49:27), and so forth; and third, he was called by words, most openly where it is said: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 22:7.)

“Apostle” is Greek; in Latin it means “sent,” according to the words: [Col. 0289B] “Behold, I shall send you to nations far away” (ibid., 21).

How he was called an apostle he makes clear by adding: “through the will of God.” “Will” is used in various ways in Scripture. Sometimes it signifies the soul; sometimes a plan; sometimes it contains the sense of the verb meaning “it pleases.” Accordingly, in this passage we appropriately understand “through the will of God” to mean “according to God’s good pleasure,” where the force of divine love toward him is shown.

For he was not called an apostle in just any manner, but through the will of God—that is, through providence and dispensation. He called himself an apostle of Jesus Christ to distinguish himself from false apostles. Whoever brings about salvation through the words or examples of others is rightly called an apostle of Christ. Conversely, whoever brings about someone’s destruction either through words or examples [Col. 0289C] is called a false apostle.

And Sosthenes. It must be asked why he associated this man with himself in the greeting. Clearly, because he was a Corinthian teacher and very solicitous for the salvation of the brothers.

But since in other Epistles he takes different people with him, the solution to this question must be sought in one that applies everywhere. It must therefore be understood that blessed Paul, just as he was more ardent and zealous than others toward his hearers, was also more humble. To leave us an example of his humility, he therefore associated this man and others with himself in the greeting.

Or certainly he did so to confirm his account, because it is written: “In the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Deut. 17:6; [Col. 0289D] Matt. 18:16; John 8:17; Heb. 10:28; 2 Cor. 13:1).

But why did he not call Sosthenes an apostle? Clearly, because he did not yet possess such authority as to be worthy of that name.

“Brother” is used in various ways in Scripture. Nevertheless, the Apostle called this man “brother” because of adoption and affection. Hence it is written: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132:1).

And note that in this Epistle, as in the others, the Apostle placed his own name first, because the person sending the Epistle possessed greater authority than those to whom it was sent. It is customary for the names of superiors to be placed first in letters, as in: “King Antiochus sends greetings to the Jewish people” (1 Macc. 15:2).

To the church of God. *Ecclesia* is Greek; in Latin it is called “assembly” or “convocation.” Appropriately so, since it calls everyone together to itself. Hence it is also called *catholic*, that is, universal or general, because it is not confined, like the gatherings of heretics, to certain regions, but, spread throughout the world, extends everywhere. “Universal,” as some wish it, derives from “one,” that is, because it gathers everyone into the unity of faith. The Church is called “general” because within it there is a general teaching for the instruction of all, concerning both visible and invisible things, earthly and heavenly; or because it gathers the whole human race under the obedience of divine piety and religion; or because it heals the sins of all without distinction. He added “of God” to distinguish it from the church of the wicked, as it is written: “I have hated the church of the wicked” [Note: [Col. 0289D] It was more permissible for me here to conjecture this text than to interpret it, for thus it stands: “O the riches!” m. Since the discussion concerned the church of the wicked, I judged that the text ought to be referred to it. Thus, although the letter *o* is read separately, as often happens, I first thought it should be read as *odivi* (“I hated”); then I thought that the letters *t i* should be deleted. Finally, it seemed to me that the letters *ae* of the word *ecclesiam*—which is often written *aecclesia*—were the initial letter *m* of the word *malignantium* (“of the wicked”); for elsewhere texts are very often expressed by their initial letters.]. Therefore, because churches of God had already been established in different parts of the world, to show to which one in particular he was writing, he added: “which is in Corinth.” It continues: “Sanctified in Christ Jesus.” He calls those sanctified who have been reborn through the water of baptism and the grace of the Holy Spirit. But to show where this sanctification takes place, he added: “in Christ Jesus”; for apart from him no sanctification takes place.

Called saints. This was said of those who persevered in the faith. He praises them so that, through the praise of these people, he might restore those who had been deceived to the state of their original faith. But how does he call them “called saints”? Were they saints when they were called? Certainly not; rather, once called, they became saints [Note: [Col. 0290D] See the Epistle to the Romans, at the beginning, on the same words: “called saints.”]. This is the same kind of expression as: “Who can find a strong woman?” (Prov. XXXI, 10).

With all who invoke the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, in every place belonging to them and to us. What did he wish to indicate by saying “in every place”? Clearly, that all believers who are found, whether among Jews or gentiles and wherever they may be found, ought to be one, because they are members of one head. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “There will be one flock and one shepherd” (John X, 16). Alternatively, as some wish, the words “who invoke the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” were spoken about priests, since it is their special duty to invoke the name of the Lord. Thus it is written in the Law: “So shall you bless the children of Israel, invoking my name over them” (Num. VI, 23); and the Psalmist says: “Samuel among those who invoke his name” (Ps. XCVIII, 6). Samuel, indeed, was not of Aaron’s lineage; but because he was born of the tribe of Levi, as we read in the Book of Chronicles, and became a priest and offered sacrifice to God, the Psalmist therefore says: “Among those who invoke,” that is, among the priests. Why, then, does the Apostle say this? To show that priests hold in the Church the place—that is, the office and function—of the apostles; hence they are also called apostles of the churches.

Therefore, because he had first said, “who invoke the name of the Lord Jesus,” lest he seem to have excluded the authority and gift of God the Father, he added: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father.” By these words he admonishes us that the Lord Jesus Christ, too, must be invoked as God; yet all grace and every gift must be referred to God the Father, from whom all things come. He thereby shows the two—that is, the two persons of the Father and the Son—who are one in divinity, and indicates that the Father’s authority must be proclaimed. Moreover, it should be understood that in these words he wishes for the Corinthians both the remission of sins and reconciliation with God. Grace is the gift by which sins are loosened; hence it is called grace because it is given freely. Peace, however, is that by which we are reconciled to God.

Therefore, because grace and peace, which are from God, are also from his only-begotten Son, he added: “and from the Lord Jesus Christ.” Nevertheless, although discreetly, the Apostle here makes mention of the whole Trinity: for grace and peace are gifts of the Holy Spirit. Thus, when grace and peace are wished for them, the Holy Spirit, who is the third person in the Trinity, is commended.

I give thanks to my God always for you. In his customary manner he began with thanksgiving, in order to urge his hearers toward better things. In this he left an example for preachers, that they should strive to give thanks to God not only for their own progress but also for that of their hearers. By saying “to God,” he teaches that if one person learns something good from another, he should ascribe it and give thanks not to the human being but to God. For the preacher’s word labors outwardly in vain unless the grace of the Holy Spirit is present to teach the mind inwardly. He added “my” to show that although God is by nature the God of all, because he is the Creator and judge of all, by will and merit he is the God of only a few—that is, of the elect—whose alone is this expression.

Therefore, because there are some who give thanks to God both in prosperity and in adversity, not continually but for a time, the Apostle added “always” to show that God must be thanked continually both in prosperity and in adversity. The Lord also taught this when he fasted continuously for forty days and nights. What he adds, “for you,” is not to be understood as “for you who are rich or powerful,” but “for you,” that is, for you who have persevered in the faith. “In grace,” that is, “for grace.” But because there are some who possess the grace of earthly riches, lest the Apostle seem to have given thanks for people of this sort, he added “of God.” Again, because they had obtained this grace not through their own merits but through divine generosity, he added: “which was given to you in Christ Jesus,” that is, through Christ Jesus.

He makes clear why he gives thanks: “Because in everything you have been made rich in him, in every word,” and so forth. “In him,” that is, through him. But we must ask with what riches he says they were enriched. With gold or silver? No, but with those of which Isaiah says: “The riches of salvation, wisdom and knowledge; the fear of the Lord is itself his treasure” (Isa. XXXIII, 6). Therefore, to show what riches he meant, the Apostle added: “in every word and in every knowledge.” Here “word” is not to be understood essentially but nominally. “In every word,” that is, in every teaching. Knowledge is present when something is apprehended through a certain method of reasoning.

It should be understood, however, that some have wished “knowledge” here to mean human knowledge. For this reason, a little later it is added: “so that you lack nothing in any grace,” since Solomon, speaking of wisdom, says among other things: “All good things came to me together with her” (Wis. VII, 11); for the wise person suffers no deprivation. But it is better to understand spiritual rather than human knowledge here. He says that they were made rich in every word and in every knowledge because, persevering in the grace they had received, they attained the teaching of spiritual knowledge. Hence it follows: “Just as the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you.” The testimony of Christ is true knowledge; it had been confirmed in the Corinthians because, strengthened in faith, they hoped for nothing from human beings and, enticed by no pleasures of the earth, had placed all their hope in Christ.

Alternatively: The testimony of Christ had been confirmed in them because what Christ accomplished in the human being was displayed in their conduct, “in the temple” [Note: [Col. 0291D] The autograph has *in templum* (“into the temple”), which I judged should be corrected to the better reading. The sense of this interpretation may perhaps refer to what the same Apostle says in this Epistle, chapter III, verse 16: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God?”; or verse 17: “If anyone destroys the temple of God … the temple of God is holy”; or to what he says in chapter VI, verse 19: “your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit”; or likewise in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter VI, verse 16: “for you are the temple of the living God.” Alternatively, *exemplo* (“as an example”) should be read.]. For just as Christ, crucified, rose again and ascended into heaven, so they, crucified to the world and to vices, rising again through virtues, ascended into heaven through heavenly desire.

How the testimony of Christ was confirmed in them is disclosed when it follows: “so that you lack nothing in any grace,” that is, in any virtue. To whom he says this is disclosed when it follows: “as you await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ.” He calls the day of judgment the revelation of the Lord Jesus Christ. Then Christ will be revealed to all, to the just and unjust, the devout and impious alike, so that the wicked, seeing what they refused to believe, may be confounded and perish; [Col. 0293A] but the good may rejoice in the gift, when they see that they have received more than they had thought.

They therefore await the revelation of Jesus Christ who, watched on every side, always keep the day of death before their eyes and await the future judgment carefully and patiently. This too should be noted: when he says “awaiting the revelation,” he shows that the gift the faithful are to receive is still hidden; it will be revealed on the day of judgment. Hence John says: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be” (I John III, 2). The same Apostle says elsewhere: “Your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Coloss. III, 3), and so forth.

It should also be understood that, seeing the Corinthians’ shamefaced minds and recognizing that the wound of their error needed to be healed, the Apostle took care to spare their modesty. Like a most skilled physician, gently touching the wound, he first offered praise; then, attempting to remove the wound, he drove in the knife of rebuke and added the harshness of repeated reproaches.

But we must ask why he rebukes so sharply those whom he had earlier called rich in every knowledge and declared to lack nothing in any grace. Hence blessed Pope Gregory says: “Tell me, I ask you, Apostle: if they were rich in everything, why do you weary yourself by writing? And if they lacked nothing, why do you rebuke those who are far away so harshly?” For behold, those whom you said lacked nothing, you show to be lacking unity and harmony. Could the Holy Spirit, who spoke through you, have uttered a lie? Certainly not. Rather, there were some among the Corinthians who, enriched in every respect, deserved to be advanced by your praise; and there were also some worthy of your rebuke.

It is the custom of a skilled physician first to touch the healthy members around a wound, and then to apply his hand to touching or cutting away the wound. Thus, plainly, the Apostle acted. He touched the healthy members around the wound when he praised the perfected Corinthians; but when he broke out into rebuking the imperfect, he struck the wound as though it were in the body. He praised the perfected precisely so that he might reach the rebuke of the imperfect more appropriately; otherwise, they might perhaps despair of their salvation.

Therefore, lest those who had persevered in the faith waver in the present life because of their own fall, he aptly added: “He will also confirm you to the end”—namely, Christ. Certain of the alacrity of their minds and confident in the hope of their conversion, he seems by these words to promise them assurance, as though he were saying: “He who by his grace granted that you should be rich in everything will, through the gift of his mercy, confirm you so that you persevere in the grace you have received.”

But whence did the Apostle have such confidence concerning their confirmation? Clearly, from their past perseverance. For those who had remained unmoved amid so many dangers of opinion and so many disturbances caused by conflicting views had plainly shown that they would persevere in the faith. And note that, while praising these people, he invites those who had been corrupted by the pseudo-apostles to correction; for, while proclaiming the faith of the former, he calls the latter to repentance.

To show how long they were to be confirmed, he added: “to the end.” “End” is not to be understood as destruction, but as perfection and completion. Christ himself can be understood by “end,” since Christ is the end of the Law; the sense would then be “until Christ,” as though he were saying: “in himself.” It may also be understood as the perfection of good works, or the day of judgment, or the day of each person’s death, according to the saying: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 22).

Without blame. Note that he did not say “without sin”; for no one in this life can be so confirmed as to be free from sin. Hence we are instructed to say daily: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Luke XI, 4; Matt. VI, 12). James says the same: “We all offend in many things” (James III, 2).

On the day of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. He calls the day of his coming the day of judgment, when the Lord will come with the elders of his people; or the day of each person’s death, when Christ, coming, summons his elect from the prison-house of the flesh to heavenly glory.

Again, lest they waver concerning their confirmation, he added: “God is faithful.” But why did he call him faithful? Who, after all, doubts this? He called him faithful because Scripture customarily calls him this; and in truth he is faithful, because he cannot be deceived and because he fulfilled what he promised. Nor can it be otherwise than as he himself said: that we who believe him to be the Son of God should be adopted as children of God and remain in the same dignity in which he remains, whom we believe to be the Son of God. For he grants what he himself is: divinity to human beings, immortality to mortals.

Through whom you were called. “Calling” here is not to be understood according to the passage we find written: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX, 16); rather, it means predestination, according to which we were chosen for fellowship—that is, for brotherhood—with Jesus Christ. Hence it immediately follows: “into the fellowship” [Note: [Col. 0293D] The Vulgate has “into the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ.”] “of Jesus Christ our Lord.” Hence John says: “God is light; and if we love him, we know that we shall have fellowship with his Son” (I John I, 5, 7).

Up to this point the Apostle has described both the thanksgivings he offered to God for the Corinthians and their praises. Now he begins the text of the Epistle and sets forth the causes of their disagreement, adding: “I appeal to you, therefore, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,” and so forth.

By these words he asks and entreats all the Corinthians to have the same mind—that is, the mind in which they were reborn through the sacrament of baptism. It should be noted that he does not say “by the authority or dignity of my apostleship,” but “by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.” For he found nothing greater by which he could frighten them, since “there is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts IV, 12). It is as though he were saying: “I appeal to you by the name of the one whose blood redeemed you, whose grace adopted you, and by whose invocation you were saved.”

“That you all say the same thing” (understand: what you received in baptism). For he was speaking to the whole Church of the Corinthians [Note: [Col. 0294D] In the autograph margin it reads “chapter II.”], so that those who had been deceived by seducers [Col. 0295A] might return to the state of their original faith when they heard that the faith of those who had persevered was being praised in them.

And that there be no schisms among you. Heresy and schism differ in this respect: a heretic is properly one who errs in faith; a schismatic, one who errs against brotherly love. [Note: [Col. 0295D] In the autograph margin it reads “chapter III.”] Hence Origen is called by some not a heretic but a schismatic, because he did not err in faith but in certain discussions of the holy Scriptures; for he understood certain passages quite differently from the Catholic Church. Thus there were schisms among the Corinthians, because they were divided from one another not only over the opinions of different teachers but also in certain other matters, as will be demonstrated below.

But that you be perfected in the same mind, that is, in the same understanding; and what should be supplied is: “which you received from me.” And in the same knowledge [Note: [Col. 0295D] The Vulgate has *sententia* (“judgment” or “opinion”).], that is, in the reasoning of evangelical teaching, where what should be supplied is: “which you heard and learned from me.”

This, therefore, is the voice only of perfected preachers, that is, of those who live rightly and preach rightly. For preachers are always faced with a twofold obligation: either not to mix falsehood with the truth by preaching badly, or not to corrupt true teaching by living perversely.

For it has been reported to me concerning you, my brothers, by those who belong to Chloe, that there are contentions among you. We must ask why the Apostle so readily believed those who reported evil about the Corinthians, since it is written in the Law: “Do not readily believe every word” (Ecclus. VI, 7). And in the Book of Jesus son of Sirach: “What your eyes have seen, speak of these things.”

It should therefore be understood that the Apostle, filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, possessed such merit that, although absent, he knew the merits of the individual Corinthians. Hence he says elsewhere: “Although absent in body, I am with you in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order” (Coloss. II, 5). He therefore believed this so readily because through the Holy Spirit he knew it to be true.

Again, we must ask why he called “brothers” those who had been corrupted by the error of the pseudo-apostles. Clearly, it was to give them an opportunity to recover their senses. Hence the Lord commanded through Isaiah that those who were with him should say to those who had been deceived by false prophets: “You are our brothers,” so that, having heard the name of brotherhood, they might be converted and, as brothers, might be unable to disagree.

Chloe’s people, as some wish, were persons who persevered in the faith and bore fruit. Therefore, because they were of great merit, their report was so readily believed. Others assert that *Chloe* was the name of a place, so that the words mean: “by those who belong to Chloe,” as though it were said: “by those who are in Antioch.” Some say that she was a woman devoted to God, in whose company there was a multitude of believers and worshipers of God; and because she possessed great holiness, the Apostle therefore readily believed those who had been sent by her.

Contention is present when irritation wears people down and truth is not sought. A contentious person is so called, as it were, from *intentio* (“striving”) [Note: [Col. 0295D] Perhaps *intensio* (“intensity” or “tension”).], because such a person strives to claim something for himself not by reason but by a certain obstinacy of mind.

Those, then, who reported perverse things about the Corinthians also indicated that there were contentions among them, in order to show that they contained diversities of mind and varieties of disposition, even in their evangelical preaching. To make those same contentions explicit, he added: “Now I mean this: each of you says, ‘I belong to Paul’; ‘but I to Apollos’; ‘but I to Cephas’; ‘but I to Christ.’”

Here it should be noted that he identifies the errors but does not identify the authors of the errors, because they did not remain in one place [Col. 0296B] but traveled through different places in order to deceive the simple and baptize them, so that they might glory in their persons. For those whom the Apostle names were holy and true preachers—namely, Paul, Cephas, and Apollos. He introduces them in order, under their guise, to rebuke the pseudo-apostles.

By these words he shows that if one must not glory in good preachers, much less may one glory in the wicked, whose perverse teaching is displayed in what follows. He also shows that only those persevered in the faith who said that they were disciples not of any human being but of Christ; these he praises above as well.

Christ has been divided [Note: [Col. 0296D] In the Vulgate this is an interrogative statement. The question mark is absent from our autograph.]. It is as though he were saying: “If matters are as you say, then Christ has been divided; for if the members are divided, so is the whole body.”

But the Apostle says that Christ has been divided because people, usurping Christ’s glory, divided him among themselves. For just as those deceived by heretics wished to be called by their names—Arians from Arius, Sabellians from Sabellius, Photinians from Photinus—so the Corinthians, deceived by pseudo-apostles, wished to be distinguished by their names; and thereby they venerated human beings in Christ’s place and stead.

Moreover, it should be understood that heretics divide Christ when they hold diverse opinions about him. Some asserted that he was God alone; some, that he was human alone; others maintained that he was both God and human but had begun from the Virgin; some said that he had been foretold by the prophets, while others said that the prophets had said nothing about him. Since the Lord Jesus Christ is both God and human, whoever holds various opinions about him divides Christ.

Thus the deceived Corinthians were dividing Christ, because they were assigning to human beings the glory of their redemption and renewal, which was owed to Christ alone. They divided Christ because they were creating different churches.

Therefore, because it is a great evil to attribute God’s glory to human beings, the Apostle aptly added: “Was Paul crucified for you?” Here it should be noted that he began with himself, lest, if he began with others, he seem to be commending his own person while refuting them.

The sense is: “If Christ, and not Paul, was crucified for you, and you were redeemed by his blood, not by Paul’s, why, to his dishonor, do you attribute so great a grace and benefit to a human being?”

“Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” The sense is: “Paul baptized, but as Christ’s minister; Christ baptized, but as God and the author of baptism. He granted the authority of baptism to none of the Church’s ministers, but reserved it for himself alone.”

Hence John, more than a prophet, says: “The one who sent me to baptize” [Note: [Col. 0297D] John I, 33. The Vulgate has “in water.”] “said to me: ‘Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’” For if he had transferred the power of baptizing to ministers, there would be as many baptisms as ministers.

He therefore says: “Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” [Col. 0297B] It is as though he were saying: “If you were baptized as believers in Christ and justified in his name, why, forgetful of so great a benefit, do you make human beings the authors of your faith?”

The Corinthians were then like the Novatians and Donatists, who attributed the authority of baptism to themselves, rejected those baptized by Catholics, and gloried in the persons of those whom they had baptized.

[Note: [Col. 0297D] In the autograph margin it reads here “chapter IV.”]

I give thanks to my God. He makes clear why he gives such great thanks: “that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius” [Note: [Col. 0297D] The Vulgate has *Caium*.].

Is it therefore evil to baptize? Certainly not. But because he had already seen that an error had arisen from his baptism, and understood that, if he had baptized more people, a much greater error would have grown, he gives thanks to God that he baptized only a few of them.

Hence he immediately added: “So that no one may say that you were baptized in my name.” Crispus and Gaius were Corinthians, whom the Apostle brings forward as witnesses in order to refute the others. For although they had been baptized by him, they attributed no glory to him but to Christ alone, through whom they obtained remission of all sins.

I baptized also the household of Stephanas. As is explained at the end of this Epistle, this household was the firstfruits of Achaia (I Cor. XVI, 15). The Apostle bears witness concerning them that they devoted themselves to the ministry of the saints, that is, so that they might minister to the saints. He brings these people forward as witnesses against the others, just as he did those mentioned earlier.

But lest anyone say that he had baptized many of the Corinthians, he added: “As for the rest, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.” The sense is: “And if I baptized anyone else among you, attribute the glory for the sacrament of baptism not to me but to God.”

He makes clear why he baptized so few of the Corinthians: “For Christ did not send me to baptize but to evangelize.” Is it therefore evil to baptize? Certainly not. Nevertheless, evangelizing is incomparably the greater good.

For in a bishop consists the dignity of all ordinations, since he is the head of all the orders. Yet not everyone who baptizes is immediately qualified to evangelize. Although the words spoken in baptism are solemn, many are nevertheless permitted to say them; but no one can evangelize unless he is a learned bishop and an instructed teacher of the Church, who knows well how to examine everyone’s behavior and to shape the words of his preaching according to each person’s manner of life.

A bishop, therefore, who possesses the dignity of all ranks may at times also perform the duty of a minister; nevertheless, when ministers are present, he ought not to baptize. Thus the Apostle Peter did not baptize the centurion Cornelius himself but ordered ministers to baptize him (Acts X, 48), because, with them present, he did not consider it fitting to do this himself.

Christ therefore did not send Paul to baptize, because he was not among those to whom it was said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19). Rather, he sent him to evangelize when he said to Ananias: “Go, for this man is a vessel of election for me, to carry my name before the gentiles, kings, and the children of Israel” (Acts IX, 15).

How he was sent to evangelize he shows when he adds: “Not in the wisdom of speech.” He says that he evangelizes “not in the wisdom of speech” because Christian preaching and evangelical teaching do not need verbal display but are commended by their own power. The disciplines of secular studies, however, because they were invented by human beings, require the charm of eloquence; since there is no power or reason in them, they require only an attractive arrangement of words.

For this reason rhetoricians, dialecticians, or philosophers of this world were not chosen to preach the Gospel; neither were the powerful, rich, or noble, but simple, uneducated people and fishermen, the poor and lowly. This was so that perverse people would not have an opportunity to say that evangelical teaching was acceptable not through its own power but rather through the cleverness and craft of human knowledge.

Whoever, therefore, attempts to embellish the faith of evangelical teaching with his own words obscures it. He does not seek that what is preached should be praised, but that he himself, who preaches, should be praised [Note: [Col. 0298D] A truly worthy judgment, which evangelical preachers should commit most deeply to memory.].

Thus the pseudo-apostles, lest they seem foolish to the wise of this world, preached God in the wisdom of speech in two ways: they cultivated eloquence in their preaching, and they carefully avoided those things that the philosophers of the world judged foolish. For they did not preach Christ incarnate as the Son of God, or born of a Virgin, or the future resurrection. The Apostle therefore rebukes them because, in the wisdom of speech, they emptied the mystery of the cross.

Hence it immediately follows: “so that the cross of Christ may not be emptied.” For whoever preaches in such wisdom of speech empties the cross of Christ, because he scatters the mystery of our redemption [Note: [Col. 0298D] In the autograph margin it reads here “chapter V.”].

For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing. In these words he plainly rebukes the philosophers of the world, who consider the word of the cross—that is, the teaching of human redemption—foolish. They judge it foolish to believe that God has a Son, that a virgin could give birth, that God could suffer or die on a cross, or that a human being could rise from the earth.

They are aptly called “those who are perishing,” because, by refusing to accept the mystery of human redemption, they will perish eternally.

Therefore, to show for whom the cross of Christ is power, he added: “But to those who are being saved”; and again, to demonstrate more clearly of whom he was speaking, he added: “that is, to us.” For to us—that is, to those foreknown and predestined to life—it is the power of God. We do not understand weakness in it, but rather that death was conquered through the power of God and the dominion of death destroyed. And because we bear the sign of the cross on our foreheads, with divine grace cooperating, we shall be saved eternally.

Therefore, because he had said that the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing but the power of God to those who are being saved, he added this prophetic testimony to confirm it: “For it is written,” namely in Isaiah: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the understanding of the understanding” (Isa. XXIX, 14).

Here we should observe that the Lord does not promise to destroy true wisdom—not his own wisdom, which he freely bestows—but the wisdom that the wise of this world arrogantly claim for themselves and boast that they possess. He destroyed the wisdom of the wise when he accomplished in deed those things that the wise of this world denied could be done.
