The prudent of this world also said that God was inactive and did not care for human actions [Note: [Col. 0299] Namely, the Epicureans, who certainly admit that God exists but treat him as an object of contempt rather than reverence.]. The Lord rejected their prudence—that is, their understanding—by doing what they considered impossible and plainly demonstrating that he cares for human beings. For he sent his Son from heaven to earth; having suffered, been crucified, died, and been buried, he redeemed the human race.

To show whose wisdom among the wise and whose understanding among the prudent the Lord meant to reject, after producing the prophet’s testimony he added: “Where is the wise person? Where is the scribe? Where is the investigator of this age?” (Isa. XXXIII, 18.)

By these words the Apostle rebukes both Jews and gentiles. The scribes—that is, the Jewish teachers of the Law—did not wish to believe that God had a Son, that a virgin had given birth, or that God could suffer or die. Because this had not been prefigured with complete clarity, they utterly refused to believe it. Likewise, the wise men of this age mocked these same things, because human wisdom does not accept what it judges foolish: that a human being could be born without the union of male and female.

By “investigator of the age” he means specifically the astrologer, who decides that the world is governed by fate and that everything happens through the configurations and movements of the stars.

But to show most conclusively that there is neither a wise person, nor a scribe, nor an investigator of the age, he added: “Has not God made the wisdom of this world foolish?” When it is said, “God made wisdom foolish,” this should not be understood to mean that God, being wise, made wisdom foolish. Rather, he made it foolish because he showed it to be foolish by doing what it itself asserted was impossible.

For because the world did not know God through wisdom in the wisdom of God, and so forth. “In the wisdom of God,” that is, in the creation of the world, which was made by God’s wisdom, the world did not know God through wisdom—namely, carnal wisdom. For the lovers of the world, or those dwelling in the world, when they saw the world’s adornment, did not recognize the Creator through the creature or give thanks to him; instead, they attributed his unique majesty to various images and elements. Some thought God was the air, others the ether, others the sun, and others things of this kind.

Alternatively: “The world, in the wisdom of God”—that is, in the Son of God, who is the Father’s wisdom—“did not know God through wisdom,” namely the carnal wisdom that the Apostle improperly calls wisdom, since it is used here for cunning. When the world saw him living among human beings as a human being, it believed him to be merely human and therefore did not know him. It did not know him because “the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John I, 5, 10, 11).

It pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe. That is, it pleased him that the Word should become flesh and dwell among us; it pleased him to establish a preaching that would appear foolish to them, so that whoever believed the things in which they themselves refused to believe might be saved, while the unbelievers might be condemned by their own condemnation.

For Jews also ask for signs. They do not doubt that such things can happen; rather, they inquire whether they happened or not. They judge that all things are possible for God, but they seek signs by which what is preached may be proved true—signs, namely, such as were performed in the Old Testament, when Aaron’s rod blossomed (Num. XVII, 5, 8) and produced almond blossoms (Num. VIII), and when Jonah lay for three days and three nights in the belly of the whale and was afterward cast alive upon the shore (Jonah II, 1; Matt. XII, 40). Above all, they seek a sign such as was shown to Moses in the fire of the bush (Exod. III, 2, 3).

The Greeks, that is, the Gentiles, seek wisdom; they consider that only those things can happen which appear compatible with human wisdom. Therefore, through wisdom they seek to discover how either a virgin could give birth or a dead man could rise again—yet they cannot comprehend this, because it transcends all human wisdom. Hence he appropriately adds: “But we preach Christ crucified: to the Jews indeed a stumbling block, but to the Gentiles foolishness.” [Col. 0300D]

Christ crucified was a stumbling block to the Jews, because they were scandalized when they heard Christ, a violator of the Sabbath, proclaimed as the Son of God, or when they heard that the Son of God could have suffered or died. To the Gentiles, however, he was foolishness, because, when they heard proclaimed those things which did not appear compatible with human wisdom, they judged them senseless, especially the birth from a virgin and the general resurrection of the dead.

“But to those who are called”: not with that calling by which those were called who, invited to the supper of the Lamb, were not worthy to come (Rev. XIX, 9; Matt. XXII, 2), but with that of which the Apostle says: “And whom he predestined, them he also called” (Rom. VIII, 30). Therefore, to the Jews and Greeks who are called, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God [Col. 0301A], because the Jews, who had previously sought signs and were scandalized, called by God’s grace to faith, understood him to be the power of God, since through him God the Father created, rules, and governs all things.

Likewise, the Gentiles, who had previously striven to comprehend Christ’s mysteries by human wisdom, and to whom they had seemed foolishness, once made believers by God’s grace, recognized him as the wisdom of God [Col. 0301B], since through him God the Father was made known. Indeed, God the Father could not otherwise have been more fittingly known than through him who was begotten by him. Hence in the Gospel: “No one knows the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. XI, 27).

Nevertheless, in accordance with this apostolic statement, we must understand that to both groups who are called, Jews as well as Greeks, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God: power refers to action, wisdom to preaching. Christ is therefore the power of God to them, because they understood that, unless he were God, he could not perform the miracles he performed; and he is also wisdom, because they recognized that no one could teach what he taught unless he were God. Hence the Jews said of him: “From where does this power and wisdom come to him?” [Col. 0301C] (Matt. XIII, 54.)

“For what is foolish of God is wiser than men, and what is weak of God is stronger than men.” He does not truly call anything of God foolish, but speaks according to human opinion. Since human wisdom could not comprehend how either a virgin could give birth, or God suffer, or a dead man rise again, people judged these things foolish, although they contained a spiritual rationale. This foolishness is wiser than men, because human wisdom cannot comprehend it.

Similarly, according to human estimation, he calls Christ’s self-emptying weak, by which he emptied himself, becoming obedient even unto death (Phil. II, 7); but this weakness is stronger than men, because his weakness is our victory and strength: through it we have been made strong. It is stronger than men because, by dying, he conquered the death which kings, giants, and the rulers of this age could not overcome; by his assault he overthrew them, bound the author of death, and opened for us the gate of eternal life. Hence the Apostle aptly adds there: “Therefore God exalted him” (ibid., 8), and so forth. [Col. 0301D]

The Apostle had begun to reject worldly wisdom; and, persisting in the intention he had begun, he added:

[Note: [Col. 0301D] In the autograph margin, chapter VI is read here.]

“Consider your calling, brothers, that not many are wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble” [Col. 0302A] (I Cor. I, 26). It is as though he said: “Recognize in yourselves what I am saying. For look: there are already many of you who believe, but there are not many who are wise according to the flesh”—that is, those who, puffed up rather than instructed by worldly wisdom, refused to submit to divine wisdom. By these words he especially rebukes the astrologers.

Notice that those whom he calls wise according to the flesh he likewise calls powerful and noble: powerful, because, exalted by worldly power, they disdained to accept in faith the weakness of Christ’s cross; noble, because they attributed the antiquity of their origin to their superstition, saying that they possessed an ancient lineage, while calling Christians newcomers, and therefore disdaining to submit to the disgrace of the cross, that is, to the divine religion.

The Apostle therefore shows by these words that God called the faithful not according to that teaching which existed among the few, but [Note: [Col. 0301D] The particle “but,” which is missing in the autograph although the sense absolutely requires it, I judged should be added.] according to that which exists among the many, namely, the evangelical teaching. [Col. 0302B]

Alternatively: “Consider your calling, brothers, that not many are wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble”—that is, weigh and consider that not many wise, powerful, or noble people were chosen through whom you might be called, but very few fishermen, uneducated men, and poor people. Hence he appropriately continues: “But God chose the foolish things of the world” [Note: [Col. 0302D] The Vulgate reads: “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong.”] “to confound the strong; and God chose the ignoble and contemptible things.” [Col. 0302D]

This statement can be referred both to the matter and to the persons. If it refers to the matter, he calls the virgin’s birth and the Lord’s passion or death weak, foolish, ignoble, and contemptible—not because they truly are so, but because they were judged so by the wise of this age. God chose these things to confound the wise and strong, when they saw many believing what the few denied. [Col. 0302C]

If, however, it refers to the persons, he calls Christ’s apostles the foolish, weak, ignoble, and contemptible things of the world, because, in comparison with the wise, strong, and noble, they were judged foolish, weak, ignoble, and contemptible by the lovers of this world.

The Lord acted with marvelous skill. He did not wish to choose wise, powerful, rich, or noble men to preach the Gospel, lest they believe that they had been chosen on account of their own merits, and lest anyone have occasion to say that Christ’s faithful and the fame of his name had spread throughout the world not by the cunning of human wisdom, or by power, wealth, or nobility. [Col. 0302D] He did not wish to convert a fisherman through an orator; rather, through a fisherman he won over an orator.

The great Cyprian was an orator; but greater than he was Peter the fisherman, through whom not only an orator but also an emperor came to believe. This is why the Lord praised Nathanael above others (John I, 45), yet did not assume him to the dignity of the apostolate.

“And things that are not”—one may indeed supply: “truly ignoble and contemptible”—“to destroy the things that are” (similarly, “truly ignoble and contemptible”).

[Col. 0303A] Alternatively, when he says “things that are not,” we should understand the despised people of this world, namely Christ’s apostles, who, because they did not possess the glory of the world, were judged as though they did not exist. Likewise, when he adds, “to destroy the things that are,” we must understand the glorious and exalted things that were thought to exist because they consisted in worldly glory.

Thus it is said: “He chose the things that are not,” that is, the despised, “to destroy the things that are,” that is, the glorious. We know that this was accomplished: at the preaching of the apostles, many kings and rulers of this age were confounded and overthrown, and submitted themselves to Christ’s humble yoke.

But why the Lord chose these things, the Apostle makes clear when he adds: “So that no flesh might glory in his sight” [Col. 0303B]. “All flesh” may be understood as all carnal knowledge, so that the sense is: “So that no flesh might glory in his sight,” that is, so that all carnal knowledge might blush and be confounded before God himself as judge. It is carnal understanding to doubt that God’s power could enable a virgin to give birth, or that a dead man could be restored to life.

More fittingly, however, “all flesh” is understood as every human being, the whole being named from a part. The sense is then: God chose the weak and despised things of the world without any preceding merits, so that no human being might have anything for which he could rightly glory in himself before God—as though he had said openly: “So that no human being might glory before him in his own merits.”

This statement therefore embraces everyone, both the just and the unjust. The unjust, because they possess nothing, have no basis for glorying; the just, although they have something in which they could glory, nevertheless glory not in themselves but in God (II Cor. X, 17).

What, then, remains for those who are to be saved? Nothing other than the grace of the one who shows mercy. But lest the saints perhaps think that they had been left without glory, he adds: “But of him you are in Christ Jesus,” as though he were saying: Do not think that you have been left without glory. You ought to glory in God through Jesus Christ, because by God’s grace you have been called to faith in Christ and made members of him. For from him—that is, from God, who is omnipotent—you are in Christ Jesus, that is, in the faith of Christ Jesus.

God’s purpose was that believers should recognize through Christ the truth and mercy of God. The truth is the mystery of the Trinity; mercy is that by which we were redeemed when we were captives. [Col. 0303D]

Therefore, to show who this Christ Jesus was, he added: “Who was made for us by God wisdom, and justice, and sanctification, and redemption.” To confirm the faithful, he shows that Christ acted in all that he did according to the Father’s will, so that they might recognize and know that through Christ they had received true wisdom, justice, sanctification, and redemption. For no one redeems anything except what belongs to him.

But when he says, “Who was made for us wisdom,” this must not be referred to his divinity, in which he did all things with the Father and in which he himself was made by no one, having been begotten by him before all ages. In the form, therefore, of his humanity, he was made wisdom for us by God, because he was conceived and born of a virgin by the grace of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0304A]

He who in the substance of his divinity was truly the Father’s wisdom was made wisdom for us through his humanity, because through him we learned true wisdom, that is, knowledge of the Trinity.

Likewise, he who in his deity was the Father’s justice was made justice for us through his humanity, because by believing in him and confessing him as the Son of God, we were incorporated into him and thereby justified. The more closely anyone adheres to him, the more he is justified. For it is just that, when all else has been rejected, the Creator alone should be venerated and adored.

He was also made sanctification, because through him we have been cleansed not only from idolatry and our own sins, but also from every defilement of mind and body. [Col. 0304B]

Finally, because this sanctification was accomplished through his passion, he appropriately adds: “And redemption.” The offering of Christ’s body was our redemption. For this was the price he gave for us to the devil: when he offered himself to God the Father on the altar of the cross, he took away from us in himself every opposition of sin. For this reason he allowed the devil, who desired to kill him, to do so, so that, when the devil handed him over, though innocent, to an undeserved death, he might lose us, whom he held under a just obligation; and thus he might free us, his captives, from the devil’s power.

[Col. 0304C] Therefore, since he showed in what the saints ought to glory, he added prophetic testimony to demonstrate this more clearly, saying: “So that, as it is written,” namely in Jeremiah, “He who glories, let him glory in the Lord” (Jer. IX, 23).

It is fitting, and very necessary, that whoever glories should glory in the Lord, since he will not be confounded forever. Thus a person glories in the Lord if he does not say or believe that all the good he recognizes in himself is his own, but rather God’s, from whom he received it—that is, if he understands that he received from him not only what he is, but also the fact that he is good, from the one who gave him existence, in accordance with James: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James I, 17).

Let all, therefore, who adore idols and glory in their images be confounded (Ps. CXVI, 7). [Col. 0304D] For, as another prophet says: “The gods of the nations do not bring rain, nor did they make heaven and earth” (Jer. XIV, 22). Hence it is written: “The gods who did not make heaven or earth, let them perish from the earth” (Jer. X, 11). Let those also be confounded who glory in men, whom they know to possess no virtue. Hence again it is written: “Vain is the hope of man” (Tob. II, 22). And likewise: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm” (Jer. XVII, 5).

[Note: [Col. 0303D] In the autograph margin, chapter VII is read here.]

## Chapter II

“And I, when I came to you, brothers, came not in loftiness of speech or wisdom, proclaiming to you the testimony of Christ.” [Col. 0305A]

What he taught above in words he now confirms by his own example (I Cor. I, 17). Since above he gradually set forth the form of our discipline, he now, recalling the past, proves that he had delivered it in no other way than he had demonstrated: namely, that he came in humility of speech and in the foolishness of preaching—as it was judged by the wise of this age—and proclaimed to them the testimony of Christ, that is, the report that God had become man, had died, and had been buried, and so forth.

It should be known, however, that in certain manuscripts one finds: “the mystery of God.” “The testimony of Christ” is appropriately called “the mystery of God,” because the Word of God, hidden while remaining God with God, was hidden from ages and generations in two ways: by foreknowledge or predestination, and in figure.

It was hidden by foreknowledge and predestination because the mystery of his Incarnation was foreknown and predestined by God the Father before the ages. It was also hidden in figure, both in the legal writings and in the prophetic writings. [Col. 0305B]

He calls “loftiness of speech” the brilliance of eloquence and the charm of words. Heretics devoted themselves to these things, and the Corinthians, deceived by them, gloried in them. Fearing that they might appear foolish to the wise of this world, they sought to commend their doctrine by perverse eloquence, following human wisdom, and thus they emptied Christ’s cross of its power.

It should also be noted that the passages in which the Apostle rebukes the Corinthians appear to be closed off. Nevertheless, it must be understood that he condemns worldly wisdom in them as contrary to divine religion.

[Col. 0305C] Wishing to show what he had preached to them, or what he had judged himself to know among them, he added: “For I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.”

Here one must ask why he says that he preached only Christ crucified [Note: [Col. 0305] The verb “says” is missing; I judged that it, or an equivalent word, necessarily had to be added.]. Did he not also preach his birth and everything that he accomplished as a man? Did he not also establish rules for their conduct?

If, therefore, he preached only Christ crucified, what is meant by his later statement: “For I delivered to you first of all what I also received: that the Lord Jesus died according to the Scriptures, and that he rose again, and that he was seen by Cephas,” and what follows (I Cor. XV, 3–5)?

Accordingly, notice that he did not say only “Christ crucified,” but “Jesus Christ”; then he added: “And him crucified.” Christ Jesus, therefore, is himself the Son of God, born of a virgin, laid in a manger, praised by angels, recognized by shepherds, and worshiped by Magi. He himself delivered the Gospel and shone forth in miracles. [Col. 0305D]

All these things belong to Christ crucified, that is, to Christ who suffered in the flesh. Hence blessed Augustine says: To evangelize Christ Jesus is not only to preach the things that must be believed about him, but also everything that pertains to forming the conduct of the faithful.

But because the salvation of the human race is contained especially in the mystery of the cross, the Apostle therefore declares that he knew nothing among the Corinthians except Christ crucified. He declares that he knew among them what they ought to learn through him; but he says that he did not know what they, because they were carnal, were unable to learn—namely, the higher mysteries of Christ’s divinity. The expression is formed in the same manner as “a blind pit,” which is so called because it is hidden. [Col. 0306A]

“And I was with you in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling.” Behold, the Apostle says that he was among the Corinthians in weakness; and this was not enough, but he added: “and in fear.” To intensify the statement, he also added: “and in much trembling.”

By these words he shows that, while announcing Christ crucified to the Corinthians in the foolishness of preaching, he aroused much hatred and persecution against himself, as though he were announcing to them a vain doctrine hostile both to Jews and Gentiles.

[Col. 0306B] “And my speech,” that is, my doctrine and preaching, “was not in persuasive words of human wisdom.” Persuasive words are words adorned with the surface brilliance of eloquence. The evangelical doctrine does not need these things, because it commends itself by its own power; human wisdom, however, needs the ornament of eloquence in order to appear to be something great, since it is supported by no reason or power.

By these words he shows that he did not wish to please human wisdom, lest he appear to be seeking its favor.

He explains in what his preaching consisted when he adds: “But in the demonstration of the Spirit and of power,” that is, in the performance of miracles, which were accomplished through the grace and power of the Holy Spirit. For he confirmed everything he taught by miracles, in accordance with the words of the evangelist Mark: “But they went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (Mark XVI, 10). [Col. 0306C]

But it should be understood that things which are foolish according to their substance are weak and of no importance; when adorned with the brilliance of words, however, they appear wise and to possess something great. Therefore the Lord did not wish to commend evangelical doctrine by words, but by the power of the Holy Spirit.

Hence the following is appropriately added: “So that your faith might not be in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God.” The sense is: Do not ascribe what you believe, the fact that you have now become believers, to human wisdom, lest you perhaps complain that you have been deceived by its cunning; rather, ascribe it to the grace of the Holy Spirit, who is the power of God.

That the Holy Spirit is the power of God, the Lord makes clear when he says: “But remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke XXIV, 49). [Col. 0306D]

Therefore, since he had said that he knew nothing else among the Corinthians except Jesus Christ, and him crucified, lest he perhaps be thought truly foolish, he added: “But we speak wisdom among the perfect.”

It is as though he said: Do not think us foolish, we who announce Christ to you in the foolishness of preaching, for we speak wisdom among the perfect.

He calls perfect those who believed, on the testimony of the power of the cross of Christ, that it was true wisdom, and who possessed faith not so much in words as in deeds—that is, those who fulfilled their faith by their works. Alternatively, he calls perfect those who spoke in the tongues of all and who, for the salvation of others, sometimes revealed the secrets of the heart by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Among these, therefore, he spoke wisdom, because he preached to them the hidden mysteries concerning Christ’s birth. [Col. 0307A]

What wisdom he spoke, he makes clear when he adds: “Yet not the wisdom of this age.” He rightly says “not of this age,” because this age cannot grasp the divine reason and wisdom on account of the weakness of earthly thought.

Notice that, by saying “not of this age,” he shows that it belongs to the age to come, in which the truth—that is, the true wisdom of God—will appear even to those who deny it. [Col. 0307B]

There is also a human wisdom which judges that only those things should be believed true which seem in some way compatible with human reason. Divine wisdom, however, transcends every limit of human knowledge.

Hence he immediately continues: “Nor of the rulers of this age.” For if it does not belong to the rulers of the age, much less does it belong to their subjects. By the rulers of the age he calls the devil and his attendants, who rule over the lovers of this age.

Divine wisdom therefore does not belong to the rulers of the age, because evangelical doctrine and the Christian religion destroy and scatter all the errors which they have implanted in the human race. Hence it is immediately added: “who are being destroyed.”

Here John says: “For this reason, he says, the Son of God came to undo the works of the devil” (I John III, 8).

“But we speak the wisdom of God” [Col. 0307C], that is, the Son of God, who is the wisdom of God the Father—or certainly the evangelical preaching, “in a mystery, which has been hidden.”

He aptly says “in a mystery,” because, as has already been said, it was hidden from ages and generations in two ways. It is called hidden because it is not in words but in the power of the Holy Spirit; it cannot be grasped by human reason, but is credible through the efficacy of the Holy Spirit.

He therefore shows that he was sent especially for this purpose: to preach a hidden meaning and hidden knowledge which neither the rulers nor the powers of this age had known, and which the world itself had not heard.

“Which God predestined for our glory before the ages.” By these words he shows that he preaches true wisdom, so much so that he asserts that it existed with God the Father before the ages and was predestined for our glory. [Col. 0307D]

For before the ages it was predestined that the Son of God should die for the salvation of human beings. He calls “our glory” the glory of those of us who have believed, both Jews and Gentiles.

It is therefore clear that, if this wisdom was predestined for the glory of believers, it was also predestined for the confusion of unbelievers.

Therefore, to show that this wisdom was hidden from the rulers and powers, he added: “Which none of the rulers of this age knew.”

The rulers of the age, both here and above, may, as some think, be understood as the elders of the Jews, namely the scribes and Pharisees, or as the various exalted powers of the Romans. [Col. 0308A]

But the elders of the Jews cannot be understood, since they were subject to Roman rule. Nor can the exalted Roman authorities rightly be understood here, since they themselves did not crucify the Lord. Of one of them it is written that he said: “I find no cause of death in this man” (Luke XXIII, 5; John XIX, 4). Hence, after taking water, he washed his hands before the people, saying: “I am innocent of the blood of this just man” (Matt. XXVII, 24).

Accordingly, both here and above, the rulers of the age are aptly understood as those whom Christ openly triumphed over in himself, namely the demons. Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and powers, against the world-rulers of this darkness” (Eph. VI, 12), and so forth. [Col. 0308B]

The Lord was crucified according to their counsel and will. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “Behold, the ruler of this world is coming, and he has found nothing in me” (John XIV, 30).

Luke the evangelist also writes, after recounting the Lord’s temptations: “And the devil departed from him until an opportune time” (Luke IV, 13).

If, then, the rulers of the age are to be understood as the devil and his attendants, what are we to make of what follows: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory,” when Luke, recounting that the Lord cast out demons, writes among other things: “And he did not allow them to speak” [Note: [Col. 0307D] Luke IV, 41. The Vulgate reads “them” (*ea*).] “because they knew him to be the Christ”; and Mark: “because they knew him” (Mark I, 34)? [Col. 0308C]

Accordingly, as some think, they knew that he was the Christ who had been promised in the Law and the Prophets; nevertheless, they did not know the mystery that he was the Son of God.

It is more properly understood, however, that when they saw the power of his miracles, they were overcome and compelled by the presence of his majesty, confessed him to be the Son of God, and recognized—or rather suspected—that he was the Christ. But they did not know that they were to be condemned by his death. Therefore the Apostle says: “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.”

Again, one must ask why he calls him “the Lord of glory” crucified, since the Lord of glory cannot suffer, be crucified, or die. Divinity is entirely impassible.

It must therefore be understood that this was said because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 14), that is, God became man and lived among human beings. Divinity was so joined to humanity that one and the same Christ was true God and true man. [Col. 0308D]

Hence in the Gospel: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven” (John III, 13).

If we attend to the distinction of substances, only the Son of God descended from heaven, and only the Son of man was crucified on earth. But if we attend to the unity of the person, the Son of man descended from heaven, was already then in heaven, and the Son of God, the Lord of glory, was crucified on earth.

He was therefore crucified not by the power of his divinity, but through the weakness of the flesh. He is called the Lord of glory not only because he himself is glory, but also because, by glorifying his saints, he makes them shine with miracles and virtues. [Col. 0309A]

[Note: [Col. 0309D] In the autograph margin, chapter VIII is read here.]

Moreover, to show to whom the wisdom of God was revealed, he also added the testimony of the prophet. The phrase “believers recognized” is understood: as it is written, namely in Isaiah: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (Isa. LXIV, 4).

By this statement he shows that God suddenly accomplished something unexpected, unheard-of, and hidden from ages and generations, sending his Son from heaven to earth, who, having been incarnate and made man, was born of a virgin. This was something that not only human perception but even angelic nature itself could not comprehend. [Col. 0309B]

What he said above he now confirms by prophetic testimony: it is not surprising that human beings did not recognize the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation, since it was hidden even from the rulers of the age.

Nevertheless, they are rightly condemned, because, although the words of the preaching caused them offense, they ought nevertheless to have given faith to the miracles. The power of signs ought to have been set above human ignorance and weakness; and they ought in every respect to have believed what appeared impossible to human reason.

This ineffable gift, therefore, the eye did not see, because it is not a color; the ear did not hear, because it is not a sound; it did not enter into the heart of man, because it is not an earthly thought.

Earthly thoughts ascend into the human heart from below; but from above every good thing descends, in accordance with James’s words (James I, 17). [Col. 0309C]

Alternatively, according to certain copies, “it did not descend into the heart of man,” because the human heart ascends there, in accordance with the words of the Prophet: “He arranged an ascent in his heart, in the valley of weeping and tears” (Ps. LXXXIII, 7).

To where? To the place which he appointed, namely, where he might taste the sweetness of heavenly glory. When this gift was therefore in John’s heart, John was already above humanity, because his heart had ascended to the appointed place.

Likewise, the eye had not seen a virgin giving birth; the ear had not previously heard: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of my Father” (Matt. XIII, 43). It had not entered into the heart of man that he should be an heir of God and a co-heir with Jesus Christ (Rom. VIII, 17).

God prepared these splendid and ineffable gifts, therefore—of which he says elsewhere, “All things have been handed over to me by my Father” (Matt. XI, 27)—that is, he preordained them, not for everyone, but for those who believe in him and love him. [Col. 0309D]

The Apostle, therefore, to show that he and those like him belonged among those who love God, added:

[Note: [Col. 0310D] In the autograph margin, chapter IX is read here.]

“But God has revealed them to us through his Spirit.” It is as though he said: We have recognized what the eye has not seen, nor the ear heard, nor entered into the heart of man, because God has revealed it—that is, made it manifest.

He revealed it plainly not because our merits demanded it, but by the grace of his mercy and kindness. This is what he means when he says: “Through his Spirit,” that is, through the grace of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0310A]

For through faith we receive the Holy Spirit, who reveals to us the will and secrets of God. The things of God cannot be known except through the Spirit of God.

Notice also that he shows himself to have been sent for this purpose: not only to preach so great a sacrament to human beings, but also to the rulers of the age, so that, through his evangelizing, those who are in the corporeal heavens and those who dwell beneath the elements of the firmament might learn how great a good they lost when, through pride, they fell and abandoned their proper dwelling.

He is therefore a unique preacher, who attained such grace. For either no one, or scarcely anyone, could so explain the mystery of the Trinity. Hence, by divine judgment, he was rightly called the vessel of election.

Therefore, lest we think that he was speaking of an angelic or light [Col. 0310B] spirit, he added:

“For the Spirit searches all things,” namely, the Holy Spirit.

The sense is: We recognize what the rulers of the age did not recognize because that Spirit teaches us—the Spirit who searches. Since the Holy Spirit is both from God and himself God, he therefore knows naturally everything that belongs to God.

He adds “the deep things of God” to show that the Spirit himself naturally knows all God’s power and foreknowledge, something utterly impossible for a creature. Thus the Holy Spirit is shown to be truly God, not a creature but the Creator.

He searches all things not because he is ignorant and seeks to find, but because he leaves nothing unknown. He searches not in order to discover, since he knows everything; rather, the Spirit who has been given to you makes you search. For what you do by his benefit is said to be done by him, without whom you cannot do it. [Col. 0310C]

To show openly that the Holy Spirit searches all things, he also added an analogy, saying:

“For who among human beings knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being, which is in him?”

Human nature consists of body and spirit, which they also call the soul. The spirit of a human being is the rational power of the soul, by which it is distinguished from animals and rules over them according to natural law.

It is of this spirit that he says: “Who among human beings knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being, which is in him?” It is as though he were saying plainly: It is not the spirit that is outside you, but the one within you—your mind—that knows all your thoughts and purposes; for these are our inner things.

Indeed, no one can comprehend these things except our mind, which the Apostle calls spirit. [Col. 0310D]

“So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God.” It is as though he said: Because the Holy Spirit is of one substance with God, he too naturally knows everything that belongs to God, and he teaches us.

He also teaches the mystery of Christ, because he is not only the Spirit of the Father but also of the Son. No one, therefore, knows the things of God except the Spirit of God, because whoever knows them knows them through the Spirit of God.

For this has been said in the same way as the statement in the Gospel: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of my Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X, 20).

[Col. 0311A] Therefore, since he had said that God revealed these things to us through his Spirit, lest anyone perhaps believe that the Apostle and those like him had received the spirit of the world, through which they might know future things, he commended the grace of God in the Holy Spirit by adding:

[Note: [Col. 0311D] In the autograph margin, chapter X is read here.]

“But we have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God.”

It is as though he said: It is proved that we have not received the spirit of the world by the fact that we know the secrets of God, which the spirit of the world cannot comprehend.

By “the spirit of the world” he means the spirit of exaltation and pride. For all who receive the spirit of the world become proud and ungrateful toward God, and therefore are made miserable. The Spirit who is from God, however, is the Spirit of charity and love.

Alternatively, by “the spirit of the world” he means the spirit of Python, that is, the spirit of divination (Deut. XVIII, 11; I Kings XXVIII, 7; Isa. VIII, 19; Acts XVI, 16), which is the chief among worldly spirits. All fanatics, diviners, and soothsayers who are without God are seized by this spirit. [Col. 0311B]

Seized by this spirit, the pythoness raised Samuel for Saul (I Kings XXVIII, 14). Through the Sibyl this spirit also spoke and foretold many things about Christ. In certain respects it even followed the thoughts of the holy prophets, cunningly wishing to secure a place among the heavenly spirits.

Although it sometimes proclaims true things, at other times, through things that resemble the truth, it is itself deceived and deceives others.

But as someone might say: “How do you prove, Apostle, that you have received the Spirit who is from God?” he added: “So that we may know the gifts that have been given to us by God.”

It is as though he said: “A servant does not know what his master is doing. But we, beloved, have received the Spirit who is from God so that we may be able to be God’s friends, and so that we may know what the Lord our God is doing.” [Col. 0311C]

We have received the Spirit who is from God so that we may not glory in God’s gifts as though we had received them through our own merits, but may give thanks to him from whom we received them.

Many people possess many gifts of God, but do not know from whom they have received them; therefore they boast in proud vanity.

If we had received the spirit of the world, we could in no way know the gifts bestowed on us by God, for inferior things cannot comprehend the counsel of superior things. Nor can a creature know the will of its Creator unless he reveals it.

It is indeed great knowledge to know from whom one has received the very gift one possesses.

[Col. 0311D] “Which we also speak.” The meaning is this: It is most clearly demonstrated that we know what has been given to us by God because we speak these very things so that others may learn through spiritual teaching. How he spoke, however, he makes clear by adding: “Not in words taught by human wisdom,” that is, words adorned with the polish of eloquence. The meaning is: Since what we speak did not come to us from rhetoricians, dialecticians, or philosophers, we do not therefore speak it in words colored by the charm of human knowledge. For the words of human wisdom cannot grasp this meaning; nor is it learned through the study of any art, but it is conceived through spiritual reasoning by faith, in accordance with the saying: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. VI, 9; Matt. XIII, 14; Mark IV, 12; Luke VIII, 10; Acts XXVIII, 26; Rom. XI, 8; Heb. XI, 3).

“But in the teaching of the Spirit,” that is, in the teaching produced by the Holy Spirit, namely, the Gospel. Alternatively: He spoke “in the teaching of the Spirit” because, through the power of the Holy Spirit, he confirmed whatever he preached by signs and miracles. “Comparing spiritual things with spiritual.” He calls spiritual those who denied that human wisdom could transmit the grace of God. For the grace of God is contained in the mystery of faith, to enlighten the understanding of well-disposed people. Therefore, all who believe what the wise men of the world judge foolish are rightly called spiritual. Hence the Apostle compared spiritual things with spiritual, because he judged those to be spiritual who believed that what the wisdom of the world denied possible could in fact be done.

“But the natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God.” Whoever lives according to the body is rightly called carnal and natural. He is carnal because he follows carnal things; natural because his soul is carried away in dissolute wantonness, since the spirit does not govern it, and because he himself does not submit to being governed by God. The natural man, then, lives according to himself; that is, he presses his understanding down upon the earth, thinking about and desiring only earthly things. For this reason he does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God, because he does not understand what benefit the cross of Christ confers. Since he believes that nothing will exist after death, he is governed neither by the restraint of self-control nor by the rational judgment of the mind, but is dragged toward earthly pleasures and desires like an animal rushing headlong. When he hears that God has begotten a Son or that a virgin has given birth, he laughs, because he does not believe that anyone can be born without the union of male and female. Again, because he considers nothing to exist after death, when he hears that bodies dissolved into corruption can be brought back to life, he mocks it.

Hence it immediately adds: “For it is foolishness to him, and he cannot understand.” The meaning is: He cannot understand because he judges foolish whatever he cannot establish by his own reasoning. He judges foolish whatever he sees that he himself does not know. “Because it is spiritually examined,” that is, judged and condemned. It is spiritually examined because, by the just requirements of his own deserts, he is spiritually blinded so that he cannot understand.

[Col. 0312D] “But the spiritual man judges all things.” The spiritual man is one who is governed by the Holy Spirit and therefore judges that all things are possible for God. The spiritual man’s reasoning and judgment are therefore true, since through his faith and the example of his good works the unbelief and conduct of the wicked are condemned, according to the saying: “But whoever does not believe is already judged” (John III, 18).

Since, then, the judgment of the natural man, that is, of the unbeliever, is false, while that of the spiritual man, that is, of the believer, is true, it appropriately adds: “And he himself is judged by no one”—that is, he is condemned by no one, because he is saved through faith.

Alternatively: “The spiritual man judges all things” because he is above all things, since he is with God. And because he is with God, he sees with the utmost purity, and whatever he sees he loves with complete charity. He judges all things because whatever he finds to be right he approves, and whatever is wrong he rejects—in the works, conduct, fasts, almsgiving, thoughts, and all other matters of the faithful that may be judged and corrected. “But he himself is judged by no one,” that is, by no human being, but by the law alone, according to which he judges all things.

Alternatively: The spiritual man judges all those things to be vain and false in which the lovers of the world delight. He judges all things because in the divine Scriptures he follows the intention of each teacher, considers the force of every word, and understands that the command must be fulfilled which the Lord gives: “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matt. V, 39; Luke VI, 29); and likewise what the Apostle says: “We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what is proper to his body, according to what he has done” (Rom. XIV, 10; II Cor. V, 10). “But he himself is judged by no one,” because none of the carnal can penetrate his understanding.

Therefore, since the Corinthians were attempting by their own wisdom to criticize what God had commanded to be done spiritually, the Apostle added, in order to rebuke them: “For who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct him?” It is as though he said: Who among you knows God’s counsel, so as to accuse or criticize him? He calls “counsel” in God the mind, will, and dispensation according to which he himself commanded things to be done, so that the wisdom of the world might be shown to be foolish when what it denied could happen did happen—namely, the Word becoming flesh. Whoever, therefore, accepts this mind of the Lord is not displeased with what has been done, nor does he seek to instruct God, that is, to correct his counsel; rather, he praises his omnipotence, according to which he did what the wisdom of the world denied could happen.

Hence it immediately follows: “But we have the mind of Christ.” The meaning is: Because you do not have the mind of Christ, you attempt to criticize God; but we praise his omnipotence because we have the mind of God—that is, by believing in God, we share in divine knowledge.

Alternatively: “We have the mind of Christ” because, while we believe in God, we judge that all things are possible for him, just as Christ says in the Gospel: “All things are possible with God” (Luke XVIII, 27). For whoever denies that God can do all things denies that he made all things from nothing.

Next follows: [Note: [Col. 0313D] In the autograph’s margin, chapter XI is written here.]

**(CHAP. III.)** “And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal.” It is as though he said: O Corinthians, when I came to you, I carefully perceived your dullness and recognized that you lacked the capacity for spiritual teaching. Therefore I could not speak to you as spiritual people—that is, the wisdom that we speak among the perfect. By these words he addresses those who were carnal because they were still serving carnal desires.

Hence he immediately repeats the same point by way of comparison, saying: “As infants in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not food.” Here the Apostle clearly teaches that the mysteries entrusted to infants in the faith of Christ must be those which they are able to grasp. If great mysteries are entrusted to them, they are immediately scandalized and the faith of Christ is extinguished in them, just as infants, unless they are nourished with milk, grow weak and die if they take solid food. Thus the Corinthians, although they had already been reborn—for the Apostle addresses those who had been reborn and therefore calls them brothers—were nevertheless not worthy to have entrusted to them what belonged to spiritual people. After receiving the faith of Christ, which is like a spiritual seed, they had not thereafter taken pains to return any fruit of good works to God, so as to deserve to hear words of perfection and spiritual teaching.

[Col. 0314B] This eminent preacher, a divine man and spiritual physician, examined the strength and capacity of each person and formed the words of his preaching according to each one’s condition. Yet he did not preach one thing secretly and another publicly, one thing to crowds and another in private rooms; his preaching was one and the same. For he did not judge that he knew anything among the Corinthians except Christ, and Christ crucified.

Thus it was said: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal,” as though it meant: You received what he spoke not as spiritual people but as carnal. For those who said, “I belong to Paul; I to Apollo; I to Cephas,” received Christ Jesus crucified in one way; those whose cry was, “But I belong to Christ,” received him in another way—and these latter he praises at the beginning of this epistle. [Col. 0314C] The former therefore needed milk; the latter, solid food.

By milk the sweetness and pleasantness of preaching are signified; by food, profound preaching, perfected according to the principles of spiritual teaching and full of heavenly mysteries. Christ, therefore, who had been the bread of angels, remaining the Word in the beginning, God with God, became milk because “the Word became flesh.”

Of these carnal and spiritual people the Prophet says: “Yours is the day, and yours is the night” (Ps. LXXIII, 16)—that is, both the spiritual and the carnal are yours; the spiritual belong to you, and the carnal belong to you. You enlighten the former with unchanging truth and wisdom; the latter you console by the manifestation of the flesh, like the moon consoling the nights. When, therefore, spiritual people speak spiritual things to spiritual people, “day pours forth the word to day” (Ps. XVIII, 3). But because carnal people too announce the faith of Christ crucified to carnal people in some fashion, “night declares knowledge to night” (ibid.).

“For you were not yet able; and even now you are not able.” It is as though he said: What wonder is it that you were unable then, when even now you remain in the same weakness of mind and infancy of faith? Why they could not is revealed when he adds: “For you are still carnal.” This sentence rebukes those who, reborn through baptism and having obtained remission of sins, nevertheless after baptism returned to the way of life of the old man, whom they had renounced.

[Col. 0315A] Therefore, to show why he had called them carnal, he added: “For since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal and walking according to man?” There was jealousy and strife among the Corinthians because they were divided by their love for human beings. There was jealousy because they envied one another; there was strife because, while each was inflamed against the other on behalf of his love for his teachers, they were worn out by various quarrels.

But it should be noted that, after saying, “Are you not carnal?” he did not add, “And do you walk according to the flesh,” but “according to man.” It must be understood, however, that walking according to the flesh is the same as walking according to man. For whoever lives according to himself walks according to man and, consequently, according to the flesh, because he satisfies carnal desires. [Col. 0315B] Since the first man walked according to himself, satisfying the pleasures of the flesh, he therefore withdrew from God.

When the Apostle was giving the reasons why he had called them carnal, he said: “And you walk according to man,” as though he were saying: Because you live according to yourselves, you walk according to man, not according to God. For if you had walked according to God, you would certainly be gods. Whoever places his hope in a human being is therefore rightly called carnal. Conversely, whoever rejects human assistance and hopes for help from God is rightly called spiritual, because God, who dwells in him, is spirit.

“When one says, ‘I indeed belong to Paul,’ and another, ‘I belong to Apollo,’ are you not human?” Paul and Apollo were united in the unity of the spirit and the bond of peace. But the Corinthians had begun to divide them and to become puffed up against one another on behalf of one or the other, not knowing the things that are of the Spirit of God. Therefore, wishing them to be angels or gods, the Apostle rebukes them so sharply because in these quarrels they did not understand what belonged to God but what belonged to human beings.

He says, then: “When one says, ‘I indeed belong to Paul,’ and so forth.” Here it should be noted that he began with his own person, lest he appear to be defaming others out of envy and wishing to commend himself. And he appropriately says: “Are you not human?” For just as those who glory in God and hope for help from him are called not only sons of God by adoption but also gods, so those who glory in human beings and place their hope in them are called not only human beings [Col. 0315D] but also carnal. The Lord shows both in one statement when he speaks through the Prophet: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High’; but you shall die like human beings” (Ps. LXXXI, 6; John X, 34)—that is, like carnal people.

Therefore, to show that it was a great evil and a great error among the Corinthians, and an insult to God when they rendered his honor to human beings, he added: “What then is Apollo? And what is Paul?” Since someone might have answered: “The Apostles are gods,” he therefore continued: “Ministers of him through whom you believed.” [Note: [Col. 0315D] The Vulgate has “to whom you believed.”] It is as though he were saying plainly: Because they are ministers, hope must not be placed in them, but in the one whose ministers they are. Honor, glory, and thanksgiving are owed to him from whom the gift also comes. For these men, who are servants, must minister even unwillingly, as Moses, Jonah, and Elijah did.

Thus, as far as God’s honor is concerned, a human being is nothing; but with regard to the office he holds, he is to be honored, though as a servant. Hence it immediately adds: “And to each, as the Lord gave” [understand: “so he ministers”]. For as the Lord gave—that is, willed, predestined, and foreknew—so he distributed the duties of ministry.

Therefore, to show the diversity of gifts and the variety of offices [Note: [Col. 0316D] The autograph has “truth” here.], he added: “I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth.” Paul planted because he evangelized the word of Christ to the Corinthians and converted them to the faith; this is what planting means. Apollo watered because he baptized them with solemn words and strengthened them in the faith of Christ; this is designated by the name of watering. For this Apollo was a Corinthian and, after the Apostle’s preaching, labored greatly among his fellow citizens by baptizing them and strengthening them in the faith.

But because the forgiveness of sins and the bestowal of the grace of the Holy Spirit belong to God alone, he appropriately added: “But God gave the growth.” Since progress and the increase of salvation come not from a human being but from God, there is no glory belonging to man. As has been said, when compared with the honor of God, a human being is nothing; but with regard to the office he holds, he must be honored—not, however, to God’s insult, as though hope were to be placed in him, but as a servant.

Hence he fittingly adds: “Therefore neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything.” It is as though he were saying: What has been planted and watered does not ordinarily reach the result of fruitfulness unless God makes it grow and supplies it with life. We who speak to you are therefore like laborers who plant, water, and apply careful cultivation; but they cannot give greenness to the bark, produce leaves, or bring forth fruit. So too we preach outwardly in vain unless the one who created and redeemed you, and through baptism bestowed remission of sins, is present.

The teacher who teaches inwardly is present; Christ teaches inwardly; Christ teaches; his anointing teaches. If his anointing and inspiration do not teach inwardly, words resound outwardly in vain. Therefore it adds: “But the one who gives the growth is God.” If God gives it, and Christ is God, then Christ, God, gives the growth.

“But the one who plants and the one who waters are one.” Whenever the word “one” is found in the divine Scriptures without anything being added, even when several are called one, one substance and one essence are to be understood—not divided or opposed. The one who plants and the one who waters are therefore one because they are of one condition, namely, servants hired for their labor; and therefore each awaits the reward of his own labor.

Hence it immediately follows: “But each will receive his own reward according to his labor.” For the more someone has labored, the greater remuneration he will receive. The meaning is: Although they are servants, although they are ministers, although all are hired laborers, nevertheless, because their offices are different, their rewards will also be different. Since planting is more than watering, the reward will therefore be unequal.

But to show why they were worthy to receive a reward, he added: [Note: [Col. 0317D] In the autograph’s margin, chapter XII is written here.] “For we are God’s assistants.” This is expressed more clearly in Greek, where it reads: “For we are participants in God’s work.” Some copies also read: “We are God’s fellow workers.” Whatever the wording, it signifies one and the same thing.

The saints of God are therefore his assistants because, by admonishing, preaching, and baptizing, they help outwardly those whom God enlightens inwardly by forgiving sins and bestowing the grace of the Holy Spirit. They are God’s assistants in office, not in power, in accordance with the saying: “As the Father sent me, so I also send you” (John XX, 21). This sentence therefore applies especially to the Apostles, for they were Christ’s vicars.

“You are God’s cultivation, you are God’s building.” They were God’s cultivation because through the Apostle’s preaching God inspired their hearts and converted them to the faith; and, after the remission of sins through the washing of baptism and the gift of the Holy Spirit, he cultivated their character so that they might bring forth the fruits of good works. They were also God’s building because the one who gave them faith increased their other virtues by dwelling within them.

Next follows: “According to the grace of God that was given to me, as a wise architect I laid the foundation.” [Col. 0317C] Since he was about to say, “As a wise architect I laid the foundation,” lest he seem arrogantly to attribute something to himself, as though he possessed what he had not received from God, he appropriately prefaced it with: “According to the grace of God that was given to me.” Here it should be noted that he does not say “according to will” or “according to choice,” but “according to grace,” because he attributes everything to God.

He says that grace was given to him by God because he was specially chosen to be sent to preach to the Gentiles; hence he was rightly called the vessel of election. According to this grace, “as a wise architect,” he laid the foundation—that is, according to Christ’s teaching, he evangelized the word of faith to the Corinthians. A wise architect lays foundations according to the will of the author.

But because many preached to the Corinthians after him, he added: “Another builds upon it,” that is, anyone who came after me. By saying “another,” he wishes all to be understood, both good and bad preachers. The superstructure, therefore, is to be understood as what was handed on to the Corinthians by teachers of this kind. Hence, warning them, he immediately adds: “But let each one see how he builds upon it”—that is, let him weigh and consider how the superstructure agrees with the foundation, how what he preaches accords with my teaching.

For if the superstructure is crooked and worthless, while the foundation remains unmoved, when the superstructure falls it will cause a great ruin. Whoever therefore preaches badly cannot destroy the foundation—that is, the name and faith of Christ—which will remain unshaken; but his perverse teaching will perish and be destroyed, in accordance with the saying: “Every planting that my heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted” (Matt. XV, 13). This sentence therefore strikes especially at the false apostles who came after the Apostle’s preaching and, unwilling to consider his intention or imitate his teaching, deceived many of the Corinthians through their false tradition.

“Another foundation no one can lay,” and so forth. No one can lay another foundation besides the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus, because although what they preach may be heretical, they nevertheless do not dare to do so without introducing the name of Christ. They cannot commend the inventions of their error unless the dignity of so great a name makes absurd and shameful things acceptable and plausible.

He therefore says: “Another foundation,” and so forth, as though he were saying: Although there are many who preach, they do not dare to preach another Christ than the one I preached; for if they did so, their errors would immediately be detected. The sound of so great a name therefore caused the inventions and sects of the heretics to be accepted.

Next follows: “But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble,” and so forth. This apostolic statement must be counted among those passages which blessed Peter the Apostle calls difficult to understand in Paul’s letters (II Pet. III, 16); hence it has been expounded in various ways by teachers.

He calls the things that fire does not destroy “precious stones.” According to the view of some, gold, silver, and precious stones signify not works but people: gold, silver, and precious stones signify good hearers; wood, hay, and stubble, bad ones. Thus the person who builds gold, silver, and precious stones upon the foundation of faith is one who instructs his hearers well; conversely, the person who builds hay, wood, and stubble is one who instructs them badly.

“But each one’s work will become manifest,” because at the future judgment good hearers and bad hearers alike will be revealed. Hence it also follows: “For the day of the Lord will declare it, because it will be revealed in fire.” The day of the Lord, that is, the day of judgment, will declare it because it will distinguish good hearers from bad. It will be revealed in fire because the Lord will come to judgment in revealing fire.

“And the fire will test what sort of work each one’s is.” The fire will test each one’s work—that is, both good hearers and bad hearers—because it will purify the good [Note: [Col. 0317D] Here he means the purifying fire, discussed more clearly a little below], but consume the bad in an eternal conflagration.

“If anyone’s work remains which he built upon it, he will receive a reward.” The meaning is: If a teacher, through God’s mercy, has won his hearers in such a way that they escape the punishment of eternal damnation and receive eternal life, he will receive a reward for their salvation, in accordance with what the Lord says in the Gospel according to Luke: “You shall be over five cities; and you shall be over ten” (Luke XIX, 17). For the more people someone has won, the greater reward he will find.

“If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss.” That is, if bad hearers are condemned because of the demands of their own deserts, the teacher, because he was less solicitous for their salvation, will suffer loss—that is, he will undergo punishments, though purifying ones [Note: [Col. 0319D] Here is as clear as daylight the doctrine of a purifying fire lasting for a time, continually preached by the Church. Let the innovators consider this, and deny it still, if they dare, as the most ancient tradition and faith of the Church concerning this doctrine.].

Hence it immediately adds: “But he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire,” because he will be saved by his own righteousness and faith, purified through fire.

Alternatively: In this passage the Apostle mentions three things that are precious and splendid in the world—gold, silver, and precious stones—and three that are vain and worthless—wood, hay, and stubble. Hence, as some wish it, gold, silver, and precious stones signify sound, good, and catholic teaching; wood, hay, and stubble signify bad, perverse, and adulterated teaching. Thus the person who builds gold, silver, and precious stones upon the foundation of faith teaches well; the person who builds wood, hay, and stubble teaches perversely.

“But each one’s work will become manifest,” because on the day of judgment both good and adulterated teaching will be revealed to all. Hence it also follows: “For the day of the Lord will declare it, because it will be revealed in fire.” For at that time perverse teaching, which now deceives some, will be revealed to all in fire.

“And the fire will test what sort of work each one’s is,” because examination is carried out through fire. Therefore fire will test each one’s teaching; for if it finds nothing that it can burn, it will be clear that the teacher was good. Perverse teaching, however, will be fuel for the fire; this is consequently signified by wood, hay, and stubble.

“If anyone’s work remains which he built upon it, he will receive a reward”—that is, if the fire finds no stain of perverse teaching in him to burn, then he, like the three boys (Dan. III), unharmed by the fire, will receive a reward: eternal life, with the everlasting glory of blessedness.

“If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss.” The work of the bad teacher will burn because perverse teaching will perish, since it is not a substance but an accidental cause. For all evil things will then perish, like “the way of the ungodly” (Ps. I, 6). To suffer loss, however, is to undergo punishments.

“But he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire.” He says that he will be saved because the substance by which he exists will not perish, but his teaching will. But it should be noted that he does not say, “He will be saved through fire,” as though he were freed from the fire unburned by the merit of the foundation. By saying “tested through fire,” he wishes to show that the person will suffer punishment, yet will not be tortured forever like the faithless and ungodly, but will at some time be freed from the fire [Note: [Col. 0320D] What follows is the clearest demonstration of the doctrine of purgatory.], so that it may be worthwhile for him that he believed in Christ.

This interpretation, however, unless it is received carefully and soberly, is close to error. For it does not appear how he can at some time be freed from punishment here, when the Lord says: “And these will go into eternal punishment” (Matt. XXV, 46). It must be understood, however, that, as blessed Augustine says, the fire in this passage is to be understood as one through which both pass: the one who builds gold, silver, and precious stones, and the one who builds wood, hay, and stubble. For he says: “If anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, hay, and stubble.”

The fire in this passage therefore signifies the temptation of tribulation, concerning which it is said elsewhere: “The furnace tests the vessels of the potter, and temptation of tribulation tests righteous people” (Sir. XXVII, 6). This fire effects in the present life what the Apostle says here; yet it is not unbelievable that after this life it may do the same thing.

Therefore, the one who builds gold, silver, and precious stones upon the foundation of faith is the person who thinks about the things that belong to Christ, how he may please God (I Cor. VII, 32)—that is, who performs the works in which God delights. Because he understands purely, his understanding is consequently signified by gold, in accordance with the saying: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” [Note: [Col. 0320D] Compare Proverbs XXI, 20: “A desirable treasure and oil are in the dwelling of the righteous.”].

His eloquence is expressed by silver, because “the Lord’s eloquence is pure eloquence, silver tested by fire” (Ps. XI, 9). His virtues and good works are signified by precious stones, because just as fire does not corrupt precious stones, so the fire of tribulation does not consume virtues and good works.

The fire will therefore test his work, but will not burn it, because he did not love in the world those things whose loss would torment him. The day of the Lord, that is, the day of tribulation, will reveal his splendid work, like gold passing through fire. And because it will be shown to be splendid and will remain unharmed, he will receive the reward of eternal blessedness for what he built upon it. He will receive precisely what he desired.

Conversely, the person who thinks about the things of the world, how he may please his wife (I Cor. VII, 34)—that is, who performs what God abhors—builds wood, hay, and stubble. Wood, hay, and stubble therefore fittingly signify worldly thoughts and such desires for secular things as, although they may be lawful, cannot nevertheless be lost without mental anguish.

His work too will be tested by fire, because the pain of secular possessions, which he loved, will burn him if it happens that he loses them in a time of tribulation. For what was possessed with great love cannot be lost without great pain. Hence it is said shortly afterward: “If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss.” The work will burn because the substance of the world will perish. If secular possessions perish, he will suffer loss—that is, temporal damage—because he has lost what he desired.

Nevertheless, by the merit of the foundation he will be delivered if he chooses to be without those things rather than without Christ—that is, if he does not abandon Christ out of fear of losing them. This is what follows: “But he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire.” Although the pain of temporal things that he loved in the world and lost burns him, it does not consume or overthrow the foundation, which is protected by the stability and incorruptibility of faith.

Nevertheless, it must be understood that if, as blessed Augustine says, worldly thoughts and desires for secular possessions are signified by wood, hay, and stubble, the same things may also aptly signify light, venial, and minor sins, without which a human being cannot exist in this life. Hence it should be noted that when he mentioned gold, silver, and precious stones, he did not add iron, bronze, and lead, by which capital and criminal sins are signified. For whoever builds these upon the foundation—that is, after receiving the faith of Christ and the sacrament of baptism—will not be delivered through the purgatorial fire of which the Apostle speaks here unless he corrects them in this life through worthy satisfaction and amendment.

But whoever builds minor and light sins will be freed from this fire all the sooner in proportion as those sins are lighter and fewer [Note: [Col. 0321D] Here is the doctrine of purgatory, consistently transmitted from blessed Augustine down to our own times. What have the innovators to say to this?]. For, as Augustine says, the faithful will be freed from this fire more slowly or more quickly according as they have loved temporal goods more or less.

It should further be understood that, as the holy teachers have handed down, fire can operate in various ways. Whoever wishes to do so will find this in their writings.

Therefore, since he had said, “According to the grace of God that was given to me, as a wise architect I laid the foundation,” he then showed what the foundation was by saying: “No one can lay another foundation besides the one that has been laid, which is Christ.” To show toward what his intention was directed, or whose temple’s foundation he had mentioned, he added: [Note: [Col. 0321D] In the autograph’s margin, chapter XIII is written here.] “Do you not know that you are God’s temple?” It is as though he were saying: Surely you are not ignorant that you are that temple whose foundation is Christ; therefore you ought to build upon it gold, silver, and precious stones.

For he desired the Corinthians and all his hearers to strive to preserve purity of heart and body, which above all good things are acceptable to God. Hence elsewhere he says: “Pursue peace and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Heb. XII, 14). Wherever purity of mind and body is lacking, there the grace of the Holy Spirit is certainly lacking.

It should also be noted that by these words the Apostle shows that the faithful are God’s temple. Since, then, it is necessary that God dwell in his temple, they ought to live in such a way that God delights to dwell in them. It should likewise be understood that when he had said, “Do you not know that you are God’s temple?” and immediately added, “And the Spirit of God dwells in you” [Note: [Col. 0322D] The Vulgate has this text in interrogative form. In our autograph the question mark is absent.], he showed that the Holy Spirit is God and not a creature, as the heretics in their madness claim, but the Creator. For just as the Creator dwells in a creature, so he himself dwells in his temple, that is, in the Church.

Then, to terrify those who lived impurely among the Corinthians, he added: “If anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him.” This sentence strikes those who, by living impurely and corrupting their bodies, violated God’s temple—especially the man who had his father’s wife (I Cor. V, 1)—so that he might first judge himself guilty before his case was brought into the open.

But what he says is exceedingly terrifying: “If anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him.” God’s temple is violated in many ways. The person who seeks to divide the unity of the Holy Trinity violates God’s temple; the person who corrupts the holy Church with perverse doctrine or tears it apart by some schism violates God’s temple. Likewise, the person who corrupts himself by living impurely, and the person who, although preserving bodily purity, is nevertheless defiled in mind by carnal desire and polluted by delight, violates God’s temple.

To speak generally, whoever commits a sin of such a kind that it drives away the grace of God from him and excludes him from the kingdom of heaven violates God’s temple. The Lord will destroy all such people—not only when he removes them by the sentence of death, but rather in the fire of everlasting condemnation.

Therefore, in order to expose those who were living chastely among the Corinthians, he added: “For the temple of God is holy, which you are.” He rightly says “holy,” because, as blessed Augustine says, they too were indeed the temple of God through faith, but not holy, [Col. 0322C] [Note: [Col. 0322D] “Just as these”—namely, those who.] like those who were violating the temple of God. And then, to terrify the wicked, he added: “Let no one deceive himself”—that is, let no one think that, by his own counsel or another’s, he can accomplish anything beneficial for himself without the grace of God.

Alternatively: “Let no one deceive himself”—that is, let no one suppose that by his own wisdom he can comprehend the hidden things of God; let no one flatter himself; let no one place his hope in human beings. For he returns to the preceding meaning, by which he reproved the wise of the world and demonstrated that their wisdom was foolishness. Hence he adds here also: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish, so that he may be wise.”

The sense is: If anyone seems to possess the grace of spiritual wisdom and understands that salvation was promised to the human race through the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation, let him become foolish in this age—that is, let him flee the wisdom of the age, so that he may be judged foolish by it; for then he will truly be wise. For one who is foolish to the age is prudent before God, while believing that God has done what the wisdom of the world cannot comprehend.

And this is what follows: “For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.” Since God does what that wisdom denies can be done, he proves that wisdom to be foolishness.

Alternatively: The wisdom of this world is to curse the one who curses, to love a friend, to hate an enemy, and to repay like for like. But this is foolishness with God, who, by loving enemies and praying for them, has shown possible what that wisdom judged incredible.

Alternatively: The wisdom of the world is that which proclaims many gods. But this is foolishness with God, because the Catholic faith believes and confesses only one God [Note: [Col. 0323D] Let the reader consider what these words, as they lie in the autograph, are intended to mean.], “as virtue bears witness” [the reading is uncertain]. Accordingly, the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30).

Therefore, in order to confirm what he had said with a fitting testimony, he continued: “As it is written” (as some prefer, in Isaiah, since there is there a certain similarity to these words). It is more credible, however, that it was written in the book of blessed Job, where Eliphaz the Temanite is speaking; for these same words are found there: “I will seize the wise in their craftiness” (Job V, 13). “Craftiness,” as blessed Augustine says, is sometimes used in place of “wisdom,” though not properly, but by misuse.

The Lord therefore seizes—that is, reproves—the wise of the age, because he shows them to be fools by doing what they doubt can be done. As for the reading found in certain copies, “wisdom,” we should understand it as “of the carnal.” But to confirm this more fully, he also added the Prophet’s testimony: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are futile” (Psalm XCIII, 11). Since the Lord knows that human thoughts are futile—for whatever a person thinks without God is futile—he reproves them by showing to be true what they judged false, and false what they considered true.
