Therefore, because the Corinthians were boasting in their teachers, saying, “I am of Paul, I of Cephas,” he adds: [Col. 0323C] [Note: [Col. 0323D] In the autograph’s margin “chapter XV” is written here; but “chapter XIV” is marked nowhere.] “Therefore let no one boast in human beings.” He is saying, as it were: Because human thoughts are futile and their plans weak and shortsighted, one must not boast in human beings, but in God, whose plan can neither be comprehended nor revoked—for whatever a person considers without God is foolish.

Why one must not boast in human beings is made clear when he adds: “Everything is yours.” The sense is: Because everything is yours, do not boast in individuals; do not defend particular teachers as belonging specially to you, since you make use of them all. Paul, Apollos, and Cephas are yours, because they proclaim one thing and all labor for your salvation. Hence below: “But we are your servants for the sake of Jesus” (II Corinthians IV, 5). For he calls them servants, that is, ministers, in accordance with the Lord’s saying: “But I am among you as one who serves” (Luke XXII, 27).

Or, “this world.” The world is yours because it was made for you, so that you might use it rightly and order its course according to God’s will. Do not think that it is governed by fate and the constellations, but by God’s providence. For a human being was not made on account of the world; rather, the world was made on account of a human being.

“Whether life or death.” Whether the present life is yours, because it has been granted to you by God so that you may live rightly, soberly, and modestly in it and conduct it to God’s glory; or death is yours, because although it was brought upon you on account of the first human being’s sin, it is nevertheless necessary that you be prepared willingly to die for Christ, in hope of the future resurrection.

“Whether things present or things to come.” Things present are yours because they have been granted to you by God, yet in such a way that you use them without offending God. Things to come are also yours, so that you may recognize them as better than things present, entrust yourselves to them rather, and hasten as quickly as possible to receive them.

“Everything is yours”—that is, everything has been entrusted and subjected to your authority and judgment. “But you are Christ’s” (understand: his servants and fellow heirs). The sense is: Just as everything has been subjected and granted to your authority, so it is necessary that you be subjected to Christ.

“But Christ is God’s” (understand: his proper Son). It is as though he were saying plainly: Just as Christ is God’s only-begotten Son, doing the Father’s will, so it is necessary that you, adopted as sons, also do Christ’s will. Why, then, do you hope for anything from a human being to his injury, or place your hope in a human being?

But because there were some who thought of the Apostle otherwise than they ought—so that they ought to think of him as did the one who chose him for the grace of apostleship—he continued by reproving them: [Note: [Col. 0324D] “Chapter XVI” is written here in the margin of the autograph.] (CHAPTER IV.) “Let a person regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God.”

He is saying, as it were: Whoever he may be who thinks of us otherwise than he ought to think, let him judge us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Since we do not preach amid a display of words or in the brilliance of eloquence, he can certainly understand that we dispense the mysteries of Christ. And indeed they could easily recognize this, since it was not words that shone in them, but power, and miracles flashed forth.

It should be noted that he has posited two things. For many are ministers of God who do not know how to be stewards of the mysteries. They are ministers of God who follow him, in accordance with his saying: “Whoever serves me, let him follow me” (John XII, 20). But those are stewards of the mysteries of God who distribute heavenly sacraments or commandments to each of the faithful according to their quality and capacity—that is, good preachers.

It should also be understood that, by calling himself and those like him stewards of the mysteries of God, he reproves the pseudo-apostles, showing that what they preached was not of God, because they departed far from the apostolic tradition.

He continues: “Here and now it is required among stewards that one be found faithful.” Some wish this sentence to be pronounced interrogatively, others affirmatively. But in whatever manner it is pronounced, it is the speech of one reproving. By this sentence he reproves not only the pseudo-apostles, but also those who were afraid, on account of fear or favor, approval, or profit, constantly to condemn wicked conduct after receiving the grace of God’s stewardship.

He says “it is required” because of its rarity, as if he were saying: Many indeed appear to be stewards of the mysteries of God, but a faithful one is found only very rarely. He himself possessed such authority, freedom, and steadfastness that he neither spared his own life, nor feared the words of detractors, nor dreaded human judgments, provided only that he might be Christ’s minister and faithfully dispense God’s mysteries.

Therefore he adds: “But to me it is a very small matter that I should be judged by you.” He is saying, as it were: I do not fear your judgments, since I see you entangled in such great crimes. And truly it was a small matter that he should be judged by those by whom not even the saints ought to be judged. For it belongs to the saints to fear not human judgments, but God alone.

Hence he adds: “Or by a human day”—that is, by laws handed down by human beings, whose judgments he did not fear, because he had surpassed all the justice of human laws and adhered only to divine justice. By saying “or by a human day,” he wishes the divine day to be understood, on which the Lord will judge the living and the dead.

Therefore, because he remembered nothing that he had done or taught for which he might be judged even by himself, he continued: “But neither do I judge myself. For I am conscious of nothing against myself.” The sense is: My conscience is pure; therefore I fear neither your judgments, nor those of human laws, nor my own. Since he had a pure conscience, he was troubled by nothing.

But because he seemed to have wished to justify himself and, as a human being, might have been able to fall into sin, he added: “But I am not thereby justified.” He is saying plainly, as it were: I fear neither my own judgments, nor yours, nor those of human laws; but I do not presume upon my merits. I fear the judgment of the one from whom the secrets of the heart cannot be hidden and whose judgments I cannot weigh.

And this is what follows: “But the one who judges me is the Lord.” Therefore, so that the Corinthians would not fall into rash judgment, he continued: “Therefore do not judge before the time.” He is saying openly, as it were: Because you will be judged, do not judge, lest you incur a double sin and be punished more severely. Rather, as faithful and holy men, await the future day of judgment.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not judge, and you will not be judged; do not condemn, and you will not be condemned” (Luke VI, 37). There he teaches especially that, whenever it is uncertain with what intention actions are performed, we should always interpret them in the better sense, lest we fall into rash judgment. For it is an insult to a judge if a servant pronounces judgment before the judge has investigated the case.

But it must be asked why he forbids judging here, when elsewhere he himself judges and commands others to judge (I Corinthians VI, 3–5). Accordingly, it should be understood that, as the same Apostle says elsewhere, there are certain deeds that precede judgment (I Timothy V, 24). We are permitted to judge these because they are open, such as sexual violations, thefts, and murders.

There are other deeds that follow judgment, concerning which we are not permitted to judge. There are also deeds that lie between these categories; because they are hidden, we must not easily judge them, especially not so as to condemn. If, however, some things have been clearly established by evidence, they must be punished.

The Lord also demonstrates this by his own example in the book of Genesis, saying: “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has been multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grave. Come, let us descend and see” [Note: [Col. 0325D] Genesis XVIII, 20. The Vulgate has: “I will descend and see.”] “whether they have completed in action the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know.”

Behold, the Lord speaks as though uncertain, although everything is open to his eyes and not even the number of the sand of the sea can escape his knowledge. He shows that we must not easily believe or judge hidden sins, especially capital ones; once proved, however, they must be punished. Hence, after the Lord led Lot out of Sodom, he overthrew the aforementioned cities by raining fire and sulfur upon them (Genesis XIX, 24).

The Apostle is therefore speaking here about hidden and doubtful matters. It should also be noted that, by saying “before the time,” he wishes the day of judgment to be understood. The present is the time of clemency, mercy, and repentance. Hence he says elsewhere: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day” (II Corinthians VI, 2).

But then it will be the time of judgment, when evil deeds can no longer be cleansed through repentance, but each person will receive according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil (II Corinthians V, 10). Then, as Isaiah says: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isaiah III, 14).

Hence he adds here also: “Until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the secrets” [Note: [Col. 0326D] The Vulgate has: “counsels.”] “of hearts.” The Lord himself is light, as John says, “and there is no darkness in him at all” (I John I, 5). He is the light of minds, but of minds that have been purified.

Therefore, because he is light, he will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the secrets of hearts, because at his coming not only deeds but also thoughts will be exposed to everyone’s eyes, as he himself says: “Nothing is covered that will not be revealed, nor hidden that will not be known” (Matthew X, 26).

There simplicity and hypocrisy will appear. Hence he immediately adds: “And then each person will receive praise from God.” He says “then” because there is not now true praise; for it is uncertain whether the one who is praised is worthy of praise or not. Hence he also says elsewhere: “For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends” (II Corinthians X, 18).

Then, however, there will be true praise for each person. For the reprobate? No. It must be understood that praise will belong to the one who thinks or acts well, because they will hear: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV, 34).

He continues: “Therefore, brothers, I have applied these things figuratively to myself and Apollos,” and so forth. To apply figuratively is to assume another’s figure, that is, person. He therefore applied these things figuratively to himself and Apollos, so that, in his own person and that of Apollos, he might nullify the perverse traditions of the pseudo-apostles.

It should be noted, however, that he reproved them not by naming them individually but by a general judgment, lest greater discord arise among the people and they, casting aside shame, become worse. For he knew that it is very rare for someone who hears his own name or the name of one whom he loves openly denounced to remain silent. If someone hears his own name, or that of the person he loves, denounced as though it had been passed over in silence, he perhaps pretends that nothing has been said against himself or his beloved.

Under this figurative application he had also previously overthrown the persons of the pseudo-apostles, saying: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.” And again: “Therefore neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth.” In this way they were to learn not to boast in a human being, not to attribute to a human being what is granted by God, and to give glory to God, not to a human being.

Hence he adds here also: “So that no one may be puffed up on behalf of one against another beyond what is written.” The Corinthians were puffed up beyond what is written—that is, they were arrogantly wise—and they were inflamed against one another because they envied one another on account of the merits of their teachers. Each of them boasted that he was the disciple of the one whom he judged superior.

It should therefore be understood that there were some among them who, because they had received more in the sacrament of baptism or in teaching, despised those who had received less. For this reason they boasted in their teachers. The pseudo-apostles also wished to justify themselves by themselves, attributing whatever they had received to themselves and not to God.

Speaking to such people, he continued: “For who makes you different?” Here it should be noted that he speaks in the singular, as though to one person, while addressing the faction of each individual member of the people. There was such great discord among the Corinthian people that there were many loyalties to different parties. Therefore the Apostle adapted his speech to all the parties without naming any particular person, so that, when his letter was read, each party would accept as directed against itself what it understood to have been said against it.

The sense, as blessed Augustine says, is this: “For who makes you different?” That is, who separated you from the mass of perdition that came from Adam, so as to make you a vessel for honor and not for dishonor? (Romans IX, 21.) The implied answer is: No one but God.

Alternatively: You who boast that you have received more, who separated you from the one who received less, except the one who gave you what he did not give to the other? It should be noted that the gifts by which the person addressed by “Who makes you different?” is distinguished are not to be understood as earthly, but heavenly—not those things that are common to good and wicked alike, but those that only the elect can possess.

But, as the same blessed Augustine says, a carnal and vainly puffed-up person could have replied, either in words or in thought: “My faith distinguishes me; my prayer distinguishes me; my righteousness distinguishes me.” Countering such words or thoughts, he continues: “What do you have that you did not receive?” The sense is: Whatever good you have, you received from God.

Again, lest he think that he had received it on account of his own merits, he added: “But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” He is saying, as it were: [Col. 0328A] You should not boast in yourself about a good that you received, but in God, because you received it not through your merits, but freely.

Alternatively: “What do you have that you did not receive?” That is: What good do you have from the pseudo-apostles that you did not first hear and receive from me? But if you received it by hearing me, why do you boast of their teaching as though you had received nothing from me? For the pseudo-apostles were attractive through the brilliance of human eloquence, whereas the Apostle seemed contemptible because he sought not his own glory but God’s.

“You are already filled; you have already become rich; you reign without us.” These words are spoken ironically. They are not the words of one affirming, but of one indignant and emotionally stirred. He says that those people reign, are filled, and have become rich, in whom he previously reproved various vices and numerous errors—not in reality, but according to their own estimation, since they thought that they reigned and had become rich and filled because they boasted that they had received everything from the pseudo-apostles.

But to show how greatly he loved them with the affection of piety, he added: “And would that you did reign.” Like a loving father, he wishes them well even though they are ungrateful children. Yet they could not reign without the Apostle, because whatever they had received from the pseudo-apostles was full of vices and errors.

“Would that we also might reign with you.” The order would have been for him to say, “that you also might reign with us.” But because he had first said, “Would that you did reign,” he was compelled to say, “that we also might reign with you.”

Who, then, are those who reign? Those, clearly, who are certain of the hope of eternal blessedness; who, secure in God’s promises, rejoice and exult in all the adversities they suffer for Christ’s name, knowing that these do not inflict loss upon them but gain for them the reward of perpetual recompense. Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (II Corinthians XII, 10). And James [Note: [Col. 0327D] “Chapter XVIII” is written here in the autograph’s margin; but “chapter XVII” is marked nowhere.]: “Consider it all joy, my brothers, whenever you fall into various trials” (James I, 2).

“For I think that God has displayed us apostles as the last.” He especially ascribes the grace of the final apostleship to his own person because, more than all the apostles, he endured innumerable persecutions and sufferings—like those who will come as apostles at the end of time, namely Elijah and Enoch. For they will be sent before Christ’s coming to preach to the people of God and strengthen the churches, so that they may not believe but resist the Antichrist. They will pay for this with many sufferings and punishments, to such an extent that they will be killed, as the reading of the Apocalypse declares [Note: [Col. 0327D] Apocalypse XI, 3 and following. Many interpreters approve this conjecture concerning Enoch and Elijah, relying especially on the testimonies of Ecclesiasticus XLIV, 16, concerning the coming of Enoch; and Malachi IV, 5–6 and Ecclesiasticus XLVIII, 10, concerning Elijah’s coming in the last times.].

Hence he adds here: “As men sentenced to death.” He compared their time with his own. But lest he seem to boast or seek human favor, he does not speak in the singular but in the plural, saying “we.”

What he says, “I think,” should be understood not as expressing doubt but as confirmation, as in the Letter to the Romans: “I consider that the sufferings of this present age are not worthy of comparison” (Romans VIII, 18).

It may also be understood that he called them “the last” in comparison with those who came before. For those whom he chose first he sent to the Jews; those whom he appointed last he sent to the Gentiles. Therefore he says: “As men sentenced to death”—that is, to death, punishments, and various persecutions.

“Because we have become a spectacle to the world.” Elijah and Enoch will be such a spectacle in the world that they will be killed in the sight of the entire unbelieving people and their bodies will be thrown into the street, to the disgrace of the faithful. In the same way the apostles became a spectacle to the world, when they were subjected to insults and tortures in the sight of those who mocked them.

He says “to the world,” not to heaven and earth, but to those inhabiting the world. Explaining this, he adds: “Both to angels and to human beings.” By angels he means not the good but the evil, of whom the Prophet says: “The sending forth of evil angels” (Psalm XXXIII, 8). Similarly, by human beings he means not the believing, [Note: [Col. 0329D] In place of *credulos*, the autograph originally read *crudelos*, which I judged should be emended in favor of the antithesis: “not believers, but unbelievers,” following the earlier “not good, but evil.”] but the unbelieving.

They became a spectacle to these because such people exulted and rejoiced in their sufferings and deaths. Blessed Augustine, however, says that “angels and human beings” may be understood as both good and evil, so that the sense is: We have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings—not only to those who reproach us, but also to those who praise us, because we possess in ourselves something pleasing to the good angels and something displeasing to the evil. In the same way, our life pleases the faithful and displeases the unbelieving.

“We are fools for Christ, but you are wise in Christ.” Because the apostles loved Christ and preached what seemed foolish to the wise of the world, they were called fools for Christ. Ebion and Cerinthus, because they denied that God had a Son, or that God could become human, or that a virgin could give birth, along with the others who preached against Christ, were called wise in Christ.

This sentence therefore reproves the pseudo-apostles, who, seeking the brilliance of human eloquence, preached what did not offend the wise of the world. For this reason he calls them wise in Christ.

“We are weak, but you are strong.” Because the apostles preached Christ freely and steadfastly, they suffered insults, hardships, and violence, and consequently were judged weak. The pseudo-apostles, by contrast, because they preached Christ in such a way as not to offend people, remained secure; therefore he calls them strong.

“You are noble, but we are dishonorable.” Those who denied that God had been promised to Abraham or announced by the prophets were considered noble, because they did not attribute all the antiquity of the promised Christ to Christ. By contrast, those who asserted that Christ was born from Abraham’s seed according to the promise and announced by the prophets were called dishonorable.

But it should be understood that the Apostle denies what he seems to affirm, and affirms what he seems to deny. These are the words of one reproving, who confesses by denying and denies by confessing; for they are spoken ironically.

“Up to this present hour”—up to this time, that is, even among you—“we are both hungry and thirsty, naked and beaten, homeless and laboring, working with our own hands.”

Because the apostles preached Christ without flattery and according to the Catholic faith, they were not popular. Therefore they received nothing from their hearers by which they might be supported, and consequently they were hungry, thirsty, and naked. They were also beaten with blows, because they were publicly mocked and reproached.

They were homeless because unbelievers drove them from place to place, lest, if they remained longer in one location, they might convert more people to the faith of Christ. They labored, working with their own hands, to obtain food by which they might be sustained—not only because, since they were not popular, they received nothing, but also because they judged it unworthy to accept anything from those whom they saw involved in such great crimes, in accordance with the saying: “Let the oil of the sinner not anoint my head” (Psalm CXL, 5).

For they knew that one sins gravely and loses the freedom to reprove when he accepts something from a person who gives it precisely so that the recipient will not reprove him [Note: [Col. 0330D] Here is a very noteworthy observation.].

He continues: “We are cursed, and we bless; we suffer persecution, and we endure; we are blasphemed, and we entreat.” They were cursed, and they blessed, because they did not repay evil with evil, so that by their patience they might convert to the faith of Christ those who treated them badly.

They suffered persecution, and they endured, because they did not resist their persecutors. They were blasphemed, and they entreated, because, after being subjected to insults and reproaches, they humbly begged that they be permitted to give an account of themselves, knowing that, if this were granted, they would more easily convert their persecutors to the faith of Christ.

He continues: “We have become as the refuse of this world.” The sense is: Because we humbled ourselves, because we did not contradict them, we were therefore considered contemptible and the vilest of all. Hence he immediately adds: “The refuse of all things” [Note: [Col. 0330D] The Vulgate has *peripsema*; in Greek, *Περιψημα*.] “even until now.”

For *peripsema* means any worthless thing, such as plucked hairs, shavings, or any other discarded material. “Even until now” means up to the present time.

He continues: “For if you have ten thousand pedagogues,” and so forth. It should be noted that the one who first lays the foundation of faith is called a father; those who follow him are pedagogues. *Pedagogue* is a Greek word, and in Latin it is called a *pedissequus*, that is, an attendant and instructor of children, restraining their wanton age.

Because he had laid the foundation of faith, he was a father. Therefore he said: “Yet not all are fathers” [Note: [Col. 0330D] The Vulgate has “many.”].

[Col. 0331A] The reason he had said this follows: “For through the Gospel I begot you” [Note: [Col. 0331D] The Vulgate has: “For in Christ Jesus through the Gospel I begot you.”]. In saying “I begot,” he shows himself to be a father. Therefore he says this so that, when they hear him called their father, they may recognize themselves as sons and understand that no one loves them as does the one who is their father—and so they may listen to him more willingly. No outsider, after all, places the love of children before the love of his own children.

“I urge you, brothers,” and so forth. It must be considered why the Apostle said to his hearers, and on what account: “Be imitators of me.” It should be noted that he endured various adversities and hardships, hunger and thirst, for the sake of their salvation. Therefore he said: “Be imitators of me,” as though saying: Just as I endured many hardships for the sake of your salvation, so you too, disregarding the pseudo-apostles, should consider their slander of little account.

For they feared the pseudo-apostles’ slanders. It is as though he were saying: If you are sons, you ought to offer your father the honor due to him and become imitators of him. The Apostle’s purpose varies in different passages when he says, “Be imitators of me,” but his purpose in this passage is as stated.

“For this reason I sent” [Note: [Col. 0331D] The Vulgate has: “For this reason I sent to you.”] “Timothy,” and so forth. Who could comprehend in his mind or express in words the depth of his affection? It was not enough for him to send them a letter; he also took care to send his own son Timothy—and not just any son, but his dearest.

For he had many sons: some dear, others dearer, and others dearest. Timothy, however, was dearest, because the more faithful he was, the dearer he was. By these words he also touches those who had withdrawn from his preaching. If they had remained, they too might perhaps have become dearest.

But why did he send this man? Perhaps because they had consigned to oblivion what the apostles had preached to them. Therefore he sent one who knew both his preaching and his letters, so that he might recall to memory what they had forgotten.

By this action preachers are admonished not to withdraw the affection of piety from those by whom they are persecuted, but, if necessity requires, to strive to die for them.

He makes clear why he sent him when he adds: “Who will remind you of my ways”—that is, he will make you mindful. He calls his “way” his preaching and his conduct.

“Which are in Christ Jesus.” [Col. 0331D] By saying “in Christ Jesus,” and “as I teach everywhere in every church,” he shows that he taught them nothing contrary or perverse. When they heard that he observed universality, they would be ashamed not to be observers themselves, since the more one sees a particular group observing something universally observed, the more one is stirred to observe it [Note: [Col. 0331D] In the autograph’s margin “chapter XX” is written here; but “chapter XIX” is marked nowhere.].

He continues: “I will come to you” [Note: [Col. 0331D] The Vulgate’s verse 18, namely, “As though I were not going to come to you, so some have become puffed up,” is absent from this autograph.], and so forth. Observe how great was the concern of this outstanding preacher. It was not enough for him to send a letter, nor even his dearest son; finally he promises his own presence, saying: “I will come to you soon.”

But see how discreetly and cautiously he speaks. For he says: “If the Lord wills.” Why does he say this, unless because he knew that God knows better what is in a human being than the human being himself? He said this so that, if God had determined that he should come, they would attribute his coming not to Paul but to God, who had determined that he come, and so that his arrival would be understood as a work of the grace of God. If he did not come, they would attribute this neither to God nor to Paul, but to their own merits, since, because their merits demanded it, God had delayed his coming.

By this action we are admonished that, whenever we promise anything, even something spiritual, we should say, “If the Lord wills”—that is, if he permits it.

[Col. 0332B] He continues: “And I will know not the speech of those who are puffed up,” and so forth. It should be noted that false doctrine remains manifest only until the true doctrine appears; when the true has appeared, the false is obscured. So it is here. At the Apostle’s arrival, false doctrine disappeared; therefore he says: “And I will know,” and so forth.

He calls “speech” eloquence, but “power” the power of signs and deeds. Why he says, “I will know those who are puffed up” [Note: [Col. 0332D] The Vulgate has “inflated.”] “not by speech but by power,” he makes clear when he adds: “For the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power”—that is, in the power of works. Just as evangelical teaching is not in display [Note: [Col. 0332D] The autograph reads *in monte*; perhaps *in sermone* was intended.] but in power, so too is the kingdom of God.

He continues: “What do you wish? Shall I come with a rod?” and so forth. For the disposition of the apostolic mind was twofold, namely, piety and severity. Earlier he had said: “As I admonish my dearest children” (I Corinthians IV, 14); now he threatens with a rod.

What is gentler or more merciful than to admonish my dearest children? And what is harsher than to threaten with a rod? By this action preachers are admonished to possess both dispositions toward their people, namely severity and piety—but in such a way that their severity is not cruel. If it is cruel, it leads to despair; if piety is too lax, it makes people negligent. Therefore piety must be joined with severity, and severity with piety.

This is why oxen and lions are also said to have been beneath the bronze sea, not only oxen (III Kings VII, 29). What is signified by the oxen except the piety of preachers? What by the lions except the terror of severity?

We learn in the preface that Paul resembles Moses; this passage also makes it clear. For just as a twofold disposition possessed this man’s mind, so it possessed Moses’ mind as well. For it is written that, when he had ascended the mountain (Exodus XXXII) to receive the Law, God said to him: “Descend from the mountain, because your people have sinned.” When Moses pleaded, God forgave the people’s offense; but when he descended, he ordered thirty thousand to be killed [Note: [Col. 0332D] Exodus XXXII, 28 says that about twenty-three thousand men fell on that day.].

Observe how the one who had mercifully wished to be blotted from the book acted, upon descending, with such severity.

(CHAPTER V.) “It is heard that there is sexual immorality among you,” and so forth. [Note: [Col. 0333D] “Chapter XXI” is written here in the margin of the autograph.]

It is said: “Such sexual immorality is heard of.” He indicates what kind it is when he adds: “Such as does not even exist among the Gentiles”—that is, among those who are strangers to knowledge; hence they are also called *Gentiles*, as though they had been born in such a condition.

It should be understood that the Apostle speaks by way of exaggeration, so that, recognizing the gravity of the crime, they might repent and be saved. By this action preachers are admonished that, when speaking about some crime, they should speak with emphasis. For there are certain wicked and perverse people, especially the simple, who, if a vice is reproved in a restrained manner, consider the offense small. For according to the manner of speech, they understand the magnitude of the sin.

Therefore they should speak with emphasis, so that, when they hear the words, they may recognize the crime as great, repent of what they have done, and be saved.

He continues: “So that someone has his father’s wife.” Earlier he had spoken generally of the crime of sexual immorality, for sexual immorality has many meanings. Therefore he added a specific instance: “So that someone has his father’s wife.”

This man had publicly taken his stepmother; therefore he said this. But note that each crime is considered worse the more rarely it is committed. A person sins more rarely against relatives, and the rarer the offense, the worse that vice is considered. This man had sinned with a relative, because he had taken his father’s wife.

It follows: “And you are puffed up,” etc. Although such a great crime had been committed among them, they did not grieve [Col. 0333C] more deeply; rather, they were puffed up. Therefore the Apostle says: “And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned.” Such fornication had occurred among them as was found nowhere even among the Gentiles; yet they did not mourn, but were puffed up. This is why the Apostle says it.

For it belongs to the saints to grieve over the sins of others, as Jeremiah says: “Who will give water to my head?” (Jer. 9:1), etc.; and Samuel is read to have wept for Saul (1 Kings 15:35). The Lord also wept over the ruin of the faithless city, saying: “If you too had known” (Luke 19:42)—that is, “you would have wept.” Hence blessed Gregory says: Since He wept over the ruin of the faithless city, it is shown that He weeps daily for the sins of His people through His preachers. But these men were not such, and therefore they were puffed up.

[Col. 0333D] It follows: “So that he may be taken away from your midst,” etc. If you have no authority to correct someone whom you know to be involved in wrongdoing, you are alien from the sin; but if you have authority and do not correct him, you are a participant in it. If, however, you have authority to correct him but there are no one who will condemn him, you ought to tolerate him, just as the Lord tolerated Judas’s crime, although He knew him to be a betrayer. And it should be noted that, if the vice is widespread, one must depart; Isaiah makes this clear when he says: “Therefore go out from their midst, and do not touch what is unclean” (Isa. 52:11). But if it is particularized in one person, he must be cast out, as the Apostle says here.

It follows: “I, indeed, being absent in body,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0333D] In the autograph’s margin, chapter XXII is written here.] He was absent in the flesh, but nevertheless present in that Spirit who fills the world by His power, not by His bulk. In another sense, he was present through that spirit by which Elisha was present to Gehazi when he said: “Was not my heart present when the man met you and bestowed such things?” [Note: [Col. 0334D] 2 Kings 5:26; the Vulgate has: “Was not my heart present?”] And in what spirit the blessed man was present to his people follows: “When you are assembled,” etc.

He rightly says, “in the name of the Lord Jesus,” because an assembly without the Lord Jesus accomplishes nothing. It follows: “I have judged,” etc.; as though he were saying: “I have already judged that he should be removed from your midst, and I judge that he should be handed over,” etc.

This passage is explained in various ways by the teachers. Some say that he was handed over to Satan—that is, to the devil—to be afflicted, so that, afflicted, he might acknowledge his guilt, repent of his deed, and be saved. Some say that he was deprived of communion, so that excommunication is understood by “Satan.” Others understand it as imprisonment; this is especially credible, because Satan is some kind of opposition or adversity. And note that this judgment proceeds not from cruelty but from compassion; therefore he adds: “So that the spirit may be saved.” Elsewhere also: “If anyone does not obey our word through this letter, take note of him, so that you do not associate with him, that he may be put to shame; yet do not regard him as an enemy, but correct him as a brother” (2 Thess. 3:14).

A little earlier he had said that they were puffed up, although they ought rather to have mourned. He repeats this in other words when he says: “Your boasting is not good.” In its place the Greek has: “Your boasting is good”; that is, “not good.” They were puffed up, although they ought rather to have mourned over the enormity of the crime that had occurred among them.

Many imitators of these people are found, who mourn neither their own death nor that of others. Some have been so deceived by the devil that they not only do not grieve over their own or others’ sins, but the greater the sins they themselves commit, or see others committing, the happier they become. Solomon speaks of such people: “They rejoice when they have done evil” (Prov. 2:14), etc.

It follows: [Note: [Col. 0334D] In the autograph’s margin: chapter XXIII.] “Do you not know that a little leaven,” etc. It is as though he were saying: “You know that not only does a large portion of leaven added to a lump corrupt it, but even a small particle or spark, if mixed into it; and since you know this, why do you not drive away from yourselves so great a crime, which can divide your community?”

The name “leaven” is commonly used for corrupt teaching, as in: “Beware of the leaven of the scribes and Pharisees” (Luke 12:1; Mark 8:15). The comparison is fitting: just as leaven corrupts a large mass of flour, so corrupt teaching corrupts the great mass of faith and of the other virtues. It is also commonly used for corrupt action. Understand it here as well, in accordance with what he has begun to say about the people. The comparison is apt, because a crime often corrupts the great mass of holy conduct and community.

This is shown to have happened frequently among the Jewish people: when Ahaz sinned, many were struck down before their enemies (2 Chron. 28:5).

Therefore he warns and exhorts them: “Purge out,” he says, “the old leaven”—that is, the conduct of the old person—“so that you may be a new lump.” By “new lump” he means the fellowship of ecclesiastical peace. It is beautifully called a lump, because just as many grains become one large mass through the addition of water, so from many sexes, ages, and social conditions one community of the Church is formed.

It follows: “As you are unleavened.” Unleavened bread is understood as simplicity. For the children of Israel, compelled by the Egyptians, took only flour with them, from which they ate unleavened bread, because they had no opportunity to leaven it (Exod. 12:39). The meaning is as though he had said: “Since you have cast away the leaven of the old person and have been renewed, be unleavened”—that is, remain in the same newness.

Hence also: “You shall exchange the firstborn of a donkey for a sheep” (Exod. 13:13). To exchange the firstborn of a donkey for a sheep is, in the beginnings of a worldly life, to surpass innocence in holiness and chastity and to offer an offering pleasing to God, because nothing unclean can be offered to God, who is pure.

Since he had mentioned leaven and unleavened bread, in order to point out the mystery of the renewal of our Passover, he added: “For our Passover,” etc. The meaning is: It was not an animal, not a lamb, but Christ who was sacrificed, and those things prefigured Him.

“Passover” and “phase” are one name. It is said to derive from passing over and, as some have wished, from suffering, because *paschin* in Greek is “suffering” [Note: [Col. 0335D] From the verb πάσχω, “I suffer.”]. Nevertheless, the joining of the two languages is shown to be most appropriate, because on the day when He suffered, He passed over to the Father. Hence John also says: “The hour has come for Him to pass over” (John 13:1).

It follows: “Therefore let us celebrate.” Some copies have: “Let us keep the feast”; others, which explain both expressions, have: “Let us rejoice.” But we cannot rightly rejoice unless we draw into imitation the things they performed in the type. For it is written that those about to eat the Passover were told: “They shall take of the blood of the lamb” (Exod. 12:7), etc. Blessed Pope Gregory says: “What this blood is, we now know not merely by hearing but by drinking.” Let the remaining matters, which are read in his book, follow as well.

And as though they had asked where they ought to celebrate, he replied: “Not with the old leaven.” Here it should be noted that the children of Israel cast away leaven and ate unleavened bread for seven days (ibid., 15). We too ought to conduct ourselves holily and innocently throughout the whole time of our life.

To show what the old leaven was, he immediately added: “Not with the leaven of malice and wickedness,” but rather: “With the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.” Sincerity is that by which every corruption is cast away; truth is that by which every deceit is rejected.

“I wrote to you in a letter not to associate with fornicators.” By these words the Apostle indicates that he had written this. But because they did not understand which fornicators he meant, perhaps they did not take offense at this man who had committed the crime and did not drive him away from themselves.

It should be known that, as some think, he had written these things in this Letter; others, however, say that he wrote them not in this Letter but in another, which is the more plausible view [Note: [Col. 0335D] Perhaps “more probable.”]. But because they did not understand which fornicators he meant, he immediately explained by adding: “Not at all meaning the fornicators of this world,” etc. He showed that he was not speaking about unbelievers, as they had understood, but about believers.

[Note: [Col. 0335D] The Vulgate, after the verse “Not at all meaning the fornicators of this world,” has: “or the covetous, or the greedy, or those serving idols” (v. 10). In my view, our author silently passed over this verse, except for a few words; otherwise, the words “otherwise” [*alioquin*], etc., would follow. Hence perhaps, because of differing readings—namely, of the ninth verse, “I wrote to you in a letter: Do not associate,” and of the eleventh verse, “But now I wrote to you not to associate”—and because of the similarity of the contents of the tenth and eleventh verses, where the covetous, etc., are mentioned, the question arose whether the Apostle wrote this in this very Letter or in another. Hence also, namely from the similarity of the texts of one verse and the other, there arose in our autograph a mixture and confusion.]

It follows: “Otherwise you would have had to leave this world.” The meaning is: If you ought to be content with the company of evil people, it would benefit you to leave the world—that is, to die. The Apostle says this because it is almost a recompense for the wicked if they depart this life quickly, lest, if they remain longer, they harm the good and afterward be punished with a more severe penalty. Since the saints knew that sin, not death, harms the wicked [Note: [Col. 0336D] The autograph has “death.”], they sentenced some to death.

He took care to make clear which fornicators he meant; therefore he added: “If the one who is called a brother is a fornicator,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0336D] The Vulgate has this conditionally: “If the one who is called a brother is a fornicator,” and continues: “or covetous, or serving idols, or reviling, or drunkard, or greedy.”]

By these words the Apostle does not prohibit eating with unbelievers, since elsewhere he says: “If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner” [Note: [Col. 0336D] 1 Cor. 10:27; the Vulgate does not have “to dinner.”] “and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you without asking questions.” Rather, he prohibits eating with a brother—that is, a believer—if he is a fornicator or possesses some such quality as he himself lists. Such a person is not merely to be denied participation in the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, but is not even to share ordinary food, so that, when he is separated from our fellowship, he may be put to shame, blush, and be corrected. For many do not understand that they have sinned greatly unless they are separated from the company of the good.

[Note: [Col. 0336D] In the autograph’s margin, chapter XXIV is written here.] It follows: “For what have I to do with judging those who are outside?” Why does the Apostle say this, unless because it does not pertain to the bishop to judge unbelievers, but rather believers—those who are fornicators, covetous, or possess some such fault? [Col. 0336D] It pertains not only to the bishop but also, appropriately, to the faithful. Therefore he adds: “Do you not judge those who are within?”

For each person it is necessary to judge individuals in the Church—that is, to learn their character, whom he should cleave to, and to whom he should entrust his faith—since not everyone in the Church has equal merit. Some are good, others better, and others best.

It should also be known that this statement is not contrary to the earlier one in which he said: “Do not judge before the time.” There he forbids judgment; here he also seems to command it; elsewhere he says: “Judge among yourselves” (1 Cor. 10:15), etc. But there is no contradiction. Either the reason is that here he is speaking about testing or discernment, whereas there he is speaking about hidden matters that the Church does not judge but reserves for God; or certainly because his intention there was to speak about superiors, whose actions are not to be judged by the judgment of their subjects but by the judgment of superiors.

Therefore he had said shortly before: “Here it is required among stewards,” etc., as though he were saying: “Why do you inquire, since their deeds are not to be judged by your judgment?” This meaning is shown in many other passages of the holy Scriptures.

It is read in Genesis that when Noah had become drunk (Gen. 9), he was uncovered in his tent, etc. Noah represents preachers; the drunkenness and nakedness represent some reprehensible action of preachers; Ham, who mocked him, represents subjects who rashly criticize the actions of their superiors; Shem and Japheth represent good subjects, who not only do not criticize but rather cover whatever reprehensible things they recognize.

This is also shown in the Book of Kings (2 Kings 6:6), where it is read that, when the oxen kicked and the ark of God was turning so as to fall, Uzzah rashly grasped it and was struck by God and died. Hence also Saul entered a cave “to relieve himself,” and the rest follows (1 Sam. 24:4). For Saul’s relieving himself means that superiors bring into action what they had conceived wrongly in their minds.

It follows: “For the Lord will judge those who are outside.” He calls those who are outside Gentiles, whom the Lord judges, in accordance with: “The one who does not believe is already judged” (John 3:18), because the one who has no hope is dead.

As for what he says, “Remove the evil,” understand either the man who committed the crime of fornication, or his evil, or indeed the evil of each one of them. If you understand it of the man who committed the crime, he was rightly driven away, because he was dead not only through pleasure but also through action. The holy Church likewise drives away not those who die through pleasure but those who die through action. The devil kills some through pleasure and others through action.

Hence it was said to the serpent: “You shall crawl on your breast and belly” [Note: [Col. 0337D] Gen. 3:14; “upon your breast you shall go.”]. He beautifully placed “breast” first, because pleasure precedes action.

The Corinthians, since they not only did not avoid the company of wicked people but also, whenever they had disputes, preferred to have them settled by unbelievers rather than by believers, were immediately reproved and marked out by these words: [Note: [Col. 0337D] In the autograph’s margin, chapter XXV is written here.] “Does any one of you dare,” and the rest; as though he were saying: “Why do you dare what ought not to be dared?”

In accordance with the Lord’s command: “If anyone wishes to go to court with you,” and the rest (Matt. 5:40), you ought not to have lawsuits. But since you do, why do you wish to have them settled by unbelievers? That he calls them “the unjust” shows that they were unbelievers.

It follows: “Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world?” It is as though he were saying: “You know.” Therefore, since you ought to have become such as to judge the world, it is astonishing that you seek its judgment.

The saints will judge the world because, by comparison with their faith, the world’s unbelief will be condemned.

It follows: “And if the world will be judged by you,” etc. The world is judged by you if none of its unbelief or wicked works is found in you. The meaning is: If you judge the world, you are not unworthy to judge its least matters; and if you judge the whole, you are not unworthy to judge particular matters.

It follows: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” By “angels” he means demons, because they sinned against nature. They did not have a body by which they might be weighed down, nor was there anyone to persuade them; therefore they are the authors of their own evils. The saints judge them when, aided by divine assistance, they exist above nature in obedience to God.

Elsewhere he also calls them “principalities,” “powers,” and “rulers of the world,” and says that they dwell in the heavenly places (Eph. 6:12). The meaning is: If we judge principalities, much more should we judge secular affairs or those who administer them.

It follows: “Therefore, secular judgments,” etc. By “secular” he means temporal or bodily matters arising from temporal goods—that is, estates, farms, and other such things.

He also calls them “contemptible,” either meaning foolish people or those who despise their own injuries. It should be known that above he used the word “business,” but did not show what kind it was. For business may be bodily, but it may also be spiritual, as in: “My fellow workers” (Rom. 16:3; Phil. 4:3)—that is, in evangelical preaching. Then he shows what kind he means: “secular judgments.”

Because he knew their heart and foolishness, and knew that they would immediately appoint fools as judges because he had forbidden unbelievers, he forestalled them, as though giving advice: “Appoint the contemptible” [Note: [Col. 0338D] The Vulgate has: “the contemptible who are in the Church.”]. And lest they think he wanted this, he added: “I say this to your shame”—that is, to your confusion—as though he were saying: “Do not think that I want this; I said it for your confusion.”

I would prefer you to appoint a wise and perfect man over this matter, one who could judge between brother and brother in accordance with the evangelical command. Therefore he added: “Is there no wise man among you?” etc., as though he were saying: “There is.”

It could have been a great disgrace if, among so many who acknowledged God, no wise man were found who could rightly judge between brother and brother.

Blessed Pope Gregory explains this passage differently. He says that the prophet says to the leaders of the Synagogue: “Seek judgment” (Isa. 1:27), whereas the Apostle says: “Appoint the contemptible to judge.” He says that the Apostle was going to exhort his people to the teaching of wisdom and prudence and to the greater gifts (1 Cor. 12:31), and above all to the gift of prophecy. Therefore he stated long beforehand: “Appoint the contemptible,” as though saying: “It is not fitting for you, who are able to penetrate greater things, to be occupied with these matters; rather, appoint over these affairs those whom you recognize as endowed with none of the greater gifts.”

And note that he calls these contemptible people wise. “There is not,” he says, “a wise man among you,” because those who are to be appointed to judge are not fools, but those who possess knowledge of earthly matters. Thus those who have greater freedom to penetrate heavenly and spiritual matters may be less occupied with earthly concerns.

Hence Moses appointed seventy men over the people in his place (Exod. 18:25; Deut. 1:15). It should be known, however, that those who surpass the merits of the general people ought not to despise the affairs of weak brothers. Rather, they should appoint over those affairs people whom they know to possess knowledge of human matters, so that the former may penetrate heavenly things more freely, while the latter, so that they may not be strangers to our works, may administer those matters whose knowledge they have received.

[Note: [Col. 0339D] In the autograph’s margin, chapter XXVI is written here.] Therefore you are altogether at fault [Note: [Col. 0339D] The Vulgate has: “There is indeed altogether a fault among you,” etc.], etc. They are condemned in two ways: either because, contrary to the commandment, they had lawsuits, or because, although they had them, they preferred to have them settled not by the faithful but by unbelievers.

And lest they think they could be free from sin if, while having lawsuits, they had them settled not by unbelievers but by believers, he added: “Therefore, altogether,” etc.; as though saying: “You sin in this one matter: that you have lawsuits.” For although you ought to have labored toward loving your brothers as kinsmen—for spiritual kinship is greater than bodily kinship—you not only do not love them, but also inflict injury upon them.

Even though it cannot be the case that a Christian has no lawsuits, contrary to the Lord’s command: “If anyone wishes to go to court with you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak also; and from the one who takes what is yours, do not demand it back” (Matt. 5:40), nevertheless those lawsuits should not be settled by unbelievers.

But perhaps someone says: “I complain justly, because I cannot survive; my possessions are being taken away and I am being proscribed. Therefore I seek the judgment of judges.” The Apostle anticipates this thought by saying: “Why do you not rather endure injury and suffer fraud?” [Note: [Col. 0339D] The Vulgate has: “There is indeed altogether a fault among you, that you have lawsuits among yourselves. Why do you not rather accept injury? Why do you not rather suffer fraud?” [Col. 0340D]] It is as though he were saying: “You do not patiently endure injuries and acts of plunder, but drag matters before human courts; indeed, by inflicting injuries, you provoke others to the same.”

And this against brothers. It is as though he were saying: “What you ought not to have done to outsiders, you inflict upon brothers as well.”

“Or do you not know,” etc. It is as though he were saying: “If the merciful are punished, much more are the unjust.” Therefore he says, “Do you not know?” as though he were saying, “You do know.” By saying “you know,” he shows that they did not act in ignorance. Therefore he added: “Do not be deceived.”

By these words he shows the authority of the law and the entrance to the heavenly kingdom. He makes clear that if any one of these people had been devoted to a single vice, he would be excluded from the heavenly kingdom.

He shows the authority of the law because divine law prohibits all these things; he shows the entrance to the heavenly kingdom because, if anyone were devoted to a single vice [Note: [Col. 0340D] I have judged that the word “were” (*existeret*), absent in the autograph, should be added for easier reading.], he could not enter the kingdom.

But what does he mean by saying, “Do not be deceived”? He wishes to show that they had known this but had consigned it to oblivion, since he had taught among them for a year and a half. Therefore he said this in order to bring back to their memory what they had forgotten.

It follows: “You know that neither the covetous,” etc., “nor the effeminate.” Some say that the “effeminate” are those who submit to this vice, while the “male prostitutes” are those who commit it. According to some, they are the effeminate—that is, the enervated—who are rooted out of the earth. Hence the prophet says: “The effeminate shall be rooted out of the earth” (1 Kings 14:24).

They are called effeminate from the prohibition—that is, without beards. The Apostle therefore prohibited this vice because divine laws abhorred it, while human laws restrained it; and for this reason they had concubines. That it is prohibited by divine law is shown where it says: “If a man lies with a male with a woman’s intercourse, let them both be put to death” (Lev. 20:13).

“Greedy.” There is a distinction between the covetous and the greedy. Every greedy person is covetous, but not every covetous person is greedy. A covetous person may cling tightly to his own possessions and yet not seize what belongs to others; but a greedy person, even if he scatters his own possessions extravagantly, is covetous because he desires what belongs to others.

“Drunkards.” A “drunkard” (*ebriosus*) is named from habitual drunkenness (*ebriositas*), while a “drunken person” (*ebrius*) is named from a state of drunkenness (*ebrietas*). A drunken person is one to whom it happens, whether because of affection or for some other reason; a drunkard is one whose drunkenness is continual.

Therefore the Apostle, speaking carefully, did not say that a drunken person is excluded from the kingdom, but that a drunkard is.

It follows: “They will possess the kingdom of God.” Terrible is this sentence in which the Apostle says that they will not possess the kingdom of God. It is terrible because he was the tongue of the Holy Spirit, and the Spirit Himself spoke through him. Therefore we must fear lest we succumb to one of these vices and thus be excluded from the kingdom.

It follows: “And such were some of you,” etc. Lest they think that he wished merely to criticize vices and not to show that they themselves had possessed them, he said: “And such were some of you.”

Note that he says “some,” not “indeed all.” If he had said “all,” he would seem to include everyone; if he had said nothing, he would exclude everyone. Therefore, speaking moderately, he said “some.”

It should also be known that by these words he instills terror in his people, but then adds encouragement by saying: [Col. 0341A] “But you have been washed,” etc.

Why does he say this? Because when people hear good things said about themselves falsely, they commonly strive to live and conduct themselves in such a way that they may truly be what they falsely hear being said about them.

It follows: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,” etc. It should be noted that they had been reborn through the sacrament of baptism and renewed through the grace of the Holy Spirit. For baptism is the beginning of religious devotion and the foundation of all piety and goodness.

Therefore he recalls their former good condition to their memory, so that, hearing it, they might grieve that they had lost it after being deceived by the pseudo-apostles, and, by repenting and living rightly, return to the same good state.

In this, preachers are instructed that, when those who had once become good hearers have become evil, they should recall their former goodness to their memory and expose their evils by exaggerating them, so that, hearing what they have lost, they may return to the same condition through repentance and right conduct.

[Note: [Col. 0341D] In the autograph’s margin, chapter XXVIII is written here. Chapter XXVII is marked nowhere.] “All things are lawful for me,” etc. Above he said that neither fornicators, nor those serving idols, nor the others would possess the kingdom. According to some, he therefore added: “All things are lawful for me,” showing that he had free will to do these things, although they were not expedient.

But what they say is contrary to the fact that all those things are prohibited by divine law, and therefore none of them is lawful. For this reason that interpretation must be rejected.

Others say that nothing is unlawful, because the Apostle says that all things are lawful. They do not understand the force of the statement, whether through forgetfulness or obstinacy. If that were so, John—whom we do not doubt was sanctified in the womb and mindful of this teaching—would never have said to Herod: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s adulterous wife” (Mark 6:18). Nor would the Lord have said: “It is not lawful to give what is holy to dogs” [Note: [Col. 0341D] Matt. 7:6. The Vulgate has: “Do not give what is holy to dogs”; see also 15:26.] or that it is not lawful to give holy loaves to laypeople, and other such things.

It should rightly be noted that the Apostle had begun to speak about the crime of fornication. Since he knew that the incentive, fuel, and material of fornication is intemperance of the appetite, he began, amid the words by which he prohibited fornication, to speak about food.

“All things,” he says, “are lawful for me”—that is, to eat every kind of food—“but they are not all expedient,” lest I fall into the evil of fornication. Therefore whoever desires to overcome the evil of fornication completely should strive to avoid intemperance of the appetite and to recognize the ways in which it tempts people.

It tempts in five ways, as blessed Gregory says. Sometimes it causes the hour of necessity to be anticipated; hence Jonathan received the sentence of death (1 Sam. 14:39, 44). Sometimes it causes people to seek richer foods; hence the children of Israel offended God in the desert (2 Kings 16:3), because, despising manna (Num. 21:5), they sought more luxurious bodily food.

Sometimes it causes them to seek more elaborately prepared foods; hence the first fault of the sons of Eli was that, at their request, the priest’s servant received not meat cooked according to the ancient custom but raw meat, so that he could prepare it more carefully (1 Sam. 2:15).

Sometimes it causes people to exceed the proper measure; hence the Lord, speaking to Jerusalem, says: “This was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: pride, abundance of bread, and fullness” (Ezek. 16:49). By these words He shows that, by exceeding moderation in eating, they reached an unbelievable ardor of lust.

Sometimes it even causes people to consume cheap food greedily; hence Esau sold his birthright for a dish of lentils (Gen. 25:33). The sale of his birthright shows with what ardor he burned to eat cheap food.

It should also be understood that sin lies not in food but in the appetite for food. Thus we often do not offend when we eat richer foods without greed, while we often sin when we eat cheap foods greedily.

The devil recognized this: he first tempted the first Adam not with meat but with an apple (Gen. 3:6), and the second Adam with bread (Luke 4:3). Hence Adam sinned by eating the apple, while Elijah preserved the integrity of his body by eating meat (1 Kings 19:21). Whoever does what he knows to be contrary to himself, like Adam, eats the fruit of the forbidden tree.

Blessed Augustine investigated this passage more deeply and made the Apostle’s intention clear. He says: “Everything that is unlawful is not expedient; yet not everything that is not expedient is unlawful.” If this is so, it is difficult to define by a general rule what the difference is between what is unlawful and therefore not expedient, and what is lawful but nevertheless not expedient.

Yet someone can quickly answer: “Everything that is unlawful is sin, and every sin is not expedient; therefore everything that is not expedient is unlawful.” Where, then, is what the Apostle says: “All things are lawful, but not all things are expedient”?

But since we do not doubt that the Apostle spoke truly, and do not dare to call certain sins lawful, it should be understood that some things are lawful which, if done, would not be sins; nevertheless, lest they impede others from the kingdom, they ought not to be done. There are also certain lawful things that are not expedient to do.

We must therefore see what those lawful things are: namely, those that are done through that righteousness which pertains to God. Those things are unlawful that the same righteousness prohibits in such a way that they are never to be done, even if they are praised by those who learn of them.

It should also be understood that, when you do not do the things that are lawful, you are not constrained by the bond of law; rather, you avoid the benevolence of free love.

To make this clearer, an example should be given. It should rightly be noted that the Lord commands nothing unjust; whatever He prohibits is altogether unlawful. He Himself does not command a man to dismiss an unbelieving wife. If He commanded it, it would otherwise be unlawful to do so, and the Apostle would never say: “I say, not the Lord.”

But the Lord permits a wife to be dismissed on account of fornication. If she may be dismissed for carnal fornication, much more may she be dismissed for spiritual fornication—that is, unbelief—of which the Psalmist says: “You destroyed all those who fornicate from you” (Ps. 72:6).

And why [Note: [Col. 0342D] The autograph has: “And what would be.” Nevertheless, in view of the words that follow, which resolve the question, “why” seems preferable.] would it be? “But for me,” he says, “it is good to cling to God.” Therefore it was lawful to dismiss a wife on account of unbelief. Yet if she were dismissed for that reason, an opportunity would be given, through the separation of the spouses, both for causing scandal and for criticizing evangelical teaching, as well as for remaining in unbelief.

The Apostle therefore addresses this necessity: although it is lawful, it is not expedient, and he commanded that she not be dismissed.

It follows: “If any brother,” he says, “has an unbelieving wife” [Note: [Col. 0343D] This verse is the twelfth verse of the following chapter—namely, chapter seven—which our author seems here to indicate as following immediately.], etc. The same meaning should be retained in all those matters that he recognizes as lawful but understands to be harmful to the person concerned.

Likewise, it is lawful for us to eat everything; but if we persist in feasting, we are drawn toward unlawful things. Therefore it is expedient that we not make use even of lawful things, lest we be drawn toward unlawful things.

To make the meaning of this passage clearer, it should be known that “all things are lawful” means what he says elsewhere: “All things are clean” (Rom. 14:20); and “not all things are expedient” means: “It is evil for the person who eats through causing offense” (ibid.).

Repeating himself, he says: “All things are lawful for me”—namely, those things that were lawful for his fellow apostles: food, clothing, and whatever else was necessary.

But because he saw that the pseudo-apostles [Note: [Col. 0343D] The autograph has “pseudo-apostles.”] were seeking an opportunity to receive something, he himself did not wish to receive anything. Nor was it appropriate for him to accept anything from people whom he had discovered to be involved in such great crimes, because, if he accepted anything, the fervor of evangelizing would grow cold.

Those who accept gifts from people who give precisely in order to incline the minds of their teachers lose the freedom to preach. Therefore, lest he lose the freedom to rebuke them, he did not wish to accept anything from them.

For this reason it follows, and he says: “But I will not be brought under anyone’s power,” as though he were saying: “I do not wish to accept anything, lest, having been given over to you through your gifts, I lose the freedom to rebuke you and be brought under your power.”

It follows: “Food is for the belly, and the belly for food” (the sense is, “is subject to food”); “but God will destroy both it and them.” The belly will indeed be destroyed when the time for sowing or laboring has passed.

This passage is directed against the false apostles, who preached for the sake of their belly.

It follows: “But the body is not for fornication, but for the Lord” (the sense is, “let it be subjected to the Lord”); “and the Lord for the body” (the sense is, “will be joined or united to it”). For just as, by despising His commandments, we withdraw farther from Him, so, by fulfilling them, we cling more closely to Him.

In another sense, “the Lord for the body” means that He will give immortality to the body when it has been raised, on account of the merit of the soul that governs it and draws it toward good works, so that the soul may rejoice with the body once it has been raised.

It follows: “But God raised up the Lord,” [Col. 0344A] [Note: [Col. 0343D] The autograph has “will raise.”] etc. This is the same meaning, which he confirms through the Lord’s resurrection. “The power of God” is the Son. Therefore, if He was raised through the power of God, He was raised through Himself. Hence He also says: “Destroy this temple” (John 2:19), etc.

The resurrection was the work of the whole Trinity. For it should be known that, just as He Himself, rising from the dead, showed His disciples the marks of the nails and the scars of His wounds in order to instruct them more firmly in faith in the resurrection (John 20:26), so He too will raise us if we have become members of Him.

Therefore let us strive to be His members, so that we may deserve to be raised with Him and by Him.

Do you not know that your bodies, etc. For the meaning and wording depend upon the intention already begun. [Note: [Col. 0343D] In the autograph’s margin, chapter XXIX is indicated here.] They had begun above to speak about the sin of fornication, and he continues in the intention already begun, saying: “You do not know,” etc. Our bodies are therefore members of Christ because God became man. For it must be understood that the whole Church spread throughout the world is the body of Christ, and individuals are members of that body, whose head is Christ. Hence the Apostle says: “Christ, the Savior of our body” (Eph. 5:23). And it must be noted that he did not assume only a soul; for, if he had assumed only a soul, our souls would be called members of Christ, not our bodies. But because he assumed and redeemed both—that is, body and soul—our bodies are therefore said to be members of Christ. It should also be observed that he did not say “you are,” or “your souls,” but “your bodies,” for the reason already stated.

And because our bodies are members of Christ, let no one despise himself, let no one scorn himself by saying: “I shall do whatever I want; I shall live according to my own inclination, since I am nothing, for all flesh is grass; I shall plunge myself into some precipice.” If such a person despises himself, let him look attentively upon Christ [Note: [Col. 0343D] Here the word *despiciat* more properly, clearly and distinctly, means “to see” or “to comprehend,” so that the sense should be taken imperatively: namely, let him attentively consider Christ who dares to despise himself; or let whoever regards his body as worthless bring Christ’s passion and redemption back to mind. It means this rather than what the word ordinarily signifies, namely, “let him despise” or “hold in contempt.” Nevertheless, it could also rightly be understood in that sense if it was said ironically and as an invective: namely, “let him despise Christ, let him regard Christ as worthless,” since he dares to think little of himself. The first interpretation is more strongly supported by what follows.], by whose precious blood he has been redeemed; and, if he does not spare himself [Note: [Col. 0344D] The autograph has *verbi* in place of *sibi*, which I judged should be corrected both from the sense and from what follows.], at least let him spare Christ, and by sparing Christ he will spare himself.

Then follows: “Taking, therefore, the members of Christ,” etc. He speaks by asking: “Taking?” and answers by denying: “May it never be!” He fittingly denies it in this way, because whoever joins his members to a prostitute makes them one body. As long as someone lives chastely and holily, he is a member of Christ; but if he is defiled by some impurity, he begins to belong to a prostitute, and when the person joined to her becomes her member, and perhaps she is a Christian woman who gives her consent to him, then, just as he becomes a member of the prostitute, so she becomes a member of the one who practices prostitution. But it must be understood that both offend Christ: neither considers the price or the gift granted to them, nor considers what kind of person—and how great a person—he is who called his servants not only brothers but also members.

For if this gift were not possessed, it would be desired; but because it is possessed, one must live in such a way as not to lose it and must give thanks to him for it.

But there were some who said that a woman’s offense against a man was the greater. Therefore, so that it might not seem to be the greater offense, the Apostle says: “Making a member of a prostitute.” Then follows: “Or do you not know that the one who clings to a prostitute,” etc. It is as though he said: “You do not fail to know this; rather, you know it.” He rightly says “one body,” because, just as there is one nature, so there is one guilt; and just as there is one act and one pleasure, so the offense is equal.

Then follows: “The two will be one flesh.” This was first said to the first man: “For this reason a man will leave father and mother” (Gen. 2:24), etc. For just as two become one body through lawful intercourse, so these two become one through illicit desire.

Then follows: “The one who clings to the Lord is one spirit.” Above, speaking about two human beings, he said “one body”; but now, speaking about different spirits—that is, God’s and man’s—he did not say “they are one,” as above. There is a great difference, however, between the Spirit of God and the human spirit. The Spirit of God is blessed and perfect without the human spirit, whereas the human spirit cannot exist without God.

What John says when speaking about the unity of the body [Note: [Col. 0345D] John 17:11, 21, and 24, concerning the unity of the body, namely the mystical body.]: “Father, I will that, just as you and I are one, so they too may be one” [Note: [Col. 0345D] Namely, joined by the bond of faith and love in imitation of the divine Persons.], is not contrary to this passage. There, because of the unequal nature, he says: “Let them be one as we are”; he does not say, “We are all one.” Here, however, because of the grace received by the human spirit, so that, joined to the Spirit of God, it wills what he himself wills, he says: “There is one Spirit,” because the human spirit is joined to the Spirit of God, not so as to will anything other than what he himself wills.

[Note: [Col. 0346D] In the autograph’s margin, chapter XXX is indicated here.] Then follows: “Flee fornication.” The Apostle also warns that fornication must be fled, because this vice is such that it makes children of God into children of the devil. The Apostle says “flee” twice, because other vices are to be met with battle, whereas this one must be fled on foot. Against other vices one must fight with the arms; this one must be avoided with the feet. Jerome says: “Death is avoided either by the shield or by the feet.” A shield must be raised against the other vices; this one must be fled with the feet. It must be understood that the Apostle intensifies his language by saying: “Flee fornication” [Col. 0345D]—against those who remain long in this vice and, because they regard it as insignificant for too long, are not corrected even when reproved by some teacher.

That this vice must be avoided is shown by examples. If Cain, who polluted the earth with his brother’s blood (Gen. 4:8), was rejected by the Lord and is called a fratricide throughout all sacred Scripture, with what rashness do you think you can escape fellowship with Christ while polluting a member of Christ? If Enoch, by living chastely and purely, was taken away (Gen. 5:24), how do you think you can enter heaven while living impurely? If Noah alone, by abandoning the company of the wicked and entering the ark, escaped the common danger of the flood (Gen. 6:7–8), how do you think you can pass through the common destruction while enjoying the company of the wicked? If Abraham alone, by leaving Ur of the Chaldeans (Gen. 11:31)—that is, the fire—merited to be blessed, how do you think you can be blessed while remaining in the fire of carnal pleasure? If Isaac left the house and went into the field to meditate (Gen. 24:63), how do you search out heavenly things while remaining in the house of carnal pleasure? If Jacob and his sons grievously resented the rape of Dinah (Gen. 34:7), how can you rejoice in the violation of your own body? If Joseph was found worthy of praise among his brothers and bore the figure of Christ [Col. 0346B] because he escaped the crime of fornication, what must you do? For it is written that, leaving his cloak behind, he fled outside from her (Gen. 39:12).

There is no other way. For if he had succumbed to this vice, he would have died—his soul would have died, in accordance with the statement: “The soul that sins” (Lev. 18:29), etc. Nor could it rightly have been said to his father: “Your son lives” (Gen. 45:6); nor could it have been said that he ruled over the whole land of Egypt (ibid.), but only over some part of it. For those who overcome all vices rule over the whole of Egypt.

That those who succumb to this vice die is testified by Susanna, who said to the elders: “For if I do this” [Note: [Col. 0346D] Dan. 13:22: “For if I do this, it is death for me.”], etc. She saw the death of soul and body, but she chose to avoid the death of the soul and to succumb to the death of the body. And whoever, following her example, avoids the death of the soul is not forgetful of David fleeing Saul and avoiding death (1 Sam. 23). For by Saul are signified the devil and vices; by David, the elect soul, which by fighting and fleeing the devil’s suggestions turns them aside.

Then follows: “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body, but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body.” This passage is understood in various ways by the teachers [Note: [Col. 0346D] On this, see the blessed Cyprian, Letter 49.]. Novatus also wished to put it forward in the form of a question.
