Some understand it as follows: they say that fornication can be committed only by two, whereas the other sins can be committed even by one. One person cannot be called a body; two, however, can already be called a body. Therefore, the one who commits fornication sins in the body of the Church.

Others understand it of husband and wife, who are one body. Hence the earlier statement: “The two will be one flesh.” Therefore, the one who commits fornication sins against his own body—that is, either the husband against his wife or the wife against her husband.

The blessed Augustine examined this question more deeply, so deeply that he said—I do not know whether fully conclusively—that nevertheless, with God’s help, many plausible things can be said about it. “We must see,” he says, “from where the Apostle’s argument descended.” A little earlier he says: “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?” etc., down to the passage where he says: “Glorify and bear God in your body.”

In this passage the Apostle is concerned with bodily purity and wishes to instill fear in the hearts of his hearers, so that they may fear making the members of Christ members of a prostitute through impurity. But the question is why he said: “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body.” Can those things that he placed a little earlier be carried out without the body’s activity? No. You may think about something carnal, but could you think without the flesh? Or could you separate what the Psalmist says, “The fool said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Ps. 13:1), from those works about which he says, “We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ” (Rom. 14:10), etc.? No, I say, he cannot, because as long as he remains in the body he can say, “There is no God.”

The same man says elsewhere: “The works of the flesh are manifest, which are fornication” (Gal. 5:19), etc.; among these works of the flesh he lists spiritual vices. If, then, that eminent preacher in faith and truth attributes spiritual vices to the flesh, why does he say: “Every other sin is outside the body, but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body”?

So that this may not appear contradictory, it must be understood that there are two kinds of fornication: one particular, which is committed in the body, and another general one, which is nevertheless spiritual.

If, therefore, he wished the particular fornication to be understood, he certainly said “he sins against his own body” by way of intensification, because the evil of this fornication is so great and so powerful that it holds the person detained by it bound and chained, and makes him a slave to the body. At the very moment of consummation, he is unable to think about anything else, direct his attention elsewhere, or turn the mind’s perception elsewhere. Therefore he says: “He sins against his own body.” This could not be said of other sins, because, even if a person commits various other sins, he can think of one thing and do another, and need not always remain occupied with that one matter. Thus, in comparison with it, the other sins are said to occur outside the body.

It can also be understood in another way. There is a general fornication, which is also spiritual, of which the Psalmist says: “You have destroyed all who fornicate away from you” (Ps. 72:26). And to show what this fornication was, he immediately added: “But for me it is good to cling to God.” James speaks of the same thing: “Adulterers” [Note: [Col. 0347D] James 4:4; the autograph reads “covetous.” I thought it appropriate to follow my reading and the sense, and therefore corrected it as an error.], he says, “do you not know that friendship with this world is enmity with God?”

By these words he shows that to be a friend of the world is to fornicate against God. Hence the Lord also says: “No one can serve two masters” (Luke 16:13). And he shows who the two masters are: “You cannot,” he says, “serve God and Mammon”—that is, be joined to me and to the world.

John likewise says: “Everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh and the desire of the eyes” (1 John 2:16), etc., down to what he says: “But the one who does the will of God remains forever” (ibid., 17).

Therefore, whoever, out of love for his carnal pleasure, follows and embraces the desires of this world and withdraws from God certainly fornicates and sins against his own body—that is, because of love for his body he withdraws from God. But if, without clinging to the world, he clings to God, despising and overcoming the world’s pleasures and desires, and nevertheless sins through ignorance, forgetfulness, sudden seizure, or some similar circumstance, he sins, as it were, outside the body. That is, he does not withdraw from God out of love for his own body.

The Apostle may have wished one of these things to be understood, or perhaps both, since it is customary in the sacred Scriptures that many things can be understood under a single word or statement.

Then follows: “Or do you not know that your members are the temple” [Note: [Col. 0348D] The Vulgate reads: “are the temple.”] “of the Holy Spirit?” For in the statement that our bodies are members of Christ and that our members are the temple of the Holy Spirit, it is shown that he himself is the Creator and not a creature, and that he is not unequal to the Father and the Son. “Whom you have from God” is said to show that they had not received him from themselves.

Then follows: “And you are not your own,” as though he said: “Because you have become children of God in baptism, live not according to your own will but according to his.” He shows why they are not their own: “For you were bought at a great price.” It is as though he said: “If a person who buys a slave for a small price demands continuous and perpetual service from him, how much more does God, who redeemed you at so great a price—that is, not with perishable gold or silver, as Peter says, but with the most precious blood of the spotless Lamb (1 Pet. 1:18), namely, our Lord Jesus Christ—wish to demand from us eternal and continuous service?”

And therefore: “Glorify and bear God in your body.” To glorify God is to live according to his commandment. We bear God in our body when we preserve his image unharmed. It was said at the beginning: “God made man in his own image and likeness” (Gen. 1:27). Therefore, when we are polluted through impurity, we violate God’s image; but through repentance and worthy fruits of repentance we can restore that same image within us.

[Note: [Col. 0348D] In the autograph’s margin, chapter XXXI is indicated here. The Vulgate, however, begins chapter VII.] (Chapter VII.) Then follows: “Now concerning the matters about which you wrote to me,” etc. The Apostle’s intention is now different. Earlier he had spoken about unlawful things; now he speaks about lawful things. In an appropriate order, he first prohibited what was unlawful—that is, the evil of fornication—and now he commends what is lawful—that is, the good of marriage. This same order is shown to have been observed in many other passages of the sacred Scriptures.

What he says, “Concerning the matters about which you wrote,” etc., can be understood in two ways, because there can also be two intentions. According to some, while the Apostle remained among them for a year and six months, he taught that the good of continence should be preserved. But because some of them were going astray into unlawful conduct, they informed him of this in writing and sent a letter to their teacher and master, seeking advice about what should be done.

Therefore he says: “Concerning the matters about which you wrote,” etc., as though he said: “It was good, as I taught; but because you have informed me that some of you are going astray into unlawful conduct, let apostolic authority come to their aid. For I do not wish to prohibit lawful things in such a way that they go astray into unlawful things.” Therefore: “Because of fornications” [Note: [Col. 0349D] The Vulgate reads “fornication.” Our text agrees with the Greek, which also has “fornications.”] “let each man have his own wife,” etc.

There is also another, more elevated intention. They had been deceived by false apostles, who, among other things, taught them to despise marriage. Yet they patiently endured the other matters and had followed only this teaching [Note: [Col. 0349D] The autograph reads *has solam secuto*, which I judged should be corrected.]. Agitated and troubled, they wrote to their teacher, asking what he himself thought.

For this reason it is said: “Concerning the matters about which you wrote,” as though he said: “What they taught is good, although they taught it neither with a proper intention nor out of devotion to faith, religion, or pleasing God, but rather so that they might appear holier and better. But because many of you are going astray into unlawful conduct, so that you may no longer go astray because of fornications, let each man have his own wife,” etc.

Note that it does not say “because of the propagation of children,” but “because of fornication.”

Then follows: “Let the husband render the debt to his wife,” etc. The meaning is: Let them share one mind according to the law of nature, lest, if one draws the other into error, the other perish. He also explains this immediately by adding: “The woman does not have authority over her own body,” because either she does not have authority to give her body to another, or, certainly, if one of them is unwilling, the other does not have the authority to maintain continence.

Therefore he adds: “Do not defraud one another.” Neither spouse should practice continence except by mutual consent. Hence he adds: “Except by mutual consent for a time.” Why? “So that you may devote yourselves to prayer.”

Although, in accordance with the Lord’s command and that of this Apostle, one ought always to pray, nevertheless this continence must also frequently be observed, so that God may be entreated more purely. For the more anyone abstains from lawful things, the more purely he can entreat God and the more easily move him to mercy. This is also demonstrated in the writings of the Old Testament.

For when the Lord was about to descend upon Mount Sinai to give the law, Moses ordered the children of Israel to abstain and to sanctify themselves (Exod. 19:20). The priest Abiathar [Note: [Col. 0350D] Abiathar, who was also called Ahimelech, son of Ahitub and brother of Ahijah, whom he succeeded in the high priesthood, etc.] also, when he was about to give the holy loaves to David and his young men, asked whether they were pure. He received the answer: “Certainly, if the matter concerns women” (1 Sam. 21:5), etc. Here one should note the value of continual and constant abstinence, since abstinence for only three days had such force.

That one should also abstain from lawful things is shown in the case of the Nazirites, who abstained even from raisins (Num. 6:4). For the more anyone abstains from lawful things, the more he shows with what ardor he wishes to obtain what he asks.

When the time of prayer has been completed, he urges them to return for a time to intercourse, when he says: “Return again to the same.” Why? “Lest Satan tempt you,” he says, etc. Satan, that is, the devil, daily seeks an opportunity to tempt, so that, as the Apostle Peter says, “like a roaring lion he prowls around” (1 Pet. 5:8), etc. But he finds an opportunity to deceive especially when one spouse wishes to practice continence while the other does not, because then he finds an opening to draw the other into the evil of fornication.

This must certainly be known: marriages are pure and holy, because they are celebrated at God’s command; they contain nothing shameful and nothing dishonorable. Therefore, if married people commit anything shameful, dishonorable, or indecent, it is not the fault of marriage but of the people. Marriage is so holy that it causes something unrelated to it to be forgiven for its sake.

It should also be noted that in the Old Testament continence gave way to marriage because of the desire for children; now, however, lack of continence is disclosed and relaxed for the sake of the good of marriage. Therefore it was said above, “because of fornication,” and not “for the propagation of children.”

Accordingly, the causes of the different degrees must be distinguished. If you distinguish them, continence has the greater merit; intercourse, when undertaken for the sake of children, is not sin; because of lack of continence, intercourse is a fault, but a pardonable one; fornication and adultery, however, are an exceptional sacrilege.

Therefore this conjugal chastity must be observed with greater care, lest, while one seeks the means by which she herself may be blessed and rewarded, the other thereby be endangered.

It should also be noted that lovers of lust commonly argue against this teaching: “Why did God make male and female and bless them, saying, ‘Increase and multiply,’ if he did not wish that same blessing to remain forever?” They should be answered that he wished that blessing to remain until the human race had multiplied; once it had multiplied, he wished it to cease, in accordance with Solomon’s statement: “A time for embracing and a time to be far from embraces” (Eccl. 3:5).

But they commonly respond to this again: “Why did God not make all human beings from the earth, as he made Adam, since there is no doubt that he could have done so?” They should be answered that one must not consider what he could have done, but what he did.

If they wish to preserve the custom of the Old Testament, let them marry daughters, as Adam did, and sisters, as Cain did. The patriarchs also took several wives, not for the sake of lust but for the procreation of children. But how absurd this is is evident to almost everyone.

It is nevertheless understood that he who orders everything in number, measure, and weight arranged what was fitting for each period: at that time, the propagation of children; now, since human beings multiply more than is appropriate, the good of continence.

The meaning of this passage, in which the Apostle says: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman,” down to where he says, “Lest Satan tempt you,” etc., is found in the writings of the Old Testament—namely, where it is read that Lot, fleeing burning Sodom after being warned by God’s command to seek the mountains, went up into the hills (Gen. 19:30).

What, then, is Lot’s fleeing burning Sodom except avoiding the incitements and desires of one’s flesh? The height of the mountains signifies the merit of those who practice continence. He stands upon the mountain who seeks fruit only in the flesh; he stands even more upon the mountain who preserves the good of continence.

There are some, however, who, although they flee burning Sodom—that is, the desires of their flesh—cannot climb the mountain. This means that they can neither preserve the good of continence nor, because of their lack of continence, seek only the propagation of children in marriage.

This is signified by what Lot says to the angel: “There is a small city nearby, to which I can flee; is it not little, and shall I not be saved and my soul live in it?” (Gen. 19:20.) This city, called Zoar, is rightly said to be small, because the life of married people is neither great nor distinguished by signs or virtues. It is also rightly said to be nearby, because it is not far from the world.

But those who flee burning Sodom and cannot climb the mountains—that is, who avoid a condemnable life but do not properly observe the laws of marriage—must be saved by prayer. Hence the angel said to Lot: “In this I have heard your prayers, so that I would not destroy the city for which you spoke” (ibid., 21). Just as he was saved by prayer, so it is necessary that these people be saved by prayer.

[Note: [Col. 0351D] In the autograph’s margin, chapter XXXII is indicated here.] Then follows: “Now I say this by way of indulgence,” etc. Where indulgence is mentioned, it is superfluous to deny that there is sin. It is as though he said: “As a physician most skilled in medicine, I do not advise those who are standing or healthy, but, as to people who are falling and weak, I give commands.”

Like a physician who, seeing a sick person impatient, allows certain fruits so that he may not turn to more harmful things, so the Apostle, seeing that the Corinthians were impatient and lacking in continence, allowed what was lawful so that they would not turn to what was unlawful. It is as though he said: “I am not speaking to those who are standing, but, as to those who are falling, I give commands so that they may not fall to the ground.”

And this must be understood: some things are commanded; some are permitted; and some are pardoned.

Then follows: “But I wish all people to be as I myself am.” See how devout and solicitous the teacher is! As far as his devout and solicitous affection is concerned, he could wish for nothing more than that everyone should be as he himself was. This ought to be the voice of all preachers.

And note that he was not envious when he wished everyone to be like himself. What sort of person he was is revealed below.

Then follows: “Each person has his own gift from God.” By these words he invites us to preserve the good of continence. He says “from God” to show that, although it is lesser, the good of marriage also comes from him—whether we should ask it of the one from whom we seek it if we do not possess it, and to whom we should give thanks if we do possess it; or to show how concerned we ought to be in asking for it, receiving it, and preserving it.

Nevertheless, our conscience is small and weak for asking, receiving, and preserving, unless it is helped by him who says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). “One in this way and another in that”: that is, one person has the good of continence, another the good of marriage.

Then follows: “Now I say to the unmarried and to widows,” etc. Who was speaking? The Apostle. To whom? To those practicing continence and to virgins. Therefore he was a virgin—not, as some have said, a married man. For if he had had a wife, he would have wished all those to whom he was speaking to lack continence. But it must be understood that he was a virgin.

This is shown by the fact that, while he was zealous for the law (Gal. 1:14), he was overtaken as a young man by the grace of God (ibid., 15). And that this was so is made clear by the Acts of the Apostles: “Witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of the young man who was called Saul” (Acts 7:57).

“It is good for them if they remain as I am.” [Col. 0352B] By these words he calls us to the good of continence, but not in such a way that, by abstaining from lawful things, we are drawn into unlawful things. It is as though he said: “I show you my desire, but I do not wish to cast a snare upon you. Let each one of you test and examine himself to see whether he can preserve continence; if not, let him marry.”

This is what he adds: “But if they do not practice continence, let them marry.” That is: if they have tested themselves and recognized that they cannot preserve continence, let them marry.

He explains this by adding: “For it is better to marry than to burn.” He says “to burn” because the person who joins his will to the heat of his flesh and is overcome by it is burning. It belongs to the perfect to feel the heat and not be overcome. For it is exceedingly difficult to join one’s will to the heat and not be overcome.

[Col. 0352C] Then follows: “But to those who are joined in marriage,” etc. Here the intention is different. But the question must be asked why, when the Lord commands that a wife not be abandoned (Matt. 5:31; 19:10; Mark 10:2, 7), Paul says, “if she departs.” If the Lord commanded it, it is unlawful; and if it is unlawful, how can Paul say, “if she departs”? Paul must be questioned. But the Lord answers on his behalf.

For he says that a wife must not be abandoned except on account of fornication (Matt. 19:9). Since the Lord permits her to be abandoned for the reason of fornication, he gives Paul room to offer counsel: namely, he says, “Let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband.”

[Note: [Col. 0351D] In the autograph’s margin, chapter XXXIV is indicated here, but chapter XXXIII is not found marked.] “And let the husband not dismiss his wife” (understood: likewise). By these words it is shown that both are bound by the same law. Accordingly, those people must not be heeded who say that the higher and lower sex, the head and the member, ought not to be bound by one law [Note: [Col. 0351D] I thought the particle “not” should be added for the sake of the sense.]. [Note: [Col. 0352D] Against the error of Ambrosiaster, who interprets this verse as meaning that a husband is permitted to take another wife because of his wife’s fornication, although the Apostle prohibits both.]

Then follows: “Now to the rest I say.” Above he had said that the Lord spoke about both kinds of believers; but the Apostle now speaks about those others who are believers on one side while unbelievers are found on the other. He makes this clear by adding: “If any brother has,” etc.

But since the Lord commands that a wife not be abandoned, why does Paul say: “If she wishes to live with him, let her not be dismissed”? It must be understood that the Lord permitted her to be abandoned on account of fornication. Therefore Paul gave the counsel not to dismiss her, because unbelief is fornication.

For if the Lord had not permitted a wife to be dismissed on account of fornication, and if unbelief were fornication, the Apostle would in no way have given the counsel not to dismiss her, since what is permitted may be done or not done without guilt.

But he does not say this so that an unbeliever may now take a believer as a spouse. Rather, at the beginning of the Church he speaks about those who had been joined before the faith, when, as the Apostles preached, some believed and others did not. He says that such spouses should not be dismissed, so that through the wife’s faith and conduct the unbelieving husband may be drawn to the faith. Thus Peter says: “If any do not obey the word, they may be won without a word through the faith and conduct of their wives” (1 Pet. 3:1).

He explains this by adding: “The unbelieving husband is sanctified,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0353D] In the autograph’s margin, chapter XXXV is indicated here.] This happened among that very people, so that a believing wife drew an unbelieving husband to the faith, and a believing husband drew an unbelieving wife to the faith.

“Otherwise your children,” etc. This also happened among that very people, so that believing parents drew unbelieving children to the faith. Therefore the Apostle did not wish separation. For if it occurred, when the children believed, they would follow their unbelieving parents, and an opportunity would be given for remaining in unbelief.

Then follows: “But if the unbeliever departs,” etc.—that is, if he rejects your faith and, seeking an opportunity to depart, departs. He must be tolerated only so long as he persecutes the faith by insulting you. But when he begins to wish to depart, let him depart.

“But a brother or a sister is not,” etc. That is, such a person is not so subject to this obligation that he should lose the faith because of it. And not only because of that person, but also not because of a father, mother, or any possessions that are owned like money. Nor should one quarrel with such people, nor enjoy their conversation. Why did he add this? “Because God has called us in peace.”

Then follows: “For how do you know, wife,” etc. This relates to what came before, where he had said that the believing husband did not wish to abandon an unbelieving wife. It is as though he said: “If God waits for faith, much more should you. You have believed now; he will believe then, because the one who has drawn you to the faith will certainly draw him also.”

Therefore he adds: “Unless it is to each one,” etc. God has divided matters so that you believe now and he then. Therefore he adds: “Let him walk in this way.” He explains this by adding: “Each one as God has called.” God has called you so that you believe now and him so that he believes then.

“As in all,” etc. In saying this, he means that they had not taught anything contrary or perverse; and while they hear that they have been taught the general doctrine, they should be ashamed not to be observers of it.

Then follows: “Was anyone called while circumcised?” [Note: [Col. 0353D] The question mark found in the Vulgate is lacking here.] “Let him not draw on the foreskin,” etc. These words depend upon the preceding statement: “Let each one walk as God has called him.”

Here the question must be examined carefully: why does the Apostle say that a circumcised person should not draw on the foreskin, when what has been cut away cannot be restored? The meaning, therefore, is this: “Let the circumcised person not draw on the foreskin”—that is, let him not live as one uncircumcised; and “the one called in the foreskin should not draw on circumcision”—that is, let him not live as one circumcised.

For example, if a Jew is called to the faith and has also become a Christian, he should not regard himself as unworthy of being called a Christian because he does not have a foreskin, thereby giving glory to the foreskin.

Likewise, if a Gentile is called to the faith and has already become a Christian, he should not regard himself as unworthy of being called a Christian unless he is circumcised, thereby giving glory to circumcision because he hears circumcised people preferred.

He must know that the Jews are not preferred because they are circumcised, but because of the faith and merit of Abraham. Indeed, they are not merely not preferred; they are made worse than the uncircumcised, because it is less serious never to have been a son of Abraham than to have ceased to be one.

It should certainly be noted that these words are not those of someone imposing a command, but rather of someone giving counsel: no Jew should be compelled to pass over to the foreskin, nor a Gentile to circumcision, but each should have the freedom to remain where he is or to pass over wherever he wishes.

To make the Apostle’s intention clearer, it must be understood that if a Jew were in a place where he would scandalize no one and wished to draw on the foreskin—that is, to withdraw completely from the carnal observances of the law—the Apostle would not rebuke him.

Likewise, if a Gentile were in a place where he would scandalize no one and wished to draw on circumcision, not because he believed it would benefit him, but to show that he did not reject the sign that had also been a sign in its own time, the Apostle would not rebuke him.

For he makes clear what the meaning and intention are when he adds: “Circumcision is nothing,” etc. By these words he shows that circumcision and the foreskin neither benefit nor harm, and that it is neither circumcision nor the foreskin but faith that commends us to God. When faith is completed by works, we merit to be saved.

It follows: “Let each one remain in the calling in which…” [Note: [Col. 0354D] In the autograph margin, chapter XXXVI is written here.] This refers to what he said above: “As God has called him, so let him walk.” It follows: “Were you called as a slave?” [Note: [Col. 0354D] The question mark found in the Vulgate is lacking here.] Do not let it trouble you. The Apostle exhorts the one who is called to the faith while a slave by condition not to be concerned that he is a slave, since his servile condition does not hinder him from attaining the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom. And lest he perhaps become sluggish and negligent toward the service of his earthly master, thereby bringing Christianity into disrepute and deservedly losing the reward of his obedience, he therefore adds: “But if you can become free, make use of it,” and so forth. As though he were saying: Do not be lazy or negligent. Although he said, “Do not let it trouble you,” serve faithfully, so that, in accordance with what the Lord says, “The one who is faithful in what is least” (Luke 16:10), you may both be rewarded by God with the prize of eternal blessedness and be granted freedom by your earthly master, since the Lord came not to change conditions but minds.

And because he could say, “How can I be the Lord’s servant, since I am a human being’s?” he added words of consolation and encouragement, saying: “For the one who was called as a slave in the Lord…” Servitude to sins is worse than servitude according to human condition. For sins make a person a slave, just as Ham became a slave through iniquity; therefore, when sins are dismissed, a person is restored to freedom. Alternatively: the one who serves an earthly master, because he acts wisely—that is, because he believes in Christ—is made free. Hence the ancients did not hesitate to define all wise people as free. Solomon likewise says: “Let free men serve the wise servant” (Prov. 17:2).

And because he was speaking about two persons, he continued by adding: “Likewise, the one who was called while free…” Freedom is harmful and bitter when one is alienated from grace; hence elsewhere: “You were free from righteousness” (Rom. 6:20). Since a human being understood that this freedom was harmful and bitter, he passed over to the praiseworthy service of Christ, who says: “Take my yoke upon you, because it is sweet, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:29).

But one must attend to what the apostolic words accomplish and what his intention is: namely, to establish and demonstrate unity. It is as though he were saying: O masters, do not exalt yourselves over yourselves; and you, O slaves, do not abase yourselves. For the one who was called as a slave in the Lord is the Lord’s freedman, and the one who was called while free is Christ’s slave. Hence he immediately adds: “You were bought with a price,” as though he were saying: Not with unequal prices, but with one; therefore do not exalt yourselves or abase yourselves, because you are brothers.

It follows: “Do not become slaves of human beings.” Certainly, it must be asked why, after exhorting slaves above to serve their earthly masters, he now says, “Do not become slaves.” It is not, I say, contradictory, because he is referring to that statement in which, much earlier, he reproved them for being deceived, since some were called followers of Peter and others of Paul. For he says: “Another says, ‘I am of Paul,’” and shortly afterward: “Was Paul crucified for you?” Therefore he says: “Do not become slaves of human beings.” Those are called slaves of human beings who are subject to human superstitions, as were the Corinthians. “Do not become slaves,” as though he were saying: It was not Paul or Peter but Christ, who is rich toward all (Rom. 10:12; Eph. 2:4), who redeemed you. Therefore, since you were redeemed not at different prices but at one price, belong to no one except the one Lord. He redeemed you at a great price and gave for you what no other could give. For even if another could shed blood, he was nevertheless not without sin, and therefore he could not abolish sins.

Therefore, if someone redeemed by another strives to serve the one by whom he was redeemed, in order to render a kind of repayment, how much more ought you, redeemed by God, to offer him perpetual service?

It should be known that some have understood this apostolic statement—“The circumcised man who was called should not bring in the foreskin,” and so forth—metaphorically. They say that he called the celibate “circumcised” and the married man “foreskinned,” so that the meaning is: “Was someone called while circumcised”—that is, without a wife—“let him not bring in the foreskin”—that is, a wife. If someone was called in the foreskin—that is, with a wife—“let him not bring in circumcision”—that is, let him not dismiss his wife. Hence the preceding passage: “If any brother…” They also wish this to be understood under the names “slave” and “free.” For he says: “Were you called as a slave?”—that is, with a wife—“Do not let it trouble you”—that is, do not dismiss her, because she does not impede you. “But if you can become free, make use of it.” By these words as well he shows that he prefers the continent to the married, and he also touched upon the direction of his intention, briefly previewing, in his customary manner, the subject about which he was going to speak at greater length.

It follows: “For the one who was called as a slave in the Lord is the Lord’s freedman.” A freedman is one who is partly free and partly a slave. Thus a married man is rightly called a freedman, because he is a slave insofar as he does not have power over his own body, but free because of works of piety and the other virtues. He is a slave because he renders what he owes to his wife; yet he is free because he has shaken the neck of his mind free from the yoke of vices and walks in the liberty of the virtues.

It follows: “The one who was called while free”—that is, without a wife—is Christ’s slave, because he is subject to Christ. For this slavery is nobler than every freedom. He repeats for the third time what he said above: “Let each one remain, brothers, in the condition in which he was called, with God.”

[Note: [Col. 0355D] In the autograph margin, chapter XXXVII is written here.]

It follows: “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord,” and so forth. Above, he had prohibited the evil of fornication. Then, after speaking about married and continent persons, he inserted the matter of the circumcised and the foreskinned. According to some, his intention regarding the slave and the free man was another matter. Now, however, he speaks about virgins, concerning whom he had also been questioned. Hence above: “Concerning those things about which you wrote…” Therefore, at this point one must supply: Concerning virgins, about whom you questioned me in writing, I have no command of the Lord, but I give advice.

He appropriately says that he does not have a command of the Lord, because the Lord himself was the author of marriage, and therefore it would not have been consistent for him to command the opposite. Here one must observe the difference between a command and advice. What is commanded cannot be violated without transgression; but if advice is violated or disregarded, there is no transgression.

He also said that he was giving advice. And how does he show this? “As one who has obtained mercy,” and so forth. This distinguished preacher, faithful in word and knowledge, gives advice; but, because he obtained mercy from the Lord, he says this—since faithful servants ought not to begrudge benefits but rather to invite others to better things—as though he were saying: I give advice according to the mercy I have received, so that I may be faithful. And note that he attributed what he was to God, not to himself.

It follows: “I consider this to be good.” What so distinguished a preacher considers should be accepted not doubtfully but without hesitation. The good he considers is being without a wife; hence above: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman.” He wishes this good to be understood not only as good because of the greater reward of the heavenly kingdom, but also as good because of the present necessity. There is no doubt that the necessity of the present time is manifold. There is the pain of the womb; the labor of giving birth, nursing, and clothing children; the suffering of their orphanhood; the building of houses; the preparation of dowries; and similar concerns. It is therefore good to remain in this condition—that is, without a wife—because one will not only receive a greater reward but will also be kept apart from these necessities of the present time.

It follows: “Are you bound to a wife?” and so forth. The Apostle had summoned his people to the good of continence. And lest the good itself consist in the dissolution of marriages, he spoke cautiously, saying: “Are you bound to a wife?” and so forth. This is the apostolic and Dominical teaching: it summons people to greater goods without despising lesser ones—that is, it draws them toward the good of continence without despising marriage. For the truth of God in the Scriptures is greater than chastity.

“If you have taken a wife,” and so forth, “and if a virgin marries,” and so forth. Neither commits an offense, because each performs a lawful act.

“Nevertheless, they will have tribulation in the flesh.” But what are those tribulations? The tribulations are these: concealing one’s wife; the wife’s subjection to her husband; fear that another may be admitted; and other matters that can be mentioned.

It follows: “But I am sparing you.” In two ways: that is, when I summon you to the good of continence, so that you may not be subjected to the aforementioned tribulations of husband and wife, I am sparing you; or I am sparing you in the sense that, if you wish to subject yourselves to them, you may do so.

And he adds why he said this: “This, then, I say, brothers: the time is short.” As though he were saying: People do not live as long now as they did at first. For scarcely does anyone remain joined to a wife for forty or thirty years, and he loses with grief the wife whom he had possessed with love. And because the time is short, what remains is this: those who have wives should be as though they did not have them—that is, they should not be overcome by carnal desires and pleasures. For then someone who has a wife does not have one, when he pleases his wife in such a way that he does not displease the Creator.

And those who weep should be as though they were not weeping—that is, they should be afflicted by temporal tribulations in such a way that they are lifted up by hope of the future reward. Someone then weeps without being overcome by grief when he is so afflicted by the tribulations of this present time that he is raised up by hope of eternal recompense.

And those who rejoice should be as though they were not rejoicing—that is, they should rejoice over earthly advantage in such a way that they remain mindful of divine judgment. Someone then rejoices without being overcome by joy when he takes pleasure in earthly advantage while fearing divine judgment.

And those who buy should be as though they did not possess—that is, they should not think that they will possess for long what they have bought. Someone is then a buyer who does not possess when he does not think that he will possess for long the things he has bought.

And those who use this world should be as though they did not use it—that is, they should disdain being held by the things they prepare for their own necessity. Someone then uses without being held by what he uses when he holds the things he has prepared for his necessity and is not held by them.

And he adds why he said this: “For the form of this world is passing away.” It is not the world but its form that passes away, because it is written: “But the earth remains forever” (Eccles. 1:4). Therefore it remains in essence but passes away through renewal. And if the form of the world passes away, much more do the things that belong to the world. As though he were saying: Why do you cling to the world and to the things that belong to the world, which are passing away, as though they and you would remain for a long time? And this shows that you are passing away, because you observe the death of others, and by observing it you recognize your own departure.

Although the end of the world is far distant, the Apostle nevertheless ought to speak in this way on account of those who would read this epistle near the end of the world. As though he were saying: You have heard of future tribulations such as have not been from the beginning (Mark 13:8), and you very much do not wish to see them. Since you lack the desire to see them, why do you not spare your children by not taking wives and not begetting children who will see them—especially since it is not the time for God to create children through intercourse but to regenerate them through baptism?

He adds why he said this: “But I want you to be without concern,” and so forth. For who does not want what the Apostle wants?

It follows: “The unmarried man is concerned with how he may please the Lord.” He rightly says, “He is concerned with how he may please his wife,” because a married man cannot serve God freely. Therefore he adds: “And he is divided.” Divided not in body but in mind. And “the woman,” it is understood, is divided as well.

And because “woman” can refer both to a virgin and to a married woman, to show which woman he meant he adds: “The unmarried woman and the virgin,” and so forth, “is holy in body”—because she is without a husband—and “in spirit”—because she is free from worldly concern.

“But the married woman…” The Apostle says that the married woman thinks about the things of the world, and the virgin about the things of God. But we observe the opposite: a married woman may think about the things of God, and a virgin about the things of the world. It should be known that marriage does not hinder such a married woman; rather, when by thinking about the things of God she surpasses her own natural condition, she will be rewarded with eternal blessedness.

But that virgin will not only fail to be rewarded for the good of virginity; she will also be condemned doubly, because she handled the work of virginity badly. For it is written: “Cursed is the one who does the work of the Lord” (Jer. 48:10), and so forth. And Paul says: “They display the work of piety, but deny its power” (2 Tim. 3:5). She had the work, namely virginity, but denied its power because she did not understand the goodness of virginity.

That the aforementioned married woman will be rewarded is testified by the action of Gideon. For it is read (Judg. 6:11) that, when he had separated the grain from the chaff, an angel appeared to him, and so forth. To separate grain from chaff signifies separating virtues from vices, better things from good things, and the best things from better things. And while he is doing this, an angel appears to him and orders a kid to be offered to him and broth to be poured over it (ibid. 19). By the kid are signified the wanton movements of the flesh, and by the broth, fluid thoughts. Therefore to sacrifice the kid and pour broth over it signifies destroying not only carnal works but also fluid thoughts, after the example of Christ.

And while this is being done, the angel touches these things with the rod of God; the person is raised up by divine assistance; fire comes forth from the rock and consumes everything (Judg. 6:21), because the ardor of divine assistance destroys in that person not only carnal works but also fluid thoughts. This is fulfilled only in good virgins and in a few distinguished continent persons.

It follows: “For your own good,” and so forth. The Apostle knew that they had been distressed by what he had said, and therefore he says, “For your own good,” as though he were saying: I know that you were distressed by what I said; but I did not say it in order to cast a snare for you, but to summon you to what is honorable. He calls the good of continence honorable because it is good and holy, and to that which grants you the freedom to entreat the Lord without impediment. He rightly says “without impediment,” because a married person cannot serve God freely and without impediment.

[Note: [Col. 0359D] In the autograph margin, chapter XXXVIII is written here.]

It follows: “But if anyone thinks that he is behaving dishonorably,” and so forth. This meaning depends on what precedes. Above, he had spoken about virgins and had praised the good of continence so highly that he seemed to reject marriage with abhorrence. Lest he appear to do so, he added: “But if anyone thinks that he is behaving dishonorably…”

There can be two interpretations at this point. First: It could have happened that the Apostle advised parents to raise their daughters chastely and purely until the time of puberty. But when they reached that age, which is suitable for marriage, if the parents chose that it was better for the girl to marry publicly than to do something of that kind secretly, from which disgrace or confusion might arise, and if the girl wished to marry, let her marry, because she does not sin if she marries.

Or, “if he thinks that he is behaving dishonorably”: if he has raised her chastely until puberty and, when she has reached that age, has not decided which of the two she should choose—whether to preserve virginity or to be joined in marriage. For “the one who stands firm in his heart,” and so forth: if someone has raised his daughter chastely until puberty, and when she has reached that age he himself has stood firm in his heart in order to preserve her as a virgin; and if the girl herself has joined her own will to that of her father, having no necessity to marry—that is, if she has chosen to remain a virgin—then, having power over her own will, that is, preserving her virginity, she does not sin.

Here it is shown that parents ought not to give their daughters in marriage against their will, since good acts should not be begrudged but rather encouraged.

There is also another interpretation of “if anyone thinks that he is behaving dishonorably”: if someone has raised his own flesh chastely until puberty, and after it has reached the age at which it can marry, he thinks that he is behaving dishonorably, lest he perhaps be reproached by his own people or by others outside the family, he does not sin if he marries.

But if, after reaching puberty, he has firmly decided to preserve virginity and is not ashamed of another person’s reproach, if he wishes to preserve virginity, let him preserve it.

The following words respond to both interpretations, that is, to the daughter and to the flesh: “What he has decided in his heart—to preserve the virgin,” and so forth.

This is that Dominical and apostolic teaching: it summons people to greater things without despising lesser ones. In this matter, three degrees are found: good, better, and best. The good is found among the married; the better among widows, that is, the continent; and the best among virgins.

“A woman is bound by the law,” and so forth. This is an evangelical meaning. For the Apostle explains the meaning of his teacher and of the Gospel that he preached. The Lord commanded that a wife not be abandoned except on account of fornication, and that neither an adulterer nor an adulteress take another spouse.

Likewise, the Apostle commanded that an adulteress should not leave her husband, whether chaste or adulterous, and take another; nor should an adulterous man do so. Why? Because he does not have power over his own body. The same applies to the woman. Therefore, lest a man who wishes to take another woman himself fall into what he reproves in his wife. Nevertheless, through repentance they can be reconciled.

“But if her husband has died” [Note: [Col. 0359D] The Vulgate reads: “But if her husband has died, she is released,” and so forth.], “she is released,” and so forth. Understand this not of one who has fallen through adultery but of one who has departed through death. Yet this is so only if she preserves chastity until she is lawfully joined to another.

But the wording of the law seems contrary to this passage, and also to the Dominical statement. For the Lord commanded that a wife not be abandoned except on account of fornication. The Apostle repeats the same thing, saying that if she departs, she should remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. Here he says: “A woman is bound,” and so forth. Yet the law says: “If a man takes a wife and has her, and then, because he finds some indecency in her, regards her with hatred, he shall write a bill of divorce, place it in her hand, and send her away from his house. But if another man takes her, and because he finds some indecency in her regards her with hatred, and dismisses her, or if he dies, the first husband may not take her back, because she has been defiled” (Deut. 24:1) [Note: [Col. 0360D] Deut. 24:1; the autograph reads “uxorem”—“wife.”]

Two contradictions are found here. The Lord says that she must not be abandoned except on account of fornication. The law says that she may be dismissed on account of some indecency. And he himself says that the first husband may not take her back. Likewise, both the Apostle and the law say: “If another man takes her,” and so forth.

This appears to be a contradiction. But if it is understood, the contradiction in the wording disappears, as in many other passages. Let the veil of the wording therefore be removed, so that the spiritual meaning may shine forth.

A person takes a woman and has her when he assumes responsibility for a temporal matter. He dismisses her and drives her from his house because of some indecency when, on recognizing sin, he casts that concern from the house of his mind. Another takes her because it commonly happens that, when that concern is extinguished in one person’s mind, it is generated in another’s. But because of some indecency he dismisses her, or dies, because he dismisses her on account of recognized sin; or it commonly happens that he extinguishes that concern, or is extinguished by it. If it is understood in this way, no contradiction is found.

“Let her marry whom she wishes”—that is, let her marry the one whom she loves. For it commonly happens that a marriage entered into unwillingly has a bad outcome. But she marries “in the Lord” when she is rightly joined to her own religion; or when she preserves chastity until she is lawfully joined to another; or if she has joined herself to another because of love for her children and human frailty. [Note: [Col. 0361D] Perhaps “sive se” should be read here instead of “sive si.”]

“I think that I too have the Spirit.” Lest they disregard him or regard his advice as the advice of an ordinary human being, he therefore says, “I think,” and so forth. As though he were saying: Do not regard my advice as the advice of an ordinary human being. Rather, since I have the Holy Spirit, my advice is the advice of the Holy Spirit; and if it is the advice of the Holy Spirit, it is God’s, because the Spirit himself is God’s Spirit.

Some say that this was said reproachfully, so that the meaning is: “Surely I do not have the Spirit of God?” Just as someone might say to a slave: “Well done; I suppose I am your master.”

[Note: [Col. 0361D] In the autograph margin, chapter XXXIX is written here.]

(CAP. VIII.) It follows: “Concerning the things sacrificed to idols” [Note: [Col. 0361D] The Vulgate reads: “Concerning the things sacrificed to idols.”]—understand, “you asked.” It should be known that the Apostle had been questioned about these matters, as in the phrase, “the things about which you wrote.” Since he responded concerning some matters—for example, “It is good for a man not to touch a woman”—and concerning virgins, here he responds to the question about the things sacrificed to idols.

An idol, according to the interpretation of its name, is an image or form, because *eidos* in Greek [Note: [Col. 0361D] εἷδος.] means “form” in Latin; and from *eidos* comes *idolum*, just as from *forma* comes *formula*. Hence *idolatry*, to which *latria* is opposed.

If an idol is called an image or form, it must be asked why the Apostle says that an idol is nothing. For whatever exists is something. It is nothing because the thing referred to is not seen with the eyes but imagined by the mind. For example, if a dog’s, sheep’s, or some other animal’s head were painted on a human body, or two faces, or the hindquarters of a fish, lion, bird, or some other creature were placed on a human chest—such an image has never been seen. Or if an image of Jupiter, Mercury, or someone else is fabricated, then, as far as the material element is concerned, it is something, because it exists; but as far as what it is said to be is concerned, it is nothing, because it is not what it is said to be. Therefore it is falsehood; falsehood is sin; and sin is nothing, because it does not subsist.

Some people say that *idolum* comes from *dolus* (“deceit”), ignorant of the nature of the Greek word. An idol is also called a *simulacrum*. As Isiodus says [Note: [Col. 0361D] That is, Hesiod in his *Theogony*.], *simulacrum* is derived from *similitudo* (“likeness”). For he relates that in the beginning human beings were warriors and builders of cities. After their deaths, their loved ones painted images of them on walls, stones, or the ground—not so that they would be believed to be gods, but so that, by remembering them, they might find consolation for their grief.

In the course of time, however, this error became so deeply rooted that the devil entered into it and spoke through these images to the faithless and deceived. A *simulacrum* is also said to derive from *simulatio* (“simulation”); the Jews maintain that it was first invented by Ishmael. The gentiles, however, say that Prometheus was its inventor and transmitter.

Among the Greeks, Cecrops [Note: [Col. 0361D] Cecrops the Egyptian, and according to some the first king of the Athenians and founder, while according to others merely the restorer of Athens. The following material he took from Eusebius’s preface to the *Chronicon*. In this our author agrees with Herodotus. Nevertheless, Lactantius should be consulted, book I of the *Institutes*, where he asserts that Melissus, king of the Cretans, was the first to sacrifice to the gods. Others say other things.] is said to have first made an image, built altars, offered a victim, and carried out many other things that had never been seen or heard of in Greece.

It follows: “We know that we all possess knowledge”—understand, human or worldly knowledge. Alternatively, the meaning is as though he were saying: Do we know this because we all possess knowledge? No. For although we all possess worldly knowledge, we do not all possess divine knowledge, so as to understand that an idol is nothing.

It follows: “Knowledge puffs up.” It should certainly be noted that he usually approaches a subject gently before later intensifying it. Thus here he begins gently, but in what follows he greatly intensifies the matter, both by marking the ignorant and by reproving the wise. For he says: “Knowledge puffs up,” and so forth. He does not indicate to whom he is speaking, but merely seems to look down upon them.

It should be known that there is a kind of knowledge by which people become swollen with pride. Because it is not seasoned with charity, it puffs up. Knowledge without charity is of no benefit, since, just as wine without admixture alienates the mind, so knowledge without charity does the same.

Some say that no simple thing, without the admixture of something else, is useful, as with food. Bread itself is not desirably consumed without the admixture of something else. Charity itself also cannot exist without the other virtues.

This passage also stands against those who, puffed up by false knowledge, believed that everything was lawful and therefore ate food sacrificed to idols, not fearing to scandalize weak brothers.

It follows: “For if anyone thinks that he knows something,” and so forth. The meaning is this: The person who thinks that he knows because he understands that everything is lawful and that what enters the mouth does not defile (Matt. 16:11, 20), yet takes what is lawful to the scandal of his brother, has not yet learned how he ought to know—that is, that even if something is lawful, it is nevertheless not expedient.

It follows: “But whoever loves God,” and so forth. The meaning is this: The person who loves God possesses true knowledge; and the one who loves God loves his brother’s salvation as his own. Such a person is known by God, because his knowledge is approved by him.

It follows: “Concerning foods sacrificed to idols”—understand, “you asked.” Up to this point he had spoken, as it were, preliminarily to others; from here he begins to explain the matter explicitly.

It follows: “We know that an idol is nothing” [Note: [Col. 0363D] In the Vulgate, only this proposition is found here: “An idol is nothing.”]. He added what had already been said—that an idol is nothing—in confirmation: “And that there is no God except one.” Therefore the image of Jupiter or of the others is not God.

It follows: “For although there are those who are called gods,” and so forth. This statement can be understood in two ways. First, according to the opinion of the gentiles, gods are said to be in heaven, such as the sun, moon, and various stars; and on earth, the images of Jupiter, Mercury, and Hercules.

Or, in the true sense, the gods in heaven are angels, and on earth the elect: “I have said, ‘You are gods’” (Ps. 81:6; John 10:34). For if human beings are called gods, much more are angels, who lack mortal flesh. But it is forbidden to call them gods in such a way that *latria*—divine worship—be offered to them, since only one is God essentially; angels and human beings are gods only by name. Hence: “Behold, I have appointed you God of Pharaoh” (Exod. 7:1), and: “He shall be brought to the gods” [Note: [Col. 0363D] Exod. 22:8; the Vulgate reads: “He shall be brought to the gods.”]

Therefore he adds: “But for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things.” This is true, I say, because whatever exists, wherever it exists, is from him. And, in order to distinguish us from those who are from him but are nevertheless not in him through faith, he adds: “And we are in him.”

It follows: “And one Lord, Jesus Christ.” Through Christ, the Son of God, all things that exist were created by the Father; therefore he says: “Through whom are all things,” as in: “All things were made through him” (John 1:3). Appropriately, after saying “through whom,” he adds: “And we through him,” because through him we were created so that we might exist, and through him we were recreated and reformed so that we might understand and believe in the one God and recognize that an idol is nothing.

It follows: “But knowledge is not in everyone.” The meaning is this: Although there are also believers, not all possess this knowledge, namely, that they should understand that an idol is nothing and recognize the one God.

It should certainly be known that there were some among the common people who, because they were still held by love of the idol, believed that some divinity or grace was present in it. Therefore he says: “But some,” that is, simple people, “with consciousness of the idol until now”—that is, with love and pleasure, while they believe that some divinity or grace is present in the idol—“eat as though they were eating food sacrificed to idols,” that is, food handed over to idols; and their conscience, being weak, is defiled because they believe that something is present in the idol.

Origen, however, says: It should be observed that the Corinthians did not eat only things consecrated to idols. They themselves were lovers of philosophical teaching and of the secular liberal disciplines, and they devoted themselves to them. But those who had been strengthened in the faith, while reading the fictions of the poets, were not corrupted by them, because they believed that there was nothing gracious or useful in them. The weak and simple, however, while engaging with them in imitation of the strong, were corrupted by the syllogisms of the philosophers and thus ate as though they were eating food sacrificed to idols.

Therefore the Apostle warns them not only to abstain from food sacrificed to idols but also not to devote themselves to the fictions of the poets, so that they might not scandalize the weak. For every utterance is consecrated either to the devil or to God. The utterance that summons us to purity, chastity, sobriety, and similar virtues is certainly consecrated to God; but the utterance that summons us to contrary things is undoubtedly sacrificed to demons.

It follows: “Food does not commend us to God.” The meaning is this: If food does not make us more pleasing to God, does not make him more favorable toward us, and if we do not offend him by abstaining from food, why do you not fear scandalizing your brothers on account of food?

It follows: “Nor, if we eat”—understand, food sacrificed to idols—“will we abound,” that is, become richer, so that we will have no need of other foods; “nor, if we do not eat, will we lack,” because there will be other foods by which we may be sustained.

It should also be known that many of the Corinthians had been so strengthened in the faith that they believed everything to be lawful for them and believed that nothing entering the mouth defiled them, as the Lord says (Matt. 15:11, 20). Therefore they did not hesitate to eat food sacrificed to idols. But the weak, seeing this, were scandalized. For that reason they abstained not only from those foods but entirely from meat and wine, since the meat sacrificed to idols was sold in the marketplace. They also sacrificed the first fruits of wine to idols and performed certain sacrifices in the winepresses themselves.

And because the weak were scandalized, the Apostle says: “See to it that this freedom of yours does not become a stumbling block to the weak,” as though he were saying: Since you know that everything is lawful, see to it that this very knowledge does not offend others.

A stumbling block occurs in two ways: either because the weak reproved them, judging them unclean, or because the weak imitated them. Hence he immediately adds: “For if someone sees you who possess knowledge,” and so forth, “will he not be built up”—that is, provoked to eat food sacrificed to idols—though not with the faith with which you eat it?

It follows: “And so the weak person will perish through your knowledge, the brother for whom Christ died,” and so forth. As though he were saying: Why do you not fear killing your brother, whom Christ redeemed by dying? Your knowledge kills him.

By these words the Apostle shows that the thing itself is not so much evil as the danger to the brother. He also shows that the one who provides an occasion for sinning incurs a greater condemnation than the one who sins in himself.

The same is demonstrated where Balak is read to have summoned Balaam the diviner to curse the children of Israel (Num. 22:23). Although he did not curse them, he nevertheless gave evil advice (Num. 24:14; Mic. 6:5; 2 Pet. 2:15). Therefore, when the Lord commanded that vengeance be exacted from the children of Israel upon the Moabites [Note: [Col. 0364D] “Vengeance” might perhaps be added; Num. 31:2 and Jude 11.], Moses spoke to the people and said: “Gird yourselves and wage war against the Moabites” (Num. 25:17). They went out and killed every male with the sword, along with Balaam (Num. 31:7–8).

Note that the children of Israel, who sinned in themselves, were punished more mildly than the Moabites, who provided the occasion for sinning. Hence those who had previously conquered six hundred thousand men were themselves overcome by twelve thousand. This was certainly accomplished by justice: as long as they possessed sin, they were defeated; once they had cast off sin and remained in righteousness, they overcame the kings, although they had been defeated by women.

Therefore you too, if you wish to overcome all your enemies, take up feet shod, the breastplate of righteousness, the shield of faith, and the helmet of salvation (Isa. 59:17; Eph. 6:14; 1 Thess. 5:8). If you are stripped of these, you can be overcome by any vice.

It follows: “Thus, by sinning against the brothers,” and so forth. Note that those who sin against the brothers are said to sin against Christ. Just as those who are under the law sin against the law, so those who sin against their brothers sin against Christ, because they err in matters subject to him.

Observe also that he did not say “against Christ” [Note: [Col. 0365D] Nevertheless, the Vulgate reads “against Christ.”] “To sin against Christ” means to deny him. He speaks of the weak conscience either in the sense of imitating or of reproving.

It follows: “But if food scandalizes my brother…” Observe how great the Apostle’s charity and love were. In order to provoke his people to charity, he set himself forward as an example. As though he were saying: I know that everything is lawful for me and everything is clean, but I abstain entirely from these things because I understand that they are not expedient. Hence above: “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient” (1 Cor. 6:12).

[Note: [Col. 0365D] In the autograph margin, chapter XL is written here.]

**(CHAPTER IX.)** “Am I not free?” etc. These are the words of an angry and agitated mind; and unless pronunciation comes to its aid, he seems to affirm what he is striving to deny. Therefore it must be read in such a way that the statement is understood as expressed through denial. Rather: “Am I not free?” etc., as though he were saying: “I am.” He was free, because he did not preach by pretense or in order to receive something. He was an apostle because he had been sent, as in: “Behold, I send you to nations far away” (Acts 22:21). He had seen the Lord, either when going to Damascus or while praying in the temple. “Are you not my work in the Lord?” That is, the work of my apostleship. For when I had preached among you for one year and six months, and had brought you over from unbelief to faith, what else is now shown in your faith than the work of my apostleship?

“And if I am not an apostle to others,” etc. By “others” he means believing Jews who, while still remaining in carnal observance, denied that Paul held precedence, because, in preaching to the Gentiles, he was abolishing the Sabbaths and the other observances of the Law. For while the other apostles, by concealing their position, preached that they should remain in carnal observance, so that they might somehow draw them to faith in Christ, and Paul seemed to teach something contrary to the apostles by abolishing carnal observance, they denied that he was an apostle. Therefore he said: “If I am not an apostle to others”—that is, if I am not one to those who still live carnally—“yet surely I am to you,” whom I brought to faith in Christ by preaching. “For you are the seal,” etc.—that is, the proof and dignity of my apostleship are you, whom I drew from paganism and unbelief to faith.

“My defense,” etc. Your faith is my defense before those who ask me whether I am an apostle or not. “Do we not have authority?” etc. He means the authority which the Lord, when sending them to preach, declares in the words: “Whoever receives you” (Luke 9:48), etc., through to “the laborer is worthy” (Luke 10:7), etc. And he showed them not only by words but also by deeds that they ought to receive what was necessary, as in: “Many were following them” (Mark 6:8), etc.

Why did he wish them to receive what was necessary? So that, occupied with small matters—that is, with necessities—they would not withdraw from the greater matter, preaching, and so that preaching might not come to them more slowly. And observe that he grants the authority not by commanding but by permitting. Therefore Paul, in accepting it, is made free from guilt, since a transgression of a command cannot exist without blame.

And to show that he had received the authority he had mentioned, he added: “As also the other apostles.” By “the others” he means all the apostles. And lest he seem to be of lesser merit, he added: “And the brothers of the Lord.” For he calls “the brothers of the Lord” those who seemed to be of outstanding merit. And, to confirm still further what he had said, he added: “And Cephas.” For Cephas, who was chief of the apostles, accepted it; and by calling him to testify, he makes the judgment concerning himself more certain.

[Col. 0366C] “Do we not have authority to lead about a sister,” etc. Some, understanding this less well and failing to understand the apostolic intention, have wrongly interpreted this passage, saying that the apostles received authority to take wives. The ambiguity of the Greek expression deceived them, since the Greek wording here can be understood both of a wife and of a woman. Nevertheless, this ought not to have deceived them. Both the preceding and the following words dispel this error. Above, he says “sister,” whereas no one takes a sister as a wife; and below he says “to lead about,” whereas no man who takes a wife says, “I led her about,” but rather, “I took her.” And if it seems to anyone contradictory that women ministered to the apostles, let him read the Gospel. There he will be able to find that it is not contradictory, since women ministered to the Lord, as in: “They were also following him” (Mark 15:41), etc. For devoted women, lovers of heavenly instruction, ministered from their resources to their teachers. This was especially not contradictory because it was a Jewish custom, although a cause of scandal to the Gentiles, which the Apostle nevertheless did not wish to use. But even if that point had deceived them, it did not deceive those who considered the Apostle’s intention.

“Or I alone and Barnabas,” etc. He says “Barnabas” because he was a fellow apostle in working—that is, in receiving support—so that he might speak more decorously. And lest he seem to wish to commend himself and reproach others, he added: “Who serves as a soldier?” etc. For these men were soldiers who served in the heavenly kingdom and fought against the devil’s ambushes; therefore they received support, just as those who serve as soldiers in an earthly kingdom customarily receive their pay. “Who plants a vineyard?” etc. These men were planters of a vineyard because they showed the ecclesiastical people the way of salvation. That the ecclesiastical people are signified by the name “vineyard” is indicated not only in the Old Testament but also in the New. In the Old, as in: “He brought a vine out of Egypt” (Psalm 79:9), etc., and: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts” (Isaiah 5:7), etc. In the New, as in the parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who went out early in the morning” (Matthew 20:1), etc., and: “He planted a vineyard” (Mark 12:1), etc.

“Who feeds a flock?” etc. By the flock the ecclesiastical people are signified, both in the Old and in the New, because he shows his own the way of salvation. In the New, as in: “And I have other sheep” (John 10:16), etc. This soldier and leader of the heavenly army, faithful in faith and truth, demonstrated by all these examples that he possessed authority to receive support. And lest anyone suppose that he had said this through human wisdom and natural ingenuity, he added: “Do I say these things according to human judgment?” As though he were saying: “Do not think that I have spoken according to human wisdom, but according to divine wisdom.” And wishing to confirm this very point by the testimony of the Law, he added: “Or does the Law itself not say this? For it is written: ‘You shall not muzzle’” (Deuteronomy 25:4), etc. In that Paul, speaking of the New Testament, takes an example from the Old Testament, he shows the agreement of the Law and the Gospel. He also shows that it must be interpreted allegorically. At the same time he makes clear that teachers ought to confirm their statements by the examples of the saints.

That there is one agreement between the Law and the Gospel is made clear here and in the writings of the Old Testament. For we read that the Lord commanded Moses to make two cherubim of purest gold (Exodus 25:18), facing one another with turned faces and covering the mercy seat (ibid., 20). What are signified by the two cherubim—[Note: [Col. 0367D] From the Hebrew word *cherub*, which sometimes signifies a calf or ox; hence in Ezekiel 1:10 and 10:20, “the face of a cherub” and “the face of an ox” are regarded as virtually synonymous; at other times it expresses one who is strong and powerful.]—who are interpreted as “fullness of knowledge,” except the two Testaments? They look toward one another with turned faces because no disagreement is found between them.

That the covering must be cast aside so that the brightness of the allegory may appear is shown where we read that Jacob took almond and poplar rods (Genesis 30:37–41), stripped them, and placed them in the channels; and when the flock came to drink, looking at the rods during the heat of mating, it conceived offspring of various colors. What is signified by the rods except the examples of the holy Fathers? By the fact that he stripped them, so that where the bark was removed the brightness appeared, while where it remained the greenness endured, it is shown that Sacred Scripture is partly to be examined allegorically, while in part reverence for its historical meaning must be preserved.

Thus we read: “You shall love the Lord your God” (Matthew 22:37), etc., and: “Wash yourselves, be clean” (Isaiah 1:16), etc. Are these to be examined allegorically? And when we read: “You shall not plow with an ox and an ass together” (Deuteronomy 22:10); and: “You shall not put on a garment” (Deuteronomy 22:11; Zechariah 3:4), etc.; and: “You shall not muzzle the ox” (Deuteronomy 25:4; 1 Corinthians 9:9; 1 Timothy 5:18), etc., are these to be understood only literally? No. The covering must be cast aside, and the brightness of the allegory must be revealed.

What is signified by the waters of the channels except Sacred Scripture? What by the rams except knowledge? What by the sheep except action and intention? The rods are placed in the channels because the examples of the Fathers are inserted in Sacred Scripture. The ram stands above the sheep because rational knowledge is preferred to our action and intention. At the sight of the rods they conceive offspring of various kinds because, when we consider the examples of the saints, we generate various actions of good works.

That they ought to confirm their statements by the examples of others is made clear where we read that the Lord commanded Moses to make silver columns (Exodus 26:27) and, around them, to cast bronze pegs by which the tabernacle would be supported, lest it be overturned by the force of the winds. By the silver columns the writers of the New Testament are signified. What is signified by the pegs except the writers of the Old Testament, and by the tabernacle the Church? The pegs therefore rest around the columns because the writers of the New Testament strive to confirm their statements by the examples of the ancients. The columns are rightly said to be silver and the pegs bronze, because silver rings and shines. The writers of the New Testament made manifest what they proclaimed; bronze rings but does not shine, because the writers of the Old Testament did not reveal what they proclaimed.

“Do you not know that those who work in the sanctuary,” etc. By various comparisons he had shown above that it was lawful for him and those like him to receive from their hearers whatever was necessary. Continuing in the intention he had begun, he says: “Do you not know that those who work in the sanctuary,” etc. Here it should be noted that he mentions two things: the sanctuary, on account of the Gentiles, who sacrificed to their gods in sanctuaries and ate from the sacrifices; and the altar, on account of the Jews, whose priests offered victims upon the Lord’s altar and shared in them.

Because there was a command (Leviticus 7:32–33) to receive the right shoulder—mystically, on account of good works—and the breast of separation (ibid., 34), namely, on account of knowledge, which ought to be kept far apart from the knowledge of the hearers, he showed that he possessed the authority. Yet he said that he had not used it, lest he seem not to need these things but rather to possess them in abundance. Therefore he added: “But I have not written these things,” etc. As though he were saying: “So that what has not been done until now may henceforth be done.”

Therefore he continues: “It would be better for me to die,” etc. He says this because he had also determined in his mind to accept nothing from his own people. He preferred to suffer the death of the flesh rather than make the Gospel appear to be for sale. He calls his “glory” that which he possessed before God through Jesus Christ, by which, condescending to all through humility, he made himself like them.

It continues: “If I preach the Gospel”—with the implied words, “so that this may happen to me”—“there is no glory for me.” Why? “For necessity is laid upon me,” that is, “I have no means by which I may be supported.” Hence he adds: “Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel”—that is, “I shall preach to my own detriment,” because I shall be tormented by hunger, having no means by which to live.

It continues: “For if I preach willingly,” etc. By these words he shows how the Gospel ought to be preached: namely, that every end should be established for the Gospel. When this is done, the preaching is voluntary, and everlasting reward will follow it.

[Col. 0369B] It continues: “But if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship.” The meaning is: If I preach because of the necessity of temporal life, a stewardship has been entrusted to me, because others receive their good through me—that is, the Gospel, which they love—and I am deprived of the reward, which is a very great evil. It is a wicked thing to preach for the necessities of temporal life, because then one seeks not the evangelical reward but a price, like a useless servant who, having received an office, gives provisions to his fellow servants, is content with food alone, and is deprived of his wage. Therefore the Gospel must be preached not for the reward of transitory life but for eternal recompense.

But since elsewhere the Apostle calls himself a steward in a good sense, while here he places “stewardship” in a bad sense, lest he seem contradictory to himself, it must be understood that there is a servant who passes into the status of a son and is also the distributor of those things of which he is master; in this sense he calls himself a steward. Here, however, he speaks of stewardship in a bad sense, in accordance with the condition of a rustic servant: he supplies provisions to servants and is content with food alone.

What follows must be read as a question, with the voice suspended until the answer is given. To make the meaning clearer, let us question the Apostle and say: “O Apostle, what is your reward, since you do not accept the reward that is given to others, though those who preach do not preach for its sake?” He makes clear what it is: “That, in preaching the Gospel, I may offer it without cost”—that is, that I may show that the Gospel is not costly and is not for sale.

He returns to the authority he had received when he says: “I have not used my authority in the Gospel.” He did not use his authority in the Gospel so that sinners might be corrected more freely. He also set himself before them as an example, as though he were saying: “Learn the example from me: because I do not understand it to be expedient, I do not use my authority in the Gospel. So you also, because you understand it not to be expedient, should not eat meat sacrificed to idols, although it is permitted.”

[Note: [Col. 0369D] In the autograph margin, chapter XLI is written there.]
