It continues: “For although I was free from all,” etc. He was free, as Scripture says: “He made himself the servant of all,” because, condescending to everyone through humility, he made himself mentally like them all. He cherished and nourished his hearers—not only those who were perverse, but also those who were sluggish in doing good—until he could summon them to the way of salvation, lest, grieving that they had been sharply rebuked, they should depart in scandal.

This must be understood: he does not say that he became all things to all people by pretending, which is characteristic of pretenders; nor by the cunning of one who lies, but through the affection of one who sympathizes; not by imitating the evils of others, but by sympathizing with all the evils of everyone and seeking the healing remedy of mercy.

It continues: “I became to the Jews as a Jew,” etc. He observed the ancient custom of the Jews not from a desire to pretend but from an impulse of sympathy, either to show that it had been given by God and, according to God’s arrangement, was to endure until the predetermined time, or certainly to separate it from the sacrilegious rites of the Gentiles.

He too, loving his neighbor as himself, did not deceive them; rather, without deceiving them in any way, he observed the aforementioned custom in order to rescue them either from the error by which they did not believe in Christ or from the error by which they hoped to obtain forgiveness for their sins through the ceremonies of the Law. He also observed it to show that he did not reject the intention with which the Fathers had observed it. Whoever preserves the intention of the Fathers does not err, provided that he does not believe he can be sanctified through the ceremonies of the Law, since all sanctification has been accomplished in Christ. Hence, while observing it with Jews, he does not impose it upon Gentiles.

It continues: “To those who are under the Law,” etc., through the point where he says: “I became weak.” He says this not through the cunning of one who lies but through the affection of one who sympathizes.

It should also be known that there were some who said that he had been ceremonially purified in the temple and had become a Jew only by pretense. But it is wholly unbelievable that a man of such authority should have done anything by pretense. Rather, with the authority and freedom with which he says: “Was anyone called after circumcision? Let him not draw over the foreskin” (1 Corinthians 7:18)—that is, let him not wish to live as one uncircumcised, covering the flesh of the stripped member, and let one called in uncircumcision not wish to live as one circumcised—he also said that he became a Jew to the Jews and a Gentile to the Gentiles.

It should be noted that the Law of God and of Christ is one, not that there is another one, as Mani claims. He also speaks of being in the Law, under the Law, and without the Law, and wants these to be understood differently. A carnal Jew is “under the Law”; a Catholic is “in the Law”; any pagan Gentile is “without the Law.”

Therefore, let those who say that he was ceremonially purified in the temple and pretended to be a Jew also say that he sacrificed fictitiously to an idol in order to pretend to be a Gentile—although he not only did not worship an idol, but rather reached the palm of martyrdom by detesting it.

Thus he became a Jew to the Jews and a Gentile to the Gentiles, not through the cunning of one who lies but through the affection of one who sympathizes, because he treated and considered the error and blindness of all of them as though they were his own, and wished to help them as he would have wished someone to help him if he himself were held in their condition.

A healthy person serves the sick if he considers the sick person’s infirmity as his own and serves him as he would wish to be served if he were held in that infirmity. He does not lie if he calls himself weak.

There were some who said that he called himself a Gentile to the Gentiles because, in accordance with philosophical teaching, he agreed with the philosophers, preaching that the world was made by God, that souls are everlasting, and that human beings are of his lineage. Thus, they said, he agreed with them so that he might summon them to faith in Christ, so that they would believe that the one appointed by God as judge of all was Christ. And just as all the preceding points depend upon this, if this is true, those statements too contain no falsehood.

How the healthy person becomes weak for the sake of the weak has been explained above. The Corinthians and others like them were weak in certain matters. The Apostle’s weakness was that he did not use an authority that was lawful. For what is weaker than learning an art he did not know and supporting himself by the labor of his own hands?

It continues: “To all”—that is, to Jews, Gentiles, and the weak—“I became all things.” He says this not through the falsehood of simulated lying, but through the piety of truthful compassion, because he understood that he could have been in all those conditions had he not been freed by divine mercy. A person truly becomes what the one is for whom he wishes to have compassion if he aids that person’s miseries as though they were his own. He also becomes what the other is, not by deceiving him, but by considering both himself and the other.

It continues: “I do everything.” Why? “For the sake of the Gospel.” For what purpose? “That I may become a sharer in it.” The meaning is: Just as the Gospel meets everyone, wishes to save everyone, and proclaims the salvation of all, so too may I act, so that my intention and that of the Gospel may be one.

[Col. 0371C] [Note: [Col. 0371D] In the autograph margin, chapter XLII is written here.]

“Do you not know that those who run in a stadium,” etc. He undertakes another subject, offering a comparison that applies not only to the Corinthians but to all Christians. The stadium was so called from *stare*, “to stand,” because Hercules ran one hundred and twenty-five paces in a single breath—that is, an eighth of a mile—and stopped; hence it was named from standing. This custom also passed to Rome, so that a stadium was said to be six thousand paces long. At the turning points of the stadium a prize, that is, a reward, was placed, and the runners competed before the emperor; the one who arrived first received the prize.

Now the stadium is compared with faith, because, just as many run there, so many run in the stadium of faith. By the one who received the prize, the unity of the Church is rightly signified. But there is a great difference between that stadium and this one. There, only the one who received the prize ran profitably; here, all who run rationally by loving, hoping, and doing good works will receive the reward of the future life.

And because he had offered a comparison, he added an exhortation, saying: “Run in such a way,” etc.—that is, “in such a way that you may obtain it.” He added another comparison, saying: “Everyone who competes in the contest,” etc. *Agon* is Greek; in Latin it means contest, struggle, wrestling, and conflict. For just as there was a custom of running, so too there was one of wrestling. But the person who was going to wrestle abstained from every food that could hinder his contest. It is also reported that he tied sheets of lead around his loins because of nocturnal temptations.

And if they abstained in this way for the sake of a perishable crown, much more ought we, for the sake of the glory of eternal blessedness, to abstain from every vice—even in thought, and especially from bodily impurity.

[Note: [Col. 0371D] In the autograph margin, chapter XLIII is written here.]

It continues: “Therefore I run in this way,” etc. After presenting the comparisons, he places himself as an example within them, saying: “Therefore I run in this way,” etc. He says “I run” with reference to the stadium, and “I fight” with reference to the contest. He ran not uncertainly, because he had heard something certain about his election. He fought not like a child. For children customarily strike the air when fighting, but he did not. He chastised his body with hunger, thirst, and similar things by which the body is worn down, and “I bring it into servitude”—to God, that is, or to the mind.

“Lest perhaps, with others,” etc. Observe how rash and foolish people are when, without fearing and while uncertain of their election, they act thus, whereas the one who had heard something certain was afraid. By this everyone is admonished to hope while fearing and to fear while hoping, so that hope may nurture those who labor and fear may spur on the negligent. Hence the Psalmist says: “Those who fear the Lord have hoped in the Lord” (Psalm 115:11).

[Note: [Col. 0372D] In the autograph margin, chapter XLIV is written here.]

**(CHAPTER X.)** After the comparisons presented above, he added an example from the Old Testament pertaining to the same matter, saying: “I do not want you to be ignorant,” etc. How this happened is clear, and how it is understood spiritually is already partly known. His intention, however, must be considered.

His intention was to show the Corinthians that baptism, reception of the mystery of Christ’s body and blood, and the other things celebrated in the Church are of no benefit if they lived negligently, just as all the things he mentions here benefited those people nothing when they lived negligently. It is as though he were saying: “Just as those people, although possessing all these things, perished by murmuring, so you too, possessing them while living negligently, will perish.” Hence he says below: “But with most of them God was not well pleased,” etc.

That these things are to be understood spiritually he makes clear by adding: “They drank from the spiritual,” etc. Here it should be observed that he does not say, “The rock signifies Christ,” but “was,” because it was not the rock but Christ who produced the water. In the fact that the rock followed them as far as the borders of the Moabites (Exodus 17:6), Christ was prefigured as one who would be born after Moses.

“All these things happened in figure,” etc. By these words he gives us an example of allegorical interpretation. We are also warned not to desire what they desired when, remembering Egypt, they longed for the eating of meat (Exodus 16:3), lest we likewise perish and become idolaters.

The Apostle recalls the passage in which Moses ascended Mount Sinai while the people remained near the mountain; they threw gold into the fire, and the head of a calf came forth; after sacrificing and eating, they rose to play (Exodus 32:4–6). Hence he says: “The people sat down.” This shows that such worship and wicked feasts incite to wantonness. We are warned not to do such things, lest we perish in the same way.

“Nor let us commit fornication,” etc. He recalls the passage in which the Moabites adorned their daughters and placed them before the sons of Israel; the Israelites desired them and sinned (Numbers 25). The anger of God burned so fiercely there that many perished; and unless Phinehas had killed the adulterers, he would have destroyed the greater part of the people (ibid., 11). We are warned not to perish by doing such things.

“Nor let us tempt Christ,” etc. When he says that they tempted Christ, it is shown that Christ existed before he was born of the Virgin, and that Moses bore the figure of Christ, for those people tempted Moses. We are warned not to perish by doing such things.

“Nor murmur,” etc. Their exterminator was the opening of the earth (Numbers 11:33); but the devil was especially the author of their destruction.

“All these things happened in figure,” etc. Here he shows that allegorical interpretation is required. But he does not say this so that we might receive the things promised by the Law, but so that evangelical teaching might be held with greater certainty. He makes clear why he wrote this: “They were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come”—that is, for us who were going to exist and believe.

It continues: “Therefore, whoever thinks that he stands,” etc. Here he touches upon those who ate meat sacrificed to idols, disregarding the scandal of a brother. He also warns them lest, puffed up by human knowledge, they fall and, through pride, enter into temptation.

Therefore he added: “Let no temptation seize you,” etc. Human temptation is thinking of some evil; diabolical temptation is carrying it into action. It is as though he were saying: “To think of evil is sin, but to carry it into action is diabolical.” In another sense, human temptation occurs when someone called upon for advice stumbles in the advice itself, so that it has a bad outcome. This is human. The same is true when someone sees a person and judges him to be good or evil without any evidence making this clear.

It continues: “God is faithful.” Temptation occurs in many ways. “He will not permit you to be tempted,” etc. He is faithful because what he promises cannot fail, for he himself does not fail. A human being is also called faithful because he fulfills what he promises, and faith is so called because something is done.

The meaning is: If you remain in faith, he will fulfill what he promised. For although he permits storms of temptation to arise for your testing, if you endure them for three or four days and he sees that you cannot bear them, he will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can endure; or else he will utterly extinguish the temptation, or provide help so that you can bear it. This is what he says: “But with the temptation he will also make a way out”—that is, he will provide consolation.

It continues: “Therefore, my beloved, flee,” etc. The meaning is: Because he does not lie, and you indeed do not lie, fulfill what you promised when you believed in him in baptism: namely, renounce the devil and his works. The more closely someone approaches idols, the farther he withdraws from God. It is also difficult for those who frequent idols not to suspect that there is something great or virtuous in them. Therefore flee not only with your feet but also in your conduct, so that you do not give the devil an opportunity.

[Note: [Col. 0373D] In the autograph margin, chapter XLVI is written here.]

It continues: “As I speak to prudent people.” He spoke to prudent people—that is, to philosophers—so that they might judge for themselves that what he was saying was true. It is as though he were saying: “If you are prudent, because you are philosophers and dialecticians, judge for yourselves; that is, by the comparisons that follow, prove that what I say is true.”

It continues: “The cup of blessing that we bless,” etc. The meaning is: If, because of the signification of one cup and one bread, which are offered under one invocation to the one God, we are one bread and one body because we partake of them; and if the Israelites, living carnally, because they eat the victims offered under one invocation to the one God upon one altar, are participants and are one—then see to it that perhaps you too, who eat meat sacrificed to idols, may be one with those who sacrifice with them.

[Note: [Col. 0373D] In the autograph margin, chapter XLVII is written here.]

But because he saw that they were crafty and cleverly responding to him, saying: “O Paul, if you are one, as you say, and carnal Israel is one with the altar because it eats the victims, and you say that we are one with those who sacrifice to idols”—[Note: [Col. 0374D] In the autograph margin, chapter XLVIII is written here.]—“then you understand something great in the idol, if participation in its sacrifices makes us one with it,” he forestalled their cunning and said: “What then? Do I say that what is sacrificed to idols is anything?” etc. That is: “I do not say this.”

And since they could reply: “Why then do you say it?” he answered: “Not because it is something, but because what the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God.” It is as though he were saying: “Although an idol is nothing, the devil is nevertheless something; deceiving simple and wicked people, he made himself worshiped in these things. And although what is offered is something, because it is God’s creature and is good, nevertheless, on account of certain invocations of demons, what is clean is made unclean. Therefore I do not want you to eat unclean things, lest you become associated with unclean demons.”

[Note: [Col. 0374D] In the autograph margin, chapter XLIX is written here.]

Therefore he immediately adds: “I do not want you to become partners with demons,” etc. The meaning is: Those who associate with demons are separated from God; those who drink the cup of demons reject the cup of the Lord; and those who love the tables of demons disparage the Lord’s table.

While they were doing these things, they were accustomed to say: “In this we imitate the Lord, because he ate with publicans and sinners.” Therefore he says: “*An aemulamur Dominum?*” (“Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy?”). As though he were saying: “If you imitate the Lord in this, because you eat with sinners, why do you not imitate him in this also, because you eat meat sacrificed to idols?” For he is never read to have eaten such meat. If it were to be eaten, he would have shown this by his own example. Therefore, since you exhibit an example that the Lord did not exhibit, are you stronger than he?

In some copies it is found: “*An ad zelandum Dominum provocamus?*” (“Are we provoking the Lord to jealousy?”). The meaning is: “By doing these things, are you not provoking him to avenge himself upon you? Or are you stronger than he, so that he cannot do so?”

It continues: “All things are lawful for me,” etc., as above.

It continues: “Whatever is sold in the meat market,” etc. He had forbidden them to eat meat sacrificed to idols and had restricted them so severely that he almost seemed to have condemned nature itself. Because meat sacrificed to idols was sold in the meat market, he yielded by granting permission, lest they be excessively constrained or nature seem condemned. “Whatever,” he says, “is sold in the meat market,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0375D] In the autograph margin, chapter L is written here.]

But why did he command them not to ask questions? So that the Christian would not be identified and so that, for the sake of mocking him, someone might say that whatever was being offered had been sacrificed. And because he wished to show that what was sacrificed to idols was good by nature, he added: “The earth is the Lord’s,” etc., as though he were saying: “If the earth is the Lord’s, that too is the Lord’s.”

For whose conscience he commanded them not to ask, he shows below: “Not your own,” he says, “but another’s.” Why, then, on account of another? Lest that person either rejoice in his idols or be given an opportunity to criticize and say: “Why does this man curse the idol whose sacrifices he eats so eagerly?”

[Note: [Col. 0375D] In the autograph margin, chapter LI is written here.]

It continues: “If someone among the unbelievers invites you,” etc. By these words he does not compel them to go, but leaves it to their freedom, so that, following the example of the Lord, if they recognize that they can be of benefit—that is, that they can win them either by example or by teaching—they may go.

It continues: “Why is my freedom judged?” etc. As though he were saying: “I am free because I understand all things to be clean and lawful. Why, by eating meat sacrificed to idols, should I give occasion for another’s conscience to judge me?”

It continues: “And if I partake with thanksgiving,” etc. The meaning is: If, under the invocation, blessing, and veneration of God, I receive lawful things with thanksgiving, why should I, by eating meat sacrificed to idols, give others an occasion to blaspheme me?

[Note: [Col. 0375D] In the autograph margin, chapter LII is written here.]

It continues: “Therefore, whether you eat or drink,” etc. By these words the Apostle most plainly curses and condemns sacrifices to idols. For what does eating meat sacrificed to idols have to do with the praise of God? When something sacrificed to idols is eaten, a greater injury, I say, is inflicted upon God.

If, in the Law, groves, altars, and shrines are commanded to be destroyed and demolished—something that pertains to the praise of God—how can eating meat sacrificed to idols pertain to praise? To celebrate simply under divine invocation and blessing, with thanksgiving, and to provide necessities to those in need pertains to the praise of God, because from this the means is given by which God may be praised.

It continues: “Be without offense to Jews,” etc. In other words: “You are an offense to the Jews because you say that you possess the Law and the Prophets and understand them, yet you eat meat sacrificed to idols, which they curse. You are also an offense to the Gentiles, because you not only do not rebuke them so that they may withdraw from these things, but you give them an occasion to remain in them, since they believe that you understand something great in idols. And you are an offense to the Church of God, because you give simple people an opportunity either to imitate you or to criticize you.”

It continues: “Just as I also please everyone in every way.” Did he please his persecutors? No. But there were believers from every class whom he pleased. He is not contradictory, because elsewhere he says that he does not please human beings, since he did not establish the end of his pleasing among human beings.

[Col. 0376B] [Note: [Col. 0376D] In the autograph margin, chapter LIII is written here.]

**(CHAPTER XI.)** It continues: “Not seeking what is useful for me,” etc., through “as I also am of Christ.” The meaning is: Just as Christ assumed flesh and endured reproaches not for himself but for our salvation, so he sent the apostles into the world not for themselves but for the salvation of the human race. So you too should strive to seek the salvation of your brothers.

It continues: “I praise you, brothers, because you remember me in everything,” etc. These words are spoken ironically.

It should be understood that among the Corinthians there was a shameful and dishonorable custom: men went about with long hair, and women prayed to God with their heads uncovered. The Apostle begins to attack and condemn this custom from the creation of the first human beings.

He says: “I want you to know,” etc. “The head of the man is Christ”; [Note: [Col. 0376D] In the autograph margin, chapter LIV is written here.] because all things are through him; “the head of the woman is the man,” because she was created from him; “the head of Christ is God,” either on account of his humanity or because he was begotten by him.

[Note: [Col. 0376D] In the author’s own manuscript margin, chapter LV is marked here.]

Then follows: “Every man praying,” that is, preaching, “or prophesying,” that is, proclaiming future things, “with his head covered dishonors his head,” because this is a disgrace to him. Then follows: “A man ought not to cover his head”; that is, he should display the freedom of his head.

Then follows: “For he is the image and glory of God.” This means that, just as there is one God through whom and from whom all things exist, so he made one man from whom all human beings derive. He is therefore the glory of God, because he was made for the humiliation of the devil, who wished to exalt himself so as to be above all things.

Then follows: “The woman is the glory of the man,” because she was made from him. He develops this at greater length up to the point where he says: “[Col. 0376D] Therefore she ought to have authority”—understand, authority expressed by a veil—“because of the angels,” that is, because of preachers; or because of the heavenly angels, who are undoubtedly present wherever divine and heavenly rites are celebrated. Or certainly, she ought to have a veil in order to display submission because of the first transgression.

Indeed, lest women should appear excessively subjected and men should be exalted too greatly over them, he therefore added: “Nevertheless, neither is the man without the woman in the Lord.” Confirming this, he says: “But all things are from God.” As for the statement “as also the man by the woman,” one should not understand this as referring to the one by whom the woman came into existence, but either to Cain, or Abel, or Christ born from the Virgin.

Then follows: “Judge among yourselves,” and so forth—as though he were saying: “If you do not wish to assent to my admonitions, namely, that it is unfitting for an unveiled woman to pray, at least return to nature, and nature itself will teach you that if a man grows his hair long, it is a disgrace to him,” and so forth.

He set before them a syllogism: if it is unfitting for a woman to pray unveiled, then it is fitting for her to pray veiled. And because he knew them to be crafty, lest they should contentious­ly say, “Paul, where do you get examples by which to confirm what you are saying?” he forestalled them and said: “If anyone seems to be contentious,” and so forth—as though he were saying: “I know that you are contentious.”

“I have shown that this is required by nature. But if you seek examples contentiously, we have no such custom, nor does the Church of God.” By “we” he means on account of the Jews, and by “the Church” on account of the Gentiles. The sense is: neither Moses nor Christ has this custom. Therefore, if you have adopted this practice, you show that you are disciples not only of Christ but not even of Moses.

In this passage Faustus is refuted, since he denied that bodies were created by God, whereas the Apostle says that all things are from God.

It should be carefully noted that the Apostle elsewhere says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Eph. 4:23), and again: “Putting off the old man” (Col. 3:9), and so forth. Here he attentively observes that, if a human being is renewed in the spirit of the mind, it is there that the human being is shown to have been made in the image of God, where no distinction of sex is displayed.

“The spirit of the mind” is spoken of in the same way as “the body of the flesh” or “the flesh of the body.” For if the human being is renewed in the spirit, woman is not excluded from this renewal, especially since the Apostle says elsewhere: “There is neither slave nor free, there is neither male nor female” (Gal. 3:28), and so forth.

But because in the body woman is distinguished from man by sex, we must understand that there is a particular and principal faculty of the soul, namely, the rational spirit, which is designated by the name “man,” while the soul itself is designated by the name “woman.” This is beautifully appropriate: just as woman is governed by man, so the soul is governed by the spirit.

This man—that is, the spirit—when he considers the things of God, directs his gaze toward heavenly things, and remains fixed upon those things that will endure, ought not to cover his head; that is, he ought not to obscure the face of the mind with the veil of temporal cares, but should always have a pure heart, so that he may contemplate heavenly things with greater clarity.

This woman, that is, the soul, when she considers the things of the world, especially those that are necessary, ought to have the veil of discernment, lest she become attached to what is superfluous.

In another sense, “man” may be understood as referring to preachers, and “women” to uneducated peoples. This too is beautifully appropriate: just as woman is governed by man, so these peoples are governed by preachers.

This man, that is, the preachers, ought not to cover his head, that is, to assume the veil of folly. The woman, however, ought to cover her head, that is, the peoples ought to assume the veil of humility and submission. Ignorance will not harm them if they humbly strive, by asking questions, to learn what they do not know.

For just as it is a disgrace for a woman not to cover her head, so it is a disgrace for the peoples, having cast off the veil of humility, to desire the proud freedom of teachers.

“This, however, I command,” and so forth. After he had rebuked the shameful behavior of the Corinthians and their corrupt way of life, he likewise rebuked their shameful custom. The men went about with long hair, and the women without veils.

There was also another shameful practice among them, which the Apostle now rebukes by saying: “This, however, I command,” and so forth. When they gathered for church, they did not wait for one another. When the presbyters arrived—for rulers had not yet been appointed—they would offer the food they had brought, then claim the consecrated portions as their own, joining them to their ordinary meals and celebrating a dinner in the church. Thus those who arrived later, as commonly happens, would either bring nothing or, lacking anything to contribute, withdraw in embarrassment.

They had been deceived by false apostles into being jealous of their own possessions.

“I do not praise you,” and so forth—that is, you come together for the worse, because you do not keep what I handed down to you.

[Note: [Col. 0377D] In the author’s own manuscript margin, chapter LVI is marked here.]

“First of all,” and so forth. He says that the first source and root of all vices is division, since no good can exist where there is division. “And I partly believe it.” The Apostle moderated his statement with these words. For he did not hesitate to say that he knew this, since he could have learned it from others, or come to know it through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, with which he was filled.

“For there must be heresies,” and so forth. This passage resembles the one in which the Lord says: “It is necessary that scandals come” (Matt. 18:7), and so forth. But neither does the Lord say this because he wishes scandals to exist, nor does the Apostle say it because he wishes heresies to exist. Rather, he says it because it was impossible that they should not come, or because, when they came, those who were chosen—men known only to themselves and to God—would be revealed, as happened with Job.

Job was a man of holy conduct, known only to himself and to God; but when temptations arose, he was revealed to others. In the same way, there were certain people among the Corinthians who were called followers of Apollos, followers of Peter, and others Christians. But when heresies arose, those who were Christians were revealed.

Augustine says: “We ought to make good use of heretics.” As long as they are in the Church, they are harmful; when they stand outside the Church, they not only do no harm but even prove beneficial—not by speaking the good which they do not know, but by stirring up the carnal to seek, and by bringing the spiritual to produce good things.

“Therefore, when you come together” [Note: [Col. 0377D] The following remarks demonstrate the real presence of Christ’s body and blood in the sacrament of the Eucharist, as well as the ancient practice of approaching it fasting.], and so forth.

The Apostle had touched upon the matter above in his customary manner; now he undertakes the same subject with greater emphasis, saying: “Therefore, when you come together.” But why does he call it “the Lord’s supper”? Because on that day the Lord supped with his disciples.

Note that he calls the mystery of his body and blood a supper, as if to say: “This is the supper.” Yet below he says that he handed it over during supper, as it is written: “While they were eating” (Matt. 26:26), that is, after the lamb had been eaten. This was entirely appropriate, since it followed that the old Passover should come to an end and that they should thereafter pass over to the new one.

Nor is the Church reproached on this account because she receives it while fasting. The reason is that the soul must first be marked with spiritual food, and only afterward must the body be sustained with ordinary food.

It is reported that this custom is observed in Egypt. On Saturdays, gathered together toward evening, some approach to receive the body while hungry, others while drunk. Certain men of reputable life have also handed down the practice that once a year, namely on the evening of the feast of Passover, for the sake of more certain reverence, they should take all ordinary food first and then receive the mystery of the body and blood, provided that they did not break their fast before the ninth hour.

It should also be noted that the Lord handed both things over to his disciples, body and blood, because he assumed and saved both soul and body. For just as the body is signified through bread, so the soul is signified through blood.

It should be understood that he handed over this sacrament at the end. For after handing it over, he immediately went to the place where he was to be handed over—as when someone, toward the end of his life, gives a beloved gift to a friend as a memorial of himself.

But when a person foresees such a thing, is he not moved to compunction, or even summoned to tears? In the same way, when we sanctify or receive this mystery, we ought to be moved to compunction and summoned to tears.

This is why the priest, when giving the mystery to someone who does not understand, says: “Receive the body; may it benefit you unto eternal life,” so that, hearing the word “body,” the recipient may tremble and receive it with reverence and shame.

But it should be understood that the Lord did not prescribe when it should be received. If he had prescribed this, it could not be done otherwise without offense. Nevertheless, he prescribed how it should be received and left to the apostles the determination of when it should be received. Hence there is no doubt that it was handed down by the apostles that it should be received in this manner.

“It is no longer to eat the Lord’s supper,” that is, you are not taking the Lord’s supper but your own. He explains this by adding: “Each one takes his own supper,” and so forth; “one is hungry, another is drunk.”

“Do you not have houses?” and so forth. It is as though he were saying: “Do you not have places where you can receive ordinary food? You do. Why, then, do you celebrate a dinner in the church? Is it so that you may display yourselves as rich, or shame those who have nothing?”

“What shall I say to you? Shall I praise you?” and so forth. It is as though he were saying: “Such an action is not considered praiseworthy; that is, you are not worthy of praise because you assemble in the church.”

[Note: [Col. 0379D] In the author’s own manuscript margin, chapter LVII is marked here.]

“For I received from the Lord,” and so forth. He received this from the Lord, not from Christ as a human being still subject to mortality, like the others, as he himself says: “I did not receive it from man, nor was I taught it” (Gal. 1:1), and so forth.

He therefore says “from the Lord” in order to impress more firmly upon their hearts what he was saying: “That the Lord Jesus, on the night when he was handed over,” [Col. 0380A] and the rest.

It should be understood that he handed both things over to the disciples, namely bread and wine, because he assumed and saved both soul and body. The body is signified through bread, and the soul through wine.

He says “the new cup” in distinction from the old one.

“You will proclaim the Lord’s death.” For what is it to proclaim the Lord’s death except to call to remembrance what takes place either when we consecrate his body or when we receive it?

“Until he comes.” He speaks appropriately, because after he has come these mysteries will no longer be celebrated.

[Note: [Col. 0379D] In the author’s own manuscript margin, chapter LVIII is marked here.]

“Therefore, whoever eats the bread,” and so forth. He receives it unworthily who does not receive it according to the authority of the one who handed it over. “He will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord,” because through receiving it he heaps the punishment of his guilt upon himself, since judgment is reserved for him in the future, when his hidden deeds will be revealed, and it will be known whether he received it worthily or unworthily.

“But let a person examine himself,” and so forth—that is, let him investigate and inquire whether he is worthy to receive it, and then let him receive it.

For this mystery is of such a kind that it brings salvation to those who receive it worthily, but punishment to those who receive it unworthily, as in the case of Judas. After Judas had received it, Satan entered into him (Luke 22:3; John 13:27).

And if one who receives it unworthily receives it to his condemnation, how much more does one receive it unworthily who is defiled by some impurity?

“Not discerning” [Note: [Col. 0380D] The Vulgate reads “judging.”] “the body”—that is, distinguishing this food from other food, or thinking that it is merely ordinary bread.

“For this reason many among you are weak,” and so forth. Since he had said above, “Whoever eats,” and so forth, he added this in order to make his account more certain: “For this reason many among you,” and so forth.

He calls them weak because some were afflicted with fever, others were weakened, and others were punished by bodily death. But why does he recall this? So that, hearing of the scourges inflicted on others, they might be corrected, in accordance with the saying: “When the pestilent is scourged, the wise man becomes more prudent” (Prov. 19:25), and: “The righteous man will rejoice when he sees it” (Ps. 57:11), and so forth.

“But if we judged ourselves,” and so forth. This is appropriate, because the person who recognizes and corrects his evil actions is not judged by God.

“But when we are judged,” and so forth. Whether it is said that we are judged by the Lord or corrected by the Lord, the meaning is that the person whose actions are scourged is reproved so that he may be corrected.

“So that we may not be condemned with the world,” that is, with unbelievers or pagans.

Hence Origen says: “Whoever receives it unworthily or shamelessly differs in no respect from an unbeliever or pagan.”

[Note: [Col. 0380D] In the author’s own manuscript margin, chapter LIX is marked here.]

“Therefore, my brothers,” and so forth. Having concluded his rebuke, he gives them advice concerning what ought to be done, saying: “Therefore, my brothers,” and so forth.

That is, let your offering be sanctified under the invocation of the one God; let it not be regarded as private, but be considered common.

“If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home.” That is, if anyone is impatient, let him receive ordinary food at home and not join a meal to the consecrated elements in the church.

“So that you do not come together for judgment,” that is, so that where you think you will find benefit, you may not instead find loss.

[Col. 0381A] “The rest I will set in order when I come.” There were many matters to be said concerning the ministry of the Church, and therefore it was not appropriate to teach them by letter. The universal Church preserves his instructions. For this reason he promises that he will come and teach what was necessary.

When he came, he set these matters in order by word of mouth. Hence there is no doubt that the ecclesiastical order was handed down by the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0381D] Note that the transmission of the ecclesiastical order derives from the apostles.].

For in the beginning of the Church there was a custom that those who believed, after being baptized and becoming members of the faithful, would receive the grace of speaking in all languages, so that people might be drawn to the faith more and more.

But because, as this Apostle says here, “signs are for unbelievers, not for believers” (1 Cor. 14:22), once the faith had been spread and many had begun to flock to belief, this custom itself began to cease.

The Corinthians, although they were already believers, still loved philosophical teaching. They therefore judged this gift greater than all the others and greatly desired to possess it. Consequently, those who possessed it despised those who did not, while those who did not possess it humbled themselves, believing that they did not belong to the body, or else envied those who lacked it.

[Note: [Col. 0381D] In the author’s own manuscript margin, chapter LX is marked here.]

(CHAPTER XII.) This is what the Apostle undertakes to rebuke in them, beginning to speak about spiritual things. He says: “I do not want you to be ignorant concerning spiritual matters” (understand, spiritual gifts).

Before speaking about these, he recalled their former way of life, saying: “You know that when you were Gentiles” [Note: [Col. 0382D] In the author’s own manuscript margin, “Sunday vacant after Pentecost” is marked here.], and so forth.

He wished them to remember their former way of life so that they would cease to be proud and strive to remain humble. Or certainly, just as previously they were dragged into various errors at the impulse of demons, so now, having been converted and possessing a teacher and instructor of evangelical doctrine, they should follow him wherever he wished to lead them.

Hence in certain copies one finds: “Bearing the form of idols.” Everyone is said to bear the form of whatever he worships. Since these people had now been converted, they ought to bear the form of the Gospel—that is, to display the light of evangelical doctrine in their conduct.

Then follows: “Therefore I make known to you,” and so forth. The sense is: Whoever has the Spirit of God perceives nothing perverse concerning the Lord; and whoever has a right understanding of anything concerning him recognizes it only through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Then follows: “And no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’” and so forth. Here a question arises: Why does he say, “No one can say,” when the Lord says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord’” (Matt. 7:21), and so forth?

But in the former passage “to say” means merely to utter the sound, whereas here it is understood to mean “to do.”

Then follows: “There are divisions of graces,” and so forth. By these words the Apostle shows that it is not the Holy Spirit but his gifts that are divided. For example, the sun diffuses its rays through different places but is not itself divided.

And so that his gifts might be attributed not to human beings but to God, they are called “graces.”

This passage stands against Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit is God. It also stands against Arius, who asserted both degrees within the Trinity and that the Son is lesser than the Father and the Holy Spirit lesser than both.

They tried to confirm this on the grounds that the Father is always placed first, whereas here the Holy Spirit is placed first and the Father last.

By “divisions of graces, ministries, and operations,” he may have intended the various offices in the Church. He shows their diversity when he immediately adds: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the benefit”—either of his own salvation or of the building up of the Church.

Then follows: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge.”

Blessed Augustine says that wisdom and knowledge differ. Wisdom, he says, is knowledge of divine things; knowledge is knowledge of human things—not of such matters as what gold or silver is, or how many estates we have and what kind they are, but knowledge consisting in the four virtues, than which nothing is more useful to human beings in life: through it we learn the understanding belonging to prudence, the holiness belonging to justice, the strength belonging to fortitude, and the dignity belonging to temperance.

Then follows: “To another, faith.” This means the faith by which a person, casting aside shame, freely confesses what he has believed.

“To another, the grace of healings,” by which he cures sicknesses and diseases. Hence Peter says: “Aeneas, the Lord heals you” (Acts 9:34).

“To another, the working of miracles” (Acts 9:34), namely, so that they may cast out demons.

“To another, prophecy,” so that they may announce future things.

“To another, the discernment of spirits,” so that, when he hears or reads something, he may discern from which spirit it comes.

“To another, kinds of languages,” so that he may speak in different languages.

“To another, the interpretation of words,” so that, when something is read or said, he may beneficially translate it into another language for the advancement of others.

Then follows: “But one and the same Spirit produces all these things,” and so forth.

By these words he demonstrates the unity of the Trinity and the Trinity of unity: the Father is called God, the Son God, and the Holy Spirit God; each individually is God, and yet the three are one God.

Accordingly, what the Father does, the Son and the Holy Spirit do; therefore the operation of the whole Trinity is one. Hence, although above he had spoken of God the Father and God the Son, he nevertheless did not hesitate to say that the Holy Spirit divides all things.

God is also demonstrated most openly by this statement, since he divides all things not by command but by will.

We should therefore also consider why the person who receives less ought neither to humble himself nor to envy another, as though someone else had seized the greater portion, since the Spirit himself divides everything to each person as he wills. If envy were appropriate, one should envy God rather than a human being.

Because he had begun to speak about the variety of spiritual gifts, in order to commend them more strongly he added the comparison of the body and its members. He says: “For just as the body is one and has many members,” and so forth.

The sense is: If there were only one member, it would no longer be a body; that is, a part would not exist within a whole. But because there are many and diverse members, one body is formed from these different parts. Hence it is called a body—or, alternatively, because when it is corrupted it perishes.

Then follows: “So also is Christ.” It is as though he had said: Christ has many members, with whom Christ is one body.

Therefore, in explaining what he had said—“so also is Christ”—he added: “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body.”

The sense is: Just as all the members of the body are given life by one spirit, so all who, reborn through the grace of baptism, come together into one body are given life by one Spirit.

Thus, if a bodily member is cut off, it is no longer given life by that same spirit; so too the person cut off from the body of the Church is no longer considered worthy to be given life.

Wishing to show from what the body of the Church is composed, he added: “Whether Jews or Gentiles,” and so forth. He said little, but through this little he wished all things pertaining to the joining and binding together of this body to be understood, except sin.

Then follows: “And we were all given to drink of one Spirit,” that is, we were all made to drink.

It should be understood that a single drink is often distributed among many people. For example, if someone has many vessels of unequal size, when he pours out the drink he considers the capacity of each vessel. So also God supplies grace to each person according to that person’s capacity.

Then follows: “For the body is not one member but many.” The sense is: If it were one member, it would no longer be a body. That is, if one person received all the gifts and all the graces, there would not be one body but many.

Then follows: “If the foot should say,” and so forth.

Blessed Pope Gregory says that, through the variety of the body and its members, the variety of spiritual gifts is signified.

The Church has some who are eyes, by foreseeing future things; others are ears, by humbly receiving the instructions of teachers; others are nostrils, by distinguishing good from evil; others are a mouth, by admonishing and exhorting; others are hands, by ministering to others; and others are feet, by going about for the salvation of others.

The heavenly organizer arranged the character of the members in such a way that all would be subject to one another. The eyes do not see only for themselves but for all the members. The same applies to the other members.

Likewise, he arranged the condition of souls so that, through humility, all the members of the Church would be subject to one another. For example, when someone sees that you possess a grace which he himself does not possess, he submits to you; and similarly, you submit to him.

Hence the Apostle Peter says: “As each has received a grace” (1 Pet. 4:10), and so forth.

Grace is administered in many forms, and it is rightly administered when the grace one possesses is, through humility, bestowed upon another. Hence Paul likewise says: “Through love of the Spirit serve one another” (Gal. 5:13).

Love frees us perfectly from the yoke of sin when we regard the graces of others as though they were our own, and administer our own graces to others as though they were theirs.

This same arrangement, for the sake of unity and harmony, is found to have been established by the very organizer throughout the regions of the world: one region abounds in grain or wine, another in oil, and so on with the rest.

It is likewise found among the elements of the world. For what is the world except one thing composed of different elements? If there were always heat, as in summer, or always cold, as in winter, the earth could not produce fruits. Therefore the very diversity of the elements creates a certain balance.

The same is true of metals: gold or silver is more precious than iron, but iron is more useful than both.

Then follows: “If the ear should say, ‘I am not an eye,’” and so forth.

By the eye and the hand the eminent members of the Church are signified; by the ear, those of intermediate rank; and by the foot, the least.

These people, because they have received a small grace, ought neither to humble themselves nor to despise themselves, nor to think that they do not belong to the body. Since they are members, they certainly belong to the body.

Then follows: “If the whole body were an eye,” and so forth. The sense is: If one person had received all the graces, how would the Church become the body of Christ?

Then follows: “But now God has placed the members,” and so forth. Who can now fail to see where the Apostle’s intention is directed? From the likeness of the human body he passes to reveal the truth of the spiritual body, that is, the Church.

He says that he placed each one of them “as he willed,” because he bestowed upon each person the grace he willed to bestow.

Then follows: “But if they were all one member, where would the body be?” That is: If everyone had all the gifts, from what diverse members would the one body of the Church be formed?

Therefore he continues: “But now there are many members,” and so forth.

Then follows: “The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I have no need of you,’” because the hands do not labor only for themselves but for all the members.

The feet likewise do not walk for themselves. Hence he immediately adds: “Or the head to the feet, ‘You are not necessary to me.’”

By the eye and the head the eminent members of the Church are signified; by the hand, those of intermediate rank; and by the feet, the least.

But those who are eminent cannot say to those of intermediate or lower rank, “You are not necessary to us,” because, unless those who serve are present, their dignity declines. The eminent are raised up through the work and service of the others.

For example, a king has a body consisting of commanders, counts, and tribunes; among these members he also has feet, namely soldiers. Yet he cannot say, “You are not necessary to me,” since he needs them even more, as feet are more necessary than the other members. For even if he has neither eyes nor ears nor nostrils, he can walk with his feet and seek food.

Therefore he added: “But much more, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are more necessary; and those which we think to be less honorable,” and so forth.

He calls the feet weaker and less honorable members. Although they appear weak and lowly in comparison with the others, we surround them with greater honor, since we cover them with garments and shoes.

Similarly, those signified by the feet, although they may appear lowly, should nevertheless be encouraged through exhortation and admonition, lest they humble themselves, believing that they do not belong to the body. Their concern need be only that they belong to the body, not which members they are.

Then follows: “And those parts of our body which we consider less honorable,” and so forth.

He calls the less honorable members the private parts, from which human sight withdraws.

Blessed Augustine says: “Far be it from us to call any part of the bodies of the elect dishonorable, not even the genital members. But because their use is dishonorable, the Apostle called them dishonorable. That use does not arise from nature but from the transgression of the first human beings; before that, they were honorable, like the other members.”

[Note: [Col. 0385D] Before the words “and beautifully,” words of the text seem to be missing—“they have greater honor,” to which the interpretation below is attached.]

“And beautifully,” because offspring are generated through them. These members have greater honor because, although we cover neither the head nor the eyes nor the other members, the private parts are often surrounded with splendid garments.

Through these members are signified those who go barefoot and wear filthy clothing. They possess greater honor because the more rejected they appear, the purer their life, the more pleasing they are in the sight of God, and therefore the more deserving of praise.

“Our honorable parts have no need of this,” that is, the eminent members, such as the head or the eyes. For a person who is vigorous in understanding and skilled in intellect does not need to be praised.

Then follows: “But God has composed the body,” and so forth.

God composed the body because he assigned particular functions to particular members; the same applies to the body of the Church.

For what purpose? So that there might be no schism in the body—that is, so that each member might supply its proper service to the others.

The members of the Church are rightly considered members when they are not perverted: that is, when one does not arrogantly wish to assume another’s grace while neglecting his own. If he does this, he both renders his own grace useless and fails to deserve the other’s.

Then follows: “But the members should have the same care for one another.”

Mystically understood: If someone in the Church suffers some evil or danger to his soul, all the faithful ought to grieve in compassion over his misfortune as though it were their own; similarly, they should rejoice over his progress.

Explaining the comparison he had introduced, he added: “You are the body of Christ,” and so forth.

Note that he says “members from a member.” A member in relation to the body is one thing—for example, the arm; a member in relation to another member is something else—for example, the hand or fingers in relation to the arm.

Explaining this also, he says: “And God has appointed some in the Church,” and so forth—prophets, meaning not those of the Old Testament but those of the New, such as Agabus and the virgin daughters of Philip [Note: [Col. 0385D] Agabus was a prophet and one of the seventy disciples of Jesus Christ. He foretold the famine that occurred under Claudius (Acts 11:28) and Paul’s imprisonment (Acts 21:10). The Greeks report that he was crowned with martyrdom at Antioch and celebrate his feast on 8 March; the Latins celebrated it on 9 February in the ninth century.] [Note: [Col. 0385D] Concerning these daughters of St. Philip the Apostle—whom Caius, an ancient priest of the Roman Church, seems not to have sufficiently distinguished and to have confused with the daughters of St. Philip the deacon—see Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book III, chapter 31, and Sozomen, book VII, chapter 27.].

Then follows: “Third, teachers.”

In the Old Testament those who taught the law to children were called teachers. This custom passed over into the ecclesiastical community. There are some who, although they do not belong to any higher order, nevertheless make the divine mysteries clear to others.

Then follows “miracles and gifts of healings,” as above, “helps”: either those who are weak and are helped by others, or those who help the weak.

“Governments” are those who are placed over the governance of souls, such as abbots in monasteries.

Note that he placed “kinds of languages” last, because they judged this gift greater than all the others. He did so to show that it was not only not greater but even lesser, and also to instruct them that they ought not to desire gifts which the wicked can possess and through which no one can be saved, but should instead ardently long for those which the wicked cannot possess and without which no one deserves to be saved.

[Note: [Col. 0386D] In the author’s own manuscript margin, chapter LXI is marked here.]

Therefore, after he had said: “Are all apostles?” and so forth, he added: “Strive eagerly for the better gifts.”

“Strive eagerly for the gifts,” and so forth. Having displayed the variety of graces, the Apostle exhorts and urges the Corinthians to strive eagerly for the greater charisms, that is, to pursue the greater gifts.

He calls prophecy the greater charism, since it pertains to the benefit of the whole prophecy [Note: [Col. 0386D] Although the words “which pertains to the benefit of the whole prophecy” produce a somewhat unsuitable meaning, I have not thought it right to emend them, since, although they yield an obscure sense, they nevertheless yield some sense. For their interpretation, consult what is read shortly afterward in the words of the epistle—“He who speaks in a tongue edifies himself,” chapter XIV—where he says that the difference between tongues and prophecy is as great as the difference between the salvation of one person and that of many, indeed of all. From this it may perhaps be inferred that the text should better read: “prophecy, which pertains to the benefit of the whole Church.” This reading is confirmed by the same words of this epistle, 14:4: “He who speaks in a tongue edifies himself; but he who prophesies edifies the Church of God.”].

They thought that the greater gift was the variety of languages, judging that there was no other gift greater. [Col. 0386C] Wishing to draw them away from this opinion, the Apostle therefore says: “Strive eagerly,” and so forth.

(CHAPTER XIII.) And in order to draw them farther onward, after saying “strive eagerly,” he did not immediately conclude but added: “If I speak in the tongues of human beings,” and so forth.

There are seventy-two human languages. But what are the languages of angels, since they have no bodily tongues, being incorporeal themselves?

He speaks hyperbolically, as though he were saying: “Even if you could speak in the tongues of angels, without love it would not benefit you.”

Or perhaps he calls the tongue of angels the tongue of teachers, for human speech differs from the speech of teachers. The sense would then be: “Even if you spoke in the languages of teachers, without love it would not benefit you.”

Someone may ask in what languages human beings will speak after this life. But this is not found, perhaps because then there will be no ignorance. The function of the tongue was granted so that human beings might make their actions known to others, since those actions are unknown. Then this will not be necessary, because ignorance will be absent.

“I have become like sounding bronze,” and so forth. Bronze is an irrational element and, unless struck, does not sound. When it has sounded, however, it provides neither edification nor benefit.

Similarly, a person who speaks in all languages without love is of no benefit.

“And if I have prophecy,” that is, if I proclaim future things, “and know all mysteries,” that is, divine mysteries, “and all knowledge,” that is, human knowledge, “and have all faith.”

Note that he calls this faith “all” faith, which the Lord compares in the Gospel to a grain of mustard seed (Matt. 17:19; Luke 17:6), not because of its smallness but because of its completeness and vitality. Thus here also mention is made of the mountain, as in that passage (Matt. 17:19).

“But do not have love, I am nothing.” He does not deny that he exists substantially; rather, he says that in the ministry of preaching he is nothing.

“And if I distribute,” and so forth. Note that he joins the distribution of possessions to martyrdom, thereby showing that the distribution of possessions is of great merit.

But because some customarily perform this very act hypocritically, he therefore added: “But do not have love, it profits me nothing.”

Understand “hypocritically” in two ways: either someone gives away his possessions or undergoes martyrdom out of a desire for human praise, or he pretends to be a friend while actually being an enemy.

Charity is patient, etc. He had mentioned charity above; now, showing the members of charity, he says: “Charity is patient,” etc. Patient, by enduring evils; kind, by bestowing good things. *Charity* is a Greek word and is interpreted as “love.” It is called love because it binds two persons together.

Charity does not envy—that is, it is not jealous, because it despises visible things—or, “does not envy,” that is, it does not puff itself up, because it is free from pride. Pride is the mother of self-inflation. It does not act wrongly—that is, perversely or crookedly—because it directs its intention toward the one in whose ordinances nothing crooked is found. It is not puffed up—that is, it is not proud. It is not ambitious—that is, it despises temporal things, or considers the honor of rule of little account. It does not seek its own—that is, it does not desire temporal and transitory things, or because it gives away its own possessions, which it could have retained without offense.

It does not think evil. Great is the virtue of charity, since it not only does not perform evil but does not even think it; nevertheless, if such a thought should enter the mind, it cuts it off. For there are some who do not perform evil, yet perish merely by thinking about it.

It does not rejoice over iniquity, whether in the one who commits it or in the one who suffers it, because it counts their losses as its own. Rather, it rejoices with the truth, whether in the one who practices it or in the one who endures it.

It bears everything, or endures everything, either by patiently suffering or by waiting for what has been promised to be fulfilled. And this is what follows: it believes everything—that is, it believes that the promises in the divine books will be fulfilled. It hopes that everything said is true.

[Note: The words “It hopes everything … is said” appear to have been corrupted by some transposition. I would judge that one should read: “It hopes—that is, that they will be fulfilled—in the divine writings, etc.; it believes everything that is said to be true.” In this way the words “believes” and “hopes” can receive their proper relation.]

Charity will never fall away—that is, it does not suffer collapse or ruin; for humility never falls, and charity cannot exist without humility. For the more humility penetrates heavenly things, the more it considers itself attached to earthly things; and the higher it ascends, the more it judges itself to remain in the lowest places. If it is joined to higher things, it falls away. [Note: The Vulgate likewise has *excidit*, namely, “falls away.”] The reading should be: “but if it is joined to lower things, it falls away.”

Or prophecies will be brought to an end, etc. Prophecies will be brought to an end in one way, tongues will cease in another, and knowledge will be destroyed in another. The first two will cease because they will come to an end in the present life; knowledge, however, will be destroyed because it will be increased in the future.

And how this happens, he adds: “For we know in part,” etc. He says this appropriately, because no mortal person living in the present life can know perfectly. Much is known here, but not everything; and therefore he says: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part,” that is, we proclaim future things. “But when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will be brought to an end.” It is not the knowledge now possessed that will be brought to an end in the future, but its partial and imperfect character will be destroyed, because that knowledge will be increased.

The expression is like what happens when a cloud comes between the sun and us and its brightness is withdrawn; but when the cloud is removed, one may say: “The brightness of the sun has been brought to an end”—not because the brightness itself has been abolished, but because the increase of brightness is said to have removed the imperfection of that same brightness.

He makes the same point clear by a subordinate comparison, saying: “When I was a child,” etc. He compares the present life to the age of childhood and the future life to the age of manhood. And rightly so, because the difference between this present life and the future life is as great as that between the age of a child and that of an adult. For just as childhood does not destroy infancy, nor adolescence childhood, but increases one’s strength, so future knowledge does not destroy the knowledge of this life, but increases it.

He adds another comparison related to the same meaning, saying: “Now we see through a mirror in a riddle,” etc. The person who sees through a mirror does not perceive the actual thing but an image resembling the actual thing. Likewise, a riddle presents something other than itself. A riddle is an obscure statement that indicates something else—that is, it is not the truth itself but a likeness of the thing, as in allegorical meanings.

Therefore, we see “through a mirror in a riddle,” because we do not yet know perfectly the joy of the future life. “Then face to face,” because we shall see our joy, our gladness, and the fulfillment of our desire. He makes the same thing clear by adding: “Now I know in part,” etc. That is, I shall know as I am known, and I shall see as I am seen, as John says: “We shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

Now there remain faith, etc.—that is, in this present life. In the future life, after the other two have been removed, charity remains, and for that reason it is greater. For hope succeeds faith, and vision succeeds hope; and that vision is charity. Charity is therefore greater, because these things end here, whereas charity remains.

It must be noted that there is a great difference between temporal and spiritual things. Temporal things, when they are not possessed, are greatly desired; but when they are possessed, they become wearisome and cheap. Spiritual things, however, when they are not possessed, are desired less; but when they are possessed, they kindle an ever greater desire within us. From this one should observe that if such things are loved now, when they are neither seen nor possessed, how greatly will they be loved then, when each of the elect possesses them? And this also must be known: each of the elect will find more than he could believe or hope for. Therefore no believer should think that he can here believe or hope for as much as he will find there.

[Note: In the autograph margin, “chapter 62” is written here.]

## Chapter XIV

It follows: “Pursue charity.” After praising charity, he exhorts and urges them to pursue it, as though he were saying: Since you have now recognized such great and such excellent charity, so that all good things consist in its goodness and no good can exist without it, I exhort you to pursue it.

After this admonition, he exhorts them also to be zealous for spiritual gifts. “Be zealous,” he says, “for spiritual things”—the word “gifts” being understood. By spiritual things he means the variety of graces. But because, on hearing “spiritual things,” they could have understood the various kinds of tongues, which they judged greater than all the other charismatic gifts and for which they were exceedingly eager, he immediately adds: “But rather, that you may prophesy.”

It follows: “For the one who speaks in a tongue does not speak to human beings,” because he is not understood by human beings, but by God, since he is understood by the one who also knows the hidden things of the heart. And therefore he adds: “No one hears”—that is, understands him—“but in the spirit,” that is, with the voice alone, “he speaks mysteries.”

But the one who speaks in a tongue speaks to God; and therefore he adds: “For the one who prophesies speaks to human beings,” because he is understood by human beings. He also explains what he says: edification, exhortation, and consolation. People are greatly edified when they hear the solution of questions; they also receive exhortation, so that they may advance toward better things; and they receive great consolation, because through hope of future goods they patiently endure adversity. Hence the same apostle says in the Letter to the Romans: “That through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Romans 15:4).

It follows: “The one who speaks in a tongue edifies himself.” He is speaking of the person who understands what he says. “But the one who prophesies edifies the Church.” By these words he shows that there is a great difference between tongues and prophecy—indeed, as much difference as there is between the salvation of one person and that of many, or rather, of all.

But because above he counted the grace of tongues among the variety of gifts, he accommodates himself to them and allows them to speak in tongues, saying: “I wish you all to speak in tongues.” And to show that this was the lesser gift, he adds: “But rather to prophesy,” as though he were saying: I urge you toward greater things in such a way that I do not forbid lesser ones.

It follows: “For the one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues.” Blessed Augustine labors greatly over this passage. He says that “tongues” should be understood in the divine Scriptures as hidden and profound things; whereas the tongue, the bodily member, names or signifies certain things without producing them. Thus hidden realities are indicated through the movement of the bodily member.

For there are many things and meanings in the divine Scriptures that are not themselves what they signify but signify something else. These too are designated by “tongue,” because the word is used figuratively. Therefore the one who prophesies is greater—that is, the one who clarifies and reveals hidden things—than the one who speaks in a tongue, that is, the one who can indeed utter hidden things but cannot reveal them.

There are, after all, images of bodily things; but the one who can interpret them is greater than the one who sees them. For example, Pharaoh saw visions (Genesis 40–41), and the cupbearer and the chief baker also saw visions; but Joseph was greater than all of them.

The one who excels in both matters is greater not only than the others but also than the person who merely gives the interpretation, as Daniel excelled in both. For he showed Nebuchadnezzar not only the interpretation but also the dream—and, greater than these, his thoughts—when the wise men of Babylon were facing the sentence of death because they had been tested and could not give a conjectural interpretation, since they did not know the dream. For Daniel says: “You, O king, thought upon your bed what would happen after you” (Daniel 2:29), etc.

The one who, although speaking in a tongue, can nevertheless interpret it, is not inferior to a prophet; and therefore he adds: “Unless he interprets.”

He also offered himself as an example to them when he added: “Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues,” etc. It is as though he were saying: Learn the example from me. If I come to you speaking in unknown tongues, I will benefit you nothing and will provide no edification unless I either explain prophecies to you, teach moral matters, or reveal some hidden things. This is what he says: “Unless I speak to you either in revelation, or in knowledge,” etc.

All these things are directed toward one benefit, since the person who understands teaches, and the person who reveals mysteries prophesies; and he does this because he possesses knowledge.

After presenting himself as an example, he adds another example drawn from irrational and insensible things: “Nevertheless, things without life that give sound,” etc. In other words, he says: If a flute, a lyre, or anything of that kind produces not a distinct but a confused sound, it will be useful to no one, because it does not delight the ears of those who hear it. Much more, then, will you provide no edification or benefit unless you speak in such a way that you are understood.

It follows: “For if the trumpet gives an uncertain sound,” etc. Note that he says “uncertain,” because people customarily blew trumpets in various ways. They blew them to rouse people to war, or to move or establish a camp, as is shown in Leviticus, Joshua, and the Maccabees; or at the beginning of the month and on solemn festivals. Hence the Psalmist says: “Blow the trumpet at the beginning of the month.”

[Note: Psalm VIII, 4: “Sound the trumpet at the beginning of the month.” *Neomenia* is a Greek word meaning the first day of the month, which the Hebrews especially observed in every month, especially by offering the sacrifices established by Moses (Numbers XX, 11).]

The meaning is this: Just as, unless the trumpet gives a definite sound for battle, no one prepares himself for battle, so when you speak, unless you speak in such a way that you are understood, no one prepares himself for spiritual combat. This is what he says: “So also you,” etc.

It follows: “You will be speaking into the air”—that is, emitting a sound like people puffed up with wind.

It follows: “There are, for example, so many kinds of tongues,” etc. The meaning is: Even if you spoke in all kinds of tongues, it would benefit you nothing unless you were understood.

It follows: “Therefore, if I do not know the power of the voice,” etc. This is true: if someone speaks to you in an unknown language, then both he is a barbarian to you and you are a barbarian to him.

The meaning is: Corinthians, you should not strive after tongues so that, when speaking in unknown tongues, you appear to one another as barbarians; rather, strive after charity, so that you may rejoice in mutual understanding.

Therefore he adds: “So also you, since you are zealous for spiritual gifts”—that is, tongues—“seek to abound for the edification of the Church,” that is, prophesy. It is as though he had said: Prophecy is an abundance of edification and benefit, not a variety of tongues.

Therefore he immediately continues: “And so the one who speaks in a tongue should pray”—that is, speak in such a way that he interprets—or “should pray,” that is, entreat God.

It follows: “For if I pray in a tongue”—that is, speak—“my spirit,” that is, my voice, “prays, but my mind is without fruit.” The apostle is speaking of the person who does not understand in his mind what he expresses in speech. For example, Latins are accustomed to delight in the sound of the Greek language; when they speak Greek because they are delighted by its sound, their minds are deprived of its fruit.

Some have said that the apostle was speaking of that Spirit who is given in baptism.

It follows: “What then? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray also with the mind,” etc.—unless I understand with my mind what I speak with my mouth, and think in my heart what I sing with my voice. A person sings or prays well only when the voice agrees with the intention.

Therefore, since the apostle has shown the remedy by which the mind may not be without fruit, these words admonish everyone, when he kneels or stands to pray, or even to sing psalms, to gather his mind together and not allow it to wander in different directions, so that he may not be deprived of its fruit.

It follows: “Otherwise, if you bless.” Whatever is said according to the rule of justice is blessed; or you bless when you pray, ask, or indeed sanctify something.

Therefore, if you bless in the spirit—that is, with the voice, because the other person does not understand—who takes the place of the unlearned person? Who will affirm either your prayer or your petitions? This is what he says: “How will he say ‘Amen’ over your blessing?” That is, he will not say “Let it be done,” because he does not know what you are saying.

It follows: “For you indeed give thanks well”—that is, you ask and pray well—“but the other person is not edified,” because he does not understand.

It follows: “I give thanks to God,” etc. It should certainly be noted that the same apostle could speak in various languages, both naturally—in Hebrew, Syriac, Chaldean, and Greek—and also by the grace of the Holy Spirit in other languages, as the other apostles did, as is read in Acts. And because the grace of tongues is a gift of the Holy Spirit, as he showed above, he rightly gives thanks to God.

It follows: “But in the Church I wish to speak five words with my understanding,” etc. This passage should be understood simply. Those who examine it too subtly and say that the five words signify the five books of Moses must also explain what the ten thousand signify.

We should therefore understand simply by five words a brief prayer, and by ten thousand an extended one. The meaning is: I prefer to speak five words with my understanding—that is, to offer a brief prayer plainly and clearly for the edification and salvation of those people—rather than to speak ten thousand words in a tongue, that is, to produce an extended discourse obscurely.

Here scholarly preachers are admonished not to seek their own display in preaching, but the perfection and salvation of their hearers.

It follows: “Brothers, do not become children in your understanding,” etc. A child is to be imitated in simplicity and innocence, in accordance with what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Unless you turn and become like little children” (Matthew 18:3), etc.

The innocence of a child is already clear; but it must be known that true simplicity is accompanied by prudence. Hence it is said of a certain righteous man: “Simple and upright” (Job 2:3)—simple because of his innocence, upright because of his prudence. For one cannot be possessed without the other.

Therefore both are to be possessed, so that simplicity may be lifted up by prudence and prudence moderated by simplicity. Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Be wise as serpents” (Matthew 10:16), etc.

And because a child is to be imitated in the absence of malice, not in understanding, he adds: “But in understanding be mature.”

It follows: “It is written in the Law: ‘In other tongues and with other lips I will speak’” (Isaiah 28:11), etc. The Lord speaks in other tongues and with other lips, in accordance with what he says through the prophet: “I will make a covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah” (Jeremiah 31:31), etc.
