A Jew sees God speaking in other tongues when he hears that circumcision is of no benefit, that the Sabbath is not observed, that prohibited foods may be eaten freely, that the observances of new moons, Kalends, and other festivals have been abolished, and that sacrifices of various kinds have passed over into the mysteries of his body and blood.

But why did he speak in other tongues? Clearly, so that they might believe. He makes this clear when he says: “And even so they will not hear me, says the Lord.” That people despised the Gospel and nevertheless rejected it.

Therefore tongues are for a sign, etc. It was customary at the beginning of the Church for the grace of tongues to be given to believers, so that unbelievers might be stirred to faith. But once the faith had spread and the number of believers had multiplied, that custom ceased.

Therefore the apostle says: “Tongues are for a sign,” etc., “but prophecy not for unbelievers, but for believers.” By these words he shows that there is a great difference between tongues and prophecy, not only in usefulness but also in duration.

Prophecy surpasses tongues in usefulness because tongues are given for unbelievers, whereas prophecy is given for believers. It surpasses them in duration because tongues cease, whereas prophecy will remain as long as the Church is a pilgrim.

It follows: “Therefore, if the whole Church comes together in one place,” etc. The meaning is: If you all gather together and all speak in unknown tongues, will you not give an occasion for reproach? For if unlearned people or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are insane and out of your minds?

But if all of you prophesy and unlearned people or unbelievers enter, he is convicted by all and judged by all—that is, he is convicted and judged because he understands that he is understood and openly recognizes that everything being said is true.

It follows: “And the secrets of his heart are made manifest.” By these words he shows that prophecy does not consist only in proclaiming future things but also in revealing hidden matters that are present. For just as future times conceal something from our eyes, so do the hidden things of minds and the absence of places.

Hence blessed Pope Gregory, speaking of the kinds of prophecy, says that one kind of prophecy is the revelation of the secrets of the heart. He also took this example from the apostle to confirm his account.

It is prophecy to show what is happening elsewhere when one is not present, as we read concerning Elisha: although he was in another place, he knew what his servant Gehazi had done elsewhere (2 Kings 5:26).

It follows: “And so, falling on his face,” [Note: The Vulgate has “on his face.”] “he will worship God,” because he hears nothing obscure, nothing dark, nothing disguised, nothing double, and nothing veiled, as in the shrines of idols.

For the priests of idols are accustomed to veil people’s faces so that they may not see the falsehood. The Church, by contrast, because it possesses no falsehood but all truth, does not veil its eyes but rather asks that they be opened, saying: “Reveal our eyes” (Psalm 119:18), etc.

It follows: “What then, brothers?” That is: What is to be said, chosen, or accepted as counsel? I will show you what counsel you need.

“When you come together,” he says, “each of you has a psalm,” etc. The meaning is: Whoever has a psalm of praise should speak praise; whoever has a teaching of exhortation should give exhortation; whoever has an apocalypse should give a revelation; and likewise the one who has a tongue and the one who has an interpretation. Let each person speak the grace he has received, but always for the edification of each person. Hence he says: “Let everything be done for edification.”

But because he counts the grace of tongues among the variety of gifts, and had seen them inclined toward this gift [Note: I judge that one should read: “inclined toward this gift.”] and judging it greater than the others, he did not wish to prohibit them from it entirely, lest they should become worse when provoked, thinking that he wished to restrain them out of envy.

Accommodating himself to them, he allowed them to speak in tongues, saying: “If anyone speaks in a tongue.” And note how temperately he speaks: “By two,” he says, “or at most three, and not at the same time, but in turn.”

He did not allow everyone to speak, so that they might not give unbelievers an occasion for reproach. Nor did he allow even three to speak at once; rather, while one was speaking, another was to remain silent, lest they occupy the entire day and leave no opportunity for speech directed toward edification.

And note that he grants this permission only on condition that someone interpret; otherwise, the speaker should speak to himself and to God alone.

Note also that he establishes a fixed number for prophets in the same way: “Let two or three prophets speak.”

[Note: In the autograph margin, “chapter 63” is written here.]

Why not all of them? Clearly, so that the others might question them. This is what he adds: “Let the others judge”—that is, if something hidden or contrary should appear, let them ask about it.

It follows: “But if something is revealed to another,” etc. He is introducing to the Gentiles among whom he was speaking the rite and custom of the synagogue.

The custom of the synagogue was that when they gathered together, the elders sat in chairs, the younger men on stools, and the least important on the floor.

[Note: “Place above,” which is incorrectly written after “floor” in the autograph, should rightly be deleted, unless we prefer to read “upon the walls,” as in Acts 20:9.]

He shows this when he says: “But if something is revealed to another,” etc. He urges the first speaker to be silent, because just as he himself cannot comprehend everything, so the other person is not excluded from everything.

And because God often reveals to the younger what he does not reveal to the older, he continues: “For you can all prophesy one by one,” as though he were saying: You all possess the grace of prophecy.

“And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets.” He rightly says “subject,” because the Holy Spirit fills everyone in such a way that all are subject to one another. For example, he fills you so that through humility you are subject to that person, and fills that person so that he is subject to you.

This sentence also refers to what he said above: “If something is revealed to the younger,” etc. Therefore he immediately adds: “For God is not a God of dissension but of peace.” He is not a God of dissension because there is no dissension in prophecy, as there is in the variety of tongues.

It follows: “As I teach in all the churches of the saints.” The apostle said this so that what he had written might be impressed more firmly upon their hearts, and so that, when they heard that he taught in other churches what he had written, they would be ashamed to be the only ones excluded from the common rule.

[Note: In the autograph margin, “chapter 64” is written here.]

Women should keep silent in the church. He returns to the intention with which he had begun. Above he had reproved the Corinthians because their men went about with long hair and their women went about without a veil. Then, after inserting certain intervening material, he returns to his original purpose in order to supply what was lacking, adding: “Women should keep silent in the church.”

So too the Law says, where we read: “You shall be under your husband’s power, and he shall rule over you” (Genesis 3:16)—either because she was the author of the first transgression or because she was formed from the man’s rib. Hence Sarah, speaking to Abraham, calls him “lord.”

But a question arises: Why does he say that women should keep silent in the church, when elsewhere he teaches them to perform the work of piety in the same instruction? The answer is this: He prohibited it in the churches but allowed it elsewhere. This is what he says: “Let them ask their husbands at home.” It would be superfluous to prohibit them in the churches unless he had permitted it elsewhere.

“For it is shameful for a woman in the church,” etc.—not only for women but also for men. And if they are required to be subject to their husbands, much more should they be subject to priests.

Did the word of God proceed from you? etc. The Corinthians were puffed up, saying that their belief had benefited the apostles more than it had benefited themselves—just as if someone possessed a commodity despised by everyone, and the last buyer assigned it value as a gift.

He refers to this when he says: “Did it proceed from you?” etc., as though he were saying: You were not the only ones who believed through my preaching, and so forth.

This is connected with the earlier passage where we read: “As I teach in all the churches of the saints.” And lest his teaching be despised as though it came from an ordinary human being, he adds: “If anyone thinks that he is a prophet,” etc., as though he were saying: Do not despise my teaching as though it came from an ordinary man, but receive it as God’s, because the commandments belong to the Lord.

He also touches upon the false apostles, who taught not the Lord’s doctrine but their own. He terrifies them also by adding: “If anyone is ignorant, he will be ignored”—that is, rejected.

Therefore, brothers. After many corrections, he calls them “brothers” so that they may be encouraged.

“Be zealous to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues.” See how temperately he speaks. He urges them toward prophecy in such a way that he does not forbid speaking in tongues.

We are accustomed to say: Be zealous for good and prohibit evil. But the apostle had counted the variety of tongues among the other gifts above, and they thought this gift greater than the others. He did not wish to prohibit them, lest they, being provoked, think that he wanted to restrain them out of envy.

Therefore he says this as though he were saying: I urge you toward greater things in such a way that I do not oppose the lesser.

But let all things be done decently and in order, etc. Decently, as he himself taught; in order, as he himself did.

And if we see someone doing anything in the church, we may apply this principle: “Let all things be done decently,” etc. For this order must be observed not only in matters pertaining to God but also in matters that seem to belong to human custom.

[Note: In the autograph margin, “chapter 65” is written here.]

## Chapter XV

It follows: “I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel,” etc. After instructing the Corinthians in conduct and life, he also rebukes their corrupt practices; in this purpose he continues here.

Above, not long before, he rebuked them because their women went about without veils, prayed to God without veils, and spoke freely in the church; and because, when they gathered together, they contentiously partook of the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood. He continues in this same purpose.

There was also among them this corrupt tradition: Some of them believed that Christ had risen but doubted the resurrection of others. The false apostles, however, denied that Christ had risen because they also did not believe that he had been born.

[Note: We have added *non*—“not”—from what is found below, column 399, near the beginning, where it says: “The false apostles … denied that he had been born.”]

Therefore the apostle’s purpose concerns the exposition of the commandment, and he argues against those who denied the resurrection both of Christ and of others, especially against those who believed that Christ had risen but nevertheless doubted the resurrection of others.

He is a good teacher, who is not afraid to repeat to his disciples what he had taught them. Such generosity is found only in accomplished teachers. Imperfect and bad teachers, by contrast, are ashamed when they recall what they have done or taught.

Note that he speaks indiscriminately: some things apply to those who had departed, and some to those who remained in the faith. When he says, “I make known,” this applies to those who had departed; when he says, “in which you stand,” it applies to those who had remained in the faith.

But lest they excuse themselves as though they had not received the teaching because he had preached it, he adds: “Which you also received.” And lest they appear to have rejected what they had received, he adds: “In which you also stand.” He further adds: “By which also you are saved”—that is, by which you believe that you attain salvation.

It follows: “In what manner I preached to you,” etc. The meaning is: I preached these things to you so that you might believe in the resurrection of all. If you hold fast to them, you did not believe in vain; but if you do not retain them, then, I say, you believed in vain.

Here he shows that the fruit of salvation is contained above all in faith in the resurrection.

It follows: “For I delivered to you first of all,” etc. What he says, “first of all,” can be understood in two ways: either he delivered first what he himself had received first, or he delivered what he had received first—not first in sequence, but in whatever order he chose.

When he says, “I received,” this should be understood either as reception through revelation, through prophecy, or through the Law.

He shows what this was: “That Christ died,” etc. When he says, “for our sins,” he shows that death had no relation to any fault of his own, but that he died for the sake of our redemption.

He says “according to the Scriptures” to show the harmony of the New and Old Testaments. Here he did not wish to confirm his account with examples, because he was eager to move on to the manifestation of the resurrection of others, especially since they did not hesitate concerning Christ’s resurrection.

Nevertheless, Isaiah had foretold his death: “Like a sheep he will be led to the slaughter” (Isaiah 53:7), etc.; and again: “He was wounded because of our iniquities” (ibid., 53:5), etc. He also foretold his burial: “He will give the wicked for his burial” (ibid., 53:9), etc.; and again: “His tomb will be glorious” (Isaiah 11:10). Concerning the resurrection, Hosea says: “On the third day he will raise us up” (Hosea 6:3), etc.

It follows: “And that he was seen by Cephas.” Note that he does not say “first,” lest he appear to contradict the evangelists.

It follows: “And afterward by the eleven,” when Thomas was absent (John 20:24).

It follows: “Then by more than five hundred brothers.” It should be noted that this appearance is not recorded in the Gospels. The evangelists likewise relate only ten occasions on which he appeared; from this it is plainly shown that he appeared many more times than the evangelists mention.

They therefore took care to describe only those appearances which they judged sufficient for instruction and the salvation of all.

When he says “at one time,” it is not sufficiently clear whether he means the eleven or twenty individually.

It follows: “Of whom many remain,” as though he had said: They can, when questioned, establish the truth.

Then he was seen by James. This was not the appearance in which he had been seen with the others, but a singular appearance. He wished to show himself by many proofs: individually to Peter, now to James, now also to the women, and afterward to all the disciples and to the others, so that the more manifest his resurrection became, the less doubt would remain in the hearts of believers.

Then by all the apostles. Perhaps above he had spoken of the eleven apostles; here he wishes the seventy to be understood, since they too were sent.

It follows: “And last of all,” etc. Since he says “last,” all the other appearances must be believed to have occurred before this one, whether before or after the ascension.

He says “last,” because Paul believed after all the others, and because Christ was by then presiding not on earth but in heaven.

We call that an abortion which is born outside its proper time. The apostle calls himself an abortion because he did not believe in the Lord’s presence, or perhaps because the synagogue gave birth to him imperfectly—that is, as one dead—or because the Church had despaired of his conversion.

It follows: “He appeared to me on the road” (Acts 9:3); he appeared in the Temple.

It follows: “For I am the least of the apostles”—not in merit, I say, nor in works, nor in grace, but in time.

“Who am not worthy to be called an apostle.” Why? “Because I persecuted the Church of God.”

Note that, although after baptism he had committed nothing for which he needed to grieve, he was already grieving over what he had committed before baptism.

He remembered, I say, the Lord’s saying through the prophet:

[Note: Isaiah 43:25–26. The Vulgate has: “Recall me to memory.”]

“I, I am he who blots out your sins like a cloud, and I will remember your sins no more” (Isaiah 43:25); “but you, remember.”

Here one should carefully observe how much we ought to grieve over the sins we have committed after baptism. For it is better to grieve over the sins committed before baptism than to consign the sins committed after baptism to forgetfulness. The former is a great good, whereas the latter is a great evil.

The apostle did this because he remembered the Lord’s saying: “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Matthew 23:12; Luke 14:11). And it was fitting that the one who cast himself down should be exalted.

[Col. 0398A] It follows: “By the grace of God I am what I am”; as though he were saying: “There are many merits, but they are evil ones”; and because good was repaid to him in place of evil, he says: “By the grace of God I am what I am”—that is, the fact that I am faithful, an apostle, and a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth is not due to my merit but to divine grace. By these words he condemns and restrains the rashness of those who boast of their free will. Yet, lest he who is commended for divine grace should appear alien to free will, he says: “And his grace toward me was not empty,” or “without effect.” Why was it not empty? Because I joined my willing to the grace that preceded me [Note: [Col. 0397D] This sentence should be noted.]. He added words belonging to the same meaning: “But I labored more than all of them.” For in saying “more,” he shows that a greater opportunity for laboring was given to him [Col. 0398B] than to the other apostles, since he received the office of apostleship among the Gentiles. The other apostles, who had received the office of apostleship among the circumcised, found that the Jews possessed knowledge of the law and the prophets and knew that there is one God. They could therefore more easily impress upon their hearts that God has a Son who, sent by the Father, assumed flesh and, by suffering, redeemed the human race, and that the Holy Spirit also exists. To him, however, the first necessity fell: to destroy idols; then to demonstrate that there is one God, creator of all things; next, that he has a Son who, also sent by the Father, assumed flesh and, by suffering, redeemed the human race; and that the Holy Spirit also exists: three names and three persons, yet one God. And therefore he “labored more than all.” [Col. 0398C] So that he would not appear to ascribe this to himself, he immediately added: “Yet not I.” When he says “not I,” he does not show that he did not labor, but that he could not labor without grace. Hence he immediately added: “But the grace of God with me.” By these words he shows [Note: [Col. 0398D] Here is the judgment of Saint Augustine concerning grace and free will.] that neither grace without free will nor free will without grace effects the salvation of a human being. Nevertheless, grace does operate without free will by preceding it, just as it called this man from heaven.

It follows: “Whether, then, it was I or they, and so forth.” Of whom is he speaking? Of those, clearly, whom he had said labored more than he did. By these words he shows that his authority in preaching was not lesser: “So we preach,” he says, “that you might believe, I say, in the resurrection of all.” “Whether it was I or they”—he says this so that they might be ashamed to be alien from the universal teaching and faith of all.

It follows: “But if Christ is preached among you as having risen from the dead, and so forth.” With an outstanding argument he concludes against them that they must either deny both propositions—that is, if they believe that Christ rose, they must also believe in the resurrection of others; and if they deny the resurrection of others, they must deny Christ’s as well. For the Apostle confirms one from the other. This syllogism is not one of the dialecticians but of the rhetoricians, and it is called imperfect because [Col. 0399A] it consists of a proposition, an assumption, and a conclusion. A perfect syllogism consists of a proposition and a conclusion; for example, if you say: “Is every virtue useful?” and answer, “Useful”; and then assume: “Is chastity useful?” and answer, “Useful”; and after this conclude: “Therefore chastity is also a virtue.” The Apostle likewise proposed and concluded, as though he had said: “Did Christ rise?” If they answered, “He rose,” he himself would conclude: “The others will also rise.” And again: “Will the others not rise?” If they answered, “No,” he would conclude: “Neither, then, did Christ rise.”

For the false apostles denied that Christ had risen, because they also denied that he had been born. In order not to be despised by lovers of human wisdom, who judged it foolish that God had become human and suffered, they deceived the simple and made them members of their party. John says of such people: “Whoever does not confess that Christ has come in the flesh, he is the antichrist” (I John IV, 3). And again: “Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father either” (I John II, 23). Although these men had deceived some and made them members of their party, there were nevertheless certain among them who believed that Christ had risen but doubted the resurrection of others. Of them he says: “How do some”—not all, but many were nevertheless deceived by this error.

It follows: “But if Christ has not risen” (with “nor have the others” understood), “then our preaching is empty,” and so forth. For he is arguing against them. Who would willingly hear that he was denying and judging useless what he had previously believed and approved as good? [Col. 0399C] And therefore he says: “Your faith is empty,” so that, when they heard this, they might be confounded and return to their former faith. This is also what he addresses below when he says: “You are still in your sins.” For who would willingly hear that he remains in sins whose forgiveness he had believed he had obtained? And for this reason he said: “You are still in your sins,” so that they might not endure it and, confounded, return to their former faith.

Therefore he says: “We are also found to be false witnesses of God,” and so forth. He does not say “enemies,” because an enemy is one who holds an opposing view or says less than the truth. These men could be false witnesses, because they had said great things about God if what they were saying were true; it is as though he were saying in other words: “We are indeed false, because he himself is also false: he promised that he would rise on the third day and grant you forgiveness through the water of baptism—if things are as you say, namely, that you are still in your sins.”

It follows: “Therefore those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished.” He says this so that, just as they could not endure hearing that they were denying what they had previously believed and were still in the sins whose forgiveness they hoped they had obtained, so they might not endure hearing that the hope of their dear ones had been frustrated. By “those who have fallen asleep” he means two kinds of people: either those who passed from this life in that hope, or those who, in that hope, handed over their bodies to martyrdom.

It follows: “If in this life only we have hoped in Christ,” and so forth. The meaning is: “We do not hope only in this life, but rather in the future one, because Christ saves his own in this life as well and rewards them happily after it. For if we had hope only in this life, we would be more pitiable than all human beings, since at least the pagans enjoy their pleasures here. But what benefit would fasting, prayer, vigils, or a chaste life be to us?” Pagans commonly say to us: “You who believe in Christ, what more do you have? You do not abound more in the goods of this life.” But we have more, I say, because we believe that a future life exists, incomparably better than this one.

After reproaching them for their confession, he undertook to manifest the resurrection. For he says: “But now Christ has risen, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,” because he himself was the first to pass over into immortality; for although others rose before him, they returned [Col. 0400B] to corruption.

Note that he attributes both death and resurrection to a human being, but not resurrection through the same person through whom death came: he is referring to the first and the second Adam. The first Adam found death through his sin; the second Adam, that is, Christ, found resurrection through his righteousness. He shows who these two were when he adds: “As in Adam all die.” Because Adam incurred death by sinning, all who descend from him incur death, both of soul and of body. But when he says: “So also in Christ all will be made alive,” lest this seem contradictory because not everyone is made alive, it should be understood in this way: all who are made alive are made alive in Christ.

[Col. 0400C] Having clearly established the resurrection, and wishing to demonstrate its order, he adds: “Each in his own order.” This order will be given not to the wicked but to those made alive in Christ. “Christ the firstfruits,” as above. It follows: “Then those who are Christ’s”—that is, those who believed at his coming (with “will rise” understood). When he says: “Then the end,” he shows that both the resurrection and the judgment of the wicked will belong to this life. The end will not be an ending but a completion.

It follows: “When he has handed over the kingdom to God” (because he is human), “and to the Father” (because he is the Son). But this expression, “he has handed over,” scandalized many who understood it less accurately; they said that, when he handed it over, he would cease to reign. If this is so, then the Father also ceased to reign, because he handed everything over to the Son, as he himself says: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father” (Matthew XI, 27). But who does not recognize how foolish it is to say this? Therefore the Father handed it over and did not lose it, because he possesses it together with the Son; the Son will hand it over and will not lose it.

What, then, does “hand over” mean? I say: to manifest it—so that the one who previously reigned in his own people through faith may reign through open manifestation, and those who previously saw him through a mirror and in an enigma may then see him face to face.

It follows: “When he has abolished every principality,” and so forth. He will abolish principality, and so forth, because he will show that there is one prince and king, and that every principality, whether in heaven or on earth, comes from him; and that trust must be placed not in those powers but in him alone. [Col. 0401A] [Note: [Col. 0401D] In the autograph, *confitendum* is read. See, reader, which is more correct.]

Some have understood in this passage the aerial powers that he will abolish, because he will condemn the devil with all his satellites, saying: “Go, accursed ones,” and so forth. These will no longer have the power to rule over human beings, subject them to their own forces, or exercise their powers, because they will have no opportunity to advance or wander anywhere; rather, there will be one city for all.

It follows: “But he must reign,” that is, it is fitting and expedient, “until he places all his enemies under his feet” (Psalm CIX, 1). This means either that he will subject those who are his enemies to the faith, so that, converted, they become friends—that is, that all who are predestined may be converted—or certainly that he will punish all who oppose the faith.

It must be understood that “until” should not be taken as indicating an end. [Col. 0401B] [Note: [Col. 0401D] That is, not as a temporal limit, but as “always”: the subjection of the enemies will not bring Christ’s rule to an end, but rather increase it.] It is also commonly taken as expressing conjunction, as in: “As the eyes of a maidservant” [Note: [Col. 0402D] Psalm CXXII, 2: “As the eyes of a maidservant are toward the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us.”]. It can also be taken here as expressing conjunction.

It follows: “But the last enemy, death, will be destroyed.” He is referring to the order of the resurrection; or, as some say, the devil is called “death”: “Death will be destroyed,” that is, the author of death will be punished. Hence the statement: “Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire” (Revelation XX, 14).

“He has subjected all things under his feet.” He has subjected all things, I say, as he himself says: “All authority has been given to me” (Matthew XXVIII, 18), and so forth; and the Apostle says: “At the name of Jesus every knee should bow” (Philippians II, 10), and so forth.

Nevertheless, it must be understood that there is one subjection of creatures and another of the Church: the former by sensing the Creator’s dominion; the latter by enjoying the grace of its Redeemer and adhering as members to the same head.

It follows: “When he says, ‘All things have been subjected to him,’” and so forth, until he says: “Then the Son himself will also be subject to him who subjected all things to him.” Here Arius pricks up his ears and says that the Son is rightly called less than the Father, since the Apostle also says that he will be subject.

But whoever is not scandalized by this statement knows that subjection is not always used to indicate inferiority, but sometimes also love. The same Apostle says: “The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets” (I Corinthians XIV, 32). Is this because of inferiority? No, but because of love. Even the one who is incomparably greater than all is said to have been subject to his parents (Luke II, 51)—not, I say, because of inferiority, but because of love.

So, too, the Son is subject to the Father in love, on account of unity, because their power is one and their essence is one, and so forth. But because the Father is from no one, while the Son is from the Father—God from God and light from light—for this reason he is said to be subject to him.

Others say that, just as he is said to hunger, thirst, and suffer together with his members, so he is also said to be subject in those same members. The Church is indeed subject to God, but not completely; and because the members and the head are one body, when all the members have been subjected, the Son also is subject to the Father in those members.

Others [Col. 0402A] say that, just as he is called less than the Father according to his humanity, so he is called subject according to that same humanity. For neither has divinity been changed into humanity, nor humanity into divinity; rather, humanity was assumed by divinity, because that humanity will always remain. Therefore he says: “Then the Son will be subject to the Father on account of the humanity assumed.” But because he sits at his right hand (Acts VII, 55; Romans VIII, 34; Colossians III, 1), he must not be believed to be less than him.

It follows: “So that God may be all in all.” That is, insofar as fellowship, blessedness, immortality, and everything else are concerned, he will be in all—that is, he will be everything to all. For he himself will be wholly the food, the drink, complete satisfaction, and whatever can be said to pertain to blessedness: he himself will be all of it.

The Apostle had begun to speak about the resurrection, and, continuing in the intention with which he had begun, says: “Otherwise, what will those do who are baptized for the dead?” By these words he most openly and most certainly demonstrates the resurrection of the dead.

Some were so certain of the resurrection that, if death had overtaken someone dear to them before he was baptized, they themselves, fearing that he might not rise or might rise badly, would be baptized on his behalf. And therefore he says: “What will they do?”—as though he were saying: “If things are so, their hope is frustrated.” Hence also in what follows he says that they are baptized for them.

It should certainly be noted that by this example he did not approve their action, but demonstrated the certainty of the resurrection. In another sense, “for the dead” may be understood as referring to their bodies. [Col. 0402C]

It follows: “Why are we also in danger every hour?” As though he were saying: “If the dead do not rise, why are we daily in danger?” That is, why do we suffer various trials, persecutions, and adversities?

But note that he does not say “Why are we,” but “Why are we also.” This particle, separating himself and his followers from those others, shows that those who were baptized for the dead were not Catholics and were not acting religiously.

It should be known that the Apostle was very concerned for the progress and salvation of the Corinthians; therefore he says: “I die daily, by your glory.” Pelagius says that “by” is not always used in an oath; for when we say, “I sent by the boy,” and similar expressions, it is not an oath.

Augustine, however, says that the particle used by the Greeks in this passage is employed in an oath, so that the meaning is: “I testify and swear by your glory.” Therefore it must be asked why the Apostle so frequently swears in this passage and in others, when the Lord says that one must not swear.

But because the Lord prohibits it while the Apostle swears, it is shown that an oath is not evil. Nevertheless, no one ought to use it, lest through its frequent use he fall into perjury. The Lord himself makes this clear when he does not say that what is beyond this is evil, but that it is “from evil” (Matthew V, 37).

[Col. 0403A] It follows: “Which I have in Christ Jesus.” It is as though he were saying: “I am indeed concerned for your salvation; but whether you wish to be perfected or not, I nevertheless have the reward of my labor, a glory stored up in Christ Jesus.”

It follows: “If, according to human judgment, I fought with beasts at Ephesus,” and so forth. He calls bestial human beings “beasts”: when they understood that the temple of Diana was to be overthrown through the Apostle’s preaching, they stirred up a popular revolt against him. Or he calls “beasts” those of whom the Psalmist says: “Do not hand over the souls of those who confess you to the beasts” (Psalm LXXIII, 19). He calls demons “beasts.” The soul has no beasts more savage than these. For whether you understand one group or the other, you will fight against both.

For what is surprising if he calls savage human beings “beasts,” when he himself calls Nero a lion? “The Lord,” he says, “rescued me from the lion’s mouth” (II Timothy IV, 17)—that is, from Nero’s, since he had been handed over to him twice.

What he says, “according to human judgment,” should be understood as meaning according to human sense and estimation.

It follows: “Let us eat and drink,” and so forth. This is read in Isaiah (Isaiah XXII, 13). The prophet speaks these words against the Epicureans, who denied the resurrection. [Note: [Col. 0403D] The opinion of the Epicureans could already have existed, although Epicurus, its founder, did not enter the world until several centuries after Isaiah.]

For Epicurus said: “When I have died, I shall no longer exist.” He also said that the highest good is for human beings to satisfy their desires; for this reason he was even called a pig.

The false apostles likewise, although they believed in Christ’s resurrection, denied that of the others. And therefore, taking up their voice, he says: “Let us eat and drink,” and so forth—as though he were saying: “If there is no resurrection of the dead, then, while we live, let us satisfy our desires.”

And lest they be deceived by their teachings, he adds: “Do not be led astray.” But because they could have said, “Do you judge us so insignificant that you think we can be deceived?” he himself added: “Bad conversations corrupt good morals.” By these words he shows that the companionship of wicked people often dissipates holy and upright morals. For this reason such companionships must be avoided, especially at the beginning of faith, of any religious commitment, and of good works, because these gifts are tender, like young trees, and like a wall not yet dried of its moisture: they can easily be overturned.

It follows: “Awake justly” [Note: [Col. 0404D] The Vulgate reads “Awake, you just.”]. He teaches wakefulness not so much of the body as of the mind. [Col. 0403D] He urges us to strive always to keep the eyes of the mind open, in order to avoid the snares of demons.

In certain copies one finds: “Awake, you just, and be sober,” and so forth. But whether *justly* or *you just* is read, attention must be paid to what kind of justice he commends—whether divine or human.

Human justice also consists in not taking what belongs to another. This justice, just as it does not condemn, so also does not justify. Therefore the Apostle commends not this justice but divine justice, by which alone human beings are justified. That, I say, is divine justice which not only does not seize what belongs to another but rather gives away what belongs to itself.

Note that he not only urged them to keep watch justly, but also urged them not to sin. For he says: “Do not sin.” Human beings sin in two ways: by committing what is forbidden and by failing to fulfill what is commanded. Because the Corinthians were sinning in these ways, he admonishes them by saying: “Do not sin.”

It follows: “For some have ignorance of God.” This refers to what he said shortly before: “Let us eat and drink,” and so forth. The false apostles also have ignorance of God, because, having lost faith in the resurrection, they believed that nothing exists after this life.

It follows: “I speak this to your shame” [Note: [Col. 0404D] The Vulgate reads “to your reverence.”]. Since they had given their faith [Col. 0404B] to those who had ignorance of God, he therefore says: “I speak this to your shame,” and so forth, so that, when they heard it, they might be ashamed and, confounded, return to their former faith.

The Apostle therefore took up the voice of those whom he had said possessed ignorance of God and said: “But someone will say: How are the dead raised?” and so forth. For those who deny the resurrection commonly ask this.

It follows: “Fool, what you sow,” and so forth. He rightly calls the one who denies the resurrection a fool, because nothing is more foolish than to deny that the one who created all things from nothing can raise the bodies of the dead from the dust of the earth.

It should be noted that he does not use legal or prophetic examples against them, since they were fools, but examples from insensible and irrational creatures. “What you sow,” and so forth—as though he were saying: “Just as what you sow first dies and afterward is made alive, so also does the human being.”

It follows: “And what you sow, you do not sow the body that is to be,” and so forth. The meaning is: “Just as you sow not a body but a bare grain, and afterward it rises with a body—that is, multiplied—so also a bare body is placed in the tomb, and afterward it will rise with increase, not in number but in improvement.”

It follows: “God gives it a body as he wills,” and so forth. In saying “as he wills,” whether with reference to each kind of seed or to the fact that he willed it, he shows that no other things arise from the earth than those that God created in the beginning. Similarly, no other bodies will rise than those that are placed in the tombs. Job clearly shows this when he says: [Col. 0404D] “Again I shall be clothed with my skin” (Job XIX, 26), and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0404D] In the margin it reads: “The eleventh Sunday after Pentecost.”]

It follows: “Not every flesh is the same flesh,” and so forth. It is as though he were saying: “What is surprising if God raises the bodies of the dead from the dust of the earth, when from one mass and substance he created and fashioned different kinds of things?”

At this point the philosophers of the pagans should be reproved, since they say that they can fully comprehend the number of the stars of heaven, the grains of sand in the sea, and the drops of water. Here they have been admonished to comprehend themselves, if they can; and if they can comprehend themselves, then let them turn to other matters. Because these people were unwilling humbly to submit themselves to divine wisdom, they did not deserve to arrive at the pursuit of true knowledge.

Through the variety of bodies, the various merits of those who rise are also signified. For just as God created different kinds of animals from one mass and substance, so he will raise human beings of one nature; nevertheless, they will not all be equal in merit.

What is surprising if variety is found among different natures, when within one and the same human nature there is great variety, to such an extent that each person is recognized by his own face?

It follows: “There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies.” He had indeed given an example from earthly things; he now gives one [Col. 0405B] from heavenly things also. Clearly, by heavenly things he wishes the bodies of those who rise to be understood, and by earthly things, those who die.

And therefore he says: “There is one glory of the heavenly,” and so forth. The heavenly bodies are the sun, the moon, and the stars. Hence he immediately continues by saying: “There is one brightness of the sun,” and so forth.

Through the variety of these bodies, the variety of the resurrection is likewise signified. For just as the brightness of the sun is greater than that of the moon and the stars, so the merits of those who rise will also differ. And therefore he says: “As star differs from star.”

It should nevertheless be noted: who will bring about this truth? Is it vices? No, virtues, because vices cannot possess that kingdom.

It follows: “It is sown in corruption,” because the body is buried for the purpose of being corrupted; “it will rise in incorruption,” because it will be restored incorruptible.

It follows: “It is sown in dishonor,” because nothing is more dishonorable than to swarm with worms, to be placed in the earth, and similar things; “it will rise in glory,” because it will pass over into immortality.

It follows: “It is sown in weakness,” because nothing is weaker than to lack all the senses, so that, even if it is moved, it does not feel; “it will rise in power,” because it will be raised by the power of God.

It follows: “It is sown an animal body.” Understand “animal” as “animated”; for we must not understand an animal body to mean the soul itself, just as a spiritual body does not mean the spirit itself.

If a spiritual body were understood to be the spirit, the Lord would not say to his disciples: “Touch and see” (Luke XXIV, 39), and so forth. Therefore an animal body is mortal, and a spiritual body immortal.

[Col. 0405D] The words of the book of Genesis explain this passage, where it says: “The Lord breathed into the face of the human being the breath of life,” and so forth. In the phrase “into a living soul” [Note: [Col. 0405D] Genesis II, 7; the Vulgate reads “into a living soul.”] he says that the human being became animal—that is, he was created mortal in such a way that he could die if he wished.

If he had not sinned, he would eventually have passed over to the glory of the angels without the corruption of bodily death. But because he himself was made mortal, by sinning he begot all those whom he begot as mortals. We all possess both animal and mortal bodies.

The Lord Jesus likewise came to us in such a body. He could have come in a heavenly body if he had wished; but because we were to be redeemed through his suffering, he deigned to come to us in a mortal body. After completing that suffering, he carried it over into immortality on the third day.

It follows: “If there is an animal body,” that is, a mortal body, “there is also a spiritual body,” that is, an immortal body. For just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ.

It follows: “As it is written: ‘The first human being, Adam, was made a living soul’” (Genesis II, 7), and so forth. Here it should be observed that the Lord Jesus humbled himself so greatly that he not only took on the frailty of our flesh but also deigned to be called a human being.

It follows: “But the spiritual was not first,” and so forth. The animal, that is, the mortal, comes first, because it dies first and afterward rises.

Shortly before he had mentioned two human beings, namely, the first Adam and the second. To distinguish their merits, he adds: “The first human being was from the earth, earthly,” clearly because he had been created from the dust of the earth; “the second human being was from heaven, heavenly,” namely because he was conceived and born not from the union of male and female but from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.

It should nevertheless be known that there were some who said that he had not taken true flesh from Mary and had not possessed a true human body [Note: [Col. 0405D] The disciples of Apollinaris, specifically, and others.], because the Apostle calls him heavenly.

Let them therefore hear what the same Apostle says: “As is the heavenly one, so also are the heavenly ones.” He calls those heavenly who imitate him, and there is no doubt that they are human beings. Therefore, if these become heavenly by imitating him, it is not contradictory for him also to be called heavenly, since he was conceived and born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.

It follows: “As is the earthly one, so also are the earthly ones,” because the corruptible begot corruptible, the mortal mortals, and the sinner sinners.

It follows: “As is the heavenly one, so also are the heavenly ones,” because, just as he was conceived and born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, so human beings also become spiritual and heavenly through the grace of that same Spirit and through the water of baptism.

Hence the same Apostle says: “As many of you as were baptized in Christ” (Galatians III, 27; Romans VI, 3), and so forth.

It follows: “Therefore, just as we have borne the image of the earthly,” and so forth. What does this mean? He is urging us that, just as we were imitators of the first Adam by dying, so we should strive to be imitators of the second by rising.

It should be noted, however, that everyone is said to bear the image of whatever he worships. Therefore we bear not only the image of the first human being by dying [Note: [Col. 0406D] The autograph reads “by rising again.”], or that of the second by rising, but also in our conduct.

Therefore those who are stained by impurity, raised up in the arrogance of pride, or corrupted by the plague of other vices bear the image of the first human being. Those, however, who strive to preserve purity of mind and body, humility, patience, and the other virtues of piety do not cease to bear the image of the second human being.

It follows: “Now this I say, brothers,” and so forth. Here also it must be asked why he says that flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God, since he had taught the resurrection of bodies above and confirmed it with various comparisons. He seems to contradict himself.

But he does not. If this appears contradictory to anyone, let him know that in the divine Scriptures one and the same word commonly has several meanings, as does “temptation” and many other words.

“Flesh” likewise is used in the same Scriptures in various ways. It is used for sin, as in: “The flesh desires against the spirit” (Galatians V, 17), and so forth; and for mortality, as in: “He remembered that they were flesh” [Note: [Col. 0407D] Psalm LXXVII, 39; the Vulgate reads “he remembered.”], and so forth.

It is also used for the truth of nature, as in: “All flesh will see the salvation of God” (Isaiah XL, 5; Luke III, 6). So in this passage “flesh” signifies corruption. Flesh will therefore possess the kingdom of God according to the truth of nature, but it will not possess it according to sin and corruption.

No one need labor over this passage, because the Apostle himself explains it when he adds: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption.”

It follows: “Behold, I tell you a mystery.” “Mystery” is a Greek word; in Latin it is called “hidden” or “unseen.” Behold, he promises to speak a mystery, and perhaps this is what follows: “We will all rise,” and so forth.

By these words he shows that there will be a resurrection of both the good and the wicked, but that only the righteous will be changed.

It follows: “In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye.” A moment is named from the movement of the stars; it is the briefest part of an hour.

By these words he also demonstrated the resurrection to be most certain and most swift. For he could not have shown it to be more rapid by other words than by saying that it would occur so quickly, like the movement of the eyelids, and in a moment.

When he says “at the last trumpet,” and “for the trumpet will sound,” this should not be understood to mean that the bodily author of the resurrection himself emits a bodily voice, or that the angel who will be the minister of the resurrection blows a bodily trumpet. Rather, a voice should be understood such as can be emitted by such a creature—that is, by a spiritual one—which all the dead will hear and rise.

Therefore he adds: “And the dead will rise incorruptible.” Distinguishing the good from the wicked, he also says: “And we will be changed.”

It follows: “This mortal body must put on immortality,” and so forth. “Must” means that it is fitting and expedient that what he promised should be fulfilled.

[Col. 0407D] “When this mortal body has put on immortality,” until the words, “Death has been swallowed up in victory.” This is found written in Hosea according to the ancient translation of the Seventy interpreters (Hosea XIII, 14).

The Apostle should be believed to have placed this testimony here, as in other passages, according to the truth of the Hebrew library, although Jerome, having learned the Hebrew language completely, does not find it in his translation.

Therefore, lest this appear contradictory, it must be believed that he placed this testimony according to the translation of the Seventy interpreters, which had already become famous throughout the whole world, so that he might not perhaps scandalize his hearers.

It should be understood that this expression, “Death has been swallowed up,” will belong to the triumphant. When they have conquered death and passed over into immortality, they will say mockingly: “Where is your victory, O death?” It has been emptied, because you, who were conquering in those who were dying, are now conquered in those who are rising.

“Where also is your victory,” by which you possessed the whole human race, so much so that even the Son of God, when he came, contended with you and overcame you, not by avoiding you but rather by taking you upon himself?

It follows: “Where is your sting,” or “goad,” by which you wounded the whole human race and possessed it in its poisoned state? Your victory was temporary; ours, however, is eternal.

He brought forth the voice of the triumphant and explained it when he added: “The sting of death is sin.” Sin is not called the sting of death because death made sin, but because sin begot death. Thus one speaks of the tree of life or of knowledge, not because it made life or knowledge, but because through it both can be preserved. The cup of life is spoken of in the same way.

It follows: “The power of sin is the law,” because whatever is forbidden by the law is possessed with greater delight.

Having uttered and explained the voice of the triumphant, he urges them to give thanks to God, because they conquered death not by their own strength but with the help of divine grace. He says “through Jesus Christ” [Col. 0408C] because every victory consists in him. For he was the first to conquer death and granted his own an example of conquering it.

Therefore, my beloved brothers: After many corrections, he calls them not only brothers but also beloved, so that, at least lifted up by this remedy, they might return to their former faith.

It follows: “Stand firm, immovable” [Note: [Col. 0407D] In some copies of the Vulgate: “Stand firm and immovable”; in others it reads “Stand firm, immovable,” without the conjunction “and”; in our autograph it read: “Stand firm, because immovable.” We judged the particle “because” should be deleted, since it seemed to yield no meaning—unless the reader might prefer to read: “Stand firm, you who have now become movable,” that is, who had appeared less steadfast in the faith of the resurrection.].

And because it is not enough to be steadfast in faith, he added: “abounding.” Because a person can abound in evil things, he added: “in the work of the Lord.” And because it is not enough to abound in the work of the Lord for a time, he added: “always.”

It follows: “Knowing that your labor is not empty.” It is as though he were saying: “Just as I know that I too will receive the reward of my labor, so know that you will receive the reward of yours, because labor in the Lord cannot be empty.”

[Note: [Col. 0408D] In the autograph margin, “chapter LXVI” is written here.]

## (CHAPTER XVI)

It continues: “Now concerning the collections that are made for the saints,” etc. A collection is an assembling of various resources. “Collections” were called those things that were gathered on each Sabbath and sent to the poor who were in Jerusalem. Concerning these we also read in the Acts of the Apostles that they sold all their possessions and brought them [Col. 0409A] “to the feet of the apostles” (Acts 4:34–35), and they were distributed to each person according to his need. Once the proceeds had been exhausted, the poor had nothing more to sell or by which they could be supported. Therefore the holy apostles—especially Paul and Barnabas—decided that collections should be made in each region and sent to the saints who were in Jerusalem. Concerning these he says: “Now concerning the collections that are made,” that is, for the saints.

The primitive Church had also begun at Jerusalem; hence it is written: “From Zion the law shall go forth” (Micah 4:2; Isaiah 2:3), etc. But since the Gentiles had received the evangelical faith and knowledge of the holy Scriptures from that same teaching, it was fitting that they should make collections and support the need of those same poor people. Hence he says elsewhere: “If the Gentiles,” he says, “have become partakers of their spiritual things” [Col. 0409B] (Romans 15:27); and in this Epistle: “If we have sown spiritual things among you” (1 Corinthians 9:11), etc.

The arrangement of the churches of Galatia could have been beneficial to them for salvation; and therefore he says: “As I directed,” etc. But because it might have been less well known, he took care to make it clear. For he says: “On the first day of the week,” etc. By “the first day of the week” he means the first Sabbath, that is, the Lord’s Day; hence in the Gospel: “On the first day of the week” (Matthew 28:1; Mark 16:2; Luke 24:1; John 20:1). He also instructed that collections be made on the Lord’s Day, when they gathered for common exhortation and progress. It was fitting that on that day too they should assemble for the relief of the poor saints.

It may also be asked why he did not command collections to be made every day or at every time. The reason is that he knew more would be collected, and that it would be less burdensome, if it were done at intervals. It continues: “Let each one of you put something aside by himself,” that is, storing it away in the secret place of his treasury. And because a voluntary gift is certainly acceptable to God, he left the matter to their discretion, saying: “Whatever he considers suitable.”

It continues: “So that when I come, collections may not then be made.” There were also many things among them that needed correction; therefore he instructed them to collect the money beforehand, lest, while occupied with those matters that needed correction, he should be unable to correct them.

“When I am present,” etc. Note that he left it to their discretion that those whom they themselves approved should be sent by letter to Jerusalem to deliver the collections. Thus they would be pleasing in two ways: both through the assignment of the gifts [Col. 0409D] and through the commendation of the letters.

It continues: “And if it is worthwhile that I should go as well,” etc. The meaning is: If a great deal has been collected, it will be worthwhile for me to go also, since it is fitting for a bishop to carry much with him, so that the need of many may be supported.

“Those men will go with me,” he says, so that they might become happier when they heard that they were to travel with the bishop.

It continues: “I will come to you,” etc. It should be noted that he promises not merely his arrival but a prolonged stay. Why, then, does he promise a prolonged stay? So that, if they heard that he had passed near them but had not come to them, they might perhaps become resentful and indignant, and, scandalized, become worse. This is what he says: “I do not wish to see you now in passing,” lest he should appear to have turned aside to them merely because of his journey and not for the purpose of staying.

In another sense, when he says that he will pass through Macedonia and remain for a long time at Corinth, he secretly praises the former and reproves the latter, as if he were saying: “I will pass through Macedonia, because there is nothing of that sort among them requiring me to remain for the sake of correction. Among you there are many things that need correction; therefore I will stay, or at least spend the winter.”

It continues: “I hope to remain with you for some time,” etc. Observe how cautiously he promised them a prolonged presence. For he says: “If the Lord permits.” But why does he speak with such caution? Clearly, so that, if he came to them and remained for a long time, they would understand that it had happened by divine dispensation; but if he did not come, they would likewise understand that this too had happened by divine dispensation, and would attribute it not to the Apostle but to themselves. This caution is also commended to us.

It continues: “I will remain at Ephesus,” etc. Why? “For,” he says, “a door has been opened,” etc., as if he were saying: “Many hearts are burning and longing, and are prepared to receive the evangelical teaching.”

It continues: “But there are many adversaries.” For just as many were stirred by the grace of the Holy Spirit to believe, so many were stirred by the prompting of demons to persecute. He himself is the door, for he says: “I am the door” (John 10:7, 9), etc.; and again: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). What, then, does it mean to say, [Col. 0410C] “A door has been opened to me,” except to say in other words: “The bosom of divine mercy has been opened wide to receive believers”?

It continues: “If Timothy comes,” etc. He promised his own arrival, and he also promised Timothy’s. Timothy was not there, because he had been sent to other churches; nevertheless, he was going to come to Corinth. Since he was a bishop and a fellow worker of great merit, the Apostle was therefore extremely concerned for him, lest the pseudo-apostles or those who believed wrongly should prepare an ambush for him and he should fall into the snare of death.

It continues: “For he is doing the work of the Lord,” as if he were saying: “He is as worthy of honor as I am, and is my fellow apostle; therefore you ought to receive him honorably.”

It continues: “See that you send him on his way in peace,” etc., [Col. 0410D] as if he were saying: “The one whom I await together with all the brothers, and who possesses such authority, ought not merely to be received honorably, but ought to be escorted to me, so that he may come in peace.”

[Note: [Col. 0409D] In the autograph margin, “chapter LXVII” is written here.]

It continues: “Now concerning Apollos, brothers” [Note: [Col. 0410D] The Vulgate reads “brother.”], “I inform you,” etc. Through these words the Apostle shows that he wished to satisfy the requests of the Corinthians. He also reveals, though covertly, that they themselves had asked him to send Apollos to them, since he belonged to them. But by delaying his coming to them, the same Apostle shows that this did not depend on himself but rather on Apollos. Thus, when they heard why he had delayed coming to them, they would understand that he had heard of dissensions and scandals among them. Understanding this, they would correct their errors and change their conduct, and would receive Timothy honorably, so that, when he returned and reported good things about them, Apollos might take the opportunity to go to them.

[Note: [Col. 0411C] In the autograph margin, “chapter LXVIII” is written here.]

It continues: “Keep watch.” He teaches vigilance not so much of the body as of the mind.

It continues: “Stand firm in the faith.” This applies equally to those who had departed and to those who had remained in it.

It continues: “Act manfully.” In the holy Scriptures, men are also usually understood as the perfect, and women as the imperfect. Therefore he says “manfully,” not in the manner of women—weakly and softly.

“Be strengthened,” that is, in that faith, and strengthen one another by consoling each other. To this also belongs what follows: “Let everything you do be done in charity,” as if he had said: “Let no one seek only his own salvation, but that of all the brothers.”

[Note: [Col. 0411C] In the autograph margin, “chapter LXIX” is written here.]

It continues: “I appeal to you, brothers: you know the household of Stephanas and Fortunatus,” etc. These men are also called the firstfruits of Achaia, because they were the first from that region to believe. They also appointed themselves for the service of the saints, because, after supplying their own needs and those of their households, they decided to distribute whatever they could have to the poor.

When he says, “that you also may be subject to them,” he does not so much wish them to be subject to these men as to imitate them, so that they might have others subject to them.

It continues: “I rejoice at the presence of Stephanas,” etc. For by preaching and confirming them in the faith, these men supplied what was lacking in them.

It continues: “For they refreshed my spirit as well,” because they supplied whatever was necessary for me; “and yours,” because they did this on account of your charity.

It continues: “Therefore recognize those who are such,” that is, honor them and show them honor. By these words he shows that those who are more devoted in the Church—whether in order to teach or to give their possessions to the poor—are to be regarded as worthy of greater honor. Hence he says elsewhere: “Let the presbyters be considered worthy of double honor” (1 Timothy 5:17), etc.

[Col. 0412A] It continues: “All the churches of Asia greet you.” It is fitting that a particular church should receive a greeting from the universal Church. Having given a general greeting, he added a particular one.

It continues: “Aquila and Priscilla greet you warmly in the Lord,” etc. These two are to be understood as husband and wife. They were also closely associated with Paul; and because they were of great faith and great merit, he conveyed their greeting. He calls those who were sustained both by their teaching and by their provisions their domestic church.

It continues: “All the brothers greet you.” It is certainly fitting that a greeting should be sent from all the other brothers to all the others, that is, that salvation should be wished for them.

After all the greetings, he added his own, saying: [Col. 0412B] “The greeting of me, Paul, in my own hand.” He confirms it with his own hand when he adds: “If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ,” etc. By these words he strikes those who, divided by their love for men, were called some Petrine and others Pauline.

“Anathema” is a Hebrew word; it is interpreted as “destroyed” or “alien.” “Maran Atha,” however, is not so much Hebrew as Syriac. But because of the unity of the languages, it is possible that, if the expression is compounded from Hebrew and Syriac, it may be interpreted as “Our Lord comes.” The meaning would then be: “If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be anathema, Maran Atha”—that is, at his coming let him be destroyed and alienated from the fellowship of the righteous. For his coming, just as it will be the glorification of the good, will also be the condemnation of the wicked.

The Apostle does not say this as the wish of one who desires it, but rather as one who proclaims it by the Spirit.

It continues: “The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you.” The meaning is: “This is what I wish: that the grace by which you were created and by which you were also redeemed may be with you.”

It continues: “My charity be with all of you.” Paul’s charity also consisted in wishing the salvation of others as he wished his own [Note: [Col. 0412C] In the autograph margin, “chapter LXX” is written here.]. Therefore he adds, “in Christ Jesus,” as if he were saying: “Love one another with that charity with which I love you,” that is, so that you may desire not only your own salvation but the salvation of all.

“Amen” is a word of confirmation, by which he confirms everything stated above.

**It ends. Thanks be to God.**

# THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 0411]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0411D]

Those who are about to read the second Epistle of the blessed apostle Paul to the Corinthians must understand that we can penetrate his intention if we remember that we are pilgrims with him. [Note: [Col. 0411] In the autograph margin, “chapter LXXI” is written here, counting the chapters of this work together with those of the first Epistle.]

For everyone who is making his way toward the heavenly homeland is a pilgrim in this world; and for as long as he makes use of this life, he dwells as though in a foreign homeland. Yet because this life is full of ineffable dangers and various calamities, it is the lot of few truly and perfectly to know or love God. That is, for very few is the commandment of the Lord “clear, enlightening the eyes” (Psalm 18:9); in other words, very few know God so perfectly that they do not offend either in the love of God or in the love of their neighbor.

But then those for whom the commandment is “clear, enlightening the eyes” recognize that “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 25:10). For whom? “For those who seek his covenant and his testimonies” (ibid.).

[Col. 0413A] [Note: [Col. 0413D] In the autograph margin, “chapter LXXII” is written here.]

This Epistle too is God’s covenant, and it contains many testimonies of God. Therefore those for whom the Lord’s commandment is clear and enlightening to the eyes, who seek God’s covenant and his testimonies, and who also recognize their own pilgrimage, can penetrate the Apostle’s intention. For in body they are held in one place, while in mind they delight in another, just as the Apostle himself did. Therefore those who cling to the world in both body and mind cannot penetrate the Apostle’s intention.

The Apostle, knowing that the Epistle he had directed toward correcting the people of Corinth on account of many of their errors had been effective, prepares to send a second one to strengthen their obedience. [Col. 0413B] He strengthens their obedience in such a way, however, as to censure the stubbornness of those who still refused to correct their evil actions.

It should nevertheless be understood that the Apostle was encouraged by this hope: he had heard that they had corrected especially those matters that pertained to ecclesiastical order and dignity. Therefore he did not despair that their vices would gradually be corrected. For since they had corrected everything pertaining to ecclesiastical order, the apostles were given hope that their vices and conduct would in time be corrected.

He also hastened to send them this second Epistle because in the first they had been rebuked rather severely and had been deeply saddened. Thus, while they heard that they were loved by the Apostle, they might become more devoted to good works and might advance in the fruit of repentance, since true repentance is to abandon evil with sorrow intervening.

This, however, was the principal reason for writing and sending the Epistle: their teachers had been more severely rebuked on account of the sins of others and had been deeply saddened. In order that they might not take this too harshly or resent it, he set himself before them as an example, as if he had said: “Do not take it too harshly or resent it if you have been rebuked for the sins of others, when I myself am daily exposed to various dangers and to death.”

Also, in order to show that he held a good opinion of them, he began in this way, saying:

## (CHAPTER I)

“Paul, an apostle.” Now, being confident of their conversion and correction, he also calls himself an Apostle, though he does not say that he was called. For when they had gone astray, they heard him called; and because they had corrected themselves, they hear only “apostles” [Note: [Col. 0413D] Perhaps the noun “called,” or something similar, is to be understood.].

In order to confirm the authority of his apostleship and show that its dignity was valid, he added: “By the will of God.” For not all who are called apostles are so by the will of God. Or he says “of God” for this reason: to show that he had been made an apostle not only by the man Christ but also by God.

The Son of God himself speaks in this way to the Jews: “I always do all the things that please him” (John 8:29). Paul, however, says that he was called an apostle by the will of God because he fulfilled the will of God in everything. Therefore those who, when they attain some degree of ecclesiastical dignity, strive to fulfill the will of God in everything are to be believed to have reached that position by the divine will.

## [THE TEXT BEGINS]

It continues: “And Timothy, the brother.” It should be observed that he calls himself an Apostle and Timothy a brother, because both are servants and both are apostles, yet they do not possess equal dignity.

It should also be understood that here he names Timothy separately. When writing to the Philippians, he joins Timothy to himself and calls them both servants. For he says: “Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus.” The Apostle did this because those people had not gone astray in anything, and therefore such authority did not need to be displayed to them. These people, however, had erred in many ways, and therefore much authority had to be demonstrated to them.

Note also that he writes the second Epistle with the one through whom he had sent the first. Why? Clearly, to show that he had heard good things about them from Timothy’s report.

It continues: “To the Church of God,” etc. Corinth is the metropolis of the province of Achaia. Therefore, when he writes to the Church of the Corinthians, he also writes to the inhabitants of the entire province.

For this reason he also adds: “Together with all the saints,” etc. Yet it should be considered why he joined the Church of the Corinthians to all the saints: clearly because he had heard that they had progressed.

In another sense, the phrase “together with all the saints” may be understood [Note: [Col. 0414D] “To be” or “to be understood” is implied.] as referring to the priests, whose first duty is to invoke the name of the Lord. Lest they appear to have been omitted by those of lesser understanding, since they had been included under the name “Church,” he therefore added: “Together with all the saints.” Similarly, when writing to the Philippians, he says: “With the bishops and deacons.”

It continues: “Grace to you,” etc. The Father and the Son have one work; therefore he says: “From God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

[Note: [Col. 0414D] In the autograph margin, “chapter I” is written here.]

It continues: “Blessed be God,” etc. With such words he began to arrange the text of his Epistle. Here it should be noted that, according to his customary manner, he took care to display the mystery of the true faith. For he speaks about God the Father and his gifts, and about the Lord Jesus Christ, and afterward he will speak about the Holy Spirit, although the Holy Spirit is also understood in his gifts.

What he says—“Blessed be God and Father,” etc.—can be distinguished and understood in two ways. “Blessed be God,” the creator of all things, “who is also the Father of our Lord” [Col. 0414D] “Jesus Christ”; that is, of the Word who was God in the beginning with the Father.

We do not say this in order to imply that there is one speaker who assumes humanity and another human being who is assumed, but on account of the distinction of nature: at one time he is proclaimed as exalted, at another as humble.

“Father of mercies.” Note that he begins from the matter itself, that is, from his very intention, saying “Father of mercies,” so that, when they heard that God was not only the creator of all things but also the Father of mercies, they might be lifted up and receive consolation.

Observe also that he does not call him the Father of one mercy but of “mercies,” namely because he not only forgives sins in baptism but also in repentance and contrition of heart; or because he not only forgives sins but also restores the dignity of one’s former rank; or because he is the forgiver not of one or a few sins but of many—indeed, of all sins.

It continues: “And God of all consolation.” Observe that, when he calls him the God of all consolation, he wishes to show that there are many tribulations, since some are inflicted by evil men and others by the devil. Because he himself liberates us from all these, he is therefore called the God of all consolation.

He immediately makes this clear when he adds: “Who consoles us in all our tribulation.” He consoles his own for the sake of the salvation of others. This is what he says: “So that we too may be able to console those who are in every affliction.”

It should certainly be understood that there are two kinds of tribulation. One is inflicted by persecutors and by all sorts of evil people; the other arises from repentance. The latter is no less than the former, because the former can be endured with joy, whereas the latter is possessed only with sorrow, since, when a person remembers his sins, he fears being punished for them.

The apostolic men were also freed from the tribulation inflicted by persecutors so that they might be able to provide consolation in repentance to others who were afflicted. This is what he says: “So that we too may be able to console them,” etc.; as if he were saying: “We are freed from persecutors so that we may provide consolation to you who are afflicted, showing that God does not wish any of those who believe in him to perish.”

It continues: “For just as the sufferings of Christ abound in us,” etc. The meaning is as if he had said: “Christ is present with us in all our tribulations. We suffer for his love, while he grants the help of his mercy and powerfully rescues us from those very tribulations. For as many sufferings as are inflicted by persecutors, so many consolations are administered by Christ.” Hence the Psalmist: “According to the multitude of my sorrows” (Psalm 94:19), etc.

It continues: “Whether we are afflicted, it is for your affliction and salvation,” etc. It should be carefully noted that the Apostle speaks generally, and this general expression applies to all apostolic men. But when he says, “Whether we are afflicted, it is for your affliction and salvation,” “we are afflicted” must be understood.

They were afflicted by the persecution suffered by all apostolic men for the sake of the salvation of their hearers, because they had drawn them to the faith by their preaching. This hatred was directed especially against them because by their teaching they had led them away from the worship of idols.

“Whether we are comforted, it is for your comfort and salvation”—“we are comforted” is understood [Note: [Col. 0415D] In the autograph the phrase reads, “and for your salvation we are comforted.” We have judged this transposition of the words to have been improperly introduced by the copyist’s pen and have corrected it.].

For it should be understood that, just as they were afflicted for the sake of the salvation of their hearers, so for the sake of their salvation they were rescued from those same tribulations and restored to them, so that the hearers themselves might be strengthened in the faith.

It should also be understood that the affliction, tribulation, and suffering of holy preachers could be a scandal to their hearers. For when the hearers saw their teachers oppressed by force and torn apart by various tortures, those who were weak in faith could also be scandalized, believing that their promise had been frustrated.

On the other hand, those who had already been strengthened in the faith, when they saw them suffering, wished to become companions in their tribulations and sufferings, so that they might be partners in their consolation. Therefore he says: “Our hope for you is firm.”

And as if they had asked, “What is your firm hope for us?” he himself answers: “Knowing that, just as you are companions in the sufferings,” etc.; as if he had said in other words: “We are so confident about you that we believe you will not only fail to be scandalized by our tribulations, but will rather rejoice to become companions in our sufferings, so that you may also be companions in consolation.”

It should certainly be understood that this was not happening only at that time; it is happening now as well. For example, there is someone in the Church who believes rightly and lives rightly. If certain tribulations, persecutions, and adversities befall him, those who are weak in the Church, when they see this, regard with contempt the life of the man whom they had previously held in veneration.

We read that this happened in the case of Job’s friends. They themselves were holy and believed that Job lived holily, until they saw him struck down. But as soon as he was tested, afflicted, and stripped of all temporal goods, they burst into reproach, believing that his good qualities were not genuinely good but feigned.
