Such things also commonly occur now in the Church. Therefore those who are weak in faith are warned to grow and become so strengthened in it that those who believe rightly may be able to say of them: “Our hope for you is firm,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0416D] In the autograph margin, “chapter II” is written here.]

“We do not want you to be ignorant,” etc. The Apostle had begun to set himself forward as an example to his own people, because they had been rebuked and reproved too severely and had consequently been saddened. Continuing in the intention he had begun, he says: “We do not want you to be ignorant,” etc.; as if he were saying: “Why should you take it badly if you have been rebuked for the sins of others, when I, for the sake of the salvation of others, am subject to various tribulations?”

He said this so that, when they heard it, they might be ashamed that they could not patiently endure the rebuke of their teacher.

### Asia

By Asia we must understand Asia Minor. Augustine says: “If you consider it by number, it is a third part of the world; if by size, it is half. For on the western side it is joined to Macedonia; on the northern side, to the Pontic Sea; on the central side, to the Egyptian Sea; and on the eastern side, to the Propontis. Thus it is an island, though it contains various provinces, namely Bithynia, Pamphylia, Lycia, [Col. 0417A] [Note: [Col. 0417D] The autograph reads “Litia.”], etc. It was named after a certain woman named Asia, who in ancient times held the empire of the East; and its name is interpreted as ‘lofty’ or ‘raised up.’”

And it is fitting that the Apostle should suffer such things there, because the humility of ecclesiastical peace is established among the proud.

“For we were burdened beyond measure,” etc. At that time persecution against the apostles had arisen to such an extent that they despaired of temporal life. This is what he means: “We were weary of living.”

“But we ourselves had within us,” etc. It must be asked what answer death had given them, or what answer it can give. They had received the answer of death because, deprived of human consolation, they were awaiting divine assistance alone.

“So that we should not trust in ourselves.” He rightly says that they should not trust in themselves, because those who trust in the Lord are accustomed to be delivered.

“But in God, who raises the dead.” The persecutions had arisen to such an extent that their rescue was called a resurrection.

He makes clear in whom they had placed their trust by adding: “Who delivered us from such great dangers, and delivers us”—that is, he freed us not only from past dangers but also from present ones. And because he also delivers from future dangers, he adds: “For he will still deliver us.”

By these words he shows that he would continue to suffer and would be rescued by divine grace, as he makes clear by saying: “With your help as well.” By these words he shows that he would continue in labor. For assistance must be given to those who are engaged in labor.

He explains how this help is given when he says: “Through prayer.” Here it is shown that persistent prayer is of great value. This is demonstrated not only here but elsewhere as well. For we read that Peter was freed from prison through prayer, since it is said: “And Peter was kept in prison” (Acts 12:5), etc.

By this event those in higher positions are warned not to disdain being helped by the prayers of those beneath them, since a man of such great authority did not disdain it. For who possessed such authority? No one.

“So that, from the faces of many persons, his …” [Note: [Col. 0417D] The Vulgate reads: “So that, from the persons of many, his …,” etc.], etc. In some copies one finds: “through the faces of many persons”; in others: “from the face of many”; in others: “through the persons of many.”

The meaning is this: From the gathering of many people, when we are freed from tribulations by the grace of God and restored to you, let thanks be given to God through many or by many.

In another sense, when we are restored to many for the sake of their salvation and draw them to the faith by our preaching, let thanks be given through many or by many. By these words the Apostle shows that they were freed for the sake of the salvation of those for whom they were also afflicted.

And when he had said above, “with your help in prayer,” and now says, “through many let thanks be given,” he shows that he wants them, while the apostles were held in tribulation, to pray for their deliverance, and, once they had been delivered, to give thanks to God.

This salutary rule, which was observed then, must also be practiced now. For when preachers are held in tribulation, their hearers ought to pray that they may be delivered, and, once they have been delivered, to give thanks to God. For every weakness or debility is located in the head; and if one member rejoices, all the members rejoice with it.

“For this is our glory,” that is, the testimony of our conscience. He said this because he was secure in his conscience. He did not preach for the sake of profit or from a desire for human praise, but fulfilled the duty of his apostleship.

[Note: [Col. 0418D] In the autograph margin, “chapter III” is written here.]

This is the voice of the perfect. Therefore they are warned to strive to live in such a way that they may properly say these things.

He begins to explain what he had called his glory, saying: “That we have conducted ourselves in simplicity and sincerity,” etc. Simplicity is free from all duplicity, and sincerity from all corruption. Two destructive evils are opposed to these two virtues: duplicity and corruption.

And to show that these two virtues do not consist in worldly wisdom, he therefore adds: “Not in worldly wisdom.” But where? He makes it clear by saying: “In the grace of God.”

By these words he touches upon the meaning he had explained at greater length in the preceding Epistle. For he had reproved the pseudo-apostles who preached for the sake of profit and, fearing to offend people, denied that God had become human, had been born, and had suffered.

The Apostle did not want to accept anything from the Corinthians, lest he seem like those whom he was reproving, or lest he lose the freedom to rebuke. What he accepted from other churches he did not want to accept from the Corinthians. Therefore he said: “But more abundantly toward you.”

And because he accepted from others, he said: “We conducted ourselves in the grace of God”; but because he did not accept from these people, he said: “More abundantly toward you.”

He did not want to accept anything, lest he provide an occasion for receiving, or lest he lose the freedom to rebuke.

It continues: “We have written nothing else to you” [Note: [Col. 0418D] The Vulgate reads: “We are writing nothing else to you.”], etc. By these words the Apostle indicates that he had written nothing other than what they had read in his writings and recognized in his actions. For a person’s devotion and purpose are revealed by these two indications.

By this example preachers are warned always to teach and strive to do those things that are sufficient for the salvation of their hearers.

It continues: “I hope that you will recognize this fully to the end,” etc. He derived this hope from their correction. For he had heard that they had corrected especially those matters that pertained to ecclesiastical order. From this correction he took hope and believed that in the future they would correct the remaining matters as well.

Therefore he says: “I hope that you will recognize this fully to the end.”

The statement “I hope” can also refer to himself, so that the meaning is: “I hope that you will recognize me to the end in the purpose you have come to know both through my writings and through my actions.”

If it refers to them, he uses these words to urge them toward the good of perseverance. But if it refers to himself, he too is confident in the good of perseverance, since a good work begun is worth nothing unless it is completed by persevering to the end.

For this reason, in the Old Testament the tail and the head were offered together in the sacrifice. To offer the tail and the head together in sacrifice is to complete a good work that has been begun by persevering to the end. Hence the Lord also says: “The one who perseveres” (Matthew 10:22), etc.

As for what follows—“Just as you have understood in part”—if it refers to his own person, he says this because no one can fully know the merit of any human being in this life. The same point is also indicated by what he says: “On the day of the Lord,” etc.

But if it refers to the Corinthians, he says “in part” because they had already corrected many things.

It continues: “For we are your glory,” etc. Once they had recognized the Apostle’s affection, the Corinthians gloried in him as in a distinguished father and a proven teacher. He too, recognizing their obedience, gloried in them as in devoted sons, obedient and honorable disciples.

Teachers, then, are the glory of their subjects when they possess such holiness and merit that they are held in veneration by the Church. Hearers, on the other hand, are the glory of their teachers when they are so obedient that, through the singular excellence of their obedience, they are venerated by everyone.

Therefore both groups must strive to live in such a way that they can be one another’s glory.

But when will this glory be revealed? “On the day of our Lord Jesus Christ,” that is, on the day of judgment. For there the teaching of all preachers and the obedience of their subjects will be revealed: “For nothing will be hidden that will not be revealed” (Matthew 10:26), etc.

It continues: “And in this confidence I wanted to come to you first,” etc. If this sentence refers to what precedes, he speaks of the confidence of hope; but if it refers to what follows, he shows what that confidence is.

“So that you might have a second grace,” he says. What he calls “a second” grace can be understood in two ways.

They had the first grace in receiving the Epistle; they would have the second in his bodily presence. His Epistle was an image; the presence of his body was the reality. Therefore those who had received him in likeness would receive him in reality.

In another way, they had the first grace because they had previously received him with joy and believed in response to his preaching. They would have a second grace if they received him bodily once again.

He shows this when he begins to disclose his plan to them: “And through you,” he says, “to pass into Macedonia,” etc. They would have been proclaimed to possess great dignity, merit, and grace if they were to enjoy the Apostle’s presence so often and for so long.

It continues: “When I intended this, did I use lightness?” It should be observed that the Apostle had promised that he would come to them. But because he did not come, and lest he appear to have fallen into the evil of lying, he begins to wipe away the charge of fickleness. Therefore he says: “Did I use lightness?” “No” is understood, as if he had said in other words: “The one who does not fulfill what he promises appears to use lightness; but I did not use lightness, because I placed usefulness before desire.”

For although covertly, he nevertheless shows why he did not come to them: the matter depended not on himself but on them.

Then follows: “Or do I think according to the flesh?” No. The meaning is this: The person who, thinking according to the flesh, does not fulfill what he has promised is the one who delays fulfilling his promise either out of reverence for some person, or for earthly gain, or for any kind of vanity or fickleness. The spiritual person, by contrast, thinking spiritually, does not fulfill what he has promised because he understands something deeper concerning the soul’s salvation; and therefore he places usefulness before his will. For it is carnal to place one’s will before usefulness, but spiritual to place usefulness before one’s will. Therefore the Apostle, understanding that it concerned their salvation more that he should not come to them, delayed coming.

Then follows: “So that there might be with me ‘Yes’ and ‘No’?” The word “not” is understood. The meaning is this: With them there is “yes” and “no”—with those who do not disclose what ought to be disclosed, and who place their will before usefulness. But with me there is no “yes” and “no,” because there is no falsehood and no changeability, and because we have not lied to you. Blessed Pope Gregory speaks about this passage as though he had said: With me there is no “yes” and “no”; that is, I am not moved by the breath of changeability, because I do not succumb to the vice of fickleness.

Then follows: “God is faithful.” Faithful, I say, because with him there is no “yes” and “no.” Note that, by calling God faithful, he wishes to show that he and those like him are faithful, as though he were saying: If he is faithful, then we too, through whom he speaks, are faithful. And therefore he adds: “For our word, which was among you,” etc. By these words he shows that his teaching is true, because the Apostle’s teaching is the Lord’s teaching.

Then follows: “For the Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, who was preached among you,” etc. First, in this passage it must be asked who this Silvanus was, and why he is placed before Timothy. Silvanus is the same person who is also called Silas [Note: [Col. 0419D] “Silas” according to the Vulgate, or “Sillas.” See Acts 15:22; likewise the beginnings of the two Epistles to the Thessalonians; 1 Peter 5:12; Acts 15:27, 41; Acts 16:11. Ado attests that this most faithful companion of Saint Paul died in Macedonia, as Saint Peter calls him in the cited Epistle; and he seems, quite probably, to be numbered among the Seventy disciples. The Greeks, honoring Silas and Silvanus as two distinct men, celebrate him on 13 July as having obtained the palm of martyrdom.] He is frequently mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles. It is also written of him that he was sent from Jerusalem by the apostles to Antioch with letters (Acts 15:27), on account of the diversity of foods and in order to remove the legal burdens from the shoulders of believers. For just as Saulus indicates Paul, so Silvanus indicates Silas. These men preached not only to the Corinthians but also to the Thessalonians.

But perhaps someone asks: Why is Silvanus placed before Timothy both in this Epistle and in that other one? Let the one who asks this know that he is perhaps placed first because he attached himself to the Apostle and to his preaching earlier, and first became a participant in his tribulation; the book of the Acts of the Apostles also makes this clear. For we read that, when he wished to carry out the task he had undertaken, he took Silas with him (Acts 15:40). After this we read that, when they had traveled through Syria (ibid., 41), strengthening the churches, they came to Derbe, and so forth. Timothy, although he was ordained bishop by the Apostle and is greatly praised by him, is nevertheless rightly placed after him. This order is also observed in the Church, since bishops have seats according to their rank.

Christ, therefore, the Son of God, has no “yes” and “no,” because there is no falsehood in him and no changeability either, as it is written: “With whom there is no change” (James 1:17), and so forth. But in him there was “Yes”: that is, unshaken truth and unchangeable goodness remain in him. Hence he also says to Moses: “I am who I am” (Exodus 3:14), and so forth. For being truly belongs to the one whose being is not otherwise or differently, but whose being is identical with the one who is. Creatures, however, because they do not have being from themselves, receive it from him, so that they may exist according to their measure.

To him, therefore, whose being is not otherwise or differently, but whose being is that which he is, nothing is contrary except that which is not. Consequently, just as every good is from him, so everything that exists naturally is from him; therefore every good is also from him. Again: Every creature is good, and every good is from God; therefore every creature is from him. Thus it must be noted that, insofar as the dignity and freedom of teachers are concerned, there ought not to be “yes” and “no” in them, but “yes” ought to be in them—that is, they ought not to place their will before usefulness, but usefulness before their will.

The Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, has no “yes” and “no,” because he wills nothing other than what is useful; and what is useful for him is not compelled, as it is for a human being. Nor is anything ambiguous against him, as it is among human beings. And therefore the Apostle adds, saying: “For all the promises of God are ‘Yes’ in him,” etc. The meaning is as though he had said: Christ is all truth, and therefore through him there is “Amen” to God, because all truth is through him—for “amen” is interpreted as “truth.” This truth was manifested through Christ, preached by the apostles, and confirmed by various signs and miracles.

That everything Christ promised is true and is fulfilled may be expressed in the conclusion of this statement as though he had said: Christ is the truth of all the promises, which is preached through us, and fulfillment follows. He fittingly adds: “For the glory of God” [Note: [Col. 0421D] The Vulgate has “for our glory.”], because it greatly pertains to the glory of God if all things are known and understood to exist from him, through him, and in him.

Then follows: “But the one who confirms us with you is the Lord Christ” [Note: [Col. 0421D] The Vulgate has: “But the one who confirms us with you in Christ” [Col. 0422D].] The word “is” is understood; for this writer was a Hebrew and was speaking to Gentiles. The meaning, therefore, is this: The Lord Christ is the one who confirms us and you in that faith which was promised to the fathers. For “he is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2:14), and joined the two walls coming from division together in one faith of his own, making peace in one man for those who are far away and those who are near (ibid., 15, 17).

Then follows: “And the one who anointed us is God.” He anointed us, I say, with heavenly and spiritual gifts and charisms, so that we might be “a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9), according to the Apostle Peter. Those who were anointed in the Old Testament bore the figure of the faithful.

Then follows: “And the one who sealed us.” He said this as something great: that is, he specially and uniquely chose and loved us above all creatures. We seal what we hold dear. Note that by these words he reveals one work of the Father and the Son, since those whom the Son is said to confirm are those whom the Father is said to anoint and seal. Therefore those whom the Son confirms, the Father also confirms; for those whom the Father anoints and seals, the Son also anoints and seals. And those to whom the Father gives his Spirit, the Son also gives him, because the Father and the Son have one Spirit. Hence the same writer says in the Epistle to the Romans: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9). This must also be noted: when he was speaking about human perfection (ibid.), he mentioned the whole Trinity, because the highest perfection consists in the Trinity.

Then follows: “And he gave the pledge of the Spirit,” etc. It must carefully be noted that a pledge is given for something entrusted or promised; and when the thing promised or entrusted is returned, the pledge is received back. A pledge is also given on account of the greatness of the thing entrusted or promised. Here one must attentively consider how much will be given to the elect when they are already immortal, since so much is granted to them while they are still mortal—that is, how great the reward and recompense of the heavenly kingdom will be, since even now so great a grace of the Holy Spirit is administered to the elect.

It must also be known that a pledge is given in order to make a person more certain. The grace of the Holy Spirit, therefore, is granted to the elect so that they may be more certain of the promise of the heavenly kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 0422D] In the autograph margin it reads here: “chapter IV.”]

Then follows: “But I call God as my witness,” etc. Earlier the Apostle had labored to wipe away from himself the charge of fickleness and to show himself free from the charge of lying. Now he begins to make clear why he did not come to them, when he says: “But I call God as my witness,” etc. By these words he shows that the fact that he did not come to them was not attributable to him but to them.

He also shows this when he says: “Sparing you,” since there were many among them who had not been corrected, whose sins had not yet been ripened by repentance. For this reason he did not come to them, so as to grant them the place and time for repentance, in order that, when he came, he would have no reason to spare them. To impress this more firmly upon their minds, he called God as a witness concerning his soul—that is, over his soul. This was fitting, because only God knows the secrets of the soul, according to what is written: “Man sees the face, but God the heart.” Therefore he also said, “I call God as my witness, sparing you,” so that those who were worthy, hearing this, would not be scandalized by judging themselves unworthy of his presence; while those who were unworthy would strive to live in such a way that they might become worthy of his presence.

“Not that we lord it over your faith.” By these words the Apostle shows that faith is voluntary, not compelled. For what is compelled must be ruled, but what is voluntary or spontaneous, such as faith, does not require domination. And therefore he adds: “For by faith you stand,” as though he were saying: It is not necessary to exercise domination as the priests of the Jews exercised domination over the people; for by faith you stand.

“Not that we are lord of your faith, but we are helpers of your joy.” It must be asked why he says that he is a helper of their joy, when earlier in the First Epistle he had said that he was exceedingly saddened. The reason is that, just as sadness arises from falling, joy arises from correction and amendment. It is as though he were saying: Because I was saddened when you fell, I rejoice when you rise again, by offering exhortation and supplying salutary remedies.

By this action preachers are instructed to strive to be helpers to those who rise again, by writing, exhorting, and offering salutary remedies.

“For by faith you stand.” Gregory explains this passage and shows that the Apostle had another intention, as though he were saying: In the fact that you stand by faith, we recognize that you are like us. For the Apostle was forgetting the authority of his precedence; hence he calls himself little in what follows, saying: “We became as little ones in the midst of you” (1 Thessalonians 2:7), and: “We are your servants” (2 Corinthians 4:5), because there was no fault.

But when fault appeared, he remembered the authority of his precedence, saying: “What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod?” (1 Corinthians 4:21), and so forth. Gregory himself says that the highest position is rightly governed when the superior rules over vices rather than over brothers.

By this action superiors are instructed that, when they prepare to rebuke a fault, they should strike at vices through discipline in such a way that they recognize themselves as like the others by nature. For nature created all human beings equal; it was fault that caused one to be placed above another. Therefore superiors must show themselves like the good, while displaying the authority of their precedence toward the wicked.

He understood this to have been the Apostle’s intention; and this meaning must be preserved unshaken by teachers.

[Note: [Col. 0423D] In the autograph margin it reads here: “chapter V.”]

**(Chapter II.)** “I determined,” etc.; that is, I deliberated and resolved. By these words he shows that he did not wish them to be saddened by him, but did wish them to be saddened and corrected, so that when he came he would have nothing in them to rebuke.

“For if I make you sorrowful,” etc. He had saddened them in the First Epistle. Now he says: “If I make you sorrowful”; but the meaning is this: You who sadden me by falling can make me glad by rising again.

“And I wrote this very thing to you.” For he had written it in the First Epistle, and he writes it also in the Second. He explains why: “So that when I came I might not have sorrow upon sorrow.” To have sorrow upon sorrow is not to rejoice in the succeeding amendment of those whose transgression has caused one sorrow. For the sorrow arising from amendment that does not follow is no less than the sorrow arising from transgression.

It is as though he were saying: I, who am afflicted and saddened by outsiders, may at least find rest among you, as a father among his children, among whom I ought to rejoice. I ought to rejoice for two reasons: either because you remain in the purpose you have begun, or because you correct and amend yourselves.

“I am confident,” etc. I am confident in two ways: I believe that you understand that your joy is rightly ordered if you perceive that I rejoice; or I trust that you love me so much that you count my joy as your own.

“For out of much tribulation,” etc. By these words he shows with what affection and love he was bound to the Corinthians. He shows that no distress or tribulation could separate him from the Corinthians.

“With many tears.” Why does he say “many”? He makes this clear when he says: “Not that you might be saddened,” etc.; as though he were saying: I do not wish to sadden you, but to show what love I have for you, so that in my greater concern you may understand my greater love. This is what he says: “More abundantly toward you.”

“But if anyone has caused sorrow,” etc. Why does he say “has caused me sorrow” and not “has saddened me”? The meaning is as though he were saying: You have saddened me, and you have not saddened me, because when you sinned, you gave me the opportunity to rebuke you, so that through my rebuke and reproach you might become better. He explains this when he says, “in part,” as though he were saying: You saddened me to the extent that you fell and suffered loss.

“So that I may not burden all of you.” There were two parts: one standing and the other falling. The Apostle seems to be speaking to those who were standing, whom he does not burden. And if he does not burden them, he burdens those who were falling, because the more people are scandalized by someone’s crime, the more gravely that person sins.

“For such a person, this punishment by the majority is sufficient,” etc. He says “by the majority” because he had been rebuked and reproved by many. For they had all risen up with one mind for his rebuke and expulsion. Therefore he says “sufficient,” as though he were saying: It is sufficient for his correction, expulsion, shame, and amendment that he is reproved by many, because a person detests his own offense to the extent that he recognizes others detesting it.

“So that, on the contrary, you should rather forgive,” etc. It is as though he were saying: Just as you all rose up with one mind for his expulsion and rebuke, so, on the contrary, rise up with one accord—or rather, with greater accord—for his reception and support, in accordance with: “I do not desire the death of the sinner” (Ezekiel 33:11), and: “At whatever hour the sinner turns to me” (ibid., 12), and so forth.

At that time the Apostle had specifically ordered that the man who had violated his father’s wife be expelled (1 Corinthians 5:1). Nevertheless, this sentence applies to all who were then expelled and are expelled now. He had expelled that man in the First Epistle; in the Second he orders that he be received, because he knew that in the course of time he had produced worthy fruit of repentance. For if he had not known this, he would never have ordered that he be received. Repentance offered with sorrow will not be without fruit, as is shown in David and Ahab [Note: [Col. 0425D] This is evidently because of the contrary outcome of their repentance. Alternatively, “Achaz” should be read, whose end was marked by despair rather than repentance.].

“So that he may not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.” It is as though he were saying: Receive him, lest, cast out from the threshold of the Church, he say: Since I have been cast out from the threshold of the Church, I do not enjoy the fellowship of the good and do not presume upon the hope of heavenly gifts; what remains except that I at least enjoy temporal pleasures? Therefore it is extremely necessary that we condescend to a brother on account of his own offense, lest the one who was expelled in order to be received, if he is not received, be dragged into blasphemy and, in despair, into the depths of unbelief.

Then follows: “Therefore I urge you,” etc. He calls that charity by which he understood that he had obtained forgiveness for all his offenses. To confirm charity in him is to show the affection of mercy, by which he may recognize that he has obtained forgiveness of sins and may presume upon the hope of the heavenly kingdom.

Then follows: “For this reason I wrote, so that I might learn your proven character,” etc. By these words he shows that they had already begun to be obedient, especially because they had corrected those things that pertained to the practice of the faith and ecclesiastical order. Therefore he wrote this so that they would receive the man, in order to test whether they were obedient in all things, since that is true obedience which resists the will of the one commanding in nothing.

Then follows: “If you forgive anyone anything,” etc. The meaning is: Since I forgave at your request, you too ought to forgive at my request. It must certainly be understood that these men did not possess as much foresight as the Apostle. He himself acted spiritually in whatever he did, because he was full of the Holy Spirit. They, however, understood that they ought immediately to grant what the Apostle requested; for if he forgave at their request, they ought much more to forgive when he requested it.

It must also be understood that he himself had urged them to expel the man who had committed the crime of fornication and to be severe toward him; therefore he now asked so earnestly that they receive him. And because he forgave at their request, he says, “for your sake.” To show that his action was acceptable, he says, “in the person of Christ,” thereby showing that his action was Christ’s, since he was acting as Christ’s ambassador. Hence he himself says: “Whatever you loose on earth” (Matthew 18:18), and so forth.

He explains why he forgave when he adds: “Lest we be outwitted by Satan.” It must be understood that a person is outwitted by Satan either when he is excessively lenient or when he is excessively severe.

For example, there are some who wish to appear gentle, pleasant, and approachable to their hearers, and therefore do not correct their errors. Such people are outwitted by Satan. There are also those who, inflamed by excessive zeal for the law, persecute their own people so severely that they drive them to despair. These too are outwitted by Satan—that is, deceived: the former by false mercy, the latter by excessive cruelty.

And because danger threatens on both sides, we must be very careful not to turn aside either to the right or to the left, according to Solomon (Proverbs 4:27; Isaiah 30:21).

Then follows: “For we are not ignorant of his designs.” Blessed Pope Gregory explains this passage as follows. He says: These are the stratagems of the ancient enemy: to deceive the unwary through immoderate goods. For he usually generates evil in one person’s heart through quarrels from the very place where he sees another neglecting to practice mercy. That which is done cannot be perfectly good if it does not take account of the evil that arises on the other side—unless, perhaps, it is such a good that it cannot be done without causing another’s scandal, and not doing it would itself be a sin.

Blessed Pope Gregory brings forward the man who committed the crime as a witness and understands him to have ordered that he be handed over to the devil when he commanded that he be handed over to Satan. For he says that it was carried out with great skill in teaching: the man who had voluntarily submitted himself to guilt was compelled to submit himself to punishment, and the one who had been the author of wickedness in guilt became the instrument of discipline in punishment.

He also explains the Apostle’s words: “If you forgive anyone, I also forgive,” as though he had said: I have joined my good to your good works, because I wish whatever good you distribute to be regarded as mine as well [Note: [Col. 0426D] The autograph has “you ask.”].

Then follows: “And if I have forgiven anyone anything,” etc., as though he had said: I have joined my good to your good, because for your sake I performed an act of mercy. To show where this joining takes place, he adds: “In the person of Christ.”

But because someone might say to him: O Apostle, why do you humble yourself so much? Why do you submit yourself so far as to compare the good of the Corinthians with your own and your own with theirs?—he therefore adds: “Lest we be outwitted by Satan.”

To show how sharply and perceptively he penetrated the devil’s cunning ambushes, he adds: “For we are not ignorant,” etc. The meaning is: With God as author, we are sharp stakes (*sudes*), because with the keen capacity of the mind we penetrate the devil’s cunning ambushes, lest he turn to an end of wickedness what the mind has begun well.

Blessed Pope Gregory says these things in the Moral Works, specifically in the passage where it is written: “He will swallow the river and will not be amazed” (Job 40:18); and shortly afterward: “He will seize him with his eyes, and with his stakes he will pierce his nostrils” (ibid., 19). There he wishes the very subtle counsels of the saints to be understood by “stakes,” and the hidden ambushes of the devil by “nostrils.”

[Col. 0426D] [Note: [Col. 0426D] Here, in the autograph margin, it reads: “chapter VI.”]

Then follows: “When I had come to Troas,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0426D] The autograph has “Troadae.”] The Apostle recounts his journey to the Corinthians when he says, “When I had come to Troas.” He reveals why he came: not for the sake of vanity, but because of the gospel of Christ. By this action preachers are instructed not to travel about for the sake of vanity, but for the salvation of their hearers.

Then follows: “I had no rest for my spirit.” He explains why he had no rest: because he had not found Titus, etc. As some think, he had no rest because, when he had sent Titus to Corinth, he was extremely anxious about him, since he did not know whether Titus would report good or bad news concerning the Corinthians.

When he says, “And a door was opened to me,” the meaning is as though he had said: The hearts of many people were ready to believe. For “door” signifies faith. Hence John says in the Apocalypse: “I saw a door opened in heaven” (Revelation 4:1). By “heaven” the Church is signified, and by “door,” faith.

Many at Troas were ready to believe, but there were more who resisted the Apostle out of jealousy toward those who believed. Therefore he had no rest, because he could not bear both concerns at once: resisting those who did not believe and strengthening those who did believe. Consequently, after bidding farewell to the believers, he left the people of Troas—or the Trojans—and departed for Macedonia, because Titus was going to come from there and because Macedonia was nearer to Corinth.

That this was the course of his journey is shown by the book of the Acts of the Apostles. It says that, when they had traveled through Mysia, they came to Troas, and so forth (Acts 16:8).

Macedonia was the region of Alexander the Great, son of Philip. It is said to be full of veins of gold and silver. It is also said to contain Mount Olympus, whose summit is struck neither by winds nor by rains.

Then follows: “But thanks be to God.” He had said that he had endured many things, and now he gives thanks to God. By this action we are instructed to give thanks to God for all things, both adverse and prosperous. He gave thanks to God either to provoke them to imitate him or to arm them for battles.

Then follows: “Who always leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus.” For God’s causing the apostles to triumph in Christ means making them victorious in the faith of Christ. They received not only a trophy but also a triumph in the faith of Christ.

It must certainly be known that among the ancients there was a great difference between a trophy and a triumph. “Trophy” is said, from a Greek word, to derive from pursuit, while “triumph” derives from exultation. Hence triumph is called exultation, and those who triumph are exultant [Note: [Col. 0427D] The autograph has “tripudiantes,” “dancing for joy.”].

But if “triumph” is a Latin word, as some think, it is said to derive from three kinds of praise, because those who not only put their enemies to flight but also killed them were praised by commanders, consuls, and the common people. They also received a golden palm because they had complete victory. Those, however, who possessed a trophy—that is, a half-complete victory—received a golden crown.

Then follows: “And he manifests the fragrance of his knowledge in every place.” He calls the fame of Christ’s name a fragrance, which is fittingly represented by fragrance, since an unseen thing is recognized by its scent. So also the fame of Christ’s name invisibly reaches the ears of believers, and God, who was invisible, was known through invisible preaching.

This fragrance was manifested through Christ and preached through the Epistle. Hence God says to God, Lord to Lord, and the Son says to the Father: “As you sent me into the world, I also sent them into the world” (John 17:18). This was also confirmed by signs and wonders, because the invisible God was believed invisibly, through the signs and wonders, in response to their preaching.

It must also be understood that the Apostle preserves the custom of the law. Whatever was offered in the law with a devout mind was burned as a most fragrant odor to the Lord. Similarly, the fame of God’s name, manifested by Christ, was scattered and breathed throughout the world by the apostles like a most fragrant odor.

Then follows: “For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God,” etc. Whoever asserts and thinks rightly concerning Christ is the good fragrance of Christ, both to those who are being saved and to those who are perishing. But whoever thinks or asserts evil concerning him is a bad odor, both to believers and to unbelievers: to believers, because they believe wrongly; to unbelievers, because they understand that he should not be believed.

Blessed Augustine says that the Apostle had begun by revealing his journey to the Corinthians; then he showed them that he had endured many things; then he gave thanks to God, especially because he was found to be such that God might triumph over him in Christ; and after this he says that the fragrance of the knowledge of God is manifested through him in every place.

Here it must be asked what this triumph is, or what this fragrance is. This triumph, or fragrance, is the victory of the martyrs, the shedding of their blood, and their steadfastness. When unbelievers saw these things, they received an occasion for saying: If the gospel of Christ were not true, they would never have been so steadfast in martyrdom; the blood of so many people would not have been shed; nor would they have endured various torments with such joy.

Thus they received an occasion for believing, especially because their confession was not delicate or filled with luxuries, but took place in hunger, thirst, and the rest. In this way the fragrance of the knowledge of God also breathed throughout the world.

But because someone could object to the apostles: If you are the good fragrance in every place, why do not all believe?—he, knowing that this could be objected to him, raised the objection himself and explained it, saying: “To some we are the fragrance of death unto death,” etc. It is as though he had said: O Corinthians, although we are always the good fragrance, to some we are nevertheless the fragrance of death unto death, while to others we are the fragrance of life unto life.

For human beings have been given free choice, so that the good would not be compelled but voluntary. If this were not so, there would be no basis either for the good to be rewarded with eternal rewards or for the wicked to be punished with eternal punishments. Again: We who are always the good fragrance are, because of the fault of those who do not receive us, the fragrance of death unto death; but because of the virtue of those who receive us, we are the fragrance of life unto life.

By “death” and “life” we must understand not the death by which we commonly die and the life by which we live together with beasts and cattle, but the death of which it is written: “The soul that sins” (Leviticus 5:1), etc.; and the life of which the same Apostle says: “When Christ, our life, appears” (Colossians 3:4).

For what is surprising if it is said of the apostles that to some they are the fragrance of death unto death, and so forth, when it is also written of Christ: “This one is appointed for the falling,” etc. (Luke 2:34; Isaiah 8:14)?

What is surprising, moreover, if this is said of the apostles and of Christ, when we can understand the same thing about the sun? The sun spreads its rays everywhere. It illuminates both clean and unclean things; it shines upon fragrant flowers as well as dung. Nevertheless, its rays are not defiled.

So too Christ, who cannot be changed, etc., cannot be changed by nature. To those who do not believe he is for falling, but to those who believe he is for resurrection. So also the apostles, who act in his place, are to some, as the Apostle says, “the fragrance of death unto death,” and to others “the fragrance of life unto life.”

It is as though he had said again: O Corinthians, do not despise this. If to some we are the fragrance of death unto death, and so forth, it is because, unless we preached, neither the life of obedience would follow for the good nor the death of disobedience for the wicked.

It must certainly be understood that the very sound of evangelical preaching is the fragrance of life to those who receive it, because, when they receive it, through it they pass into life. To those who do not receive it, however, it is the odor of pestilence, because just as people pass through pestilence to death, so those who do not receive the hearing of God’s word generate death for themselves and pass into it. Hence the Lord says through Ezekiel: “If you announce the sins of the wicked man,” etc. (Ezekiel 3:19).

Then follows: “And who is sufficient for these things?” That is: Who is so capable as to manifest the fragrance of the knowledge of God as we do? Not, I say, the pseudo-apostles, to whom you have given your faith.

Alternatively: “Who is so capable for these things?” That is: Who possesses such prudence or understanding that he can explain why some believe at our preaching and others do not; why some both wish to believe and are able to do so, while others neither wish to believe nor are able? “O man, who are you to answer back to God?”

Then follows: “For we are not like so many, adulterating the word of God.” In this passage he touches upon the pseudo-apostles, who adulterated the word of God. For, having abandoned the meaning of God’s word, they preached according to human understanding; or at least they understood the word of God differently from what it was.

They were such lovers of the Jewish sect that they thought wrongly about Christ, and therefore he shows them to be less capable [Note: [Col. 0429D] “Less known,” perhaps “less capable,” from the words shortly above: “Who is so capable for these things?”].

Again, an adulterer does not seek offspring in intercourse but loves pleasure. Therefore those adulterate the word of God who seek in it not the offspring of good works but the offspring of human praise. To adulterate the word of God also means to seek not the praises of God but the display of one’s own wisdom.

Then follows: “But from sincerity”—that is, from simplicity and purity of heart. To speak the word of God from sincerity and simplicity is to understand that what one speaks has been received from God. To speak before God is, while speaking, to place the divine presence before one’s mind.

But because there are some who, although they understand that they have received from God what they speak, nevertheless place human favor before the divine presence, he therefore said not only “from God” but also added “before God.”

This too must be noted: At the end of this chapter mention is made of the whole Trinity: “from God,” of the Holy Spirit; “before God,” of the Father; “in Christ,” of the Son.

[Note: [Col. 0430D] In the autograph margin it reads here: “chapter VII.”]

**(Chapter III.)** “Do we begin again,” etc. Earlier he had said: “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph,” and the words that follow, up to where he says: “We are not adulterating the word of God.” Immediately he added: “Do we begin again,” etc.

Earlier he had said great things, and such things that he might appear to be puffed up. Therefore he says, “Do we begin again,” lest he appear to be puffed up. It is as though he were saying: We do not praise ourselves to you for the purpose of seeking your commendation, but so that you may be withdrawn from the teaching of false teachers.

But why does he say “again”? Because in the First Epistle he had said many things with that intention—for example: “Am I not free?” or “Do only I and Barnabas?” and so forth. Therefore he says “again,” as though he were saying: We do not display our authority for the sake of our own praise, but for the sake of your salvation, so that the pseudo-apostles, to whom you have given your faith, may be shown to possess no authority, and so that you may abandon them and follow me.

Some wish this passage to be pronounced interrogatively, where he says, “Do we begin” [Note: [Col. 0430D] This is how it is read in the Vulgate.], etc. They think this especially because the Apostle adds: “Or do we need, as some do,” etc., as though he were saying: We do not need them.

Those whom grace, reputation, or familiarity commends do not need to be commended by the letters of others. Conversely, those whom nothing of this kind commends need such letters. The apostles, because they were commended by grace, the performance of miracles, the power of signs, and the sincerity of their preaching, did not need commendation. The pseudo-apostles, by contrast, because they lacked all these things, needed commendation.

The Lord speaks of such people: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who devour widows’ houses” (Matthew 23:14), and so forth.

There are also some priests and bishops established in the Church whom neither reputation nor teaching commends; therefore they need the praise of another so that they may be commended.

“To you, or from you.” He says “to you” because the Corinthians were being commended by the letters of others; “from you” because they were being commended by the Corinthians to others. By these words it is shown that those men traveled here and there so that they might take away not only people’s possessions but also their salvation. The apostles, on the contrary, not only did not take away their possessions but also brought them salvation.

Our letter is you, etc. For a letter is a sign of salvation. The Corinthians were indeed a letter in the hearts of the apostles, because their memory was continually present in them, and they ceaselessly desired their salvation; hence, in the First Epistle: “You are the seal of my apostleship” (1 Cor. IX, 2). And rightly are those called a letter whose memory is continually in the hearts of others, who also ceaselessly desire their salvation.

Which is known and read, etc. He rightly says, “by all people,” because it was known to everyone that they had believed when those men preached to them. Or: “You are a letter of Christ, delivered by us,” because you believed when we preached and received the Holy Spirit: “not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God.” That which is destroyed and erased is said to be committed to ink; that which remains, however, is committed to the Spirit of the living God. Faith, because it is perpetual, and the things promised by the apostles, are commended by the Spirit; but the teaching of the pseudo-apostles, because it is transitory, is commended by ink. In these words he distinguishes the true and false preachers of the Law and of grace.

Not on stone tablets. In these words the Apostle refers to the Law. For the Old Law was written on stone tablets, whose breaking signified the abolition of the written Law. And rightly on such a material, because they were to remain in hardness of heart. But did the Law itself intend this? No. But because it was going to happen, it was foreshadowed.

But on tablets of fleshly hearts. He calls the tablets “tablets of the heart” and “fleshly.” And rightly so, because flesh perceives, while the heart discerns. By these tablets, therefore, the merit and dignity of those who were to believe in Christ were signified. For there was a difference between the one and the other: to the former the Law was given outwardly, to terrify; to the latter, inwardly, to justify. The former, whether they wished it or not, were under the Law so that they might not be punished; the latter were willingly under the Law so that they might be justified.

And just as their hardness of heart is signified here by the name “stone,” so in what follows their blindness of heart is signified by the name “veil.” The difference between the preachers of this Law and of that Law is as great as the difference between the two Testaments. Hence, in what follows, the Apostle says that he preached a greater mystery and possessed a glory even greater than Moses.

Then he continues: But we have such confidence, etc. He shows what sort of confidence he had toward God through Christ when he adds: “Not that we are sufficient to think anything,” etc. It must certainly be understood that, according to the present ordering of things, unless we are governed by God, we cannot subsist, much less be saved. And if we cannot even think anything good, much less can we accomplish it—especially since he himself says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5). If no capacity for any good thought can exist in us, then much less can there be capacity for perfecting anything.

When he says, “Not that we are sufficient,” etc., the sense is as though he had said: We, few and uneducated as we are, could not convert and draw the world to the faith unless he were helping us. It should also be observed that he prefaced his words with humility because he was about to say something great. Since he had said, and was about to say, great things, lest he appear to exalt himself and seek his own glory, and thus remove the charge of arrogance, he first spoke humbly: “We have,” he says, “such confidence,” etc.

When he says, “Our sufficiency is from God,” this means that all our ability comes from him, who also made us competent ministers of the New Testament. For when he says that he and those like him are competent, he indicates the pseudo-apostles, since some of them were so enamored of the Jewish sect that they taught that the Law was to be observed in a fleshly manner. The sense is: We are ministers of the New Testament, not of the Old, as Moses was, or as those are who teach the fleshly observance of the Law. Therefore he added: “Not of the letter, but of the spirit,” that is, serving not the letter of the Law but the spirit of grace.

Why not? “Because the letter,” he says, “kills.” But one may ask why he said that the letter kills when he added that the spirit gives life. Perhaps someone might say that he meant the one commandment of the Decalogue which says, “Remember to keep the Sabbath day,” since one who observes the Sabbath in a fleshly manner dies. But who is so ignorant as to say that the letter kills because of this one commandment? Therefore he says this because of the whole Law. For what does he mean elsewhere when he says: “I would not have known covetousness” (Rom. VII, 7), etc.? And: “Taking occasion, sin,” etc.? The same is meant here when he says that the letter kills.

It kills because it can command but cannot help. For when it commands that evil not be done, although it is done, and that good be done, although it is not done, it kills. Such a Law had to be given to the proud, who trusted in their own powers and believed that they could be saved by their own effort, so that, enclosed and constrained by this Law, they might seek the grace by which they would be saved. The letter kills because, while it merely commands, it brings death; but the spirit gives life because it not only commands but also helps, for it justifies sinners themselves. The former merely demands a hearer; the latter seeks a doer.

[Note: [Col. 0431D] In the author’s own manuscript margin, chapter VIII is marked here.]

Then he continues: But if the ministry of death, etc. Here Faustus the Manichaean pricks up his ears, for he called the Law evil, to the extent of calling Moses himself evil. He says that unless the Law were evil, the Apostle would not call it “a ministry of death.” But he did not attend to the Apostle’s intention or understand his meaning. For the one who calls the Law a ministry of death says elsewhere: “The Law indeed is holy” (Rom. VII, 12), etc. He is not contradicting himself, even though the words appear to clash.

The Law is called a ministry of death because, while it reveals sin, it increases covetous desire. There are three stages: it reveals sin, increases covetous desire, and makes even those who recognize it commit a graver offense, since transgression is greater when committed knowingly. Hence he says elsewhere: “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. IV, 15). Therefore he says: “If the ministry of death was in glory.” And as though asked what that glory was, he explains it, saying that the children of Israel could not gaze, etc. The Book of Exodus makes this sufficiently clear when it says: “Because Moses’ face was made radiant from his converse with God” (Exod. XXXIV, 29), etc.

If, therefore, this was a ministry of death, much more is the ministry of the Spirit. But since we know what that glory was, we must now see what this glory is. They could not look upon the glory of Moses’ face because they were sinners and were going to remain in unbelief. This is the glory which the apostles saw on the mountain (Matt. XVII, 4; Mark IX, 1; Luke IX, 28)—namely Peter, James, and John. To show that it was incomparably greater than the former, when Moses and Elijah withdrew, Jesus alone remained in glory.

Then he continues: For if the ministry of condemnation is glory [Note: [Col. 0433D] The Vulgate reads: “For if the ministry of condemnation.”], etc. It should be noted that he calls both the ministry of condemnation and the ministry of justification glorious. For if the Law, which justly punished even its transgressors, possessed great glory, merit, and dignity, grace possesses incomparably greater glory, merit, and dignity, since it justified those transgressors of the Law who had become deserving of death.

For even that which was glorified [Note: [Col. 0433D] The Vulgate reads: “glorified.”], which became glorious, etc. Faustus again pricks up his ears, asserting that the Law was evil. He says that, to show that the Apostle had not truly said that the Law had been glorified, the Apostle therefore added: “For even that which was glorified.” He does not consider that, if the Law were evil, a greater glory would not be compared with its glory, nor would it punish its transgressors, since they would not exist.

Therefore, we must observe how carefully the Apostle spoke. He did not say merely: “Nor that which was glorified,” but added: “In this respect,” as though he had said: The Law had glory, but in its own time; in comparison with this present respect, however, its glory is not glory. For example, the moon also has the glory of light during the night; but when the sun has risen, although it does not lose its light, it seems to lose its glory.

For if that which was made void was through glory, etc. Note that the Law is said to be made void, not through abolition, but through improvement and increase, like infancy and childhood in relation to youth, or a lamp lit during the night in relation to the brightness of the sun, and similar things.

It should also be known that there are certain things in the Law which must be interpreted exactly as they are written, such as the Decalogue itself. Whoever interprets it allegorically opens the door to vices, because he destroys every moral improvement. Other things must be interpreted only historically; still others must be interpreted in both ways. But whether you understand the Law in one way or in both, it is nevertheless made void, because its meaning is changed, and what is required is not the Law commanding but grace helping.

The good things also that the Law promises are made void because they are temporal and transitory; but the things grace promises are heavenly and spiritual, and for that reason they will also remain forever. Therefore he says: “Much more that which remains is in glory.”

[Col. 0433D] [Note: [Col. 0433D] In the author’s own manuscript margin, chapter IX is marked here.]

Then he continues: Therefore, having such a hope—namely, that the ministry of the Spirit is much more glorious—we use great confidence, trusting in him who made us competent ministers. Having this hope, we use great confidence, so that he does not speak to us, as Moses placed a veil over his face so that the children of Israel might not gaze upon his face (Exod. XXXIV, 33), with a veil interposed; rather, with the veil cast aside, we hear him speaking openly. Therefore, we have received the greater dignity insofar as we hear God himself speaking.

For they could not hear a servant speaking unless a veil had been interposed; but we have been deemed worthy to hear the Son of God himself speaking. By these words the Apostle wishes to show that we, who have received such great dignity from God, ought to repay him in kind—that is, we should strive to serve him with greater fervor in proportion as we have received greater dignity from him.

It should also be known that he had begun to speak of the difference between the Law and the preachers of grace—both theirs and his—and he continues in the intention he had begun. Then he continues: But their minds were hardened. They remained hardened as long as the hardness remained: “until this present day.” He says this because, when the Apostle wrote or sent this letter, a large part of that people still remained in unbelief.

And to show that the veil by which Moses’ face was covered signified their hardness of heart, he therefore added: “But the same veil remains unremoved in the reading of the Old Testament.” But because this veil is revealed in Christ, he therefore added: “For it is made void in Christ”—that is, in faith in Christ, because Christ is the end of the Law. And this is what he says below: “But when he shall have turned to the Lord.” This turning is to be understood as faith in Christ and confession. For to turn to God is to believe in Christ; therefore Christ is also God.

When he says: “As long as Moses is read,” etc., this is what he says in the Epistle to the Romans: “Blindness in part has happened in Israel” (Rom. XI, 25). What follows—“But when he shall have turned,” etc.—is what he says there: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter,” etc.

Then he continues: “But the Lord is the Spirit.” No one is unaware that the Holy Spirit is God. These words also show that Christ gave the Law through the Holy Spirit, which is called both “Spirit” and “spiritual.” For this Law is not seen by the eyes but grasped by the mind; it is not heard by the bodily ears but understood by the heart. Nevertheless, it is uncertain to which Person he wished to refer when he says: “The Lord is the Spirit,” because the Father is called Spirit, and so is the Son.

Then he continues: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom,” as though he had said: Freedom is not in that Law which was written on stone, or which is covered by a veil, or whose glory is passing away; it is in the Law which is spiritual.

[Col. 0434D] It must certainly be understood that true freedom exists where charity is perfect. Hence blessed Pope Gregory says that true freedom exists where there is no pleasure in sinning. Therefore the person who is restrained from sin by fear does not enjoy this freedom, because, if he could sin with impunity, he would sin altogether. His very will therefore testifies that he does not sin for this reason: he recognizes that he cannot sin with impunity.

It should also be understood that this person does not enjoy this freedom, nor does the person who does good out of fear.

[Note: [Col. 0433D] The preceding remarks are highly worthy of note, namely because they reveal what this eminent man thought, many centuries ago, concerning the necessity of charity toward God and the servile fear involved in the remission of sins. [Col. 0434D]]

[Col. 0435A] Then he continues: But we. He speaks of himself and his companions, as though he had said: They have a veiled face, but we have an unveiled face—that is, an illumined one—contemplating the glory of the Lord; that is, contemplating through a mirror or from a mirror. The Greek expression used at this point does not have this ambiguity, but has the following sense, as though he had said: “Contemplating,” that is, beholding from afar.

And this is what follows: “From glory to glory of grace” [Note: [Col. 0435D] The word “of grace” is not found in the Vulgate text.]; or, from the glory of sons to the glory of the likeness of God, so that, as John says, “We may see him as he is” (1 John III, 2).

Then he continues: “As from the Spirit of the Lord”—with “led” understood—as though he had said: We are led as it is fitting that God should lead us. Here one must carefully consider what great dignity will be ours when we arrive, since such grace is granted to us that each one of us receives the pledge of the Holy Spirit.

(CAP. IV.) [Note: [Col. 0435D] In the author’s own manuscript there is here a sign which seems to indicate the beginning of a chapter.]

Then he continues: Therefore, having this ministry. He calls the ministry the office of preaching, concerning which he said above that he made us competent ministers. And lest this appear to be attributed to their own merits, he added: “According to the mercy which we have received,” as though he had said: We undertook the office of preaching not through our merits but through his compassion. Therefore, in the afflictions and persecutions that befall us, we do not fail.

Those who fail under afflictions are the ones who do not undertake the office of preaching according to mercy, but preach according to their own desire.

Then he continues: But we renounce the hidden things of shame. Shame pertains to disgrace. For it is exceedingly dishonorable and disgraceful to sin after having received the faith of Christ. The Apostle speaks as though he had said: Not only do we not fail, but we renounce the hidden things of shame; that is, we extinguish within ourselves not only wicked actions but also wicked and dishonorable thoughts.

It should be understood that these words appear to be narrative, although the sense of exhortation can be understood beneath them. Therefore those who pass over to the faith of Christ are admonished not only to reject wicked deeds from themselves but also to extinguish shameful thoughts.

Then he continues: Not walking in cunning. To walk in cunning is to remove the meaning of the word of God and introduce a human meaning.

Then he continues: By the manifestation of truth. The manifestation of truth is opposed to cunning, or adulteration, just as truth is opposed to falsehood or lying. It should be noted that he declares himself so firmly to be an advocate of truth that he was known to the consciences of all people—that is, not only of the good but also of the wicked—as preaching the Gospel of Christ in truth. For even those who were unwilling to accept his preaching understood that he preached truthfully, since he gave no one any opportunity to suspect anything evil about him: he did not preach for profit or for human praise.

He did not preach for profit because he accepted nothing from them; nor did he preach for human praise because he mortified himself.

A great point follows: “Before God.” It would have been significant if he had said this only about human beings; but because human beings can be deceived, he added something incomparably greater. Certain and confident that he had preached the Gospel in the manifestation of truth, he invoked God as a witness to confirm his claim.

[Note: [Col. 0436D] In the author’s own manuscript margin, chapter X is marked here.]

But if it is also veiled, etc. Above he had said that he did not walk in cunning or adulterate the word of God, but preached in the manifestation of truth, so that he commended himself to the consciences of all, even before God. And because someone might reply: Why do you say that your preaching is commended to the consciences of all people, when not all who heard it believed?—he answers: “But if it is also veiled,” etc.

Do not be troubled by my saying that my preaching is commended to the consciences of all, even though not all have believed. For although the Gospel is veiled, it is veiled in those who did not believe; but in those who believed, it is manifest because God has revealed it.

And wishing further to show in whom it is veiled, he added: “In whom the god of this age.” Here the Manichaean pricks up his ears and understands the god of this age to be the devil or evil. For he asserted that there were two natures, good and evil: the good from God, the evil from the devil. Hence he also maintained that Moses had served the devil, saying that the Law had been given by the devil because it produces wrath.

But it should be understood that the devil is called the god of this age in the same way that the Psalmist says: “The demons are the gods of the nations” (Ps. XCV, 5), and Paul says: “Whose god is their belly” (Phil. III, 19). This shows that neither the belly, nor the demons, nor even the devil is called God except as “the god of this age”; or he is called the ruler of worldly people—not because they are human beings, but because they are wicked.

But since this interpretation is close to error, we should understand the true God and distinguish the words in this way: “In whom God”—that is, the Almighty, Creator, and True God—“has blinded,” etc. And if it seems harsh to anyone that God is said to have blinded them, let him observe that elsewhere he says: “I have come so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John IX, 39); and Paul says: “God handed them over” (Rom. I, 24), etc.

God is said to have illumined or not handed them over when he delivers them; and he is said to blind them when he does not deliver them. But those whom he saves from this lost mass, he saves by gratuitous mercy; those whom he condemns, he condemns by his most hidden and perfectly just judgment.

So that the illumination of the Gospel might not shine upon them, etc. That is, so that they might not be illumined by believing in the light of the Gospel. Whose Gospel? Of glory. Whose glory? Of Christ. Which Christ? He who is the image of God, who is the form or character of God, as in the saying: “Who, being the radiance of glory” (Heb. I, 3), etc.

His radiance is called his image because he differs from the Father in nothing, so that whoever sees the Son also sees the Father, as he himself says: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV, 9).

For we do not preach ourselves, etc.; that is, not for our own sake but for the sake of Jesus Christ—that is, out of love for him, because we do not preach for profit or gain. For although the pseudo-apostles preached Jesus, they did not preach for his sake, because they taught for the sake of profit or their own praise.

But we are servants for Christ, etc. He was so humble that he called himself a servant. He also used “servants” for “ministers”; but, to speak more humbly, he said “servants.” When he says “for Jesus,” he means “out of love for Jesus,” showing that he did not call himself a servant because of his own dignity or their merits.

It should be understood that the saints sometimes avoid honors lest they be exalted, and sometimes seek them in order to be imitated, as the Apostle does here. For when he calls himself a servant and, below, a little one, elsewhere he says: “In what anyone dares—in foolishness I speak” (2 Cor. XI, 21), where he also says that he was caught up to the third heaven. Why does he do this, unless to be imitated? It should also be noted that he praises himself in order to exclude the false apostles; for if he had kept silent about himself, he would have commended them.

For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” etc. He calls the hearts of unbelief—which they themselves once possessed by remaining in unbelief—“darkness”; but he calls the doctrine of spiritual understanding “light.” The sense is: Concerning these darknesses he said, that is, he commanded the light of spiritual doctrine to shine forth; or, from the darkness of the written Law, he commanded spiritual understanding to proceed.

Why this is so, he makes clear when he says: “For the illumination of knowledge,” that is, so that we might illumine others with the same doctrine [Note: [Col. 0437D] In the author’s own manuscript: “that he might illumine me,” which we have considered an error requiring correction] “in the face of Christ”—that is, in the place or person of Christ. For “face” is used for “person”; hence in certain copies [Note: [Col. 0438D] Namely, in the Greek copies.] “person” is found instead of “face.”

But we have this treasure, etc. The Apostle proceeds to show why he had earlier called himself a competent teacher and why he endured persecutions. He does this against the pseudo-apostles, who were saying that he possessed neither merit nor faith and suffered persecutions for that reason.

He therefore calls spiritual understanding a treasure, and fragile bodies earthen vessels. The sense is: We have a treasure, etc.; that is, we carry spiritual understanding in fragile bodies. Hence it often happens that we become weak precisely where we save others.

Why? So that, insofar as we carry divine mysteries in fragile bodies, the surpassing greatness of God’s power may be shown all the more clearly. And rightly is spiritual understanding displayed by the image of a treasure: just as a treasure is not revealed to people by whom it is possessed, so spiritual understanding is implanted in the hearts of the faithful but concealed from unbelievers.

“In all things,” whether places or times—for much may be understood—“we suffer tribulation,” that is, affliction; but “we are not distressed,” because we are enlarged by hope of the future life.

“Aporiamur” is derived from the Greek word *aporia*, meaning “we are anxious.” The sense is: We are anxious, but we are not abandoned—that is, we are not forsaken by God. In certain copies one finds: “We suffer want, but are not abandoned,” because we are fed by God the shepherd.

We suffer persecution from evil and wicked people, but we are not abandoned by God. We are cast down by the powerful and the exalted; we are hurled headlong as though from a mountain or a roof, so that we might be destroyed; but we do not perish, because we are not destroyed for the sake of your salvation.

That these men endured all the things mentioned above and were nevertheless believed to be joyful is made clear by the Book of the Acts of the Apostles, where it is written: “They went forth rejoicing” (Acts V, 41), etc. And when Paul and Silas had been scourged and thrown into prison, and their feet had been fastened in stocks or bonds, they remained all the more joyful and glad in praising God.

Always carrying about the dying of Jesus (Acts XVI, 25), etc. What does all this mean except that he says, in other words: We are prepared to die for Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may be manifested in our bodies—that is, so that we may pass over into immortality? It should be understood that Jesus dies, is crucified, and rises again daily in his members, and that his members are given life in him.

[Note: [Col. 0438D] In the author’s own manuscript margin, chapter XI is marked here.]

He pursues the same meaning at greater length, saying in other words: For we who live are always, etc. He says “for Jesus” and means “for the body of Jesus,” because the Church is the body of Jesus: “so that the life of Jesus,” etc.—that is, so that we may pass over into immortality.

Therefore death is at work in us, etc. He seems to say: While we preach life to you, because you are alive, we stir up against ourselves the savagery and persecution of both the Gentiles and the Jews, to such an extent that we are dragged toward death.

It may also be delivered as a rebuke, so that the sense is: “Therefore death is at work in us,” etc.? No. That is, we will not always die while you live. He speaks against those who had given their allegiance to the pseudo-apostles, who said that the Apostle had no authority and suffered persecution for that reason, as though he had said: Will your preachers always live while we die? No. The order will be changed: those who now live will die, and we who are dying will live.

Then he continues: Having the same spirit of faith—that is, the spirit of the Fathers. When he says “the same,” he intends the patriarchs and prophets, and all through whom sacred doctrine was administered, to be understood. By these words he shows that he too is saved by the faith by which the Fathers were saved, because they believed that what was future, whereas these men believed that it had already happened.

He wished to confirm his account by an example, and therefore added: “As it is written: I believed, and therefore I spoke” (Ps. CXV, 10). David was speaking, but he was speaking what he believed, since no sane person wishes to affirm to others what he himself has not believed.

Then he continues: And we also believe, etc. The sense is: Because we believe, we speak what we believe.

And as though someone had asked, “What do you believe, since you also say that you speak?” he answered: Knowing that he raised Jesus. There were some among the Corinthians who doubted the resurrection, and therefore he speaks about it against them. He remains engaged in this argument for some time, against those whom he had addressed in the First Epistle.

In what he says—“who raised”—there is no contradiction whether you understand the Father or the whole Trinity.

Therefore, to show that the resurrection celebrated in the Head will also be celebrated in the members, and that what preceded in the Head will also follow in the members, he added: “He will also raise us with Jesus.” And to show that those whose faith is one will also have one dwelling together in the house of peace, he added: “And will establish you with us.”

Then he continues: For all things [are endured] for you, with “I endure” understood. Why he would endure these things for them, he explains: “So that grace,” he says, “abounding through many,” etc. The sense is as though he had said: God does not wish anyone to be deprived of his gifts, nor does he wish anyone to perish; he does not rejoice in the destruction of those who are dying, but rather wishes to save everyone.

Therefore, so that many acts of thanksgiving might be offered to him, he himself bestowed many gifts upon those who believe and promised them to those who would believe. Thus, just as it is exceedingly dishonorable and disgraceful for a person to prepare a large and sumptuous dinner, invite many people, and finally have only a few guests, so it is exceedingly dishonorable and unworthy for God to have only a few praisers.

For this purpose—that is, to acquire many—the Apostle labors daily. Hence we must consider how great his merit and dignity were, since he even regarded temporal life as of little account in order to acquire many who would give thanks to God.

Then he continues: For this reason—that is, because of faith in the resurrection, or certainly so that we may acquire many—we have not failed amid afflictions and sufferings.

But because someone might say, “How do you not fail when many among you are being destroyed?” he therefore added: “But although our outward man is corrupted,” etc. The sense is: The more the outward man is worn down, the more the inner man is renewed [Note: [Col. 0439D] The author’s own manuscript reads “is revealed,” which may well be correct, since, so to speak, when the outer shell is worn away, what is inside is revealed more clearly.]; and the greater the dangers suffered by the exterior man, the greater the gains it acquires and the greater the rewards it accumulates for the interior man.

Then he continues: For that which is momentary and light in the present, etc. What does “in the present” mean? Bodily tribulations, persecutions, and similar things. They are rightly called momentary and light because they quickly pass away and, as it were, pass by in an instant. Nevertheless, they produce an eternal weight of glory beyond measure.

He says “beyond measure” because there is no comparison. No earthly thing can in any way be compared with heavenly things, temporal things with eternal things, or perishable things with things that remain.

It should certainly be understood that he preserves the metaphor when he compares something momentary and light with the weight of glory. The meaning of this passage is also contained in the Epistle to the Romans, where he says: “For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison” (Rom. VIII, 18), etc.

He also shows which tribulations produce the weight of glory when he adds: “While we do not contemplate the things that are seen,” etc. The sense is: We are not concerned with temporal things, which pass away, but with eternal things, which remain. He explains this when he adds: “For the things that are seen are temporal,” etc. The sense is: Content only with what is necessary, we direct the mind’s gaze toward what will remain forever.

[Note: [Col. 0439D] In the author’s own manuscript margin, chapter XII is marked here.]

(CAP. V.) Then he continues: If our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, etc. He calls mortal bodies an earthly house. “Not made by hand” refers to the same bodies, but now made immortal.
