The sense is: We persevere in persecutions and sufferings and endure them cheerfully because we are certain of the resurrection, since, if we depart from this life, we will pass into immortality.

When he says, “An eternal house not made by hand,” he intends the earthly house to be understood as made by hand. It is appropriately called made by hand because mortal bodies are formed through visible growth. The heavenly one, however, is called not made by hand because the same bodies will be made spiritual invisibly by the Spirit of God.

Then he continues: For in this also [Note: [Col. 0439D] The Vulgate reads: “For even in this.”]—that is, for this purpose or because of this—we groan, desiring to be clothed over with our dwelling, which is in heaven—that is, with immortality.

He explains how we are to be clothed over: “provided that we are clothed with Christ” [Note: [Col. 0440D] The Vulgate does not contain the word “Christ.”]. Hence he himself says: “As many of you as have been baptized in Christ” [Note: [Col. 0440D] Gal. III, 27. The Vulgate reads: “For as many of you as have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ,” etc.], etc.

We are also to be clothed with faith and pious works, and not to be found naked of these.

Then he continues: For we who are in this tabernacle—that is, in the mortal body—groan, being weighed down by persecutions and various calamities, because we do not wish to be unclothed—that is, to deny the faith and thereby be naked of Christ—but to be clothed over—that is, to be granted not only immortality but also transformation.

Hence he says elsewhere: “We shall all rise” (1 Cor. XV, 51), etc. Then he continues: “So that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life”—that is, so that life may swallow up death.

But when will these things be fulfilled? When “this mortal has put on immortality” (ibid., 53), etc. And to show who grants them such a gift of perseverance, he added: “He who accomplishes this very thing in us is God,” with “is” understood.

Then he continues: “Who gave us the pledge of his Spirit,” namely, so that he might make us more certain of the promises.

[Note: [Col. 0440D] In the author’s own manuscript margin, chapter XIII is marked here.]

Then he continues: “Daring [Note: [Col. 0440D] The Vulgate reads: “being confident.”], therefore.” The sense is: Amid various dangers and countless adversities, we are always confident and at rest.

“For while we are in the body,” etc. But a question arises: How can he say, “We are pilgrims away from the Lord,” when he himself says in the Acts of the Apostles: “In him we live and move and are” (Acts XVII, 28)? If this is true, how then are we pilgrims away from the Lord?

We are pilgrims because, although he is present with us, we do not see him. But when we have come to him and see him openly, we will be pilgrims away from the body. He explains this when he adds: “For we walk by faith,” etc.

Then he continues: We are confident, and we have a good will—that is, we are more willing to depart from the body and be present with the Lord. And why are we confident? Because we also have a good will [Note: [Col. 0441D] In the author’s own manuscript margin, the Twelfth Sunday after Pentecost is marked here.].

But from where did the Apostle derive such confidence? From good will, certainly, and from pious works. Therefore this statement cannot belong to the imperfect, who know that they have an evil will and a bad case in judgment. Hence he says elsewhere: “To be dissolved and to be with Christ is much better” (Phil. I, 23), etc.

Then he continues: And therefore we strive—that is, we labor and fight, and all our effort strives toward this: whether absent or present, to be pleasing to him. He calls the mortal “absent,” and the immortal “present.”

It should be understood that, if the discipline of ecclesiastical peace is maintained, we can fulfill both conditions: that is, please him both while absent and while present. For those who please him here will not displease him there. Hence he also explains what he said above: “We are pilgrims away from the Lord.” For just as, while absent, we are pilgrims away from him, so, while present with him, we will be pilgrims away from the body.

[Col. 0441C] [Note: [Col. 0441D] In the author’s own manuscript margin, chapter XIV is marked here.]

Then he continues: For we must all be manifested before the tribunal. It must certainly be understood that, in proportion to the greatness of the one who presides, there must be fear and examination of the mind. And lest perhaps anything be added, he added: “of Christ,” because “the Father judges no one” (John V, 22), etc.

By these words the Apostle also demonstrates what he says elsewhere: “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. X, 31).

Then follows: “That each may receive what is proper to the body,” etc. Here one must inquire most carefully why he says that each person will receive what is proper to the body, since many things that can exclude us from the heavenly kingdom are done without the activity of the bodily members, by the consent of the mind alone, as in the passage: “The fool said in his heart” [Col. 0441D] (Psalm 13:1), etc. But there is no contradiction, for it may be resolved thus: each person will receive those things which he did while in the body, or while still placed in a mortal body. For as long as he remains in a mortal body, he can do things either for which he will be rewarded or for which he will be condemned. When he dies, he leaves the body, which nevertheless he will receive again at the end of the age. Yet he will no longer have the freedom to do good or evil, but only to receive what he did.

[Note: [Col. 0442D] In the autograph margin, chapter XV is marked here.]

Then follows: “Knowing therefore the fear of God, we persuade men”; that is, we impress this upon the hearts of men—namely, that they should correct their actions, abandon evil, and do what is good. If, therefore, we live otherwise than we preach, we are manifest to God. In saying this also, he touches on the matter he had begun to introduce, which he makes clearer when he adds: “And I hope that we are also manifest in your consciences.” As though he had said: “I know that the false apostles have said many bad things to you about us. For they say that we do not have as much authority or as much merit as they do, nor are we learned by those who followed the Lord, as they themselves are. They say this so that they may more easily withdraw you from apostolic teaching. But I am certain that you will believe your consciences more than their barking or their slanders.” He said this because he had given them no occasion to suspect anything evil about him: he did not preach for the sake of profit, since he accepted nothing from them; nor did he preach for the sake of human praise. For not only did he openly accept nothing from them, but he accepted nothing secretly either, so that he might be honored by the congregations and inwardly be regarded as deceitful and an impostor.

[Note: [Col. 0442D] In the autograph margin, chapter XVI is marked here.]

Then follows: “We do not commend ourselves again to you”; as though he had said: “We have already told you, and now we tell you again, that we are not saying this because we wish to commend ourselves, but for the sake of your salvation.” And as though someone had asked: “If you do not wish to commend yourself, why then do you say it?”—“And therefore we say it: to give you an occasion to glory on our behalf, so that you may have an answer against those who glory in appearance and not in the heart” (that is, an answer or something to say). For the pseudo-apostles gloried in their lineage, nobility, wisdom, and learning; but all their glory was outward, because they did not preach out of a desire to please God. The Apostle, however, announced great things about himself to them in order to exclude them; for if he remained silent about himself, they would appear to be the ones commended.

Then follows: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God,” etc. This passage may be understood in two ways. “Whether we are beside ourselves”—that is, if we preach to you in pride and exaltation, we are left to God; “or whether we are sober”—that is, if we preach in simplicity and sincerity, recognize that we are benefiting you, Corinthians. Alternatively: “Whether we are beside ourselves”—that is, while we contemplate great things, we are carried away to God; “or whether we are sober”—that is, temperate and moderate, preaching things small and humble, we are so for you.

Then follows: “The love of Christ urges us.” For just as the love of Christ raises certain minds to contemplate heavenly things, so also, through compassion and humility, it recalls them so that they may condescend to their neighbors. Then follows: “Judging this, that if one died for all.” The meaning is: Just as love drew Christ to suffering so that he might redeem us, so it also draws us to condescension. But what he says—“All have died”—may be understood in two ways. “They have died,” that is, they became mortal in Adam; [Col. 0443A] and therefore one died for all, in order to recall them to immortality. Or: all were dead in soul; and therefore one who was living—that is, dead to sin in the flesh—died in order to give them life. “So that those who live may no longer live for themselves”; that is, those who live as redeemed and renewed people should not live for themselves, meaning that they should not satisfy their own desires. Alternatively: “So that those who live,” through hope of heavenly promises, “may not live for themselves,” through hope of temporal things.

[Note: [Col. 0443D] In the autograph margin, chapter XVII is marked here.]

Then follows: “Therefore from now on we know no one according to the flesh.” He says “from now on,” that is, from the time when Christ rose and gave the pattern that those who live should not live for themselves; from that time we know no one according to the flesh. Why he said “according to the flesh” he makes clear when he adds: “And even if we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer.” Here Manichaeus pricks up his ears, denying that Christ assumed true flesh. He says that if Christ had possessed true flesh, the Apostle would by no means have said, “Even if we knew.” But blessed Augustine says: “It should be noted that the Apostle does not say, ‘Even if we suspected,’ but ‘we knew.’ One suspects a matter that one holds to be doubtful, not one that one knows.”

But here a question arises: why does the Apostle say, “Yet now we know him no longer,” when the Lord himself, rising from the dead, said to his disciples: “Touch me and see” (Luke 24:39), etc.? But there is no contradiction. For it must be known that in the divine Scriptures “flesh” is used both for mortality and for the truth of nature. Therefore Christ God has flesh according to the truth of nature, but he does not have it according to the mortality of weakness, because, “having risen from the dead, he dies no more” (Romans 6:9), etc.

If this can be understood of Christ, why did he say above, “We know no one according to the flesh”? Was he himself not in the flesh, or were those to whom he spoke not in the flesh? They were, and they were not, in the flesh. They were not, because they did not remain in hope of worldly things or temporal honors, since they understood that they would not remain here long; but because they hoped and believed that they would eventually pass over into immortality, they regarded what was certain under hope as though it had already happened.

He himself makes clear that a thing held under certain hope is regarded as though it had already happened, when he says: “If you have risen with Christ” (Colossians 3:1), etc. He did not mean that they had risen with the resurrection by which Christ himself rose; rather, their certainty under hope remained, because what had gone before in the Head would follow in the members. Again: “He saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal” (Titus 3:5), etc. Is that salvation of the resurrection which is prefigured in baptism accomplished in baptism itself? No. But although it is future, it is held through hope as though it had already happened.

A little earlier he had said: “From now on we know no one according to the flesh.” Why he said this he shows: “For even if we knew according to the flesh, we no longer know Christ,” etc.; as though he were saying in other words: “We do not know him according to the flesh, because we know him as new.” For this reason also we know no one according to the flesh, since the newness that exists in him in reality also exists in his members, though in them it is present in hope.

Of this newness he speaks when he adds: “If therefore anyone is a new creation in Christ.” He calls the ecclesiastical people a new creation: they are new either through the renewal of baptism, which they possess in reality, or through the renewal of the future resurrection, which they possess in hope; and the restoration of this latter is the renewal of baptism. It will then be perfect when the victorious have said: “Where, O death, is your victory?” (1 Corinthians 15:55), etc.

Then follows: “The old things have passed away”; that is, the hope of temporal things and earthly promises has passed away, because the old law promised temporal goods and earthly kingdoms; and therefore they are rightly said to have passed away. But now, because the grace of the Gospel promises not earthly but heavenly things, not temporal but eternal things, not transitory but abiding things, it therefore follows: “Behold, all things have become new.”

Then follows: “But all things are from God.” He says this beautifully: “All things are from God,” because although the passion of the cross properly pertains to the person of the Son, the work of our redemption and renewal belongs to the whole Trinity. Again: “All things are from God,” that is, both the new and the old, because both Testaments were given by him according to the variety and character of the times. Therefore the God of both Testaments is one. This is directed against those who said that the God of the New Testament was one and the God of the Old Testament another.

[Col. 0444C] Then follows: “Who reconciled us to himself through Christ.” The first man, once created, had been deceived by the cunning of the devil. But so that he might not perish forever, God sent his Son to reconcile him to himself, so that through him he might redeem the human being through whom he had also made the human being.

Then follows: “And he gave us the ministry of reconciliation.” He had said that he was reconciled; he also says that he received the mystery of reconciliation, since the order was such that he first sent his Son, who would redeem humanity and reconcile it to himself. After completing everything for which he had come, he took him up and, in his place, entrusted the apostles with the ministry of reconciliation—that is, the office of preaching. This happened when he said: “Go and teach” (Matthew 28:19), etc.

[Col. 0444D] Then follows: “For God was indeed in Christ”; that is, the Father was in the Son. But was he in the Son as he was in the patriarchs and prophets? No. Nor was he in him as he was in the angels, because in them he was present by grace, but in this one by nature. Hence Christ himself says: “The Father who remains in me, he does the works” (John 14:10); and again: “I and the Father are one” (John 17:11); and again: “He who sent me is with me” (John 8:29), etc.

Then follows: “Reconciling the world to himself.” He also calls the elect “the world,” of whom the Lord says: “I did not come to judge the world” (John 12:47), etc. For throughout the whole world there is a world: the world pursues the world, the defiled pursues the cleansed, the lost pursues the redeemed, the condemned pursues the saved. From this lost world comes the chosen world; hence the Lord says: “I chose you out of the world” (John 15:19), etc. “Not counting their trespasses against them”: freely and undeservedly, by the grace of baptism, he forgave them their sins, with no preceding merits.

Then follows: “And he placed in us the word of reconciliation.” This is what he had said above, “the ministry of reconciliation.” For this reason he adds: “Therefore we act as ambassadors for Christ,” that is, in Christ’s place.

Then follows: “Be reconciled to God.” But from what does this reconciliation arise? Clearly, from enmity. Yet sins, not nature, produced these enmities.

[Col. 0445B] Then follows: “He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us.” But one must ask why he says, “He made him to be sin,” when it is written of him: “He committed no sin” (Isaiah 53:9; 1 Peter 2:22), etc. The meaning is this: “He made him sin for us,” because he offered him as a sacrifice for our sins. For the victim that was offered for sin in the Old Testament was called “sin.” Again, “He made him sin for us,” because through the flesh—that is, through the likeness of sinful flesh—he condemned sin in us. Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “God, sending his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Romans 8:3), etc.

“So that we might become the righteousness of God in him”—that is, in the Church, which is his body, of which he himself is also the head. Note that he says “the righteousness of God.” For the Jews, because they sought their own righteousness, did not become the righteousness of God, since they were not subject to it. He says “the righteousness of God,” not ours, and “in it,” not in us; for just as he was made sin—not his own but ours—not in himself but in us, so we have been made his righteousness, not our own, and in it, not in ourselves.

Blessed Augustine says that in corrupt copies it is found written: “He who knew no sin,” etc.; but in more reliable copies: “He who knew no sin was made sin.” Yet the reading “Him who knew no sin,” if we consider what precedes, is not contradictory. Above he had spoken about the Father, saying: “God was in Christ,” and similar things, and of the Father he says: “He made.” But if one reads only, “He who knew no sin,” “was made” sounds better than “he made.”

Nevertheless, one must note why he says, “who knew no sin.” If he did not know sin, how did he accuse it confidently? We can say altogether that he both knew it and did not know it. He knew it through wisdom, but did not know it through experience. Whom ought the first man to have believed? He ought to have believed this one, so that he would not come to know sin through experience; for if he had not committed it, he would in no way have known it.

(CAP. VI.) [Note: [Col. 0445D] In the autograph margin, chapter XVIII is marked here.]

Then follows: “But as helpers,” etc. Above he had said that he had received the ministry and word of reconciliation, and therefore acted as an ambassador for Christ; for this reason he also showed that he had entreated them. He now begins to exhort them, so that he may fulfill his office. For he says: “But we are helpers,” namely, by praying, “and we exhort,” by admonishing.

Then follows: “That you do not receive the grace of God in vain.” Many receive the grace of God in vain. Those who join the effect of their will to divine inspiration do not receive grace in vain. Likewise, one who receives wisdom from God, if he labors in it in order to please God, does not receive God’s grace in vain. The same may be understood of faith and of the other things that a person receives from heaven.

For it must be understood that if a person had lost his own will, exhortation would be of no benefit; and if the will alone were sufficient, the same Apostle would certainly not say elsewhere: “His grace toward me was not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:10).

The Apostle wished to confirm his account by an example, and therefore he added—understand, “Isaiah said”: “At an acceptable time I heard you” (Isaiah 49:8), etc. He calls the acceptable time and the day of salvation the state of the present life, in which each person can work out his salvation. He himself explained what this time was when he added: “Behold, now is the acceptable time,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0445D] In the autograph margin, chapter XVIII is marked here.] “Behold, now” refers to the time of the Lord’s Incarnation, because the prophet had foretold it in the person of God the Father, as though he had said: “At an acceptable time,” that is, at the Incarnation of my Son. For God the Father had especially predestined that, at the time of the Incarnation of his only-begotten Son, he would grant grace and salvation to believers.

This saving time and day is followed by the night in which no one will be able to work. Concerning it the Lord says in the Gospel: “The night will come” (John 19:4), etc. Hence Solomon also says: “The sluggard, because of the cold, would not plow” (Proverbs 20:4), etc.; and again: “Go to the ant, O sluggard” (Proverbs 6:6), etc.

Then follows: “Giving no one any occasion for offense”; that is, neither the faithful nor the unfaithful—namely, Jews and Gentiles. He speaks of “any offense,” both in small matters and in great ones.

Then follows: “So that our ministry may not be reviled.” It would be reviled if they lived otherwise than they preached. The ministry of Christians is also reviled now if a Christian lives otherwise than is fitting.

Then follows: “But in everything let us show ourselves,” etc. Note that he does not say “in some things,” but “in everything.” Some people are diligent only in small good works, while others are diligent only in great ones; therefore he says, “in everything.” The minister of God shows himself in everything in such a way that he can please God. Therefore, whoever possesses wisdom, riches, or whatever else is given by God should be so diligent in these things that he may be able to please God.

Then follows: “In great patience.” Note that he does not say merely “in patience,” but “in great patience.” For where adversities are numerous, much patience is necessary. Patience is indeed a great virtue, by which the Corinthians were saved; for unless the Apostle had patiently endured them, after receiving them in such great offenses, they would have perished entirely. Through God’s patience, however, the world was saved.

Then follows: “In tribulations.” They were greatly afflicted, but they were rescued by God from their tribulations.

“In necessities.” It was necessary for them to preach the Gospel even amid tribulations; or by “necessities” he means the necessities of other matters.

“In distresses.” They were distressed by various persecutions, but were enlarged by hope of the heavenly kingdom.

Then follows: “In stripes.” Stripes are so called as though from *flagae*, because they are inflicted by a blast (*flatu*). That he was worn down by various stripes he himself makes clear when he says: “Three times I was beaten with rods” (2 Corinthians 11:25); and again: “Five times I received forty lashes less one” (ibid., 24).

“In prisons.” The book of the Acts of the Apostles shows that he himself was confined in prisons.

Then follows: “In riots.” A riot concerns citizens, whereas war concerns enemies. A riot is so called because citizens, disagreeing among themselves, fight one another. The aforementioned book makes clear that a riot arose against him.

Then follows: “In labors.” He showed himself to be God’s minister through labors, because he obtained food by the labor of his own hands, or because he labored greatly in evangelical preaching.

“In watchings.” He kept watch even through the nights while laboring to obtain food for himself; or certainly he kept watch because it was not enough for him to preach during the day unless he also spent the nights awake in preaching. Hence we read in the Acts of the Apostles that, when he prolonged his discourse through the night, a young man fell from the upper room and died (Acts 20:9).

“In fastings.” This means both voluntary fasts and necessary ones, and in both he gave thanks to God.

Then follows: “In purity,” not only of body but also of evangelical preaching. Because he maintained purity in both respects, he aroused many adversaries against himself, especially the pseudo-apostles.

“In knowledge.” Note that he numbers knowledge among the other virtues. Yet he does not mean the knowledge of human literature, which he criticizes in the First Epistle; rather, he means knowledge of the meaning of the Law and the Gospel.

“In long-suffering.” A person is called *longanimus* from *longanimitas*. He is called long-suffering because he has a long spirit for enduring many evils.

“In gentleness.” He showed himself to be a minister in gentleness because, although he rebuked sinners, he nevertheless added words of exhortation after their correction, so that he might draw them from bitterness to love of himself. For truly gentle is the person who provokes others to anger neither by frivolity of speech nor by agitation of mind.

“In the Holy Spirit” (understand: “let us show ourselves,” following his grace and fulfilling his will in everything).

Then follows: “In sincere love.” A person has feigned love when he abandons someone whom he says he loves while that person is in tribulation. The Apostle did not have such love, because he regarded all the losses and persecutions of others as his own; thus he himself says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Corinthians 11:29), etc.

Then follows: “In the word of truth.” Christ is the truth. Therefore, by “the word of truth” he means the word of evangelical preaching.

Then follows: “In the power of God.” This may be referred to what precedes, so that the meaning is: “Let us show ourselves in everything in the power of God,” that is, through his power, because we cannot do so by our own strength. Or it may be referred to what follows: “In the power of God, by the weapons of righteousness, let us be fighting on the right and on the left.”

Weapons are so called because they diminish the shoulders (*armos*), and there are two kinds: one by which the shoulder is protected, and another by which the enemy is struck. Since weapons are used both for good and for evil, he therefore adds: “of righteousness.” Thus by “the weapons of righteousness” he means an abundance of virtues.

By “the right” prosperity is customarily signified; by “the left,” adversity, according to the usage of sacred Scripture. Therefore, like a very strong soldier equipped with weapons and advancing among the ranks of the enemy, he struck down adversaries on every side, because he was neither lifted up by prosperity nor cast down by adversity.

What he meant by “on the right and on the left” he makes clear by adding: “through glory and dishonor.” To those who understood glory and honor in the Gospel, the Apostle declared that he too was blameless and truthful. Conversely, to those for whom the Gospel was disgraceful and dishonorable, he likewise showed himself blameless and truthful.

Then follows: “Through evil report and good report.” Report is so called because it travels through the ears by speech. There is report as long as a matter is not manifest; once it is manifest, it is no longer report but the fact itself. There is report of both good and evil things. To believers he was of good report, because they said that he possessed great merit; to unbelievers he was of evil report, because they said that he was a deceiver. But he himself walked unharmed between both parties, neither being lifted up by the praises of the former nor cast down by the slanders of the latter.

Then follows: “As deceivers and yet truthful.”

To believers they seemed so truthful and possessed of such great merit that they were thought to be gods; to unbelievers they seemed deceivers, that is, impostors. And what wonder, when it was said of the Lord: “We remembered that that deceiver, while he was still alive” (Matthew 27:63), etc.?

Then follows: “As unknown and yet known.” They were known to the faithful, who recognized that they possessed such great merit and dignity; but they were unknown to the unbelievers, who did not recognize what sort of men they were.

“As if dying,” etc. Augustine says: “The expression ‘as if’ applies to those matters in which there is no truth or which are transitory, just as if someone dreaming were to say, ‘I thought that I was as if in a certain place.’” They were as if dying because they were persecuted in such a way that they despaired of the hope of this present life.

“And behold, we live.” They lived because they were not extinguished, as the book of the Acts of the Apostles makes clear. For we read that when Paul came to Lystra and had been stoned so that he was thought to be dead, he rose and began to preach (Acts 4:18). Or they were “dying” because they were persecuted so severely that they thought they would yield; but they lived because they did not yield. For if they had yielded, their souls would have died.

“As chastened,” etc.—as above.

“As if sorrowful,” etc.; that is, they showed themselves severe in expression, but rejoiced in hope of the future life.

“As needy,” etc. They were needy because they were poor. They made many rich because they abounded in spiritual gifts. For *locuples* is derived from *loculus*. A *loculus* is a small purse. They were rich because they had many small purses—that is, spiritual gifts—with which they enriched others.

“As having nothing, yet possessing everything,” etc. This was glorious for the saints: to possess everything without anxiety and without the title of possession, so that they ruled not only over the things themselves but also over their owners, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, where they sold everything and offered the proceeds, etc. (Acts 6:34).

[Note: [Col. 0449D] In the autograph margin, chapter XIX is marked here.]

“Our mouth is open.” After he had said above that we know no one according to the flesh and had added why—namely, because, even if we knew Christ according to the flesh, we now know him no longer—and after he had also said that he had received the ministry of reconciliation, by which he acted as an ambassador for Christ, and had added admonition and exhortation through which the world is reconciled to God, he burst into praise of the Corinthians, saying: “Our mouth.” The meaning is: “Your correction, amendment, and salvation have made me so joyful that I cannot keep silent.”

“Our heart is enlarged.” The heart is enlarged in two ways: either through confidence in a good way of life or through hope of the resurrection. It is as though he were saying: “Your amendment and correction have made us so joyful that our heart has been enlarged and our mouth opened, so that we cannot keep silent.” Here it is shown that the obedience and correction of good subjects make teachers so joyful that they speak to them such things as they had not thought they would hear from them.

[Col. 0449C] “You are not restricted,” etc. These words show that evil hearers cannot harm good preachers who proclaim good things. Therefore the Apostle says: “You are not restricted in us,” as though he were saying: “If you have not corrected yourselves, this does not harm us, who preach good things, but you, who refuse to do them.”

And this is what he adds: “You are restricted in your own inward parts”; but you will have the same recompense (understand: “you will have it”). As though he were saying: “If you run the same course as we do, you will have the same recompense.” And as one who has the same recompense, and as a father admonishing his children, “be enlarged.” For just as we stretch out a sack if it cannot contain what is valuable, so the Apostle urges the Corinthians to be enlarged, so that they may become more capacious and may be able to contain the precious things he was about to say.

And therefore he says: “Be enlarged,” as though he were saying: “You are capacious, but become more capacious, so that you too may be able to contain them.” For he does not say “you,” but “you also,” as though he were saying: “We have already been enlarged so as to bring forth good things; you, too, be enlarged so as to receive them.”

Then follows: “And do not enter into partnership under the same yoke,” etc. A yoke is used as a figure for association, because oxen are yoked together by someone, and horses to a chariot. The meaning is: “Do not enter into partnership under the same yoke,” etc.; that is, do not enjoy association with unbelievers.

And wishing to confirm his account by comparisons and prophetic example, he added: “For what partnership has righteousness,” etc.? The Law preaches righteousness, which is contrary to iniquity. The meaning is: “What partnership does righteousness have with iniquity?” None. Thus there should likewise be no association between the faithful, etc.

What follows refers to what precedes: “Or what fellowship does light have with darkness?” Light preaches truth, and truth itself is light; this light drives away the darkness of error, and therefore there can be no fellowship.

“But what agreement does Christ have with Belial?” Belial is interpreted as “without a yoke.” It signifies the devil, who wished to be like God by refusing to bear his yoke. The Law, in figures and obscurities of the letter, preaches Christ, who drives the devil from the hearts of the faithful—the one who wished to be like God—and therefore there is no agreement.

“And what agreement does the temple of God have with idols?” It should be noted that nothing is more opposed to a Christian than idolatry and idols. For these customarily separate human beings from God and lead them to denial. Therefore, although all vices must be detested, this one especially must be detested, since it separates people from God.

For this reason he concluded by adding: “For you are the temple of the living God,” etc.; as though he were saying: “If, by believing, you are the temple of God, then those who do not believe are the temple of the devil; therefore take care lest through unbelief you become his.” He says “the temple of the living God” to distinguish it from dead temples.

Then follows: “For I will dwell,” etc. To confirm his argument, this outstanding preacher, faithful in word and truth, draws upon prophetic testimony. Here preachers are instructed to take care to confirm their own statements by examples from others.

But one may ask why he says, “I will dwell, and I will walk,” when God is everywhere and all things are in him. The meaning is this: He walks and dwells in the hearts of the elect when he causes them to progress from unbelief to faith and through increases in virtue. For just as the external human being has his feet, so also the inner human being has feet with which he can walk.

The journey from unbelief to faith and through increases in virtue is indeed a great one. It cannot be accomplished suddenly, but only through intervals of time. Yet it must be understood that only those make progress who are deemed worthy to enjoy his grace.

This is the general meaning; but one must consider what the specific meaning is. First of all, one must ask whether this is Christ’s voice, for the prophet was speaking in his voice when he said: “For I will dwell” (Leviticus 26:12), etc. But Jeremiah later shows how he would dwell. He was seen on earth and lived among human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0449] Jeremiah 31:9, 11. This text, which appears to be attributed to Jeremiah in the autograph, is Baruch 3:38.]

But the evangelist sets out more clearly how he did so, saying: “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14), etc.

“And I will be their God.” That he is God is likewise stated by Jeremiah: “This is our God, and no other will be reckoned beside him.”

[Col. 0451A] “And they will be my people.” He means the ecclesiastical people, that is, the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0451D] Again Jeremiah is cited in place of Baruch, who has this at 3:36.]

Isaiah says: “As I live, says the Lord, you will be clothed with all these things as with a garment” (Isaiah 49:18). If the elect are Christ’s garments and are clothed by him, then his people are the Church.

“Therefore come out,” etc.; as though he were saying: “If God dwells in you, and is your God, and you are his people, therefore come out from their midst”—not bodily, but mentally; not by moving from one place to another, but by devotion.

And as though they had asked how one should come out, he replied: “And do not touch what is unclean.” Hence Augustine says: “The Apostle explains in these words what he had said above: ‘Come out.’ But who touches what is unclean? Certainly the one who either commits what is unclean or gives assent to those committing it.”

And for this reason it is written in the Old Testament: “Whoever touches a dead body will be unclean” (Leviticus 11:24; Numbers 19:11; Deuteronomy 14:8). This was said because burying the dead is a work of mercy.

[Note: [Col. 0451D] In the autograph, *immundum* (“unclean”) is indeed written; but additions above and below the letters, together with several points indicating the obliteration of certain characters, seem to suggest a correction, so that *idolum* (“idol”), or perhaps *malum* (“evil”), should be read instead of *immundum*.]

[Col. 0451B] “And I will receive you.” The meaning is: “If unbelievers expel you, or if you yourselves depart, I will receive you.” The sense is like that of the passage: “They will put you out of the synagogues,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0452D] John, chapter 16, verse 2. The Vulgate reads *absque synagogis* (“outside the synagogues”).]

“And I will be a father to you”; as though he were saying: “If perverse and unbelieving parents expel you, you will have me as an everlasting father.”

“And you will be sons and daughters to me.” He says “sons and daughters” either because of both sexes or because of the strong and the weak.

“The Lord Almighty says this.” He added these words to confirm what precedes. For it is the custom of the prophets to add such statements so that they may make us more certain about what has gone before.

But who was the one who said this? Christ; therefore he is Almighty. That he is Almighty he himself makes clear: “Whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise” (John 5:19). Therefore the Son cannot do anything that the Father cannot do. But this Son is competent to say to the apostles: “With God all things are possible” (Matthew 19:26). And if all things are possible, then he too is Almighty, because he is God.

[Note: [Col. 0452D] In the autograph margin, chapter XX is marked here.]

(CAP. VII.) Then follows: “Therefore, having these promises.” He refers to the promises made above: that he himself would be our Father and that we would be his sons and daughters. Therefore, exhorting them, he continues:

[Col. 0451D] “Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh.” It must carefully be noted that he does not say merely “from defilement,” but “from every defilement,” because there are many kinds of defilement, invented both by the devil and by his members. Therefore, whoever desires to have God as his Father and wishes to be his son should abstain not only from every work of defilement but also from the very pleasure of the flesh.

But because many things are done by the consent of the mind alone and exclude us from fellowship with the sons of God, he therefore adds: “And of spirit,” that is, of the mind.

Then follows: “Perfecting holiness.” Here too he preserves an excellent order. He first set forth the promises; then he added the exhortation, saying: “Let us cleanse ourselves,” etc.; and after correction he urged that holiness be maintained, because holiness cannot exist where there is no purity.

This order is preserved in the divine Scriptures. Hence the Apostle James says: “Putting away all filthiness and abundance of wickedness” (James 1:21), etc. Hence the Psalmist: “Turn away from evil” (Psalm 36:27), etc. Hence the Lord says to Jeremiah: “Behold, I have appointed you to uproot” (Jeremiah 1:10), etc.

And because holiness cannot exist without the fear of God, he adds: “In the fear of God.” The evangelist shows that holiness does not exist without the fear of God when he says of Simeon: “He was righteous and devout” (Luke 2:25). For just as righteousness cannot exist without fear, neither can holiness.

Next: “Make room for us.” It is found more clearly in the Greek copies from which this was translated. For the verb used here has the sense as though the Apostle had said: “Be capacious toward us.” This can be understood in two ways. The sense may be: “Grasp the force of our words,” which also refers to what he said above, “Be enlarged”; or alternatively: “Make room for us,” that is, imitate our life and conduct.

And as though someone had asked, “What is your conduct, which we ought to follow?” he therefore adds: “We have wronged no one,” and so forth—as though he had said: “Bring this to mind; recall it to memory, because such was our conduct among you.”

By these words he indicates those whose false teachings had deceived them. For they had wronged them, because they had exercised authority over them; hence below he says: “You gladly put up with it if someone strikes you in the face” (2 Cor. 11:19–20). They corrupted them in the faith by teaching falsehood; they circumvented them, exhausting both their possessions and their salvation. And lest they themselves think that he was excusing himself in order to condemn them—for often, when someone excuses himself, he condemns others—he therefore adds: “I do not say this to condemn you,” as though he had said: “I am not excusing myself in order to condemn you; for one who spares does not condemn, but I say this for the sake of your salvation, so that you may not give your faith to those who deceived you.”

And because he wished to assure them that he had not excused himself for the purpose of condemning them, he recalled their former good deeds to their memory. For he says: “We have already said that you are in our hearts,” and so forth—as though he had said: “Recognize from your former good deeds that we did not say this for the purpose of condemning you; for we do not wish to condemn those whom we desire to have as companions in life and in death.”

By this example preachers are instructed that, when they rebuke their hearers, lest those hearers perhaps think that they have been rebuked out of bitterness or revenge, they should recall their former good deeds to them.

[Note: [Col. 0453D] In the autograph margin, “chapter XXI” is written here.]

Next: “I have great confidence in you,” and so forth. But from where did the Apostle derive this confidence? From the first Letter, after it had been sent and he had heard of their correction. Therefore he gloried confidently, saying: “I have much boasting on your account.”

Next: “I am filled with consolation,” and so forth—as though he had said: “I who was exceedingly saddened by your fall am now filled with consolation because of your correction, and I overflow with joy because of your amendment.”

By this example, too, preachers are instructed that, just as they are saddened by the fall of their people, so they should rejoice at their correction. It should also be observed how great was the charity in the Apostle’s mind: he regarded all adversities as insignificant in comparison with the correction of the Corinthians.

Next: “For when we had come to Macedonia,” and so forth. The Apostle relates to the Corinthians the persecutions and adversities that he endured for the salvation of others. But why does he do this? Clearly, in order to draw them to imitate him, so that, when they saw their teacher suffering for others, they would not be reluctant to endure adversities for his sake as well.

Teachers also commonly make known to their hearers the adversities that they suffer for various reasons. It should be understood that the flesh, like a brute animal, suffers amid adversities, whereas the rational spirit rejoices, because it is lifted up by the hope of the heavenly kingdom. His flesh had no rest, because as soon as one tribulation departed, another followed.

Next: “But we suffered every tribulation.” He says “every,” that is, much; for the book of the Acts of the Apostles makes clear what it was. For he says that, when they departed from Troas (Acts 16:11) and came to Macedonia (2 Cor. 1:16), which was nearer to Corinth, and from there Titus was to come (2 Cor. 2:13), many believed through their preaching. But they received the greatest consolation from a certain woman (Acts 16:14), who believed with her entire household.

Then it happened that the Apostle expelled the spirit of Python from the slave-girl of certain people—a spirit by which she practiced divination and brought great profit to her masters (ibid. 16). For this reason he was seized and, before Titus arrived, suffered great tribulation (ibid. 19).

Next: “Outwardly, battles,” that is, scourges and blows; “inwardly, fears,” namely because they were very anxious and feared that their hearers might be scandalized when they saw their teacher suffering such things.

Alternatively: “Outwardly, battles,” that is, the gathering of the faithful and the unbelieving; “inwardly, fears,” because, being placed in prison, they feared that they might be punished with more atrocious penalties, since there is no one who does not fear.

[Col. 0454A] Next: “But he who consoles the humble.” The sense is: God is the consoler of the humble, in accordance with the saying: “The Lord is near to those who are brokenhearted” (Ps. 33:19); and again: “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth” (Ps. 144:18). Therefore he who consoles the humble consoled us through the arrival of Titus, who became a participant in our tribulation; for it is a great consolation to have companions in tribulation.

Next: “Not only through his arrival.” The sense is: We were consoled not only because he became a participant in our tribulation, but also because he brought us good news about you—namely, your longing, as you advanced toward what was better; your weeping, in making your request [Note: [Col. 0453D] Perhaps “in asking,” or “in suffering,” or perhaps the text should stand as it is: passively, in enduring an attack.]; and also your zeal on my behalf.

It is as though he had said: “When he returned, he reported that, having recognized my charity, you also imitate me by defending me against those who had said many evil things about me.”

Next: “So that I rejoiced even more”; that is, I who had been greatly saddened by your fall rejoiced all the more because of your correction—or I rejoiced more over your correction than over the consolation brought by Titus.

Next: “If I saddened you, I do not regret it.” The sense is: I do not regret it because you, who were rebuked on account of the sin of others, corrected them and advanced toward what is better.

Next: “And if I did regret it,” and so forth—as though he had said: “If, because charity required it, it could have happened that I regretted having saddened you on account of the harshness of the first Letter, I would not regret it, because that Letter saddened you only for a time. And now I rejoice because of your correction.”

This is related to what follows: “Not because you were saddened,” and so forth. “But you were saddened according to God.” These are the words of one rejoicing. For the Apostle was greatly glad in his heart because everything he had done toward the Corinthians had reached their advancement and a praiseworthy conclusion. Therefore he says: “So that you may suffer no loss in anything,” as though he had said: “I rejoice exceedingly because everything has reached its intended improvement.”

The same thing should also now be done morally. For example, when someone begins to teach something good, he does not know the outcome; but if it happens to reach a praiseworthy conclusion, he must rejoice and give thanks to God.

Next: “For the sorrow that is according to God,” and so forth. Sorrow according to God exists because the sinner is ashamed and grieved, fearing that he may be punished by God. Consequently, having received consolation, he hastens toward correction. This also produces repentance leading to steadfast salvation, because it brings one to the remission of sins.

Next: “But the sorrow of the world produces death.” The sorrow of the world exists because the sinner too fears being stripped bare and [rectum, “the right/just one”; the reading is uncertain] [Note: [Col. 0454D] Perhaps “guilty,” or “guilt,” or perhaps the text should stand as it is: namely, he fears comparison with the upright or punishment by him.]. For he is sad because he fears being punished, either by an earthly judge or, if there is no earthly judge, by God. While such a person remains in a life-giving sorrow, receiving no consolation, he plunges himself into despair.

Alternatively, the sorrow of the world consists in earthly losses, or certainly in seeing the possessions of others without having acquired them.

Next: “For behold, this very thing, your being saddened according to God,” and so forth. In this sentence, as far as the rule of Latin is concerned, the conjunction “but” is superfluous; therefore it should be understood as having been placed in the sense of “and.” According to the rule of the Greek language as well, it has its proper composition and construction.

It should be carefully noted that, shortly before, he had said that he was saddened according to God. To show what fruit sorrow according to God had produced, he added the rest: “For behold, this very thing,” and so forth—as though he had said: “See that sorrow according to God produces great earnestness in you.”

And he says beautifully: “Earnestness,” because in repentance a person is very anxious lest he sin again; and where earnestness exists, sluggishness and negligence are driven away.

“But defense.” As though he had said: “Not only earnestness, but also defense—not merely of evil, since it produced confession of evil, but rather of the truth.”

“But indignation”: understand this as the indignation with which they were indignant against themselves on account of their sins; or certainly understand it as the indignation of others, which they aroused against themselves when they began to correct themselves.

Next: “But fear.” The person who is in repentance fears greatly lest his sin perhaps not have been forgiven him by God. Whether he means chaste fear or servile fear is uncertain; nevertheless, we can understand both.

Next: “But longing,” that is, longing to advance toward what is better.

Next: “But zeal,” namely, for good works—as though he had said: “You who until now were imitators of evil, strive to become zealous for what is good.”

Next: “But vengeance”: either the avenging of sins in themselves, or certainly the punishment of evil people; for one who punishes the wicked seeks not to destroy the good [Note: [Col. 0455D] In the autograph it reads: “For he who punishes the wicked seeks to destroy the good”; perhaps “to restore the good,” or “to make them good,” not “to destroy them,” is intended; or finally, “not to destroy the good,” as it seems to us it should be read.].

For he touches briefly, as is his custom, on the matter that he explains more openly when he adds: “In everything you have shown yourselves to be undefiled in the matter” (that is understood to mean, “in the matter of iniquity”).

The Corinthians, having been rebuked by the Apostle, were stirred up to drive wicked people from their fellowship. Therefore they had expelled all those whom he had marked out in the Letter. In doing this, they had shown themselves to be undefiled.

It is as though he had said: “When you expelled the wicked, you showed yourselves to be undefiled by the matter of iniquity, because one who is defiled loses the freedom to rebuke.”

Next: “Therefore, although I wrote, it was not on account of the one who did the wrong.” By these words he indicates the man who wronged his father by taking his wife (1 Cor. 5:1).

Likewise, when he says: “Nor on account of the one who suffered it” [Note: [Col. 0456D] In the Vulgate, “him.”], he indicates all those who were suffering wrongs and frauds, about whom he himself says in the first Letter: “But you do wrong and defraud, and this to your brothers” (1 Cor. 6:8).

For if they were disagreeing in some matter, or if they were inflicting some wrongs, they were taking their disputes before the judgments of unbelievers. He might have said this in other words: “I did not write only on their account, but also to make our concern manifest.”

For he had great concern for them: while he washed away the defiled, he raised up the oppressed, he recalled the rejected, and he showed that he cared for everyone. For when one person repents, many are saddened; when one person is afflicted, many are scandalized, because if one member suffers with another, all the members suffer with it.

It should also be noted that he says three things: “for you,” “to you,” and “before God,” to show that nothing was lacking from his concern.

And it should be understood that there are some who are concerned for others, but not toward those others, because their concern does not arise from those things that bring it to perfection. There are others who are concerned both for others and toward them; but because their intention is not pure, they are not concerned before God.

Next: “Therefore we were consoled,” that is, because of your correction, or because of our concern.

Next: “And in our consolation I rejoiced still more over the joy of Titus.” He himself was concerned, both openly and secretly, to guide his disciples so that he might learn the conduct of his hearers. Therefore, after he had sent Titus and Titus had found them corrected and amended, he rejoiced; and so he says: “I rejoiced over the joy of Titus.”

He might have said in other words: “Titus, who had been greatly saddened by your fall, rejoiced when he found you corrected; and I also rejoice, because his joy is mine.”

“For he was refreshed,” that is, he was filled by all of you. When he says “by all of you,” he shows that they had concord and unity, whereas in the first Letter he showed that they were divided, to the point of saying: “Is Christ divided?” (1 Cor. 1:13).

Next: “And if I have boasted to him about you in any respect.” By these words he clearly shows that he had told Titus many good things about the Corinthians before sending him—things that he had learned from those through whom he sent the Letter, or from others, since many people were frequently traveling about.

And the Apostle was not put to shame, because Titus found that matters were not otherwise than the Apostle had said.

Next: “But just as we have spoken everything to you in truth,” and so forth. Note that he repeats what he had said above: “There is no ‘Yes’ and ‘No’ in me.” The sense is: “Just as we have spoken everything to you in truth, so everything that I told Titus beforehand was true.”

Next: “And his affections are more abundantly toward you.” That is, all his members long for you. For example, just as all the bodily members desire one another’s functions—that is, hearing desires sight, sight desires smell, and so forth—so all his members desire you, remembering the obedience of you all.

The sense is: “Because your obedience was pleasing to him and made you pleasing, he loves you so much that the memory of you never departs from his mind.”

[Col. 0457A] Next: “How you received him with fear and trembling.” Titus had been sent to them with the purpose of observing their conduct; and when he suddenly appeared among them, they were afraid, recalling that they had been rebuked by the Apostle for many vices.

For they understood that he had sent them a suitable minister who would report their entire conduct to him. Therefore they received him with such fear and proved obedient to him, as though the Apostle himself had come to them.

Next: “I rejoice that I have confidence in you in everything,” as though he had said: “I rejoice not only over the correction of those who fell and rose again, but also over your progress, you who have stood firm in the faith.”

Or alternatively: “I rejoice because you who began to correct those things that pertain to the cultivation of the faith and to ecclesiastical order, and which deserve correction, will correct them.”

## Chapter VIII

“But we make known to you, brothers.” Above he had recounted to the Corinthians the persecutions and afflictions that he had suffered in the churches of Macedonia. Then he had said: “If I rejoiced over the joy of Titus.” After this he concluded his discourse and expression with praises; now he undertakes another subject, saying: “We make known to you, brothers,” and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0457D] In the autograph margin, “chapter XXII” is written here.]

But the question arises: Why did he begin his discourse with the work of mercy? [Note: [Col. 0457D] The verb “began” is understood, or something similar.] It should be understood that the Apostle acted ingeniously and in an admirable manner: namely, by soothing them with praise, he would more easily provoke them to the work of mercy.

Morally, proud and powerful people should be admonished in this way: if there is anything good in them, it should be brought forth in praise, or what might be present in them should be mentioned, so that what requires correction may more easily be corrected.

For this reason he brought forward the example of the churches of Macedonia: when the Corinthians heard that others were devoted to the work of mercy, they would be ashamed not to be devoted themselves.

Morally, teachers are instructed that, whenever they wish to provoke their hearers to good works, they should set before them the examples of the saints, so that they may draw them more quickly toward the good things they desire.

With the same intention he also calls them “brothers.” It is beautifully said: “The grace of God that has been given,” because grace is given by God and is given to none but the churches.

Next: “That amid a great testing of tribulation, their abundance of joy was more than sufficient” [Note: [Col. 0458D] The Vulgate reads “was.”]. The sense is: When they saw us suffering many adversities, they were not scandalized or made to waver in the faith; rather, through the testing of our tribulation they received a fullness of joy, because they understood that such steadfastness in persecution was not without reason.

Alternatively: When they saw us suffering, they themselves were also stirred up to rejoice in suffering with us; and they suffered because they understood that in those same tribulations, under the hope of the future resurrection, there was a fullness of joy.

“And their very deep poverty,” and so forth. By “very deep” he means profound and great. In these words he shows their purpose and devotion, as though he had said:

“Although their means were meager, they were so devoted that they were ready to give beyond what their strength and resources allowed.” Therefore he says: “It abounded into the riches of simplicity.”

He calls them “simple riches” because they did not give for the sake of human praise, or to redeem their teachers so that they would not be rebuked by them, but out of a desire to please God.

For those who give for the sake of human praise do not act simply; and those who receive from such people lose the freedom to rebuke, because it is written: “Gifts and presents blind the eyes of judges” (Ecclus. 20:31).

Next: “For I bear them witness according to their ability,” and so forth. The order is inverted, for it should be: “I bear them witness because they gave according to their ability, and beyond their ability they were willing.”

To show how this happened, he adds: “With much exhortation,” as though he had said: “They did what they could, and they desired to give more than their means allowed. But we judged that it ought not to be accepted, lest, if they suffered want, they should regret it and lose the fruit of their reward.”

They, however, with exhortation, tears, and prayers, begged that they might receive the grace and participation of the ministry that is performed for the saints—that is understood, “that they might receive it.” But when we saw that, having disregarded all temporal things, they were intent only on heavenly things, we later decided to accept what we had previously judged should not be accepted.

Next: “And not as we hoped,” that is, “they did more than we had hoped.”

Next: “But they gave themselves first to the Lord,” that is, by correcting their former errors and changing their life and conduct.

“Then to us,” namely, by providing the necessary expenses.

And because they did this simply, he therefore adds: “By the will of God.”

Next: “So that we asked Titus,” and so forth—as though he had said: “You too showed such devotion that we asked Titus to come to you.”

But why Titus and not someone else? Because he was known and pleasing to them, and they had advanced in many ways through his exhortation, so that through him they might also advance in this work of mercy.

Morally: When someone must be taught or urged toward some good work, he should be taught by someone who is pleasing to him and whom he himself loves.

[Note: [Col. 0458D] In the autograph margin, “chapter XXIII” is written here.]

Next: “But just as you abound in everything—in faith,” and so forth, “so also abound in this grace,” that is, in the work of mercy.

For he makes clear in what things they abounded: in faith, because they had already been strengthened; in speech, because they possessed varieties of languages; in knowledge, because they were wise; in all earnestness, because they had been rebuked and therefore were anxious lest they be rebuked again; and in all your charity toward us, that is, concerning us.

Next: “I do not speak as one commanding.” The sense is: “I am not extorting this from you as though I were compelling you, nor do I want your work to be involuntary rather than voluntary.”

Next: “But approving the good disposition of your charity through the concern of others.” This can be understood in two ways.

First, as though he had said: “So that, through the zeal of other faithful people, the good disposition of your charity may be approved,” that is, may be stirred up to the work of mercy.

Or by “others” he means the poor who were in Jerusalem, as though he had said: “Lest perhaps the poor who are in Jerusalem be anxious because of their want, let the good disposition of your charity be shown to be genuine,” that is, “be stirred up so that you may relieve their need with your wealth.”

Next: “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ,” as though he had said: “You know the example of the one who gave freely, because for your sake he became poor,” and so forth.

He might have said: “He rejected what was his for your sake; why, then, do you not give what is yours for his sake?”

Again: “If he gave what was his, why do you not give what is yours, and return to him, for your sake, what belongs to him?”

Again: “Although he was rich, he became poor, not so that he might grow, but so that you might grow. For he became what you were, so that he might make you what he was. He became poor so that he might make you participants in the riches of his divinity.”

Again: “He became poor so that, through his one poverty, he might make you rich in faith here and afterward heirs of the heavenly kingdom.”

This passage also stands against Photinus.

Next: “And I give advice in this matter.” Above he had said: “I do not speak as one commanding.” The same is meant by what he now says: “I give advice,” as though he had said: “I do not demand it; I give advice.”

The advice of so great a teacher, therefore, should not be disregarded. As though someone had asked, “Why do you give advice?” he himself explains: “For this is useful for you,” and so forth.

By these words he shows that a work can be involuntary, either because the one asking becomes wearied or because the one commanding gives orders.

It should also be understood that he praises them by reproving them. He praises them when he says: “You began”; he reproves them when he says: “Last year,” as though he had said: “You began late.”

He acted like a skilled physician who applies medicine to a sick person: the very same medicine soothes what is healthy and bites what is putrid.

Next: “But now complete it also in deed,” as though he had said: “Let your will be shown in your work.” For the end of every matter must be considered; just as a good work done under compulsion is not accepted by God, so neither is a slackened will.

Next: “So that, just as the readiness of mind exists,” and so forth—as though he had said: “Complete your ready will in action.”

And because he had urged them to the work of mercy, lest he seem to demand as much from the poor as from the rich, he adds: “Give from what you have.”

It should be understood that if the rich person gives as much as he can and the poor person gives as much as he can, they are equal. But if the rich person gives as much as he can while the poor person gives more than his means permit, then the poor person surpasses the rich—just as that poor widow who, as we read in the Gospel, put all her livelihood into the treasury (Mark 12:41).

For if the will is ready, that is, devoted, and a person gives according to what he has, that is, according to the extent of his means, the gift is acceptable to God. One must not demand from her what she does not have.

For this reason Tobias also says when admonishing his son: “My son, if you have much, give much,” and so forth (Tob. 4:9).

Next: “For it is not that there should be relief for others,” and so forth. These are the words of one accommodating himself to their weakness. For he knew that they were weak, and therefore accommodated himself to them, as though he had said:

“I am not advising you to give so much that you relieve the want of others while you yourselves suffer want. For it is written: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ Rather, I advise equality: that you relieve their want without yourselves suffering want.”

It should be understood that elsewhere, when accommodating himself to the weak here, he urges the strong toward greater things, saying: “He who sows sparingly” (2 Cor. 9:6), and so forth.

In the present passage he says this because in this present life things are distributed in turns: some are rich and others poor.

Next: “Let your abundance supply their want,” and so forth. By “their” he means the poor who were in Jerusalem.

When the holy Apostles sent preachers to the Gentiles, they also charged them to remember the poor. Therefore they urged collections to be made, by which the want of the poor saints might be relieved.

For it should be understood that the condition of the faithful Jews and of the faithful Gentiles was not the same, although they had one dwelling-place. The former, having renounced all temporal things, came to the faith; the latter—that is, the Gentiles—came with their households and the possession of their ancestral goods.

The former had chosen what was greater, namely, to devote themselves entirely to vigils and fasts; the latter were still occupied with earthly affairs.

Therefore he admonished them to relieve the want of the former with their wealth, so that they might become participants in their riches. It was as though he had said:

“You rich people, strive to relieve their poverty with your earthly wealth, so that in the future you may deserve to be relieved by their riches. For those whom you now see as poor you will one day see as rich; and you who are now rich, if you are negligent in giving, will be poor.”

All who give away their possessions here in order to receive greater things in the future act like cultivators of the earth, who cultivate it in order to receive a more abundant harvest.

Next: “So that there may be equality,” as though he had said: “Just as there is equality in God, who makes his sun rise equally upon the good and the wicked” (Matt. 5:45), so there should also be equality among you, so that they too may share in your riches and you in their good things.

[Col. 0460D] But because he wished to confirm his account by an example, he added: “As it is written: ‘He who gathered much did not have too much,’” and so forth (Exod. 16:18).

This is written in Exodus. A command had been given to the children of Israel that, while each person gathered manna according to the measure of one gomor for each head, it should be said: “He who gathered much did not have too much.”

For the person who, distrustful that he might not be able to find manna on the following day, gathered more than a gomor did not have more, because it swarmed with worms; and the person who gathered less had enough.

It should be understood that what was done then is also done now. For whoever, out of fear of future poverty, keeps back his riches, produces worms for himself through that very distrust—worms that will not die. Hence the Lord says: “Their worm shall not die,” and so forth (Isa. 66:24).

But we must consider the Apostle’s intention in bringing forward this testimony. He did so so that the rich would not be deceived by a false hope, believing that they would be rich in the future in the same way as they are now. For even if they possess much, salvation and life do not consist in the abundance of their riches.

The poor, too, who possess little should not be cast down, because that poverty will not harm them; rather, it will benefit them.

“But thanks be to God,” and so forth. The Apostle gives thanks to God, who had placed concern for the Corinthians in the heart of Titus, and who had made them obedient to him. He says that Titus had the same concern that he himself had, like a father.

For he was a true father, since by his preaching he had drawn them from unbelief into the light of faith. Whatever concern the one who was their father had, Titus had as well; therefore he says “the same.”

By this example preachers are instructed that, if they see one of their people concerned for souls, and those for whom he is concerned proving obedient, they should strive to give thanks to God, as the Apostle does here.

“For he indeed accepted the exhortation,” that is, the consolation, so that the one who had first refused to come would now hasten willingly to come.

“But having become more concerned,” and so forth. At first he became concerned by hearing; afterward he became more concerned by seeing, to the point that he desired of his own will to go to them.

“We also sent with him a brother,” and so forth. He commends this man, who was less well known, by praise; Titus, however, who had also become a close companion, had no need of praise.

But because he says: “Whose praise is in the Gospel,” and the rest that follows, the teachers say that this man was Luke. They say this because he wrote the Gospel wonderfully and afterward the book of the Acts of the Apostles, as he himself says: “The former account I composed,” and so forth (Acts 1:1).

He is called “a companion of the journey,” that is, of evangelical preaching; “in this grace,” that is, in the preaching and reconciliation “which is administered by us.” It is as though he had said: “We received this grace of preaching so that we might administer it to others” [Note: [Col. 0461D] This word appears to have been corrected in the autograph, so that it reads “we might make it known” (*manifestaremus*).]; therefore it is administered by us.

“From the glory of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0461D] The Vulgate reads “to the glory of the Lord.”] means from the salvation of souls, because the more people are saved, the more his glory increases.

“And to fulfill our appointed will,” that is, our arranged and ordered purpose.

But observe how great his love was. He regarded the tribulations and adversities of the present life as insignificant in comparison with the ministry of the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0462D] It is likewise corrected to read “of manifestation.”].

“Avoiding this,” and so forth. This suitable teacher, sufficient for preaching, avoided being blamed in the matter of mercy under discussion if it were not carried out. Or he was guarding against the reproach of those churches that had been led to the faith by others, lest he himself be reproached because by his preaching he had led them to the faith.

Therefore he took care to send suitable ministers who, by their wisdom and knowledge, would provoke them not only to the perfection of other good works, but also to the work of mercy.

Or he was guarding against their reproach, because they were such lovers of the Jewish sect that they observed the Law according to the flesh, lest they say: “These are not true Christians, since Jews give them even greater gifts.”

“For we provide what is good,” and so forth. “Before God,” because he preached the salvation of souls; “before human beings,” because he had sent ministers so suitable that they would not tear apart the hearts of the Corinthians, but by their knowledge and wisdom would provoke them not only to other good works, but also to the work of mercy.

“We also sent with them,” and so forth. By these words he shows that they had advanced in the faith, as though he had said:

“O Corinthians, you can recognize your progress in this: you have been found worthy to receive so many and such ministers.”

Some wish this man to have been Apollos, because in the first Letter Paul says that he had asked him to send Apollos to them (1 Cor. 16:12); but it is uncertain who he was.

“Now much more concerned,” as though he had said: “At first he was concerned, but afterward he became more concerned, placing great confidence in you,” either because Titus reported good things about you, or because the others reported them—those whom he also calls “the apostles of the churches, the glory of Christ.”

For many were going and returning, whether sent by the apostles or traveling of their own accord, and they could report these things to them.

“My companion.” Titus was his companion because he had been ordained a bishop; the other brothers were helpers of the Gospel.

By the fact that the Apostle sent such men, preachers are instructed that, when they wish to draw someone toward goodness, they should send someone whose mind is not, and will not become, corrupted by any disease.

“Therefore, the demonstration,” and so forth. By these words the Apostle commends them, so that they may prove obedient and devoted toward those men. It is as though he had said:

“I will be able to recognize your conduct and faith in this: if you receive them honorably in the presence of the churches,” that is, “in the sight of the churches.”

## Chapter IX

“For concerning the ministry,” and so forth. It appears that the Apostle is beginning another kind of discourse.

Some say that up to this point the Apostle has spoken about almsgiving in earthly goods, but that he is now speaking about the almsgiving of the word of God, which is greater than earthly almsgiving; therefore this almsgiving should be diligently practiced toward believers.

Others say that until now he was addressing laypeople, whereas he is now addressing priests, to whom both kinds of mercy must be commended.

Others say that from the beginning of this discourse to the end he has spoken about almsgiving in earthly goods.

But if he is speaking about this, why does he repeat it so frequently? A person commonly repeats a matter that he recognizes and practices so that he may impress it more firmly upon the hearts of others.

This is shown in Peter, whom the Lord, recognizing that he possessed the love of his ardor [Note: [Col. 0462D] Perhaps the better reading is “the ardor of his love.”], asked whether he loved him (John 21:15).

Or he repeats it in order to show what affection he has toward his hearers. With this intention the Apostle repeats it, adding: “For I know your ready disposition,” and again: “It is superfluous for me to write to you,” that is, “my heart has been enlarged to write to you.”

“For Achaia has been ready,” and so forth. With the same intention with which he had put forward the Macedonians as an example, he also puts forward the Achaians—that is, so that they would be ashamed not to imitate them.

But were these not also Achaians? They were. Yet he puts forward certain neighboring churches as examples.

What does it mean to say: “Your zeal has stirred up very many,” unless he means, in other words: “Your correction and amendment have stirred many to correction,” that is, to imitation?

To such an extent that they said: “If the Corinthians, who fell, rose again in such a way that they were praised by the Apostle, how much more can we correct our conduct so that we may please God and the Apostle, since we have not fallen?”

But we have sent the brothers whom he mentioned above, so that we may not be found otherwise than we boast. The Apostle had praised the Corinthians to the Macedonians; and, lest they should find them different from what the Apostle had said, he therefore took care to send suitable ministers who would urge them to the work of mercy, so that the Macedonians might not find them otherwise. And therefore he added: “So that, just as I said, you may be ready,” and so forth. He rightly says: “Let us be put to shame,” because, if the Macedonians should find them otherwise, the Apostle would be ashamed—especially the Corinthians; for the one who sees another put to shame on his account is usually more ashamed than if he himself were ashamed on his own account. “So that we may not say that you are [Col. 0463D] in this substance” [Note: In the Vulgate these words, “so that we may not say that you are,” are read as a parenthetical expression.]—that is, that we should not deny that you are engaged in this work of mercy [Col. 0463C].

Therefore I considered it necessary. As if he were saying: “O Corinthians, do not regard it as insignificant that I am sending so many and such important ministers; for I judged it necessary to send such men, so that they might prepare the blessing that had been promised.” Those who prepare a blessing must indeed be suitable. He calls it “the promised” blessing, referring to what he had said above: “For Achaia also has been ready since the previous year.” He calls it a blessing because those who give deserve to be blessed either by God or by those to whom they give. For each person is perfected through the contemplation of the one according to whose command he gives. Beginning from God’s cause, and insofar as human custom is concerned, the Apostle commends propriety: “as a blessing,” and so forth.
