[Col. 0463D] Earlier, condescending to the weak, he said: “Not that there might be relief for others,” and so forth; now he urges the strong, saying: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly.” Since the Apostle, condescending to the weak, earlier said: “Not that there might be relief for others,” and so forth, he now, rising to a higher level, urges the strong, the capable, and the wealthy to greater works of piety, saying that they should prepare the promised blessing, “not as though out of avarice.” He also brought forward an analogy from earthly matters, saying: “But I say this: Whoever sows sparingly,” and so forth—as if he had said: “Just as the one who sows little also reaps little, so you too, if you give little, will receive a small recompense of eternal happiness.” It should certainly be understood that the Apostle often presents his hearers with various analogies: now that of a soldier, now of a farmer, now also of a physician, now of a merchant. Likewise, here he sets forth an appropriate analogy of a sower, both in quality and in quantity. In quality, namely, because what one sows, that one also reaps; in quantity, because as much as one sows, so much also one reaps. It should also be noted that he calls the miser “the sparing one,” from whom something is, as it were, extorted and demanded so that he may contribute; for this reason he is slow to give, because he does not see the fruit of his reward.

It follows: “And whoever sows in blessings,” and so forth. To sow in blessings means, with gladness of heart [Col. 0464B] and in hope of future recompense, to perform an act of mercy, in accordance with Solomon’s saying: “In every gift make your face cheerful” [Note: [Col. 0463D] This text is found written in the book of Ecclesiasticus by Jesus son of [Col. 0464D] Sirach, XXXV, 11, not by Solomon.]. This can also be understood of the almsgiving of God’s word, since whoever gives the alms of the word to his hearers must administer it with sincerity of heart, lest he perhaps be deprived of its fruit. It should certainly be noted that, if the one who sows in blessings will reap in blessings, then conversely the one who sows in curses—that is, in sadness—will also reap in curses; for it is written: “Whatever a man sows, that he will also reap” (Gal. VI, 8).

But the Corinthians, because they had long before promised that they would make the collection, are addressed in this manner when he adds: “Each one according to what he has determined in his heart” [Col. 0464C]—that is, according to what he has deliberated, decided, and arranged (with “let him give” understood). Nevertheless, let him not regret it, lest he perhaps be deprived of the fruit; and therefore he adds: “Not from sadness or from necessity.” The Corinthians could give out of sadness or necessity while they saw the other Churches making their collections, because they were ashamed to act otherwise. For they could say: “Look, while others are giving, if we do not give in return, we shall be marked out and judged worse than the others.” Therefore, lest the work of piety be deprived of its fruit, they are warned by the Apostle that it should not proceed from sadness or necessity.

Morally speaking: There are many in the Church who, when they see the community doing something good, are ashamed to act otherwise, lest they be regarded as blameworthy.

It follows: “For God loves a cheerful giver.” That is, from among all those who give what is theirs, God loves those who give with gladness of heart, and he also prepares them for recompense. Here it should also be observed that, if he loves those who give with gladness of heart, then he certainly hates those who give with sadness of heart.

It follows: “Now God is able to make every grace abound in you.” In these words the Apostle wishes God’s grace to be present with them, so that, just as his grace had conquered all vices, so they might also be found perfect and devoted in the work of mercy, supported by his aid.

It follows: [Col. 0465A] “Having always all sufficiency in all things,” and so forth. He also invokes God’s grace upon them, so that they may abound in every good, to such a degree that they lack nothing pertaining to the salvation of the soul. This happens when people choose sufficiency—that is, when, after meeting their own needs and those of their household, they give what remains to the poor, as it is written: “He scattered; he gave to the poor” (Ps. CXI, 9), and so forth. By this example he greatly urges them toward the work of mercy. Here it should also be observed that he says: “He scattered; he gave to the poor,” and so forth. For if his righteousness remains forever who gives to the poor, how much more does that of the one who gives to the righteous remain? Thus there is a distinction between the poor and the saints: the poor are those who are publicly in need; the saints are those who devote themselves to all fasts [Col. 0465B] and vigils, like Anna [Note: Concerning her, see the Gospel of Luke II, 36–37]; or certainly those who distribute their possessions, like the apostles.

It should certainly be understood that righteousness is so called as if it were “the state of right” (*juris status*). Therefore that person practices righteousness who understands that all temporal goods have been given by God in common to everyone. That person, I say, is an imitator of God’s righteousness who, in imitation of him who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and so forth, gives indiscriminately to friends and enemies alike whatever he has in abundance.

It follows: “But he who supplies seed to the sower,” and so forth. Note that the seeds and growing things belong to God, since by his will they are both sown and grow for the sustenance of human beings. It should also be understood that by these words he supplied them with great confidence for giving, as if he had said: “If the seeds and growing things belong to him, why are you sluggish about giving to him what belongs to him? For, if you give, you will make him your debtor.” And because he had said two things, he repeats two things: “And he will multiply your seed,” and so forth. The meaning is: “He who supplies seed will also multiply it, and he who provides bread will also increase the growth of the crops.” Therefore do not be sluggish about sowing—that is, about distributing to the poor—for if you sow once, you will reap twice. To reap twice means both to receive in the present life an abundance of temporal goods with which we may relieve the poverty of the poor, and in the future to receive the reward of eternal recompense.

Note that crops are called “of righteousness.” Nevertheless, the crops of righteousness belong to the righteous, who distribute them well; for the unjust, however, the crops are certainly crops of injustice.

[Col. 0465D] It follows: “So that, enriched in all things,” and so forth. Those are rich in all things who abound both in temporal and in spiritual goods. He says “for all simplicity,” because those who give ought to do so simply—that is, they should not wish those to whom they give to be subject to them, nor seek any service from them on that account. For whoever desires any of these things receives his own reward; hence the Lord says: “Truly I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI, 2).

In what he says—“which works through us thanksgiving to God”—the meaning is this: The simplicity of administration works through us thanksgiving to God [Note: Perhaps: “the simplicity of the administration of thanksgiving,” and so forth.] [Col. 0466A]. That is, when we exhort and you give, others are moved to give thanks to God.

It follows: “For the ministry of this service,” and so forth. By “the ministry of the service” he means the ministry of the collection. The meaning is: Whoever fulfills the ministry of this service will be rewarded not only because he relieves the poverty of the saints, but also because he urges others who see him to give thanks to God. Thus he will be enriched by the gift of two rewards.

It follows: “By the testing of this ministry.” The meaning is: By this test you will show that you are truly Christians, if you become fulfillers of this ministry—that is, of the collection.

It follows: “Glorifying God in the obedience of your confession.” The meaning is: In the obedience of your confession—that is, through the fulfillment of your promise—you will be glorifying God in the Gospel of Christ [Col. 0466B].

It follows: “And in the simplicity of your sharing.” By “the simplicity of sharing” he means also sincerity of mind—that is, that nothing other than what ought to be sought should be sought. He says “toward those who were in Jerusalem,” and “toward all,” referring to those to whom they themselves were giving, or certainly to those who saw this and lived in other places.

It follows: “And by their supplication for you, longing for you.” In these words the Apostle shows, although indirectly, that the Corinthians were commended to God not only by the merits and prayers of the saints who were in Jerusalem, but also by those of all the others who saw them and, for the sake of the Corinthians’ salvation, desired the Corinthians to be subject to their needs [Col. 0466C]. Therefore he says: “For you, longing for you.” For what saint would not desire someone to be subject to his needs for that person’s salvation? If the one who gives wishes the one to whom he gives to be subject to him, he certainly loses his reward. And therefore the saints always desire people to be subject to their needs, lest they lose their reward.

He shows why they long for them by adding: “Because of the surpassing grace of God”—that is, so that God’s grace may be present in you in a surpassing way; for the humbler you are, the more exalted you will be.

Alternatively: “Because of the surpassing grace,” namely, of knowledge, charity, and similar gifts. The meaning is: “So that you who already abound in all other things may also abound in this grace of generosity.”

[Col. 0466D] It follows: “Thanks be to God for his indescribable gift.” It should be noted that in giving thanks he concludes his discourse on the work of mercy, which he had also begun with praises. The meaning is: “I give thanks to God, who by his mercy has enriched you with his ineffable gifts.”

If, however, this is referred back to what precedes, the meaning is: “Giving thanks to God, who undeservedly bestowed his indescribable gifts upon you.”

**(CHAP. X.)** But I myself, Paul, and so forth. There were some among the Corinthians who thought that he possessed lesser authority, and this suspicion could impede his preceding exhortation concerning the work of mercy [Col. 0467A]. Therefore the Apostle inserted an assertion of his authority, saying: “But I myself,” and so forth—as if he were saying: “I myself, the father, preacher, and teacher who throughout the whole text of this Epistle have admonished you like a father admonishing his children; or rather, I myself, who am not one person when present in body and another when absent in the Epistle; or rather, I myself, who am humble in appearance among you but, when absent, am confident regarding you.”

“I appeal to you,” and so forth—as if he were saying: “By the gentleness and modesty of the one who, although he could avenge himself upon his enemies, endured patiently, I appeal to you.” But when he says “I appeal” and “I am confident,” he seems to address the good, though on account of the wicked. What he was confident about he makes clear by adding: “But I ask that I may not dare when present.” For there were some among the Corinthians who still remained uncorrected; there were also pseudo-apostles by whom they had been deceived. Therefore he speaks as if he were saying: “I ask you to bring yourselves into such a state that, when I come, I may have nothing to rebuke—whether by excommunicating you or separating you from unity—but may be glad, like a father among his children, because of that confidence,” and so forth.

Whom he was addressing he makes clear when he adds: “Those who think that we are walking according to the flesh”—that is, remaining in the flesh and living carnally; or, while reading the Law, not understanding it correctly. For they said that the Apostle did not understand correctly, and therefore that faith ought not to be placed in him.

He responded to these two accusations by adding: “For although we walk in the flesh,” and so forth—that is, while existing in mortal flesh, we live according to the divine commands, with carnal desires put to death; or, possessing the same Law as the Jews, we understand it spiritually [Col. 0467C].

“For the weapons of our warfare,” and so forth—as if he were saying: “Our weapons are not a shield, sword, or material and visible things, but are powerful through God.” They are powerful because by words we can do what others cannot do with swords; or they are powerful because with these weapons we fight against the kingdom of iniquity. For just as Christ fights against the kingdom of iniquity, so we too, enriched with his gifts, both possess weapons and are ourselves weapons, and we labor to destroy the kingdom of iniquity.

Why are they powerful through God? He adds: “For the destruction of fortifications.” By “fortification” he means the teaching of the pseudo-apostles, who fortified it by their cunning and deceptions; nevertheless, the fortification itself was destroyed by the apostles’ battering rams, just as a visible wall is usually demolished by battering rams [Col. 0467D].

“Destroying counsels,” and so forth. He calls the height of the ancient enemy the snares that insert themselves into human counsels and, as it were, build a fortification; nevertheless, they are destroyed by apostolic teaching. For these people, wishing to establish their own knowledge, refused to submit themselves humbly to God’s knowledge.

“And taking captive every understanding,” and so forth—that is, we overcome the pseudo-apostles, who take captive and subject to themselves every understanding prepared for the service of Christ.

There is also another, better meaning: Once the truth has been manifested, to destroy falsehood.

“And having readiness,” and so forth. “In readiness” means “openly,” or “in plain view.” As if he were saying: “We are ready to avenge every disobedience when your obedience has been fulfilled.” For the obedience of believers condemns the disobedience of unbelievers. This happens when those who had been advocates of falsehood begin to be confessors of the truth [Col. 0468A].

“Observe what is according to appearance”—that is, notice what is open and manifest. He then explains what those things are: “If anyone is confident that he belongs to Christ,” and so forth.

There were some among the Corinthians who said that they belonged to Christ—that is, the pseudo-apostles against whom the Apostle speaks, saying: “If anyone is confident,” and so forth—as if he were saying: “If you say that you belong to Christ, we also belong to him.” But he greatly humbles himself, since he does not put himself forward. For how presumptuous is the person who wishes to make himself equal to the Apostle? And if that is greatly presumptuous, how much more presumptuous is the one who even wishes to place himself above him.

But although he humbles himself here, he immediately adds the authority of his apostleship, saying: “For even if I should boast somewhat more,” and so forth—as if he were saying: “If I, who have humbled myself, should not be ashamed to make the authority of my apostleship known, saying of myself that it was said concerning me: ‘This man is a chosen vessel for me’ (Acts IX, 15), because I do not act against the saying, ‘Let another praise you’ (Prov. XXVII, 2), and so forth—for I say this not for my own praise, but for your salvation, so that you may not put your faith in the pseudo-apostles.”

It is clear with what intention, after the exhortation concerning the collection, he inserted the authority of his apostleship. Continuing in this same intention of commending his authority, he says: “But that I may not be considered as though wishing to terrify you through letters”—with “I say” understood.

Those who have no grace by which they are commended, and who possess neither authority, office, nor teaching, terrify people through letters; they terrify the absent because they fear the present. The Apostle, on the contrary, was not like this, nor were those who were with him. He was commended by authority, because he was filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit and sent by the Lord to the office of preaching; therefore he did everything according to the disposition of the Holy Spirit.

He then adds the words of those who thought that he terrified the absent through letters: “For his letters,” they say, “are weighty and strong,” and so forth.

It should certainly be understood that the presence of the saints seems weak to the puffed-up and proud, and their speech contemptible. Why? Because it is characteristic of the saints not to display their authority unless compelled. Therefore, the weaker they see them appear, the more they think them to possess no authority. The faithful, on the contrary, think differently: the more lowly they perceive them to be, the more exalted and authoritative they understand them to be, and therefore they fear them all the more [Col. 0468D].

It follows: “Let such a person consider this”—that is, one who is of this sort of opinion should consider that, “what we are in our letters when absent,” and so forth. It is as if he had said in other words: “I am not one person and another; I am not divided, because I am not presumptuous. It is characteristic of the presumptuous to threaten what should not be threatened and to promise what should not be promised. But even if we say anything by threatening or promising, we can indeed fulfill it through the one who dwells in us” [Col. 0469A].

Therefore the humble perceive me as humble, while the proud recognize me as stern and strong.

It follows: “We do not dare to insert ourselves,” and so forth. The meaning is: “We do not dare boastfully to put forward concerning ourselves things that are not in us, nor to despise God so far as to compare ourselves with the pseudo-apostles, who are commended not by God’s grace but by their own presumption.”

It follows: “But they, measuring themselves by themselves and comparing themselves with themselves,” and so forth [Note: The Vulgate reads: “But they, measuring themselves by themselves and comparing themselves with themselves.”]. It is as if he had said: “We measure ourselves by ourselves,” because we do not extend ourselves beyond the measure of the divine rule—that is, of God’s disposition—nor do we confine ourselves below that measure, because we do not compare ourselves with the pseudo-apostles.

It follows: “We will not boast beyond measure.” This is, as it were, an exposition of the preceding words. To boast beyond measure is to extend oneself beyond the limits of the divine disposition.

It follows: “But according to the measure of the rule that God measured out to us.” The meaning is: “We extend ourselves to preach, but according to the boundaries and limits that God established for us.” But because you are contained within [Note: See whether *infra* should here be read *intra*.] the measure of the divine rule—that is, of his disposition—we have extended ourselves as far as you. This is what he means by “the measure of reaching as far as you,” as if he had said: “We did not come to you through presumption, but were prompted by divine revelation.”

You also believed because of our preaching; hence he says in the First Epistle: “You are the seal of my apostleship” (I Cor. IX, 2), and again: “I begot you through the Gospel” (I Cor. IV, 15).

It should also be understood that, prompted by divine revelation, he came to the Macedonians and Corinthians. It should further be noted that by these words the Apostle shows that regions and provinces had been divided among preachers, so that each might have a particular sphere in which to glory.

It follows: “For we do not extend ourselves beyond you as though we did not reach you.” To extend oneself beyond measure is to wish to exceed the limit of the divine rule. Nevertheless, it should be understood that throughout this entire statement the Apostle’s purpose is to show the Corinthians that they ought not to despise him, since he received, according to the measure of the divine disposition, the task of drawing them to the faith by his preaching—as if he had said: “You ought not to despise your own father, teacher, and instructor, nor prefer to him the pseudo-apostles, who boast beyond measure.”

It follows: “As far as you we have reached in the Gospel of Christ.” He says “of Christ” to distinguish it from those who preached not Christ’s doctrines but their own false teachings.

It follows: “Not boasting beyond measure.” What it means to boast beyond measure he immediately shows when he adds: “In the labors of others.” The Apostle did not boast in the labors of others but in his own, since the Corinthians had been drawn to the faith through his preaching. The false apostles, however, boasted in the labors of others [Col. 0470A]—that is, in peoples who had believed through the preaching of others. They did not even dare [Note: Perhaps, instead of *non audebant*, one should read *eludebant*. In the autograph it is written in this way: “*Aliaudebant*,” which I have judged should be emended.] to go over to unbelievers who demanded signs, because they could perform none; and therefore they went over to believers who did not demand signs.

It follows: “Having hope in the growth of your faith,” and so forth. The meaning is: “We do not yield to persecutions or sufferings, because we have a sure hope that, when your faith has grown, we too shall be rewarded by God. And therefore we seek neither your gold, nor your silver, nor anything else of yours, since we shall await our reward from God.”

It follows: “According to our rule, in abundance, even to evangelize in the regions beyond you.” In these words the Apostle promises that he will not be content to remain forever in Corinth, since the measure of the divine rule has not been extended only as far as them, but also to those places to which he intends to travel and preach, which had been encompassed by the divine line. Therefore he says: “Those beyond you.”

At that point, however, lest he appear to glory in the labors of others or to build upon another’s foundation, he says that he will evangelize where no one had previously laid a foundation and where Christ had not yet been named. This is what he means by: “Not according to another’s rule”—that is, doctrine, or, better, people.

Hence he immediately adds: “To glory in those things that have been prepared.” It should be understood that whenever the Apostle sent Epistles to those Churches that had come to the faith through another’s preaching, he did not threaten severity but sent exhortation and admonition, pointing out their sin so that they might be corrected. To those, however, who had come to the faith through his own preaching, he also threatened severity.

By doing this he fulfilled the commandment of the Law, by which it was ordered that, if anyone passed through another’s field, he had the right to pluck ears of grain with his hands and rub them, but not to put in a sickle (Deut. XXIII, 25).

It follows: “But whoever boasts, let him boast in the Lord.” Since he had said above that he did not boast beyond measure or in the labors of others, he also added the matters for which someone might suspect him of seeking his own glory. Therefore he added: “But whoever boasts”—that is, whoever boasts in doctrine, or in the multitude of believers, or in the progress of his hearers, let him boast in the Lord; that is, let him refer everything to the Lord’s praise and to the Lord’s gain.

It follows: “For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved,” and so forth. The one who is approved is the one commended not by his own presumption but by the Lord’s grace. The pseudo-apostles were not approved, since they were commended by no virtues whatever.

**(CHAP. XI.)** It follows: “Would that you could bear with a little of my foolishness,” as if he had said: “You Corinthians, who for a long time endured false preachers boasting, bear with me at least a little.” Note that he calls himself foolish because he was about to say great things about himself, and such boasting could appear to belong to foolishness.

It follows: “For I am jealous over you with God’s jealousy.” The meaning is: “I am not stirred against the false apostles by envy; rather, burning with fatherly affection, I am jealous for you, so that I may present you to God immaculate and undefiled.” Hence he immediately adds: “For I betrothed you to one man as a chaste virgin,” and so forth.

By “one man” he means Christ; by “a chaste virgin,” either the holy Church in general, or specifically the faithful soul, which, when reborn through the water of baptism, becomes Christ’s bride and, so that it may admit no other, is worthy to receive the pledge, the earnest of the Holy Spirit.

It should be understood that a bride who judges another to be more beautiful, nobler, and wiser than her bridegroom is no longer chaste but rather corrupted. Likewise, the soul that is Christ’s bride corrupts itself when it loves gold, silver, and other things more than Christ himself.

But we must consider what chastity the Apostle wished to be understood: bodily chastity or chastity of mind. If you understand bodily chastity, very few are those who preserve it; but if you understand chastity of mind—that is, integrity of faith—many possess it.

It should be known that there are some who preserve bodily chastity but do not preserve virginity of mind, as heretics do. Likewise, there are some who possess chastity of mind but not of body, as married people do; marriage itself is no obstacle to them. Again, there are some who preserve virginity of mind but do not possess bodily chastity, because they rush headlong through the precipices of vices. These people, together with the heretics, are held under one rule: corruption must be avoided in mind just as in body.

More appropriately [Note: In the autograph the reading is “Vel connius”; suspecting a corrupt transposition, we judged that it should be read thus.], however, an example of this passage is compared with the place where it is written in the Apocalypse: “These are they who have not been defiled with women” (Apoc. XIV, 4). There he understands “women” as heretics, and “virgins” as the faithful of all the Churches, who follow the Lamb wherever he goes—that is, passing from corruption to incorruption.

Blessed Augustine, however, explains that passage according to bodily virginity. For he says that only the hundred and forty-four thousand who have not been defiled with women can sing the song [Col. 0471D]. To sing the song means that those who have not been defiled with women rejoice above all the faithful in the incorruption of the body. They follow the Lamb because the flesh of the Lamb is virgin.

But who would separate Peter from this praise, or the other apostles, who, according to the opinion of the holy teachers, were all married except Paul and John?

It follows: “But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning” (Gen. III, 4), and so forth. In these words he shows his jealousy and ardor, since he admonishes them even by expressing fear.

The serpent deceived Eve in this way. When God had commanded the first-formed humans not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, the serpent came to them and said: “Why did God command you not to eat from the tree of knowledge?” Eve replied: “Because on whatever day you eat, you will die.” The serpent said to them: “It will not be so; but God knows that on whatever day you eat, you will be like gods,” and so forth—as if he had said: “He commanded this for the purpose of frightening you; yet he will not do what he threatened.”

Similarly, the Apostle feared that the Corinthians might be deceived in this way. For the pseudo-apostles came to them and said: “Why do you not observe the Law?” They replied: “Because, since grace has been given, the Law is no longer in force.” They, on the contrary, said: “Grace was not given so that the Law might be abolished, but so that even in this way the Law might be fulfilled; and its fulfillment alone is sufficient for salvation.”

There are also some in the Church who are signified by the name of serpents. For they say that there is no eternal fire, and that what was said—“These will go into eternal punishment” (Matt. XXV, 46)—was said so that people might be afraid; nevertheless, God would not allow his creature to perish forever. Although these people are themselves lost, they destroy others. For if the one who comes preaches another Christ, and so forth, up to the point where he says: “You would rightly bear with it.”

The meaning is: “You would rightly bear with the pseudo-apostles being preferred to me if they had conferred something greater than what I conferred upon you. But because they preached the same Christ as we did, and the same Spirit, the same Gospel, and the same baptism, it is not, I say, right for you to prefer them to me.”

Nevertheless, a question arises: Why did he say to the Corinthians, “You would rightly bear with it,” when he says to the Galatians: “If anyone should preach another Christ” (Gal. VIII, 9) besides the one we preached, “let him be anathema”? How can those people be accursed when he says to these that it would be right? The matter is resolved in this way: Since these Corinthians were believers, they could not preach another Christ except the one who had been crucified for our redemption. He says “let him be anathema” to the Galatians because, if they preached another Christ, it would no longer be a superior Christ but one incomparably worse than all others.

It follows: “For I consider that I have done nothing less than the great apostles.” Above he spoke against the false apostles; now he speaks on behalf of the true ones, saying: “I consider,” and so forth—as if he had said: “Why do you wish to prefer the false apostles to me, when you ought not even to prefer the great apostles? For the other Churches received nothing more from the great apostles than you received from me. Nothing more, I say—especially since he labored here more than all the others and saw the Lord both on the road and in the Temple.”

It follows: “And if I am unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge.” It should certainly be understood that the Corinthians had been deceived by many errors. Some favored the pseudo-apostles, others the true apostles, and still others those who spoke elegantly. They favored all these people for the purpose of overthrowing him and showing him to possess lesser authority [Col. 0473A].

Therefore, having spoken against the false apostles and on behalf of the true ones, he now also speaks against those who sought brilliance of eloquence in preaching. “If I am unskilled in speech,” he says, and so forth—as if he had said: “Why do you wish to prefer to me those who seek brilliance of eloquence in preaching? You ought not, I say, to prefer them to me. For although they are skilled, they are skilled in a place where there may be danger; whereas, although I am unskilled, I am unskilled in a place where there is no danger. For if I am unskilled in speech, I am nevertheless not unskilled in knowledge.”

Someone can indeed possess perfect faith and knowledge while being slow in speech. Nevertheless, one may ask why he calls himself unskilled when Festus says of him: “Paul, great learning is driving you mad” (Acts XXVI, 24). It should be understood that, according to what Festus said, he was instructed in extensive learning; nevertheless, out of humility he called himself unskilled.

It follows: “In every way we have been made manifest to you”—that is, it has been made clear that I did not preach for the sake of empty praise or earthly profit, but for the sake of your salvation. I have also been made manifest through signs and wonders, or because of the abundance rather than the poverty of my words.

It follows: “Or did I commit a sin,” and so forth—as if he had said: “I committed no sin among you for which you ought to prefer the pseudo-apostles to me, unless perhaps I sinned in this: that I did not take what belonged to you. And if I committed this fault, forgive me, I beg you.”

For this very reason they feared him more, because he accepted nothing from them. For this reason also they preferred the pseudo-apostles to him, because they thought that they were loved more by them [Note: Perhaps one should read “believed or understood themselves to be loved.”]. They believed themselves holier to the extent that they were more pleasing to them, and therefore they became more willing to give to them.

It should be understood that he beautifully says: “Humbling myself.” For what is humbler than not using a power that has been received? This humility also greatly concerned the Corinthians’ freedom [Note: Perhaps “generosity.”]. Therefore he says: “So that you may be exalted,” since they were being freed from the domination of the false apostles.

And because someone might say, “How did you humble yourself so that we might be exalted?” he himself replies: “Because I freely preached the Gospel of Christ to you.” The meaning is: “Accepting nothing from you for a year and six months, I announced the Gospel to you.” And, lest this should perhaps seem incredible, he added: “I robbed other Churches,” and so forth—as if he had said: “I received support from other Churches so that I could preach to you.”

Therefore, lest what [Note: In the autograph, *ne* is read in place of *quod*.] he had received from other Churches for their salvation seem insignificant, he used this word, namely, “I robbed.” It should also be understood that the less he showed himself to have received from them, the more heavily this burdened them.

Next follows: “And when I was with you and was in need,” etc. It should certainly be noted that he not only did not wish to receive anything from them when he abounded through the labor of his own hands or by the resources of other churches, but did not do so even when he was suffering want. Hence blessed Pope Gregory says: “For who can comprehend or recount Paul’s compassion? Indeed, while he was supplying the Corinthians with nourishment for their spiritual food, he did not wish to receive from them nourishment for his bodily food.” For which of us would now draw some rich man to the faith by his preaching, if he saw him being miserly toward himself and would not rebuke, indeed would not even reprimand him? “For what was lacking to me,” etc.; that is, what I could not obtain by the labor of my hands, the brothers supplied. For from the first hour of the day until the fifth he worked with his hands to acquire food for himself; but from the fifth until the eleventh he preached, and so vigorously that, overcoming the pagans who resisted him, he drew them to the faith. “Those who came from Macedonia.” But why did he accept from these people? Because they had not been deceived by the false apostles. From the Corinthians, however, he did not wish to accept, lest he give the false apostles who were among them an opportunity to receive.

“And in all things without honor” [Note: [Col. 0474D] The Vulgate has *onere* (“burden”); the autograph, however, has *onore* twice. Indeed, the word *honor* and its derivatives are almost always written without the letter *h*.], etc.; that is, not only in food or drink, but also in service, attendance, and other such matters, I was without honor. And lest they suppose that he had said this because he wished to receive from them, he therefore added: “I have kept myself so, and will keep myself so”; as if he were saying: Far be it from me, who once decided not to receive, ever to receive. Or, according to some: “I will keep myself so” as long as you have the false apostles among you.

“The truth of Christ is in me.” As if he were saying: Just as in Christ there is no “yes” and “no,” so also in me, who am considered his member. I am the member; he is the author. I am the recipient; he precedes, and I follow. Why he said this, he adds: “This glory of mine,” etc. He calls it his glory that he did not use the authority he had received. Here he also shows that what he had not accepted was glory, not sin; hence earlier: “Have I committed a sin?” “It shall not be hindered,” etc.; that is, I shall not accept, for it would then be hindered if I had accepted. But one must ask: since earlier he had urged them toward the work of mercy, why does he now say, “It shall not be hindered in me”? For this reason: he did not accept for the sake of his own need, but for the sake of the poor who were in Jerusalem. His glory would then have been hindered if he had accepted for the sake of his own need.

[Col. 0474D] “Why?” As if he were saying: Perhaps it will be broken because I do not love you, and therefore will not accept? No. I love you, and I love you more by not accepting than by accepting. And to show that he loves them, he adds: “God knows”; so that, when they heard that he had summoned as witness the one who knows the hidden things of all hearts, in order to demonstrate his love, they might be made certain of his affection. “What I do, I will also do”; that is, just as I have not accepted until now, I will not accept—and this is what he had said earlier: “I have kept myself so, and will keep myself so.” Why does he make this clear? “To cut off the opportunity,” etc. The false apostles wanted the Apostle to accept, so that they themselves might acquire an opportunity to receive [Col. 0475A]—if he accepted bread, they would accept gold—and therefore, under the pretext of this opportunity, he did not wish to accept. “So that in what they boast, they may be found to be like us.” These men boasted of accepting gifts, because they thought themselves holier insofar as they became more pleasing to those who gave to them more willingly; they would be found to be like the apostles if they accepted.

[Note: [Col. 0475D] In the autograph’s margin it says here: “Chapter XXIV.”]

“For such men,” etc. They are deceitful: those in whom evil lies hidden, that is, those who contemplate one thing in their minds but perform another in their deeds, as the false apostles did. For they preached Christ and baptism, etc., but with another intention; and therefore he adds: “Transforming themselves into apostles of Christ,” because they preached for the sake of gain and profit, whereas Christ’s apostles preached for the sake of the salvation of souls.

[Col. 0475B] “And it is no wonder,” etc. As if he were saying: Why is it surprising if the members are transformed, when even the head is? For the devil is an angel of darkness, and if he appeared in the form he actually has, he would not be received; therefore he transforms himself into an angel of light, so that he may commend himself more easily. For this reason the elect are made vigilant, so that, when he appears, they may carefully inquire whether he truly belongs to the light or not. Hence Joshua, seeing the angel, said: “Are you one of ours or one of our adversaries?” (Josh. V, 13). And when the apostles saw the Lord walking upon the sea, they thought it was a phantom and cried out (Mark VI, 49; Matt. XIV, 26). Peter, seeing him upon the waves, said: “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you,” etc. (Matt. XIV, 28). “Whose end was,” etc. Just as the belly and the things belonging to the belly perish, along with all other transitory things, so these men also will perish; and whatever end adulterers and murderers are destined to have, the same will also befall these men who only pretend to be good [Note: [Col. 0475D] Perhaps *habere* (“to have”) should be supplied.]

“Again I say.” Earlier he had said: “Would that you would bear with me a little,” etc., and immediately wished to take up this matter. Nevertheless, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit he inserted certain words; after inserting them, and diverting his line of thought, he returns to the order he had begun, saying: “Again I say” (so that no one may think me foolish). He says this because he was about to say things in what follows that might appear to pertain to his praise; as if he were saying: Do not think that I say this for the sake of my own praise, but for the sake of your salvation, because I speak under compulsion. Or: Let no one think me foolish because I speak the truth, or because I do not say everything that I know. And therefore he adds: “Otherwise receive me as a fool”; as if he were saying: If you consider only the words, because I seem to praise myself, you will think me a fool; but if you weigh my intention, you will recognize that I am not foolish but wise, because I am acting for the sake of the salvation of others—so that, like them, I may boast a little, since they boast much.

“What I speak, I do not speak according to God”; that is, insofar as my voice is concerned, when I praise myself I do not speak according to God. For one who praises himself does not by that praise win God’s favor, since he will receive from him not exaltation but humiliation, not praise but rejection. He explains this by adding: “But as though in foolishness,” etc.; as if he were saying: As far as the voice is concerned, I speak in this substance of glory. It appears to be foolishness, because it is foolishness to wish to praise oneself, as in the saying: “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth” (Prov. XXVII, 2). As far as intention is concerned, it is not foolishness; and therefore he says: “As though in foolishness,” not truly so.

“Since many boast,” etc. By these words he indicates the Jews who believed and boasted of the nobility of their lineage, putting themselves before believers from the nations. This was perverse, because it is not descent according to the flesh but conduct and imitation that make children of Abraham. Here it is shown how great is the rashness of those who, through the sacrament of baptism, have become children of God, yet boast of the nobility of the flesh that had generated them as children of the devil.

“You gladly bear with,” etc. Continuing the intention he had begun, he reveals the ministry and dignity of his authority, by which he seemed to surpass not only the false apostles but even the magicians [Note: [Col. 0475D] A word among the Arabs, Idumeans, and Chaldeans referring to a philosopher and wise man. See Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, and Book III, *Against Marcion*; Saint Justin Martyr, *Dialogue with Trypho*; Saint Epiphanius, *Epitome of the Catholic Faith*; and, among more recent writers, Tostatus, Mariana, Barradius, Grotius, Cornelius à Lapide, and many others.]—and he continues: “You gladly bear with,” etc. For he calls those foolish who boasted of the nobility of their lineage and of circumcision, since it is foolishness to boast of such things. As for his saying “wise,” some say that it was spoken ironically, and that it should therefore be pronounced in such a way that a negation is understood; for every expression is distinguished either by its meaning or by its pronunciation. Similar words can have dissimilar meanings: for example, if I say, “You acted through your wisdom,” it may be said in praise, but it may also be said in reproach. This passage should therefore be pronounced interrogatively, so that the negation may be understood.

There are also some who think that the Apostle said this straightforwardly, because there were certain wise men among the Corinthians whom he had praised in the First Epistle and said were rich in all things; these men also tolerated the false apostles. The Apostle speaks against them, saying: “You gladly bear with,” as if he were saying: I wonder why, since you are so very wise, you tolerate the false apostles so greatly. For they wished to endure the false apostles so that they might be regarded as more glorious, and the Apostle grieved over this, as if he were saying: Why do you bear with these men and refuse to bear with me? [Col. 0476D] etc. It should be noted that the elect patiently endure evil people in two ways: either so that they may draw them to the way of truth, or so that, if they cannot do so, their patience may at least be rewarded.

“For you bear with,” etc. He now begins to identify those whom they tolerated, adding: “If someone brings you into servitude,” that is, to the law, since they labored to subject them to the servitude of the law; or “into servitude,” because the priests of the Jews exercised that domination over the people which bishops now exercise over the people [Note: [Col. 0476D] The autograph has *damnationem* (“condemnation”).] [Col. 0477A]. “If someone devours you”; that is, if someone consumes what belongs to you, for they preached concern for the belly; hence the same Apostle says: “Their god is the belly” (Phil. III, 19). “If someone takes”; that is, if someone seizes what is yours. Hence the Greeks also call robbers *harpagers* [literally “snatchers”], and we call those birds that are eager to seize other creatures *hawks*. These men likewise “took,” because they robbed. “If someone exalts himself.” They exalted themselves because they boasted of the superstition of their nation and of circumcision. “If someone strikes you in the face.” To strike someone in the face means openly to disparage and heap insults upon him.

“I speak according to dishonor.” Because he was about to say such things in what follows, and therefore could appear to be boasting, he prefaced it with “according to dishonor,” since it pertains to foolishness for someone to boast about himself. “As though we had been weak in this respect”; that is, in the matter of boasting. As if he were saying: If they wish to boast, we too can boast, because we are not weak in those matters of which they boast. “In whatever anyone dares”—“to boast” is understood. As if he were saying: If anyone dares to boast in this, I too dare. “I speak in foolishness.” Since he was about to praise himself, he therefore prefaced it with “I speak in foolishness.”

“They are Abraham’s seed,” etc., up to where he says: “They are ministers of Christ.” And because he was going to say, “I am more a minister,” he therefore first said, “as though less wise.” Why he would say “more,” he begins to make clear: “In very many labors.” [Col. 0477C] He had begun by speaking about the false apostles, but what he says can also be referred to the good apostles: “In very many labors,” for he shows that they devoted themselves to labors, but himself even more. With this statement he includes everything that follows.

“In prisons more abundantly.” By saying “more abundantly,” he also shows that they had been imprisoned, but he had been imprisoned more abundantly, because by his persistent preaching he aroused the hatred of others against himself, and therefore was kept in prison. “In wounds beyond measure”; that is, and so forth—these wounds were beyond measure. “In deaths frequently,” etc. Now he explains what he had said above, “in wounds,” by saying: “From the Jews five times,” etc.; that is, as a transgressor of the law. For the commandment of the law was that, if someone proved to be a transgressor of it, he should be brought before the elders; and if they decided that he should be flogged, the flogging itself was not to exceed the number forty, lest the brother, shamefully scourged, should lie before his eyes (Deut. XXV, 3). Later, however, it was handed down by their elders that thirty-nine blows should be given, lest, by counting, the number forty be exceeded and the transgressor thereby be made a violator of the law.

Bede says that in a book which his own departing [Note: [Col. 0477D] Perhaps *abiens* (“when departing”).] servant had brought him from the city of Rome to his own province, he had seen a torturer depicted standing and holding a four-pronged whip. With one prong and its handle he held the victim, while with the other three he struck him; and the man lay prostrate before him. This shows that with ten blows he completed a total of thirty, while with three he completed nine. For if he had struck with four, he would have completed forty.

But if you ask about the mystery [Note: [Col. 0477D] The autograph has *ministerium* (“ministry”).]—why the law commanded this—it should be noted that the number forty signifies the struggle of the present life. Appropriately so: spread throughout the four quarters of the world, it fights against the snares of the devil with the Decalogue, so that it may wipe away the vices that have been committed.

“Three times I was beaten with rods.” Having been flogged five times by the Jews, he had received thirty-nine blows on each occasion; but, because the nations did not observe the same law, he was beaten with rods by the Gentiles. “Once I was stoned” (Acts XIV, 18), as happened at Lystra. [Col. 0478B] “Three times I suffered shipwreck” (Acts XVII, 41). Because he traveled by sea frequently, he suffered shipwreck; for this commonly happens to those who sail often. “I was in the deep of the sea by night and by day.” If you wish to accept the testimony of the ancient teachers, it should be understood exactly as it sounds: namely, that he was hidden beneath the sea’s waves. But no one should think it incredible that he was not drowned by the waves or consumed by sea beasts and monsters, since by divine mercy he was brought out—especially because Peter walked upon the waves of the sea. That was a great deed, but this one was no less than it.

But if you wish to refer it to the mystery [Note: [Col. 0477D] The autograph prefers *ministerium* (“ministry”).], Paul, lying hidden beneath the waves after shipwreck and raised up by divine mercy [Note: [Col. 0478D] From what follows, perhaps *erutus* (“rescued”) should be read.], signifies those who are to be rescued—those who are afflicted not only by external adversities but also, when they come to death or are covered by worldly affairs, are delivered by divine mercy. For by Peter, who, while walking upon the waves of the sea, doubted and therefore began to sink, but was immediately sustained by the divine hand, the saints are signified: those who, having been entrusted with faith, are trampled down by the adversities of this present life [Note: [Col. 0478D] The autograph has *calcant* (“trample”).], and, if it happens that they are shaken in some respect, are nevertheless raised up by divine mercy, like human beings. Some understand “the deep of the sea” to mean a place not far from land.

“On journeys often”; because he traveled from place to place in order to draw unbelievers to the faith and strengthen believers in the faith. “In dangers from rivers.” It could happen that he traveled in winter, when rivers exceed their usual limits, so that they might present an obstacle to one wishing to cross, and hence there were dangers. “In dangers from robbers.” The devil saw his eagerness: he wished to save many by his preaching, and many were still to be saved, as many had already been saved. Therefore he stirred up robbers against him, so that the one who could not be extinguished in the city might at least be extinguished by robbers. In this he shows that he carried nothing valuable for the robbers.

“In dangers from my own people.” The Jews grieved because they recognized that the man whom they had known as a defender of the law and a zealous imitator of ancestral traditions (Gal. I, 14), even to the point of receiving letters so that, if he found any Christians (Acts IX, 2), etc., was opposing all these things; and therefore they inflicted persecution upon him.

“In dangers from the Gentiles.” The Gentiles grieved because he preached Christ’s passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven; and because he impressed knowledge of the one God upon people’s hearts and destroyed idols, they therefore inflicted persecution upon him.

“In dangers in the city.” For example, in Damascus, where he was so closely confined that he could find no means of escape; but, placed in a basket, he was lowered by the brothers through a window in the wall (II Cor. XI, 33).

“In dangers in the wilderness.” The devil stirred up [an uncertain object] against him, etc.

“In dangers at sea.” One must ask: since above he had said, “By night and by day I was in the deep of the sea,” why does he repeat, “In dangers at sea”? Since he repeats it, we should understand this as referring to the danger that occurred when he appealed to Caesar (Acts XXV, 10) and was sent to Rome with the others. While they were sailing, the ship struck a sandbank [*syrtis*] (Acts XXVII, 41), and the soldiers decided to kill the watchful men [*pervigiles*], so that none might escape by swimming; but the centurion prevented this on Paul’s account (ibid., 43).

“In dangers from false brothers.” He calls those who believed from among the Jews “false brothers”: although they had believed, they nevertheless observed the ceremonies of the law. Hence they were false, and they too inflicted persecution upon Paul.

“In labor”; that is, whether of the hands or of preaching. For from the first hour of the day until the fifth he acquired food for himself by working; from the fifth until the eleventh he preached. [Col. 0479C] And because labor can exist without hardship—that is, without need and poverty—he added, to show that the labor was destructive: “In hardship.” “In many sleepless nights,” whether of preaching or of work, in order to acquire food. And rightly did he devote himself to sleeplessness, because it is necessary that one who is wearied by distress should keep watch, so that he may be worthy to have God as his deliverer.

“In hunger and thirst,” whether necessary or voluntary, because he fled from place to place and therefore could not be free from hunger. And to explain what he had said, “In hunger and thirst,” he adds: “In many fasts” [Note: [Col. 0479D] The autograph has “in vigils.” I judged that repetition to be erroneous and avoided it, following the Vulgate in reading “in fasts.”], whether voluntary or necessary.

“In cold and nakedness.” You have an example in the Acts of the Apostles, where it is written that, when Paul was sailing (Acts XXVIII, 1–2) and had come to the island of Malta [Note: [Col. 0480D] The autograph has “Miletus.”], a viper attacked his hand while he was making a fire from bundles of grapevines because of the cold.

“Besides those things,” etc. By “those things” he means the external afflictions that he had enumerated above. And to show that they were lighter, he said: “The daily pressure”; for the more frequently adversities occur, the more lightly they are endured. “The daily anxiety,” etc. From what custom did this arise? Certainly from the ancient tradition of the Fathers. For they themselves warned that hearers ought to be admonished without interruption, and therefore he exercised such great concern.

Blessed Gregory says: “Who can penetrate Paul’s compassion?” Externally he was afflicted by adversities, but inwardly he was tormented by anxiety, remembering what he had urged: “not looking each to his own interests” (Phil. II, 4). For he was tormented more by concern for others than by concern for himself. He feared that they, seeing their teacher scourged, might be scandalized. Who can explain in words the virtue of the man who, at one and the same time, is wearied outwardly by adversities and inwardly tormented by anxiety?

“Who is weak,” etc. He said this out of compassion, not in pretense. “Who is scandalized,” etc. By “scandal” he means a movement of the flesh, which usually occurs in two ways: either by looking upon the beauty of another person or through the ardor of one’s own flesh. But let such a person not yield or succumb when he hears that the Apostle sympathizes with him. Likewise, if someone is assailed by some wavering, let him not lose confidence that he can make God favorable toward him, since the Apostle sympathizes with him and also says that he himself burns.

There are some who wish to understand “faith,” so that the sense is: “Who is weak, or who is scandalized, and I do not suffer?” Likewise they understand it of charity and the other virtues. For he had said great things above, but these things are no less. Yet someone may perhaps say: How was this man righteous, when he reported his own good deeds in this way? Since God inserts his own praises into the divine Scriptures, he is not contradicting himself when he says: “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth” (Prov. XXVII, 2), etc.; rather, he reveals these things so that they may be recognized. For if they were not revealed, they would not be recognized; if they were not recognized, they would not be loved; if they were not loved, they would not be followed, nor would he reward those who followed. Paul reported his good deeds with this intention.

Next follows: “If it is necessary to boast,” etc. The sense is: If it is necessary to boast, I will boast in nothing other than my infirmities. Note that he calls the adversities he described above “infirmities”: “In hunger,” he says, “and thirst,” etc. Why, then, does he boast in these things, when nothing in them appears glorious, but everything mournful? Yet, if you attend carefully, it is very glorious to boast in those things for which an eternal reward of life remains.

Next follows: “The God and Father of our Lord,” etc. He was about to say great things about himself, and therefore prefaced them with an affirmation. For he was about to say things that might appear incredible. Who would believe him if he said that the leaders of the nations, together with the Jews, had risen up against him and that he had been able to escape? Or perhaps he prefaced his affirmation with an oath so that those who thought him to possess lesser authority might more readily place faith in his words.

Next follows: “The governor of Damascus under King Aretas” [Note: [Col. 0480D] The autograph has “Aratae.”], etc. This governor of Damascus, too, because he had understood that the Jews had conspired to kill Paul, sought to apprehend him, so that what they desired to accomplish through malice he might accomplish through power; or so that he might favor the Jews, or certainly so that, by destroying the disturber of peace, he might show himself the more zealous in the office entrusted to him.

Next follows: “And through a window I was let down in a basket by the wall,” etc. With dangers threatening him on every side, he had been so hemmed in that scarcely any place of escape could be found. Therefore he was lowered through a window by the brothers, in a basket, so that he might escape the hands of his persecutors even in this way.

Hence blessed Pope Gregory says: “Perhaps someone asks how this righteous man could so diligently avoid the fury and death of his persecutors. Yet he was altogether righteous, because he avoided death for this reason: he understood that there would be no fruit in it. He avoided death, not in order to preserve life for himself, but rather to supply life to others.” He himself shows this to be so when he says: “I am ready not only to be bound in Jerusalem, but also to die” (Acts XX, 22), and when he came to Rome to suffer.

The same aforementioned pope also says that all the things we do ought to be done under the great moderation of discernment. It is very necessary to attend to this carefully. If the magnitude of the fruits comes first, then, I say, one cannot avoid labors without danger to oneself; but if the magnitude of the labor comes first, one can avoid the labors of death without danger to oneself. The Apostle considered this, and therefore diligently avoided death. He acted like a very brave soldier who, shut in on every side by a siege, seeks the field of battle so that by his preaching he might overthrow more adversaries of the sacred faith [Col. 0481C]. Nevertheless, it should be understood that the person who avoids labors without danger to himself is the one who patiently bears the conduct of others.

**(Chapter XII.)** Next follows: “If it is necessary to boast.” He says this, nevertheless, because he escaped their hands. Yet it is not expedient, because it is not beneficial: God is not made favorable by boasting but by humiliation. Next follows: “But I will come to visions,” etc. Note that he attributes infirmities to himself but revelations to the Lord.

Next follows: “I know a man in Christ fourteen years ago,” etc. Note that, compelled by great necessity, he revealed what he had concealed in silence for fourteen years. Observe also that he says “a man,” so that it might not be thought to be a fantasy. He says “in Christ,” so that it might not be believed to have been done by the devil.

When he says “the third heaven,” we should not understand the place where the moon is situated. Rather, he says “up to the third” to show that it is above every creature and all the elements. The spiritual heaven, therefore, should be understood as the firmament and the throne above. Since this revelation also occurred twice, he therefore added: “And I know such a man,” etc.

He calls the heavenly paradise Jerusalem, which is our mother, and where the angelic powers and the souls of the saints are; its entrance the thief also heard [Note: [Col. 0481D] Perhaps “the thief entered its entrance” should be read. The meaning is sufficiently clear, although an error has crept into the wording.]. Those, therefore, who doubt that resurrected bodies can exist in heaven or in paradise should hear that the Apostle says he does not know whether he was in the body or outside the body. By asserting that he did not know, he shows that either possibility can exist.

He calls the words “secret words” things that are not permitted for a human being to speak: either “not permitted” because one cannot speak them, or, if one can, because it is nevertheless not lawful. One should also carefully consider how it can be true that the Lord says: “No human being shall see me” (Exod. XXXIII, 20), etc.; and yet if the same vision is granted to any mortal, it is entirely true that those who saw him died to the world.

Blessed Augustine says: “It may be asked what the Apostle says he does not know, or what he knows. But let us connect the words, so that perhaps from their connection we may be able to recognize what he knows and what he does not know. The order of the words is therefore this: he says that he knows that a man was taken up into heaven or paradise, but he says that he does not know whether this occurred in the body or outside the body. Since what he says is true, either he knew both things or he knew neither” [Note: [Col. 0481D] These words have the character of an objection and seem to mean the following: If what the Apostle says he saw is true—as it most certainly is—he ought to have known both things. For if he saw it, then he knew that he was present in the body; or he knew neither, meaning that it is false that he saw anything. He begins to answer this objection and absurdity in the words that follow: “But it should be known.”]

But it should be understood that the paradise or heaven shown to him was corporeal; therefore he saw it with bodily eyes, since a corporeal thing is ordinarily seen by bodily eyes, and a spiritual thing by spiritual eyes. If, however, a spiritual thing is seen by bodily eyes, it is not seen through that mode or by that vision by which corporeal things are seen by bodily eyes and spiritual things by spiritual eyes; rather, it is seen through a certain special vision that surpasses all others.

For example, a spiritual thing is seen by spiritual eyes, such as justice and similar things. Who, when considering justice, asks what it tastes like or smells like, and so forth? No one asks this, and yet it is spiritual [Note: [Col. 0482D] Perhaps read: “for it is indeed a spiritual thing.”] Moses, however, spoke with God face to face; nevertheless, he understood that the thing he saw was not God, since God is incorporeal, and therefore he sought to see what God truly was.

Blessed Augustine also says that perhaps Paul did not know this: whether, with his body temporarily dead, his soul had also been taken away and seen this, or whether, while remaining in the body like the prophets, he had recognized it in an ecstasy of mind. Nevertheless, it should be understood that, if what was shown to him was certain and substantial—as it must most truly be believed to have been—then he saw what was said through that vision which surpasses all others.

Next follows: “On behalf of such a man I will boast” (the word “man” is understood); “but on my own behalf, nothing.” He says this because he spoke as though about another person.

Next follows: “For even if I should wish to boast, I would not be foolish.” Why not? “For I will speak the truth.” Here he openly shows why he had said above: “So that no one may think me foolish.” It should certainly be understood that the person who reveals gifts bestowed upon him from heaven is not foolish, and the person who conceals them is not imprudent.

Next follows: “But I spare.” It should be noted that the Apostle knew much greater things which, lest he appear to be exalted, he did not wish to reveal; therefore he says: “But I spare,” that is, I conceal. Why? “Lest anyone think more of me than he sees in me” [Note: [Col. 0483D] The Vulgate has “in me.”], namely, in my activity, or hears from me, namely, in my preaching.

Blessed Pope Gregory says that he moderated his preaching under great providence [Note: [Col. 0483D] Perhaps “prudence.”]. For he said certain things for the sake of his hearers and kept certain things silent, lest he seem exalted in their eyes; he said certain things in order to give life to his own people, but kept certain things silent in order to preserve his own.

Next follows: “Lest the greatness of the revelations exalt me,” etc. Note that he does not say, “The greatness of the revelations exalted me,” but “lest it exalt me,” because it was not given in order to wipe away a fault that was already present, but to prevent one that could arise.

It should also be understood that, as blessed Pope Gregory says, God orders the hearts of his saints under a provident dispensation. Thus he enriches them with his many gifts and grants them victory over many vices, yet allows some things to remain in them against which they must struggle and be tested. In this way, when they are unable to overcome small things, they recognize that they have not conquered great things by their own strength—like the people of Israel, who, after exterminating many nations, were unable to exterminate the Philistines. Hence it is written: “The Philistines were left so that Israel might be tested” (Judg. III, 4). It should also be understood that God scourges a human being in five ways, as is shown in this passage.

Next follows: “A thorn was given to me in my flesh,” etc. In this passage different people understand different things: some understand the thorn as afflictions, others as headaches, and still others as the lust of the flesh.

Blessed Augustine, however, who was more eloquent than all the teachers of Roman eloquence, says as follows: “Paul, a disciple of Christ—not Pelagius, a disciple of the Antichrist—says that the evil of lust is present in him, and in the clearest words he reveals the evil of lust. Recognizing that the incitement of his flesh and an internal civil war existed within him, and finding no place of escape except the grace of God, he cried out, saying: ‘Wretched man that I am!’ (Rom. VII, 24), etc.” Behold, he understood that he could be liberated only by the grace of God. Pelagius, however, believes that by his own powers he can both abandon evil and rise toward good.

“Lest the greatness of the revelations,” etc. Augustine himself says: “O terror and trembling! Who would not now fear to be exalted, if such a great man fears that he may be exalted?”

Next follows: “A thorn was given to me,” etc. It is a saving antidote by which the poison is overcome. And what else should I call this but *theriac*, which is prepared from viper’s venom? [Note: [Col. 0483D] The autograph has *sisidriacum*.] A thorn of lust was given to him so that the swelling of pride might be driven out; Satan was given so that Satan might be overcome. Thus the jaw of Behemoth [Note: [Col. 0483D] Job XL, 10 and following. *Behemoth* in Hebrew generically signifies a large animal, whether an elephant or something else. The Fathers, however, commonly understand the devil by this name.]—which is the devil—was pierced. For, as blessed Pope Gregory says, “By the means through which he strikes, he saves”; for through the very means by which he tempts the saints, wishing to destroy them, he saves the tested against his will.

Next follows: “For this reason I besought the Lord three times,” etc. If he asked and was not heard, where is what the Lord says: “Before you call, I will say, ‘Here I am’” (Isa. LVIII, 9), etc.; and again: “Whatever you ask, I will give you” (Matt. XXI, 22; John XIV, 13)? Was he not present while he was not hearing him? He was indeed present, like a physician who cuts out a sick person’s wound while the patient cries out under his hands. The physician is more present by not sparing him than if he spared him. Likewise, the Lord was more present by not granting the request than if he had granted it. For although he did not hear him according to his wish, he heard him according to his salvation. Indeed, he heard this man more than he heard the demons whom he allowed to go into the pigs (Matt. VIII, 30; Mark V, 11; Luke VIII, 32).

Next follows: “My grace is sufficient for you,” as if he had said: You labor, you hesitate, you fear that you may perish; but my grace is sufficient for you—that is, my calling and my predestination are sufficient for you. You have been predestined; you cannot perish [Note: [Col. 0484D] These words, which so clearly demonstrate the power of predestination, deserve very careful attention.]. Therefore do not fear. “For power is made perfect in weakness”; that is, the more a person is worn down by persecutions, the more he is lifted up [Note: [Col. 0484D] The autograph has *revelatur* (“is revealed”).].

It follows: “Therefore I will gladly glory,” as though he had said: Because I have deserved to hear that power is perfected in weakness, I will gladly glory in my weaknesses. Why? “So that the power of Christ may dwell in me.” “For this reason I take pleasure in...” He had said above, “I will gladly glory,” and therefore he added, “For this reason”—that is, because power is perfected in weakness—“I take pleasure in...” It should be observed that he had said many things above and was also about to say certain things below; yet both those things mentioned above and those to be mentioned below prevail over weakness. And because the things he had said above could appear to pertain to his praise, for that reason he fixed the eyes of his mind upon weakness, under whose name he embraced all the things mentioned earlier.

“In insults,” that is, not in honor; “in necessities,” that is, not in riches; [Col. 0484D] “in persecutions,” that is, not in rest or relief; “in distresses,” that is, not in exaltation or elevation; “for Christ,” that is, I endure these things not for crimes or sins, as heretical robbers suffer them. Hence the Lord says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution” [Note: [Col. 0484D] Matthew 5:10, where persecution for righteousness is under discussion], and so forth.

“For when I am weak...” The more he was afflicted by blows, the more he was strengthened; for in the saints, the more the outward person is afflicted, the more the inward person is strengthened. This is why the holy martyrs were so exceedingly strong in tribulations.

“I have become foolish...” Observe that he calls himself foolish and compelled, because, out of necessity—that is, for the sake of the salvation of his hearers—he had praised himself; and therefore he says: “You compelled me.” It should be understood that it is characteristic of fools, not of saints, to glory willingly.

This is the point of what he adds: “I ought to have been commended by you,” as though he had said: You ought to have resisted the pseudo-apostles, who are my detractors and persecutors. “For I was inferior in nothing” [Note: [Col. 0485D] The Vulgate has: “For I was inferior in nothing to them”], and so forth. It is as though he had said: I was inferior in nothing to Peter, Andrew, and the others, because I labored more than all. For if you refer the matter to teaching, they taught nothing different from me; if to the performance of miracles, likewise they did nothing greater. For although I am later in time, I am not inferior in dignity or merit.

By these words he shows that those who are greater in merit must not be preferred to those who are greater merely in age or time. For example, did John not preach before Christ? Or did Christ baptize John, rather than John baptize Christ? Yet John was not therefore greater. And did Andrew not follow Christ before Peter? Nevertheless Christ entrusted the Church to Peter also, saying: “You are Peter,” and so forth.

You also have an example in the Old Testament. Moses was younger than Aaron, yet God appeared to Moses in the bush, saying: “I am the God of Abraham” (Exodus 3:6), and so forth—especially although Aaron was more eloquent (Exodus 4:10), and so forth. Canonical authority likewise teaches that those who are greater in wisdom and merit are to be preferred to those who are greater in time. The same is true here.

“Although I am nothing...” Thus he humbles himself in order to raise himself up; and therefore, after saying, “I am nothing,” he added: “Yet the signs of an apostle” [Note: [Col. 0485D] The Vulgate has: “of apostleship”]. Observe also that he says “with all patience.” With this patience he had endured the Corinthians, and by the medicine of prodigies and signs he had corrected their errors. It is as though he had said: Insofar as I am a human being, I am nothing; insofar as I am an apostle, I am something.

“For what is there...” It is as though he had said: The other churches received no more from Peter or Andrew than you received from me, except perhaps this one thing: that I did not burden you by accepting payment. But if even this was a fault, forgive me—that is, pardon me this wrong. For it should be understood that it is characteristic of fools to reproach an act worthy of praise. He shows that they are fools.

And lest they should think that he, who had accepted nothing at the beginning of his preaching, might later wish to accept something, he therefore added: “Behold, this is the third time...” [Note: [Col. 0485D] In the autograph, the margin here reads “Chapter XXVIII”; but nowhere are Chapters XXV, XXVI, and XXVII found.] It is as though he had said: Do not think that I wish to accept something, since up to now I have accepted nothing. “For I do not seek what is yours,” and so forth.

By these words he urges them toward love of him, so that, hearing that he sought them, they might love him. It is as though he had said: The pseudo-apostles seek what is yours; do not love them. But I seek you; and since that is the greater thing, love me.

“For children ought not...” By these words he shows that he is their father. For, according to human custom, parents lay up treasures for their children, not children for their parents, but for themselves or for their own children. In spiritual matters, however, the opposite is true: children lay up for their parents, not parents for their children, because the children provide what is necessary.

And because this is the custom, he said this as though he had said: Since such is the practice both in carnal and in spiritual matters, I have acted contrary to it, because I accepted nothing but stripped other churches (2 Corinthians 11:8) in order to preach to you.

This is also the point of what he adds: “But I will most gladly,” that is, most devotedly, “spend,” that is, whatever I can receive from those churches, so that I may be sufficient to preach to you. “And I will be spent,” that is, I will be handed over to death by others for your salvation. There is no love greater than this. Hence the Lord says: “Greater love” (John 15:13), and so forth.

“Although, loving you more...” This depends upon what was said above. He had said: “I will be spent,” and therefore he added: “Although you...” I love you more than my other people, or more than others are loved by the other apostles, yet I am loved less by you than by my other people, or than others are loved by their own apostles.

“But let it be so: I did not burden you...” That is, I did not burden you financially in person. “But being crafty...” It is as though he had said: I did not refrain from accepting anything in order to receive more later. For deceit is called fraud or pretense; for that person is deceitful who thinks one thing inwardly but does another outwardly. The Apostle would then have wished to catch them by deceit if, for the sake of gaining much, he had refused to accept little.

“Did I take advantage of you through any of those...” It is as though he had said: None of those whom I sent to you said, “Give money worthy of his status, if you wish to keep him peaceful; you will not be able to keep him peaceful unless you give a suitable amount.” And if anyone had said to Paul, “I have sinned,” he would have tormented him.

“I appealed to Titus...” It is as though he had said: Titus did not defraud you, because he sought nothing from you, just as I did not; for those whose devotion is one also have one will. And therefore he added: “Did we not walk in the same spirit?” That is, in the same teaching and in the same footsteps, because we accepted nothing.

“Have you thought all this time...” It is as though he had said: For a long time you thought that we did not wish to accept a gift because of the gift itself, and not [Note: [Col. 0486D] The autograph has: “us”] because our intention was simple. But the pseudo-apostles were introducing this error, saying: “He refuses to accept small things so that he may receive great things.” For this reason he adds an affirmation under oath, saying: “Before God,” and so forth.

It is as though he had said: What I do not accept is not for the sake of greater profit, but for your salvation; or, for the sake of your salvation [Note: [Col. 0486D] The reason is perhaps to be supplied], I do not bend the rigor of my preaching. For it is of great benefit to the person who is rebuked if he does not receive anything from his teacher; for, while the teacher accepts nothing, the person believes that the teacher cannot be reconciled with him unless he amends his ways.

It follows: “For I fear that perhaps, when I come...” By these words he also shows that many among them were still uncorrected. Therefore he expressed the fear by which he would terrify them, lest, when he came, he should find them such as he did not wish them to be—that is, uncorrected—and therefore exercise the authority of his rule over them, while they themselves would find him such as they did not wish him to be—that is, rigid and severe.
