By this action preachers are warned that, if they hear of anything blameworthy concerning the peoples subject to them, they should first direct fear toward them, so that they may be corrected, lest they come and, finding them uncorrected, exercise the authority of their rule over them.

[Col. 0487B] It follows: “Lest perhaps there be contentions, jealousies...” Why he feared, he made clear in these words: namely, lest the things that follow should be found among them. “Contentions” are so called as though arising from every kind of striving, because a person defends something according to his own purpose—not from the desire to learn the truth, but rather to conquer.

“Jealousies” are envies. Nevertheless, as blessed Augustine says, there is a difference between jealousy and envy. Jealousy occurs when a person is tortured by pain over something that another has acquired and he himself has not acquired, and when the thing in question is such that it can be possessed by only one person. Envy, however, occurs when someone is tortured by pain over another’s happiness, and grieves over something that another acquires although he himself does not even desire it.

“Animosities” are anxieties, since *animosus* is understood as anxious or suspicious, that is, jealous. “Dissensions” are divisions, quarrels, and separations.

“Detractions” are so called as though they were withdrawals, because a detractor is one who says that another’s good is evil, or certainly says that what is great is small. For, while doing this, he strives to obscure his brother’s good reputation and, as it were, draws it back from the other’s heart, so that he will not be believed to be such as he had previously been believed to be.

“Whisperings,” or “whisperers,” are named from the sound made in the ears, because a whisperer is one who, speaking not to a person’s face but into his ear, detracts from another.

“Inflations” are also called swellings, because one who is inflated is called, as it were, wind-filled; for, just as a wineskin is stretched by wind, so his mind is swollen by bitterness, indignation, or some form of exaltation, as though by wind.

It follows: “Sedition.” It should be understood that there is a difference between sedition, war, and incitement. Sedition concerns citizens; war concerns enemies; incitement refers to a fight stirred up by the burning of one’s own flesh. Although all these things are different, they nevertheless tend toward one end: the division of love. Therefore, because they had been divided, lest they become divided again, the Apostle directed fear toward them so that they might guard themselves against all these things.

[Col. 0488A] It follows: “Lest again, when I come, God humble me among you...” In this passage, when he says, “and I mourn many,” he shows that some had already been corrected through repentance and had been recalled to fellowship with the holy Church. Nevertheless, many still remained uncorrected, and he feared that because of them he would be humbled.

For what father would not rejoice in beloved children, or who would not grieve over evil ones? Therefore he directed fear toward them so that they might be corrected, lest, if he came and found them unamended, he should be humbled and mourn because they had not done penance—for if they had done so, they would have obtained forgiveness.

This also works against the Novatians, who, after someone falls into the evil of fornication, deny that he can rise again through repentance. Repentance would indeed be imposed in vain if the fruit of forgiveness did not follow.

It should also be understood that he mentions three things: fornication, uncleanness, and shamelessness. Of all these, shamelessness is the worse, because shamelessness is called, as it were, monstrous uncleanness, practiced in uncertain matters or in things done against nature, as in the case of the man who took his father’s wife (1 Corinthians 5:1).

The chaste person is called modest; the shameless person immodest—that is, one who, having lost modesty, engages in detestable sexual acts. “Uncleanness” is called whatever is contrary to purity. “Fornication,” however, in this passage should be understood as that which is committed bodily; “uncleanness” can also be understood as that which is committed through bodily pleasure or through the deliberation of the mind.

**(CHAPTER XIII.)** It follows: “Behold, this is the third time I am coming” [Col. 0488C] [Note: [Col. 0487D] The Vulgate has: “I come”]. He had come twice, and now promises that he will come a third time, because shortly before he had said that he was ready.

But it may be asked why he joined the testimony of the Law to his coming. Clearly, he did so because, according to the precept of the Law, a person is either justified or condemned on the testimony of two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 17:6). Since he had warned them twice to correct themselves, he therefore brought forward this testimony, so that, if they did not correct themselves, they might understand that he would no longer spare them.

Hence he immediately added: “I have already said, and I say beforehand...” He had warned those who had sinned formerly, both while present and while absent, as well as all the others; and he warned those who had not yet completely corrected themselves that, if he came again, he would not spare them. The Apostle spares them, as it were, by not sparing them, because he first introduces fear, lest he should find something for which to exercise his authority.

It follows: “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” The meaning is: You wish to test by experience whether I am able to do this, and therefore you do not wish to correct yourselves. You seek proof of Christ speaking in me, to discover whether he can accomplish through me what I say, so that, if he accomplishes it, you may henceforth be afraid, but, if he does not accomplish it, you may remain secure.

In saying “who speaks in me,” he shows that his speech and teaching belong to Christ.

It follows: “Who is not weak among you...” The meaning is: If he is not weak among you, much less is he weak among us, and he will be powerful among us [Col. 0489A] [Note: [Col. 0489D] The autograph also has: “he may have been able among us.” In my judgment this reading lacks sense and should be corrected from the Vulgate, so that the meaning is: “Who is not weak among you, but is powerful among you, and will be powerful among us.”]

For Christ was not weak among them, because he had performed many signs among them through the apostles: they had seen the blind given sight, lepers cleansed, and so forth. It is as though the Apostle had said: If Christ was not weak among you, why are you not afraid, since he can accomplish what I say?

Because someone might respond to this by saying, “How was he not weakened, since he was crucified?” he added and said: “For even if he was crucified through our weakness” [Note: [Col. 0489D] “Our” does not occur in the Vulgate], and so forth.

It is as though he had said: He was crucified and suffered through the weakness of our flesh; he died and, ascending into heaven, opened the way to the heavenly kingdom, so that those departing from this life might enter without any delay into the happiness of that same kingdom [Col. 0490D] [Note: Perhaps *integre*—“completely”—should be read]. What he says, “through the power of God,” refers either to the Father or to the same Son.

It follows: “For we also are weak in him.” This is the voice of the apostles and of perfected men alone. “We are weak in him,” that is, we suffer and are afflicted for him. “But we shall live with him through the power of God among you.” It is as though he had said: We are weak among unbelievers, because the greater the things they make us suffer, the weaker they think us to be; among you we live, because you understand us to be stronger the greater the things you see us suffer.

According to the reading “we shall live,” the meaning is: “If we suffer death with him, we shall also reign with him” (Romans 8:17).

It follows: “Test yourselves...” That is, examine one another, and also bring before your eyes the dangers of temptations, and consider whose faith and virtue you possess [Col. 0489C].

It should be carefully understood that there is a temptation of testing and a temptation of deception: the temptation of testing comes from God, while the temptation of deception comes from the devil; nevertheless, both occur through the human being. Here, however, temptation should be understood as testing.

It should also be understood that this mutual testing and examination is of great value, in accordance with Solomon’s saying: “Iron is sharpened by iron” (Proverbs 27:17), and so forth.

It follows: “Or do you not recognize that Christ is in you?” It is as though he had said: If you bring the dangers of temptations before your eyes and recognize whose faith or virtue you possess, you will know whether Christ is in you or not—and you can recognize this. But if you do not do so, you will not recognize it; and that is to be reprobate. Therefore he says: “Unless perhaps you are reprobate.”

It follows: “But I hope that you will recognize...” By these words he urges them toward firmness in faith and holy conduct. It is as though he had said: If you recognize, as I have said, that Christ is in you, you will also recognize that we are not reprobate—that is, double-minded or of divided intention. This statement refers to what he said above: “For a long time you have thought,” and so forth.

It follows: “But we pray to God...” As usual, the Apostle prays for his people, that they do no evil.

It follows: “Not that we may appear approved” [Col. 0490A]. He would appear approved if he found them uncorrected—that is, such as would allow him to exercise his authority over them. But the Apostle did not want this; therefore he added: “But that you may do what is good. We, however, may be reprobate” [Note: [Col. 0490D] The Vulgate has: “but that we may be reprobate”].

But what does it mean that he wishes them to do good, while he wishes himself to be reprobate? Does he wish evil upon himself? No. Rather, he calls himself reprobate—that is, humble. The Apostle would then be reprobate, that is, humble, if he found them corrected, because he would be unable to exercise his authority over them.

Hence, explaining this, he added: “For we cannot do anything against the truth.” It is as though he had said: If you correct yourselves, we cannot exercise our authority over you, because we can do nothing against the truth, since the truth is in you. But if you do not correct yourselves, we can exercise our authority against you, because we fight for the truth, though for your sake.

It follows: “Yet we rejoice when we are weak” [Note: [Col. 0490D] The Vulgate has: “because we are weak”], “but you are powerful.” By these words the Apostle shows that he rejoices in their good works. It is as though he had said: If you resist vices vigorously and powerfully, we rejoice, because then we are weak—that is, humble. But if you do not resist vices, we are powerful and you are weak, because we can exercise over you the authority of our rule.

Preachers should also act this way now: if their hearers are powerful, the preachers should be weak; and if their hearers are weak, the preachers should be powerful.

It follows: “This also we pray for,” that is, that you may be [Note: [Col. 0490D] That is, powerful or weak, as he explained above, according to what is appropriate; or perhaps one should read: “as you know”]. And this is what follows: “Your completion,” that is, your perfection.

It follows: “Therefore I write these things while absent, so that I may not act more harshly when present.” By these words he instilled fear in them so that they might be corrected, lest, when he came, he should act more harshly—that is, exercise the power of his apostleship severely against them.

And this is what follows: “According to the authority that the Lord gave me for building up and not for tearing down.” Behold, he says that he has received authority. And fittingly he says “for building up,” because preachers receive authority for this purpose: to save by correcting, not to destroy by failing to correct.

[Col. 0490D] Having finished the commendation of his own person—which he had begun at the point where he had concluded his discussion of the collections, in which commendation he had labored greatly for two reasons, namely, either to show that he was not of less authority than the others, or to remove from himself the charge of greed—he now undertakes another matter. That is, he adds an exhortation together with a narrative.

[Col. 0491A] [Note: [Col. 0491C] The autograph margin here reads “Chapter XXIX.”]

“Finally,” he says—that is, for the rest, moreover—“brothers, rejoice; be perfected; exhort one another,” that is, admonish one another. For through this exhortation, by which vices are overcome through hope of future things, perfection arises; from perfection comes joy, because no one can rejoice and yet fail to be perfect unless he overcomes vices.

It follows: “Think the same thing.” He touches upon this because he had also mentioned it at the beginning, where he said: “I appeal to you to say the same thing” (1 Corinthians 1:10). This is what he says here: “Think the same thing,” that is, do not think differently about me or in relation to me, whether in faith or in conduct.

It follows: “Keep peace.” He commends peace to them on account of those who were inflicting fraud and injury upon their brothers and, for this reason, dragging them before the judgments of unbelievers, as he says in the first letter: “But you do injury and defraud” (1 Corinthians 6:8), and so forth.

It follows: “And the God of peace and love will be with you.” Having completed the exhortation, he added the narrative: “The God of peace,” he says, and so forth.

God is called the God of peace because he himself is the author of peace, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Christ is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2:14). And the Lord says: “I leave you peace; I give you my peace” (John 14:27).

He is the God of love, in accordance with the saying: “I give you a new commandment: that you love one another” (John 13:34), and again: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (ibid., 35).

The meaning is: If you have peace and love, you will possess the author of peace forever. For this is the true and secure peace, which the wicked cannot possess. Hence the saying: “There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isaiah 57:21).

Nevertheless, even if the wicked possess peace, it is very far from the peace that the Lord distinguishes when he says: “I give you a new commandment: that you love one another” (John 14:27), not such peace as the world gives.

Moreover, in saying “the God of peace,” and so forth, the Apostle wished it to be understood that, if they had hatred and quarrels, the author of hatred and quarrels—that is, the devil—would possess them forever.

It follows: “Greet one another with a holy kiss.” A greeting is an indication and a wish for salvation. He calls this greeting and this kiss a holy kiss, but the kiss of those others is an indication of corruption and, as it were, of restoration and satisfaction. Therefore, whenever the Apostle commends a kiss, he always adds a qualifying word.

It follows: “All the saints greet you.” It is as though he had said: Not the powerful, not princes, but all the saints.

It should be considered why he directed the saints’ greeting to them. Clearly, he did so to urge them toward the good of holiness, so that those who were greeted by the saints might become holy; or certainly to invite them to return the greeting to one another, so that those who were greeted by the saints might greet the saints.

Observe that he does not merely say “the saints,” but adds “all,” because it belongs to the saints to wish that everyone be saved. Therefore, whoever does not desire the salvation of all should understand that he too is not included in this greeting.

[Col. 0492B] It follows: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ...” Having also completed the greeting, he added a prayer: “The grace of the Lord,” he says, and so forth.

It should especially be noted that at the end of this Epistle the love of unity is commended. And fittingly so, because the highest perfection consists in the unity of the Trinity.

For the love of the Father sent us the Savior, that is, Jesus, by whose grace we have been redeemed. This love and grace are also preserved for us through the fellowship of the Holy Spirit, since the Holy Spirit perpetually guards and defends those who are loved by the Father and redeemed by the Son.

This passage also works against Arius, who likewise said that the Son was inferior to the Father because, wherever the Father and the Son were mentioned, the Father was always placed first.

It should also be noted that he does not say merely “with you,” but “with all,” clearly to show how much love he had, since he wished grace not only for those who had been corrected but also for those who had not been corrected.

It is as though he had said: You can recognize how much I love you by the fact that I wish grace not only for those who have been corrected but also for those who have not yet been corrected.

Or he says “with all” so that no sex, age, social status, or language would be excluded; but just as the blood of Christ redeemed everyone, so everyone might possess the grace of Christ.

“Amen” is a word of confirmation, which confirms everything.

**The end. Thanks be to God.**

# HERE BEGINS THE EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS

[Col. 0491]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0491D]

Observe that just as, in these latter times, when the Word of God, clothed in the flesh of the Virgin Mary, came forth into the world, the appearance of his humanity was open to everyone, while knowledge of his divinity was granted to very few—that is, only to the elect—so, when the words of the Law and the Prophets are brought forth to human beings, they are covered with a veil.

There the flesh was the veil; here, the letter. And just as divinity lay hidden beneath the veil of flesh, so spiritual understanding lies hidden beneath the veil of the letter. And just as those eyes were blessed which recognized that divinity lay hidden in the flesh, so also are those blessed who recognize spiritual understanding as hidden in the letter.

Those who had believed from the circumcision certainly did not possess these blessed eyes, since they did not withdraw from observing the carnal Law and believed that they were justified by its works. Indeed, they even criticized the Apostle, saying that he was not a true apostle because he had not followed the Lord in the flesh and taught things contrary to the other apostles.

By this cunning and trickery they had subverted the Galatians, who also did not possess spiritual eyes, because they did not penetrate the mysteries of circumcision, the Sabbath, or the other legal observances.

If these people had eyes by which the divinity of the Word is recognized, they would answer those persuading them to observe carnal practices as Susanna answered the elders when they dragged her toward sexual violation: “If I do this, it is death for me; but if I do not, I shall not escape your hands” (Daniel 13:22).

So these people too would say: If we do this—that is, if we prefer the carnal Law to grace—we shall incur the death of the soul; otherwise we shall not escape the hands of your criticism. But it is better, by living Catholicly and understanding the Law and the Prophets spiritually, to remain in the freedom of grace than, by departing from it, to incur God’s displeasure together with your grace.

Therefore God must be entreated to drive away from the eyes of our heart the darkness of all vices and the cloud of every defilement, by which those eyes themselves are often accustomed to be blinded, so that we may be able to penetrate the mysteries of the Law and the Prophets and, what is now especially necessary, the intention of this Apostle.

It should be understood that the Gauls were first called by the whiteness of their bodies, because Greek *gala* is called *lac* in Latin. Hence the Sibyl, “then binding their milk-white necks with gold” [Note: [Col. 0493D] Virgil, *Aeneid* 8.660–661: “they are entwined with gold”]. He could have called them white, but he wished to preserve the propriety of the expression.

Mountains and the severity of the climate exclude the heat of the sun, and therefore the color of their bodies cannot be discolored.

The province of Gaul also has mountain ridges to the east; to the north, the waters of the Rhine and Germany; to the south, the steep peaks of the Pyrenees [Note: [Col. 0493D] The autograph has: “of the Pyrenean river”]; and to the west, the Ocean Sea. Its beginning is Belgica and its end Aquitania.

For, having been summoned by the king of Bithynia [Note: [Col. 0493D] Perhaps “Bithynia,” which is related to Galatia] to assist him, they divided the kingdom with him after victory had been achieved. Thus, mingled with the Greeks, they were called Gallo-Greeks, and their region Gallo-Greece.

Nevertheless, the earlier name remained and still remains, so that they themselves were called Galatians and their region Galatia [Note: [Col. 0493D] This is now Çankırı. Concerning the Galatians, or Gauls, who at that time were scattered throughout Asia, see 2 Maccabees 8:20: when the Macedonian allies hesitated, only six thousand Jews in Babylonia killed one hundred and twenty thousand Galatians, with help given to them from heaven].

It should not, however, appear contrary to reason if people from the western regions, with many kingdoms lying between, crossed into the eastern regions and established settlements there, since peoples from the East and Greece reached almost to the furthest limits of the West.

For, as Marcus Varro says, Massilia was founded by the Phoenicians [Note: [Col. 0493D] Jerome calls them Phocaeans, or Phocenses, following Justin, Book 43. See Pomponius Mela, Book 2, *On the Situation of the World*; Strabo, Book 4 of the *Geography*; Aulus Gellius, Book 10], whom he also says were trilingual.

Rhodes too, from which come the *Rhodoani*, was founded by Rhodian colonists. And why should this be surprising, when Italy itself, occupied by Greeks, was called Greater Greece?

It is also established that the Romans themselves, descended from the stock of Aeneas, were of Asian origin.

I also wish to point out that the Apostle marks each province in his Epistles according to its particular character, and this can easily be recognized in them.

Nevertheless, the traces of the virtues or vices of those same provinces remain to this day.

In each of them, for example, he greatly praises the faith of the Romans: “I give thanks,” he says, “to my God” (Romans 6:17), and so forth. For what nation is more ready to believe, or what people more devoted to ecclesiastical worship?

Yet he marks them as being held by the vice of pride: “Do not be high-minded” (Romans 11:20), and so forth; and again: “Do not think more highly” (Romans 12:3), and so forth. This trace remains in them to this day.

He strongly marks the Corinthians. For he reproves their various evil customs, namely, that their women prayed without veils (1 Corinthians 11:5), that they held banquets in the churches (ibid., 22), and that, puffed up with human wisdom, they denied the resurrection of the flesh. Whoever knows Corinth knows that this remains there even now.

He likewise places the Macedonians foremost in praise, because they were greatly devoted to the grace of hospitality and generosity in almsgiving. Hence he also says: “Concerning brotherly love” (1 Thessalonians 4:9), and so forth.

Nevertheless, he reproves them because some of them went about idly: “For we hear that some among you walk disorderly” (2 Thessalonians 3:11); and again: “When we were with you, we commanded you this” (ibid., 10).

As for the Galatians, with whom we are now concerned, he marks them as exceedingly foolish—a trait that remains in them to this day. Hence Jerome says: “Whoever knows with me the norm of my metropolis knows certainly that the Galatians are foolish and deceived by various errors” [Note: [Col. 0493D] I have nowhere found this text literally in the Veronese edition of Saint Jerome [Col. 0494D]. It is certain, and worth observing, that an error has crept into the transcription of this text, whoever its author may be. The words “whoever knows with me the norm of my metropolis,” since they convey no suitable sense, should be read differently, perhaps more correctly: “whoever knows with me the norm of their metropolis,” namely Ancyra. In fact, the words that alone can appropriately correspond to this text from Saint Jerome are found in his commentary on this Epistle, Book 2, chapter 3, p. 430 of volume 7 of the aforementioned Veronese edition, as follows: “Anyone who has seen Ancyra, the metropolitan city of Galatia, knows with me that the Galatians have been declared foolish and senseless, and knows how it is still torn apart by so many schisms and corrupted by so many varieties of doctrines.”]

It should also be understood that the Apostle’s purpose in this Epistle, as in the one addressed to the Romans, is to make clear both the abolition of the Law and the dignity of grace.

The difference is that in the Epistle to the Romans he uses more subtle arguments, because they were prudent; in this one he speaks in more explicit words, because they were foolish. He does not so much [Note: [Col. 0495D] The autograph has: “notam.”] address them by teaching as by rebuking, so that authority might recall those whom reason did not persuade.

And although the abolition of the Law and the dignity of grace are made clear in all his Epistles, they are especially clear in these two.

It should also be understood that the Apostle is not addressing those who had believed from the circumcision and, having been deceived by false apostles, had passed from the freedom of grace into the slavery of the Law. These false apostles said that Paul was not a true apostle, especially because he acted one way in Jerusalem and taught the Gentiles to act another way, and because the other true apostles observed the Law while he destroyed it.

The Galatians had acted like a man who, after being freed from the hand of a gladiator, hands himself over to a trainer. The Apostle Peter was also deceived by their pretense, as the Apostle mentioned above makes clear in this Epistle (Galatians 2:11).

## [THE TEXT BEGINS]

**(CHAPTER I.)** “Paul, an apostle.”

It is a sign of great authority that Paul, at the beginning of his Epistles, calls himself an apostle of Christ. For just as earthly judges assume in their letters the names of princes and kings whose intimacy they enjoy, so that they may be held in greater veneration and receive greater service, so Paul also called himself Christ’s apostle, in order to show whose authority he possessed, to be held in greater veneration, and to cause all Christians to be struck with fear at the beginning of his Epistles.

This is why, at the beginning of the Epistle to the Hebrews, he does not call himself an apostle, although he does so in all the other Epistles: in what follows he was going to describe Christ as the great high priest and apostle.

For *apostle* in Greek means “one who is sent” in Latin; in Hebrew it is said to be *silas*, a name likewise derived from sending.

It should be understood that the Hebrews say that apostles and prophets are those to whom the word of sending is directed, as Moses was, to whom it was said: “Come, and I will send you” (Exodus 3:10), and so forth; and as Isaiah was, who said: “Behold, here am I; send me” (Isaiah 6:8); and the other prophets likewise.

John the Baptist is rightly also called an apostle and prophet, because it is written of him: “There was a man sent from God” (John 1:6).

It continues: “Not from human beings.” It should be understood that there are four classes of apostles. There are those who are sent neither by human beings nor through a human being, but by God—such as Moses, all the prophets, and the apostles. Again, there are those who are sent by God but through human beings, such as Joshua. Again, there are those who are sent not by God but through a human being [Note: The words “such as those … through a human being” are written in the upper margin of the manuscript, in the same script but with less black ink [Col. 0495D; 0496D], and appear to have been excerpted from the beginning of Book I of Saint Jerome’s *Commentaries*.]—such as those whom we see in the Church obtaining ecclesiastical ranks through the distribution of gifts, for the sake of popular favor. Finally, there are those who are sent neither by God nor by human beings nor through human beings, but come for their own purposes—namely, earthly profit, the belly, or human praise—as were all false apostles.

But the Apostle, in order to show that he belonged to the more excellent rank, says: “Not from human beings,” that is, he was not ordained an apostle by the apostles. For apostles used to ordain apostles in order to strengthen the Churches, just as, on the contrary, they sent their own men against the zealots of the Law in order to destroy the faith of the Church. Hence he himself says: “Nor through a human being,” that is, he was not ordained by a wicked apostle, whether a Jew or Jews.

It should certainly be understood that these words seem to some to be words of pride. Nevertheless, they are not; rather, they are words of necessity. For he said this because he was compelled by necessity—namely, so as not to give the pseudo-apostles an opportunity, and to demonstrate the authority of his apostleship. In this he opposes those who said that he was not a true Apostle and preferred the other apostles to him.

But lest the defenders of the Law should have an opportunity to say that he was not a true Apostle because he taught differently from Peter and the others, he himself says: “Not from human beings,” and so forth—as though he had said: “I learned the Gospel from the one from whom Peter and the others learned it; therefore I am not inferior to them.”

It should also be noted why he says: “Nor through a human being.” Does he deny that Christ is human? No, I say; he denies that He is merely human. Or he denies “a human being” because, although He was human, He gave commandments as God.

It continues: “But through Jesus Christ,” and so forth. It should be understood that in this passage the Apostle simultaneously refutes the errors of Arius, Manichaeus, and Photinus. It should also be noted that Christ is said to have been raised by the Father (Acts III, 15), as is likewise read in the Acts of the Apostles, and yet He is related to have raised Himself. The explanation of this question is evident.

It continues: “And all the brothers who are with me.” It should certainly be noted that, whereas in his other epistles he joins to himself sometimes Sosthenes, sometimes Silvanus, and at other times Timothy, in this Epistle he associates all the brothers with himself. He did this because a greater authority was then necessary, so that, when they heard the greeting of all the brothers, they might understand that all had been troubled and stirred up against them, recognize that they had committed a monstrous crime, and take refuge in correction. For the agreement of many is very powerful in correcting the crimes of the wicked: the more someone is reproved by many, the more seriously he recognizes that he has sinned and the more easily he is corrected.

It continues: “To the Churches of Galatia.” It should be noted that he does not say “to the Church,” but “to the Churches,” in order to show that he had written not merely to the urban populace but to the inhabitants of the entire province.

Observe that he calls those “Churches” which he later notes to have been deceived by various errors. Hence it is shown that there is a perfect Church having neither spot nor wrinkle, and an imperfect Church which, although its virtues have not yet been completed, is nevertheless gathered in the name of Jesus and has been corrupted by some error [Note: In the autograph, “gathered” is masculine plural (*congregati*). It seems to me that the verb *est* (“is”), or another equivalent, is missing here.]

Likewise, “wise” is used in two ways. There is one who is perfectly wise, such as those of whom the Lord says: “Behold, I shall send you wise men” (Matthew XXIII, 34). There is also one who is imperfectly wise [Note: In the autograph it reads, “for he is perfectly wise.” I judged this should be corrected, both on the basis of what follows—where the matter concerns reproof, which one does not need if one is perfectly wise—and on the basis of the cited text, which confirms this part of the distinction. Saint Jerome, who sets forth this distinction at the beginning of his *Commentaries on this Epistle*, has the following: “The perfect are meant by: ‘I shall send among you wise men’” (Luke XI, 49); “the foolish by: ‘Reprove the wise man, and he will love you’” (Proverbs IX, 8). “He who possesses complete and perfected virtue does not need correction.”] Hence Solomon says: “Reprove the wise man, and he will love you” (Proverbs VIII, 9). Certainly, the perfectly wise person does not need reproof [Note: That is, the perfectly wise person, for whom there is no occasion for the reproof mentioned by Solomon in the cited passage.]

What is said about wisdom can likewise be understood of chastity, fortitude, and the other virtues, because some are found at their completion, while others are still making progress.

It continues: “Grace to you and peace,” and so forth. It should be understood that, with deeper counsel and more subtle ingenuity, the Apostle uses these expressions in this Epistle more than in the others. He wished grace for them in order to show that they could be justified not by works of the Law but by the grace of God; for if they were justified by works of the Law, grace would no longer be grace. He also wished them peace, to admonish them that they ought to remain in the freedom they had begun to possess, because where there is no peace there is no freedom. Grace is that by which sins are forgiven, and so forth.

It continues: “Who gave Himself for our sins.” What he says—“Who gave,” and so forth—contributes greatly to his purpose. For he says this so that, when they heard that Christ had been handed over for sins, they might understand that they could not be justified by works of the Law. If they were justified by works of the Law, Christ would have handed Himself over for sins in vain.

The function of the Law was to reveal sins, but not to abolish them. Christ’s mercy, dignity, and power, however, consisted in revealing sins and abolishing them alike. Therefore Love handed itself over so that it might free us from impiety, Justice from injustice, and Equity from iniquity.

Hence he immediately adds: “So that He might rescue us from the present evil age.” It may be asked why he calls the age evil. “Age” is the course of the sun and moon and the revolving succession of years. All these things were created by God and are good. Thus an evil age is spoken of in the same way as an evil goodness, an evil city, and an infamous forest, because blood is shed there, and in the same way as “evil days.” Hence the Apostle says: “Redeeming the time” (Ephesians V, 16), and so forth. And Jacob said to Pharaoh: “The days of the years of my life are one hundred and twenty [Note: Genesis XLVII, 9, where the reading is not “one hundred and twenty,” but “one hundred and thirty”] years, few and evil,” and so forth. There he called “days” the hardships and pressures by which he had been afflicted.

The Apostle, however, in order to show that the handing over of the Son was valid and worthy, and to confirm the same, said that it had been done according to the Father’s will: “According to the will,” he says, “of God.” Here he shows that neither did the Son act without the Father’s will, nor did the Father hand Him over without the Son’s will, since, just as their nature is one, so also their will and operation are one.

He also shows that the Son fulfilled the Father’s will in all things. The Son Himself makes this clearer when He says: “I have not come to do my own will” (John VI, 38), and so forth. For the Apostle likewise did this—not, as he himself says, seeking to please human beings (Galatians I, 10), and so forth. Therefore let no one strive to fulfill his own will, but that of the other; and let no one seek his own glory, but that of the other.

It continues: “To whom is glory,” and so forth. Infinite praises are owed for infinite benefits. It was an infinite benefit that the Father handed over for the sins of human beings not an angel, not an archangel, but His own Son. Therefore, returning infinite praises, he says: “To whom is glory throughout the ages of ages.”

“Ages of ages” is said in the same way as “Song of Songs” and “King of Kings.” There are, in fact, ages which, through the gathering together of many ages, are called “ages of ages.” And when he says “throughout the ages of ages,” he uses it in place of “for infinity.”

It is also used for a finite period, as in: “He shall be your servant forever” (Exodus XXI, 6). In certain copies “for eternity” is found, where “age” refers to the jubilee year. For just as the end of the age will be the termination of all temporal causes and things, so the jubilee was the complete termination of buying, selling, and exchange [Note: The jubilee year, however, was the fiftieth year (Leviticus XXV, 10–11). On this matter, consult Vallartius’s note below, “Jerome’s Vindications from the Book of Jerome’s Questions,” on page 378 of volume VII of Saint Jerome’s works.]

Hence also the Psalmist says: “His mercy is forever” (Psalm CV, 1; CVI, 2).

“Amen” is a Hebrew expression. It is interpreted as “truly,” “faithfully,” or “may it be so.” With this expression the Apostle confirmed his preface, just as the Lord also confirmed those statements which He wished to impress more firmly upon the hearts of His hearers.

[Note: In the autograph’s margin, “chapter II” is written here.]

“I marvel that so quickly,” and so forth. Having completed the preface, he begins the text of the Epistle. That text begins with a rebuke, when he says: “I marvel,” and so forth.

It should be noted that the verb “to transfer” is used both in a good and in a bad sense: in a good sense, as in “Enoch was transferred by God” (Sirach XLIV, 16); in a bad sense, as with Ahab by Jezebel [Note: In the autograph it reads “Acaph by Zezabel,” which I judged should be corrected as an error, since these names are nowhere mentioned in the sacred text in this connection. Ahab is not said to have been transferred, but to have been carried to Samaria after his death, where the dogs licked his blood. See 3 Kings XXII, 38. The sacred text is silent as to whether his body was transferred by his wife Jezebel. Saint Jerome, however, interprets this “transfer” as Ahab’s transgression, persuaded by Jezebel—namely, when he descended from true worship to idolatry (3 Kings XXI, 26).] [Col. 0499A]. But those who are transferred by God are not found, as it is written of Enoch: “He was transferred, and he was not found” (Genesis V, 24; Hebrews XI, 5). Those, however, who are transferred by the devil are found by their enemies. The Galatians had been transferred in this way, and the Apostle teaches and marvels concerning their transfer [Note: Perhaps the reading is “he says,” or “he grieves.”]

There is also another kind of transfer, according to the judgment of human writings. When someone passes from one doctrine to another, he is said to have been transferred. Thus we read of a certain man [Note: Saint Jerome calls him Dionysius, whom he mockingly says was surnamed *Metathemenus*, that is, “the transposed,” “the transferred,” or “the one who changed sides,” because he defected from the Stoics to the Cyrenaics.] who, before experiencing pain, said that pain was nothing, but, worn down by afflictions, declared pain to be the greatest evil.

The Apostle marvels at the Galatians’ transfer, and at how quickly it occurred, because the guilt of those who are transferred under compulsion is not equal to that of those who transfer themselves willingly. Likewise, the guilt of those who deny God after being afflicted by various tribulations is not equal to that of those who deny Him without having been wearied by any adversities.

Or they were transferred quickly because not much time had passed since they had believed and withdrawn from the apostolic preaching.

“He who called you,” and so forth. This passage is understood by hyperbaton in the following way: “I marvel that you are transferring yourselves so quickly from Christ Jesus, who called you into His grace.” He says “grace,” not “merit,” because they had been drawn from unbelief to faith by divine grace. Hence the Lord says: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Mark II, 17).

“Into another Gospel,” and so forth. It must be asked: if it is another Gospel, how is it not another? It should be noted that a thing which truly exists has substance, and because the Gospel truly exists and contains truth, it is therefore not another. Those things, however, which do not truly exist are nothing.

Examples show that this is so: “Do not hand over, Lord, your scepter to those who are not” (Esther XIV, 11). Paul likewise says: “I say to everyone who is among you” (Romans XII, 3). He was addressing those who were among them [Note: That is, our author wishes the Apostle to have had in view and addressed only certain persons as existing among them, while neglecting the others as though they did not exist.]

“Unless there are some who are troubling you,” and so forth. Observe that, although he had said “those who are troubling you,” he did not add “they are changing the Gospel.” This is because they themselves could be troubled, whereas the nature of the Gospel could in no way be changed, since it is immutable.

“But even if we, or an angel from heaven,” and so forth. This passage is understood hyperbolically. The Apostle did not say this because he himself would change or because an angel would preach something else. Rather, speaking by way of exaggeration, he said it as though he were saying: “If it could happen that I, or an angel from heaven, preached something other than what I have preached—which could not happen—you ought in no way to withdraw from what you once received.”

The Apostle invokes an anathema upon himself in order to repel from himself the charge which certain people brought against him, saying that he acted one way in Jerusalem but taught the Gentiles that they ought to act otherwise. He invokes an anathema upon the angel also, so that the preaching of Peter and the other apostles would not be highly esteemed if they had preached differently. For if an angel, who possesses greater authority, would incur an anathema by preaching differently, how much more would the apostles?

The Apostle also invokes an anathema upon himself because, if he acted with any negligence, he could be rejected, in accordance with what he himself says: “Lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Corinthians IX, 27). He invokes an anathema upon the angel because the angel too could be changed: having abandoned his dwelling, he was cast into this wretched life and is accustomed to be transformed into various forms.

It should also be understood that he expressly names himself and the angel, but indicates the others generally, lest he seem to wish to rebuke them; nevertheless, he secretly points them out [Note: In the autograph: “to make manifest.”]

“Anathema” is also found in the ancient books. We read that, when Jericho had fallen, Joshua placed everything belonging to it under the name of anathema [Note: Joshua VII, 1. This word is also used elsewhere in the sacred text: Numbers XXI, 3; Deuteronomy VII, 26; XIII, 17; and many other places.] Paul also placed this in his Epistles [Note: In the autograph: “let him place”; perhaps “he places” or “he used to place.”]. It is also used in the canonical ordinances, so that whoever does this or that may be anathema.

“Anathema” is also a Hebrew expression [Note: Saint Jerome likewise says of this word: “Moreover, *anathema* is properly a word of the Jews.” In reality, however, in the sense in which we now use it, this is a Greek word, rendered “set apart,” “separated,” or “devoted”; for us it denotes something torn away from the communion of the faithful. It also signifies the assignment of any object whatsoever to destruction. This word, which in Hebrew is *cherem*, is also used in the sacred text for something consecrated to God and not to be converted to profane uses (Leviticus XXVII, 28–29).], and in Latin it is interpreted as “destruction” or “alienation.”

“As we said before,” and so forth. As some wish to understand it, the Apostle had said this when he was physically present. He says it also in this Epistle, and says it again in the same Epistle, so that he might impress more firmly upon their hearts what he had said. It is the custom of sacred Scripture to repeat frequently what it wishes to impress more firmly.

It should not, however, seem contradictory that the most patient man, who calmed the hearts of troubled people, becomes indignant and angry against the Galatians. He did this because, just as a father grieves over his sons, so he grieved over the Galatians’ transgression. The interpretation of their province’s name also suits them, for “Galatia” means “transfer” [Note: Saint Jerome likewise has this interpretation; Vallartius notes that it follows the etymologies of the books of names then commonly accepted, citing 1 Corinthians. In any event, everyone recognizes that “Galatia” is a Greek, not a Hebrew, word and signifies nothing other than the region of the Galatians; their etymology is derived *apo tou galaktos*, “from milk.”]

[Col. 0501A] [Note: “Chapter III” is written here in the margin of the autograph.]

“For now do I persuade human beings,” and so forth. It should be noted that no one can persuade God, since all the secrets of hearts are manifest to Him. One can, however, persuade human beings. Yet the person who rightly persuades human beings does so because he pleases them in such a way as to draw them into God’s service. The person who does not persuade rightly pleases human beings in such a way that he makes the goal of pleasing consist in them themselves.

Finally, let us not think that the Apostle is teaching here that human judgments should be despised. If he were doing so, he would contradict himself, since elsewhere he says: “Knowing therefore the fear of the Lord, we persuade human beings” (2 Corinthians V, 11); and again: “Be without offense to Jews and Gentiles” (1 Corinthians X, 32), and so forth.

He advises each person to please human beings in such a way as not to displease God. Otherwise, let them strive to please God alone, because it is one thing to please human beings and God, and another to please human beings alone.

Here, however, he says that he once pleased them. Hence he adds: “If I were pleasing human beings”—that is, the Jews—“I would not be Christ’s servant,” because the one who pleases them displeases Christ. This is his intention. Nevertheless, it can be applied generally to everyone, since whoever pleases human beings for some unjust reason displeases God.

[Note: “Chapter IV” is written here in the margin of the autograph.]

It continues: “I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel,” and so forth. He now shows why he said that he had become an Apostle not from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ, when he says: “I make known to you,” and so forth—as though he were saying: “If you are ignorant of from whom or how I learned the Gospel, I want you to know that it is not according to a human being,” and so forth.

By these words the Apostle does not deny that Christ is human, but denies that He is merely human, because He was more than human—that is, God and human being.

The Apostle’s intention is to show the Galatians that he did not learn the Gospel from the apostles, but learned it from the one from whom Peter and the others also learned it.

If, then, he did not receive it from a human being, from whom did the Galatians receive it? Was it not from a human being when they received it from Paul? Was the Church not receiving it from human beings when it received the Gospel from the apostles? No, I say, because they were gods. Hence it is written: “I said, You are gods” (Psalm LXXXI, 6), and so forth. Whoever has the Spirit of God is called God.

He refers to the revelation that took place on the road, when he was going to Damascus (Acts IX, 2).

[Note: “Chapter V” is written here in the margin of the autograph.]

It continues: “You have heard of my manner of life,” and so forth. This account could greatly benefit the Galatians, and they could make great progress through it when they heard that the man who had once been a zealot for the carnal Law—and not just any zealot, but a savage [Note: The autograph reads *servos* (“slaves”), which I judged should be corrected as an error.] persecutor of the faithful—had now been converted and had become a preacher of the Gospel. They could therefore marvel at him all the more.

In this account the weight and gravity of the words should be considered. “You have heard,” he says, “of my manner of life,” not “of my grace”; “formerly,” not “now”; “in Judaism,” not “in the Law of God.” He says “beyond measure,” not merely “to some extent.” He says “the Church of God,” not “the Church of Christ,” as he had then supposed it to be [Note: The manuscript reads *credatur* (“is believed”), but I judged this should be corrected on the basis of Saint Jerome’s text, from which this passage appears to have been taken. Jerome does not say “the Church of Christ,” as Paul then supposed it—Christ, whom he held in contempt and persecuted—but, as he now believes Him, “the Church of God.” That is, our author, following Jerome’s cited text, says: “He calls it the Church of God, not Christ’s, as he had then supposed it to be.”] For the one who was then despised is now believed to be God [Note: I judged that the particle “not,” which in our manuscript improperly precedes the verb *expugnabam*, should be deleted.], “I was destroying”—that is, I was ravaging it like a savage marauder.

“And I was progressing in Judaism.” Observe that he attributes his progress not to the divine Law but to Judaism. He says “beyond many,” not “beyond all,” and “of my contemporaries,” not “of the old men,” both to show the zeal he had for the Law and to avoid boasting.

It continues: “Being a more abundant zealot,” and so forth. This could produce even greater amazement, because the man who had been a more ardent zealot for the carnal Law and ancestral traditions, and had been a savage persecutor, was converted and became a preacher of the Gospel. Through this he wished to show the Galatians that his Gospel was true, so that they might understand that he could have been changed from such great Judaism and zeal for the Law not by his own merits, but only by divine grace.

“But when it pleased Him who set me apart,” and so forth. He is read as having been set apart not only here but also in the Epistle to the Romans (Romans I, 1). Jeremiah too was known in the womb (Jeremiah I, 5). And concerning the Lord, as some say, it is written: “From the womb of my mother,” and so forth [Note: Psalm XXI, 11. Saint Jerome has “from my mother’s womb”; there is often some difference between his textual reading and that found in our manuscript.]

There is also a wicked womb and belly. Hence it is written: “I was conceived in iniquities” (Psalm L, 7), and so forth. Again: “Sinners have been estranged from the womb” [Note: Psalm LVII, 4. Saint Jerome reads “from the vulva” instead of “from the womb,” as in our Vulgate, which he corrected. These differences may be observed very frequently.]

Thus “setting apart” is used both in a good and in a bad sense. Therefore those are set apart by God from their mother’s womb who are withdrawn by divine grace from the custom of carnal parents, as this Apostle was.

Or he says that he was set apart by God’s foreknowledge, because he was set apart not only from the womb but before the foundation of the world. Therefore what God foreknew would happen, He fulfilled when He appeared to him on the road as he was going to Damascus [Note: It is worth noting here that our Atto, who up to this point has religiously followed Saint Jerome’s footsteps in this Epistle, did not wish here to support his opinion that this occurred through God’s foreknowledge: namely, that God loves the one whom He knows will become righteous before he comes forth from the womb, and hates the one who will be a sinner before he sins. This view is approved by theologians who follow Augustine’s position, but Atto apparently avoided it lest he seem to depart even slightly from the opinion of Saint Augustine, which he had embraced completely in the preceding Epistles.]

The mother synagogue may also be understood, since it gave birth to him imperfect. He was set apart from his mother’s womb when he was separated from Judaism, of which he had been a zealot [Note: In the autograph: “he had fled, a zealot, and was separated.”]

It continues: “So that He might reveal His Son in me.” When he says “in me,” some understand it as “to me”; others, as “through me.” Or the meaning may be that, since a human being has a nature capable of understanding this teaching, what he possesses nevertheless remains hidden within him. If, however, through divine mercy what is hidden is revealed to him, so that he understands the things of God, the Son of God is revealed to him. This is shown to have happened to Paul.

It continues: “Immediately I did not consent to flesh and blood.” Some understand “flesh and blood” to mean the apostles. Hence Porphyry says: “The enlightened Apostle disdained to pass over to human beings in order to learn anything from them” [Note: Saint Jerome, adducing this example, says: “After the revelation of Christ.” It may perhaps be read: “The Apostle, enlightened because of the revelation of Christ.” In the manuscript it is written in abbreviation as *Apls*. The reader will see.]

But Jerome says: “Far be it from me to call Peter, Andrew, or the others human beings, since they were gods.” Rather, it was said of those concerning whom it is written: “My spirit shall not remain in a human being,” and so forth (Genesis VI, 3); and again: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you” (Matthew XVI, 17).

The meaning is: “I did not consent to flesh and blood,” that is, I did not agree with carnal people, nor did I cast my pearls before swine, and so forth (Matthew VII, 6). Hence the meaning is better represented in Greek—that is, *contuli* (“I conferred” or “I communicated”). The sense is: “I did not consent to flesh and blood,” that is, I did not communicate anything to carnal people, because I did not associate myself with them; rather, I endeavored to draw them to the faith by my preaching.

And because someone might say, “If you did not consent then, you consented afterward,” the word “immediately” must therefore be joined to what precedes. For if “flesh and blood” were to be understood as the apostles, he would have added “Nor did I go to Jerusalem” in vain.

It should be noted, however, that this account seems contrary to Luke’s account. For he reports (Acts IX, 5, 26 and following) that, after being enlightened and acting boldly in Damascus, Paul returned to Jerusalem and attempted to join himself to the disciples, along with the other things read there about him.

To prevent this from seeming contradictory, it could have happened that, after acting boldly in Damascus once he had been enlightened, he returned to Jerusalem when persecution arose against him—not to see the apostles, but to escape the attack of his enemies, as though he were taking refuge in another city.

Or, when persecution arose, he left Damascus and went to Arabia; but, since he had done nothing there worthy of his apostleship—which is why Luke omitted the matter—he returned to Damascus. That he did nothing worthy in Arabia was not due to laziness but to divine dispensation, since he was prevented, just as he was when he wished to go into Asia (Acts XVI, 6–7).

Afterward, having spent many days in Damascus—which he here calls three years—he went up to Jerusalem to see Peter.

But perhaps someone says: “What benefit is this apostolic account to me, in which he says that he went and returned?” Yet, lest it seem empty of meaning, it compels us to seek its mystery. Since in what follows (Galatians IV, 24–26) he interprets the Old Testament through Arabia, Mount Sinai, and Jerusalem, the enlightened Apostle, recognizing Christ through revelation, went to Arabia—which is interpreted as “humble” or “western”—that is, he returned to the Law and the Prophets, which were in decline, in order to investigate whether he might recognize Christ as having been foretold there as well.

Having recognized Christ there, he returned to Damascus—which is interpreted as “the blood of the people” or “of the kiss” [Note: Saint Jerome has: “He returned to Damascus, that is, to the blood and passion of Christ.” Some believe that Abel was killed by his brother near this city, and that the name Damascus was given to the place because of Abel’s blood. They say that in Hebrew *Dam-sacb* refers to a sack of blood. Others may judge how reliable this account is.]—that is, he returned to the mystery of the Passion. Having been strengthened, he sought the place of peace and vision.

[Note: “Chapter VI” is written here in the margin of the autograph.]

It continues: “Then, after three years,” and so forth. It should be noted that he says he came to Jerusalem not to learn the Gospel—which he had preached for three years—but to see Peter. He did not come to see Peter out of vanity—that is, to discover whether he was bald or long-haired, lean or fat—but with a spiritual purpose, namely, to pay honor to the chief of the apostles.

It continues: “And I remained with him fifteen days.” This contributes greatly to his purpose. Those who study numbers say that this number is sacred and signifies complete knowledge and perfect teaching. There are fifteen psalms [Note: The word *carmina* (“songs” or “poems”) is missing; this word appears in Saint Jerome’s interpretation.] which begin with tribulation and reach the courts of the house of the Lord, which likewise has fifteen steps. The Lord’s solemnity also begins on the fifteenth day (Exodus XII, 14). And fifteen years were added to King Hezekiah’s life (Isaiah XXXVIII, 5). These examples show that the number is sacred. Therefore, through the number of days during which the Apostle remained with the chief Apostle, his perfect teaching is demonstrated.

But lest someone say that, even if he did not learn from Peter, he nevertheless learned from the others, he immediately added: “I saw none of the other apostles.” He did not fail to see them because he held them in contempt, but because they had already been scattered for the purpose of evangelizing.

His reason for seeing James was that James had been ordained by the Apostle as bishop of Jerusalem. We should understand “the brother of the Lord” not, according to the heretics, as Joseph’s son born after the Lord from Mary, or as a son born from another wife, but as the Lord’s kinsman, in accordance with the custom of Scripture.

The other disciples are also called the Lord’s brothers [Note: “Are called” is understood.] Hence He Himself says: “Go, tell my brothers” [Note: John XX, 17, where the reading is not “Go, tell,” but “Go and say.”]; and: “I shall declare your name to my brothers” (Psalm XXI, 23; Hebrews II, 12).

Perhaps this man is specially called the Lord’s brother because he was of such remarkable holiness and such great renown that people eagerly sought to touch the fringe of his garment [Note: Saint Jerome is the source of this account in his commentary on this Epistle.]

He was thrown from the pinnacle of the Temple and killed by the Jews. Simeon succeeded him, and they also crucified Simeon for the Lord’s sake [Note: See Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities*, Book XX, chapter 16.]

“As for the things I am writing to you,” and so forth. This statement can be referred both to what precedes and to what follows, and to everything he writes. If one attends to it simply, these words are those of a person swearing [Note: Perhaps “of one who swears.”], intended to show that everything he had said was true. For he was not lying, since it was not his practice to lie.

It should be understood, however, that the Apostle does not desire an oath as though it were the highest good. Nor does he act against the Lord’s command, which says: “Let your speech be: Yes, yes; no, no” (Matthew V, 37). Rather, this is done because of the slowness of understanding among his hearers.

If one looks more deeply, the sense is as though he were saying: “Everything I write is worthy of the divine presence, because everything is just and true.” He himself makes this clear when he says: “I do not lie,” since it is written: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Psalm XXXIII, 16); His gaze is excluded from sinners.

“Then I came,” and so forth. He therefore came into the regions of Syria in order to establish Churches, because, once enlightened, he did not wish to remain idle.

“Syria” is interpreted as “high” or “sublime.” He therefore came into the regions of Syria in order by his preaching to make lofty what had been cast down, and sublime what had been lowly.

“Cilicia” is interpreted as “taken” or “a mournful calling.” He therefore came into Cilicia in order by his preaching to take up that region; such taking-up cannot occur without the lamentation of repentance.

“But I was unknown,” and so forth. He was known by face to the Churches of Syria, Cilicia, and Arabia because they were Gentile Churches, and he had received the ministry of preaching among the Gentiles. But he was not known by face to the Churches of Judaea, only by report, as he himself says: “They had only heard” (Galatians I, 23).

Observe also that he says “to the Churches” because believers were not found only in Jerusalem, but also in other places, to such an extent that they formed Churches and refused to join with the Gentiles.

“And in me they glorified [Note: The Vulgate reads “they made glorious.”] God.” What does the Apostle wish to demonstrate by these words? He wishes to make his teaching known and to show that he is a true Apostle. For they would certainly not glorify God in him, whose persecutor he had been, unless by their own judgment they recognized his teaching to be true.

[Note: [Col. 0505D] In the autograph: “was making manifest.”]

**(CHAPTER II.)** “Then, after fourteen years,” etc. He had said above that after three years he had come to Jerusalem [Col. 0506A] for the purpose of seeing Peter. Here, however, he says that after fourteen years he came to Jerusalem in order to confer about the Gospel. But perhaps someone is troubled about why he came after so many years had passed. He himself resolves this question when he adds: “According to a revelation.” He went down then when it had been revealed to him—that is, when it was expedient. But why had it been revealed to him? Because dispute and dissension had already arisen in the churches. For the Galatians had already turned back to the servitude of the Law; and therefore it was revealed to him so that the conference concerning the Gospel might show that his Gospel and that of the other apostles were one, and might recall them from servitude to the Law.

And note that he associates Barnabas and Titus with himself, so that “in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word might stand.” He wanted to take these men with him [Col. 0506B] so that, if any question arose, he would have witnesses to whom he could make clear the meaning and judgments of his intention [Note: [Col. 0505D] In the autograph: “he made manifest.”]. And observe that he does not say, “I learned the Gospel from them,” but “I conferred,” to show that he was not of lesser authority. For conferring belongs to equals, whereas learning belongs to inferiors.

“Privately,” etc., refers back to what he had said above: “I conferred.” But perhaps someone will say: Why privately? Had he lied in public and wanted to speak the truth privately? It is not so. His ministry was not to lie; hence he also says that he is a teacher of the Gentiles “in faith and truth” (1 Tim. II, 7; II Tim. VII, 11). Rather, what he was about to say more profoundly and subtly—what those to whom he had spoken publicly could not grasp, as in: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people” (1 Cor. III, 1), etc.—he therefore discussed privately with these men, because they were able to understand it. But what was that more profound matter? The abolition of the Law and the dignity of grace.

“Lest perhaps I should run in vain,” etc. The Apostle was certain that he was not running in vain; but for the sake of the others, who were uncertain, he wished to confer about the Gospel, so that they might be assured that he was not running [Note: [Col. 0506D] The words “but ... run” are found at the bottom margin of the manuscript.], or had run, in vain.

“But neither Titus,” etc. The intention is as though he were saying: If we were not compelled—although we were in a distinguished city among apostles and advocates of the Law, and among those who thirsted for our blood—to have Titus circumcised, why have you, O Galatians, [Col. 0506D] when you had suffered violence from no one [Note: [Col. 0506D] The manuscript reads *intulistisse*. I judged that *intulissetis* should be read, in accordance with the text. Since, however, our author seems to have wished to express the experience of suffering violence, not the infliction of it, I have preferred this reading.], passed from the freedom of grace to servitude under the Law?

“But because of the false brothers who had been secretly brought in.” He calls those people false brothers who had believed in such a way that they did not withdraw from carnal observance; in what follows he also calls them spies. For it belongs to a spy to put forward one thing outwardly while thinking another inwardly. He says that they wanted to spy out his freedom, because they wanted to discover whether they were observants of the carnal Law. And why do they reveal it? “So that they might bring us into servitude,” that is, by stirring up persecution, they might drag us into servitude under the Law.

“To whom we did not yield even for an hour.” [Note: [Col. 0507D] Above the word *neque* the word *ad* appears to have been written in the same character. From what follows it may be seen that our author used several readings, especially the old Latin reading—called the Italian—and that which is more accurate, derived from Greek and Latin manuscripts and called the Hieronymian; he seems, however, to have conformed himself rather to the latter.]

This passage is read in two ways. In the true Greek copies it reads: “to whom we did not yield even for an hour”; in certain Latin copies: “to whom we yielded for an hour.” But if you read it according to the Greeks, the meaning is as though he were saying: O you Galatians, if we had yielded so that Titus might be circumcised, you would have had an opportunity to say: “Apostle, why do you compel us to withdraw from circumcision and the other observances, when you were unable to prevent your beloved Titus from being circumcised?” He explains why he would not have yielded when he adds: [Col. 0507B] “So that the truth of the Gospel might remain among you.”

But if you read it according to the Latins—“we yielded”—this must not be understood of circumcision, but of the persecution that arose from Antioch to Jerusalem concerning this question. For it is reported that the Antiochenes said that no one could be saved without observing the Law. And therefore the Apostle yielded, so that he might be sent concerning a matter certain and necessary, in order that this question might be confirmed by the judgment of the elders [Note: [Col. 0507D] The blessed Jerome, in his commentary on this Epistle, from whom this interpretation has been taken, has as follows: “Or if the authority of a Latin copy pleases anyone, we ought to understand it according to the preceding sense, so that the yielding for an hour concerned not the circumcision of Titus but the journey to Jerusalem. Namely, Paul and Barnabas yielded to the subjection of going to Jerusalem because sedition had been stirred up at Antioch over the Law, so that their judgment might be confirmed by the apostles’ letter, and the truth of the Gospel might remain among the Galatians—a truth that was not in the letter but in the spirit, not in carnal sense but in spiritual understanding, and not in manifest Judaism but in what is hidden.”].

And therefore he yielded so that the truth of the Gospel might remain among the Galatians. But if you understand it of circumcision, the meaning is this: We yielded for an hour so that Titus might be circumcised, yet not with the intention they had, but while proclaiming that circumcision was worth nothing. And therefore we yielded because danger was pressing and death was imminent; and if we had been killed, the truth of the Gospel [Col. 0507C] would not have remained among them, since there would have been no one to proclaim it.

The blessed Jerome says: “The conjunction *autem* (‘but’) is superfluous” [Note: [Col. 0508D] The blessed Jerome, in his commentary on this Epistle II, 3–5, Vallarsi edition, vol. VII, col. 401.], because it has nothing answering to it or bringing it to a conclusion. Therefore it should be read in this way: “But neither Titus,” etc. “Because of the false brothers who had been secretly brought in,” he says. For by these words he shows by whom he had been compelled to circumcise Titus.

It follows: “But from those who seemed to be something,” etc. It is as Jerome says, as though he had declared: Although Peter, James, and John had been taken up by the Lord, had seen him transfigured, and he had laid the foundations of the Church upon them; nevertheless, it makes no difference to me, because I am not speaking against those who followed the Lord in the flesh, but [Col. 0507D] against those who prefer the Law to grace. I do not disparage my predecessors or accuse my elders; but I confidently say that God does not accept a person’s status, but calls everyone impartially to the grace of salvation. And therefore it makes no difference to me—that is, my authority and doctrine do not differ from theirs—because there is one teacher who taught both them and me.

Nevertheless, I do not place myself above them, nor do I criticize what they were like, because God does not accept a person’s status, nor judge the past, nor consider what each person once was, but what he is. “For who will accuse those whom he has chosen? Or who will condemn those whom he justifies?” (Rom. VIII, 33–34.) Yet he who was able to make those who were ignorant and without the glory of the Law learned and glorious was also able to fill me, who was skilled and glorious in the Law, with the same Spirit, so that just as I had been glorious in the Law, so also I might be glorious in this respect.

Some understand this to have been said not of the apostles, but of those who were distinguished and [Col. 0508B] greatly influential among them, yet were advocates of the Law; and therefore, he says, it makes no difference to me—that is, I do not care what they once were, because now they think wrongly.

It follows: “But those who seemed to be something contributed nothing to me,” that is, those who possessed great authority were unable to disclose anything to me. Yet it must be noted that above he said, “I conferred,” and now he says, “They contributed nothing.” Perhaps by these words he wishes to show that he had conferred upon them certain important things that he had done or taught, things of which they were ignorant; whereas they had contributed nothing to him that was hidden from him.

“But on the contrary” [Note: [Col. 0508D] Vulgate: “but conversely.”], “when they saw that the Gospel had been entrusted to me,” etc. The apostles recognized that the Lord and teacher who had taught them had also taught Paul, and that Paul had learned the Gospel from the one from whom Peter had learned it; therefore his Gospel was not different. Nevertheless, it had been arranged by divine dispensation that there should be two: one among the circumcised, the other among the uncircumcised, lest faith should be delayed.

For if Gentiles of mature age were tortured by the sign of circumcision, which would be of no benefit, and were forbidden their customary foods, they would be slow to come to the faith. Likewise, if the Jews were forbidden circumcision and the ancient custom of the fathers—through which they boasted of their glory and which was for them almost a second nature—they would certainly be slow to believe. Therefore Peter received the special office of preaching among the circumcised, while Paul received it among the uncircumcised, so that any Jews who believed would have Peter [Note: [Col. 0508D] In the autograph: “as a guide.”] to follow; [Col. 0508D] likewise, those believing from the Gentiles would have Paul. Thus, despite differing observances, the Gospel would not be different but one.

[Col. 0509A] It follows: “He who worked through Peter.” The meaning is: My authority is not inferior to his, and my Gospel is not different but one, because there is one teacher who taught us. For I received apostleship from him among the Gentiles, just as Peter received it among the circumcised; because he who worked through Peter also worked through me.

The fruit and usefulness of this entire account must be considered. The Apostle makes this clear to the Galatians so that they themselves, as well as all who are present or will come later, might recognize that, despite differing observances, the Gospel is not different but one.

It may also be asked what Peter would do if he encountered a Gentile, or what Paul would do if he encountered a Jew. We may answer that, although Peter received the special office of preaching among the circumcised and Paul among the uncircumcised, their zeal nevertheless remained impartial; therefore they took care to draw to the faith anyone and everyone whom they could, from whatever people they came.

It follows: “And when they had recognized the grace that had been given to me,” etc. It must be noted that above he had said, “those who seemed to be something”; here he explains this when he calls them “pillars.” They were called pillars because they had been taken up by the Lord on the same day, both at his transfiguration and at the raising of the daughter. To one of them the Lord said: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVI, 19); to the other he said: “The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God” (Rev. III, 12). James too possessed great authority, as much is read concerning him.

It may also be asked why these men are called pillars, when the Church is called a pillar; hence Paul himself says: “So that you may know how one ought to conduct oneself in the house of God” (1 Tim. III, 15), etc. There is no contradiction, because the body consists of members, and the members belong to the body.

It must be noted that he says Peter received the office of preaching among the circumcised, and associates with him distinguished men, while he says that he himself received it among the Gentiles, with Barnabas associated with him. Yet the Apostle reserved the apostolic office itself for himself alone [Note: [Col. 0509D] In the autograph: “the apostolic office itself.”]. Someone may perhaps ask why Titus was not associated with him. Evidently, it was because he did not possess sufficient authority for such a distinguished man to be joined to men of such stature.

It follows: “They gave me and Barnabas the right hand,” namely, as a sign of fellowship and agreement, recognizing that the Gospel was not different but one.

[Col. 0509D] “That we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcised,” etc. It must be understood that, when the apostles were sent out to preach, they were given this command: that they should remember the poor saints, especially Paul, who was destined for the Gentiles.

By “the poor” we should understand those who were in Jerusalem; or certainly those who, as Jerome says [Col. 0509D] [Note: The words “or certainly those ... Jerome” are found in the lower margin of the manuscript.], were cursed by their fellow countrymen because they believed in a crucified man; or those of whom the Lord says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. V, 3), etc.; or, certainly, those poor in virtues, as Origen says, concerning whom Paul, being solicitous, declared: “If a person is overtaken” (Gal. VI, 1), etc. He shows his concern for the poor not only in this Epistle but also in others.

[Note: [Col. 0509D] In the autograph’s margin: “here read chapter VII.”]

It follows: “When Peter had come to Antioch” [Note: [Col. 0509D] Here, as in certain readings and in the commentaries of the blessed Jerome, the reading is “Peter,” not “Cephas,” as in the Vulgate.], etc. He continues the intention he had begun, showing that the Gospel is not different but one.

For he rebukes Peter because he was observing Jewish customs and compelling the Gentiles to Judaize. He also rebuked him not so much for his own sake as for the sake of those whose fear had led him into simulation, [Col. 0510B] so that, when they saw the chief of the apostles corrected, they might also be corrected themselves.

And note that he writes “reprehensible” with hesitation, because Peter was not so much reprehensible in Paul’s eyes as in the eyes of those who might be scandalized when they saw him withdrawing from them. He says that certain men came from James [Note: [Col. 0509D] The manuscript reads *vere* (“truly”), but I judged that *venire* (“to come”) should be read in accordance with the text of the Epistle. Since the Epistle reads “when certain men came,” it is sufficiently clear that here, where the manuscript reads *quosdam vere*, *venire* should be read. In these ancient manuscripts, syllables are very often omitted or transposed.], because James had been appointed bishop at Jerusalem, where, and in which city, there were many believers who were nevertheless advocates of the carnal Law.

Before these men came, Peter ate with the Gentiles; after they came, he withdrew. He was so carried away by this simulation that the other brothers also agreed with him, and Barnabas was led into the same simulation.

It follows: “But when I saw” [Note: [Col. 0510D] Vulgate: “but when I had seen that they were not walking rightly.” The blessed Jerome, in his commentary on this passage: “but when I had seen that they were not walking with a straight foot.”] “that they were not walking rightly,” etc.

The blessed Augustine says that Peter acted like a man who, having both feet sound, pretended to limp with one.
