It must be understood that he refuted him by an unavoidable syllogism, saying: “If you, although you are a Jew,” etc.; as though he had said: If, by nature a Jew, you understand that one ought to Judaize, why did you join yourself to the Gentiles? And if you understand that one ought not to Judaize, why do you withdraw from the Gentiles? For the Gentiles could both reproach him and be scandalized, supposing that they could not be justified by faith alone without the works of the Law.

It may be asked why he reproved him openly, when it is written: “Reprove him between yourself and him” (Luke XVII, 3). But he had to be rebuked publicly, especially for the sake of those whose fear had led him into simulation.

Again, someone asks why he rebuked him, when Peter was doing the very thing Paul himself says: “I became to the Jews as a Jew” (1 Cor. IX, 20), etc. We can answer that Peter and Paul did this with different intentions. Peter acted by simulation, whereas Paul acted not with the cunning of one who lies, but with the affection of one who shares another’s weakness.

Furthermore, some have said [Note: [Col. 0510D] Saint Clement of Alexandria, in the fifth book of the *Hypotyposes*; Eusebius Pamphilus, *Ecclesiastical History* I, 12. Dorotheus of Tyre agreed with these in the fourth century; he lists Cephas, whom Paul rebuked, not among the apostles but among the seventy disciples. Also the blessed Chrysostom, vol. V, homily 64; the blessed Jerome in his commentary on this Epistle; and Saint Gregory the Great, *Homilies on Ezekiel* 18, together with many others. Most Latin writers, however—Cyprian, Tertullian, Hilary the deacon, Gregory the Great, Thomas, and a great number of later interpreters, as well as Augustine himself—judged Peter and Cephas to be one and the same person.] that this Peter whom Paul rebuked was not that apostle.

But they say this too carelessly, failing to consider what precedes in this Epistle, where he says: “He who worked through Peter in apostleship also worked through me,” etc. Again, some say that the Epistle called the Second Epistle of Peter, in which Paul is preferred with praise (2 Pet. III, 15–16), was not written by the same Peter, claiming that he would never have praised so highly the man by whom he had been so sharply rebuked.

They likewise consider the words of that Epistle too carelessly. For in it he says: “A voice having come to him from the magnificent glory: This is my Son” [Note: [Col. 0511D] First Epistle of Peter I, 17, where he renews the memory of the Transfiguration (Matt. XVII, 5), and in the following verse, namely 18, asserts himself to have been its witness, as in the cited chapter of Matthew.], etc. This example shows that the Epistle is indeed his.

It follows: “We are Jews by nature,” etc. The Jews applied this name—namely, “sinners”—to the Gentiles; for they called all Gentiles sinners. The meaning is: We are Jews by nature, but sinners—not among those whom we call sinners. Therefore we cannot be justified by works of the Law. Hence he immediately adds: “Knowing that a person is not justified by works of the Law,” etc.

The meaning is: Since we know that we cannot be justified by works of the Law, but only through faith in Christ, we believed in Christ so that we might be justified through faith. This is what he adds: “And we too have believed in Christ Jesus,” etc.—that is, we who are Jews by nature.

It follows: “For this reason no flesh will be justified by works of the Law.” It must be understood that, as some interpret it, he said “no flesh” because only that people who were found in the province of Palestine was justified by the works of the Law; but now, since the Church has spread throughout the world, not one flesh—that is, one nation—but every flesh is justified.

According to his proper intention, however, he said “no flesh,” meaning no one, because the Law brought no one to perfection (Heb. VII, 19).

[Note: [Col. 0512D] In the autograph’s margin: “here read chapter VIII.”]

“But if, while seeking to be justified,” etc. What the Apostle says is as though he were saying: If, while seeking to be justified through faith in Jesus Christ and not by works of the Law, we are found to be sinners, then we would have sought in vain, if we were righteous.

In another sense: If we believed that we were justified by the works of the Law, and, after being justified, seek to be justified through faith in Christ, we are found to be sinners, because we seek something other than what should be sought. For the righteous person who seeks something other than what should be sought is found to be a sinner.

For if the Gentiles cannot be justified by faith in Christ alone [Note: [Col. 0512D] In the autograph: “alone.”], then Christ is a minister of sin. And therefore he adds: [Col. 0511D] “Is Christ therefore a minister of sin?” The Apostle presses and constrains them so that they must either confess that justification is possible through faith in Christ alone or confess that Christ is a minister of sin, just as the Law is; for the Law could reveal sins but could not abolish them. [Col. 0512A]

This even those advocates of the Law who had believed from circumcision did not dare to confess [Note: [Col. 0512D] Autograph: *quid* (“what”).]. Constrained and bound by this argument, the Apostle speaks in the name of all: “Certainly not.”

“For if I build again what I destroyed,” etc. Had Paul destroyed faith? Had he labored to destroy it and then wished to rebuild it, so that he might become a transgressor? No. For faith can in no way be destroyed, any more than the Gospel can, since it is the truth. Hence above: “They want to turn the Gospel” [Note: [Col. 0512D] In this Epistle I, 7, where the reading is *convertere* (“to turn”), not *converti* (“to be turned”).].

What, then, had he destroyed? The pride of the Jews in themselves, which they possessed because of the Law. And if he wished to rebuild this [Note: [Col. 0512D] Autograph: “or certainly, were to build.”], he would make himself a transgressor. For one who fights against the destruction of the truth, acknowledges that he can destroy it, and returns to it so that it may be rebuilt in him, would constitute himself a transgressor.

“For through the Law I died to the Law,” etc. Who was this person speaking? He was a Jew. And what was he saying? “Through the Law I died to the Law.” To which Law? Through the spiritual Law he had died to the carnal Law.

For the Law had been his pedagogue until divine grace was withdrawn from it. Once he had been drawn away, he died to the carnal Law through the spiritual Law. It is like a child nourished at the breast: when he leaves the breast, he is said to have died to the breast. Or, if the comparison is helpful, a ship carries people until they reach their homeland; when they arrive, the ship is said to have died for them.

“So that I might live for God.” The sinner lives under the Law; the righteous person lives under God. And as though someone had asked, “How did you die to the Law?” he answered: “I have been crucified with Christ” [Note: [Col. 0512D] Autograph: “Christ.”], that is, crucified together with him.

For the one who is crucified desires no evil and covets nothing earthly. So too this man was crucified with him, as it is written: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh” (Gal. V, 24), etc.

He acted according to the example of the man who said: “Remember me, Lord” (Luke XXIII, 42), etc., who deserved to hear: “You will be with me in paradise.” For to exist with Christ is to reign with Christ.

“But I live—not I.” These words appear contradictory: “I live” and “not I live.” But the savage persecutor did not live; the devout preacher lived. Hence the blessed Gregory says: “I do not live: in myself I have been extinguished; but I live, because I have not died in essence. Nor did he live through wickedness; he lived through essence.”

And he explains why he does not live: “Christ, however, lives in me,” that is, piety, justice, goodness, and so forth; for all these things are Christ, and through them he dwells in the elect.

“But insofar as I now live in the flesh.” It must be observed that it is one thing to be in the flesh and another to live in the flesh. To be in the flesh belongs to the wicked; to live in the flesh belongs to the good.

That being in the flesh belongs to the wicked is shown by the same Apostle: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God” (Rom. VIII, 8); while he said to the good: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit” (ibid., 9).

This man, who was not in the flesh, lived in the flesh, because his soul remained within the prison of the flesh; nevertheless, in mind he served God, as he himself says: “Our citizenship, however” (Phil. III, 20), etc.

And to show where he lived, he adds: “In faith,” etc.—that is, in good and everlasting spiritual realities; for God promises his own not temporal things but eternal things, so that they may live in those realities in which they now reign by grace, later more openly; in which they now reign through hope, later in possession.

[Col. 0513B] And wishing to show in whose faith alone he lived, he adds: “Who loved me,” etc. Admirable and ineffable is this love: that God should die for humanity, the Creator for the creature.

And when he says, “he gave himself,” etc., he shows that he himself was a sinner, and that Christ died for sinners. Hence the Lord says: “I have not come to call the righteous” (Mark II, 17; Luke V, 32; Matt. IX, 13), etc. For he would have given himself in vain for a righteous person, unless that person were a sinner. And because he gave himself for me, I do not reject the grace of God.

A person rejects it in two ways: either when he passes from the freedom of grace to servitude under the Law, or when, having received the remission of sins through the sacrament of baptism, he is defiled by the same vices again.

“For if righteousness comes through the Law,” etc.—as though he were saying: If justification came through the Law, [Col. 0513C] Christ would have died for nothing. The Apostle has taken up one part of a syllogism, to which another member must be added so that it may be complete, in this form: Christ did not die for nothing. The conclusion, however, is this: A person will not be justified by the righteousness of the Law.

[Note: [Col. 0513D] In the autograph’s margin: “here read chapter IX.”]

**(CHAPTER III.)** It follows: “O foolish Galatians.” He calls them foolish for two reasons: either because they had returned from the Spirit to the flesh, or because he is marking them according to the particular character of their province [Note: [Col. 0513D] See what Atto says about the Galatians at the beginning of this Epistle.].

It follows: “Who has bewitched you?” Note that he does not address them with deeper arguments, as he does the Romans, but rather with the common word “bewitched,” as one speaks to fools. For this word is found in the divine Scriptures. In the book called the Wisdom of Solomon it is also written: “The fascination of worthlessness obscures good things” (Wis. IV, 12).

Among ordinary people, *fascinum* is said to be the evil eye cast upon little children who are not yet able to walk with steady steps. Hence Virgil:

“I do not know what eye,” etc. [Note: *Eclogues* 3, verse 103:

“I do not know what eye bewitches my tender lambs.”

This is an example of the very frequent transposition of syllables in our manuscript: where *teneros* (“tender”) should stand, it reads *terenos*.]

This belief was current concerning the Galatians: they were still tender, nourished with milk and not with solid food. Therefore he says: “Who has bewitched you?” As though he were saying: You were still little children and tender; perhaps, therefore, you have been harmed by bewitchment.

Whether the *fascinum* has such power according to popular belief, God alone knows. Nevertheless, we should not doubt that there are certain kinds of demons assigned to this task—for there are different kinds of demons—which disturb children in body and mind.

It follows: “Before whose eyes Jesus Christ was portrayed.” It is no small praise of the Galatians that Christ is said to have been portrayed before their eyes—that is, announced beforehand—because, by diligently reading the Scriptures of the Old Testament, they recognized that Christ was destined not only to be crucified but also to suffer everything that was to happen to him.

Therefore Jesus is said to have been portrayed before the eyes of all those who know the sequence of the Old Testament.

It must be understood that in some copies the reading is *proscriptus* instead of *praescriptus* [Note: [Col. 0513D] The text of the blessed Jerome in the edition of Vallarsi cited above has *proscriptus*. In the interpretation of this passage immediately attached to it, however, he consistently has *praescriptus*. Vallarsi rightly thought that Martianus should read *praescriptus*, just as Jerome prefers it in the exposition appended below and says that he found it in his own manuscripts. Our copies, on the contrary, affirm the reading printed here, which in fact neither differs from Jerome’s interpretation nor from the Greek text, προεγράφη (*proegraphē*, “was written beforehand/portrayed beforehand”). Victorius consistently reads *proscriptus*. Vulgate: *praescriptus*.]

For *proscriptus* means alienated or cast away. Those who prefer to read *proscriptus* understand it in this way: Jesus was proscribed before their eyes because, abandoning the freedom of grace, they passed over to servitude under the Law.

But as far as the particular situation of the Galatians is concerned, the earlier meaning is more appropriate, because they sinned not deliberately but through ignorance. Therefore, whenever we see someone sinning deliberately, we may use this verse.

It follows: “This alone I wish to learn from you,” etc.—as though he were saying: You could have been questioned about many things by which I might compel you to prefer grace to the Law; but since I have called you foolish, I will ask not many questions, nor profound ones.

From what does he question them? “Did you receive the Spirit,” he says, “from works of the Law?” etc.

It must be understood that at the beginning of the Church there was a custom whereby baptized believers received some gift of the Holy Spirit quite openly, by which it was shown that they had received the grace of that same Holy Spirit in baptism. Thus, concerning the twelve mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles: “Some were speaking in tongues, others were prophesying” (Acts XIX, 6–7), etc.

For, as Paul taught, the Galatians likewise had received such gifts of the Holy Spirit. Therefore they are asked whether they received the Holy Spirit from works of the Law or from hearing with faith.

As though he were saying: If the Holy Spirit were given through works of the Law, it would follow that he would be given only to the circumcised. You, therefore, who believed through my teaching and received the Holy Spirit while still remaining in the uncircumcision—why did you pass over to circumcision of the flesh?

It follows: “Are you so foolish?” etc. The meaning is: It is an excellent order to ascend from lesser things to greater; it is a perverse order to descend from greater things to lesser.

But you are so foolish that you are carried from greater things—that is, apostolic grace—to something very small—that is, carnal understanding. Here it is shown morally that all who descend from greater things to lesser are consumed [Note: [Col. 0515D] The manuscript has *consummuntur* with two m’s; perhaps *consummantur* (“are brought to completion,” or “are consumed”) should be read, in accordance with the text whose interpretation it serves.].

It follows: “Have you suffered so many things in vain?” etc. It must be understood that at the beginning of the faith it was customary for believers to suffer many things from unbelievers. In accordance with this custom, the Galatians, remaining in love of faith and charity, suffered many things; therefore he says: “You have suffered many things,” etc.

“ If indeed in vain” is not a statement of doubt here but of affirmation, so that the meaning is: “If indeed in vain,” that is, certainly in vain, because you were deceived. That this expression is used to indicate certainty is shown by the same Apostle: “But it is not righteous before God to repay tribulation to those who trouble you,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0515D] 2 Thess. I, 6, where it reads: “If indeed it is righteous,” etc., not, as in the autograph, “But it is not righteous,” etc. It is permissible to suspect that the autograph’s reading is corrupt.]. 

Others understand the expression as the customary speech of one who doubts, with this meaning: “If indeed in vain,” that is, if you persevere, then you suffered in vain.

It follows: “Therefore, the one who supplies the Spirit to you,” etc. “Supplies” means “administers,” and it is in the present tense; the verb that follows is also in the present tense.

By these words the Apostle shows that at all times, days, hours, and moments, the grace of the Holy Spirit is given to the faithful so that they may progress. He also shows that the Galatians had received gifts of the Holy Spirit and varieties of grace, which are enumerated in the Epistle to the Corinthians: “To one,” he says, “is given through the Spirit a message of wisdom” (1 Cor. XII, 4 ff.), etc.

But because they had not received discernment of spirits, by which they could distinguish the apostolic Spirit from that of false apostles, they were deceived. Yet because the same variety of graces still remained in them, they are asked: “Did you receive the Spirit from works of the Law?” As though he were saying: Not from works of the Law, but from hearing with faith; just as Abraham believed while uncircumcised and was deemed worthy to be justified (Gen. XV, 6; Rom. IV, 5; Jas. II, 23).

It follows: “And it was reckoned to him as righteousness,” because in the promise he received all the nations as an inheritance—that is, so that whoever believed while uncircumcised and became imitators of his faith might be his children.

[Col. 0515D] It follows: “You recognize” [Note: [Col. 0515D] Vulgate: “recognize.” The blessed Jerome, in his commentary on this Epistle: “you recognize.”] “therefore that those who are of faith are the children of Abraham.”

The meaning is: If until now you have not recognized this, then, once these testimonies have been brought forward, you can understand that all who believe while uncircumcised and imitate Abraham’s faith unquestionably become his children.

“Therefore, foreseeing,” etc. By “Scripture” we should understand not ink, characters, or parchment, but the Holy Spirit or the power of that same Scripture.

Therefore Scripture, foreseeing that the Gentiles would believe while uncircumcised and imitate Abraham’s faith, announced it beforehand to them, saying: “In you all the nations will be blessed” (Gen. XII, 3; Sir. XLIV, 20).

“In you,” that is, not in Isaac, not in Jacob, but in Christ. Therefore it is in Abraham, because Christ is from his seed.

It follows: “Therefore those who are of faith,” etc. Note that he does not say “those who are of circumcision.” The meaning is: Abraham, believing while uncircumcised, before he knew the sign of circumcision, was deemed worthy to be blessed.

You, therefore, who believe while uncircumcised, have become children of Abraham and have been deemed worthy to be blessed. Why, then, did you pass over to circumcision of the flesh, when the uncircumcised are children of Abraham?

[Note: [Col. 0515D] In the autograph manuscript, “chapter X” is read here.]

Next: “We imitate the faith” [Note: [Col. 0515D] The author cites the words “we imitate the faith” as though they were the text of the Epistle, although these words are found nowhere except perhaps borrowed from the Epistle to the Hebrews 6:12, where it says, “Imitators of those who [Col. 0516D] through faith,” etc.; or from chapter 13:7, where it says, “Imitate the faith of your leaders.”]; and the whole point is to show that the circumcised does not possess more than the uncircumcised. “For whoever,” etc., depends on what precedes. For earlier he had said: “But Scripture, foreseeing,” etc.; and from that statement he had foretold: “They will be blessed,” taking occasion to say: “For whoever,” as though he were saying:

“O Galatians, why do you wish to pass from uncircumcision to circumcision, when those who believe in uncircumcision, imitating Abraham, are blessed, while those who are under the law are under a curse, because the law cannot command in a carnal manner—and for that reason they are under a curse?” Hence Peter says: “Why do you wish to place a yoke upon them again?” etc. (Acts 15:10).

And because he had earlier said something great [Note: [Col. 0516D] I suspect that an error has entered here, and that instead of *magnum*, which is found nowhere above, *maledictum* should be read, since it occurs a few words earlier. It is also possible that *magnum* should be retained, that is, “a great matter.”], wishing to confirm this very testimony, he added: “As it is written: ‘Cursed’” (Deut. 27:26), etc. In some copies *omnis* (“everyone”) is found, and in all copies; in others, it is not. But the sense is one and the same. For Moses’ intention was to instill terror in his hearers, and Paul likewise intended to terrify the Galatians.

[Note: [Col. 0516D] In the autograph manuscript, “chapter XI” is read here.]

“But because in the law,” etc. In saying “no one,” he shows that there are some who [Note: [Col. 0516D] The word *qui* (“who”) is missing in the manuscript, but it must be added, as is abundantly clear from the relation of the second member of the sentence to the first.] are not justified, namely, transgressors of the law; and there are some who are justified, [Col. 0516D] but not before God, such as observers of the law, provided that they keep the law with fear. For the law says:

“Whoever does this or that shall surely die” [Note: [Col. 0517D] This occurs several times in Exodus and Leviticus, so that it need not be cited as a single particular text.];

and:

“Whoever lies with a male as with a woman shall surely die” [Note: [Col. 0517D] Leviticus 20:13. The Vulgate reads: “Whoever lies with a male in a woman’s intercourse.”].

There are also others who are justified, but before God—that is, those who, by believing in him, require nothing besides him. And wishing to show who the righteous person before God was, he added: “It has been manifested” [Note: [Col. 0517D] The Vulgate reads *manifestum* (“manifest”).], etc. This is indeed read in Habakkuk (Hab. 2:4); but in some copies, according to the Septuagint, it is found as “by my faith.” Aquila, however, gives “by his faith,” with “of God” [Note: [Col. 0517D] Consult Vallartius’s note on this text in the commentary of Saint Jerome on this Epistle, p. 431 of volume 7 of Saint Jerome’s works.] understood.

For in saying, “The righteous person lives by faith,” he shows that the righteous person who [Note: [Col. 0517D] I judge that the word *qui* (“who”) should be added for the sake of the sense.] does not have faith does not live, just as Paul did not live by faith. For he himself was righteous, since he lived blamelessly under the law; yet he did not live by faith, because he did not possess the one who said: “I am [Col. 0517B] life” (John 14:6).

Thus one says, “The righteous person lives by faith,” just as one can say, “The chaste, prudent, and temperate person lives by faith,” for someone may possess all these qualities without faith. It may also be parsed differently: “The righteous person lives by faith,” that is, the one who is from faith—that person lives.

“But the law is not from faith.” It should be noted that through faith a person awaits spiritual goods, since faith concerns things that are not seen. In the law, however, there is no faith, because what it grants to those who observe or despise it is temporal and visible. If it inflicts punishment on those who despise it, that punishment is visible; if it grants a reward to those who observe it, that reward is temporal.

“But [Note: [Col. 0517D] Leviticus 18:5: “Keep my laws and judgments, which, if a person does, he shall live in them.”] whoever has done it” [Note: [Col. 0517D] The Vulgate reads: “Whoever has done them.” Saint Jerome and Augustine also read it this way in their commentaries on this Epistle.], etc. Note that [Col. 0517C] after saying *eam* (“it”), he added not “in it” but “in them,” to show that “the law” is used for the commandments. And he rightly says “he will live,” because those who observe the law obtain the prolongation of life through their observance.

[Note: [Col. 0517D] In the autograph manuscript, “chapter XII” is read here.]

Since he had said above that they were under the curse of the law, wishing to show how they would be rescued from it, he added: “Christ redeemed us,” etc., as though he were saying:

“Since you have now passed into freedom, why did you wish to pass again into slavery?”

To show how they were redeemed, he added: “Having become a curse for us.” It should be noted that he is called a “curse” in the same way that he is called “sin.” Yet in one sense sin is the transgression itself, to which punishment is owed; in another sense sin is called death, that is, the punishment of sin. This shows that we sin by transgressing, but that we do not sin by dying. For one thing is called by one meaning and another by another meaning, just as “tongue” can mean the bodily member that moves in the head, or the Greek or Hebrew language; and just as “hand” can mean a bodily member, or writing, as when I say: “Bring me your hand,” or “Give me your hand.”

And because what he had said seemed harsh, wishing to confirm it by testimony, he added: “Cursed is everyone” (Deut. 21:23), etc. Note that he does not say “this one or that one,” nor simply “someone,” but “everyone.” Hence Augustine says: “Even Christ?” [Note: [Col. 0517D] On this Epistle, volume 3 of the Works, p. 954.] “Certainly—even Christ, because it says ‘everyone.’”

He himself also says:

“O heretics, Moses foresaw no less the saints who would be on the cross; rather, he rightly foresaw that heretics would deny Christ’s death.”

It is as though he were saying:

“O heretics, why do you struggle and strive to deny that he was accursed, when even Moses had foreseen that he would die?”

In some copies it is found: “Cursed is everyone to God” [Note: [Col. 0518D] See Saint Jerome’s commentary on this Epistle concerning this matter.]. Nor is this contrary, since, unless he had been destined to die for sins and for our death, he would by no means have sent his Son to undergo our death, so that he might free us from the debt of death. When he says “everyone,” “everyone who dies and hangs” is understood.

Confess, therefore, O heretic, that he was accursed; for if you deny that he was accursed, you deny that he died. And why was he accursed? [Note: [Col. 0518D] The words “because … accursed” are found in the upper margin of the manuscript.] He adds:

“So that the blessing of Abraham might come upon the nations,” etc., that is, so that the nations, believing in uncircumcision through the faith of Christ, might be blessed.

“So that we might receive the promise of the Spirit,” etc., that is, so that what they preserved through fear, we might preserve through the love of faith. He says “Spirit” because this grace of the promise was made through him.

[Col. 0518C] [Note: [Col. 0518D] In the autograph manuscript, “chapter XIII” is read here.]

Next: “Brothers (I speak according to human terms).” That is, not according to God, nor according to hidden wisdom or solid food, but according to the tenderness of one who, because of weakness of the stomach, is nourished with milk and dew [Note: [Col. 0518D] Saint Jerome, from whom this comparison was taken, has in Vallartius’s edition “milky dew.”].

Next: “Even a human testament, once confirmed, no one rejects,” etc. He introduced a comparison from earthly affairs, and therefore, as some say, prefaced it with: “I speak according to human terms.” Hence Jerome says:

“And for this reason, because they say that Paul was speaking about a human testament, he prefaced it with ‘according to human terms.’”

Yet especially because he says in what follows, “in seeds,” he says:

“I have examined the whole of the Old and New Testament, and I have found seeds placed in the plural neither in a good nor in a bad sense” [Note: [Col. 0518D] The sense, though not the actual words, of Saint Jerome is being reported.];

or because he used not “covenant” [Col. 0518D] [Note: [Col. 0518D] Through an error, *fictum* (“fabricated”) is written here and *factum* (“made”) a little later [Col. 0519C]. But neither *fictum* nor *factum*, but *pactum* (“covenant”), should be read in both places. Saint Jerome’s interpretation of this passage proves this, since he maintains that the Hebrew word *berith* means “covenant,” not “testament.”], but “testament.” For the Hebrew word called *berith* [Col. 0519A] does not [Note: [Col. 0519C] I think the negative particle, which was missing, should be added in order to satisfy both the sense and Saint Jerome.] mean a human testament, but a covenant [Note: [Col. 0519C] The autograph has *factum* (“made”). *Pactum* (“covenant”) should be read, as is clear from what was said above.] . No interpreter has translated it otherwise.

But because he was addressing them not in deeper but, as it were, in common words, he therefore prefaced it with “according to human terms.” It should indeed be known that as long as a person lives with a testament, it can be rejected and corrupted; but if he dies, it can neither be corrupted nor altered.

[Note: [Col. 0519D] In the autograph manuscript, “Sunday, the thirteenth after Pentecost” is read here.]

Next: “The promises were spoken to Abraham,” etc. It should be known that what death accomplishes in the confirmation of a testament, the inviolable promise of God accomplishes; for if the former cannot be corrupted, much less can the latter be corrupted by a word. Or this may be understood in the following way: just as a human testament is confirmed by death, so the promises were fulfilled and confirmed by the death of the Lord Jesus.

It should also be known that, although he had used “promises” in the plural, he used “seed” in the singular because those who live spiritually will not be blessed in the same manner as those who are carnal. For whoever wishes to be blessed must be joined to Christ. All the righteous are joined to him, and all are his members, while he himself is also their head. For the Apostle commonly asserts that head and members are one body.

“But this I say: a testament confirmed by God.” The sense is:

“I call those promises that were made to Abraham a testament confirmed by God.”

He compared a human testament, once confirmed, with God’s promises.

Next: “Which came four hundred and thirty years afterward.” But this has been found by only a few [Note: [Col. 0519D] Saint Jerome speaks of this reckoning of the years as follows: “For it is not a small matter, and although many have sought it, I do not know whether it has been found by anyone.”]. Nevertheless, it should be known that it can easily be recognized in the following way.

Abram was seventy-five years old when, at God’s command, he departed from Ur of the Chaldeans (Gen. 12:4). After this, in the twenty-fifth year—which was the hundredth year of his life—he received Isaac (Gen. 21:5). Isaac, when he was sixty years old, begot Jacob (Gen. 25:26). Adding these together gives eighty-five years.

Jacob, when he was ninety-one [Col. 0520A] years old, begot Joseph [Note: [Col. 0519D] As is clear from Genesis 47:9. Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh (Gen. 41:46). Seven years of abundance and two years of the Egyptian famine had already passed when Jacob came with his sons to Egypt (Gen. 45:6, 11). Joseph was therefore thirty-nine years old when Jacob came to him, and Jacob said before the king that he was one hundred thirty years old (Gen. 47:9). If Joseph’s thirty-nine years are subtracted from Jacob’s one hundred thirty years, it is established that Jacob begot Joseph in his ninety-first year.]. In his one hundred thirtieth year—which was Joseph’s thirty-ninth year [Note: [Col. 0519D] Instead of *nonus* (“ninth”), the manuscript reads *natus* (“born”), which should be corrected. Both the sense and the accuracy of the calculation, as well as what follows, require this.]—he entered Egypt. When all these figures are added together, they amount to two hundred fifteen years.

The children of Israel also remained in Egypt for the same number of years. This too can be proved in the following manner. After Jacob entered Egypt, Joseph lived seventy-one years [Note: [Col. 0520C] Genesis 50:22, 25 says that Joseph died at the age of one hundred ten. If his thirty-nine years are subtracted—the years he had already completed when his father came to him, as stated above—seventy-one years remain for completing his age of one hundred ten.].

Between Joseph’s death and Moses’ birth there were sixty-four years [Note: [Col. 0520D] The manuscript reads sixty-six years, but the following calculation shows that sixty-four should be read. It was an especially easy error to write VI instead of IV. Joseph’s seventy-one years after his father’s arrival therefore provide the certain portion of the calculation. Moses is said to have been eighty years old when he stood before Pharaoh (Exod. 7:7). These two periods together make one hundred fifty-one years. What remains to be proved is the period of sixty-four years between Joseph’s death and Moses’ birth; concerning this there are as many opinions as there are heads. See Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities*, book 13. I myself favor the opinion of those who assume a longer period, as more suitable to the extraordinary multiplication of the Jews.]. Moses, however, was eighty years old when he appeared before Pharaoh. Adding all these figures together gives two hundred fifteen years. Thus the apostolic statement is shown to be true: the law was given after four hundred thirty years.

But this account, according to which the children of Israel are said to have stayed in Egypt for two hundred fifteen years, seems contrary to what the Lord says to Abraham:

“Know beforehand that your seed will be a stranger in a land that is not theirs, and they will afflict them for four hundred years” (Gen. 15:13).

The statement that they would be strangers for four hundred years is not contrary if you understand this to include the sojourning during which they lived as strangers in the land of Canaan, since the land of Canaan was not theirs until they received it by lot through Joshua (Josh. 13).

Nor is the statement “They will afflict them for four hundred years” contrary, because it may be understood through hyperbaton, so that the sense is:

“Your seed will be a stranger in a land that is not its own for four hundred years, and they will afflict them”—with “in the final part of those years” understood.

Scripture also makes this clear when it says that as long as Joseph lived, [Col. 0520C] and those who knew him were alive, the children of Israel were not afflicted (Exod. 1:7). It also relates that Moses, who was born at the beginning of the affliction, was eighty years old when he appeared before Pharaoh (Exod. 7:7).

The following also seems contrary: Moses says:

“The dwelling of the children of Israel, during which they dwelt in Egypt, was four hundred thirty years” [Note: [Col. 0520D] Exodus 12:40. According to the Hebrew text, the Septuagint, and the Samaritan text [Col. 0521D]—all of which express these 430 years as reckoned from Abraham’s sojourning—and according to nearly all the Fathers and the Apostle himself, learned interpreters think that the text should be read here as: “The sojourning of the children of Israel, who—not ‘during which’—dwelt in Egypt, was 430 years.], etc.

But this is not contrary, because it is to be understood through the figure called synecdoche. A part of the number encompasses the whole number. For this law, which was given after so many years had passed, is not able to nullify the promises, because it is not able to fulfill them.

Next: “For if the inheritance is from the law,” etc. The sense is:

“If the law could fulfill the promise, the promise would be nullified, and the inheritance would be given through the law.”

“But it is not so,” he says, “for God granted it to Abraham through a promise.”

But because the Apostle knew that the Galatians could object and say:

“O Apostle, if the matter is as you assert, then the law is useless,”

he anticipated them:

“What then is the law?” he says, etc.

That is: “Why was it given?”

[Note: [Col. 0521D] In the autograph manuscript, “chapter XIV” is read here.]

He himself answers:

“It was established because of transgressions” [Col. 0521B].

It should indeed be known that, since all [Note: [Col. 0522D] Perhaps “people.”] had refused, through free choice, to obey God and to await patiently the time when they would be justified through faith in Jesus Christ, the law was given to restrain them. For after the making of the calf, its sacrifice, the murmuring, and various other transgressions, the law was given.

Next: “Until when?” “Until,” he says, “the seed should come to whom he had made the promise.” That is, Christ, through whose faith they would be justified.

Next: “Ordained through angels.” This agrees with the statement of Stephen:

“He was in the wilderness in the assembly of God, with the angel who spoke to him” (Acts 7:38).

But it seems contrary to what is read elsewhere:

“The law was given by God.”

For it is read that “the Lord descended upon Mount Sinai” (Exod. 19:20), and likewise: “The Lord spoke with Moses” (Exod. 2:10), along with many other passages.

Nevertheless, this is not contrary. Since God is invisible and incorporeal, he cannot be seen, nor can he speak; therefore he spoke through a created being subject to him. Nor is this contrary to his saying:

“Let me alone, that my anger may burn” (Exod. 32:10);

or:

“Make me a tabernacle” (Exod. 25:8–9);

or anything similar. For the angel spoke in the person of God, just as a reader, when reading, says: “I am the God of Abraham,” etc.

Next: “In the hand of a mediator”—that is, in the power of the Son, who was a mediator, though not of God and human beings, until he assumed the flesh of our mortality.

And lest, on this account, he seem to be separated from the divinity of the Father, he added: “A mediator is not of one, but God is one,” because although he is not one in person, he is nevertheless one in the substance of divinity.

In saying “of one,” “of one party” is understood [Note: [Col. 0522D] The autograph has “of the Father.” But “of one party” should be read, as what follows proves.]. This is directed against the Galatians, as though he were saying:

“Why do you all wish to be one people—that is, the circumcised—when the mediator is not of one party, but rather joins one people from two peoples in his faith?”

For this mediator accomplishes between the giver and the recipient what the law accomplished between the promise and its fulfillment.

A little earlier, lest the law seem useless, he posed the question to himself:

“What then is the law?”—that is, “Why was it given?”

“Because of transgressions,” he answered.

So now, posing the question to himself, he says:

“Is the law therefore contrary to the promises of God?”

It is as though he were saying:

“Could such a law have been given by the one through whom the promises were made, a law that would be contrary to the promises?”

“No,” I answer.

The law is shown not to be contrary to the promises in two ways. If it were such a law, so great and powerful that it could fulfill the promises, it would be altogether contrary to them; or it is not contrary because it does not teach anything opposed to them. For just as John’s baptism was not contrary to baptism, but rather a preparation for it, so the law was not contrary to grace, but rather its preparation.

[Note: [Col. 0522D] In the autograph manuscript, “chapter XV” is read here.]

Next: “For if a law had been given,” etc. According to the first sense of the preceding statement, what follows may be understood as follows:

“If a law had been given,” that is, if the law had been so great and powerful that it could give life—that is, make people children of God, since they would become children of God if they were given life—then righteousness would indeed be from the law, because the promise would be fulfilled through the law.

Next: “But Scripture confined everything under sin.” What does he mean by saying “confined,” since Scripture cannot confine? “To confine,” therefore, means “to manifest.” Human beings, blinded by sins, did not acknowledge themselves to be sinners. Thus, lest they boast that they were righteous and sighted, fail to seek a physician, or ask him for salvation, the law was given to manifest everyone as sinners, so that, while all acknowledged themselves to be sinners, they might flee to the physician.

And this is what follows:

“So that the promise from faith in Jesus Christ,” etc.

Next: “Before faith came”—namely, the faith of Jesus Christ, that is, knowledge of him—“we were being kept under the law, confined.” That is, we were constrained as though by the bonds of prisoners [Note: [Col. 0522D] The autograph has *carceraribus*.].

It should nevertheless be noted that the law, by which it constrained the wicked, was not therefore the author of evil, since its duty was to show evil, not to abolish it. It is like a judge who thrusts the wicked into prison: he is not the author of evil, but it is his duty to thrust the wicked into prison so as to show them guilty; it is also within his power to release them.

Likewise, it was God’s role through the law to manifest them, and it was likewise within his power through faith in his only-begotten Son to release them. This is what he means by “into the same faith” [Note: [Col. 0522D] The Vulgate reads “into that faith.”], that is, until we should come to the faith that was to be revealed. For by saying “to be revealed,” he shows that it had been hidden.

[Col. 0523A] Next: “Therefore the law was our pedagogue.” *Paedagogus* [Note: [Col. 0523D] That is, Greek *Παῖδαγωγός*, formed from *παῖς*, “child,” and *ἀγωγός*, “leader.”] is a Greek compound word, formed from two words, namely, from the idea of leading children. It restrains an unruly age, so that a child abstains from whatever he desires until he reaches mature age.

Therefore the law is rightly compared to a pedagogue, because it was given to restrain the wicked and curb the unruly until we should come to Christ. This is what he means by “in Christ,” that is, “to Christ,” so that we might be justified by his faith. When Christ came, leaving the pedagogue behind, we passed into the freedom of grace. This is what follows:

“But when faith came,” etc.

Next: “For you are all sons of God,” etc. The sense is:

“O Galatians, if we who were under a pedagogue until Christ came, when he came, left the pedagogue behind, believed in the Lord Jesus, and, justified by his faith, became sons, why do you, who believed in uncircumcision and all became sons of God, wish to remain under a pedagogue?”

[Note: [Col. 0523D] In the autograph manuscript, “chapter XVI” is read here.]

Next: “For all of you who were baptized in Christ,” etc., as though he were saying:

“And if you, O Galatians, through the grace of the Holy Spirit and the water of baptism, were reborn and put on Christ, why do you wish to pass from the freedom of grace into slavery to the law?”

By these words the Apostle shows that Christ is the clothing of all believers—not only here, but also where he says:

“Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 13:14).

The Apostle also wishes subtly to show that if those who are baptized put on Christ, then those who are not baptized do not deserve to put on Christ.

Why those who are baptized in Christ put on Christ he explains when he adds:

“There is neither Jew nor Greek.”

For he shows that the circumcised possesses no more than the uncircumcised, provided only that he believes in Christ and is baptized. Hence elsewhere he says:

“Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything,” etc. (1 Cor. 7:19).

Next: “There is neither slave nor free”—that is, they are not distinguished by social status, but by the merit and rational character of faith. Hence a slave often possesses more than his master.

Next: “There is neither male nor female.” It should be known that male and female are distinguished by sex and weakness; nevertheless, they are not divided in faith, because faith belongs to the inner person, and faith is where there is no sex. Hence men are often led to salvation through women, and conversely women through men. Paul teaches this more fully in the Epistle to the Corinthians (ibid., chapter 14).

Therefore one may ask why he says that neither Jew nor Greek is divided in Christ, etc., when both he himself and the other apostles gave specific instructions to Jews and Gentiles, slaves and masters [Note: [Col. 0523D] The words “Therefore one may ask why he says” are written at the bottom margin of the manuscript [Col. 0524D].].

But this is not contrary, because one thing is necessary for us in this life, as on a journey, and another is necessary in order to come, or by which we may come, to the kingdom. Distinctions are also necessary in this life, and for that reason they gave specific commandments, lest the name of Christ or of Caesar be blasphemed by their teaching.

Hence the Lord says to Peter:

“Nevertheless, lest we offend them, go to the sea,” etc. (Matt. 17:26);

and again:

“Give to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s” (Matt. 22:21; Mark 12:17; Luke 20:25);

and Peter says:

“Be subject,” etc. (1 Pet. 2:18);

and Paul likewise:

“Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities,” etc. (Rom. 13:1).

He shows why there is no division in Christ when he adds:

“For you are all one in Christ”—that is, one body, because Mother Church gives birth to all into one infancy [Col. 0524B].

[Note: [Col. 0524D] In the autograph manuscript, “chapter XVII” is read here.]

Next: “But if you are Christ’s,” etc. The sense is:

“If you, O Galatians, who believed in uncircumcision, were baptized, put on Christ, and are his children, then you are Abraham’s seed, because he too is from Abraham’s seed.”

For all who believe in Christ after receiving the seed of evangelical preaching, when they are baptized and put on Christ, become both his children and Abraham’s children—that is, seed from seed.

It should be known, however, that whenever Christ is called Abraham’s Son, this is to be understood carnally; but whenever the Galatians or other believing Gentiles are called his children, this should be understood not carnally but spiritually.

It should also be noted that when the promises are said to have been made to Christ, they are put in the plural. Hence the earlier statement:

“To Abraham the promises were spoken,” etc.

But when the promise is said to have been made to the faithful, it is put in the singular. It is a beautiful transition from the plural number to the singular, because the ecclesiastical people have been gathered from different nations, sexes, and ages.

[Note: [Col. 0524D] In the autograph manuscript, “chapter XVIII” is read here.]

**Chapter IV.** Next: “I say, however: As long as the heir is a child,” etc.

This comparison could have been very familiar to the Galatians and to everyone. For when a father departs for a distant region from which he might be expected—or certainly not expected—to return, or when death approaches him, he entrusts his son to guardians and administrators, and also establishes a time. As long as the son is under guardians, he differs in nothing from a slave, because they dine together, play together, and are kept under the same discipline, although he is lord of everything—“destined to be” is understood—until the time appointed by the father arrives.

When the appointed time comes, he passes into freedom, while the slave remains in slavery.

The Apostle himself explains this comparison when he says:

“So also we, when we were children”—namely, in sense and understanding—“were under the elements of the world.”

The “elements” are understood by some as the prophets, by others as angels, because human beings are governed through the ministry of angels. Hence the Lord says:

“Their angels always see the face of my Father,” etc. (Matt. 18:10).

Others understand them as the letter of the law; some understand them as the ceremonies of the law, namely circumcision, observance of the Sabbaths, and so forth.

But let us understand the elements as the letter of the law, because letters are also called elements.

One may ask why he says “of the world.” He says “of the world” because these things are performed in the world. For “world” often stands for the things that take place in the world. Hence:

“I did not come to judge the world” (John 12:47);

and again:

“The world did not know him” (John 1:10).

“But when the fullness of time came.” He calls the fullness of time the time fixed by the Father, when he had predestined to send his Son from heaven to earth for the salvation of the human race.

[Note: [Col. 0525D] In the autograph manuscript, “chapter XX” is read here.]

Next: “God sent his Son.” This sending is to be understood as the incarnation. For he makes clear what kind of sending it was when he says:

“Made from a woman.”

He says “made” because of the frailty of our flesh. And note that he does not say “through a woman,” because of the heretics [Note: [Col. 0525D] Marcion in particular and others who wished Christ’s flesh to have been merely apparent; the Apostle perhaps wished to forestall their heresies.], but “from a woman,” that is, from the substance and seed of a woman.

Understand “woman” as referring to sex, not to corruption. It is also a characteristic of the Hebrew language to call someone “woman” on account of the distinction of sex, just as Eve, immediately after she was created, was called “woman” (Gen. 2:22).

Next: “Made under the law.” He was made under the law because he was circumcised, because legal offerings were presented for him, and because he observed the other legal ceremonies. He is also read to have been subject to his parents until the thirtieth year of his life (Luke 2:51).

But he destroyed all these things, especially when the time of his passion was approaching, because grace was to be manifested. He shows why he was made under the law: [Col. 0525C]

“To redeem those who were under the law.”

What is surprising if he was made under the law in order to redeem those who were under the law, when he was made mortal in order to free us from death?

Next: “So that we might receive the adoption of sons.” In these words he distinguishes our dignity from Christ’s: he is the proper Son, whereas we are adopted; he is so by nature, we by grace.

And note that he does not say “we might receive” in the sense of receiving something never possessed, but “we might receive again.” A person receives what he does not have and receives again what he has lost. Thus he says “we might receive again” the dignity that we lost in Adam.

But if this comparison is applied to the Gentiles, it has another outcome. A little earlier he compared the law to a pedagogue; then he compared the guardians and administrators to the elements of the world.

This lesser people, that is, the ecclesiastical people, because it was gathered not from one people but from two, was therefore compared to a pedagogue through the Jews and to guardians through the elements because of the Gentiles, since they had served the elements—that is, the sun, the moon, and the others.

But if this is applied to the Gentiles, it should not seem contrary that he says “so also we,” because the teacher and master joined his own person to the persons of his hearers.

Nor should what we said—that some understand by “the elements of the world” the letter or ceremonies of the law [Note: [Col. 0525D] The words “that some understand by ‘the elements of the world’” should be added for the sake of the sense [Col. 0526D].]—seem contrary, because just as there was slavery in the worship of idols, so there was slavery in the ritual of the legal ceremonies.

But if this comparison, like the preceding one, is applied to the Jews, especially since he was speaking about circumcision, then, lest the Gentiles seem to be excluded, he added:

“Since you are all sons” [Note: [Col. 0526D] The word “all” is not found in the Vulgate.].

It is as though he were saying:

“Just as we, O Galatians, who were serving under the elements of the world, withdrew from them and by believing became sons of God, so you, believing in uncircumcision, have all become sons of God. Why, then, do you wish to pass into slavery to the law?”

He shows how they became sons when he adds:

“God sent the Spirit of his Son,” etc.

It should certainly be known that at the beginning of the Church it was customary for some special gift of the Holy Spirit to be given most visibly to believers. With this gift and grace, blessed Peter silenced the brothers who were murmuring because he had entered to a man who was uncircumcised:

“Who was I,” he said, “that I could hinder God?” (Acts 11:17)

That is, how could I prevent those who had received the Holy Spirit from being baptized? When they heard this, they fell silent, etc. (ibid., 18).

He says “the Spirit of the Son” against the heretics, to show that just as the Spirit proceeds from the Father, so also from the Son.

He says “crying out,” that is, “causing us to cry out.”

*Abba* is a Hebrew and Syrian word, while “Father” is Greek and Latin. For this reason the Apostle used both, because he foresaw that all nations would believe, so that each might recognize the characteristic expression of its own language and praise God in that language.

[Col. 0526C] Next: “Therefore he is no longer a slave but a son.” It is as though he were saying:

“O Galatians, since you have received the Holy Spirit and become sons of God, why do you wish to pass from freedom into slavery?”

And if you are sons, you are also heirs, because inheritance is owed to sons. But so that the Apostle might exclude everything except grace, he added “through God,” as though he were saying:

“Not through your merits, nor through your effort, nor through the law, but through God’s grace—”

“But at that time, indeed,” etc. It is as though he were saying:

“When you were ignorant of God, you served idols, and for that reason you then more easily obtained indulgence. Those who sin knowingly will be punished more severely than those who sin unknowingly.”

This is like the case of Abimelech, who took Sarah as Abraham’s wife, when God had struck [Col. 0526D] his household’s womb [Note: [Col. 0526D] Genesis 20:18. Perhaps *perclusisset* (“had closed”) should be read. The Vulgate has *concluserat* (“had closed”), but the present reading is also correct.]. He said:

“Lord, will you destroy a righteous and ignorant nation?” (Gen. 20:4)

It is as though he were saying:

“If I sinned unknowingly, what justice is there in my not obtaining indulgence?”

This should be understood not only of this matter but of every matter.

How are you turning back again, etc. Above he had said “elements,” and had added “of the world”; but now he calls them “empty,” because at first, while ignorant of God, they served idols, but afterward, having acquired knowledge of God, they were returning to their former errors. Rather, having been known [Note: Through error, *cognovistis* (“you came to know”) is read instead of *cogniti sitis* (“having been known”), as will be clear from what follows.], etc. For what he says must not be understood as though God came to know something unexpectedly, suddenly, or in the course of time; rather, it is said in the same way as John’s words: “Let us love God” (John IV, 19), not because we loved him, but because he first loved us. For we were known before we came to know, since we were drawn by him (John VI, 44).

“You observe days,” that is, Sabbaths; “and months,” namely, new moons, that is, the new moon—for they reckoned the months by the moon; “and seasons,” that is, the three periods of the year [Note: Exodus XXIII, 14 and following: namely, the feast of Unleavened Bread, the feast of the firstfruits of the harvest, and the feast at the end of the year.], during which they celebrated different observances (Exodus XXIII, 17), when it was also commanded that every male should appear in the presence of the Lord; “and years,” that is, the seventh year, namely the sabbath of sabbaths, and the jubilee.

“I fear for you,” etc. See how moderately he speaks. He did not say, “I have labored in vain,” lest he reject them utterly; rather, he said, “lest perhaps” in vain, because he neither wished to cast them off completely nor to leave them uncorrected. For if he had cast them off completely, they would have despaired; if he had left them uncorrected [Note: Perhaps “if they had remained uncorrected,” or after *uncorrected* one should supply “he would have left them.”], they would have provided others with an example of destruction. By these words he shows that he does not doubt their conversion and that he wishes them also to recover their senses.

“Become as I am.” As though he were saying: “I ask you, all my brothers: abandon the legal observances and become imitators of me. For I, who was once a zealous adherent of the law and a defender of ancestral traditions, have counted all those things as filth, dung, and refuse. For I too am as you are”—that is, just as you are human beings, so I too, as a human being, have come out from these things, and you will be able to come out from them as well.

[Note: In the autograph margin, “chapter XXI” is written here.]

“Brothers, I beseech you,” etc. After many corrections and rebukes, he recalls their former good qualities to memory, saying: “You have done me no wrong,” etc. As though he were saying: “Remember that, at the beginning of my preaching, when your understanding was less developed, you did me no wrong; why do you do so now, when you understand more?” He said this so that, hearing of their former good conduct, they would not despair. By this example preachers are admonished that, when they rebuke their people, they should recall their former good deeds, lest, through despair, they be swallowed up by excessive sorrow.

[Col. 0527D] “You know, however,” etc. He calls the weakness of their flesh their limited understanding, as though he were saying: “I did not preach deeper matters to you, but only what you were able to grasp. And my temptation,” etc. What he calls “temptation” should be noted: at the beginning of his preaching the Apostle endured many adversities and was afflicted by many tribulations. This could have been a temptation to the Galatians, who might say: “What purpose or fruit can there be in such teaching, when its preacher himself is afflicted by so many torments?” When he says, “in my flesh,” the sense is as follows: “Though I was humble, despised, and contemptible, knowing nothing except Jesus Christ” (I Corinthians II, 2), you did not reject me; rather, you received me as an angel of God—that is, as a messenger of heavenly gifts—and not merely as such, but as Jesus Christ himself. Note that he places Christ before the angel, whereas the Psalmist, conversely, places the angel before Christ, as in: “You made him a little lower” (Psalm VIII, 6); there, because of his humanity, here, because of his divinity.

“Where, then, is your blessedness?” As though he were saying: “Where is the devotion, religious reverence, and affection of charity toward me that you once possessed?” He spoke in this way to bring them to shame, as they heard what they had been and recognized themselves as blameworthy [Col. 0528B]. By this example preachers are admonished to act similarly toward their people.

“For I bear you witness,” etc. This passage must be understood hyperbolically. He wishes to display the greatness of the charity they showed at the beginning of his preaching; therefore he speaks as though saying: “You loved me so greatly that, if you could have given your eyes in return for the Gospel, you would have wished to deprive yourselves of them and count your loss as my gain.” For what is dearer among the members of the head than the eye? Nothing. Why, then, does he say this? A true preacher and disciple of truth cannot lie. But, as we have said, he speaks in this way to magnify their charity.

[Col. 0528C] “So I have become your enemy?” etc. Some wish this passage to be delivered interrogatively; others narratively. If interrogatively, the sense is: “Why have I become your enemy by telling you the truth?” If narratively, it is: “I have become your enemy by telling you the truth.”

[Note: In the autograph margin, “chapter XXII” is written here.]

“They are zealous for you,” etc.—that is, they are envious, because you have passed to the knowledge of Christ without circumcision. This is because Christ, who had been promised to them, was preached to them and also took flesh from them. Why this is not good, he himself explains: “They wish to exclude you so that you may be zealous for them”—that is, imitate them.

“But be zealous for what is good in a good way,” that is, with good intention, and not temporarily, but always. For in each word he strikes at the Galatians, who had already imitated what was good with good intention, but not always, because they had withdrawn. This is what he adds: “And not only when I am present with you”—as though saying: “Do not imitate me only when I am present, but also when I am absent.”

[Note: In the autograph margin, “chapter XXIII” is written here.]

He continues: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor,” etc. It should carefully be noted that he does not say, “for whom I am in labor,” but “again,” because, when the Apostle taught, the Galatians believed, and, after receiving the seed of evangelical preaching, Christ was conceived in their hearts. But because he was not strengthened, he was easily extinguished by the preaching of the false apostles; therefore the Apostle labored to restore him once more after his extinction. It should also be noted that the one who had assumed a father’s affection by saying, “Through the Gospel I begot you” (I Corinthians IV, 15), here assumes that of a mother when he says, “I am in labor.” In order to show himself the father and mother of his hearers, he assumed the affection of both parents.

Yet who can express in words the affection of parents? Hence Origen says: “Human nature is not horrible, but venerable. For who can comprehend what care there is, or what labor belongs to parents, when the father begets or the mother conceives and gives birth?” They are no less diligent in nurturing. Just as a seed is sown, received in a furrow, covered by earth, germinates, grows into grasses and stalks, and continues up to the fruit, so the seed of a human being is sown in the womb, then conceived; afterward, dried by its own moisture, compacted, and formed until it is brought forth into the light, and, once brought forth, is nourished. Likewise, the seed of the word of God is sown in the heart; thus Christ is conceived in the mind and afterward formed.

The blessed Pope Gregory explains this affection of parents more fully in the passage where the Lord says to Job: “Do you know the time when the wild goats give birth on the rocks?” (Job XXXIX, 1). The Apostle was a hind of God and bent down in order to give birth.

It should be known, however, that the difficulty of conception or birth sometimes arises from the man, sometimes from the woman, and sometimes from both; likewise, the ease of the process may arise in the same ways. The same applies to preachers. This preacher was indeed a competent preacher, and the Galatians competent hearers; nevertheless, they had been deceived through ignorance.

It should also be noted that, so long as a birth is tender, it can easily be extinguished. Since Christ had not been strengthened in the hearts of the Galatians, as has been said, he was therefore easily extinguished. For this reason the Apostle diligently labored to restore him once again. By this example preachers are admonished that, if they see any virtue extinguished in one of their hearers, they should be no less diligent in reviving it than they were in creating it.

[Col. 0529D] He continues: “I would like to be present with you now and to change my voice.” The Apostle also knew that the Scriptures are beneficial when they are read, but much more beneficial when something is commended in a living voice. For the Scriptures do not possess the power to manifest the grief of the heart, assume a voice of rebuke, or bring forward now one point and now another with emphatic force. Therefore he said: “I would like to be present with you now”—as though saying: “I cannot write as much as you deserve to hear; and, unless I were constrained by the bonds of confession” [Note: Perhaps Atto followed the subscription of the Greek manuscripts, which would have this Epistle sent from Rome. This is less likely, since this Epistle makes no mention of chains, whereas he mentions them in the other Epistles that he wrote from Rome in chains. More probably, and as authors generally hold, it was written from Ephesus, where he remained for two years in the school of a certain tyrant and learned that the Galatians had been deceived by false brothers. The meaning of “the bonds of confession” is therefore very obscure, unless he wished the duty of preaching to be understood as these bonds, or unless we read *confusion* instead of *confession*, in view of what follows: “I am ashamed on your account.”], I would wish to be with you and to change my voice.

He says “to change” it because, having called them his children, he did not want them to become worse after being scandalized by harsh rebukes, if he assumed a rebuking tone toward them, thereby showing that they were not worthy of such honor as to be called his children. He explains why he would change his voice: “Because I am ashamed on your account.” Just as parents reject foolish children so as not to be put to shame, so he says here, “I am ashamed.” In Greek manuscripts one finds “I am in need” [Note: The Greek word Ἀπόρουμαι signifies need or want rather than shame, which is expressed by αἰσχύνη or σύγχυσις.], but the sense is the same. The Apostle’s shame consisted in the fact that his teaching did not abound in them, but rather was in need.

He continues: “Tell me, you who wish to be under the law,” etc. He was about to speak of great matters and interpret the law; therefore he prefaced it with: “Tell me,” etc., as though saying: “You Galatians, who wish to be under the law, why have you not read the law? Or, if you have read it, why have you not paid attention to what the law says?” For, as though someone had said, “Produce the law,” he himself replies: “For it is written,” etc. (Genesis XVI, 15). Note that he calls the historical narrative of Genesis “the law,” against those who say that the law consists only of what is commanded or prohibited. And what is surprising if he called the history of Genesis the law, when the entire sequence of the Old Testament is called law?

[Col. 0530C] He continues: “But he who was born from the slave woman according to the flesh”—that is, according to carnal custom and union, namely, of male and female—and therefore is called a son of the flesh. He continues: “But he who was born from the free woman, through the promise,” namely, born from an old and barren woman, and therefore called the son of promise.

This is not contradicted by what is written: when the angel found Hagar in the wilderness, he said to her, “You will bear a son, and you shall call his name Ishmael,” etc. (Genesis XVI, 11). Why, then, is Ishmael not also the son of promise? Because God’s promise differs greatly from an angel’s promise: when the sun rises, the moon is darkened.

This solution may, however, seem to be contradicted by what the Lord himself promised Abraham. He said to him: “And concerning Ishmael I have heard you; I will multiply him exceedingly,” etc. (Genesis XVII, 20). To prevent this from appearing contradictory, it should be understood that it is one thing to speak of someone conceived or born, and another to promise that someone will be conceived; likewise, it is one thing to multiply someone greatly and enrich him with temporal goods, and another to establish him within a covenant [Note: Genesis XVII, 21, where “covenant” is read, from the Hebrew *berith*, which the blessed Jerome, in his exposition of this Epistle, calls *testamentum* (“testament”) when citing this passage.].

[Col. 0531A] He continues: “These things were spoken allegorically,” etc. Here he offers an example of allegorizing and seeking figures. Through the mothers and their sons he shows that two covenants and two peoples are to be understood. All authorities agree on this, although the Apostle does not interpret it openly, but merely indicates the path of interpretation.

He continues: “For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia,” etc. As far as the historical account is concerned, the Arabian mountains are connected with those of Jerusalem. Mystically, however, through the difference of places he indicates the distinction between the two covenants. Fittingly, the law that was to pass away is represented through Hagar, and Hagar is interpreted as “sojourn” or “pilgrimage” [Note: In Greek, παροινία.]. Who does not know that a pilgrimage is far removed from a perpetual inheritance? It is also rightly said that the law itself was given at Sinai and in Arabia, because Sinai is interpreted as “temptation,” while Arabia is interpreted as “western” or “declining.” He says, therefore, “It is joined to the one that is now Jerusalem,” because the people who received the law around Sinai afterward became inhabitants of earthly Jerusalem.

He continues: “But the Jerusalem above is free,” etc. He distinguishes earthly Jerusalem, which is enslaved with her children, from the heavenly one. Jerusalem is to be understood as the holy Church, which partly makes its pilgrimage on earth and partly reigns with God in heaven. Although it dwells on earth, it is nevertheless heavenly, because its way of life is in heaven. It is also rightly called the mother of all the faithful, because through the water of baptism she brings them all forth into one infancy.

And because he had mentioned two mothers, he wished to confirm his account by an example; therefore he added: “It is written”—in Isaiah, that is—“Rejoice, you barren one,” etc. (Isaiah LIV, 1). These are words of exhortation. The prophet exhorted her to rejoice, break forth, and cry aloud: “For the children of the deserted woman are many,” etc.

He calls her “deserted” by the first man when he sinned, for as soon as he sinned he abandoned the fellowship of the citizens above. Or “deserted” because she did not yet have a time for giving birth, whereas the synagogue had a husband, a time for giving birth, and bore many saints.

It should be known that, until Abraham begot Isaac—that is, until God the Father sent his Son to earth for the salvation of the human race—the synagogue was fruitful. But when he came, she who had been barren became fruitful, because through faith she clung to Christ; while she who had been fruitful became weak, because through unbelief she withdrew from Christ and lost her commitment to virtue. Hence the prophet says: “Those who have been waiting for me for many days” [Note: Hosea III, 3: “For many days you shall wait for me.”], etc. This is why Hannah says: “The barren woman has borne seven” [Note: I Samuel II, 5; Jeremiah XV, 9. The number “seven” is found in Jeremiah in the cited passage, whereas in the corresponding place in the Book of Kings “many” is read.], etc.

He continues: “But we, brothers,” etc. He speaks of himself and those like him [Note: The pronoun *se* (“themselves”) is not found in the text. Nevertheless, both the text itself and the blessed Jerome’s treatment of this passage led me to add it.], while Origen says that it should be read “you” [Col. 0532A]. This is not contradictory, because the Apostle had foreseen by prophetic spirit that the Galatians would return to their former faith, especially since they had sinned not deliberately but through ignorance.

He continues: “But just as then he who was born according to the flesh,” etc. It is not found in the historical narrative of Genesis that Ishmael persecuted Isaac. Nevertheless, it is written that, when the two were playing together, Sarah took this very badly and said: “Cast out the slave woman and her son,” etc. (Genesis XXI, 10). The Apostle calls that play “persecution.” But why? He was a teacher of the law and had learned the law at the feet of Gamaliel. Because he understood the force of the law and that the play was not simple, he called it persecution.

Sarah likewise understood that Ishmael might be trying to draw Isaac into buffoonery, so that Isaac would become like Ishmael and Ishmael could be given precedence in the inheritance; or perhaps he wanted to draw him toward an idol; or, as learned authorities more commonly suspect [Note: Through a prone error, the manuscript reads *suscipiantur* (“may be received”) instead of *suspicantur* (“they suspect”).], he wanted to claim the rights of the firstborn. For this reason she took it badly.

When he says, “So it is now also,” this may refer to the Galatians and the zealous adherents of the law, or to the whole Church and all carnal people.

He continues: “But what does Scripture say?” These are words intended to frighten. He added this example to frighten the Galatians, as though saying: “You who wish to be sons of the slave woman, why do you not pay attention to what Scripture says?” Thus, when they heard that the slave woman and her son had been cast out, they would be frightened and fear being excluded from the perpetual inheritance.

It should certainly be known that, although iniquity may be exalted, and although heretics—or powerful people against the humble and poor—may swell with pride, they are nevertheless slaves and sons of a slave woman.

“Therefore, brothers, we are not sons of the slave woman,” etc. He either speaks of himself and those like him, as above [Note: I have judged that *ut supra* should be read here; the abbreviation *usp.* was written compactly, especially since the discussion shortly above concerned the son of the slave woman and of the free woman, and the interpretation of himself and those like him.], or else joins his own person to the Galatians, because he foresaw that they would return. To show from whom, or through whom, this freedom had come, excluding everything except grace, he added: “With the freedom by which Christ freed us.” As though saying: “Not merits, not the law, and not circumcision, but Christ”—that is, as he himself says: “If the Son makes you free,” etc. (John VIII, 36).

[Col. 0532D] (CHAPTER V.) “Stand firm.” Because they had not fallen completely. Therefore, whenever speech or admonition is directed to the good, this expression should be used; toward the wicked, “rise.” That “standing” refers to the good is shown by the prophet: “The Lord lives, before whom I stand” (2 Kings V, 16); and by the Lord to Moses: “Stand here with me” (Deuteronomy III, 31); and by Stephen: “I see Jesus standing” (Acts VII, 55). Because he was standing, Stephen saw him standing. The Psalmist likewise says: “He set my feet upon a rock” (Psalm XXXIX, 3)—that is, he placed the steps of my intention upon Christ—and: “Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall” (I Corinthians X, 12); and: “Stand firm in the faith,” etc. (I Corinthians XVI, 13).

By all these examples he makes clear that standing belongs to the good, while lying down belongs to the wicked and unbelieving. Hence the prophet says to unbelievers: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem” (Isaiah LX, 1); and: “Rise, you who sleep” (Ephesians V, 14); and: “It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Romans XIII, 11).

“And do not”—this depends on what precedes. Above he had said: “We are not sons,” etc. Therefore he adds: “Do not,” etc., as though saying: “O Galatians, since you have been made free, why do you wish to subject yourselves again to slavery?” It should be known that whoever understands the law carnally [Note: The words “the law … carnally” appear in the lower margin of the manuscript.] and lives carnally, or whoever understands it spiritually [Note: “Understood” is perhaps to be supplied.], yet nevertheless lives carnally, is held under slavery.

He says “again” because above he had said that they had been servants of the elements of the world, and now they wish again to serve the elements of the letter of the law.

[Note: In the autograph margin, “chapter XXIV” is written here.]

“Behold, I, Paul,” etc. The Lord says: “Whoever hears you hears me” [Note: Luke X, 16. The manuscript reads “whoever hates you hates me.” Apart from the fact that this text is found nowhere, the present correction also seems to be supported by the fact that “whoever hates you” has nothing to do with our subject, whereas “whoever hears you” is highly relevant, as appears from the following text and interpretation.]. Paul likewise says: “Do you seek proof of the one who speaks in me?” (2 Corinthians XIII, 3). Therefore, after saying, “To the rest I say, not the Lord” (I Corinthians VII, 12), lest his words be despised, he added: “I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (ibid., 40). Thus it is shown that whoever hears Paul hears Christ. Consequently, his words must be observed no less than those who said, “Thus says the Lord.”

[Col. 0533C] Why does he say, “Behold, I,” when he had already shown above that he was an apostle? He wishes to manifest his authority, as though saying: “I, Paul, speak—by my authority asserting both that the law must be abolished and that circumcision is of no benefit. I am the one who commanded my beloved disciple Timothy to be circumcised, not to show that circumcision is beneficial, but for the sake of the salvation of others.”

“For if you are circumcised,” etc. But why does he say here that circumcision is of no benefit, when he says to the Romans: “Circumcision is beneficial if you observe the law” (Romans II, 25), and elsewhere: “What advantage does the Jew have, or what is the benefit of circumcision? Much in every way” (Romans III, 1–2)? One must examine the intention. There his purpose was to admonish those who had believed from circumcision not to be compelled to return to the foreskin, and those from the foreskin not to be compelled to circumcision. Here, however, he admonishes the Galatians not to turn to circumcision, since it is of no benefit.

“But I testify,” etc. This is directed against those who were zealous for the law and were compelling the Galatians to turn to circumcision. As though saying: “If you turn to circumcision, you must also observe the other practices.”
