He also speaks against the Ebionites, who said that faith was of no benefit without circumcision [Note: It seems preferable to read “faith without circumcision”: such was the error of the Ebionites, who wished to join the New and Old Testaments, that is, the simplicity of the Gospel with the observances of the law.], and who denied that Paul was a true apostle, saying that he acted one way with the Jews but taught the Gentiles to act differently.

As though saying: “If you observe this one thing, you must observe the others as well, because the one who gave this one also gave the rest.” They could have replied: “Let us follow what is possible and abandon what is impossible.” Yet this is not the Apostle’s meaning, because he wants them to observe everything.

“You have been alienated from Christ”—that is, estranged, cast down, and separated—“you who are justified in the law,” etc.; that is, you who believe yourselves justified by the higher things [Note: Perhaps “by the superstitions” of the law.] of the law have been alienated from grace, that is, separated from it.

“But we” [Note: The Vulgate reads *enim* (“for”).] “through the Spirit,” etc. He sets the Spirit against the letter and calls Christ the hope of righteousness. The sense is: “We, by the Spirit and through faith, await the hope of righteousness, the Lord Christ, at whose coming there will be not mercy but justice; for he himself is every virtue.”

The Apostle and those like him awaited this coming when they said: “May your kingdom come.” Then, when he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father, God will be all in all, so that, just as he now reigns particularly in each person, afterward he may reign universally in all.

[Note: In the autograph margin, “chapter XXV” is written here.]

“For in Christ Jesus,” etc. He says that circumcision is of no value because of the Galatians’ turning toward it. Why mention the foreskin, when no one is unaware that it is of no benefit? He mentions it because of those who had been grafted from the wild olive into the good olive (Romans XI, 17), lest they should glory against the circumcised, saying that they were of greater dignity because Abraham believed while uncircumcised. Thus, avoiding the danger on both sides, he said that neither circumcision nor the foreskin is of any value.

“But faith,” etc. Great is the power of faith, which works through charity. The Lord demonstrates its greatness by speaking of the man who owed five hundred denarii (Luke VII, 41), where he adds concerning the woman: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (ibid., 47), and: “Your faith has saved you” (ibid., 50). This shows how great faith is before God, since through it one can obtain forgiveness of one’s sins.

[Note: In the autograph margin, “chapter XXVI” is written here.]

He continues: “You were running well,” etc., by following the light of truth rather than the shadow of the law. “Who hindered you?” That is, “By what perverse teacher have you been deceived?” Anyone may use this verse if he sees someone passing from holy conduct to disapproved conduct and say: “You were running well; who hindered you?” The blessed Jerome says: “It is useless not to obey the truth,” just as above, where he says: “O foolish Galatians,” etc.

“Your persuasion,” etc. From what he says, “from him,” it should be understood as referring either to God or to some teacher—that is, to those who call you, not to the one who calls you back. Some interpreters, deceived, said that “from him” means from God alone [Note: The blessed Jerome says concerning this passage: “It is better, therefore, to read the verse as follows: ‘Your persuasion is not from him who called you.’ For one work is God’s, another that of human beings.” The sense is somewhat obscure; yet from the cited text of the blessed Jerome Atto’s meaning is apparent. When blessed Paul says that this persuasion is not from him, this should be understood of God or of the teachers or apostles who call you, but not of those who call you back—that is, the pseudo-apostles, whose persuasion this truly was. Atto says that some were deceived because they interpreted “from him” not of the teachers but of God alone. He may have feared that God’s calling would appear empty and ineffectual among the Galatians, who had departed from the call, if “from him who calls you” were understood only of God’s call. The blessed Augustine says concerning this Epistle: “For this persuasion is carnal.”]

“A little leaven,” etc. They could have said: “O Apostle, why do you rebuke us so harshly and severely, when not all of us have been deceived?” He answered: “A little leaven,” etc., as though saying: “O Galatians, although those who came down from Jerusalem were few, do not despise them, because a little leaven—that is, their small number—can disturb your whole region.”

They could also have said: “Why do you rebuke us so harshly and severely, when we have turned only toward one commandment, namely circumcision?” He answered: “A little leaven,” as though saying: “O Galatians, that one commandment can corrupt the whole mass of your faith.” Origen treats this passage at greater length. He says:

“Just as a falling spark sets fire to a house, walls, and cities, runs through broad forests, and one member infects the whole body, while one sheep defiles the entire flock, so one commandment, if fulfilled, corrupts the whole mass of your faith unless it is cut away—just as the spark must be extinguished, the member cut off, and the sheep excluded.”

Jerome says [Note: In his treatment of this passage of the Epistle.]: “Arius was a spark; if it had been extinguished, it would never have traveled through so many regions of the world.” This expression is found in the Epistle to the Corinthians (I Corinthians V, 6), but there it refers to some small vice, whereas here it refers either to circumcision or to those who came down from Jerusalem.

“I am confident,” etc. This outstanding preacher had foreseen by prophetic spirit that the Galatians would return to their former faith; therefore, adding the name of the Lord, he said, “I am confident.” If he had learned this through human reasoning or perception, he would not have said, “in the Lord.”

When he adds, “You will be of the same mind,” what is written in the Epistle should be supplied. By these words he gives them hope of recovering their senses. From this preachers are admonished that, when they rebuke their people, they should grant them hope of recovery.

“But whoever troubles you,” etc. Some say that he spoke of Peter, because shortly above he had called him blameworthy. But it does not follow that, when the churches were already disturbed, he would rebuke the chief of the apostles so harshly—especially since Peter had been drawn into the matter not as a cause of dissension but under the pretext of peace.

It is more reasonable to understand him as referring to someone of great authority among the apostles, perhaps in Jerusalem, who was also regarded as possessing great authority among the Galatians. Therefore the Apostle, by withholding the name, identifies the person according to his office.

When he says, “troubles,” the sense is this: they were troubled because some wished to place the letter above the Spirit, while others placed the better law above grace; and some [Note: This adverb is read in this way in the Allobrogian manuscript; it could perhaps be read *alii* (“others”), *aliter* (“otherwise”), or *allegorice* (“allegorically”). See, reader, which reading pleases you more. In what is almost prophetic spirit, one might say that our author foresaw grace as volatile—or, as modern theologians say, versatile—and sought in advance to whistle it down and oppose it. See what he frequently says about grace in his exposition of the Epistle to the Romans.] maintained that volatile and false grace, having no roots in truth, was genuine.

“He will bear judgment,” etc.—whether in the present life or in the future. For it is a great evil to give another an occasion for sinning. The Lord makes this clear when he says: “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble,” etc. (Mark IX, 41). Those who were held guilty of the greater crime were punished with such a penalty [Note: Namely, as in the Gospel, by having a millstone placed around the guilty person’s neck and being thrown into the sea.]. Since the Galatians were little ones in faith, and this person had given them an occasion for stumbling, he ought to bear judgment.

[Note: In the autograph margin, “chapter XXVII” is written here.]

“But I, brothers,” etc. Here one must ask why the Apostle says that he preaches circumcision, since throughout the whole Epistle he has labored to destroy it. It should be understood that he is not preaching circumcision; rather, he is referring to the one about whom he had said above: “He had sown this,” saying: “Paul does not reveal the truth to you, because Peter, James, and John preach and observe circumcision, and Paul does likewise; for he circumcised his disciple Timothy and purified himself with the Jews in the temple.”

Therefore he says: “And I, if I preach circumcision,” etc., as though saying: “If it is as that man says, why am I suffering persecution?” In other words: “I do not suffer persecution because I preach Christ as born and having suffered, but because I teach that circumcision must be abolished.”

[Col. 0537A] “Then the scandal of the cross has been abolished” [Note: The manuscript reads *evacuandum* (“to be abolished”), which I have corrected to *evacuatum* (“has been abolished”) in accordance with all the Greek and Latin texts.], etc. The Apostle preached Christ Jesus crucified, which was indeed a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles who did not believe (I Corinthians I, 23). Therefore he says: “Then the scandal has been abolished,” etc. For if circumcision does not save, I preach in vain that circumcision is beneficial.

“Would that those who are troubling you would also cut themselves off,” etc. Why does this disciple of truth, who had said, “Pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matthew V, 44), and the same Apostle, “Bless those who persecute you” (Romans XII, 14), and “Neither will slanderers inherit the kingdom of God” (I Corinthians VI, 10), invoke mutilation upon these people?

The difficulty is resolved as follows. It could have happened that, grieving over the Galatians’ deception—they who had been redeemed by the precious blood of Christ—the Apostle, irritated and indignant, said: “Would that they would cut themselves off,” that is, “Would that those who trouble you were destroyed from your midst, so that you might be saved.”

In another sense: “Would that they would cut themselves off,” that is, “If there is any salvation in circumcision, would that the member in which salvation lies were cut off, so that they might be made eunuchs”; hence the Lord says: “It is better to enter with one eye,” etc. (Matthew XVIII, 9; Mark IX, 46).

“For you were called to freedom,” etc. As though saying: “You who have passed into freedom, take care not to live according to your own desire on account of that freedom.” Or, because you have passed into freedom, take care not to pass freely into circumcision [Note: The manuscript has *a circumcisione* (“from circumcision”), but the words that immediately follow prove that it should be read as corrected.], and obey the pseudo-apostles so that you may be subjected to them. For this is why they want you to turn to circumcision: so that you may be subjected to them, and render what you offer through fear as something you offer through love. Therefore he adds: “But through charity,” etc.

[Note: In the autograph margin, “chapter XXVIII” is written here.]

The blessed Gregory says: “Charity then makes us perfect in freedom from the yoke of slavery whenever it subjects us in turn, through love, to the service of one another; or, charity makes us perfect in freedom from the yoke of slavery whenever we share our goods with others and count the goods of others as our own.”

The whole law, etc. As though he were saying: O Galatians, why do you wish to turn to legal observances, when everything is fulfilled in one saying? And he adds what that saying is: “You shall love your neighbor,” etc. For just as he says in the Epistle to the Romans, “Love of one’s neighbor works no evil” (Rom. XIII, 10), and, “Love is the fullness of the law” (ibid.), so also here. But why does he say that the fullness of the law consists solely in love of one’s neighbor, when the Gospel says, “On these two commandments the law and the prophets depend” [Note: [Col. 0538D] We judged that the words “the Gospel says,” namely Matthew XXII, 40, “on these two commandments”—that is, in love of God and of one’s neighbor—should be added.]? For this reason: one depends upon the other, and neither can exist without the other. Therefore whoever loves his neighbor loves God, because he loves God’s commandment. For God’s commandment is to love one’s neighbor; and whoever loves God likewise loves his neighbor. And since one depends upon the other, why is love of God not expressly proposed? Because a person is more readily proved by love of one’s neighbor than by love of God. Someone can say, “I love God”; and if he does not love him, this remains unknown. But if he says this to his neighbor, it can more easily be proved, since, if he inflicts the evil he is able to inflict and does not bestow the good he is able to bestow, he plainly shows that he does not love his neighbor. And therefore he set down love of one’s neighbor, not love of God.

But if you bite and devour one another, etc. From various disputes—some saying that the law was better than grace, others that the letter was better than the spirit, some that open Judaism was better, others that hidden Judaism was better, and so forth—various conflicts arose. But by then some were circumcising themselves so that they might be preferred to others; in doing this they envied others, drew others into envy, and by doing this were consumed. And therefore the Apostle said this. In another sense: “But if you bite one another,” that is, if you turn to the carnal circumcision of the law, you bite one another because you demand vengeance. For the law says, “An eye for an eye,” etc. (Lev. XXIV, 20); and while you seek vengeance, you will be consumed, since now not one but two perish. But how could the Jews free themselves from all the things mentioned above unless they lived spiritually?

[Note: [Col. 0538D] In the autograph margin, chapter XXIX and the Fourteenth Sunday after Pentecost are written here.]

And therefore he adds: “Walk by the Spirit.” For the one walks by the Spirit who does not carry out the works of the flesh; and the one does not walk according to the flesh who does not carry out the works of the flesh, because the spirit resists. Likewise, the works of the flesh are not carried out when the spirit resists; and the works of the spirit are carried out when no resisting movement of the flesh is found in us. What he says here—“You shall not fulfill the desires of the flesh”—is equivalent to what he says in the Epistle to the Romans: “For the will to do good is present with me, but I do not find the means to accomplish it” (Rom. VII, 18). For just as there he speaks of good things, so here he speaks of evil things.

But it must be noted that doing good is one thing and accomplishing it is another. To do good is to resist desires; to accomplish it is not to desire. Likewise, not sinning is one thing, and being without sin is another. We can refrain from sinning—that is, resist desires—but we cannot be without sin, because we desire. Likewise here, having the desires of the flesh is one thing, and not fulfilling them is another. We cannot avoid having the desires of the flesh, because we desire; yet we do not fulfill them, because we resist our desires. But this will be perfect when “death has been swallowed up in victory” (I Cor. XV, 54), and when “this mortal nature has put on immortality” (ibid.).

For the flesh desires, etc. “What we do not wish, that we do” (Rom. VII, 16), and we desire it. In this way teachers generally use the example to confirm their position. But one must work very carefully lest the Apostle seem to have unusually departed from the intention with which he began. For he often touches beforehand upon the subject that he later develops at greater length. His intention, then, is as follows. He had begun to destroy carnal observances of the law; still persisting in that intention, he says: “Walk by the Spirit,” that is, understand the law spiritually, because if you do so, you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh—that is, you will not demand vengeance. “The flesh desires,” that is, the carnal sense desires against the spiritual, and the spiritual against the carnal. And if it should happen that the carnal is overcome by the spiritual [Note: [Col. 0539D] In the autograph, “is separated” is written.], the whole person is called spiritual; and likewise conversely. This occurs not only in two people but in one person, for it often happens that the spiritual prevails over the carnal, and the carnal over the spiritual. “Whatever you wish,” etc.—that is, do not seek vengeance.

But if you are led by the Spirit, etc.—that is, if you are driven and moved by the Spirit of God, you are not under the law, because the law is not laid down for the righteous. Or: you are driven by the Spirit of God if you understand the law spiritually; then you are not under the law, because you will not demand punishment. For what else does afflicted flesh desire except vengeance? But understand it spiritually, and do not seek it.

Now the works of the flesh are manifest, etc. But one must ask why the Apostle says that all these things belong to the flesh, when some seem to belong to the spirit, namely rivalries, conceits, and so on. This question is resolved by a figure of speech in which one part includes another, so that “flesh” is understood as the whole person. The meaning is therefore: “The works of the flesh are manifest,” that is, the works of any human being. But some say that the flesh is the incentive and origin of all vices. Blessed Augustine, however, says: Those who said this did not understand the order of nature. For corruptible flesh did not make the soul sinful; rather, the soul became the author of the sin of corruptible flesh, which is the punishment of sin. Nevertheless, the flesh has the *fastus* of heaviness, by which the soul is weighed down [Note: [Col. 0539D] In the autograph it reads: “The flesh has the *fastus* of heaviness, by which the soul is weighed down.” We judged that “by which” should be read instead of “by whom.” What is meant by *fastus* is not entirely obvious, unless, with Alinus, we understand the Latin expression *fastum facere* as “to inflict injury,” so that the meaning is: “The flesh has *fastus*; that is, the flesh suffers the injuries of heaviness,” which seems to be confirmed by the text cited below.], as in the words: “The body, which is corrupted, weighs down the soul,” etc. (Wis. IX, 15). He himself says: These vices must be attributed to the soul, lest the devil, who is without flesh, seem to be excluded from all these things. For he is called an adulterer and a murderer because he is the author and instigator of them all, and of similar things. For he does not say these things [Note: [Col. 0540D] That is, he does not say that “these things”—that is, not merely the works of the flesh—are what blessed Paul is enumerating, lest those things be thought excluded, namely the sins of the spirit mentioned above, which separate human beings from the kingdom of God no less than those other sins.], lest those things appear to be excluded which separate human beings from the kingdom of God.

“These things I foretell to you.” He foretold them when he was present bodily, and he foretells them through this Epistle; or he had foretold them in the Epistle to the Corinthians, where he enumerates these things, since it could have happened that it reached their hands. Nor is it contrary that he says “to you,” because he wrote his Epistles to all the churches.

But the fruit of the Spirit, etc. Note that he calls vices the works of the flesh, and virtues the works of the spirit [Note: [Col. 0540D] The word “spirit” is absent, and I judged that it should be added.], because the former can be destroyed, whereas the latter increase. “Against such things there is no law.” He does not say “against these,” lest the remaining things appear to be excluded. He says, “Against such things there is no law,” because those who remain in such things are not under the law, since the law is not laid down for the righteous but for the unrighteous; or, there is no law against spiritual people and those who live spiritually. But it must be understood that above he placed the vices first and then the virtues. It is necessary first to destroy vices and then to perform good deeds, as the Psalmist says: “Turn away from evil,” etc. (Ps. XXXVI, 27); and Jeremiah: “I appointed you to uproot,” etc. (Jer. I, 10); and James: “Therefore, having put away all uncleanness,” etc. (Jas. I, 21).

He listed more vices than virtues because there are more of them. But who would fail to notice that each vice is destroyed by its corresponding virtue? Fornication, what else is it but adulterous thought, which separates people from God? But no virtue destroys it better than the virtue of love. Uncleanness, shamelessness, and the other things that the apostles are ashamed to name (Eph. V, 3; Col. III, 5) so that they might make the children of Israel modest and ashamed [Note: [Col. 0540D] The manuscript reads *facite* (“make”); I judged that it should be emended to *facerent* (“they might make”). Reader, consider whether this is correct.], are destroyed by nothing better than the spiritual sword.

But those who belong to Christ, etc. Origen joins this passage to the preceding in the following way: “Against such things there is no law,” because they crucified the flesh of Christ. For it must be noted that the Word of God, by taking flesh, united us to himself; our flesh is his, and our members are his. Therefore we have been crucified with him; therefore we ought not to cling to earthly things but to dwell upon spiritual things, following the example of him who said: “Remember me, Lord,” etc. (Luke XXIII, 42). But if you say separately, “His own flesh,” etc., it must be understood not of Christ’s flesh but of someone else’s, as though he were saying: O Galatians, since you have already crucified yourselves, why do you wish to turn to circumcision, when circumcision is of no benefit to those who have been crucified?

[Note: [Col. 0540D] In the autograph margin, chapter XXX is written here.]

If we live by the Spirit, etc. What does he mean by this, or who says it? The inner person does, as though it had happened that this person were separated: from the spirit he is called spiritual, just as from the flesh he is called carnal. Someone may use this verse if he sees someone behaving carnally.

“Let us not become,” etc. This depends upon what precedes, because he had said: “If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit; let us not become vain-glorious,” etc. For they were provoking and envying one another, some saying that the law was better than grace, and so forth, as above; and those who envied were doing this. Many books of the pagans exist concerning this expression, which is “glory.” It is also found in divine writings. But it is used both in a good and in an evil sense: in an evil sense, as in, “They do all their works so that they may be glorified [Note: [Col. 0541D] The Vulgate reads “may be seen.” Blessed Jerome himself, in commenting on this Epistle and citing this passage from Matthew, reads “may be glorified.”] by human beings”; in a good sense, as in, “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord” (I Cor. I, 31; II Cor. X, 17), and, “I do not seek my own glory” (John VIII, 50). And therefore, because it is used both in a good and in an evil sense, he added the word “vain”: we ought indeed to be desirous, but not of vain glory. For example, someone gives alms: if he does so in order to please human beings, he seeks vain glory; if he does so for God, he seeks substantial glory. Someone approaches martyrdom: if he does so so that his members may be held in veneration and so that he may be called a martyr, he seeks vain glory. Hence, where we read, “If I hand over my body so that I may burn” (I Cor. XIII, 3), the Greek has the better reading, “in glory” [Note: [Col. 0541D] The Greek text does not have “in glory” but “that I may glory.” It was easy, however, to confuse *καυθήσομαι* (“I may burn”) with *καυχήσομαι* (“I may glory”), since the two are distinguished by only one letter, and to take one for the other.]; but if he does so in order to receive recompense from God, he seeks substantial glory.

[Note: [Col. 0541D] In the autograph margin, chapter XXXI is written here.]

(VI.) Brothers, and if someone should be overtaken, etc. He calls them brothers because they are spiritual; he calls the person “a human being” because he is fragile, and by that very name he shows that the person deserves pardon and indulgence. For he says “a human being,” that is, a fragile and sinful person. And note that he says “overtaken.” The person is overtaken who sins not intentionally, not after reflection, and not after deliberation, but by accident. And note that he does not say “in many things” but “in one thing,” because the one who is overtaken in one thing ought to be corrected in a spirit of gentleness.

“You who are spiritual”—that is, you who are more than merely human—“restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness,” that is, of meekness, so that you may not be rigid, savage, or cruel. For if you are severe and cruel, you are not an imitator of him who descended from heaven to earth for the salvation of the human race. But a question arises: why does he say that the person should be corrected in a spirit of gentleness, when in the Epistle to the Corinthians he says, “Shall I come to you with a rod?” etc. (I Cor. IV, 21). The answer is easy. Those who sin intentionally, after reflection and deliberation, must be corrected with the rod of severity; those who sin accidentally must be corrected in a spirit of gentleness. This may be referred to what precedes, so that the meaning is: If someone comes to the faith slowly from paganism or Judaism, he must be tolerated until he progresses. And why had he said, “in a spirit of gentleness”? He adds: “Considering yourself,” etc., as though he were saying: Consider that you are a fragile human being, capable of sinning and having sinned. [Col. 0541D] And note that he does not say, “lest you fall,” but “lest you be tempted.” For falling or not falling is within our power [Col. 0542A] together with God’s help [Note: [Col. 0541D] Observe how cautiously our author, truly Augustinian, drew this text from blessed Jerome’s exposition of this Epistle and chapter. Where blessed Jerome says, “For at times it is within our power to be conquered or to conquer,” Atto added, “together [Col. 0542D] with God’s help.”]. Being tempted, however, is not within the power of the person tempted, but of the tempter.

But perhaps someone, already worn out by many years, says: “For that reason he is afraid to correct severely [Note: [Col. 0542D] The meaning here is somewhat obscure. It seems to me that the order and sense of the words are as follows: Someone says, worn out by old age, “The Apostle is therefore afraid to correct severely because he fears being tempted; but I am already safely in the harbor of tranquility, and so I can correct severely.” Our author replies: “But if that person fears, how much more does this man fear—namely, the old man—because he knows,” etc. See blessed Jerome on this passage.]; I am already safely in the harbor of tranquility, and I can correct severely.” But if that person fears being tempted while correcting severely, this one does so all the more, because he knows through how many and how great dangers he may have reached the harbor of tranquility. Someone approaches martyrdom and escapes, and sees someone else, afflicted by various tortures, deny the faith: he does not marvel that the other denied it, but that he himself was able to escape.

“Bear one another’s burdens.” This admonition is salutary. For we bear burdens when, by our own firmness, we support another’s weakness, and by our wisdom sustain another’s foolishness. [Col. 0542B] “And thus you will fulfill,” etc. He calls the commandment of Christ the law of Christ, namely the commandment in which he himself says: “This is my commandment, that you love one another” (John XV, 12). He so strongly emphasizes this commandment that he says below [Note: [Col. 0542D] That is, in what follows, not the text cited but a similar passage, XIII, 34: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another.” Verse 35, which follows immediately, belongs with it: “By this all will know,” etc., the text cited below.]: “By this all will know that you are my disciples,” etc.

For if anyone, etc. For example, someone sees a foolish person and wishes to be wise by comparison with that person’s foolishness; likewise, someone sees an unjust person, and so forth. When a person thinks himself to be something while he is nothing, he deceives himself. This may be referred to what precedes, so that the meaning is: If someone thinks that circumcision amounts to something when it is nothing, he deceives himself. What follows also belongs to what precedes: “But let each one test his own work,” etc., as though he were saying: If he searches his inner self, he can recognize and know whether he has anything in himself of which to glory. For no one is closer to him than he himself; therefore, if he searches himself, he will not measure his own strength by another’s strength.

“Each one,” etc. This appears contrary to the earlier passage, where he had said, “Bear one another’s burdens,” etc. But it is not contrary, because there he was speaking of works of piety and chastity, whereas here he is speaking of merit. The meaning is: “Each one will bear his own burden,” that is, each one will receive recompense according to his own merit. It may also be referred to the statement “Bear one another’s burdens,” so that the meaning is: Who are you that you do not hesitate to support another’s weakness? You will not be defiled in his place, because each one will bear his own burden. It may also be referred to the other statement, so that the meaning is: Do not be lifted up by another’s praise, so that you think yourself to be what you are said to be, because both you will bear your own burden and he will bear his.

[Col. 0543A] [Note: [Col. 0543D] In the autograph margin, chapter XXXII is written here.]

“Let the one who is instructed in the word share,” etc. Until now he had addressed the strong, who were able patiently to tolerate the weakness of others. Now he addresses the subordinate members, explaining how they ought to conduct themselves toward their preachers. For it often happens that, while giving themselves to preaching, they suffer poverty. And therefore the Apostle admonishes the hearers to share all good things with their preachers, that is, to provide food and clothing. The same Apostle says elsewhere: “Having food and clothing, with these we are content” [Note: [Col. 0543D] I Tim. VI, 8, where the text reads: “Having food and coverings, with these,” etc.].

But it must be understood that the same Apostle calls temporal goods “goods” according to human custom. And why is this surprising, when the Lord also says to disciples who had not yet reached perfection, at the conclusion of the Sermon [Note: [Col. 0543D] That is, of the mountain, on whose summit Jesus Christ stood and taught; blessed Jerome allegorically interprets the summit of that mountain as the summit of perfection in his exposition of this Epistle.]: “If you, then, although you are evil,” etc. [Col. 0543B] (Matt. VII, 11)? Perhaps Job had called temporal things goods in response to his wife, who said: “Bless God and die” (Job II, 9), and he replied: “If we have received good things,” etc. (ibid., 10). He had called bread a good thing. The things he endured were evil. For that man of God, full of God, knew that nothing could be called good except the virtues that make us blessed, and nothing evil except what makes us miserable. But he was speaking according to human custom. For when Sacred Scripture speaks according to its own manner and language, it affirms that virtues or vices are good or evil.

“Do not be deceived,” etc. Someone could have answered: “O Apostle, I cannot do this, because my field has dried up this year from drought; hail has destroyed my vineyard; taxes have exhausted my income [Col. 0543C] and royal levies; I cannot do what you say.” To this he replies: “Do not be deceived” [Note: [Col. 0544D] In the autograph margin, chapter XXXIII is written here.], as though he were saying: Do not say this, because in saying it you are deceived; for although you can deceive a human being, you cannot deceive God. He himself knows your granary, your cellar, and all your possessions.

And lest that person think he was losing what he had given, he therefore adds: “For whatever a person sows,” etc., as though he were saying: Do not think that you are losing what you grant, because you will receive recompense. And it must be understood that there are two fields: one spiritual and one carnal. When we do spiritual things, we sow in a spiritual field; when we do carnal things, we sow in a carnal field.

And because he gives the image of a sower, he wishes to make that image clear. He adds: “For the one who sows in his flesh,” etc. Those sow in the flesh who satisfy their carnal pleasures, that is, lusts, and so forth. They reap corruption, that is, the punishment of eternal damnation. But those who sow in the spirit—those sow in the spirit who sow virtues—and by sowing virtues they will reap eternal life. And note that he says “in his own flesh,” with an addition, but says simply “in the spirit.” The reason is that we can sin by our own efforts, whereas we cannot perform good deeds at all by our own efforts. Some have wished to understand the Holy Spirit [Col. 0544A], so that the meaning is: Whoever gives something out of love for the Holy Spirit will receive recompense from him. This may be referred to what precedes, so that the meaning is: Whoever sows in his flesh, that is, whoever understands the law carnally, will reap corruption, because what the law promises is temporal; but whoever sows in the spirit, that is, whoever understands it spiritually, will reap eternal life.

“And while doing good,” etc. This is a salutary apostolic teaching, for in these words he urges us to the good of perseverance. He knew that some began well but did not complete their work by persevering in faith; therefore he speaks in this way. And because there are some who expect to receive recompense here for the good they do, he therefore adds: “For in due time we shall reap,” etc. It is as though he were saying: The time of sowing is one thing and the time of harvest another; we do not sow and reap at the same time. Likewise, now we ought to do good, but afterward receive recompense. For the one who receives it here is deprived of reward in the future. Hence the Lord says: “They have received their reward” (Matt. VI, 5, 16); and Solomon: “An inheritance to which one hastens,” etc. (Prov. XX, 21). And note that he says, “Let us not grow weary,” and “without growing weary,” because those who perform good works without weariness will receive recompense without weariness.

[Note: [Col. 0544D] In the autograph margin, chapter XXXIV is written here.]

Because he had said above, “Whatever a person sows,” up to “without growing weary,” he therefore adds: “Therefore, while we have time,” etc. It is as though he were saying: If we must receive then, we must sow now, but in fertile soil, according to the prophet: “Break up new ground,” etc., and “circumcise the foreskin,” etc. (Jer. IV, 3; Hos. X, 12). “All,” that is, both pagans and Jews, because he has granted all temporal things to everyone in common. “Especially,” that is, those who share with us the same religion, devotion, and faith; and your household, and each person in his own order. This apostolic teaching must not be despised but desired with the greatest eagerness. For each person ought to take care to labor lest he lose the time granted and given by God by spending it in idleness. Indeed, certain pagans were so diligent that they regretted having lost a single day. It is said that Titus, son of Vespasian, after Jerusalem had been destroyed and while returning victoriously to Rome, said one night at dinner to his companions: “Friends, I have lost a day.” If that man, who was a pagan and had neither the law nor the prophets, regretted losing a day in which he had not labored for the stability of the kingdom or the people, with what face will you, who are a Christian, behave? It is also said that John, worn out by advanced age and unable to deliver a sermon at the assembly, would say, when his attendants carried him in their arms: “Little children, love one another.” When he was asked why he kept saying this, he gave an appropriate answer: “Little children, because this one commandment of the Lord is sufficient if it is fulfilled.”

[Note: [Col. 0544D] In the autograph margin, chapter XXXV is written here.]

“See with what large letters,” etc. From this point to the end he wrote with his own hand, for the following reason: Some people were saying that he was not a true apostle, because Peter, James, and John preached and observed circumcision according to the flesh, while Paul circumcised his disciple and purified himself with the Jews in the temple. They had been deceived by this one matter. Wishing to wipe away this accusation, he writes with his own hands; and he wrote especially with his own hands to those among whom he knew there were people who would fight against his truth and teaching. Or he did so in order to display his authority and show that he did not fear his detractors, as though he were saying: O Galatians, you can recognize from this that I do not fear my detractors, since I have written the letters with my own hands.

[Col. 0545B] “All who wish,” etc. By “flesh” we may understand either the carnal Jews, any carnal person, or even carnal vices [Note: [Col. 0545D] The manuscript reads “devoted to carnal vices.” I would have thought that *deditum* or *deditos* should be added, had he not already used “carnal” in what I take to be this sense. I therefore judged that the passage should be emended.]. “Only so that they may not suffer persecution for the cross of Christ.” It must be noted that Gaius [Note: [Col. 0545D] Blessed Jerome has “Gaius.”] Caesar, Octavian Augustus, and his successor Tiberius established by public laws that throughout the Roman world the Jews should use their own laws. Therefore some believers turned to circumcision so that they might not suffer the scandal of the cross. “For not even those who are circumcised,” etc., as though he were saying: They do not circumcise themselves in order to keep the law, because the law cannot be fulfilled carnally; but they do not wish to understand it spiritually, so as to fulfill it. “But they wish you to be circumcised,” etc. It is as though he were saying: They compel you to be circumcised so that they may glory in the sign of circumcision on their shameful members. And this is like what is written in the Epistle to the Romans: “Their god is their belly,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0545D] This text is not in the Epistle to the Romans but in the Epistle to the Philippians III, 19. A similar passage, equally relevant here, is found in Romans XVI, 18: “They do not serve Christ our Lord but their own belly.”] For these people rejoiced in having many disciples. The Lord reveals with what eagerness they wished to draw people to circumcision when he says: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who travel around sea and land to make one proselyte,” etc. (Matt. XXIII, 15). And if they were eager to draw one person, how much more the whole province of Galatia?

[Note: [Col. 0546D] In the autograph margin, chapter XXXVI is written here.]

“But far be it from me,” etc. The Apostle distinguishes his glorying from theirs in these words, as though he were saying: They glory in circumcision; I glory in the cross. It is like the words: “They went away rejoicing” (Acts V, 41), etc. And he shows whose cross it is when he says: “In the cross of the Lord.” [Col. 0545D] For it must be noted that there are those who die to the world, and the world has died to them. The Apostle was one of these.

“For in Christ Jesus.” In this passage he openly shows his intention, as though he were saying: I, Paul, who earlier dictated these words while someone else wrote them, am now writing with my own hands so that you may know that I do not fear my detractors. As for what he says, “Neither circumcision is of any avail,” etc., as above, he calls the ecclesiastical people renewed through the sacrament of baptism a new creation. But this renewal is effective only if one keeps what one has promised; for if one withdraws, one is not included in this renewal.

“And whoever follows this rule,” etc. Note that the Apostle directs everything toward the rule, so that if anything crooked or perverse should be found, it may be removed. For he calls the apostolic teaching a rule [Col. 0546B], and he shows its great authority when he says: “Peace be upon all who follow this teaching,” etc. Peace is that by which we are reconciled to God; mercy is that by which sins are forgiven. He says “upon the Israel of God” to distinguish it from carnal Israel, for there is an Israel that is not God’s; hence in the Apocalypse: “Those who say that they are Jews,” etc. (Rev. II, 9).

[Note: [Col. 0546D] In the autograph margin, chapter XXXVII is written here.]

“From now on,” etc. It is as though he were saying: Since the truth has been made clear, let no one provoke me to argument. This is like what he says in the Epistle to the Corinthians: “If anyone is contentious among you” (I Cor. XI, 16). Hence the Greek has the better reading: “Let no one cause me trouble.”

“For I bear the marks,” etc. Note that he says “marks,” not circumcision; and he says “of Jesus,” not the marks of the law. For marks are signs of punishments by which slaves are branded [Note: [Col. 0546D] The manuscript reads: “knots of punishments by which slaves are unknotted.” Blessed Augustine, however, says in his exposition of this Epistle: “Marks are certain signs of servile punishments,” etc.; therefore we judged that the text in our manuscript should be emended.]. He calls the dangers of prisons, stonings, shipwrecks, and the other sufferings recounted in the catalogue of his virtues marks in his own body.

“Grace,” etc. He says not of the law but of the Lord; not with the flesh but with the spirit; not with just anyone but with the brothers; and not with others but with the true ones. This is what “Amen” means, for *amen* is interpreted as “truly” or “faithfully.” With this expression the Apostle confirmed his account, just as the Lord does in the Old Testament: “As I live, says the Lord” (Num. XIV, 28), and in the New: “Amen, amen, I say to you” (John I, 51). So also does he. And that it is used in the sense of “truly” is shown in the Epistle to the Corinthians, where he says: “How will he say ‘Amen’ over your blessing?” [Note: [Col. 0546D] Perhaps the same passage, or perhaps a reference to it; I Cor. XIV, 16.]

The Epistle to the Galatians ends.

THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS BEGINS.

[Col. 0545]

ARGUMENT.

[Col. 0545D]

The Ephesians are Asians. Having received the word of truth, they persevered in faith. The Apostle praises them highly, writing to them from prison at Rome. Some maintain that, although they had been preached to by another, they were strengthened by the Apostle. Others will say that they first received the word of faith from the Apostle. But however the matter may stand, it must nevertheless be understood that they had believed both from the Jews and from the Gentiles. Therefore he first addresses the Jews, explaining to them the mysteries of Christ, namely the Incarnation and what follows. Then he turns to the Gentiles and urges them not to be ungrateful for such great benefits. Afterward he gives them all, jointly, the moral precepts [Note: [Col. 0547D] The autograph reads “mortality.” I judged that this obvious error should be corrected to “morality.”] that apply not only to them but also to all Christians. Among other things, he teaches what masters and servants, fathers and sons, men and women ought to do. The chief point at the beginning is that he may show that Christ existed before the world and that hope must be placed in him. Concerning the admonition: everyone who progresses in understanding ought also to progress in love, according to the saying, “Whoever adds knowledge adds sorrow” [Note: [Col. 0547D] Ecclesiastes I, 18 reads: “Whoever adds knowledge adds toil also.”]. What sorrow? That he should be displeased with himself, restrain himself, and grieve that he is held amid the dangers of the world. Although these things are necessary for Christian people, they especially suit those who investigate the mysteries of Scripture.

THE TEXT BEGINS.

(CHAPTER I.) Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus. Concerning the fact that he begins in such a way as both to suggest Christ and to make clear that he evangelizes him, note how he writes to the Romans: “Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus.” Compare the two passages, and you will find that he is the apostle of the one whose servant he is. He says “through the will of God,” as also in the Epistle to the Galatians, to show that he was changed not by his own will but by God’s: for we are saved not by our own effort but by God’s mercy. But why does he say “to the saints and faithful,” unless because there are faithful people who are not saints, such as catechumens, who have faith but have not been reborn? Alternatively: He does not write to everyone, but to those who preserve holiness in faith. A pagan can also be faithful if he returns what has been entrusted to him [Note: [Col. 0547D] That is, the entrusted property, as blessed Jerome has it in this passage; or perhaps *commodatum* (“what has been lent”) should be read: the word has been written compactly as *comdatu* [Col. 0548D].], if he does not reveal a secret; and yet he is not holy, because he does not believe in Christ. Alternatively: He bound them to a definite religion when he said that they were holy and faithful in Christ, so that they might not accept anything new and alien to Christ. For whoever is holy in Christ ought to love and cherish nothing but Christ. Concerning the fact that he says “grace and peace” to them: grace belongs to the Father, when he sends his Son to earth; peace belongs to the Son, when, through him, we who have been redeemed are reconciled to God the Father. In this explanation the Trinity is shown, since the Holy Spirit is designated by the names of grace and peace, because he himself is called the gift of God.

He continues: “Blessed be God,” etc. With keen intelligence he urges his hearers to praise God. This passage can be read in two ways, as has already been said in the Epistle to the Corinthians.

He continues: “Who blessed us,” etc. Note that he says not “in one” but “in every,” that is, not in a few but in all; and not in earthly things but in spiritual things. There is an earthly blessing. An earthly blessing is to have children, to abound in riches, and to rejoice in health and honor (Lev. XXVI, 9), things promised in Leviticus to those who observe the law; that is, to lend to foreign peoples at interest, to have granaries full of grain, and so forth. Such blessings are not spiritual. Hence they did not possess them who wandered in sheepskins and goatskins, in poverty, in caves, avoiding the attacks of persecutors (Heb. XI, 37). Therefore everything must be understood spiritually, and spiritual blessings must be awaited not in earthly things but in heavenly ones.

Then follows: “Just as he chose us in him,” etc. Augustine: Who, I ask, could hear these things attentively and intelligently, and dare to doubt this truth so clearly established, which we defend? For God chose the members of Christ before the foundation of the world, predestining them in him [Note: [Col. 0548D] Here is Augustine’s view of predestination, most evidently asserted by the blessed Paul as an exceedingly clear truth, about which no one could dare to doubt.]. Not, as Pelagius says, because he foresaw that the saints would become such and therefore chose them [Note: [Col. 0548D] These statements should be joined to those found very frequently in the Epistle to the Romans and elsewhere concerning predestination.], but he chose them in order that they might become such. For the Apostle cries out: “That we should be”; when he predestined us, he foreknew his work, by which he makes us holy and blameless. For what purpose did he foreknow us? For adoption as sons. Whom? Us, who were far away. Why? For the praise of glory. He says, “according to the purpose of his will,” so that in so great a benefit of grace we might not boast of the merits of our own will. In this will, certainly, he “graced” us. The expression “graced” is derived from grace, just as “justified” is from justice; that is, he made us pleasing. In whom? That is, in Christ: “we have redemption.” For this is grace: that in Christ, through his blood, we should have redemption and forgiveness of sins. For he redeemed us from carnal works and desires in order that we might serve him—which is to live spiritually.

Then follows: “According to the riches of his grace.” It abounded to such an extent that he not only redeemed us from death, but also gave us such wisdom that we might know his mysteries.

Then follows: “In all wisdom and prudence.” The Stoics say that wisdom concerns divine and human matters, but prudence concerns human matters alone.

Then follows: “That he might make known to us the mystery of his will.” We have understood the will of God’s mystery—that is, of our redemption—because he revealed it. “According to his good pleasure”: not according to our good will, which could not have been good unless he himself had come to our aid so that it might be good [Note: [Col. 0549C] Here is prevenient grace.].

He says “for the dispensation of the fullness of times” because it had been determined when the Father would send his Son here; hence he says elsewhere: “When the fullness of time had come” (Gal. IV, 4). Then follows: “To restore all things” [Note: [Col. 0549C] In this Epistle the blessed Jerome reads differently from the Latins: instead of *instaurare*, “to restore,” he reads *recapitulare*, “to recapitulate,” from the Greek ἀνακεφαλαιόω, which means “I gather the heads,” or “I repeat the principal points”; from it comes ἀνακεφαλαίωσις, “a reduction to a summary,” or “recapitulation.” The blessed Jerome is followed by Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book V, chapter 17, and by the translator of Saint Irenaeus, book I, chapter 1.]. Some understand “heaven” as the soul and “earth” as the body. Others understand “heaven” as the Jews and “earth” as the Gentiles. Others understand “heaven” not as the angels, but as their knowledge, which advanced from the time of Christ; for, as though ignorant, they asked: “Who is this King of glory?” (Ps. XXIII, 8.) But it is better to say that their number was fulfilled through the salvation of human beings.

Then follows: “In whom we have also been called by lot”; that is, foreknown beforehand—but first the lost sheep [Note: [Col. 0549D] That is, the Jews.], [Col. 0549B] and afterward the Gentiles. “He who works all things,” etc. This does not mean that everything that occurs in the world occurs according to God’s will, but that everything he does, he does with counsel and by his will. Otherwise evils too could be attributed to God.

“That we should be for the praise of his glory”: that is, if we believe in him and become spiritual by following Christ, we shall be for the praise of the glory of that God, so that through the signs we perform God’s glory may be praised. Then follows: “We who first hoped”: we apostles, or the Jews, who believed first.

Then follows: “In whom you also,” etc. He turns to the Ephesians, so that this benefit might not seem to belong to others and not to those to whom he was writing the Epistle. He says, “This is yours also, for you too are included in it.” “In whom you also, when you believed,” etc.; that is, whoever hears the word of truth and believes is sealed by the Gospel, or by Christ. For there are many who hear and do not believe, and therefore do not receive the seal of the Holy Spirit. “The seal of God”: just as the first human being was formed according to the image of God, so in the second regeneration whoever has received the Holy Spirit is sealed by him.

Then follows: “Who is the pledge of the inheritance”: that is, he gave the pledge itself so that we might be secure concerning the inheritance. “For redemption”: that is, so that we might be redeemed from these earthly and bodily evils and acquired as adopted sons. “And this for the praise of his glory”: not because God needs the praise of anyone, but because it benefits those who praise him.

[Note: [Col. 0549D] In the author’s manuscript margin, chapter II is written here.] Therefore, I too, having heard, etc. He moves from this point specifically to an exhortation of the Ephesians. “Having heard your faith,” he says, “I love you; having heard of your love, I too will take care to give thanks to God for you.” Every prayer is either for things received or for things to be received, and either for ourselves or for others. This concerns the past. He then speaks of the future: “That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ.” He is called “the Father of glory,” as though Christ were the glory of the Word, of wisdom, or of peace, as in: “Awake, my glory” (Ps. CVII, 3), and: “The glory of the Lord appeared over the tabernacle” (Lev. IX, 23). This glory fashioned a temple for itself from the Virgin’s womb. The God who is the Father of glory becomes the Father of this temple. Therefore, may this God of the assumed human being—while the Father of glory, wisdom, and truth—grant the saints what follows: “May he give you the Spirit of wisdom,” etc. How can he wish wisdom for the Ephesians when he says to the Corinthians that wisdom puffs up (I Cor. VIII, 1)? There he is pointing to carnal wisdom; here, however, he commends spiritual wisdom, and whoever possesses it will be able to become humble rather than puffed up. But how does he pray that they may have knowledge of God, when above he had praised them? He prays that they may know more perfectly that they were saved by God’s grace, not by their own merit, and that nothing can be hidden from God. For whoever knows this perfectly cannot sin. Concerning [Note: [Col. 0549D] Here our author, or his copyist, seems to have left an incomplete sense in the example he intended to introduce. Nevertheless, I would suppose that he had in mind what is read in I Kings II, 12: that the sons of Eli, “sons of Belial,” who did not know the Lord, had so departed from the priestly office and committed a very great sin before the Lord because of this very ignorance of God.] the sons of Eli.

Then follows: “Having been enlightened,” etc. He says this because the inner person has his members and his eyes, concerning which the Psalmist also says: “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” (Ps. XII, 4); and again: “The eyes of the wise are in his head” (Eccl. II, 14). Knowledge concerns those things that we previously did not know; recognition concerns those things that we remember after having forgotten them.

[Note: [Col. 0549D] The blessed Jerome also introduces this distinction in his treatment of this Epistle, as one accepted by some.]

Then follows: “That you may know,” etc. It is as though he were saying: If, knowing to what hope you have been called, you easily despise every hope of the world, and if you see the riches of God’s inheritance, every earthly inheritance will seem filthy to you; for no one who hopes for such riches would care to possess lead [Note: [Col. 0549D] An error has certainly crept in here. I have not wished to correct it because a very extensive alteration of the words would have been necessary to restore the sense, while the genuine phrasing is highly uncertain. I promise myself a safer correction if I bring forward the source of this interpretation, from which it has been taken almost word for word. It is the commentary falsely ascribed to the blessed Jerome but more correctly attributed by the learned to Pelagius, on the testimony of Saint Augustine—among other places, in book III of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 1—and also on the testimony of Marius Mercator, Cassiodorus, and the author of *Praedestinatus*. There we read: “If you knew to what hope you have been called, you would easily despise every hope of the world; and if you saw the riches of God’s inheritance, every earthly inheritance would seem horrible to you. For no one who hopes for the kingdom with its riches considers himself a steward and deigns to possess a modest substance.” In the entire sequence of the text there is scarcely a difference of one or two words. From this commentary, too, our author had taken the example of the sons of Eli a little earlier. All these things together prove that our Atto had this commentary, along with the others, very much before his eyes.]. And rightly he says “in the saints,” not “in all human beings.” For who can comprehend the greatness of God’s goodness, which he has bestowed on believers from Jews and Gentiles, so that they might become adopted sons and members of Christ? And rightly he says: “According to the working [Note: [Col. 0551D] The Vulgate adds “of his power.”] of his power, which he worked in Christ,” because to know these things we need that power which God also used in his Son, raising him from the dead—not raising him once only, but continually from the dead—and making him free from death, undefiled by any contamination of death. Christ rises daily from the dead in those who repent. Concerning the fact that God himself is the inheritance of the saints: thus it is said of the sons of Levi, “I am the Lord, their portion” (Num. XVIII, 20; Josh. XIII, 14); likewise, “The Lord is their inheritance” (Deut. XVIII, 2); and, “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. LXXII, 26); and, “You are the portion of my inheritance,” etc. (Ps. XV, 5).

Then follows: “Raising him up”; that is, insofar as he was able to die. Concerning the fact that “right hand” is used for honor: in God there is nothing left, because he is not corporeal. For the Father too is at the right hand of the Son, as in: “The Lord at your right hand has shattered,” etc. (Ps. CIX, 5). Concerning the fact that the Apostle had learned these names from Hebrew tradition—or, certainly, by understanding the Law spiritually, he perceived something more sublime—and that what he read concerning kings, leaders, tribunes, and centurions in Numbers and in the Books of Kings he recognized as implying that, just as there are different dignities in the heavens, so it is necessary that they have subjects who are subordinate to them and fear them. For if a human being, soon to be reduced to dust, when chosen as king possesses these offices, how much more does the King of kings possess various offices of dignity?

But how does he say that all things have been subjected to him, when elsewhere he himself says: “We do not yet see all things subjected to him”? “He must reign,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0551D] I Cor. XV, 25 and following, where the negative particle *necdum*, “not yet,” although admitted by the blessed Jerome when he cites this passage in his interpretation of this Epistle, is not found at all.]. Either he says this according to foreknowledge, or, if he is speaking of the past, we must understand that some things were subjected to him by will, such as good things, and others by necessity, such as evil things. Such are the Jews, the pagans, and the demons themselves, who were created good by God but became evil and are subjected unwillingly. Alternatively: “all things” may not refer to the whole, as in: “The whole city cried out” [Note: [Col. 0551D] I Kings XIV, 20: “the whole people.”]; and the Apostle himself: “All seek their own interests” (Phil. II, 21); likewise: “All abandoned me” (II Tim. IV, 16); and in the Psalm: “All have turned aside” (Ps. XIII, 3); likewise: “Every human being is a liar” (Col. III, 16); and: “Teaching every human being” (Ps. CXV, 2). In these testimonies, a part is understood: “all” means all those about whom he is speaking.

[Col. 0551D] Just as the head has members subject to it, some healthy and others sick, so Christ, who is the head, has both evil and good people in the Church. The saints are subject to him willingly, but the evil are subject to him by necessity. In this passage “the Church” should be understood to include not only human beings but also angels and all rational creatures. This statement—“who is filled with all things in all things”—must not be understood exactly as it sounds. For he does not say “fills,” but “is filled.” One verb belongs to the agent, the other to the recipient. Just as an emperor is filled when peoples submit to him, so Christ, when human beings believe in him, is himself filled in all things—yet in such a way that he may be fulfilled as all things in all: that is, so that those who believe in him may be full of every virtue, and may make him advance in age, wisdom, and grace before God and human beings (Luke II, 52).

Alternatively: “Who is now present in parts among individuals”: in one there is justice, in another chastity, in another wisdom [Note: [Col. 0551D] The words “in another … wisdom” are found in the side margin.], because it is difficult for anyone to possess all these things. But at the end, when all things have been subjected to him, “all things in all” will be fulfilled [Col. 0552B] so that, just as God is full of every virtue, “all things in all” may be filled [Note: [Col. 0551D] These words, “so that … in all,” are also found in the margin.], and all things may be in all.

[Note: [Col. 0552D] In the author’s manuscript margin, chapter III is written here.] (CHAPTER II.) Then follows: “And you, when you were,” etc. The order is: “You, when you were dead through your trespasses and sins, God made alive together with Christ in his mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us. And when we were dead through trespasses, in which at one time,” etc., up to “made alive together with Christ.” The causal conjunction *autem*, “but,” was either added by the unlearned or by the Apostle, who was unskilled in speech [Note: [Col. 0552D] But not in knowledge, as the blessed Jerome says, whose interpretation this is.]. Concerning the fact that Scripture understands death in two ways. Here he speaks of the death of the soul, which comes through trespasses—that is, through pleasures—for sins are spoken of as works. Beautifully he says “you walked,” not “you walk.”

[Col. 0552C] “According to the age of the world”: that is, according to worldly people. Or certainly, “the age” is the evil spirit who works in unbelievers; for he cannot work in those who are believers. They are called “sons of disbelief,” just as “sons of Gehenna” and “sons of wrath.”

Then follows: “In which”: that is, not only you Gentiles, but also we Jews, lived in the desires of the flesh—not merely desiring, but doing whatever evil thought had suggested.

“And we were by nature children of wrath”: that is, by a nature corrupted through vice, not one created upright. Since human beings were under this wrath through original sin, and all the more gravely and harmfully insofar as they added greater or more numerous sins besides, a mediator was necessary—that is, a reconciler—who would appease this wrath by a unique sacrifice, of which those sacrifices were types. Concerning the wrath of God [Note: [Col. 0552D] That is, the passage should be understood as referring to the wrath of God. See the note below on chapter III of this Epistle, no. 1037.].

[Note: [Col. 0552D] In the author’s manuscript margin, chapter IV is written here.] Then follows: “But God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0552D] The words “who … us” are found in the side margin of the manuscript.] He is rich not only in power but also in mercy, as in: “You have mercy on all” [Col. 0553A] (Wis. XI, 24), etc. Concerning the fact that his love was great in handing over his Son for the redemption of a servant.

Then follows: “And when we were dead.” Dead not only through original sin but also through actual sin: he made us alive together with Christ through baptism. Let us not despair concerning ourselves because what happened in the head has happened. Let us consider that in the head, not yet in ourselves, it has already happened in certain hope.

Then follows: “That he might show in the ages to come the abundant riches of his grace,” etc. The greatness of the benefit by which he rescued us from many dangers is shown especially by this: in future ages he will show his glory over us not to one rational creature but to all rational creatures. The other statement, “that he might show in the ages,” refers to the understanding that we were saved not by our own merit but by his grace. And greater love is shown by dying for sinners than for the righteous.

[Note: [Col. 0553C] In the author’s manuscript margin, chapter V is written here. There also appears: “Vercellinus the deacon, with several words that cannot be read because they have been partly cut away from the bottom margin and partly obliterated by the passage of time.” Yet several words later one can read: “from his hand.”]

Then follows: “By grace you have been saved,” etc.; that is, he will show the riches of his goodness in the ages yet to come because you have been saved by grace. And when he said: “Through faith—not from yourselves, but it is God’s gift,” the faith itself is meant. Concerning the faith of Cornelius [Note: [Col. 0553D] Our author is referring to the faith of Cornelius, who accepted the angel’s vision and summoned Peter: Acts X, 1, 2 and following. As we shall note shortly below, he introduces this example merely to preserve it in memory, in case he should have occasion to explain these Epistles to himself or to others.]. And he rightly adds: “Not from works,” lest some hidden thought creep in: if we were not saved through works, then certainly we were saved through our faith, and in another respect our salvation is ours. Faith is not from us, so that we may glory not in ourselves but in God. He shows this even more clearly when he says: “For we are his workmanship.” We become truly free for good when God fashions, forms, and creates us—not as human beings, which he has already done, but so that we may be good, according to what is said: “Create a clean heart in me, O God” (Ps. L, 11). This occurs “in Christ,” that is, in baptism, and “in good works”; or, the works foreknown but now assigned to the saints [Note: [Col. 0553D] Something is lacking here for a complete sense, or the passage must be emended. Perhaps after “foreknown” one should read “he commemorates,” “he understands,” or some similar verb. For through these “foreknown works” he seems to have wished to interpret what the Apostle says in this verse: “in good works, which God prepared beforehand so that we should walk in them.”]. Therefore, let us walk in them confidently.

[Note: [Col. 0553D] In the author’s manuscript margin, chapter VI is written here.] Then follows: “Therefore remember.” He recalls from how great an ignobility they had been led to nobility, so that they would not be ungrateful for God’s benefits. He adds: “That formerly you Gentiles,” that is, you thought carnally and therefore lived carnally. And note that he says “in the flesh,” not “in the spirit,” concerning the Gentiles. Concerning the fourfold division of circumcision [Note: [Col. 0553D] Concerning this fourfold division between Jews and Gentiles, the blessed Jerome writes as follows in his treatment of this Epistle and of this verse: “Jews and Gentiles are therefore divided into four groups. Some are circumcised in the flesh and in the spirit, such as Moses and Aaron, the apostles, and Nathanael, whose hidden Judaism the Lord perceived when he said (John I, 47): ‘Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.’ Others are circumcised neither in flesh nor in spirit, such as Nebuchadnezzar and Pharaoh, and today the multitude of barbarian and Roman peoples who do not believe in God. A third group is circumcised only in the flesh and has an uncircumcised spirit; to them the prophet says (Jer. IV, 4): ‘Be circumcised for your God, and do not circumcise the flesh of your foreskin’; and elsewhere (Jer. IX, 26): ‘All the nations are uncircumcised in flesh, but the house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart.’ The last group is the one of which it is now said: ‘You Gentiles formerly in the flesh, who were called the foreskin by that which is called circumcision in the flesh made by hands’; such is now the whole multitude of believers, and the entire world from the Gentiles is full of them.”]. Who are called “the foreskin.” From what source? From that which is called circumcision made by hands. This does not mean that circumcision is true unless it is spiritual; but it pleased them to call the stripping away of the flesh by this name. By comparison with circumcision made by hands, another circumcision is called “not made by hands,” that is, spiritual.

Note that he says: “Having no hope,” that is, the hope which the Jews had; and “without God”: for although they had various gods, they were without the true God. He says “in the world” because, in God’s foreknowledge, they were not without God, but they were without God in the world.

[Note: [Col. 0554D] In the author’s manuscript margin, chapter VII is written here.] Then follows: “You who formerly,” etc. Since God is everywhere and wholly everywhere—everywhere, as in: “Am I a God nearby and not a God far away?” (Jer. XXIII, 23); and again: “If I ascend into heaven” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 8), etc.—how are the Gentiles said to be far from God? Clearly in the sense of: “Salvation is far from sinners” (Ps. CXVIII, 155). Therefore it is near to the righteous. Note that no one approaches God without the Lord’s blood. Note also that he is our peace just as he is our justice or truth. Just as justice justifies us, so peace makes us peaceful, as in: “I leave you peace” (John XIV, 27), etc., so that we may say: “With those who hate peace” (Ps. CXIX, 7), etc. If Christ is the peace of the elect, those who are without peace consequently do not have Christ.

But concerning what he said above, “alienated from the commonwealth of Israel,” we should know that he said this because the true commonwealth exists when we think according to the Spirit, live according to the Spirit, and are circumcised in Christ from carnal desires (Jer. IV, 4). He also called them “strangers to the covenants,” because even if some from the Gentiles had believed, they were called proselytes—that is, foreigners—among the Jews.

Concerning the fact that Augustine says that Christ is designated under the name “peace,” because he cannot be divided, torn apart, or in any way doubled. Now, whoever makes both one is all the more one with the Father and the Holy Spirit; and since he is not divided, he is therefore one with the Father and the Holy Spirit. This word is written with three letters [Note: [Col. 0554D] Namely, *pax*, “peace.”], and it does not admit a plural number. Consider, therefore, that the Father is represented by *p*, the Son is designated by alpha, because just as alpha is the first element, so Christ is called the beginning; for when he was questioned, he says that he is the beginning (John VIII, 25). This syllable is long and first. Its length signifies Christ’s eternity, not temporality; that it is a syllable signifies that the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son, and that they are one; and that it is first signifies that the Son is not second, as in: “I am alpha and omega, the first and the last” (Rev. I, 8). He is “last” because he wished to be born and to die. The Greek letter χ (*chi*), however, is the third letter from the end; it signifies the Holy Spirit, who does not tend toward an end [Note: [Col. 0555D] In the manuscript, *fidem* is written; I have corrected it as an error.] but always excels in heavenly majesty. Therefore the Apostle says: “Think on the things that are above” (Col. III, 2). For this reason we are admonished to keep our hearts raised upward every day. I have no doubt that the Apostle, dwelling in the glory of this supreme excellence, would speak in this way: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue,” according to my intention, “toward the prize of the heavenly calling of God” [Note: [Col. 0555D] Phil. III, 13. The Vulgate reads: “But one thing I do: forgetting indeed the things behind and stretching myself toward the things before, I pursue toward the designated goal, toward the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus” (v. 14).].

Therefore, in order that peace may be formed, the vowel *a* is joined to *p*, so that *p* may not remain mute, because the Father is always joined to his voice and Word. But in order that it may be *pax*, *x* is added; this letter is written as a double letter in place of two consonants because it is shared by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. These letters differ from one another in their names and persons. Why? Because one is called *p*, another *a*, and the third *x*. *P* is a letter substantially; likewise *a* is a letter substantially, and *x* is a letter substantially. So the Father is naturally God, etc. Just as “peace” is written with three letters, so God is Trinity; and just as “peace” has a singular number, so God possesses the singular number of divinity. In this joining of the letters, [Col. 0555C] the division of the three is not admitted, so that peace may be complete. For if you remove even one, there will be neither Trinity nor peace.

Then follows: “Who made both one,” that is, Jews and Gentiles, as in: “And I have other sheep” (John X, 16), etc.

Then follows: “And the middle wall,” etc. The middle wall, and the barrier dividing the two peoples, were the burdens of the Law, which deterred the Gentiles from being joined to the Israelites. The wall itself—that is, the letter of the Law—is here called “enmity,” because he annulled the Law of commandments in decrees, that is, circumcision and similar practices, which were demanded not so much by God’s will as by the people’s stubbornness. The Lord removed these enmities by annulling the letter of the Law. For the Lord of the Sabbath removed the bodily observance of the Sabbath.

[Col. 0555D] “That he might create the two,” that is, receive the two peoples into his faith as one new human being. These are the two walls coming from opposite directions to the cornerstone, so that they might be one in faith and in name—that is, Christians. An angel brought one wall—that is, the shepherds (Luke II, 9)—to Christ, and a star brought the other—that is, the magi (Matt. II, 1). The latter came from far away, the former from nearby [Col. 0556A]. And beautifully he adds: “By the cross, killing the enmities in himself.” By the cross Christ killed the enmities—that is, everything hostile to the soul. And where? “In himself,” that is, in his flesh: through the flesh he conquered flesh and the carnal observances of the Law. “And he came and announced,” [Note: [Col. 0555D] The Vulgate reads: “and coming he evangelized.”] etc. This was because the Gentiles were far away, worshiping idols, whereas the Jews were near because of their knowledge of the Law.

Then follows: “For through him,” etc. “Both” [Note: [Col. 0556D] The Vulgate reads *ambo*, “both”; the blessed Jerome, in his treatment of this Epistle, reads *uterque*, “each.”], that is, Jews and Gentiles, have access through him—that is, through Christ—in one Spirit, that is, through the love of the Holy Spirit, in whom we cry: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Rom. VIII, 15).

[Note: [Col. 0556D] In the author’s manuscript margin, chapter VIII is written here.] Then follows: “You are no longer strangers,” etc., that is, outsiders, foreigners, and proselytes. For the Lord did not separate you from his people, as Isaiah says: “Let not the son of the foreigner say, ‘The Lord will surely separate me from his people’” (Isa. LVI, 3). Concerning the fact that he now responds to what he had said above, “strangers to the covenants”: “You are no longer strangers,” etc. And to what he had previously said, “alienated from the commonwealth of Israel,” he now returns: “But you are fellow citizens of the saints,” etc. They are called citizens because they come together in one heavenly city. Since the Lord is ruler and prince in that same city, they are therefore “members of God’s household,” because the saints are those who have seen God in some way: either in mind, as Abraham did, or in mind and body, as the apostles did. Those who believe without either of these are not fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household.

[Col. 0556C] Then follows: “Built upon,” etc. By these words he openly shows that some are saints and others citizens. For he says that these people have been built upon the foundation of the apostles—that is, so that they may observe Christ’s commands. These commands are the apostles’ foundations, and upon these foundations there is a superstructure formed from life, conduct, and discipline. Concerning the fact that the first foundation is to believe in Christ and to have hope in him. Hence follows: “With Christ himself as the chief cornerstone,” etc. Christ is the foundation. He is called the cornerstone because he receives two peoples into his faith. He is called both foundation and chief because the Church is founded and perfected in him. In him, he says, the whole building grows.

Concerning the fact that unholy stones cannot be placed in the holy temple, by comparison with Solomon’s temple: if a joined building grows into a holy temple, let us strive to be living stones rolling upon the earth [Note: [Col. 0556D] That is, like the stones of which Zechariah says IX, 16: “Holy stones are raised above the earth.” Nevertheless, the blessed Jerome, who cites this text from Zechariah in his treatment of this verse of the Epistle, reads *volvuntur*, “roll,” just as our author does, instead of *elevantur*, “are raised.”]. For when we have become living and polished, we shall be built into a holy temple, and within us there will be an ark, cherubim, the mercy seat, and all the heavenly mysteries.

[Col. 0557A] Then follows: “In whom you also,” etc. He brings this exhortation to the Ephesians with great moderation, urging them to supply what they lacked and, once corrected, to become God’s complete temple.
