Here he destroys the error of those who assert different natures, since the Apostle instructs those whom he had said were without God to become God’s temple. There are also those who understand by the constructed building not human beings alone but angels as well, because the Church of the good angels and of the holy souls is one.

[Note: [Col. 0557C] In the author’s manuscript margin, chapter IX is written here.] (CHAPTER III.) Then follows: “For this reason,” etc.; that is, because of the matter I mentioned above: that the Son of God saved the Gentiles and the Jews and made them one, not because of their merits but by his grace. Concerning the fact that he calls himself a prisoner: either because of chains, or because of Christ’s love, or because of the burden of the body; for he was held here by his love for the Gentiles, while he desired to depart and be with Christ (Phil. I, 33). By saying that he is a prisoner, he confirms Christ’s Gospel, showing how great his hope is, since he endures such things even though he could have been honored among the Jews and enjoyed the dignity of a teacher.

What does “if indeed,” etc., mean, up to [Note: [Col. 0557C] The phrase *etc.* may be missing, either to the end or something similar, so that it should perhaps be read: “up to the end, up to,” etc., or in some comparable manner.], unless you hold firmly within yourselves, according to the divine dispensation and not according to human doctrine, that I say that Jews and Gentiles are one in Christ? We can find no other answer. For he did not say: “For this reason I did this or that, I taught this or that,” but, leaving the reasoning suspended, he passed on to other matters. Unless, perhaps, we excuse him on the ground that he himself confessed, saying: “And if I am unskilled in speech” [Col. 0557C] (II Cor. XI, 6), etc., and seek in him an order of ideas rather than of words. The passage can be rendered as follows: “For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and a prisoner for you who are from the Gentiles, came to know the mystery, so that I might also hand it on to you, just as I spoke a little earlier in this same Epistle. You ought, however, to hear of the dispensation of God’s grace that was given to me for you who are Gentiles, for whom I am also a prisoner.” He could have said: “For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles, came to know the mystery, as I said briefly,” etc.

Concerning the fact that whoever attends to the preceding parts of this Epistle will see that the mysteries revealed there have been mentioned only in part. I did not say as much as I could, but as much as they could grasp. For no Epistle contains such deeply hidden meanings as this one, meanings which the Apostle boasts of knowing and shows us briefly indicated, so that we may seek more attentively [Col. 0558B] what has been written.

Then follows: “Which in other generations was not made known,” etc. Did Abraham, Jacob, Moses, David, Isaiah, and the other prophets not know this? Concerning examples of these men [Note: [Col. 0557C]

From this incomplete clause, which produces an unfinished sense, we shall take the occasion to discuss the incomplete expressions and interrupted propositions that occur frequently throughout this Epistle, and indeed the adverbial phrase “concerning the fact that it can be found,” which never or only very rarely occurs in the other earlier Epistles. Apparently, for the sake of brevity, our Atto wished to compose a summary of the exposition rather than an exposition in full, intending that preachers, or others who wished to meditate on or explain the Epistles of the blessed Paul for themselves or for others, should find in condensed form the points that the holy Fathers had written at greater length. Thus, whenever he says—and often excessively—“concerning the fact that,” one should understand: “see the blessed Jerome, Augustine, or others”; or also: “understand,” “note,” “speak,” or something similar.

The examples that follow, cited from the blessed Jerome, will provide evidence for this assertion; our author alludes to them in the incomplete clause “concerning examples of these men.” For the blessed Jerome writes at this point as follows:

“Whether Abraham, Jacob, Moses, Isaiah, and the other prophets did or did not know this is a question. Scripture records that the coming of Christ and the calling of the Gentiles were foretold by them. Abraham indeed saw his day and rejoiced, and it was said to him (John VIII, 56; Gen. XXII, 18): ‘All nations shall be blessed in your seed.’ Jacob too speaks prophetically of him who would arise from Judah (Gen. XLIX, 10): ‘And he himself shall be the expectation of the nations.’ Moses likewise considered the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt (Exod. XI, [the citation is corrupt]); Isaiah says: ‘Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son’ (Isa. VII, 14); and elsewhere: ‘There shall be a shoot of Jesse, and he who shall arise to rule the nations; in him the Gentiles shall hope’ (Isa. XI, 10). And, lest this become lengthy, it is enough to mention a few things from the Psalms (Ps. XXI, 28): ‘All the families of the nations shall worship in his presence’; and again (Ps. XVII, 11): ‘All nations shall serve him.’ And still more clearly concerning the people of Israel and the Lord the Savior (Ps. LXX, 15–16): ‘Visit this vine and perfect it, which your right hand planted, and upon the son whom you strengthened for yourself.’ The dispensation of his body is also indicated in what follows (ibid., 18): ‘Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the son of man whom you strengthened for yourself.’”

Of whether, according to Montanus, we should say that the prophets were ignorant of what they said, or whether we should examine why the Apostle said this: note that he did not say that it was hidden from all the sons of men—that is, not from those who are gods, but from the carnal.

[Note: [Col. 0558D] Here is another instance drawn from the imperfect discussions noted above. Namely, in the passage which he sends to Saint Jerome at the cited place, where he says: “Either, according to Montanus, we must understand that the patriarchs and prophets spoke in ecstasy and did not know what they said; or, if this is impious—for the spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets—they certainly understood what they spoke. And if they understood, the question arises how Paul can now say that what had not been known to other generations was revealed to Christ’s apostles. Either, then, this must be answered: that Paul carefully and expressly testified that the mystery was unknown to the sons of men, not to the sons of God, to whom he speaks: ‘I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’ (Psalm 81:6); namely, that those who received the spirit of adoption, among whom the patriarchs and prophets belonged, knew the mystery of God.”]

And if this interpretation seems forced to anyone, it must be said that he did not assert definitively and generally that it was unknown, but unknown in the way in which it has now been revealed to the Apostles. For it is one thing to know beforehand in the spirit what is to come, and another to see what has been completed. Hence John is called “more than a prophet” (Luke 7:26). [Col. 0558C] And the Savior says: “Many prophets [Note: [Col. 0558D] Luke 10:24: “many prophets and kings”—Saint Jerome, in his commentary on this Epistle, reads “the righteous” in place of “kings”] wished to see what you see, and did not see it; and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it,” etc.

What is this mystery? Certainly, that the Gentiles are fellow-heirs and fellow-members of the same body.

Concerning the fact that the Gentiles are fellow-heirs with Israel, or rather with Christ—who is called our inheritance—and are fellow-heirs of Christ (Deuteronomy 18:2; Psalm 15:5), as in the passage: “Heirs indeed of God” (Romans 8:17), etc.

Concerning examples of inheritance.

[Note: [Col. 0559C] Namely, see Saint Jerome on this Epistle concerning the passages cited above, namely Deuteronomy 18, Psalm 15, and Romans 8.]

Likewise, concerning the example of the members, in relation to what he says: “fellow-members.”

[Note: [Col. 0559D] Thus Saint Jerome: “‘Fellow-members’ signifies that, just as in one body there are many members—for example, eyes, hands, ears, feet, the belly, and knees—and although they are in one body they have their own distinctions and rejoice and grieve for one another, so, although those who believe in Christ have different gifts, they are nevertheless gathered together in the one body of the Church. In the preceding two words, namely, when he says ‘fellow-heirs and fellow-members,’ one might suspect that something different was intended in one body. But when he adds, ‘and fellow-partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus,’ every distinction is entirely removed. For where there is one common participation, everything is shared.”]

Concerning the fact that, in the two expressions, something different could be suspected in one body: in what follows, “and fellow-partakers,” every distinction is removed. Where there is common participation, everything is shared.

Concerning the fact that, by saying “through the Gospel,” etc., he excludes pride: for by saying this he attributes it not to himself but to the grace of God. A disciple of humility could not pride himself on knowledge when he recalls that he was a persecutor of Christ and a ravager of the Church. For there are those who reproach him because he said that what the prophets had not known was revealed to him.

Next: “To me, the least of all,” etc. And rightly was this grace given to one who had been humbled, since “everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Matthew 23:12; Luke 14:11).

Concerning the fact that, if they are “unsearchable,” how are they proclaimed, and how is what was hidden brought forth? This is resolved in two ways: either because, before Christ’s coming, they were unsearchable and hidden, but after the Lord’s coming they were revealed; or because things which by their nature were unsearchable to human beings became known when God revealed them. For it is one thing to reach a secret by one’s own ingenuity—something which, once discovered, ceases to be unsearchable—and another to know, through God’s revelation, what cannot be discovered by itself. When you have learned it and told it to others, it nevertheless remains unsearchable, just as it was for you until you came to know it. Hence the Psalmist says: “How great is the multitude of your sweetness” (Psalm 30:20), etc.

It may also be understood in this way: that the ages themselves were ignorant of it—that is, rational and spiritual human beings in the world.

Concerning examples from “the age.”

[Note: [Col. 0560C] Saint Jerome, in his commentary on this Epistle: “For ‘the age’ is frequently understood of those things which are occupied in the world, as Paul speaks to the Galatians, saying: ‘That he might deliver us from the present evil age’ (Galatians 1:4). And elsewhere: ‘That he might show in the ages to come’ (Ephesians 2:7), in place of ‘those things which were to come in the succeeding ages.’” [Col. 0560D]]

Next: “So that it might now be made known.”

[Note: [Col. 0560D] The Vulgate has: “so that it may be made known.” Saint Jerome, however, in his commentary on this Epistle, has: “so that it might be made known.”]

According to the gift of God’s grace, which was given to the Apostle so that he might proclaim the unsearchable riches of Christ. For this reason the mystery itself was revealed to him, so that through the Church the manifold wisdom of God might be made known not only to the Gentiles but also to the principalities and powers. This wisdom, formerly destined according to the purpose of the ancient ages, now appears to have been brought to completion in Christ.

The manifold wisdom of God has also now been revealed through the Church to the principalities and powers. God had formerly determined in his mind that it would exist, and from what we see we recognize that it has now been perfected.

Concerning the fact that the cross opened to us, and also to the angels, a mystery which they did not know; hence, when he returned with his body to heaven, they say: “Who is this who comes from Edom?” (Isaiah 63:1), etc.

Concerning the fact that this wisdom is manifold and distinguished by great variety.

[Note: [Col. 0560D] See Saint Jerome, from whom this explanation was excerpted and reduced to a summary.]

Look at Christ’s cradle; look also at heaven. See him crying in the manger; hear the angels praising him (Luke 2:13–14). Herod persecutes him (Matthew 2:3); the magus worships him, while the Pharisees are ignorant of the one whom the star reveals (Matthew 2:3). He is baptized by a servant, but praised by the Father. He is plunged into the waters, but the dove descends—or rather, the Spirit in the form of a dove. He comes to his passion and fears to suffer; he wishes the cup to pass from him (Matthew 26:39), and rebukes Peter because he fears the cup. What is wiser than this foolishness, more distinguished by variety, or more obscure than the wisdom which he manifested in Christ Jesus our Lord?

There are those who understand this joining of the words as referring to the Church as having been made.

[Note: [Col. 0560D] Saint Jerome, in his commentary on this Epistle: “Although many may understand, according to the order and connection of the words, that the Church was made, and also the πρόθεσις—that is, the proposition, which in Latin we have expressed in its natural gender as propositum—nevertheless, ‘wisdom made in Christ’ may resound more appropriately than the rest. For ‘the foolishness of God is wiser than men’ (1 Corinthians 1:25). See the discussion against the Arians.”]

Next: “In whom we have boldness,” etc. There is nothing from which we can derive greater confidence than from a pure conscience, as in the passage: “If our heart does not condemn us” (1 John 3:21), etc. It is a great thing to have boldness; but to have confidence in that boldness makes our approach more secure, so that, when we approach, we may receive something of his majesty, as from a ray of the sun we receive heat and brightness.

Concerning the fact that one who possesses wisdom should understand wisdom in Christ: the same may likewise be understood of righteousness, truth, peace, and chastity.

[Note: [Col. 0560D] See Saint Jerome at this place.]

[Note: [Col. 0560D] In the autograph margin this is marked “chapter X.”]

Next: “For this reason I ask,” etc.

Concerning the fact that one may read either “that I may not fail” or “that you may not fail,” because of the ambiguity of the Greek expression. But if you read “that I may not fail,” the sense will be: I see the world coming to faith through my preaching and the temples of idols being filled with filth, and for this reason the snares of the devil have been aroused against me, so that, wearied by temptations, I may cease preaching.

[Note: [Col. 0561C] The verb “I may cease” is lacking. Relying on Saint Jerome’s authority, I have ventured to add it.]

Therefore I ask earnestly that I may not succumb—and this for your sake, because what I suffer and what afflicts me happens for the sake of your salvation. These tribulations are your glory, since in Judaism I could have been glorious; I would by no means endure such things unless I were certain of the reward.

But if you read “that you may not fail,” the sense will be: I ask that you not fail amid my tribulations—that is, that you not suffer a scandal to your faith because of my tribulations. He fears wounds of the mind in his disciples more than wounds of the flesh in himself. Hence he says to the Galatians: “You did not despise your trial in my flesh” (Galatians 4:14). Surely they are moved by this? Hence the Psalmist says: “But my feet had almost slipped” (Psalm 72:2), etc., up to: “Therefore in vain have I justified” myself. For he himself makes clear that he suffered many things for the Ephesians when he says: “If, after the manner of men, I fought with beasts” (1 Corinthians 15:32), etc. Likewise: “I do not want you to be ignorant of our tribulation which occurred in Asia” [Note: [Col. 0561D] The words “Likewise … Asia” are written in the bottom margin.], etc.

He asks perfectly that the Ephesians not fail amid the tribulations which he endured for them, because he preached the Gospel to them. These pressures were punishments among unbelievers, but glory and victory among believers, because the one who does not yield to his adversaries conquers.

Next: “For this reason I bow,” etc. Just as the eyes are members, so are the knees of the inner person, as in the passage: “Strengthen the weak hands and make firm the feeble knees” (Isaiah 35:3), and: “At the name of Jesus every knee” (Philippians 2:10), etc. This does not mean that angels or souls possess bodily knees; rather, by kneeling, the submission of the mind is understood.

Concerning the fact that one who serves God bends the knee to God, while one who serves lust, avarice, and anger bends the knee to the devil, as in the passage: “I have left for myself seven thousand men” (1 Kings 19:18), etc.

But these statements do not abolish bodily kneeling, since the Apostle also prayed on the shore with his knees bent (Acts 21:5); and the Church is instructed to bend the knee.

[Note: [Col. 0561D] In the Old Testament we frequently read that prayer and worship were performed in this way: Mordecai refused to do so before Haman (Esther 3:2), whereas Daniel did so before the true God, bending his knees three times a day (Daniel 6:10). In the New Testament we read several times that this worship was performed before Jesus Christ, and finally by the Son of God himself before the Father (Luke 22:41), where it says: “And kneeling down, he prayed.” There he handed down that divine pattern of prayer in these words: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me; nevertheless, not my will but yours be done.”]

Concerning the four qualities of kneeling.

[Note: [Col. 0561D] I would rather think that “of the four” should be read, if our author intended, as is customary, to refer the reader to Saint Jerome; otherwise, I confess that I entirely fail to understand his meaning. Saint Jerome, in fact, brings forward four examples of kneeling which is done to the devil through sin: through lust, anger, avarice, and gluttony.]

Concerning the fact that some copies have only “to the Father,” so that he is the Father not only of Christ but of all rational creatures: note that he does not say, “Every fatherhood was born or created,” but “is named,” since it is one thing to deserve the name of fatherhood and another to share in nature.

Note that just as the name of essence is attributed to human beings, as in: “He who is sent me” (Exodus 3:14), or the name of goodness, as in: “No one is good except God alone” (Luke 18:19), so that they are said to exist and to be good, so also the name of fatherhood, as in: “who was the son of Seth, who was the son of Adam, who was the son of God.”

[Note: [Col. 0562D] Luke 3:38. For an understanding of this exposition, consult Saint Jerome on this Epistle. He says that just as God imparts the name of his essence and substance even to the other elements, so that they too are said to exist—not because they exist according to nature, for there was a time when none of them existed, and again, if he wills, they will return to nothing, but because in his goodness he has granted that they be called existent—so he has bestowed the name of fatherhood from himself. Understand the same concerning fatherhood and essence with regard to goodness, which belongs by nature to God alone but may be attributed to the other creatures by participation.]

But how “in heaven”? Just as we call Abraham and the prophets our fathers, so the angels rejoice in calling the archangels fathers. For the virtues, dominions, and powers would not be called such unless they had others subject to them.

Next: “That he may grant you according to the riches,” etc. It is as if he says: For this reason I bend my knees, so that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, power—that is, participation in his majesty—and strengthen you through his Spirit, but in the inner person, since it frequently benefits us for the outer person to be afflicted. And may you have Christ dwelling in your hearts, and this through faith; but let faith be made firm by love—that is, being rooted and grounded—as in the passage: “You are God’s cultivation, God’s building” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

For then, as you begin to comprehend with all the saints, etc. And when these things have been fulfilled, then you will be filled with all the fullness of God.

[Note: [Col. 0562D] The Vulgate has “into all the fullness.” Saint Jerome, however, agrees with our text in this Epistle, although others read according to the Vulgate.]

Perhaps the length of heaven and earth may be understood as extending from west to east and from south to north. But since, according to Ecclesiastes, heaven is said to be round (Ecclesiastes 1:6) and to revolve in the manner of a sphere, a sphere has neither breadth nor height, since it is equal on every side. What, then, should we understand by height except the angels, and by depth except the demons, and by length and breadth except those who occupy the middle? Those who progress toward better things possess length; but those who, living carnally, tend downward possess breadth, because “broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction” (Matthew 7:13).

Christ also possessed depth by descending to the lower regions; height by penetrating the heavens (Psalm 67:19); breadth and length by sending the apostles to all the nations, as in: “Into all the earth” (Romans 10:18; Psalm 18:5), etc.

Concerning the fact that these words reveal the form and mystery of the cross, about which much has already been said.

After this, let us take care to learn not merely an eminent love, but Christ’s love which surpasses knowledge. Here we must observe that Christ possesses a great and immeasurable love of knowledge—that is, love for those who desire to know him, who meditate on his law day and night (Psalm 1:2), and who turn words into deeds. Whoever is such as to be worthy, through his knowledge, of possessing Christ’s surpassing love ought to think of nothing besides knowledge. In this way he will be filled with all the fullness of God, not only in the present age but also in the future: here understanding, there enjoying more fully.

[Note: [Col. 0563D] Here the autograph margin reads “chapter XII”; chapter XI appears nowhere.]

Next: “Now to him,” etc. The order is this: Glory to him in Christ, glory in the Church, and glory throughout all generations, to him who is able to accomplish more than what we ask or think. He will accomplish it according to the power that works in us, namely, Christ’s power, according to which I also work.

Alternatively, this may all be referred to God. Since the Apostle knows that we do not know how to pray as we ought, and knows that God grants more than is asked and more than we can understand, he says: “Now to him,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0563D] In the manuscript, “he erred” appears in place of “now to him.” Since the former occurs nowhere in the text and yields no suitable meaning, while having considerable literal similarity to the words of the text, “now to him,” I judged that it should be corrected as an obvious error.]

He will grant according to the power that works in us—that is, just as he now surpasses our prayers and merits, giving greater things than we ask, so also may he grant the other things which the mind cannot even conceive.

[Note: [Col. 0563D] In the autograph, “which neither” is written. According to Saint Jerome, who has these very words there—“so also may he grant the other things which neither the mind can conceive”—this should be read.]

To God himself be glory in the Church, which has no stain; then in Christ, in whom all the fullness of divinity dwells. May this glory not extend only through the present age and end in the ages to come, but exist throughout all the generations of the ages.

Concerning the fact that, up to this point, he has spoken about the mystery of Christ’s incarnation and the joining together of the two peoples; from here onward he begins to set forth moral precepts.

[Note: [Col. 0564D] In the autograph margin this is marked “chapter XIII.”]

(Chapter IV.) Next: “I beseech you,” etc.

Concerning the fact that he may be understood to be bound by chains and imprisonment, or by the love of Christ, as in the passage: “The soul of David was bound to the soul of Jonathan.”

[Note: [Col. 0564D] 1 Samuel 18:1, where the wording is not “bound,” as here and in Saint Jerome’s exposition of this Epistle, but “knit together.”]

He may also be called bound by the frailty of the flesh, since, although he desired to depart and be with Christ, he remained in a corruptible body for the salvation of his hearers.

Let us see with how much humility hearers ought to speak, when the teacher of the nations says: “I beseech you.” But what does he beseech?

[Col. 0564A] Next: “That you walk worthily,” etc.

Concerning the fact that one walks worthily who enters by means of the one who says: “I am the way” (John 14:6; Isaiah 30:21; Proverbs 4:27; Psalm 36:23), etc.; who does not turn to the right or to the left; who turns his foot away from every evil way (Psalm 118:101); and in whom it is fulfilled that “the steps of a man are directed by the Lord” (Psalm 16:5).

And appropriately he adds: “With all,” not “with some,” humility. For one who considers himself earth and ashes will never be lifted up by pride; and one who, having contemplated God’s eternity, considers the brevity of this life will always have everlasting destruction before his eyes and will be humble and cast down.

Gentleness is that which is disturbed by no passion, and to it the possession of the earth is promised (Psalm 36:11). These people also bear with one another in love. Philosophers bear with one another, but not in love.

Concerning the fact that the perfected do not need this precept.

[Note: [Col. 0564D] Saint Jerome, from whom this interpretation is taken, has “the holy” in place of “the perfected.”]

For they have nothing that requires bearing. But among so great a multitude there were some who had to be borne with. The meaning of this passage was given above, where he says: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2); and we showed that this should be understood both of bodily and of spiritual infirmities (Romans 15:1).

“Being careful to preserve,” etc.

Concerning the fact that the person who possesses something is charged with carefully preserving it, while the person who does not possess it is given the command to acquire it. For this reason he says these things to the Ephesians, because they had already received the gift of the Holy Spirit.

This passage is directed against heretics who, having shattered the bond of peace, claim that they preserve the unity of the Spirit. But how can there be many gifts (Romans 12:3; 1 Corinthians 12:4; Ephesians 4:7) if the Spirit is one? The gifts of the Spirit are various, but the Lord is the same.

We are one body—that is, either the Church or the body taken from the virgin, lest you believe that he was incarnated as many times as he is said to have appeared in the Old Testament. Alternatively, “one body” refers to works, while “one Spirit” refers to the contemplation of knowledge.

It is asked how there can be one hope of calling if there are many dwelling places in the Father’s house (John 14:2). But there is one hope of one house and one kingdom, in which there may be a variety of merits. Alternatively, the one hope of calling is the resurrection and the transformation that is to come.

Concerning the fact that there are some who, in this passage, do not understand the Holy Spirit but an affection of the mind designated by the name “spirit,” as in the passage: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32); and concerning the widow: “So that she may be holy in body and spirit” (1 Corinthians 7:34).

He preserves the unity of the spirit who is not carried about by every wind of doctrine (Ephesians 4:14) and is not changed like the moon (Sirach 27:12), serving now God and now the devil. But he has one body of good works.

[Note: [Col. 0564D] According to Saint Jerome, “of works” should be added.]

And he presents his own flesh as a temple to God, and has one spirit, thinking the same things, in one hope of calling, never doubting the promises.

[Note: [Col. 0565C] In the autograph margin this is marked “chapter XIV.”]

Next: “One Lord,” etc.

Concerning the fact that heretics think that the Son should be called Lord, not the Father, and likewise that the Father is God, not the Son. But far be it from us to believe that dominion exists without divinity or divinity without dominion.

“One faith” is said because we believe equally in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and “one baptism” because we are baptized not in names but in the name of the Trinity.

[Note: [Col. 0565C] Saint Jerome’s commentary on this Epistle gives greater clarity to this exposition: “‘And one baptism’; for we are baptized in the same way into the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. We are immersed three times, so that the one mystery of the Trinity may be manifested. And we are not baptized in the names of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, but in one name, which is understood to be God. And I wonder by what logic Arius, Macedonius, and Eunomius, united in impiety though divided in discord, suspect a diversity of nature in one word, one work, and one sacrament, and, holding a muddy font belonging to the creature in the Son and the Holy Spirit, have drawn out different streams of heresy. ‘One baptism’ is also directed against Valentinus, who maintains that there are two baptisms, and against all heretics, so that they may know that they do not possess baptisms, but that in the one Church of Christ there is one living fountain. ‘One baptism’ may also be said in this way: although we are baptized three times because of the mystery of the Trinity, nevertheless it is reckoned as one baptism. There is also one baptism in water, in the Spirit, and in fire. And concerning this the Lord speaks: ‘I have a baptism with which I must be baptized’ (Luke 12:50); and elsewhere: ‘With the baptism with which I am baptized you shall be baptized’ (Mark 10:39).”]

This passage is directed against Arius, who says that there is not one sacrament but that the nature of the Trinity is unequal. It overthrows Valentinus, who says that there are two baptisms.

Concerning the fact that the various prepositions—“above,” “through,” and “in”—create distinctions of meaning, so that the Father is said to be “above all.”

[Note: [Col. 0565D] The Vulgate has “above all people.”]

For he is the source of all; the Son is “through all,” because all things were made through him and he runs through all things.

[Note: [Col. 0565D] John 1:3. Saint Jerome explains this distinction concerning the Son as follows: “through all: the Son, because he passes through everything and goes through all things.”]

The Holy Spirit is “in all,” because he is given to believers, without whom nothing is done.

When it is said “God and Father,” he is not therefore called God and Father of all in the same way, since he is the Father of rational beings, while he is God of all. For example, if one man has ten men, five sons and five servants, and you say, “Of all these one is Lord and Father,” he would be Father to the five sons and Lord to the five servants—that is, Father to some and Lord to others.

[Note: [Col. 0566C] Saint Jerome has “men.”]

[Note: [Col. 0566C] In the autograph margin this is marked “chapter XV.”]

Next: “But to each one,” etc.; that is, although God is above all, through all, and in all, grace is nevertheless given to believers according to their measure—not because the Spirit himself can be measured, but because each person receives from him according to his capacity.

Concerning the likeness of the sea and the diversity of vessels.

[Note: [Col. 0566C] The autograph reads “males” (masculorum). In view of Saint Jerome’s text, which we have brought forward both to clarify the meaning of this incomplete discussion and to demonstrate the need for correction, we judged it should be emended. Saint Jerome’s text is as follows: “To make this more evident, let us take an example, although it is imperfect and does not fully correspond to the comparison, but through which what is said may nevertheless be understood. The sea is certainly immense, and its capacity is known to God alone. If someone wished to distribute from it to many people according to what they could carry, it would be necessary for him to give to each according to measure, and their portions would receive a measure, although the whole is immeasurable. So too the Holy Spirit is indeed immeasurable and enclosed by no limit; nevertheless, he is given to each according to what is beneficial.”]

Note that this is called the grace of Christ’s gift. Hence it follows: “For this reason he says: Ascending on high” (Psalm 67:19).

Concerning the fact that he wished to confirm his account by an example.

For Christ, ascending on high, led captivity captive: because he freed us, who were held captive, and took the devil captive. He bestowed various gifts on those whom he freed, as in the passage: “He gave gifts to men”; or, “he received.”

[Note: [Col. 0566D] In the cited Psalm, “you received.”]

The Psalmist says “he received,” because it was still future; Paul says “he gave,” because he recounts what had already occurred. Both were true, because he gave from heaven and received on earth: he gave inasmuch as he is the head, and received inasmuch as he is the body. Hence the passage: “Saul” (Acts 9:4), etc.; likewise: “As long as you did it to one of the least of these” (Matthew 25:40), etc.

Concerning the fact that the Apostle recounts these things with the intention that, since he had said: “bearing with one another” (Ephesians 4:2), etc., up to “of peace” (Ephesians 4:3), he might teach the Church to be harmonious in diverse gifts and not divided because of the diversity of gifts; for just as there is one Lord, so the Church is one body.

Next: “But what does ‘he ascended’ mean,” etc.? That is, by the fact that he descended, he ascended. He calls “the lower parts of the earth” the underworld, to which Christ descended in soul in order to free from there the souls of the elect. Hence, when he rose, many bodies of the saints are said to have risen with him (Matthew 27:52).

When he says “to fill all things,” the following is understood: the things written in the Law and the Prophets, and other hidden dispensations which he alone knows with the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0566D] “Knows” is understood.]

For we cannot know how Christ’s blood benefited both the angels and those who were in the underworld; nevertheless, we cannot fail to know that it did benefit them. He descended and ascended so that what was empty might be filled.

At this point those who said that Christ did not exist before Mary are refuted.

[Col. 0566C] Next: “And he himself gave,” etc.

For while he here says that the Son gave what, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, he says the Father gave, he destroys the heretics.

[Note: [Col. 0566D] Namely, Ebion and Photinus.]

They said that the persons of the Father and the Son were not of one nature or one operation.

[Note: [Col. 0566D] Saint Jerome, from whom this exposition was taken, has the following: “And from this passage it is most clearly demonstrated that the Father and the Son have one divinity. For what Christ is now described as having bestowed, God the Father is related to have given in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: ‘God has appointed in the Church, first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then powers, gifts of healings, helps, governments, kinds of tongues’ (1 Corinthians 12:28). Sabellius, not understanding this, confuses the Father and the Son by refusing to believe that the operation of different persons is the same.” [Col. 0567C]]

Concerning the fact that, at the beginning of the Church, all these offices existed—that is, apostles and prophets; not those who existed before Christ’s coming, but such men as Agabus.

[Note: [Col. 0567C] One of the Seventy, according to the Greeks, and a disciple of Jesus Christ, who foretold that a famine would occur throughout the whole world (Acts 11:28). Saint Luke testifies at the cited place that it occurred during the reign of Claudius, in the fourth year of his reign and the forty-fourth year of Christ. Among pagan writers, Suetonius mentions it in Claudius, chapter 18, and Josephus in Antiquities, book XX, chapter 2.]

And now there are evangelists, whose feet are blessed (Isaiah 52:7). There are also teachers and pastors today. The teachers are themselves pastors, because the one who teaches truly feeds.

[Note: [Col. 0567C] At the bottom margin appear these words: “and … teachers.”]

In the beginning all taught or baptized; this is not now permitted, lest the mysteries of the Church become cheap.

What purpose do the different offices serve? For the building up of the body of Christ. But until when?

Next: “Until we all arrive,” etc. Whom does he mean by “all,” except believers? The sense is: these offices are necessary until the whole Church reaches the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ. This is partly fulfilled in the present life, but is completed at the end. It is fulfilled here when we are so established in faith and love that we are not carried about by every wind of doctrine. It is completed when the whole body is filled.

But why does the Apostle call himself little? Out of humility, or because he sees in part and prophesies in part? (1 Corinthians 13:9.) For in comparison with Judaism he was perfect, as in the passage: “When I was a child” (1 Corinthians 13:11), etc.; but in comparison with the understanding that is to come he was little, because he knows in part.

The person who says that he uttered this not from humility but from the awareness of his own condition says: The Apostle, sharp of intellect, fought against errors and, standing as though at the stern and holding the rudder, shattered the foaming waves of heresies through the security of faith. Yet he did not look out securely and fearlessly upon the winds blowing from every side; his victory was not secure.

[Note: [Col. 0567D] The manuscript reads “sacred.” Both common usage and Saint Jerome’s words on this passage recommend the more correct reading.]

Nevertheless, he hoped that, with God’s help, once doubt had been driven from his mind, he would firmly believe the truth and increase it in love for Christ, whom he knew to be both his own head and the head of the whole Church.

It should be known that this passage becomes clearer in Greek, because when the word is transferred word for word, the meaning becomes obscure.

[Note: [Col. 0567D] Because in Greek they are said μεταφορικῶς, “metaphorically.” Every metaphor, when transferred from one language into another, sometimes loses its meaning and almost always loses its force and elegance.]

[Col. 0568A] Next: “From whom the whole body,” etc.

Concerning the fact that, when at the end we see the Lord and arrive at the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, then his whole body—which now appears dispersed and torn apart—will be restored to its proper structure and joining.

An example is given of a human being divided into parts, with bone not joined to bone, and with a physician placing the members in their proper locations before the person is healed.

[Note: [Col. 0567D] For an understanding of this scarcely indicated and incomplete comparison, it is useful to cite Saint Jerome’s text on this passage: “Let us understand all rational creatures by the example of one rational animal; and whatever we say about its members and parts, let us know that it is to be referred to each rational creature. Let us imagine this animal so torn apart through its limbs, veins, and flesh that bone does not cling to bone and sinew is not joined to sinew; the eyes lie separately, the nostrils apart, the hands occupy one place, the feet have been thrown elsewhere, and the remaining members are dispersed and divided from one another in this way. Imagine someone coming who is a physician of such knowledge that, according to the tales of the pagans, he could imitate Asclepius and raise Virbius to a new form and a new name. He would necessarily restore each member to its proper place, join structure to structure, and, with the parts restored by a kind of glue, make one body.” [Col. 0568C]]

There is also the likeness of a child whose members are filled out and whose stature is completed without your seeing it.

[Note: [Col. 0568C] “Let the child grow and, with age progressing secretly, mature into perfect adulthood. His hands will have their own increase; his feet will feel their growth; his belly will be filled while we do not know it; his shoulders will broaden while the eyes are deceived; and all the members will grow in parts according to their measure, yet appear to increase not for themselves but for the body.” Thus Saint Jerome at that place. [Col. 0568D]]

So Christ, the almighty physician, joins feet to feet and eyes to eyes so that the body may be perfected; and all the members are joined together in him through love.

[Note: [Col. 0568D] In the autograph margin, “chapter XVI” is written here.]

It follows: “Therefore I say this,” etc. Concerning the fact that he perseveres in the intention he has begun, that is, in regard to the precepts of morality [Col. 0568B], and that he now binds by invocation of the Lord’s name those whom above he had entreated. The sense is: “I say to you, O Ephesians, and I adjure you: since you are to come to the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age, do not walk as the Gentiles walk,” that is, “in the vanity of their mind,” because they are not of the weighty people in whom God is praised. For this reason they became darkened in mind, that is, blind; for through creation they could have recognized the Creator, and because they are unwilling to do so, they are alienated from the life of God. For there is no life except in God; departing from him, they move toward nonbeing, because of the ignorance that is in them.

Note that blindness of mind produces contempt for God. Note that a person is called unlearned and blind only when he can know and see. Thus we call neither a brute animal unlearned nor a stone blind. The nature of the Gentiles, however, was capable of knowing God. But if only they had been content to sin—or had repented, even late! But what does he say? “Who, having despaired of themselves” [Note: [Col. 0568D] According to Saint Jerome, *desperantes* is less correctly translated from the Greek ἀπηλεγοῦντες ἑαυτούς: for in Greek those who despair are called ἀπηλγοῦντες, whereas ἀπηλεγοῦντες are those who, after they have sinned, do not grieve; feeling no sense at all of their ruin, they are carried headlong and, like beasts that see the sword, rush toward death—namely, without pain, or “insensible.” For one of the philosophers, Dionysius surnamed Metathemenus, also proclaimed ἀναλγησίαν, that is, insensibility.], that is, those who despair of the future life, or who believe that there are no punishments for evils [Note: [Col. 0568D] I might almost say that divination was needed to understand these words and restore them to their correct reading. For in the codex they appear written as follows: *malorum supplicationes se credunt* (“they believe the supplications of evils”). Whether I have reached the intended meaning or not, I gladly leave to the judgment of readers. I will add only this: in my judgment I have introduced nothing into the formation of these words except the letter *i* between the two letters *c* of the word *supplicia*, which is written *supplica*. The negative particle immediately following, although it might rather be referred to *tion*, and although no point appears above the letter *i* here—as scarcely anywhere else—seems capable of being read without difficulty as *tion*, since the two small letters *t i*, joined by the little stroke of the upper line that usually cuts through the letter *t*, form *ti*.], therefore they hand themselves over to impurity, doing whatever the body wishes, the flesh desires, and lust suggests. They do this in avarice, since they are never satisfied by their indulgence, nor does their pleasure have an end; for beyond the permitted union of man with woman they climb to greater excesses, males committing shameful acts with males and receiving within themselves the recompense of their error.

The Apostle demonstrates, in writing to the Thessalonians, that the whole practice of impurity belongs to “avarice,” understood not simply in its ordinary sense, as the wording seems to say, but as lust. For he says: “For this is the will of God” (I Thess. IV, 3), etc., up to: “And that no one overreach or defraud his brother in business” [Note: [Col. 0569C] I Thess. IV, 6. Saint Jerome also interprets this passage so that Saint Paul’s intention was to summon us to chastity and to warn those who have wives to be content with their own wives and not dare to abuse a brother’s wife or intrude into another’s marriage-bed. Here I am pleased to report Saint Jerome’s observation concerning this Epistle, which he also gives at its beginning: among all Paul’s Epistles, this one is especially involved both in wording and in meaning.]. For what consistency would there be, either here or there, for him to speak of impurity and then suddenly discuss avarice? [Col. 0569B]

[Note: [Col. 0569D] In the autograph margin, “chapter XVII” is written here.]

It follows: “But you,” etc. For if everyone heard or learned Christ—those who seem to hear him—he would not say, “if indeed,” etc. For one knows Christ who knows wisdom, prudence, justice, and truth. Such a person cannot walk in the vanity of his heart, nor can he be blind, because he sees the light; he does not give himself over to impurity, because he sees the lover of purity.

Let us learn Christ; that is, let us come to him who can truthfully say: “Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” [Note: [Col. 0569D] II Cor. XIII, 3: “Or do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?”], etc.; for in him we hear Christ. Indeed, through hidden inspiration he also teaches whenever he wills.

“As there is truth in Jesus.” This name sometimes signifies a human being, as in: “You shall call his name Jesus” (Luke I, 31); sometimes the Word, as in: “But for us there is one Lord Jesus, through whom are all things” (I Cor. VIII, 6). It may also be understood in this way: “As there is truth in Jesus”—truth was in none of the patriarchs, prophets, or apostles except in Jesus alone; for the others knew only in part (I Cor. XIII, 9). Truth appeared in Jesus alone, who confidently says: “I am the truth” (John XIV, 6).

Concerning the fact that this truth is understood not in the valley but on the mountain, together with the Law and prophecy, it is apparent from the fact that Moses and Elijah are seen on the mountain when the Lord was glorified (Matt. XVII, 2).

It follows: “That you put off,” etc. The order of the words is: “You, however, did not learn Christ in this way, if indeed you heard him or were taught in him to put off,” etc., up to “error”; and then to add: “As there is truth in Jesus.” The sense is: As there is truth in Jesus, so it will be in you who have learned Christ and have been taught to put off the former way of life.

Note that what must be put off is conduct, not nature: that is, the evil life of the old person, who is corrupted daily and tends toward worse things. Note that this corruption is not the one of which it is said: “Even if our outward person is being corrupted” [Note: [Col. 0569D] II Cor. IV, 16: “Even if our outward person is being corrupted, yet the one who is inward is renewed from day to day.” “For,” says Saint Jerome, “the corruption of the outward person is the renewal of the inward person; and conversely, the corruption of the inward person is the restoration of the outward person.”], etc.

It follows: “But be renewed in the spirit of your mind” [Note: [Col. 0569D] The text agrees with the Vulgate reading, as does the exposition that follows. The interpretation attributed to Saint Jerome from Pelagius’ work on this Epistle also agrees: in both places it reads “in the spirit of the mind.” But Saint Jerome reads *in spiritu sensus* (“in the spirit of the sense”) in the text and continues his interpretation according to that reading. He says: “We are renewed neither in the mind without the spirit, nor in the spirit without the mind; rather, we are renewed together in the spirit of our mind, so that just as we sing with the spirit, we also sing with the mind; we pray with the spirit, and we also pray with the mind. Thus may we be renewed in the spirit of our mind: when the mind has become clean and purified, free from every stain of foul accumulation, then the spirit is joined to it, and they are united by a certain bond of unity, so that it is no longer called simply spirit, but the spirit of the mind. When we have been renewed in the spirit that is the spirit of our mind, then we shall put on the new person, who has been created according to God.”], etc. Concerning the fact that we are renewed neither in the mind without the spirit nor in the spirit without the mind. Just as we pray with the spirit, so we also pray with the mind. Thus we are renewed in the spirit of the mind when the mind has become clean; then the spirit is joined to it, and we put on the new person.

For what is not new in the Savior? His conception [Note: [Col. 0570D] To serve Saint Jerome, the author of this exposition, I have emended this passage, for the text stands thus in the Constantinopolitan codex: *novus cept.*, that is, the word *conceptus* divided into two parts, with *novus* perhaps written by error between them in place of *nativitas*.], birth, delivery, teaching, life, cross, resurrection, and ascension to heaven. He is “in righteousness,” etc. Whoever imitates him has put on the new person.

Concerning the fact that in Latin *creatio* signifies generation or birth, whereas in Greek it means *factura*, a making [Note: [Col. 0570D] Saint Augustine, however, in Book I of *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*, chapter 23, asserts that Scripture uses *factum* and *creatum* indifferently, whether of things produced from some material or of those produced from nothing. This usage is also attested several times by profane authors. Our author agrees with Saint Jerome.]: Hence it is not understood by many when Wisdom says: “The Lord created me at the beginning” (Prov. VIII, 22; Sirach XXIV, 14).

Concerning the fact that *creatio* and *conditio* are used only of great things [Note: [Col. 0570D] Thus Saint Jerome: “The world is said to have been created; a city is said to have been founded; but a house, although large, is more properly said to have been built or made than founded or created.” [Col. 0571C]].

Alternatively: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind”—not because the spirit is one thing and the mind another, but because not every spirit is a mind. God is called spirit; a voice is called spirit; the wind and the life of animals are called spirit; likewise the body is called flesh, as in: “In the putting off of the body of the flesh” (Coloss. II, 11)—not because flesh is something other than body, but because not every body is flesh, since there are heavenly bodies, etc.

What he says, “Put off the old person,” etc., up to “truth,” is what he says elsewhere: “Having put off the old person with his deeds, put on the new person, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of the one who created him” [Note: [Col. 0571C] Coloss. III, 9, where the Vulgate does not read *Dei* (“of God”) after *agnitione* (“knowledge”).]. These words should be compared. This renewal takes place in the mind, in which the image of God exists. Certainly this renewal is not instantaneous, as is the renewal in baptism.

[Col. 0571B] It follows: “Therefore,” etc. A lie is a false representation accompanied by the will to deceive [Note: [Col. 0571C] A brief and most apt definition of a lie.]. That is: Put away the lie of worldly writings and speak the truth of God’s law. By “with his neighbor” he wishes every human being to be understood. “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” (Exod. XX, 17). If neighbors are acquaintances or believers, then are the wives of others to be desired? Since all who are born from Adam are neighbors, do not consider what an unbeliever is, but what you wish him to become. For the parable of the wounded man (Luke X, 30), who fell among robbers, reveals who is a neighbor.

Moreover, what follows—“because we are members of one another”—shows that the mysteries are to be disclosed to believers and to those who wish to receive them, because what is holy must not be given to dogs (Matt. VII, 6). Likewise, just as bodily members do not tear one another, so those who are in the body do not injure one another.

[Note: [Col. 0571C] “Chapter XVIII” is written here in the autograph margin.]

It follows: “Be angry,” etc. Concerning the fact that there are two kinds of anger: a natural impulse and the will to take revenge. Be angry at your own faults or those of others, and do not sin.

It follows: “Let not the sun go down,” etc. He is not speaking simply of this physical sun, since from morning until evening a person can commit so many evils that he could scarcely expiate them with tears throughout the days of his life. The sense, therefore, is: Let there not be such great anger that it extinguishes in you the sun of justice and truth.

Concerning examples involving the sun [Note: [Col. 0571C] It is useful to present Saint Jerome’s text, so that our author’s passage may be supplemented here. “Since, therefore, the true sun, just as it sets upon evil prophets, according to what is written (Amos VIII, 9), ‘The sun shall set at midday upon your prophets,’ so also it sets upon all sinners, granting them none of the light of its rising, the Apostle now commands us not to do such things, overcome by fury, through which the sun may set for us and the governing principle of the heart be enveloped in darkness. Some think this should be understood simply, as is also that passage of the fourth Psalm, from which this seems to have been taken (verse 5): ‘What you say in your hearts, and in your chambers be pricked,’ that is, whatever you sin in the day by deed, speech, or thought, cleanse these things through repentance when night comes; and let anger be brief and not be postponed until the following day.”].

It follows: “Do not,” etc. In Greek, *diabolus*; in Latin, “accuser”; in Hebrew, Satan. Concerning the fact that just as Christ stands at the door and knocks, and if anyone opens to him he enters and dines with him (Rev. III, 20), so the devil knocks like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour (I Pet. V, 8); and when you have given him room, he enters. But he usually sends temptation beforehand, as a messenger; if you receive it and nourish it, he himself also enters.

An example from Judas [Note: [Col. 0571D] Here is an example taken from Saint Jerome: “Finally, in Judas Iscariot he first shot an arrow into the heart, so that he might betray the Savior. If that wretched man had not cherished the arrow after receiving it, Satan would never have entered him after the dipped bread in the dish. At the same time, observe carefully that the devil did not find room to enter Judas, whose breast he had already struck, except at the Savior’s meal. For we are then especially delivered into his power when we are conquered neither by the humanity, clemency, nor gentleness of the one whom we unjustly hate.”].

“Do not give him room,” as in: “If a spirit possessing authority rises against you, do not leave your place” [Note: [Col. 0572D] Eccles. X, 4. The Vulgate likewise reads so; Saint Jerome, however, has: “Do not give him room.”].

[Col. 0572B] It follows: “Let the one who stole,” etc. Theft is anything acquired to the detriment of another. Therefore nothing is safer or more secure than to live by the work of one’s hands and to help others, because occupations cannot be free from sin. There are people who work only so that they will not be in need, but they do not fulfill this commandment; for it does not say, “Work so that you may not be in need,” but “so that you may have something to give to those suffering need.”

Alternatively: There is spiritual theft, as in: “Everyone steals the words of his neighbor” (Jer. XXIII, 30); and: “All who came before me” [Note: [Col. 0572D] John X, 8: “All who came, as many as came, are thieves,” etc.; where neither *extra me* (“outside me”) nor *ante me* (“before me”), as Saint Jerome has it, is read.], etc. Let the one who stole sacred utterances cultivate the field of his mind, so that he may not only abound himself but also be able to give food to his fellow servants at the proper time. This is why they think this [Note: That is, the interpreters, including Saint Jerome.], because “good” is not said of something temporal.

There are those who sew pillows for themselves out of theft, while the Lord’s tunic is seamless [Note: That is, as Saint Jerome says, those who gather scraps of Scripture here and there in order to make a torn tunic, which is “from below,” not “from above.” For the Church’s tunic—that is, Christ’s body—is woven from above and seamless in every part, and it cannot be torn even by enemies.].

[Note: [Col. 0572D] “Chapter XIX” is written here in the autograph margin.]

It follows: “Let no evil word,” etc. A good word is spoken when virtues are taught as things to be pursued; conversely, an evil word is spoken when someone is provoked to vices.

Concerning grace, occasion, and the quality of speech [Note: [Col. 0572D] Here too we are compelled to report Saint Jerome’s words. They are as follows: “In place of what we have set down, ‘for the building up of the occasion,’ which in Greek is expressed as τῆς χρείας, the translator altered it in the Latin manuscripts for the sake of euphony and wrote ‘for the building up of faith.’ Whenever someone benefits from our speech and, in accordance with the suitability of the place, time, and person, builds up those who hear, a good word has proceeded from our mouth. But whenever we speak either at the wrong time, in an unsuitable place, or not in a way appropriate to our hearers, an evil word proceeds from our mouth, for the destruction of those who hear. Let us therefore consider what we say, because we shall have to give an account for every idle word on the day of judgment. And even if we do no harm, yet if we do not build up, we shall have to pay the penalty of an evil word.”].

It follows: “And do not grieve,” etc. Concerning the fact that these passions properly belong to us, since we suffer them even unwillingly, whereas they do not occur in God and are therefore attributed to him metaphorically. For if someone has defiled the house of the Holy Spirit, the Spirit departs—not grieving for himself but grieving over that person.

Alternatively: The Spirit grieves when those who possess charity grieve over the sins of the wicked. Thus he is said to be grieved, to grow angry, to repent, and to cry out with groans [Note: [Col. 0573D] Phrases with which the sacred writings are filled.].

“He sealed” [Note: [Col. 0573D] The Vulgate reads *signati* (“sealed”).], he said, because through the Holy Spirit the image and likeness of God are received. They are sealed with this Spirit for the purpose that they may strive to be by imitation what he is by nature and may in no way be corrupted.

It follows: “All bitterness,” etc. Bitterness is opposed to sweetness. Fury [Note: [Col. 0573D] The Vulgate does not have *furor* (“fury”), but Saint Jerome does.] is anger beginning. Anger is a movement of the mind. Clamor consists of abusive words. Blasphemy is worse than perjury, because in perjury God is invoked as witness to a false matter, whereas in blasphemy God himself is blasphemed.

But what would it accomplish to restrain these things if the root remained? Therefore he adds: “With all malice.”

It follows: “But be toward one another,” etc. These things are set against bitterness. “Giving to yourselves” [Note: [Col. 0573D] In place of *vobismetipsis*, the Vulgate has *invicem* (“one another”). Our author reads the former with Saint Jerome, and this also opens a more suitable path for the exposition that follows.] he says, because the person who grants something to another has more compassion for himself than for that other person.

Alternatively: If, having abandoned bitterness, we have passed over to gentleness, this has been given to us by God.

Alternatively: He commands us to forgive another’s sins, just as our sins have been forgiven us by God.

Concerning the fact that sins are debts: there is the example of the two debtors, and also: “Forgive us our debts” [Note: [Col. 0573D] He refers this to Saint Jerome, who says concerning this passage: “Another person will understand what he says, ‘forgiving one another,’ simply, so that just as it is said above, ‘Be kind to one another,’ so now it may be said, ‘forgiving one another,’ in place of ‘forgiving each other’: just as God forgave us our sins in Christ, so may we also forgive those who have sinned against us. To prove that the forgiveness of sins is called a gift in Scripture, he will take the example written in Luke (Luke VII, 41), where one creditor had one debtor owing five hundred denarii and another owing fifty; when he had forgiven both, and the Savior asked which of them had greater love, the one questioned replied that it was the one to whom more had been forgiven. It is also said in the Lord’s Prayer (Matt. VI, 12): ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.’ God forgave us in Christ, not standing outside him but dwelling in him, because the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father. Nor is the one in whom forgiveness is given immediately inferior to the one who forgives in himself, since the Apostle also says (II Cor. II, 10): ‘If I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven it in the presence of Christ and God.’”].

[Note: [Col. 0574D] “Chapter XX” is written here in the autograph margin.]

(CAP. V.) It follows: “Be imitators of God,” etc. Note that he says to the Corinthians: “Be imitators of me” (I Cor. IV, 18). This is evidently because they were carnal and could not immediately become imitators of God, as those who were spiritual could; a distinction that preachers ought to observe.

Concerning the fact that we are imitators of God if we forgive others as God forgave us. This is what he says: “And walk in love, just as God [Note: [Col. 0574D] The Vulgate has “Christ.”] loved us.” Such is this commandment that all things are fulfilled in it.

In what he says, “And he handed himself over for us,” we are admonished to be ready to die for our brother. Concerning the fact that he is said to have been handed over in many ways, according to various intentions. Because he had come to fight against the aerial powers, he was therefore a victim; and because he returned victorious to the Father, Christ became an offering.

Concerning “for a sweet-smelling fragrance”: those sacrifices that were offered as a sweet-smelling fragrance in the Old Testament especially prefigured this [Note: [Col. 0574D] In these passages, perhaps for the sake of brevity, our author intends merely to point out to preachers and to all who undertake to expound the word of God the sources from which they might draw.].

[Note: [Col. 0574D] “Chapter XXI” is written here in the autograph margin.]

It follows: “But fornication,” etc. Concerning the fact that we are imitators of God if, after casting these things away, we preserve purity of mind; hence he himself says: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Lev. XI, 44).

Concerning the fact that he would not have joined impurity to fornication unless there had been a certain philosopher [Note: Apparently one of the Cynics.], who taught that the titillation of the flesh and the emission of semen should not be avoided.

Avarice in this passage, however, is to be understood not of money but of lust. By saying “as befits saints,” he shows that those who are found in any impurity outside fornication are not saints.

Concerning the difference between foolish talk and buffoonery: foolish talk has nothing honorable in it, whereas buffoonery proceeds from an intelligent mind and, through rustic words—that is, through joking—provokes people to laughter. These things must be entirely avoided by holy men, who should rather weep and mourn, as the Lord is said to have told the apostles in the Hebrew Gospel [Note: The Hebrew Gospel of the Nazarenes]: “And never be joyful except when you see your brother in love.”

But what does he mean by: “But rather thanksgiving”? It should be understood that “thanksgiving” here does not mean the kind by which we give thanks to God, but the kind by which we are witty (*salsi*), gracious [Note: [Col. 0574D]

The codex reads *falsi*, which we have judged should be emended in accordance with the correction of Saint Jerome’s text, where this same word, which was also read in various forms, has been corrected. That correction, as well as what follows, is strongly supported.

It is worthwhile also to quote here Saint Jerome’s words in confirmation of this interpretation: “Since among the Greeks it is not customary except among the learned to use εὐχαριστίαν, in distinction from eucharistia, to mean being gracious and giving thanks, I therefore think that the Apostle, as a Hebrew of Hebrews, used a familiar word and wished to explain his meaning by another sense of the word—especially since among the Hebrews, as they say, ‘gracious’ and ‘giving thanks’ are expressed by the same word. Hence I think it is written in Proverbs (Prov. XI, 16): γυνὴ εὐχάριστος ἐγείρει ἀνδρὶ δόξαν, ‘A gracious woman raises glory for her husband,’ meaning ‘a woman who is gracious.’ We would seem to do violence to Scripture and boldly take ‘a woman giving thanks’ for ‘a gracious woman,’ unless the other editions also agreed with our opinion. For Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus read: γυνὴ χάριτος, that is, ‘a gracious woman,’ and not εὐχάριστος, which refers to the giving of thanks.”]

and lovable, and pleasant among human beings. For it is not fitting for a Christian to be a buffoon or a foolish talker, but to have speech seasoned with salt, so that it may confer grace on those who hear.

It follows: “But know this,” etc. Note that, of the six vices named, he repeats three, and whoever is subject to them will not have a share in the kingdom of God. For if a foolish talker and a buffoon, as such, were excluded from the kingdom of God, God’s judgment would seem cruel, since it would condemn even speech uttered in jest. Nevertheless, if someone possesses these faults without the greater ones, he will not have the place he would have had if he had not been a buffoon or foolish talker.

Concerning the fact that shamefulness occurs when the mind is inflamed toward lust and the fire is kindled by the titillations of the flesh, but is restrained and extinguished by fear of God, remembrance of death, and the judgment of the mind. Therefore it ought not to have been named with those things by which people are excluded from the kingdom of God.

Note that those who understand avarice as impurity say that it would not follow for the Apostle, while discussing impurity, suddenly and disorderly to pass to something else. Conversely, those who understand avarice as love of money say that the Apostle wished to join avarice to fornication in order to show how great an evil avarice is.

Concerning the fact that the person who turns away from God through love of money is rightly called an idolater, because just as the belly is the god of the gluttonous, so money is the god of the avaricious. This is the general form of fornication, as in: “The sons of Israel fornicated after foreign gods” (I Par. V, 25; Hosea IV, 12).

Note the distinction not of substance but of persons in the phrase “of Christ and of God.” For the kingdom of Christ the Son and of God the Father is one. Alternatively: “God and Father” refers to one person, as in: “When he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father” (I Cor. XV, 24), “then the Father will not be, but God will be all in all” (ibid., 28). Wherever “God” occurs, both the Father and the Son may be understood. Some say that, because of Arius, he named Christ as well as the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0576D] “Chapter XXII” is written here in the autograph margin.]

It follows: “Let no one deceive you,” etc. Note that words that deceive are empty, whereas those that build up are full and abundant. Empty words are spoken by those who say that there is no hell or no other life, or who make punishments lighter by saying that punishment does not come from outside but is the consciousness of sin, like a fever attacking inwardly and inflicting pain. For God is angry about nothing so much as the fact that a sinner is proud and does not repent.

And rightly he says: “Because of these things”—whether deeds or words—the wrath of God has come, that is, the flood or the fire upon Sodom.

“Upon the sons of disobedience” [Note: [Col. 0576D] Or “of unpersuadableness”: ἀπείθεια may, according to Saint Jerome, be understood as deriving more from persuasion than from trust, in the contrary sense.], that is, of the devil; as if he were saying: “sons of wrath, of death, of Gehenna,” etc. The sense is: Learn the future from the past. If he spared sinners at the time of the flood and the inhabitants of Sodom, will he spare you also? [Note: [Col. 0576D] These words, almost ironically, our author took word for word from the commentary attributed to Saint Jerome from Pelagius, where “he will spare you” is interrogative.].

It follows: “Therefore do not become partners with them,” that is, if you become partners in sins, you will also be companions in punishments.

Concerning the fact that heretics are refuted here, those who say that there are two natures, whereas the Apostle says that those who had been darkness became light; for those who imitate the devil are sons of darkness and sons of night, while those who follow Christ, who says, “I am the light” (John VIII, 12), are sons of light. For God is light, and he says, “My little children” (John XIII, 33).

Note that those who were darkness in themselves become light not in themselves but in the Lord.

Concerning the example of one who walks at night [Note: That is, John III, 20: “The people sitting in darkness and seeing nothing.”].

And as if someone were to say, “In what virtues must we walk?” he answered: “The fruit of light consists in all goodness,” etc. For whoever walks in goodness, justice, and truth is a son of light. But whoever walks in wickedness, injustice, and falsehood is a son of darkness. Such people do not know what is pleasing to God.

Note that he says, “Proving.” For it is not easily found; therefore he says “proving,” an ability especially possessed by spiritual persons and by those who meditate day and night on the law of the Lord.

An example from the money-changer, who recognizes a coin by seeing its weight and its ringing sound [Note: This example is Saint Jerome’s. He says that we ought to act like the most prudent money-changer, who tests an engraved coin not only with his eye but also by its weight and its ringing sound.].

Concerning the fact that the order seems confused, it can be resolved as follows: “Therefore do not become partners with them, proving what is pleasing to God; for although you were once darkness,” etc., up to “truth.”

It follows: “And do not participate,” etc. Note that, through what he has said should be done, he turns to what should not be done. He had spoken of the fruit of light; now he speaks of “unfruitful works.” Likewise in Galatians he used the word “fruit” for good things and the word “flesh” for vices, precisely because there is no fruit in vices.

And because it is not enough not to do evil unless it is also corrected, he adds: “But rather expose them.”

Concerning the fact that exposing evil belongs to a clear conscience—that is, to one who cannot be told: “Hypocrite, first remove the beam” (Luke VI, 42). Concerning the fact that a prelate shares in the evils of his subjects if he does not expose and correct them.

[Col. 0577A] It follows: “For the things that are done by them in secret,” etc. Concerning the fact that this is joined to what precedes, namely, to the sons of disobedience: for the things that the sons of disobedience do secretly in houses or bedrooms are shameful to mention. He rightly said this when he added: “It is shameful even to speak of them.”

Then follows: “But all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light” [Note: Saint Jerome likewise has it: “But all things that are reproved by the light are made manifest.”]. What are all these things, except those done secretly? For this reason they are reproved, so that they may be recognized and abandoned. For whatever is made manifest is light. There are people who judge great crimes, or small ones, or no crimes at all. But when they are exposed and reproved, they are recognized; and those who were previously darkness begin to be light. Therefore he says: “Rise, you who sleep,” etc.

This concerns those who think that the words are taken from Isaiah, where it says [Note: Someone may ask, says Saint Jerome, who it is that says, “Rise, you who sleep,” etc., or whose testimony the Apostle has misused. Certainly, anyone satisfied with a simple answer will [Note: Surely, says Saint Jerome, the commentator in the Veronese edition, Saint Epiphanius thought this testimony was cited from the apocryphal Elijah (*Heresies* 42, p. 372). George Syncellus, in the *Chronography*, p. 21, assigns it to ἐκ τοῦ Ἱερεμίου λεγομένων ἀποκρύφων, “from apocryphal writings said to be Jeremiah’s.” Conversely, others think that they can find it in the authentic books. Saint Thomas derives it from Isaiah 60: “Arise, be illumined, Jerusalem, for your light has come.” Others prefer an allusion to Isaiah 26:19: “Your dead shall live; my slain shall arise . . . for your dew is a dew of light”; or finally to Isaiah 9:2: “The people who walked in darkness saw a great light; for those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, light arose for them.” Consult the interpreters of that passage.] say that he brought forward into discussion something read in the hidden prophets and in writings called apocryphal—as it is clear that he did elsewhere as well—not because he approved the apocrypha, but because he used verses of Aratus, Epimenides, and Menander to establish at the appropriate time what he wished to prove. Yet not everything these men wrote is holy merely because he testified that they had said something true.]

“Rise, shine,” etc.; for it was customary among the apostles to take from Scripture not so much its words as its meaning. There are likewise those who say that this was taken from the apocrypha—not because he approved the apocrypha, any more than he approved the fables of the pagans, from whose books he takes examples. Thus Jude too uses the book called Enoch (Jude 14). But such things should be read by those who, being full of the Holy Spirit, can distinguish truth from falsehood.

But why does he say “you who sleep” and “from the dead”? Some think that this is because souls die. For the spirit is not said to die [Note: Thus Saint Jerome: “Therefore, since there is also the spirit of man, which we always remember to be written of in a good sense, and the soul, whose weaknesses and deaths of sinners we read about, what is now said—‘Rise, you who sleep’—should be referred to the spirit; and what follows—‘rise from the dead’—should be fitted to the soul. For the soul that has sinned shall itself die; but we never read anywhere that the spirit dies.”]. Others say that the wicked sleep with God and must be raised; in relation to human judgments they are dead, as Lazarus was.

This concerns what Jerome says: someone among the people explained that these words were spoken because Christ was crucified over Adam’s tomb. Just as the dead Elisha raised a dead man, so now Christ would illumine Adam—that is, [Note: I judged that the particle “not” should be added, in accordance with the cited text of Saint Jerome, which I am glad to reproduce so that our text may be illuminated by a clearer light: “I know that I heard someone disputing this passage in church, who, in order to display to the people a theatrical miracle in a form never before seen, offered this testimony as though it were pleasing, saying that it was spoken to Adam, buried at the place of Calvary, where the Lord was crucified. It was called Calvary for this reason: there the head of the ancient man had been buried. Therefore, at the time when the Lord was crucified and hung over his tomb, [Note: As the cited commentary says, we have also seen above that Jerome marks this same unnamed person in his commentary on Matthew 27:33. The opinion devised to create a popular miracle—that Adam was buried at Calvary, where Christ was crucified—is certainly such; and it is plainly paradoxical that he should have put these words to Adam: “Rise, you who sleep,” etc. Moreover, Saint Ambrose, in his commentary on this epistle, and Augustine, on Psalm 3, read “and he will touch you,” a reading Jerome approves. Erasmus, followed by Victorius, conjecturally made the Greek ἐφάψεται (*ephapsetai*, “he will touch”) in place of ἐπιψαύσει (*epipsausei*, “he will touch lightly”). Chrysostom, Homily 18 on this passage, says: Οἱ μὲν φασί· Καὶ ἐπιψαύσεις τοῦ Χριστοῦ, οἱ δὲ φασίν· ἐπιφώσει σοι ὁ Χριστός, μᾶλλον δὲ τοῦτο ἔτι: “Some say, ‘And you will touch Christ’; others say, ‘Christ will shine upon you’; but the latter is still more so.”] this prophecy was fulfilled, saying: ‘Rise, Adam, you who sleep, and rise from the dead’; and not, as we read, ‘Christ will shine upon you’—that is, ‘Christ will arise for you’—but ‘Christ will touch you.’ For by the touch of his blood and of his hanging body he would be quickened and rise; and then that type would also be fulfilled in reality, when the dead Elisha raised a dead man” (2 Kings 13). Whether these things are true or not I leave to the reader’s judgment. Certainly, at that time they pleased the people and were received with a kind of applause and rejoicing. I will say only what I know: this interpretation does not agree with the meaning and context of the passage.”]

—not, “Christ will arise for you,” but “Christ will touch you.” He says that this interpretation does not fit the passage.

And because he had urged them to reprove, he now urges them to see how they should do so, saying: “See,” etc. There are people devoted to the faith who are severe; if they are reproved, they stir up persecution in the Church. Therefore he adds: “Not as fools,” etc. It belongs to the wise to consider to whom, how much, and in what manner one should speak.
