Alternatively: The Ephesians had passed from the darkness of unbelief into the light of faith. He urges them to walk carefully. This concerns the person who walks carefully, who walks in the law of the Lord and says: “Perfect my steps, so that they may not stray” (Psalm 16:5), etc.

[Note: In the autograph manuscript the margin reads here: chapter 23.]

Then follows: “Redeeming the time,” etc. All these days are evil; therefore let us redeem evil times through patience and forbearance, so that the time which is hostile may cease to be so.

Alternatively: O Ephesians, who have risen from sleep, see that you walk carefully and wisely. This concerns Joseph, who redeemed one period of his life from many circumstances; likewise Job [Note: That is, as Saint Jerome says, Joseph had one purpose: to please God. This purpose was never changed by any variation of time or circumstances—not by the envy of his brothers, the condition of slavery, the temptations of youth, his mistress’s promises, the squalor of prison, or finally the arrogance of Egyptian power. The same should be understood of Job. Both of them redeemed time for themselves and turned evil days into good ones. The Apostle urges us to do the same.].

Then follows: “Therefore do not become foolish,” that is, because the time is called evil, or so that you may walk carefully. The days are evil, like an evil house [Note: That is, a house in which some evil is committed. So it is in the commentary often attributed to Saint Jerome.].

Then follows: “And do not,” etc. Just as we cannot serve two masters (Matthew 6:24; Luke 16:13), so we cannot be filled both with wine and with the Holy Spirit. Drunkenness from wine is followed by lust and uncleanness; the Holy Spirit, by chastity, purity, and so forth.

Then follows: “Speaking,” etc. A hymn is sung when God’s praise is sung; a psalm is connected with an instrument; but a canticle is sung by one who discusses heavenly things. Accordingly, the psalm refers to the body, while the canticle refers to the soul [Note: These words are Saint Jerome’s. It is worthwhile to reproduce a few of his very beautiful remarks about ecclesiastical singing: “Not in the manner of tragedians, with the throat and jaws smeared with sweet medicines so that theatrical melodies and songs may be heard in church, but in fear, in works, and in knowledge of the Scriptures. Even if someone is, as they customarily call such people, κακόφωνος—that is, harsh-voiced—if he has good works, he is a sweet singer before God. Let Christ’s servant sing in such a way that it is not the singer’s voice but the words being read that please, so that the evil spirit who was in Saul may be driven out from those who are similarly possessed by him, and may not be introduced into those who have made the house of God into a stage for the people.”

Very similar to this is what the blessed Aelred, abbot of Rievaulx in England and a contemporary of Saint Bernard, has in *The Mirror of Charity*, book 1, chapter 23. It depicts, too vividly and beautifully to be omitted, certain kinds of singing and sounds admitted too freely into churches: “What purpose, I ask, does that terrifying blast of the bellows serve, expressing rather the crash of thunder than the sweetness of a voice? What purpose does that contraction and breaking of the voice serve? One sings below, another above, another sings over it, another divides and cuts up certain middle notes. Now the voice is tightened, now broken, now struck, now expanded in a broader sound. Sometimes—shameful to say—it is forced into the neighing of horses; sometimes, having laid aside masculine vigor, it is sharpened into the thinness of a woman’s voice; sometimes it is twisted and untwisted by a kind of artificial winding. At times you may see a man with open mouth, as though his breath were blocked, exhaling rather than singing, and by a ridiculous interruption of the voice seeming to threaten silence; now imitating the struggles of the dying or the ecstasy of those suffering. Meanwhile the whole body is shaken by theatrical gestures: the lips are twisted, the eyes roll, the shoulders play, and the movement of the fingers answers each individual note. This ridiculous doubling of sound is called religion; and where such things are practiced most frequently, it is loudly proclaimed that God is being served most honorably. Meanwhile the standing crowd, trembling and astonished, admires the sound of bellows, the clashing of cymbals, and the harmony of pipes, but watches the lascivious gestures of the singers and the meretricious alternations and breaks of their voices with laughter and mockery, so that one might think they had gathered not for the oratory but for the theater, not to pray but to watch. Nor is that dreadful Majesty feared before whom they stand, nor is reverence shown to that mystical manger which they serve, where Christ is mystically wrapped in cloths, where his most sacred blood is tasted from the chalice, where the heavens are opened, angels stand in attendance, earthly things are joined to heavenly things, and human beings are associated with angels. Thus what the holy Fathers established to stir the weak to an affection for piety is turned there into an occasion of illicit pleasure. Sound should not be preferred to understanding; rather, sound together with understanding should generally be admitted as a stimulus to greater devotion. Therefore the sound should be such, so moderate and grave, that it does not capture the whole mind for its own delight, but leaves the greater share to understanding.” Thus far Aelred. See what Saint Thomas Aquinas, Saint Charles, and other holy men say about this singing, as well as what has been wisely and frequently decreed in various places by synods and councils.]

Notice that he says, “in your hearts.” Let young men and those entrusted with the duty of singing hear this: one must sing not with the voice but with the heart. Let Christ’s servant sing in such a way that it is not the singer’s voice but the words being read that please.

Then follows: “Giving thanks,” etc. Notice why he says “always” and “for everything”: not merely because he has given us the sun, moon, earth, water, animals, and the rest, but so that in everything we may say: “Blessed be God; I suffer less than I deserve.” In comparison with my sins, these things are nothing. Such a person is a perfect Christian. Through whom are thanks to be given? Through Jesus Christ. And to whom? To God the Father, because through the Son we have access to the Father.

[Col. 0580A] Then follows: “Being subject to one another,” etc. Let bishops, priests, and the rest hear this, so that they may be subject to their subjects, just as Christ was when he washed the apostles’ feet (John 13:5). This subjection is not practiced in vanity but in the fear of Christ, since whatever is done either by superiors or by subjects must be done equally in the fear and love of God.

[Note: In the autograph manuscript the margin reads here: chapter 24.]

Then follows: “Wives to their husbands,” etc. What he had commanded generally—that is, subjection—he now commends with respect to particular persons. He commands that, just as the Church is subject to Christ, so the wife should be subject to her husband. Thus we read that Sarah called Abraham “my lord” (Genesis 28:12). For just as there is a holy union in Christ and the Church, so there should be a holy fellowship between husband and wife.

It should not seem contrary to this passage that he said to the Corinthians, “Let the husband render the debt to his wife” (1 Corinthians 7:3), etc. The Corinthians were being nourished with milk like children, whereas these were being fed with solid food like mature people. Let each follow whom he wishes [Note: That is, as Saint Jerome says, each person is free either to follow the Corinthians, as little children still drinking milk, or the Ephesians, already mature in faith.]. Nevertheless, let him know that those who nourish [Note: That is, as Saint Jerome says, what the Savior says: “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in that day”—that is, the day of judgment—“for these are properly the works of marriage.” Therefore every effort must be made to imitate the Ephesians rather than the Corinthians, lest we be found, as in the flood, buying and selling, marrying and being given in marriage; instead, with our loins girded, let us hold lamps in our hands.].

Then follows: “Husbands, love,” etc. The Apostle does not preach divorce in these words [Note: The particle “not” is absent in the autograph; it should be added, both because of Saint Paul’s text and because without it the sense of the exposition would become absurd and inconsistent with the text. Saint Jerome’s exposition of these words also supports its addition. From the sanctity of this love, compared with Christ’s love for the Church, heretics took occasion to dream that the Apostle had forbidden marriage. The answer, briefly, is that he forbade not marriage but its abuse—namely, meretricious lust and uncleanness.], but teaches that marriages ought to be holy. Just as Christ was prepared to die for the Church, so husbands should be prepared to endure dangers for the salvation of their holy wives.

For what follows—“Thus husbands,” etc.—is also written in Genesis from Adam’s perspective: “This now is bone of my bones,” etc.

Then follows: “For no one has ever,” etc.—unless perhaps someone suffers from the royal disease or cancer. Even such people hate not the flesh but the disease. When he says that we are his members, this should not be understood of the bones and flesh assumed from the Virgin, but of our participation in his grace.

Then follows: “Therefore,” etc. Christ left the Father because he appeared not in the form in which he is equal to the Father (Philippians 2:6–7); and he left his mother—either the heavenly Jerusalem or the Synagogue—and joined the Church to himself. When he says that this sacrament is great, but that he is speaking of Christ and the Church, he shows that not all sacraments are equal.

This concerns his saying, when addressing the Ephesians, “Nevertheless, you also,” as though he were saying: Although I say that this prophecy has been fulfilled in the union of Christ and the Church, nevertheless you too must love your wives; but let the wife fear, etc. Here love is accompanied by fear, so that affection may be preserved with honor: the husband should love his wife, and the wife should fear her husband. But we must ask: with what kind of fear? [Note: That is, the fear of reverence, or what they call perfect fear—the fear by which the one who fears is made perfect, and of which Psalm 34:9 says: “There is no want for those who fear him.”]

[Note: In the autograph manuscript the margin reads here: chapter 26.]

**Chapter VI**

Then follows: “Children, obey your parents,” etc. Continuing with a particular admonition, he urges children to obey their parents—but good parents. Hence Moses says: “Those who said to their parents, ‘We do not know you,’ kept your commandment” (Deuteronomy 33:9).

When he says that this is “the first commandment,” this is to be understood as referring to the second tablet [Note: Some, as Saint Jerome says, read—as in the Vulgate—“the first commandment with a promise.” This commandment, taken from Exodus 20:12, is fifth in the Decalogue. It is the first, however, to which explicit promises are attached: “That it may be well with you and that you may be long-lived,” etc., although the Apostle has omitted the final words. Saint Jerome’s observation seems less exact, however, because promises are also found in the second commandment of Exodus 20:5–6 and Deuteronomy 5:9–10: “Showing mercy,” etc. Perhaps, then, because the Decalogue was the first law given to the people leaving Egypt, each commandment of the Decalogue should be called a first commandment in comparison with the precepts later written in the law. If you want anything further, consult Saint Jerome, who discusses the matter at greater length.

As for what our author says, “on the second tablet,” this seems to me to convey the Apostle’s genuine meaning much better. Perhaps he has in mind the first commandment of Leviticus 19:3, where this commandment truly occupies first place: “Let everyone fear his father and his mother.” Our author calls the commandments delivered by the Lord to Moses in Leviticus the second tablet, in relation to the first tablets delivered by the Lord and broken by Moses (Exodus 32:15, 19); or rather because the first of the two tablets contained the three commandments referring to God, while the second contained those beginning with the fourth, which commands children to honor their parents and concerns one’s neighbor. See Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book 6, near the end; Augustine on Exodus, question 71, and letter 119, chapter 11; and Saint Thomas, *Summa* I–II, question 100, article 4.]

What he said—“that you may be long-lived upon the earth”—must not be understood of the accursed land of Judea (Jeremiah 20:14), lest it conflict with the Psalmist, who says: “Woe is me, that my sojourning has been prolonged” (Psalm 120:5), or with Solomon, who prefers the dead to the living (Ecclesiastes 4:2–3). Rather, it refers to the land of which the Psalmist says: “I believe that I shall see” (Psalm 27:13), and again: “My portion” (Psalm 142:6), etc.

[Note: In the autograph manuscript the margin reads here: chapter 27.]

Then follows: “And fathers, do not,” etc. It is the sin of children if they do not obey their parents; but it is the sin of parents if they provoke either small children to anger or adolescents and older children by imposing burdensome commands [Note: On this duty of parents, see Saint Jerome, who speaks somewhat at length and very beautifully about this passage.].

[Note: In the autograph manuscript the margin reads here: chapter 28.]

Then follows: “Servants, obey your masters,” etc. Just as he warns the Corinthians that a believing husband or wife should not leave an unbelieving spouse (1 Corinthians 7:13), lest he seem to preach divorce, so here he warns believing servants to obey their masters, lest the Lord’s teaching be blasphemed because of contempt. For Christ did not come to change social conditions but morals.

He foresaw that if servants despised their masters, the masters would not only refuse to allow other servants to come to the faith but would also regret those whom they had already allowed to do so. If, however, they recognized that believing servants were more devoted and humble, they would rejoice that others believed, and perhaps they themselves would believe as well.

Someone may ask why he says “with fear,” when fear is not in charity. Someone answers that he says this to the imperfect. But if they were perfect, chaste fear should be understood, just as above he says of the wife that she should fear—that is, honor—her husband.

He rightly says: “Not with eye-service,” as those do who wish to please human beings, but “as servants of Christ”; for whatever is done at Christ’s command is done for Christ. They also do his will from the heart when they turn necessity into willing service.

This concerns the fact that in many matters the will of masters agrees with the will of God, since they wish to have chaste, humble, and faithful servants. If it should be otherwise, one must obey God rather than man [Note: Perhaps *aliter* should be read in place of *alias*, although *alias* in the sense of *aliter* is supported by a shorter form.].

[Note: In the autograph manuscript the margin reads here: chapter 29.]

Then follows: “And you, masters, do the same things to them.” What same things? That is, let them command with simplicity of heart, remitting threats, as though he were saying: Threaten for the sake of discipline, but withdraw the threats for the sake of mercy, knowing that both your Lord and theirs, etc.

This concerns the fact that servants and masters must be admonished differently. Servants should be admonished always to keep before their eyes the humility of their condition; masters, not to lose the memory of the nature they share equally with their servants. Servants should be warned not to despise their master by proudly resisting his ordering; masters should be warned that, if they grow proud against God because of the gift he has given them, and if they do not recognize those whom their social condition holds subject to them as their equals by their common nature, etc.

To the former it is said that they should be obedient; to the latter it is commanded that they withdraw their threats, because both were redeemed at one price and are journeying toward one homeland. Great and heavenly are these rights. Therefore the Church receives servants and free people, learned and foolish, great and small, equally. The Church knows them all as children. Hence holy men, recalling the beginnings both of their first and of their second birth, never call their household servants “slaves,” but “brothers,” and invite them to the kiss. For they abhor a name produced not by nature but by iniquity.

Servants did not become servants because of Ham, whose curse was fulfilled in the Canaanites (Deuteronomy 7:2), from whom kings arose [Note: That is, in Palestine and Syria, Sidon and Phoenicia. Kings arose from those peoples—namely, the Jebusites, Amorites, Hivites, and many others—who were exterminated by Joshua according to the Lord’s command, because of the curse pronounced by Noah.], but because of injustice and the iniquity of the world. What more does a master have than a servant, or what less does a servant have than a master? They are distinguished only by name. The Lord did not conduct his judgment on behalf of servants and masters, but on behalf of the good and the wicked. For the good servant is a son and friend of God; the wicked master is a son and servant of the devil, and worse than any slavery.

[Note: In the autograph manuscript the margin reads here: chapter 30, and shortly afterward: the twenty-third Sunday after Pentecost.]

Then follows: “Finally,” etc. After admonishing particular groups, he immediately adds a general admonition, saying: “Be strong,” not in yourselves but in the Lord; not in your own power but in his.

This concerns how the Apostle, like a commander arming soldiers for battle, arms and directs his hearers toward a special conflict. For he says: “Put on the armor of God.” Why “of God”? Because just as one who fights visible enemies takes visible weapons, so invisible weapons are necessary against invisible enemies. To say, “Put on the armor of God,” means nothing other than: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 13:14)—that is, truth, righteousness, piety, and the other things understood in Christ.

Then follows: “Our struggle is not” [Note: The manuscript reads *conculcatio*; I judged this should be corrected in accordance with all the readings.] “against flesh and blood,” that is, not against human beings, who consist of flesh and blood, but against “principalities and powers”—that is, those who claim dominion over wicked people; against “the rulers of this world,” meaning of darkness, not of heaven and earth. For demons are rulers not of the world but of those who love the world.

But thanks be to God, who has rescued us from darkness. Let us therefore remain in light and freedom. Hence it is said to them: “You were once darkness” (Ephesians 5:8), etc.

Someone may ask where the Apostle found the occasion for saying these things. Perhaps it was in the battles narrated in ancient histories as having been fought by the children of Israel against the Ammonites, Moabites, and Canaanites, as though he were saying: O Ephesians, what you read about Israel’s battles against the nations seems to speak of our flesh, etc., so that from those accounts we may understand that our struggle is not against flesh—that is, against human beings—but against demons [Note: This exposition is taken from Saint Jerome. Where it reads “our flesh,” it should perhaps rather be corrected to “the flesh of the nations,” or “their flesh.”].

When he says “in the heavenly places,” he means the air, from which we call the birds “birds of heaven,” because this air is filled with unclean spirits.

Then follows: “Therefore take up,” etc. He repeats the exhortation because victory is difficult: they must put on the armor of God. For what purpose? “So that you may be able to resist on the evil day”—that is, on the day of temptation, or in the time of the present age, as in: “The days are evil” (Ephesians 5:16); or in the future, as in: “Why do you want the day of the Lord? The day of the Lord is darkness and not light” (Amos 5:18). Likewise: “The day of wrath, that day” (Zephaniah 1:15), etc.

When he says, “and having perfected everything, to stand,” “in everything” should be understood as referring to all that I instructed above.

Then follows: “Stand therefore,” etc.—that is, like the one who said: “He set my feet upon a rock” (Psalm 40:2), etc. It is good that your enemy find you standing, not lying down; girded, not ungirded.

This concerns the fact that the inner person has loins, whence the Lord says: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35), etc.

Then follows: “Having put on the breastplate of righteousness.” Righteousness is rightly designated by the name of a breastplate, because just as a breastplate is made complete by many rings, so righteousness is made complete by many virtues.

“And having shod your feet.” These are the feet of the soul. We must shoe them—that is, fortify them—with the examples of the holy Fathers, so that we may proclaim the Gospel without fear; as in: “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace” (Isaiah 52:7; Nahum 1:15; Romans 10:15).

This concerns his calling faith a shield: just as all darts are extinguished by a shield, so all adversities are overcome through faith. The helmet of salvation protects the head—that is, the understanding of the inner person. For if you are clothed with all these things but do not have a sword, you may defend yourself to some extent, but you cannot destroy your enemy. Therefore he adds: “And the sword of the Spirit.” Hence elsewhere: “For the word of God is living” [Note: Hebrews 4:12: “For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart.”], etc.

If you do not have the sword of the word, you will not easily overcome the deceptions of heretics. Just as a soldier without a sword does not go into battle, so all righteousness is unprotected without the word.

Then follows: “Through every prayer,” etc. This concerns the distinction between prayer and supplication. They say that supplication is made for past or present sins, whereas prayer is made to obtain what we hope for.

And because we greatly need God’s help to defeat the deceits of the ancient enemy, he therefore adds: “Praying at all times in the Spirit.” He rightly says “in the Spirit,” so that we may not merely speak words learned by heart or written down, but so that the inner person—that is, the spirit—may pray with full desire and pray at all times.

Notice that he says “through every.” Prayer is manifold: sometimes for ourselves, sometimes for others, sometimes for things belonging to the future [Note: These words—“sometimes . . . future”—are written in the margin.], and sometimes for things belonging to the present life.

Notice that when the words cease, the spirit ought to pray; and he shows how this is so when he says, “at all times.” Since a definite time might have been understood—namely, the days given to human beings for work [Note: Perhaps “for prayer.”]—he therefore adds: “and keeping watch in it with all perseverance,” lest, like sleeping people, we merely recite things we have read or memorized. For just as a sleeping person does not know what he is saying, so does the one who prays in such a way that he is thinking about something else.

Notice that he urges them to pray for the saints and for himself. Inflated and proud people disdain requesting the prayers of the saints. Notice also that he himself prays for the Ephesians and asks them to pray for him. Here we learn that superiors should pray for their subjects and subjects for their superiors.

But observe that he does not ask them to pray for bodily health or for temporal possessions, but that speech may be granted to him—that is, that the word may abound and that his mouth may speak more openly and confidently, without any hesitation. Notice that this very thing would benefit those whom he urges to pray. Here we learn to pray for those whom we teach in the Lord.

Then follows: “For which,” etc.—that is, for the Gospel. He is an ambassador of Christ, and although he is in chains, he still carries out the duty of evangelizing. But he prays that he may not be overcome by suffering [Col. 0585C], because all ministers of the word must endure such things. Hence follows: “So that in it,” etc. What else should he have asked for amid adversities and punishments except that confidence be given him to make the Gospel known? Notice that confidence is greater when something is said fully and reasonably.

[Note: In the autograph manuscript the margin reads here: chapter 31.]

Then follows: “But so that you also may know,” etc. Notice that he says two things: what concerns me and what I am doing. What concerned him, except chains? And what was he doing, except teaching diligently? He discloses none of this through the letter but communicates everything through the messenger, that is, Tychicus [Note: The manuscript reads “Titicus.”]. In showing his person, he also commends his journey. When he says “the beloved brother,” he shows him to be of great merit, since he is called Paul’s beloved. But why beloved? Was it because he was his minister? He says: “A minister in the Lord”—that is, in preaching.

Then follows: “So that you may know what concerns us,” etc.—that is, what punishments and chains we endure. “To comfort your hearts,” so that you may not be troubled by concern and anxiety about me.

This concerns the great consolation it could have been to hear that Paul, in Rome, the mistress of cities and the citadel of Roman power, was triumphing from prison and chains. For this reason Tychicus was sent to announce Paul’s life and conduct to them. It could indeed have been a great consolation for those wishing to imitate him to know everything the Apostle was doing.

[Col. 0586B] Then follows: “Peace,” etc. The final part of the letter is a prayer. He prays and wishes peace for the brothers, then love, and afterward faith. These are the things that make a perfect Christian. But love is greater than peace (1 Corinthians 13:13), because there are people who endure those whom they do not love.

Notice that without faith the remaining virtues are possessed uselessly, as in: “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Romans 14:23). Notice also that faith itself, together with the other virtues, is given by the Lord.

Then follows: “But grace be with all,” etc. Heretics have a corrupted faith because they do not think rightly about Christ. Others also have a corrupted faith because they serve him with an improper intention. Still others have a corrupted faith because they hope in Christ only in this life. Some have understood “corrupted” to mean those who engage in sexual intercourse, who are commonly called corrupt. But how are holy marriages excluded from this grace? Therefore corruption means the domination of any sin. To love the Lord “in incorruption” means that sin does not reign in our mortal body, etc.

He placed “Amen” at the end as a confirmation of everything written above. Through this Hebrew word he shows that what has been written is true and faithful.

**The Epistle to the Ephesians ends.**

**The Epistle to the Philippians begins.**

[Col. 0585]

**Argument.**

[Col. 0585C]

[Col. 0585D] The Apostle preached the word of faith to the Philippians after being admonished in a vision, as is related in the Acts of the Apostles, to go to them and open their ears to hear the word of God (Acts 16:19). For he remained among them many days, until he had fully instructed them and made them firm in the faith. And because after his departure they were not transferred to something else, as were the Galatians, they are praised by the Apostle. The praise of these men is also the condemnation of others, namely, the Corinthians. For when they had believed through the Apostle’s preaching, they advanced so far in faith and knowledge that they even preached the Gospel and defended it against the attack of the false apostles. For this reason he also receives expenses from them, so that he might be able to preach to others.

While praising them together, he admonishes them not to be terrified by his sufferings. Through these the Gospel of Christ is not destroyed but confirmed, because he could not endure so much for a false or doubtful cause. Yet although they are praised, there were imperfect people among them. Nor is this surprising, because the holy Church is mixed: it is a threshing floor, and the grains will remain mixed with the chaff until they are cleansed by the winnowing of just discernment. This was signified by the fact that the Jebusites lived with the Jews in Jerusalem (Judges 1:21). For what is signified by Jerusalem, which is called “vision of peace,” except the Church? [Col. 0587B] And what is signified by the Jebusites, whose name is interpreted as “those who trample,” except the wicked?

Morally: What is a holy soul except Jerusalem? Although it possesses works of piety and holiness, is it not nevertheless completely free from evil? Since, therefore, there are Jebusites in a holy soul—that is, contrary affections—it must labor for this purpose: because it feels desire, it should not consent to desire, so that even if it murmurs behind one’s back, it does not resist openly. Thus, I say, the one who wishes to be praised with the Philippians and to penetrate the Apostle’s meaning must necessarily live.

Regarding the fact that the Philippians are Macedonians, and Macedonians are Greeks: this province was first called Emathia, after Emath; then Macedonia, after the Macedonian king. They are the Ionians, named after Javan, the son of Japheth.

Regarding the position of this province: [Col. 0587C] it has the Aegean Sea to the east, Dalmatia to the west, Asia to the south, and Mysia to the north.

## THE TEXT BEGINS

### (CHAPTER I)

“Paul and Timothy.” By the fact that the Apostle joins the names of others with his own, it is shown that through the mouths of many the Holy Spirit expresses one meaning and forms one doctrine. Nor is this surprising, since the heart of the multitude of believers was one (Acts 4:32). From this preachers should learn to praise God with one voice.

Regarding the fact that he places his name at the beginning of his letters in the manner of kings, so as to display the dignity of his apostleship. Regarding the fact that he does not call himself an apostle, because he was writing to people who thought rightly about him.

Regarding moral instruction. Regarding the fact that he discloses his condition when he adds “servants”—not servants of vices, but of Jesus Christ. This condition is nobler than every dignity, because a servant of Christ is a servant of righteousness, wisdom, chastity, and things of this kind.

Since Paul and Timothy are writing, it must be considered to whom he says “to all the saints”: not to all the Philippians, lest they cast pearls, and so forth (Matt. 7:6), but to the saints who are “in Christ Jesus.” Heretics are not holy in Christ, because they do not think rightly about Christ.

It follows: “Who are at Philippi.” Regarding the fact that Philippi [Col. 0588A] is a city of Macedonia. These people, having received the word of truth, remained steadfast in the faith and did not accept false apostles. He praises them together, writing to them from prison at Rome through Epaphroditus.

When he says “to bishops and deacons,” he does not wish pontiffs to be understood, but presbyters under the name “bishops.” For there was no reason for there to be several bishops in one city. At that time presbyters were called bishops.

What he wishes for the saints he shows when he adds: “Grace to you and peace from God.” And appropriately so, because the memory of the saints is celebrated with thanksgiving. Grace is that by which sins are forgiven; peace is that by which people are reconciled to God. Thus far the greeting.

It follows: “I give thanks to my God,” and so forth. Notice that he begins with thanksgiving. Notice also that he displays his love toward those for whom he prays without ceasing. Observe that he instructs us to praise God not only for our own progress or that of our own people, but for the progress of everyone.

And because they were righteous, he says, “making supplication with joy,” since he prays differently for the Galatians and differently for the Philippians. In the former there was sorrow, because they had departed; in the latter joy, because they were standing firm. We too pray with joy for the good, but with sorrow for the wicked. Notice that he calls this joy spiritual, not bodily.

He explains for what he gives thanks when he says, “for your fellowship”: that is, because you share with me in preaching the Gospel. When he says “from the first day,” this is to be understood as from the time when you believed; as though he were saying: You are persevering in the good that you began. [Col. 0588C]

[Note: [Col. 0587D] In the autograph margin it reads here: chapter II.]

Because he confidently trusts in God’s mercy that they will persevere, he says: “Being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you,” and so forth. Notice that here he refutes those who say that we begin the good from ourselves. Behold, he says, “he who began”; and the Lord says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5); and the Psalmist: “His mercy will go before me” (Ps. 58:1); and: “Your mercy will follow me” (Ps. 22:6). For he himself goes before us so that we may will, and he himself follows us so that we may not will in vain. [Note: [Col. 0587] See the other Epistles, especially that to the Romans, where he treats of divine grace.]

Notice that he calls “the day of Christ” either each person’s death or the day of judgment. Notice also that by these words he urges them to perseverance. And notice that he says it is right for him to feel this because he has them in his heart and in his bonds—as though he were saying: I love you so greatly that neither bonds nor scourges can remove your memory from my heart.

In the defense and confirmation of the Gospel he calls them his companions, in accordance with what he had said above, “for your fellowship.” Notice that in two respects he places the Philippians before the Ephesians: first, because he is certain of their perseverance, and second, because they devoted themselves daily to reading.

And appropriately he calls them companions of his joy, as though he were saying: Just as you are companions in labor and teaching, so you will be companions in joy.

[Col. 0589A] It follows: “For God is my witness,” and so forth: that is, “to be incorporated,” [Note: [Col. 0589D] In the autograph it reads incorporali. It seemed preferable to read incorporari, “to be incorporated,” so that the exposition would be more suitable and more consonant with the Apostle’s thought. For the Apostle says: “God is my witness, how I long for all of you in the bowels of Jesus Christ.” By the verb “to be incorporated,” namely, into Christ, our author perhaps wished to express the whole idea. The text cited below also seems to support this reading.]

as in the saying: “Whoever eats my flesh” (John 6:57), and so forth; or, “I love you as though you were the bowels of Christ.” [Note: [Col. 0590D] Here he had before his eyes the Commentary of Jerome, or rather that of Pelagius.]

When he invokes God as witness, he does not act against the Lord’s command, because he swears from necessity. For he wants them to trust him, to love the one who loves them, and to cherish the one who cherishes them. He desires them not with carnal but with spiritual love. [Note: [Col. 0590D] These repeated expressions provide increasingly strong confirmation that incorporari should be read above instead of incorporali, so that no place may be given to empty repetitions, of which our interpreter is entirely free.]

It follows: “And this I pray,” and so forth. Notice that he not only commands what they should do, but prays that they may do it, because it is not enough to know what must be done unless the assisting grace is present by which it can be accomplished.

It follows: “In knowledge,” and so forth. Notice that he prays that knowledge be given to those who already possess knowledge, because without knowledge no one can possess sincerity—that is, integrity—nor approve the better things, that is, the more useful things, and abound in the fruit of good works. And to what end is this? Is it so that this may be praised? No, but for the praise of God, according to the saying: “Let your good works be seen,” and so forth (Matt. 5:16).

[Note: [Col. 0590D] In the autograph margin it reads here: chapter III.]

It follows: “But I want you to know, brothers,” and so forth. By these words he consoles them concerning his tribulations. The meaning is: They not only do no harm, but even help, when I suffer not for a crime but for Christ.

It follows: “So that my bonds,” and so forth. It is a great praise to be bound for Christ in every praetorium and in all other places—that is, before kings and in the other places where judges sit. Praetorium is said as though from praeciptorium, “place of command,” because the praetor sits there to examine cases. Praetors are called as though they were praeceptores, “commanders,” because they give commands—that is, they are prefects, as though they were those set over others.

[Note: [Col. 0590D] In the autograph margin it reads here: chapter IV.]

[Col. 0589C] It follows: “So that many,” and so forth, as though he were saying: Many brothers, following the example of my bonds, have cast aside fear and freely preach Christ.

And because people preach Christ with various intentions, he therefore adds: “Some indeed,” and so forth. Here he shows four kinds of persons who preach Christ. The first and the last preach out of malice; the two in the middle preach with good intention. But we must see how they differ from one another.

The first is malicious because of envy: they grieve that he alone should claim the knowledge of preaching; they preach in order to take away the glory he has among believers. They envy him because they perceive that he has been chosen by God.

The last is evil because they do not proclaim Christ chastely or holily, but in order to harm the Apostle. Since they openly denied Christ, they pretended to preach Christ so that the Apostle might experience tribulation and greater pain. Or they preached with the intention of burdening the Apostle, as though they were making more disciples and filling the world with their teaching, thereby heaping greater envy upon him.

Notice that the two good kinds are opposed to the two contrary kinds. The second answers the first, for good will is contrary to envy. The third is opposed to the fourth, because charity toward Christ—or toward Paul—cannot preach Christ for the sake of Paul’s persecution.

The wicked seek what is their own in preaching, not what belongs to Jesus Christ (Phil. 2:21). But good and faithful people obediently listen not to just any human being, but to the Lord himself, who says: “Do whatever they tell you,” and so forth (Matt. 23:3). Therefore they profitably hear even what is not profitably done. They strive to seek their own interests, but they do not dare to teach their own interests.

It follows: “What then?” and so forth. The meaning is: Why should I be moved, or why should I be cast into tribulation, when I rejoice altogether that Christ is proclaimed in every way?

There is an “occasion” when Christ is preached not for his own sake but for the sake of something else; there is “truth” when Christ himself is loved for his own sake. But whether he is proclaimed in the former or the latter way, he says that he rejoices because Christ is named and Christ is proclaimed.

Paul therefore rejoiced because the truth was preached through deceitful men and Christ was announced through the mouths of the wicked. Many benefit by teaching what they do not practice; but far more would benefit if they sincerely loved what they taught. The first joy is in the brothers who preach with good will; the second is in those who preach Christ with evil will.

He explains why he rejoices when he adds: “For I know that this will turn out for me,” and so forth. The meaning is: What they proclaim as the cause of my destruction, I know will result in my salvation—but through Christ’s action, since he governs everything for my salvation and turns adversity toward prosperity.

Even if they proclaim Christ for the purpose of making me suffer and tormenting me, my hope is nevertheless in Christ, because from all these things I expect a reward, and I endure them so that they may be converted.

This passage should not be understood, as some think, to mean that the Apostle granted heretics permission to preach Christ however they wished. Rather, because at the time when the Apostle was teaching there were people who preached Christ in order to stir up greater persecution against him, he says that he rejoices either because Christ is proclaimed in whatever manner, or because his reward is increased through tribulations.

It follows: “Because in nothing shall I be put to shame,” and so forth—that is, in no manner by which Christ is proclaimed. For I will never be ashamed, but will rejoice in both ways.

He says that both now and always Christ is magnified in his body, because while his body was being afflicted with punishments, he did not cease to preach Christ. [Col. 0591A] This is what he adds: “Whether by life or by death.” It is as though he were saying: If I live by enduring punishments, Christ will be preached; and if I die through punishments, Christ will be preached even more, [Note: [Col. 0591D] The words “and if … Christ” are found in the lower margin.] when they see that I was neither worn down by punishments [Note: [Col. 0591D] Or perhaps “frightened away.”] nor recalled by death, but persevered in preaching.

It follows: “For to me, living is Christ,” and so forth. The meaning is: I have no desire to live here except in order to build up the body through my example. I do not fear death, because to die is gain for me. To live is Christ for me, because whoever hopes in him always lives, both now and afterward.

Therefore, nothing that they do matters. Whether they kill me or tear me apart with punishments, none of these things harms me, because “to me, living is Christ,” and so forth.

But if living, and so forth. Since he had said above, “To me, living is Christ,” and it was uncertain what life he meant—this life or the future one—he therefore added that he meant this present life, which is in the flesh.

“When I am in the flesh,” he says, “the fruit of my labor is for me.” What fruit? That I preach Christ, that many may be saved, and that the world may be enlightened. These are the fruits of one who lives in the flesh.

It follows: “And what I shall choose, I do not know.” The meaning is: If I die, I have gain, because I go to the one whom I love. On the other hand, if I live here, I have the fruit of my labor by evangelizing Christ and bringing many to the faith. Therefore, he says, I do not know whether I should desire death or remain in this life.

It follows: “But I am constrained by the two,” and so forth. Regarding the fact that blessed Augustine says it is uncertain whether, “having desire” for the two [Note: [Col. 0592D] The Vulgate reads desiderium, “desire.”] he means “having desire for the two,” or whether “I am constrained by the two” is to be taken separately.

The phrase should be connected with what follows: “Having the desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.” But since he then adds, “for it is much better” [Note: [Col. 0592D] The Vulgate reads “much better” rather than “much more excellent.”], the particle “for” resolves the ambiguity. The interpreters who removed this word were led by the view that he seemed not only to be compelled by the two alternatives, but also to desire both.

The passage should therefore be punctuated as follows: “What I shall choose, I do not know; but I am constrained by the two.” This punctuation is followed by: “Having the desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.” And as though someone had asked why he had the desire for this, he says: “For it is much more excellent.”

Why, then, are you constrained by the two? Because there is a necessity of remaining in the flesh. Behold: although he is constrained by the two, he has a desire to die and also a necessity of remaining in the flesh.

O how great was this man’s affection of love toward believers! For the sake of others he chose not what was best for himself, but what was necessary for others, saying: “And having this confidence,” and so forth.

Who, desiring the third heaven, would not despise earthly things? Who, eager for paradise, would not reject all these things? Who, remembering words of mystery, would not scorn human eloquence? Who, laboring through so many persecutions, would not choose rest?

But because he placed charity first, he chose what would benefit others, saying: “I know that I shall remain.” [Col. 0592A] Truly, like a father, truly like a servant of God, constrained by two desires, he chose to remain for the sake of others.

“I shall remain,” he says—that is, I shall remain until completion; that is, for the sake of your progress, through my presence with you again; that is, so that while present I may perceive how your glory rejoices and abounds in Christ: that you love Christ, that you serve Christ, and that you, as servants of Christ, rejoice.

It follows: “Only live worthily of the Gospel of Christ.” He wishes them to conduct themselves worthily, lest he regret having wished to remain in the flesh. One conducts oneself worthily of the Gospel who lives according to its commands and places his hope in it.

He explains this conduct when he says: “So that whether I come.” To stand with one spirit and labor together with one mind is to live worthily of the Gospel. The order is: Live worthily, so that I may hear worthy things about you, because you stand in one spirit. I may hear this while absent, or see it while present.

And as though someone had asked why he so strongly commends unity of spirit and labor, he explains when he adds: “In nothing be terrified.” Here, like a commander, he teaches his own people to be united and not divided, so that they may gain victory and not be terrified by their adversaries.

Why? Because for those who suffer tribulation for Christ, it contributes to salvation; but for those who cause the tribulation, it contributes to destruction.

And because this conflict is manifold, he says: “In nothing be terrified”—that is, neither by crafty disputes, nor by sufferings, nor by insults. This passage strengthens both martyrs and the members of Christ who contend among the members of the devil.

It follows: “And this is from God,” and so forth—that is, God works this, so that what is destruction for others may be salvation for you.

In whom does he work this? In you, to whom it has been granted, and so forth. Although the Apostle diligently exalts God’s grace in everything, what he says nevertheless contributes to the praise of the Philippians: it was granted to them by God the Father to believe and to suffer for Christ.

For he neither permits nor grants this except to those who love Christ, whom he himself has caused to love him. Many possess faith, but not faith so great that they could suffer for Christ. And because he had said that it had been granted to them to suffer for Christ, he added: “the contest.”

It follows: “The same contest,” and so forth—that is, I do not want you to be ignorant of this struggle. It is the one you saw in me or heard about from me: prison, chains, scourges, and other things of this sort.

Regarding the fact that they had seen some things—that is, among themselves—and had heard other things, namely, what he had endured either at Jerusalem or at Rome.

### (CHAPTER II)

It follows: “If there is therefore any consolation,” and so forth.

When he is about to ask a favor—that they complete his joy, namely, by thinking the same thing and differing from one another in nothing—he first sets forth, as it were, the grounds of their merits, by which he may obtain what he asks.

The grounds of their merits are these: they have been summoned and consoled in Christ, and they have the comfort of charity, and so forth.

The order is excellent. First, by believing, they are summoned and consoled in Christ. Then it remains for them to have the comfort of charity. Afterward, through love, the fellowship of the spirit is acquired. Finally, they become the inner parts of one body and possess compassion.

The meaning is: If there is any consolation in Christ, complete my joy. The same should be understood with each phrase, as though he were saying: If these things are in you, complete my joy, so that you may think the same thing.

Where? By having the same love and being united in spirit.

The things he enumerates above will then be true if they fulfill the things he commends below. Notice how he binds them together: if they do not preserve these things, they will not appear approved in the others either. Since they did not wish to be regarded as strangers by him, they should preserve these things so that they might be perfect.

And because there were quarrels among them—for in a great house there are golden vessels and wooden ones—he therefore adds: “doing nothing through contention” [Note: [Col. 0593D] Saint Ambrose has “doing nothing according to irritation.”], and so forth.

Some have a compulsion to contend; others have a desire to contend. Because both are vicious, the Apostle prohibits both. And because some contend for the sake of boasting, he adds: “nor through empty glory.”

Full glory is the desire to please God; empty and vain glory is the desire for human favor. This does not befit a Christian. He now adds the contrary of the second kind.

It follows: “But in humility,” and so forth. True humility exists when you believe another to be better than yourself. Then you will be able to preserve patience, like a servant or son, because servants know their master and sons their father to be superior.

And so that you may be able to fulfill this, consider that in the one who is evil there may perhaps be hidden some good for which he could be preferred to you, or that some evil may perhaps lie hidden in you which you do not recognize. Likewise, perhaps he will turn from evil to good, and you from good to evil.

It follows: “Not seeking what is their own” [Note: [Col. 0593D] The Vulgate and Pelagius, under the name of Saint Jerome, have “considering”; Saint Ambrose has “contemplating.”], and so forth.

If we think only about ourselves—that is, about our own liberation—we may benefit ourselves. But this is little. We truly act for ourselves when we help others. Since we are one body, we ought to labor for the whole body like members laboring for the whole.

[Note: [Col. 0593D] In the autograph margin it reads here: chapter V.]

He confirms this admonition by an example when he adds: “Have this mind among yourselves,” and so forth. The meaning is: Do not seek what is yours, but what belongs to others, just as Christ did not seek what was his.

Although he was the Word, equal to the Father, he wished not only to become human for the sake of human beings, but also to take their sins upon himself. How much more ought you, a human being, to bear human weakness, both of mind and of body, since you too can become weak as a human being.

Therefore, offer him what you wish to have offered to you, just as this one did, who says: “I have become all things to all people,” and so forth (1 Cor. 9:22).

[Col. 0594A] It follows: “Who, being in the form of God,” and so forth. Although he was equal to the Father in the form of God, [Note: [Col. 0593D] In the manuscript ut, “so that,” is read in place of non, “not”; this must be emended, since everything that follows cries out that it is a sheer error utterly foreign to the author’s thought.] he did not lose the form of God in the form of a servant. For “in the form of God” and “in the form of a servant” refer to one and the same being.

Therefore, in the form of God he is greater than himself; in the form of a servant he is less than himself: as in the saying, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and again, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). [Note: [Col. 0594D] The words “in the form … than himself,” in the same hand, are placed in the lower margin.]

Hence Augustine says: The Son of God is therefore equal by nature to God the Father in the form of God; in the form of a servant he is less than the Father.

Therefore, because the form of God received the form of a servant, he is wholly God and wholly human. He is wholly God because of the one who received God, and wholly human because of the human being who was received. For by that assumption one was not changed into the other: neither was divinity changed into humanity, nor humanity into [Col. 0594B] divinity.

It follows: “He did not regard it as robbery,” and so forth. It was not necessary for him to seize by robbery what he possessed by nature.

It follows: “But he emptied himself,” not by emptying his substance, but by concealing his honor.

It follows: “Taking the form of a servant,” not by losing what he was [Note: [Col. 0594D] This more and more proves that the reading above should have been emended from “so that he might lose the form of God” to “not lose it,” since everything that follows cries out against the former reading.], but by assuming what he was not, so much so that he washed the disciples’ feet (John 13:5).

It follows: “Made in the likeness of human beings,” and so forth. Augustine says:

We use the word habitus, “form” or “state,” in many ways: the state of the mind, as when it denotes the acquisition of some art; the state of the body, as when we say that one person is more handsome or stronger than another, which is more properly called habitudo, “condition” [Note: [Col. 0594D] It seemed right to read habitudo instead of habitatio, so that the sense might be restored.]; and the state of things fitted to our limbs, from which we speak of being clothed, shod, and armed.

In all these cases, however, habitus derives from the verb habere, “to have.” Habitus is therefore said of something that comes about so that it can be possessed, and without which we can exist.

Nevertheless, there is this distinction: some things change but are not themselves changed, such as wisdom; some both change and are changed, such as food, for what is consumed does not retain the same form, and the one who consumes it becomes strong from being weak; some are changed and do not change, such as a garment when it is removed, for it does not retain the same beauty that it had when worn; there is a fourth kind, which neither changes nor is changed, such as a ring. If you examine this kind carefully, it either does not exist or is extremely rare.

This habitus does not belong to the first kind, because human nature did not change the nature of divinity; nor to the second, because neither divinity was transferred into humanity nor humanity into divinity; but rather to the third.

For he was assumed in such a way that he was changed for the better and was formed by him ineffably more excellently and more closely than a garment is formed by a human being when it is put on.

By this term, therefore, the Apostle shows that he put on a human being as though he were a garment. By uniting and conforming him to himself [Note: [Col. 0595D] In the autograph: veniens, “coming.”], he joined him to immortality and eternity.

For the Greeks call the habitus that consists in the acquisition of wisdom ἕξις (*hexis*, “habit” or “disposition”), from ἔχω (*echō*, “I have”). But this other kind, in the sense in which we say “shod,” “armed,” or “clothed,” they call σχῆμα (*schēma*, “form” or “figure”). [Note: [Col. 0595D] From the Greek ἕξις, “habit,” and ἔχω, “I have.”] [Note: [Col. 0595D] Greek: σχῆμα.]

From this we understand that the Apostle spoke of the latter: where we have habitus, they have σχῆμα. By this term it must be understood that the Word was not changed by the assumption of humanity, just as limbs are not changed by clothing, although that assumption ineffably joined the one assumed to the one who assumed him.

But because human words can be adapted to ineffable realities, so that God, who assumed humanity, would not be understood to have changed, it was chosen that this assumption should be called in Greek σχῆμα and in Latin habitus. [Col. 0595B]

“Found as a human being”: that is, by possessing a human being he was found to be human, or “as a human being,” so that by an intermediate meaning he might be shown to be more than human.

It follows: “He humbled himself,” and so forth. Because there are many kinds of death, he therefore adds “of the cross.” For concerning this death the wicked say: “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death” (Wis. 2:20).

This contributes to what he had admonished above, namely, that they should not seek what is their own. Behold: the immortal one dies for mortals. In that he endured everything for us, he shows that we should seek not what is ours but what belongs to others. And because we understand humility, obedience, and things of this kind in Christ, let us strive to live in such a way that we may have the same mind among ourselves.

[Col. 0595C] It follows: “Therefore God exalted him,” and so forth. Divinity is not exalted, because it could not be humbled; this must be understood according to his human nature.

It follows: “And he gave him a name,” and so forth—a name that could be compared with the name of the Son. The Father gave this name to the human being who had been assumed, so that he might be the proper and natural Son.

It follows: “So that at the name of Jesus,” and so forth. At what name does every knee bend except that of Christ Jesus—of those in heaven, of angels, of those on earth, of human beings, and of those beneath the earth, of demons?

By the bending of the knee a certain submission of the mind should be understood, since angels are incorporeal.

It follows: “And every tongue should confess,” and so forth—that is, confess his same glory.

Notice how he commends the same one as both human and God, so that there may be one person and God may be a Trinity, not a Quaternity. For just as the person is not doubled when the soul is joined to the flesh, so the number of persons is not increased when humanity is joined to the Word, so that there is one Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0596D] In the autograph margin it reads here: chapter VI.]

Therefore, beloved, and so forth. After admonishing them to seek what belongs to others, and confirming this very point by the Lord’s example, he adds an exhortation that they love one another.

Notice that he calls them “beloved” because they are obedient.

But why “with fear and trembling”? Some think that fear belongs to the soul and trembling to the body. But why “more and more”? Is it because the day of death is approaching, or because one who admonishes is more fearful in his absence?

We must attentively hear the mystery of this passage: namely, that when we counsel others and take care of others, we work salvation for ourselves even more; and then, that there is power in us to work salvation for ourselves. Thus he says: “Work out your salvation.”

But lest pride arise, he immediately adds: “For God is the one who works,” and so forth, so that he would not give an opening to heretics who say that we ourselves are able to work the good.

He says that God works, and that we also work. The good work belongs both to God and to us. God works the willing by inspiring and persuading, and by promising rewards; and he works the accomplishing by saying: “The one who perseveres,” and so forth (Matt. 10:22).

[Col. 0596B] It follows: “Do everything without murmuring,” and so forth. By these words, if you refer them to what precedes, he teaches that when, in seeking the salvation of others, we grow weary and are unable to fulfill what we desire, we should neither murmur nor doubt the reward.

Alternatively: He had previously admonished them to seek the salvation of others; now he teaches that, when we wish to fulfill the legal, prophetic, and evangelical commands, we should not murmur by complaining about their burden, because “blessed are the meek” (Matt. 5:4), nor act with doubt, because “not a hair of your head will perish” (Luke 12:7).

It follows: “So that you may be without complaint”—that is, without reproach—and “simple children,” because the simple divine nature wishes for simple worshipers, as in the saying: “Be holy, because I am holy,” and so forth (Lev. 11:44; 1 Pet. 1:16), without the reproach of crime.

It follows: “In the midst of a crooked generation,” and so forth. While we are in this life, we must strive to surpass the conduct of the wicked by living well, doing everything without reproach. Then you will shine like lights in the world, like the sun. Just as the stars are obscured by the splendor of the sun, so our bright life will obscure the conduct of the wicked.

He says “the word of life,” because the wicked possess dead words, while those who hold the word of life cling to what they say. And he appropriately adds “for glory,” because the glory of teachers is the progress of their disciples.

But when? “For the day of Christ,” that is, the day of judgment. For then the good preacher will hear: “Be over ten cities,” or “five cities” (Luke 19:17). Then it will be revealed that they did not labor in vain. Now they seem, in the eyes of unbelievers, to labor in vain, but then it will be shown that by preaching they acquired many people for the Lord.

Notice that “I labored” is a general term, while “I ran” is a specific one.

It follows: “But even if I am offered,” and so forth. The meaning is: If I am killed, because I have offered to God the sacrifice and service of your faith, the joy of your salvation overcomes the sorrow of my death, since you believed through my preaching. Therefore you too should rejoice and congratulate me in the same way—that is, have the same concern for me as I have for you.

[Note: [Col. 0596D] In the autograph margin it reads here: chapter VII.]

It follows: “But I hope in the Lord Jesus,” and so forth. Notice that after the Epistle he promises to send Timothy. This shows that he has great concern for them.

Notice the gravity with which he makes the promise. For he says: “I hope in the Lord.” And why he is sending him he explains by saying: “So that I too may be encouraged”—that is, so that I may rejoice when I hear of your progress.

Why he is sending this man he explains when he says: “For I have no one so like-minded”—that is, no one who has the same mind. Here you have one reason. You have another: “Who will be sincerely concerned for you”—that is, he must be sent who is dear to me and who will also show concern for you.

It follows: “For all seek what is their own, not what belongs to Jesus Christ”—that is, their own advantages or rest, unwilling to endure tribulation for the salvation of others.

[Col. 0597B] There were many who cared for others, but it happened that at the time when he sent Timothy they had been directed elsewhere, and he had no one with him except hirelings—that is, people seeking their own interests.

It follows: “But you know his proven character,” and so forth. The meaning is: Timothy served with me in the Gospel. But he briefly shows how: as a son serves his father, with charity and devoted love.

Notice that he is not called most dear because he served him in chains and prison, but because he served with him in preaching.

It follows: “I hope, therefore, to send him to you.” Notice that after praising his person, affection, and diligence, he says that he will send such a man, but with the gravity mentioned above: not immediately, however, but when he has seen what concerns him.

[Col. 0597C] It follows: “But I hope,” [Note: [Col. 0597D] The Vulgate reads “I trust.”] and so forth. With great affection and great love he promises to come after Timothy’s arrival, since his own coming will not be without purpose.

[Note: [Col. 0597D] In the autograph margin it reads here: chapter VIII.]

It follows: “But I considered it necessary,” and so forth. Although he had promised Timothy’s arrival, because there would be a delay he meanwhile sends Epaphroditus, whose person he commends.

This is a commendation of his person: “my brother,” he says, and “fellow soldier”—a brother in faith and law, a fellow soldier in the camp, or in teachings. He calls him “your apostle,” that is, one sent to you, because others had been sent to others. For everyone who is sent on account of the Gospel is called an apostle.

He then adds the reason why he is sending him: “because he was longing for you all.” He says this so that they may love Epaphroditus all the more.

It follows: “And he was distressed,” and so forth—that is, he was distressed because of your sorrow, since he had heard that you were excessively saddened on account of his illness. He was troubled by this distress and greatly desired to see you.

It follows: “For indeed he was ill almost to the point of death,” and so forth. Here he shows why he was troubled and distressed: in such an illness, longing and anxiety are great.

“He was ill,” he says, “to the point of death; but God had mercy on him.” Behold, the benefit of God is shown when we are preserved in life. Moreover, we should not hasten toward death. Everything we do here for the sake of life is done well if it benefits both ourselves and others.

It follows: “Do not cause sorrow,” etc.; that is, lest the sadness of imprisonment increase the sadness of desolation. Note that he distinguished the dispatches. But why did he send him? “So that, when you see him again,” etc.; that is, on account of whose absence you were sad. “And I may be without sadness”: I, who had been sad on account of your sadness; or, I who could have been sad over his absence, may become joyful through your consolation. Note that we ought to pray for the life of those through whom others are helped.

It follows: “The more quickly,” etc. But someone asks [Col. 0598B] how he could have fallen ill in the presence of one who raised the dead. Let him know that signs are not for believers but for unbelievers (1 Cor. 14:22). Someone likewise asks how he says that he was sad over the disciple’s illness, when he warns others not to be saddened over those who sleep (1 Thess. 4:12). Let him know that the sadness of despair is one thing, and the sadness of desolation another.

It follows: “Receive him,” etc. He says this either so that they may be more ardent toward him, or on account of those who were less spiritual. “In the Lord”: that is, you who belong to the Lord, receive his servant and love him with all rejoicing.

It follows: “And hold such men in honor”; that is, not only such a man, but all who possess this merit.

[Col. 0598C] But why “with honor”? It follows: “Because for the work of Christ,” etc.; that is, he labored so greatly in preaching that he incurred illness. Alternatively: He handed over his life to me, clinging to me and serving me in chains; or, preaching freely: “His life unto death,” according to the saying, “Whoever loses his life,” etc. (Mark 8:35; Matt. 16:25; Luke 17:33).

It follows: “That he might supply what was lacking on your part,” etc. As though he said: Because I was occupied with others, he completed what was lacking in my service. Alternatively: He himself served me on your behalf.

[Note: [Col. 0597D] In the autograph’s margin, chapter IX is read here.]

(CHAPTER III.) It follows: “Finally, brothers, rejoice in the Lord”; that is, not in the world.

[Col. 0598D] It follows: “To write the same things to you,” etc. That is, it is not burdensome for me to write the same things that I taught, because I understand them to be necessary for you on account of the false preachers, concerning whom he also adds:

[Note: [Col. 0597D] In the autograph’s margin, chapter X is read here.]

It follows: “Beware of dogs,” etc. By these words he warns them to keep away from the Jewish zealots for the Law, because they are workers of iniquity: for what the apostles were building, since they believed salvation to consist in works of the Law, they were attempting to destroy [Note: [Col. 0598D] I have dared to add, even at the risk of the mark of rashness, the words “they were attempting to destroy,” which the sense absolutely required and which are lacking in the autograph; for in the exposition taken from the commentary of Saint Jerome—or rather, of Pelagius—this passage is read as follows: “Beware of evil workers, who are attempting to destroy what we have well built.” [Col. 0599D]].

[Col. 0599A] It follows: “Beware of the concision” [Note: [Col. 0599D] Ambrose has “circumcision.”]. What is “concision” except cutting off? For he designates those who, envying the Gentiles, perverted the Galatians by the wickedness of their arguments, persuading them to be circumcised. He rightly calls them dogs, who first bark and then tear the flesh with a savage bite.

It follows: “For we are the circumcision, who serve the Spirit of God” [Note: [Col. 0599D] The Vulgate has “who serve God in spirit.”]. This concerns the servants of Christ, who circumcise all their senses. As though he said: We cut away every evil from our hearts; but they remove the skin from only one member.

It follows: “And we glory.” In the Law? No. But in Christ Jesus, “and we place no confidence in the flesh”; that is, we do not place our hope in carnal circumcision, as do those who locate their salvation in it. [Col. 0599B] And lest they seem to say this because he himself had no reason for boasting, he added: “Although I myself,” etc.; that is, I too can boast in the flesh, if I wish.

[Note: [Col. 0599D] In the autograph’s margin, chapter XI is read here.]

It follows: “If anyone else thinks he has confidence in the flesh, I have more.” Here he teaches why he has confidence in the flesh: namely, because he is a Jew by circumcision, ancestry, tribe, nation, Law, administration in the Law, and also by zeal and manner of life; yet he says that all these things are loss to him on account of Christ.

It follows: “Circumcised on the eighth day,” etc. By these words he makes clear why he could boast in the flesh more than the others: to show how great his zeal for Judaism had been, he says that he persecuted the Church of God and lived in the Law without reproach. [Col. 0599C] But what I formerly considered gain I understood to be loss to me; and because I recognized that those things had no value at the present time, I therefore regard all of them as worthless, like refuse, on account of Christ—those things by which I had thought to acquire life. I cast them away as impediments for Christ’s sake, and I regard them as dung, so that I may gain Christ. What is “I suffered loss” except “I was made into losses”? [Note: [Col. 0600D] Perhaps “I was made into losses,” that is, I endured losses in my body. Otherwise the interpretation would become more obscure than the text.]

It follows: “And may be found in him,” that is, in Christ, “not having my own righteousness,” that is, the righteousness of the Law; as though he said: My righteousness was connected with my own effort; I believed that I could please God through works of the Law.

It follows: “But that which is through faith in Jesus Christ”: this righteousness, which is through faith in Christ, not that which is from works of the Law.

[Col. 0599D] For what purpose is this righteousness? It follows: “To know him and the power of his resurrection”; that is, so that I may perfectly recognize his benefit and the power of his resurrection—he who rose for this reason, that we might rise—and “the fellowship of his sufferings.” The power of the resurrection is fellowship in sufferings. And because resurrection is the reward of sufferings, resurrection has perhaps therefore been mentioned first.

[Col. 0600A] It follows: “If by any means I may attain,” etc. He speaks of the resurrection of the perfect, not fellowship with the wicked. For he teaches that if in this life we have been companions in suffering, at the resurrection we shall meet the Lord (2 Cor. 1:7; 1 Thess. 4:16).

It follows: “Not as though I had already received,” etc. With respect to the perfection that the saints possess in this life, Paul was perfect; with respect to the future perfection, he was imperfect. Since he had praised the Philippians, lest they become proud or remain sluggish, he says that he is imperfect, so that when they heard this they might say: If the Apostle is not perfect, who among human beings can be perfect in this life?

And therefore it follows: “But I pursue, if I may apprehend,” [Col. 0600B] etc. This man, who was laying waste to the Church of Christ, was apprehended when Jesus appeared to him on the road (Acts 9:3). Note that Christ did not free all his followers from all their sufferings, and in a certain sense apprehended all those who follow him. Therefore the one who follows Christ and wishes to apprehend Christ must follow him in all his sufferings, so that he may apprehend Christ in that very condition in which Christ apprehended him.

[Note: [Col. 0600D] In the autograph’s margin, chapter XII is read here.]

It follows: “I do not consider myself,” etc. Concerning his earlier statement that he had not received and was not perfect, and now that he had not apprehended: with respect to the perfection of the future life, he was imperfect; with respect to comparison with others living in the flesh, he was perfect. But [Col. 0600C] he says that, following the example of an archer, he directs his arrows toward the goal and the mark, lest the arrow’s deviation to one side reveal the archer as inexperienced. He asserts that he forgets what lies behind and stretches toward what is more fitting [Note: [Col. 0600D] The Vulgate has “what lies before,” and this is the better reading. The repetition of the text below also confirms it.]; through this he teaches that past things are to be neglected and future things sought, so that what he considered perfect today may, as he progresses, be found imperfect tomorrow; and so that, remaining not in a stationary position but in the race, we may arrive at perfect righteousness.

Since the Philippians, hearing these things, could say: If the Apostle still calls himself imperfect, how much more imperfect are we? He therefore says that, afflicted by many tribulations, he had not apprehended, because he was still alive; for dying for Christ is a great participation in sufferings. And because he is alive, [Col. 0600D] he says that he has not apprehended. Concerning the interpretation that all temporal things are to be understood by “what lies behind,” and the desire for eternal things by “what lies ahead”: everything that passes is behind; what comes and remains is future.

It follows: “But stretching myself toward what lies before,” etc. As though he said: I know that I progress daily in the house of God, and, not counting my former labor, I hasten toward what lies ahead. For the intention of one who seeks continues until that toward which we strive is apprehended. But the right intention is that which advances [Note: [Col. 0601D] Perhaps “profits” or “progresses.”] toward faith. Faith begins a sure knowledge, which will be perfected not in this life but in that one, when we shall see, etc. (1 Cor. 13:12). Let us therefore think in this way, so that we may know that the outcome of truly seeking is safer than presuming unknown things to be known. Let us seek as though we shall find, and let us find as though we shall seek; for when a person has completed something, then he begins.

It follows: “Therefore, as many as are perfect,” etc. What ought we to think except that we are imperfect and have not yet apprehended? But tell us, Paul, how can you be both perfect and imperfect? This is the true wisdom of human beings: to know that one is imperfect. For [Col. 0601B] the perfection of all the saints in the flesh is imperfect, because perfect perfection cannot exist in this life, in which the flesh desires against the spirit. Here we are commanded not to obey the desires of sin; there it will be that we do not possess desires of sin. Yet, thirsting for that perfect perfection, he calls himself imperfect; and again, knowing that he does not have the will to sin, although he sins unwillingly, he calls himself perfect. The perfect person is one who is not ashamed of his own imperfection.

It follows: “And if you think anything differently,” etc.; that is, if God has revealed something to you in another manner, so that you consider it as belonging to the practice of a better way of life, regard it as God’s gift, lest you become inflated.

And lest presumption arise here, and what had not been revealed by God be thought to have been revealed, he therefore added: “Nevertheless, let us think the same thing to which we have attained.” That is, in the conduct of faith, do not think outside the rule of discipline; rather, think what is common and honorable in the truth of the Gospel. Alternatively: If there is anything concerning this very matter that we have mentioned which you receive differently, think and understand that it is granted to you. Therefore, you who are perfect, even if you think something less perfectly, wait humbly and ask it of God; for he can reveal it to those who walk. And therefore he adds: “Nevertheless, let us think the same thing to which we have attained.” What is “to which we have attained”? Namely, that, forgetting what lies behind, we strive toward what lies before. For this he repeats here by saying: “Let us walk in the same way.” To those who walk, what is lacking is thus revealed.

[Note: [Col. 0601D] In the autograph’s margin, chapter XIII is read here.]

It follows: “Be imitators of me,” that is, of the things that I do or teach.

It follows: “And observe those,” etc. This concerns the two meanings of “observe”: either to imitate, as here; or to avoid, as in Romans: “Observe those who cause dissensions and offenses” (Rom. 16:17).

It follows: “For many walk,” etc. Here he marks out the false apostles. Heretics are also marked out [Note: [Col. 0601D] Especially Jovinianus.], [Col. 0602A] who turned bodily torture into feasting and luxury.

It follows: “But now I tell you even weeping,” etc. Note how great his love was. He instructs not only his own but also mourns for outsiders. Those who rejoice when their own are perishing are far removed from his concern.
