He explains whom he mourns: “Enemies,” he says, “of the cross of Christ.” These are those who do not understand, according to the Gospel, Christ as passible and impassible, uncircumscribed and local, eternal and temporal. Alternatively: They are “enemies of the cross of Christ” who either do not believe that he died, or, thinking that he was merely a human being, mock his cross, which became the salvation of humanity.

It follows: “Whose end is destruction”; that is, the end of the false [Col. 0602B] apostles and heretics. Because he was filled with the Holy Spirit, he knew that they would persist in evil, something not granted to others to know; and therefore we should not judge hidden matters.

It follows: “Whose god is the belly.” Why is the belly their god? Because they preached for the sake of food; or because they believed that God took pleasure in the consumption of clean foods. “Their glory,” however, we say, “is in their shame,” because they gloried in their shameful members, and because they are those who set their minds on earthly things and therefore trust in carnal circumcision.

It follows: “But our citizenship,” etc. As though he said: O Philippians, you have been so cautious that you have not been led astray by false teachers, but have conducted yourselves with us in heaven. Note that a person who says that he dwells in heaven is still in the flesh, because in one place he was detained by the flesh, while in another he was present in mind. Note that this peace [Note: [Col. 0601D] Perhaps the word is “voice,” that is, “speech”; for our author often uses “voice” for “speech.” Nowhere does he mention peace.] does not belong to the wicked. Therefore it must be seen to it that we do, speak, and think such things as accord with them.

It follows: “From there also,” etc.; that is, from heaven. For he ascended there. From there we believe that he will come, after the example of the people who awaited the priest to emerge from the Holy of Holies. Whom? The one “who will refashion,” etc. That is, by rising he gave hope of resurrection, since what we possess in hope we shall possess in reality after the resurrection has been accomplished: when the mortal puts on immortality, etc. (1 Cor. 15:53). And lest you despair that a human being will rise from dust, he added: “According to the operation by which he was able” [Note: [Col. 0602D] The Vulgate has “by which he is also able” instead of “by which he was able.”] “to subject all things to himself.” Then the conformity will take place, when, having been made like him, we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2).

It follows (CHAPTER IV): “Therefore, my most beloved brothers,” etc. By these words he warns them to remain in the same faith, which cannot happen unless they have one love. O Philippians, if you do this, you will be my glory and crown: glory in the present, crown in the future. For in the progress of good hearers there is joy for preachers.

It follows: “I urge Euodia” [Note: [Col. 0602D] The Vulgate has “Euodia”; elsewhere “Euhodia.” It is uncertain whether the person was a man or a woman, for some manuscripts have the masculine name “Euodius”; but the printed editions and nearly all manuscripts have the feminine name “Euodia,” Εὐωδίαν. Some maintain that Syntyche was a man and Euodia his wife. Nevertheless, in the Martyrology, among the holy women, on July 22, Syntyche is listed. Therefore the more common opinion is that they were two women.], etc. This concerns women who possessed knowledge, whom he invites to greater prudence, so that just as they had progressed in the works of the Gospel, they might also progress in knowledge. He rightly says that they should think the same thing “in the Lord,” that is, correctly perceive and understand the things written concerning Christ.

It follows: “I also ask you,” etc. Germanus was a proper name [Note: [Col. 0603C] Nevertheless, in the printed edition we commonly see it printed with a lowercase initial, as though “germani” were a common noun rather than a proper name.], and he was a companion of equal dignity, just as Epaphroditus is called Paul’s fellow soldier. Note that he does not say, “I command.” Here teachers are instructed to teach good hearers by addressing them rather than commanding them. And he rightly says: “They labored with me in the Gospel,” either by working or by teaching—teaching, that is, not among men but among women, not in the church but in the home. “Together with Clement and my other helpers.” This Clement was a man of great learning, formerly a philosopher, and presided over the Roman Church [Col. 0603B] [Note: [Col. 0603D] More should be said about this saint than concerns us here. Nevertheless, it will not be out of place to say that the better part of the Fathers and interpreters have wished this to refer to the Clement who presided over the Roman Church after Saints Linus and Cletus. Grotius considers this Clement to have been merely a presbyter of the Philippian Church. The things reported about him in his Life, in the book of the Recognitions, and in the Apostolic Constitutions are more numerous; but the critics have sufficiently discussed the authority of those books. Saint Chrysostom, Homily 1 on 1 Timothy, maintains that this Clement was the Apostle’s constant companion. Saint Irenaeus, Saint Clement of Alexandria, Origen, and other ancient writers attest that he was a disciple of the apostles. Saint Epiphanius, Saint Jerome, Rufinus, Bede, and others write that Peter and Paul, occupied with their journeys, entrusted the Roman Church to him, Linus, and Anacletus, after appointing them bishops [Col. 0604C]. Indeed, Rufinus reports that the Apostle Peter chose him as his successor. In the Constitutions, book VII, chapter 46, we read that Saint Linus was ordained by Saint Paul. Saint Epiphanius, however, thinks that this Clement was chosen bishop of Rome by Peter, voluntarily resigned that office, and was compelled to resume it after the deaths of Saints Linus and Anacletus. This opinion is commonly embraced by writers, so that Linus succeeded Saint Peter, Anacletus Linus, and Clement Anacletus, in the year of Christ 91, the tenth year of Domitian; Irenaeus, book III, chapter 3; Eusebius, book III, chapters 3, 4, and 21, Ecclesiastical History. See Calmet, Dictionary of Sacred Scripture, under “Clement.” A copy of the book of the Recognitions of this holy Clement is preserved in a very ancient codex in the archive of the Vercellian Eusebian chapter.]. And he rightly says: “Whose names are in the book of life,” so that it may not matter that they are not written in this Epistle [Note: [Col. 0604D] In the codex it is read, “so that they may not mention.” Perhaps it should have been written, “so that they may not take offense,” according to the exposition frequently attributed to Saint Jerome, which reads: “So that they might not be troubled by their names,” etc.]. This concerns the fact that Moses (Exod. 17:14), David (Ps. 39:8; 68:29), and the Savior in the Gospel (John 20:30; 21:25) mention this book; for those who save themselves and others by admonishing them are the apostles’ helpers.

[Note: [Col. 0604D] In the autograph’s margin, chapter XIV is read here.]

From this spiritual commendation he passes to a general admonition when he says: “Rejoice in the Lord,” etc. Because the Apostle was joyful at their works and faith, he urges them, for the increase of joy [Note: [Col. 0604D] The preposition “for” is lacking; the frequently cited exposition of Saint Ambrose, or of Hilary the deacon, suggested that it be added, where it reads “for the increase,” etc.], to rejoice themselves also. But where? “In the Lord”: that is, not in the world, and not at intervals of time, as some understand it; rather, always—that is, in prosperity, in adversity, and in all the other circumstances ordinarily mentioned in this connection.

[Col. 0603C] It follows: “Let your moderation,” etc. This concerns the word “moderation,” so called because it keeps to a measure. It greatly contributes to the merit of future life if we live moderately. And when he says “in all things,” he means both when Jews and Gentiles are persecuting, so that your moderation may convert them.

It follows: “The Lord is near,” etc. This is a great exhortation. Since the end of each person and the day of judgment are imminent, we ought to hasten to live with good morals and great moderation. Or, because the Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth (Ps. 144:18), you ought not to be anxious about worldly affairs, because God both provides all that is necessary for you and gives better things in the life that is to come. Or: Do not fear your persecutors, because the Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart (Ps. 33:19).

It follows: “But in every prayer,” etc. Prayer is for obtaining what we hope for; supplications are for past or present sins; thanksgivings are praises for benefits bestowed. All of these are contained in the office of the Mass.

[Col. 0604B] It follows: “Let your petitions,” etc.; that is, whoever asks should ask for such things as it is fitting for a believer to ask, since the things we do are already known to God; and, as we have said, they should be made known in such a way that they are things fitting for a faithful and righteous man.

It follows: “The peace of God,” etc. This has been stated with great force and precision. For when the peace of God comes into us, we shall understand God; and when we have understood God, we shall do nothing dissonant or perverse as before, but everything will be so peaceful that all our understanding will be with us. Peace means now to rest and possess security. God grants us this peace when all understanding is already with us. For the one who understands God understands everything; and by understanding everything, he possesses the peace of God, through which the heart [Col. 0604C] and all the inner parts of the heart are guarded. Note that he says: “Let your petitions be made known.” This knowledge is produced by persistence and vigilance in prayer. Then, after speaking of the fortifications of his peace, which surpass every mind, he says: “It will guard your hearts.” He says this because the one who has peace with God [Note: [Col. 0604D] The word “peace” is lacking; Saint Ambrose’s exposition, whose words these are, suggested that it be added [Col. 0605D].] does not fear every hostile mind.

[Col. 0605A] [Note: [Col. 0605D] In the autograph’s margin, chapter XV is read here.]

“Finally, brothers,” etc. What does “finally” mean except: After you have come to know these things, think in such a way that you receive and consider whatever things are true? What are those true things? Certainly, those spoken in the Gospel. It follows that what is true is chaste, for truth is not corrupted; and what is not corrupted is chaste. Then the things that are true and chaste are also just. Next he enumerates things that are lovely and of good reputation, although one does not love according to the good that is spoken of one. Likewise, things of good reputation do not contain envy. Of all these, the former belong to virtue itself, while the latter belong to the fruit of virtue. Virtue is loving what is true, chaste, just, and holy; the fruit of virtue is what is lovely and of good reputation. Therefore he adds these two: “If there is any virtue, if there is any praise.” But just as virtue does not come from us, so neither does our praise come from us, but from God. “Think about these things”—namely, those things that you learned through my teaching. It follows: “And received”; again, from where did you receive them? “You heard and saw”; that is, you heard them from me and saw them in me. He says this because he was not merely an admonisher but an example of every good thing. It follows: “Do these things.” Above he had said, “Think”; for good thought is not sufficient without action [Note: [Col. 0605D] The words “it follows … without action” are written in the lateral margin.].

It follows: “And the God of peace will be with you.” Note that this reward was especially necessary for the Philippians: namely, that they should all think as one and thereby have with them God, who loves and teaches peace.

[Note: [Col. 0606D] In the autograph’s margin, chapter XVI is read here.]

It follows: “I rejoiced greatly in the Lord,” etc.; that is, you bloomed again with the flower of good work, which had not withered through forgetfulness but had been impeded by occupation. And therefore he adds: “For you were occupied.”

It follows: “Not as though because of want,” etc. What is implied is: so that you might send me what is necessary for me. The sense is: I do not say this, he says, because of want; for I do not wish you to think on my behalf what you thought previously—that I wanted you to send things to me—or that what I now want you to send is being requested because of want. For afterward he says: “Not because I seek the gift, but I seek the abundant fruit in your account” [Note: [Col. 0606D] The Vulgate has “in your reckoning,” and likewise elsewhere.] (below, 4:17). I do not therefore seek this because of poverty, but so that there may be abundant fruit in your account.

It follows: “For I have learned in whatever state I am to be sufficient.” I have learned to be content with what I have and to be sufficient for myself [Col. 0605D] in whatever condition I am [Note: [Col. 0606D] The words “I have learned … to be sufficient” are written in the lateral margin.]. This should not be referred only to expense, but to everything that one person can provide for another. Accordingly, he included here not merely money but all necessities.

It follows: “I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound; everywhere,” etc. To suffer want is common to all kinds of people, but to know how to suffer want belongs to the great. Likewise, anyone can abound; but to know how to abound [Col. 0606A] belongs only to those whom abundance does not corrupt.

It follows: “I can do all things,” etc. He testifies that he does not rejoice in their work for his own sake, but rejoices in their progress. Blessed Pope Gregory says that unless it were an art to know how to abound and to hunger, and other things of this sort, the Apostle would not say so emphatically, “I know” or “I have learned.” Note that he attributes these things not to himself but to the Lord. “I can do all things,” he says—not some things—“in him who strengthens me,” not in myself. This manner of conduct must also be observed by the faithful: they should place their ability in divine strength.

It follows: “Nevertheless, you did well”; that is, you became participants or came to my aid in tribulation, because my composure ought not to have prevented your reward. Note that he was not among those who seek what is their own; for he says that he does not seek the gift but seeks the fruit. Those who can imitate him should rejoice; those who cannot should support their own needs from the milk of their sheep, but should not neglect the weakness of their sheep.

[Note: [Col. 0606D] In the autograph’s margin, chapter XVII is read here.]

It follows: “You also know,” etc. Here he openly explains what was said above: “You shared in my tribulation,” that is, you provided assistance by supplying necessities. But when he says “in the account of giving and receiving,” this should not be understood as though the one who received had himself given something; rather, when a gift is given, there is an account of giving and receiving. What money could Paul have given? But since the account of giving and receiving belongs to money, he continues: “For even to Thessalonica,” [Col. 0606C] etc. Behold, he shows that he knew how devoted they had been in their service: they had ministered not only to the Apostle preaching among his own people, but also when he was far away.

And lest he seem to say this because he wanted to receive something from them, he added: “Not because I seek the gift, but I seek the fruit.” I do not seek, he says, even these necessities, but the fruit of your goodwill. He calls the thing itself “the gift,” and devotion “the fruit.” Hence he also adds: “I have all things and abound”; that is, I do not seek the gift because I have everything. And many have everything, but do not abound.

Finally, he continues in order to show the abundance: “I have been filled by what I received from Epaphroditus.” Lest what abounds seem to belong to someone else, he says that it also belongs to those who sent it. [Col. 0606D] “I have been filled,” he says, “when I received what you sent through Epaphroditus.” Just as above he seeks nothing except the fruit, so here too, when he says that he has been filled, he does not rejoice in the things sent but in the devotion of those who sent them. And “an odor of sweetness” is not in the thing offered but in the devotion of the mind, just as Noah’s sacrifice is said to have been “an odor of sweetness” (Gen. 8:21), although God does not take pleasure in the flesh and blood of animals. He does not say these things without reason: the gift seemed to have been made either less carefully [Col. 0607A] or less generously than was customary for them, so that, by recalling their former works, they might know that they had done less than they had begun to do. Note that almsgiving is called a sacrifice; and just as an offering made by saints is accepted, so an offering made by the wicked is rejected. Having finished his account of almsgiving, he prays for them.

[Note: [Col. 0607B] In the autograph’s margin, chapter XVIII is read here.]

It follows: “But my God.” Note that this is the voice of the righteous, whose God he is by grace. He speaks of their desire because he knew that their hearts were good. He says “according to his riches,” not according to the riches of the world. God’s riches are spiritual. And he says “in glory, and in Christ,” in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. Note that this blessing is not inferior to the blessings of the patriarchs.

It follows: “Now to God and the Father,” etc. To God the Father be glory, [Col. 0607B] and in Christ Jesus let there be eternal glory for him—that glory which is owed to both persons together with the Holy Spirit, who is one God. This concerns the fact that, having finished the Epistle with praise, he passes to the salutation.

[Note: [Col. 0607B] In the autograph’s margin, chapter XIX is read here.]

It follows: “Greet every saint.” It is a fearful thing that he greets only the saints. He calls them saints because they are free from crimes, not from sins [Note: [Col. 0607B] Here he establishes the distinction between crime and sin, or the desire of sin, which he also sets forth elsewhere [Col. 0608B].]. It follows: “All the brothers who are with me greet you”—with me in the flesh, with you in mind. The saints of more eminent merit also greet you, but especially those who are of Caesar’s household. Why does he single these out? Because he wished to show them as more devoted, and so that, when they heard that powerful people had come to faith, they might become more joyful; as though he said: Do not fear preaching the Gospel, whose power is so great that even those who could have been proud, putting aside the world’s arrogance, have taken upon themselves Christ’s humble yoke.

“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ,” etc. Because there were various questions concerning Christ, to confirm the solidity of Christ’s divinity he earnestly asks that his grace be with their spirit. This concerns grace, by which sins are forgiven; he wishes it to be with their spirit because the inner person is nobler than the outer.

“Amen” confirms everything he had said above, because “amen” means “true.” For it is exceedingly impious to doubt in any respect the words of so great a Teacher.

[THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS.]

[Col. 0607]

HERE BEGINS THE SUMMARY OF THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS [Note: [Col. 0607D] This title is written in letters which, as they say, are partly capital and partly contained within the body of the text.].

[Col. 0607C] 1. Because he prays for them, praising their faith: that they have been made worthy to share in the lot of the saints in Christ, in whom all things have been created, whether thrones, etc.

2. Because, although they were enemies, they have been reconciled to God for service, which had been hidden from the ages, and while teaching every person; and because all the treasures are hidden in Christ.

3. So that they may not be deceived by philosophy, since they have been buried with Christ in baptism. He has erased the bond written against us. And let no one judge you in food or drink. And so that they may not be led astray in the humility of angels.

4. If you have died to the elements, why do you still make judgments as though you were living? And think on the things above. And mortify the members that are upon the earth. And put on the new human being, where there is neither Gentile nor Jew.

5. If anyone has anything against another, let him forgive. And let there be psalms and hymns [Note: [Col. 0607D] It is written “vmnis.”]. And let everything be done in the name of the Lord. And let women be subject to their husbands, and let husbands love their wives; let children and servants obey.

6. Prayer must be persevered in for him; and one must walk in wisdom toward those who are outside, and let speech be seasoned with salt. And concerning those whom he greets.

[Note: [Col. 0608D] All the titles that follow in this Epistle are written in what are called uncial letters in the autograph.]

WHICH SAINTS THE APOSTLE PAUL MENTIONS IN THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS.

[Col. 0607]

[Col. 0607D] Epaphras, whom he says is a faithful minister from among them, and Tychicus, whom he calls a most beloved brother.

Onesimus, a most beloved and faithful brother, whom he says was one of them. Aristarchus, whom he calls his fellow prisoner.

[Col. 0608D] Mark, Barnabas’s cousin, concerning whom they had received instructions. And Jesus, who is called Justus. These are helpers from the circumcision.

Luke, the most beloved physician. And Demas; Nympha, and the churches in her house. Archippus, whom he admonishes to look to the ministry that he received.

ARGUMENT TO THE COLOSSIANS.

[Col. 0609]

[Col. 0609A] The Colossians, like the Laodiceans, are Asians. They too had been anticipated [Note: [Col. 0609A] The codex has “to be supplied.”] by false apostles. The Apostle himself did not visit them; but he corrects them through the Epistle. For they had heard the word from Archippus, who had also received the ministry among them. Therefore the Apostle, already bound, writes to them from Ephesus [Note: [Col. 0609A] Perhaps “from Onesimus” should be read instead of “from Ephesus,” namely, because the Epistle was sent through him and Tychicus. Or, more consistently with the truth, “and” should be read instead of “from,” so that it reads: “He writes to them, and from Ephesus.” For these two Epistles—or rather, the Epistle to the Philippians—are considered to have been written and sent from Rome while he was in chains, just as shortly afterward this one is specifically said in our codex to have been “written from Rome.” This cannot in any way be reconciled with the words “from Ephesus.” This will become clearer from what is found somewhat below in the argument of the Epistles, where it is asserted that the phrase “to those who are in Colossae” has been wrongly written as “from Ephesus.”].

The Epistle to the Colossians, written from Rome, ends here. It contains 208 verses.

HERE BEGINS THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS.

[Col. 0609]

ARGUMENT.

[Col. 0609A]

False apostles were striving to overthrow the Colossians, [Col. 0609B] who sought, after Epaphras’s or Archippus’s preaching, to entangle the simplicity of their minds in philosophical arguments. The Apostle warns them not to place their hope in the principles of the elements, by which human life is, as it were, governed. For this reason the Apostle exhorts and admonishes them through the Epistle not to think that hope exists anywhere apart from Christ, lest they be deceived [Note: [Col. 0609D] This argument, so that we may assign each part to its proper author, has been taken almost word for word from Saint Ambrose, or Hilary. I say “almost” because there is a difference in several words, namely in the passage that Saint Ambrose’s text has as follows: “they should entangle the simplicity of their minds, lest they despise the principles of the elements, by which, as it were, the governor,” and so forth. In that text, the words “lest they despise the principles,” etc., seem to present this as an admonition of the false apostles. In our text, however, after the words “the simplicity of their minds,” [Col. 0610D] one reads: “The Apostle admonishes them not to hope in the expressions of the elements, by which, as it were,” etc. Here the admonition “not to hope” belongs to the Apostle. It seemed necessary, however, to correct *nec* (“nor”) and read *ne* (“lest”), for the sake of elegance of expression. We have also judged that *in orationes* (“in expressions”) should be read *in rationibus* (“in principles”). For what are “the expressions of the elements”? What hope is there in them? The Epistle’s text itself, as well as Saint Ambrose’s cited argument, speaks of the principles of the elements.]

[INCIPIT TEXTUS.]

(CAP. I.) Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Timothy, a brother. In the other Epistles, Sosthenes and Silvanus are sometimes included, and at times Timothy as well. Timothy appears in only four, because either they were dictated at the same time, or the other Epistles too were dictated in Timothy’s presence. This is thought to have happened for two reasons: both so that the Epistle might possess greater authority, since it was not written by one man alone, and because the Apostle had no jealousy if, while he was dictating, the Holy Spirit happened to suggest something to others. Without any sadness, Paul would add to the letters he was dictating, in accordance with what he himself instructed the Corinthians: “If something is revealed to another while another is prophesying, let the first one be silent” (I Cor. XIV, 30). Thus he himself also fulfilled his own command by his actions; and, because others had suggested a few things, he dictated both his own words and those of another as his writing.

To those who are in Colossae. The Colossians, like the Laodiceans, are Asians. They had heard the word of the Gospel from Archippus, who had also received the ministry among them. The Apostle himself had not come to them, but wrote to them—not from Ephesus, as is mistakenly found written in the arguments of the Epistles, but from Rome, from prison. [Col. 0610A] First, he praises them, saying that he has heard of their great faith. Then he warns them not to be led astray either by philosophy or by the ceremonies of the Law.

[Col. 0610B] To the holy and faithful brothers in Christ Jesus. Grace to you and peace from God our Father. Not every faithful person is holy, since catechumens too can be called faithful because they believe in Christ, although they are not yet holy, having been sanctified through baptism. This may nevertheless be understood in another and perhaps better way: that he calls the priests and ministers of the Church holy, while the rest of the faithful multitude are called faithful. We give thanks to God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, always praying for you. He begins with praise of God, because God has granted them the gifts described below.

Hearing of your faith in Christ Jesus. This too has been placed with the greatest care for the sake of distinction: there are many faithful people, but not in Christ Jesus. And of the love that you have for all the saints. It should certainly be noted that, just as he subtly rebukes the Corinthians for their stinginess, so he praises these people for the generosity of their love. For the proof of love is the exhibition of a deed.

Because of the hope that has been laid up for you in heaven. As though he were saying: The more intensely you love God in heaven, the more abundantly you bestow good things upon your neighbors on earth, since you know that you are storing up treasure there “where moth does not corrupt, and where thieves do not break in and steal” (Matt. VI, 20).

Which you heard in the word of the truth of the Gospel. What he had earlier called “the word of truth,” he now repeats as “the Gospel,” because truly no other preaching is true except that which is supported by the authority of the Gospel.

[Col. 0610D] Which has come to you, just as it is in the whole world, [Col. 0611A] and bears fruit and grows, just as it does among you. Although the Gospel had not yet possessed the whole world, he said that it bore fruit and grew throughout the whole world, in order thereby to signify how far it would eventually come through bearing fruit and growing. If, then, it is hidden from us when the entire world, as the Church bears fruit and grows, will be filled from sea to sea, it is undoubtedly also hidden from us when the end will be; for it will not come beforehand. For this reason he eagerly continues, as an example of the other nations, [Note: [Col. 0611D] In accordance with Saint Ambrose’s text, from which this exposition was borrowed, Following Saint Ambrose’s text, from which this exposition was borrowed, I thought that the reading should be: “for this reason these people grow as an example of the other nations”; whereas in the autograph it read only: “for this reason these people grow among the other nations,” and so forth.] to speak of their growth and the production of living fruit, so that, having received the grace of God, they might advance both in number and in works, adding to their faith those who, drawn by the example of their good works, would become their brothers in Christ.

[Col. 0611B] From the day on which you heard and recognized the grace of God in truth. That person recognizes the grace of God in truth who is not ungrateful for God’s grace: who attributes nothing to his own merits if he does anything worthy, but gives glory to the One whose gift is whatever goodness exists in human beings.

Just as you learned from Epaphras, our most beloved fellow servant, who is a faithful minister of Christ Jesus on your behalf. This Epaphras is the same person who is called Epaphroditus in the Epistle to the Philippians [Note: [Col. 0611D]

Philipp. II, 25, and IV, 18. I do not know what reasoning led our author to confuse Epaphras with Epaphroditus and merge two persons into one. For according to Theodoret, Epaphroditus was bishop of the Philippians, or, as Saint Paul calls him at Philipp. II, 25, the apostle of the Philippians. Perhaps he was even one of them; at least he was very well known and dear to them, as can be seen from verse 26 of the same chapter, and he was at times their envoy to the Apostle, as we infer from the same Epistle, IV, 18, and the bearer of the apostolic Epistle. Among the Greeks his feast is celebrated on the eighth or ninth day of December, and additionally on March 29 and 30; he is also listed among the apostles, or the seventy-two disciples, as well as among the bishops of Andriaca or Andraca. Let us pass over in silence Epaphroditus, bishop of Tarracina, initiated by Saint Paul, whom it is not established to be the same as this man; he is mentioned in a sermon attributed to Metaphrastes and in the Roman Martyrology on March 22.

This Epaphras, however, was from Colossae, as is made entirely clear from the Epistle to the Colossians IV, 12. Indeed, he is believed to have been their first bishop, a view for which the Apostle provides grounds both in the cited chapter and in chapter I, 7 of the same Epistle. He is also mentioned in the Epistle to Philemon, verse 23, and in the Martyrologies on July 19, where it is related that he suffered martyrdom at Colossae.]

He was the one who ministered to them the grace of Christ in the place of the Apostle, whose person he commends by praising him and saying: “Our most beloved fellow servant.” He then adds the reason: “Who is a faithful minister of Christ Jesus on your behalf.”

He also made your love known to us in the Spirit. He praises them in every respect because they were merciful toward those who had set out from the circumcision for the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, to preach from nation to nation and from kingdom to another people. Hence he continues:

For this reason, from the day on which we heard, we too have not ceased praying for you and asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will. Hearing of their devoted and eager disposition toward the faith of Christ, the Apostle prays for them, so that, having more fully recognized the will of God, they might complete through rational action the devotion they had learned after hearing the faith of Christ, lest the faithful building of their mind [Note: [Col. 0612D] In the manuscript it reads: “nor so faithful a building of the mind, and strength,” etc. I have restored the correct reading by correcting the error through the work of Saint Ambrose, or Hilary, whose verse this is.] and the strength of their faith, if they undertook something rashly and unskillfully, should lose the fruit of their labor. For that which is done with a devoted mind and prudently is readily accepted.

[Col. 0612A] In all wisdom and spiritual understanding. He prays for the Colossians, as he does for all the churches, that they may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding. He explained what he had said obscurely: how God grants the will, assists and strengthens it, both by inspiring and by teaching; granting wisdom and understanding through his grace, and restoring and strengthening freedom of choice through his constant grace.

So that you may walk worthily of God, pleasing him in every way; bearing fruit in every good work and growing in the knowledge of God; strengthened with every power according to the might of his glory, in all patience and long-suffering with joy. See how the good teacher gradually raises them to higher things, so that they may walk worthily of God, [Col. 0612B] pleasing him in every way—that is, persevering in every good work. Then he has them bear fruit through the growth of virtues and grow, not in bodily form, but in the knowledge of God. After this he adds: “Strengthened with every power according to the might of his glory, in all patience and long-suffering with joy.” All these peaks and rewards of the virtues would invite those whom adversities might otherwise deter. He wants the increase of their works to take place through knowledge, so that they may not be ignorant of the hope of their faith. They are then firm and stable if they understand what has been promised through faith and how great is the power of the glory of God’s majesty in patience: that, through long expectation, he bears with the human race, which by its irreverence not only neglected the Creator but also persecutes those who love him. They too must therefore be patient, bearing insults and curses if oppression should come, awaiting God’s judgment and not doubting concerning it, but rather rejoicing with thanksgiving to God in the promised life, as he says:

Giving thanks to God the Father. Why, and for what reason? Explaining this, he added: “Who has made us worthy to share in the lot of the saints in light.” As though he were saying: He has deigned to summon and bring the nations into the promise of the Jews, which is eternal light—that is, everlasting truth. The Apostle sometimes uses darkness to signify unbelief and light to signify faith, as he says elsewhere: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephes. V, 8)—that is, you were once unbelievers, but now you are believers through the Lord. We frequently find “lot” used to mean inheritance in the Holy Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0613D] Among many other examples, where Joshua divided the land by lot.].

Who delivered us from the power of darkness. For, liberated from the condition of darkness—that is, rescued from the power of unclean spirits and the fellowship of the wicked, by whom we were held because of Adam’s own sin [Note: [Col. 0613D] Saint Ambrose has “both from our own sin and from the sin of Adam, who is the father,” etc., in his treatment of this text. Therefore either “from our own sin and from Adam’s sin” should be read, or we must suppose that our expositor intended to speak only of original sin, which passed into all human beings and became the personal sin of each one, and thus subjected us to the devil.], who is the father of all sinners—we have been transferred through faith into the heavenly kingdom of the Son of God, as he adds next.

And transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love [Note: [Col. 0613D] So Saint Ambrose. The Vulgate, however, has *dilectionis* (“love”) instead of *charitatis* (“love”).]. He wished to show us with what love God loves us, when, lifting us from the depths of Tartarus, he brought us into heaven with his true Son. Even now all believers who are devoted with steadfast minds, departing from the world and guided by the angel of the right hand, are brought into [Col. 0613B] heaven, which had not been granted before death was conquered. He did not say “of his Son”; if he had said that, he would have spoken most truly, just as he has spoken most truly wherever he often said it. But he says: “of the Son of his love.” Therefore the Son is also the Holy Spirit, if there is no love of God in that Trinity except the Holy Spirit. But since that is utterly absurd, it remains that the Holy Spirit is not the only one who is love there, but that he is properly called so for the reasons I have sufficiently discussed [Note: [Col. 0613D] Namely, in the earlier Epistles, where he discussed the Trinity, especially in the Epistle to the Romans.]. What has been said—“the Son of his love”—should be understood as nothing other than “his Son,” and finally [Note: [Col. 0613D] “Finally,” that is, as the final and truer interpretation [Col. 0614D] it should be understood as “the Son of his substance,” because the Father’s love, and the other matters that follow.] “the Son of his substance.” For the love of the Father, which is in his ineffably simple nature, is nothing other than his very nature and substance, as we have often said and are not reluctant to repeat often. Accordingly, the Son of his love is none other than the one begotten from his substance.

In whom we have redemption [Note: [Col. 0614D] The Vulgate has “redemption through his blood.” In the text, however, “through his blood” is not found, although the exposition of the text mentions the blood of Christ. Saint Ambrose, Saint Chrysostom, and Jerome, or Pelagius, likewise do not have “through his blood” in the text. It is also worth noting Saint Chrysostom’s observation that in the Greek text not merely λύτρωσιν (*lytrosin*, “redemption”), but ἀπολύτρωσιν (*apolytrosin*, specifically “full and complete redemption”), is read, so that we might no longer perish or become mortal.], the forgiveness of sins. In this redemption the blood of Christ was given as a price for us. When the devil received it, he was not enriched but bound, so that we might be released from his chains. For the forgiveness of sins makes us free, so that, freed from our debts, we cannot be held liable. For no one has been saved without the faith of Christ.

Who is the image of the invisible God. Image, equality, and likeness must be distinguished. Where there is an image, as in a mirror, there is immediately likeness, but not immediately equality, as in equal eggs. Where there is equality, there is immediately likeness, but not immediately an image. Where there is likeness, there is not immediately an image or equality, as with eggs of different kinds; in a mirror there is [Col. 0614A] an image, because it has been expressed from the thing reflected. Likeness is necessary, but not equality, because many things belonging to the original are absent from the image [Note: [Col. 0614D] In the autograph, *desunt* (“are absent”) was read as *sunt* (“are present”), which the sense showed must be corrected.]. Where there is equality, there is immediately likeness, but not immediately an image, as with two equal eggs: there is equality and there is likeness, since whatever is present in one is present in the other; yet there is no image, because neither has been expressed from the other. Where there is likeness, there is not immediately an image or equality: every egg is like every other egg insofar as it is an egg, but although a partridge egg is like a hen’s egg insofar as it is an egg, it is not its image, because it was not expressed from it; nor is it equal, because it is smaller and belongs to another kind of animal.

There can therefore be an image in which there is also equality, as is found in parents and children: there is an image in which there are both equality and likeness, if the interval of time were absent. For the likeness of the son has been expressed from the parent, so that it is rightly called an image, and it can be so great that it may rightly also be called equality, except that the parent precedes in time. From this it is understood that equality can sometimes possess not only likeness but also an image, as was shown in the preceding example. There can also sometimes be likeness and equality even though there is no image, as we said of equal eggs. There can be likeness and an image even though there is no equality, as we showed in the mirror. There can also be likeness where there are equality and an image, as we mentioned in the case of children, except for the time by which parents precede them. Thus we call one syllable equal to another even though one comes before and the other follows.

In God, however, since the condition of time is absent—for it cannot rightly be thought that God begot the Son in time, since through him he created time—it follows that the Son is not merely his image, because he is from him, and likeness, because he is an image, but also equality, and such equality that not even an interval of time can impede it.

The firstborn of all creation. He testifies that the Son was begotten before every creature, not created, in order to distinguish his birth from the making of creation. And to make this completely clear, he added:

Because in him all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible. This is what the evangelist John testifies at the beginning of his Gospel, IV, 3, saying: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” For if none of the created things was made without him, it is plainly evident that he himself is not a creature, through whom every creature was made. But it must be understood that whatever is believed to have been made through him is also ruled and sustained through him.

According to the flesh, he was made first of every rational creature. He says “firstborn,” not “first-created,” so that he may be believed to have been begotten by nature and first in perpetuity. Or certainly, “firstborn from the dead” (below, verse 18), because he was the first to rise. And to explain more openly what and how great the Son’s power is according to divinity, he shows what things exist through him: thrones, dominions, principalities, powers. All things were created through him and in him; and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him. Thus it is to be believed that there is absolutely nothing less in him than there is in the Father.

And he is before all things. [Col. 0615B] So it is, because he alone was born from God the Father, from God’s unbegotten substance. Through his power, which possesses generation, the other creatures came into being from the Father—not so that they might share substance with him, but from nothing, by the will of God the Father, they began through the Son.

For the “thrones” are those hosts over which almighty God perpetually presides in order to exercise judgment. Since in Latin we call thrones *seats*, those are called thrones who are filled with so great a grace of divinity that the Lord sits in them and issues his judgments through them. Hence the Psalmist also says: “You sit upon the throne, judging equity” (Ps. IX, 5). But when he says, “and all things hold together in him,” this is to be understood as follows: without him they are nothing; for unless they have been subjected to him, they will become, through wandering error, subject to destruction.

And he is the head of the body, the Church. Christ is the head of the Church, provided that all heavenly and earthly beings have one mind, so that they constitute the Church—that is, are of one faith. Otherwise, severed from the head, that is, from the Creator of all bodies and of the whole body [Note: [Col. 0615D] Either these words have been added incorrectly, or something is missing that disrupts the sentence, although the author’s meaning is sufficiently clear [Col. 0616D].], they rave in a kind of madness and vanity. For just as the head has many members subject to it, so our Lord Jesus Christ, since he is the head of the Church, has as his members all those who are gathered into the Church.

Who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead. That is, through him those things that had become ruined through a certain negligence were to be restored anew, lest it be counted as an injury to him if his work were restored through another; [Col. 0615D] so that, just as he was born before all things, so he might again be first before all through the resurrection by which the former life was restored to the dead. For he was born before all things from God, in order to create what did not exist. Again, he was born in the flesh from the Virgin, in order to abolish the sin that had entered the world through the virgin Eve. Born, therefore, and having died, he rose again, so that he might afterward recreate what he had first made, because through error those things had become as though dead, and so that he might always be first and chief in every life.

Behold two natures indicated [Note: [Col. 0616D] That is, signified.] in the one person of the Lord Jesus Christ: the Beginning, through whom all things were made; the firstborn in grace, because he rose from the dead before all the saints and, having conquered death, now reigns in heaven. He is rightly called the firstborn of these brothers, because in dignity he surpasses all adopted sons, including those who preceded the time of his incarnation by being born.

So that he might hold the first place in everything. For, just as through divinity he is the beginning and head of the angels, so through the assumption of flesh he is the head of all the elect among human beings.

Because in him he was pleased to make all fullness dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself. For the Lord was full of the Holy Spirit, full of grace and truth (John I, 14); from his fullness [Col. 0616B] we have all received according to the measure of our capacity, because grace has been given to each of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift (Ephes. IV, 7). For it could be said of the sole mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and piety; and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. II, 2–3). All the saints, however, do not receive the fullness of his Spirit, but receive from his fullness as much as he grants. “To one,” indeed, “through the Spirit is given the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another the grace of healings in one Spirit; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another the discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of speeches. But all these things one and the same Spirit works, distributing to each as he wills” (I Cor. XII, 8–11).

Therefore, since we have received from the fullness of our Creator not merely some portion but whatever good we possess, we must take the greatest care lest anyone, heedless, exalt himself because of his good action or thought; otherwise, if he remains ungrateful to the giver, he will lose the good he received.

Making peace through the blood of his cross, whether the things on earth or the things in heaven. The things in heaven are made peaceful when what fell among the angels is restored from human beings. The things on earth are restored when the human beings predestined to eternal life are renewed from the oldness of corruption. Thus, through that singular sacrifice in which the Mediator was offered—one sacrifice foreshadowed by the many victims of the Law—the heavenly things are made peaceful with the earthly, and the earthly with the heavenly.

For, as the same Apostle says, “it pleased him to make all fullness dwell in him, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether the things on earth or the things in heaven.” This peace surpasses, as it is written (Phil. IV, 7), all understanding, and cannot be known by us until we have come to it. For how are the heavenly things made peaceful except through us—that is, by being brought into agreement with us? There is always peace there, both among all rational creatures and with their Creator; and, as was said, that peace surpasses all understanding—our understanding, certainly, but not that of those who always see the face of the Father (Matt. XVIII, 10).

As for us, whatever human understanding we may possess, “we know in part, and we see through a mirror, in an enigma” (I Cor. XIII, 12). But when we have become equal to the angels of God, then, like them, we shall see “face to face” (ibid.); and we shall have as much peace toward them as they have toward us, because we shall love them as much as we shall be loved by them. Thus their peace will be known to us, because ours too will be of such a kind and so great; nor will it then surpass our understanding.

The peace of God, however, which is there toward them, surpasses without doubt both their understanding and ours; for every rational creature that is blessed is blessed from him, not he from it. Hence, according to this, what is written is better understood: “the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding.” In saying “all,” even the understanding of the holy angels cannot be excepted—only God’s understanding can be excluded; for his peace does not surpass even his own understanding.

And you, although you were once alienated and enemies in mind through evil works, he has now reconciled in the body of his flesh through death. He recalls what a great gift of God has been granted to the nations, so that he may show that they are deeply indebted to God in thanksgiving. When we were alienated and enemies, God, through his plan by which he decreed to visit the human race, visited and reconciled us in the body of his flesh. He therefore granted all these things so that we might not nullify his benefit and become enemies again, as we once were when we were involved in idols and wicked works. For they worshiped the works they had made.

But the mercy and providence of God sought them out, so that they might obtain God’s grace as a free gift, returning to him with a clean conscience. Thus, on the day of judgment, when no trace of their former error was found in them, they might be joined to their Creator, who, in order to benefit the human race, was made incarnate and became human, so that in his flesh he might conquer death.

To present you holy, immaculate, and irreproachable before him. Behold the virtues in which the preacher of the nations wants them to be conspicuous. Holiness refers to chastity; purity to integrity; irreproachability to prudence: they were to be irreproachable in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation and to shine among them through the work of virtue, like lights in the firmament of heaven. It should be noted that he said that they had once been alienated from God in evil works, not that they were so at the time when he was writing these things.

If indeed you remain grounded and steadfast in the faith and immovable. He wanted them to know that Christ’s passion would benefit them if they remained in the faith they had received; and that they would become immaculate if the perverse teaching [Col. 0618A] or examples of human beings did not deceive them, but if they firmly believed the future things they had heard from the Apostle.

From the hope of the Gospel, which you have heard. Those who do not live according to the Gospel cannot possess the hope of the Gospel. As the same Apostle says elsewhere: “For if we have been planted in the likeness of his death, we shall be planted also in the likeness of his resurrection” (Rom. VI, 5).

Which has been preached in every creature that is under heaven. By the name of “every creature,” every nation of the Gentiles can and should be signified. For earlier the Lord had told the apostles not to go along the road of the Gentiles (Matt. X, 5). Later, however, they were commanded to preach the Gospel to every creature (Mark XVI, 15).

Of which I, Paul, have become an apostle [Note: [Col. 0617D] The Vulgate has “I, Paul, a minister,” and likewise in the other readings.], and a minister, who now rejoice in sufferings for you. [Col. 0618B] He confesses that he rejoices in the tribulations he endured because he sees their progress in faith among the believers. Tribulation is not fruitless when it gains for life the one for whom he suffers. He says that these sufferings are inflicted upon Christ, whose teaching they persecute, thereby burdening the faithless with the cruelty of their impiety [Note: [Col. 0618D] Ambrosius, or Ambrosiaster, has “credulity.”], while proclaiming to the faithful the love of God, whose Son continues even now to suffer injuries for us.

And I complete in my flesh what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ, for his body, which is the Church. The meaning is this: Christ was led to death by the Jews alone; I suffer for his Church at the hands of both Jews and Gentiles. Christ began the passion but did not complete it; it is now completed in his body, that is, in the Church, while we suffer for you in order to build you up, [Col. 0618C] just as he did, who suffered first and left us an example, so that we might follow his footsteps.

Of which I have become a minister according to the dispensation of God that was given to me for you. He confidently says that he was made a minister of the Gospel among the Gentiles by God through Christ, so that the mystery begun by the Lord might be fulfilled through a suitable and effective servant—something that had been hidden for ages. He says that he was made a minister of the sacred Gospel, not just any kind of minister, but one of those about whom the Lord had said: “Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord appointed over his household, to give them their measure of grain at the proper time?” (Luke XII, 42).

It should be noted that he covertly rebukes those who came from the circumcision, whom the Lord had not chosen for this work. They, pursuing shameful profit, did not serve Christ the Lord but their own belly, and through sweet words and false blessings they corrupted the hearts of the innocent.

To fulfill the word of God. This word contains many prophetic statements concerning the calling of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jewish people, such as: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship him” (Ps. XXI, 28). The word of God is fulfilled in you who believe when the prophetic declarations are seen to have been fulfilled. Hence he continues:

The mystery that was hidden from ages and generations. It should be considered that the Apostle did not say that the mystery of the calling of the Gentiles had been hidden from the sons of God—that is, from the patriarchs and prophets—but from ages and generations, that is, from the philosophers and wise men of the world. For the holy prophets knew these things well and foretold that they would be fulfilled in us. Hence he continues:

But now it has been made manifest to his saints. For they did not become saints when the apostles came to the Gentiles, but were made saints through evangelizing. Thus it is written in the Gospel according to John (II, 52): “Jesus was about to die for the nation, and not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the children of God who were scattered.” They were not yet children of God except in predestination; but the only Son of God suffered for them and made children of adoption from children of wrath. For them he also adds:

[Col. 0619B] To whom God willed to make known the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ in you. He asserts that the mystery which had been hidden for ages was now revealed—that is, made known in the time of the apostles—because the Gentiles too were to be admitted to the faith of Christ without circumcision of the flesh, although Christ had been promised to the Jews. Earlier, before the preaching of the faith, it had been commanded that Gentiles be circumcised if they wished to approach the Law. Now, however, by the mercy of God, they were commanded to be received into the faith as they were. The Jews considered it unworthy that Christ, in whom the hope of the Jews lay, should also make the Gentiles participants in his glory.

The hope of glory, whom we proclaim. Christ is called the hope of glory because through him those who believe in him will attain glory. Rebuking every person [Col. 0619C] and teaching every person in all wisdom, so that we may present every person perfect in Christ Jesus—that is, Jew and Greek, slave and free—for “there is no partiality with God” (Ephes. VI, 9), but “in every nation, those who fear the Lord and practice righteousness are acceptable to him” (Acts X, 35).

He calls this the true wisdom, which exists in the Lord’s discipline, when Christ is recognized. The Apostle testifies that he himself carries this out with great care, so that by instructing every person in this wisdom he may present that person perfected before God in the understanding of Christ, so that he may attain the mystery of the birth from God, the birth from Mary, and the whole work of Christ, both heavenly and earthly.

It should also be noted that he wants to present everyone perfect according to that perfection of which he says elsewhere: “As many as are perfect, let us think this” (Phil. III, 15), although he had said earlier: “I do not consider myself to have comprehended it” (ibid., 13). There is, then, a certain imperfect perfection: that a person should know that in this life he cannot be perfect.

In which I also labor, striving. Just as above he proposed two things—rebuke and teaching—so here too he proposes two: labor and struggle. Rebuke pertains to the wicked; teaching to the humble. Likewise here, labor pertains to the work of preaching, while struggle pertains to those who resist.

According to his activity, which he works in me [Col. 0620A] with power. He says that his struggle against the faithless is accompanied by signs of power, so that unbelief may be subdued through them. For whoever has dared to contradict with a certain subtlety of diabolical cunning must, overcome by shame, yield to power. And lest the preacher prove ungrateful to divine grace, whatever he had said above about himself he now attributes to the One from whom he received it, saying: “according to his activity.”

Until now he has spoken generally about all; now, however, he addresses the Colossians themselves and says:

## Chapter II

“For I want you to know what concern I have for you, and for those who are in Laodicea, [Note: [Col. 0619D] In the Laudocian manuscript: Laudociae; elsewhere Laodiceae; and so also Saint Chrysostom and Jerome, or Pelagius; [Col. 0620D] in Greek, of course, Λαοδικεία (Laodicea),] and for all who have not seen my face in the flesh, so that their hearts may be comforted.”

He testifies that he is no less concerned for those whom he had never seen in the flesh than for those to whom he was preaching in person, so that they might know that he loved them with no less affection because he had not seen them than he loved the others among whom he was present. Thus he might cherish their spirits in love, and they might become ready through the letter to receive knowledge of the mystery of God in Christ. After the Apostle had recalled and commended how great a struggle he had for them, for those who had been in Laodicea [Note: [Col. 0620D] Again, in the manuscript: Laudociae,] and for all who had not seen his face in the flesh, so that their hearts might be consoled, he added:

“Being instructed in love and in all the riches of the fullness of understanding, for the knowledge of the mystery of God the Father and of Christ Jesus.”

They should observe that these are the riches of wisdom and knowledge: that Christ is recognized as worthy of worship in the fullness of his divinity. Therefore the whole mystery of God’s sacrament is in Christ. He is the one in whom every creature will perish unless it has hoped; thus all power is in him, and whoever knows him seems to possess knowledge of everything that exists. No other is to be sought for worship, because the power of all authorities is in him. For all receive their being from him. Since he is one, he can do all things. Therefore he is also called the head of all, so that all things may be seen to subsist through him.

The people to whom he wrote were in danger of being led astray by the shadows of things under the attractive name of knowledge and of being turned away from the light of truth that is in Christ Jesus our Lord. He saw that they had to beware of this care for vain and superfluous observances under the name of wisdom or knowledge, especially of the superstition of paganism [Col. 0620D] and of those who were called philosophers, as well as of Judaism, where the shadows of future things had to be removed, since Christ, their light, had already come.

“In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.”

Therefore all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are rightly said to be hidden in him. The whole rationale of the knowledge of every creature, heavenly and earthly, must be in him, because he is the head of them all. Whether of angels or of all other beings, all knowledge of them is in their author, so that whoever recognizes him seeks nothing further—not wisdom, not power—[Col. 0621A] because he has recognized the one in whom there is perfect power and perfect wisdom. Whatever he may think he has found elsewhere, he will find fully and abundantly in him.

For who was wiser than Solomon? Who was more prudent than Daniel? God gave them wisdom above others precisely to make known to unbelievers that he is the author of all wisdom. Accordingly, Nebuchadnezzar, admiring Daniel’s wisdom, says to him: “Truly, your God is himself the living God and the one who reveals mysteries” (Dan. II, 47).

This is hidden from every unbeliever: that all wisdom is in Christ. They do not read astrology in the Gospels, geometry in the Apostle, or arithmetic and music in the prophet. These disciplines are despised by our people for this reason: they do not pertain to salvation but rather lead into error [Col. 0621B] and turn people away from God, so that while they devote themselves to such arguments of calculation, they neglect the care of their souls. For what wisdom is so true as to know what is beneficial and despise what is harmful? It is harmful because it prevents the soul from caring for itself.

Not without reason, then, does the one who has recognized Christ find the treasure of wisdom and knowledge: he has recognized what is useful to him, so that he should not merely fail to admire every word or thought that is apart from Christ, but should also count it as folly.

“But I say this so that no one may deceive you with lofty speech.”

“I say this,” he says, “so that no one may circumvent you with plausible argument.” Because they were led by love of the truth, he feared that they might be deceived by plausibility. Therefore he commended Christ to them, in whom they possessed their sweetest treasure, namely, wisdom and knowledge, and whose name and promise could be used to lead them into error. He warns them lest their understanding be carried away by the conversations of evil men and by the cunning of iniquity. For the wise men of the world seek by a certain art and by the minutiae of argument to ensnare the souls of the simple, so that through reasoning about worldly things they may draw them away from the hope that is in Christ.

“For although I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit.”

He feared for them because he saw what they still lacked. Hence it follows:

“Rejoicing and seeing your order, and supplying what is lacking in the usefulness [Note: [Col. 0621D] The Vulgate does not read this way, but rather: ‘rejoicing and seeing your order, and the firmness of your faith, which is in Christ.’ The Vulgate agrees with the Greek reading of Saint Chrysostom. Our author transcribed this text from Saint Ambrose or Hilary, together with a large part of this exposition of the Epistle.] of your faith.”

He plainly saw a kind of spiritual structure, as he says elsewhere: “You are God’s building” (I Cor. III, 9). In it he saw both what gave him joy and what required his labor. He rejoiced because he already saw the building; he labored because he understood that it still had to be built up to the summit of perfection.

See how he wanders, as it were, through holy longing. Here he is held in body; there he is led in spirit. To those present he displays the affection of a father’s love; to those absent he makes it known. To those before him he devotes his works; to those listening he expresses his wishes. He is effectively present with those among whom he was, yet not absent from those among whom he was not.

[Col. 0622A] We understand this wandering of his more clearly if we consider further his words to the Corinthians. For he says: “I will come to you when I have passed through Macedonia; indeed, I shall pass through Macedonia. Perhaps I shall remain with you, or even spend the winter” (I Cor. XVI, 5).

“Therefore, as you received Christ Jesus our Lord, walk in him, rooted and built up in him, and established in the faith, just as you were taught, abounding in him with thanksgiving.”

He urges and exhorts them not to let their devotion diminish or withdraw from the faith they had attained, and not to be overturned by wicked fables so that they should receive Christ otherwise than they had learned. For many corrupters of the faith were going about to seduce the simple, announcing Christ deceitfully and hypocritically. He warns them to avoid such people with great care, so that, stable and firm upon the foundation of the Trinity, they might offer abundant thanks for God’s mercy in the hope of future things.

He nourishes them so that they may be capable of sharing in the treasures of knowledge and wisdom hidden in Christ, lest, as though unfit for these things, they be captured by plausible argument and turn aside from the way of truth. Therefore he adds:

“See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ.”

By “philosophy” he means an earthly philosophy, by which those who wish to be considered wise in the world are accustomed to be seduced. It is composed of arguments and the subtlety of certain minutiae, as though it had investigated physical causes, while containing certain additions that serve as exhortations to a good life or as instruction. Sometimes it is arranged around measurements and numbers, sometimes around the qualities and quantities of the elements.

Whoever falls into its arguments will scarcely and rarely escape. He is held by plausible causes and invented notions, considering nothing so true as what is seen and understood in the elements. And because present things, visible to the eyes, appear pleasant and attractive, they seduce some who think that spiritual reasoning must be despised and mocked in despair of the future. They assign all power to the stars, being subject to carnal reasoning, lest they should believe that heavy things can be lifted into heaven, light things descend to earth, or anything bodily be generated without mixture with other things. Thus they resist the power [Col. 0622D] and providence of God.

They know that many things are recorded in the sacred ancient Hebrew books, performed through Moses, which human reasoning cannot grasp. Likewise, in the new books there are deeds performed by the Lord or through the apostles that carnal reasoning forbids them to believe. [Note: [Col. 0622D] The manuscript reads “saying” (*dicentes*); since this lacks grammatical connection and order, we judged it should be emended. Yet that reading, *dicentes*, together with several following verses, is read word for word in the frequently cited commentary of Pelagius, where *dicentes* refers to the philosophers of his time.] They say that nothing can come from nothing; that the soul either has no beginning or is mortal; that a virgin cannot give birth—or, if she has given birth, as they claim, she is not a virgin; and they maintain that it is foolish to believe that God was born from a human being, died, and rose again.

He therefore calls this tradition, or philosophy, deceptive and empty, because it was not ordered by the power of God but by the weakness of human reasoning, which confines God’s power within its own knowledge, refusing to believe that he can act otherwise than carnal reason allows. By this reasoning they assign a diversity of divinities to the individual elements for worship, in order to bind the minds of the ignorant and prevent them from extending themselves toward the true God. For this reason he warns them to avoid this tradition: it is a worshipper of the world, not of God, who is one; and it does not lead to Christ but draws people away from Christ.

“For in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily.”

Divinity is not bodily. But because he calls the sacraments of the Old Testament “a shadow of future things,” he says, by comparison with those shadows, that the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Christ, since in him all the things represented by those shadows are fulfilled. Thus, in a certain sense, he himself is the body of those shadows—that is, he himself is the truth of those figures and signs.

The Apostle therefore used a transferred expression, as though God had dwelt in a temple made with hands, not bodily but in the manner of a shadow, that is, through signs prefiguring the future. For he also calls all those observances “shadows of future things” by the same transferred expression (Coloss. II, 17). The Most High God, as it is written, does not dwell in temples made with hands (Acts XVII, 24; Isa. LXVI, 1).

Or “bodily” was said because God dwells also in Christ’s body, which he assumed from the virgin, as in a temple. Hence, when the Jews asked for a sign and he said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II, 19), the evangelist, explaining what this meant, says: “But he was speaking of the temple of his body” [Note: [Col. 0623D] Through perhaps a copyist’s oversight, this text is lacking in the manuscript, so we have ventured without hesitation to add it.].

We therefore think that the distinction between the head and the other members is this: in any member, however eminent—even in some great prophet or apostle—however much divinity may dwell, the whole fullness of divinity does not dwell there as it does in the head, which is Christ. For in our own body sensation is present in each member, but not as much as in the head.

“And you have been filled in him, who is the head of every principality and power.”

By making Christ the head of all, he wished him to be understood as the beginning of all, just as he himself said when asked, “Who are you?” (John VIII, 25). He answered: “The Beginning, who also speaks to you.” [Col. 0623D] “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I, 3).

He wonderfully wishes them to despise these things as though they were marvelous, when he shows that they have been made the body of that head, saying: “And you have been filled in him, who is the head of every principality and power.” The sense, or order of the words, is this: If you are instructed by the knowledge of the one who gave a beginning even to invisible creation, what can those contribute to you who understand nothing more than what they see?

More is signified as being given to believers than can be detected in the elements, because whoever is in Christ is filled with the abundance of divinity, which the elements do not possess. Finally, the Holy Spirit dwells in believers, something that cannot be granted to the elements; for it was unworthy and incongruous that the invisible should dwell in visible substance, and the incorporeal in things that are perceptible.

Let their worshippers therefore hear, come, and believe in Christ, so that they may become greater than those whom they now worship.

From this point he mocks the Jews and the pseudo-apostles, lest they be seduced by them, and says:

“In whom you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made by hands.”

To prevent them from being seduced by Jewish shadows, he adds: “In whom you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made by hands,” that is, by which you stripped off the whole old man. Those are circumcised in Christ who, having cut away the worship of the whole human tradition, are joined to Christ—circumcised in heart, not in flesh; that is, serving in spirit, not in flesh—so that they may be turned from earthly things to heavenly, from human things to divine, and from error to truth.

“In the stripping off of the body of flesh.”

He did not intend two things to be understood, as though flesh were one thing and the body of flesh another. Rather, “body” is a name applied to many things, one of which is flesh. For, apart from flesh, there are many heavenly bodies and earthly bodies. He said “body of flesh” because in this passage he wished “body” to be understood as flesh. Hence it follows:

“Buried with him in baptism, in which you also rose through faith in the operation of God, who raised him from the dead.”

They rose through faith in God, believing that, after the example of Christ, he would raise them from the dead. In baptism the old man is laid aside and the new man is assumed; one dies to sins [Note: [Col. 0624D] The words “and the new man … dies” are found in the lower margin,] so that one may live to righteousness, be joined to Christ, and hold the pledge of the future resurrection in the example of the Savior, who rose from the dead.

“You have risen,” he says, “to new life, believing and understanding that this is his work.” See how here also he shows them the body of Christ, so that they may despise these things, adhering to their great head, the mediator between God and human beings, Christ Jesus, and seeking no false or ineffective intermediary through whom to adhere to God.

He therefore exhorts them to persevere in renouncing the pomp and magic arts [Note: [Col. 0624D] Perhaps “of magical arts” is better.] of Satan. Satan urges them to worship the elements for this reason: to draw them away from God, wishing to make human beings participants in his apostasy. Since he cannot persuade them to worship under his own name—for his name itself is abhorred—he attempts to accomplish his will under another’s name.

“And you, when you were dead in offenses and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, he made alive together with him.”

He says that the Gentiles were dead, first because they refused to receive the law of Moses, which was given as a testimony to the Creator and to condemn vices; and then because of their sins, since they were unworthy of life. Thus he distinguished them from the Jews, as though they had been enemies of the one God.

The Jews, however, living in confession of the one God, learned with the coming of Christ the mystery of God, which they had awaited for their justification. In Christ they received remission of sins through faith in Jesus Christ and the grace of the New Testament—what had been taken from them, since it is impossible to be without sin.

Therefore he includes the Jews also, saying: “Forgiving [Note: [Col. 0625D] The Vulgate has “you”; Saint Ambrose has “us,” as in the autograph.] us all offenses,” so that after the particular case he might add the general one, because he forgave all people all offenses.

But since, as the Lord says, “The one to whom more has been forgiven must love more” (Luke VII, 42), the Gentiles were alike subject to eternal death not only because of their sins but also because of circumcision (he called uncircumcision the carnal sins from which we must be stripped). Although they were doubly guilty, they became fellow heirs of the children [Note: [Col. 0625D] This sense is somewhat obscure. Since an emendation might have departed from the author’s intention, we thought it better to adhere faithfully to the reading and leave it to the judgment of the reader.].

For this reason he exhorts the Gentiles, so that, considering the causes of their evils and what grace they received from God in Christ, they may devote themselves wholly and diligently to the service of the one by whom they have been delivered from the different punishment of death.

“Forgiving you all offenses,” that is, taking away the causes of death and the sins.

“Erasing the bond written against us [Note: [Col. 0625D] Chirographum in the manuscript.] of the decree that was contrary to us.”

Thus he erased it when he removed it from the midst. He removed it from the midst when, as he says, he fastened it to the cross. He said that this meant stripping the principalities [Note: [Col. 0625D] “Principatus” ought to be read, in accordance with the text of Saint Paul [Col. 0626D] and his interpreters.] and powers publicly and triumphing over them in himself.

These things appear obscure and therefore must be clarified with care. This is the protection that the Apostle explains through the significance of various causes. He recalls many things that were done so that the human race might attain forgiveness: not only that he might forgive us our own sins, but also that he might remove the sin resulting from Adam’s transgression. He called this “the bond of the decree,” which did not permit us to rise from the dead, because the law made us guilty; it had entered so that sin might abound (Rom. V, 20).

Some say that *chirographum* means something like a written document: for *cheir* [Note: [Col. 0626D] Greek χείρ, “hand,”] in Greek means “hand,” and *graphia* [Note: [Col. 0626D] γραφὴ, “writing,”] means “writing.” Thus *chirographum* in Greek means “handwriting.” For this reason the Apostle here calls the sin of the human race a *chirographum*, as though it were a kind of document kept with God, a record of sins.
