Hence he himself says in the Song: “Are these things not stored up with me and sealed in my treasures?” (Deut. XXXII, 34.) All these things were erased on the cross by forgiving sins and abolishing the record of offenses. This could not have happened unless he had fastened sin to the cross. For when the Savior, by not sinning, conquers the sin that held humanity guilty, and, moreover, is killed by that sin though innocent, sin itself is crucified. Sin is said to be slain when it has been defeated. The cross is not the death of the Savior but of sin. For the innocent man who is killed makes those by whom he is killed guilty.

And to show what it means to erase, he adds:

“And he took it away from the midst, fastening it to the cross”: by offering himself to death for sinners, he not only put sins to death on the cross but also gave the rewards of immortality through an undeserved death.

“Stripping the principalities and powers, he led them forth confidently, openly triumphing over them in himself.”

Other manuscripts read: “Stripping himself of the flesh, he displayed the principalities and powers confidently, triumphing over them in himself.” These were not good principalities but evil principalities and evil powers, namely, diabolical and demonic powers. He displayed them—that is, he made them an example—so that, just as he stripped himself of flesh, he might show that his own people were to be stripped of the carnal vices through which those powers dominated them.

Through this mortality of the flesh the diabolical powers of envy, which dominated us, were defeated; having been conquered by the Savior, they were stripped of the souls they held [Note: [Col. 0626D] The autograph has this text as follows: “For through this mortality of the flesh the diabolical power of envy dominated us, because, having been conquered …” Let the reader judge whether we have emended it correctly.].

They held them with authority because they had sinned. But the powers themselves were found to be still more wicked when they killed the one who had conquered them without sinning. Thus they are rightly to be stripped, as he said, publicly—that is, on the cross—and openly triumphed over by Christ.

He is said to have led them forth, not by killing but by dying; not by inflicting force but by enduring, so that, with all pride broken, he might give us an example of conquering. For, as already stated, in himself our head provided an example that will be completed in his entire body, which is the Church, when it is finally delivered from the power of the devil in the resurrection.

“Therefore let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a festival, a new moon, or Sabbaths.”

He speaks generally against those who, having come from the Jews to believe in the Lord and Savior, wished to observe Jewish ceremonies. On this matter a considerable dispute was also raised in the Acts of the Apostles. Hence it follows:

“Let no one judge you” concerning those who boast that they are teachers of the law—concerning food and drink, as though some things were clean and others unclean; or concerning a portion of a festival day, as though some days were festivals and others not.

For us, who believe that Christ has risen, there is a perpetual and eternal festival. Or concerning a portion of a new moon—that is, of the Kalends and the new month—when the waning moon comes to an end and is covered by the shadows of night. The light of Christians is eternal, and they are always illuminated by the rays of the sun of righteousness.

Or concerning a portion of Sabbaths, so that they should not perform servile work or carry burdens. We have been granted freedom in Christ, and we have ceased to carry the burdens of sins.

“All these things,” he says, “are a shadow of future things and images of coming happiness.” In these matters the Jews, according to the letter, cling to the earth and are held there; but we, according to the Spirit, pass over to Christ, who, in distinction from the shadows, is now called the body. Just as there is truth in a body and falsehood in the shadow of a body, so in spiritual understanding we should await the whole world, food, drink, the entire festival, perpetual Kalends, and eternal rest.

“It is shameful,” he says, “and utterly incongruous, and foreign to the nobility of your freedom, that, although you are the body of Christ, you should be led astray by shadows and appear to be convicted as sinners, as though you were neglecting these observances.”

“Which are a shadow of future things, but the body is Christ.”

They were given through Moses so that they might be a shadow or figure of future things; when the truth appeared, the figure ceased. Just as, in the emperor’s absence, his image has authority, but in his presence it does not, so these observances had to be kept in their proper time before the Lord’s coming, but in his presence they have no authority.

“Let no one deceive you, affecting humility and the worship of angels, intruding into things he has not seen, vainly puffed up by the sense of his flesh.”

The Greek manuscripts do not have “let no one deceive you” but “let no one convict you” [Note: [Col. 0627D] Saint Chrysostom has neither one nor the other in the text. Saint Ambrose has: “Let no one deceive you.”]. Where we have “intruding into things he has not seen, vainly puffed up by the sense of his flesh,” they have “inculcating” [Note: [Col. 0627D] Neither one nor the other appears in Saint Chrysostom’s text. In place of “intruding,” Saint Ambrose has “exalting himself.” It will not be irrelevant to bring Saint Ambrose’s reading into consideration: “Let no one deceive you, wishing [Col. 0628D] in humility of spirit and superstition toward angels to exalt himself in the things he sees, vainly puffed up in the mind of his flesh,” and so forth.].

We ask what he intended by “humility and religion toward angels.” Truly, it is a humble and pitiable notion to believe that God delights in the blood of goats and bulls and in the odor of incense, which human beings often avoid. “The body, therefore, is Christ.”

“Let no one convict you, wishing to appear humble in heart.” If this had been expressed by the Greek word, it would also sound more familiar in ordinary Latin usage. Thus in common speech one says *thelodives* of someone who wants to be rich, and *thelosapiens* of someone who wants to be wise, and other expressions of this kind. Therefore here too: *thelohumilis*, that is, “wishing to be humble,” aspiring to humility. This is understood as “wishing to appear humble,” aspiring to humility.

For this is what the human heart does in such observances: it makes itself appear humble toward religion. He added “the worship of angels,” or, as some manuscripts have it, “the religion of angels,” which in Greek is called *theresheia* [Note: [Col. 0628D] Θρησκεία, as Saint Chrysostom has it.]. By angels he wishes the principalities to be understood—those whom they believe to have been appointed over the elements of this world and to be worthy of worship in these observances.

“Therefore,” he says, “let no one convict you, although you are the body of Christ, wishing to appear humble in heart in the worship of angels, inculcating what he has not seen.”

Either he intended “inculcating what he has not seen” because people practice these things according to suspicions and opinions, not because they have seen that they ought to be done; or else, “inculcating what I have seen,” because he considers them important after seeing them observed by human beings in certain places, whose authority he trusts even without a rational explanation. Thus he seems important to himself because he has happened to see the secrets of certain sacred rites.

But the clearer meaning is: “inculcating what he has not seen, vainly puffed up in the mind of his flesh.” For he wonderfully says “puffed up in the mind of his flesh” precisely where above he had said *thelohumilis*, “wishing to be humble.” In strange ways it happens in the human soul that it becomes more puffed up through false humility than it would if it openly displayed pride.

In this matter it should be noted that the excellent preacher joins the appearance of humility to superstition. When the flesh is worn down through abstinence more than necessary, humility is displayed outwardly, but inwardly one grows gravely proud of that very humility. And unless the mind often became swollen through the virtue of abstinence, the arrogant Pharisee would never have deliberately counted it among his great merits, saying: “I fast twice in the Sabbath” (Luke XVIII, 12).

It follows:

“And not holding fast to the head, from whom the whole body, joined and supplied through its connections, grows with the increase of God.”

What he earlier warned them to avoid under the name of philosophy he now teaches more openly that they must avoid: those who, devoted to earthly wisdom, assert that the things lying before their eyes or appearing to them are to be worshipped. Thus souls held by the worship of these things are kept bound beneath the firmament, lest they extend themselves above the firmament toward the higher heavens to worship God, the God of all.

This is accomplished by the work of the enemy, who always seeks to keep souls humbled upon the earth, where he knows that he himself has been cast down from heaven and will remain there by God’s just judgment. He pretends to be religious, although this is the greatest sacrilege.

They are puffed up because they observe the movement of the stars, which they call angels—not by divine authority but by human superstition. This contributes nothing except harm, since they refuse to hold the faith of Christ, who is the Creator and Lord of all. For all things receive their origin from him.

Just as the members of a body are joined from the head to the feet, so whoever does not believe in Christ, the head of all the saints, is outside this body and, however much he boasts, does not live; just as the members have no life except in the head.

It follows:

“If you have died with Christ to the elements of this world, why, as though living in the world, do you submit to decrees?”

That is: if you have been baptized with Christ and in baptism have died with Christ to the elements of the world, why do you not say with me: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI, 14)?

Everyone who is baptized in Christ dies to the world. For he renounces all errors of superstition in order to worship only the faith of Christ. When those things that belong to natural righteousness have been removed, the discipline given by God remains, through which one lives to God by the hope that is in Christ.

He dies, however, to those things to which he had been subjected through error, while denying those whom he had presumed to exist [Note: [Col. 0629D] In the Maurist edition of the works of Saint Ambrose, after *quos* they added *deos* (“gods”) from several manuscripts, as they say. In our text, although this exposition of the verse was taken from that source, the word *deos* is not present.].

Thus, through the enmity of renunciation, human beings and the worship of the elements are said to be dead to one another. By “world” he signifies the error of the flesh. Everything that is seen is assigned to the flesh.

Hence the Apostle John also says: “Do not love this world, nor the things that are in this world” (I John II, 15)—that is, let us not love either the elements from which the world is composed or the errors invented by human tradition, but only Christ, who died for us so that he might join us, though lost, to his body.

Those who have been buried with Christ have died to the elements, so that they concern themselves with none of these things. For they have learned to hold fast to heavenly things, which can give the former life [Note: [Col. 0630D] The text of Saint Ambrose, from which this exposition was taken, has “perpetual.”].

These things neither give the present life nor permit the future life to be grasped. But whoever, after baptism, is uncertain about certain things, thinking that some of the ancient practices are to be venerated, shows himself to be living according to the elements, which he decides are to be worshipped or hesitates to despise. Thus he will remain within the circuits of the world, alienated from God, because, clothed in the old man, he will not be able to pass beyond carnal things.

After these words he inserts the sayings of those who, through these observances, pronounce decrees concerning this world as though they had been made rational by vanity and puffed up by humility. Conversely, as though living in the world, they say:

“Do not touch, do not taste”—that is, do not touch the body of a dead man, nor a garment, nor the stool on which a menstruating woman has sat; do not taste pork, hare, moray eel, eel, cuttlefish [Note: [Col. 0630D] The manuscript has *sipiam*.], or any fish that does not have scales and fins (Lev. II; Deut. XIV).

“All these things are destined for destruction through use itself.”

That is, all these things are subject to corruption and destruction, and through the act of being consumed they are digested into excrement.

“According to the precepts and teachings of human beings.”

According to the precepts and teachings of human beings—namely, those for which the Lord rebukes the Pharisees, saying: “You have made void the commandment of God because of your tradition” (Matt. XV, 6; Mark VII, 9).

“Which indeed have an appearance of wisdom.”

Why does the Apostle say that the things he condemns have an appearance of wisdom? Let us nevertheless say what we can often observe in the Apostle’s own words: wisdom is also applied to the things of this world, which he more explicitly calls “the wisdom of this world” (I Cor. III, 19).

Nor should it trouble us that here he did not add “of this world.” In another place, when he says, “Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe?” (I Cor. I, 20), he adds “of this world,” so that the meaning is: “Where is the wise man of this world?” Yet the same sense is understood here.

Such, then, is this appearance of wisdom. Nothing is said in these superstitious observances except what appears to offer some rational account according to the elements of this world and the nature of things [Note: [Col. 0630D] In place of *ubi*, *quamvis* may perhaps be better read.].

Hence he also says: “Beware lest anyone deceive you through philosophy” (above, 8), and yet he does not say “of this world.” And what is philosophy in Latin except the pursuit of wisdom?

“These things,” he says, “have indeed an appearance of wisdom”—that is, they are things about which some account is given according to the elements of this world and according to principalities and powers, in the observance and humility of the heart. For these superstitions have the effect of humbling the heart through vice.

Thus Jewish observances appear to the ignorant and to the common populace to possess an image of human reason and wisdom, because they have humble thoughts.

It follows:

“Not for sparing the body.”

This means that they do not spare their bodies when they are deprived of these foods, which they are compelled to abstain from. For the Jews do not spare their bodies in taking food, sometimes rejecting what they have and seeking what they do not have. From this necessity they sometimes contract weakness and illness. Nor do they honor themselves, since “all things are clean to the clean” (Rom. XIV, 20; Titus I, 15), and nothing can be polluted when it is received with thanksgiving, since it was created by the Lord to invigorate and sustain human limbs through the nourishment and filling of the flesh.

By the elements of the world—to which, or rather by which, we have died—we must understand the law of Moses and the whole Old Testament. Through these elements, as through beginnings of religion, we learn about God; and through the elements of the letter, which is being destroyed, we are led to the life-giving Spirit.

Since we have died to the world and to its elements, we ought not to observe the things that belong to the world, because in one there is a beginning, and in the other perfection.

It follows:

“Not with any honor for the satisfying of the flesh.”

This does not mean that one food satisfies the flesh more honorably than another, since satisfying its need requires only that it be restored and supported by whatever food is suitable for health.

## Chapter III

“Therefore, if you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth.”

For this reason you should desire nothing earthly and seek nothing transitory or mortal, but pursue heavenly wisdom, not earthly wisdom. The resurrection nevertheless has two forms: first, the soul rises from earth to heaven; then, having received the body, it rises, caught up to meet Christ (I Thess. IV, 16).

For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. Your life—that is, your blessedness—is hidden, not so that it may not be seen, but so that it may be preserved, as it is written: “When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord” (Ps. 126:4). Here labor is required, but the reward is reserved for the future. Hence what follows:

[Col. 0631A] But when Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory. Christ is our life, because he is indeed the true God and eternal life; without his grace, whoever believes himself to be living is dead while alive. Therefore all the faithful ought not now to seek their own glory here, since they are sons of God, yet what they are to be has not yet appeared. For what does it mean to say, “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory,” except what John the Evangelist, his fellow apostle, also wrote to the faithful in his epistle: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be; for we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2)?

[Col. 0631B] Therefore put to death your members that are upon the earth. Since he indicates in the Epistle to the Romans that all sins together constitute a body (Rom. 6:6), he therefore calls individual offenses “members,” so that, after receiving and preserving the understanding of the Gospel from the fullness of the Savior, they might devote themselves to a good life, abstaining from every disgraceful act and evil desire, by which they might avoid losing the fruit of divine knowledge. He speaks figuratively, naming the effect by the means producing it, because he does not command the body’s constitution to be destroyed, nor the members—which are the soul’s instruments for performing good works—to be abolished. Rather, as is customary, he calls the evil use of the members “members.” For elsewhere the same Apostle says of our body: “No one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it” (Eph. 5:29). How, then, are we commanded to love our neighbors according to this pattern, if we ourselves have acted unjustly toward ourselves? What the Apostle commands to be put to death he immediately explains, saying:

Fornication, impurity, lust. These are what the Apostle commands to be put to death, not the body’s constitution, which, if rightly governed, is our aid. The habit or appetite of the vices must be restrained, not the body killed. Every lack of self-control may be called impurity and lust.

And evil desire. The Apostle would not have said “and evil desire” unless there were also a good desire, as he himself testifies concerning himself: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23). Where it is directed toward evil, it is a vice; where it is directed toward good, it is not a vice but an affection.

[Col. 0631D] It follows: And greed, which is the service of idols. Greed is rightly compared with idols, because while people serve immoderately the metals of gold and silver from which idols are made, they revere gold in place of God. Yet he compared greed with idolatry in order to show that nothing is more criminal than it. Under one name he designated two most evil and impious kinds of wrongdoing, which must be avoided by every means. Idolatry is first and foremost a grave crime. For what is so pernicious and disastrous as, to the injury of God the Creator, to attribute the honor due to him to wood, stones, or other metals, when human beings themselves do not tolerate a slave’s being called by the name of “lord,” although it is not nature but a certain condition that subjects him to slavery? The other crime is greed: not different in wickedness, but different in name. Hence he says to Timothy: “For greed is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:10) [Note: Saint Ambrose likewise has this reading; the Vulgate, however, has “desire.”]. It is capable of every offense, seeking to fulfill the impossible desire of its avidity, always drinking and always thirsting. Therefore he rightly displayed both evils under one name. They are nearly fulfilled by one and the same action: just as idolatry attempts to take glory away from the one God, so that what belongs peculiarly to him—the name of divinity worthy of him alone—may not be heard of him alone, so greed also reaches into God’s possessions, so that, if it could be done, one person alone might appropriate his creature, which God made for all. Hence God says through the prophet: “The gold is mine and the silver is mine” (Hag. 2:9). Both, therefore, are enemies of God; for each denies God what belongs to him.

Because of these things the wrath of God is coming upon the sons of distrust. Or, as other books have it, upon the sons of unbelief [Note: Saint Chrysostom likewise has this reading, namely ἀπείθεια, which has been rendered by “unbelief” in the translation. It was plainly easy to write one Greek word in place of the other, since “distrust” is written in Greek as ἀπιστία.]. He calls the Sodomites and those who perished in the Flood, or those who were unbelieving toward God’s word in the wilderness, “sons of unbelief.” He says that God’s judgment will come because of the evils mentioned, so that vengeance may be taken upon those who, having despised God and his law, preferred to follow what had been forbidden. The meaning, or order of the words, is this: Future things must be feared on account of past things, because you will rightly be called the children of those whose imitators you have been.

It follows: In these things you also once walked, when you were living in them. When he said, “when you were living in them,” he showed that they had lived wickedly for a long time, as if he were saying: “Do not now live in this way, lest you appear to have believed in vain.” He does not conceal how great a benefit God’s grace through Jesus Christ conferred upon them, so that they might rejoice at having escaped the wrath that will suddenly come upon the unbelieving of the whole earth, and might present themselves in such a way that they could obey the commands of him by whom they had been freed from the second death.

But now you also must put away all anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy, and shameful speech from your mouth. Now he forbids what seem to be lesser sins, lest, because he previously commanded the graver sins to be put to death, they should think that these were permissible or need not be avoided as though they were not dangerous. Such indiscipline is unworthy even of the sons of men who have been well instructed; how much more is it unworthy of the sons of God?

Do not lie to one another. For it is not fitting for the children of truth to lie, since all lying comes from the devil, who was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth.

It follows: Stripping off the old person with his deeds, and putting on [Note: [Col. 0633D] Our codex, together with Ambrosiaster, has “put on”; the Vulgate, with Jerome or Pelagius, has “putting on.”] the new, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him. Both in wording and in action, he named this image more clearly in the Epistle to the Ephesians, giving the same command in other words: “Strip off,” he says, “the old person with his deeds, and put on the new, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him” (Col. 3:9–10). Thus what is read there—“put on the new person, who was created according to God”—is expressed here as “put on the new person, who is renewed according to the image of him who created him.” There he says “according to God”; here, “according to the image of him who created him.” In place of what he there wrote, “in righteousness and holiness of truth,” here he wrote “in the knowledge of God.”

This renewal and reformation of the mind therefore takes place according to God, or according to the image of God. But it is said “according to God” so that it may not be thought to take place according to another creature; it is said “according to the image of God” so that it may be understood to take place in that which bears the image of God, namely, in the mind. In the same way we say “dead according to the body,” not according to the spirit, which departs from the body when a believer and righteous person dies. For what do we mean by “dead according to the body” except dead in body or with respect to the body, not dead in soul or with respect to the soul?

Certainly this renewal does not take place in one instant during the course of one’s life, as that renewal in baptism takes place in a single instant through the remission of all sins. If, then, we renew the spirit of our mind—and it is this spirit that is the new person, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him—there is no doubt that the human being was made according to this rational mind, where knowledge of God can exist, not according to the body or according to any other part of the soul. Through this renewal we also become sons of God by the baptism of Christ; and by putting on the new person, we put on Christ through faith.

Who, then, is the person who excludes women from this fellowship, since they are heirs together with us in grace, and since the same Apostle says elsewhere: “For you are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus. For all of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female. For you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Gal. 3:26–28)? Have believing women, then, lost the sex of their bodies? No; but because renewal according to the image of God takes place where there is no sex, namely, in the spirit of their mind.

Where there is neither Gentile nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free, but Christ is all and in all. It is as though he plainly said: Before God, neither sex, condition, race, nor province is prejudicial; only conduct together with right faith is required. Scythia is a remote province beneath the north, stiff with cold and barbarous in its customs. For this reason, it is said that its people were called Scythians.

It follows: Therefore, as God’s chosen [Note: [Col. 0634D] Other readings add “holy and beloved.”], put on compassion, kindness, humility, modesty, and patience. To possess and fulfill these things is to strip off the old person with his deeds and to put on the new, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of him who created him. He urges them to do these things, which establish merit before God. Abstaining from sins is produced by fear: a person fears that, by doing evil, he may be subjected to punishments. But the things he now urges them to do pertain to the progress of merit; they are done from the will, not from necessity. Therefore, whoever abstains from what is unlawful has praise; but whoever restrains himself from what is lawful has both praise and reward.

Bearing with one another, after the example of Christ, who bore our weaknesses, both spiritual and bodily. And forgiving one another—that is, showing indulgence and pardoning each other—as Christ also forgave all, even his persecutors.

If anyone has a complaint against someone else, just as the Lord forgave you. It is as though he said: If the one who can avenge himself forgives, and spares, in whom no sin can be found, how much more ought you to do so, who cannot live without sin and whose vengeance is either small or nonexistent? Therefore do not exact small matters from your fellow servants, lest the many debts of sin that have been forgiven you be demanded of you.

Above all these things, have love. Since love is greater than all things, he urges them to devote themselves especially to it. For then all the things he commanded above to be observed can be brought to the fruition of reward, if they walk the way of the law under love’s guidance. Whoever does something out of love acts with the whole mind. There is no hypocrisy or pretense in love, as John says: “Fear is not in love” (1 John 4:18); for whoever fears is not perfect, since perfect love casts out fear. Hence the Lord preferred to be loved rather than feared.

For this is what embraces unity; this is what makes all one body; this is what possesses true peace, which it preserves with a pure heart. Peace can exist in name without love; but love always possesses peace with it.

[Col. 0634D] Which is the bond of perfection. Love is called the bond of perfection because every good work that is done is bound by it, so that it may not perish. For anything whatsoever is quickly torn away by the tempter if it is found detached from the bond of love. But if the mind is bound by love of God and neighbor, then, whenever the movements of temptation suggest anything unjust to it, love itself sets up a barrier against them and breaks the waves of persuasion against the gates of virtue and the bar of inward love.

And let the peace of Christ rejoice in your hearts. The peace of Christ is such as he had with himself, for he had no sin in himself. Whoever possesses peace within himself, the more perfectly he possesses it, the more greatly he will endure affliction in the world, as the Lord himself testified to his disciples, saying: “I have spoken these things to you, so that in me you may have peace” (John 16:33). “But in the world you will have affliction.” The peace of Christ is war against the world.

[Col. 0635A] In this peace you were also called in one body; and be thankful [Note: [Col. 0635D] Various readings occur here. The Greek of Saint Chrysostom, as well as that of Saint Ambrose and the Vulgate, and also the reading of Saint Jerome or Pelagius—which should not be omitted—have “be grateful.” In the exposition cited most recently, Saint Jerome says: “In some copies it reads, ‘be grateful.’” From these copies, therefore, our Atto took the text, reading the abbreviated form gratia, namely gra[tia estote] (“be grateful”). The exposition also corresponds to this reading.]. That is, do not be imitators of the ancient law, which returns injury for injury; rather, be imitators of the grace of the Gospel, which not only forgives enemies but also intercedes for them so that they may be forgiven.

Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, in all wisdom. The word of Christ consists of the Gospel commandments, which not only priests but also faithful laypeople ought to possess, not merely sufficiently but abundantly. They must also admonish and teach one another, as follows:

Teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. He urges them always to meditate on things that resound with Christ; to keep in their hearts things that continually give thanks to God the Father, so that the melodious voice may serve him, the psalm praise him, and the hymn exalt him. And let him alone know this—he who sees through the hidden things of the mind—from whom the reward is hoped for: psalms of David, songs of Moses and of all the prophets; hymns, such as the melodies of the three youths in the furnace. We say these things so that the edification of the Church may be brought forth by you wisely and rationally. What distinction there is among psalms, hymns, and songs (Eph. 5:19) has already been discussed in the preceding Epistle to the Ephesians.

It follows: Singing in your hearts to God in grace—that is, sing not only with the mouth but also with the heart, so that the heart may agree with the voice and you may be able to understand what you sing. He commanded that they sing in their hearts so that it would not be done for human approval and they would not lose what has been built up.

Whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Whether you teach or perform some good work, do nothing for your own glory, but do it for the Lord. Above he commanded that God be praised in the heart and thanks be given to him; now he urges that the name of the Lord Jesus be praised and exalted both in word and in deed, throughout our whole manner of life, so that when our words are free from blame and our works are good, the Lord Jesus may be magnified, whose instruction makes his disciples irreproachable. We then truly give thanks to God if we observe the manner of his commandments.

Giving thanks to God the Father through him—that is, giving thanks to God, who deigned to send his Son to inspire and teach these things.

Wives, be subject to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord. Thus he commands that women ought to be subject to their husbands, as God commanded among other things when he said to the woman: “Your desire shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you” (Gen. 3:16). In this manner and discipline, she should fear her husband as her lord, from whom she began to exist. He feared that, when the function of the flesh ceased in many cases, either subjection in women or the affection of love in men might cease. The husband and wife are bound according to the pattern of Christ’s authority in the Church. After this he turns to husbands, in order to command them in the same way what they should do with their wives. For he continues and says:

Husbands, love your wives [Note: [Col. 0636D] The following explanation is taken from Saint Gregory, Homily 37 on the Gospels.]. Behold, the disciple proclaims that a wife must be loved, while the Master says: “Whoever does not hate his wife cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:26). Does the judge announce one thing and the herald proclaim another? Or can we both hate and love at the same time? But if we weigh the force of the command, we can do both through discernment: we should love those who are joined to us by bodily kinship and whom we recognize as our neighbors, while we should hate and avoid those whom we suffer as adversaries on the way of God. In a certain sense, the one who is wise according to the flesh is loved through hatred: when he brings evil things upon us, he is not obeyed.

To show that this hatred toward our neighbors does not proceed from affection but from love, the Lord immediately adds: “And even his own life.” We are therefore commanded to hate our neighbors and to hate our own life. It is clear, then, that the neighbor must be hated out of love, since he is hated in the same way as oneself. We hate our own life properly when we do not yield to its carnal desires, when we break its appetites and resist its pleasures. What is led to something better by being despised is loved, as it were, through hatred.

So we must display toward our neighbors a discerning hatred, so that in them we may love what they are and hate what obstructs us in the way of God. Far be it from a faithful person, when hearing the Apostle say, “Love your wives,” to love in his wife the desire of the flesh, which he ought not to love even in himself, while hearing the other Apostle say: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world; for if anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (1 John 2:15).

And do not be embittered against them. The preacher of the new life would never urge a natural requirement unless they had begun to exercise self-restraint—a requirement which nature itself demanded; this has already been noted more fully by us in the Epistle to the Ephesians.

Children, obey your parents in all things, for this is pleasing in the Lord. He prepares them for discipline, since he commands them to be instructed by their parents according to God, so that they may show one another the reciprocal duty of love. Children can have God favorable to them if they render their parents the honor due to them in their obedience.

Fathers, do not provoke your children to indignation. Thus, just as the reward of obedience and submission has been demonstrated in children, so moderate authority is commanded of parents, so that they may know that they preside not over slaves but over sons. Nor is he content with this limit to the command; he adds that parents ought to be gentle toward their children, lest, being constrained by them, they sin against them and offend God—which they do not wish to do. For anger is an inconsiderate thing, so much so that sometimes the person who is angry does not even spare himself. Fathers ought to remember that they too were once sons; children, however, should consider that they will become fathers, so that, with the counsel of both sides balanced, children may be subject and fathers gentle.

So that they may not become fainthearted—that is, lest, being exasperated, they become angry, but may always learn through your example to be patient.

Slaves, obey your earthly masters in all things. Here the Apostle wisely foresaw that the teaching of our Savior might be blasphemed in some respect if believers proved useless to their masters, and that someone who might otherwise have allowed his slaves also to become Christians might begin to regret those who had already become so. But if he saw them progressing toward what was better and changing from unbelievers into believers, he would not only wish his other servants to believe but would himself likewise be saved through faith.

Not serving merely for appearance, as those who please people. Do not serve merely for appearance, as those do who desire to please people; rather, turn necessity into willingness and obtain a reward from the Lord for human service, especially since the master of the flesh imposes no command different from that of the Creator and Lord. Since God cannot be served otherwise than with a pure heart—he sees through the hidden things of souls—he likewise commanded that people serve human beings in this way. Whoever serves merely for appearance does something else in secret; whoever serves with the mind is the same outwardly as inwardly. If, therefore, he is faithful in this service, he will win the Lord’s favor. For this reason he wishes the slave to be just and obedient in relation to his earthly master, so that he may also be faithful and obedient in the things of God. If he proves capable in the present situation, where he knows that there are no rewards except corruptible ones, how much more eager will he be in devotion to God, whom he knows will give immortal rewards to the faithful?

But in simplicity of heart, fearing the Lord, who always sees everywhere and hates all pretense; for the human eye can be deceived. Therefore act in such a way that you turn the necessity of your condition into the willingness of religion, so that, when everyone sees that you have progressed toward what is better since becoming Christians, thanks may be given to the Lord for your good works.

Whatever you do, perform it from the heart, with all humility, having laid aside your former pride and pretense.

As for the Lord, and not for people. Whatever we do for people out of love for him, we do for the Lord, not for people. Knowing that you will receive from the Lord the repayment of the inheritance, with whom there is no partiality. To make them ready in obedience and faith, he promises that they will receive from God in the kingdom of Christ the reward of good works. In order that this may be proved and accepted, he wishes them to obey as they would obey the Lord, from whom they expect their reward. Otherwise, if someone acts unjustly, he offends not only a human being but also God, whom he has despised through the fraud committed against his earthly master. But if he acts well, he will not be regarded by God as a human slave, as though more contemptible, but will be rewarded as a free person among human beings—a slave of Christ, which is a name of dignity.

Serve the Lord Christ. Whoever faithfully serves a human being for love of the Lord Christ serves the Lord Christ. Whoever does an injury will receive what he has done unjustly; and there is no partiality with God. Whether it is a slave who has despised his master or a master who has treated his slave unjustly, he should know that such an injury will not go unpunished before God.

[Col. 0638B] (CHAP. IV.) Masters, provide your slaves with what is just and equitable—that is, you ought to consider yourselves fathers rather than masters, because the ancient custom is that good masters are called heads of households.

Knowing that you also have a Lord in heaven. Before him you are so entirely one that you have been bought equally, and one inheritance has been promised to both; therefore, whatever kind of Lord you wish him to be toward you, be such toward your fellow servants, rather than toward slaves. So that earthly masters may not be inflated with pride, presuming upon their lordship, he moderates and restrains their minds, so that, having considered the matter, they may recognize that God the Creator made all human beings free, not slaves and free persons. But this arose through the world’s iniquity: when one person invades another’s territory, he then takes free people captive. Hence the ancients called them manucapti, “seized by the hand,” and from this came mancipia, “slaves.”

This misfortune and condition is still visible today. Some are ransomed; others remain slaves. Before God, however, the one who has sinned is considered a slave. Indeed, because of sin Ham was called a slave. The ancients agreed with this judgment, defining all wise people as free and all foolish people as slaves, because the wise person abstains from sins, so that the one who follows what is right is free, while the slave is the one who, through the lack of wisdom that is foolishness, subjects himself to sin. Thus Ham was called a slave because of his foolishness: he foolishly laughed at his father’s nakedness (Gen. 9:22).

He therefore shows masters that they are not truly masters but masters only in appearance: they are masters of bodies, not of souls. For only the Lord, the invisible God and creator of all things, rules both bodies and souls. Considering this, let them exact just service from their slaves—such service as they themselves wish to be exacted from them by the common Lord. For although they do not serve God as they ought, while they do not deny that he possesses power over all things and that his daily gifts and the services of creation are provided for human use, they exact from their equals—indeed, I will not say from their brothers—such burdensome service that it cannot be endured. They do not bear in mind that they too, willingly or unwillingly, are slaves, and that they should consider of what merit they are.

Devote yourselves to prayer, keeping watch in it. He says “keeping watch in it” because a sluggish and negligent petition cannot obtain anything even from a human being, much less from God. Now that the Colossians already believe [Note: [Col. 0639D] In the autograph: “the prudent.”] in the mystery of the Lord Christ, he shows that they must devote themselves to prayer in avoiding the sins of vice, so that their merits may increase as the adversary’s temptations diminish. He considers them worthy to such an extent that he judges that they can even assist him with their prayers, boldly asserting the Gospel that he had received the commission to make known.

In thanksgiving—that is, both for all the things granted to you and even amid adversities, which occur through his administration. Praying at the same time for us, that the Lord may open to us a door for the word, so that we may speak the mystery of Christ. How is the door of the word opened except when the understanding of the hearer is opened, so that he believes, having made a beginning in faith, and accepts what is preached and discussed for the building up of sound doctrine, rather than, through unbelief, rejecting and driving away what is said?

For what does it mean to say, “Praying at the same time for us, that God may open to us a door for the word,” except that it most plainly demonstrates that even the beginning of faith is a gift of God? It would not be requested from him in prayer unless it were believed to be granted by him. This gift of heavenly grace had descended upon the seller of purple, whose understanding God had opened, as Scripture says in the Acts of the Apostles, and she attended to what was spoken by Paul (Acts 16:14); thus she was called to believe. God does what he wills in human hearts, whether by helping, judging, or inspiring, so that through them too what his hand and counsel predestined to be done may be fulfilled [Note: [Col. 0639D] A very noteworthy statement about predestination and grace, to be joined with the passages most frequently read in the exposition of the Epistle to the Romans.].

For this I am also imprisoned—that I may make it known as I ought to speak. That is, that he himself may grant what, to whom, and when I ought rationally to preach; for, while we preachers speak outwardly to the ear, he works inwardly in the heart.

Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside, making the most of the time. Since it is necessary for us to walk among the faithful [Note: [Col. 0640D] Our codex has “the faithful”; we judged that it should be emended on the authority of Saint Ambrose.] and to mingle in conversation for the sake of worldly association, this is what he urges: let your conduct itself be accompanied by wisdom, on account of the scandal of the Gentiles, lest they receive from us an occasion for blasphemy and be stirred up to persecution. For what need is there to speak with someone whom they know to be unmanageable and obstinate in mind, ready to offer insult?

He therefore gives this advice so that, with modesty as the teacher, words of religion may be spoken at a suitable place and time; or, if such a person is present in the midst of others, one should remain silent. One must act one way with the powerful of the world, another way with people of moderate standing, and another with the humble. Again, one must act one way with the gentle and another with the irascible, to whom one ought to yield [Note: [Col. 0640D] In the autograph: “to be yielded to.”]. This is what it means to make the most of the time. For when, in the face of one lying in wait for the Lord’s words and raging with the audacity of the moment, you yield, you turn the injuries of a hostile time to profit. If the head—that is, the king—assents, there is freedom for the body to speak God’s words with gentleness, so that they may be summoned to goodness. Yet one must always yield to those who are clamorous and passionate for abuse. You conquer when you yield.

Let your speech always be seasoned with grace, as with salt—that is, always possess within yourselves the reasoning of wisdom, lest our religion be judged foolish by philosophers and Gentiles. So that you may know how you ought to answer each person. This is what blessed Peter the Apostle also wrote to the faithful in his epistle, saying: “Always be ready to make a defense to everyone who asks you for a reason concerning the hope that is in you” (1 Pet. 3:15). Nevertheless, one must answer pagans in one way, Jews in another, heretics in another, philosophers in another, and the other unbelievers in yet another.

Everything concerning me will be made known to you by Tychicus, the most beloved brother, faithful minister, and fellow servant in the Lord: “brother” in the law; “faithful minister” of the sacred Gospel; “fellow servant” in labor.

I have sent him to you for this very purpose, so that he may learn what concerns you and encourage your hearts, together with Onesimus, the most beloved and faithful brother, who is one of you, and who will make known to you everything that is being done here. From this we can infer that he wrote these four epistles from prison in Rome: to the Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, and Philemon.

To the Ephesians, because he says: “So that you also may know what concerns me and what I am doing, Tychicus, the most beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, will make everything known to you; I have sent him to you for this very purpose, so that you may know what concerns us and he may encourage your hearts” (Eph. 6:21–22). This Tychicus, who was sent to the Ephesians, is also sent to the Colossians with Onesimus.

At that time Onesimus accompanied him, when Onesimus was carrying personal letters to Philemon on his own behalf (Philem. 10). To the Philippians, because he says: “All the saints greet you, especially those of Caesar’s household” (Phil. 4:22).

This, however, is distinctive to the present Epistle to the Colossians: Onesimus, who is commended by letter to his master Philemon (Philem. 10), was also the bearer of this Epistle, since he says later: “Everything concerning me will be made known to you by Tychicus, the most beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord, whom I have sent to you for this purpose, so that he may learn what concerns you and encourage your hearts, together with Onesimus, the most beloved and faithful brother, who is one of you.”

But if Philemon, to whom that epistle was written, was Onesimus’s master—or rather, if through being a master he became his brother (Philem. 16)—and Onesimus is said to be one of the Colossians, reason itself and the order of events instruct us that Philemon too was a Colossian. At that time Onesimus carried a common epistle to the whole Church, when he had taken private letters to his master commending himself [Note: [Col. 0640D] A most elegant argument by which it is proved that this Epistle and the Epistle to Philemon were written at the same time and from imprisonment in Rome.].

There is also another indication: Archippus is named in this Epistle, to whom, together with Philemon, it is written here: “Say to Archippus: See to the ministry that you have received in the Lord, so that you may fulfill it” (Philem. 2:17).

Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you—that is, one who is held in chains with me and shares my suffering through the affection of love. This Aristarchus appears to be a man of good conduct and merit, designated as a participant in the Lord’s devotion and a companion of the Apostle’s labors.

And Mark, the cousin of Barnabas (Acts 15:36). He does not fail to mention Mark, in order to indicate what commendation he possesses: once he is known to be related to the praiseworthy man Barnabas, he may be regarded as honorable. We think that he was the writer of the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0641D]

Here the discussion concerns that Mark who was also called John Mark (Acts 12:12), the faithful son of a certain woman named Mary, in whose house the faithful and the apostles customarily gathered. He was the disciple and cousin of the blessed Barnabas (Acts 15:37). He attached himself to Saints Paul and Barnabas when they returned to Antioch (Acts 12:25), and he also accompanied them as far as Perga in Pamphylia. When Paul and Barnabas planned to return to Asia in order to visit the churches, Barnabas wanted to take him as their traveling companion, but Paul opposed this. Paul therefore went alone into Asia, separating from Barnabas and this John Mark, who went to the island of Cyprus. Moreover, Mark gave great assistance to Paul when he was detained in prison. In Asia he joined Timothy in his labors (2 Tim. 4:11). The Latin and Greek Church celebrates his feast on September 27. He is said to have been bishop of Byblos and is called an apostle by the Greeks. Where or by what death he died is very uncertain; perhaps at Ephesus, where his famous tomb was venerated. See Eusebius, book 3, chapter 39, and book 7, chapter 25; Chrysostom, Oration 67, p. 504, no. 6.

From this, the opinion seems rather weak—not only that of our author but also that of others, which has now almost entirely fallen out of use—that this same John Mark was identical with Saint Mark the Evangelist, the disciple, companion, and son of Peter (1 Pet. 5:13). It would be too long and foreign to our purpose to report what so many ancient and modern writers have said about this matter. See Calmet, Sacred Historical Dictionary, under the entry “Mark.”]]

They are called cousins, as though sororini, that is, those who are born from individual sisters.

If he comes to you, receive him. For this reason he instructs [Col. 0641B] the Colossians to welcome Mark kindly and not reject him, because they knew that he had departed from Paul through disobedience.

And Jesus, who is called Justus, who are of the circumcision. As if he were saying: “These are the only ones now with me”; or, “These alone of the circumcision are my fellow workers in the New Testament, through which one reaches the kingdom of God.” This Jesus, whom he calls Justus by name, he mentions as one of those alone for whom he bears witness, because these men of the circumcision had assisted him, agreeing with him and sharing his judgment, so that they now proclaimed that circumcision ought no longer to be practiced. Therefore he calls them his partners in the kingdom of God. But to proclaim that one must be circumcised and that Sabbaths and new moons must be observed is not spiritual but earthly [Note: [Col. 0642D] The words are read in the lower margin.].

This is what we said above [Col. 0641C]: that the Epistle to the Colossians was written at the same time, and by the same bearer of the letters, as the Epistle to Philemon, as is also shown by the names of those who are greeted. For it is written thus: “Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you, and Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, and Epaphras, who is from among you, a servant of Christ”; and a little farther on: “Luke, the most beloved physician, greets you, and Demas”; and: “Tell Archippus: See to the ministry that you received in the Lord, so that you may fulfill it”; and: “Remember my bonds.” But if anyone thinks that the letters were not written together because only a few names appear in the letter to the Colossians that are not recorded as having been added to the letter to Philemon, let him know that not everyone is a friend or acquaintance of everyone else; [Col. 0642A] and that one letter is addressed privately to a single person, while another is addressed publicly to the whole Church.

Epaphras, who is from among you, a servant of Christ Jesus, greets you. Who Epaphras was—the man who is written in Paul’s letter addressed to Philemon as Paul’s fellow prisoner (Philem. 23)—we may conjecture from the addition there, “in Christ Jesus,” that he endured at Rome the same bonds for Christ as Paul did, and that he could consequently be called both Christ’s prisoner and his fellow prisoner. Or certainly the reason may be that he too was a person of distinction among the apostles, like Andronicus and Julia, concerning whom he writes to the Romans: “Greet Andronicus and Julia [Note: [Col. 0642D] Rom. 16:7. The Vulgate has Junia.], my kinsmen and fellow prisoners, who are distinguished among the apostles and who were in Christ before me.” So much concerning Epaphras.

As for his fellow workers in the Gospel and in his bonds [Col. 0642B], when he was also writing the Epistle to Philemon (Philem. 24), he lists Mark, whom, as I said, I think to have been the writer of the Gospel; Aristarchus, whom we mentioned above; Demas, concerning whom he says elsewhere, “Demas has deserted me” (II Tim. 4:9); and Luke the physician, who handed down the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles to the Churches in writing. He makes the Epistle more dear to them when he bears witness to one who is from among them.

A servant of Christ Jesus, always concerned for you in his prayers. He is truly proved to be a servant of Christ who is always found to be concerned for Christ’s body. He testifies that he desires such salutary things for them that he shows the man who is their fellow citizen and especially dear to them through the affection of mutual unity to be a participant in his advocacy for their benefit. [Col. 0642C]

That you may stand perfect and complete in every will of God. What is “that you may stand” except “that you may persevere”? Hence it is said of the devil, “He did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44), because he was there but did not remain. These men, certainly, were already standing in the faith. For when we pray that one who stands may stand, we pray for nothing else than that he may persevere.

For I bear him witness that he has much labor for you, and for those who are in Laodicea and Hierapolis. Laodicea and Hierapolis are cities of Asia Minor. Because he was concerned for the Church, he is therefore called a servant of Christ Jesus; and the Apostle publicly celebrates his great testimony: “I bear him witness that he has much labor [Col. 0643A] for you,” just as he also testifies about himself that he had been in many labors. To make them attentive to his greeting, he shows how great the vigilance of others is on their behalf. For, I think, a person becomes more concerned when he sees another laboring in his own cause.

And tell Archippus: “See to the ministry that you received in the Lord, so that you may fulfill it.” What ministry did Archippus receive from the Lord for the people? We read elsewhere: “And to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the Church that is in your house” (Philem. 2). From this we think either that he was bishop of the Church of Colossae, whom he is admonished to govern diligently and carefully, or that he was a preacher of the Gospel. Or, if this is not so, for the present this is enough for me: that Philemon, Archippus, and Onesimus himself, who carried the letter [Col. 0643B], were Colossians; and that, as we said earlier, four letters were sent from Rome at the same time.

Luke the beloved physician, and Demas, greet you. Luke was truly beloved by the Apostle, because, setting everything else aside, he always followed the Apostle; he is also said to have written the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles.

Greet the brothers who are in Laodicea, and Nympha, and the Church that is in her house. Since he was similarly concerned for those who are in Laodicea, in his letter he instructs them to be greeted, considering Nympha especially dear and greeting her household as well. For she appears to have been so devoted that her entire house was marked with the sign of the cross. [Col. 0643C]

And when the Epistle has been read among you, arrange for it also to be read in the Church of the Laodiceans, and read the one that is from Laodicea. Because the Apostle’s instructions are general and his letters were written for the benefit of everyone, he therefore also commanded that this Epistle be read to the Laodiceans, so that through it they might learn what they ought to do; and he instructed the Colossians to read the letter of the Laodiceans, in accordance with the sense stated above. [Col. 0644A]

And tell Archippus: “See to the ministry that you received in the Lord, so that you may fulfill it.” Through them he admonishes their superior to be concerned for their salvation. And because the Epistle is written for the sake of the people alone, he addresses it not to their ruler but to the Church. For after Epaphras, who instructed them, this man received their Church to govern.

The greeting in my own hand—Paul’s. All the letters that he did not write with his own hand he confirmed by subscribing his own sign at the end in Hebrew letters, so that they would not be corrupted by false brothers. Hence elsewhere he says: “The greeting of me, Paul, with my own hand; this is the sign in every letter” (II Thess. 3:17). [Col. 0644B]

Remember my bonds. He says this to remind them, so that they may keep in mind the sufferings he endured for the salvation of the Gentiles, and may show themselves such that he would not regret suffering injuries on their behalf. As if he were saying: “Since I suffer these things for your sake, imitate my example.”

The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. Amen. Grace is so called as something given freely; for grace is truly with those who, after receiving it and remaining in it, do not exalt themselves on the basis of their own merits.

[Col. 0644C] Thanks be to God. Amen.

# THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS

[Col. 0643]

## ARGUMENT [Note: [Col. 0643D] This title is lacking in the manuscript.]

[Col. 0643C]

In order to encourage others, by the example of these people—that is, the Thessalonians—to advance in faith, he praises them because, remaining in the grace they had received, they had increased toward the attainment of a greater reward by pursuing better things, so that they might strive toward perfection and so that the dignity acquired through their virtues might inspire the rest. For they had so thoroughly imbibed the spirit of faith that, through hope in the future—even in the case of their fellow citizens, the Macedonians—they endured the persecutions inflicted for the name of Christ with devoted hearts. Thus, in order to record in writing their merit and his own joy at their progress, he writes to them as follows [Note: [Col. 0643D] This argument is by Saint Ambrose, or by the deacon Hilary; indeed, it is a complete exposition of the Epistle.].

## [HERE BEGINS THE TEXT]

### (CHAPTER I)

Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, to the Church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and in the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace to you and peace. The letter contains the names of three bishops, but its meaning [Col. 0644C] and words belong to the Apostle alone. Because they rejoice with great gladness in the progress of these people, the Epistle is written with their agreement to the people in the exultation of God the Father and of our Lord Jesus Christ, wishing them peace and grace.

We give thanks to God always for all of you, making mention of you [Col. 0644D] in our prayers, unceasingly remembering your work of faith, and the labor of love [Note: [Col. 0643D] The Vulgate has “labor and love.”], and the expectation [Note: [Col. 0644D] Instead of “expectation,” the Vulgate has “and steadfastness of hope.” Our translator reads the text with Saint Ambrose.] of our Lord Jesus Christ before God and our Father [Note: [Col. 0644D] The Vulgate has “before God and our Father.”].

Since all good things come from God, they first give thanks to him for the progress of these people, who deemed it worthy not only to give his gift to human beings subject to sin, but also to adopt them as sons, assisting them at the same time to endure every hardship, so that they might become more worthy. Therefore they say that they remember them in their prayers because they were increasing in the work of faith [Col. 0645A] beyond the other Churches, so that by God’s will they might bring the work they had begun to completion, ready in their zeal for love and endurance, and in hope of the Lord’s coming before God, who deigned to incarnate his Son for the salvation of humanity. For it is God’s good pleasure that one should advance in Christ.

Knowing, beloved brothers of God, your election: for our Gospel did not come to you in word [Note: [Col. 0645D] The Vulgate has “in speech.”] alone, but also in power, and in the Holy Spirit, and in great fullness, just as you know what sort of people we were among you for your sake [Note: [Col. 0645D] Instead of “for your sake,” the Vulgate has “on your account.”].

They indicate that they had been humble among them, so as to give them an example of gentleness—not that they lacked great things that could urge them toward faith, since the power of signs and wonders in the Holy Spirit supplied strength to the Gospel teaching; that is, not in appearance but in the truth of fullness, [Col. 0645B] so that assistance would be lacking in no necessity, but grace would appear abundant both in teaching and in conduct and in the healing of the sick. Thus the perfect work of the Holy Spirit might become evident in the Churches of the Thessalonians, so that, seeing themselves inferior in nothing to the Churches of the Jews, they might rejoice in the gift of God, who had deemed them worthy to become participants in the promise made to Abraham.

And you became imitators of us and of the Lord himself [Note: [Col. 0645D] The Vulgate does not have “himself.”], receiving the word in great affliction [Note: [Col. 0645D] The Vulgate has “receiving the word in much tribulation, with joy,” and so forth.], with joy in the Holy Spirit, so that you became an example to all believers [Note: [Col. 0646D] The Vulgate has “so that you became a model.” It is enough to have said once that the text of this Epistle agrees in every detail with the text of Saint Ambrose.] in Macedonia and Achaia.

Eager for belief, they endured the insults and injuries they suffered from their fellow citizens, trusting in what was to come. Hence they are also called imitators of the apostles and of the Lord himself, because the Lord likewise suffered these things from the Jews, and the apostles, [Col. 0645C] following the faith of God, endured persecutions, rejoicing because they were considered worthy to suffer insults for the Lord’s name (Acts 5:41), knowing that great rewards had been promised for these things. For a servant is proved faithful when, for the name of his master, he provokes his master’s enemies. Remembering this, they rejoiced in the hope of the promise amid affliction.

Thus it is a great exhortation to progress when he says that they have become like Christ and the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0646D] Ambrosiaster has “the apostles”], to serve as an example to the other believers in those places, where their reputation was spreading.

For the word of the Lord has been proclaimed from you, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but your faith in God has gone forth in every place. This is like what he says in Romans 1:8: “Your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world.” But this statement goes beyond that, because not only their faith but also the work of their faith reached every place.

So that we have no need to say anything. For they themselves announce concerning us what kind of entrance we had among you, and how you turned to God from idols, to serve the living and true God, and to await his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus, who rescued us from the coming wrath.

They say that [Col. 0646A] the reputation of their arrival and of the Thessalonians’ conduct, together with the preaching of the Gospel, had spread everywhere, so that it was unnecessary to recount these things. For it is superfluous to speak of matters that are known. The news had reached everyone in the surrounding region, so that they too announced to others with what devotion the Thessalonians had received the apostles. And because they had been ready to accept everything they had heard from them, they abandoned dead gods and awaited Christ from heaven—Christ whom they had heard had died for the sake of human salvation, had risen after conquering death, and had been taken up with flesh into heaven, the cloud serving him, to the shame of the world’s wise men. These men, after considering worldly things, think that the nature of flesh, which is heavy, cannot possibly be raised into heaven. Through this result of the Holy Spirit, earthly wise men are put to shame.

[Col. 0646B]

### (CHAPTER II)

For you yourselves know, brothers, our entrance among you, that it was not fruitless, but that, after first suffering and being afflicted with insults, as you know, at Philippi, we dared, with freedom of speech, in our Lord, to speak the Gospel of God to you amid great conflict.

He suffered the affliction he now recalls at Philippi with Silas [Note: [Col. 0646D] Or Sila.], on account of the python spirit that he had driven out of the girl (Acts 16:18), as has already been said in its proper place. He did not yield to this affliction but proved stronger, daring to preach and not fearing to speak, trusting in the promised reward, so that they too might be secure in persecutions and rejoice because of the future recompense. He therefore says that it is a sign of a devoted and faithful preacher if he does not fear to speak the word of God amid affliction, calling the person empty who, overcome by present terror [Col. 0646C], is afraid to preach. For one who is secure in the promised hope does not yield, so that he may be crowned.

For our exhortation was not from deception, nor from impurity, nor in deceit; but just as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the Gospel, so we speak—not as pleasing human beings, but God, who tests our hearts. He says this on account of the false apostles, who preached in deceit and deception without being sent, so as to ensnare the Gentiles into serving the law of works. But he proves by many facts that he was chosen and sent to preach: he was found stronger in afflictions and blameless in conduct, so that there was nothing in him that seemed less worthy of God, with signs following.

Some preached Christ for the sake of gain, serving human favor, [Col. 0646D] because they were more lax in rebuking, since they possessed no authority, and weak in tribulation, because their message came not from the heart but from deceit. For everyone who acts without hope gives way when tribulation arises.

For we never conducted ourselves with a word of flattery, as you know, nor with an occasion for greed; God is witness. Here he makes clear what he indicated above when he said, “not with an occasion for greed,” calling [Col. 0647A] God as witness because he did this also from the heart, not in hypocrisy, as though he despised small offerings so that perhaps larger ones might be presented. Hence he appeals to them as people who knew and approved that he had flattered no one. For the false apostles wanted to be afforded an opening for greed, so that, under that pretext, when they saw the true apostles accepting everything offered, they themselves could plunder the simpler people without provoking envy.

Nor seeking glory from human beings [Note: [Col. 0647D] The Vulgate and Saint Ambrose read “from men.”], either from you or from others, although we could have been burdensome as apostles of Christ. He presses the case against the false apostles so strongly that he says he refused what he was permitted to request—support—in order to confound those who had neither the right nor the shame, yet claimed honor for themselves. For they wanted themselves, rather than God’s teaching, to be commended. But the Apostle, who sought glory not in the present but in the future, made himself humble so that God’s preaching might be exalted. [Col. 0647B]

But we were little children in the midst of you, as a nurse cherishes her own children; so, longing for you, we desired to impart to you not only the Gospel of God but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us. He shows that he had such affection for them that, because it was genuine, he wanted it to be demonstrated more by deeds than by words. Deception can lie hidden in words, so that those who were prompted by these exhortations might place all their feelings in the Apostle’s love.

For you remember, brothers, our labor and toil; [Col. 0647C] working night and day so as not to burden any of you. This is what he says in Acts of the Apostles 20:34: “These hands,” he says, “provided what was necessary for me and for those who were with me.” Hence in another Epistle he says: “If anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat” (II Thess. 3:10). He says this also against the false apostles, who pretended to be preachers so that they might eat while idle. In order to give an example of how the Christian life ought to be governed and at the same time expose the impostors, he persisted in human labor, casting the false apostles into shadow; moreover, those who devote themselves to labor turn away from evil thoughts, occupying their minds and preventing them from falling into dangers.

We preached to you the Gospel of God. You are witnesses, and God, how holy, just, and blameless we were toward you who believe; as you know how we exhorted and counseled each one of you, as a father does his children [Note: [Col. 0648D] The Vulgate, Saint Ambrose, and Saint Chrysostom have “comforting.”], that you should walk worthily of God, who calls you into his own kingdom and glory. These things are clear. He reminds them of how they had believed when he preached, of what kind of person they had found him to be, and of what commands he had given them, so that they might become worthy of God, who had called them from earth into heaven in order to awaken their joy.

And for this reason we also give thanks to God without ceasing: that when you received from us the word of the hearing [Col. 0648A] of God, you accepted it not as the word of human beings but, as it truly is, the word of God, which is also at work in you who believe. They give thanks to God because he opened their understanding to receive his Gospel. For the glory of those who preach is that their hearers readily believe. They received the word with such devotion that they proved themselves to have understood God’s teaching.

For you, brothers, became imitators of the Churches of God that are in Judea, in Christ Jesus, because you too suffered the same things from your fellow citizens as they did from the Jews, who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets, and persecuted us, and did not please God, and are hostile to all people, forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles so that they may be saved, thereby [Col. 0648B] always filling up their sins; but the wrath of God has overtaken them to the end.

He complains of the impiety and unbelief of the distrustful Jews, who are not only enemies of their own salvation but also of that of others, forbidding them to believe and be saved—murderers from the beginning. For they ought at least to have spared the Lord, who was common to all, since they did not spare their fellow servants and rulers. Their sins are filled up to such an extent that they may never deserve to obtain mercy. Therefore he says that the Thessalonians, having suffered the same things from their fellow citizens, imitated the endurance of the saints and of our Lord Jesus Christ. He presents the Jews as the authors of this crime, so that both the great glory of those who suffer for the Lord’s name and the vengeance prepared for hostile and faithless people may be recognized.

[Col. 0648C] But we, brothers, having been separated from you for a time, in presence but not in heart, hastened all the more eagerly to see your face, with great longing. For this reason we wanted to come to you—I, Paul, both once and again—but Satan hindered us.

They say that they were separated from them not in spirit but in body. Love is neither divided nor separated; nevertheless, because their instruction would be more complete, they say that they long to see their face. In divine matters, the faculties of understanding fail to grasp what can be said. A single day is not enough for the pen to set down what can be expressed in one hour—not to mention that certain mysteries of our religion, because of carnal understanding, ought not easily to be made public lest they cause scandal, since not everything is to be said to everyone, but words must be measured according to each person’s capacity [Col. 0648D]: one way for the inexperienced and another for those firmly grounded. Therefore the presence of the body is required, because in this way the truth of love is perfected. Although love is not divided, the absence of the body produces longing. Finally, the will is fulfilled through kisses and the embrace of souls.

He asserts that Satan was an impediment to this, because Satan also stretched out his hands against the apostles, so that the truth might not be disclosed to human beings. For he stirred the minds of the faithless so that they would hold the apostles with blows and bonds and prevent them from speaking the word of God. The leading Jews said to the apostles: “Did we not expressly command you not to speak [Col. 0649A] in the name of Jesus to any human being?” (Acts 5:28). But because what is not from God cannot stand (ibid.), Satan’s obstacles are dissolved.

For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Is it not you, before our Lord Jesus at his coming? For you are our glory and joy. It is clear that the perfection of disciples is the joy and crown of the teacher. They are the ones who will eat the fruits of their labors. For the fruit of the teacher is an obedient disciple; when the disciple’s good conduct benefits the teacher, the teacher reaps the fruit of his labor. The disciple’s labor in a good work gives a crown to the teacher before Christ the judge.

For this reason, no longer able to endure it, we thought it best to be left alone in Athens; and we sent Timothy [Col. 0649B] [Note: [Col. 0649D] The manuscript has “Titus”; this had to be emended according to all the readings.] our brother and fellow worker of God in the Gospel of Christ, so that he might strengthen you and exhort you on behalf of your faith, lest anyone be shaken by these afflictions; for you yourselves know that we are appointed for this. For even when we were with you, we told you beforehand that we would suffer affliction, as indeed happened, and you know it.

He has expressed the reasons for the longing mentioned above. They wanted to be present with them for this reason: to strengthen their minds, lest any of them be scandalized by the apostles’ afflictions—lest those who performed such great signs should at some point become weak and be so humbled as to be subjected to blows and bonds. To address this matter, he testifies that Timothy [Note: [Col. 0649D] Here “Timothy” is clearly read.] was sent, a suitable teacher who could show that Christians’ merits increase if, after suffering for the Lord’s name [Col. 0649C], they give thanks to the one from whom they expect the reward for this, and that at the same time they might pour out prayers to God that they remain steadfast.

They had proclaimed that they would suffer this persecution so that, by professing beforehand that they possessed foreknowledge of the matter, they might show that they could escape and avoid these injuries. But because there is great hope in these things, he says that they willingly endure what was inflicted [Note: [Col. 0649D] We have added the verb “says” from Ambrosiaster.] Therefore I too, no longer able to endure it, sent him for this purpose: to learn about your faith, lest the tempter should in some way have tempted you and our labor become fruitless.

He says this on account of certain people who might be led astray by Satan’s cunning.
