For in every congregation there is a firm part and a weak part, and he was concerned for their sake lest he should lose the fruit of their belief. And because he could no longer endure being ignorant of what was actually happening among them, [Col. 0649D] he sent [Note: [Col. 0650D] Again, “Timothy” is clearly read.] Timothy, the bishop whom he had appointed, through whom he could learn the truth.

But now that Timothy has come to us from you and announced to us your faith and love, and that you have a good remembrance of us, always longing to see us just as we long to see you, for this reason, brothers, we have received consolation in you beyond all our need and affliction, through your faith, because now we live if you stand firm in Christ.

He has explained why he writes to them in such an eager tone. Therefore, when the messenger arrived and declared the firmness of their devotion in faith and their love for the Apostle, he became joyful at their common harmony and wrote to them, confident in the fruit of their faith and good conduct. [Col. 0650A]

For what thanksgiving can we render to God concerning you, for all the joy with which we rejoice because of you before our God, night and day praying most abundantly that we may see your face and complete what is lacking in your faith? He says that nothing is worthy enough to compensate for the salvation acquired by the Gentiles. And because they had advanced through perseverance in faith and the practice of a better life, he desires more and more to see them, so that they may learn what pertains to their perfection—namely, the mysteries of spiritual realities, [Col. 0650B] which ought not easily to be made public—so that they may know whom, and how immense a one, they hoped would be their judge.

For it is one thing to receive faith and another to receive an exposition of the faith. One discussion concerns the nature of the Father and the Son, and another concerns the persons. The Father is unbegotten, whereas the Son is begotten. With regard to the persons they appear different, although the unity of nature is indivisible. For unity is not in the person but in the substance. The Holy Spirit, however, must not be thought degenerate because he is named third. Therefore whoever does not doubt concerning the second person also admits the third.

But may God himself, and our Father, and our Lord Jesus Christ direct our way to you. He asks that their journey be arranged in proper order: first [Col. 0650C] by God the Father, because all things are from him; then by the Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things exist. Thus the power and providence of the Father and the Son might commend his arrival, make it acceptable to those who hear him, and remove the devil’s obstacles so as to direct his journey.

And may the Lord multiply you and make you abound in love for one another and for all, just as we do for you, so as to strengthen your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints. To increase the joy that he has in them, he desires that they be multiplied in every good thing, so that, when he comes to them, he may find in them more worthy of praise than he had heard from Timothy, and so that they may be found blameless with the saints in the love [Col. 0650D] of God the Father and at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, when the examination of each person before his tribunal begins to approve them. He calls him God because of the terror of his majesty, but Father because of the kindness by which he deigns to adopt those who believe in him as sons; this will be manifested at the Lord’s coming.

### (CHAPTER IV)

Therefore, as for what remains, brothers, we ask and exhort you in the Lord Jesus that, just as you received from us how you ought to walk and please God, as you are walking [Note: [Col. 0650D] The Vulgate has “so you may walk.”], you should abound [Col. 0651A] more and more. This is what I said above: that, in order to increase his joy, he wants them to grow in good works according to the apostolic commands.

For you know what instructions we gave you through the Lord Jesus Christ. For this is the will of God: your sanctification; that you abstain from fornication; that each one of you know how to possess his own vessel in holiness and honor, not in the passion of desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God; that no one transgress or defraud his brother in business, because the Lord is an avenger concerning all these things, just as we told you beforehand and testified.

Although he praises them throughout the whole Epistle, he nevertheless admonishes them not to be led by any stealthy intrusion into unlawful things and so incur the vengeance that they had learned would avenge evils, [Col. 0651B] knowing that this pleases God if they keep their bodies undefiled; but also to deal simply with their brothers, lest, found to be like the Gentiles, they be disowned under the name of adoption.

For God did not call us to impurity but to holiness. Therefore whoever rejects these things rejects not a human being but God, who gave the Holy Spirit into you [Note: [Col. 0651D] The Vulgate has “into us,” as do Ambrosiaster and Hieronymiaster.]. To bind them more firmly to what he teaches, he introduces the person of God, saying: Whoever transgresses the commandments rejects not a human being but God. He says that God gave us the Holy Spirit for this reason: so that we might live holy lives, because the Holy Spirit does not dwell in a body subject to sins (Wisdom 1:4–5).

Concerning brotherly affection, we have no need to write to you. For you yourselves have been taught by God [Col. 0651C] to love one another. And indeed you do this toward all the brothers throughout the whole of Macedonia. Although he praises them for doing this as well, he nevertheless admonishes them to practice it more eagerly. By saying that they have been taught by God himself, he indicates that they ought to be more ready in brotherly love. For because of his great love God had mercy on us; having become his imitators, we rightly show that we have been adopted by God as sons.

But we exhort you, brothers, to abound more and to strive to be quiet, to attend to your own affairs, and to work with your hands, as we commanded you, so that you may walk honorably toward those who are outside, and that you may desire nothing from anyone. Again he exhorts them in the same way to abound in good works deliberately. To indicate that this truly is what pleases God, he frequently gives this admonition. The way of justice must be followed, so that one may rightly reach mercy: those who are inferior in material possessions should work with their hands, so that by this very intention they may be lifted away from common unrest and from evil thoughts, so that their discipline may also be praised by unbelievers and they may be drawn to the faith.

But [Col. 0652A] we do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the others who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus.

The reason is clear: if the future resurrection of the dead is believed, those who depart bearing the sign of the cross are not to be mourned. Rather, the unbelievers are truly to be mourned, because from here they pass into Gehenna, where they will learn that what they refused to believe was true. The faithful, however, are those who will rise to glory; those who depart through Jesus—that is, under the hope of this faith—will be brought with him at his coming, so that they may be seen by all.

Yet although he forbids the mourning of the deceased’s departure, elsewhere he says, “lest I should have sorrow” [Note: [Col. 0651D] That is, in the exposition of the cited text addressed to the Philippians.]. But this has also been resolved in its proper place (Phil. 2:27).

For this we say to you by the word of the Lord: we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, together with them, will be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ the Lord in the air, and thus we shall always be with the Lord. Therefore comfort one another with these words.

He professes that he speaks by the Lord’s instruction when he says, “We say this to you by the word of the Lord.” In order to demonstrate the firm hope and assured glory of the resurrection promised to the saints, he explains the very order in which it will occur, with the will of Christ the Judge being made known by the Holy Spirit, so that those who have sent their loved ones ahead may not grieve in that very hope, learning that at the coming of the Lord those who die in Christ will rise first.

Christ the Lord himself, by the will of the Father, will descend from heaven like the first angel with the heavenly army, as is contained in the Apocalypse of the apostle John, to wage war in the name of the Lord against the Antichrist. When he has been destroyed, the dead will rise at Christ’s command. Thus “to descend with the trumpet of God” means to wage war in the name of God. For he is, as he himself said to Jesus son of Nun (Joshua 5:14), the commander and prince of the army of the Lord; for this reason he is called an archangel.

When he descends with the trumpet of God, he is God, because Scripture contains both truths. Thus, in Exodus, we read that the angel appeared to Moses in the flame [Note: The Vulgate has “the Lord” where “the angel” occurs. But see Acts 7:30, where Stephen, recounting what happened to Moses, says: “An angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai in the flame of a burning bush.”]. Immediately afterward we recognize that he himself is God, for the same Scripture says (ibid. 6): “And Moses approached and turned away his face, because he could not look upon the face of God.” He is therefore God, because he is the true Son of God. He is commander and prince because he is the head of all things, and because all things are through him.

When, therefore, those who died in Christ have risen first, then we who are alive will be caught up together with them, borne by the clouds, to meet Christ in the air, so that all may come with the Lord to battle and he may see alive those whom he had killed. For just as the clouds served the Lord, so also they serve those whom he deigned to call his brothers. “And thus we shall always be with the Lord.”

In that very catching up, death will occur, as though through sleep, so that the soul, having departed, may be restored in an instant. For when they are taken up, they will die, so that, when they reach the Lord, they may receive their souls in the Lord’s presence, since they cannot be dead together with the Lord. With this hope he commands those who, still following pagan custom, thought that the passing of their loved ones ought to be mourned to comfort one another.

## (Chapter V)

“Concerning the times and the seasons, brothers, there is no need for anything to be written to you. For you yourselves know carefully that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. And when they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them, as labor pain upon a pregnant woman, and they will not escape.”

This is what the Lord spoke in the Gospel, saying: “Watch, because you do not know the hour at which your Lord will come” (Matthew 24:42; Mark 13:33; Luke 12:37). And again: “If anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ,’ or, ‘There,’ do not believe it” (Matthew 24:23; Luke 17:21). For he will appear suddenly and unexpectedly, just as a flash appears from east to west, bringing with him the army of the army of God the Father, for the destruction of the Antichrist and his followers.

When the wicked have become secure in the devil’s kingdom, after the saints—namely Enoch and Elijah—have been killed, and when they rejoice in victory, sending gifts to one another, as the Apocalypse says, then sudden destruction will come upon them. At his coming Christ will destroy all of them, so that the surviving saints, seeing this, may exult.

“But you, brothers, are not in darkness, so that that day may seize you like a thief. For you are all sons of light and sons of God; you are not of the night or of darkness.”

By darkness he signifies ignorance and falsehood; by day, knowledge and truth. For this reason he says that Christians are not in darkness, but that pagans and unbelieving Jews are sons of darkness, because they are worshipers of falsehood. Accordingly, he indicates that the faithful ought to be secure, because they do not remain ignorant of the future coming of the Lord but await it attentively, so that it may come. Those who are ignorant, however, distrust him; the day will suddenly seize them unprepared and destroy them.

“Therefore let us not sleep, as the others do, but let us watch and be sober. For those who sleep sleep at night, and those who become drunk are drunk at night. But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love, and as a helmet the hope of salvation. For God has not appointed us to wrath, but to the acquisition of salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us, so that, whether we sleep or watch, we may live together with him. Therefore encourage one another and build one another up, just as you are doing.”

What he says is clear. He warns them not to act carelessly because they are secure in the name of the Savior; therefore he says that we must be armed with three defenses: faith, hope, and love. While faith remains, it arouses hope; hope is necessarily attentive to the promise and does not sleep; and love offers devotion to the Lord. Love admits nothing hostile. For this reason the Lord Jesus died for us and rose again, so that, whether we watch—that is, live—or sleep—that is, die—we may enjoy eternal life together with him.

This is what he said above: at the coming of the Lord the faithful, both dead and living, will be taken up to meet the Lord and will always live with him. He teaches that we must meditate upon this, so that we may build one another up in this understanding.

“We ask you, brothers, to recognize those who labor among you in the Lord and admonish you, and to hold them in the highest honor in love because of their work. Be at peace among yourselves.”

This is what he also says in another Epistle (1 Timothy 5:17): presbyters who labor in word and teaching are to be honored with double honor. For a person suffering want may become weary of carrying out a ministry that benefits his hearers. What benefit is there in receiving honor without fruit? Or what great thing is it to offer material things to one who provides spiritual things? For just as riches produce neglect of salvation, so poverty, while seeking to be satisfied, turns away from justice. For this reason Solomon asks neither to be made excessively rich nor destitute (Proverbs 30:9).

Nevertheless, he says that this must be done in love, so that the honor shown to a priest arises not more from fear than from affection, and so that it may also benefit the one who gives it. For what is not done willingly does not reach its proper effect. Although for the present it benefits the recipient, it will bring no benefit in the future to the giver. And because disagreement produces many evils, he urges them to be peaceable.

“We ask you, brothers: correct the disorderly, comfort the fainthearted, support the weak, and be patient toward all. See that no one repays evil for evil to anyone, but always pursue what is good toward one another and toward all. Rejoice always in the Lord. Pray without interruption. Give thanks in all things. For this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.”

Since there must be some people in the congregation who are disorderly, others fainthearted—that is, fearful—and still others weak in faith, he therefore urges those who are disciplined, courageous, and firmly grounded in faith, with a prayer, to care for such people, so that by bearing with them they may be able to advance and may not become worse if evil is repaid with evil.

For this reason he urges them to pursue nothing but what is good, not only in the affairs of the brothers but toward everyone. Unbelievers can be drawn to faith by good works, so that they may always rejoice in the Lord—that is, in what is good. They are also to pray without interruption. Persistent prayers move the mind of the Judge to grant mercy. In all good actions they are to give thanks to God, who has granted this teaching in Christ Jesus our Lord.

“Do not extinguish the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies. Test everything; hold fast to what is good. Abstain from every kind of evil.”

He says this so that no one who speaks by the Spirit may be forbidden too readily. The Spirit is extinguished when the fervor of one beginning to speak is stifled by contradiction, lest, because they do not understand that spiritual things are being spoken through him, they insult the Holy Spirit and sin through ignorance.

Nor does he mean that someone who appears to reveal the Scriptures should not be heard patiently; rather, all statements must be examined and then judged, lest, while rejecting the grace given to a brother, they oppose its author. He therefore urges that everything said be tested, and that whatever has been spoken soberly and well be retained.

Whatever agrees with the words of the apostles and of the Lord himself is to be regarded as well spoken and retained. But one must abstain from whatever appears hostile to the faith. For worldly spirits often deceitfully speak good things as though in imitation, and among them introduce evil, so that through the good things they may be accepted and the evil things may be accepted as well. Because the sayings are thought to come from one spirit, they are not distinguished from one another; instead, what is unlawful is commended through what is permitted, by the authority of the name rather than by the truth of the virtue.

They often teach even abominable and contrary doctrines under the name of the apostles and of the Lord himself. Therefore he urges that everything be tested, because the utterances of the Lord cannot be contradictory. Hence also the Epistle of the apostle John says: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are from God” (1 John 4:1). For if a spirit says many good things but in some matter puts forward what is contrary to the faith, it must be recognized as not being the Holy Spirit. No error can be found in the Holy Spirit.

Either, through a kind of exercise in eloquence, it presents some things as spiritual and others as carnal—for every error is assigned to the flesh—or, certainly, by some artifice of cunning it pretends to be good in order to insert evil into it, as I mentioned above. Thus, in Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla, the prophets of the Cataphrygians, the worldly spirit, by a kind of imitation, pretended to be good, so that through many things resembling the truth, and even through genuine truths, it might falsely claim to be the Holy Spirit.

“May the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, so that your spirit, soul, and body may be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Christ is the God of peace. For he says: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27). Since everything the Father has belongs to the Son, the Apostle wishes him to sanctify us, so that he may enlighten us through his pious clemency and direct all our desire toward perfection, so that the spirit given to us may be whole.

It is whole when we devote ourselves to a good life, possessing a clean soul and a blameless body, so that the entire human being may be perfect. For the body may be clean while the soul is polluted by an evil thought; therefore he says that everything in a person must be clean.

But if an evil life or thought intervenes, the spirit will not be whole, because it abandons the person subject to sins. When soul and body disagree, although the body is without consciousness, they become alienated from him; and, as though he were losing them, the spirit will not be whole. For this reason the spirit is given to a person, so that it may remain and be, as it were, his head. It will not therefore be whole, because it loses its members when a person withdraws from it by doing what the Holy Spirit hates.

“God is faithful, who called you, and he will also act. Brothers, pray for us.”

He calls God faithful in his promises, so that they may conduct themselves rightly with confidence in the reward. And because those who live rightly according to the Gospel can readily obtain what they ask, he urges them to pray for him. For many readily obtain what they desire.

“Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss.”

Holy kisses belong to Christian greeting; all others are carnal, because whatever is done without Christ is carnal and therefore mortal. For one who despises the author of life is in death.

“I adjure you by the Lord that this Epistle be read to all the brothers.”

He binds them to be diligent in reading the Epistle to all the brothers, so that they may know both his praises and his admonitions, through which they may become perfect.

“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.”

He wishes them to advance in good works in such a way that the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ may remain in them forever.

The end. Thanks be to God. Amen.

## The Second Epistle to the Thessalonians

[Note: The argument and exposition of this Epistle, as also of the first Epistle to the Thessalonians, are by the same person, the blessed Ambrose, or Hilary the deacon. Since the title is lacking in the manuscript, we judged that it should be supplied.]

[Column 655]

### Argument

[Column 655D]

Since, in the first Epistle given to the Thessalonians, he wrote, among other things, about the coming of the Lord and the resurrection of the saints, he now writes another Epistle to them. In it he indicates, though obscurely—for he could not write openly—the abolition of the Roman kingdom, the appearance and condemnation of the Antichrist, and the disorderly conduct of certain brothers.

### The Text Begins

#### (Chapter I)

“Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, to the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

He writes to them in the customary solemn manner. For, as usual, the beginning of the Epistle is contained in these words; and the same three persons are named as its authors, just as in the first Epistle.

[Column 656D]

“We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is fitting, because your faith is growing exceedingly, and the love of each one of all of you for one another is increasing.”

They declare themselves indebted to God in thanksgiving for their progress. And to show that this debt was not insignificant, he says, “as is fitting,” so that they might testify that very great thanks ought to be returned to God for so immense a gift. After receiving the first Epistle, they continued to be better than they had been, so that they appeared rich and abundant in the very thing that, after devotion to the Lord and God, we have been commanded to possess: that we should love one another.

“So that we ourselves boast about you in the churches of God for your patience and faith in all your persecutions and afflictions that you endure, as an example of the just judgment of God, so that you may be considered worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you also suffer.”

They testify that their glory consists in the conduct of these people and in their endurance of persecution, to such an extent that their example is presented before the other churches, so that by imitating them those churches may increase in devotion to suffering for Christ and may deserve to obtain what has been promised to the saints on the day of God’s just judgment. For love of that judgment they did not hesitate to despise the world.

The afflictions themselves are examples of future merits in those who suffer for glory; in those who persecute, however, they are examples leading to destruction.

“Indeed [Note: The Vulgate has ‘if nevertheless’; hence perhaps *si quidem* should be read.], it is just before God to repay affliction to those who oppress you, and to grant rest with us to you who endure affliction, at the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven with the angels of his power, in flaming fire, bringing vengeance upon those who do not know God and upon those who do not obey the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ. They will suffer the penalty of eternal destruction, away from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his power.”

Because he says that the example of God’s just judgment will appear both in the good and in the wicked, he therefore continues: “Indeed, it is just before God that he repay each person according to his works.” What is more just than that those who in this world oppress the good and make them exiles through persecutions should in the future suffer the same things that they inflict, while the others should be at rest with the remaining saints—those who, coming from the great tribulation, will receive an eternal kingdom at the coming of the Lord from heaven?

He will come with the heavenly army and with fire as his minister, to bring vengeance upon the pagans who are ignorant that God the Father is the Father of Christ Jesus, and upon the Jews who, although they say that they know God, do not believe the Gospel of Christ, which God the Father gave him to hand on to his servants.

The presence of the Lord and the glory of his majesty will burn all of them with fire, so that they may pay the deserved penalty of eternal destruction, always experiencing it but not utterly ceasing to exist, so that the punishment itself may in some way continually generate them for the purpose of consuming them.

“When he comes to be glorified in his saints and to be marveled at in all who have believed, because our testimony to you was believed on that day, the day of the Lord’s coming.”

It contains a twofold meaning [Note: We have supplied the verb from the works of the blessed Ambrose.]. For he will come to punish the wicked and glorify the good. He will appear glorious and marvelous to those who believe, by the example and faith of the apostles, when they have been crowned, while the Gospel bears witness for them on the day of the Lord. But he will appear severe to unbelievers when they begin to be confined by eternal punishments. For the crown of the disciples is the glory of their teacher, and his truth is the punishment of unbelievers, because they did not believe what was preached.

“For this reason we also always pray for you, that our God may make you worthy of his calling and fulfill every good purpose and work of faith in power, so that the name of our Lord Jesus Christ may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God and of the Lord Jesus Christ.”

He adds prayers to his joy, so that, since they are devoted, God may deign to help them complete the work they have begun, to the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that the perseverance of the disciples may serve as the teacher’s testimony to his glory. For the authority of the teacher consists in the confidence of the disciples when they make themselves more worthy of the grace they have received.

#### (Chapter II)

“Now we ask you, brothers, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and by our gathering together to him, not to be quickly shaken from your understanding or disturbed, either by a spirit, or by a word, or by a letter supposedly sent by us, as though the day of the Lord were at hand. Let no one deceive you in any way, because unless the apostasy comes first and that man of sin, the son of destruction, is revealed—he who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshiped, so that he sits in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God—”

He begs them not lightly and readily to accept the opinion that the coming of the Lord is imminent. He gives such commands that even if someone should speak as a prophet through the Spirit, he should not be believed; nor should assent be given to a discourse or a letter perhaps written in the name of the apostles.

For deceivers often fabricate a letter under the name of some distinguished man in order that the authority of the name may commend what could not be accepted from the person himself. This is so that, in the very disturbance, while the unwary are caught off guard, they may be seduced into worshiping the devil. He will boast of these things for this reason: appearing under the name of the Savior and deceiving the saints, he will wish to be worshiped, in order to deceive those who believe in Christ.

But so that this most shameless Satan may not have the place or opportunity for deception that he thinks he possesses, he has designated the time and signs of the Lord’s coming. For the Lord will not come before the Roman kingdom has fallen and the Antichrist appears, who will kill the saints after restoring liberty to the Romans, though under his own name.

Knowing that the Lord will come to restrain him, he will usurp the Lord’s name, so that both his kingdom may appear genuine and he may draw along with him those who will perish together with him. He will sit in the seat of the Lord, in the seat of Christ, and will assert that he himself is God, not the Son of God.

Therefore in the Gospel the Lord says to the Jews: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; if another comes in his own name, you will receive him” (John 5:43). For this reason it is to be expected that he will come from the circumcision, or as one circumcised, so that the Jews may have confidence in believing him. Thus, when the Apostle writes to the Thessalonians, he teaches that everyone ought to be cautious in a matter of this kind.

“Do you not remember that, while I was still with you, these things were being told you? And now you know what is restraining him, so that he may be revealed in his own time.”

He says that what remains is for the one who will come before the Lord to be revealed, so that the Lord’s coming may now be expected. Above he spoke of this, as though under a veil, saying: “Unless the apostasy comes first.” By this I have indicated above that the abolition of the Roman kingdom is to be understood, so that when it has fallen and the Antichrist has come, then the coming of the Lord may be believed to be near.

“For the mystery of iniquity is already at work; only let the one who now restrains continue to restrain, until he is removed from the midst.”

The mystery of iniquity also began with Nero, who, in his zeal for idols and at the instigation of his father the devil, killed the apostles. It continued up to Diocletian and finally Julian, who by a certain art and subtlety could not complete the persecution that had begun, because it had not been granted from above.

Satan uses such ministers so that, while the Roman kingdom continues, under the multitude of gods he may mock the manifestation of the one true God in order to seduce human beings. This is what he said: “Until he is removed from the midst.”

[Column 659B]

“And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the brightness of his coming” (Isaiah 11:4). “His coming is according to the working of Satan, with every power and signs and lying wonders.”

He says that the Antichrist will appear after the fall of the Roman kingdom, as has been mentioned. For at the very end of time, knowing that destruction is threatening him, when the Roman kingdom has fallen and he has been cast down from heaven to earth, as is said in the Apocalypse of the apostle John, the devil will provide himself with a person through whom and in whom, by performing certain displays of power with the permission of the just God, he may commend himself so that he will be worshiped as though he were God.

He will imitate the Son of God. Just as the Son of God, born or made human, demonstrated his divinity through signs and powers, so Satan will appear in a human being, displaying himself as God through lying powers, as was said above.

The revelation of the mystery of iniquity is this: when the Antichrist appears, he will be recognized as the god, so to speak, of those whom the common people previously worshiped as gods at his command. He will be their first or highest god; he will make this credible through the powers of his signs.

For this reason he called them lying portents: he wants people to believe through signs that he is what he is not, in order to deceive those whom he is going to ensnare. This was foretold to the saints so that they might know what to avoid.

“With every deceit of iniquity for those who are perishing, because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved.”

He says that the deceit of his iniquitous wonders benefits those who are destined to perish. Because they rejected the truth through which they could have been saved, while the apostles were preaching, they were handed over to the devil. For, unwilling to be saved, they are abandoned by God.

“And for this reason God sends them a working of error, so that they may believe the lie, in order that all who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity may be judged.”

The working of error is entrusting belief to falsehood, so that those who were unwilling to acknowledge the brightness of light as day may think that darkness ought to be called day. Thus, having incurred a more serious guilt, they may be condemned without objection, as enemies of the truth but doers of iniquity [Note: The printed editions of the works of the blessed Ambrose read *fautores* (“supporters”) here.].

[Column 660A]

“But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, because God chose you from the beginning for salvation through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth, to which he also called you through our Gospel, for the acquisition of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Here God’s foreknowledge is made prominent: he knows the minds of all people before their birth. For nothing is hidden from him concerning those who will believe. Therefore from the beginning he knows that these will be faithful, those who by believing increase their faith rather than diminish it. Sanctified through faith in the truth of the Gospel of the Son of God, they are acquired for the increase of the glory of Christ’s body, as he says in another Epistle: “So that all things may grow for the increase of God” (Ephesians 4:15; Colossians 2:19). For all who, abandoning the devil, flee to faith in Christ contribute increase to God in the body of Christ, though previously they had caused diminution.

“Therefore, brothers, stand firm and hold fast to our traditions, which you learned either through word or through our Epistle.”

So that God’s foreknowledge may remain directed toward their salvation, he urges them to stand firm and persevere in the tradition of the Gospel, so that they may be attentive and, by growing sluggish through idleness and leisure in God’s works, fail to complete what they began. For one is foreknown as believing and able to remain faithful if one is stirred by frequent admonition.

“May our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal consolation and good hope through grace, console your hearts and establish you in every good work and word.”

Since the Father and the Son are one power, one divinity, and one knowledge [Note: In the printed works of the blessed Ambrose, *substantia* (“substance”) is read here instead of *scientia* (“knowledge”); perhaps *essentia* (“essence”) should be read in the manuscript.], he did not hesitate first to name our Lord Jesus Christ and then God our Father through his gracious condescension, not by the truth of nature. He loved us so greatly that he gave his Son for us: God for human beings, the Lord for servants, the true Son for adopted children. Thus his death is our life, his resurrection our justification, and his second coming the rest of our life and our glory forever. This hope is therefore the consolation of present afflictions, through which, established in good works, they may grow also in teaching.

#### (Chapter III)

“Finally, brothers, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may run and be glorified, as also among you, and that we may be delivered from wicked and evil people. For not everyone has faith.”

He asks that God may direct his teaching in an unhindered course and pour it through the mouth of his Apostle into the ears of his hearers; that he may restrain and quiet the uprisings of evil people who distrust the truth; and that the Apostle’s confidence in speaking may grow, for its fruit and for the conversion of many.

“But the Lord is faithful. He will strengthen you and guard you from evil.”

Because God has promised that his help will not fail the faithful and those who live well in their time of need, for their strengthening—and because they were zealous for good things both in faith and in action—he calls God faithful in his promises, since his providence was directed toward them.

“We have confidence in the Lord concerning you, that you are doing and will do what we command.”

Because he trusted that they deserved to be kept safe under God’s protection, he did not doubt that they were carrying out and would continue to carry out, in the Lord’s name, what he commanded them.

“May the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God and the expectation of Christ.”

He wishes this for them from God, and does not doubt that it can be granted: that their hearts may advance in the love of God toward awaiting the Lord’s coming, so that, once the world has been condemned [Note: The printed editions read “despised” (*contempto*) here.], they may desire the coming of the one who conquered the world.

“We command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to separate yourselves from every brother who walks disorderly and not according to the tradition that they received from us.”

Since not everyone in the congregation obeys the word of teaching, but follows his own desire and judgment rather than the law, he therefore commands them to avoid such people, so that they may recognize that they are in error.

“For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we did not live disorderly among you, nor did we eat anyone’s bread without payment. Instead, in labor and toil, working night and day, we acted so as not to burden any of you—not because we did not have the authority, but so that we might give you ourselves as an example to imitate.”

He says that they were not unaware of his work and labor, which he diligently undertook so that he would not need another’s bread, in order to give them an example to imitate. It would not have been blameworthy for him to receive bread from those to whom he supplied spiritual food for their souls, food that would also secure immortality with glory for the body.

For liberty can then truly be exercised if a person subjects himself to no one for the sake of his belly or money, content with his own bread. This is especially beneficial for praise when, although he has permission and the ability to take, he exercises restraint. Such a person can benefit his hearers. For they will respect this strictness, and what he commands will not be able to be disregarded.

“For even when we were with you, we commanded you this: if anyone is unwilling to work, neither should he eat.”

He taught not only by words but also urged them by his actions. For a teacher is competent when he fulfills in his deeds what he teaches in words. They then learn that what they hear is true when they see that it is not neglected by their teacher. Although what is taught is plainly known to be true, if the teacher begins to neglect it, those who hear make little progress. Deeds persuade more than words.

Therefore those who progress both in action and understanding through words alone, while their teachers are negligent, deserve greater rewards. He was an example for those in the congregation of moderate or limited means, so that they might learn not to lose their freedom. Hence Solomon also says: “Rarely set foot in your friend’s house, lest, being filled with you, he hate you” (Proverbs 25:17).

For one who frequently comes to another’s table must, being devoted to idleness, flatter the person who feeds him, whereas our religion calls people to freedom. Therefore, he says, if anyone refuses to work, let him abstain from eating, so that, since no one can live without food, he may devote himself to working and, living according to his own judgment, may have God favorably disposed toward him.

“For we hear that some among you are walking disorderly, doing no work but acting as busybodies.”

Those who wish to remain idle do this so that an opportunity may arise by which they can make their entrance desirable into the houses of the rich. Going about, they carefully gather reports of what people say, knowing what they wish to hear about each matter, so that they may be readily fed when invited and questioned. This conduct is utterly foreign to the Lord’s discipline. Their belly is their god, and they provide necessities through shameful concern.

“Now to such people we command and exhort in the Lord Jesus Christ that, working quietly, they eat their own bread.”

To make the exhortation easier for them to accept, he introduces the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and urges them to obey what is useful for them.

“But you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good. If anyone does not obey our word in this Epistle, take note of that person and do not associate with him, so that he may be put to shame. Do not regard him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.”

Because above he commanded each person to eat his own bread, lest some of them seize the opportunity for stinginess and inhumanity, he immediately added: “But you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good” (Galatians 6:9). For the person who is humane in giving is not subject to reproach; rather, it is the person who, although able to endure labor, wishes to spend his life in idleness.

If the authority of the Epistle does not correct him, he commands that this person be noted and that others not associate with him, so that, put to shame because everyone avoids him, he may submit to the Apostle’s commands. He wishes this to be done without anger or insult: they should patiently withdraw from him, but if circumstances require them to speak with him, they should admonish him to allow himself to be corrected and no longer to despise the Apostle’s commands. They should likewise not maintain familiarity with him until he becomes obedient.

For if he is provoked to anger by insults, he will become worse. He will be incited to contention and will begin to defend his error; he may also be ashamed to correct himself, lest he appear afterward to admit what he had previously excused.

“May the God of peace himself give you peace always and in every place. The Lord be with all of you always.”

He follows them with a good wish as though they were his dearest sons, desiring that they may always have peace, for peace is the guide to eternal life. For the Lord promised that he would be with those who are peaceable.

“The greeting is in my own hand—Paul’s—which is the sign in every Epistle; this is how I write.”

Because of interpolators and corrupters of the Scriptures, he testifies that in every Epistle he always adds a greeting written in his own hand, so that a letter not subscribed by his hand cannot be accepted as having been written in his name.

[Column 664A]

“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all.”

This greeting was written by the Apostle’s hand, in which he wishes the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ to be with them. Amen.

The end of the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians.

## The First Epistle to Timothy

[Note: The argument and exposition of this Epistle, as also of the two preceding ones, are by Hilary the deacon.]

[Column 663]

### Argument

[Column 663A]

Timothy was the son of a faithful Jewish woman and a Greek father, because of whom he could not be circumcised as a child. Through the diligence of his mother he learned the sacred writings, and, applying himself to them, he ordered his life well. When the Apostle wished to take him with him, knowing that he would be a suitable steward of the evangelical truth, he was compelled, because of the Jews, to circumcise him. They insisted that one born of a Jewish mother should not be accepted uncircumcised for the ministry of teaching, on account of the testimony of his ancestry. Having therefore already been made a bishop, Timothy is instructed by this Epistle how he ought to order the Church.

## [HERE BEGINS THE TEXT]

### (CHAP. I)

Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus according to the command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope, to Timothy, his genuine son in the faith: grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.

He shows that he was made an apostle by the command of the Father and the Son, so that he might proclaim salvation in God the Father and hope in Christ, his Son. Since no one denies that salvation is in God, nor should anyone doubt that hope is in Christ Jesus, whom he recognizes as having been raised from the dead and as having given an example of this hope. He writes to Timothy in this way so that he might be confident about his ordination, since he was chosen by the command of the Father and the Son for teaching. Paul calls him a true son, but in the faith, as he says to the Corinthians: “For in Christ Jesus,” he says, “through the Gospel I begot you” (1 Cor. 4:15). This is a true and firm generation, which knows neither decline nor diseases nor pestilence, and which knows neither hunger nor thirst. He says that in the kingdom of God no one will be in need, because glorious immortality will be given by God in the kingdom of God and of Christ. He prays that their grace, mercy, and peace may remain with Timothy.

As I urged you to remain in Ephesus when I was going to Macedonia, so that you might charge certain persons not to teach otherwise, nor to attend to myths and endless genealogies, which provide controversies rather than the edification of God, which is in faith.

A son ought not to be asked by his father, but because of the affection of charity, and in order to show him an example of humility, the bishop entreats his fellow bishop not to allow the Jews to teach the people anything other than what was handed down by the Apostle. He does not want them to take pleasure in the myths which the Jews are accustomed to relate about the genealogies of their origins from Abraham, Isaac, and the other patriarchs, and about circumcision and the things later handed down by Moses, lest they be ensnared into observing these things, which had been given carnally. What need is there to mention genealogies, which are plainly infinite through descent, or what was done under each of them and to what extent, rather than seeking salvation more briefly through faith? For controversies arise when it is examined what was done, when, how, and why; and this matter impedes salvation.

The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith. Some, having strayed from these things, have turned aside to empty talk, desiring to be teachers of the law, though they understand neither what they say nor the matters about which they make assertions.

Because charity is greater than all things, he said that this is the end—that is, the perfection and completion—of all the commandments, provided that it proceeds from a pure heart and a good conscience. True charity cannot possess an evil life or a feigned faith; in these the whole law and the prophets are fulfilled. Certain Jews, however, ignorant of the mystery of the law and of the prophets—that these had been handed down to be observed until Christ—went astray after Christ had been preached, maintaining that the law of works must still be observed in new moons, circumcision, and the distinguishing of foods. Therefore he says that they have turned aside to empty talk, because they wished to teach what they did not understand.

We know that the law is good if someone uses it lawfully, understanding this: that the law is not laid down for the just, but for the unjust and disobedient, the impious and sinners, the criminal and profane, those who kill fathers and mothers, fornicators, men who have intercourse with males, kidnappers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is opposed to sound teaching, which is according to the Gospel of the glory of the blessed God, which was entrusted to me.

He does not deny that the law given through Moses is good, but only on condition that its meaning be understood and that it be received according to the manner in which it was given. For he knows the law, and the reason for which it was given, who, after Christ has been preached, abandons it in that aspect in which it is called the law of works, but uses it with regard to the love of God, maintaining and affirming that the things spoken by the Savior are found in the law and the prophets. He uses the law lawfully who can distinguish the things given for a time from those that are perpetual, and who understands that the things pertaining to the mystery of Christ ought no longer to be observed in the future, as though the one believed to be coming had not already come.

If, therefore, everything is understood in its proper place, the things are good; if not, they will be evil for the person who asserts them perversely. For it is sin to explain each thing without regard to its proper place. Moreover, since the just have no need of the law—that is, those who, having received the remission of sins, have been justified, so that they no longer live under the law from which they have been freed by God’s gift through faith in Christ—they should thereafter observe the law of nature, which has received the knowledge of the Creator and urges them not to sin, and await the day of judgment. On that day the just will be rewarded, since they have kept the natural law. If the human race had had this law as its guide, the law written in letters and given through Moses would not have been given.

But because the natural law was treated with contempt, as though it had no authority, Scripture was confirmed, so that it might be known that the law was to be observed both for the present time and because the one who confirmed it will in the future call to account those by whom it was neglected and those by whom it was observed. Thus he says that the law was given not only because of evil acts and bodily vices, but also because of the faithlessness by which they despised the Creator, so that they might learn to live well and give thanks to the Creator.

And I give thanks to him who strengthened me, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he considered me faithful and appointed me to the ministry, although previously I was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man. But I obtained mercy because I acted ignorantly, while I had not yet believed. The grace of our Lord overflowed exceedingly, together with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.

For this reason every unbeliever suffers weakness of mind, constrained by carnal reasoning not to believe what is spiritual. Therefore he says that he gives thanks to Christ, because the manifestation of his majesty strengthened the weakness of his mind. Paul had thought it impossible that what was preached concerning the Lord’s power, his twofold birth, his resurrection, and his hope could be true. Once strengthened, he appeared to be one who was worthy and able to be the steward of the Lord’s mystery, so that he might confirm by the law those truths which, through love of the law, he had previously judged incredible. He could rejoice in the persecutions which he had formerly inflicted on believers as though justly, grieving because he had inflicted them and rejoicing because he suffered them.

For he had learned such great hope in the one whom he had formerly denied that he rejoiced more in suffering than he had previously exulted in persecution. He had not acted out of wickedness but out of error, and when a person repents, forgiveness can readily be granted.

[Note: In the works of Ambrosiaster it is read with an emendation. In the margin: “he was able, when he repented.”]

But whoever knows that the things he denies are true acts not through error but through ill will.

[Col. 0665D] His wound is incurable. For envy compels him to call false what he knows to be true.

The saying is trustworthy and worthy of all acceptance: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the first. But for this reason I obtained mercy, so that Christ Jesus might display in me all patience and magnanimity, as an example to those who would believe in him for eternal life.

What is as welcome and pleasing as proclaiming forgiveness to sinners? For who is without sin, so that he would not receive this gift with a common thanksgiving, honoring and praising God as its author in Christ?

[Note: In the printed works of Saint Ambrose, the reading is not “with all.”] In order to wash humanity from sins, Christ descended from heavenly things to earthly ones, took the flesh of sin, mingled himself with earthly existence so as to make humanity heavenly, and allowed himself to die so that, having rescued it from death, he might restore it immortal to paradise.

Who would not praise without limit these benefits that God bestowed on humanity, the Lord on the servant, the Creator on the creature—benefits by which he did more for humanity than when he made what did not exist? For after he had been abandoned, despised, and attacked with insults, he added to his benefits, without being sought, so that he might be more gratefully and more highly honored when he restored humanity than when he created it, and might show that he alone was able to do all these things.

Thus Christ brought aid to humanity without violating or losing his purity or power. He willed to be born a human being, knowing for certain that contact with flesh could not defile him. He mingled with human society, knowing that he could not be corrupted by sins. He allowed himself to be killed, not because he was unaware that death could not rule him, but because he knew that he would crush it by his own power. He did all these things to teach that he was able to do everything.

This humility does not diminish him but contributes to his glory, and not only to his glory but also to the glory of those who believe in him. For it is an honor to be the servant of one who is powerful. Although many Jews had already believed before the Apostle, including some of those who had killed the Lord himself, the Apostle nevertheless humbles himself and, still grieving over his unbelief, calls himself the first of all sinners.

Because, more than others, he had steeped himself in the Savior’s mystery and had drawn nearer to understanding his magnificence, he accused himself all the more: he had recognized such great goodness late, and not of his own accord, but after being anticipated by the Savior’s mercy. Thus he became himself a witness to the divinity of the one whom he had previously judged to be a dead man.

His accusation is the Savior’s praise: the Savior called his persecutor to grace as an example to other believers, so that through his patience he might display his magnanimity in him. He who was so benevolent toward an enemy would show himself to be equally benevolent toward those who hastened to him.

To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory for ever and ever.

These words pertain to the person of God the Father. He calls him alone immortal and invisible because all immortality comes from him, so that immortality belongs to him most truly. Whoever is immortal does not possess this from himself but from him. Likewise, God alone is invisible, because no one has ever seen him.

For he does everything through the Son, whom we therefore say was seen, although he appeared otherwise than he is.

[Note: In the Ambrosiaster printed by the Maurists it is likewise written *apparuisse*; the editors noted that some manuscripts less correctly read *apparuisset*. Our manuscript correctly reads *apparuisse*.]

He therefore proclaims honor and glory in truth to God the Father, by whose goodness and providence Christ delivered sinners from death.

This charge I entrust to you, my son Timothy, in accordance with the prophecies previously made concerning you, so that you may wage the good warfare in them, possessing faith and a good conscience. Some, having rejected these, have suffered shipwreck with regard to the faith. Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I handed over to Satan so that they might learn not to blaspheme.

After recalling what and how great were the benefits of God the Father and of Christ his Son toward sinful humanity—although they deserved punishment, God not only forgave them but justified them and adopted them as his children—Paul now shows in the following passage the order by which Timothy should instruct the people in ecclesiastical discipline. He exhorts holy Timothy, mindful of his election, to fulfill the task to which he was appointed.

He was predestined when he was taken up by the Apostle for this purpose: to be ordained, judged worthy to become a bishop, and to fulfill the evangelical warfare in faith and a pure conscience. Whoever teaches faithfully cannot have a bad conscience. He shows faithfulness in preaching if he abstains from every contrary practice, since by the example of good works he provokes many to cruelty, trusting in the hope of the preaching.

For whoever despises the faith is plainly of bad conscience. He is either a hypocritical preacher or an open blasphemer, as Hymenaeus and Alexander were. By abandoning the faith, they suffered shipwreck—that is, they were stripped of the truth or deprived of life. For what is truth except life?

He says that he handed them over to Satan so that they might be cleansed because of their blasphemy.

[Note: In Ambrosiaster, “that they might be corrected.”]

This handing over took place because the Apostle, provoked by their blasphemies, pronounced a sentence against them. The devil, who is prepared for this purpose—to take into his power those who have turned away from God—hearing the sentence, seized them, so that they might understand that they were subjected to punishments for this reason: they had blasphemed.

Hence it is said, among other things, in the Gospel: “Now do not sin any more, so that something worse may not happen to you” (John 5:14). This shows that bodily illnesses are sometimes inflicted because of sin. That they occur through the devil as minister, the Lord declared when he said, among other things: “And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound for eighteen years, to be released from this bond on the Sabbath day?” (Luke 13:16).

### (CHAP. II)

Therefore, first of all, I urge that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings, and for all who are placed in high positions, so that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life in all piety and chastity. For this is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

This is the ecclesiastical rule handed down by the teacher of the nations, which our priests follow: they plead for everyone and make supplication for the kings of this world, so that they may keep the nations subject, and so that, living in peace, tranquility of mind, and quietness, we may be able to serve our Lord.

They also pray for those to whom exalted authority has been entrusted, so that they may govern the commonwealth in justice and truth, with an abundance of resources supplied, so that, once the disturbance of sedition has been removed, joy may take its place. “Bread strengthens the heart, and wine gladdens the mind” (Ps. 103:14).

They petition for those who are in various kinds of need, so that, rescued and delivered, they may praise God as the author of their safety. They also offer thanksgivings for the things that God’s providence supplies to us daily for life, so that in all these things God the Father may be praised, from whom all things come, and his Son, through whom all things exist.

Thus, when everything hostile and inimical to this government has been quieted, we may be able to serve God in a spirit of piety and chastity. Disturbance and captivity preserve neither piety nor chastity. For how can one be pious who is stripped of everything? And how can there be chastity where a person is not master of himself?

Therefore, in order that these things may be preserved, quiet is necessary, so that acceptable service may be rendered to God, who wishes all people to be saved and to know the truth. As he says: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3).

If God, who is called omnipotent, indeed wishes all people to be saved, why is his will not fulfilled? But in every statement a meaning and a condition are concealed.

Hence the apostle Peter says (2 Pet. 1:20): “Every Scripture requires interpretation.”

[Note: The Vulgate reads: “No prophecy of Scripture is made by its own interpretation.”]

God wishes all people to be saved, but only if they approach him. He does not wish them to be saved against their will, but wishes them to be saved if they themselves also desire it. For the one who gave the law to everyone certainly excluded no one from salvation.

Does not a physician make his remedy publicly available for this reason, to show that he wishes to save everyone, provided that the sick seek him out? For salvation is not genuine if it is given to someone unwilling to receive it. Nor can a person rejoice in the salvation he has received if, unwillingly—assuming such a thing is possible—he accepts the medicine. Not to mention that medicine cannot have an effect unless the sick person applies his mind to it.

Because this medicine is not bodily but spiritual, it benefits neither the doubtful nor the envious. For it is faith that gives salvation. Unless the mind receives it with its whole will, it will not only profit nothing but will also harm. The grace of faith has the power to pour divine healing into those devoted to it, but to inflict upon the undevoted a disease through which the whole person perishes.

For there is one God and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.

He signifies that God and Christ have one will in saving humanity. Thus he confesses one God the Father, because all authority comes from him, and one mediator between God and human beings, Christ Jesus.

Sent by the Father and made an arbiter, he reconciled God and human beings by reforming them into the knowledge of God. Because the Father and the Son are one—not one person, but one undivided nature—the Son became an arbiter.

The Son of God, having assumed flesh, was born a human being, so that, as mediator between God and human beings, Christ Jesus might be human—not without divinity, since in God there was humanity and in humanity there was God. Thus, by being from both, he might be mediator and reconcile both, accomplishing this first in himself.

He could not be called the mediator of God and human beings while preserving the unity of God, as though there were another God who would restore to favor the human being estranged from God. Rather, he who had not transgressed the law that had been given became the arbiter between the one who had sinned and the one who knew no sin, so that the latter might forgive and that the human being might thereafter remain in the faith of God.

He gave himself as a ransom for all. This testimony was given at its proper times, and for this I was appointed a herald and apostle—I speak the truth; I do not lie—a teacher of the nations in faith and truth.

Once reconciled to God, humanity was still subject to infernal death and could not ascend to the one to whom it had been reconciled. Therefore the Savior, in order to bring his arbitration to completion, allowed himself to die contrary to what was due. Descending to the underworld, he condemned death for the impiety it had committed against him, taking away those whom death held, so that thereafter no one bearing its mark could be held by it.

He displayed testimony to this at the time when he rose. For the destruction of death is the resurrection of the dead. This Apostle was sent to proclaim this hope to the nations, so that they might learn from him what hope there is in Christ. For this reason he was appointed as a teacher, to teach faith and truth.

Therefore I wish men to pray in every place, lifting holy hands without anger or dispute.

The mind must be peaceful in prayer, so that the prayer may be brought to fulfillment. Hands are holy when the heart is pure. Nevertheless, he commands prayer in every place in such a way that a suitable place is understood—not an unsuitable or filthy place, especially since the Lord forbids praying in public (Matt. 6:6). Rather, he warns them not to think that prayer should take place only in the Church.

Likewise, women should dress decorously, with modesty and chastity, adorning themselves not with braided hair, gold, pearls, or costly clothing, but—as is fitting for women who profess piety—through good works.

Women ought to pray in humble dress, not ostentatiously. Whoever wishes to be heard ought to humble himself, removing pomp from himself in order to provoke God’s mercy. Proud dress neither obtains what is sought nor makes a person rightly believed. For what prudent person would not shrink from a woman dressed ostentatiously? How much more would God the Creator, seeing the body he made free bound with metals, reject it?

Humble clothing corresponds to a good profession, so that a woman may be judged to be what she appears to be. But a woman who prefers to be seen with pomp in the house of God achieves what she wants not for God’s sake but for the sake of human beings: she appears glorious, but receives nothing from God except a stain. The more splendid she seems to human beings, the more she is despised by God.

Let a woman learn in silence, in complete submission. I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man, but to remain in silence.

He commands not only that a woman have humble dress, but also that authority be denied her and that she be subjected to the man, so that both in dress and in obedience she may remain under the power of the man from whom she derives her origin. For Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, became involved in transgression.

But she will be saved through the bearing of children, if they remain in faith, love, and holiness with chastity.

[Note: The Vulgate reads *permanserit* (“if she remains”); the Greek editions, however, have *si permanserint* (“if they remain”), with which our text agrees.]

He places the man before the woman because he was created first, so that the woman may be inferior because she was created after and from the man. There is also another reason: the devil did not deceive the man but the woman; the man, however, was deceived through the woman. Therefore no boldness may be granted to her, but she ought to remain in humility, because through her death entered the world.

But she will be saved, he says, through the bearing of children, provided that they remain in faith, charity, and a pure life. By “children” he means those who are regenerated through faith in Christ. For if they persevere in their generation, she will be delivered when they rise from the dead—not that she will be delivered by them, but that through their generation, when those destined for eternal life believe, they reach the resurrection from the dead. She will be saved when they believe and lead chaste lives.

[Note: That is, through their upbringing and instruction, which is the principal duty of women; if they neglect this, they cannot be saved. Nevertheless, it must not be denied that the interpretation of this passage is obscure.]

For the resurrection remains suspended until all who are predestined to salvation believe.

### (CHAP. III)

This saying is trustworthy: “If anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work.”

Because a bishop must be a man of good life, the one who desires the episcopate desires a good work. In desiring this, he appears to desire a good life, provided that he does not turn aside from the requirements set out below, lest he seem to have acted from ambition or desire for money.

Therefore a bishop must be above reproach.

[Col. 0670D] He describes what a bishop ought to be, so that no one may seek the episcopate unless he is trustworthy and able to abstain from everything contrary, so that he may not be unworthy of his profession.

The husband of one wife.

Although having a second wife is not forbidden as a matter of number, nevertheless, in order that someone may be worthy of the episcopate, he ought to reject even what is permitted because of the dignity of the office itself. The person who desires that seat must be better than the others.

Sober, chaste, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not addicted to wine, not violent, but moderate; not quarrelsome, not harsh; managing his own household well, having children subject to him with all [Note: The Vulgate and Ambrosiaster read “with all chastity.”] love.

He says that a person who observes the qualities he enumerates ought to be made a bishop. These are signs of episcopal dignity. But if someone pursues higher things and dedicates both body and soul to God, refusing to bind himself in marriage, he will be all the more worthy. He placed the lesser requirement first so that no one might doubt the greater.

But if anyone does not know how to preside over his own household, how will he take care of the Church of God?

It is clear that someone can then be proved a suitable ruler if he has first governed his household rightly: “The one who is faithful in very little is also faithful in much” (Luke 16:10).

Not a recent convert, lest, being lifted up with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil.

This is true, because those who are inexperienced in the faith are accustomed to be puffed up with pride, especially if they receive an office. Novelty and power inflate them, and they think themselves more worthy than others. Seeing that honor has been conferred on them in the first year after their spiritual birth, they think they have been called not so much for their own advancement as for that of others, as though they were giving a benefit to religion rather than receiving one from it. Through this, being puffed up, they fall into the devil’s snare.

When Satan finds an opportunity in their pride, he casts them down. Therefore it is read in Solomon: “God resists the proud” (Prov. 15:21; Wis. 15:14; Sir. 10:21). Hence the same Apostle says in another Epistle: “Whoever thinks he is something deceives himself” (Gal. 6:3). And the Lord says: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11).

He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside.

Following the Lord’s teaching, he says that the future bishop ought to have a good reputation among outsiders, because “the one who is faithful in very little is also faithful in much,” as the Lord says (Luke 16:10). “If you were not faithful with another’s wealth, who will give you what is your own?” (ibid., 11.)

Thus, if someone is not found faithful in worldly matters and human conduct, there can be no doubt that he will not be suitable in divine matters either. If he has shown faithfulness to human beings, much more will he show it to God.

If a bishop does not keep the fear of God before his eyes, commending himself more to the present age, God abandons him as unfaithful and a false prophet. He appears deformed and stained to everyone because he acts otherwise than he preaches, accusing himself by his own words, since he has been assigned to Satan’s flock.

He proves that he truly preaches if he attempts also to practice what he preaches. Therefore the person who is to undertake the governance of God’s household must be chosen with great care. If suitable stewards of earthly matters must be sought, how much more of heavenly matters?

Deacons likewise must be chaste, not double-tongued, not devoted to much wine, not occupied with shameful profits, holding the mystery of the faith with a pure conscience. Let these also first be tested, and then let them minister without blame.

When he commands that deacons be chosen with such care—although they are known to be ministers of the priests—what kind does he wish bishops to be, except, as he himself says, irreproachable? They must not engage in public, shameful, or base business. He knows that they engage in trade in order to seize profits, and that they profess nothing other than what they practice. They are exposed as shameful when they present themselves as pure.

After the bishop, he places the ordination of the diaconate. Why? Unless because the ordination of bishops and presbyters is one and the same. Both are priests. But the bishop is first, so that every bishop is a presbyter, though not every presbyter is a bishop. The bishop is the one who is first among the presbyters.

Finally, he indicates that Timothy was ordained a presbyter; but because he had no one before him, he was a bishop. Hence he also shows how a bishop should be ordained. For it was neither right nor permitted that an inferior should ordain a superior. No one gives what he has not received.

Women likewise must be chaste, not devoted to discord, but sober and faithful in everything.

Because he commanded that the bishop be made holy, and likewise the deacon, he certainly does not wish the people to be different, especially since the Lord says: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Lev. 19:2). Therefore he also wishes women, who appear to be inferior, to be without blame, so that the Church of God may be pure.

But the Cataphrygians, seeking an opportunity for error, defend with empty presumption that women themselves ought to be ordained deacons, because he addresses women after the deacons. Yet they know that the apostles chose seven deacons. Was no woman then found suitable, when we read that holy women were present among the eleven apostles? But in order that heretics might appear to support their own opinion by words rather than by the meaning of the law, they oppose the Apostle’s words to the Apostle’s meaning: when he commands that a woman remain silent in the Church, they, on the contrary, claim for her authority in the Church’s ministry.

Let deacons be husbands of one wife, managing their children and their own households well. For those who have served well acquire for themselves a good standing and much confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.

He now adds what he had said less fully about the ordination of the diaconate. He also shows that these men ought to be husbands of one wife, so that those may be chosen for God’s ministry who have not departed from God’s established order. God appointed one wife for a man, with whom he might be blessed. No one is blessed with a second wife.

If they have governed their children and households well—that is, their servants or household members—they can become worthy of the priesthood and have confidence before God, knowing that they can obtain what they ask, since thereafter they restrain themselves from intercourse with women.

For this reason wives were formerly permitted to Levites or priests: they had much free time away from their ministry or priesthood. There was a multitude of priests and a large number of Levites, and each served the divine ceremonies at a fixed time according to David’s institution.

He established twenty-four divisions of priests so that they might serve in rotation. Thus Abijah belonged to the eighth division, and Zechariah exercised the priesthood in his course, as is contained in 2 Chronicles 13. When it was not their turn to serve at the altar, they took care of their households. But when the time of their ministry approached, they purified themselves for several days and came to the Temple to offer service to God.

Now, however, there ought to be seven deacons and a certain number of presbyters, two in each Church, with one bishop in each city. Accordingly, all ought to abstain from intercourse with women, because they must be present in the Church every day and cannot have a delay in which to purify themselves lawfully after intercourse, as the ancients did.

An offering must be made every week, and, even if not daily for travelers, at least twice a week for residents. There are also people who are baptized while sick almost every day.

The ancient priests were permitted this because they were not seen in the Temple for much of the time but lived as private persons. If he commands laypeople to abstain for a time for the sake of prayer, so that they may devote themselves to prayer, how much more ought Levites or priests to pray?

They must therefore be purer than the others, because they are God’s agents.

I am writing these things to you, hoping to come to you soon. But if I delay, I am writing so that you may know how one ought to conduct oneself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth.

As far as his knowledge was concerned, this consisted in the fact that he expected to see Timothy soon. But since it commonly pleases God to do something else, whose providence is known to him alone, he says: “In case I delay, I am writing to you,” so that Timothy may know how to order the Church, which is the house of God.

Although the whole world is God’s Church, nevertheless it is called his house, whose ruler today is Damasus.

[Note: Pope Damasus was created in the year of Christ 366 and died in 384. Saint Ambrose was made bishop in 374 and died in 397. Hilary the deacon lived in 362. Having already been Lucifer’s companion in the embassy to the emperor Constantius, he adhered to the Luciferian schism until the rebaptism of those who had been baptized by the Arians. This schism, with Hilary himself as its author, soon perished, according to Fleury, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 15, no. 29. Here, however, Damasus is presented as a living pontiff. The frequent citation of Saint Gregory and many other arguments—which it would be too long and irrelevant to report here, and which are set out more fully in the preface—prove that the other Epistles, except these two to the Thessalonians and the two to Timothy, were expounded long after Hilary and Saint Ambrose. In particular, the exposition of Romans, Corinthians, Galatians, and so forth, through Philippians, is very different from that of Ambrosiaster.
