What are we to say about these Epistles to the Thessalonians and Timothy? We are very uncertain. The mention here of Damasus has the appearance of referring to a contemporary. Nevertheless, this could be one of those interpolations that interpreters very often introduced. See the preface on this matter.]

For the world is disturbed in transgression by various errors. Therefore it is necessary that the house of God and the truth be said to be located where God is feared according to his will, and where his servants profess concerning him what he has deigned to teach.

In case his words should be denied to be his, he confirmed them by works of power—things that no one else can do—so that, being convicted by these signs, unbelief might perish without excuse. The foundation of the truth consists in these signs and wonders.

And indeed, by the confession of all, great is the mystery of this piety. He does not deny that every one of the faithful admires the mystery of the truth preached in the Church, which he calls piety. For through his magnanimity and mercy, God grants divine gifts to those who come to know him, excepting the forgiveness of sins, which he bestows in the present life.

What was manifested in the flesh was vindicated in the spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, and taken up in glory. The sacrament of God’s mystery, which is Christ in the flesh, says that what had been hidden in the spirit was made manifest. For the Son of God, born as a human being—he who was secretly with God—made himself known to creation by his works and preaching. And this is what it means for him to have been vindicated in the spirit: that through works and power he showed who he was, though he was in the flesh. Then he appeared to the angels, no longer in the humility of his form, but in power. For he appeared humble to the sight through the flesh until, having conquered death, he rose from the dead and his majesty was seen [Col. 0674B]—he who, though born as a human being, was not wholly merely human. Thus, recognizing the mystery that had previously been hidden but was manifested in the flesh, the angels bend the knee before him, giving thanks to him as God, because they have learned the truth that was proclaimed to the nations, so that they might be freed from error; and through it the world advances, so that it may not be condemned. For this is why God’s sacrament was believed in the world: so that its unbelief could not obtain pardon for its error. As the Lord says concerning the Jews: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin. But now they have no excuse for their sin” (John 15:22). For what they despised as weak and deformed was taken up in glory. After his person and power had been manifested following the cross, the Savior openly ascended gloriously into heaven, with the clouds attending him.

[Col. 0674C] **(CHAP. IV.)** Now the Spirit expressly says that in the latter times some will depart from the faith, paying attention to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars whose consciences are branded, who forbid marriage and command abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who have come to know the truth; for every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving. For it is sanctified through the word of God and prayer.

The Holy Spirit does not conceal what he has revealed as future, for the instruction and warning of the churches, so that the churches, having been forewarned, may be vigilant lest they be deceived by such people. What could he have announced in a voice clearer and more explicit for avoiding—or rather, for condemning—[Col. 0674D] the men of this pestilential doctrine, except that he should call their false assertion a deceptive and simulated doctrine of demons, [Col. 0675A] so that, when the words of this assertion are heard, it might be known that this doctrine had been devised by the devil? The Holy Spirit had foretold it: the doctrine asserts falsehoods about the Savior’s incarnation, as is now denounced among the Marcionites, although they have almost disappeared, and among the Patricians [Note: [Col. 0675D] These did not survive beyond the fifth century, as Phylaster and Augustine testify; both mention survivors of this sect. This, together with many other evidence, proves that the expositions of these four Epistles—to the Thessalonians [Col. 0676D] and to Timothy—were either taken from Ambrosiaster or filled with interpolations from other earlier writers. See the preface.], or especially among the Manichaeans. For they deny that Christ was born, prohibit marriage, and teach that people must abstain from foods.

He says that their conscience is branded—that is, corrupted by hypocrisy. For just as a branding iron corrupts the leather and leaves a mark on it, so deceit marks the conscience that, through the fraud of malice, knows one thing but professes another, marking it for destruction. He now denies that these people can be changed so as to be saved: just as a brand cannot be altered, so their mind cannot be corrected. For nothing is worse than hypocrisy. [Col. 0675B] They are like those Jews who understood that Christ worked by God’s power but said that these things were done by him through Beelzebul (Matt. 12:24; Mark 3:22; Luke 11:15). For although they do not regret having been born, they treat the Maker of humanity maliciously: they prohibit marriage, deprive Christ of flesh, and, in order to injure him, teach abstinence from the things he established for our use, so that, by despising them, they may make them appear evil and invented by an evil author. This is why the Apostle shows that all things made by God are good, provided that they are received with thanksgiving. For they will be unclean to one who does not praise the Creator in them. Nor can those things benefit such a person rightly if he receives them in a way that mistreats their Author.

[Col. 0675C] In presenting these matters to the brothers, he says: “You will be a good minister of Christ Jesus, nourished by the words of faith and of the good doctrine that you have attained.” What could be truer, clearer, or more provident than that Christian teaching should be transmitted incorruptibly, so that its fruit may be praised as fertile and sound in the Lord’s threshing floor? That is, so that on the day of judgment he may not be judged reprobate and condemned to be burned in the fire. This belongs to a good teacher and capable minister of the Lord Jesus Christ, especially since he says that Timothy was nourished by the words of faith and good doctrine, which he asserts that Timothy had attained from childhood. For Timothy, who had been instructed in all the intact books of the Hebrews, became a perfect teacher once he had received the faith.

“But reject profane and old-womanish fables, training yourself for piety.” Profane words are understood as hostile or contrary words; old-womanish fables are certain ravings. Some people customarily turn these into controversies through the clamors of their disputation, as though an empty matter were being treated whose outcome is nothing but vanity. He therefore warns that one must turn away from things that are contrary, and similarly from those that are old-womanish and composed with a kind of vanity. For there are some who, heated in spirit, throw themselves [Col. 0676A] into such disputations. He urges devotion to piety, because it produces great progress. Those who practice mercy toward the elderly, repaying their parents in kind, both do not deprive them of God’s assistance in the present life and will possess immortality with glory in the future.

He says that bodily exercise is useful only to a small extent. To fast and abstain from foods, while the Creator’s authority remains intact, is of little benefit unless piety is added to it—piety whose works, aided by the prayers of many, obtain God’s favor. Finally, the Gospel testifies that those who are generous toward their brothers and serve them in various ways advance toward eternal life, while those who dissent from this work go into eternal fire. Bodily exercise is nothing other than restraints upon the flesh. [Col. 0676B] If someone, then, because mercy is a great matter, nevertheless suffers the flesh to become slippery and undisciplined, what will happen to such a person? Without doubt he will be punished, because the former must be done and the latter must by no means be neglected. But if he has had only bodily exercise, he will suffer everlasting punishments, just as the Lord promised in the Gospel. For the whole substance of our discipline consists in mercy and piety.

Carnal people and spiritual people nevertheless practice different bodily exercises. Carnal people fatten and nourish their bodies with rich food, so that they may advance swiftly toward destruction; spiritual people moderate their bodies through fasts and abstinence, so that, having become sluggish with regard to desires, they may be worthy of the future resurrection. The spiritual person chastises his body because of hope for the future; the carnal person cherishes it because of despair concerning the future, caring for it temporarily so that it may move more quickly toward sinning. [Col. 0676C]

“This saying is trustworthy and worthy of all acceptance.” For this is why we labor and suffer persecutions: because we hope in the living God, who is the Savior of all human beings, especially of believers. It is entirely worthy and should be accepted for the sake of the hope that is in God that we suffer persecutions, because in the present life hope is fleeting, whereas in God’s promise it is firm and stable. He is the salvation of all, because from him and through him all live, insofar as the present life is concerned; but insofar as the promised salvation is concerned, the faithful live. For he has promised those who know him another life after this life—which ends in death—a life that will flourish in immortality. [Col. 0676D] Therefore he says, “especially of believers.”

“Command these things and teach them. Let no one despise your youth, but be an example to the faithful in speech, conduct, love, faith, and purity.” Timothy was young with regard to age, but with regard to character and conduct he was mature and serious. He therefore admonishes him in this way, so that his progress in every respect might be an example of good works; so that in a young man disciplined and serious conduct might appear remarkable; so that his actions might excuse his age, and he might be regarded not as a young man but as an elder; and so that older men might be ashamed [Col. 0677A] if they did not show themselves, in conduct and character, to be serious in accordance with his example, while young men would have their contemporary as their teacher. Remarkable was the most holy young man Timothy, whose example should restrain undisciplined youth and punish the irreverence of elders.

“Until I come, attend to the reading, exhortation, and teaching. Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery.” He wants Timothy to be attentive and devoted to the practice of reading, striving with every care and diligence to exhort and teach. Exhortation occurs when, by gentle speech, we summon people to a good work. Teaching occurs when we disclose to the minds of hearers things that lie hidden. For if the ruler of the people neglects these things [Col. 0677B], he neglects the gift given to him. A leader is appointed over the people for this purpose: to care for their salvation by admonishing and teaching, so that his ordination may bear fruit. God appointed him for this very reason, so that he might advance the salvation of his people. Therefore anyone placed in this authority who is negligent will be regarded as a despiser of God, called least in the kingdom of God (Matt. 5:19). For one who does not consider himself worthy to teach will not be able to accomplish this.

Yet the statement that the gift is given signifies that he is ordained through prophecy and the laying on of hands. Prophecy is the means by which someone is chosen as a future teacher, as one who will be capable; the laying on of hands consists of mystical words by which the person chosen for this work is confirmed, receiving authority, with his conscience as witness, so that he may dare to offer sacrifice to God in the Lord’s place.

[Col. 0677C] “Meditate on these things; devote yourself to them, so that your progress may be evident to all. Attend to yourself and to your teaching; persist in them. For by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you.” He admonishes him to be an example to everyone not only in good works but also in the practice of teaching. For he signifies that the progress of his discipline must appear not only in teaching but also in deeds. “A good tree produces good fruits” (Matt. 7:17); likewise, good teaching cannot produce evil works. When good works are seen, they should be understood as the fruit of divine instruction, and hearers should be able to advance. For they understand that what is said is true and to be feared when they see it carefully observed with great reverence by the very person who teaches it. This benefits the ruler of the people in two ways: he will receive a reward both for his own good works and for those who hear him. But if he has been negligent, how will he give an account both for himself and for them? [Col. 0677D]

**(CHAP. V.)** “Do not rebuke an older man, but exhort him as a father; younger men as brothers; older women as mothers; younger women as sisters, in all purity.” Out of respect for age, an older person should be summoned to good work with gentleness, so that he may more readily accept admonition. For, once admonished, he may fear being rebuked later, which is disgraceful for an older man. Among all peoples, old age is certainly held in honor. Hence both the Synagogue and later the Church had elders, without whose counsel nothing was done in the Church. I do not know through what negligence this practice has grown obsolete, unless perhaps through the laziness of teachers—or, more likely, through their pride, since they wish to appear to be the only ones who matter. He considers that younger men should be admonished as brothers, with an affection born of love, so that, seeing that they are admonished out of love, they may correct themselves more readily, especially when they see that his actions do not differ from his preaching.

Older women, he says, should be treated as mothers. When they see themselves being instructed in gentle speech, they should not take it harshly, since they are advancing honorably. It is harsh for elders to be rebuked by younger people; he wishes this to be softened by a certain moderation, so that both the speaker and the hearer may make progress. He instructs that younger women should be admonished and taught as sisters, so that they may readily accept the discipline of good conduct. For when they see that matters pertaining to a good life are not imposed upon them imperiously, they consent, presenting themselves humbly to the one who admonishes them. [Col. 0678B] Things that cannot be obtained by authority are usually obtained by gentleness. For even animals, when they are jealous of their limbs, yield nevertheless to caresses.

“Honor widows who are truly widows.” He says that those widows are to be honored who have deliberately become widows: women who, although they could marry, rejected a second marriage so that they might be better and worthy of God, knowing that marriage is blessed only once. They are rivals of the most holy Anna, who served God with fasts and supplications night and day, having experienced intercourse with one man (Luke 2:36–37).

“But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let her first learn to manage her own household piously and to repay her parents in kind. For this is pleasing in the sight of God.” He says that a widow must first be tested in this life and conduct, so that only then may she be worthy of being called a widow of the Church—one who submits to ecclesiastical discipline not for the sake of profit but for the sake of protection. Merits must come first, so that the honor given to one who approaches may be seen to be deserved. A woman who has treated her dependents piously and governed her household well has observed God’s law and has been made worthy of the Church’s reward.

“For she who is truly a widow and desolate hopes in God and persists in prayers night and day.” A widow who has children or grandchildren should not readily be admitted to the Church’s support, because if she has governed her household piously and carefully, her own family must repay her in kind, just as she repaid her relatives. But if, as often happens, impiety has caused her relatives to despise an old woman whom she treated piously, it is fitting that she be received by the Church, because she has lived faithfully according to the Lord’s law. A widow, then, who is desolate or despised by her relatives hopes in God. Seeing that she has support from no quarter, she is wholly devoted to God and expects the assistance of life and salvation from him alone.

“But she who lives in luxury is dead while she lives.” He signifies that a woman called a widow because she is a widow must be such that she devotes herself to prayer in order to win the Lord’s favor, serving God night and day, and showing that she rejected a second marriage for this reason: to devote herself to discipline. If, under the name of widow, she devotes herself to luxury or wantonness, she must be regarded as dead while she lives. For it is a kind of imposture to do one thing and profess another: to desire the honor of widowhood rather than the service and devotion of God. The profession of the name itself indicates that she rejected a husband and chose God, to whom she should serve with her whole mind for the sake of the promised life.

“And command these things, so that they may be irreproachable.” He wants a widow to maintain such diligence in her actions and conduct that she cannot be criticized. Removed from hope in worldly association and from the task of caring for the body, she has turned to God for this purpose: to lead a life worthy of approval. Once the occasions that commonly open the way to sins have been removed, good conduct can remain unharmed.

“But if anyone does not care for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.” He says that this widow, who was negligent toward her dependents and did not raise them in the discipline and admonition of the Lord, is to be dishonored [Note: [Col. 0679D] The verb “says” is missing in the manuscript; it should be supplied, as the sense and the Maurist edition of Ambrosiaster suggest.], because, like the faithless, she did not obey God’s law. It is necessary that the person who acts under the law and fear of God yet despises it be considered worse than one who is not subject to the law. The latter does not know; the former knowingly despises.

“Let a widow be chosen who is not less than sixty years old, the wife of one man [Note: [Col. 0679D] The words “who has been” are understood, as in the Vulgate.], having a testimony of good works: if she has raised children, if she has shown hospitality, if she has washed the feet of the saints, if she has assisted those suffering affliction, if she has pursued every good work.” Since a widow is commended by the distinction of her past works, he teaches that such a woman should be chosen. Her name is entered, by the Lord’s judgment, in the Church’s records, and her earlier life declares her worthy. Instructed in divine service and wearing away her life in these duties, she should be received into the bosom of the Church, to whose lawful services she once devoted herself. [Col. 0679C]

“But refuse younger widows. For when they have lived in luxury, they want to marry in Christ.” He prohibits the acceptance of young widows into this profession. Faith should not readily be entrusted to an unstable age, especially since examples exist of women who, after professing this way of life, through the allurements of luxury possess the name but not the works of widowhood, and, turning back, are enticed by marriage. Anyone who thinks he can live a life of luxury in Christ does not remain innocent. Luxury draws him toward its own members, so that he becomes subject to sin. For luxury is the gateway to sin. One who loves a dissolute life cannot be unaware of where it leads.

“They incur condemnation because they have nullified their first faith.” He shows what awaits such women, so that they may not rashly undertake what is difficult to fulfill. Or, if the mind is devoted to this way of life, let it retain the intention privately for the time being, since it has learned that it is rash to profess what should not yet be entrusted to a youthful age. For one becomes liable to condemnation by turning away from what one had rightly done. The more praiseworthy it is to fulfill what is believed to exceed one’s strength, the more deserving of punishment one will be if, through reckless presumption, one dares to impose upon oneself what one cannot bear, [Col. 0680A] and this should not be counted as deserving pardon, because from the beginning one has proved faithless.

“At the same time [Note: [Col. 0680D] The manuscript reads *simulatae* (“simulated”), where we read *simul autem* (“at the same time, however”).] they are idle, learning to go around from house to house; and not only idle, but also talkative and curious, speaking about things that ought not to be spoken.” Certain virgins and widows, commended by their profession—for the name of this way of life is glorious—are welcomed in the houses of the rich. They act in order to conform to the wishes of those people, going about and seeking things to bring them that will please them, so that, while idle, they may receive gifts and, according to a bad custom, seek more through stories than through what they do with their hands. Thus they go out proud and adorned, acting contrary to their profession. Such conduct is often harmful to them even in this life, for what they always think hidden is revealed. What else does it mean for them to speak about things that ought not to be spoken? They are close to marriage, sharers in many secrets, flatterers, and complainers about servants.

“Therefore I want younger women to marry, bear children, and manage their households. For this is to govern a household [Note: [Col. 0680D] Ambrosiaster does not have the words “for this is to govern a household.”].” They should give no occasion to the adversary for reproach. For some have already turned aside after Satan. Since the things he mentioned above concerning such women are contrary and unlawful, they will lead them to death. He therefore gives counsel and commands that what is lawful be done. It is better to care for one’s own household than to flatter in another’s household. It is also much better to marry than to walk about conspicuously under a good and pious profession. It is better to seek one’s livelihood with modesty by the work of one’s hands [Col. 0680C] than shamelessly to await another’s provisions in idleness. Thus Satan finds an opportunity to overthrow unwary souls when those who profess piety behave unjustly. Nothing is more dangerous than for conduct to contradict one’s profession. Satan does not envy an open evil, because he rejoices in it; but the person whom he sees deceiving others he will cause to reveal that he is his child, not God’s. Such a result does not displease God.

“If any believing man or woman has widows, let him or her provide sufficiently for them, so that the Church may not be burdened and may have enough for those who are truly widows.” What is surprising if apostolic authority was able to foresee what would happen? For what he said is now evident: the widows of believers greatly burden the Church. Those who appear wealthy in the world, and who, on account of old age, withdraw these women from the work of spinning, take away from them both clothing and food—not entirely, but in part—so that, driven by poverty, they turn to the Church in order to live. Such people ought not merely to give generously to their own needy relatives; they ought also to feed and clothe other poor women. This is greatly harmful. When support is given to these women, it is given either less or not at all to others who deserve it more and who are worthy of being supported at the Church’s expense. The Church is burdened when it is compelled to clothe many whom it ought to clothe only in small numbers, and the people, who could willingly and frequently provide for a few, are forced to dismiss many, either grumbling or responding more slowly. For although he commands that a widow be chosen who was the wife of one man, now among them are found not only wives of two or three husbands but also women who have lived more shamefully. Sometimes this happens through negligence, sometimes through the influence of power. [Col. 0681A]

“Let the presbyters who preside well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching.” Good and faithful stewards should be judged worthy not only of exalted honor but also of earthly support, so that they may not be saddened by lack of resources but may rather rejoice in their faith and teaching. For a person is more zealous when poverty does not humiliate him, and his authority increases when he sees that even in the present he receives the fruit of his labor—not so that he may abound, but so that he may not lack.

For Scripture says: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing” (Deut. 25:4; 1 Cor. 9:9); and, “The laborer is worthy of his wages” (Matt. 10:10; Luke 10:7). The reward of one who proclaims the kingdom of God should be such that he is neither saddened nor exalted by it.

“Do not accept an accusation against a presbyter.” Since the honor of this order is exalted—for such men are vicars of Christ—an accusation against such a person should therefore not readily be admitted. It ought to seem unbelievable that this man, who is God’s bishop, should be a most disgraceful stage-player [Note: [Col. 0681D] In the printed works of Ambrosiaster, after the words “who is God’s bishop,” one reads “who has behaved criminally,” [Col. 0682D] followed by “as it is credible that he is a stage-player,” and so forth.].

“But rebuke those who sin in the presence of all, so that the others may have fear.” An accusation of crime concerning a presbyter should not readily be believed; nevertheless, if it is proven or manifest that he has behaved irreverently, he commands that the man be rebuked publicly, so that the others may be terrified. This benefits not only those who have been ordained but also the people. For when they see an honorable man rebuked on account of error, they must necessarily take care for themselves.

“I testify before God and Christ Jesus and the elect angels that you observe these things without prejudice, doing nothing by partiality. Do not lay hands hastily on anyone, nor share in the sins of others. Keep yourself pure.” He brings forward a solemn testimony before God the Father, Christ his Son, and the elect angels, whom the Lord calls holy in the Gospel. They are called elect because there are others who are reprobate, who are not God’s angels but the devil’s, consenting to his apostasy.

Under this solemn testimony, then, he commands that the matters pertaining to the ordering of the Church be observed without partiality. No one should readily receive ecclesiastical dignity unless his life and conduct have first been examined, so that a minister or priest may be appointed only after being approved as worthy. Otherwise, if he later appears blameworthy, the leader of the people may perhaps regret not having fully judged what the person deserved when he ordained him improperly. Nor should one whose sins are suspected be ordained, lest the ordainer be stained by his vices and transgressions. [Col. 0682A] If the transgressions are entirely hidden, the ruler will be free of guilt, because his conscience is clear. Suspicion causes anxiety. He sins if he does not investigate but ordains in this way. The person who is to be ordained must be proved better than the others. It is not enough for him to be without a crime, because his merits in good works must come first, so that he may be considered worthy of ordination. By observing these things, the bishop will present himself as pure before religion and will receive the reward for this in the future.

“Do not continue drinking water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses.” He now gives particular advice, so that Timothy may govern himself by sound teaching. For God wisely wishes to be served, not by people who become weak through excess and then have to seek the assistance of physicians. One must practice moderation, so that, if possible, the service once begun may be advanced gradually rather than diminished through thoughtlessness. Lack of moderation unsettles the soul itself, so that when it is anxious about illness it is not wholly devoted to divine service. Lack of foresight therefore causes harm. For when the soul is placed in tranquility, it raises its whole heart to God, entreating with undivided judgment for the things that should be requested.

“The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment, while those of others follow afterward. In the same way, good works are manifest; and those that are otherwise cannot remain hidden.” He wants it understood that there will be no excuse for those who attach themselves to people whose sins are publicly known, so that, although such people ought to be avoided, they may instead be treated as honorable. This therefore signifies that the man of God, especially Christ’s steward, must separate himself from such people; he has authority even to rebuke them. If they promise to amend themselves, they are to be retained.

He shows that the evil works of others follow them, because, while they are considered good when alive, they are exposed after death, so that those who previously presented themselves as suitable are afterward revealed as impostors. By the same reasoning, just as evil deeds become manifest, so do good deeds. A good life and modest actions cannot be hidden; when piety is added, they make people perfect. Yet just as certain evils are hidden for the present, so are certain good things. No one can know everything about other people; rather, one proves and judges from what one sees and hears. He weighs whether the things said correspond to the person of whom they are said, whether they are good or evil. What is hidden from human beings, however, will be made public on the day of judgment. This is why these things were said: so that they may know that such people have a more serious case than others. For the person who, while evil, presents himself as good is worse than the one who is openly evil.

**(CHAP. VI.)** “Let all who are under the yoke of slavery consider their masters worthy of all honor” [Note: [Col. 0682D] The Vulgate reads *quicumque*, “whoever,” instead of *quotquot*, “all who.”], “so that the name of the Lord and the doctrine may not be blasphemed.” He wants masters to give thanks to God for the service of their slaves. For when slaves have rendered faithful service to them according to God’s discipline, perhaps the masters themselves may submit to this discipline.

“But those who have believing masters must not despise them because they are brothers; rather, they must serve them all the more, because they are believers and beloved, receiving the benefit.” If he commands that profane masters be served with complete diligence, how much more must believing masters be served? A person then proves that he is subject to the fear of God if he obeys a believing and temporal master with his whole heart. He must not consider such a master contemptible because he is called a brother on account of the common faith. Indeed, the person who thinks that a believing master should be despised will deserve the harsher rebuke.

“Teach and exhort these things.” He wants the Lord’s teaching to be made manifest, so that its detractors may take care, since there is nothing in it that can be criticized. At the same time, they should consider the shameful things hidden in their own sacred practices and blush at the very means by which they will be without excuse.

“If anyone teaches otherwise and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the doctrine that accords with piety, he is conceited and knows nothing, but is sick with disputes and battles over words, from which arise envy, contentions, blasphemies, evil suspicions, and conflicts among people who are corrupted in mind and deprived of the truth, supposing that piety and the worship of God are a means of gain—withdraw from such people.” He commands that those who differ from Catholic discipline be despised, especially those who, although convicted and rebuked, refuse to assent because of the disorder of their perverse mind and who delight in and feed upon disputes. A proud person does not allow himself to be defeated, especially since he erupts into conflict in order to seek approval. This must be avoided by gentle and good men. Dispute is never without strife; and it would be a small matter if strife alone arose, but blasphemies and enmities arise as well. Such things are alien to God’s servants.

Those whose minds are corrupted and who have been deprived of the truth consider this useful. They regard the worship of God and piety as a means of gain, expecting nothing concerning the future but making provision for how they may get through the present, like the worldly sects that are known to have been founded for the sake of present profits. He is not unaware that some people are pleased to hear that they should flourish in this life; therefore he commands withdrawal from such people.

“But piety with contentment is great gain.” He calls it great wealth and acquisition if a believer is content with his own condition. A pious person is so toward himself and others when, hoping to acquire God’s mercy for the future life, he considers what he has sufficient for the present, without hesitating to give from it. For every greedy person is impious, harming both himself and others.

“For we brought nothing into this world; and it is certain that we can take nothing out of it. But having food, we will be content with these things.” He openly declares the folly of mortals who mock abundance and wish to become rich, even though they know that they possess nothing as their own in the world. What does human greed accomplish except that it becomes its own enemy? No one brought anything into the world; no one will be able to take anything away. A person who imposes anxiety upon himself and seeks to accumulate will depart from here as he came. Job also wrote this and confessed it in his own suffering, saying: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I must return to the earth. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21). If the greedy did not retain possessions to their own destruction, a few people would store up what could suffice for many, with benefit even to themselves.

“For those who want to become rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is the root of all evils, and by desiring it some have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many pains.” Nothing is so harsh and destructive as for a member of the Church—especially one who occupies an exalted position—to pursue the riches of this age, because he harms not only himself but also others. He offers people an example contrary to the faith, and many imitators must necessarily follow him to their destruction. The more honorable his rank, the more he urges others to imitate him, especially in a matter toward which life in this world is inclined. Greed can admit every evil. It is therefore the root of all evils: in order to satisfy its desires, which cannot be satisfied, it commits sorcery, murders, obscenity, and every kind of crime, and it is not even secure in the present, because it is always desiring and is condemned in the future.

“But you, man of God, flee these things.” He urges and commands the man of God to cut himself off from greed, so that he may be secure both here and be rewarded with divine prizes in the future. [Col. 0684C] For it is not without reason that the person who rejects greed—which persuades many—should be crowned.

“Pursue righteousness, piety, faith, love, patience, and tranquility of mind. Fight the good fight of faith; take hold of eternal life, to which you were called and for which you confessed the good confession before many witnesses.” Since greed is an unjust thing, he commands the man of God to reject it and pursue righteousness, piety, and the other virtues he mentions. For he cannot avoid greed unless he clings to the things opposed to it. How can a greedy person be faithful, when by his works he denies what he appears to confess in words? How can he be a lover of the brotherhood whose hands are dry? How can he be patient when he is always reaching out toward what belongs to others? Or how can he possess tranquility of mind when day and night he is inflamed by the avidity of desire?

But since this iniquity was alien to Timothy, the man of God, he is commanded to undertake the good fight of faith. Victory belongs to faith when all vices and crimes are subdued, so that one may attain the rewards of eternal life. His confession is contained in the Church’s records from the very beginnings of his faith, when the one questioning [Note: [Col. 0683D] We supplied from the other manuscripts the word *interrogante*, “when the one questioning,” which is missing in our manuscript. [Col. 0684D]] and the one responding bore witness to it.

I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who bore witness under Pontius Pilate to the good confession, that you keep the commandment unstained and irreproachable until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ, whom the blessed and only Sovereign will display at the proper times [Col. 0685A] [Note: [Col. 0685C] In the manuscript: “the pontiff.”]—the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone possesses immortality and dwells [Note: [Col. 0685C] The word “dwells” is missing.] in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen nor can see; to him be honor and eternal power. Amen.

With great vigilance and foresight he gives these instructions to the ruler of the Church. For in his person the salvation of the whole people is contained. He is not so careful because he is anxious about Timothy’s conduct, but because of Timothy’s successors, so that they might preserve the Church’s order by Timothy’s example. Finally, he says, “that you keep the commandment unstained until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ.” He binds this obligation so tightly that he testifies that he commands it in the presence of God and Christ. To inspire fear, he recalls Christ’s passion. Whoever despises that for which Christ suffered must necessarily become answerable for his passion. Nor did he pass over the day of judgment, which will come at the time ordained by God’s will: he declares him alone blessed and powerful, King of kings and Lord. For he alone possesses blessedness, power, dominion, and kingship in himself and from no one else; likewise, immortality. The Father possesses all these things, and the Son likewise receives them from the Father. The inaccessible light, however, belongs to the Father alone, because he has never appeared to anyone. Hence he adds: “whom no human being has seen nor can see”—not because the Son’s light is different, since it is written in the Psalm, “In your light we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV, 10), that is, that the Father’s light is in the Son, but because no one has seen the Father, and therefore he dwells in inaccessible light. No one has the right to see the Father except Christ, who is from God: he sees God. The Son, however, because he himself does all things, is said both to appear and to be seen. Therefore what was stated above is peculiar to the Father: “to whom be honor and eternal power.” Amen—that is, truly.

Command those who are rich in this present age not to think arrogantly [Note: [Col. 0685C] The Vulgate reads “not to be proud.”], nor to place their hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who provides us abundantly with everything for enjoyment; command them, in their readiness for good works, to be rich in good deeds, generous in giving, sharing with others, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future [Col. 0686A], so that they may take hold of the true life.

That is the true life which we hope will come, a life bounded neither by decay nor by time. For it is eternal, and rightly called true. This present life is an image of life, not the truth. And because an image is not altogether emptiness, that life is acquired in this one; and, so that we may hasten toward it, from the image—which the truth surpasses—we learn what cannot be attained through pride or hope in riches, but through humility and hope in God, who promised it. For our hope must be placed in him, because he provides what is necessary for our needs—not in riches themselves, but in their author. What hope can there be in something perishable and uncertain? Indeed, some depart from these riches; while those who appear to remain in them gain no profit from them for the future [Col. 0686B], but loss, unless they share them with those in need. For they are not eternal, so that they should be preferred to the future life. They make people proud, as though they promised immortality. We have the example of resurrection in Christ, and many do not love Christ as they love riches, although no example can be seen of riches having delivered anyone from death. Christ redeemed us, not riches. He showed the way to the future life, so that, rejecting all these things, we might follow him and come to immortal and heavenly riches. Therefore we must strive for this: to be rich in good works and to acquire spiritual riches from these earthly resources. Let us sow on earth, so that we may reap in heaven, where an eternal treasure is stored.

“O Timothy, guard the deposit entrusted to you” [Note: [Col. 0686C] The Vulgate reads “the deposit.”], avoiding profane novelties of words and oppositions of falsely named knowledge [Note: [Col. 0686C] The Vulgate reads “of falsely named knowledge.”], which some professing have missed the mark concerning the faith. Grace be with you.

He again urges that what was said above be preserved, while things contrary to religion are to be avoided—things that usurp merely the name of knowledge and are deceptive in their profession, so as to deceive the simple. They pretend to have faith, from which they have fallen away, in order to introduce faithlessness. And he subscribed with his own hand, saying, “Grace be with you.” Amen.

End of the First Epistle to Timothy.

# THE SECOND EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY

[Col. 0685]

## ARGUMENT [Note: [Col. 0685] The Argument and exposition of this Epistle are by the same author as those of the three preceding Epistles, namely, Ambrosiaster.]

[Col. 0685D]

He writes another Epistle to Timothy, now instructed in ecclesiastical discipline, so that by his own example he might summon him to martyrdom and teach him what hope the promise contains; for some would eventually turn away from sound doctrine because it seemed harsh to them and turn instead to myths, that is, to human inventions.

## [THE TEXT BEGINS]

[Col. 0686D] (CHAPTER I.) “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God according to the promise of life which is in Christ Jesus, to Timothy, his beloved son.”

For this reason he indicates that he was called an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God: to teach what and how great the promise in the future is through faith in Christ, so that by his preaching he might increase the number of those being saved through the Lord’s discipline. For those are worthy servants who, by their diligence and [Col. 0687A] faith, enlarge their masters’ affairs. He writes this to Timothy as to a most beloved son so that he may imitate him in this matter, handing the same things on to others, in order that, through an unbroken succession, he may be a capable teacher through whom the truth he has affirmed may win many to the promised life.

“Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.”

He wishes for him the Father’s grace in mercy, so that it may be present with him, and the grace of Christ Jesus our Lord, because God bestows his grace through Christ, so that the grace of both may be one.

“I give thanks to my God, whom I serve with a pure conscience from my forefathers, because I have an unceasing remembrance of you in my prayers, longing greatly to see you night and day, remembering your tears, so that I may be filled with joy as I recall the sincere faith that is in you, which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice; and I am certain that it dwells in you as well.”

Since it is fitting to remember good people, he therefore gives thanks to God because he remembered Timothy, a remarkable man, so that this too may be understood as a gift of God. For one who thinks about good men does not do so without merit. And because the God of Christians is the same God who was the God of the Jews, he declares that he gives thanks to that God whom he served from his forefathers. For when his ancestors hoped for what Paul had begun to preach, their faith was one and the same. And because he entered into the service of his parents, and because he was still among them when they served God, he rightly says: “whom I served and serve from my forefathers.” How? “With a pure conscience,” he says. For in this way he once persecuted the Church [Col. 0687C], so that he did it out of love for God, not out of ill will. For similarly it is written in the Epistle to the Hebrews that Levi, who received tithes (Heb. VII, 9), gave tithes to Melchizedek; because, he says, Levi was in Abraham’s loins (ibid., 10) when he offered tithes to Melchizedek [Note: [Col. 0687D] The words “because … Melchizedek” are found written in the lower margin.]. Thus here too he says that he served God from his forefathers, because Levi is also said to have offered tithes in his forefather. For Jacob is Levi’s father, Isaac his grandfather, and Abraham his great-grandfather. Accordingly, he professes that he remembers Timothy very much and eagerly longs for him because of the memory of his tears, which he had shed out of love for the Apostle, as may be understood, when the Apostle was departing from him. Therefore he rightly longs for one who loves him, so that he may be filled with joy through their shared happiness, on account of the sincere faith which he indicates was in both Timothy’s grandmother and mother [Col. 0687D], and certainly in Timothy as well. Thus all this affection is because of the faith that was inviolate in them.

“For this reason I remind you to rekindle the gift of God that is in you through the laying on of my hands. For God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.”

For this reason he indicated that he had remembered the sincerity of his parents’ faith, so as to make Timothy stronger. For who, hearing the praise of those whose very participation he shares, would not grow, adding courage to such strengths? Thus he rekindles in him the gift of God’s grace received [Col. 0688A] through the ordination of the presbyterate, while he warms his spirit with the joy of his mind, rejoicing in himself, just as there is joy in the freshness of ordination. Finally he adds: “For,” he says, “God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power.” The renewed human being emerges from fear, receiving a spirit of joy because of justification, since every unjust person is in fear, not strong but weak, not in love but in hatred, not in soundness of mind but wounded by error. If, however, he is freed from these things through faith, he will be strong, beloved, and self-controlled.

“Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me, his prisoner.”

He teaches that steadfastness is required and that one must not tremble in confession. There is no reason to be ashamed of it, because although Christ was seen as a human being [Col. 0688B], by his deeds he nevertheless appeared to be God; and although he was crucified, he nevertheless rose from the dead and, with many looking on, ascended into heaven as the cloud received him. Therefore this is not a cause of weakness but of power, because where weakness is supposed, power appears. Thus the one who is proved to have conquered is foolishly said to have been weakened.

In the same way, there is nothing in the Apostle that should cause shame. For although he is said to have been humbled by afflictions and beatings, in that very respect he confounds his detractors, because in signs and wonders he is seen to be manifestly extraordinary by God’s will [Note: [Col. 0687D] The words “because … extraordinary,” which are missing from the manuscript [Col. 0688D], we have judged should be added from the printed editions.], so that it may be understood that he was humbled not through weakness but willingly, for a certain advancement in merit. For this reason God permits his servants to be humbled by the wicked, lest he appear to award them rewards unjustly.

“But share in suffering for the Gospel according to the power of God, who saved us.”

Since death was conquered by God’s power, so that we might be saved, it is therefore fitting that we repay our Redeemer in some measure. Since we cannot respond to all his benefits, let us at least faithfully and diligently carry out his commission.

“And he called us with a holy calling.”

The holy calling occurs when people are chosen to govern God’s holy people. The elder is called to holiness when he is chosen as the leader of holiness.

“Not according to our merits.”

This is true, because if one investigates the matter thoroughly, no human being can appear worthy to be Christ’s representative. All whom he chose had previously been sinners. Thus, insofar as comparison with others is concerned, they were found worthy; but insofar as the matter itself is concerned, all are unworthy.

“But according to his own purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before the ages of the world.”

Since God in his condescension determined long ago to save sinners—for God knew beforehand what would happen in human beings, before he made them and they sinned—he predestined how they would be restored, at what time, through whom, and by what method they could be saved, so that this gift might appear to be granted neither through the merit of those who are saved nor through that of those by whom they are called, but through God’s [Col. 0689A] grace, by faith in Christ.

“But now revealed through the illumination of the advent of our Savior, Christ Jesus.”

He testifies that God’s gift, which had been hidden in mystery before the ages of the world, was revealed through Christ’s incarnation and appearing, when human beings began to receive the remission of sins.

“Who indeed destroyed death, but brought eternal life to light through the Gospel, in which I was appointed a herald, an apostle, and a teacher of the nations.”

He shows by what means Christ saved his people, saying that he destroyed death, which was hostile to humanity, so that humanity could not rise from the underworld; then at last he brought life to light through immortality, so that once risen from the dead it could no longer die. For the life bounded by time is obscure, while it is drowsy, ignorant, and badly conducted. He shows how life is brought to light: through the Gospel, eternity is given to believers, with the teacher of the nations preaching.

“For this reason I also suffer these things.”

While preaching God’s gift, he experiences the devil as an enemy, who arouses afflictions against him because he has snatched the people from the devil’s jaws.

“But I am not ashamed.”

Secure in this, because a great promised reward is set aside for tribulations, he is not ashamed but glories in afflictions.

“For I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to guard my deposit for that day.”

This is what he means: he is secure through hope and confidence in the Savior’s greatness, because what he entrusts to him is safe [Col. 0689C]. What does he entrust to him except his salvation, so that, suffering here for him, he may find salvation with him when he begins to judge, and, while punishing the faithless, declare this man worthy of eternal life?

“Having the pattern of sound words which you heard from me in faith and love that is in Christ Jesus, guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us.”

He calls his instructions, together with his deeds, the pattern of saving doctrine, and commands Timothy to follow and preserve them with the Holy Spirit’s assistance.

“You know this: that all who are in Asia turned away from me, among whom are Phygellus and Hermogenes.”

Those whom he mentions were full of deceit. They pretended to be friends of the Apostle so that, by attaching themselves to him, they might learn [Col. 0689D] how to slander him or bring accusations against him through others; but after they saw that they had been exposed, they withdrew from him.

“May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chain.”

This refreshment should be understood in two ways: he refreshed him with his comfort during the hardship of imprisonment, and, if the Apostle had any needs, he supplied them, or ministered to those in need. Because of the hope of the things promised, he was not ashamed to approach and seek out a man held in custody. Those whom he mentioned above, however, because they were ashamed of Christ’s cross, abandoned the Apostle in his need.

[Col. 0690A] “But when I was in Rome, he searched for me diligently and found me. May the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day.”

When the Apostle came to Rome and appealed to Caesar, he was guarded by soldiers. At that time Onesiphorus [Note: [Col. 0689D] In the manuscript: “Onisiphorus.”], out of love and respect for his teaching, searched for him with great diligence and found him. His visit was so pleasing to the Apostle that he commends him to the Lord in this way, so that he may find mercy before God on the day of judgment: just as he found the Apostle by searching for him, so may he find mercy by seeking it from the Judge. For this is what he prays: that the Lord, the Father of heaven and earth, grant him to find favor with the God of the human race, namely, the Son. This is like that passage in Genesis: “And,” it says, “the Lord rained sulfur and fire upon Sodom and Gomorrah from God out of heaven” (Gen. XIX, 24) [Col. 0690B].

“And you know very well how much he ministered at Ephesus.”

Since some people are accustomed to serve persons rather than causes, wishing to please the powerful, the Apostle displays Onesiphorus’s general goodness, so that he would not seem perhaps to have commended him merely because he had ministered to the Apostle, when it was clear that he had been magnanimous toward everyone.

## (CHAPTER II.)

“Therefore, my son, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus, and the things that you heard from me through many witnesses, entrust these to faithful people who will be capable of teaching others.”

He commands Timothy to be steadfast and strong in teaching the grace of God that is in Christ Jesus. He wishes not only the grace but also the mysteries concerning Christ, the secrets, to be entrusted to faithful [Col. 0690C] and worthy people who can teach others, not indiscriminately to ordinary and negligent persons. For a teacher must be chosen with great care.

“Labor as a good soldier of Christ. No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself.”

What he says is clear, because no one can serve two masters (Matt. VI, 24). Secular business must serve greed, and unless people have lied, they cannot carry it through. Thus it is a sin, though a slight one. The ecclesiastical servant, however, proves himself to God for this reason: so that, devoted to him, he may fulfill the duty he promised, diligent in God’s affairs and separated from secular business. For it is not fitting for one person to have a double profession.

“And if someone competes, he is not crowned unless he competes lawfully” [Col. 0690D].

He wants the soldier of God to be so practiced in God’s works and in the office assigned to him that he may attain the reward of glory, watching with his whole mind over divine service, scorning present things, and loving heavenly things. For he proved himself for this purpose, so that, laboring here, he might be rewarded in heaven.

“The farmer who labors ought to receive first from the fruits. Understand what I say. For the Lord will give you understanding in everything.”

Saint Timothy was so abstinent that he even refrained from what was permitted. This is what he wants understood: he abstained from sharing in the treasury, although the Lord had decreed that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel [Col. 0691A]. Therefore the Apostle first commanded him to take from it, since he was first, and then distribute to the others.

“Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, from the seed of David, according to my Gospel, in which I labor even to chains, as though a robber; but the word of God is not bound.”

Since many future sons of the devil would deny that the Son of God had become incarnate, he recalls this, because they strive deceitfully to assert it under the name of apostles. He added, “according to my Gospel,” to exclude the false conversations of a corrupt mind. For the heretics should not be believed about the apostles more than the apostles themselves are to be believed when they testify to their own preaching.

He complains that he carries out this preaching with labor. He was afflicted by pressures and prisons because, as it seemed to them, he offended both Jews and Gentiles by preaching incredible things. He made the Jews angry because he taught that the Law had come to an end. He made the Gentiles enemies because he preached one God in Christ. Hence they treated him as a criminal, binding and imprisoning him so that he might be silent, not knowing that they could not bind the word of God. Indeed, often when imprisoned he suffered no loss but gained profit. He was not without someone to whom he could preach in prison, so that, unable to invite people freely to the faith, he might nourish them with the word of God while held in chains.

“Therefore I endure everything for the sake of the elect, so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, with heavenly glory.”

So that by his preaching he might save people predestined to life, he was subjected to destruction [Col. 0691C], knowing that he would obtain the salvation he sought for them.

“For if we have died with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him.”

He indicates that it is possible to attain immortality and Christ’s glory if we remain in the form of baptism, where all sins die, so that, renewed, we may flee all former vices and crimes and, following the author’s footsteps, appear dead to sins. If, moreover, it is added to this purpose that we do not endure tribulations and afflictions for the Lord’s name with reluctance, then, enduring these things together with him, we shall reign together with him. For it is fitting that the one who suffers reproaches or dangers for him should appear glorious in his kingdom.

[Col. 0691D] “If we deny him, he will also deny us.”

This is true: if we have not confessed him before human beings, then he too will say to us in the necessity of the coming judgment, “I do not know you.” This signifies punishment.

“If we do not believe, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself.”

No one can take away from the Lord what he possesses. For who is stronger than he, through whom all things came into being? Nothing can be added to the perfect one, because the person who believes in him contributes nothing to him; nor does the person who does not believe take anything away from him. Whatever is done, therefore, concerns our progress, so that we may not remain in ignorance. He is not made firm by us, since he is firm in himself and with himself.

[Col. 0692A] “Remind them of these things, testifying before the Lord. Do not quarrel over words; it is useful for nothing except the ruin of those who hear.”

He warns that disputes must be avoided. Instructions should instead be given under the fear and dread of God, because disputation can produce scruples in those who are not yet firmly established. In disputes, people often bring forward such arguments, drawing the sword of malice, that they disturb the minds of foolish brothers.

“Take careful charge of yourself, so that you may present yourself to God as a proven worker, unashamed, rightly handling the word of truth.”

Since some people say that disputation is beneficial, while the Apostle knows that it is more harmful, he commands each person to take care that, rejecting quarrels, he may make himself approved, calling those who rely on disputes “unashamed.” For disputation necessarily extorts something—or rather, many things—that are said against one’s conscience, so that inwardly one loses in spirit while outwardly departing victorious. No one tolerates being defeated, even if he knows that what he hears is true. But the person who speaks to those who are willing and peaceable rightly handles the matter and has a good conscience. Therefore there should be discussion among God’s servants, not quarrelling.

“Avoid profane novelties of words, for they will advance greatly toward emptiness. Their speech spreads like gangrene.”

He continues the same point, that disputes should be avoided. It is not fitting for people of one faith to quarrel, but in discussion they should bear with one another and agree on good statements. If something seems unacceptable, it should be passed over peacefully. Adversaries and dissenters usually provoke one another; among them one is Catholic and the other profane. The Catholic, then, whom the Apostle commands to despise and avoid empty myths, ought to be quiet, always bringing forth words from a good conscience and not allowing impious words to be uttered in his presence. Such things give some people an opportunity to advance toward worse things. For there are people who, hearing profane words, conceive an evil thought; therefore disputation is harmful.

“Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have strayed from the truth by saying that the resurrection has already occurred, and they are overthrowing the faith of some.”

Now he reveals the names of those whose case prompted his warning to avoid disputes. He designates them as profane and impious, straying from the truth. For they denied what is the chief teaching of Christians: that they will rise from the dead in the future [Col. 0692D]. But, as we are taught from another Scripture, they said that the resurrection occurs in children, and there were people who gave perverse assent to this against the faith they had received at the beginning.

“Nevertheless, God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: ‘The Lord knows those who are his,’ and, ‘Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity.’”

God’s foundation is faith, which contains the things God promised. This faith cannot be overthrown by the inventions of the faithless and heretics. Although they deny the future things we believe, God will nevertheless give what we believe he will give, as his promise testifies [Col. 0693A]. Our faith, therefore, is the seal of God’s promise; it confirms God’s words. On the day of judgment God will recognize those who bear his sign and dissent from the iniquity of the faithless and heretics, which imagines that it can weaken God’s promise. For nothing is so iniquitous as to oppose God’s faith.

The same was said to Dathan, Abiram, and Korah by Moses when they dared to offer sacrifices against God’s command. “The Lord knows those who are his.” By saying this he showed what destruction awaited those who perverted God’s words.

“In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and earthenware, some for honor and some for dishonor.”

By this he signified that there are different kinds of people in the Church [Col. 0693B]: some good and eminent, whom he wants understood as gold; some merely good, whom he designates as silver; and others not good, whom he calls wooden and earthen vessels. I think this is clear to everyone. For the frequent language of the Apostle’s rebuke demonstrates it in the Church of Corinth. Now it is obvious in our own Church; and in the temple at Jerusalem, which was a type of the Church, it is confirmed by clear readings.

There were Sadducees among them, from whose root Hymenaeus and Philetus arose. After the Apostle had spoken about their perverse opinion, he immediately added this, so that it would not be surprising to see dissenting people in the Church. In the Church of Corinth too, which I mentioned, there were some who denied the resurrection in their dissent.

But the insane Novatian, [Col. 0693C] to flatter his own error, teaches that this must be understood differently, so that the great house is believed to signify the whole world, because it contains a diversity of people. Yet it is clear that the Apostle used the example of a rich and wealthy house which, although it is well supplied, [Note: [Col. 0693D] In the printed manuscripts, after “although it is well supplied,” we read “nevertheless has wooden and earthen vessels.” The same applies here to the Church: although it is called holy, it nevertheless has these and [Col. 0694D] the other things that follow.] nevertheless has vicious people and people of perverse opinions, as I mentioned above. He shows that these deserve dishonor, but not that they will perish; rather, they are to be purified through fire, because they are in some respect necessary to the household.

Novatian, however, puffed up with pride, wishing to defend the truth and universal holiness of his church, decided that this should be understood as though the Church existed with him and contained everyone purified, on account of those matters for which he accuses us, though we are innocent. But why was there any need in this passage to say something about the world, or why should he assert that the world signifies a great house? For the Lord says to the apostles: “You are not of the world. But I chose you” (John XV, 19). How, then, are those to be enclosed within the world who are said not to be of the world? And therefore the Apostle says: “What have I to do with judging those who are outside?” (I Cor. V, 12.)

In one house, all are under one name. For all are reckoned under the name of their one master. The world, however, contains people of different professions, so that they profess to have different gods and lords. Therefore he did not call the world a great house, but the Church [Col. 0694A], in which all are under the name of one Lord.

“Therefore, if anyone cleanses himself from these things, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work.”

Here another heresy is refuted by its own fraud: it asserts that some souls are evil by nature and cannot be compelled to goodness, whereas this passage says that bad people can be changed into good and the impure purified. Hymenaeus and Philetus could have cleansed their minds if they had wished, so as to become a sanctified vessel prepared for honor.

“Flee youthful desires.”

Youthful desires are hostile things. They are worldly pleasures given over to every kind of enticement and therefore to be fled by God’s servant.

[Col. 0694B] “But pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace with those who call upon God from a pure heart.”

He commands the pursuit of these things, which seem strange and harsh to youthful age. Whoever chooses righteousness does nothing contrary to it; whoever loves faith keeps the commandments. Whoever follows love is humble toward everyone. The guardian of peace provokes no one to quarrel.

“But avoid foolish and uneducated questions, knowing that they generate disputes.”

Senseless questions belong partly to the faithless and partly to the heretics; some arise from the side of the faithless and compel modest people to quarrel. For modest people are unsettled by the excessive contradiction of their impiety and, in anger, say something contrary to their purpose. Some heretics pretend to patience, although they cannot hear anything harsh from a Catholic, so as to commend their perverse conversations; therefore one must dissemble toward them.

“The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, teachable, patient, and modest, correcting those who think differently, in the hope that God may perhaps grant them repentance [Note: [Col. 0694D] All the readings have ‘repentance,’ but in our manuscript ‘patience’ is written.] leading to the knowledge of the truth, and that they may come to their senses, having been captured by him to do the devil’s will.”

These words need no interpretation, for they are clear. Yet he has shown how beneficial modesty is. If humility has been pleasing in certain heretics because they appear humble, how much more praiseworthy and fruitful will it be in a Catholic, if he is gentle, in whom both useful understanding and conduct worthy of imitation are seen?

## (CHAPTER III.)

“But know this: in the last days difficult times will come. People will be lovers of themselves alone, lovers of money, insolent, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, impious, without faith, without love, slanderers, incontinent, harsh, hostile to goodness, treacherous, reckless, conceited, lovers of pleasures rather than lovers of God, having the appearance of piety but denying its power. Avoid such people.”

This is a prophecy of the holy Apostle, in which he foresaw how many evils would come from the heretics and also from the Jews. For all these things, which are hostile to the faith, are marked out in them [Col. 0695A]. The Apostle himself said: “What have I to do with judging those who are outside?” (I Cor. V, 12.)

Those who think wrongly about God and, without fear, profess what belongs to his dishonor—how can they be benevolent in human society? Therefore he says, “having the appearance of piety but denying its power,” because they profess themselves Christians while being utterly wicked in conduct and perverse in understanding. The praise and power of God are found not more in profession than in deeds.

“For among them are those who slip into households and take captive little women burdened with sins, led by various desires, always learning and never arriving at the knowledge of the truth.”

Although this applies to all heretics, since they enter households and ensnare women with cunning and deceitful words so that through them they may deceive men, after the manner of their father the devil, who deceived Adam through Eve, it applies especially to the Manichaeans. For none are so intrusive, so deceitful, or so ensnaring as they. They are known to worship one thing and profess another, to carry one thing within and claim another outwardly.

They defend chastity and uphold it by their own law, yet live shamefully. They praise mercy, although they are found to be unjust among themselves. They assert that the world must be despised, yet always appear carefully groomed. They boastfully proclaim that they devote themselves to fasts [Note: [Col. 0695D] The words “they devote themselves … proclaim” are found in the upper margin.], while all appear well fed—except that they are seen to be pale through some artifice, so as to deceive.

The Apostle therefore prophesied these things especially about them [Col. 0695C], although it is clear that they did not exist in the time of the apostles, just as the Arians did not; for the emperor Diocletian identifies them in an edict, saying: “This filthy and impure heresy, which,” he says, “has recently emerged from Persia.” They find women who, out of vanity, desire to hear something new, and through agreeable things they persuade them to accept shameful and unlawful matters. For they are eager to learn but lack the judgment to test what they hear. This is to be always learning without possessing the knowledge of truth.

“Just as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses (Exod. VII, 11), so these also resist the truth [Note: [Col. 0695D] The words “so … the truth” are missing from the manuscript, but we have added them from the Vulgate and Ambrosiaster.], people corrupted in mind and disqualified regarding the faith, but they will not advance any further. For their ignorance will be evident to everyone, as theirs also was.”

[Col. 0695D] This example is taken from the apocrypha [Note: [Col. 0695D] The divine Chrysostom, in Homily 8 on this passage, says: “Who were these magicians in Moses’ time? And how are their names found nowhere else? Either the traditions were unwritten, or Paul learned these things through the Spirit.”]. Jannes and Mambres were brothers, Egyptian magicians or sorcerers, who thought that by the counterfeit rivalry of their magic they could resist the power of God working through Moses. But when the power in Moses’ works increased, they were humbled and, with the pain of their wounds, confessed that God was working through Moses.

Accordingly, he says that these people too will advance no further in asserting their impiety, because their incompetence and deception will become public; and although unwillingly, they will nevertheless confess their ignorance at the end.

“But you have followed my teaching, conduct, purpose, faith, patience, love, endurance, persecution, and sufferings.”

He wants Timothy to imitate the things he enumerates. For these things will ultimately lead not to repentance but to joy.

“Such things as happened to me at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra: what persecutions I endured, and from all of them the Lord delivered me. But wicked people and deceivers will advance from bad to worse, themselves wandering astray and entangling others in their errors.”

Therefore he recalls what and how much he suffered, in order to display the aids of God, by which he defended and kept his servants safe from Satan’s cunning, making them secure and strengthening them, so that they would not fear what might be inflicted by the treacherous, but would be cheerful in persecution, confident that all who live rightly in Christ are hated even by the members of their own body. But evil people will advance from bad to worse, when they see many agreeing with them, so that they lead the rest into error. For when they are known to be evil and deceptive, yet nevertheless flourish and prosper in the world, they attract some people to become their imitators, to be punished not only for their own errors but also for those of the people whom they destroy by their example.

“Nevertheless, continue in the things that you have learned and that have been entrusted to you, knowing from whom you learned them, and because from infancy you have known the sacred writings, which are able to instruct you for salvation.”

He indicates that possessing knowledge of the Old Testament is of great benefit. For he calls them the sacred writings that point to the person of Christ and declare his Incarnation for the redemption and salvation of humanity. He urges him to advance in these writings. Antiquity is the strength of novelty; knowing from whom he learned, he possesses firm authority. For he saw signs and wonders performed by him, before which every argument gives way.

“All Scripture is divinely inspired and useful for teaching, for reproof, for restoration, and for instruction in the righteousness that is in it, so that the man of God may be prepared and perfected for every good work.” [Col. 0696D]

It is clear that all Scripture whose author is shown to be God is useful. For it was given to benefit the unlearned and to restore those who have been disfigured, drawing the wicked toward righteousness, so that the man of God may be perfect in every good work. For, progressing step by step in the new man, it establishes him as a man of God.

## Chapter IV

“I testify before God and Christ Jesus, who is going to judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom: proclaim the word; be urgent [Col. 0697A] in season and out of season; reprove, exhort, rebuke, with all patience and teaching.”  
[Note: The word *importune*, which is absent from the manuscript, has been restored from the Vulgate and the other witnesses.]

He commands so earnestly that God’s gift be preached without violation that, with God the Father and Christ his Son called as witnesses, he urges and insists that this be carefully undertaken, so that by constant preaching and frequent reproof he may call people to better progress, at the proper time. And so that they may more readily agree with the one who reproves them, he urges that this be done without bitterness.

“For there will be a time when they will not endure sound teaching, but, itching in their ears, they will heap up teachers for themselves according to their own desires; and some will turn away their hearing from the truth and turn instead to myths.”

This too is a prophecy of the holy Apostle, who, foreknowing the future, commanded that one must apply oneself diligently to teaching, so that those strengthened in faith and instructed in good works might remain firm in sound discipline. Thus, in the last time, when some begin to turn from truth to error, they may remain unmoved. He says that there will be people who want to be taught according to their desires, turning from steady and truthful teachers to those who teach them what they willingly hear, because truth seems harsh to them; and, abandoning sound doctrine, they devote themselves to myths. They do not wish their evil works to be reproved. Therefore they want teachers who serve their habits. Their ears itch to hear myths of vanity, composed under the name of doctrine, in which they take delight. Nothing is more characteristic of this than the Manichaeans, who possess various inventions of I know not what kind, designated by inflated names, [Col. 0697C] although they are trivial matters and certain ravings.

“But you, be sober in all things, be patient, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry. For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand.”
