He admonishes and urges him to keep watch, to act courageously in ecclesiastical discipline, and to explain the Scriptures, so that the prudent and instructed may avoid empty myths. For the Apostle, knowing that his passion was near, wishes to leave in the holy Timothy an example of devout conduct and sound teaching, so that capable teachers might never be lacking through succession. Yet he calls his passion a libation. For he is being offered as a sacrifice to God, since he suffers for God’s righteousness.

“I have fought the good fight, I have completed the course, I have kept the faith. What remains is that the crown of righteousness has been laid up for me, [Col. 0697D] which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award me on that day—not only to me, but also to those who love his appearing.”

He recalls that he preserved everything useful and prosperous for himself and for others. For he offered himself to his hearers as a model not only in words but also in deeds, so that he might be a faithful steward to his author through the truth of his preaching, and, having struggled with every care and skill against the rulers and powers of the world, might leave an example of how they could be conquered. He also did this so that his inviolate teaching and the lawful contest of the struggle might make them worthy to be crowned, [Col. 0698A] because God, the righteous judge, will give the greatest rewards to those who love him and await his Son from heaven.

“Make every effort to come to me as soon as possible. For Demas has deserted me, loving this present world, and has gone to Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia; Titus to Dalmatia. Luke alone is with me. Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me in the ministry. But I have sent Tychicus to Ephesus.”

Although the whole instruction of ecclesiastical law is contained in the letter, nevertheless, because of his great affection, he desires Titus’s presence. He bears witness to Mark for this reason: he remembers his former labors.

“Bring the cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus [Col. 0698B] when you come, and the books, especially the parchments.”

The Apostle was by nature a Jew, and he possessed nothing foreign to himself. How, then, did he have a cloak? But since he was from Tarsus, and since it is established that those from there were received into Roman society so that thereafter they would be called Roman citizens, it is therefore necessary that they also have a curia in which, according to Roman custom, they might assemble wearing cloaks. For whoever at that time went out to meet the Romans with gifts were granted perpetual immunity and were called Roman citizens, as were their brothers, as the same Apostle testifies. It may therefore be that, if it was not his own—for he had devoted his entire self to the Law—he had his father’s cloak.

“Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils. May the Lord repay [Note: The Vulgate reads *reddet*, ‘will repay’.] him according to his works. You also avoid him, for he strongly resisted my words.” [Col. 0698C]

This Alexander and the Demas mentioned above were colleagues. At first they were with the Apostle, pretending friendship toward him; but when they were proved deceitful in time, both withdrew from him. This man, the coppersmith, who was bolder in evil, withdrew from him in such a way that he also became a contradicter of his words. Therefore, since he dared to contradict the Apostle, he rightly warns that he should be avoided, leaving him to God’s judgment.

[Note: The words “this man … in such a way” were added from the printed manuscripts.]

“At my first defense no one stood by me; everyone deserted me. May it not be counted against them.”

He calls the pressure and tribulations inflicted upon him his defense. For suffering is life for Christians, and persecution is defense. The pressure inflicted for righteousness will defend him on the day of judgment, making the treacherous guilty. Thus, at the very beginning of the pressure inflicted upon him, he complains that he was deserted; and because he knows that this is customary, he does not want it counted against them, since the disciples also deserted the Lord when he was seized by the Jews. For it is written in the prophet: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Zechariah 13:7).

“But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the proclamation might be fulfilled and all the nations might hear it.”

For this reason he says that he was fortified by the help of the Lord Christ and increased in power, so that he might fulfill the preaching among all the nations. Therefore he asks that those who deserted him in his time of need be forgiven, so that, accepted by God, he might not seek vengeance. For he believes that he was helped by God all the more because he was deserted by human beings.

“And I was delivered from the lion’s mouth. The Lord will deliver me from every evil work and will save me in his heavenly kingdom. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.”

His fellow Apostle Peter says similarly that our adversary the devil prowls about, roaring like a lion and seeking whom he may devour (1 Peter 5:8). But because he found no opportunity in the Apostle by which he could deceive him, he stirred up pressure and punishments against him through his own children, so that, if not as a sinner, then at least as a righteous man, he might nevertheless be removed from this life, lest he encourage many to the faith. When he had nearly accomplished this, the Apostle, delivered by God’s providence, mocks him and testifies that he is weak, since he was snatched from his mouth: what he desired to accomplish, he could not. Thus he rejoices that he was rescued from death by God’s help and is so confident in the Lord’s providence that he believes he will be delivered from future temptations—not merely delivered for the present, but also saved on the day of judgment and destined to reign with the Lord Christ throughout the eternal ages.

“Greet Prisca and Aquila and the household of Onesiphorus. Erastus remained at Corinth. I left Trophimus sick at Miletus. Make every effort to come before winter.”

Aquila and Prisca are the people with whom he stayed as a guest and worked with his hands. Onesiphorus is the man to whom he bears witness in the Second Letter. Yet how could Trophimus have become sick while the Apostle, who raised the dead, was present? But signs were performed for unbelievers. And because merit is placed before God for various reasons, whether someone gives thanks to God in tribulation or in sickness, provided that he seeks no aid from the opposing side, he advances in merit before God. Because of the rains and cold, he urged him to come to him in autumn.

“Eubulus greets you, and Pudens, and Linus, and Claudia, and all the brothers.”

As usual, the letter is completed with the greeting of the brothers.

“The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Farewell.”

This is the Apostle’s subscription; he says that it is a sign in every letter. And because the Son of God is also the same Son of Man, and is called both Jesus and Christ, so that both man and God may be signified, he is designated by two names. Yet in both names the dignity is indicated, according to the reason for which the names were given.

*End of the Second Letter to Timothy.*

# The Letter to Titus Begins

[Col. 0699]

## Summary of the Letter to Titus

[Col. 0699C]

1. He instructs Titus concerning the kind of bishops he should ordain, and that he should rebuke the Cretans harshly.

2. Since all things are clean to the clean, and that old men, old women, young men, and young women should preserve chastity, and that slaves should obey their masters.

3. Since the grace of God has appeared, instructing us to live devoutly; and that he should rebuke with all authority, so that they may be subject to the powers and be modest.

4. Since we too were once foolish. But the kindness and humanity of God saved us, not because of our works; and that he should avoid foolish questions and a heretical person after one correction.

## Preface to Titus

[Col. 0699]

[Col. 0699C]

He reminds and instructs Titus concerning the establishment of presbyters, spiritual conduct, and the avoidance of heretics, who believe in the Jewish Scriptures. [The final words, *bens ei ab urbe Roma*, are corrupt or uncertain in the supplied text; literally they read approximately “good to him from the city of Rome.”]

## The Text Begins

[Col. 0699D]

### Chapter I

“Paul, a servant of God.”

What are we to make of the fact that our Savior and Lord said to the Apostles, “Now I will no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15:15), while the disciple of that same teacher—indeed, the Apostle in whom Christ was speaking—called himself a servant? Yet in another place the same Lord said to the same Apostles: “Say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were obliged to do” (Luke 17:10). And since both statements were spoken by Christ, one must carefully consider how they should be understood.

From these words of the Lord it is evident that there are two kinds of good servitude: one of fear and the other of love; one belonging to servants who fear, the other to those who love and please as sons. A maidservant fears lest she be flogged; a married woman fears lest she offend her husband’s mind. But the fear of servitude, which contains punishment, casts out perfect love (1 John 4:18). Perfect fear of servitude, however, not only contains no punishment, but is reached through joy, as the Psalmist testifies when he urges and says: “Let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name” (Psalm 85:11); and again: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever and ever” (Psalm 18:10).

The holy angels also possess this fear, and certainly the holy Apostles possessed it as well, through the coming of the Holy Spirit, through whom love descended into our hearts. Therefore the Lord did not call them servants but friends, although they were called servants both by themselves and by the Lord: clearly, not because of fear, but because of their love of pleasing God.

“But an Apostle of Jesus Christ.”

He distinguishes servitude from apostleship, because not everyone who is a servant is immediately also an apostle, whereas everyone who is an apostle is also a servant. Paul, however, is an apostle because he had been sent to preach Jesus Christ himself. And this must be understood: if the Father and the Son are one, then whoever believes in the Son also believes in the Father, because whoever does not believe in the Son does not have the Father. Therefore the servitude of the Apostle Paul must be referred indifferently both to the Father and to the Son.

“According to the faith of God’s elect”—that is, of those who have not merely been called but also chosen. There is also great diversity among the elect themselves, according to the variety of times, understandings, and expressions. Nor does someone immediately, simply because he is God’s elect, possess faith according to election, or possess knowledge of the truth according to faith. But [Note: In the margin, in the same script as the text, the letters *an* are written beside this sentence. Let the reader determine what these letters signify. A little farther below, sentences of St. Jerome also seem to have been noted.] according to the faith that he himself infuses and by which he makes people believers—those whom he also chose in his foreknowledge—as he says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16).

“And the acknowledgment of the truth that is according to godliness.”  
[Note: In the margin, as noted above, this appears in the following form: *Ih*, that is, Jerome or the so-called Jerome, whose sentence or interpretation this is.]

It is asked why, after saying “according to the faith of God’s elect and the acknowledgment of the truth,” he added, “that is according to godliness.” Is there, then, some truth that is not placed in godliness, and is the acknowledgment of truth now introduced to distinguish it as “the truth that is according to godliness”?

There plainly is a truth that does not possess godliness. If someone knows the art of grammar or dialectic, so that he possesses the method of speaking correctly and can distinguish between false and true, he possesses truth. Geometry, arithmetic, and music also contain truth within their own knowledge, but that knowledge is not the knowledge of godliness. The knowledge of godliness is to know the Law, to understand the prophets, to believe the Gospel, and not to be ignorant of the Apostles. Conversely, many possess a true knowledge of godliness, but do not immediately possess knowledge of the other arts mentioned above, or knowledge of those disciplines according to truth. [Note: These final words may have been added incorrectly, since they obscure the sense.]

“In hope of eternal life.”

This truth, therefore, whose acknowledgment is according to godliness, is placed in the hope of eternal life, because it immediately grants the reward of immortality to the person who comes to know it. Without godliness, however, knowledge of the truth gives pleasure for the present but has no reward in eternity.

“Which God, who does not lie, promised.”  
[Note: In the margin it is noted as follows: *AN*, namely Augustine.]

If he does not lie, acknowledge the truth, and the truth will free you; for the truth is Christ, and he gives nothing other than what he promised, both to the righteous and to the unrighteous, although this may seem harsh to human beings. [Note: This brief exposition, attributed to Augustine in the marginal note, is found almost word for word in the commentary of Pelagius attributed to St. Jerome.]

Or it may be understood in this way: what he promised to Abraham—that all nations would be blessed in him—he fulfilled in Christ through the preaching of the Apostle Paul and his fellow Apostles.

“Before the times of the ages. But in his own times he manifested his word in the preaching entrusted to me.”  
[Note: Here it is noted in the margin as *ag*, namely Augustine again.]

See: he said that there were eternal times, although they were not coeternal with God. For before the times of the ages—that is, the eternal times—he not only existed but also promised eternal life, which he manifested in his own times, that is, at the appropriate times. What else is “his Word”? For he himself is eternal life. But how did he promise it, since he surely promised it to human beings who did not yet exist, before the eternal times? It is because in his eternity, and in his Word, coeternal with him, what was to occur in its own time had already been fixed in predestination. [Col. 0702C]

“According to the command of God our Savior.”

No other Savior God is meant here than the Son. For he is one and the same with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one true Savior and God.

“To Titus, his beloved son.”

He calls Titus his son through teaching, example, instruction, and discipline, but not by nature, “according to the common faith.”

[Note: *Ih*, namely Jerome.]

Did he call the faith common to all who believed in Christ, or common only to himself and Titus? It seems more likely that the faith of the Apostle Paul and Titus was called common than that of all believers, among whom, because of the diversity of their minds, the faith could not be common but was diverse.

“Grace and peace from God the Father and Jesus Christ our Savior.”  
[Note: *Ag*, namely Augustine.]

He commends the grace of God, as in the other letters, through which our sins are forgiven so that we may be reconciled to God; and peace, through which we are reconciled to God.

“For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might correct what remains to be corrected.”

He left Titus, his disciple, in Crete to strengthen the beginnings of the newly born Church and to correct whatever seemed to be lacking, while he himself proceeded to other activities in order once again to lay the foundation of Christ among them. When he says, “so that you might correct what was lacking,” he shows that they had not yet come to a full knowledge of the truth; and although they had been corrected by the Apostle, they nevertheless still needed correction.

“And appoint presbyters in each city, just as I arranged for you.”  
[Note: The words that follow, up to the text beginning “if anyone is without fault,” belong to St. Jerome’s exposition of this Letter. Consult the responses of theologians and canonists on this question, which refute the heresy of Aerius.]

Let us carefully attend to the Apostle’s words: “so that you might appoint presbyters in each city, just as I arranged for you.” In what follows he explains what kind of presbyter ought to be ordained, namely: “If anyone is without fault, the husband of one wife,” and so forth. Later he adds: “For a bishop must be without fault, as God’s steward.” A presbyter, therefore, is the same as a bishop. Before factions arose in religion at the devil’s instigation, and people began saying, “I am of Paul, I of Apollos, and I of Cephas” (1 Corinthians 1:12), the Churches were governed by the common counsel of the presbyters.

But after each person began to regard those whom he had baptized as his own rather than Christ’s, it was decreed throughout the whole world that one of the presbyters should be elected and placed over the others, so that responsibility for the entire Church would belong to him and the seeds of schisms would be removed.

If someone thinks that the opinion that a bishop and a presbyter are one and the same is ours rather than that of Scripture, let him reread the Apostle’s words to the Philippians: “Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are in Philippi, with the bishops and deacons: grace to you and peace” (Philippians 1:1–2), and so forth. Philippi is one city of Macedonia, and certainly there could not have been several bishops in one city, as they are now considered to be. But because at that time the same people whom they called presbyters were also called bishops, he spoke indifferently of bishops as presbyters.

This might still seem ambiguous to someone unless it is confirmed by another testimony. In the Acts of the Apostles it is written that, when the Apostle Paul had come to Miletus, he sent to Ephesus and summoned the presbyters of that Church, to whom he later said, among other things: “Pay attention to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you as bishops to shepherd the Church of the Lord, which he acquired through his blood” (Acts 20:28). Here too one must carefully observe how, after summoning the presbyters of the one city of Ephesus, he later called these same men bishops. Let us therefore see what kind of presbyter, or bishop, ought to be ordained.

“If anyone is without fault.”

The difference between sin and crime is that every crime is a sin, but not every sin is a crime; and in this life many can be without crime, but no one can be without sins. Therefore the holy preacher, when describing a man worthy of priestly grace, did not say, “If anyone is without sin,” but, “If anyone is without fault.” Who can be without sin, when John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8)?

In this distinction between sins and crimes one must consider that certain sins pollute the soul, whereas crimes extinguish it. The priest elected for the Church must not merely be without any crime at the time when he is to be ordained, having erased his former stains through a new way of life; rather, from the time [Note: The words “from the time …” are written at the bottom margin of the manuscript.] when he was reborn in Christ, he must not be pierced by the consciousness of any sin. For how can the head of the Church remove evil from its midst if he himself has fallen into a similar offense? Or with what freedom can he rebuke a sinner, when he silently answers himself that he has committed the same acts that he rebukes?

“The husband of one wife.”  
[Note: *Ag*, namely Augustine.]

What food is to the health of the body, intercourse is to the preservation of the race. Neither is free from bodily pleasure. The diverse practices of the Fathers were caused only by the diversity of times. Thus it was necessary for even non-carnal prophets to engage in bodily intercourse, just as it was necessary for even non-carnal Apostles to eat bodily food.

Those who understood more sharply the rule concerning the steward of the Church judged that no one should be ordained unless he was the husband of one wife; they even judged that a man who, while a catechumen or pagan, had had another wife should not be ordained. [Note: This is not an absurd opinion, and it is sufficiently approved by the passages that follow. St. Jerome, however, criticizes it in this place, saying: “Many, more superstitiously than truthfully, think that even those who, while pagans, had one wife, but after losing her married another after Christ’s baptism, should not be chosen for the priesthood.” See what follows.]

For the issue concerns a sacrament, not sin. For in baptism all sins are forgiven. But because of the holiness of the sacrament, just as a woman, even if she was violated while still a catechumen, cannot after baptism be consecrated among God’s virgins, so it did not seem unreasonable that a man who had exceeded the singular number of wives had not committed some sin, but had lost a certain sacramental norm—not necessary for the merit of a good life, but necessary as the mark of ecclesiastical ordination.

“Having faithful children, not accused of debauchery or disobedient.”  
[Col. 0705A]  
[Note: *Ih*, namely St. Jerome.]

First, it must be said that the name of the priesthood is so holy that even matters outside us are reckoned to us—not so that we should fail to become bishops because of our own vices, but so that we should be barred from this rank because of the lack of restraint of our children. For with what freedom can we rebuke other people’s children and teach what is right, when the person rebuked can immediately answer us, “First teach your own children”? Or with what face can I rebuke a stranger who commits fornication, when my own conscience answers me, “Then disinherit the fornicating son; cast away your children who serve their vices”? When an evil son lives with you under the same roof, do you dare to remove the splinter from another’s eye while not seeing the beam in your own? (Matthew 7:5; Luke 6:41.)

Therefore a righteous man is not polluted by the vices of his children. But the Apostle reserves for the ruler of the Church the freedom to be such a man that he is not afraid, because of the vices of his own children, to rebuke strangers who are delinquent.

“A bishop must be without fault.”  
[Note: *Ag*, namely Augustine.]

No minister could rightly be ordained in the Church if the Apostle had said, “If anyone is without sin,” or if he had said, “Having no sin,” rather than what he says: “Having no crime.” Many baptized believers are without crime; but in this life I would say that no one is without sin.

“As God’s steward.”

If trustworthy stewards of human laws are sought, what sort ought those to be who administer divine laws? They must not eat and drink with the drunken, strike servants and maidservants, and await the Lord’s coming uncertainly, but must give their fellow servants food at the proper time. The only difference between a steward and the household is that a fellow servant has been placed over his fellow servants. Let the bishop and presbyter know that the people are fellow servants with them, not slaves.

“Not arrogant”—that is, not swollen with pride and pleased with himself because he is a bishop, but acquiring the position of a good steward, whose work benefits many.

“Not quick-tempered.”

A quick-tempered person is one who often becomes angry and is stirred by the slightest breath of an answer or offense, like a leaf by the wind. Someone who becomes angry occasionally is not necessarily quick-tempered; rather, that person is called quick-tempered who is frequently overcome by this passion.

“Not addicted to wine.”

The Apostle also forbids the bishop to be addicted to wine, lest, with his senses occupied, he either heighten his laughter beyond the dignity of gravity and burst into loud laughter with loosened lips, or, if he recalls some slightly sad matter, break out amid his cups into sobs and tears.

“Not violent.”

This, understood simply, also edifies the hearer, so that he does not readily extend his hand to strike or, in madness, rush upon another’s face to beat it. But he who placed his back beneath the lashes and, when cursed, did not return a curse for a curse condemns a bishop who is a striker. Better, however, let us say that the bishop is “not a striker” if, being gentle and patient, he knows at the proper time what should be said and what should be kept silent, and does not strike the consciences of the weak with useless speech.

“Not greedy for shameful gain.”

The desire for shameful gain must also be alien to the man who is to become a bishop. For many teach “things that ought not to be taught, for the sake of shameful gain”; they overturn entire households and think that godliness is a means of profit. “Better,” according to Solomon, “is a little possession with righteousness than great revenues with iniquity” (Proverbs 16:8); and a good name in poverty is to be preferred to a very bad name in riches (Proverbs 22:1).

The bishop who wishes to imitate the Apostle, having food and clothing, ought to be content with these alone. “Those who serve at the altar live from the altar” (1 Corinthians 9:13). He says “live,” not “become rich.” Therefore money is shaken out of our belt, and we wear only one tunic (Matthew 10:9–10; Mark 6:8–9), so that we do not think about tomorrow (Matthew 6:34). The desire for shameful gain is to think about more than the present.

Thus far the Apostle has taught, by his words, what a bishop or presbyter ought not to have. Now, conversely, what he ought to have is explained.

“But hospitable.”

Above all, hospitality is enjoined upon the future bishop. If everyone desires to hear the Gospel say, “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me” (Matthew 25:35), how much more does the bishop, whose house ought to be the common lodging of all? A layman who receives one, two, or a few people has fulfilled the duty of hospitality. A bishop is inhuman unless he receives everyone.

“Kind,” so that he may receive guests kindly. He is called *benignus*—kind—as though “exceedingly good.”

“Sober,” that is, temperate.

“Chaste,” free from every crime.

“Just,” in judgment.

“Holy,” in action through self-restraint.

“Self-controlled.”

He says this so that, because he had said “the husband of one wife,” no one might think that he had thereby made room for lack of self-control. Therefore, just as gentleness, patience, sobriety, moderation, abstinence from the desire for profit, hospitality, and kindness ought especially to be found in a bishop, and ought to distinguish him above all laypeople, so too chastity ought properly to belong to him—and, so to speak, priestly modesty—so that he not only abstain from impure action but also keep his eyes and thoughts free from error, since his mind is to confect the body of Christ.

The bishop must also be just and holy, so that he may exercise justice among the people over whom he presides, giving each person what he deserves and showing no partiality in judgment. The difference between the justice of a layman and that of a bishop is that a layman may appear just among a few, whereas a bishop must exercise justice among the many whom he has under his authority.

“Embracing the faithful word that accords with the teaching.”  
[Note: *Añ*.]

That is, he must love the teaching and always speak from it, rather than pursue vain and idle myths.

“So that he may be able to exhort in sound teaching.”

Sound teaching is that which heals its hearers, so that a person is not ungrateful for what he possesses as God’s gift by attributing it to himself.

“And to refute those who contradict.”

Such a person must be chosen as the bishop of the Church: one who can exhort those who waver and refute those who contradict—that is, convict them by the testimonies of Scripture. Even if this statement stood alone, it could suffice against those who say that innocence of life can be sufficient for teachers of the Churches without knowledge of Scripture.

[Note: *Ih*.]

“For there are many who are insubordinate, empty talkers, and deceivers of minds.”

The man who is to become the leader of the Church should unite eloquence with integrity of life, so that his works are not silent without speech and his words do not blush because his deeds are lacking—especially since such people are not few but many, and are not submissive but insolent. The teacher of the Church, to whom the souls of the people have been entrusted, must overcome such people by the reasoning of the Scriptures and impose silence upon them by the weight of testimonies.

“Especially those of the circumcision.”  
[Note: *Añ*.]

Those who speak human traditions rather than divine commandments.

“Whom it is necessary to refute”—that is, it is necessary to convict them prudently by the testimonies of Scripture.

“Who overturn entire households”—that is, they overturn not one or a few households, but all of them, together with their masters and servants.

“Teaching things that ought not to be taught”: distinctions concerning foods, concerning the Sabbath, which has already been abolished and rendered idle [Note: Vallarsius reads “abolition” in St. Jerome’s exposition, from which this interpretation derives; where we read *aboliti otio*, “abolished and rendered idle.” Our reading is better supported by what follows in the exposition of the verse “evil beasts,” where it says that for this reason they gladly admit festivals and idleness], and concerning the insult of circumcision—things that are now superfluous in the time of Christ, namely, the ceremonies of the Jews.

[Note: *Ih*.]

“For the sake of shameful gain.”

Because their belly is their god, they want to make their own disciples for the sake of shameful gain, so that, as teachers, they may be supported by their followers. We can also interpret what is said, “for the sake of shameful gain,” in another way: the Apostle may have used a common expression by which all heretics, when teaching perverse doctrines, are accustomed to claim that they are gaining people, although it is not gain but destruction to kill the souls of the deceived.

“Someone among them, their own prophet, said: ‘Cretans are always liars.’” What he says, “their own prophet,” should not be referred specifically to the Jews and those who are of the circumcision, but to many who are not subject, and who are empty talkers and deceivers of minds. Since they were in Crete, they must certainly be believed to have been Cretans—lovers of falsehood, and not merely liable to fall into it as usually happens, but always the same, continually liars [Note: [Col. 0707D] Who this prophet was, of whom the Apostle speaks—Callimachus or Epimenides—see Saint Jerome on this passage, with Vallarsius’s notes.].

“Evil beasts, idle bellies” [Note: [Col. 0707D] In the margin of this exposition it is noted as follows: “Añ.” These words, however, are taken from Pelagius’s frequently cited commentary.], that is, idle gluttons, and therefore they readily accept holidays and leisure [Note: [Col. 0708D] In the margin: “Ag.”]. This was said of a certain Epimenides, who was a Cretan, in whose books this hexameter verse is found, which stands in Greek according to metrical feet; in whose books it is found [Note: [Col. 0708D] I have not ventured to correct the error, or rather errors, that have crept into this text, because of the extensive alteration of wording that would have been necessary. See Saint Augustine, *Against the Adversaries of the Law and the Prophets*, Book II, §13, Paris edition, vol. 8, col. 588, where these words are missing, although the whole of this verse is found in his text.]; this man is not found among the prophets of God. Nor does it belong to those utterances of God which He says were entrusted to the Jews. For this reason the Apostle did not mention his name, as he usually mentions the prophets of God [Note: [Col. 0708D] Saint Augustine, in the cited passage, continues after those words as follows: “Sometimes saying, ‘as David also says’ (Rom. IV, 6); ‘But Isaiah dares and says’ (Rom. X, 20); ‘as Hosea also says’ (Rom. IX, 25); or, with their names suppressed, when he says, ‘as it is written,’ and that Scripture is understood in which, etc.”—which is also found in our text.] in whom God’s authority resides.

“This testimony is true” [Note: [Col. 0708D] “Ih.”]. Not the entire poem from which the testimony was taken, but only this testimony, this verse, by which they are called liars. And surely, since he approved one part only of the poem [Note: [Col. 0708D] Saint Jerome agreed.], he must be considered to have refuted the rest [Col. 0708C].

“For this reason rebuke them sharply, so that they may be sound in faith.” Since they are liars and evil beasts, persuading others of falsehoods and thirsting for the blood of the deceived like wild animals, rebuke them for this reason, so that they may be sound in faith. Concerning this soundness of faith he speaks in what follows: that old men should be sober, honorable, chaste, sound in faith, love, and patience; and by analogy with the soundness of faith, doctrine too is called sound.

“Not attending to Jewish fables and commandments of men who turn away from the truth.” These are the human traditions for which the Jews are reproved in the Gospel (Matt. XV, 9–14) through Isaiah (Isa. XXIX, 13): honoring God not with the heart but with the lips.

[Col. 0709A] “Those who turn away from the truth”—that is, from the grace of the New Testament, which was revealed and proclaimed in the Gospel, either through figures or through words and deeds in the Old Testament. [Note: [Col. 0709D] “Ih.”]

“All things are pure to the pure.” Since above he had said, “For there are many who are not subject, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those who are of the circumcision,” and had subsequently added concerning those who had been deceived by them, “Rebuke them sharply, so that they may be sound in faith, not attending to Jewish fables and commandments of men who turn away from the truth,” and since, as is argued most fully in Galatians and Romans, they thought there was a distinction among foods, some appearing pure and others impure, he therefore now adds, “All things are pure to the pure”—namely, to those who believe in Christ and know that every creature of God is good, and that nothing is to be rejected which is received with thanksgiving.

“But to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure” [Note: [Col. 0709D] “An.”: this exposition belongs to Pelagius.]. The defiled and unbelieving are those who do not believe that Christ, by giving faith, removed from the necks of believers the yoke of the Law—that is, all the things that had been given temporarily in figure [Note: [Col. 0709D] Perhaps “and the things that…,” is missing.]. They called these things impure.

“But both their mind and their conscience are defiled” [Note: [Col. 0709D] “Ih.”]. For this reason even things that are pure by nature become impure to them—not because anything becomes impure in itself, but according to the condition of those who partake, so that what is pure becomes pure to the pure and impure to the contaminated. Otherwise, even bread of blessing and the Lord’s cup do not benefit unbelievers and the polluted, because whoever eats that bread and drinks from that cup unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself (I Cor. XI, 27). For at Christ’s coming all things were cleansed.

“They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him.” They say that no one knows Christ as they do, since He was promised to them through the Law; but by their deeds they deny His coming [Note: [Col. 0709D] This is Pelagius’s, or the so-called Hieronymianist’s, text, which reads: “They say that they know Christ better, as promised through the Law; but by their deeds…” It should therefore be read, or rather understood, of the Jews, who asserted that no one knew Christ as well as they did.], while they think that they cannot be justified without the aid of the Law.

“Being detestable, disobedient, and unfit for every good work” [Note: [Col. 0710D] “Ih.”]. Just as someone honors God with his lips while remaining far from Him in his heart, so someone confesses God in speech and denies Him by his deeds. But one who denies God by his deeds, with a feigned confession, is rightly called detestable and profane; and, persuaded by no consideration of truth, is called disobedient and unbelieving. Hence it happens that he is unfit for every good work; for even those things which, perhaps overcome by natural goodness, he has done well are not good, since they are disapproved by the perversity of his mind.

**(CHAPTER II.)** “But you speak what is fitting for sound doctrine.” The Apostle now teaches Titus, his son and disciple in Christ, to speak those things that accord with sound doctrine, because doctrine is sound when the teacher’s teaching and life likewise agree.

[Note: [Col. 0710D] “AN.”] “That the old men should be sober.” Here he calls the elders of the Church “old men”; they must provide an example to all, lest they give a bad example to the younger.

“Respectable, prudent, sound in faith, in love, in patience” [Note: [Col. 0710D] “Ih.”]. At first he generally instructs Titus what he himself ought to say to everyone in the words, “But you speak what is fitting for sound doctrine.” Now he explains, species by species, what is fitting for each age: first what is appropriate to elderly men; then what is appropriate to old women; third, what is suitable for young people, namely both for young men and for young women. Although, in the command concerning old women, he appended instructions about young women, he was not so much teaching the young women himself as explaining what they were to be taught by the old women. Finally, concerning slaves, and through each age and condition, he establishes the commands so appropriately that his speech becomes a rule of life and conduct.

“Similarly, old women in holy attire” [Note: [Col. 0710D] “Añ.”]—that is, women who were chosen as an example to others. There is therefore also an unholy attire, of which he says elsewhere: “Not with braided hair or costly clothing” (II Tim. II, 9).

“Not slanderers”—that is, they must not bring the sins of others, whether known or unknown, before others’ faces as insults.

“Not enslaved to much wine,” but drinking a little, with sobriety, for the health of the body.

“Teaching what is good.” He permitted them to teach, but women, and not in church; rather, privately and among their own sex.

“Young women, to love their husbands.” So that they would not love other men; or because some were continent, lest, if they did not love their husbands, the word of God should be blamed as though it preached discord.

“Prudent, chaste, sober, managing the household,” lest they distress their husbands in any way.

[Col. 0710D] “Kind, submissive to their husbands, so that the word of God may not be blasphemed”—lest they themselves blaspheme it if they were negligent, or lest others, seeing them become worse than they had been before the faith, disparage the Christian religion [Note: [Col. 0710D] In the codex: “the Christian religion.”].

In what he said above, “Similarly, old women” [Note: [Col. 0710D] “Ih.”], this means that, like elderly men, they should be sober, honorable, chaste, sound in faith and chastity [Note: [Col. 0711D] Saint Jerome has “love.”], and patience; so that they are not accusers, are not enslaved to much wine, and teach what is good. Their distinctive requirement, in their own sex, is that they be holy in attire.

“Likewise exhort the young men to be sober.” Just as, in what he had commanded above when he said, “Similarly, old women in holy attire,” we said that the likeness of the old women was to be referred to the old men, so now, in what he adds, “Exhort the young men similarly, that they be chaste,” we think that the likeness of the young men is to be applied to the old women and through the old women to the old men: they should have the sobriety of the old men, and be honorable, chaste, and sound in faith, love, and patience. They should be chaste in all things—in mind as well as body, in deed as well as thought—so that there may be no suspicion of shamefulness in a young man.

“In all things present yourself as an example of good works.” For it is of no benefit for someone to be practiced in speaking and to have worn out his tongue in talking, unless he teaches more by example than by word.

“Slaves are to be subject to their masters in everything, pleasing them in all things, not answering back, not defrauding, but showing complete good faith, so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior.” Since our Lord and Savior, who says in the Gospel, “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI, 28), considers no condition, age, or sex excluded from blessedness, the Apostle therefore now establishes commands for slaves also, since they are a part of the Church [Col. 0711C] and members of Christ’s body. And just as above he taught what Titus ought to instruct old women, young women, and young men, so now he establishes commands suited to slaves: first, that they be subject to their masters in everything. This applies to all things that are not contrary to God: if a master commands something that is not opposed to the holy Scriptures, the slave should submit to his master; but if he commands something contrary to them, the spirit should obey rather than the master of the body. Pay close attention to how he assigns commands suitable to each person: “Slaves,” he says, “are to be subject to their masters in everything.”

“For the grace of God our Savior has appeared to all men, instructing us.” After the catalogue of instruction given to Titus concerning what he ought to teach old men, old women, young women and young men, and finally slaves [Col. 0711D], he rightly adds now: “The grace of God our Savior has appeared to all men.” For there is no difference between free and slave, Greek and barbarian, circumcised and uncircumcised, woman and man; rather, we are all one in Christ. We are all called to the kingdom of God; after our offense, we are all to be reconciled to our Father—not through our merits, but through the grace of our Savior. Either Christ Himself is the living and subsisting grace of God the Father, or this is the grace of Christ, who is God and Savior; and we have been saved not by our merit, according to what is said elsewhere: “You will save them for nothing” (Ps. LV, 8). This grace appeared to all men for the purpose of instructing us.

[Note: [Col. 0711D] “Añ.”] “To renounce ungodliness and worldly desires.” Every carnal desire and every temporal ambition is worldly, as God Himself says: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation, drunkenness, and the cares of this life. Let us live soberly, justly, and piously in this age” (Luke XXI, 34). The same blessed Apostle admonishes us elsewhere, saying: “Not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sobriety” (Rom. XII, 3). Nevertheless, in this threefold division, in which he says that we should live soberly, justly, and piously, it seems to me that the person lives soberly who does not pursue the pleasures of luxury; justly, the person who in no way harms his neighbor and, insofar as he can, bestows benefits upon him; piously, the person who in no way withdraws from the fellowship of ecclesial unity, but, placed within the Church, firmly holds whatever he knows with certainty to belong to the knowledge of the true faith, while whatever he does not know or about which he is uncertain he investigates humbly and patiently, until, if he thinks differently, he comes to know it when God reveals it to him.

These sobriety, justice, and piety, which ought to be present in all the faithful, are so closely joined to one another that if one of them is lacking, the other—which appears to be present—cannot benefit at all. For sobriety, by which someone abstains from wrongdoing in himself, is not fruitful unless it is also pious and just—that is, unless he believes rightly in God. Nor is justice fruitful, by which each person bestows on his neighbor what he desires to have bestowed upon himself, if it is not sober and pious. Piety too is dead, by which God is rightly believed, if either sobriety of conduct or love of neighbor is not maintained. True salvation of the soul is therefore acquired when piety in faith, justice in love, and sobriety in chastity and moderation are maintained.

[Note: [Col. 0712D] “Añ.”] “Awaiting the blessed hope.” The person who has lived as the same Apostle teaches above awaits these things with confidence. No other blessed hope should be believed more fittingly than what the Lord will say on the day of judgment to those who will be at His right hand: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV, 34).

“And the coming of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.” Christ is the great God, as the Prophet testifies when he says: “Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise in the city of our God, on his holy mountain” (Ps. XLVII, 2). He is also the Savior of all, especially of the faithful. His coming in glory is not to be understood as that by which He comes invisibly each day with the Father, not without the Holy Spirit, to the faithful and abandons the impious. Rather, it is to be understood as the coming when He will come in His own majesty and that of the Father, with all His angels, and will send them to gather His elect from the highest heavens to their farthest boundaries; and they will gather all nations before Him, and He will separate them from one another as a shepherd separates sheep from goats (Matt. XXV, 31), and so forth.

[Col. 0713A] “Who gave himself for us.” If He gave Himself—that is, offered Himself to be crucified by the hands of the impious—and the Father handed Him over, because He did not spare His own Son but handed Him over for us all (Rom. VIII, 32), then, although the passion accomplished for our salvation was personally the passion of the Son alone, our salvation is nevertheless shared by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

“That he might redeem us from all iniquity”—that is, from all actual and original sins. Let those who exalt themselves on account of their own merits hear this: Christ died for the impious in order to free us from all iniquity.

“And cleanse for himself an acceptable people, a follower of good works.” The people acceptable to God are followers of good works, who do not exalt themselves because of their good works, but, because they do what is good, glory in the Lord and not in themselves.

“Speak these things, exhort, and rebuke with all authority.” He recommends not authority of power, but authority of life. For one teaches with all authority when one first does what one says. Conscience impedes the tongue and removes confidence from teaching. He therefore did not instill in him the power of elevated speech, but confidence in good action. Hence it is also written of the Lord: “For he was teaching as one having authority” (Matt. VII, 29; Mark I, 22; Luke IV, 32), not as the scribes and Pharisees. For He alone, uniquely and principally, spoke with good authority, because through weakness He committed no evil [Col. 0713C]. By the power of His divinity He possessed what He bestowed upon us through the innocence of His humility.

We, who are weak human beings, when we speak to human beings about God, ought first to remember what we are, so that from our own weakness we may consider in what manner of teaching we should care for our weak brothers. Let us therefore consider whether we are such as those whom we correct, or whether we were once such; and if, through the operation of divine grace, we are no longer such, let us correct with humility of heart all the more gently, insofar as we recognize ourselves in those whom we correct. But if we are neither such nor have ever been such as those whom we still wish to correct, let us, lest our heart become proud and fall more grievously because of that very innocence, bring before our eyes some of their other good qualities while correcting their faults.

We must also consider how we speak. Often words that bring one person back to salvation wound another. Hence the Apostle Paul, who admonishes Titus by saying, “Rebuke with all authority,” exhorts Timothy by saying, “Rebuke, entreat, rebuke in all patience and doctrine” (II Tim. IV, 2). Why does he command authority for one and patience for the other, unless he perceived one to be of a gentler spirit and the other of a more fervent one? Severity of speech had to be enjoined upon the gentle person through the authority of command; but the one who burned with fervor had to be tempered by patience, lest, if he became more ardent than was proper, he should not bring the wounded back to salvation but wound the healthy.

We must also take care how much we speak, lest, if we prolong a word of exhortation or rebuke to someone unable to bear much, we lead our hearer to disgust.

[Note: [Col. 0713D] “Ih.”] “Let no one despise you.” I do not want you to present yourself in such a way that anyone could rightly despise you. Thus what is now said to Titus has this meaning: no one among those in the Church should live in such a way, while you act sluggishly, that he thinks himself better than you. For what sort of edification will a disciple have if he understands that he is greater than his teacher? Hence not only bishops, presbyters, and deacons must take the greatest care to precede the whole people over whom they preside in conduct and speech, but also those of lower rank—exorcists, readers, church attendants, and all who serve the house of God. For it greatly destroys the Church of Christ when laypeople are better than clerics.

**(CHAPTER III.)** “Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities.” Since he had said, “Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities,” an opportunity for denial could be given to those who fear torments, if, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement, they claimed that they were subject to rulers and authorities and would do whatever they commanded. Therefore he added:

“To obey commands, to be ready for every good work.” They are to obey for every good work: if what the emperor or governor commands is good, let them comply with the will of the one commanding; but if it is evil and contrary to God [Col. 0714C], let them answer with what is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts V, 29). Let us understand the same concerning slaves in relation to their masters, wives in relation to their husbands, and children in relation to their parents: they ought to be subject to masters, husbands, and parents only in those things that do not conflict with God’s commands.

What follows, “to be ready,” may be read in two ways: either “to be ready for every good work” is understood; or this phrase is joined to what precedes, so that “to obey for every good work” ends there, as though “to be ready” were another distinct and special command, according to what is written in Leviticus: “The goat that is sent away, bearing the people’s curse, shall be handed over to the hand of a ready man” (Lev. XVI, 21).

[Col. 0714D] “To blaspheme no one” [Note: [Col. 0714D] “Añ.”]—that is, not even those who deserve to be blasphemed, but rather to fulfill what the same Apostle commands elsewhere, saying: “Bless those who persecute you; bless, and do not curse” (Rom. XII, 14).

“Not quarrelsome, but gentle.” A quarrelsome person, by returning evil for evil, does not extinguish but provokes strife. A gentle person is one who remains mild and tranquil amid injuries, and not only does not return evil for evil but also returns good for evil.

“Toward all people.” Not only toward the good but also toward the evil, so that he strives to conquer the evil by goodness.

[Col. 0715A] “For we too were once foolish and unbelieving.” So that they would not despair of correction, he offers his own example: “We too,” he says, “were such; therefore we ought to bear patiently with the folly of those who are such.” It should also be noted what sort of people Christ found us, and what sort He made us, so that we do not presume upon our merits or glory in the goodness of nature.

“Going astray, serving various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another.” Behold what we were before grace, through the freedom of free choice. Some understand this passage differently, thinking that it was not spoken about Paul and the apostles, but about others under the persona of the apostles: just as, under his own persona and that of Apollo and Cephas, he spoke about the dissension and schism with which he reproved the Corinthians (I Cor. I), so also in the present passage, naming himself and the apostles, he showed what all who believed in Christ had been before the regeneration of the life-giving washing.

At the same time, his humility is admirable: he rightly remembered that he had served all vices without Christ, having despised, as refuse and filth, all the humility and righteousness of the Law.

“But when the kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared: not from works of righteousness that we had done” [Note: [Col. 0715D] “Añ.”]. What works of righteousness did we Jews do—how much less the Gentiles, who served wood and stone? It should be noted that the Apostle says He saved us not from works of righteousness, because we were saved through no merits of ours, but solely through the mercy of the Redeemer. [Col. 0715C] Let those who overthrow free choice rather than defend it be silent.

“According to his mercy he saved us.” According to His mercy, which both precedes us by inspiring us in every good work and follows us by assisting us—not according to our diligence or labor.

“Through the washing of regeneration.” Through that regeneration of which the Lord says: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John III, 3).

“And renewal of the Holy Spirit,” of which the Apostle says elsewhere: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who was created according to God” (Eph. IV, 23). This renewal does not take place in a single moment, as the remission of all sins takes place in a single moment in baptism.

“Whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior.” The name “pouring out” signifies the abundance of graces among the heirs of the New Testament, greater than among the earlier righteous.

[Note: [Col. 0715D] “Ih.”] Let us attend more carefully, and we shall find in this chapter the most manifest Trinity. The kindness and mercy of God our Savior—of no one other than God the Father—through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom He poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, justified us for eternal life. The salvation of believers is the mystery of the Trinity.

[Note: [Col. 0715D] “Añ.”] “So that, having been justified by his grace.” It must be observed that we are justified by His grace, not by our merits.

“That we might be heirs according to the hope of eternal life. Heirs indeed of God, and fellow heirs of Christ” (Rom. VIII, 17). It should be noted that we are justified, or made heirs of eternal life, according to God’s grace, not according to carnal inheritance, as the Jews assert, nor according to our merits, which we did not previously possess as good ones, as the Pelagians arrogantly claim.

[Col. 0716B] “The saying is trustworthy; and concerning these things I want you to insist, so that those who have believed in God may be careful to excel in good works. These things are good and useful to people” [Note: [Col. 0716D] “Ih.”]. What he says, “The saying is trustworthy,” is to be joined to what precedes, where he had stated: “So that, having been justified by his grace, we may become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.” The saying concerning the inheritance of God and the hope of eternal life is worthy of faith [Note: [Col. 0716D] The words “The saying … eternal life” appear at the bottom of the margin.]. Therefore one ought to believe it without doubt or fear and to insist that others believe it as well. Not only this, but this too must be affirmed along with the rest to those who wish to believe. Therefore he says: “And concerning these things I want you to insist.” Those who have believed these things to be true must necessarily take care to excel in good works, through which the inheritance of God and the hope of eternal life are prepared.

“But avoid foolish questions, genealogies, contentions, and disputes about the Law, for they are useless and vain.” When he says, “Avoid genealogies, contentions, and quarrels that arise from the Law,” he particularly strikes at the Jews, who boast and think that they possess knowledge of the Law if they retain the names of individuals. Since these names are foreign, and we do not know their etymologies, we often pronounce them incorrectly. And if we happen to err in accent, in the length or shortness of a syllable, either lengthening short syllables or shortening long ones, they customarily mock our ignorance, especially in aspirates and in pronouncing certain letters with a scraping of the tongue.

[Col. 0716D] “Avoid a heretical person after one and a second admonition, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment.” In the codices one reads—and Pope Athanasius too approved this as correct—“after one and another admonition.” This means that it is not enough to rebuke or admonish only once someone who has been corrupted by some error; a second instruction must also be given, and every word must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.

But why he is to be avoided after the first and second admonition, he explains by saying: “Because such a person is perverted and sins, being condemned by himself.” For someone who, after being rebuked once and twice and hearing his error, does not wish to be corrected considers the person correcting him to be in error; and, on the other hand, preparing himself for verbal disputes and quarrels, he wishes to win over the person by whom he is being taught.

He is said to be condemned by himself because fornicators, adulterers, murderers, and those guilty of other vices are expelled from the Church by priests; but heretics pronounce sentence upon themselves, withdrawing from the Church by their own choice. This withdrawal appears to be a condemnation by their own conscience. They think that the difference between heresy and schism is that heresy possesses a perverse doctrine, while schism separates itself from the Church because of disagreement with the bishop; this can indeed be understood to some extent at the beginning. But in fact no schism fails to invent some heresy for itself, so that it may appear to have withdrawn from the Church rightly.

“When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, hasten to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to winter there.” Since, after the foundations of other churches had been laid, Titus was necessary to build the structure upon them, Paul writes to him that, once he had sent Artemas or Tychicus—one of the two who had been with him—to Crete to fill his place, Titus himself should come to Nicopolis, declaring that he intended to winter there. From this we may recognize Paul’s fatherly affection for the Cretans. He needs Titus for the ministry of the Gospel, yet he does not want him to come to him before Artemas or Tychicus, his successor, has arrived in his place. Nicopolis is the city that received its name because of Augustus’s victory, since he defeated Antony and Cleopatra there.

“Diligently send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way, so that they may lack nothing.” This is the Apollos about whom it is also written to the Corinthians: “Each of you says, ‘I am of Paul,’ ‘I of Apollos,’ ‘I of Cephas’” (I Cor. I, 12). He was an Alexandrian man of Jewish origin, very eloquent and accomplished in the Law, and bishop of the Corinthians. Because of the dissensions that existed in Corinth, he should be thought to have crossed over with Zenas, a teacher of the Law, to the nearby island of Crete; and, after Paul’s Letter had calmed the dissensions that had arisen at Corinth, to have returned again to Corinth.

Who Zenas, the teacher of the Law, was, we cannot say from any other passage of Scripture, except that he too was an apostolic man and had undertaken the work that Apollos carried out: building up the churches of Christ. He therefore commands Titus, since they were going to sail from Crete to Greece, not to let them be in need of provisions, but to ensure that they had what was necessary for the journey.

“But let our people also learn to excel in good works for necessary uses, so that they may not be unfruitful.” Above he had said: “Diligently send Zenas the teacher of the Law and Apollos on their way, so that they may lack nothing.” Since an unspoken objection could arise—so that Titus, or anyone reading the Letter, might say, “From where should Titus give provisions to those who have none?”—he resolves this question and, as though no objection had been made, removes it by saying: “But let our people also learn to take the lead in good works for necessary needs, so that they may not be unfruitful.”

He calls “our people” his own people [Note: [Col. 0717] In the autograph it reads “uses,” but we have determined that “their own,” following Saint Jerome, should be read.], those who have believed in Christ. Since they belonged to Christ, they rightly deserved to be called Paul’s and Titus’s as well. “You have authority,” he says, “over the disciples: teach them not to be unfruitful, but to minister to evangelists and apostolic men who serve through good works; and to minister not in just any matters, but in those that are necessary.” “Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content” (I Tim. VI, 8); and “those who serve the altar live from the altar” (I Cor. IX, 13). Those who have become participants in our spiritual things ought to share their material things with us. And lest they perhaps easily disregard either Paul’s Letter or Titus’s command, he calls all who have not ministered to evangelists unfruitful.

“All those who are with me greet you.” Either he followed his customary practice of saying that Titus was greeted by everyone who was with him, or else he was speaking specifically about Titus, because he was such a man that he deserved the love of all who were with Paul. It is indeed great praise for Titus that he was greeted by all through Paul.

“Greet those who love us in the faith.” If everyone who loves did so in the faith, and there were no others who loved without faith, Paul would never have added faith to love by saying, “Greet those who love us in the faith.” Mothers also love their children, so that they are ready to die for them, but they do not love them in the faith. Wives also love their husbands, and very often die with them, but that love is not the love of faith.

Only the love of the saints loves in the faith, to such an extent that even if the person who is loved is an unbeliever, the saint nevertheless loves him in the faith, according to what is said: “Let everything of yours be done in faith [love]” (I Cor. XVI, 14). And elsewhere: “Love your enemies” (Luke VI, 35). The saint loves his enemies, and therefore loves them in the faith, because he believes in the One who promised that He would reward the fulfillment of the commandment.

“God’s grace be with all. Amen.” It should be known that in the Greek codices it is written, “Grace be with all of you,” so that neither “of the Lord” nor “of our Lord” is found in the authentic books. Thus he invokes grace collectively upon the saints and believers, Titus and the others who were with him. And just as the patriarch Isaac blessed his son Jacob (Gen. XXVII, 27–29), and Jacob himself blessed the twelve patriarchs (Gen. XLIX, 1–28), so the Apostles, when they entered a house, used to say: “Peace to this house” (Matt. X, 15). If the house was worthy, their peace rested upon it; but if it showed itself unworthy, the peace returned to those who had invoked it. So now, at the end of his Letter, the Apostle invokes grace upon the believers [Col. 0719A]; though offered as a prayer, it took effect, and this lay in the believers’ power, if the person blessed wished to show himself such as the person blessing him wished.

[Col. 0720A] The Letter to Titus ends, written from Nicopolis. It contains 117 verses.

# THE LETTER TO PHILEMON BEGINS

[Col. 0719]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0719B]

He writes Philemon a familiar letter on behalf of his slave Onesimus. He wrote to him from the city of Rome, from prison; and this is its beginning:

[THE TEXT BEGINS.]

“Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ.”

In no Epistle did he use this designation, although in the body of his Epistles—namely, those to the Ephesians, Philippians, and Colossians—he testifies that he is in chains for his confession. Yet it seems to me a mark of greater boldness to call himself “a prisoner of Jesus Christ” than “an apostle.” For the apostles gloried that “they were deemed worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41); but the authority of bonds was necessary. Since he was about to make a request for Onesimus, the one asking had to be such as could obtain what he sought. Truly blessed is the one who glories not in wisdom, riches, eloquence, or worldly power, but in the sufferings of Christ. Yet not everyone who is imprisoned is a prisoner of Christ; rather, whoever is bound for the name of Christ and for confessing him is truly called a prisoner of Jesus Christ. And the blood poured out makes a martyr only when it is shed for the name of Christ.

“And Timothy, a brother.” This is included so that we may know that this letter too was dictated from prison and amid chains, where Timothy always remained with him, at the time when the Epistles to the Philippians, Colossians, and Ephesians appear to have been dictated.

“To Philemon, beloved and our fellow worker, and to Appia, a most beloved sister.” Paul and Timothy therefore write to Philemon, most beloved and a fellow worker, who is called most beloved because he is engaged in the same work of Christ. They write also to Appia, a sister, who is believed to have been either his sister or his wife. Between two men—both apostolic men, between Paul’s fellow worker and his fellow soldier—the name of Appia is inserted, so that, supported by such companionship on either side, she may seem to possess not the rank of her sex but that of her merit.

“And to Archippus, our fellow soldier.” We should suppose that this Archippus fought alongside Paul and Timothy against the adversaries for the name of Christ and emerged victorious. For this reason he is now called a fellow soldier: he had prevailed in the same contest and warfare.

“And to the church which is in your house.” He writes to the church that is in his house. Yet it is ambiguous whether this means the church in the house of Archippus or that in the house of Philemon. But, as is more likely, it is thought to refer not to Archippus but to Philemon, to whom the Epistle itself is also addressed.

“Grace to you and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.” He is still writing from two persons to several; and in nearly all the Epistles the opening is the same, invoking grace and peace upon them from God the Father and from Christ the Lord. From this it is shown that the Son and the Father have one nature, since the Son can bestow what the Father can, and what the Son bestows is said to be bestowed by the Father. “Grace” is mentioned because we are saved by no merit or work of our own. “Peace” is that by which we have been reconciled to God through Christ. Although Paul and Timothy write jointly to Philemon, Appia, and Archippus, what follows shows that Paul alone writes to Philemon and converses with him alone.

“I give thanks to my God, always making remembrance of you in my prayers.” Here he no longer speaks as Paul and Timothy to Philemon and the others, but Paul alone speaks to Philemon alone. We can find this manner of writing in his other Epistles as well: although several persons are mentioned in the preface when the letter is addressed to several, afterward one speaker is introduced throughout the body of the Epistle.

When he says, “I give thanks to my God, and always make remembrance of you in my prayers,” it is ambiguous whether he means that he always gives thanks to God, or that he always makes remembrance of him in his prayers. Yet both meanings can be understood. The one who instructed others to give thanks to God in all things could not be constrained by any distress so that he himself failed always to give thanks to God. If Paul always prayed for the saints and for those who were especially worthy—and Philemon too is a saint, possessing such faith and love in himself that he was known not merely by report but also by his deeds—it is credible that Paul always prayed for Philemon, so that the faith and love he possessed in Christ and toward all Christ’s saints might, through the sharing of faith and the working of the knowledge of every good thing, be preserved by Christ’s mercy.

“Hearing of your love and the faith which you have in the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints.” It is not difficult to interpret the statement that Philemon had love in the Lord, since after God we are commanded to love our neighbors. Nor should we think that faith and love toward God and his saints are sufficient for us unless what we believe is completed in action.

“So that the sharing of your faith may become evident in the knowledge of every good thing in Christ Jesus.” By how many stages and advances the apostolic discourse rises toward higher things! Whatever good is praised in Philemon is taken from the example of the apostles, and is good for this reason: because it is drawn from Christ’s fountain.

“For I have had great joy and consolation in your love, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you, brother.” He explains more fully and teaches why he said, “I give thanks to my God, always making remembrance of you in my prayers.” It was indeed fitting always to give thanks to God for Philemon’s love, since by receiving the saints’ inward affection and the deepest recesses of their hearts he had refreshed them.

“Therefore, having great confidence in Christ Jesus to command you what is fitting, and because of love I rather appeal to you—being such a one as Paul, an old man, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.” After first praising Philemon with many commendations, Paul could, given the nature of the matter for which he was about to ask—a matter useful to the one for whom it was requested and to the one making the request—have commanded rather than asked. This confidence arose from the fact that one who had accomplished such great works for Christ could not be unequal to himself in other matters. Yet he wishes rather to ask than to command, presenting the petitioner’s great authority, by which the Apostle appeals as an old man and a prisoner of Jesus Christ.

Everything for which he asks is this: Onesimus, Philemon’s slave, having compounded flight with theft, had plundered some of his master’s household property. Going to Italy so that he might not easily be apprehended in the vicinity, he had squandered his master’s money in extravagance. Let no one think that we have invented this rashly or arbitrarily; he will learn it from what follows. Paul would never have said, “If he has wronged you or owes you anything, charge it to me. I, Paul, have written this with my own hand; I will repay it,” nor would he have become surety for property that had been taken unless what had been taken had been squandered.

Thus, while Paul was imprisoned at Rome for confessing Christ, Onesimus believed in the Lord Jesus and was baptized by him. Through worthy repentance he wiped away the stains of his former life, so completely that the Apostle became a witness to his conversion—the same Apostle who had once rebuked Peter for not walking with a straight step in the truth of the Gospel (Gal. 2:11). Therefore, insofar as the sin and crime by which he had injured human beings are concerned, he does not deserve pardon. But insofar as the testimony of the Apostle is concerned—who knows that he has been fully converted—the one who is asked is weighed down by a great obligation, since the former fugitive and thief had become the Apostle’s minister. (What other ministry did the Apostle have than that of the Gospel of Christ Jesus?) Therefore, as a fellow servant and fellow evangelist, not as though from the Lord but as from a fellow servant, he should be forgiven, since Onesimus was likewise a servant of Christ and a minister.

“I appeal to you for my son, whom I have begotten in chains, Onesimus.” Wishing to obtain what he asks, he now asserts that he is pleading not for Philemon’s slave but for his own son—and for that son whom he begot in the chains of the Gospel, that is, in the sufferings he endured for Christ’s Gospel.

“Who was once useless to you.” “To you alone,” he says, “not to others.” Now, on the contrary, by the comparison of his usefulness—since he is useful both to his master himself and to Paul, and through Paul to others—he deserves more love than he had previously deserved hatred. Hence he says:

“But now he is useful both to you and to me.” He is useful to his master because he could serve Paul on behalf of his own master; he is useful to Paul because, while Paul was detained in prison and in chains, Onesimus could minister in the Gospel as well.

“But receive him—that is, receive my own heart.” “Heart” signifies inward affection and a complete willingness from the soul, when everything that is within us is received by the person being entreated. In another sense, all children are to be understood as the hearts of their parents.

“Whom I wished to keep with me, so that he might minister to me in the chains of the Gospel.” He repeatedly emphasizes and reiterates that Onesimus is his son, the son of his chains, and the minister of the Gospel while he is in chains, so that Philemon—wisely and deliberately praised so highly in the preface—would not dare to refuse, lest he appear unworthy of his own praises.

“But without your counsel I wanted to do nothing, so that your good might not be as though compelled, but voluntary.” The Apostle Paul could therefore have kept Onesimus for his ministry without Philemon’s consent. But if he had done this without Philemon’s will, the act would indeed have been good, but it would not have been voluntary. What is not voluntary was, in another respect, judged not to be good. For nothing can be called good unless it is freely undertaken. Here we must consider the Apostle’s prudence: he sends the fugitive slave back to his master so that he might benefit his master, which he could not do if he were kept away from him.

“Perhaps for this reason he departed.” By adding “perhaps,” he beautifully tempered the statement. God’s judgments are hidden, and it is rash to pronounce as certain what is doubtful. “Perhaps,” he says, “for this reason he departed”—cautiously, hesitantly, tremblingly, and without taking an entirely firm step. Otherwise, if he had not inserted “perhaps,” all slaves would have been obliged to flee so that they might become the apostles’ disciples.

“For a time from you.” Since he joined the words “for a time,” we should understand “time” as a period. In comparison with eternity, every period of time is brief.

“So that you might receive him forever, no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother.” No master is eternal to his slave. His power, and the condition of both, end in death. Onesimus, however, who through the faith of Christ has become eternal, became a brother to the eternal Philemon—who himself had believed in Christ—after receiving the spirit of freedom. He was no longer a slave but a brother: from a slave, a most beloved brother; an eternal brother to the Apostle, who was himself eternal, and to his master, to whom Onesimus was afterward joined much more closely in spirit than his former condition according to the flesh had joined him.

At that time, when he was subject to him in the flesh, he was not joined to him in the Lord. Now, however, he is joined to him both in the flesh and in the Lord. From this we understand that a slave who believes in Christ is bound to his twofold master by a twofold law: for a time he is joined to him by the necessity of the flesh, and forever he is united to him in spirit.

“Therefore, if you consider me your partner, receive him as you would me.” He means: If you wish to have me as your partner, have Onesimus also, whom I regard as my associate, my son, and my own heart. If you are unwilling to receive him or to have him, you yourself understand that you cannot have me either.

“But if he has wronged you or owes you anything, charge it to me.” As an imitator of his Lord, with Christ speaking within him, Paul ought to do, according to his strength, what Christ did. For if Christ bore our weaknesses and grieved over our wounds, the Apostle rightly takes his stand for Onesimus and guarantees what he owes. As we said above, the whole matter concerns what had been taken by theft and lost through extravagance, which could not be absolved except by compensation. Philemon made that compensation at great cost when, in exchange for a fugitive slave and lost money, he received a most beloved brother and an eternal brother, and through him made the Apostle his debtor.

“I, Paul, have written this with my own hand; I will repay it.” Whatever Onesimus seized by theft, I guarantee that I will repay. This Epistle and my own hand are witnesses to the guarantee. I did not dictate it in my usual manner but wrote it out myself.

“I will not say to you that you owe me even your own self.” Because of the word of Christ that I preached to you, through which you became a Christian, you owe your very self to me. If you are mine, and everything that is yours is mine, then Onesimus too, who is yours, is mine. I could therefore treat him as my own; but I leave the matter to your will, so that you may have the reward of forgiving him.

“Yes, brother, may I enjoy you in the Lord.” If he had not added “in the Lord,” but had said only, “May I enjoy you,” he would have placed the hope of his blessedness in him, although even in ordinary speech “to enjoy” is used of taking delight in someone whom one loves. When the beloved is present, delight necessarily accompanies that presence.
