If you pass through that delight and refer it to the place where one ought to remain, you make use of it and are said, improperly and abusively, to enjoy it. But if you cling to it and remain in it, placing the end of your joy in it, then you are truly and properly said to enjoy it. This must be done only in the Trinity, that is, in the supreme and unchangeable good.

[Note: [Col. 0723D] “Ih.”]

“Refresh my heart in Christ.” Just as he wishes to enjoy Philemon in the Lord, so he wishes his own heart—Onesimus, whom he also called by this name above—to be refreshed through Philemon.

“Trusting in your obedience, I have written to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say.” The person who presumes upon the one whom he is about to ask in a certain way prejudges the matter, so that the one asked will not be permitted to refuse what is requested. Moreover, if the petitioner knows that the person asked will do more than he has requested, he asks for less so that the one asked may have a voluntary reward greater than the request itself. If Philemon does these things in response to a human command, how much more will he do them out of love for God! Therefore he is rightly praised by the Apostle’s voice because he fulfilled his commands in action.

“At the same time, prepare a lodging for me as well.” He says this so that, while Philemon awaits his coming, he may be more inclined to do what has been requested. Paul knew that, when he came to a new city to preach the crucified Christ and to bring unheard-of teachings, very many people would flock to him. It was therefore necessary that the house be in a prominent part of the city, where people could easily gather. It should also be free from every nuisance and spacious enough to accommodate many listeners; it should not be near places of public spectacle, lest its proximity be disgraceful; finally, it should be situated on level ground rather than in an upper room. For this reason I think that Paul also remained for two years in Rome in a rented dwelling. Nor, I believe, was the lodging small, since crowds of Jews gathered there every day.

“For I hope that through your prayers I shall be granted to you.” God grants a son to his father when asked, and a brother is often preserved through a brother’s prayer. The Apostle, however, is granted to the prayers of the whole Church for the benefit of those who are about to hear him. This gift is said to concern not so much the one who is delayed—prepared as he is from martyrdom for martyrdom—as those to whom the Apostle is sent.

That Paul was often in prison and was released from his chains, he himself says elsewhere: “In prisons frequently” (2 Cor. 11:23). Sometimes, by the Lord’s help, he was released because the persecutors themselves found no cause worthy of death in him. Nero’s sword had not yet consecrated Christian blood. But because of the novelty of his preaching—whether through envious Jews or through those who saw their idols being destroyed—when the crowds had been stirred to madness, Paul and his companions were sent to prison, and then, once the violence and fury had subsided, they were released.

The Acts of the Apostles testify that this happened as we say. There Agrippa says to Festus that Paul could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:32). No cause had been found against him except certain questions concerning their own religion and a certain Jesus whom Paul asserted to be alive. From this we understand that Paul could likewise have been released by the other judges, with the Lord arranging matters so that the new preaching might be spread throughout the whole world.

“Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you; so do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers.” What we said at the beginning—that the Epistle to the Colossians was written at the same time and carried by the same letter-bearer as the Epistle to Philemon—is also taught by the names of those who are greeted. For in that Epistle too it is written: “Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you, and Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, and Epaphras, who is from among you, a servant of Christ” (Col. 4:10). A little farther on: “Luke the most beloved physician greets you, and Demas; and say to Archippus: See to the ministry which you have received in the Lord, so that you may fulfill it. And remember my chains.”

If anyone does not think that the two Epistles were written at the same time because the Epistle to the Colossians contains several names that are not listed here, let him know that not everyone is a friend or acquaintance of everyone else, and that a private letter to one person differs from a public letter to the whole Church.

Who Epaphras, Paul’s fellow prisoner, was may be conjectured from the addition here of the words “in Christ Jesus”: perhaps he endured at Rome the same chains for Christ as Paul did, and, being a prisoner of Christ, could also be called Christ’s fellow captive. Or perhaps the meaning is that he too was distinguished among the apostles, like Andronicus and Junia, of whom Paul writes to the Romans: “Greet Andronicus and Junia, my relatives and fellow prisoners, who are distinguished among the apostles and who were in Christ before me” (Rom. 16:7).

This is what concerns Epaphras. As for the fellow workers in the Gospel and in his chains, when writing the Epistle to Philemon Paul mentions Mark, whom I think to be the writer of the Gospel [Note: These words are Jerome’s. See, however, what we have noted on Colossians concerning this Mark—or John Mark—as another person than the evangelist.]; Aristarchus, whom we mentioned above; Demas, of whom he says elsewhere, “Demas has deserted me” (2 Tim. 4:10); and Luke the physician, who handed on the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles to the churches in writing.

For just as the apostles, from fishermen of fish, became fishers of human beings, so Luke was transformed from a physician of bodies into a physician of souls. Of him he says elsewhere: “I sent with him the brother whose praise in the Gospel is throughout all the churches” (2 Cor. 8:18). Whenever his book is read in the Church, his healing does not cease.

“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.” When divine grace is in the spirit, it makes the whole person spiritual, so that he clings to the Lord in mind and body, and what is written may be fulfilled in him: “The one who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17).

According to the Hebrews, Paul is interpreted as “admirable”; Timothy, “beneficent”; Philemon, “wonderfully gifted,” or “mouth of bread,” from *os* (“mouth”), not from *os* (“bone”); Appia, “self-controlled,” or “freedom”; Archippus, “length of work”; Onesimus, “answering”; Epaphras, “fruitful,” and “seeing,” or “growing”; Mark, “exalted by command”; Aristarchus, “a mountain of greater work”; Demas, “silent”; Luke, “himself rising.”

If we wish to understand all these names according to their interpretations, it is not difficult to see that he writes especially to the admirable and beneficent one, to whom all things have been granted and whose mouth is open toward the heavenly bread. Then he writes to the self-controlled and free woman, and to the one characterized by length of work, who never ceases from holy labor. He writes on behalf of the one who answers to his testimony, and to the one to whom the Epistle is especially dedicated, greeted by the abundance of one who is continually increasing. He writes also to the one who has been exalted through commands, and to the one who has grown through greater works even as far as a mountain; and to the one who has set a guard over his mouth and fortified his lips with a door—who perhaps remained silent because he had abandoned the Apostle for a short time. Finally, he writes to the one who, rising by his own power, increases daily and makes progress as his Gospel fills the world, growing as often as it is heard or read.

[Col. 0726C] The Epistle to Philemon, written from Rome, ends here. It contains 34 verses.

# THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS

[Col. 0725]

## THE CHAPTER SUMMARY OF THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS BEGINS

[Col. 0725D]

1. That in the last days the Father spoke in the Son, who is the radiance and representation of his substance and sat at the right hand, having become superior to the angels.

2. That we must heed what we have heard, lest perhaps we drift away; and that Jesus was made a little lower than the angels; and that he is not ashamed to call them brothers, so that through death he might destroy the devil and become a faithful high priest.

3. That we should consider the Apostle and High Priest Jesus, who is faithful, as Moses was in the house; and, “Today, if you hear his voice”; and that we should fear lest, by provoking him, we fail to enter into rest.

4. Concerning the Sabbath rest; and that he again establishes a day; and that the word of God is living; and that Jesus the great High Priest has had compassion on us.

5. Concerning Melchizedek; that solid food belongs to the mature; that it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened to be renewed; and concerning the earth that drinks in the rain falling upon it.

6. Concerning the Hebrews, that they ministered to the saints; and concerning the oath, by which we have an anchor; and concerning Melchizedek, where he met Abraham; according to whose priesthood Jesus, innocent and undefiled, remains forever.

7. That the law brought nothing to perfection; and concerning the true tabernacle; and concerning the statement, “Behold, the days are coming.”

8. Concerning the tabernacle and the things that were in it; and that it is not the blood of goats but the blood of Jesus that cleanses believers, and that without blood there is no remission.

9. That Jesus will not enter into things made by hands but into heaven, at the consummation of the ages; and that under the legal sacrifices there was a remembrance, not a cleansing, of sins; and concerning the statement, “You did not desire sacrifice and offering.”

10. That the flesh of Christ is a veil; and concerning baptism; and that for those who sin voluntarily and trample upon the Son of God there will be a fearful expectation of judgment; and concerning the Hebrews, who had compassion on prisoners; and that patience is necessary until the one who is to come arrives.

[Col. 0727A]

11. Concerning the faith of the saints who were pilgrims on earth and awaited a city.

12. Concerning the tribulations and deaths of the saints, whose patience we ought to imitate; and that, looking upon the passion of Jesus, we should persevere in discipline as sons.

13. That we should raise up our weakened hands, pursuing peace and holiness; and concerning Esau; and that we have approached not a blazing mountain but Zion; and that we should not disregard the one who speaks from heaven.

14. That we should receive an unshakable kingdom, because God is a consuming fire; and concerning love, hospitality, and an undefiled marriage bed; and concerning leaders; and concerning Jesus Christ, yesterday and today; and concerning foods that are of no benefit.

15. Concerning the altar that we have; and that Jesus suffered outside the camp; and concerning leaders.

## INTRODUCTION TO THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS

[Col. 0727]

[Col. 0727A] The Hebrews were called by the proper name of their race: those who had believed in Christ from among the Jews. Their churches had been founded by the Apostle throughout Judea. Concerning them this same Paul, writing to the Galatians, says: “I was personally unknown to the churches of Judea that are in Christ” (Gal. 1:22).

These people, terrified by the exceedingly bitter persecution of the other Jews who had not received Christ, were in haste abandoning the Christian religion handed down to them by the apostles. The Apostle Paul, strengthening them by his exhortation, recalls them to their former faith. He writes to them from Italy through Timothy. For this reason he did not place in this Epistle the usual preface concerning his name: he himself had been sent especially to the Gentiles, whereas the other apostles had been sent to the Jews.

## THE PROLOGUE TO THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS BEGINS

[Col. 0727]

[Col. 0727B] First of all, it must be said why the Apostle Paul, in this Epistle that he wrote to the Jews—whom he wished to call Hebrews rather than Israelites—did not follow his customary practice of writing either his name or the dignity of his office. The reason is that he writes to those who had believed from the circumcision, as the Apostle of the Gentiles and not of the Hebrews.

Knowing their pride, and demonstrating his own humility, he did not wish to place the merit of his office first. Since among the Hebrew churches he was regarded, under a false suspicion, as a destroyer of the law, he wished, under an unnamed identity, to explain the figures of the law and the truth of Christ, lest hatred of his name, because of the prominent title placed at the beginning, exclude the benefit of the reading.

Others understand it this way: Paul did not place either his name or the title “apostle” at the beginning in his customary manner because he was going to speak about Christ, saying: “Since we have Jesus, the High Priest, Priest, and Apostle of our confession.” It would not have been fitting for Paul also to be called an apostle where Christ was to be called the Apostle.

It is said that the Apostle sent this Epistle to the Hebrews written in the Hebrew language. Luke the evangelist, retaining its meaning and arrangement, composed it in Greek after the blessed Apostle’s departure. The whole purpose of the Epistle was to summon the Hebrews—that is, his own people—to faith in Christ and to distinguish the excellence of the grace given through the Son from the shadows of the legal rites, which had appeared to the fathers through angelic ministrations.

Therefore, he first stated that the prophets had spoken to the fathers in various ways, saying:

## CHAPTER 1

“God, who formerly spoke to our fathers in the prophets in many portions and in many ways [Note: [Col. 0727D] The Vulgate does not have ‘our’], in these last days has spoken to us in his Son.”

[Col. 0728B] Writing this at the very beginning to the Hebrews, blessed Paul made a sufficiently good start. By saying “in many portions and in many ways,” he shows that even the prophets did not obtain the grace of seeing God, since none of them saw him as he is, as it is said elsewhere: “I multiplied visions, and in the hand of the prophets I was represented” [Note: [Col. 0728D] The Vulgate reads “assimilated”]. But it is clear that the only-begotten Son has been seen.

Consider this carefully. First, he strives to establish the Son’s superiority through the prophets. Then, as though this had been granted, he argues and declares that God spoke to them through the prophets, and afterward through angels, since angels too spoke to the Jews. It is as though he said: What is so great if he sent prophets to our fathers? To us he sent his own only-begotten Son, and through that only-begotten Son he deigned to speak.

We are superior also in this respect and possess much more, because the Lord himself spoke to us, while to them it was servants and fellow servants—that is, either prophets or angels. By saying “formerly” and “in these last days,” he indicates that, after a long interval had passed in between, when we were already near punishment, when all the gifts had fallen silent, when there was no longer any hope of salvation, and when we were thought to be inferior to everyone, then we proved to be superior.

It should be noted that the preposition “in” can also be understood as “through.” He did not say, “Christ spoke,” although it is clear that he did speak; rather, because the souls of those to whom he was writing were still weak and could not yet fully understand Christ, he said that God spoke to us through his Son. See how he makes this a common cause, joining himself to the apostles on equal terms when he says, “He spoke to us in his Son.” The name “son” is common:

[Col. 0729A] Wherever “proper Son” is understood, he is higher and more excellent: “Whom he appointed heir of all things,” that is, of the whole world. Jacob is no longer merely the Lord’s portion, nor Israel merely his inheritance, but all nations altogether. That is, he appointed his Son, our Lord, heir of all things, just as Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles: “God made him both Lord and Christ” (Acts 2:36).

He uses the name “heir” in order to establish and show that he is the proper Son and that there is no loss of dominion for him. Then he carries the discourse to higher things, saying: “Through whom he also made the ages,” showing that the same one who came into the world in these last days is the one through whom the world was made. He thus displays the greatness of the one who was the bearer and author of the New Testament.

Where now are those who say, “There was a time when he was not”? What the evangelist John says—“All things were made through him” (John 1:3)—this writer signifies by saying, “Through whom he also made the ages.” Thus he too declares that Christ existed before all ages and that he was their creator.

After this, using several elegant stages, he reaches what is much greater than all that he has said above, and sounds forth: “Who is the radiance of glory and the representation of his substance, bearing all things by the word of his power, making purification of sins.”

We understand many true things about God that we are entirely unable to express. We also say many things that we are not capable of understanding. For example, we know that God is everywhere, but we do not grasp intellectually how he is everywhere. Likewise, we know that there is some incorporeal power that is the cause of good things for all, but we utterly do not know what it is or how it is.

Behold, we say something about it, yet we cannot understand it. I have said that it is everywhere, but I do not understand how; I say that it is without beginning, but I do not understand how it is so; I say that it begot the Son from itself, but I do not know how to grasp this intellectually, so that the one begotten is not later than the one who begot him.

There are also things that cannot be said, although they can be grasped by the mind. The mind understands, but it cannot express them. This is especially so when we speak or hear something about God. You can even see Paul himself weakened in the face of certain such matters, unable to explain them fully. For neither is the tongue sufficient to speak, nor is the intellect strong enough to comprehend.

And why do I speak of the tongue or the intellect, when not even the higher part of the mind itself—which is far superior to both—can fully comprehend anything when divinity is being discussed? If the peace of God surpasses every mind (Phil. 4:7), and if the things prepared for those who love him have not entered the human heart (1 Cor. 2:9), then he himself—the God who nourishes [Note: [Col. 0729D] Perhaps “peace” should be read] and who is the creator of all things—far more immeasurably surpasses our thoughts.

Through the radiance of his glory, he declares the essence of his divinity. He also used one thing to demonstrate the three persons, since in fire there are the fire itself, radiance, and heat. Therefore he adds:

“Who is the representation of his substance.” A representation is one thing distinct from the one whose form it declares, but here the distinction concerns not every aspect, only the person. For even here the representation gives a complete indication of equality with that whose representation it is, and certainly admits no suspicion of a corrupt dissimilarity.

He called this a “representation” which elsewhere he calls “form,” when he says: “Who, though he was in the form of God” (Phil. 2:6). “Form” there and “representation” here declare one equality of essence.

“Bearing all things by the word of his power”—that is, governing them. For he holds together things that are falling and tending toward nothingness. It is no lesser thing to sustain the world than to create it. But, if one must speak more boldly, it is even greater. In making, the essences of things were brought forth from things that did not exist; in sustaining, what has been made is held together so that it does not return to nothingness.

While these things are governed and things opposed to one another are fitted together, a great and truly wondrous sign, and an indication of immense power, is displayed. By saying “bearing,” he wished to indicate the ease with which he sustains all things. He did not say “governing,” using the metaphor of those who move or accomplish something with a finger without any labor.

Just as John said, “What was made in him was life” (John 1:3), wishing to distinguish him from all creatures, since it is clear that he himself is the life of all, so he too says, “bearing all things.” He does not speak as the pagans do, who claim that God is deprived of participation in the creation and providence of things. By saying, “by the word of his power,” he signified that he sustains everything without labor.

After such a display of divine majesty in the Son, he now descends to the humility of his incarnation, saying: “Making purification of sins.” After stating those great and exceedingly wondrous things above, he now speaks of the care and concern he exercises for human beings.

Although the former statement is universal, since he sustains all things, this latter is much more universally significant insofar as it concerns all who have believed in him. Hence John also says: “In him was life” (ibid., 4). But, revealing his providence, he says again that he is light: “Through him,” he says, “light.” [The text appears defective here.]

“Making purification of our sins”: in this passage he signifies two things of greater importance—that he cares for us, and that he has cleansed our sins—and also that he accomplished this work through himself. In many passages you will find him glorying especially in this: not merely that we have been converted to God, but also that this was accomplished through the Son.

And truly this is a great gift and an even greater achievement: that it has been bestowed upon us through the Son.

After this, he immediately instructed us concerning his resurrection and ascension, to raise our minds toward heavenly things and contemplate [Col. 0731A] his ineffable glory. Hence he adds: “He sits at the right hand of Majesty on high.” Observe the kinds of names he uses, since he could not find the proper names of realities, nor the proper names of majesty or glory that he desired. As I said above, certain things often present themselves to us which we indeed understand but cannot express. For as yet no term has been established that indicates the essence itself, nor can any proper term be found for it. And why should it be surprising that this is so with God, when you will not even find a proper name for an angel that declares his essence? I believe, moreover, that no suitable designation has been found for the soul either. For it does not seem to me that this name fully displays its substance; indeed, you will find the same reality called both soul, heart, [Col. 0731B] and mind. “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 50:12). You will also frequently find it called “spirit.” Here, then, “right hand” signifies honor, not that God is to be believed corporeal. For the Father too is written to be at Christ’s right hand: “The Lord,” he says, “at your right hand will shatter [Note: [Col. 0731D] The Vulgate has ‘shattered.’] kings on the day of his wrath” (Psalm 109:5). Both, therefore, are at the right hand, because there is nothing left-handed in the Divinity, since the human being who was raised has now been taken up and is one with God [Note: [Col. 0731] The words “in … is” appear in the upper margin.].

What does “on high” mean? Does it confine God to a higher place? Far from it. But, as I have already said, by “right hand” he did not deform God but demonstrated a likeness of honor. Therefore, by saying “on high,” he does not confine him to a place, but shows him to be higher and more exalted than all [Col. 0731C]—that is, that he has reached the very throne of the Father’s glory. Therefore, just as the Father is on high, so also is the Son. For the sitting together—that is, the seat of both Persons—indicates nothing other than equality of honor. And he proceeds to show the same Son’s excellence when he says: “Having become so much superior to the angels, as he has inherited a name more distinguished than theirs.” In what he said, “having become,” we must understand “having become” as “having been assumed,” as though he were saying: “He has been assumed in a manner superior to the angels.” And on what basis does he assert this? From the name itself. You notice that the name “Son” customarily discloses its proper character. Indeed, unless he were the proper Son—that is, one begotten from the Father himself—how could you establish the greatness of his honor from this? [Col. 0731D] For if the Son were so by grace, he would differ not only from the Father but would also be lower than the angels. “How do you say this?” he asks. Because righteous human beings too have been called sons of God. Therefore, unless the name “son” indicates its proper character, it cannot show what distinction exists between creatures and the Creator.

“For to which of the angels did he ever say: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’?” (Psalm 2:7.) “To none” is understood. But when he said, “You are my Son,” he makes nothing else manifest except that he was begotten from the very essence of the Father. For this reason he used the present tense, “today,” because for God there is neither past nor future, but everything is always present [Col. 0732A]. This saying can also be understood according to the flesh, because just as flesh shares in higher things, so the divinity graciously consented to share in humble things.

And again: “I will be a Father to him, and he will be a Son to me” (2 Samuel 7:14). This is said without any doubt concerning the Son’s incarnation; for this reason he used the future tense: “I will be a Father to him, and he will be a Son to me.” And he adds: “And again, when he brings the Firstborn into the world, he says: ‘And let all the angels of God worship him’” (Psalm 96:7). “Entering,” therefore, he calls the assumption of flesh. What he calls “entering” here, he called “going out” in the Gospel: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John 16:28). And elsewhere: “The sower went out to sow” (Luke 8:5). Rightly, then, he calls the manifestation of his incarnation a “going out.” We were outside, away from God; for he went out to us—that is, taking flesh, he spoke with us when he gave us commandments, and thus, cleansing us from sins, he turned us toward God. For this reason he calls the coming of his incarnation a “going out,” whereas Paul calls it an “entering.” For by saying, “When he brings the Firstborn into the world,” he means this: when he entrusts the world to him. Understand this as said not of the substance of the Word but of the form of a servant, in which form he is the firstborn among many brothers (Romans 8:29). For if he was in the world, and, according to John (1:10), the world was made through him, in what other way is he brought into it except according to the flesh? Then [Col. 0732C] he possessed the whole world, when he was acknowledged by all.

“And let all the angels of God worship him.” That is, God the Father commanded all the angels to worship Christ according to the flesh. But someone may ask: Were only the angels commanded to worship him? No, but every creature, as Paul himself says elsewhere: “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:10).

“And concerning the angels, indeed, he says: ‘He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flame of fire’” (Psalm 103:4). It is as though he were saying: He gave the one whom he commanded the angels to worship the power that, whenever he wishes, he may make angels from spirits; and his ministers a flame of fire, because he makes those who stand daily in his presence burn and blaze with love for him. It should be understood, however, that “angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature. They are always spirits, but they cannot always be called angels. If you ask for the name of their nature, it is “spirit”; if you ask for the name of their office, it is “angel.” In respect of what he is, he is a spirit; in respect of what he does, he is an angel, because *angelos* is called *nuntius* (“messenger”) in Latin, just as “human being” is the name of a nature, while “soldier” is the name of an office. Thus he makes those who were already created as spirits by God the Creator into angels by sending them to announce what he has commanded.

[Col. 0733A] “But to the Son: ‘Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever’” (Psalm 45:7). Observe how he distinguishes them, and with what clarity he separates creatures from the Son. He would not have called the Son by a more distinguished name if the name had the same meaning. “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever.” Here you have the insignia of kingship. “A scepter of equity,” he says, “is the scepter of your kingdom.” Here you have another insignia. The scepter signifies the rule of divine equity, which is rightly called straight because it is bent by no crookedness. The scepter rules the righteous and strikes the wicked; but this scepter is unconquered strength, the most upright equity, and inflexible discipline. The ancients called this scepter of the kingdom, the emblem of honor, a staff or royal scepter, signifying in it the king of virtues, the Lord and Savior.

[Col. 0733B] “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity.” This is the straight scepter and the dominion of rulers: to love righteousness and hate iniquity. No one perfectly loves righteousness except the one who abhors evil deeds, for whom love of truth is hatred of falsehood.

But what rewards were given for this love of goodness and hatred of iniquity, he explains below, saying: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you.” The repetition in the words “God, God” reveals a proclamation of great love. But how is God, whose throne is for ever and ever, anointed by God—unless he is Christ Jesus, who received the name “Christ” from this very anointing? For *chrisma* means “anointing,” and *Christus* means “anointed.” Christ the Anointed signifies both king and priest, since these dignities were conferred through the most sacred [Col. 0733C] anointings. Indeed, as has already been said, the very name “Christ” is derived from the holy chrism. But he is said to be anointed in that nature in which, through the dispensation of the flesh, Christ is truly said to have been born, to have died, and to have risen again. His divinity, however, had no need of assistance from any gift or honor.

“With the oil of gladness”: he indicates in two ways that this holy anointing came about. It was not visible oil, but the invisible grace of the Holy Spirit, of which the blessed apostle Peter testifies in the Acts of the Apostles (10:38), saying: “Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power.” And in prophecy: “I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him” (Psalm 88:2), signifying the Holy Spirit by “holy oil.” Or the oil of gladness for him was having no stain of sin. Hence the conscience of the saints is always gladdened, since it is not gnawed by any harshness of recollection.

“Beyond your companions.” It is therefore said, “beyond your companions,” because he was portrayed as having received this blessing above the whole human race—whether kings or priests in the Old Testament, or apostles and martyrs in the New—and as having been uniquely anointed so that he might anoint, that is, sanctify, the others. For in him is the fountain of blessing, from which it flows among all the elect as he himself sees fit.

After speaking, then, of the excellence of his humanity, by which he is above the children of God, the apostle again turns to the eternity of divinity in the same Son of God and begins to cite the testimony of another psalm. For he says: “And: ‘You, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth.’” Lest, on hearing “when he brings the Firstborn into the world,” you suppose that the gift was subsequently bestowed upon him, he adds: “And: ‘You, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth’” (Psalm 101:26). You are shown to have existed not now but from the beginning, through the power of divinity, the Creator before creatures, without any beginning.

“And the heavens are the works of your hands.” Here we should understand “hands” as the power of God’s command. For elsewhere he says: “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Psalm 148:5).

“They will perish.” They perish from the state in which they now exist, as creatures are changed for the better. “But you remain.” Just as he showed the Lord’s eternity before he created all things, so after the heavens have been changed he says that he remains in the glory of his majesty. “And all of them will grow old like a garment.” That grows old which, like clothing, is worn away by age, as human flesh is worn away by death—though it will nevertheless be changed for the better in the resurrection. He also adds: “And like a cloak you will change them, and they will be changed.” Just as anyone wraps up and changes a cloak, so he will likewise change the world [Note: [Col. 0733D] The manuscript reads *iñ maturus est*.], and he will be able to effect its condition and transformation into something better as easily as anyone wraps up and changes a cloak.

“But you are the same, and your years will not fail.” For just as he said to Moses, his servant, “I am who I am,” so in these three verses the Prophet has described, with admirable brevity, the transformation of creation and the Lord’s eternity.

After speaking again of the divine majesty’s eternity in the Son, the blessed Paul turned his discourse to the glorification of his humanity, saying: “But to which of the angels did he ever say: ‘Sit at my right hand’?” (Psalm 109:1.) To the victorious Son, and through the holy incarnation the conqueror of the whole world, there is granted, after the glory of the resurrection, the honorable shared seat at the Father’s majesty [Col. 0734D], so that through this position the glory of the humanity he assumed might be declared. “Until I place your enemies.” That the enemies are subjected to the Son by the Father signifies not the Son’s weakness but the unity of nature, whereby one acts in the other. For the Son too subjects enemies to the Father, because he glorifies the Father on earth. “As a footstool for your feet.” By the Lord’s feet eternal stability is signified, where he stands, as though with his footsteps planted, in the full power of all his might. Those are destined to be placed beneath these feet who, daily abandoning the opposition of vices, return to the Lord and, like a footstool beneath the feet, bow before his preaching. [Col. 0735A] Without doubt he speaks of those enemies who, after being converted, are placed at the right hand. Here the adverb “until” does not indicate the certainty [Note: [Col. 0735D] The manuscript reads “the certainty of times.” Perhaps “end,” to which the following eternity refers.] of some period of time, but demonstrates the power of eternity.

“Are they not all ministering spirits sent out for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?” It is as though he were saying: He appointed the angels as ministers, but caused the Son to sit at his right hand, something he never granted to any angel. The Son too was sent, but not as a minister, nor to perform the duties of any office, but as the only-begotten Son. The Son saves as Lord; these, as servants, serve those who are saved through faith. They are plainly made ministers for our salvation, although they are superior to us; nevertheless, they provide service for our salvation. Their function makes this clear, since *angeli* in Greek means “messengers” in Latin. They are sent everywhere on our behalf; they labor on our behalf; they hasten on our behalf; they perform their office for us. The books of the Old and New Testaments are full of examples of these things. Angels proclaimed the Gospel to the shepherds (Luke 2:9); an angel came to Mary (Luke 1:28); and we read many similar accounts in the divine Scriptures. At the same time, he also lifts their minds, showing the great honor God has graciously bestowed upon us. Understand, then, how great an honor exists for us: God sends his angels to us as ministers, just as he sends them to friends.

**Chapter II.** Having thus introduced the ministry of the angels, through whom even the light itself was administered, he immediately [Col. 0735C] adds a discussion of the excellence of the grace brought to us through the Son of God, saying: “Therefore we must pay closer attention to the things we have heard.” Why did he say “closer”? That is, more closely than we were accustomed to under the Law. He did not mention the name “Law,” but he makes this clear in his argument. And why must we pay closer attention to the things we have heard? Are both those things and these things not from God? He therefore said “closer,” either meaning more closely than they were accustomed to under the Law, or perhaps “more fully,” lest he should disappear from view [Note: [Col. 0735D] Perhaps: “or certainly more fully—not that he should disappear from view,” and so forth; that is, lest they be led to believe that God is absent because he no longer appears. The sense is very obscure.]. But because the Old Testament had for a long time possessed great authority among them, whereas these teachings were presented to them as though new, he shows that they should not judge them contemptible: on the contrary, we must observe more closely the things we have heard through the Son of God, because of their greater abundance. In his customary manner he joins his own person to theirs in saying “we have heard.” He then follows this by adding: “lest we drift away”—that is, lest we perhaps perish, lest we perhaps fall away—unwilling that the sense of those listening should flow away from what they had heard into empty things. He explains this also in the words that follow, saying: “For if the word spoken through angels [Col. 0736A].”

Some say that here he touches upon Moses, because he received the Decalogue of the Law from the Lord on Mount Sinai, as it is written there: “Moses spoke, and the Lord answered him” (Exodus 19:19); and elsewhere: “The Law was given through Moses” (John 1:17). But here the Apostle teaches that it was given through angels. Likewise, in the Epistle to the Galatians (3:29), he says in a similar way: “Arranged through angels by the hand of a mediator.” And again in the Acts of the Apostles (7:53): “You received the Law at the direction of angels, and you did not keep it.” It is shown in very many passages that it was given through angels. Or, because he was speaking of all the things that were said or done in the Old Testament—or certainly because God was in the angels—the word “was made firm [Note: [Col. 0735D] The sense here is somewhat obscure. It nevertheless seems to be interpreted as follows: either the word spoken through angels was made firm because all the things said or done in the Old Testament were made firm, since, as stated below, they were faithfully verified; or else, because God was in the angels, it was made firm.]” was used. What does “was made firm” mean? [Col. 0736B] Clearly, “true,” as though he were saying, “faithful in the proper time.”

“And every transgression and disobedience received a just reward of retribution.” That is, nothing remained unpunished: whatever he promised, or whatever he said in threatening, everything that had been foretold received a just recompense of reward. But why did he say “recompense of reward,” when “reward” is ordinarily used of something good? It is the Apostle’s custom not to be overly concerned with the precise propriety of words, but to use interchangeably terms that refer either to good or to evil, as when elsewhere he said: “Bringing every thought into captivity to obey Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5); so here too he says “recompense of reward.”

[Col. 0736C] “How will we escape if we neglect so great a salvation?” By these words he sufficiently indicates that there was not as great a salvation in the Old Testament as there is in the grace that the Son of God brought to us. For now God promises us not, as he promised them, the riches of the earth, but the glory of heaven. He has granted us victory not over earthly enemies but over spiritual ones. He has given us not a life that miserably perishes but an eternally blessed and everlasting life. He briefly indicated all these things by saying: “If we neglect so great a salvation.” Then he added the preeminence of what was spoken through the Son of God: “Which, having first been announced through the Lord”—that is, these things we speak of received their beginning from the very source. For what we proclaim was not brought to us by human beings or even by angels, but the only-begotten Son himself bestowed it upon us.

“It was confirmed to us by those who heard,” that is, those who heard from the Lord confirmed it to us by their own powers. Luke also said this at the beginning of his Gospel: “As those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word delivered them to us” [Col. 0737A] (Luke 1:2). “It was confirmed to us,” he says: it was believed and brought to completion. This salvation, which was given to us through the same Son, remains forever.

“God also bearing witness [Note: [Col. 0737D] The particle *etiam* (“also”) is not found in the Vulgate, but does occur in the text of Ambrosiaster, from whom many passages have been excerpted here and there.] by signs and wonders [Note: [Col. 0738D] The Vulgate has “portents.”], and by various powers.” How does God testify? Not by word or voice, but by powers and wonders. At the same time, he signifies the abundance of graces that were not present among the ancients: neither such great signs nor such varied wonders as were given after Jesus was glorified. He therefore shows that they did not simply believe them, but did so through signs and wonders. After this he adds: “And by distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his will.” He attributes everything to the divine will and counsel [Col. 0737B], as though he were saying: He himself knows what benefits each person, or what is beneficial for whom; therefore he distributes grace to each one. He says the same to the Corinthians: “God placed each one as he wished” (1 Corinthians 12:18). And again: “The manifestation of the Spirit is given to each one for the common good” (ibid., 12:7).

“According to his will.” He therefore shows that gifts are given to each person according to God’s will, so that they may not be lifted up into pride, puffed up by the vanity of boasting, or made more negligent by the greatness of the gift. For whoever considers himself master of a virtue does not think that the gift came to him from the grace of the giver, but from the debt owed on account of his own merits. Such a person is consequently puffed up by the vanity of pride. Therefore God wisely distributes everything [Col. 0737C]. We can observe this also occurring in the Church, when one person has the ability to speak for teaching, while another cannot even open his mouth. Let the one who has not received a similar grace not be distressed, knowing that “the manifestation of the Spirit is given to each one for the common good.” For if a human head of a household knows to whom he ought to entrust any particular task, much more does God, who knows the minds of all human beings and knows everything before it happens.

“For he did not subject to angels the world to come, of which we are speaking.” Is he discussing another world? No, but this one. For this reason he also added “of which we are speaking,” so that he would not allow the hearer’s mind to wander while another world was being sought. How, then, does he call it “to come”? The world was “to come” in order to be made—that is, in order to believe. This world to come, then, he subjects not to angels but to Christ. For he did not subject to angels our salvation, which took place in the world at the end of the ages, and which had long before been foretold by the prophets as future, but to his Son, to whom, as was shown above, the Father’s voice sounded, saying: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.”

He confirms this also with prophetic examples, saying: “Someone testified somewhere, saying” (Psalm [Col. 0738A] 8:5). Why did he not place the Prophet’s name first, but conceal it? He does this in other testimonies as well, as was read above. I think that he did this not to conceal but to make a point: he shows that they possessed extensive knowledge of the Scriptures, so that he did not need to state the name of the speaker, but could introduce the testimony as concerning something evident and readily at hand, saying: “What is man, that you are mindful of him?” The word “man” must be pronounced with contempt—that is, as referring to fragile and perishable Adam’s descendant, bound by the general corruption of the ancient sin. The Lord is mindful of him when he forgives his sins and bestows the gifts of his mercy upon him. “Or the son of man, that you visit him?” Here the voice should now be raised, because this signifies the Lord and Savior, who was not born like other mortals from two human beings, but proceeded from the Holy Spirit and the womb of blessed Mary, ever-virgin, like a bridegroom from a glorious bridal chamber. And consider that above he said, “You are mindful”; then he added, “you visit.” He was mindful when he had mercy from heaven upon the patriarchs; he visited when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). For we speak of “visiting” when a physician enters among the sick, and it is clear that this was truly fulfilled in the Lord’s coming.

“You diminished him.” From this point the humility and glory of the Lord and Savior are recounted. He was made lower, not by any necessity of service, but by the voluntary choice of his own compassion, as the Apostle says: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians [Col. 0738C] 2:7).

It follows: “A little lower than the angels.” The Creator of the angels was made lower than the angels in that respect in which he accepted the cross for human beings. He rightly said “a little lower,” because although he assumed a mortal body, he nevertheless had no sin.

“With glory and honor you crowned him.” He was crowned with honor when, after the resurrection, God exalted him—inasmuch as he had become human—and granted him the world’s astonishing recognition. He was crowned with glory in the resurrection and ascension, and with honor in the granting of the Father’s majesty.

“And you appointed him over the works of your hands.” Above, his glory and honor were recounted; now power is also set forth, so that the perfect fullness of Christ the Lord’s majesty may be recognized [Col. 0738D]. For by saying “over the works of your hands,” he shows that every creature is subject to him, because just as nothing is excluded from the Lord’s work, so nothing is shown to be divided off from Christ’s power.

“You subjected all things beneath his feet; for in subjecting all things, he left nothing that was not subject to him.” By saying “all things,” he appears to have excluded neither earthly nor heavenly things. And the one whom he had previously said was made a little lower than the angels because of the humility of the flesh, he now says, after the ascension, to have had all things subjected beneath his feet, so that this distinction might both remove doubt from those who waver [Col. 0739A] and display the glory of the holy incarnation. He says “beneath his feet” so that every creature may rightly be seen to honor and worship him.

“But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him.” He says this concerning those who do not believe in him, because the preaching of the Gospel has not yet obtained all things. Above he said that nothing was left not subject to him; here he asserts that not yet all things appear subject to him, because there he indicates universal subjection, whether voluntary or necessary, whereas here he indicates only voluntary subjection, by which they faithfully [Note: [Col. 0739D] Perhaps *fideles* (“the faithful”) should be read instead of *fideliter* (“faithfully”).] believe in him.

“But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death.” Here he shows that the cross of Christ is glory and honor, for which he was made a little lower than the angels, just as the Lord himself always calls it, saying: “That the Son of Man may be glorified” (John 18:4). If he calls the things he suffered for servants “glory,” much more, human being, when you suffer, you ought not doubt that it pertains to your everlasting glory. And he adds: “So that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.” He himself called it grace, because he tasted death for the salvation of all. It was not owed to us that the Son of God should taste death for us, but grace accomplished this. He indeed died for all. But what if not all believe? He nevertheless fulfilled what was his to do. He said specifically, “tasted death,” because he remained in it for a short time, so that, having immediately conquered it, he might rise again [Col. 0739C].

“For it was fitting that he, for whom and through whom all things exist, who had brought many sons to glory, should perfect the author of their salvation through suffering”—that is, bring the salvation of all to completion. “For whom are all things”: through his death both the things in heaven and the things on earth were restored, through him by whom all things were also created. You see how much there is among us. The Son himself is a Son, and we are sons: he is the proper Son, we are adopted; he saves, and we are saved. You see how he both joins us together and distinguishes us. “Many sons,” he says, bringing them to glory: here he joined them together. “The author,” he says, “of their salvation”: here he distinguished them.

[Col. 0739D] “For the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one.” Here again observe how he joins them together, honoring and consoling them, and calling them Christ’s brothers, in accordance with his statement that they are from one. Then, strengthening his argument and showing that he was speaking of the one who is according to the flesh, he adds: “The one who sanctifies”—that is, Christ—“and those who are sanctified”—that is, us. Consider how great the difference is. He sanctifies; we are sanctified. And he adds, “all from one.” For there is one God, from whom all things come; but he is so in one way, and we in another: he as the proper Son, we as adopted sons. Nevertheless, we have one God as Father; he, as the proper Son, sanctifies; we, as adopted sons, are sanctified.

[Col. 0740A] “For which reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying.” In saying that he is not ashamed to call them brothers, he demonstrates that this is not a matter of natural reality but solely of his mercy and great humility, since he chose us as brothers for himself. He also confirms this with prophetic testimony, lest it be thought something new and not foretold long before. For he says: “I will proclaim your name to my brothers” (Psalm 21:23). After the sacred passion and resurrection, he says that the glory of his divinity would be proclaimed throughout the whole world. For “I will proclaim” means “I will cause it to be announced,” just as in the Gospel he says to the women: “Go, tell my brothers” (Mark 16:5). They are called brothers who love and are loved. And he adds: “In the midst of the Church I will praise you.” In the midst of the saints, the Lord’s praise resounds through him who says: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Luke 10:21). For the true praise of the Lord is proclaimed not only by the mouth but also by the heart and by the conduct of one who fulfills the Lord’s commandments.

“And again: ‘But I myself trust in him’” (Psalm 17:3). This was said of the human being he assumed, whose entire confidence is undoubtedly in God the Father, just as he himself says in the Gospel concerning those for whom he prayed: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24). He also exhorted them to have confidence, saying: “Take courage, because I have conquered the world” (John 16:23).

“And again: ‘Behold, I and the children whom God has given me’” [Col. 0740C] (Isaiah 8:18). The Apostle brought forward this testimony from Isaiah, referring it to Christ and the apostles, whom he called children on account of their innocence. Concerning them the Lord himself says: “Let the little children come to me, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (Matthew 19:11).

“Therefore, since the children shared in flesh and blood, he himself likewise shared in the same.” Pay attention to his likeness according to the flesh, in which he himself shared with the children. Let all heretics be ashamed; let them be covered with confusion and embarrassment, those who say that he came only apparently and not truly. For he did not merely say that he shared in these things and stop, although even if he had said that, it would have been sufficient; but he added “the same.” He is clearly shown to have added something more, namely something closer: he did not come in the fantasy or image of others, but demonstrated true brotherhood with them and humanity in Christ that was not fictitious. For just as the children consist of flesh and blood, so he likewise shared in flesh and blood, so that he might have something with which to taste death for the salvation of the children.

He immediately adds the abundant reason for this dispensation, saying: “So that through death he might destroy the one who held the power of death, that is, the devil.” Here he reveals something astonishing: by the very means through which the devil held power, he was also defeated. The weapons that had been strong against the world—that is, death—were the means by which Christ struck him. Here he intimates the greatness of the power of the one who conquered. Consider what a great good death accomplished. “So that he might free those who throughout their whole life were subject to slavery through fear of death” [Col. 0741A]. Why do you tremble? Why do you fear what has already been condemned? It is no longer terrifying but desirable, as the end of labors and the beginning of rest. Why does he say, “Throughout their whole life they were subject to slavery through fear of death”? They were indeed slaves of death because they feared death, and they had not yet been released from the fear of death, whose laws held them bound. Now, therefore, the saints mock it; after the contest has been completed and death defeated, they are about to pass into the kingdom. Hence Paul himself says: “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23).

“For he did not take hold of angels, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham. Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect.” For this reason our Redeemer became not an angel but a human being: without doubt, what he redeemed had to be what he became, so that by not taking hold of the fallen angel he might leave him behind, while by taking hold of the human being in himself he might restore him. Desiring to demonstrate God’s great mercy and the love he had for the human race, after the Apostle said, “Therefore, since the children shared in flesh and blood, he himself likewise shared in the same,” he develops this meaning further: how he came to share in flesh and blood. He says: He did not take hold of any angel, so that the Son of God might be joined to their nature in one person; rather, God, the Son of God, bestowed this honor and dignity upon human nature, so that God and man might be one person. Why did he not say “he assumed”? [Col. 0741C] Clearly, he used this word, “took hold,” because we were like people withdrawing from him and fleeing far away; he pursued us, took hold of us, and conformed the nature of our frailty to himself in one person. Wonderful is the union in which a mortal was joined to the eternal and immortal! He shows how eagerly he hastened toward human nature, and that God has great concern for it. Thus here too he places something much greater by way of comparison. For he did not take hold of any of the angels; and truly it is a great, wondrous, and astounding thing that our flesh should sit above and be worshiped by angels, archangels, cherubim, and seraphim. This, therefore, must be frequently turned over in the mind and greatly praised. For he did not say simply “human beings,” but “the seed of Abraham.” Here he honors the patriarch and those who are descended from him, to whom this Epistle was written. He recalls God’s benefits, their carnal kinship with Christ, and the promise spoken to Abraham: “To you and to your seed I will give this land” (Genesis 12:7). For all are from one: from Abraham come Christ according to the flesh and those to whom he is speaking here.

“Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect.” What does “in every respect” mean? He was born, brought up, grew, suffered, and even died, so that in every respect he might be like his brothers, who are subject to such a condition. For above he says that he is the radiance of glory and the likeness of the Father’s substance, through whom he made the ages [Col. 0742A], and that he sits at the right hand of the Father. Yet this one, so great, so wondrous, and so glorious, took such care for our salvation that he became our brother in every respect. For this reason he in a manner left the angels and the other heavenly powers, in order to seize us and carry back to the heavenly homeland the lost sheep, found through his passion, after placing it upon his shoulders (Luke XV, 4–5). This one, so great and such a priest, also willed to become our priest before the Father, offering himself for us.

Accordingly, he continues and adds: “so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people.” “For this reason,” he says, “he assumed our flesh, solely out of mercy, so that he might intercede for our sins.” There is no more remarkable explanation for the whole of this dispensation than this alone. For he saw [Col. 0742B] the human race lying in the smoke of wrath, bound by the chains of sins, subject to death, and suffering tyranny; and he had compassion on it as a faithful high priest. Therefore the only reason he was made like his brothers in every respect was that he might be a faithful high priest. “Faithful,” he says—that is, true and powerful. For it is the priest’s duty to be faithful, so that he may be able to free from sins those whose priest he is.

Accordingly, having next spoken of his power, he adds: “For in that which he himself suffered, having been tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted.” “In that”—that is, as a human being—in which he suffered, he is able to free the bound and to help the tempted, so that they may not be overcome; for he knows our temptations not only as God, but also as a human being, having learned them by experience in himself. [Col. 0742C] And although God in his own nature is incapable of suffering, nevertheless in the nature that he assumed the same Son of God was capable of suffering and was made like our nature. In the flesh that he assumed he endured many savage sufferings. He knows what tribulation is; he knows what temptation is; but through endurance he conquered. He himself was tempted, but not overcome. What, then, does he mean when he says, “He is able to help those who are tempted”? It is as though he were saying: “With great eagerness he stretches out his hand to share in their suffering.”

## Chapter III

“Therefore, holy brothers, partakers of a heavenly calling, consider the Apostle and High Priest of our confession, Jesus.”

He is still speaking about the mystery of Christ’s incarnation. For in the Gospel he himself also testifies that he was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt. XV, 24). The Greek word *apostolos* is rendered in Latin as *missus*, “sent.” Know what Jesus is and what kind of one he is, and you will have no need of any other consolation or comfort. He called him the High Priest of our confession—that is, of our faith—to whom this new people has been entrusted, just as the former people was given to Moses to govern. But greater things, or things far better, have been entrusted to this one.

For blessed Paul the apostle wishes to raise the minds of the Israelites toward the excellence of God’s promises, so that they may prepare themselves attentively to receive what God has graciously promised to bring them. He calls them beloved brothers, called to heavenly things, sharing with Christ in God’s inheritance, “who is faithful to him”—that is, to God the Father—“who made him.” He is speaking of his humanity, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh, not of his divinity, which was not made but begotten by the Father, of one substance with him.

“As Moses also was in all his house (Num. XII, 7).” Intending to place him above Moses by comparison in the matter of the priesthood under the Law, he introduced this statement, asserting that he was faithful in his house. Faithful—that is, devoted, protecting what belongs to him and not allowing it to be corrupted. We are that house, as he says in what follows: just as Moses was faithful in his house—that is, in the former people.

Immediately he goes on to show how we ought to be his house. For he says: “Whose house we are, if we hold firm to the confidence and glory of hope until the end” [Col. 0743B], because “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 22). He calls the inhabitants “the house,” just as he calls “the Church” not the stones or buildings but those who are called together in the church. He adds: “We are God’s house”—that is, God’s work, created in Christ Jesus.

Up to this point he has compared Christ’s incarnation with Moses. From here he turns to narrate Christ’s superiority, saying: “For this one has been considered worthy of greater glory than Moses, just as the one who built the house has greater honor than the house.” He did not say that the craftsman has greater honor than the works, but that the one who built the house has greater honor than the house. You see that he is speaking not of a temple but of the whole people: first of the people whom Moses led out of Egypt [Col. 0743C], and then of those whom Christ freed from the devil’s slavery and acquired for himself as a house.

“For every house is built by someone, but the one who created all things is God.” Here he distinguishes the builder from the thing built, intending it to be understood that God is the author of both houses, though in different ways: of the house over which Moses presided in one way, and of the house over which Christ is known to be leader and Lord in another. Therefore he continues: “Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony of the things that were to be spoken; but Christ as a son over his own house, and we are that house, if we hold firm to the confidence and glory of hope until the end.”

This one—that is, Jesus—enters into the Father’s possessions as a son; but the other—that is, Moses—enters his house as God’s servant. Here again he urges them to stand firm and not be overthrown. We shall be God’s house if we hold firm to the confidence of hope and its glory until the end. He rightly said “the confidence of our hope,” because all good things are possessed by the saints in this life only in hope, until they arrive at the vision of perfect blessedness: “For in hope we were saved” (Rom. VIII, 24). We cannot have the good things promised to us in this life of punishment except in hope, while patiently awaiting that one and holding firm hope until the end [Note: [Col. 0743D] We have judged that the words “holding firm hope,” which are missing in the manuscript, should be supplied from the text of Ambrosiaster.].

[Col. 0744A] “Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says: Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts (Ps. XCIV, 8–11).” Above, the blessed Apostle spoke of hope, because we ought to hope for what is to come. But hope that is seen is not hope.

The history that the Prophet recalls here is very well known. When the Israelites had gone out from the land of Egypt (Num. XIV, 1–4), had traveled a long way, and had received many signs of God’s power in Egypt, at the Red Sea, and in the wilderness, they decided to send scouts (Num. XIII, 1–4) who were to inspect the nature of the land that had been promised to them. They went forth and returned, greatly admiring the land and saying that it produced very large fruits, but that the province was inhabited by men who could not be conquered [Col. 0744B] and who were strong.

But the Israelites were ungrateful and foolish. They ought to have remembered the many benefits of God: how he had rescued them from danger when they were enclosed in the midst of such a great Egyptian army; how he had supplied them without interruption with springs of water; how he had given them manna; and how he had performed the other miracles that we believe God performed. Yet they neither believed God nor remembered any of these things. Instead, they were terrified by fear and said, “Let us return to Egypt.”

God therefore became angry with them because they had so quickly forgotten God’s benefits and his miracles. He swore that that generation would not enter the rest once promised to their fathers. Thus all perished in the wilderness except two men only (Num. XIII, 18–34; XIV, 5–45).

Why, then, did David later say these things, speaking after that generation: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts,” lest you suffer the same things as your ancestors and be deprived of the promised rest? Because there is another rest [Note: [Col. 0744D] It appears that *alia* is missing, so that the reading should be: “For there is another rest, namely an eternal and heavenly one,” as is found below.]. For if they had already received the rest that was in Palestine, why does he again say to them, “Do not harden your hearts, as your fathers did”? What, then, is this other rest except the kingdom of heaven, of which the Sabbath is an image and shadow?

The Apostle therefore mentions three rests in this Epistle: the first, the Sabbath, on which the Lord rested from his works; the second, the rest in Palestine, into which the Israelites were to enter so that they might rest from great misery and labors; and the third, the true rest, namely the kingdom of heaven, which we have already discussed above. Those who happen to reach it will truly rest from their labors and afflictions. Concerning it the Prophet speaks to the true Israelites, saying: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.”

At one time your fathers heard his voice through Moses, and they hardened themselves. Thus he then spoke through a herald, when you hardened your hearts against God. Now he speaks through himself: “Let your hearts become gentle.” The one who formerly sent heralds has deigned to come himself. With his own mouth he speaks—the one who spoke through the mouths of the prophets. At the voice of the one who sent heralds and now cries out through himself, do not close your hearts.

[Col. 0745A] Remember how your fathers were hardened and how they did not enter the promised rest, but, embittered and murmuring against God, perished in the wilderness. They were your fathers who perished; do not imitate them. And they will not be your fathers, although you were born from them, knowing that “God is able from stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. VII, 9).

“For forty years I was offended by this generation.” He chastised them in many ways, yet they always went astray in their hearts. The Lord fasted for forty days in the wilderness in order to triumph over the one against whom they had murmured for forty years in the desert. After completing the whole glory of his victory through his passion and resurrection, he remained with his disciples for forty days before ascending into heaven.

During the first forty days he displayed the temptation of this pilgrimage; during the later forty days, the consolation that the saints will have in their homeland. For his body—that is, the Church—must suffer temptations in this world. Yet that consoler is not absent, who said: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20).

“To whom I swore because of their unbelief that they would not enter into my rest.” That God speaks is a great thing; how much more that he swears! He wished the oath to serve as confirmation. By whom did God swear except by himself? He has no greater by whom he might swear. By himself he confirms his threats. As what he promises is true, so what he threatens is certain.

He swore that they would not enter his rest [Col. 0745C], and yet some must enter that rest. Therefore, after they have been rejected, we shall enter, because although some branches were broken off on account of dissimilarity and unbelief, we are grafted in because of faith and humility. The apostolic exhortation to the people concerning entering the rest follows.

For he says: “See to it, brothers, that perhaps there may be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, causing you to depart from the living God.” Indeed, unbelief is born from hardness, and just as hardened and rigid bodies do not obey a word [Note: [Col. 0745D] Ambrosiaster, from whom this example is taken, has it thus: “And just as hardened and rigid bodies do not obey the hands of physicians, so hardened souls do not obey the word of God.”]. If your fathers, he says, because they did not hope as they ought to have hoped, suffered the things recorded in the history we mentioned earlier and perished in the wilderness because of hardness of heart, you have much greater reason to fear such things, just as they experienced them.

For this word was addressed to those who were present or would be present. Therefore he says “today.” For “today” always exists as long as the world endures.

He goes on to say more about “today,” adding: “But exhort one another each day, as long as it is called ‘today,’ so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.” That is: build one another up and correct yourselves, lest similar things happen to you [Col. 0746A], lest anyone among you be hardened by the deceit of the sin of unbelief. You see that unbelief produces sin. For just as unbelief gives birth to an evil life, so also the soul, when it has entered into the depths of evils, despises (Prov. XVIII, 3). But when it despises, it does not permit itself to believe, so as to free itself from the fear of eternal death.

Then the Apostle adds: “For we have become partakers of Christ.” “We share in him,” he says—that is, we have become one with him. For he is the head, and we are the members; we are co-heirs and members of the same body with him, according to the spiritual human being who was created in him.

“If indeed we hold the beginning of his substance firm until the end.” What is “the beginning of his substance”? [Col. 0746B] It signifies faith, through which we subsist and are born from God as sons, becoming, so to speak, sons of his very substance. This must be observed most carefully, lest we be corrupted by the stain of any doctrine.

Then the Apostle continues to speak about “today,” saying: “when it is said”—he says—“Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in that provocation,” continuing “from the things they heard.” Here the Apostle begins to explain the prophetic testimony that he set forth above. For he said: “Today,” he says, “if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in bitterness.”

Whom does he mean when he mentions those who were hardened? Surely those whose corpses were cast down in the wilderness [Col. 0746C]? What he says amounts to this: They also heard, he says, just as we have heard, but hearing the word did them no good. Therefore do not think that merely hearing the preaching provides entry into God’s rest. They too heard through Moses, but hearing brought them no benefit, because they did not believe, and what they heard was not joined to faith.

He distinguished those who believed the word of the preaching from those who did not believe. For he says: “But not all.” Caleb and Joshua, however, who did not agree with the unbelievers, escaped the punishment inflicted upon the others. Nor was it the only gift granted to them that they escaped the death by which the others perished: they were also granted entry into the promised land and the honorable inheritance of their portion.

“Today,” he says [Col. 0746D], “if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” For “today” always exists. Let none of you be hardened by the deceit of sin or by the deceit of the devil. It is truly deceitful to hope for nothing concerning the future, thinking either that we shall render no account of the deeds and actions we perform here, or that there will be no resurrection, or that, even if they were believers [Note: [Col. 0745D] The manuscript has *quasi*; I judged this to be an error to be corrected from what follows [Col. 0746D]. There the direct address appears to be directed to the Hebrews whom the divine Paul was addressing: although they were believers, they were nevertheless still excessively attached to the Law. Perhaps the reading should more correctly be: “or that, although they were believers,” and so forth.], they nevertheless retained great devotion toward Moses.

In this also he shows that their hearts must not be hardened as the hearts of those of whom these things are said were hardened. To say, “What now? Once I have sinned, do I have no hope of recovering myself?” is deceit. Then he aroused hope in them, just as he said above, “we have become partakers [the transmitted reading *ponae* is uncertain],” saying: Since he loved us so greatly and deigned to make us his body, he will not despise us as we perish.

Let us understand, I say, what we have been made into. We and Christ are one. Let us not prove unbelieving toward him. Let us fear the destruction of those people and dread the just judgment of God, who will repay each person according to his works: eternal rest to those who have faith, provided that it is the faith that works through love; but to those who do not believe, everlasting punishment.

Therefore, lest we abandon the promise that we made to God in baptism and return again to the works of unbelief, which we renounced before many witnesses, let each person labor for himself, lest he be found less worthy to enter God’s rest. For it has been announced to us how we ought to enter God’s rest, just as it was announced to them—yet to us through the Son, and to them through a servant. You see how he distinguishes the work from the Maker, and the servant from the Son. The former enters into the Father’s possessions as Lord; the latter as servant.

## Chapter IV

Immediately the Apostle adds words of exhortation, saying: “We shall enter the rest, we who believe,” just as he said: “As I swore in my anger: If they shall enter into my rest.” He urges us to enter the rest, lest it perhaps be said to us, as it was to them: “If they shall enter”—that is, “They shall not enter into my rest.”

For he hastens to show that the rest to which we have been called is another rest, namely the heavenly one. He does not say that we shall enter the rest that is in Palestine, but that they did not enter it because of the hardness of their hearts.

He therefore added a discussion of the first rest, saying: “And indeed, the works were completed from the foundation of the world. For somewhere he spoke about the seventh day in this way: And God rested on the seventh day from all his works (Gen. II, 2). And again in this passage: If they shall enter into my rest.”

Since, therefore, it remains for some to enter it, and those to whom it was first announced did not enter because of unbelief, he immediately added the second rest, which was promised to the people of God. Just as he himself rested, so he promised us rest. This does not mean that he rested because of any weariness from labor, but that “he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. XXXII, 9; XIV, 5). In the same way, after laboring through the six ages of the world, he will bring us to rest: “And again in this passage,” he says, “they shall not enter into my rest.”

The conjunction “if” can be understood as affirmation, negation, or doubt. Above it was used in the sense of negation, where he said that because of their unbelief God swore that they would not enter. He added, “If they shall enter”—that is, “They shall not enter.”

Here, however, “if they shall enter” can be understood affirmatively, as though he were saying: “If they enter, they shall fare well.” Therefore he added: “Since it remains for some to enter it.” He means the rest that was in Palestine. Only a few entered it—namely, Caleb and Joshua—out of all those who journeyed from Egypt. Accordingly he says: “And those to whom it was first announced did not enter because of unbelief,” referring to those who departed from Egypt, whose corpses were cast down in the wilderness.

Then he begins, though obscurely, to discuss the third rest promised to those who believe in Christ. “Again,” he says, “he appoints a certain day, ‘today,’ saying in David, after so much time, as it was said above: Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts. For if Jesus had given them rest, he would never afterward have spoken of another.”

Here he shows that there is a third rest, about which David said “today.” He does not mean the rest into which Jesus led the people, but indicates that there is another rest, far more excellent than that one, into which the true Jesus, not the symbolic one, leads those who belong to him.

Let us hear whether this is certain. After so many years, he says, he again says: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” For if Jesus son of Nun had granted true rest to the people whose leader he was [Note: [Col. 0748B] Ambrosiaster has *ductor*, “leader.”], he would certainly not have spoken afterward of another day. It is therefore certain that some will receive the rest signified by the rest that was in Palestine, into which the true Jesus will lead his people.
