“Therefore a sabbatism remains for the people of God. For whoever has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, just as God did from his.”

God’s rest must be understood as the perfection of his works: on the sixth day, after the original creation of things had been completed, he ceased on the seventh day from creating new natures. Through that rest of God, which is eternal [Note: [Col. 0748C] Our manuscript has “which is not eternal.” We judged this should be corrected both from what follows and from Ambrosiaster’s text [Col. 0748D].], he earnestly calls us to eternal rest. He called it *sabbatismus*, “sabbath-rest,” because he was speaking to Jews.

In this passage he did not use the ordinary word for “rest,” but *sabbatismus*, its proper name, toward which they rejoiced and hastened [Col. 0748D] [Note: [Col. 0748D] After these repeated words, some text is read with a variation, as follows: “*sabbatismus*, its proper name, toward which they rejoiced and did not hasten.” This seemed to us to require deletion.]. He calls the kingdom of God a *sabbatismus*. For just as the Sabbath commands everyone to abstain from all evils, yet orders them to do those things that pertain to the service of God—things performed by the priests and things that benefited the soul, and nothing else—so he does not wish the Sabbath in God’s kingdom to be understood in such a way that anyone should afterward return from it to laborious works, as they did on the bodily Sabbath.

Whoever enters this Sabbath of God will rest perpetually from his works, just as God did from his. [Col. 0749A] Wishing, therefore, to instruct them about the resurrection and eternal rest, he inserted “today” very frequently, so that they would never despair of entering, as though he were saying: If anyone sins while it is still “today,” let him have hope of returning. Therefore no one should despair as long as he lives.

It follows: “Let us therefore hasten to enter into that rest, so that no one may fall into the same example of unbelief.” Faith is indeed a great and saving thing. Without it no one can be saved, as it is said: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI, 6).

Accordingly Paul also admonishes those who have been worthy to be received into the dignity of the mysteries [Note: [Col. 0749] In Ambrosiaster’s manuscripts this explanation appears as follows: “who have been worthy to receive the ministry worthily.”], saying: “Let us hasten to enter into that rest.” “Let us hasten,” he says, because faith is not sufficient; a life worthy of faith must also be added, and great diligence must be applied [Col. 0749B], lest faith be idle.

For if those who committed fornication and murmured against God were not deemed worthy to enter the land, how shall we deserve to enter heaven if we live carelessly like the nations? Anyone who wishes to possess heaven must adorn his faith with good works. And the one who lives badly suffers not only this loss—that he does not enter the kingdom of God—but also something more terrifying: he is handed over to everlasting punishment.

Therefore he added: “So that no one may fall into the same example of unbelief.” He terrified his hearers with the destruction of those who perished in the wilderness, lest they fall under the same judgment, as though he had said: We are sufficiently instructed by our ancestors, so that, if we fall into similar things, we may not suffer what they suffered—that is, the same example of unbelief.

[Col. 0749C] Then, in order to strike greater fear into sinners, he adds: “For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword.” Here he shows that the same one himself performed those deeds, that he lives and has not been extinguished, and that we have the same judge who condemned them because of their unbelief.

For he said: “The word of God is living.” The Word of God is the Son of God, who says of himself: “If anyone keeps my word, he will never see death” (John VIII, 31). Just as they, if they had kept the word of God, would have lived and entered the promised land, so we too, if we keep his word, shall live and enter the heavenly rest.

“For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword.” A sword can divide the limbs from the body and penetrate the secret and hidden places of the flesh; but the word of God is much sharper, “reaching to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow.”

We live by the soul; by the spirit we understand. Bodily life is shared with animals; spiritual reason with angels. God’s judgment is so effective that it distinguishes bodily sins from spiritual ones, discerning with what mind or desire a person acts or serves in his heart. His insight is so penetrating that he knows all that we do or think more certainly than we ourselves do.

We always have as the witness of our actions and thoughts the one whom we shall have as judge. Let us fear the presence of the one whose knowledge we cannot escape in any way. Therefore he also added: “And he is the discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart.”

The word of God distinguishes joints and marrow because it discerns the thoughts and intentions of the heart. Bones are joined to bones through joints. Often, while we act with a right thought, we suddenly turn toward the desire for praise and do for the sake of praise what we had initially begun to do for the sake of truth. Since thoughts are joined to thoughts, a kind of network of joints is formed in the spirit.

But the bones joined in a joint also have marrow. The holy preacher explains this more clearly when he adds: “And he is the discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” Our thoughts are the joints; our intentions are the marrow. Often we think one thing, while the aim of our thought is something else.

For example, suppose someone defends the case of an orphan or widow in exchange for a reward and, perhaps entering a church, says to God in his prayers: “You see that I defend the cause of the orphan and the widow.” Without doubt he knows what he is thinking, but he does not know what his thought is aiming at. He thinks one thing but intends another. For he is seeking not the defense of the orphan or widow but payment in money. Take away the temporal reward, and he will not defend the orphan or widow.

The word of God, therefore, is the discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart, because it does not look merely at what a person thinks within himself; through the marrow of the joints—that is, through the intention of the thought—it penetrates the whole person [Col. 0750C]. Nor is it surprising that, being wholly present everywhere, it knows its entire creation, whether spiritual or bodily, since nothing that has been made was made without it (John I, 3).

Therefore he added: “Nor is there any creature invisible in his sight.” By this he especially terrified them, lest, while still standing in the faith, they should fail to complete the works of faith with complete satisfaction. For he himself discerns what is in the heart; there he examines, where he considers, repaying each person according to his works.

“But all things are naked and open to his eyes.” Often we fear appearing disorderly in our outward actions before the eyes of human beings, yet in our inner thoughts we do not fear the gaze of the one whom we do not see, although he sees everything. We are much more visible inwardly to God than outwardly to human beings.

Therefore all the saints look around themselves both outwardly and inwardly, either reproving themselves externally or fearing the one before whom they are invisibly seen internally. And what we say about human beings applies equally if one speaks of angels, archangels, Cherubim, Seraphim, or any other creature: everything is revealed to his eyes, everything is open and manifest, and nothing can be hidden from him.

“All things are naked and open to his eyes, to whom our word is directed”—that is, to whom we shall render an account of our actions.

[Col. 0751A] “Therefore, since we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God.”

Shortly before, when discussing his divinity, he said: “All things are naked and open to his eyes.” Now, however, because he is speaking about the flesh, he discusses him as high priest, since he offered himself for our salvation and was the first of all to enter into rest.

“We have,” he says, “a great high priest who has passed through the heavens.” Thus Moses, the leader of the people to whom a temporary rest was promised, did not enter the rest that he so often promised to the people. But our priest, the guarantor of a better promise, making a way for those who believe in him, was the first to enter the rest promised to the people entrusted to him.

He shows him to be a great priest because he possesses an everlasting priesthood, always living to intercede for us. He also shows this same one to be the Son of God when he says: “Jesus the Son of God.” He never wished to say this of Moses, but presented Moses as a servant. Above he testified to them under the name Jesus that the name announced by an angel sent from God to the Virgin signified that he was truly the Son of God, and therefore the great priest.

“Let us hold fast to the confession.” What confession does he mean? That he is the Son of God; that Christ is God; that he suffered, was buried, rose on the third day, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come from there to judge the living and the dead; and that through him we possess every good thing—redemption, resurrection, and an everlasting inheritance with him. Let us confess these things.

That these things are true is clear from the fact that the high priest has been established within the inner veil. For he enters sprinkled with blood—his own, not another’s—as did the former high priests, who were sprinkled with the blood of a red heifer.

“For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses.” He does not ignore what concerns us. He came by way of the human condition, in every respect without sin, bringing with him nothing for which he would be liable to death, as he himself testifies in the Gospel, saying: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John XIV, 30).

Many high priests do not know those who are placed in tribulation, nor do they know what tribulation is in any particular person. For it is impossible for one who has not experienced affliction and has not endured everything in a tangible way to know the sufferings of the afflicted. Our high priest, however, appropriately endured first all the things that were inflicted upon human misery after the sin of the first man, and then ascended through the inner veil to the throne of the Father’s majesty.

“Tempted in every respect according to the likeness, without sin.” He was tempted in various ways, but not overcome. Tested in tribulations, he was everywhere a glorious victor. He was tempted according to the likeness of flesh, without sin—according, therefore, to the likeness of sinful flesh; yet his flesh was entirely without sin.

Accordingly, from the Scriptures I recognize him as unlike us; from the Scriptures, recognize him with me as like us. He is not unlike us for the same reason that he is like us; the one statement has one cause, and the other another cause. Yet let us demonstrate both.

Christ is unlike a human being because he is God, for it is written of him that he is “God blessed above all, forever” (Rom. IX, 5). And Christ is like a human being because he is human, since it is likewise written of him: “The mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (Gal. III, 19).

Christ is unlike a sinner because he is always holy; and Christ is like a sinner because “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and condemned sin in the flesh because of sin.” Christ is unlike a human being born through intercourse, insofar as he was born from a virgin; but Christ is like a human being born, insofar as he too was born from a woman, to whom it was said: “What will be born from you as holy will be called the Son of God” (Matt. I, 20; Luke I, 35).

Christ is unlike a human being who died because of his sin, insofar as he was without sin and died by his own power; but again Christ is like a dead human being, insofar as he too died a true bodily death.

This is the temptation by which he was tempted. He suffered the persecution of many; he received spitting; he was accused; he endured insult; he suffered slander; he was rejected by his own people; finally, he was crucified.

“According to the likeness,” he says, “without sin.” When he says “in the likeness of flesh,” he does not mean that the likeness of an imagined flesh was in him, but that he assumed true flesh. Why, then, did he say “in the likeness of flesh”? The nature that he assumed is like our flesh, but he had none of the sin that our flesh contracted from its parents.

For original sin was of such a kind in the flesh of the first man that from it both punishment and remedy could arise. Sin and punishment exist in the whole human race, except in Christ, in whom there was salvation and remedy. The sinful flesh was not so prejudged that a remedy could not arise from it. The power of God foreknew how, from the same substance, justice, equity, mercy, and devotion could come forth.

“Let us therefore approach with confidence the throne of grace, so that we may obtain mercy and find grace for timely help.” Let us therefore approach with confidence—that is, let us approach through faith to his throne of grace. Let us have confidence that, although we are sinners, we can be reconciled through his grace, provided that we produce fruits worthy of repentance and hold firm faith to the end. But now our high priest, Jesus the Son, sits upon the throne of grace; he is ready to forgive our sins at the opportune time of help. The opportune time is the time of his help and mercy, as this outstanding teacher said elsewhere: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI, 2). And the prophet, signifying this same opportune time of help long beforehand, said: “At an opportune time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you” (Isa. XLIX, 8). Even now, for sinners to find mercy after baptism, if they have repented, is the work of him who sits upon the throne of grace. [Col. 0753A] But that he was made high priest for us is a great indication of the humility that he assumed from our nature—not of his substance, which he possesses eternally with the Father. To him let us bring our faith, together with confidence in his goodness, at this opportune time, while he sits upon the throne of grace and grants everything that may contribute to our salvation. Now is the time of gifts; let no one despair of himself. Let us fear his throne of equity when he comes to judge all things according to justice. Then will be the time of despair for those unwilling to turn to the seat of grace, when the bridal chamber will be closed, and only those who bring lamps shining with good works will remain with the bridegroom.

**(CHAP. V.)** “For every high priest taken from among human beings is appointed on behalf of human beings in matters relating to God.” Blessed Paul now wishes to show that this Testament is much better than the Old, because nothing in it is imaginary—as, for example, no bodily temple, no carnal victims, no legal observances—but everything is higher and more perfect, since the whole meaning of this Testament consists in spiritual things. But because spiritual matters do not introduce the weak to faith in the same way as bodily matters, he began his discussion with bodily things, saying: “For every high priest taken from among human beings is appointed on behalf of human beings.” He first defines what a high priest is, and shows what belongs to the high priest, what his ministry is, and what the signs of the high priesthood are: namely, “that he may offer gifts and sacrifices of propitiation, and that he may be able to sympathize with those who are ignorant [Col. 0753C] and erring, since he himself also is surrounded by weakness.” It was necessary to establish faith through earthly excellences, so that they might reach higher spiritual realities and, from the customary practice of the priests under the law, be led to something higher—that is, to Christ’s priesthood—since they were still weak and almost carnal.

The duty of the high priest, therefore, is to stand between God and the people and to entreat God on behalf of the people’s sins. This is what Christ did: offering himself for our sins, always living to intercede for us—once taken from among human beings, but always interceding on behalf of human beings. Here the Apostle sets down certain things Christ has in common with priests and certain things that are higher. Thus, what he says, “Every high priest taken from among human beings,” is common; so also, “is appointed on behalf of human beings,” and “to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.” This too is common, but not in its entirety. The remaining point is not common: “He is able to sympathize with those who sin in ignorance.” This is already an excellence, about which he discussed more fully above in the earlier statement. Therefore he added: “And because of this he ought to offer for sins on behalf of himself just as on behalf of the people.” This applies more to the legal priests than to Christ, unless someone should say that Christ and the Church are one body, and that when he offers for the Church, he also offers for its members. But this interpretation may appear forced.

Next he begins to discuss [Col. 0754A] how one ought to approach the priesthood: “No one,” he says, “takes the honor for himself, but the one who is called by God, just as Aaron was.” Here too he strikes at priests desirous of honor and eager for the priesthood, not for the salvation of the people but for worldly ambition. Aaron, therefore, was called by God through the sign of the flowering staff; it was shown that he had been chosen by God as priest, and this was also demonstrated by the burning of those who wished to envy his high priesthood.

“So also Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest, but the one who said to him: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’” This is what he himself says in the Gospel: “For I have not come from myself, but he sent me” (John VIII, 42). And again: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing; it is my Father who glorifies me” (ibid., 54). It should be noted [Col. 0754B] that *glorify*, *honor*, and *make glorious* are three words but one reality, expressed in Greek as *doxain* [Note: [Col. 0753D] From the verb δοξάζομαι, “I am glorified,” and δόξα, “glory.”]; because of the variety of translators, however, it has been rendered differently in Latin. What is called “I glorify” in the Gospel, the Apostle here calls “making glorious.”

The Son was therefore glorified by the Father when, after he had been baptized, the Father’s voice was heard from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17; Luke III, 22). This making-glorious, or glorification, had been foretold long beforehand through the prophet, inspired by the Holy Spirit: “The Lord said to me: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’” (Ps. II, 7). “The Lord” signifies the Father. Let us attend to the words he used: “He said to me, ‘You are my Son,’” which he was also going to say to him after his baptism: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” Thus, so that you might understand Christ as one person and the only-begotten Son of God, he added: “Today I have begotten you.” This has nothing in common with the others who are called sons and who are called priests, of whom it is said: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’” (Ps. LXXXI, 6; John X, 34). Rather, it belongs entirely and uniquely to the only-begotten Son.

“Just as he also says in another place: ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek’” (Ps. CIX, 4). To whom was this said—who is according to the order of Melchizedek? To no one else, but only to our high priest, that is, Christ. For all the priests who existed at the time when this prophecy was uttered were under the law. Writing to the Hebrews, the Apostle inserted this discussion. They could point to no other person at all except our high priest, that is, Christ.

According to the legal commandments, Melchizedek was not a priest; rather, he was one according to the dignity of a distinctive priesthood, offering bread and wine to God, not the blood of brute animals. Christ was made a priest according to the order of this priesthood—not a temporal priest, but an eternal one. To him was said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” All the others were priests under the law; he alone was according to the order of Melchizedek, because he was born from a virginal womb before the morning star [Col. 0755A]—not according to the fact that, as God, he was born from the Father and was with the Father, coeternal with the one who begot him and consubstantial with him—but as priest because of the flesh he assumed and because of the sacrifice that he offered for us, received from us: namely, his flesh and blood. Concerning this sacrifice he himself says in the Gospel: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you do not have life in yourselves” (John VI, 54).

But in this flesh and blood let the human mind conceive nothing bloody and nothing corruptible, as the Apostle says: “For whoever eats the body of the Lord unworthily eats judgment upon himself” (I Cor. XI, 29). Rather, let it conceive a life-giving and saving substance, granted to us in bread and wine; when these are received worthily, through them the forgiveness of sins and possession of the kingdom of God are bestowed upon us. [Col. 0755B] Melchizedek, the most righteous king, established the order of this sacrifice through a mystical likeness when he offered the fruits of bread and wine to the Lord. For it is clear that the sacrifices of sheep and cattle, which belonged to the order of Aaron and not of Melchizedek, have perished; but this institution remains, the one celebrated throughout the world in the distribution of the sacraments.

Christ is called priest above all because he offered himself once for us to be sacrificed, just as Scripture speaks once of Melchizedek and of his priesthood. When “forever” is said, the Lord Christ himself is signified, who remains in everlasting glory.

“Who, in the days of his flesh, offered prayers and supplications with a loud cry and tears to the one who was able to save him from death, and was heard because of his reverence.” Here the Apostle more clearly expresses what our high priest accomplished in his priesthood, saying: “Who, in the days of his flesh.” The days of our Lord Jesus Christ’s flesh are the days in which he assumed flesh, in which he was tempted and suffered, in which he offered prayers and supplications to the one who was able to save him from death. Everything Christ did in the flesh consists of prayers and supplications for the sins of the human race.

The holy shedding of his blood is the loud cry in which he was heard by God the Father, because of his reverence in undergoing that same passion without sin for the sake of our salvation. Though he had no sin, he was made sin for us—that is, an offering for our sins. He accomplished all this with great reverence and perfect love: he who first loved us and handed himself over for us as an acceptable sacrifice to God. He was therefore heard by God because he offered God an acceptable sacrifice—that is, himself.

What is said here is therefore like what is read in the Gospel, that he “offered prayers and supplications with a loud cry and tears to the one who was able to save him from death,” since there he is read to have said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me. Nevertheless, not my will but yours be done” (Matt. XXVI, 39; Mark XIV, 36; Luke XXII, 42). For he did not come to do his own will, but the will of the one who sent him (John V, 30). He placed the will of the Father’s dispensation above the will of his flesh, in order to show in himself the true nature [Col. 0756A] of our humanity.

Blessed Paul says here that he poured out prayers and supplications, not from fear of death but for the sake of our salvation. Hence, in another passage also, he says that the blood of Christ cried out for us more effectively than the blood of Abel, which cries from the earth to the Father to accuse his brother’s crime.

“And although he was the Son of God, he learned obedience from what he suffered; and, having been perfected, he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him, having been called by God a high priest according to the order of Melchizedek.” I think enough has been said above about the likeness of Melchizedek’s priesthood. Now let us see what the Apostle wishes to be understood by saying: “Although he was the Son of God, he learned obedience from what he suffered.” This obedience, which he says the Son of God learned—that is, voluntarily assumed—he also demonstrates elsewhere, where he says: “He became obedient” to the Father “unto death, even death on a cross; therefore God also exalted him” (Phil. II, 8).

In saying, “and, having been perfected, he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him,” “perfected” means “made perfect.” He shows how great is the gain of his passion, which is sufficient for everlasting salvation to all believers. Therefore, if the obedience of the Son is the cause of human salvation, how great is our necessity to obey God, so that we may be found worthy of the salvation that he granted us through his own Son?

“Concerning this we have much to say, and it is difficult to explain [Col. 0756C], since you have become weak in hearing.” He gives the reason why what he had undertaken to say about the incarnate Son was difficult to interpret: namely, because they were weak and of fragile understanding in grasping the deep mysteries of God. Although, considering the time, they ought to have become teachers, they had again come to need someone to teach them the first elements of God’s utterances, and had become people needing milk rather than solid food. The difficulty of interpretation lay in their slowness, not in apostolic wisdom, to which the mysteries hidden for ages had been revealed, as he demonstrates fully in the Epistle to the Ephesians.

Then he added: “For although you ought to be teachers by this time, you again need someone to teach you the first elements of the utterances of God, and you have become people needing milk, not solid food.” He is therefore speaking to those who, through the law and the prophets, ought to have possessed an exercised understanding of Christ’s coming and of the grace brought through him to believers. If they had believed, they could also have become teachers of others through the mysteries of God given to them.

But now they have become like infants to whom the first elements of letters are handed for reading. Whereas they ought to have been strong in faith and eager for knowledge, ready to receive the customary food of wisdom belonging to the mature, they have now become people needing milk. He calls milk a humble discourse, which he testifies they needed because they could not ascend to the higher secrets of God’s mysteries.

For example, one who cannot understand what the Gospel says—“The Word became flesh” (John I, 14)—how can he reach the height of that statement where it says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”? (ibid., 1.)

“For everyone who partakes of milk is inexperienced in the word of righteousness, for he is a child. But solid food belongs to the mature, to those who, through habit, have their faculties exercised for discerning good and evil.” The palate distinguishes the flavors of foods; the soul, however, tests the discourses of various teachings. Concerning these he says later in this Epistle: “Do not be led astray by various teachings” (Hebr. XIII, 9). Just as an infant does not know how to distinguish one food from another, and often suffers harm by taking harmful things if an elder does not restrain him, so every unlearned person, not knowing how to distinguish teachings, is easily deceived and endangered on the path of error.

What milk and solid food are in relation to each other, the unlearned and the wise are in relation to each other. Just as milk suits infants and solid food suits those mature in age, so a humble discourse suits the unlearned, while it is fitting for the wise who appear to have exercised faculties to know the mystery of God’s secret things. How, then, can our faculties become exercised? Certainly through practice and frequent reading of the holy Scriptures. Hence the Psalmist calls blessed the person who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night (Ps. I, 2).

**(CHAP. VI.)** “Therefore, leaving behind the beginning of Christ’s discourse, let us advance toward perfection” [Note: [Col. 0757D] The Vulgate has *perfectiora*, “more perfect things.”]. Therefore—that is, because you ought to have faculties exercised in the law of the Lord—let us leave behind the discourse concerning the beginning of Christ. What is the discourse concerning the beginning of Christ except the beginning of faith? Just as one who is brought to the teaching of letters must first hear the elements, so a Christian must first of all be instructed in the catholic faith, which is the foundation of our salvation.

But if someone needs to be taught about the faith, he does not yet possess the foundation. This foundation must be firm and fixed in the Christian’s heart, so that from it he may become worthy to be transferred to the perfection of the other virtues. But if someone has heard the word of truth and has been baptized, and after several years needs to hear again about the faith—because he must still be taught about faith, the resurrection, and the future age—he does not yet possess the foundation; he is seeking again the beginning of Christianity.

Because faith is the foundation, while the other things are superstructures, as the blessed Apostle shows in the words that follow, saying: “Not again laying the foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith in God.” We call that person perfect who possesses a rightly ordered life together with faith. If either of these is lacking, he will not be perfect. If both are lacking, he may rightly be called a child; and just as an infant is taught letters, so this person must again be instructed in the faith.

He secretly wishes to weaken the law and call his hearers to the grace of Christ. Whoever is going toward virtue must first reject the wickedness of sins, [Col. 0758A] cleanse the works of death through repentance, and thus approach God.

“Of the doctrine of baptisms, of the laying on of hands, and of the resurrection of the dead and eternal judgment.” It is not enough for repentance to cleanse sinners unless they are immediately baptized, as blessed Peter is read to have replied to the people in the Acts of the Apostles: “Repent, brothers, and let each of you be baptized in the name of the Lord” (Acts II, 38). For what a human being cannot accomplish by himself he can receive through God’s grace in baptism.

What does “the doctrine of baptisms” mean? It should not be understood as though there were many baptisms, but as referring to one, because just as there is one faith, so there is one baptism (Eph. IV, 5). He said “baptisms” because of the variety of those who receive it. “The laying on of hands” is that by which the Holy Spirit is believed to be received; after baptism it is customarily performed by bishops for the confirmation of unity in the Church of Christ.

When these matters have been perfectly received in the Church, one must possess faith in the resurrection and in the future judgment. To live like the angels and to lack nothing of the things belonging to this life is the promise of this life made to us through the Holy Spirit. The fruit of this promise is the presence of that same life. These two things—that is, faith and judgment—remain for the one who has been baptized once; he is not to be baptized again.

“And this we will do, if God permits.” In this faith of baptism, resurrection, and future judgment, with God’s permission we will fully instruct you.

[Col. 0758C] So that no one might in any way suppose that a second or third baptism could be performed after sins, he immediately adds: “For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have also tasted the heavenly gift, who have become participants in the Holy Spirit, who have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and then have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to contempt.”

“It is impossible,” he says—not difficult. By saying “impossible,” he consigns to despair the possibility of their being baptized a second time: for impossible is what cannot be done, whereas difficult is what, although laborious, can nevertheless be done. “Once,” he says, “you were enlightened through the grace of the Holy Spirit and tasted the heavenly gift”—that is, you received the forgiveness of sins [Col. 0758D]—“and became participants in the Holy Spirit” through the distribution of God’s gifts, which the same blessed Paul enumerates in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, XII, 8–10; “and you tasted the good word of God.” Here he means evangelical teaching. “And you came to know the powers of the age to come.” What is the power of the age to come except the resurrection and the blessed life promised to the saints?

You received and came to know all these things through the teaching of faith and the grace of God, having been enlightened through baptism. Know with complete certainty that, if you fall again into sins, it is impossible for you to be renewed again to repentance. He said “to repentance,” that is, “through repentance.” [Col. 0759A] What, then? Is repentance excluded after baptism? Certainly not. But renewal cannot take place a second time through the washing of sacred baptism. He said “renewed,” that is, “made new.” For sacred baptism makes a person new, concerning which the prophet says: “Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. CII, 5). Its power—that is, the power of sacred baptism—is established in the cross and burial of Christ.

Therefore he added: “Crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to contempt.” This means that our old person was crucified together with Christ, as he says elsewhere: “For we have been made conformed to his death” (Rom. VIII, 29). And again: “You were buried with him through baptism into death” (Col. II, 12).

For just as it is impossible for Christ to be crucified a second time—and this is what it means to hold him up to contempt—so the person who thinks he can be baptized a second time demands that Christ be crucified a second time, although he was crucified once, died, rose victorious over death, and ascended into heaven in triumphal glory.

Just as Christ died once in the flesh on the cross, so we die once in baptism—not in the flesh, but to sin. And just as he cannot die again, so we cannot be baptized again, except perhaps through the tears of repentance, not through the washing of regeneration.

“So,” you say, “there is no repentance?” There is. But there is no other baptism. Repentance exists and possesses great strength, even for one who is deeply overwhelmed by sins. If he wishes, he can be freed from the burden of sins and bring the one in danger to safety, even if he has reached the very bottom [Col. 0759C] of iniquity.

This is evident from many testimonies. “Does not the one who falls rise again?” (Ps. XL, 9.) “Or will the one who turns away not return?” (Ps. XIII, 7.) What, then, is this medicine of repentance, and how is it prepared?

First, by reproving one’s own sins. He says: “I have not hidden my iniquity, and I will declare my iniquity against myself to the Lord, and you have taken away the impiety of my heart.” Second, by lamenting one’s sins with great humility and thereafter producing fruits worthy of repentance, so that one may never again fall into the same sins. Then one who possesses worldly means should begin to redeem himself through many acts of almsgiving, as it is written: “A man’s riches are the redemption of his soul” (Prov. XIII, 8). Finally, one must be angry with no one, return no evil for evil, and forgive all who sin against him, as the Truth himself says: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke VI, 37).

“For the land that drinks in the rain often falling upon it and produces suitable vegetation for those by whom it is cultivated receives a blessing from God. But if it produces thorns and thistles, it is rejected and near to a curse, and its end is burning.” Let us hear the words of God with trembling. These are not Paul’s threats, nor are they the words of a human being; they belong to the Holy Spirit, to Christ speaking through Paul.

Here he makes a comparison between the soul making progress in the teaching of God and the soul neglecting its salvation. [Col. 0760A] He compares the soul making progress to fertile earth watered by heavenly rains and flourishing with the blossoms of holy shoots, saying: “For the land that drinks in the rain often falling upon it.” Here he makes clear that those to whom he was speaking had received and absorbed the word of heavenly teaching, and had received it repeatedly through the law and the prophets, yet even so had not become ready to produce shoots of faith.

He adds something further about the good land into which the seed of God’s word fell: “Producing,” he says, “suitable vegetation.” Nothing is as suitable as faith in the Son of God and an excellent life. Such land receives a blessing from God, so that it may bear thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and even a hundredfold fruit (Matt. XIII, 23).

It should also be noted that all abundance in the crops of the earth and in the fruits of trees can advance the cultivators’ purposes in no other way than through God’s blessing. It was not the work of farmers to awaken the earth to fruitfulness, but the command of God, as the same Paul says elsewhere: “I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth” (I Cor. III, 6). He appropriately offered this example concerning a soul flourishing in virtues through God’s blessing.

Immediately he added another example [Note: [Col. 0759D] A Greek word: that is, “an example.”] concerning the person who neglects his salvation, saying: “But if it produces thorns and thistles, it is rejected and near to a curse, and its end is burning.”

Who is clean from these thorns? Even if we were clean, we still ought not to be presumptuous, but to fear and tremble lest the thorns of sins perhaps spring up in us. [Col. 0760C] How could a soul or flesh full of thorns be proud? Would it not need to uproot them with the greatest care?

What are the thorns? Let us hear Christ speaking about thorns: the anxiety of this world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word and render it fruitless (Matt. XIII, 29). He said “producing thorns,” not “generating” them; such a person is near to a curse. O what consolation this statement contains! He says “near to a curse,” not “cursed.” The person who has not yet fallen under the curse but is near to it can also be brought far away from it. He not only consoles them in this way, but also in what follows. For he did not say: “The rejected land, being near to a curse, will be burned.” What did he say? “Its end is burning.” [Col. 0760D]

This burning will occur only if each person remains in his sins to the end. For on whatever day the sinner turns back, “he shall surely live and shall not die” (Ezek. XVIII, 21). But if we cut away the thorns, through repentance we can enjoy a thousand blessings and become approved, sharing in God’s blessing.

After rebuking them sufficiently, terrifying and striking them, he again cares for them, so that he will not make them despair. He neither flatters them in everything nor strikes them in everything. Nor do we say this as though we considered you full of thorns, but because we fear that you may become such. It is better to terrify you with words, so that you may not suffer through the facts themselves.

“But we are confident about you, beloved, of better things [Col. 0761A] and things nearer to salvation, although we speak in this way.” Since blessed Paul had no present grounds on which to praise those to whom he wrote, he begins to commend them in terms of future hope, saying: “We are confident about you, brothers, of better things and things nearer to salvation, although we speak in this way.” It is as though he had said: We are confident concerning you of the very best things, and of things that advance your salvation. We did not mean that what I said above about the rejected land and its nearness to burning applies to you, because we believe better things about you.

He also brought their past to mind, so that through their past he might draw them toward every good thing. Therefore he added: “For God is not unjust, so as to forget your work and the love that you showed in his name, when you ministered to the saints and continue to minister.” [Col. 0761B] See how he revived and strengthened their souls by recalling ancient things to them; he made them understand that God had not forgotten them or his past benefits toward them. For it is necessary that the person who lacks hope for the future fall into sin.

Then he urges them to hope for future things in every respect. For who could strengthen someone concerning future things if he despairs of God’s present benefits, believing that he has nothing from God? He makes a similar reproach to the Galatians (V, 7), saying: “You were running well. Who bewitched you?” And again: “Did you suffer so many things without cause?” (Gal. III, 4.) Yet, to soften the same statement, he immediately adds: “If indeed it was without cause.”

So also here he tempered his statement, saying: “For God is not unjust, so as to forget your work,” since you showed such love toward the saints. For we wish you to be imitators of those who through faith and patience “inherited the promises” [Note: [Col. 0761] On the basis of what follows and of the text of Ambrosiaster, *haereditaturi* (“who will inherit”) should be read.]

Why he desired their salvation he shows in the following argument, saying: “For we desire each one of you to show the same diligence toward the fulfillment of hope to the end, so that you may not become sluggish.” “We desire,” he says, “that you conduct yourselves not only in words but also in virtues—not as though we were blaming your former conduct, but warning you to be concerned about the future; that is, whatever sort of people you were at first, we desire you to be such now and in the future.”

He did not say “I wish,” which expresses the authority of teaching, but used language expressive of paternal affection. [Col. 0761D] This is what he means: We desire each one of you to have the same diligence that you once possessed, directed toward the fulfillment of hope—that is, the diligence you ought to have for the eternal resurrection.

“But imitators of those who through faith and patience will inherit the promises.” He urges his hearers to await God’s promises and the inheritances he promised to his saints with unfailing faith and perfect patience.

He also seeks to strengthen this more firmly through examples, saying: “For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom he could swear, he swore by himself, saying: ‘Blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you.’ And thus, having patiently endured, he obtained the promise.”

The wisdom of blessed Paul is remarkable. Alternately he raises those to whom he writes through praise; alternately he terrifies them through the warnings of the preceding history, so that they would not be faithless or insufficiently trusting in God’s promise; and alternately he urges them through the examples of others toward patience and faith, so that they may believe without doubt not only God when he speaks but also when he swears by himself.

Although he had many examples of saints who through patience inherited God’s promises, he especially brings forward faithful Abraham, both because of the dignity of his person and because this occurred in him in an especially significant way. By patiently enduring, he obtained the promises in his children—not only the promises of the past, which were fulfilled among the people of God, but still more the future promises concerning children [Col. 0762B] whom God’s goodness raised up from among the nations and made children of Abraham in faith.

Patience, I say, brought about the promise for the one who heard and awaited the promised inheritance; the fainthearted and unbelieving did not obtain it, just as a very great multitude of them perished in the desert. How impious it is not to believe God when he swears! God swore by himself because he had no one greater by whom he could swear.

Here the person of God the Father may be understood in this oath, since he promised the patriarch concerning his Son, saying: “And in your seed all the nations of the earth will be blessed” (Gen. XXII, 18). He does not say “in your seeds,” as blessed Paul demonstrates in another Epistle (Gal. III, 16), but “in your seed”—that is, in Christ.

Christ himself also swears in the Gospel, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you.” He too swears by himself, because he likewise had no one greater by whom he could swear. “Blessing I will bless you”—this can be understood as referring to the stars of heaven, by which the saints who were to come from his seed are signified. “Multiplying I will multiply you”—this can be understood as referring to the sand of the sea, by which the sinful people of that nation can be signified. For Scripture records the Lord saying both, when it says: “Your seed will be like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the shore of the sea” (Gen. XXII, 17).

“For human beings swear by one greater than themselves, and the end of every dispute among them, for confirmation, is an oath.” If, then, human beings are to be trusted concerning the future—although the prophet says of them, “Every human being is a liar” (Ps. CXV, 2)—how much more ought God’s oath to be believed, since he is truth and can neither be deceived nor lie?

Human beings swear by one greater than themselves, and the end of every dispute among them, for confirmation, is an oath—as though he were saying: Through this the discussion of the entire dispute is resolved, not merely of some single matter but of the whole dispute. It was indeed necessary to believe God without an oath, but he says that God swore.

“Accordingly, wishing to show more abundantly to the heirs of the promise the immutability of his purpose.” Therefore he also mentions this promise, which has been made common to us: “He interposed an oath.” Since among human beings something appears trustworthy when an oath has been introduced into their disputes, he did this. Yet it is not the same thing for a human being to swear by himself and for God to swear. A human being does not possess authority over himself, but God possesses authority over all that exists.

Because the human race is unbelieving, however, he stooped to our level. Just as he swears for our sake, although it is unworthy of him not to be believed, so above it was said: “He learned from what he suffered,” since human beings consider it especially worthy of belief when someone passes through experience into faith.

“So that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we may have the strongest consolation—we who have fled for refuge to hold fast the hope set before us, which we have as a safe and firm anchor of the soul.” He speaks of two things, signifying the promises of God the Father concerning his Son and the Son’s coming into this world for our salvation.

The hope set before us is the truth of the events that were promised to the patriarchs and fulfilled, so that from things already accomplished we may believe in things that are still to come. “This hope,” he says, “we have as a safe and firm anchor of the soul.” Just as an anchor, once cast, does not allow a ship to be carried about, even if the winds shake it, but makes the ship firm, so faith strengthened by hope brings us into the vision of the realities that we presently grasp through faith and hope.

Therefore he added, saying: “And entering even into the interior of the veil.” For a storm and heavy rain shake a vessel, but an anchor does not permit it to sink. So too our hope, which we have fixed in the interior of the veil, cannot be submerged by any unbelief, if we truthfully say with the Prophet: “Cast your care upon God, and he himself will nourish you (Ps. LIV, 23).” If we did not possess this hope, we would be wholly submerged, not only in spiritual matters but also in bodily ones, because, as the Apostle says, “he who ploughs ploughs in hope; and all our labor is comforted by hope of whatever reward (I Cor. IX, 10).” Hope penetrates the interior of the veil when it believes the heavenly realities without any doubt, and hopes and loves them; by its works it shows what it loves, what it believes, and what it hopes.

And in order to add a firmer hope for us, he continued: “Where Jesus, the forerunner, entered for us, having been made High Priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” A forerunner is the forerunner of someone, as John was Christ’s. For he did not simply say, “he entered,” but “where the forerunner entered for us”—where, without doubt, we ought to follow our forerunner. A forerunner and those who follow ought indeed to be on the same road. This, however, is said of him according to the flesh, who offered himself as a sacrifice to God for a pleasing fragrance. He was made High Priest according to the order of Melchizedek. Therefore those whose High Priest he is ought also to be better; and whatever difference there is between Aaron and Christ, there is, in a certain sense, the same difference between Jews and Christians.

The sacrifices too are superior. Let us offer such things, namely, as can be offered in that heavenly sanctuary—not sheep and oxen, not blood and fat. All these things have been abolished, and in their place “rational worship” has been introduced (Rom. XII, 1). What is rational worship? It is what is offered to God through the soul and through the spirit. “God is spirit,” he says, “and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth (John IV, 24).” What is it to worship God in spirit, except in charity, in perfect faith, in undoubted hope, and in the holy virtues of the soul, which the Apostle abundantly enumerates elsewhere?

## (CHAP. VII.)

“Now this Melchizedek”—Melchi means “king,” while sedech means “of righteousness.” And what else is “king of righteousness” than our Lord Jesus Christ, of whom it was already said above: “You loved righteousness and hated iniquity (Ps. XLIV, 8)”?

“King of Salem.” He also received this name from the city that he inhabited. For Salem means “of peace,” which again pertains to Christ. He himself makes us righteous; he himself made peace between the things in heaven and the things on earth; he is our peace, “and made both one” (Eph. II, 14).

“Priest of the Most High God.” Melchizedek is called priest of the Most High God to distinguish him from other gods, so that he might be understood to be the priest of God the Creator, not of idols.

“Who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings.” The Hebrews report that this man was Shem, the son of Noah, and that at the time of Abraham’s birth he was 392 years old [Note: [Col. 0763D] Ambrosiaster says 290. We may incidentally observe here that this opinion concerning Melchizedek—namely, that he was the same person as Shem—also has many supporters among modern writers. If you desire further information, consult P. Calmet’s *Historical and Biblical Dictionary*, under the entry “Melchizedek,” [Col. 0764D] where you will find almost all the opinions and their authors on this matter.], and that at the time of Abraham’s death he was 565 years old. Thus he survived Abraham by forty-five years, after which all the days of his life amounted to six hundred years.

It is not surprising, then, if Melchizedek went out to meet Abraham in victory, offered bread and wine for the refreshment both of Abraham himself and of his warriors, blessed him—as he owed this to his great-grandson by the right of fatherhood—and received from him tithes of the spoils and of the victory. But there is no need to labor at length over this literal interpretation, because it has been sufficiently explained in the commentaries on the book of Genesis that I wrote some years ago concerning spirit and letter [Col. 0764D] [Note: [Col. 0764D] He asserts that he wrote commentaries on the book of Genesis. Would that we possessed so great a treasure!].

“And he blessed him.” For the one who blesses is greater than the one who is blessed. Hence the priests born from Abraham’s offspring blessed their brothers—that is, the children of Israel, to whom those priests gave tithes according to the command of the law—as persons truly greater and more eminent than themselves.

“To whom Abraham divided a tithe of everything.” Abraham would in no way have given tithes to the foreigner Melchizedek, an uncircumcised priest, unless Melchizedek’s honor had been very great.

Then he introduces another distinction, saying: “Without father, without mother, without genealogy.” Because his name is introduced suddenly, and it is not at all stated from what stock he was born, nor is anything reported or indicated about the beginning or end of his life, either before or afterward, he therefore adds: “Having neither beginning of days nor end of life.”

How did he have neither beginning of days nor end of life? How else than because Scripture does not narrate his genealogy, as we have already said above? Christ likewise, by his very nature, is without beginning and without end. Just as we know neither the beginning of this man’s days nor the end of his life because they were not written, so we know neither the beginning nor the end of the Son of God. He alone was begotten from the Father without a mother according to divinity; he alone was born from a mother without a father according to humanity; and he is also the eternal Priest, to whom it is said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

“He has been likened to the Son of God.” In this passage, likeness is not used for equality but for figure. Just as in images something similar and something dissimilar are represented—the likeness lies in the arrangement of the colors, while the difference is clearly shown—so there are shadow and truth, figure and the thing signified.

“He remains a priest perpetually.” The Apostle wants this to be understood of Christ the Lord, not of Melchizedek [Col. 0765C], because Melchizedek died and was not a priest forever. His figure, however, lives forever in Christ.

Hence it follows: “Now contemplate how great this man is, to whom even the patriarch Abraham gave tithes from the chief things.” The great patriarch Abraham gave tithes of his substance to the priest Melchizedek after the blessing, knowing that a priesthood was destined to arise spiritually among the Gentiles, better than the Levitical priesthood that was to arise from him in Israel. The priesthood of the Church, possessing the foreskin, was destined to bless the priesthood of the Synagogue, which possessed circumcision.

The Apostle Paul impresses this upon the Jews to whom he sent this Epistle and says: Look and understand how great this priest Melchizedek is, who bore the figure of Christ; to him so great a patriarch as Abraham gave tithes from the chief things—that is, from the better things that he possessed.

“And indeed those who receive the priesthood from the sons of Levi have a commandment to take tithes from the people according to the law, that is, from their brothers, although they themselves also came from the loins of Abraham.” Such, he says, is the excellence of the priesthood that even those who were like their forebears and had the same forefather were nevertheless judged far better than those from whom they received tithes. And although the priests of the tribe of Levi take tithes from their brothers, this man who took tithes from Abraham was not a priest from the tribe of Levi. Therefore he would in no way have given tithes to a foreigner unless Melchizedek’s honor had been very great.

“But his genealogy is not counted among them,” that is, among the sons of Levi. Melchizedek, as he says above, was “without mother and without genealogy.” In a significant way, Christ’s generation according to divinity is not counted among them, in accordance with the saying: “Who will declare his generation?” He took tithes from Abraham and blessed the one who had the promises. “Without any contradiction, the lesser is blessed by the better” (Isa. LIII, 8).

In these two respects Melchizedek’s priesthood surpasses the entire priesthood of the Old Testament: first, because he was worthy to receive tithes from Abraham, the father of all the priests; and because he blessed the one who had received the promises. In this way Melchizedek could not more openly prefigure Christ in the Old Testament.

The great patriarch gave tithes of all his substance to the priest Melchizedek after the blessing, knowing spiritually, as we have said, that a priesthood among the Gentiles was destined to be better than the Levitical priesthood that was to arise from him in Israel, and that the priesthood of the Church, possessing the foreskin, was destined to bless the priesthood of the Synagogue, which possessed circumcision.

“By the better he is blessed,” that is, by the greater. Blessing is an abundance. Therefore no one can bless unless he is greater, and no one can be blessed unless he is lesser. You see how great the difference is between Abraham and Melchizedek, who bore the figure of our Savior. Melchizedek is shown to be better than Abraham, and his priesthood better than that of the Levites. Christ is shown to be better than Melchizedek, and than all the prophets, patriarchs, and saints. These were holy as human beings; he is God and human being. They were adopted sons; he is the proper Son.

He scatters and launches this distinction throughout the whole text of this Epistle, wishing to demonstrate how great the difference is between Christ and the patriarchs or prophets. For this reason he chose Melchizedek, because, as we have already said, he bore the figure of our Savior more openly and clearly. And, as he himself affirms, “without any contradiction, the lesser,” Abraham, “will be blessed by the better,” that is, by Melchizedek. Abraham gave tithes, which pertains to the priesthood of Melchizedek. Melchizedek in turn blessed him, which belongs to superior excellence.

In writing this, and in examining the matter, the Apostle strongly condemned and excluded Jewish arguments. Therefore he said: “For you have become weak (Heb. V, 11),” because he wanted to overturn this, so that they would not glory in those things. Such is the wisdom of the Apostle Paul. He first makes a great disturbance, and then proceeds to the matters he wants to demonstrate, saying: “And here indeed mortal men receive tithes.”

By “mortal men” he means the priests, the sons of Aaron from the tribe of Levi, because they were mortal. “But there he bears witness that he lives.” “There,” that is, in the passage where the priesthood of Melchizedek is mentioned, he bears witness that he lives when he says: “You are a priest forever,” and so forth.

“And, so to speak, through Abraham even Levi, who received tithes, was tithed.” “He received tithes” means Levi received them from his brothers; he “was tithed,” namely, “in the loins of Abraham,” because Abraham gave tithes to Melchizedek.

“For he was still in the loins of his father when Melchizedek met him.” How was he still in the loins when Melchizedek met him? Levi was present in Abraham, although he had not yet been born.

[Note: [Col. 0767D] At the beginning of this line the seventh reading is recorded, although no other six readings are noted anywhere.]

“If, therefore, perfection was through the Levitical priesthood—for under it the people received the law....” Here he begins to show the difference between one law and another, and between one priesthood and another: namely, between the law of Moses and the law of the Gospel, and between the priesthood of Aaron and the priesthood of Christ. He establishes that everything received by that people was given symbolically. The Apostle understands the tabernacle, the sacrifices, and all the other things figuratively throughout the text of this Epistle.

When he says, “the people received the law under it,” he means under Moses and Aaron, their descendants, who were to come in the fourth generation.

“What further need was there for another priest to arise according to the order of Melchizedek, and not to be called according to the order of Aaron?”

“For when the priesthood is transferred, it is necessary that a transfer of the law also take place.” By the transferred priesthood he means the transfer from Levi and Aaron to Christ; that is, he excluded the priesthood of Aaron. For he would certainly not say that a priest should arise according to the order of Melchizedek if that priesthood were the better one. If, therefore, that priesthood must be introduced, it is necessary that the law also be transferred. A priest cannot exist without a covenant, without a law, and without commandments. The priesthood has been transferred; therefore the law also has been transferred.

“For the one concerning whom these things are said belongs to another tribe, from which no one attended the altar. For it is evident that our Lord arose from Judah, a tribe concerning which Moses said nothing about priests.” “The one concerning whom these things are said”—that is, Christ—is the one in whom the law was transferred, as he has already said; he says that the tribe also was transferred. The tribe likewise had to be changed.

And how was the priesthood transferred? From tribe to tribe, from the priestly tribe to the royal tribe, so that the same tribe might be both royal and priestly. Observe the mystery. At first it was royal; afterward it became priestly. So too Christ was always king, but became priest when he assumed flesh. Without any priestly genealogy, he became human among humans—not from the tribe of Levi, but from the tribe of Judah, a tribe from which Moses received nothing concerning priestly commandment.

This occurred on account of the mystery of the sacrament that Christians are commanded to celebrate: not according to Aaron, with sacrifices of animals, but by offering in sacrifice the offering of bread and wine [Col. 0768A], that is, the sacrament of his body and blood.

“And it is still more evident if another priest arises according to the likeness of Melchizedek.” “Still more evident” means that he will arise not only from another tribe, but with higher honor, and manifestly according to the order of Melchizedek. Once the priesthoods are compared, Melchizedek is shown to be better than Levi, who preceded as an image of the high priesthood that Christ was destined to receive forever.

“Who was made not according to the law of a carnal commandment, but according to the power of an indissoluble life.” Christ, he says, was made priest not according to the law of a carnal precept. For the law was carnal in many respects. What is a “carnal precept”? “Circumcise the flesh,” it says; “wash the flesh; cleanse the flesh.” Its promises were long life, milk and honey, and peace. Aaron received the priesthood from this law.

Christ, he says, was made priest according to the power of an indissoluble life. He says “according to power,” not according to law. For in the law there was weakness, since the Old Testament was a shadow; therefore power could not remain in it. This life, however, is indissoluble, because it is not a figure but the truth. Therefore the Gospel is characterized not by weakness but by power and indissolubility according to that power.

“For he bears witness: ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.’” In this order of Melchizedek Christ is called priest forever, because Melchizedek offered no carnal victims, but only bread and wine. So Christ, offering to God the Father the offering of bread and wine—that is, his body and blood—we offer and receive that offering daily upon the altar.

“There is indeed a setting aside of the preceding commandment because of its weakness and uselessness. For the law brought nothing to perfection.” That setting aside is the one of which Isaiah says: “Do not continue to offer sacrifice in vain; incense is an abomination to me. I will not endure your new moon, Sabbath, and other festivals; your assemblies are wicked. My soul has hated your new moons and solemnities (Isa. I, 13).”

Some argue here concerning what he said, “because of its weakness,” for elsewhere also he shows its weakness when he says: “In what was weak through the flesh (Rom. VIII, 3).” Therefore the law itself was not made weak, but the law brought nothing to perfection, because it could neither make the obedient person perfect, nor remove sin, nor conquer death.

But why could it not fulfill this, in which it was weak through the flesh? By commanding the weak without helping them, it becomes weak. It was weak “through the flesh,” that is, through the desires of the flesh arising from sin, which a human being cannot conquer by free will alone unless accompanied by preceding grace; therefore he cannot become a doer of the law [Note: [Col. 0767D] These statements concerning grace and free will should be joined to those frequently made on the same subjects in the exposition of the Epistle to the Romans.].

And this is what the same Apostle says next: “For the law,” he says, “brought nothing to perfection.” The implied meaning is that perfection has been completed in Christ.

The statement that the law was weak and brought no one to perfection can also be understood in another way. The love of God and of one’s neighbor is commanded there, in accordance with what we read in the Gospel: the Lord answered the interpreters of the law, “The first commandment is: You shall love the Lord your God. The second, which is like it, is: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend the whole law and the prophets (Matt. XXII, 37; Mark XII, 29).”

If everything is contained in these commandments, how was perfection absent there? Because love of one’s enemies was not found established in it. Hence the Lord says: “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” [Col. 0769B] (Matt. V, 17). And afterward: “Love your enemies and do good to those who hate you (ibid., 44).” Therefore perfection is found not in that law but in the New Testament.

“But the introduction of a better hope, through which we draw near to God.” They too had hope, but not such hope. They hoped for carnal promises: namely, to possess the land in a state of favor and to suffer no evil. We, however, hope that, being pleasing to Christ, we will possess not earth but heaven.

It is better still that we should receive that life which, in the words of Paul, “no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not entered the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him (I Cor. II, 9).” It is better to abide with God, to reach his paternal throne, and to minister with the angels.

“And insofar as it is not without an oath.” How great, then, is this priesthood of Christ—or this introduction, or our hope—which is not without an oath? All those earlier things were promised, but this priesthood, confirmed with an oath, remains a great priesthood forever. Since Scripture testifies that, while God’s word remains, heaven and earth will pass away (Matt. XXIV, 35), how much more is this true when he added an oath?

“Others indeed were made priests without an oath,” and therefore their priesthood does not remain forever. Just as there are many priests who are mortal, so there is one who is immortal. Through Christ’s priesthood the better hope has been found.

“This one, however, with an oath, through him who said to him: ‘The Lord swore and will not repent; you are a priest forever.’” By saying this he shows that Christ’s priesthood remains forever. He says “with an oath” so that our human nature might more readily believe what is said.

The question arises how he can say, “The Lord swore and will not repent,” when elsewhere he says: “I repent that I made human beings on the earth (Gen. VI, 7),” and, “I repent that I made Saul king” (I Sam. XV, 11). This does not mean that God repents of anything, but that he caused those who do not fulfill his commandments to repent, just as those who did not listen to Noah repented in the Flood. Or “he will not repent” means “he will not change.”

“To such an extent Jesus became the guarantor of a better covenant” [Col. 0770A], because his priesthood remains perpetual and he himself intercedes for us.

“And indeed others became priests in greater number, because death prevented them from remaining.” Here he shows that the priesthood according to the order of Levi does not remain. For how can one who does not always live save? During the time in which he lived, he prayed for them, as we read that many others did, as in the case of Samuel. Afterward, however, they died.

“But this one, because he remains forever, has an everlasting priesthood. Hence he is also able to save forever those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them.”

This one, however, is not like the others, but saves forever. Christ’s priesthood is perpetual and gives salvation to the human race; therefore he can save forever, since he himself is eternal. Yet this applies to those who “draw near,” not to those who withdraw, “through him to God”—that is, “no one comes to the Father except through me.”

“To intercede,” not to judge, “for them”: that is, he intercedes for those who draw near, not by voice but by his presence.

“For such a one was fitting for us to have as high priest: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens.” “Such a one was fitting.” By this he does not commend our holiness, but the enormity of the iniquity that no one could heal except him. The greatness of the physician is shown by the gravity of the illness cured.

“Holy” in the inner person; “innocent” in his hands; “undefiled” in body, because he was without any opposition from sin and without the seed of a man; “separated from sinners,” that is, from consent to sin, because he had no sin and no deceit was found in his mouth; “made higher than the heavens,” because he ascended above all the heavens and presides over every creature, ruling, sustaining, governing, and exercising dominion.

“He does not have daily need, as the priests do, first to offer sacrifices for his own sins and then for those of the people.” The priests of the Old Testament, because of their own crimes, had to offer sacrifices. First they offered for themselves and then for the people (Lev. XVI, 6). This one, however, made himself a sacrifice for our sins: “He did this once, offering himself.” He did not do so daily, as the priests mentioned above did, but, once placed upon the cross, he offered himself to the Father as a sacrifice for the sin of the people.

“For the law appoints as priests men who have weakness; but the word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints the Son, perfected forever.” It is as though he were saying: As long as priests were chosen from among human beings, they could not be without weakness—that is, without sin. For they were sinners and transgressors, because “the law brought nothing to perfection.”

The “word” of which he spoke must be understood of Christ. Hence the Prophet says: “The Lord swore and will not repent; you are a priest forever (Ps. CIX, 4).” “After the law” means after the giving of the law; “the Son, perfected forever” means not merely without sin now, but forever. He who was chosen for the priesthood never sinned. He was without sin, because he had no sin and no deceit was found in his mouth (Ps. XXXI, 2).

## (CHAP. VIII.)

“Now the main point of the things being said is this: We have such a High Priest.” “Main point” is a diminutive expression: understand it as meaning, “Let us recapitulate from the head the things we have said above.” We have, he says, such a high priest as I showed above—namely, one according to the order of Melchizedek—“who sat at the right hand of the throne of Majesty in the heavens, a minister of the holy places and of the true tabernacle, which God established and not man.”

By saying that he sits at the right hand, he means the prosperity of eternal life. “A minister of the holy places”: hence the Lord himself says, “The Son of Man did not come to be ministered to but to minister (Matt. XX, 28).”

In this passage he calls heaven the tabernacle, which God established, as it is written: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth (Gen. I, 1).” It is therefore the true tabernacle because the Lord established it, and not figurally, as was the tabernacle made by Moses’ hands. It is called true because it was not a figure.

“For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices.” He is speaking of the Levitical priesthood, whose priests offered carnal sacrifices for their own sins and those of the people.

“Therefore it is necessary that this one also have something to offer.” It is necessary that Christ have something to offer: namely, his body and blood, offering them daily through his members, in whom it is necessary that he be a priest for us.

“If, therefore, he were on earth, he would not be a priest, since there were those who offered gifts according to the law.” If the Lord were now dwelling here on earth in a carnal and visible manner, it would be necessary for priests to exist carnally according to the law. The symbolic sacrifices could not be removed before that sacrifice of the Holy of Holies, which is his body, had been offered. For he had not yet offered his own holocaust in the Passion.

Nor was it proper for the shadow to be removed before the thing signified had been confirmed by the testimony of the apostles who preached and of the peoples who believed.

“Who serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things. As Moses was instructed when he was completing the tabernacle: ‘See,’ he says, ‘that you make everything according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain (Exod. XXV, 40).’”

Everything—whether priesthood, tabernacle, or sacrifices—was a shadow and a copy. They displayed a figure of heavenly things and serve heavenly things [Note: [Col. 0771D] That is, the shadows.]; that is, the works of the New Testament, which are called heavenly works of the Church because through them heavenly things are obtained.

The Church was constructed according to the pattern of the tabernacle. Just as the tabernacle was established in the wilderness, so the Church has been established in the wilderness of this life, concerning which the Psalmist says: “For he hid me in his tabernacle in the day of evils (Ps. XXVI, 5).”

The tabernacle is therefore furnished with various kinds of things, some precious and some less valuable. This demonstrates that some in the Church are saints and others sinners, although all the faithful are constituted within the body of the Church.

“But now he has obtained a better ministry, just as he is also the mediator of a better covenant, which has been established upon better promises.” Christ has obtained a better ministry than the one Moses administered. Do you see, he says, how much better this celebration is than that one? That was a copy and a form; this is the truth.

He is the mediator of a better covenant to the extent that he has obtained a better ministry: the ministry of the new covenant, in which our sins are forgiven and eternal life is promised. It is better because under the old law they possessed rest, but only for a time, and sins were not forgiven.

But in order to make his hearers rejoice more, he says: “Which has been established upon better promises” [Note: [Col. 0772D] The Vulgate has *sancitum*; Ambrosiaster has *sanctificatum*.] From this it is certain that it is based upon better promises, because the former has been excluded and this has been introduced in its place. For this reason it excels: because it is better. “Has been established,” he says—that is, it is holier than that covenant, and its promise is better: the promise of eternal life is better than the promise of earthly goods.

“For if that first covenant had been without fault, there would have been no occasion sought for a second.” If the law of the Old Testament had healed our faults, a second law would not have been required [Col. 0772C], as the prophet says here:

“For finding fault with them, he says: ‘Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete a new covenant over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah (Jer. XXXI, 31).’”

Because of the offense of the old person, which was not healed by the letter that commanded and threatened, that covenant is called old. This one is called new because of the newness of the spirit, which heals the new person from the defect of oldness.

Finally, attend to what follows: “Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers (Jer. XXXIV, 13).” That covenant was old; this one is new. How, then, is that one old and this one new, when the same law is fulfilled through the New Testament that said in the Old, “You shall not covet” (Exod. XX, 17; Deut. V, 27)? It is because what was prohibited there is fulfilled here.

“On the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt.” He defined the time to which he was referring when he called it a covenant. He did not say, “the covenant that I made with their fathers,” lest they should perhaps think that the covenant made with Abraham or Noah was the one in question. Therefore he added: “On the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt.”

That covenant, then, was old, because this one is new. Why, then, is that one old and this one new, when the same law is fulfilled through the New Testament that said in the Old, “You shall not covet”? “Because they,” he says, “did not persevere in my covenant, and I disregarded them, says the Lord.”

Thus, because of the offense of the old person, which was not healed by the letter that commanded and threatened, that covenant is called old; this one is called new because of the newness of the spirit, which heals the new person from the defect of oldness. Heaven is likewise called new even though it is the same heaven that must remain, because some aspect of it must be excluded and another aspect remain; therefore it is called new.
