It is as though he were saying: I will bring about perfection where not a figure but the truth itself is displayed. The expression “to take by the hand” demonstrates his power and their assistance.

“Because they did not remain in my covenant, and I disregarded them, says the Lord.” By “I disregarded them” he means, as it were: I left them to the desires of their hearts.

“For this is the covenant that I will establish with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: by putting my laws into their minds, and writing them upon their hearts.”

He will write his laws in their hearts, not on stone tablets but on tablets of fleshly hearts. The promises of the Old Testament are earthly. Apart from the sacraments that were shadows of future things—such as circumcision, the Sabbath, other observances of days, ceremonies concerning certain foods, and the various rites of sacrifices and sacred things, which suited oldness, the carnal law, and the servile yoke—it nevertheless contains commands of righteousness such as we too now command people to observe.

These are expressed especially on those two tablets, without the shadowy signification of a figure, as in: “You shall not commit adultery, you shall not commit murder, you shall not covet.” There is also another commandment, which is recapitulated in this saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

Nevertheless, because, as I have said, earthly and temporal promises are recounted in that covenant—things that are good for this corruptible flesh, even though they prefigured eternal and heavenly things belonging to the New Testament—now the good of the heart itself is promised, the good spirit of the mind, that is, intelligible good, when it is said: “Putting my laws into their minds, and writing them upon their hearts.”

Thus he indicated that they would not possess the laws externally, but would love the righteousness of the law itself.

[Col. 0773D] Then he added the reward as well: “And I shall be their God, and they shall be my people.” What is better than this good, what more blessed than this happiness? To live for God, to live from God, with whom is the fountain of life, and in whose light we shall see light! Of this life the Lord himself says: “And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the one true God” (John 17:3). He also promises this to those who love him, saying: “Whoever loves me keeps my commandments; and whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I shall love him, and I shall show myself to him” (John 14:21)—that is, in the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father, not in the form of a servant, in which he also showed himself to the ungodly. Then what is written will come to pass: [Col. 0774A] “Let the ungodly be taken away, and let him not see the glory of the Lord” (Isaiah 18:26), since “the wicked will go into everlasting fire, but the righteous into everlasting life” (Matthew 25:46). This eternal life, as I have mentioned, is defined as being that they may know the one true God.

Hence John also says: “Beloved, we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). This likeness is now beginning to be restored, so long as the inner person is renewed day by day according to the image of him who created him. But what, or how great, is this in comparison with the perfection of that exalted state which will then come to be? Indeed, the Apostle, applying to ineffable realities whatever example he could draw from familiar things, compared a child’s age with that of a grown man: “When I was a child,” he says, “I spoke like a child, I understood like a child, I thought like a child; but when I became a man, I put away the things of a child” (1 Corinthians 13:11).

Showing in due course why he said this, he continues: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face. Now I know in part; but then I shall know as I am known” (ibid. 13:12). Accordingly, through this prophet also, whose testimony we are expounding, this is added so that in it the reward, the end, the perfection of happiness, and the sum of blessed and eternal life may consist.

For when he had said, “And I shall be their God, and they shall be my people,” he immediately added: “And each person shall not teach his neighbor, and each person his brother, saying: Know the Lord.” Certainly the time of the New Testament is already here, to which the promise was made in these words that we have recalled from that prophecy. Why, then, does he still say that each person is to say to his neighbor and his brother, “Know the Lord”? Or perhaps this is not said when the Gospel is preached, and its very proclamation is made so that this is said everywhere? For why does the Apostle say that he is a teacher of the Gentiles, unless what he himself says is being fulfilled: “How shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how shall they believe in him whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Romans 10:14).

Since, then, this preaching is now spreading everywhere, how is this the time of the New Testament, of which the prophet said: “And each person shall not teach his neighbor, and each person his brother, saying: Know the Lord, because all shall know me, from the least to the greatest of them”? It is because, in promising and joining to that same New Testament its eternal reward—that is, the most blessed contemplation of God himself—he spoke of that reward.

What, then, does “all, from the least to the greatest of them” mean, except all who belong spiritually to the house of Israel and to the house of Judah—that is, to the children of Isaac, to the offspring of Abraham? For this is the promise about which it was said to him: “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” (Genesis 21:12). “For not all who are descended from Israel are Israel, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring.” “Because all shall know, from the least to the greatest of them.” All Israel and the house of Judah—for not all who are from Israel are Israel, but all to whom it is said in the psalm: “For the morning reception” (Psalm 21:1), that is, for the new light of the New Testament: “All the offspring of Jacob, magnify him; let all the offspring of Israel fear him” (Psalm 24:25).

The whole offspring, certainly—not every offspring, but the offspring of those who were promised and called: “those who are called according to his purpose.” “For those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Romans 8:28, 29). Therefore it is from faith, so that the promise may be firm according to grace for all the offspring—not only for the one that is from the law, that is, the one that comes from the Old Testament into the New, but also for the one that is from faith, which was not promised to itself by the law. It is from the faith of Abraham—that is, the sons who imitate Abraham, who is the father of us all—as it is written: “I have appointed you the father of many nations” (Genesis 17:5). All these, therefore—predestined, called, justified, and glorified—shall know the Lord by the grace of the New Testament, from the least to the greatest of them.

“For I shall be merciful toward their iniquities, and I shall no longer remember their sins.” By “their iniquities,” which he says will now be shown mercy in the New Testament, and by their sins no longer being remembered, he means their idolatry: that which they formerly practiced, when they worshiped foreign gods.

“But by saying ‘new,’ he made the first old. And what is becoming old and growing aged is near to destruction.” By saying “new,” he showed that the first was old. See how he honored the law and refused expressly to call it old. Nevertheless, he said this: for if that one were new, he would certainly not afterward have called this covenant new as well.

**(Chapter 9.)** “The first covenant indeed had ordinances of worship and an earthly sanctuary.” He shows that the priesthood and the covenant—and therefore the tabernacle itself and the Holy of Holies—were destined to have an end. For he demonstrates that everything was figurative. The earlier judgments [Note: [Col. 0775D] Perhaps “signs.”] belonged to that period, when everything was done through sacrifices.

What, then, did it have? It had, indeed, the first covenant. What is the covenant? Clearly, the ordinances of worship. What are the ordinances? The signs that existed then, which, he says, are not possessed now. He shows that it has ceased. He calls it an earthly sanctuary because everyone was permitted to enter; and that place in the tabernacle was open, where the priests stood, as well as Jews, proselytes, Gentiles, and Nazoraeans. Since it was accessible even to Gentiles, he calls it earthly.

“For a first tabernacle was made, in which were the lampstand, the table, and the presentation of the loaves, which is called the Holy Place. Behind the second veil was a tabernacle called the Holy of Holies, having a golden censer and the ark of the covenant covered on every side with gold; in it was a golden urn containing manna, and Aaron’s staff that had blossomed, [Col. 0776A] and the tablets of the covenant, above which were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat.”

These were signs of the world. For everything was venerable, and clear indications of greatness, and safeguards [Note: [Col. 0776D] Perhaps “memorials”], and the tablets, he says, of the covenant—for he had broken them—and the manna: for they had murmured, and so, that its memory might be handed down to posterity, he commanded that it be preserved in a golden urn. And Aaron’s staff, he says, which had blossomed.

Moses was figuratively displaying the manifold mysteries of the Church of Christ. Yet he was not able to set them forth openly to the people whom he was instructing; rather, he signified them through the figure and work of the lampstand and its vessels, until the Lord and our Redeemer himself should come in the flesh, and, having bestowed the grace of the Holy Spirit, disclose to the Church the inner meaning of that same figure. Thus, by dying on the cross, he would tear the veil of the temple and reveal the sacred mysteries that had been concealed; and after his resurrection, appearing to the disciples, he would open their understanding so that, with the eyes of their minds spiritually enlightened, they could perceive these and the other secrets of Scripture.

The tabernacle, then, signified the Church of God, of which the Psalmist says: “For he hid me in his tabernacle on the day of troubles” (Psalm 26:5). The lampstand, the tabernacle, and likewise the table signify the universal Church of the present age. For this reason they were placed before the veil, in front of the ark of the covenant: because the Church has not yet deserved to be admitted to the vision of its Redeemer in heaven.

Thus the table is that by which it daily supplies heavenly nourishment to those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, so that they may not fail amid temptations. This table—that is, sacred Scripture—is said to have been made of acacia wood (Exodus 25:23), that is, constructed from the strong words and deeds of the holy Fathers. To its unity the people of God are gathered from the whole world by apostolic voices.

The lampstand is holy preaching, because it shows light to those who are wandering. It is both table and lampstand, because, instructed in sacred writings, it has learned both to satisfy the hungry soul with good things and to supply the lamp of the word to those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. When it humbly subjects itself to this lamp—restraining itself from its own pleasures in order to do what God’s word commands, and raising itself above visible joys in order to hope for and love what he has promised—it becomes, as it were, his lampstand. For in all things it places heavenly authority above its own desires, and, humbling itself, displays the brightness of God’s word to everyone both by preaching and by doing.

The presentation of the loaves is the body of the Lord, which is to be received daily in the ministry. The first tabernacle, as we have said, signifies the condition of the holy universal Church, which is partly already reigning with the Lord in heaven, and partly still dwelling away from the Lord as its members depart this life and others succeed them. By the second tabernacle we may understand the heavenly Jerusalem.

He calls the Holy of Holies heaven (Hebrews 12:24), and the veil heaven, and the flesh entering within the veil (Hebrews 6:19), that is, the veil of his flesh (Hebrews 10:20). The golden censer is Christ himself. The ark of the covenant fittingly signifies the incarnation of our Lord and Savior himself, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. It was covered on every side with the purest gold because the human nature assumed by the Son of God was inwardly full of the power of the Holy Spirit, and outwardly openly displayed the works of the Holy Spirit to human beings.

We also understand the golden urn—that is, the flesh of Christ, pure and undefiled—which preserves within itself the manna of perpetual divinity and bears the enduring heavenly sweetness of that angelic bread. Likewise, Aaron’s staff signifies the life-giving standard of that same supreme and true high priest, our Lord Jesus Christ alone, and the ever-green, blossoming vitality of immortal memory.

The stone tablets also fittingly signify the perpetual firmness of the two covenants. The mercy seat signifies none other than the Lord and Savior—more particularly, it signifies in him the bowels of compassion—of whom the Apostle says: “Whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood” (Romans 3:25). For this reason also he placed it above, because mercy is exalted above judgment; hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies are over all his works” (Psalm 144:9).

At its right and left stand two cherubim. This is the fullness of knowledge, namely, love of God and of neighbor, through which the Lord is revealed. For no one can reach the Lord except through love. The fullness of the law is love.

Others understand these same two cherubim as the two covenants, which overshadow the mercy seat of God—that is, the mysteries of Christ—as the prophet testifies: “You shall be known in the midst of the two living creatures” (Habakkuk 3:2).

“Of these things we cannot now speak individually.” Perhaps because they required a lengthy discussion, he therefore said: “Of these things we cannot now speak individually.” For these were not merely things that were seen, but enigmas. To these mysteries we have endeavored to draw near insofar as he has granted it—he who opens the mouths of the mute and makes the tongues of infants eloquent (Wisdom 10:21).

[Col. 0777D] “When these things had been arranged, the priests were continually entering the first tabernacle, accomplishing the services of the sacrifices.” After these things had been ordered in advance, as the Apostle narrated above, the priests continually entered the first tabernacle, until the Mediator of God should come, who entered once for all.

These things certainly existed, but the people did not enjoy them, for they did not see what they prefigured. Therefore they had been established no more for them than for those to whom they were prophesied.

“But into the second tabernacle once a year the high priest alone entered, not without blood, which he offers for himself and for the ignorance of the people.” You now perceive the forms set forth earlier. [Col. 0778A] So that they might not say, “How is the sacrifice one?” he shows that this had been the case from the beginning, since what was holier was one. “Then,” he says, “the high priest offered once,” and we believe that our Mediator was offered once in his Passion. And he rightly said, “not without blood”—that is, we were redeemed not without the Passion of our Savior.

“This the Holy Spirit signified”—understood as being through Moses—that Christ would suffer once for the human race: “the way into the holy places had not yet been disclosed” (Exodus 30:10; Leviticus 16:2). For this reason those things still remained, because the realities signified through those shadowy images had not yet appeared.

“While the first tabernacle still had its standing. This is an illustration of the present time.” For that tabernacle [Col. 0778B] was a figure of the present time, that is, of the present Church, which now exists in the New Testament.

“According to which gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the worshiper with respect to conscience, but only in foods and drinks and various baptisms and ordinances of the flesh imposed until the time of correction.” Observe that the law brought nothing to perfection. For they could not be cleansed by the ancient sacrifices; the stains of the soul were not removed, but these concerned only the body, according to the law of a carnal commandment. It could not forgive adultery or murder. Its concern was this: eat this; do not eat that. “Only distinctions in foods and drinks.” “Drink this,” he says; [Col. 0778C] “this is not permitted.” “And various baptisms and ordinances of the flesh.” This was the righteousness of the flesh. In this way he diminishes those sacraments, showing that they possessed no power. And they continued until the time when they were corrected, until the old things passed away—the shadows and figures that had existed—and the new things came.

“But Christ, appearing as high priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle not made with hands—that is, not of this creation—entered once for all into the holy places, not by the blood of goats or calves but by his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption.”

“Christ,” he says, “being present,” or, as some manuscripts have it, “coming” [Note: [Col. 0777D] Or, in others, “approaching”]—that is, coming for this very purpose, not succeeding another. He did not first come and then become this, but came as this at once. And he did not say, “coming as the high priest of sacrifices,” but “of good things,” as though he were unable to express everything in a single phrase.

By the tabernacle not made with hands he means the flesh of our high priest, and truly it is not of this creation, because the whole Trinity worked in it. It is not from these created things, but spiritual, from the Holy Spirit. Hence it is greater and more perfect, because the entire operation of the Holy Spirit dwells in it, since in him all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily.

“By his own blood,” he says, “he entered once for all into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption.” When he says “having obtained,” he shows that the others did not obtain it. The other priests, entering frequently, did not obtain it; this one, through a single entrance, obtained eternal redemption.

“Holy places” in this passage he calls heaven, into which he entered. Observe how he calls the tabernacle, the veil, and heaven itself the Lord’s body. Why does he do this? According to one meaning and another. For example, what I call the veil is heaven. Just as a wall separates the holy places by means of the veil, so the flesh conceals the divinity. The tabernacle, veil, and heaven alike conceal inside whatever they contain, so that it does not appear outside; thus the flesh conceals the divinity, as we have said.

“For if the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer, sprinkling those who are defiled, sanctify for the cleansing of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works, to serve the living God?”

“If,” he says, “the blood of bulls can cleanse the flesh, the blood of Christ washes away the soul’s filth much more.” Here he shows the difference between the two cleansings, and how one is exalted while the other is humble. And rightly so, since the one cleansing is by the blood of bulls, while the other is by Christ’s blood.

Nor is it enough for him merely to mark this by name; he also sets forth the difference in the manner of the offering: “who,” he says, “through the Holy Spirit offered himself without blemish to God”—that is, the sacrifice was without blemish, clean from sins. This was accomplished through the Holy Spirit, not through fire or the blood of a calf.

“And he will cleanse,” he says, “our conscience [Col. 0779C] from dead works.” He rightly said “from dead works.” Here, if someone touches a dead work, he is defiled; there, if someone touched a dead person, he was polluted.

“To serve,” he says, “the living God.” He calls him living to distinguish him from dead gods. Here he makes clear that those who possess dead works cannot serve the living and true God. No one, therefore, who possesses dead works can enter to the Father.

For if one who touched a dead body was not permitted to enter the temple, how much more one who has dead works? For defilement is exceedingly grievous. Dead works are those that have no life, that produce no outward effect. Just as a dead body is useful to no sense and even distresses those who approach it, so sin immediately strikes our reasoning faculty and does not allow the understanding itself to rest; rather, it disturbs it, agitates it, and immediately leaps upon the soul.

Do you not see those who suffer from disease, how they are afflicted with a kind of swelling, how they turn themselves this way and that, how they are filled with foul odors, how their faces are deformed, how they are unclean throughout? Such also are sinners, even if they are not visibly so.

“And therefore he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that, with death having intervened for the redemption of the transgressions committed under the first covenant, those who are called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance.”

The various victims that were killed under the law signified the one death of Christ, which was accomplished for us through gratuitous mercy, so that, with his death intervening, the guilt of our consciences might be washed away—guilt that could not be cleansed by the blood of irrational creatures.

Therefore our Lord and Savior became the mediator of the New Testament, so that through his undeserved death both the shadows of the law and the guilt of human beings might come to an end. “For the redemption of the transgressions committed under the first covenant”—that is, so that through the grace of Christ they might receive forgiveness of sins, which, although the first covenant commanded it, they could not obtain because it did not assist them—and so that they might receive the promise of the eternal inheritance [Note: [Col. 0779] Between “eternal” and “inheritance” a ninth reading is recorded], that is, so that in the Church they might receive through Christ what the law displayed but could not give to its followers.

“For where there is a covenant, the death of the covenant-maker must necessarily intervene. For a covenant is confirmed over the dead; otherwise it has no validity while the one who made it is alive.”

Perhaps many who were more weakly disposed could, precisely because Christ died, be especially inclined not to believe his promises. The Apostle explains this by drawing examples from ordinary custom. What sort of example is this? “Therefore,” he says, “it is necessary to have confidence, because covenants are not confirmed and strengthened while their makers are alive, but when they are dead.” A covenant becomes firm after a person has departed from this world; while he is alive, he will change it whenever he wishes.

Thus Christ’s death confirmed the New Testament. For this reason he asserts that the New Testament was confirmed for us in Christ, and that the Old Testament was its likeness, in which the death of the covenant-maker was prefigured through victims.

If, then, it is asked how, according to the words of the same Apostle, we are “co-heirs with Christ, and sons and heirs of God” (Romans 8:17), since an inheritance is also secured by the death of the one who leaves it, and an inheritance cannot be understood in any other way, the answer is that we became heirs when he himself died, since we have already been called his sons: “The children of the bridegroom,” he says, “do not fast while the bridegroom is with them” (Mark 2:19).

We are therefore called his heirs because he left us possession of ecclesiastical peace through faith in the temporal dispensation that we possess in this life, as he testified when he said: “I give you peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14:27).

For we were under condemnation; we ought to die; he died for us and made us worthy of the covenant. But because we had become unworthy, a covenant was no longer sufficient; punishment was required. “Why then do you boast in the law?” (Romans 2:23). For he placed us in such sin that we could not otherwise be saved unless the Lord died for us.

We become his co-heirs when, at the end of the world, “death is swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15:54). “Then we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

We do not obtain this inheritance through the death of his Father, who cannot die, since he himself is our inheritance, according to what is written: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Psalm 15:5). But because, when we were called, we were still children and insufficiently capable of contemplating spiritual realities, divine mercy extended itself even to our lowest thoughts, so that we might attempt to perceive in some fashion what we did not see clearly and distinctly.

That very thing which we perceived enigmatically dies when we begin to see face to face. For what is taken away is rightly said to die: “When the perfect comes, the partial will be done away” (1 Corinthians 13:10). Thus, in a certain sense, the Father dies for us in the enigma, so that he himself may be our inheritance when he is possessed face to face (ibid. 13:12). Not because he himself dies, but because our imperfect vision of him is destroyed by perfect vision.

Nevertheless, unless that earlier vision nourishes us, we would not become capable of the other, fullest and clearest vision. And if a devout understanding is admitted concerning the Lord Jesus Christ—not according to the Word who in the beginning was God with God, but according to the child who advanced in age and wisdom—then, with that unique assumption preserved which he does not share with other human beings, it is clear that he possesses a fitting inheritance. For we cannot be his co-heirs unless he too is an heir.

But if a devout interpretation is not admitted [Note: [Col. 0781D] The meaning is very obscure], perhaps the Lord’s humanity may be understood as an heir first in part and then wholly; although he is said to advance in wisdom, he may be understood to be an heir in his body, that is, in the Church, whose co-heirs we are, even though it is composed of us. [Col. 0781C]

Yet again it may be asked: through whose death are we also the inheritance of God, according to the statement, “I shall give you the nations as your inheritance” (Psalm 2:8), unless perhaps it is through the death of this world, by which we were formerly held as though it ruled over us? But afterward, when we say, “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14), Christ possesses us, once the one who possessed us has died—when we renounce him and die to him, and he dies to us.

“Therefore not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.” What does “was inaugurated” mean? It means “was made firm” and “was strengthened.” In that covenant also there was blood, just as there is blood here. If the blood there was not Christ’s blood, do not be surprised. It was a type. Hence he said: “Not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.” Therefore it was necessary for the solemnity of the covenant to be completed also through death.

“For when every commandment of the law had been spoken by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying: ‘This is the blood of the covenant which God commanded for you’” (Exodus 24:8). “And he likewise sprinkled the tabernacle and all the vessels.”

Why, then, tell me, is the book of the covenant sprinkled, and the people as well, unless the precious blood was being proclaimed from the beginning through that figure? The blood of the calf is the blood of Christ, which he offered as a sacrifice for us. The blood of the goats likewise prefigured that same blood of Christ, [Col. 0782A] because he was offered for our sins.

The water prefigured baptism. The scarlet wool signifies the love of Christ, through which he suffered for us; hyssop signifies the humility of Christ, or repentance; the book signifies sacred Scripture.

“This is,” he says, “the blood of the covenant which God commanded for you.” This blood prefigured that blood which flowed from Christ’s side on the cross. With this blood Christ sprinkled us through the word by which it was said: “This is the blood of the New Testament for the forgiveness of sins” (Matthew 26:28; Mark 14:24; Luke 22:20; John 5:6 [reference as printed]). This utterance, stained with blood through hyssop, sprinkles.

There the body was cleansed externally, for the cleansing was bodily; here, because the cleansing is spiritual, it enters the soul and cleanses—not merely by being sprinkled, but like a fountain flowing into our hands. With that blood, which had been smeared on, the one sprinkled was again washed; for he did not continually walk about covered in blood. But it is not so with the soul: the blood is mingled with its very substance, making it strong and clean and leading it to indescribable beauty.

He then shows that death was not only for the sake of confirmation but also for cleansing. Since death seemed to be an impure thing, and especially the death that occurred through the cross, he says that this death cleansed and continues to cleanse all the more, and that this cleansing is precious and held in the highest regard.

Therefore the sacrifices came beforehand, because of this blood. Therefore the lambs, and everything else, were done because of this. The tabernacle signifies those of whom the prophet says: “I shall dwell in them and walk among them” (Leviticus 26:12; 2 Corinthians 6:16). The various vessels signify the multitudes of the faithful, all of whom are cleansed through Christ. For this is what follows:

“And almost everything is cleansed with blood according to the law, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.” Why did he say “almost”? Why did he express it in this way? Because among those things there was neither perfect cleansing nor perfect forgiveness. Perfect cleansing and forgiveness are in the blood of Christ, which was shed for us for the forgiveness of sins; and without that blood—that is, Christ’s blood—we have not been redeemed.

“Therefore it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly realities to be cleansed by these things, but the heavenly realities themselves by better sacrifices than these.” Or, as it is read in our translation: “Therefore it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be cleansed by these things, but the heavenly things themselves by better sacrifices than these” [Note: [Col. 0782D] The words beginning “Or, as in our translation” and ending “than these” are written in the same script at the bottom margin].

How are they copies of heavenly things? Does he call heaven itself, or the angels, “the heavenly things”? Nothing of the kind. He means the cleansing itself of Christ, for it is heavenly, although it is celebrated on earth. It was necessary that the world be cleansed through this spiritual sacrifice.

Therefore, if brute animals were not worthy victims for the sake of the rational animal—that is, the human being—a heavenly victim had to be sought: a human being who should be offered for human beings, so that a rational victim might be slain for a rational sinner.

But since a human being without sin could not be found, and the victim offered for us could cleanse us from sin only if it were itself free from the contagion of sin—for what was defiled could not cleanse the defiled—it was necessary, if the victim was to be rational, that a human being be offered, and, if the human being was to cleanse humanity from sins, that he be a human being without sin.

If he descended from the mixture of sin, he would not save those who were lost. Therefore the Son of God came for us into the womb of the Virgin. There he became human for us. He assumed nature from her, not guilt. He made his body a sacrifice for us. He presented for sinners a victim without sin, which could die by virtue of its humanity and cleanse by virtue of its righteousness.

When the ancient enemy saw him after his baptism, he immediately attacked him with temptations and sought to break into his interior through various approaches. He was defeated and overthrown by the invincible integrity of Christ’s mind.

But because he could not reach his interior, he turned to his exterior, so that, since he had been defeated by the strength of his mind and could not deceive him through temptation, he might at least seem to overcome him through the death of his flesh. And, as we said earlier, he was permitted to act against him in that which the Mediator had received from us mortals.

But where he was able to do something, there he was defeated on every side. From the place where he received the outward power to kill the Lord’s flesh, there his inward power—the power by which he held us—was itself killed.

He was defeated inwardly while he acted outwardly as though by force. And he who had held us justly liable to death justly lost his claim to death [OCR “nortis” corrected contextually to “mortis”] over us, because through his agents he sought to destroy Christ’s flesh, in which he found nothing owing to the debt of guilt.

Our Lord, therefore, paid for us an undeserved death, so that the death owed by us might not harm us. Thus it was rightly said: “Wisdom struck down the proud one” (Job 26:12).

“For Jesus did not enter into holy places made with hands [Note: [Col. 0783D] In the Vulgate: ‘For Jesus did not enter into holy places made with hands, copies of the true realities’], copies of the true realities, but into heaven itself, now to appear before the face of God on our behalf.”

Just as above the Apostle set every cleansing, or redemption, against the death of Christ, so here also he sets heaven itself in the place of a temple. “For,” he says, “Jesus did not enter into holy places made with hands, copies of the true realities.” Therefore those are the true realities, while this is the copy.

The temple was established in such a way as to resemble heaven. For God had commanded it to be made with great dignity, so that bodily eyes might be drawn to it more strongly. We say that Jesus entered insofar as he is human. For insofar as he is God, he is everywhere and fills all things. He did not enter into things made by human hands, but into heaven itself, created at the Lord’s command.

He shows not only this difference, but also that the high priest was brought near: “that he might appear,” he says, “before the face of God.” For he does not enter the holy places as the other priests did through certain signs; rather, he sees God himself there.

Accordingly, he shows something venerable not only in heaven but also in the entrance: “that he might appear before the face of God on our behalf.” What does “on our behalf” mean? “When he ascends with the sacrifice,” he says, “he makes the Father propitious” (Romans 3:25), just as John says in his Epistle: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, and he is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:1–2). Why are you now surprised that he intercedes, when he appointed him as a priest, as he says in what follows?

“Nor that he should offer himself repeatedly, as the high priest enters the holy places every year with another’s blood. Otherwise he would have had to suffer repeatedly from the foundation of the world.” He himself, therefore, is both sacrifice, priest, and victim. For if this were not so, many sacrifices would also have had to be offered. He would have had to be crucified more than once. “Otherwise,” he says, “he would have had to suffer repeatedly from the foundation of the world.”

“Now, however, once, at the consummation of the ages, he has appeared to abolish sin through his sacrifice. And just as it is appointed for human beings to die once, and after this comes judgment.” He would have had to suffer more frequently, because it would have been necessary that, if he had wished, he should have suffered from Abel onward, whenever they sinned in each successive generation, and should always have had something to redeem. But he did not wish to die except once, because redemption was accomplished by one death. “Once,” he says, “at the consummation of the ages.” Why at the consummation of the ages? After many sins. For if it had happened at the beginning, no one afterward would have believed; yet he ought not to die a second time, and everything would have been fruitless. But because he suffered afterward, when many sins had accumulated, he rightly appeared then. He says the same thing elsewhere: “So that he might show in the ages to come the riches of his grace” (Rom. IX, 23; Eph. II, 7). And this happened once, at the consummation of the ages, through his own blood, not through another’s. The blood of another could only investigate sins [Note: Perhaps *expiate* should be read, as at the beginning of the exposition of chapter X, where he says: “sins were expiated for a time,” [Col. 0784D] “they were not forgiven.”]; it could not save. But Christ’s blood is his own, not another’s, since it is neither the blood of goats nor of lambs, as had been commanded in the Law; and it can not only expose sins but also save.

“It is appointed,” he says, “for human beings to die once.” What, then? Do we no longer die? We die that death, but we do not remain in it; indeed, this is not really death. For the tyranny of death—and death truly is death—is when the dead are never permitted to return to life. But when there will be life after death, and a better life, that is not death but sleep. Since death was therefore going to hold everyone, he died in order to free us. “And after this, judgment”: that is, because each person will receive according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.

“So also Christ, having been offered once, was offered to take away the sins of many.” By whom was he offered? It is clear that he was offered by himself. Here he calls him not only priest but also victim and sacrifice, offered by himself. “He was offered once,” he says, “to take away [Note: Perhaps *exhaust* should be read, since he repeats the wording above.] the sins of many,” that is, to remove them. [Col. 0785A] Why of many, and not of all? Because not all believed. He did not take away the sins of all, because they did not wish to believe.

“He will appear a second time, without sin, to those who await him for salvation.” Just as it is necessary for each of us, after death, to receive according to his works, so it is right that Christ, having conquered death and obtained the kingdom, should appear a second time to those who await him for salvation, and should justly avenge his own people, although he suffered unjustly at the hands of others. This appearance to those who await him for salvation is better than the common vision of him, of which it is said: “Every eye will see him, even those who pierced him” (Rev. I, 7).

But what does he mean by saying that he will appear a second time without sin? Did he come the first time with sin, although it is written: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Ps. XXXI, 2)? And he himself says of himself: “For the ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John XIV, 30). Thus, “to appear a second time without sin” means that he will no longer be seen in the likeness of sinful flesh, nor will he be bearing the sins of others in his body upon the wood, as he did at his first coming; nor will he any longer intervene on behalf of sins, but will exercise vengeance upon sinners.

## Chapter X

“For since the law possesses only a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the realities, it can never, by the same sacrifices that they offer continually year after year, make those who approach perfect. Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered, because the worshipers, once cleansed, would have had no further consciousness of sin? But in those sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year. For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.”

It showed only a pattern, not the power itself. Just as an image has the pattern of a human being, but not the human being’s power, so it was a shadow, not the truth itself. Through the shadow—that is, through a figure—it displayed in many forms the mysteries of Christ and the Church, until the truth itself should come, reveal to his Church the inner meaning of that same figure through the grace given by the Holy Spirit, and disclose all those mysteries by dying on the cross.

Sins were expiated for a time, but they were not forgiven. For it could never make those who approached perfect; otherwise they would have ceased to be offered. How could they continually seek to remove sins through the same sacrifices? If they had been freed from all sins, sacrifices would certainly not have been offered every day for the whole people, both in the evening and during the day. Accordingly, what occurred was an accusation of sins, not their cancellation; an accusation of weakness, not a manifestation of power. Since the first sacrifice accomplished nothing, it was offered a second time as well, although it too accomplished nothing. In the fact that they were offered, there was a rebuke of sins; in the fact that they were offered continually, there was a rebuke of weakness. Therefore, he says, he commanded them always to be offered because of weakness, and so that a remembrance of sins might be made.

What about us, then? Do we not offer every day? We do offer, but we do so in remembrance of his death, and this is one sacrifice, not many. How is it one and not many? Because it was offered once. That sacrifice was offered in the Holy of Holies, while this sacrifice is a pattern of that one; we always offer the same sacrifice. Nor is it now one lesser sacrifice, another today, and another tomorrow, but always the same; therefore this sacrifice is one. Otherwise, on this reasoning, since it is offered by many, there would be many Christs. Certainly not: he is one everywhere, fully present here and fully present there, one body. For just as the one who is offered everywhere is one body and not many bodies, so too there is one sacrifice.

[Col. 0786B] Our high priest is the one who offered the sacrifice that cleanses us. We offer that same sacrifice now, the one that was offered then. Once offered, it cannot be consumed. But what we do is done in remembrance of what has taken place. “For do this,” he says, “in remembrance of me” (Luke XXII, 19; I Cor. II, 24). We do not make another sacrifice, as though there were another high priest [Note: That is, as though there were another high priest.], but we always make the same one. Rather, we perform a remembrance of the sacrifice.

“Therefore, when he enters the world, he says: ‘Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but you prepared a body for me; burnt offerings and offerings for sin did not please you’” (Ps. XXIX, 7) [Note: In the cited Psalm: “burnt offering and offering for sin you did not request”; but the Vulgate has the following in this Epistle, X, 6: “burnt offerings for sin did not please you.”]. “Then I said: Behold, I have come; in the heading of the book it is written concerning me, to do your will, O God.” Having first said, “You did not desire sacrifices, offerings, burnt offerings, and offerings for sin, nor were the things offered according to the Law pleasing to you,” he then says: “Behold, I have come to do your will, O God.” “He takes away the first in order to establish the second. By this will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ” [Note: The Vulgate adds *once* after these words.].

He shows that the earlier sacrifices were useless for complete cleansing and that they were rather a form, and were not acceptable. They did not please him from the beginning, as he says through the prophet Jeremiah: “Your burnt offerings are not acceptable, and your sacrifices did not please me” (Isa. I, 11; Amos V, 21). But if they did not please him, neither was it his will that they be offered. How, then, did he command that they should be offered?

The Apostle, as a creature following the Creator, expressed the matter in this way: “I want all people to be as I myself am” (I Cor. VII, 7), in conscience; and again: “I want the younger women to marry and bear children” (I Tim. V, 14). Behold, he establishes two wills, but they are not both his will. First he says, “I want all people to be as I myself am”; then, “I want the younger women to marry.” So here too it was not his will that the preceding sacrifices should be made. Rather, as he said above, he not only did not will this, but did not even desire it. Therefore, they sacrificed against [Col. 0787A] [Note: It might perhaps more appropriately be read *contrary to*.] the will of God. This practice was reproved; it possessed no power, but was fruitless and useless. For the sacrifices were forms of the future realities of Christ and the Church. They offered them so that, while sitting without a sacrifice, they would not fall into the worship of foreign gods when they saw others offering sacrifices. It had been imposed upon them as a form of servitude, not of justification.

Accordingly, sacrificing is not the will of God [Note: This is what most strongly proves what we said a little above: instead of *against the will*, one should read [Col. 0788D] *contrary to the will*.]. Since those sacrifices did not please him, he immediately came, as it is written: “Then I said: Behold, I have come”—words spoken of no one other than Christ.

But if they were forms, how did they not cease and disappear when the truth came? They could not be removed before that holy sacrifice of the Holy of Holies, which is the body, had been offered. For those who afterward sacrificed those sacrifices always resisted the Holy Spirit. Nor were the things offered according to the Law pleasing to him: “Neither sacrifice nor offering nor burnt offering nor offering for sin pleased him.” He demonstrates this not again from the New Testament but from the prophets, bringing forward testimony from earlier times that these things were going to cease.

He therefore commanded the sacrifices already mentioned to be offered because they were figures pointing toward the true sacrifice, which would free the whole world from sin. For this reason they are rejected, because the true sacrifice was now approaching. And the Prophet says: “Behold, I have come; in the heading of the book it is written concerning me” (Ps. XXXIX, 7)—that is, in Leviticus, the book that commands and recounts the sacrifices.

Since I am the principal and only sufficient sacrifice, I am therefore in the heading—that is, at the beginning—of the book of sacrifices written about, just as it says: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. I, 1). What does “to do your will” mean? To hand myself over: this is the will of God, “by which will we have been sanctified.” Or did he mean something else: that it is not sacrifices that cleanse human beings, but the will of God? “He takes away the first in order to establish the second,” as though he were saying: He rejects the old and affirms the new.

“And every priest stands daily ministering and offering the same sacrifices repeatedly, which can never take away sins. But he, having offered one sacrifice for sins, sits forever at the right hand of God, from now on waiting until his enemies are placed as a footstool for his feet” (Ps. CIX, 2) [Note: The Vulgate has: “But he, having offered one sacrifice for sins,” and so forth.]. “For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are sanctified.”

To minister is a sign of ministry; therefore, to sit is a sign that ministry is being rendered to him. Those priests, by offering many sacrifices every day, could not take away sins. But he offered himself for us and sat forever at the right hand of God. To sit at the right hand demonstrates his judgment. “From now on waiting.” What is the reason for this delay? So that his enemies may be placed as a footstool for his feet. His enemies are the Jews, heretics, and all unbelievers, who are to be placed under his authority. Here, indicating the extent and power of subjection, he did not say “let them be subjected,” but “so that they may be placed beneath his feet.” Let us therefore not become part of the number of his enemies. For his enemies are not only those who are unbelievers, but also those who are filled with an unclean life. “The mind of the flesh is hostile to God” (Rom. VIII, 6); “it is not subject to the law of God.”

“For by one offering he has perfected”—that is, he speaks of what the Lord says: “After those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws into their hearts, and I will write them upon their minds; and I will no longer remember their sins and iniquities. Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer an offering for sin” (Jer. XXXI, 33).

What the Holy Spirit testified through the prophet has been fulfilled. Those sacrifices immediately disappeared, because when the truth came, the shadow disappeared. “Where there is forgiveness of these,” the Apostle says, “there is no longer an offering for sin.” And the Apostle argued this not only without written proof but also with written proof, adducing the prophetic statement: “You did not desire sacrifice and offering” (Ps. XXXIX, 7), and in this passage: “This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws into their hearts, and I will write them upon their minds”—not on tablets of stone, as among the ancient people, but on tablets of fleshly hearts. “And I will no longer remember their sins and iniquities.” It is as though he were saying: Where there is no remembrance of sins, there is no longer any need for a sacrifice to be offered. Hence he adds in what follows: “Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer an offering for sin.”

[Col. 0788C] “Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Christ, a new and living way which he inaugurated for us through the veil, that is, through his flesh, and since we have a great priest over the house of God…”

He shows the distinction and great difference between the high priest, the sacrifices, the tabernacle, the covenant, and the promise up to the present time. Those things, he says, were temporal, but these are eternal; those were soon to perish, but these remain; those were weak, but these are perfect; those were a form, but these are the truth. For he says: “He was not made priest according to such a carnal commandment, but according to the power of indestructible life” (Hebr. VII, 16). And again: “You are a priest forever” (ibid., 17): behold the priest’s perpetuity.

Of that covenant he said that it was old; “but what becomes old and grows aged is near to disappearing.” This new covenant possesses the forgiveness of sins, whereas the other had nothing of this kind; for the Law perfected nothing (ibid., 19). The former had the blood of goats, not Christ’s; this one has Christ’s own blood. The former had a tabernacle made by human hands, but this one has one not made by human hands; for he says: “Jesus did not enter into holy places made by human hands” (Hebr. IX, 24).

Since, therefore, he declares all those things lesser and these greater, he says that we have greater confidence to be cleansed through Christ’s blood than those who offered sacrifices in a carnal manner. We have confidence to the extent that we have become greater fellow-heirs and enjoy such great love.

By “entrance into the holy places” we must understand heaven, or access to spiritual realities. For no one can attain the gifts of the Holy Spirit except through faith. “Which he inaugurated,” he says, “a new way”: that is, he gave us the beginning of using it. He calls it a new way because he himself went along it, giving us an example of humility: not following the ceremonies of the Law, but the fulfillment of hope.

By calling it “new,” he attempts to show that we possess all things in a greater way, since the gates of heaven are now open—something that did not happen even to Abraham. But he called it living, that is, perfect and enduring, through the veil [Note: The manuscript reads “thus perceived, through the veil”; immediately above, however, after the words “through the veil,” appears “enduring.” Perhaps the transposition of the words would yield a more suitable sense, as follows: “enduring, perceived through the veil” [Col. 0790D].]—that is, his flesh. For this flesh first cut open that way. He himself dedicated it, because he went along it. He rightly called it a veil, because it conceals the divinity: when he was raised into heaven, then the heavenly things appeared.

“Let us draw near with a true heart in the fullness of faith, our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our body washed with pure water. Let us hold firmly to the confession of our hope without wavering—for he who promised is faithful—and let us consider one another for the provocation of love and good works.”

With what should we draw near? With the holiness of faith, with spiritual worship, with a true heart, in the fullness of faith, because none of these things is visible [Col. 0789C], nor is the priest visible as in the old Law—although even that priest did not enter into the holy places. But because we too have entered, we must do so through the assurance of faith, without hesitation. Many now say that some will be resurrected and others will not; this, he says, is not faith. We must believe this way concerning invisible things, and even more. Here we perceive with the senses; there, with the spirit.

“Having our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience.” He shows that not faith alone is required, but also a virtuous life, so that no one is conscious of any wickedness in himself. Those who are not so disposed do not receive the holy things in the fullness of faith. No one entered the holy places unless he had been washed. And no profane person enters that heavenly vision unless he has first been washed through repentance.

They sprinkled the body; we sprinkle the conscience. Why did he not say “cleansed and sprinkled”? Wishing to show the distinction of the sprinkling, he therefore used the word “sprinkled.” One thing is God’s, another is ours. To wash and sprinkle belongs to God; to draw near in truth and in the fullness of faith, with his grace, belongs to us.

“And washed,” he says, “the body with pure water.” Here he means the washing of baptism, because outwardly we are washed with water, but inwardly we are cleansed by the Holy Spirit. What does “let us draw near with a true heart” mean? It means without hypocrisy. Woe to the sinner who enters by two paths. Let there be nothing false in you, he says. Let us not say one thing while thinking another. This too is not a true heart. Such wicked falsehood belongs to the fainthearted; for faintheartedness arises from unbelief. This is what it means to sprinkle the heart through faith.

“For he who promised is faithful; and let us consider one another for the provocation of love and good works.” He is faithful because he does not deceive. Hence he says elsewhere: “God is faithful, by whom you were called” (I Cor. I, 9; I Thess. V, 24). For we must go there and enter the kingdom. Therefore, do not investigate everything, nor await explanations; our circumstances require faith:

[Col. 0790B] “Let us consider one another for the provocation of love.” What does “let us consider” mean? It means “let us understand,” as it is read in certain manuscripts. It is as though he were saying: If someone is endowed with virtue, let us imitate him; let us direct our attention toward him, so that we may love and be loved. For good works arise from love.

What does “for the provocation of love” mean? To love and be loved more. “And of good works”: so that in this they may have a rivalry. To do is a greater virtue than to speak. As far as teaching is concerned, you too have many teachers in your community who do this through their works themselves.

“Not abandoning our gathering, as is the custom of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the day approaching.” Here he not only admonished certain people but also silently reproved them. Love is increased through gathering together. Hence the Lord says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matt. XVIII, 20); and Ecclesiastes says: “A brother helped by a brother is like a fortified city” (Prov. XVIII, 19).

Gathering together is a great good. It makes love itself more fervent; from it all excellent things are generated. Nothing good is done except through love. Let us therefore strengthen one another in this. Love is the fullness of the Law. We do not need toil or sweat. If we love one another, a spontaneous path leading to virtue is laid open before us.

By “the day approaching,” he means what the same Apostle says elsewhere: “The Lord is near; do not be anxious about anything” (Phil. IV, 5, 6). Now, he says, he is near to us [Note: Rom. XIII, 11: “For now our salvation is nearer than when we believed.”]; the time of salvation has already been shortened (Rom. IX, 23).

“For if we sin willingly after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sin.” There is no second sacrifice. Here again those who remove repentance arise. For by this he does not exclude repentance, nor the propitiation that takes place through repentance, nor does he repel and cast into despair those who sin. He is not an enemy of our salvation in this way. What, then? He excludes a second washing. He did not say, “There is no further repentance,” nor did he say, “There is no longer forgiveness,” but he says, “There is no sacrifice”—that is, there is no second cross. He calls the cross a sacrifice. For one sacrifice perfects forever those who are sanctified (Hebr. X, 14), unlike the Jewish sacrifices.

Those who examine this Epistle more carefully understand the passage in this way: the statement “there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins” is not to be understood of the sacrifice of a contrite heart through repentance, but of the sacrifice about which the Apostle was then speaking, namely, the burnt offering of the Lord’s passion, which each person offers for sins at the time when he is dedicated through faith in that same passion and, having been baptized, is initiated under the name of a Christian believer.

The Apostle signifies that thereafter, once a person has sinned, he cannot be cleansed again by being baptized. With this understanding, the opportunity for repentance is not shut off. It is to be understood, however, that those who have not yet been baptized have not yet received the full knowledge of the truth, so that the baptized person is understood [Note: This sense is concealed beneath such a tangle of words that we have almost left it unintelligible. If conjecture is permissible, it seems to us that it should be read as follows: “Thus, let this statement—‘he has not yet received the full knowledge of the truth’—be understood of the one who has not yet been baptized, who cannot possess it as the one who has already been baptized can. Hence, instead of *ut etiam*, we have thought *ut et iam* should be read. What follows, however, namely *non autem*, seems to signify that not all baptized people possess the whole knowledge of the truth, either because of the later progress of some, which he adds, or because of the pitiable negligence of others, which either hinders or destroys knowledge in them. For the rest, we willingly leave the matter to the patient reader of sharper understanding.].

But not every baptized person has also received the knowledge of the truth, because of the later progress of some or the miserable negligence of others. Nevertheless, that sacrifice of which he was speaking—the Lord’s burnt offering, which is in a certain sense offered for each person when he is marked with his name in baptism—cannot be offered again if he sins. For those who have once been baptized cannot be baptized again, even if after baptism they have sinned through ignorance of the truth.

[Note: What follows is no less obscure. It nevertheless seems to be understood as follows, if there is room for conjecture: “Thus it happens that, since no one is rightly said to have received the knowledge of the truth without baptism, everyone who has received it, precisely because he has received it, cannot be baptized again. Yet not everyone who does not receive the knowledge of the truth through instruction should therefore suppose that he can offer that sacrifice on his own behalf.” I flatter myself that I have grasped the author’s meaning and the more coherent sense of what was said above. Let the reader judge.]

Thus it follows that, since no one is rightly said to have received the knowledge of the truth without baptism, it is nevertheless the case that everyone who has received it has no sacrifice left for sins—that is, he cannot be baptized again. Yet not everyone who does not receive the knowledge of the truth through instruction should therefore suppose that he can offer that sacrifice on his own behalf.

“If he has already been washed”: that is, if he has already received within himself, through baptism, the sacraments of that same truth, he cannot be baptized again. It is as though we were to say that every human being is not a four-footed animal; nevertheless, not every animal that is not a human being must therefore be four-footed, and so forth.

We say that those who have already been baptized are better healed than renewed through repentance, because renewal takes place in baptism, where repentance indeed operates, but as upon a foundation that remains. Thus a building can be repaired from its foundation; but if someone wishes to lay the foundation again, he must necessarily overturn the entire building.

For this reason he says this to the Hebrews, because they appeared to have turned back from the New Testament to the old priesthood. “Therefore,” he says, “leaving the word of the beginning of Christ, let us press on to perfection, not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith in God, of the teaching of washings, of the laying on of hands, of the resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment” (Hebr. VI, 1, 2).

All these things are handed down in baptism, and he denies that they are to be repeated—specifically, in the consecration of the faithful. For in the exposition and teaching of the word of God, they must be stated not only once but often, as the opportunity presented by the matters under discussion requires.

“But there is a certain fearful expectation of judgment and a zeal of fire that will consume the adversaries.” Here the Apostle most clearly declares the final day of judgment, or everlasting fire. “Which will consume the adversaries.” By “adversaries” he means not only unbelievers but also those who act contrary to virtue—namely demons, heretics, and all evildoers—whom it will burn up; or, since that same fire also receives both household members and intimates, it will consume those who oppose them as well.

[Note: In the margin, chapter XXVI is written here, although no preceding chapters appear to be marked with numbers.]

“He who sets aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deut. XVII, 6). “Without mercy,” he says, so that there is no pardon and no mercy—although that law was Moses’ law, for he himself had established many things. What does “before two or three” mean? If two or three have testified, they immediately deliver judgment.

[Col. 0792C] If, then, in the Old Testament, where the law of Moses is set aside, sinful human beings were condemned to such a great and severe punishment, “how much worse punishment do you think will be deserved by one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, considered the blood of the covenant common or profane, by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace?”

How does someone trample underfoot the Son of God? When someone partakes of him through the sacraments unworthily, does he not commit sins? Does he not trample him underfoot? Does he not despise him? Just as we regard the things we trample underfoot as worthless, so those who sin consider Christ worthless. You have become the body of Christ, yet you hand yourself over to the devil in order to trample Christ underfoot.

“And considered the blood,” he says, “of the covenant polluted”—or, as it is found in Greek, “judges it common” [Col. 0792D]. “Common” may mean unclean, or something that possesses nothing more than other things. Those who receive heretical teaching into themselves, rather than Christ’s teaching, pollute Christ’s blood; through their sins they drive Christ out of themselves, and they insult the Spirit of grace when they do not believe that forgiveness of sins takes place in the Church. As it is said: “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Luke XII, 10; Matt. XII, 32; Mark III, 29).

Indeed, the person who does not exercise what the Spirit grants also insults the Spirit of grace. For whoever does not accept a benefit wrongs the benefactor. He made you a son; yet you wish to become a slave? He came to dwell with you; yet you bring him evil thoughts? Christ wishes to be firmly established in you; yet you trample him underfoot through gluttony and drunkenness.

Let us who partake of the sacraments unworthily listen. Let us who approach that table unworthily listen to what follows:

“We know what he said: ‘Vengeance is mine, and I will repay.’ And again: ‘The Lord will judge his people’” (Deut. XXXII, 35; Ecclus. XXVIII, 1). This was said concerning enemies who do evil, not concerning those who suffer evil. Here he also consoles them, saying: “I will repay.” For God remains forever and lives; therefore, even if they do not receive their recompense now, they will receive it later. They must lament, not we. We have fallen into their hands, but they have fallen into the hands of God. For it is not the one who suffers who suffers some evil, but the one who does it.

[Col. 0793C] “It is terrible to fall into the hands of the living God.” They fall into the hands of the Lord who, fearing human judgments, regard God’s judgments as insignificant. But you too, whoever you are, if you do not repent, will fall into the hands of the Lord. That is what must be feared: the judgment of God. This other thing—the judgment of human beings—is nothing.

Therefore, when we see someone being punished here, let us not tremble at present things, but let us tremble at God’s future judgments. According to his mercy, his indignation also exists, and his fury always rests upon sinners who fall into his hands.

“But remember the former days, when, after you had been enlightened, you endured a great struggle of sufferings, at one time being made a public spectacle through reproaches and tribulations.”

The best physicians, when they have cut away an illness and increased the pain through the incision, immediately bring comfort and a remedy to the place where the pain is present and troubling, and they restore the disturbed soul. Once they have revived it, they do not add another incision. Indeed, they use milder and effective medicines to soothe and comfort the extent of the pain caused by the incision already made.

The Apostle did the same. After he had shaken their souls and pierced them with the mention of Gehenna, proving that in every way the one who insults God’s grace must perish, teaching this from the law of Moses, affirming it further through other testimonies, and saying that it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God, he then consoled them, lest he cause a soul overcome by excessive fear to be swallowed up in despair. He consoled them with praises and exhortations, setting before them the sacrifice of their own household as an offering:

“Remember,” he says, “the former days, when, after you had been enlightened, you endured a great struggle.” It is as though he were saying: Although you were introduced among those who had not been part of the order of the disciples, you displayed such eagerness and such courage; now, by recalling it, I ask you to persevere in the same spirit, so that, continuing in tribulations, you may be an encouragement to each person.

He divides up how they endured temptations or struggles, which is the greatest title to praise. Then he explains it in detail, expanding his discourse [Col. 0794B] and presenting many praises. How so? “At one time,” he says, “you were made a public spectacle through reproaches and tribulations.”

Reproach is a grave matter, capable of overturning the soul and blinding the mind. For hear what the Prophet said: “When they say to me every day, ‘Where is your God?’” (Ps. XLI, 4). And again: “If an enemy reproached me, I would have endured it” [Note: Ps. LIV, 13: “An enemy had cursed me; I would certainly have endured it.”].

Since the human race is exceedingly desirous of glory, it is easily taken captive by reproaches as well. He did not simply say “through reproaches,” but intensified the statement by adding “made a public spectacle.” For when someone is reproached in secret, he is distressed; but much more so when it happens before everyone. How great was the evil that, after they had departed from Jewish weakness and passed over to the best way of life, and had rejected their ancestral traditions, they suffered many evils at the hands of their own people and had no one to defend them.

“I have nothing to say,” he means, “because although you suffered these things and perhaps grieved, in fact you rejoiced even more. Not only,” he says, “were you not ashamed of your own sufferings, but you also became companions to others who suffered in the same way.” I think this was said concerning the apostles.

“But at another time you became companions of those who behaved in this way.” It is as though he were saying: You who ministered to them are their companions in the reward.

“Indeed, you showed sympathy toward those in bonds, and with joy accepted the seizure of your possessions, knowing that you have a better and lasting substance.” You see that he speaks of himself and of the other prisoners. For you did not regard those bonds as bonds, but stood firm like athletes, strong; you not only had no need of encouragement or consolation in your own sufferings, but became encouragement and consolation to others as well.

“And with joy you accepted the seizure of your possessions.” By “seizure,” he means that you accepted with joy what those who had taken their goods away from them had seized, because of the eternal reward. He satisfies and confirms the point wonderfully. For perhaps that seizure could be attributed to the violence of the plunderers. No one, perhaps, could have prevented the violent men, although you could have done so; for if you had wished it not to be seizure, you could have denied the faith. But you did something far greater than this: you endured these things with joy. This was entirely apostolic conduct, worthy of those courageous souls, that they should rejoice when scourged. “They were returning” [Note: [Col. 0795D] In place of *remunerabantur*, one seems to have to read *revertebantur*, or something similar, as is clear from the text cited below.]—he says—“from the presence of the council, rejoicing, because they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41). For whoever bears something with joy shows that he has his reward. By saying, “you accepted,” he made clear that their endurance was voluntary. “Because you accepted,” he says, “knowing that you have a better substance in heaven, permanent, and possessing something firm and stable, something that cannot perish, unlike these earthly things, which perish.”

[Note: [Col. 0796D] In the margin of the manuscript, chapter 27 is written here.]

“Therefore do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward. For you need endurance, so that, after doing the will of God, you may receive the promise.” He did not say, “because you have thrown it away,” but “do not throw it away.” For what is lost requires much labor to be acquired again; but what is retained, and is accompanied by fear, must also possess courage. Do not fail amid tribulations, because the reward is great.

For he exhorts them in order to make them stronger and to give them a stable and firm faith. He speaks differently to the Galatians and differently to the Hebrews: to the former, so that Christ might be formed in them; to the latter, so that their stability might become firm. To the former he says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19). And rightly so. For they were being afflicted above all; therefore they needed a reproving manner of speech. These, however, were somewhat colder, and therefore needed a gentler manner of speech.

“Therefore do not throw away,” he says, “your confidence.” It is therefore evident that they possessed much confidence toward God. “Which has,” he says, “a great reward.” For this reason he anticipated almost their entire thought, saying: If you understand that you have a better substance in heaven, ask for nothing else; only endurance is needed here—not so that you may fall, but so that you may remain in those same things; so that you may not cast away what has been bestowed upon you. You need nothing else except to stand firm, as you have stood firm, so that, when you reach the end, you may receive the promise. You need only to persevere and await the future, not to fight again. You have been brought close to the crown itself; you have endured all the contests, bonds, and tribulations; your possessions have been plundered. What remains, then, except that you stand firm for this purpose, so that you may be crowned? Await this alone: the arrival of the crown.

Oh, what greatness of exhortation and consolation! It is as if someone said this to an athlete who had defeated all his opponents and had no one left to compete with him, while the time of his crowning was then prolonged into the future until the judge of the contest should arrive to give him the crown. But the athlete, bearing this impatiently, might wish to go out and flee, unable to endure it in this way and fearing the flames of the heat. This, then, he himself also indicated, saying: “For yet a very little while: the one who is to come will come, and will not delay” (Habakkuk 2:4). “The one who is to come will not delay”—that is, Christ.

And lest they perhaps say, “When will he come?” he consoles them from the Scriptures. For he consoles them as though only a short time remained: “For now our salvation is nearer” (Romans 13:11). He does not say this from himself, but from the Scriptures. “But my righteous one will live by faith” (Habakkuk 2:4; Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11). “But if he withdraws, my soul will not be pleased with him.” We, however, are not children of withdrawal, leading to destruction, but of faith, leading to the gaining of the soul.”

The righteous person lives by faith, because your soul is the life of your body, and your faith is the life of your soul; whoever withdraws himself from it will not please God. “You have labored,” he says; “you have endured many contests. Await the blessed hope. Do not seek here the things for which you have hoped, because the righteous person lives by faith.”

## Chapter 11

“Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen. For by it the elders received testimony.”

Faith, then, he says, is a vision of things not seen, leading to the same assurance as though they were visible. Accordingly, neither credulity nor unbelief can be spoken of with regard to things that are seen; nor can faith be spoken of except when someone has assurance concerning things that are not seen. For when the things that are in hope are thought to be without substance, faith gives them a pure substance. The resurrection has not yet taken place and does not yet exist in substance, but hope makes it subsist in our soul. This is what he meant by “substance.”

If, then, faith is the proof of things not seen, why do you wish to see it already, so as to fall away from the presence of salvation? It is perfectly clear that faith is the proof of things that cannot appear. For things that appear no longer require faith, but recognition. When Thomas therefore saw and touched, why was he told, “Because you have seen me, you have believed” (John 20:29)? He saw one thing and believed another; for divinity could not be seen by a mortal human being. He therefore saw the human being and confessed him to be God, saying, “My God and my Lord.” By seeing, therefore, he believed: observing the true human being, he exclaimed that he was God, whom he could not see.

[Col. 0796D] What follows brings great joy: “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (ibid.). In this saying we are especially marked out, we who have not seen him in the flesh but retain him in our mind. We are marked out if we follow our faith with works. For the one who truly believes is the one who practices by his actions what he believes. By contrast, concerning those who retain faith in name only, Paul says: “They profess that they know God, but in their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16).

“By faith we understand that the ages were prepared by the word of God, so that the visible things came to be from the invisible.” Faith requires a strong and manly spirit, one that rises above all sensible things and passes beyond the weakness of human reasoning. No one can become faithful in any other way unless he withdraws himself from ordinary custom.

Since, then, the souls of the Hebrews were weak, and although they had begun from faith, were made fainthearted by the sufferings of their tribulations, bore them with too little patience, and were shaken, he first exhorted them from their own experience, saying, “Remember the former days”; then from the divine Scripture, which says, “The righteous person lives by faith”; then from reasoning, saying, “Faith is the substance of things hoped for,” the conviction of things not seen.
