Now he begins to speak of the ancestors, of great men, presenting them to us wonderfully as examples, because just as all of them were saved through faith, so we too are all saved through faith.

For when the soul finds a companion in the same sufferings, it rests and breathes again. This commonly happens both in faith and in tribulation. “Therefore,” he says, “let mutual faith be a consolation among you.” For the human race is very fragile and excessively hesitant in its thoughts.

The apostle therefore exhorts them through the ancestors. First, from common understanding, he says that it is manifest from the beginning that God brings into being the things that exist from things that do not exist: visible things from invisible things, substantial things from things that do not exist. And how do we know this? Because he made this by his word. Reason contributes nothing to us in this matter. From where do we know that God made it? Reason does not assist us. No one was present when these things were being made. How, then, is it certain? It is manifest that this is a matter of faith.

“By faith,” he says, “we understand that the ages were prepared by the word of God.” By faith we believe that they were prepared—that is, perfected or made—because the things that are seen were made not from visible things but from invisible things. This belongs to faith. For the invisible things existed, since “darkness was over the abyss” (Genesis 1:2). They became visible, since all things received their form.

[Note: [Col. 0797D] In the margin of the manuscript, chapter 28 is written here.]

“By faith Abel offered to God a greater sacrifice than Cain, through which he received testimony that he was righteous, God bearing witness to his gifts; and through it, though dead, he still speaks.”

First he presents the one who suffered evil, and this from his brother. He set before them an example proper to their situation: “For you,” he says, “have suffered the same things from your fellow countrymen.” He exhorts them so that, just as Abel was unjustly killed by his brother and did not refuse persecution, so they would not refuse it if they suffered unjustly at the hands of their fellow countrymen.

“Abel offered a greater sacrifice than Cain”—not because that sacrifice was materially greater, but because Abel brought to God, through faith and with a willing mind, whatever best thing he had. From this his possessions were multiplied for him. We understand that by this he pleased God. For he received testimony that he was righteous—whether because fire descended from heaven, as Theodotion reads, and the Lord kindled it over Abel and over his sacrifice; or through that sentence of the Lord by which God remembered the first martyr, Abel, even to the last, to take vengeance upon those who exact vengeance on his servants, as we read in the Gospel: “From the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah” (Matthew 23:35; Luke 11:51), “the son of Barachiah, whom they killed between the temple and the altar” (2 Chronicles 24:22).

“And through it, though dead, he still speaks,” as it is said: “The blood of Abel cries out to me from the earth” (Genesis 4:10). Or, “he still speaks”: that is, he was indeed killed, but his glory was not killed with him. It is as though he were saying: He is not dead; therefore neither will you die.

The apostle did all this to make them more receptive to faith and stronger in enduring. Therefore he multiplies so many signs, so many miracles, and so many consolations. The more fiercely someone has suffered, the more his glory increases. When he still speaks, this is evidence that he lives: he is on everyone’s lips, and everyone admires and blesses him. Whoever admonishes others to be righteous speaks. For speech does not achieve as much as his suffering. Just as heaven, simply by appearing, speaks, so does he when he comes to mind. He would never have been held in such admiration if, while alive, he had possessed a thousand tongues, as he is now admired. This glory is not acquired without dangers.

“By faith Enoch was transferred so that he should not see death, and he was not found, because God transferred him; for before his transfer he received testimony that he pleased God. Without faith it is impossible to please God. For whoever approaches God must believe that he exists and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him.”

Enoch did not say to himself: What need is there to endure labors and dangers? Abel has died for the love of God, and has not yet attained the resurrection; but his desire is manifest, and the things that had to be done by him have been done. The things that are hoped to be given have not yet been bestowed upon him. Nor has the murderer received punishment. God threatens him, but has not yet repaid him. What benefit will this bring him?

But, passing beyond this kind of delay, he understood that if God exists, there will certainly be retribution. “You too, therefore,” he says, “pay attention to yourselves; and if you see that you receive nothing here, do not be troubled. If those pleased God who had no examples set before them, how much more ought we to please him, for whom so many shining stars have appeared, until the true Sun should come?”

“By faith,” he says, “Enoch was transferred.” Enoch pleased God through faith, so that just as the earlier ancestors did not see him before his coming but believed, so we too, knowing this, must believe what we do not see, in order to receive as they received, as it is said: “Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face continually” (Psalm 104:4).

The cause of his being transferred was that by which he had pleased God. But the cause of Enoch’s pleasing God was faith. For unless he had known that God would repay, how could he have pleased God?

“For without faith it is impossible to please God.” How did he believe these things? He believed that if someone believed that God exists, he would also receive retribution. “How, then, does he please God?” “It is necessary,” he says, “to believe that he exists.” Does he exist? If faith is required because he exists, then reason is no more capable of comprehending what he is. In the same way, because he is the one who rewards, faith is required, not reasoning. How could matters pertaining to his essence be comprehended by reasoning? What sort of reasoning could reach such things?

Many people ask where Enoch was transferred, and why he was transferred, and why neither he nor Elijah died; whether they still live, and how they live, and in what condition. But it is superfluous to inquire into these matters. Scripture has said that one was transferred and the other taken up; but it has not added where or how they are.

They say that this happened so that, at the very beginning, Enoch might immediately be recalled, so that the human soul might receive hope: that death is dissolved and the devil’s tyranny condemned. First, through Abel, he permits death to occur, wishing by terror to show that the sentence remains truly firm: “You are earth, and you will go into the earth,” lest those who trusted become sluggish. Through Abel he terrifies; through Enoch he arouses people to strive to please him. For to those who seek good works, he becomes a rewarder through their understanding of the reward.

“By faith Noah, having received an oracle concerning things not yet seen, and fearing, prepared an ark for the salvation of his household; through which he condemned the world and was made heir of the righteousness that comes through faith.”

“Concerning things not yet seen,” he says—that is, concerning the rains—he constructed the ark, fearing. For reason suggested nothing of this in the present life. “They were marrying,” as the Lord says in the Gospel, “and giving in marriage” (Matthew 24:38); the air was clear, and there were no signs. Nevertheless, he feared and, through faith, fearing the things that were not yet seen, constructed the ark for the salvation of his household.

“Through which”—that is, through faith—“he condemned the world”; that is, he condemned it by comparison with himself, since the world had no faith. He was made heir through faith, not through the law, since he alone held the faith of the ancestors while the others were turning away from him. For he showed them worthy of this punishment because they were not corrected even by that construction.

“And he was made heir of the righteousness that comes through faith.” He is called heir of the kingdom of heaven, or heir of the world, because through his offspring the world was restored. He appeared righteous because he believed God. This belongs to the soul that is genuinely disposed toward God and judges nothing more delightful than his words, just as unbelief does the opposite when it is opposed to him. Faith certainly produces righteousness.

Just as we have received an oracle concerning eternal Gehenna, so Noah received one concerning the condemnation of the world. Although he was mocked, he continually prophesied. The meaning is this: If you suffer persecution, you must endure it, lest that day overtake you like a thief.

The example of Enoch was an example of faith alone. The example of Noah was an example both of faith and of unbelief. This is perfect consolation and exhortation: that not only those who believed are found to have been approved, but that unbelievers also suffer the opposite consequences.

“By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed by going out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance; and he went out, not knowing where he was going.”

That is, Abraham himself also pleased God through faith. He did not know where he was going, because the place of habitation in that land was unknown. Insofar as he walked, he walked by faith. Or he did not know where he was going because he had no one to imitate. For it had been said: “I will give this land to you and to your offspring.”

He saw his son dwelling there as a stranger; he saw his grandson; he saw himself living as a stranger in a foreign land, and he was not troubled. This was how things were arranged with Abraham so that afterward the promise might be carried forward into his offspring, although it had also been said to him, “I will give it to you and to your offspring”—not always to you alone, but to you and to your offspring.

And yet neither he, nor Isaac, nor Jacob possessed this promise; their descendants did. Therefore he says, “By faith Abraham, who was called.” For he was not so called when he obeyed God; therefore it says, “who was called Abraham.”

“By faith he dwelt as a resident alien in the land of promise, as in a foreign land, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, fellow heirs of the same promise.”

Abraham’s faith is doubled because of the greatness of his faith; hence he is called the head of faith. For just as he went out by faith, not knowing where he was going, so by faith he remained in his own land.

A *casa* is a house; *casulis*, a diminutive expression, means that he lived in little dwellings or tents with Isaac and Jacob. He himself taught them faith.

“Fellow heirs of his promise.” The promise made to Abraham was also made to Isaac, and the promise made to Isaac was also made to Jacob. All were fellow heirs and jointly heirs of Abraham’s promises, because the promise was made to all, as it had been made to Abraham.

To Abraham it was said: “In you all the thoughts of the earth will be blessed, and in Isaac your offspring will be called.” To Isaac: “I will fulfill the oath that I swore to Abraham your father, and I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven, and I will give all these regions to your descendants, and in your offspring all the nations of the earth will be blessed.” To Jacob it was said: “I am God Almighty; grow and multiply. Nations and peoples will come from you, and kings will come forth from your loins. The land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you and to your offspring after you.”

“For they were awaiting a city having foundations, whose architect and founder is God.”

Observe that they received these promises by awaiting and trusting. If, then, trust is reception, we too can receive. For although they possessed none of these things, they contemplated them with desire. They did not pay attention to the promises made concerning the earthly land; they were seeking the future rest. Let us be ashamed, then, who seek earthly things.

They showed themselves worthy of greater things. He did not permit them to receive this, but bestowed greater things upon them, wishing to show us that they were worthy of greater things. Unwilling to be bound to earthly matters, they drew their minds away from the earth with such devotion that they did not even accept the things that were being given. This is why their descendants received them. They were worthy of the earth, not of that city whose architect and founder is God.

[Note: [Col. 0801D] Here the margin reads chapter 29.]

“By faith Sarah herself also received power to conceive offspring” [Note: [Col. 0801D] Between the words “power” and “to conceive,” the manuscript reads “twelve.”] “even beyond the proper time of life, because she considered him faithful who had promised. Therefore from one man—and one who was as good as dead—there arose descendants as numerous as the stars of heaven and as innumerable as the sand on the seashore.”

Someone might perhaps say: How was this by faith, when she laughed (Genesis 18:12)? For although that laughter was laughter of joy, it was not laughter of complete faith. Later she was also confirmed in faith by the same angel; therefore the cause of her doubt was removed and faith was introduced.

“She received power to conceive offspring.” She was already deadened and barren; there was a double obstacle. One was temporal, for she had already grown old; the other was natural, for she was barren. But she received power both to receive and to retain the seed.

Women commonly become barren for two reasons: either when the womb does not possess the power to receive the seed, which happens in old age when the feminine functions fail, or when the womb is closed even in youth, so that the seed does not reach the places of conception. Against both—namely, barrenness and old age—God gave power. The seed reached the place of conception immediately, and after it arrived, he gave the woman the firmness necessary for childbirth. By the solidity of faith, the unsoundness of the womb was strengthened, so that all things might be possible for the one who believes (Mark 9:22).

“Therefore,” he says, “from one there arose descendants for him.” That is, from the one Isaac there arose for him two sons, or afterward an innumerable multitude of people; or from the one body of Abraham and Sarah there arose innumerable peoples [Note: [Col. 0801D] Or, if we may add something of our own—which we do not do without fear and reverence—perhaps by “from one there arose descendants, and from one who was as good as dead, as the stars of heaven,” the apostle could have intended to signify the Old Testament and the Jewish people, and the New Testament and the Christian people, which succeeded the former when it was as good as dead. May the apostle kindly pardon our boldness, as we admire and venerate his divine meanings with bowed heads.].

Therefore all were also born from one—not merely to signify that she gave birth, but also that she became the mother of as many as even fertile women could not produce. “And from one who was as good as dead,” he says—or, “from one who was as good as dead,” with the feminine form. For he was not dead as regards life, but dead as regards a woman. An old man can indeed emit semen, but he lacks the firmness of the seed necessary to beget children, unless perhaps with a young woman, as some relate.

“Like the stars of heaven,” he says, “or the sand of the sea.” This is said hyperbolically. By the stars of heaven, the good are to be understood; by the sand, the wicked. For the multitude of that one nation, which according to the flesh was born from Abraham through his grandson Jacob, grew so greatly that it almost filled every region of the world; and therefore it could also, according to the hyperbole, be compared to the multitude of sand. This alone is innumerable to human beings, not to God; to God, even the sand of the earth is not innumerable.

If in this life such promises of God are so readily fulfilled—if they are so wonderful, glorious, and magnificent—what will those things be of which these are additions? What, then, is more blessed than attaining them, or more wretched than failing to attain them? If someone expelled by human beings from his homeland is judged miserable, and anyone who has lost an inheritance seems pitiable to everyone, what good can you suppose remains for the one deprived of heaven? With how many tears must such a person be mourned? For when someone, by his own will, drives himself into this condition, he deserves not only tears but lamentation as well.

“All these died in accordance with faith, not having received the promises, but seeing them and greeting them from afar, and confessing” [Note: [Col. 0802D] The Vulgate reads “confessing.” Indeed, this should be the reading, as what follows in this passage sufficiently proves.] “that they are strangers and sojourners upon the earth. For those who say such things make it clear that they are seeking a homeland. And if they had remembered that from which they had gone out, they would certainly have had time to return; but now they desire a better one, that is, a heavenly one.”

Two matters here deserve investigation. Since he had said above that Enoch was transferred and was not found, lest he should see death, here he says that all these died according to faith. And since he had again said that they did not receive the promises but saw them from afar, above he said of Abel that he received testimony that he was righteous and that through it, though dead, he still speaks; of Enoch he said that he was transferred; and of Noah that he was saved from the condemnation of the world and made heir of the world.

It seems to me that the matter can be resolved in this way. All died in accordance with faith. In this passage he says “all” not because all died, but because he means all those whom we know to have died. As for what he said, “not having received the promises,” this is true, because in certain respects they did receive them. Enoch received the promise so that he would not see death; Noah received it so that he would be saved; and many others received similar things. But these were merely libations and first tastes of future realities.

For God bestows upon us not only the things that are future but also those belonging to this life, as he said to his disciples: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:33; Luke 12:31).

“Seeing from afar”—that is, the promises which Christ, when he came, proclaimed: that if someone should leave houses, brothers, sisters, father, or mother, he will receive a hundredfold and eternal life (Matthew 19:29).

Or they saw from afar his coming and greeted it—that is, desired it—as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Many kings and prophets desired to see the things that you see, and did not see them, and to hear the things that you hear, and did not hear them” (Luke 10:24). Thus they confessed concerning those things that they also greeted them.

He said this by a metaphor drawn from sailors, because from afar they see the desired cities, and before entering them, they greet them in advance and make them familiar to themselves. They saw in faith and confessed in their words that they were strangers and sojourners, as it is written: “I am a stranger, like all my fathers” (1 Chronicles 29:15; Genesis 23:4; Psalm 38:13).

Where does Abraham confess that he is a stranger and sojourner? It is necessary to inquire into this, though perhaps we shall also find that he himself confessed it. David certainly confessed it, as we have said: “I am a stranger,” he says, “like all my fathers.” He is called a stranger from *peregre*, “from abroad.” For we say *peragrare*, “to travel through” or “to walk about,” because they lived in tents, while they purchased tombs with money.

It is certain that they were strangers, since they did not even have a place in which to bury their own. What, then? Did they mean that they were strangers in that land in which the Philistines lived? Certainly not, but strangers throughout the whole world. And rightly so. For they saw none of the things they desired in it; everything was foreign and alien to those who wished to worship the power of God.

How, he asks, were they strangers? Their concern was not with the things of this world; and they demonstrated this not only in words but also in the things themselves and in their actions. God said to Abraham: “Go out from your land,” which was thought to be his homeland. He immediately went out and was not held back by love of his own people; he departed as a stranger and came to a foreign land. God said to him: “Offer me your son.” He offered him as though he did not possess human nature.

“For those who say such things make it clear that they are seeking a homeland”—that is, a heavenly one. And lest anyone say that the land of the Chaldeans was their homeland, he added: “And if they had remembered that from which they had gone out, they would certainly have had time to return”—that is, they had the opportunity to return to Chaldea, from which they had come; but they desire a better one, that is, the heavenly Jerusalem.

The first virtue is to be a stranger and sojourner in this world, to have nothing in common with the kings of this age, and to be removed from them as a stranger. But that excellent preacher did not call himself a stranger; he called himself dead to the world. “The world,” he says, “has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14).

[Col. 0803D] “Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a holy city for them” [Note: [Col. 0803D] The Vulgate does not have the epithet “holy.”].

This is great—truly great—and an indication of much blessedness. Let us therefore praise his essence ineffably and love his mercy, because he deigned to bear the name of mercy, saying, “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” although his name is eternal.

For him it is a disgrace when he is called the God of wicked people, and he himself also brings disgrace upon them. Just as he is glorified when he is called the God of kind and excellent people who cultivate virtue, so conversely he is dishonored in the deeds of the wicked. But those men were so illustrious and so full of confidence that he was not ashamed to be called their God.

He is called the God of the earth and the God of heaven, indeed the God of the nations, and not only of the nations but of the whole world, because he himself created and built everything. But he is not called the God of those saints in the same way; he is called their God as a friend. Even now he is called the Lord, the God of Christians, and yet this name surpasses our dignity.

“By faith Abraham offered Isaac when he was tested, and he was offering his only-begotten son, who had received the promises—to whom it had been said, ‘In Isaac your offspring shall be called’—reasoning that God was able even to raise him from the dead.”

Thus, in one and the same deed of blessed Abraham, Jacob praised the greatness of his works [Note: Jacob the Apostle’s praise of Abraham is indicated in his Catholic Epistle, II, 21 and 23 [Col. 0803D], where first his works, namely in verse 21, and then his faith, in verse 23, are praised.]. Paul praised the steadfastness of his faith, yet Paul did not set forth a different or divergent opinion from Jacob. Both knew that Abraham was perfect both in faith and in works; and therefore each proclaimed more fully in him that virtue which he saw his own hearers needed more greatly.

Since James was writing to those who held faith without works to be idle, he appropriately brought forward that example in which Abraham’s outstanding faith—also previously praised, as Scripture testifies—was made evident: his faith had not lain dormant and idle in his heart, but had already burned eagerly toward obedience to the divine commands. Paul, however, was instructing people who exalted themselves in their own works without the grace of faith. He showed that without faith it is impossible to please God. And, in refuting and correcting their [Col. 0804C] rashness, he collected examples of all the patriarchs and clearly taught that all had been approved by the testimony of faith.

Hence, speaking specifically of Abraham, he added that he offered Isaac by faith, “reasoning,” he says, “that God was even able to raise the dead.” He therefore joined the deed to faith: Abraham wished to offer his son immediately because he believed that God would immediately raise him; and he believed that God would raise him after death because he held as true what he had heard: “In Isaac your offspring shall be called.”

Just as he believed, without relying on human reasoning, that God could give a son from a dead womb and from an old man, already naturally unfit for begetting, so by that same faith he believed that the slain son could be raised. He knew with complete certainty [Col. 0804D] that God could not be deceived, and that, even if the boy were killed, God’s promise would nevertheless remain secure.

Therefore this Apostle, too, had learned through the Spirit of God what Abraham had held within his mind when, praising his faith, he says: “Abraham’s faith did not hesitate when he offered his only son, in whom he had received the promises, thinking that God was even able to raise him from the dead.”

Great indeed was Abraham’s faith. In Abel, Enoch, and Noah there was reasoning; but in Abraham it seemed to surpass all reasoning. For God’s commands appeared to conflict with God’s commands; faith seemed to oppose faith; and God’s command was contrary to the promise. Consider, for example, what he had said: “In Isaac your offspring shall be called”—and Abraham believed it; and then he said again: “Sacrifice him to me,” although the whole world was to be filled from his offspring.

Observe the conflict between commands and promises. He was commanding things contrary to the promises. Yet that righteous man neither became stupefied nor said that he had been deceived. No one could say, “Since he had another son, Abraham hoped to fulfill the promise through him, and therefore, trusting in that, he offered this one.” The Apostle says that he was offering his only-begotten son, who had received the promises, insofar as the substance of the promise was concerned. For this reason the Apostle added “only-begotten,” wishing to show that the one who had received the promises was the only-begotten son, as it is written: “In Isaac your offspring shall be called.”

Then, lest anyone think that Abraham did this in despair, and that through this command he had lost faith in the promise, let everyone recognize that he also possessed that faith, although it might seem to conflict with this command. Yet it did not conflict: he did not measure God’s power by human reasoning, but carried everything out by faith. Therefore the Apostle is not afraid to say that God was also able to raise him from the dead.

“You,” he says, “you cannot say this, because he promised you rest in the future and tribulation in the world. ‘In the world,’ he says, ‘you will have tribulation’ (Matt. XXIV, 9); and, ‘Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me’ (Matt. X, 38; Mark VIII, 34; Luke IX, 23); and again, ‘They will bring you before rulers and governors because of me’ (Matt. X, 18; Mark XIII, 9).”

The opposite happened to Abraham. He was commanded to do something contrary to the promise, yet even so he was neither troubled nor stunned, nor did he think himself deceived. You suffer nothing beyond what was promised, and yet you are disturbed. He, however, heard something contrary to the promise from the very one who had made the promise, and he was not disturbed.

“By faith,” he says, “Abraham offered Isaac.” What then? Did God not know that this man was strong and approved? Why, then, did he test him? Not so that God himself might learn this, but so that he might demonstrate it to others and make Abraham’s strength manifest to all.

Here he also reveals the purpose of temptations, lest they think that they suffer these things as people abandoned by God. If, then, temptations are imposed upon those who have been approved in such a way that God exercises his athletes even when no cause exists, how much more ought you to endure everything bravely for a reason.

With elegance he warned them to learn the example of good faith from the patriarch himself, urging those who had believed from among the Jews to follow, as good offspring, the deeds of their first and greatest ancestor. Since he was admonishing them not to fail in temptations and to prove their faith through works, he appropriately set forth an example from the patriarch by which he could instruct them in both virtues.

For what greater temptation can occur—apart from those involving wounds to one’s own body—than for an old man to be compelled to kill his only and most beloved son? How can someone hesitate to give his tunic or his food to the poor for love of God, if he did not hesitate immediately to hand over to death, at the Lord’s command, the son whom he had received in old age as his heir?

The phrase “reasoning that God was even able to raise him from the dead” may be understood as having been said for the sake of those whom he wished to lead toward hope in the resurrection, and who dared to say, “He promised us good things after death; perhaps he deceived us.” He shows that God is able to raise the dead; and if God is able to raise the dead, then surely he will restore everything that he promised.

“Therefore he also received him in a parable.”

He received him in a parable because Isaac was saved when the ram had been killed (Gen. XXII, 13). Isaac was slain insofar as Abraham’s will was concerned; afterward God gave him back to the patriarch in a parable, that is, in the likeness and figure of Christ’s Passion.

Everything was a likeness: the things enacted in Abraham were certain figures which the true Abraham, that is, God the Father, was to enact for us at the end of the age. Abraham bore the figure of God the Father, while Isaac bore the figure of Christ.

For just as Abraham offered his only and beloved son as a sacrifice to God, so God the Father handed over his only Son for us all. And just as Isaac himself carried the wood upon which he was to be placed, so Christ carried upon his shoulders the wood of the cross on which he was to be crucified. The ram is the flesh [Col. 0806C] of Christ. Isaac was offered but was not killed; only the ram was killed. Likewise, Christ was offered in his Passion, but his divinity remained incapable of suffering.

“By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning future things.”

“Future things” does not mean the future age, but the things that were future within this age, of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Many prophets and kings desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke X, 24).

If the Son was not revealed to some because of their weakness, since they were unable to receive him, nevertheless he was revealed to those who were radiant with love of virtue. The Apostle also says this: Isaac blessed them by faith, foreseeing the things to come. Jacob bore the figure of Christ, or of the Christian people, while Esau bore the figure of the Jewish people [Note: [Col. 0805] These points strongly support our exposition of the words in verse 12 of this chapter, “and are all descended from one,” which was given above.].

“By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph and worshiped the top of his staff.”

Indeed, Jacob himself also blessed each of Joseph’s sons, Ephraim and Manasseh—that is, only two sons—by faith. They are called “each” because he blessed each of the two separately.

Through the elder, Manasseh, he wished to prefigure the Jewish people; through the younger, the Christian people. He first wished to mention the blessing of the two sons so that his faith and prophecy, worthy of worship through the top of the staff, might be revealed.

In that staff which Jacob worshiped, and at whose top he placed his lips, he worshiped the kingdom of Christ, which he had foreseen in the Spirit and which was to come at the end of the age. He foresaw it being ruled by the true Joseph, that is, the Lord Christ.

Or perhaps he foresaw that Christ would later be born from the same stock as those who had received the staff of the kingdom. Others understand the passage differently, though this seems to us beside the point: they say that a king would arise from Ephraim [Note: [Col. 0807D] The same as Ephraim, Psalm LXXVII, 9.], who afterward ruled over the ten tribes; and therefore Jacob worshiped the top of Joseph’s staff.

“By faith Joseph, when dying, mentioned the departure of the children of Israel and gave orders concerning his bones.”

Joseph did not say, “Since my father and my grandfather did not receive this land while they were alive, although he greatly valued their virtue, will God now make them worthy to receive what they were made worthy to receive?” He said none of this, but hoped for everything, because through faith he foresaw what was to happen.

Hence he himself says: “God will visit you after many days; carry my bones with you” (Gen. L, 23; Exod. XIII, 19). He would never have given orders concerning his bones unless he had hoped with full faith that they would be brought back to the land of promise.

The righteous did not concern themselves with tombs. We should not become faint-hearted wherever we are buried, especially since we do not know where the bodies of many brave saints lie buried. How much less ought we to concern ourselves with this matter?

[Note: [Col. 0807D] Here, therefore, reading XIII.]

“By faith Moses, after he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they had seen that the child was beautiful, and they did not fear the king’s edict.”

If they did not fear, how did they protect him? It is as though, had they not feared, this were reckoned to them. From where, then, did they hope to save the child, except through faith?

From the very beginning, from his infancy, much grace had been infused into that righteous man. Nature did not bring this about, making him a handsome little child; rather, it was divine grace that also stirred up that barbarian Egyptian woman to love him, to take him, and to seize him.

In these circumstances faith had no adequate evidence. What was there, then—and how much was there—for them to believe merely from his appearance? But you, he says, possessing so many pledges of faith, believe on the basis of the very things you hear, so that you may receive with joy the plundering of your possessions, even though your faith may extend through many periods, as did Abraham’s. These people, too, by faith did not fear the king’s edict.

“By faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to have the enjoyment of temporary sin, considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt; for he was looking toward the reward.”

It is as though he were saying to those to whom he was writing: “None of you has abandoned a royal palace—spacious, splendid, and magnificent—nor such treasures; none of you, when able to be a king’s son, despised them as Moses did; and he not only despised them but also renounced them.”

Having preferred heaven, he did not wish to admire the beauty of the Egyptian kingdom. He chose rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the pleasures of sin. He regarded refusing to suffer with the others as a sin.

If, then, he judged it a sin not to suffer gladly with the others, how great a heap of sin will those have who abandon the assembly? You suffer for your own sake; but he, looking toward the reward not only for himself, chose this also for the sake of others, so that the accumulation of his reward might grow greater. He voluntarily cast himself into such great dangers, although he could have lived piously while also enjoying worldly goods.

“Considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt.” He judged it better to endure reproach for Christ [Note: [Col. 0807D] That is, reproach similar to the reproach Christ endured; or “for Christ,” namely, for the people from whom Christ was to be born [Col. 0808D]; or for the coming Christ, in whom the righteous hoped.] than to live in luxury.

What is “the reproach of Christ”? It is the kind of reproach Christ endured, the kind you now endure, and the reproach Moses endured for Christ. By rejecting the errors of our fathers, we endure reproach, just as Moses also endured reproach when he heard: “Do you intend to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?” (Exod. II, 14).

This is the reproach of Christ: when someone endures reproach from members of his household, or from those to whom he does good, just as Christ himself heard reproach from those for whom he was crucified, when they said: “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross” (Matt. XXVII, 40).

Moses suffered these things because of his benefaction, just as Christ did. For this reason he aroused them, showing that Moses had also suffered the same things as Christ. Christ suffered and endured everything while they shook their heads. Yet he neither sent forth lightning bolts nor wished to avenge himself, so that he might show us an example of humility.

“By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the king’s anger; for he endured as seeing the invisible one.”

Accordingly, even the fact that he turned to flight belonged to faith. Why did he not remain? He says: so that he would not hurl himself into open danger. For this would already have been the act of one who was testing God, rushing into the midst of danger and saying, “Let us see whether God will deliver me.” The devil said this also to Christ: “Throw yourself down” (Matt. IV, 6; Luke IV, 9).

You see that this is diabolical: for someone needlessly and gratuitously to cast himself into danger in order to test whether God will save him. Moreover, Moses could no longer remain there to govern them, since they were so ungratefully afflicting the man who had done so much for them. It was foolish and senseless to remain there.

“By faith he celebrated the Passover and the shedding of blood [Note: [Col. 0808D] The Vulgate has “and the shedding of blood” expressed differently: *et sanguinis effusionem*.], so that the one destroying the firstborn might not touch them.”

The same Apostle often argues several things within the very passages he speaks, and he is dense in his statements; such indeed is the grace of the Holy Spirit. His few statements do not contain a profusion of words; rather, within the brevity of his words he possesses a great and abundant meaning.

It is as though he were saying to them: “If the blood of a lamb, amid the Egyptians and in the midst of such destruction, preserved the Jews unharmed (Exod. XII, 7), how much more will it save us—not our doorposts, but our souls?”

The angel feared that blood, for he knew whose type it was. He trembled, understanding the Lord’s death; therefore he did not touch the doorposts. Although what was being done was itself nothing, what was prefigured through it was great.

What was taking place was the shedding of blood; what was prefigured was salvation, protection, and prevention of destruction—namely, the leading of us out of Egypt, that is, out of the darkness of idolatry. Yet you, possessing the blood of the Lamb himself, are not ashamed.

“Let us put on the weapons” (Rom. XIII, 12), that is, that sacrifice, because the destroyer prowls in the deep night. Observe, then, how, while arguing and wishing to instruct them under the guise of exhortation, he explains whose figure and type the blood had been.

The doorposts of the Israelites were smeared with the blood of a lamb, so that the destroying angel would not dare to inflict ruin. The faithful people are marked on their foreheads with the sign of the Lord’s Passion for the protection of salvation, so that only those who have been marked in heart and forehead with the blood of the Lord’s Passion may be freed from destruction. They also say with their mouths: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Ps. IV, 7).

Hence the solemnity itself is called *Pascha*, which we can call “passing over,” because, as we proceed from worse things to better, we abandon dark Egypt.

[Col. 0809C] “By faith they crossed the Red Sea as though on dry land; when the Egyptians attempted it, they were swallowed up.”

Consider that everywhere faith exceeds human reasoning and rises above human weakness and lowliness. By believing, they even avoided punishments. From this it clearly appeared that the water was real, since those who entered it were swallowed up. From this it appeared that it was not an illusion but the truth of events, since the Egyptians, attempting the crossing, were swallowed up.

It is as though he were saying to those to whom he was writing: “We must hold faith so firmly that, whenever our spirit is tossed about in some despair, we should then also be people of faith, so that we may be delivered. Even if we come as far as death, even if everyone despairs of us, then we must hold faith all the more firmly.”

What hope could they have had? Surrounded on every side, if they wished to flee, they would either perish in the sea or fall into the hands of the Egyptians. Yet through faith they conquered everything.

The same sea forgot its nature for these people; for the others it was armed against them. In a typological sense, what is signified by the Red Sea except baptism, consecrated by the blood of Christ?

The pursuing enemies, together with the king, who die behind them, are past sins that are blotted out, and the devil, who is drowned in spiritual baptism. The Egyptians press, sins pursue and close in, but only as far as the water.

“By faith the walls of Jericho fell after they had been encircled for seven days (Josh. VI, 20).”

It was not the sound of trumpets that cast down the stones of the walls—as though someone might blow trumpets for ten thousand years. Faith accomplishes everything. Things are not all changed by any necessary sequence of events or by the law of nature; rather, everything happens because of hope.

Accordingly, here too everything happens because of hope. The Apostle confirms, above and below, that it is necessary to believe in the things hoped for in the future. He therefore extended this discourse at such length, showing that miracles were not obtained and accomplished by faith only now, but from the beginning.

Figurally, Jericho signifies the world. Jericho, by interpretation, is called “the moon.” The moon, however, represents the appearance of this world, because just as the moon wanes through its monthly cycles, so this world, running toward the completion of the ages, will fall through daily decline.

The ark signifies the Church; the bronze trumpets signify strong preachers. The Israelites therefore carry the ark around this city of Jericho for seven days while the bronze trumpets sound. Its walls fall through the presence of the ark and the sound of the bronze trumpets.

For in this period, which revolves through the succession of seven days, while the ark is carried—while the Church moves around the world—at the voices of the preachers, as at the sound of trumpets, the walls of Jericho, that is, the lofty and proud obstacles of the world’s unbelief, collapse, until at the end of time the last enemy, death, is destroyed.

Then he increases the consolation and exhortation of his discourse, directing it toward weak persons. It is not surprising that such admirable persons endured these things bravely; but the fact that a prostitute believed so faithfully offers you a remarkable example [Col. 0810C]. The passage continues:

“By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with the unbelievers, having received the spies in peace (Josh. II, 3).”

It is as though he were saying openly: “It is shameful if you are more unbelieving than a prostitute.” She merely heard men announcing these things and immediately believed. You, however, hear not only men but also the voices of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath.

The effect of faith also followed in Rahab’s case: while all the others perished, she alone was saved. She did not say to herself, nor did she reason logically: “Since I am among many people, can I be wiser than wise men who do not believe, while I believe?” She did not think in this way, but believed their words—that these things could happen.

Rahab bears the figure of the Church, which has been gathered from foreign and alien nations. Previously she lived in the desires of the flesh and prostituted herself to idols. To her the Lord Jesus Christ sent the two Testaments to examine human conduct.

For this reason, so that he might more fully test the faith of believers or the stubbornness of rebels before the arrival of his judgment, he sent the Law and the Gospel as two spies.

Up to this point he has spoken of the lawgiver, of the ancient fathers, and of Moses’ successor, Joshua, son of Nun. Now he is going to speak of the judges of Israel, mentioning their names because of the brevity of his discourse—those who fought through faith and conquered very many nations.

“And what more shall I say? For time will fail me as I tell of them.”

The time allotted for writing the epistle is failing me. This is what I had proposed in my heart, whether by narrating their deeds or their history; but, having ended with the prostitute and brought before them the shameful quality of her person, I no longer take pleasure in recounting histories.

Yet, lest he seem to prolong his discourse, he does not explain these matters but runs through them, doing both things very wisely: avoiding the loss of time while not removing the density of his statements. He was neither completely silent nor did he become tiresome by speaking. He does both. Whoever wishes to burden a believer with the length of his discourse incurs the reputation of seeking display. One must look to usefulness and adapt oneself to it.

“Of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets, who through faith conquered kingdoms.”

The reason they are all mentioned together is that the deeds of each were performed by the same faith, through which these men likewise conquered by faith.

Gideon ruled, receiving a sign in the fleece, in order to overthrow Zebah and Zalmunna (Judg. VIII, 40). Barak acted to crush Sisera and all his chariots (Judg. IV, 6, 15, 16, 21). Samson, at his death, killed more than he had killed while alive (Judg. XVI, 30). Jephthah fought against the sons of Ammon and offered his daughter (Judg. XI, 30). David killed the Philistine and received a promise concerning Christ (1 Kings XVII, 50). Samuel killed Agag, king of Amalek (1 Kings XV, 33).

“They practiced righteousness”: because they completed in works what they believed. “For they obtained the promises,” because they were worthy to have them promised to them.

Or they obtained the promises because, when David had received an oath-bound answer that Christ would arise from him according to the flesh, he did not doubt but believed. Thus it is written: “The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not disappoint it: ‘From the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne’” [Note: [Col. 0811D] Psalm CXXXI, 11: “The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not frustrate it; from the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne.” This promise is found especially in 2 Samuel VII, 12 and the following verses.].

And elsewhere: “Once I have sworn by my holiness, I will not lie to David: his offspring shall remain forever. And his throne shall be like the sun before me” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 36–37).

And in 1 Chronicles XVII, 11–13: “When your days are fulfilled,” he says, “and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come forth from your womb, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build me a house, and I will establish his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son; and I will not remove my mercy from him, as I removed it from the one who was before you.” We see that this has now been fulfilled in Christ.

“They shut the mouths of lions; they quenched the violence of fire.”

“They shut the mouths of lions” through faith: Daniel did so (Dan. XIV, 39), as did Samson (Judg. XIV, 6) and David (1 Kings XVII, 34–37).

“They quenched the violence of fire” through faith, as did the three youths in the fiery furnace (Dan. III, 93). This is faith: when things turn out contrary to us, we then believe that nothing contrary has happened, but that everything has been ordered consistently.

“They escaped the edge of the sword, grew strong from weakness, became mighty in war, and routed the armies of foreigners.”

They escaped the edge of the sword through faith—that is, the David already mentioned, or Gideon, or many others whom it would take too long to enumerate. We know that through faith they were strong in war and routed the armies of foreign nations.

They grew strong from weakness through faith, as did Hezekiah (2 Kings XX, 5–6). They became mighty in war, as did Judas and his brothers [Note: [Col. 0811D] 1 Maccabees III, together with the other chapters recounting the valor of Judas and his brothers.].

“Women received their dead back by resurrection.”

The Apostle is recalling the events that took place through Elijah and Elisha. At the request of those women, they were asked through faith to raise their dead, as the Apostle remembers.

Elijah raised the son of the widow of Zarephath of Sidon and returned him to his mother [Note: [Col. 0811D] 1 Kings XVII, 17. The opinion that Jonah was the son of the widow of Zarephath long prevailed among certain rabbis, because of what is read in the same chapter, verse 24: “Now by this I know that you are a man of God, and that the word of the Lord in your mouth is true.” For the son of Amittai is called Jonah; and *Amittai* in Hebrew means “truth.” On this opinion see St. Jerome, Preface to Jonah; Pseudo-Epiphanius; and Dorotheus, *On the Death and Life of the Prophets*, Question to Antiochus, question 65, among the works of St. Athanasius. But Jonah flourished under Joash and Jeroboam II, kings of Israel. How, then, could he have been the son of that widow, since Elijah was taken up sixty years before the reign of Joash?]. Elisha raised the son of the Shunammite woman (2 Kings IV, 35).

“Others were stretched out, refusing redemption, in order to obtain a better resurrection.”

“Stretched out,” that is, extended—namely, stretched out on the wood of the cross by ropes. Or, as others say, they bent down the tops of trees and stretched and broke the bones of martyrs, because they despised present things and desired eternal release.

“Others experienced mockeries and scourges, and in addition bonds and prisons.”

We read of some of these things as fulfilled in Jeremiah and Amos. Thus, when the Apostle writes of these or others, he describes what commonly happens to those upon whom evils are inflicted.

First they mock them—hence the term *delubria* is derived—and after they have been scourged, as Micah was by Zedekiah [Col. 0812D] (1 Kings XXII, 24), bonds and prisons follow (ibid.).

“They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were tested, they died by the killing of the sword.”

They were stoned, as Jeremiah was [Note: [Col. 0812D] The opinion that Jeremiah was stoned, and that the Apostle intended to speak of him here, has been supported by many ancient writers [Col. 0813D] and reinforced by Hebrew tradition. See Tertullian, *Against the Gnostics*, chapter 8; Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, book II; Epiphanius, *On the Life and Death of the Prophets*; and Dorotheus, *Synopsis*.], or Naboth (1 Kings XXI, 13), or Zechariah [Col. 0813A] [Note: [Col. 0813D] There is a well-known and more extensive question concerning this Zechariah, too long to discuss here. See the *Biblical Historical Dictionary*, under the entry “Zechariah,” where the question and the authors who treat it are supplied.].

They were sawn in two, as Isaiah was [Note: [Col. 0814D] It is the opinion and tradition of Hebrews and Christians that Isaiah was cut apart with a saw and died at the beginning of the reign of Manasseh, king of Judah. See Origen on chapter XXIII of Matthew; Augustine, *City of God*, book XVIII, chapter 24; and many others.].

They were tested—that is, proved—as Abraham and Jacob were. They died by the killing of the sword, as Uriah did (2 Kings II, 24) and Josiah (2 Kings XXIII, 29; 2 Chronicles XXXV, 23).

They endured all these things through faith, despising the present so that they might be raised to heavenly things. There are two miracles of faith: it commands great things, and it suffers great things, counting suffering as nothing.

“They wandered about in sheepskins (*melotis*) and in goatskins, needy, oppressed, afflicted.”

Here we should understand Elijah. He is clearly indicated; but not only he, also others who lived in this way: afflicted on every side by want, oppressed by tribulations, and needy through poverty, so that through affliction they might reach the desire for eternal things.

Some say that *melotes* was a garment hanging down on one side only, made from skins, such as the monks in Egypt used [Note: [Col. 0814D] Cassian, *On the Habit of Monks*, chapter 11.], and which Elijah is also said to have worn (2 Kings I, 8).

“Of whom the world was not worthy.”

Here “the world” means people deceived by love of the world and, by clinging to creation, turned away from recognizing the majesty of their Creator. Of this he says elsewhere: “Now the ruler of this world will be cast out” (John XII, 31).

He shows that the devil is ruler of sinful human beings, not of God’s creatures. Whenever the figure of the world is used in an evil sense, it indicates the lovers of this world, not God.

Far be it from us to believe that he is the ruler of heaven, earth, and all creatures, which are generally called by the name “world.” The whole world therefore serves its Creator, not its deceiver; its Redeemer, not its destroyer. It is governed by divine providence; it is not overturned by the cunning of the enemy, except insofar as the people belonging to that portion of humanity subject themselves to the devil by their own will and not by any necessity.

Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the powers of this world and the rulers of this darkness” (Eph. VI, 12)—that is, against sinful people who remain in the darkness of iniquity.

The world is rightly not worthy of such people. This is why the Lord says in the Gospel: “If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you. But because you are not of the world, and I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you” (John XV, 18).

Such people the world—that is, the people of the world—cannot receive, because they are not worthy. An enemy cannot receive one who has been reconciled; one condemned cannot receive one who has been saved; one defiled cannot receive one who has been cleansed.

“Wandering in deserts and mountains, and in caves and hollows of the earth.”

He means Elijah, or the other people who lived through deserts, under the earth, and in the hollows of the earth.

“And all these, approved by the testimony of faith, did not receive the promise, since God had provided something better for us, so that they should not be made perfect without us.”

Who are all these except those mentioned above, whose faith, so clear and praiseworthy, has been recalled: Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, the Israelites who crossed the sea, Joshua, Rahab, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets?

They were sons of God, the light of the world, the salt of the earth, stars of the firmament, earthly human beings and heavenly angels, living stones and splendid pearls. Their deeds testify to their faith, because without faith it was impossible for them to please God.

Yet, although approved, they did not receive the promise. Someone might say: “What benefit did it bring them to serve God, if they remain without reward to this point?” Far be it from us. May our Lord God remove this thought from the minds of Christians, that we should believe that those who, while still surrounded by mortal flesh, have received the great reward of seeing and knowing God remain without reward.

Finally, hear what is written about them in Revelation VI, 9–11: “I saw beneath the altar the souls of those who had been killed because of the word of God, and they cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘How long, O Lord, [holy and true,] will you not judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?’ And individual white robes were given to them, and it was told [Note: [Col. 0814D] The Vulgate has “it was said.”] them [Col. 0814C] that they should rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers was fulfilled.”

At present the souls of the saints have individual robes, rejoicing in their blessed immortality; when their bodies rise again, they will possess a double portion in their own land, according to Isaiah (Isa. LXI, 7).

At present, however, their desire for the resurrection is not denied them; it is postponed because of the increase of their brothers who are to be gathered in. The joy of the souls themselves can also be represented by white robes, since, through the Lord’s revelation, they have learned both that the wicked will be condemned at the end and that, until the end of the age, many will be joined to their number through martyrdom.

Overflowing with eternal love, they preferred to remain content with this consolation and to defer their own joys until the number of their brothers should be completed.

[Col. 0814D] [Note: [Col. 0814D] In the margin of the manuscript, the reading here is “Lesson XIV,” and “Chapter XXX.”]

## (Chapter XII)

“Therefore, since we too are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, laying aside every burden and the sin that besets us, let us run with perseverance the contest set before us.”

Here he calls the patriarchs and prophets, or the faithful saints, witnesses; because of the height and multitude of their merits, he calls them a cloud. For just as a cloud is inflamed by a fiery ray, so the soul oppressed by evils is inflamed and refreshed by their example. And he does not say that it appears above us, but that it is “laid upon us.” Since we have such great examples, let us lay aside everything, as one who is running and hastening toward a contest—that is, sleep, anxiety, weak thoughts, or every human activity—and let us run with perseverance, so that, just as they endured, we too may endure. For let us run toward the contest set before us, as the Prophet says: “I have run the way of your commandments” (Psalm 118:33). The Apostle did not say, “Let us add to our course,” but, “Let us remain in the same contest set before us.” For he commanded that they should not give up, but remain in it.

“Looking to the author of faith and its perfecter, Jesus, who, for the joy set before him, endured the cross, despising shame.” Christ himself also frequently commended this to his disciples: “If they called the master of the house Beelzebub,” he says, “how much more his household?” (Matthew 10:25). And again: “A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master” (ibid., 24). Let us look to our Savior, since he is recognized as the author of the salvation of our souls, and learn to run. For just as sons attend to their parents, and disciples to their teacher in contests, shaping their minds according to what they learn from their instructors and taking certain rules from them through sight, so here too, if we wish to run and learn [Col. 0815C] how to run well, let us look to the author, or perfecter, Christ, because he is both the author and the perfecter. For he himself infuses faith into us. Indeed, he said to his disciples: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16). He himself also laid the beginning in us; he himself will establish the end, or perfection. For in him we all possess perfection.

“Who, for the joy set before him, endured the cross.” He endured it because of what he foresaw at the end. For it was possible for him to suffer nothing, if he had wished. No sin or deceit was found in his mouth. It was therefore possible for him, if he had wished, not to come to the cross, as he himself says in the Gospel: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:17–18). Nevertheless, despising shame, he endured the cross—that is, he endured it without embarrassment or shame. If, then, he who had no necessity to be crucified was crucified for our sake, how much more is it right for us to endure all things courageously? For this reason the Lord appeared in the flesh: to rouse human life by admonition, to draw near by providing examples, to redeem it by dying, and to restore it by rising again. For he died for no other reason than to teach us to regard as nothing the glory bestowed by human beings; therefore, although not subject to death, he accepted death, teaching us to presume against death.

“And he sits at the right hand of the throne of God,” that is, in the prosperity of eternal life. Even if there were no promise, the example alone that the Apostle presents here concerning Christ would have been sufficient to persuade us to endure all things. Now rewards are also promised—and not ordinary ones, but exceedingly great and ineffable ones. For after he conquered, giving an example to his followers, he sits at the right hand of the Father. What went before in the head must also follow in the members. First, therefore, we must endure mockeries, insults, and reproaches, as he endured them, and afterward return to the heavenly realms.

Accordingly, whenever we have suffered anything of this kind, let us think of him, because his whole life [Col. 0816B] was filled with much dishonor. He continually heard from the Jews that he was insane, a deceiver, a magician, and a criminal; that he was mad and had a demon. They accused him of magic when they said: “By Beelzebub he casts out demons” (Luke 11:15). He heard this from those to whom he was doing good. If he had heard such things while doing nothing, it would not have been astonishing; but while teaching what pertained to the truth, he heard that he was a deceiver, and while expelling a demon he was said to have a demon. Not only this, but they also disparaged him on account of his family and homeland: “Is this not the son of the carpenter, whose father and mother we know? Are not all his brothers among us?” (Matthew 13:55; Mark 6:3; John 6:42). And again they said: “Search and see that no prophet arises from Galilee” (John 7:52). And again they said: “Does Scripture say that the Christ will come from the village of Bethlehem?” (ibid., 42).

Do you also wish to hear of the mockeries? They came, he says, to the very cross, worshiped him, struck him, slapped him, and said to him: “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross” (Matthew 27:40). Moreover, a servant of the high priest struck him on the cheek (John 18:22); and mocking him, they clothed him in scarlet, and spat in his face. They also repeatedly subjected him to temptations, rebukes, and accusations. Because of all these things the Apostle admonished them to look to the author of faith and its perfecter, Jesus.

“Consider him who endured such contradiction from sinners against himself, so that you may not grow weary, fainting in your souls.”

Remember him who endured such things from sinners, although he had no sins, so that you, who are known to be transgressors and sinners, may endure. For if you are his disciple, he says, imitate the teacher; this is what it means to be a disciple. But if he went through tribulations while you wish to go through repose, you do not wish to travel the same road by which he traveled, but another. How, then, will you follow him if you do not follow? How will you be a disciple if you do not follow in the teacher’s footsteps?

[Col. 0817A] “Contradiction against himself” means that he allowed them to do whatever they wished, contradicting them in nothing. By this name he indicated the blows he received, the mockeries, injuries, insults, reproaches, and derisions—all of them. Therefore he insists that they should not fail amid tribulations, since they had not yet reached martyrdom and the shedding of blood. Hence he adds:

“For you have not yet resisted unto blood, struggling against sin.”

There are two kinds of reasoning that are thought to be opposed to each other, although they provide one another with much assistance. The Apostle here trampled down both kinds. One occurs when, in tribulation, we think that we have suffered very much, as we also read that blessed Job did when he was under affliction. The soul somehow rests when, placed in tribulation, it remembers its sufferings, just as the Apostle recalled above: “Remember the former days, in which, after being enlightened, you endured a great contest of sufferings.”

The other occurs when we say that we have suffered nothing significant. The former kind makes the soul that is being overwhelmed by sorrows rest and recover; the latter turns the negligent and supine soul around, causes it to lay aside arrogance, and draws it back. Therefore, lest exaltation should arise in them from that testimony, consider what he says: “You have not yet resisted unto blood, struggling against sin,” as if he were saying: “You have not yet endured death; you have suffered only the loss of property; you have merely been harassed and undergone persecution. Christ shed his blood for you, but you have not yet suffered anything of this kind for yourselves. He struggled for the truth unto death, fighting for you; but you have not yet reached the dangers that threaten destruction.”

By saying “struggling against sin,” he shows that sin was fiercely attacking them and armed in various ways.

“And you have forgotten the consolation that speaks to you as sons, saying: My son, do not neglect the discipline of the Lord, nor grow weary when you are rebuked by him.”

He exhorts them from the testimonies of Scripture, so that they may not fail while being rebuked. This can bring them no small consolation, when they recognize that enduring such things one after another is the work of God. Certainly these are God’s words. For by his permission the righteous suffer various pressures. You cannot say that someone is righteous because he exists without tribulation, since he chastises every son whom he receives. Therefore all the righteous must pass through pressures and tribulations.

The sentence of the Lord Christ is: “Broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction, but narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life” (Matthew 7:13–14). If, then, one comes to life by that way, and cannot arrive there otherwise than through hardships and tribulations, we must endure, since all who have been led to life have passed through this road. There are those who serve the Lord in prosperity but fall away in adversity. Therefore the Apostle, who taught them to live well in prosperity, also exhorts them in correction not to fail, lest, when weakness, poverty, or human persecution comes upon them, they lose the devotion they appeared to preserve in tranquility.

“For whom the Lord loves, he chastises” (Proverbs 3:12; Revelation 3:19). “He scourges every son whom he receives.” The Apostle asserts these testimonies so that, just as sons are scourged by their fathers in order that they may be worthy to approach their paternal inheritance, so these people too may patiently endure corrections from God, with a cheerful spirit, in order to reach the true and eternal inheritance. Therefore, the less we ought to murmur about the scourging by which we are chastised, the more certainly we hold in it the pledge of paternal love. Hence he himself also says: “I rebuke and chastise those whom I love” (ibid.).

[Col. 0818B] “Persevere in discipline. God offers himself to you as to sons.”

“Persevere,” he says, “in discipline.” As if he were saying: “It is better for you to pass into life through discipline than to go into torments without discipline.” Since they thought that they had been abandoned, he tells them that they should rather believe that they have not been abandoned, as if he were saying: “Because you have suffered so much, you think that God hates you or has abandoned you. If you were not suffering this, then you would have more reason to think so. For if he chastises every son whom he receives, the one who is not chastised is certainly not among the sons.”

“But,” you say, “do the wicked suffer no evils?” They certainly do suffer. When he says that every son is scourged, he does not say that everyone who is scourged is a son, but that every son is scourged. For he always and everywhere chastises and disciplines the son. There are indeed many wicked people who are scourged, such as murderers, robbers, sorcerers, and plunderers of tombs; but they suffer punishment for their iniquity. They are not scourged as sons, but punished as the worst of people, not as sons. The tribulations of the faithful are thought by the reprobate and lovers of the world to arise from sin alone; but they consider themselves righteous because, abandoned to the perversity of their own judgment, they have hardened without the scourge.

“For what son is there whom his father does not correct?”

In households, a father commonly neglects the children of others but chastises or corrects his own children, lest harmful negligence overwhelm them. If, then, fathers do this for their own sons, lest negligence overwhelm them, we ought to rejoice when we are chastised, since this is done for true sons. Therefore God deals with us as with sons, and so you cannot say that we are unable to endure such things.

“But if you are without discipline, of which all have become partakers, then you are illegitimate children and not sons.”

The meaning of this sentence, with what is implied, is as follows: If all good sons, who have endured the discipline of Christ, have become partakers of discipline, then all the negligent, who despise God’s discipline, are reckoned illegitimate children and not sons.

“Furthermore, we had the fathers of our flesh as instructors, and we revered them; shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits and live? For they instructed us for a few days, according to their own will; but he does so for what is beneficial, in order that we may receive his sanctification.”

If carnal children revere their fathers, how can you not revere the heavenly Father? The difference between them is not merely a distinction of persons, namely, that these are earthly and he is heavenly, but also a difference in the very purpose. For they did not instruct us toward the same purpose or toward spiritual realities, but according to what seemed good to them—that is, fulfilling their own will and desire.

“They,” he says, “instructed you so that you might be useful to them, perhaps at times even without cause; for their will was not useful in everything. But he instructs, teaches, and chastises us for what is beneficial, so that he may make us receptive to his gifts.” Since carnal parents instruct us for a short time, how much more does our Creator do so for what is beneficial and perfect, so that we may receive his sanctification—that is, his purity—and become worthy of him?

Discipline, therefore, is participation in holiness. For it excludes the customs of worldly things [Note: [Col. 0819D] Perhaps “desires” (*amores*).] and draws spiritual grace toward itself. If we consider the righteous, all of them have become illustrious through tribulations.

“Now every discipline, at the time, seems not to be a matter of joy but of sorrow; afterward, however, it yields the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.”

Every discipline, he says, both human and spiritual, when it is being practiced, does not seem to be a matter of joy but of sorrow. He calls all of this both spiritual and human discipline because whatever is said is called discipline; conversely, what is done with a joyful and wicked disposition does not appear to be discipline.

In spiritual discipline there is sorrow first, so that joy may follow; but in the crime of iniquity there is joy first, and sorrow follows. In the latter there is pleasure first, and distress follows; in the former there is sadness first, and then gladness is produced. The former, therefore, must be pursued: one is first saddened and afterward enjoys joy. The latter must be rejected: one first rejoices and afterward falls into sorrow.

In spiritual discipline there is always joy arising from everlasting gladness, although one is afflicted by tribulation, just as the same eminent preacher says elsewhere: “We glory in tribulations” (Romans 5:3). In the one, fear of future sorrow disfigures present joy; in the other, hope of future gladness removes present sorrow. Do not be sad, then, if discipline itself is accompanied by injury; it will nevertheless yield sweeter fruits.

“Afterward,” he says, “it will yield the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it”—not merely one fruit, but an abundant multitude of fruits. Those who are trained by it: he rightly said “those who are trained by it,” that is, those who patiently endure for a very long time. Afterward they will receive the fruit—that is, after it has been completed, it will yield the fruit of righteousness, namely, a reward. “Those who sow in tears shall reap in exultation” (Psalm 125:5). “The most peaceful fruit,” that is, the most delightful.

Therefore we ought to hope for better things at the end. For in trees the bark is almost always bitter and rough, but the fruits themselves are delightful in their sweetness. Those who drink bitter antidotes patiently endure an initial unpleasantness, and then experience the sensation of health. If, then, it is right to hope for such things, and you are suffering and enduring sorrow, you are failing with regard to the better things that you ought to endure. You must endure. You must not become so weakened by tribulation, but bear it courageously. This is why he says in what follows:

[Col. 0820B] “Therefore lift up the hands that hang down and the weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not go astray but rather be healed.”

“Therefore,” that is, because the reward of recompense is given for discipline and joy follows, we must make straight paths and lift up weakened knees. Here he touches upon their hesitations, and he touches upon them so that they might persevere without such hesitations. If discipline pertains to love, as the Apostle demonstrated above both by events and by words, and if at the end it has received a better outcome [Note: [Col. 0820D] Perhaps “will receive a better outcome,” that is, fruit], why are you becoming slack? Why do you not make straight paths for your feet?

This was what happened to those who were failing through despair and were not strengthened by any hope of the future. “Walk straight,” he says, “and let lameness not increase further, but rather let it be restored to its former condition.” He commands that the hanging hands and weakened knees be raised, as Isaiah says: “Strengthen the slack hands and make firm the weak knees” (Isaiah 35:3).

“Straight paths,” that is, thoughts. Hence the Prophet says: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Psalm 118:1). “What is lame,” as he says elsewhere: “Why do you limp between me and Baal?” (1 Kings 18:21). “But rather be healed,” as if he were saying: “Whoever does not believe rightly should believe more firmly and steadfastly, so that in every way you may obtain healing.”

“Pursue peace with all, and holiness, without which no one will see God.”

There are many things that display the form and distinction of Christianity; but above all, and better than all else, are the affection of mutual love and the peace that unites human hearts. Therefore Christ also said: “My peace I give you” (John 14:27). And again: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another” (John 13:35). Therefore the Apostle also says: “Pursue peace with all and holiness” (2 Corinthians 13:11), that is, in body and spirit, so that “blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). [Col. 0821A] “Without which,” that is, without peace and holiness, no one will see God.

“Watching carefully lest anyone be lacking in the grace of God,” as it is found in certain manuscripts [Note: [Col. 0821D] So the Vulgate reads]. He speaks to them as though they were traveling long journeys in a group and company of travelers, as if he were saying: “Take care of yourselves, lest any one of you remain behind. I do not ask only that you yourselves arrive, but also that you look after the others, lest anyone among you,” he says, “be lacking in the grace of God.”

He calls the grace of God faith, hope, love, and excellent conduct. Or the grace of God is that by which our sins are forgiven, so that we may be reconciled to God, while peace is that by which we are reconciled to God [Note: [Col. 0821D] This definition of grace and peace occurs frequently in the commentaries on the other Epistles, especially the commentary on Romans]. Everything, indeed, is God’s grace. Do not say that only one person has perished. For he died on behalf of one person. You, therefore, neglect the one for whom Christ deemed it worthy to die.

“Watching carefully,” he says, that is, carefully examining, visiting, and recognizing, “lest any root of bitterness spring up and cause trouble, and through it the many be defiled.”

He did not say “a bitter root,” but “a root of bitterness.” A bitter root can produce sweet fruits; but a root, source, or purpose of bitterness can never produce anything sweet, because everything there is bitter, everything grievous, everything marked by crime and the worst abomination; they bring nothing of sweetness or delight. “And through it,” he says, “the many be defiled,” because “a little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Corinthians 5:6; Galatians 5:9).

I want this not only for the sake of the person in whom iniquity may be found, but also because of the harm that may spring from his propagation. That is, if there is any such root, do not allow any shoot to rise from it, but cut it off before it defiles others. He rightly said that sin is bitter. Truly, nothing is more bitter than sin. Those who, after committing sin, are tormented by the sorrow of conscience and consumed by truly dreadful bitterness know this.
