The bitterness of wrongdoing sometimes overturns understanding and reason itself, as we read happened in what follows concerning Esau.

“Lest there be any fornicator or profane person, like Esau, who for one meal sold his birthright” (Genesis 25:33).

The term “profane” is given as *castri margus* [Note: [Col. 0821D] I confess that I do not know what this means, unless, instead of *castri margus*, one should perhaps read *quasi margus*, or, in Greek, μάργος, meaning foolish, insane, or senseless—*margos*—so that he may have intended to signify that Esau was almost a foolish seller]. Or it refers to one who sold what was useful in exchange for what was useless.

Through his own negligence and desire he sold the honor he had received from God, and for a small pleasure he lost great honor and great glory. Because of his love for temporal things, he went so far as to sell his birthright. Therefore the first became last, and the second became first. The latter became first through perseverance, while the former became last through negligence. Accordingly, insofar as this pertains to prefiguration, the birthright belongs to us, not to the Jews.

It seems to me that he signifies certain people among them who lay under this vice of fornication, but whom he did not wish to accuse publicly; rather, he pretends ignorance, and afterward, if they persisted, it would then be appropriate to rebuke them. Hence later in this Epistle he says: “For fornicators and adulterers God will judge” (Hebrews 13:4). And at the beginning of this sentence: “Pursue peace and holiness.” The Apostle calls Esau a fornicator because, against his father’s will, he took foreign wives.

“For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected; for he found no place for repentance, although he sought it with tears.”

Above he demonstrates why, when Esau desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, and why he did not find a place for it as his brother Jacob did. Although he sought it with tears, he could no longer reach that place of blessing as his brother had.

Here he does not exclude repentance. Otherwise, if he had condemned repentance, how could he earlier admonish and exhort the sluggish? How could he invite those who had become lame, slack, and weakened—which is the beginning of ruin—to rise? For in this way he blamed himself. If he groaned with great lamentation, why did he not deserve to find a place for repentance? Because that repentance was not salutary, just as Cain’s sorrow did not proceed from repentance. Here too the opportunity concerning his brother appeared [Note: [Col. 0822D] Perhaps one should read: “And here he, namely Cain, disclosed the killing of his brother,” that is, he did not deny it].

What, then, shall we say except that he did not repent as he ought? For this is how repentance must be carried out appropriately [Note: [Col. 0822D] The words “it is necessary” or “it is fitting,” or something similar, may perhaps need to be added here]. Those tears were not tears of repentance, but of a violent spirit and indignation, as is revealed by his deeds. Let those who suppose that sins remain unpunished consider and attend to why Esau could not obtain forgiveness: namely, because he did not repent as he ought.

Do you wish to see complete repentance? Consider Peter and how he repented after denying Christ. The evangelist, recounting his story for us, says: “And going out, he wept bitterly” (Matthew 26:75; Luke 22:62). His great sin was forgiven because he carried out repentance as he ought.

The Apostle may also have said this, as some suppose, in order to press them down under grave fear, lest they fall again into the lapse of wrongdoing—as if he were saying: “Whoever has fallen will no longer be able to deserve any consolation.”

[Note: [Col. 0822D] Here the manuscript reads “Lesson XV.”]

“You have not come to a tangible [Note: [Col. 0822D] The Vulgate reads “a tangible mountain.” In the manuscript, “mountain” is missing [Col. 0823D], although it is repeatedly mentioned later in the exposition] and accessible [Vulgate: “burning”] fire, and to storm, darkness, gloom, tempest, the sound of a trumpet, and the voice of words. Those who heard it excused themselves, lest the word should also be spoken to them. For they could not bear what was being said. And if a beast touched the mountain [Vulgate: “death”], it would be stoned. And so terrible was what appeared that Moses said: ‘I am terrified and trembling.’ But you have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to the assembly of many thousands of angels, and to the church of the firstborn, who are enrolled in heaven, and to God, the judge of all, and to the spirits of the righteous [Note: [Col. 0824D] The Vulgate adds “perfect”], and to Jesus, the mediator of the New Testament, and to the sprinkling of blood that speaks better than Abel.”

That is, you have not approached visible and tangible light, as we read in the case of the ancient Jewish people [Col. 0823B], but the invisible and incomprehensible Lord. These things are reported to have occurred on Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:9, 18): fire, darkness, gloom, and tempest appeared; God was seen, he says, on Mount Sinai.

The New Testament, however, was not given to us with anything of that kind, but was bestowed through Christ’s simple word alone. Observe, then, how he makes a comparison between both these people and those, and how he placed it at the end, in order to show how much higher the grace is in the New Testament, while also announcing that grace through the Old Testament.

Those who make comparisons lower one side so that the excellence of the other side may stand out. Thus here too the Apostle declares by comparison with them that our realities are greater, better, gentler, and full of the utmost wonder. [Col. 0823C] They are better in two ways, since they are at once greater and brighter. There the shadow rested; here the truth is held and revealed. Therefore our realities are more accessible and clearer.

Writing this also in the Epistle to the Corinthians, he says: “But we, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord” (2 Corinthians 3:18), and not as Moses placed a veil over his face. “They,” he says, “did not deserve to receive such things as are known to have been bestowed upon us.” For what did they deserve to see except darkness and gloom? They certainly heard a voice; but you too have heard a voice—not one coming through a cloud, but through Christ’s flesh. You were not thrown into turmoil or confusion, but stood and spoke with the Mediator.

Then Moses was afraid; [Col. 0823D] now no one is afraid. Then the whole people stood below; now, as sons hearing their father, we have heard Christ speaking. It is as if he were saying: “Those things were indeed terrible and dreadful—things that hearing itself could not bear, and to which not even a beast would dare approach. Nevertheless, they were not like the things that have now occurred.”

For what is Mount Sinai in comparison with heaven? What is a tangible fire in comparison with an untouchable one? For the prophet says: “God is a consuming fire” (Deuteronomy 4:24). What are tempest and the sound of trumpets in comparison with those words of the Lord by which he taught his disciples on the mountain, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:3; Luke 6:20), and many other words that are far brighter than the sun?

There Moses is present; here, Jesus. There are the names of peoples; here, thousands of angels. He calls the firstborn those believers who believed first, who are enrolled in heaven.

“And God, the judge of all”—as if he were saying: “Not merely the judge of the Jews or of the faithful, but clearly of the whole world.”

He says that the spirit of the righteous and perfect has approached—that is, the Holy Spirit whom they received in baptism. Or he calls the spirits of the righteous and perfect the souls that have proved acceptable before God.

He calls the blood of sprinkling the passion of Christ, which speaks better than Abel, because Abel’s blood accuses, whereas Christ’s blood excuses, as in the Gospel: “So that upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar” (Matthew 23:35).

The blood of Jesus speaks better than Abel’s because Abel’s blood demanded the death of his brother’s murderer, whereas the Lord’s blood obtained life for his persecutors. Therefore, so that the sacrament of the Lord’s passion may not be useless to us, we must imitate what we receive and preach to others what we revere.

“See that you do not refuse him who speaks. For if those did not escape who refused him who spoke on earth, much more will we not escape if we turn away from him who speaks to us from heaven.”

Beware of refusing Christ’s teaching, because he sits at the right hand of God the Father. When the Jews, terrified, refused God, who was speaking with Moses on earth, saying, “You speak with us, and do not let God speak with us, lest perhaps we die” (Exodus 20:19), how much more will we be struck by a greater vengeance if we turn away from him who speaks to us from heaven?

“Whose voice then shook the earth, but now promises, saying” (Haggai 2:7): “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also heaven.”

He who then shook the earth and gave the law to Moses now promises that he will shake once more not only the earth but also heaven. Therefore, the greater the works he promises to accomplish, the more he must be feared. By saying “once,” he shows that they will never again be shaken.

“But the expression ‘yet once more’ indicates the removal of things that can be shaken, as things that have been made, so that the things that cannot be shaken may remain.”

He indicates the removal of things that can be shaken, in accordance with what David says: “In the beginning you founded the earth, O Lord, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain, and all things will grow old like a garment. And like a covering you will change them, and they will be changed” (Psalm 101:26).

It is plainly established that on the day of judgment he will change and transform the world’s condition for the better, and that this will be as easy as anyone’s folding up and changing a covering. But if he changes these things, his power, strength, kingdom, and power [Col. 0825A] will remain immovable in his saints. He said all these things so that we might know that, the more we understand the things that exist to be subject to change, the more we ought to seek the things that cannot be shaken, as he said.

“Therefore, receiving an unshakable kingdom, let us have grace, by which we may serve God acceptably, with fear and reverence.”

As if he were saying: “We have grace”—that is, grace freely given in the New Testament—“by which we can please God.” He says “with fear and reverence,” that is, with the fear of dread and the reverence of love. Whoever can both serve God and please him possesses the grace of God. He calls the unshakable kingdom the kingdom of Christ, that is, the Church.

“For our God is a consuming fire” (Deuteronomy 4:24).

God is called fire because through this fire the rust of sins is consumed. He does not consume the material that he made, but burns away what we have drawn upon ourselves from sin externally. He does not consume what he himself made, but what human wickedness has introduced.

Concerning this fire the Truth says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it should burn?” (Luke 12:49). Earth is the name given to earthly hearts; while they continually heap weak thoughts within themselves, they are trampled by evil spirits. But the Lord sent fire upon the earth when, through the breath of the Holy Spirit, he set the hearts of carnal people ablaze. The earth burns when the carnal heart, cold in its perverse desires, abandons the passions of the present age and is kindled with love for God.

### (Chapter XIII)

“Let brotherly love continue among you [Col. 0825C]. And do not forget hospitality. For through this some pleased [Vulgate: remained hidden or unnoticed], having received angels as guests [Note: [Col. 0825D] Genesis 18:3; 19:2—namely, Abraham and Lot].”

For he did not say, “Become lovers of the brethren,” but, “Let brotherly love continue.” And again he did not say, “Become hospitable,” as though they were not already so, but, “Do not forget hospitality”; as if he were saying: Let perseverance in love and hospitality continue—something which, because of their tribulations, they might perhaps have forgotten. And not merely hospitality, but also love of hospitality, which is expressed more distinctly in the Greek. He did not use ξενοδοκίαν [Note: [Col. 0825D] He does not say ξενοδοχεῖον, or κατάλυμα, that is, an inn or lodging-place, but φιλία, or φιλοξενεία.]—a word signifying hospitality—but *philo*, which conveys love of hospitality; as if he were saying: “Do not simply receive guests, but do this with love and charity,” as blessed Peter also says: “Be hospitable to one another without grumbling” (I Peter 4:9).

“For through this,” he says, “some pleased,” or, as it is found in the Greek, “remained hidden,” while receiving angels as guests. Consider what honor and what profit it is, through receiving human beings, to attain to evangelical hospitality. What does “remained hidden” mean? It means that, without knowing them to be angels, they received them as guests, as we read that Lot did; and this very event is also recalled by the Apostle in this passage.

[Col. 0826A] “Remember those who are imprisoned, as though imprisoned with them, and those who are suffering, as though you yourselves were also dwelling in the body”; as if he were saying: “Remember them as though you too were imprisoned with them; and,” he says, “remember those who are suffering as though you yourselves were also in the body”—that is, as though you yourselves had been dwelling for a long time, and should therefore endure as they endured.

“Marriage is honorable in all, and the marriage-bed undefiled.” He commanded that marriage be honored, as blessed Peter says: “Showing honor to the female vessel as to the weaker one” (I Peter 3:7). It is called *connubium* because they are joined together. “According to knowledge,” moreover (ibid.), so that they may know what God desires and may give honor to marriage—or, as blessed Peter says, to the female vessel. For if we abstain from intercourse, we give honor; but if [Note: [Col. 0825D] The particle *si*, absent in the autograph, is required by the sense and has therefore been added.] we do not abstain, it is clear that intercourse is contrary to honor, as the same Apostle Paul says elsewhere: “Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (I Corinthians 7:5).

Therefore I must never be continually devoted to marriage, lest I be hindered for even a single hour from prayer, to which I am commanded always to apply myself, as the Apostle instructed elsewhere. And “the marriage-bed,” he says, “undefiled”—that is, lawful intercourse, free from fornication. The Jews did not consider the marriage-bed undefiled, for they thought marital intercourse polluted [Note: [Col. 0826D] In the manuscript, *collutum*. The following context shows that this should be emended.] it. For they said that a man rising from the marriage-bed could not remain clean. Therefore, O most ungrateful and senseless Jew, what is permitted by nature is not polluted, but what proceeds from a perverse will. For if marriages are honorable, they are also clean. Why, then, do you think that pollution arises from them?

“For God will judge fornicators and adulterers.” First he said, “Marriage is honorable and the marriage-bed undefiled”; then he added, “God will judge fornicators and adulterers.” For he showed that fornicators and adulterers are justly judged. If marriage has been permitted, then the fornicator is justly punished, and adulterers are justly punished. For fornication is understood not only as intercourse with women, but also as worshiping idols. Adulterers are not only those who fornicate with another man’s wife, but also heretics, because they adulterate the words of God.

[Col. 0826D] “Let your conduct be without avarice, content with what you have.” For he did not say, “Do not possess,” but, “Let your conduct be without avarice.” An avaricious person is one who is tight-fisted in giving and eager in receiving. A certain wise man admonished this, saying: “Do not stretch out your hand to receive and close it when giving” (Ecclesiasticus 4:36). Perhaps, after the depletion of their possessions, they wished to gather wealth again under the pretext of almsgiving. I think that this is why the Apostle admonished them to let their conduct be without avarice [Col. 0827A], so that they would be content only with present necessities, as he himself says elsewhere: “Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content” (I Timothy 6:8).

And lest they perhaps say, “What shall we do if the means necessary for us should fail?” he immediately added consolation, bringing forward testimony from the Book of Joshua 1:5: “For God himself [Note: [Col. 0827D] The Vulgate does not have *God*.] said: ‘I will never leave you nor forsake you.’” He does not lie in any way if we place our hope in him. Therefore we ought confidently to say: “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me” (Psalm 117:8). “Man” means the flesh, or the ancient adversary, or some affliction. He is called “man,” as the Prophet says: “Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil man” (Psalm 139:2); he is called man because he deceived humanity.

For in all temptations and tribulations we ought to cry out this verse of the Psalmist, or of the Apostle, so that, having God favorable to us, we may mock all human things. For just as, if God is angered, it will not benefit us even if all armies stand with us, so, if God loves us, we will have no need and suffer no injury even if all our enemies pursue us with hostility.

“Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you; considering the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith.” When you offer sacred sacrifices to God for them, always remember those who spoke the word of God to you. Constantly considering their end—that is, turning it over in your mind—and carefully examining yourselves, scrutinize the outcome of their way of life, namely, their perseverance to the end. Since their way of life had a good end, therefore imitate their faith. By “faith” he means their firmness or perseverance, which proceeded from a pure life: that is, hold fast to their examples and persevere to the end.

“Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today, and forever.” Do not think that he acted only then and does not act now, or that he existed then and does not exist now. The same one who was yesterday is also today, and forever. “Yesterday” signifies past time; “today,” the present; and “forever,” the future without end. As if he were saying: Before the ages, throughout the ages, and after the age, he will always remain, as the Prophet bears witness concerning him: “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Psalm 101:28).

“Do not be led away by various and strange doctrines.” “By various doctrines,” he says, “and new ones, do not be carried about.” He calls “new doctrines” those which they had not heard from them. For they did not possess anything firm, but were manifold through a variety of differences. By this command he reproves those who introduced observances concerning foods, as he makes clearer in what follows when he says:

“For it is best to establish the heart by grace, not by foods, which did not benefit those who walked in them.” [Col. 0828A] It is good, he says, to establish the heart by the grace of the New Testament that has been given to us. It is better to retain faith and works than the foods of the Old Testament, in which those who walked had no benefit. For there is one observance: namely, to abstain from sins. Abstaining from foods is of no benefit. Although they devoted themselves earnestly to such observances, nevertheless, because they did not have faith, that observance of foods benefited them nothing. Their keeping of the law benefited them; their abstaining from food benefited them nothing. Everything depends upon faith, if faith itself is strengthened in you; for the heart will be fortified if faith confirms all things.

“We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no authority to eat.” We have an altar [Col. 0828B]—that is, heaven, where Jesus daily presents himself before the Father on our behalf—or the altar, that is, [Note: [Col. 0827D] The manuscript reads *fidem* (“faith”).] the holy Church, where [Note: [Col. 0828D] The manuscript reads *unum* (“one”); we judged it should be corrected as an error.] daily, in the ministry, we receive the blood and body of Christ; from this those who serve the tabernacle, that is, their own body, have no authority to partake. For he had said above: “The heart ought to be established by grace, not by foods, which did not benefit those who walked in them.” Lest it be thought that he was abolishing those things, he therefore said: “We have an altar and a tabernacle.” For that prefigured what we hold in truth. “We,” he says, “observe such things in truth as that was prefigured in figure.”

“For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the sanctuary for sin by the high priest are burned outside the camp.” The bodies are burned outside the camp [Col. 0828C] if we remain in disgrace before everyone. We are the animals if we offer our bodies amid disgrace and persecutions, imitating the example of the Lord, to whom it was said: “Hail, King of the Jews,” and many other things. Or the bodies are burned outside the camp when they are consumed outside the fellowship of worldly people through divine love. And our blood is brought into the sanctuary by the high priest, that is, by Jesus Christ; for it is brought into the sanctuary, that is, into heaven. Blood is brought in through Jesus, as John says: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the propitiation for our sins” (I John 2:1). Those animals prefigured this: their blood was brought into the sanctuary for sin. For they were types of these things, since they were not instituted simply, but were an arrangement signifying this meaning.

“Therefore Jesus also, to sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate.” These things spoken above are known to have been done in figures; Jesus our Savior then showed that this was accomplished in truth, both in himself and afterward in his members. In order to redeem the people through his own blood, he suffered outside the gate—that is, he was crucified outside Jerusalem.

“Therefore let us go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach.” Let us therefore go out to him, despising the present and loving the future, rejecting visible things, as the Apostle says elsewhere: “The things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (II Corinthians 4:18). “Bearing his reproach,” he says—that is, sharing with him, so that just as he endured reproach, so may we also endure it. Let us commune with him, share with him, and suffer the same things; for that reproach is not reproach but sanctification. His reproach is his sign, which we bear on the forehead or in the mind, as Christ himself says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16:24; Luke 9:23). For often, through human shame, we abstain from many good works; and again, often, through human shame, we abstain from many evil works.

[Col. 0829B] “For we do not have here a lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come.” We do not have an earthly dwelling here. Therefore let us go outside after the Lord into reproaches, for his sake, so that we may dwell in the city that is to come [Note: [Col. 0829D] In the autograph, *habemus*; the sense requires emendation.]—that is, the heavenly Jerusalem.

“Through him, therefore, let us continually offer a sacrifice of praise to God”—through him, that is, through Christ, we ought to offer a sacrifice of praise to God—“that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name,” as the Prophet says: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (Psalm 49:14). They offered sheep and calves and gave them to the high priest; but we offer none of these things, only thanksgiving. Let our lips bring this forth. “By such sacrifices,” he says, “God is pleased.” Let our voice resound with nothing blasphemous; let it contain nothing [Note: [Col. 0829D] Perhaps *non improperium*, “not reproach,” or *non propter tuum*, “not for your sake,” in accordance with the Apostle’s teaching in I Corinthians 13:5 and Philippians 2:21, where he teaches that one should not seek one’s own things; for the words stand here as *nonpropt uum*. It may perhaps be preferable to read *non protervum*, “not insolent.”] violent, insolent, or arrogant. Let us give him a sacrifice, so that he himself may offer it to the Father. It is offered in no other way than through the Son, and even more fully through a contrite mind.

“And do not forget beneficence and fellowship, for by such sacrifices God is pleased.” Even if others have seized your possessions, do not forget to give alms from what you have, as the Prophet says: “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor” (Psalm 40:2). Do not think that the one whose hand you see is the recipient; the recipient is the one who commanded you to give. You give bread on earth; God receives it in heaven. You give to one who will consume it; he receives who will repay it. Nor will he repay what he received. You gave earth; you will receive heaven. You gave temporal things; you will purchase eternal things. The bread you gave has been consumed; the bread [Col. 0829D] that he will give will refresh and will not fail.

[Note: [Col. 0829D] In the autograph’s margin this is marked “Chapter XXXVII.”] “Obey your leaders and submit to them. For they keep watch, as those who will have to give an account for all of you [Note: [Col. 0829D] The Vulgate reads “for your souls.”], so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning.”

The Apostle commanded them to lend an ear to their leaders. For we ought to obey the commands of our elders. If they prove wicked, we should not act as they act, but as they teach (Matthew 23:3). If they prove contrary in the faith, they are not only to be avoided but even fled. If they differ in conduct, hear Christ saying: “The scribes and Pharisees have taken their seat on Moses’ chair. Therefore observe and do everything they tell you, but do not act according to their works; for they say and do not do” (ibid., 2–3). As if he were saying: “Pay attention not to their life but to their words.” As far as conduct is concerned, no one can be harmed. Why? Because their works are manifest to all (Galatians 5:19; I Timothy 5:24). In matters of faith, however, what is taught is not manifest to all. [Col. 0830B] Nor does a wicked person hesitate to teach contrary things. Nevertheless, those who are sound in faith must be obeyed, as the Apostle commanded, because they keep watch and give an account for our souls.

For they do not merely watch, but keep watch continually. Therefore be subject to them, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning. O what danger awaits those unhappy and wretched men who thrust themselves forward to govern others and cast themselves into the abyss of so many punishments, since they will have to give an account for all their subjects! After such a great warning, in which we see negligence threatened, what a burden and what difficulties of governance there are for the many who rush forward and thrust themselves into it [Note: [Col. 0830D] I have judged that this text should be somewhat emended. It stood as follows: “After such a great communication, which we see imposed on negligence, for many who rush forward and thrust themselves into so great a burden, so great a difficulty of governance.” It seemed to convey no suitable sense.]!

For if those who are compelled by necessity can have no refuge and find no excuse when they have managed affairs badly or carried out their administration negligently, how much more severely will those be punished who seek leadership eagerly and ambitiously and thrust themselves forward! Such a person closes the place of pardon to himself much more completely. Saul, who had initially refused governance, fell into dangers after he had refused it; how much more the man who thrusts himself forward in ambition for leadership?

Therefore one must fear, both on account of conscience and because of the burden and magnitude of the responsibility. One should neither refuse when drawn into leadership nor, when no one draws him into it, thrust himself forward. But when considering the great eminence of such dignity, one ought to flee it; [Col. 0830D] once one has taken it up, however, one ought to show obedience and reverence. Nothing should be done immoderately [Note: [Col. 0830D] Truly a golden admonition, and worthy of so great a bishop!].

“Pray for us, for we are confident that we have a good conscience, wishing to conduct ourselves well in all things.” As if he were saying: “I do not want you to bring any accusations against me.” “Our conscience,” he says, “condemns us in nothing, nor are we conscious of anything against ourselves.” “We are confident,” he says, “that we have a good conscience in all things”—not only among the Gentiles, but also among you. We do nothing for the sake of commerce; we have brought forward nothing with deceit. “I write these things,” he says, “not as an enemy or as a foe, but as a friend.”

For this passage appears to be a supplication, as though he were writing to those who had been grieved and who were treating him as a transgressor, unwilling even to hear his name. This is also shown by what follows: “I urge you even more to do this, so that I may be restored to you more quickly.” This too is the prayer of one who loves greatly—not simply, but with complete intensity and every possible earnestness. “May I come to you quickly,” he says. This is the disposition of one conscious of nothing against himself: he hastens to come to them quickly.

He urges them to pray for him. To obtain this for himself, he first asks their assistance in prayer; then he himself also supplicates every good thing for them.

“May the God of peace, who brought back from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the eternal covenant, our Lord Jesus Christ”—do not therefore dissent from us, if you wish to have the God of peace favorable to you, from whom all his peace proceeds, as he himself says: “I leave you peace; I give you my peace” (John 14:27). He himself is the great shepherd, as he says in the Gospel: “I am the good shepherd, and I know my sheep, and mine know me” (John 2:14).

[Col. 0831C] “May he make you fit in every good work, so that you may do his will, working in you what is pleasing before him through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.”

May he make you fit for every good work and word, so that you may have a life and correct doctrines according to his will. “Working,” he says, “in you what is pleasing before him.” For he says elsewhere: “It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13). And this is through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

“But I ask you, brothers, to bear with the word of consolation. For indeed I have written to you very briefly.” He did not say, “I ask you to bear with a word of admonition,” but “a word of consolation”—that is, a word of comfort, a word of exhortation. “No one,” he says, “can reject the length of a discourse except through impatience.” This was what he did not wish to reveal to them, but he said it covertly, as if he were saying: “Even if you are faint-hearted—for it is characteristic of such people not to endure a lengthy discourse.” Nevertheless, it is especially appropriate for the weak to hear few things, those which they are able to grasp and which pierce their minds with the pain of repentance.

For if a discourse of exhortation is delivered to them at one time in many forms, since they cannot retain many things, they lose everything together. Thus physicians also apply poultices to the stomachs of the sick, spreading them with suitable and delicate medication; [Note: [Col. 0831D] Perhaps read *ne si* (“lest if”).] otherwise, if they are filled with too much medicine, instead of strengthening the weakness of the stomach and relieving the sick person, they oppress and aggravate him. Yet although the Apostle wrote so much, he said that it was little in comparison with what he was going to say, as he said elsewhere: “As I wrote briefly, so that when you read you may understand my insight into the ministry [Note: [Col. 0831D] The Vulgate reads *mystery*.] of Christ” (Ephesians 3:3–4).

“Know that our brother Timothy has been released”—that is, he is understood to have been released by us, or he means that he was released from Athens—“with whom I shall see you if he comes more quickly.” This was suitable for making them gentler: he said that he was prepared to come to them.

“Greet all your leaders and all the saints.” He treats this exhortatively, since he was writing to them through those leaders.

“Those from Italy greet you” [Note: [Col. 0832D] The Vulgate adds “the brothers.”]. He clearly shows that he wrote this Epistle in Rome.

“Grace be with you all. Amen.” He means the grace of faith, which we received in baptism; or he wishes them the grace of repentance or perseverance—which is common to all. For grace is the remission of sins, through which, by his gift, we may deserve to be cleansed.

I alone am not sufficient to give thanks for your grace, nor is any creature sufficient to give thanks, eternal God, without beginning and without end: through whom all things were made, both those above in heaven and those below on earth. You do not will and make some things while willing but not making others; rather, whatever you will, you make.

Your works are marvelous, your judgments fearful, your promises to be believed. You willed to be called the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and you said: “This is my name forever, and this is my memorial from generation to generation.” Without quality, good; without quantity, great; without need, creator; without position, present; without location, wholly everywhere; without time, eternal; without change, making changeable things; suffering nothing; alone the good King, alone excellent, alone just, almighty and eternal.

You show mercy through gratuitous compassion and undeserved goodness. You condemn and harden sinners through truth, without any injustice; yet through your undeserved mercy you have pity on human beings, because you are powerful. You overlook human sins for the sake of repentance. You make the clean from the unclean, conceived from seed; you wipe away iniquities like a cloud and sins like a mist. Your goodness toward the undeserving and the deserving does not flow sparingly, but lavishly and abundantly.

You placed in my heart the desire, for the taste and sweetness of this holy life of Scripture, to leave my people and my homeland, so that I might taste something of its sweetness and thereby come to know you, because truly your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths.

But your unfailing compassion, abundant clemency, immeasurable mercy, and eternal goodness have given me more than I asked and granted me more than I sought. You gave me not only the heavenly bread that I myself might eat, but also caused me, through an unworthy servant [Col. 0833A], to distribute it to your faithful servants.

For this reason I, an unworthy servant, ask that those useful servants into whose hands these little works of my labor may come refer to God the Author whatever excellent thing they find; and whatever is less satisfactory, may they forgive me. I also ask that, for my sins, they not disdain to request at least in one word God’s undeserved mercy for me, so that when the crown of reward has been given to the just by the merciful Judge, he may grant me, a sinner, however little pardon through God’s undeserved mercy.

Thanks be to God. Amen.

[Col. 0833]

## Sermons of Atto, Bishop of Vercelli

[From the Vatican manuscript, in Mai, *New Collection of Ancient Writers*, vol. VI, part II, p. 11.]

## Sermon I: On the Advent of Our Lord Jesus Christ

[Note: [Col. 0833D] This sermon, together with four others—on Pentecost, Saint Eusebius, the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin, and the Nativity of the Forerunner—was published by the distinguished Jo. Dominicus Mansi in the appendix to volume II of Baluzius’s *Miscellanies*, Lucca, 1761, from this same old and very rare Vatican manuscript. However, being disturbed by haste, that otherwise most learned man wrote and carelessly published many disgraceful errors contrary to the manuscript’s testimony; I shall now correct them.]

[Col. 0833B]

To celebrate the nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, dearest brothers, prepare your hearts even now, order your conduct, and direct your life, so that, when he comes, he may not judge us for negligence but may deem us worthy of reward on the basis of [Note: [Col. 0834C] Mansi reads *ex* (“from”).] worthy works [Note: [Col. 0833D] Mansi distorted these clauses.] Blessed Paul the Apostle cries out: “It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Romans 13:11). He therefore calls negligence “sleep.” Shaking it from our hearts, we ought frequently to devote ourselves to the diligence of good works [Note: [Col. 0834D] The upper margin of the manuscript has been destroyed by damp; approximately two lines have perished on each page. Let readers use this rule to estimate the following lacunae.] … diligently to acquire [Note: [Col. 0834D] Mansi incorrectly reads “and almost.”] … worthy … if I should negligently offend in anything … he might appease him. Behold, indeed, the heavenly … has come, in a certain special way, to visit … whose advent it is much more fitting for us [Col. 0833C] to await with salutary foresight. Through fasts, vigils, prayers, abstinence, almsgiving, and the other virtues, let us carefully wash away the stains of past guilt from the house of our mind, and let us not intend to return to them again.

It is not at all sufficient, when some festival intervenes, to lay aside our iniquity if, after it has passed, we consider returning again to the same thing. For the coming Guest will wish to judge future things just as present things, hidden things just as manifest things [Note: [Col. 0834D] Mansi incorrectly reads “past things.”]

Finally, the Psalmist says: “The Lord is near to all who call upon him, to all who call upon him in truth” [Col. 0834B] (Psalm 144:18). Although the Lord is proved to be everywhere, he is nevertheless undoubtedly said to be near to those to whom he deigns to be favorable—namely, those who call upon him in truth.

Those call upon him in truth who worthily ask for what is beneficial. But those who presume to ask him for superfluous things [Note: [Col. 0834D] Mansi reads “superfluous matters.”], or who do not ask for what they seek with their inmost hearts, plainly do not call upon him in truth, nor do they deserve to have him near, in accordance with the saying: “Salvation is far from sinners” (Psalm 118:155). For whoever seeks God deceitfully will never deserve to find him [manuscript: “to be found”]. Hence it is written: “The Holy Spirit will flee deceit” (Wisdom 1:5).

This was also well declared when angels announced the Lord’s nativity to the shepherds, saying [manuscript: “while saying”]: [Col. 0834C] “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). Good will consists not only in doing no evil, but also in not desiring it. Therefore Christ’s peace is rightly announced to such people.

But those who pretend for a time to avoid murders, hatreds, adulteries [Note: [Col. 0834D] Mansi omitted this word.], thefts, perjuries, and other vices, while already conceiving in their hearts a return to these same things, are certainly not people of good will, and Christ’s peace is not granted to them [Note: [Col. 0834D] Mansi incorrectly reads “is not granted to him.”].

A soldier lays down his weapons, restores his body, and refreshes his limbs so that, when the proper time comes, he may recover his strength and fight again with the same weapons. Not so … to deserve to put on … to reach … let us rejoice [Note: [Col. 0834D] Mansi incorrectly reads “to wound.”].

## Sermon II: On His Nativity

[Col. 0835A]

Let us all rejoice, dearest brothers; let all nations be glad and exult. It is not merely the visible sun that has illumined this day, but rather its invisible Creator. On this day, God became man; heavenly things serve earthly things; angels and human beings are recalled to harmony.

For when God was in the beginning, as the Gospel reading tells you, “All things were made through him” (John 1:3). But the enemy of the human race attempted to rise up against his Creator, saying: “I will set my throne toward the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:14). Because of this pride, both he and all his followers, who wickedly attempted to ascend, were cast down by divine judgment. To repair their fall, the Lord placed human beings in paradise. The angels also, awaiting from them the restoration of their own order, received them with great joy and abundant love.

But after the transgression of Adam, the first man, hatred and discord grew to such an extent that scarcely any root of the former affection remained. The angels no longer considered themselves our companions, because they served God without any offense. Whenever they appeared to human beings, they permitted themselves to be worshiped as by a subject creature.

Thus Christ, God before the ages and made man in time in order to redeem us, assuming the form of a servant, reconciled heaven and earth, angels and human beings. After his incarnation, the angel forbade himself to be worshiped by a human being, [Col. 0835C] saying: “See that you do not do this; I am your fellow servant and that of your brothers” (Revelation 19:10).

This is that day on which the laws of nature are changed: a virgin conceived, a virgin gave birth, and the Word became flesh (John 1:14). For he whom the immensity of heaven cannot contain is placed in the narrow confines of a manger.

Today angels appeared to the shepherds, instructed them concerning the Lord’s birth, strengthened them so that they would not be afraid, announced great joy to them, and first sang “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2:8–15). The angels announced the Lord’s birth first to the shepherds because those who know how to preside over faithful flocks with care deserve, more than others, to see sublime things.

Let us therefore rejoice today, dearest brothers … [lacuna]

## Sermon III: On the Feast of the Lord’s Octave

[Col. 0835D]

We always celebrate this day on the Kalends of January [codex: of the Januarys], as you know, beloved brethren. But we must not pass over in silence the fact that certain false Christians disturb the solemnity of so great a day by sacrilegious mixture, so that they seem to celebrate the divine offices in the churches, while at home they do not cease to engage in various magical practices [Note: On the superstitions spreading through Italy in the Middle Ages, see Muratori’s Dissertation 59 in *Annals of the Middle Ages*, vol. V. It would certainly have been fuller if Muratori had known Atto’s previously unpublished sermon here.]. Moreover, they do not fear observing the traditions of the January festivals and the rites of the pagans [Col. 0836A]. They even drive the grace of charity so far from themselves that on this very day they do not wish anyone to enter their house for the first time unless he has arrived laden with offerings; they refuse to receive anyone as a guest and do not wish to give or lend anything at all from their house [Note: Similar superstitions are mentioned in the little work of Martin of Braga, which I recently published, much more accurately and with an unpublished opening, in the third volume of *Classical Authors*, p. 379.].

O faithless and misguided man! It would be better for you to receive Christ or the poor as guests in your house than peasants whom you and your household have oppressed and equipped with gift-baskets or wine-vessels. For the same Lord says: “Whatever you did for one of the least of these, you did for me” (Matt. 25:40). And again: “Give alms, and everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41).

Likewise, on the Kalends of March such people commonly rave through many magical tricks [as the codex reads]; above all the days of the year, the devil still exercises his colony among them [Col. 0836B]. We shall explain to you where we believe this originated. Mars and Janus were wicked and wretched men: one was a murderer and adulterer; the other was so vain and insane that he even burned himself in the flames. After their deaths, statues were fashioned for them, according to the custom of the pagans, and because of the enormity of their crimes it pleased demons to dwell in them. To deceive human beings more easily, the demons chose to invent for themselves the names of those men, and thus boasted that they were alive and were gods. They declared that the beginnings of the two months should be consecrated to them and ordered that those same months—March and January—be called by their names, from Mars and Janus; they also taught how solemn rites should be celebrated on each of their Kalends and what forms of worship should be performed [Col. 0836C].

This error grew through continual practice to such an extent that it was almost worshiped by all who had been led astray. From this, I think, comes the practice that persists among peasants to this day.

We have also learned that the names of the months, and likewise of the constellations, still remain among some people as compositions of various fictions devised by the most ancient pagans—for example, Aries, Taurus, and the rest. If their names are carefully investigated, they are recognized as false, because the forms of animals are never seen in the stars; rather, pagan curiosity undertook to elaborate these ravings according to the will or praise of its divinities, and more truly of its demons.

We can establish this from a few examples. The pagan philosophers called the constellation *Arctos*, that is, “the Bear” [Col. 0836D], and wrote that it had been placed among the stars by Jupiter; our peasants have called it “the wagon.” What they assert to be the head of a bull, these people call a hen. But what they identify as the belt of Orion, our people loudly call a reaping sickle. Let no one therefore judge these interpretations inferior, as though they had represented the impiety less accurately. In the end, neither does ἄρκτος [codex: *Arcton*], “the Bear,” display a bear better than a wagon; nor does that other constellation designate the head of a bull more appropriately than a hen [Col. 0837A]. And as for what is called Orion’s belt, it is evident to everyone that it resembles a reaping sickle better than a belt.

We are compelled to speak of such matters because we have learned that many people led astray by perverse teaching observe them to an excessive degree. For almighty God established the stars in the heavens so that they might serve human beings on earth. They temper the darkness, indicate the divisions of the hours, and mark out the regions of the world for travelers and sailors. There are also certain stars by which we can sometimes foresee periods of rain or calm. The Creator of all things imposed this law upon them in the beginning; they are not able either to help or to harm beyond it. Yet there are mathematicians who teach that the stars rule those being born, dominate marriages [as the codex reads], and must be observed by builders [Col. 0837B].

But what they assert concerning birth is sufficiently refuted in the homilies on the Epiphany [Note: Presumably those of Augustine.]. Let us meanwhile record what we think concerning marriages. We have often seen countless men and women who were sterile, and although various investigations of times, or the most diligent study of the constellations [lacuna], may have been made, they have fathered children by different spouses.

As for buildings, we can at least gather the truth from the present fire at Pavia [Note: Muratori relates this fire in his *Italian Annals* under the year A.D. 1004. Burontius understands it of another, earlier fire at Pavia, which Luitprand mentions under the year 924. [Col. 0838D] *Editor of the Patrologia edition.*]. What city in this kingdom had buildings that gleamed with more splendid structures, as you saw? No calculation of the stars, ancient or modern, could be discovered under which a house had not been built there; yet in a single day it was consumed by fire, like a judgment from God.

Those who say that offspring are conceived through some observation of the stars or lost through negligence [Col. 0837C]; or who assert that houses erected under the rising of certain stars are burned by fire while those erected under others remain unharmed; or who contend that something comes from venerating the stars—all are shown by these testimonies to be deceivers.

But the enemy of the human race, perceiving the various weaknesses of human beings, seeks to attack us through various snares. Just as he suggests robbery to the powerful, fraud to the cunning, lust to the pleasure-loving, and pride to the strong, so he hardens the wound of unbelief in the foolish and the rustic, spreads the poisons of superstition, defends them by custom, and fortifies their hardness.

Even if they excuse themselves in some fashion from the foregoing vices, they are nevertheless struck down by these arrows. Such people must therefore be asked whether they ever recite, attend to, or ponder the creed of faith [Note: *Credulitas* is commonly used by the ancient Fathers in the sense of “faith”]. If they reject it, they should be separated from our fellowship until they amend their ways [Col. 0837D]. But if they claim that they practice these things frequently, let them say with what mouth or heart they assert that they believe in almighty God, whose will they are thought to obstruct by such practices.

For concerning such people the Lord says through the prophet: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13). He alone is almighty who can do all things. Concerning him the Psalmist says: “Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the deeps” (Ps. 134:6). And the apostle Paul says: “For who has resisted his will?” (Rom. 9:19).

Therefore, my brothers, it is plainly evident that such practices can greatly harm those who observe them. Eradicate them from your minds as though they had never been in your ears. Rather, according to the blessed apostle Paul, whatever must be done should always be done in the name of the Lord (Col. 3:6). If anyone despises this, let him be separated from the company of Catholics, so that those who are entangled in the bonds of [lacuna] mathematics [or astrology] may deserve to be gathered among your sons [lacuna].

## SERMON IV. ON THE EPIPHANY

To those celebrating the feast of the Epiphany, we wish to make known what the Epiphany is. For *Epiphany* is Greek; in Latin it is called “appearing above” (*superapparitio*). When our Lord Jesus Christ was born, a star appeared above the lodging where he was staying with his mother. It invited the Magi from distant regions to adore the Lord, and from this it consecrated the name of this day.

Although the Lord adorned this day with various miracles, this event nevertheless held the chief place in its name, either because it was the first or because it was the greatest of all. For this star aroused the firstfruits of the nations for Christ the Lord, compelled them to believe, and taught them to adore him. From their multitude, now spread throughout almost the whole world, one Church is called forth.

The other miracles that the Lord deigned to perform as the years revolved, on the same annual occasion, all look toward this event as toward their beginning or head, as the sequence of the Scriptures also declares [Col. 0838C]. At the same time of year the Lord was baptized in the Jordan, was revealed by the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove, was marveled at by the waters, and was pointed out even by John’s finger: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). Then he changed water into wine at the wedding (John 2:8), just as afterward he satisfied five thousand people with five loaves and two fish (Matt. 14:21).

What else were all these things than the star that would lead human hearts, dwelling in distant regions, to recognition of the true God, our Lord Jesus Christ? Just as by a guiding light we examine what is obscure through the darkness of night, so by seeing the miracles people more easily understood God hidden in the likeness of a human being.

Therefore, if we attend more closely to the miracles mentioned above, we understand that all these things were prefigured in the Magi themselves, which the Lord afterward [lacuna] when they understood that the Son of the heavenly King had joined himself to them there through the mystery of the incarnation.

Again, when they receive from the Jews, bearers of the five books, some indication of the Lord’s birth, they find, as it were, five loaves. But as they labor on the journey and reach him, and enjoy his presence, the five loaves, as though being broken, increase, and they are filled with their delights [codex: “he is filled with their delights”].

The two little fish are attested by the books of the Psalms and the Prophets, which are also rightly eaten through these events, because certain of their statements are fulfilled in them. For the Psalmist says: “The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba shall bring presents” (Ps. 71:10). Isaiah likewise said: “All shall come from Sheba, bringing gold and frankincense and proclaiming the praise of the Lord” (Isa. 60:6).

Holy baptism is finally signified in them by the fact that, in the number of themselves and of their gifts, they first received the confession of the Holy Trinity before they deserved to adore the Lord; or because through the same gifts they declared him to be God, king, and mortal human being—without this confession no one can be granted the grace of baptism; or because after their adoration they were warned not to return to Herod but to go back to their own country by another way (Matt. 2:12).

This adoration has in a certain way made baptism known to us [as the codex reads]. Our country is paradise. From it we were expelled through the fault of the first human being, and for a long time we wandered in the country of Herod, that is, in the power of the devil. But after we confess God according to the Catholic faith, and immerse our head in the baptismal font in order to adore him, we are warned by all the teachings of Holy Scripture not to return to Herod.

Herod signifies the devil, as the interpretation of his name makes clear. Thus we are urged by divine admonitions to return to our homeland by another way, so that we who fell by following the byways of vices may ascend by the path of virtues to the highest [lacuna].

## SERMON V. ON THE BEGINNING OF THE FAST

Whenever, dearest brethren, [lacuna] the abundance of preparation also [lacuna] those who [lacuna] recognizes [lacuna] from which [lacuna] who abound more richly in costly garments or more luxurious foods and drinks [lacuna], may make the miserable appetites and contempt [of such things] render people happier. Much more, therefore, beloved, now that the time of [lacuna] and observance is approaching, we must prepare ourselves in every way with fitting devotion.

But because, according to the blessed Apostle, “One person judges one day to be different from another, while another judges every day alike” (Rom. 14:5), those who indulge more eagerly in pleasures on ordinary days ought to abstain from them more strictly during these forty days. For the soul that dies through an abundance of food sometimes rises again through the observance of fasting. Food should be taken only from necessity; fasting should be embraced for the greatest benefit.

Know therefore, beloved, that on the fourth day of the present week we shall devoutly celebrate, with Christ’s mercy consenting, the beginning of the sacred fast, so that the flesh which in its enjoyment drew us into sin may now, afflicted, lead us back to forgiveness. This must be begun with great diligence, so that we may deserve to reach its end without stumbling. For a thing that has not been well begun will scarcely have a perfect conclusion.

Therefore, beloved, set aside worldly business, frequent the churches, make tearful confession of your sins to God and to the priests, and labor throughout that entire day in God’s service, so that you may learn more fully how, with God’s help, to complete the work you have begun in a salutary manner.

But because the way of life proposed to all is not the same, the life of clerics must be removed from the conduct of laypeople. According to the blessed Pope Telesphorus, those who ought to anticipate others in fasting [Note: Atto takes this from the constitution of Saint Telesphorus, which may be seen in the Roman edition, vol. I, p. 79. The matter is also mentioned by Anastasius in *The Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, and by Jerome—not Eusebius, in whose authentic edition nothing of the kind is said—in the *Chronicle*. Nevertheless, Baronius, under the year 154, wisely notes that the Lenten fast originated not with Telesphorus but with the apostles.] must not fail first to cleanse their own sins by repentance, so that they may purify the people more worthily on the appointed day. For one ordinarily soils rather than cleanses something by touching it with polluted hands.

Therefore, before all else, let us wash our hands: that is, let us correct our evil deeds through the zeal of a good manner of life. Then, through divine service, let us labor to wash away the stains of others’ sins, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whose blood we have been redeemed and by whose providence we are governed. Amen.

## SERMON VI. ALSO ON THE BEGINNING OF THE FAST

[lacuna] suitably through [lacuna] he asks [lacuna] concerning the fortieth, or rather [lacuna] a [lacuna]-cesimum [number; reading uncertain], or a fast of some other number more [lacuna], which is readily clear if we consider the times mentioned above or the authorities. Four [lacuna] still reach the sum of the number [Col. 0840C].

Moses therefore acted rightly: when receiving the law of the Decalogue, he fasted forty days, to show by this that there is no perfection in the Decalogue unless it is illumined by the grace of the holy Gospel, which is described in fourfold form.

This fast was also granted to the prophet Elijah, because he was both a preacher and witness of the Old Testament and was reserved to appear also as one belonging to the New. Our Lord Jesus Christ likewise deigned to observe this fast because, as he himself says, “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5:17); or so that he might show himself to be the author of both the Old and the New Testaments, since the four holy Gospels do not destroy the Decalogue but rather strive to strengthen it; or because the same Lord had come to release the Decalogue, previously sealed and enclosed among the Jews, and to proclaim it through the four regions of the world.

Following such examples and teachings of our fathers, all Christians ought to revere this kind of fast with devoted mind, pure heart, and pious affection. No time could be more appropriately chosen for it than one bordering upon and contiguous with the Lord’s resurrection.

For these forty days signify the whole period of the active life, which requires self-restraint: we must fast from the allurements of this world, meditating only on the things of God and ruminating upon divine nourishment, so that we may deserve to reach the contemplative life, which is understood through Easter joy, exulting.

The number ten signifies the perfection of blessedness, while four signifies fullness. The whole world is spread out under the four winds and is raised upon four elements; the seasons of the year also change in fourfold succession. Thus, ten multiplied by four produces forty.

By this number it is shown, beyond dispute, that we must abstain and fast here from every temporal pleasure, so that we may attain heavenly delights. The Lord clearly signified this in the exodus of the Jews: they were led through the desert for that many years, sustained almost solely by the nourishment of manna, so that they might reach the homeland of promise.

But those who, on account of the desert [lacuna], therefore, dearest brethren, [lacuna] must be guarded most diligently. If it begins only in the sixth week before Easter [lacuna], it is clear that it will not be a forty-day fast: six weeks contain forty-two days. After subtracting six Sundays, we know that no more than thirty-six days remain in abstinence, four short of the present number.

Therefore four days of the preceding week are taken so that the number may rise to the aforesaid total. Today, then, is the beginning of this fast, the Wednesday of the seventh week. From today until the holy resurrection of the Lord, except only for Sundays, it is fitting to observe the strict fast in every respect [Col. 0841C]; if it is broken in any way, it will no longer be a forty-day fast.

If Holy Scripture rebukes those who, even on days that are in some manner free from fasting, indulge in pleasures and delights, what harsh sentence will those receive who neglect even these days? Or with what conscience will anyone dare to approach the eating of the spotless Lamb during the Easter festival? How will he be able to communicate in the Lord’s body who has neglected to adorn himself, even for a time, with good morals, when he hears: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11:29)?

Let us therefore abstain from worldly profits and business; let us abstain from carnal pleasures that wage war against the soul (1 Pet. 2:11), and prepare in our minds a dwelling worthy of God.

Above all, beloved, make a true confession of past evils to God and to the priests [Note: In the margin: “let us make [it],” and likewise shortly afterward, “let us do [it].”], and perform worthy penance, because it is greatly harmful to join splendid buildings to perishable foundations.

Consider also the prudence of the serpent, which does not dare to drink the water of a spring until it has poured out all its venom. Medicine likewise does not benefit a wound if the iron still remains in it.

Therefore, brothers, be assiduous in your duties, prompt in vigils, constant in prayers, moderate in food, sober in drink, generous in almsgiving, honorable in chastity, abstaining even from the marriage bed, removed from all games and idle words, because things permitted on other days are regarded as crimes on these days.

Moreover, frequent the churches, visit the sick and those in prison, pay the debts of debtors, console the sorrowful, give to the poor [lacuna].

## SERMON VII. ON PALM SUNDAY

By the promise of our Lord Jesus Christ, dearest brethren, we are confident that no terror has oppressed your hearts concerning his glorious resurrection and no doubt has entered your minds. For the fear of the apostles and of the other saints of that time was nourished by the darkness of unbelief. Their weakness, however, became an increase of our perfection.

Thus the things that during the days now past seemed to emit rays, as it were, through shadowy leaves are now proclaimed in a clear voice [Col. 0842B]. From this you can gather that the more we announce the Lord’s passion, the more swiftly you approach the celebration of his resurrection.

Six days, in fact, are counted until the joy of that feast; the sixth week has also passed since we proclaimed the beginning of the fast. Therefore, beloved brothers, strive during these six weekdays to recover whatever you may perhaps have neglected during the preceding six weeks.

There are some who judge certain days of this week—namely Thursday and Saturday—to be freer than the other days of Lent. This is contrary to the decrees of the canons and is confirmed by no authority of Holy Scripture; nor does it seem right to us.

For the nearer we come to Easter joy, the more purely we must prepare ourselves through fasts, prayers, vigils, and every work of mercy, and moreover wash away past sins with continual tears.

Even if someone does not believe that his own crimes are worthy of tears, at least the injury done to the Lord should pierce him during these days. For although he was God before the ages, when he came in the form of a servant he received spittle and blows from the impious and did not disdain to lay down his life in time for the salvation of us and of them as well.

Therefore, my brothers, let each one show compassion toward those who bear reproaches and weep over the blindness of those who inflict them. He himself said in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5).

A little mourning is useful now, so that we may rejoice more freely in the holy resurrection. The Psalmist also says: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115:12–13).

The cup may be understood as either open persecution or hidden groaning; in either form, every Christian ought to drink it.

Let us therefore prepare ourselves for the coming feast [Note: Codex, first hand: “for the coming festival,” and below, “to which,” without correction. Recall the beginning of Sermon 4: today in Italian we say *la festa*.], beloved, to which we may worthily reach [lacuna] the Lord. Let us rejoice [lacuna]. Not foods of luxury but works of justice and fairness must be sent ahead [lacuna].

It is more suitable to acquire three ordinary, equally good tunics, by which you can clothe both yourself and Christ’s poor, than to acquire for yourself one costly garment alone [Col. 0843A]. It is better for you to acquire simple food, by which you can welcome several needy people to your table, than to spend a great deal of money on luxurious foods while you eat drunkenly alone in your house and Christ’s poor perish in your presence, afflicted by hunger or nakedness.

For the blessed apostle John says: “Whoever has the substance of this world and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him—how does the love of God abide in him?” (1 John 3:17).

Therefore flee avarice and love charity, without which no one will deserve to see God (Heb. 12:14). May charity, peace, and joy be with you forever. May he deign to grant this, whose kingdom [lacuna].

## SERMON VIII. ON THE DAY OF THE HOLY RESURRECTION

Today, dearest brothers, we celebrate the day of the Lord’s resurrection, on which our Lord Jesus Christ, having destroyed the dominion of death, rose from the dead. We also call it “Passover.”

*Passover* is therefore a Hebrew word; in Latin it means “passing over.” This was prefigured long before the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

When the children of Israel were oppressed by Egyptian servitude, they cried out to the Lord to rescue them from the hand of Pharaoh, that is, the king of the Egyptians. The prophet Moses was sent to him and warned him, by the Lord’s command, not to oppress the Lord’s people but to let them serve God alone, and not to prevent them from going wherever they wished.

Because Pharaoh refused, God visited the Egyptians with the greatest plagues, through many signs and various wonders. Yet even then they did not heed the Lord’s voice [Col. 0843C] and did not release the people; rather, they oppressed them more severely.

But the Israelites cried out to the Lord more and more, asking him to rescue them from the hand of their oppressors. Their cries ascended before the Lord.

The Lord had given them a sign: in every household they were to slaughter a lamb and mark all their doorposts with its blood. For he indicated that he would pass through the midst of Egypt [as the codex reads] and announced that all its firstborn would be struck down. He promised to save and free from their enemies those whose doorposts he found marked in this way.

He also commanded them each year [lacuna] the Red Sea, on the following day [lacuna] the Egyptians, so that they might pursue them. When the children of Israel saw them, they were greatly afraid.

Nevertheless, the Lord opened the sea for them, dry land appeared, the waters became like a wall on their right and left, and they walked on dry ground in the midst of the sea. Their enemies, however, pursued them and were drowned, and not one of them survived (Exod. 14:28).

All these things were therefore a type and figure of what you now see fulfilled in reality. For the Passover in which that lamb was slaughtered signified this Passover, in which the true Lamb, that is, our Lord Jesus Christ, was killed. Unless our doorposts—that is, our mouths—are marked by his blood, we cannot be saved.

As the children of Israel were freed from Egyptian servitude through the slaughter and blood of that lamb, so we have been redeemed from diabolical servitude through this true Lamb.

And just as they could in no way escape the danger of their enemies except by crossing the Red Sea, so we can in no way avoid the devil’s snares except through the washing of baptism. As all their enemies were drowned and perished, so all the vices within us are extinguished in baptism.

Let us therefore celebrate, beloved, the true Passover. Let us pass from vices to virtues. Let us pray the Lord to free us from the hand of Pharaoh, that is, from the power of the devil. Let us rise from death to life, that is, from sin to righteousness. Let us hasten to the holy Church, which is the holy city Jerusalem, so that we may deserve to share in the company of those who rose with him and appeared to many in the holy city (Matt. 27:53).

Let us therefore rejoice and exult in him, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit [lacuna].

## SERMON IX. ALSO ON WHITE SUNDAY

“Praise the Lord, all nations, and praise him together, all peoples” (Ps. 116:1).

It is worthy and just that the Lord should always be praised by us, as the Psalmist testifies when he says: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33:1).

The praises of the Lord are always fitting for our mouths, but especially on this great festival. For to the King who shattered hell, led back captives, restored life, and took away death, a new song is justly owed, and it is fitting that his praise should resound magnificently.

Come now, dearest brothers, sing with the Prophet a new song to the Lord: “His praise is in the assembly of the saints” (Ps. 149:1). We must praise the Lord together not with bronze cymbals, not with the little songs of the streets [Col. 0844C], not with the blare of trumpets, but with a new song—that is, with the song of the New Testament.

Thus it continues: “The saints shall exult” (ibid., 5) [lacuna] “let him glory in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10:17) [lacuna] with joy, because, as the apostle himself testifies, “the world and its desire are passing away” (1 John 2:17) [lacuna] in God—that is, surely, “they shall rejoice in their resting places,” namely, in their pure conscience and clean heart, by which they will deserve to see God.

They do not rejoice in theaters like actors, nor in wedding songs and ditties like mimes, nor in dances and the circus like performers or worshipers of idols—whom, alas, some Christians still imitate in many ways.

For what is more pitiable in old men, more shameful in young men, or more destructive in adolescents than to sing of the violation of virgins and the lusts of prostitutes through shameful gestures and seductive voices, so that by such snares they may provoke their spectators to their own corruptions? Thus those who have not yet fallen, being protected by divine grace, or who have risen through repentance by God’s mercy, may stumble into the whirlpools of lust [Col. 0844D].

Indicating the prostitute, Solomon says: “A woman is loud and wandering, unable to endure quiet, unable to keep her feet at home; now outside, now in the streets, now lying in wait near the corners” (Prov. 7:10–12), and many other things of this kind, which cannot be enumerated because of their multitude.

Dina also, the daughter of so great a father, Jacob, suffered rape when she went out to see the women of the region. We have both read and heard of many other women who, in a similar manner, grievously mourned the loss of their irrecoverable virginity.

For theatrical entertainment is a robber of chastity. We also read that the games of the circus had Liber and Venus, the most infamous demons, as their founders.

Therefore let every Christian flee the service of those whose merits he does not wish to imitate, especially during these feast days. It profits little to have lamented our downfalls during the season of Lent if now, by polluting the Easter festival, we fall again into the same things.

We will scarcely be able to escape unless we take care to cleanse our minds of such things, because, according to the Apostle, “bad conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:33).

Hence Solomon says: “Death entered through the windows” (Jer. 9:21). Our windows are the five bodily senses, through which the death of the soul enters us, as though through windows. May he deign to free us from it, whose kingdom [lacuna].

## SERMON X. ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

[Note: Burontius published this sermon from the Vercelli codex, p. 310, but it differs in very many ways; it would be far too laborious to record them. Without the Vercelli codex, however, I cannot determine where the editor may have gone wrong. I therefore faithfully reproduce only the reading of the Vatican codex.]

The Lord and our Savior, dearly beloved brothers, after rising from the dead, wished to remain with his disciples on earth for forty days, so that he might wipe from their hearts the sadness of those forty hours during which he had rested in the tomb; or because, just as he freed the children of Israel from Egyptian slavery and from the depths of the Red Sea, led them through the desert for forty years, and meanwhile instructed them concerning the establishment of the tabernacle, the offering of sacrifices, and the observance of ceremonies, and afterward, once the proud nations had been destroyed, brought them into earthly Jerusalem, which is called the land of promise,

[Col. 0845C] so also, rising from the dead, he raised from the darkness of hell those who were being unjustly detained, bringing them into the light; and leading his disciples from the darkness of unbelief to the knowledge of the true light, he remained with them for forty days, so that meanwhile he might instruct them more fully concerning the establishment of the holy Church and the knowledge of the holy Scriptures, and afterward, with all the aerial powers destroyed, might ascend before them to the holy heavenly Jerusalem. This too is called the land of promise, which he promised to those who love him (James 1:12), as the Psalmist says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 26:13).

Those forty years, therefore, can well signify these forty days, and from them we can explain so great a similarity. Today, after completing his mysteries on earth, the Lord ascended triumphantly into heaven, with many seeing—and indeed rejoicing—as it is written: “God has ascended amid jubilation, and the Lord with the sound of the trumpet” (Psalm 46:6). Jubilation occurs when such great joy is conceived in the heart that the power of speech cannot express it fully. He said this because the apostles, seeing such a miracle, were filled with inexpressible joy of heart: they saw our Redeemer, whom they truly believed had already risen from the dead, ascending bodily to that place.

Therefore they did not doubt that everything he had promised them could be granted, nor did they distrust that they would follow him, as he had promised, to immortal and heavenly glory, a glory they rejoiced to see that he had already attained. They also awaited the Holy Spirit with all the greater confidence because they saw that everything else he had foretold had been fulfilled.

Certainly, by what follows—“with the sound of the trumpet”—we understand the crash of the angelic proclamation, like a resounding trumpet, when it said: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11). This was proclaimed so that no sorrow might remain for the apostles when they saw the Lord taken away from them in bodily presence, and so that they might not doubt his going into heaven, since they saw the angels ministering to him.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, because we have already been brought out of Egyptian slavery, crossed the Red Sea, and long ago risen together with the Lord, having been buried with him in death—for through these things the grace of baptism is represented—let us now pray earnestly that, placed in this solitude of mortal life, he may deign to instruct us in the commands of the Gospel and of the Decalogue, which the forty years or days signify, so that, with our vices destroyed, we may joyfully deserve to reach the heavenly Jerusalem.

Thus, through the intercession of the holy apostles, let us strive to celebrate the Lord’s ascension in such a way that we may be able to await the gifts of the Spirit which they received, as it is written: “Ascending on high, the Lord led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings” (Ephesians 3:8). He led captivity captive when, having conquered death, he removed its infernal spoil and triumphantly led it to the heavens. He gave gifts to human beings when he bestowed the Holy Spirit upon the apostles—and not only upon the apostles, but also upon the other righteous.

It is fitting for us to beseech this with the greatest reverence, so that we may be worthy to obtain such things and continually observe what we have obtained; and whatever we have neglected to fulfill throughout the whole time, let us at least observe during this coming decade. Let us wash away the stains of our wicked hearts, drive away every evil, and live in this festival in such a way that we may joyfully be able to receive the coming Pentecost.
