For if the Holy Spirit finds us purified, without doubt he will prepare a dwelling for himself within us. May he himself grant this, whose kingdom and dominion endure forever.

## SERMON XI. ON PENTECOST

[Col. 0846D] Dearly beloved brothers, we celebrate Pentecost as a feast-day, which we count as the fiftieth day from the Lord’s resurrection. For *Pentecost* in Greek means “fifty” in Latin; five decades make up this number. This day is therefore held as the most celebrated among the festivals of the year, because on it the Holy Spirit, namely the Paraclete, coming from heaven, deigned to strengthen the apostles so greatly that he cast from their hearts all the fear by which they had previously been confined in silence behind closed doors; and immediately, rejecting those same barriers, they proclaimed Christ publicly to all nations in a free voice and in various languages (Acts 2:4).

It is fitting that his coming is separated from the paschal glory by so many days, because the gifts of this Spirit are seven: seven times seven comprises the number of days that intervene. Yet this one day—the fiftieth—is rightly added and placed before them, because although the gifts are diverse, the Spirit is nevertheless one and the same (1 Corinthians 12:11). We extend his feast over seven days because ecclesiastical custom has dedicated one day to each gift.

Nor were there lacking heretics who said that this Spirit proceeded not from the Father and the Son together, but from the Father alone. We can appropriately answer them with testimonies from Truth itself [Note: Let us note Atto’s refutation of the error of the Greeks.]. For he says to his apostles in the Gospel: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father” (John 15:26). And again: “If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come; but if I go away, I will send him to you” (John 16:7). . . . By these words it is sufficiently and clearly “demonstrated” that the Spirit proceeded “not only” from the Father, but equally from the Son.

But since the perfidy of the heretics is thereby utterly refuted, let us turn our attention to the proclamations of the feast already begun [Note: Mansius reads incorrectly: “let us proceed.”]. For the number fifty signifies remission, as we can gather from the Old Testament. In the fiftieth year, which was called the jubilee [Note: M. reads *jubilaeus*]—that is, the year of remission—debts were remitted to debtors, and servitudes were freely released for slaves who were approaching freedom.

This fiftieth day, therefore, can rightly also be called a jubilee, because when the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles, he granted them remission of all sins and made them free from the frailty of their former contagion [Note: M. incorrectly reads “of all.”]. This day was also celebrated as a feast in the Old Testament, and on it the first loaves made from new crops were annually presented in the temple. Mystically, among us too, on this very day, loaves made from new crops—that is, the new virtues of the Holy Spirit, by which we are nourished and live—were first handed down to the nations through the apostles [Note: M. incorrectly reads “them.”].

It is not without reason that, on the fiftieth day after the Lord struck Egypt in its firstborn, destroyed the power of its rulers, and freed the children of Israel from their slavery and from the depths of the Red Sea, he resolved to give through Moses the law which he was to proclaim to the peoples. And on the fiftieth day after he struck hell in its firstfruits, destroyed the power of its rulers, and brought out from the depth of death all who were being unjustly detained there, he arranged through the Holy Spirit to make known to the apostles how they should act and instruct others.

But divine providence wished to entrust one law to the Israelite people through Moses and another to us through the holy apostles. The former threatens destruction; the latter continually teaches repentance. Moses showed this when, after the law had been given, he descended from the mountain and returned to the people. When he found that the people had sinned by worshiping the golden calf, he said:

“Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Let each one place his sword upon his thigh, and let each one kill his brother, each his neighbor, and each his kinsman” (Exodus 32:27).

But blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, together with the others, after [Note: M. incorrectly reads “through.”] the coming of the Holy Spirit, boldly said even to those who had crucified the Lord himself:

“Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:38).

For our Redeemer, tempering the harshness of the Old Law, made its bitter drink potable through his incarnation. Indeed, in the Old Testament it is written:

“The person who does anything of these abominations shall perish from his people, says the Lord” (Leviticus 18:29) [Note: What follows is lacunose in Mansius.].

In the New Testament we find:

“There will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance” [Thus the manuscript] (Luke 18:7).

See, brothers, that we do not lose the time for repentance, which has been granted with such great indulgence [Note: Mansius incorrectly reads *totum* (‘the whole’) and shortly afterward *indulgentiae* (the genitive ‘of indulgence’).] For we call the fruit of repentance whatever good work we undertake, in satisfaction for sin and in striving toward reconciliation with God [Note: M. incorrectly reads “we proceed.”]: fasts, vigils, abstinence, prayers, works of mercy, and the other virtues.

Christ has prepared many paths for us by which we can avoid the pits of destruction [Note: M. incorrectly reads “places before us”; M. also reads “may be able” for “can.”]. Yet the more means there are of escaping, the more pitiable are those who descend into the pit. Although, therefore, during these days that have passed [Note: M. omits “these”], we have lived in pleasures, as though at a wedding, for the sake of the continuing solemnity, and while standing have offered the vows of prayer to the Lord, let us now throw ourselves upon the earth and pour out tears; let us devote ourselves to fasts and vigils, and hasten to take up the burden of repentance [Note: M. incorrectly reads “sacrament.”].

For the Lord says in the Gospel:

“The children of the bridegroom cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them. The hour will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days” (Matthew 9:15) [Note: M. ridiculously reads “daughters” for “sons.”].

During the time that has passed, in a certain way we had the Lord present with us bodily; but now he has ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father. He has poured the promised Spirit into the hearts of the faithful. The Spirit urges them unceasingly to pray, fast, and perform other good works, so that although they cannot now touch the one whom they had bodily, they may everywhere experience his consolation.

But those who have deserved to receive such a gift must live in such a way that they are never separated from him. It is fitting for us sinners to follow their footsteps in all things [Note: M. reads “of the pious.”], and to prepare ourselves so that, if we have not yet deserved to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit, or if we have rejected it through sin after receiving it, we may be found fit to receive—or even to receive anew—and likewise to preserve it [Note: Mansius reads *suscipiendam*, contrary to the manuscript.].

Let us take care to entreat the Savior of all with a pure mind, a devoted mouth, and worthy works [Note: M. incorrectly reads “let us persist.”], so that he may deign to remain with us forever [Note: M. omits “forever”], though not bodily, by his aid, he who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and is glorified as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## XII. The Same Sermon Abbreviated, So That Common People Would Not Become Bored

Pentecost, dearly beloved brothers, is the holy day we celebrate, which we count as the fiftieth from the Lord’s resurrection. For *Πεντηκοστήν* in Greek means “fiftieth” in Latin [Col. 0849B]; five decades make up this number. This day is therefore held as the most celebrated among the festivals of the year, because on it the Holy Spirit, namely the Paraclete, coming from heaven, deigned to strengthen the apostles so greatly that they cast from their hearts all the fear by which they had previously been held in silence behind closed doors; and immediately, rejecting those same barriers, they proclaimed Christ publicly to all nations in a free voice and in various languages.

This day was also celebrated as a feast in the Old Testament, and on it the first loaves made from new crops were presented in the temple. Mystically, among us too, on that very day, loaves made from new crops—that is, the new virtues of the Holy Spirit, by which we are nourished and live—were handed down to the nations through the apostles.

It is not without reason that, on the fiftieth day after the Lord struck Egypt in its firstborn, destroyed the power of its rulers, and freed the children of Israel from their slavery and from the depths of the Red Sea, he resolved to give through Moses the law which he was to proclaim to the peoples. And on the fiftieth day after he struck hell in its firstfruits, destroyed the power of its rulers, and brought out from the depth of death all who were being unjustly detained there, he arranged through the Holy Spirit to make known to the apostles how they should act or instruct others.

But divine providence wished to entrust one law to the Israelite people through Moses and another to us through the holy apostles: the former threatens destruction, while the latter continually teaches repentance. Moses showed this when, after the law had been given, he descended from the mountain and returned to the people. When he found that the people had sinned by worshiping the golden calf, he said:

“Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Let each one place his sword upon his thigh, and let each one kill his brother and each his neighbor” (Exodus 32:27).

But blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, together with the others, after the coming of the Holy Spirit, boldly said even to those who had crucified the Lord himself:

“Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:38).

For our Redeemer, tempering the harshness of the Old Law, made its bitter drink potable through his incarnation. Indeed, in the Old Testament it is written:

“The person who does anything of these abominations shall perish from his people, says the Lord” (Leviticus 18:29).

In the New Testament we find:

“There will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance” (Luke 15:7).

See, brothers, that we do not lose the time for repentance, which has been granted with such great indulgence. For we call the fruit of repentance whatever good work we undertake, in satisfaction for sin and in striving toward reconciliation with God: fasts, vigils, abstinence, prayers, works of mercy, and the other virtues.

Christ sets before us many paths by which we can avoid the pits of destruction. Yet the more means there are of escaping, the more pitiable are those who descend into the pit. Although, therefore, during these days that have passed, we have lived in pleasures, as though at a wedding, for the sake of the continuing solemnity, and while standing have offered the vows of prayer to the Lord, let us now throw ourselves upon the earth and pour out tears; let us devote ourselves to fasts and vigils, and hasten to take up the burden of repentance.

For the Lord says in the Gospel:

“The children of the bridegroom cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them; the hour will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days” (Matthew 9:15).

During the time that has passed, in a certain way the Lord was present with us bodily; but now he has ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father. Therefore let us entreat him with a pure mind, a devoted mouth, and worthy works [Col. 0850C], so that he may deign to remain with us forever, though not bodily, by his aid—he who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and is glorified as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XIII. ON THE ANNOUNCEMENT OF THE BLESSED FORERUNNER AND MARTYR OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST, JOHN THE BAPTIST

After [Note: M. incorrectly reads “through.”] the Gospel reading, dearly beloved brothers, the birth of the most blessed John, the forerunner of our Lord Jesus Christ, has been announced to us. It now seems necessary to teach something about its preparation, because every effort must be made lest the people pollute through ignorance what the highest obedience requires them to observe. If they sin in such matters unknowingly, the same judgment will involve us together with them; but if they despise what we teach, we shall mourn their alienation in such a way that we need not thereafter fear danger for ourselves.

Let your prudence therefore know that, in many places, a wicked custom has grown up concerning so glorious a solemnity: certain little prostitutes abandon the churches and divine offices, and spend the night here and there [Note: M. reads “partly”] in streets and crossroads, even at springs and in the countryside; they establish choirs, compose songs [Note: M. reads “little songs”], cast lots, and pretend to predict whatever is supposed to happen to anyone in such circumstances.

Their superstition generates such madness that they dare to baptize herbs or leafy branches, and afterward presume to call one another godfathers and godmothers, carefully preserving those objects hung in their homes for a long time afterward, as though for religious purposes.

Blessed John is called the Baptist because he first preached to human beings the baptism of remission and undertook the ministry of baptizing; he even deserved to wash the Author of all things with his baptism. The rest . . . They also customarily defile the feast of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, with such dirges. Some of these women serve such vanities for the sake of magic, others for the sake of sexual misconduct [Note: M. reads “take part” instead of “serve.”].

Consider, therefore, dearly beloved brothers, how much disgrace such people inflict upon us, their superiors, and how much harm they inflict upon themselves; and so let each of you at least cleanse his own house of such errors [Note: M. reads “all shamefully.”]. Let us share the burden [Note: M. omits “and”], and let us also share the reward [Note: M. reads “immediately”]. Each of you [Note: M. reads “of us”] ought to preside over his household as a bishop, because *bishop* means “overseer.” For from each person as much will be required as has been entrusted to him [Note: M. reads “is required.”]. See that there is no one to whom something has not been entrusted, and from whom something will not be required.

Let us therefore invite one another to the observance of so great a festival; let us wipe away errors and repel every heresy. Let us hasten forward with fasts, vigils, and prayers, so that we may deserve to celebrate devoutly the feast of so glorious a martyr, through our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: The Codex reads *festam*, “feast” in the feminine, though this occurs elsewhere as well.].

## SERMON XIV. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE SAME SAINT

[Col. 0851C] Today, dearly beloved brothers, the birth is celebrated of him concerning whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “Among those born of women none has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Luke 7:28).

By “those born of women” he means those born from the softness of desire; for *woman* is so called from *softness*, because this sex is easily softened toward sin. It should certainly be noted that the Lord does not include his own birth under this testimony. Although his Mother was naturally called a woman, she was nevertheless masculine in continence: without human desire she bore offspring and brought forth the Savior for the world.

Among all other most holy and eminent men, begotten, of course, through male seed, no Catholic would doubt that blessed John is in every respect to be compared with them. His birth was announced by an angel in the temple; his mother, barren and already an old woman, became fruitful; the mute tongue of his father was released; before he was born, the Lord’s mother recognized him; and Christ’s presence was also gladdened by him. Through the prophet he had even deserved to be proclaimed long beforehand, concerning whom it was said:

“Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you” (Malachi 3:1).

Consider, therefore, beloved ones, how great an honor is due to him who, sent by God the Father, deserved to precede the coming of the Son. From this ministry he also took the name “forerunner.” He preceded the Lord in birth, preaching, death, and descent to the gates of hell.

He was so greatly honored by him that he deserved to be glorified by his testimony and to be called more than a prophet. To magnify his glory further, the Lord added:

“From the days of John until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11:12).

The kingdom of heaven suffers violence and the violent seize it when some wicked person, perversely for a long time [lacuna], mercifully escapes the punishments he deserved through evil living and [lacuna] enters joyfully into the lofty [lacuna] things of heaven.

It is rightly said, “from the days of John,” because he first preached the baptism through which sins are forgiven and the gates of the heavenly kingdom are opened.

May the merciful Lord deign to receive us there through the merits and intercessions of this most blessed forerunner and martyr of his, whose kingdom and dominion endure forever.

## SERMON XV. ON THE FEAST OF THE HOLY APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL

Today’s solemnity, dearly beloved brothers, admonishes us to embrace fervently the footsteps of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul. They denied themselves and despised the whole world, and thereby obtained judicial authority over it. Because they refused to succumb to the world, they were exalted to heaven: Peter became its key-bearer, and Paul its usher.

O how fitting and glorious it is that Peter should be the key-bearer of heaven while Lucifer should experience the prison of hell! A human being rose to eternal glory; an angel fell to everlasting punishment. The one, exalted and lifted high in himself, was made the lowest of all creatures created by God; the other, humble and despised, became even the first of the apostles. Pride cast the former down; humility raised the latter up.

How aptly he was called Simon, because *Simon* means “obedient”! His companion Paul followed him not far behind even in his own name. For we call Paul “little”; the name seems to signify great obedience, since a man so illuminated by divine light and instructed in such great heavenly teachings that he deserved to be called by the Lord himself a chosen vessel for carrying his name (Acts 9:15) considered himself worthy to be named “little.”

He could therefore be called great whom the Lord himself called and taught after his ascension into heaven, whom he consecrated as his apostle (Galatians 1:1), who was caught up to the third heaven and deserved to hear a divine secret (2 Corinthians 12:3).

Both therefore possess the glory of splendor, because both possessed the humility of love. Both live with Christ, because they did not fear dying for him. Peter did not shrink from the twisted cross; Paul did not fear the armed hand. The former inclined his head toward the earth so that he might raise it toward heaven; the latter was beheaded so that he might rather increase.

Rightly they obtained such rewards, for they endured such torments. Let us reflect very frequently, dearly beloved brothers, upon their deeds, and take care to imitate them insofar as we can. Let us reject earthly and passing things and embrace heavenly and enduring ones, because it profits a person nothing to gain the whole world if he suffers the loss of his soul (Matthew 16:26).

Let us rejoice in humility and flee pride, because everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 18:14). [lacuna] is the one who loves [lacuna] [uncertain surviving fragment: *-cio*] into eternal life will receive it. Therefore, with every effort and [lacuna] let us strive to entreat you, men, [lacuna] so that what our frailty cannot obtain, their holiness may obtain for us, and that through their prayers they may bring us there where they have gone before us by their merits, through our Lord Jesus Christ.

## SERMON XVI. ON THE DEPOSITION OF THE MOST BLESSED EUSEBIUS, BISHOP OF VERCELLI

[Note: Mansius published this sermon from the Vatican manuscript in 1761; Burontius likewise presented it as previously unpublished in his 1768 edition. Burontius clearly did not know Mansius’s work on Atto, as is evident from Burontius’s edition, in which he printed nothing from Mansius. Burontius himself, on page XXV, expressly calls this sermon on Saint Eusebius unpublished, though falsely.]

[Col. 0853B]

Dearly beloved brothers, we must always say something to the common people about the principal solemnities, so that they may learn through our speech what they strive to celebrate according to custom. But in this festival we can say nothing more fitting to them than to discuss more closely the deeds of our patron [Note: Mansius incorrectly reads “more correctly.”] [codex 1, in the hand: “festive”].

We have learned, therefore, that the most blessed Eusebius, whose feast we celebrate today, was of Sardinian origin [Note: Thus the codex; M. reads *natum*, “born”]. Nevertheless, we have learned that he was washed in the waters of baptism at Rome, received from the sacred font by the supreme pontiff himself, and deserved to acquire his name.

That name aptly corresponded to grace, for he was pious from infancy. *Eusebius* means “pious,” as the Greek interpreters explain.

But the man regenerated by the blessed pope Eusebius was ordained bishop by his successor Julius [Note: M. unfaithfully reads “Saint Julius.”]. At that time the city of Vercelli was almost the great heresiarch of all Italy [Note: M. reads “overcome by heresy,” contrary to the manuscript]. Eusebius was sent there, endowed with faith, word, and deed.

The enraged assembly of Arians despised him so greatly because they saw that he was an advocate of the true faith [Note: M. incorrectly reads “assembly”]. And because they did not fear blaspheming the Redeemer, they even dared to reject his shepherd [Note: M. unfaithfully reads “herald”].

They shut themselves inside the doors of the church of the blessed Mother of God, which Constantine of pious memory had built from its foundations. They secured the entrance with bars and bolts, so that by this means they might prevent the shepherd’s arrival [Note: Mansius perversely reverses the order: “prevent the arrival of the shepherd.”].

But the outstanding shepherd shattered everything by the sign of the cross. He came with a free voice to preach the holy Trinity [Note: Mansius reads feminine *praedicandam* for the transmitted neuter *praedicandum*, ‘to preach.’]; and because he did not fear to testify that the Son of God was equal to the Father, he deserved to enter when the doors of his Mother opened before him [Note: The codex and M. read “with the doors opening.”].

The Arians, struck with such terror, withdrew and went in confusion to the most cruel emperor. For Constantius, the emperor of that time, was an especially dangerous subverter of the Catholic faith; and because they knew him to be a heretic, they freely accused the Catholic.

He soon fraudulently summoned all the bishops to Milan for a synod, so that he might secretly extinguish the holy faith [Note: M.’s reading is corrupt: “so that he might secretly extinguish the holy Father.”]. Blessed Eusebius delayed going there, for he was not unaware of what had to be done [Note: M. reads “instead of going.”].

The emperor praised a document composed by the heretics according to their faith, which proclaimed the Son lesser than the Father [Note: This is how Atto speaks elsewhere; M. reads “lesser than the Father”]. At first the Catholics opposed it, but finally, terrified, all who were present signed [Note: Several words following this, lost in a lacuna of the Vatican manuscript, are taken from Burontius’s edition. I disregard Burontius’s variants in this sermon because I have the Vercelli manuscript far away.].

When blessed Eusebius heard this, he poured forth indescribable groans from his heart. He could no longer restrain himself from going to the aforementioned council to contend for the faith [Note: M. shamefully reads “to recall it to memory”; the manuscript reads “to contend.”].

Carrying the precious relics of the holy Gospel [Note: Understand the famous codex of the Gospels still preserved at Vercelli], he hurried and soon reached the river Siccida [Note: M. reads “Sicidem,” and incorrectly places the punctuation earlier]. The boat by which people customarily crossed was then waiting on the opposite bank [Note: M. reads “and the boat”]. When he called it, it came to him of its own accord; it received him, crossed the waters, and carried him safely across [Note: M. reads “which used to cross.”].

Proceeding from there to the great metropolitan city, he mourned deeply with the Catholics. Wiping away their grief [Note: M. reads “extinguishing.”], he spoke wisely and granted forgiveness to all the brothers if they would thereafter follow his footsteps.

The emperor received him and feigned great humility, so that by such means he might seduce his holiness into sacrilege [Note: M. reads “security”]. He said: “Sign, brother, what we have signed; confirm what we all confirmed long ago” [Note: M. reads “write.”].

But the prudent Father [Note: M. incorrectly reads “brother.”] detested doing this. He refused to place his name before all the others on the document; he proclaimed that it should be destroyed and another made, one on which he could sign first [Note: M. reads “proclaimed”]. Thus, by divine providence, he was able to outwit the tyrant, whom the tyrant had cunningly tried to deceive.

Without delay, permission was granted for that document to be burned, and another was ordered to be prepared in its likeness [Note: M. very badly reads “it was not ordered”]. Once composed in this way, it was entirely as blessed Eusebius had dictated [Note: M. reads “discovered”]. The Catholics agreed to it; all, with one mind, signed after him. They promised to contend for this faith and pledged not to deny it even under the injury of death.

When the emperor saw that their steadfastness could not be broken, he turned nearly all his madness against blessed Eusebius [Note: M. reads “converted”]. Then he resolved to afflict him with various dangers [Note: M. shamefully reads “with a plan”; the following six words are omitted by Mansius]. Finally he ordered him to be carried away into prolonged exile.

He endured harsh prisons and chains [Note: M. reads *acerbos* for *acerbas*]; for a long time he suffered from hunger and thirst. There he was manifested through signs and miracles and was often strengthened by angelic consolations. Yet even when placed in such dangers [Note: M. reads “nevertheless”], he did not, as a good shepherd, forget his flock. For from distant regions he visited them constantly by letters and continually strengthened them in perseverance in the Catholic faith.

But by now the Catholics were almost yielding, for the heretics had persecuted them for a long time. At last the Lord took pity and destroyed the wicked tyrant, and brought blessed Eusebius alone back to his own place [Note: M. reads “taking pity”].

On that journey, the Lord showed him a vision [Note: Mansius reads nominative *ille* (‘he’) for dative *illi* (‘to him’).], from which he might recognize the dissolution of his body. In a vision he thought he was standing on the summit of a mountain, and he believed that he flew on wings higher toward a certain palace, brighter than the sun.

He immediately understood that he would ascend from the lofty conduct of the present life to the reward of eternal glory [Note: Several words following this, lost through a lacuna in the Vatican manuscript, have been supplied from Burontius.].

Meanwhile, returning to Vercelli, he was received by his people with great joy [Col. 0855C] and the highest honor, and he preached the faith of Christ to them with steadfast speech. He declared that he would soon depart from the world, and foretold that they would suffer many things after his departure [Note: Thus the Vatican manuscript]. Nevertheless, he urged them to endure these things patiently; he set before them examples of his own steadfastness and passion, and moreover promised them the joys of eternal reward.

Nor was the Arian uprising lacking in compelling the martyr to his crown. They rose against him with clubs and swords and did not fear to overwhelm him with stones. Their blows fractured his skull; he died and thus returned his holy soul to God.

He was buried by his disciples in the church which he himself had once built, driven by divine love, in honor of the martyr Theonestus [Note: Mansius reads “Theonectus”]. There many benefits are granted to all who entreat blessed Eusebius with pure prayers.

May he also free us through his prayers from eternal punishment—the one who today, on the Kalends of August, was freed from the prison of the flesh.

## SERMON XVII. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED MOTHER OF GOD, EVER-VIRGIN MARY

[Col. 0856A]

We celebrate today the Assumption of glorious Mary, ever-Virgin, whom, placed upon the heavenly throne, we adore with devoted minds [Note: [Col. 0855D] M.: “with faithless prayers.”]. For God himself and the Lord, whose Mother we honor [Note: [Col. 0856D] M.: “all of us for her.”], says in the Gospel: “If anyone ministers to me [Note: [Col. 0856D] M.: “will minister to me”], let him follow me; and where I am, there also will my minister be” (John 12:26).

For above all mortals the holy Mother of God ministered to Christ the Lord. She followed him so closely that she grieved with him in his grief and suffered with him in his suffering. Yet concerning his Passion it had been foretold to her: “And a sword will pierce your own soul also” (Luke 2:35). Truly, therefore, she remains in heaven with him whom she served diligently on earth.

Again, elsewhere he says to his disciples: “On that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you” (John 14:20). Again: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); so you and I shall remain one [Note: [Col. 0856D] M.: “we and I shall remain one”]. For what he said to the apostles must also be understood of the other righteous. What wonder, then, if those who are in him abide in heaven? Or what great thing is it if blessed Mary deserved to be heavenly, when the blessed Apostle said of all the righteous: “As is the heavenly one, so also are the heavenly” [Note: [Col. 0856D] M. adds: “they are”] (1 Corinthians 15:48)?

Christ is heavenly, for he descended from heaven; and by imitating him [Note: [Col. 0856D] M. reads shamefully, “by giving”], through participation in him, the other righteous also deserve to be heavenly [Note: [Col. 0856D] M.: “deserved to be”]. Nor should it seem contrary that the Lord says in the Gospel: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man” (John 3:13). For Christ is God, the Son of God and of man; he alone descended from heaven—indeed, he alone ascended.

But the others who are in him are one, and are no longer separate, but are his members. Therefore he alone ascended [Note: [Col. 0856D] Mansius here wrongly posits a lacuna], while those who are in him, or those who … dwell in heaven [lacuna]. For the apostate angels, who had been in heaven and withdrew from God, from there … [lacuna]. Human beings, if they cling to God [Note: [Col. 0856D] M. reads “in” for “if”; M.: “if they clung to God”], will be raised into heaven [Note: [Col. 0856D] M.: “in heaven”]. This must especially be said of blessed Mary, in whom the Lord remained above all mortals. Therefore we have no doubt whatever that she remains in him. Since he also deigned to take flesh from her body [Note: [Col. 0856D] M.: “only”; M.: “from his body”], there is no doubt that he joined her to himself as a member; and her to whom he adhered above all others on earth, he joined to himself above all others in heaven.

We do not dare at all to assert that her body has already undergone resurrection [Note: [Col. 0856D] M.: “his body”], because we do not know that this was declared by the holy Fathers [Col. 0857A] [Note: [Col. 0857D] “Understand the ancient Fathers; for somewhat later writers, such as Gregory of Tours, Ildefonsus of Toledo, Fulbert, Peter Damian, Peter of Blois, Andrew of Crete, and John of Damascus, affirmed it, as Benedict XIV observes in his treatise *On the Feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary*, chapter 8, section 15. There Benedict proceeds, learnedly as is his custom, to confirm the matter from other theological passages.”]. Finally, in the valley of Jehoshaphat the place of her burial remains, but her body is not found there. Yet he who ineffably drew flesh from her knows what has become of her body [Note: [Col. 0857D] M.: “what her body is”].

Nevertheless, whether in the body or outside the body, we confess that she was exalted in heaven above the choirs of angels. For if we truly believe that all the righteous will at some time rise with their own bodies, and that they will be caught up to meet God in the air, and thereafter remain forever with him, according to what the blessed Apostle Paul says (1 Thessalonians 4:16), what wonder is it if the Lord, through an act of compassion, granted the Mother in advance what he will give all the saints at the end of the world, when he clothes mortal bodies with immortality?

Finally, it is written: “There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars” (1 Corinthians 15:41). By the glory of the sun the Apostle taught us to understand the resurrection of the Savior, of whom it is written: “For you who fear God, the Sun of righteousness shall rise” (Malachi 4:2). By the moon we may also understand his Mother. For just as the moon is especially illuminated among the heavenly bodies by the sun, so she too is undoubtedly more brightly illumined by the Lord than the other righteous. When he added “of the stars,” he made known the resurrection of the other saints [Note: [Col. 0858D] “Thus also on page 17, at the final line.”].

It follows: “As star differs from star in glory, so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15:41–42). For difference in life produces variety in resurrection. Perhaps the resurrection of the Mother of God could precede that of the others, anticipating those whom she had surpassed on earth by the merit of her life.

Nor should we fabricate any doubt concerning her death, which we recognize also in the humanity of her Son. Yet she did not deserve to remain long subject to death, since the flesh taken from her he had already conquered by rising again [Note: [Col. 0858D] Mansius: “in the flesh”]. Indeed, since her Son ascended into heaven by his majesty, he could take his Mother there by his piety [Note: [Col. 0858D] M.: “his Mother’s”]. There is no doubt that he shared his glory with her [Note: [Col. 0858D] M. omits “with her”] and established her as mistress of the whole world.

For he who [lacuna] father and mother [lacuna] fulfill [lacuna] we can prove by examples from Scripture [Note: [Col. 0858D] M.: “I can prove”] [lacuna]. Therefore the holy Virgin attained dignity when she deserved to become the Mother of God. A virgin bore a child; a woman gave birth to God. She was made pregnant by the Holy Spirit and made fruitful by the Creator of the world [Note: [Col. 0858D] M.: “made pregnant”]. She was exalted above the choirs of angels in the heavenly places [Note: [Col. 0858D] M. omits “in the heavenly places”], to which may the merciful Lord [Note: [Col. 0858D] M. lacks “merciful”], through the intercession of this same Virgin, deign to lead us, whose etc.

## SERMON XVIII. ON THE BEHEADING OF THE MOST BLESSED FORERUNNER OF CHRIST, JOHN

The magnificent John, the forerunner and martyr of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose birthday the world celebrates today, was brought forth holy from his mother’s womb, as it is written: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you, and appointed you a prophet among the nations” (Jeremiah 1:5).

He had guarded this sanctification with such great abstinence that scarcely any stain of sin clung to his life. For he drank neither wine nor strong drink, and ate nothing unclean. Moreover, he had chosen to dwell in the desert, lest even the gathering of people pollute his life. He continually preached the word of the Lord to those who came to him; when they departed, he devoted himself to unceasing prayer. His manner of life was most humble, his clothing most harsh, and his food most poor.

For we read in the Gospel that he had a garment of camel’s hair and a leather belt around his waist; his food was locusts and wild honey, and he was in the desert preaching a baptism of repentance (Mark 1:6). For the sake of his preaching he practiced remarkable discipline, so that he himself completely did what he preached and fulfilled what he commanded. He preached baptism and baptized those who came to him. He taught repentance and displayed its standard in himself.

O what a great man was this, who was conceived when an angel announced it and was sanctified from his mother’s womb; who always lived in abstinence and wept for the sins of others as though they were his own; who never ceased preparing the way for the Lord by preaching; and who did not hesitate to lose his head for proclaiming the truth!

His holiness grew so greatly that many believed him to be the Christ. Yet, as a guardian of humility, he rejected this as though poison of death had been offered him. He confessed that he was the voice of one crying out. He preached that Christ would come after him, and declared him to possess such authority that he did not consider himself worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal (Mark 1:7).

He was an advocate of truth. Neither the vanity of human praise had compelled him to utter a lie, nor tyrannical fear been able to turn him away from bearing witness to the truth, nor had the queen’s flattery made him tolerate wickedness. By forbidding Herod the marriage-bed of his brother, thus his … adulterer … “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s adulterous wife” (Mark 6:18). Hence he was shut up in a dreadful prison … until such a reputation should cease [uncertain]. Yet the more the athlete of Christ was afflicted by chains, the more he detested unlawful deeds. Finally, his head was cut off, and he departed to the Lord, since he had not consented to conceal the testimony of the truth.

For God is Truth, as he himself says in the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). Whoever does not fear concealing the truth in some way strives to conceal God; and whoever is afflicted here for its testimony will be crowned eternally by Truth itself, which is God.

Therefore, dearest brothers and sisters, let us flee falsehood and its father, the devil. Let us imitate the truth, which we confess to have proceeded from God. By his merits and intercessions may we obtain this, whose festival we all celebrate together today, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ.

## [ATTO’S POLYPTICUM]

## NOTICE ON THE WORK THAT FOLLOWS, BY MAI

To publish all of Atto’s unpublished writings that are in the Vatican manuscript, there remained the *Polypticum*, written twice by the author. The first version was written in a very obscure manner, so that it would not be understood by the uninitiated (*ἀμύητοις*); the second was somewhat clearer. This second version was extracted from the same manuscript by John Mansius.

The first version is illuminated by no explanations in the manuscript; the other is supplied with glosses and scholia, some of which Mansius brought to light. I am now publishing the first version, but I have also taken the glosses and scholia from the second, without which my edition would be useless, since absolutely nothing could be understood.

The cause of the obscurity is not single. For the work contains barbarous and abnormal words, and poetic meter is often mixed with prose in an unpolished fashion. But nothing so darkens and overwhelms this writing as the perverse arrangement of the words, which the author habitually scatters deliberately outside every rule of speech.

I give one example from the final chapter: “This, from which it is fitting that Augustus beware, he prepares to possess as a censorship in name.” The author corrected this perversity in the second writing of the *Polypticum* as follows: “From which it is fitting that he who is prepared to possess it in the name of Augustus beware of this censorship.”

Furthermore, one might be allowed to wonder at Atto, now using a style obscure to the point of marvel, although in his other works he is so lucid—unless the grammarian Virgil, whom I recently published from a Neapolitan manuscript, conveniently taught us that this is one of the twelve kinds of Latin that he enumerates in his epitomes and mentions more than once in his didactic letters.

He calls this an unusual and mystical kind of Latin. In the second chapter of the *Epitomes*, where he discusses the division of speech, he gives several examples from authors whose method our Atto entirely followed. Virgil also records the causes of what he calls “scinderation,” among which he regards as the chief that mystical matters, which ought to be disclosed only to the knowledgeable, should not easily be discovered by the lowly and foolish.

But I now refer my reader to the book of that grammarian. In accordance with it I have also published in type another old little work composed in arcane Latin, entitled *Hisperica Famina* [Note: [Col. 0859] “The little work discussed here has been reprinted in volume 90 of Migne’s *Patrologia*, in the appendix to the Venerable Bede. EDITOR.”].

Atto’s *Polypticum* is a kind of satire or censure of his own times, directed especially against rulers, whose ambition and other vices it chastises at length.

## ATTO, BISHOP OF VERCELLI: *POLYPTICUM*, WHICH HE CALLS *PERPENDICULUM*, WITH ANCIENT GLOSSES AND SCHOLIA

[Note: [Col. 0859B] “*Polypticum* means a description of many things. For it does not speak specifically about only one person, but reproves the vice of many.”]

(In Mai, *New Collection of Ancient Writers*, vol. VI, part II, p. 43.)

### THE LETTER BEGINS

To the highly revered Bishop Fulano [Note: [Col. 0859] “As far as concerns me, that is, in my conscience.”] [Note: [Col. 0859B] “Among the Spaniards *Fulanus* is used in place of any individual’s proper name when the name is lacking.”].

Fulano [Note: [Col. 0859] “That is, I.”], desiring for myself such a blessed end as that of the most fortunate shepherd Silvester. You are dead to some, but to me you are not dead; rather, you are alive—indeed, vivid and alive to me [Note: Thus also Atto in the second edition of the *Polypticum*. But Mansius unfaithfully reads “in me.” There is no time to expose Mansius’s many other errors and divergences from the manuscript. MAI.].

As we run through the path of this labyrinth [Note: [Col. 0860B] “By labyrinth he means this age”], either teach us how, by standing firm, to avoid the abyss, or where those lifted up safely may reach delights. You will see what I perceive. But thus my [thoughts], compared with yours, are like *cantabries* [Note: [Col. 0861C] “*Cantabries* are the thinnest impurities, resembling scales, rising with itching from the surface of human skin in hairy places, especially on the head, and falling away without any ulceration.”] compared with flour [Note: [Col. 0861D] “*Pollinis* is a very fine and exceedingly white kind of flour, sifted through oxhide. It is called *pollinis* because it surpasses the other kinds of flour.”].

There: what I have, and what you have, return happily [Note: [Col. 0861] “Restore it—that is, answer my little book.”]. Amen. The letter ends.

### ARGUMENT

The sophists do not unravel chaos by humming [Note: [Col. 0861D] “The glosses and scholia on the following two verses have perished in the manuscript. MAI.”]. I shall pursue the leftward course continually for the world; not idle matters shaken by this trustworthy pen, nor will little bones be pounded. Tired now, I shall set down the *Perpendiculum* [Note: [Col. 0861D] “He wishes to call this little book the *Perpendiculum*, in which he intends to refute harmful things and establish honorable ones”]. No hard iron [Note: [Col. 0861] “Hard metal”] will be able to silence its voice, nor will Attic *zema* [Note: [Col. 0861D] “*Zema* is a Greek little broth. Greece abounds in spices with which *zema* is flavored.”] be in the rumen [Note: [Col. 0861D] “In the throat. For the rumen is a part of the throat, whence also comes ‘to ruminate’.”]. The argument ends.

### 1

This is the sickness of the present age, and it is sought; it is a plague, and it is pursued in every way. It smiles at its approach; when it creeps in, it delights; in its youth it involves great labor; when it swells, it lays one low; and when it withdraws, it is cursed.

For it usually makes its clients ignoble and those who despise it glorious. This is astonishing: although up to now it has been a ruin for nearly all who have desired it, the arrogant still do not fail, nor is the harshness of those who are raised up restrained.

They deceive themselves into thinking they are superior to the men of old [Note: [Col. 0861] “They lie”], whom prudent censure accuses of being so much more sluggish. If their bundles are gradually begun to be unraveled, I judge that those worthy of being listed first are the ones whom stiff garlands [Note: [Col. 0861] “Crowns”] display crowned.

Do the chroniclers deny this, especially those who loudly proclaim the supreme woe [Note: [Col. 0861] “Calamity”] and all their joy [Note: [Col. 0861] “Pleasure”]? They do not make a noisy procession [Note: [Col. 0861] “Multitude”] who, proceeding along the tangled straight path, have drawn a red line [Note: [Col. 0861D] “A line painted red; that is, those who lived happily in secular honor with such wisdom that, by instructing posterity through their example, they made it blessed”] for their followers.

Although they depict their number as inextricable [Note: [Col. 0861] “They write the number”], those who endure [Note: [Col. 0861] “Live with the greatest harshness”] neither lived on as survivors nor rejoice, poor wretches [Note: [Col. 0861D] “The dead. The ancients called only a happy life ‘living,’ but a sorrowful one ‘enduring.’ Thus, when recording the years of the dead, they wrote: ‘He lived so many years; he endured so many.’”].

Yet I do not think it sincere [Note: [Col. 0861] “Pleasant or prosperous”] to describe now the appearance of their deeds [Note: [Col. 0861] “Qualities”] or to record them privately [Note: [Col. 0861] “By name”]. For even now, while still boys [Note: [Col. 0861B] “Boys”] in a fresh age, they see clearly and have often swallowed these things belched forth by their fathers, and they retain them more securely because they have been impressed upon them [Note: [Col. 0861C] “They hold them in memory”].

It is now easy to reckon the members [Note: [Col. 0861] “Kinds”] of the wickedness already mentioned [Note: [Col. 0861] “Foretold”], according to what a mind passing over them [Note: [Col. 0861] “A thought running through them”] has brought the inner parts [Note: [Col. 0861D] “The heart”] back into description by the pen.

### 2

The height of the matter we are explaining [Note: [Col. 0861] “Discussing”] rises through a threefold distinction. Some even add an as [Note: [Col. 0862D] “An as, that is, one, which is also a fourth distinction. For if one is added to three, there will plainly be a fourth. Since this fourth mode of ascent is extremely displeasing to the wise, he says ‘some.’”].

Either, when the ruler of powers [Note: [Col. 0861] “The governor of authorities”] marks someone whom he wishes to advance with his clear nods, the voice of everyone calls him forth [Note: [Col. 0861] “Summons him”]; or when the same person is granted the enjoyment of a throne by the powerful right of his parent; or when wicked labor and mad battles meet triumphs, they hasten to rise savagely against another, whom the herald had already proclaimed, while the conspirators support the accursed with profane hands.

What then? The rival is completely emptied, through whose benefit the first soldiers are enriched. They do not seek an inviolate treaty [Note: [Col. 0862D] “They seek truces, so that, secure for a while, they may be free from military service”] in which the lord’s sleep may find sweetness.

Meanwhile, however, it is pleasant to pass the released time, and for both to enjoy what they have obtained. The two princes are terrified by opposing threats [Note: [Col. 0861] “They are threatened”] into hostilities [Note: [Col. 0861] “Enmities”], lest the soldiers dare to gape powerfully [Note: [Col. 0861] “That is, to yawn or open the mouth; the expression is taken from birds”] against them, or forbid anything that remains in a pitiable [Note: [Col. 0861] “Lowly”] name, so that the princes may flourish so greatly that they are rather not even masters of private property.

Then they secretly discuss with their associates the return of these stratagems [Note: [Col. 0861] “Frauds”], taking care to repay them diligently. For this reason they are not reluctant secretly to frequent the olive branches [Note: [Col. 0861] “Since the olive is a sign of peace”] [Note: [Col. 0862D] “Seeing that the princes very much wish to rule their subjects, they choose rather to make peace in whatever way than to be troubled by such injuries from their subjects. Although they hope that mutual aid will suffice to suppress them, they nevertheless seek external support to join to their own, lest the others later be able to summon their own forces to their aid.”].

Through mounted messengers [Note: [Col. 0862D] “Messengers. Mounted messengers are envoys carrying something, so called from *vehere*, ‘to carry’], they murmur cautiously [Note: [Col. 0861] “Whisper”], supported by clever men lest anything trivial occur through which the soldiers might be stirred at the first inquiry. They also request foreign commanders and their cooperation, heap gifts upon them, and quickly promise greater things [Note: [Col. 0861] “They promise things increased beyond measure”].

Why does the fortune of the powerful not yet promise something extorted from the outermost regions, which the intermediaries [Note: [Col. 0861] “Go-betweens”], or these men themselves, eagerly desire to taste beforehand?

They burn to bring their own forces together with them and subdue their proud men; or, if these are idle or sluggish, they then rage through arms and deny aid to the oppressed, for they themselves will rage.

There remains also a specimen of the deceit by which the tribunes, overwhelmed at the bottom [Note: [Col. 0863] “Deficient superiors”], are struck down. When their soldiers seek the flattering airs of the court, and return from there to their own homes with loaded shoulders, the men called “fortifiers” [Note: [Col. 0863] “Often called the king’s counselors”]—the arbiters and masters of these soldiers—do not even bear benefits in the giving, lest they first be properly repaired, if the commanders should place them before themselves in generosity.

They lend [Note: [Col. 0863] “They enrich”] them, immune from their own loss [Note: [Col. 0863] “Immune from their own, that is, from their property, because they enrich them from another’s loss”], and promote them as faithful to themselves through another’s loss. They take those through whom they advance, but not from those by whom they do so [Note: [Col. 0863] “That is, from the masters”].

If chance separates them, or if they themselves bring them together better, they remain silent until matters spoken against one another have been brought forward against one another. They decide to investigate them and prepare themselves. They spread individual trifles through households like seeds, from which they often reap and learn what is useful beforehand.

Hence the soldiers first dissolve their loyalty to their masters [Note: [Col. 0863B] “They scatter or evacuate”], and now make firm their observance of a second loyalty—the loyalty that will be lacking to the princes. Then they brand themselves with infamy, undermine their masters, and do not refuse to swear falsely by the heavenly power.

Thus, enticed by shameful desire, they are sometimes expected to provide favorable things [Note: [Col. 0863] “Prosperities”] to sorrowful masters [Note: [Col. 0863] “Sad masters”]. Whenever chance postpones some danger, they bring it upon them from their own resources and, by heaping it up [Note: [Col. 0863] “That is, by filling the danger”], overthrow them.

### 3

Therefore the princes add rough things through what they have gnawed away, and decide to fortify all the shallow places [Note: [Col. 0863D] “They establish camps on steep mountains, or set guards at river crossings, so that no access to cross may be open to anyone unknown to them”], so that no stranger may transfer anything to himself.

Those who possess very strong fortifications they either oppress with hostages or try to remove. If by chance you trust someone’s estate to them, that they may preserve it for you, or if you undertake to place any title of men upon their heirs, they immediately hold this as an accusation to be measured out against its owners. They claim for themselves whatever is useful from everything, and do not permit any part to be distributed among those who had at least once prepared it.

[Note: [Col. 0863C–D] “*Elogia* are called disgraceful accusations or marks of crimes. *Alogia* are banquets; appropriately so, because the ancients dined in silence and quiet. Modern people, using wine at banquets, with which it is not lawful to preserve silence, seek amid their cups the stories that poems may tell.”]

They build fortresses of counsel, so that no attack may terrify them, but so that whatever they have calmly devised may be carried out against anyone there. They establish an *aumatia* [Note: [Col. 0863D] “*Aumatia* are secluded places in a theater. Mansius incorrectly reads *humatia*. MAI.”] and arrange three-sided spaces within it.

But after they have firmly planted their slipping feet, they store the quarrels of the nobles in their minds, declaring themselves allies of both opposing sides. They perversely act as traitors toward the one, and accuse rivals of being rival plagiaries [Note: [Col. 0863D] “Deceivers. A plagiary is called *plagiator* from *πλάγιον* (*plagion*), ‘oblique,’ because he does not walk by a straight road but entices through tricks.”], charging them with such a crime that the unjust quiver [Note: [Col. 0863D] “Here he calls the quiver a deceitful mind bearing various ambushes”] is not exposed and may bite anyone indiscriminately who is ungrateful [Note: [Col. 0863] “Hateful”].

They sing of those summoned as most distinguished, and prolong the rupture by calling upon sacred things [Note: [Col. 0863] “By swearing by sacred things”], lest they return with them together to their former friendship [Note: [Col. 0863D] “Return to the earlier friendship”] while they remain at the bottom. Nor are the informers themselves separated [Note: [Col. 0863] “Authors”], as they strive in the same way to turn these matters around.

Then Alecto claps her serpent hair [Note: [Col. 0863] “With serpent hair”].

### 4

But if some clever and crafty person should foresee these schemes, let him whisper that these things will be deserted and rendered ineffective, so that the innocent, whom even the law [Note: [Col. 0863] “Censure”] does not weary, may not suffer.

Then the throat [Note: [Col. 0863] “The prominent part of the throat”] is constricted by terror, and a thin voice escapes toward the air, hissing between the doorposts [Note: [Col. 0863] “Teeth. The doorposts of the mouth are the teeth”], while, with livid pupils, he presses upon the edicts through polished tricks [Note: [Col. 0863] “Affected devices”].

Here the assertor of truth is marked with a rabid stigma, so that the prey may be torn apart as quickly as possible. Clothed in *mastrugae* [Note: [Col. 0863D] “A *mastruga* is a garment made from the hides of wild animals. It is called *mastruga*, as if ‘monstrous,’ because those who put it on seem transformed into the appearance of beasts. It is suitable for hunters, especially archers; for beasts deceived by such an appearance easily approach them.”], they set forth, with scorpions, *tragelaphs* [Note: [Col. 0864D] “A *tragelaphus* is the same as the *plataceron* in Deuteronomy: an animal with broad horns, almost like a deer in appearance, but with shaggy shoulders, an elongated chin, and a bristling beard. These animals are found near the Phasis. In Latin, a he-goat-deer.”].

How, like the Parthians, the one leading the way and advancing captures the airs of death; then, with himself as leader, twisting herds of beasts through the air, he drives them away. The bow-bearer charges that not everyone had fallen before the one to whom each had been prostrate; he blasphemes, cursing only the one whom he also wearies by restraining, if someone among the commanders who knows how to recognize such frauds should bring them into the open.

They order things consonant with *abscides* and curved forms to be engraved on flashing molds, and frequently summon *martisium* [Note: [Col. 0864D] “*Martisium* is food made in a mortar, whence it takes its name”], pounded foods [Note: [Col. 0864D] “*Intritum* is likewise a food prepared from bread by culinary art. Bread is placed in water and left there for a while until it is completely soaked. Then it is taken from the water and broken down with a pestle in a mortar. It is then mixed with oil, a little honey, and spices, and placed in a cauldron on the fire until it reaches its proper consistency. It is called *intritum*, as if ‘crushed’”], and *hemistes* [Note: [Col. 0864D] “*Hemistes* are vessels from which one drinks in a single breath”], so that while they are preserved in their preparation they may loosen themselves.

They study how to distribute, bit by bit [Note: [Col. 0865] “In small portions”], even among the rather coarse things [Note: [Col. 0865] “Ugly things”] that they strive to open up [Note: [Col. 0865] “Distribute”] to the enemy, while they draw talents from blood or leave behind whatever things destroy whomsoever they ruin.

Until this advancement [Note: [Col. 0865] “Increase”], they provide it from the loss of others. Among them there are also those who envy the fortune attained by others. They weary them with these tricks, display feigned or fabricated griefs [Note: [Col. 0865] “Introduced or fictitious”], and bring forth the hardships of the princes to those who had increased them. They reveal that it is right to exclude them, but refuse to exact vengeance upon them, and explain what is possible [Note: [Col. 0865] “Possible”].

While those men strive to accomplish this, they seek rather such methods as the *amphifarii* prescribe [uncertain]. If they await someone who can strike down the commanders, they ask from where they may now be able to do so. Then they seek profit from it. But if they wisely place guards, they arrange for themselves to withdraw. They expose to associates the devices by which they undo each other.

From others they first teach these things, and later claim that they themselves had withdrawn when summoned in order to betray them. They demand that what the rebels possess should be attributed to their faithful men, remaining as rewards for treason and for the perjuries of fraud.

Meanwhile they watch the commanders. Then they yield what they had also wished to tear away from the old arrangements, while the supports [Note: [Col. 0865] “Aids”] of the stripped and submerged battle lines have been removed, along with those who flourish through skill.

Then these men too suffer losses, and, through their grim success, are deprived of advantages and receive strength from no one. In turn they howl. Nor will there be lacking a title for the crime by which misery may be stirred against the others—alas, poor cannibals [Note: [Col. 0865D] “Anthropophagi. Because of their excessive cruelty these men are also called *ambrones*] whom the rapacious have exposed.

### 5

Then the death and ruin of the others are also thrown before these men. They accuse the incentives to crime; they had made these men commanders, and they are ashamed of the disgrace spread throughout everyone, yet they do not try to bring back those who have been exposed [Note: [Col. 0865] “Recall those who have been made public”]. They seek only to be able to inflict these hatreds.

Rumor tells of a certain savage bird which, while it chirps with growing heat during the breeding season and flatters with relaxed wings, receives a mate of a different kind and not of the same nature. When the bird senses that she has been made pregnant by him, the joined female [Note: [Col. 0865] “United in intercourse; for *dos* is the term for the mating of mute animals”] pursues him, rejoicing to tear open her bridegroom’s entrails.

So the commanders grow fat on spoils [Note: [Col. 0865D] “On plunder. Just as the aforementioned bird, fertilized by the seed of her mate, seeks to be satiated with his entrails, so the commanders, made magnificent by the aid of the nobles, desire also to be enriched by their wealth”]. They gape at rising against one another, lest empty desire be hindered from every crime it covets.

While the restless guardians [Note: [Col. 0865] “Administrators; for the nobles usually serve as the commanders’ guardians”] drag different things, hating one another, the two do not share one purpose, and the individuals cannot resist, adorned wherever they proceed; they await only whom the urn [Note: [Col. 0865] “The lot”] may summon.

It is a shame for anyone to breathe any spirit through the upper airs. Each holds whatever he has to be removed, and the happier man is the one betrayed who has already escaped unharmed.

They reject kisses [Note: [Col. 0865] “They reject their spouses”], and some do not fear to leave their children exiles behind [Note: [Col. 0865] “Children appear to be left orphans when their surviving parents abandon them”]. Others wound their livid entrails with *pascema* [Note: [Col. 0865D] “*Pascema* is a very small Egyptian loaf by which the monks of that region are sustained.”].

There are also the idle, gazing at the pyramid and at the cave-image [Note: [Col. 0865] “A hollow rock that returns the image of the one who cries out”] or at a hollow, watching for the knot. There remain also those whose sight is defrauded of the sun, or those whom the severed name of their parent seems to preserve as boys [Note: [Col. 0865] “The beardless appear to retain the father’s severed name”].

From some is taken the part that carries four senses [Note: [Col. 0865] “The head”] and tests them [Note: [Col. 0865] “Experiencing or testing; for in the head things are approved or rejected”]. In another, what has been torn away restrains the fifth [Note: [Col. 0866D] “Represses it.” The author says that some leave their wives and children and go into exile; others, setting aside secular life, choose monastic life; others submit their necks to the punishments of prisons. Many are deprived of their eyes; others are castrated; sometimes their heads too are cut off, and these carry four senses; when torn away, the fifth—touch—is also destroyed.].

Here the suppressed hatreds are pressed down in this way, and they pursue whatever remains of the offspring. Some indeed pay the penalties deservedly, but while furious desire enjoys the guilty, it rages without sparing anyone who should be exempt from wickedness, and unbridled drives the honorable themselves toward the precipice.

After they have restrained the distinguished men, once the ruined have gaped open through advantage [Note: [Col. 0865] “Utility”], the mockers of those men become entangled in weariness. And those who once rejected them through an empty oath now seek the deceived right hands which they would previously have gladly entrusted to prosperous masters—if they had kept their first agreements—now to be endowed with no estates or resources.

Even if birth produced these men noble, unless they obey the authors of wickedness continually, the latter compel them to follow as shipwrecked men on white feet [Note: [Col. 0866D] “Either barefoot or covered with white leather. The footwear of nobles is usually made from blackened leather”]. And they complain as dependants [Note: [Col. 0865] “Obligated”], so that, even unwillingly, they may make good what they had promised when rewarded [Note: [Col. 0865] “Rewarded”].

### 6. What are the judges to choose?

They take pleasure neither in relating what has been examined nor in examining what is set down in ancient volumes. They brandish their masters’ contrived commands and frame laws tainted by money, so that justice’s evenly balanced scale may weigh no one fairly. The same [Col. 0866C] law is not proclaimed for everyone: even if it strikes someone they love, he will escape unharmed; but someone they hate, or a possessor of wealth, will fall, broken by intrigue or force and driven out [the wording around *excuset et exodiunt* is damaged]. Nor does a single, enduring judgment often answer the same case: what it now condemns, it soon extols with praise, and then denounces the same things as profane and worse still.

But the insolent builder of the lofty citadel rises, indeed, crowned and resting on a rich throne. Filled with his own thoughts, he seeks to deceive the surviving company with crude syllogisms. He rejoices if their last day removes any of them, so that he may enter as an accidental heir. As for the widows left by them, they are given no choice whether to remain so; unless they ransom themselves, they must prepare to marry again. These undeserved marriages are either bought by needy men or elevate the king’s foolish [Col. 0866D] clients, who do not hesitate to dishonour stepchildren or [Col. 0867A] cast out the mothers who have spent their wealth.

Sometimes the ruler will take into the palace, for his use, a mosaic pavement marked with shameful figures [the agreement in the supplied wording is defective]. Then he forces the surviving consuls and the others to live as private men. He drives out natives who have been advanced, expecting needy men to be generous to him, and installs foreigners in chosen curule seats. And sacred things or citizens—provided Mammon separates out the babblers—are to render service and obey his commands in everything [the construction of this sentence is uncertain]. “These great things are no strangers to us: our native ancestry produced them.” Thus they applaud in astonishment, ignorant of what shines in the ceremonial robe or of what the bordered toga taught [the connection of the clauses is obscure].

Obsidian deceives them; they commonly prefer the liquid driven from soda by heat to the precious stones of India and the Caucasus. When they raise the insignia of a commander of a thousand, they do not know how to fit them together properly.

[Col. 0867B]

### 7.

When the people consult them, they bear down upon them with snarling and braying, following barbarous habits. They disdain what the laws proclaim and terrify their subjects with the din of their own bellowing. At first they delight in displaying their pomp amid unaccustomed successes. But once they begin to examine fortune’s ways, although outwardly they put off their cares, a wound pricks within their breast. Thus, after surrendering themselves to rest on lofty, furnished couches, they are not allowed to enjoy the fruit of deepest silence. They look up at the Stephadium, go out beneath the sky, and repeatedly consult the water clocks by lamplight, even though they err in taking their measurements.

Their minds toss as they investigate these unfamiliar matters: now sudden riches, now a fall from favour terrifies them, as the experience of their predecessors has taught them, when they thought the prince’s favour secure. They regard what they have overlooked as no pardonable matter, [Col. 0867C] and no measure excuses it, while every service is exacted from them as from undeserving stewards [the syntax is uncertain]. Authority excuses no one out of regard for his station, nor does reputation drive away insult. Dignity and ancestral praises engraved in catalogues fail to restrain those who act against them. They try to conceal any stain their birth has given them and to shine solely by the dignity they have received.

They spur themselves on with this. But consciousness of their lowly descent torments [Col. 0868A] their minds, which fear binds ever more tightly. They ponder their insolent master and reconsider their predecessors, the former consuls. They survey the possessions they have seized and subjected, and fear to lose office. Hence they seek one another as allies [a few words are missing] ... is accomplished by a threat. Prolonged security now prepares an unguarded fall, as the instructive sequence shows.

They do not disclose their agreements while gathering the soldiers they have enlisted into a single body, so that none may stand apart and seek someone able to resist [the transmitted *ut sit ne exul ... nequis* is uncertain]. With one front they burst out in accusation against the ruler. They grant him indulgence and keep their pledged faith if he is permitted to withdraw. But should he cast a stain upon the people, or even murmur, they will force him into silence with bonds, making him pay for it; or they painfully shut him off from the light, compel him to travel the bitter road, and to behold unknown ages.

Thus their spirits sink [Col. 0868B] when they become masters as the king’s accidental heirs [the wording of the first clause is obscure]. They often celebrate feast days with proud display, and at banquets invite one another to drink from splendid cups. They give one another bracelets and exchange Sabaean sashes heavy with glittering bosses. Again they bind themselves with renewed pledges of loyalty. They exchange brides from their families and receive one another’s children from the sacred font, preserving their alliance by such a pledge, so that their compacts may at least endure. Others swear by the Lord of spirits and by the urns of his most faithful witnesses, wrought in polished gold. Thus they divide country and people among themselves, ruin the poor, and do not shrink from profaning anything sacred.

### 8.

It is said that the Hericine antelope, when it begins to batter down the foliage, entangles itself to its death and at last [Col. 0868C] betrays itself by its own cry. So it happens to those who presume to violate sacred things.

Meanwhile retaliation does not cease. Although injuries suffered long ago are thought forgotten, or their commands were not carried out, opportunity takes vengeance upon the offenders [the subjects are not consistently expressed]. They moreover commit threefold the wrongs for which they once professed to expel the ruler. Their household goods are plunder; few complain about them to the court, since no one in the court makes a sound. [Col. 0869A] Mercy looks on from afar and sees no share of herself in these men, surrounded by youthful companions. Amid their applauding band you will hear a mutterer, if he wishes to dine lavishly with them, utter things from which truth has been effaced. O times that bring no one before an acknowledged judge, though the peasants press their complaints!

I recall the tombs of our forefathers, but do not judge them to be like these consuls, who think to weigh everything by prosperous circumstances [the supplied wording is tangled]. As they prolong their banquets, music resounds through the city, blown, echoed in measures, and struck upon taut strings. A tuneful voice joins it; Istria supplies the dancing. The cupbearers watch ceaselessly, mingling clarified wines with nectar, and serve wheat beer and other strong drink, to drive away restraint and loosen their drunken bodies. Hence—[Col. 0869B] shameful crime!—they fill the air with wanton laughter that reveals them, and spur one another on by exchanging lascivious tales. Enticements then suggest debauchery and incest. All around, servants spend the night revelling and gratifying their masters in these things.

### 9.

Yet they cannot enjoy these things long without another’s jealousy, since they are their fellows’ equals in rank but greatly surpass them in dignity. For hardship produces concord; insolence, division. The lesser men hurry to join together apart from the others, to the detriment of the greater. They claim that much of what the greater retain is owed to them, and insist upon equalization. The former excel in numbers, with their strength at full heat; the latter possess more mature judgment, greater wealth, and the protection of lofty walls. Yet they consider it [Col. 0869C] impossible to extinguish the rising turmoil unless they appoint a prince, though they refuse to place themselves beneath him.

At last they resolve to set a fool over themselves, through whom they may secure their own advantage, one who will investigate none of their actions or dare refuse them. They even make him attest this by divine rites. In vain: for if, once appointed, he remains dull, he will settle no conflict. The younger men will go on vigorously disparaging the elders. They do not spare the master either unless he separates himself from the latter. The eloquent elders, in turn, threaten worse things against the inexperienced, press the master [Col. 0870A] and demand his promises, urging him to rise against their adversaries. What will he do? Can he escape the ruin threatened on both sides? Nor will ingenuity aid the fool. He can only flee his enemies and live privately.

But if he originally presented himself as a dullard by design, and his prudence shines forth once the diadem favours him, then, frightened, they secretly try to quiet their mutual hatred and whisper of coming together again, so that by this agreement they may unravel their master’s oppressive power once more. With his clear understanding, their schemes cannot remain hidden from the ruler; he prepares to abolish their foolishness along with the fools. They, opposing him, eagerly seek to thrust him from his lofty throne. What has happened before, instructing the ruler, greatly hinders them: they reckon it something to fear, and think they may fail in the attempt themselves [the final construction is uncertain].

[Col. 0870B] Then the nobles dispatch treasures afar to enlist allies. From this they expect increased assistance. They even prepare to raise up a powerful foreign leader and submit their necks to him. Then indeed [several words are missing] ... support, and first through deputies, if assemblies cannot lawfully be held, in which the arrangements may be communicated; these incomplete proceedings may falter for a while [the clause following the lacuna remains defective].

### 10.

Meanwhile the present ruler’s furious onslaught will not cease to rage or grow sluggish in devouring the guilty. He will strive all the harder to reduce the strongest resisters to the level of the overthrown [*in supernum* is obscure]. And those whom they once sought to advance by frequent greetings may prepare to help them; but as soon as they hear the first whisper of their falling fortunes, they turn aside. Instead they report to the ears of the prevailing ruler that his own soldiers have earnestly sought their help in a plot. [Col. 0870C] No one, they say, could win their assent; abandoning their friendship, they deny what fear had washed away [the latter clause’s wording is uncertain].

With such fabrications they expect profits from his side, although the faithless nobles had earlier promised them privileges, purchased by sworn pledges. But the prudent ruler gives them little and rebukes them calmly: “It would have helped if these matters had been disclosed to us earlier by your side, while they still lay hidden.” He scorns their feeble limbs and mocks their faint hearts.

There are also foreign military chiefs under another ruler. When they hear the complaints through messengers, they immediately require pledges that the disaffected men will never return to the favour [Col. 0871A] of their old ruler. In return they promise them assistance on the same terms. Then they cautiously and very quickly send envoys to that king, revealing the soldiers’ proposals but concealing their own pledges, in order that he may give handsome gifts and the agreements already made may be annulled. Let him rage against his own men: they will not tolerate peace among them. And if he takes steps to heap up gifts, he will be able to stir those purported helpers into enemies for the others’ destruction; then, if advantageous, they conclude treaties with a return offered [the objects of *cumulare* and *talione* are not explicit].

Others, when asked to invade another’s dominion, roar, rage, and utter stern boasts; armed, they hasten to make a covert attack upon the ruler. But once they cross his frontiers and see him surrounded by a glittering host, they halt, [Col. 0871B] lose heart, and seek pretexts to withdraw. Even if they see their own army standing firm, should the ruler send peaceful messengers laden with gifts to them from afar, they deliberate in private, complain that they were misled, and denounce as faithless the consuls who engaged them. They accuse those men of deceit, abandon them, and consign them to death. Then they try to return unharmed and carry their gains back to their own land.

### 11.

Rarely, however, someone is brought in who openly and resolutely attacks the ruler, determined to overthrow him, and does not desist until he gains either death or victory; or, after the devastation of war, he divides the territory with the other, and, content with their portions, they enter a single treaty, each secure in subduing his own subjects.

What will the soldiers who invited him gain? If in such danger [Col. 0871C] he breathes his last, the survivor will seek them out for punishment. If he escapes victorious, he too will compel them to the same penalty; remembering what occurred, he will not consider his throne inviolable unless they are deprived of authority.

There are provinces ruled by a single prince.
