If he gravely injures any men whose breasts swell with arrogance, they immediately approach the dreaded wearer of the triple diadem, inciting him to remove the ruler, who commands forces unequal to his. Even if they can accomplish this, they will have no return to their own homes; however successful, they will finally receive their deserts [the construction of *explicent ... recursum* is defective]. Commanding the various nations’ battle lines, he will bring scattered words [Col. 0871D] into obedience. They know no sparing way of life, [Col. 0872A] but plunder every better thing, even reducing matrons to prostitution in holy places [the supplied *nec vivere parce quae noscitant* has defective syntax].

Once they perceive the country devastated, their stay is not prolonged: troops cannot long be kept in foreign lands. Nor is it fitting for the ruler to remain so far from his own army with a scanty force among those whose loyalty he greatly doubts. He returns to his own soil, rejoicing to see it again. Those who brought him in may resolve to accompany him: if they do, they choose an exile marked by lasting sorrow and humiliation; otherwise they are left to a disgraceful ruin.

Meanwhile the ruler of the country where these things occur, inferior in troops, is in exile or laments, shut deep within the walls of a strongly fortified city. But when he learns of the enemy’s departure on that longed-for day, he summons into battle formation the scattered men whom conspicuous loyalty had marked out. He instructs his chief officers [Col. 0872B] and prepares to give each his due: joys to the faithful, bitterness to the hostile. Those who summoned the tyrant against him receive the greatest penalty, with punishment added to punishment. Nor does the ruler alone hate them: the troops also fix their hatred upon them for the humiliation they endured. They strive to impoverish not only those men but their dependants as well, until the passage of the years gradually destroys the whole affair.

### 12.

There remains this too: if death cuts them off amid these things, they cannot rejoice in a future age as the present slips away. Yet the vice does not perish. Others arise and turn again through the same cycle.

But there are men who were never trained in school, who could not reach even the fringe of Wisdom’s shining veil, and to whom it means nothing if rulers are carried on a bier to the grave, [Col. 0872C] provided they themselves may return home unharmed, loaded with spoils [the supplied sentence has an incomplete construction]. You are deceived, erring man, in trying with subtle devices to confound things distinguished by ages beyond yourself. Whether practised or poured out, what you put forward is worth nothing; then let barren nature abandon her own gifts [the connection remains obscure]. If you can imagine a noble and a camp-follower to have the same station, you will be able to see heaven, earth, and Cocytus in one and the same condition.

Why do you disparage rulers’ offices? Can you obscure the supports which the Almighty himself chose to sustain a failing world? Do you not cite the books of Kings? Do you not applaud the man to whom the chorus of virgins awards a trophy for ten thousand enemies [the placement of *decem milium* is awkward]? [Col. 0872D] Do you not prefer this to the *hecaton per phoneuma* sacrifice? [Col. 0873A] Or him for whose eyes the sun recalled its course by twice five steps? Do you not mention the temple’s adorn­er, Coheleth, who also removed abominations [*procanum ... coheleth*; the identification and construction are uncertain]?

Now let the New Testament come in its order: Helena’s son, vigorous in victorious arms, who removed the sufferings of Christ’s worshippers and confirmed the rights of their office. Nor, O Theodosius, great ruler, are you brought forward by this man’s lips for your great triumphs: rejecting heresies, you scattered barbarian weapons, destroyed shrines, and decreed the removal of their priests, so that no underground haunt of a demon might remain in which something of the old cult could lurk, but everything might serve the one Creator.

Nor, deluded man, do you reckon his namesake grandson exalted, who tempered burning coals with a burning coal, and frost again with a burning coal: he subdued fury and lust by doctrine, was faithful to Charity, and [Col. 0873B] neither remained sluggish nor yielded to dejection, more often supplicating the Eternal than triumphing in arms.

What can the common multitude accomplish? It cannot even subsist on its own when deprived of leaders. The earliest ages indicate this, though not readily; we must give it attention here. From Adam’s first descendants strong limbs grew, and fruitful offspring produced abundant multitudes, increasing through frequent succession and rare deaths. But they lacked a ruler equipped to instruct the untrained companies how to avoid the danger of the surging flood. The Abrahamic people itself, God’s people, was led to triumph while living obediently under disciplined leaders; when it strayed and despised them, it was exiled far from its threshold and became an unprofitable stock. This applies not to it alone but to every earth-born being. Why mention only human beings, whose [Col. 0873C] noblest part, the mind, we confess to be with God?

There are also small, provident winged creatures, vigorous in their skill, granted a perpetual celibate life through the air. They honour a commander among themselves and render him his due. When the others are lively, [Col. 0874A] they show him to be safe; if he dies, they mourn his funeral. If he leaves his home, all abandon their occupations; they do not shrink from seeking their former dwelling places with him. A little people prospers under an industrious and wise leader; without him, an equipped legion is brought to nothing.

### 13.

Cease your undertaking now, and use our judgment. It pleases me to rebuke these fools with such craft. O men for whom it suffices to squander what is poured into your half-casks! To what purpose? That you may at least be table-contributors to the great. In return for soothing trifles, your lung cannot hold out: when pressed, it seems able to utter only panegyrics paid for with princely dishes [the sentence concerning *pleumon* has damaged agreement].

Gluttons! If one dining room excludes you from its preliminary meal, you soon go shamelessly from house to house to pursue breakfast [Col. 0874B] elsewhere, sip wine outside, and make the rounds after a dish or a contribution at a tavern. Should this fail, you take thought how to obtain it when the prey has been removed by departure or deprived of office [the construction remains broken]. Your drunkenness is not postponed, however much the overburdened belly expels its bitter load. The only brotherhood among you, you yourselves confess, is an Arval brotherhood [an association here linked with feasting].

Already your excess flesh would leave you unfit to bear burdens; but the wound eating into your breast consumes it into thin liquid, and from it does not cease to fill you with black bile [the syntax around *sarciam ... staret* is defective]. O that sarcophagi now held you embalmed for burial—or, earlier, the infants’ graves beneath the eaves! If a jester wishes you to be carried forth as decrepit old men, he does not wait until the coffin, nor does he scan the undertakers’ cheerful faces [the relationship of the clauses is obscure].

For even if by the rain-stones you could change [Col. 0874C] the face of heaven, you cannot corrupt a man’s judgment. Revelling with grim jaws, you threaten to abolish the truth, pulling your lips awry in jealous grimaces and opening your mouths to bark. The Arretine pots clattered as they boiled: as the damp vessels take in fire, so drunkenness may drip into fools [Col. 0875A] themselves [*stitiat* is uncertain].

I reject their silent winking, scorn their chirping, and count their chatter as nothing. My tongue does not descend to two-obol ditties, nor does my pen answer your insult in that fashion [the wording of the second clause is defective]. But if they bring written charges, let our pages be brought before a gathering of honourable men. No obelus will mark mine; it will deserve [several words are lost] ... wax ... one ... a diligent tower ... lest a harmful mark adhere to the point [the remaining syntax is broken, and part of the gloss is lost].

### 14.

By your babbling you have spread rumours among the people, though you now try to quiet them. If they subsequently spring up among any frivolous cultivators, it will then be proper to uphold what was promised long ago. Can judges with weak daylight sight discern clearly even the tiny flower of a plumb-line [the image and syntax are uncertain]? They seek to gnaw like caterpillars, not for any flavour in their mouths but to destroy by devouring. [Col. 0875B] As a gardener, I take care to bar their way with fences. Let them visit the seller of ointments, choose eye-salves, and put their dark sleeping screens in order, so that afterwards they may distinguish light from darkness.

I am not so lethargic as to presume to abolish rulers’ offices: I admonish that they must not be violated. As I have already told you, fool, it is a grave matter to climb to the summit of the assembly, subdue one’s country into captivity, and deprive another of his throne. Fornication and plunder will follow, however anyone denies it. It is preferred to expel the chief rather than to take away a lawful spouse and introduce an unlawful one [the wording *amplexum ... jugalem ... inelegum* is obscure].

Does not the man dragged from his own threshold into exile bear it more lightly than the one oppressed within his home like a hired labourer, while another rustic heaps up stores he had amassed for himself, and he may not so much as taste what the other holds without right [the *promos* clause is damaged]? Or the man confined in fetters and kept from drink while [Col. 0875C] everything is ruined? One sees his own wife caressed with kisses, and feels that a descendant of his family is forced into a corrupted marriage; even the women’s suitors are deceived by a delusive hope of alliance. Let anyone argue that invading a kingdom is a slight matter, if these things follow [printed *difficile*, “difficult,” makes the argument uncertain].

The man who delights in the war arising from this may meanwhile fall and descend into the abyss. He who longs to prepare for others the sorrows described either knows nothing of Avernus or awaits it without fear. The Creator of all will bring him under judgment, so that he leaves this age dishonoured and enters the punishment of the next.

Therefore, the man whom the Almighty [Col. 0876A] wishes to show worthy by his signs, or whom the united assembly of all the nobles seeks to advance, and whom honourable love of country supports in this, may lawfully ascend a vacant throne if he excels. But let him take care that his ascent increases no distress among the people, and let him remove every suspension of justice, should there be any. Those who reach kingship by such a beginning may perhaps attain a happy last day, having blessed their country. The others, stripped of tyranny, will pay the penalty which they prolonged while holding it. The book of both Testaments can unfold these scraps for you in the school; if you choose to turn its thousand leaves, it will put no obstacle before my witnesses but will itself support me with its writings.

### 15.

But let my pen return to the very persons whom you took care to single out. O foolish company, had Jesse’s offspring [Col. 0876B] aspired beforehand to exchange the shepherd’s crook for the royal staff, when, through the prayer of the mystical seer, the power of the sought anointing was bestowed upon his head [*Isai* is Jesse; the supplied construction is difficult]? I recall that Hezekiah and Josiah came forth as kings from royal blood, with their native people’s favour.

Was not Helena his mother, and his father the one who had rested in the seat of kingship? When arranging a colleague for himself, providence willed the son [the Helena–father–son sentence is syntactically damaged; the source note names Constans and Constantine]. Theodosius too sprang from distinguished soldiers of Spain and, by the aid of the supreme Godhead, restored the world to safety from the barbarians. When signs first indicated that he too would be raised to the highest place, he saw himself in a vision clothed in the imperial robe by the upright Meletius, who placed the diadem upon him. He was able, without anyone identifying him, to recognize that previously unseen man when he eventually beheld his face, by the evidence of the vision.

[Col. 0876C] Soon advanced by the emperor Gratian, he became his colleague, as the vision had foretold. Amid the pressing wars which he brought to rest, it was then fitting for his namesake grandson, matching him in merits, peacefully to occupy his father’s and grandfather’s throne. If the royal seat comes to anyone in this manner and he occupies it, guilt will not attach to him, provided he judges himself adequate to the title of such great majesty. But he must not yet exult that he remains secure. Initial auspices alone do not suffice to confer happiness; worthy though they are, they require further growth.


#### Source notes and glosses

These entries follow the supplied source’s order. The exact source gloss is retained beside its English translation; the English identifies the relevant term or passage.

1. **§6.** [Col. 0865] Indices.

   On *arbitri*: the gloss reads *Indices* (“indicators” or “informers”; possibly a corruption of *iudices*, “judges”).

2. **§6.** [Col. 0865] Revera.

   On *quin*: indeed.

3. **§6.** [Col. 0865] Suis perversis cogitationibus adimpletur.

   On *foetatur*: he is filled with his own perverse thoughts.

4. **§6.** [Col. 0865] Populum superstitem.

   On *cohortem*: the surviving people.

5. **§6.** [Col. 0865] Eventicius heres.

   On *caducarius*: an accidental heir.

6. **§6.** [Col. 0865] Dehonestare.

   On *obfuscare*: to dishonour.

7. **§6.** [Col. 0867D] Postquam omnem substantiam, tam suam quam etiam filiorum in proprium usum expenderint, tum eas abjiciunt ut alias, si fieri potest, nobiliores vel pulchriores aut etiam ditiores ducant uxores.

   On casting out the mothers: after spending all the property, both theirs and their children’s, for their own use, they cast the women aside to marry other wives, if possible nobler, more beautiful, or richer.

8. **§6.** [Col. 0867] Parvulis crustis ac variis tesselis elaboratam.

   On *litostratam*: worked with little pieces and various tesserae.

9. **§6.** [Col. 0867] Garrulos et stultos.

   On *buccos*: babblers and fools.

10. **§6.** [Col. 0867D] Genus est lapidis translucidum, et reddens imagines.

   On *Obsius*: a translucent kind of stone that reflects images.

11. **§6.** [Col. 0867D] Tradunt qui de vitri natura scripserunt, quod ex cocto nitro et littorea harena, ejus sit reperta materies. Dicit eos novitate honoris adhuc incogniti, nec vilia contemnere, nec eligere pretiosa.

   On the liquid from soda: writers on the nature of glass relate that its material was discovered from heated soda and shore sand. He says that, because their new honour is still unfamiliar, they neither despise cheap things nor choose precious ones.

12. **§6.** [Col. 0867] Millenarius qui mille militibus praeest.

   On *chiliartica*: a commander of a thousand, who commands a thousand soldiers.

13. **§6.** [Col. 0867] Copulare ordinate.

   On *coaptare secunde*: to join together in due order.

14. **§7.** [Col. 0867] Inutiliter loqui. Rudere proprie asinorum est.

   On *rudere*: to speak uselessly. Braying properly belongs to asses.

15. **§7.** [Col. 0867] Mores.

   On *sequellas*: habits.

16. **§7.** [Col. 0867] Palam.

   On *foris*: openly.

17. **§7.** [Col. 0867] Procrastinent.

   On *perendinent*: let them procrastinate.

18. **§7.** [Col. 0867] Pungit; inspicare enim proprie est faces infindere.

   On *inspicatur*: it pricks; *inspicare* properly means to split torches.

19. **§7.** [Col. 0867] Ornamentis lectorum.

   On *fulcribus*: with the furnishings of couches.

20. **§7.** [Col. 0867D] Stephadium signum est in coelo, quod rustici praesepe dicunt. Et dicitur stephadium quasi stipadium; sic enim praesepe prius dicebatur, a stipitibus ex quibus fiebat.

   On *Stephadium*: a sign in the sky that country people call the Manger. *Stephadium* is so called as though *stipadium*: the manger was formerly called this from the stakes (*stipites*) of which it was made.

21. **§7.** [Col. 0867D] Vasa aquarum, quae judices habent pro horis nocturnis metiendis.

   On *clepsydras*: water vessels which judges have for measuring the hours of the night.

22. **§7.** [Col. 0867] Candela quae lucet in umbra.

   On *lucubro*: a candle that shines in the dark.

23. **§7.** [Col. 0868D] Decipiantur. Quamvis etenim spatia horarum in his discernere nesciant, sed quia maesticia somnum capere non possunt, haec tamen inquirere illis saltim tranquillitas est.

   On *fallantur*: they are deceived. Although they do not know how to distinguish the intervals of the hours in these vessels, their sadness prevents sleep, and at least studying them gives some tranquillity.

24. **§7.** [Col. 0867] Scilicet ab honore.

   On *exire*: namely, from office.

25. **§7.** [Col. 0868D] Desunt pauca verba.

   A few words are missing.

26. **§7.** [Col. 0867] Maculam.

   On *lentiginem*: a stain.

27. **§7.** [Col. 0867] Vinculis.

   On *vincilibus*: in bonds (*vinculis*).

28. **§7.** [Col. 0868D] Circumspicere. Haec quippe omnia periphrasis sunt mortis. Denique si suam considerans culpam, exilium subeat, fortasse quiescent persequentes. Quod si ipsis coeperit crimen innectere, vel si murmuraverit, aut carceri mancipatur, aut etiam interficitur.

   On *lustrare*: to look about. All these expressions are a circumlocution for death. If he acknowledges his guilt and goes into exile, his persecutors may perhaps desist. But if he begins to accuse them of a crime, or murmurs, he is imprisoned or even killed.

29. **§7.** [Col. 0867] Dies festos.

   On *caltudias*: feast days.

30. **§7.** [Col. 0867] Conviviis.

   On *alogiis*: at banquets.

31. **§7.** [Col. 0867] Splendida.

   On *nibara*: splendid.

32. **§7.** [Col. 0867] Invitant.

   On *conducunt*: they invite.

33. **§7.** [Col. 0867] Armillas.

   On *calbas*: bracelets.

34. **§7.** [Col. 0867] Ex sacro fonte.

   On *delubro*: from the sacred font.

35. **§7.** [Col. 0868D] Dicit eos laborare ut inter se inviolabilem possint firmare amicitiam, alii per nuptias, alii per comparatica, alii vero quod superest jurejurando per Deum et sanctorum corpora.

   On their oaths: he says that they strive to establish inviolable friendship among themselves, some through marriages, some through baptismal sponsorship, and others, as a remaining means, by oaths sworn by God and the bodies of saints.

36. **§7.** [Col. 0867] Auro.

   On *ofaz*: in gold.

37. **§8.** [Col. 0868D] Animal acerrimum nimis, habens cornua longa, serrae figuram habentia.

   On the antelope: an exceedingly fierce animal, with long horns shaped like a saw.

38. **§8.** [Col. 0869D] Ops dicitur misericors, eo quod libenter opem ferat.

   On *Ops*: Mercy is called *Ops* because she willingly brings aid (*opem*).

39. **§8.** [Col. 0869D] Speculatur; nullam namque partem in his prospicit, quam in se recognoscat, cum illos crudeles, se misericordem intelligat.

   On *prospectat*: she observes. She sees no part in them that she recognizes in herself, understanding them to be cruel and herself merciful.

40. **§8.** [Col. 0869] Juvenes.

   On *buteones*: young men.

41. **§8.** [Col. 0869] A mutire seu mutire MAI.

   On *mucissonem*: from *mutire*, or *mutire* (“to mutter”; the supplied note repeats the same form). Mai.

42. **§8.** [Col. 0869] Sepulcra majorum quae nunc ipsis mortuis posuit.

   On *busticeta*: the forefathers’ tombs, which he has here used to signify the dead themselves.

43. **§8.** [Col. 0869D] Locum pro habitatoribus posuit; ex ea enim provincia sunt homines nimiae atque incredibilis velocitatis.

   On *Istria*: he has put the place for its inhabitants, for that province produces people of extraordinary and incredible agility.

44. **§8.** [Col. 0869D] Caelia est potio ex succo tritici per artem confecta.

   On *caelia*: a drink artificially prepared from the juice of wheat.

45. **§8.** [Col. 0869] Manifestantium.

   On *prodentium*: of those making manifest.

46. **§9.** [Col. 0869] Monent.

   On *castigant*: they admonish.

47. **§9.** [Col. 0869] Impossibile.

   On *invalidum*: impossible.

48. **§9.** [Col. 0869] Excusant, scilicet a minis vel a derogationibus. [Cod. exipiunt.]

   On *excipiunt*: they excuse, namely, from threats or disparagements. The manuscript has *exipiunt*, a spelling variant of “they exempt.”

49. **§9.** [Col. 0869] Juvenibus vel imperitis.

   On *rudibus*: the young or inexperienced.

50. **§9.** [Col. 0869D] Pernicies ab utrisque partibus pollicitas. Minores minantur principi ni segregetur a majoribus, et suis consiliis adquiescat: at contra majores admonent ut in minores saeviat, sibique ut promiserat [Col. 0870D] in omnibus pareat. Minores quoque in aliquibus superant, majores vero in quibusdam excellunt.

   On the two ruins: destruction threatened from both sides. The lesser men threaten the prince unless he separates himself from the greater and agrees to their counsels; the greater, conversely, urge him to rage against the lesser and obey them in everything, as promised. The lesser excel in some respects, the greater in others.

51. **§9.** [Col. 0870D] Quae neutrum absolutum est, id est quae res. Dicit enim, quia si ante adsumptum honorem, stultum se princeps simulaverit, et potestatem adeptus suam ostenderit sapientiam, cuncti proceres ejus pavore clam ad concordiam revocantur, ut ejus a se jugum facilius simul excutere valeant: non enim volunt imperantem habere dominum, sed potius obsequentem.

   On *quae*: an independent neuter, that is, “which thing.” He says that if a prince feigned stupidity before assuming office, then displayed his wisdom after obtaining power, all the nobles are secretly brought back into concord through fear of him, so that together they may more easily shake off his yoke. They want an obedient lord, rather than one who rules them.

52. **§9.** [Col. 0869] Sublimi.

   On *aucto*: lofty.

53. **§9.** [Col. 0870D] Prioris principis dejectio.

   On *praecedentia*: the deposition of the former prince.

54. **§9.** [Col. 0870D] Scilicet in dominica expulsione.

   On *in ipsis*: namely, in the expulsion of their lord.

55. **§9.** [Col. 0869] Auxilia magnificanda.

   On *augenda solatia*: assistance to be increased.

56. **§9.** [Col. 0870D] Desunt verba aliquot.

   Several words are missing.

57. **§10.** [Col. 0869] Toleratores, qui sunt et potentiores. Majoribus vero fulti praesidiis magis praevalent adversa tolerare.

   On *perpetitores*: those who endure, who are also the more powerful. Supported by greater resources, they are better able to endure adversity.

58. **§10.** [Col. 0869] Aequare.

   On *hostire*: to make equal.

59. **§10.** [Col. 0869] Promovere.

   On *producere*: to promote.

60. **§10.** [Col. 0869] Lucra.

   On *foenora*: profits.

61. **§10.** [Col. 0871] Honesta.

   On *lepida*: honourable.

62. **§10.** [Col. 0871] Fines.

   On *margines*: frontiers.

63. **§10.** [Col. 0871] Destinant.

   On *distingunt*: they consign.

64. **§10.** [Col. 0871] Terra propria.

   On *solo privato*: in their own land.

65. **§11.** [Col. 0871] Expetet ad poenam.

   On *expetet*: he will seek them out for punishment.

66. **§11.** [Col. 0871] Ipse.

   On *isdem*: he himself.

67. **§11.** [Col. 0871D] Etiam in sacratis locis, hoc est in ecclesiis. Pro nimia enim multitudine hostium quia castra vel urbes raro defendendi adsumunt fiduciam, nobiles feminae contemptis omnibus ad ecclesias confugiunt, ut saltim pudicitiam inibi religionis valeant reverentia custodire. Sed nefandissimus hostis non eas tantum extrahere, sed inibi etiam commaculare praesumit.

   On *in sacris*: even in consecrated places, that is, churches. Because enemies are so numerous, people seldom feel confident of defending forts or cities; noble women abandon everything and flee into churches so that reverence for religion may at least preserve their chastity there. But the utterly wicked enemy presumes not merely to drag them out but to defile them even there.

68. **§11.** [Col. 0871] Prolongatur.

   On *traducitur*: is prolonged.

69. **§11.** [Col. 0871] Deducere proprie est amicum abeuntem prosequi.

   On *deducere*: properly, to accompany a departing friend.

70. **§11.** [Col. 0871] In qua ista aguntur.

   On *praesentis*: in which these things take place.

71. **§11.** [Col. 0871] Ad egestatem perducere.

   On *egestare*: to reduce to poverty.

72. **§12.** [Col. 0871D] Cirrati sunt scholastici a cirris capillorum dicti. Nam antiquitus scholares pueri usque ad adulescentiam non tondebantur.

   On *cirrati*: scholars, named from curls of hair. In ancient times schoolboys were not shorn until adolescence.

73. **§12.** [Col. 0872D] Carbasus genus veli tenuissimi et perspicui ex lino. Bene sophia carbaso tegitur, quia nec ex toto latet sapientibus, nec omnino nuda conspicitur. Stultis vero nec ad ipsius etiam veli perscrutationem patet accessus, quia ejus disciplinae non susceperunt intellectum.

   On *carbasus*: a very fine, transparent linen veil. Wisdom is aptly covered with such a veil, since she is neither wholly hidden from the wise nor seen entirely naked. Fools cannot even approach the examination of this veil because they have not acquired understanding of her teaching.

74. **§12.** [Col. 0871] Domum ire.

   On *domoitionem*: to go home.

75. **§12.** [Col. 0871] Extra te. Non poteris namque adprobare quae nisus es confirmare.

   On *prae te*: outside yourself. You will not be able to prove what you strove to establish.

76. **§12.** [Col. 0871] Separata.

   On *singillata*: separated.

77. **§12.** [Col. 0871] Astutiis, quasi subtilibus telis.

   On *sutelis*: by tricks, as though fine webs (*subtilibus telis*).

78. **§12.** [Col. 0871] Summates.

   On *summati*: nobles (*summates*).

79. **§12.** [Col. 0871] Terrae.

   On *aridae*: of the earth.

80. **§12.** [Col. 0871] Eundem statum.

   On *unum*: the same condition.

81. **§12.** [Col. 0871] Retro subpedias.

   On *subpetias*: earlier, *subpedias* (“supports”); the note refers back to that form.

82. **§12.** [Col. 0871] Libros regum.

   On *malachim*: the books of Kings.

83. **§12.** [Col. 0871] Testaris.

   On *confiteris*: you bear witness.

84. **§12.** [Col. 0872D] Hecaton per phoneuma genus est sacrificii. Si quis centum hostes interfecisset, Marti de homine sacrificabat; et dicebatur hoc sacrificium per phoneuma (a φονεύω).

   On *hecaton per phoneuma*: a kind of sacrifice. If someone killed a hundred enemies, he sacrificed a human being to Mars; this sacrifice was called *per phoneuma*, from φονεύω (“I kill”).

85. **§12.** [Col. 0873] Procanus est ornator aedificiorum.

   On *procanus*: an adorner of buildings.

86. **§12.** [Col. 0873] Omnimodis pati.

   On *pancratiari*: to suffer in every way.

87. **§12.** [Col. 0873] Tutulos dicebant sacerdotes brevium templorum.

   On *tutulos*: *tutuli* was the name for priests of small temples.

88. **§12.** [Col. 0873] Seducte.

   On *inducte*: deluded one.

89. **§12.** [Col. 0873D] Haec omnia per hexegesin in subsequentibus invenies explanata. Nam pruna ignis est adhuc ardens, unde etiam a pruritu dicitur, id est ab ardore, vel ἀπό τοῦ πυρός cujus vis diversas in scripturis habet significationes: aliquando enim significat doctrinam, aliquando iram, aliquando libidinem, aliquando praeceptum caritatis et cetera. Pruina est frigus, cujus nomen ab igne est, sicut et prunae, quia paene unum effectum habent: urit namque ignis, urit et frigus: quod etiam quamvis varias habeat significationes, saepius tamen in malo ponitur. Vere ergo Theodosius prunas pruna temperavit, quia per doctrinam, quam didicerat, iram et libidinem devicit. Rursus pruna pruinas edomavit, quia per ignem caritatis segnitiem et accidiam superavit. Haec siquidem duo vitia bene pruinae comparantur, quia prudentiae ignem minime capiunt: naturaliter etiam in corporibus hominum ex frigidissimo [Col. 0874D] humore, id est, melancholico nascuntur. (Theodosii senioris vitia haec, verene an potius falso? notat Eunapius ethnicus in excerptis vaticanis script. vet T. II. p. 281. Editor.)

   On *prunas pruna ... pruinas ... pruna*: all this is explained by exposition in what follows. *Pruna* is fire still burning, named from *pruritus*, that is, heat, or ἀπὸ τοῦ πυρός (“from fire”). Its power has various scriptural meanings: doctrine, anger, lust, the commandment of charity, and others. *Pruina* is cold; its name, like *pruna*, comes from fire because their effects are almost the same: fire burns and cold burns. Though it too has various meanings, it is more often used adversely. Theodosius truly tempered coals with a coal, since by the doctrine he learned he overcame anger and lust. Again he subdued frost with a coal, since by charity’s fire he overcame sluggishness and acedia. These two vices are aptly compared with frost because they do not admit the fire of prudence; physically they arise in human bodies from the coldest, melancholic humour. The editor adds: “The pagan Eunapius attributes these vices to the elder Theodosius—truly, or rather falsely?—in the Vatican excerpts, *Scriptores veteres*, vol. II, p. 281.”

90. **§12.** [Col. 0873] Deo qui karitas est.

   On *karitati*: to God, who is charity.

91. **§12.** [Col. 0873] Saepius.

   On *subindius*: more often.

92. **§12.** [Col. 0873] Exessu, morte. [Malim excessu.]

   On *exessu*: death. “I would prefer *excessu*,” meaning “departure” or “death.”

93. **§12.** [Col. 0873] Moderatis. Stitiosi siquidem dicuntur instituta servantes: unde et superstitiosi qui super instituta observant.

   On *stitiosis*: disciplined. Those who keep established rules are called *stitiosi*; hence *superstitiosi*, those who observe beyond what is established.

94. **§12.** [Col. 0873] Deviatus.

   On *exorbitatus*: having strayed.

95. **§12.** [Col. 0874D] Ideo mentem hominis cum Deo esse dicimus, quia inter omnes mortales solus de divinis noverit cogitare.

   On the mind being with God: we say the human mind is with God because, among all mortal creatures, the human alone knows how to think about divine things.

96. **§12.** [Col. 0873] Magistrum militiae.

   On *stratilatem*: a military commander.

97. **§13.** [Col. 0873] Stultos.

   On *pecuatos*: fools.

98. **§13.** [Col. 0874D] Hemicadium est vas olearium: dicitur autem hemicadium eo quod non plenum cadum contineat; cadus quippe Graece amphora est.

   On *hemicadium*: an oil vessel, so called because it does not hold a full *cadus*; *cadus* in Greek means an amphora.

99. **§13.** [Col. 0873] Symbolones a symbola, quae vulgo dicitur confersa.

   On *symbolones*: from *symbola*, commonly called a shared contribution (*confersa*).

100. **§13.** [Col. 0873] Vicissitudine quae vobis redditur.

   On *talione*: the return made to you.

101. **§13.** [Col. 0873] Tuccetae dicuntur escae principum.

   On *tuccetis*: *tuccetae* are the dishes of princes.

102. **§13.** [Col. 0873] Edulium est praegustativa comestio.

   On *edulium*: eating beforehand as a tasting.

103. **§13.** [Col. 0873] Catillare est alienas domos infrontate gyrare.

   On *catillare*: shamelessly to make the rounds of other people’s houses.

104. **§13.** [Col. 0873] Confer am.

   On *obolam*: the supplied gloss reads *Confer am*, probably *conferam*, “a contribution.”

105. **§13.** [Col. 0873] Sarcia est superfluum carnis incrementum, quo ultra modum corpora saginantur.

   On *sarcia*: a superfluous growth of flesh, by which bodies are fattened beyond measure.

106. **§13.** [Col. 0873] Implere.

   On *foetare*: to fill.

107. **§13.** [Col. 0874D] Ad augmentum quidem suae invidiae, quicquid comedunt, in felle destillat.

   On black bile: whatever they eat drips into gall, increasing their envy.

108. **§13.** [Col. 0873] Funeris obsequio perunctos.

   On *polinctos*: anointed in the rites of burial.

109. **§13.** [Col. 0873] Sepulchra infantium nulla obsequia promerentium.

   On *subgrundaria*: graves of infants who receive no funerary observances.

110. **§13.** [Col. 0874D] Pegaso homo jocularis aut vilis persona, et declinatur pegaso pegasonis. Pegasus vero apud paganos fingitur equus fuisse pennatus.

   On *pegaso*: a jester or lowly person, declined *pegaso, pegasonis*. *Pegasus*, however, is imagined among the pagans to have been a winged horse.

111. **§13.** [Col. 0874D] Manales dicebantur petrae, quas antiqui in modum cylindri per limites verrere solebant pro pluviae commutanda inopia.

   On *Manales*: stones which the ancients used to roll like cylinders along boundaries to remedy a lack of rain.

112. **§13.** [Col. 0873] Valgiae sunt labellorum obtorsiones in supinatione tractae.

   On *valgiae*: distortions of the lips, drawn back and turned upwards.

113. **§13.** [Col. 0873] Latratum, et est proprie canum. Baubare tamen nunc eos dicit supervacua et vilia loqui.

   On *baubatum*: barking, properly belonging to dogs. Here, however, he calls their useless and worthless speech barking.

114. **§13.** [Col. 0873] Vasa fictilia dicta ab Aretio civitate, in qua plurima fiunt.

   On *Aretina*: earthen vessels named from the city of Arretium, where very many are made.

115. **§13.** [Col. 0873] Fervendo sonant. Cacabare enim a [Col. 0875] qualitate soni dicitur.

   On *cacabant*: they sound as they boil. *Cacabare* is named from the quality of the sound.

116. **§13.** [Col. 0875] Semnion Grecae, Latine conventiculum honestorum dicitur.

   On *semnion*: in Greek, what Latin calls an assembly of honourable men.

117. **§13.** [Col. 0875D] Perierunt verba aliquot. MAI.

   Several words have perished. Mai.

118. **§13.** [Col. 0875] Perierunt in lacuna glossae.

   Part of the gloss has perished in the lacuna.

119. **§14.** [Col. 0875] Excolensibus.

   On *harpagantibus*: those cultivating [printed *excolensibus*].

120. **§14.** [Col. 0875] Luscinii dicuntur in die parum videntes.

   On *lusciniorum*: *luscinii* are those who see poorly by day.

121. **§14.** [Col. 0875] Vasa somniaria et obscura, conopeis similia. Dicuntur autem alucinaria quasi a luce alia, id est luce privata.

   On *alucinaria*: dark furnishings for sleep, like mosquito nets. They are called *alucinaria* as though “other than light,” that is, deprived of light.

122. **§14.** [Col. 0875] Fornicatio.

   On *pornia*: fornication.

123. **§14.** [Col. 0875] Fortis mercenarius.

   On *baro*: a strong hired man.

124. **§14.** [Col. 0875] Ita cod. At Mansius primos. MAI.

   On *promos*: thus the manuscript. Mansi, however, has *primos*. Mai. The former suggests provision-stewards or stores here; the latter means “the first” or “foremost.” The sentence is damaged.

125. **§14.** [Col. 0875] Vincula quibus quadrupedes alligantur.

   On *nummellis*: fetters with which quadrupeds are bound.

126. **§14.** [Col. 0875] Bellum.

   On *polemum*: war.

127. **§14.** [Col. 0875] Pandecte, liber Vetus et Novum Testamentum continens.

   On *pandecten*: a *pandecte*, a book containing the Old and New Testaments.

128. **§14.** [Col. 0875] Ramentum dici voluerant antiqui quasi quoddam projecticium purgamentum.

   On *ramentum*: the ancients intended this to mean something thrown away, a kind of refuse.

129. **§14.** [Col. 0875] Folia.

   On *facies*: leaves.

130. **§15.** [Col. 0875] Specialiter.

   On *in faciem*: specifically.

131. **§15.** [Col. 0875] Stulta.

   On *pelingna*: foolish.

132. **§15.** [Col. 0875D] Scipio virga regalis est. Romani siquidem scipionem vocabant virgam quam triumphantes cum sceptro in manu gerebant, ad imitationem victoriae Scipionis.

   On *scipio*: a royal rod. The Romans called the rod carried in the hand with the sceptre by triumphators a *scipio*, in imitation of Scipio’s victory.

133. **§15.** [Col. 0875D] Constans enim imperator filium suum Constantinum favore populi etiam secum regnare compulit.

   For the emperor Constans compelled his son Constantine, with the people’s favour, to reign alongside him as well. [The names are retained as supplied.]

134. **§15.** [Col. 0875D] Meletius quidem episcopus fuit Sebastes Asmeniae civitatis, qui merito sanctitatis maximus [Col. 0876D] ab omnibus dicebatur. Postea etiam ad Antiochenam translatus est ecclesiam.

   Meletius was bishop of Sebaste, a city of Armenia [printed *Asmeniae*], and was called “the greatest” by everyone because of his holiness. He was later transferred to the church of Antioch.

135. **§15.** [Col. 0876D] Theodosius cum a Gratiano imperatore directus contra barbaros triumphasset, vidit se in somnis a Meletio episcopo imperiali more ornatum; et non longe post ab eodem Gratiano ad imperii susceptus est culmen. Sed postea cum synodum Constantinopolim centum quinquaginta episcoporum congregare fecisset, nullo prodente, inter omnes et sola sui somnii memoria eundem cognovit Meletium.

   When Theodosius, sent against the barbarians by the emperor Gratian, had triumphed, he dreamed that Bishop Meletius adorned him in imperial fashion. Not long afterwards Gratian raised him to the summit of imperial power. Later, after assembling a synod of 150 bishops at Constantinople, he recognized that same Meletius among them, without anyone identifying him, solely from the memory of his dream.

[Col. 0877A] **16.** Hence, since “pasture” has been mentioned [Note: Excellent; hence we also say *pastophoria*], I now wish to set forth certain principles. “By the word of the Lord”—Saul was raised from humble Israel in order to protect it [uncertain]. From this point he drove out the Philistines and, having captured the surrounding nations hostile to him at the beginning of his reign, began to empty them through easy victories. But greed [Note: Avarice] compelled him to covet what was forbidden; soon his once-supple arms withdrew from battle through weariness. His fearful mind, daring not even to look upon the enemy’s battle line, struck itself with its own weapon and incurred Aetnaean punishments.

Eudoxus [Note: A king of good renown] had also brought King Manasseh forth, as a prince from his blood [Note: Reviving: for after God had added fifteen years to Hezekiah’s life, Manasseh was born]. His father judged that he should succeed to the throne and be extinguished meanwhile [Note: Meanwhile, that is, until the end. He said “meanwhile” because of Manasseh’s final conversion. It should certainly be noted that he believed the example of these three kings sufficient to explain what he had proposed. For although they had lawfully assumed power, they afterward behaved most wickedly; only Manasseh repented, while the others, persisting in the same course, reached an unhappy end. In them he showed that no one ought to be secure because of righteousness, nor despair because of crimes]. For him he decreed that the things for which he himself burned, and those which he presented as cast-off, should be expiated; attacking the Theusebian [uncertain], he restored the rites and shrines of the demons.

His colleague Licinius, while [Note: For he marched with the soldiers in the army] he continued to entice their minds with his “scytales” [Note: The *scytale* is a kind of serpent whose back shines with such a variety of markings that the sight of it delays observers; and because it is slow in crawling, it captures by the wonder of its appearance those whom it cannot overtake. Licinius is therefore aptly called a *scytale*, because by fraudulent pretence he won the favor of others so completely that they voluntarily placed themselves beneath him; later many perished through his poisonous deceptions], obtained their support to the point that they pressed him forward by their vote [Note: The ancients, holding pebbles in their hands, counted numbers [Col. 0878B] with them. *Calculus* is also said of the attainment of the highest position or of victory, because whenever the number reached a thousand, calculators appropriated the thousandth pebble to themselves and said that they had obtained as many pebbles as they had counted thousands. And because a thousand is the highest number and cannot be counted beyond it, if someone had attained the summit of anything, they said that he had obtained the *calculus], foolishly to seize the empire, while they composed songs in his honor and remained silent beneath him with impunity.

He had mocked the diligent Augustus [Note: A diligent Augustus means faithful and without deceit. He means Constantine, as he will indicate in what follows], so that he himself might support him. He also took him as his associate [Note: He adopted him. When Constantine heard him praised so greatly by the soldiers, he associated him with himself in the empire and gave him his sister in marriage. At first Licinius falsely made himself modest; at last he fell into every crime and, moreover, declared war against Constantine, who immediately expelled him from the empire], despising him and refusing to yoke his sister to his marriage bed [Note: Despising him].

The toga that had for a time covered him, still crude, was deceitful; he breathed favorable airs toward orthodoxy and then plunged into demon-worship. He suppressed the Delphic rites [Note: He had suppressed them] and utterly crushed the roof-rites [Note: Magic rites, in which sacrifices were offered upon rooftops]. He renounced the accomplices and practitioners of trickery [Note: Fraud], and of the art; the ancient archons [Note: Rulers] had drawn them to themselves as followers and executioners, so that they might handle sacred vessels [Note: Sacred vessels] together with suitable men, and he had constrained them with them.

“Anna” [Note: This is the interjection of one entreating, as though he said “would that” or “I beseech you”] had not yet begun, but had been made void [Note: Had emptied what had never been begun]; it had been established by the authority of the elders [Note: Strengthened by the authority of the elders] throughout the regions of the world [Note: Throughout the parts of the world]. But when his present dominion [Note: Rule] became foolish, he began to reject it through antitheses [Col. 0878A], and then the recent bloody decrees were proclaimed [Note: Brought forward], holy [Note: Holy].

If anyone now confessed Jesus, he first assigned him to the executioners and afterward to the butchers. Soon he also gave them over to revel with Bromius, and likewise with Cynthius, their accomplices, and with Incubus, all the way to the end. Moreover, he raised the imperial sword against Constantine, from whom he had received his kingdom, and he also assailed his co-ruler and kin [uncertain]. Immediately, when these things had been made public [Note: Published], the divine power opposed him and removed him, and, having cleansed the laws, established them firmly [Note: He overthrew his abominable laws and put worthy laws in their place to be observed].

**17.** A worthy form scarcely grows from a sluggish stock, or perhaps never from such a lineage. Nor does what proceeds from an illustrious source [Note: Noble] arise without distinction; rather, it often declines from an excellent origin, and it is a crime to fall from what has been proclaimed beforehand [Note: Predicted] and has thundered toward the scepters [Col. 0878B]. Yet no one will perfect himself merely by dedication; nor will honorable equality, extending dignity even to those imbued with lesser qualities, make the great great enough to ascend an eternal kingdom.

These redeemed ones [Note: The redeemed are all Christians, whom Christ deigned to redeem from the devil’s possession with his own blood and reconcile to himself] and the phylacteries of Christ [Note: Observances] are owed to all. In the measure of life, let each person preserve what belongs to him with modesty. Let him put ambition outside; let him be humble [Note: Humble], and not a hoarder [Note: Hoarders are those who pile up or gather the goods of others for themselves].

Let it be enough that he possesses benefits justly: what the ancient ones had left behind, he should expend; and let household generosity provide what is required by unstained service, lawfully and exactly from what his own cultivation produces, and let his skill duly bring forth what has been entrusted to it. Let them delegate duties, and, if the greater ones are diligent, let him supply what is lacking—not pomp, but enduring zeal. If they return profit, let him repay eternal praise and service equally.

Even if he suffers ruin, let him not cease to demand the same one, without hope; nor let him blaspheme in poverty, unaware of what judgment has struck him [Note: Struck by judgment]. Can unexpected changes not occur? Let the self-glorifier [Note: Beyond measure] not gape before the ungrateful man [Note: One who gives no thanks]. For if you are to be increased [Note: Augmented] by miseries [Note: Miseries; they also say this is the name of a Fury], say “by hardships,” [MAI]—this crushed man will be able to be cast down and thrust back into Erebus.

**18.** “Patagine” [Note: There is this difference between *patago* and *patagium*: *patago* is an ulceration of the mouth which, when swollen, nearly makes a person speechless; *patagium* is a cloak variegated with gold and purple] poured out—“hem” [Note: When written with aspiration, *hem* is the interjection of someone grieving, as though “alas for me.” Without aspiration it is an adverb of display, as though “behold me.”]—but why should I, like an emphatic herald, explain the rule [Note: Regulation] of a dissolving age, whose eloquent tongue cannot even conjecture its diseases?

Yet once it was languishing still worse: bedridden and sunk in filth, repeating dirges, it was wasting away in a desperate state [Note: Despaired of] with its health already abandoned. Above it stood the chief thief [Note: The devil], also destroying it with poisonous bites. Meanwhile, seeing the afflicted one, he came to his aid; but the one who had smeared him with his palm shook him from his mouth, and, disarming him—he had also made him toothless [Note: Made him without teeth]—emptied him [Note: Emptied him], restored the loosened world to solidity, and then strengthened the weakened man so that he could stand.

He made known both what must be avoided and what must be used for salvation. But because the sick man transgresses this, associates with harmful things, and refuses what is salutary, he is often seen to relapse. Yet the maker, physician, and author of salvation himself also provides a remedy for the ungrateful: he has often stretched out costly antidotes and *lixopyrites* [Note: Poultices. He calls antidotes and *lixopyrites* works of mercy].

Now let us earnestly pray that he will not withdraw his hand, nor, moved by anger, press the surgery further, but that he will pour in and apply ointments from the highest *dynamidia* [Note: Medical books. *Dynamis* means the power and force of herbs; hence *dynamidia* are books in which their medicines or cures are written. Here *dynamidia* properly signifies divine mercies], by which he may drive away the wasting disease; that the time for surgery may come, so that, after a brief delay, he may find what he ought either to burn or dare to cut.

May the Church, dedicated to Christ’s marriage bed [Note: The Church. For all washed by the water of the sacred font are known to be the body of the holy mother Church, the bride of Christ. Therefore he prays that no Christian may be torn from her body, lest, mutilated in some part, she appear to be brought to grief], not mourn the cut-off portions [Note: Cut-off parts are pieces of the body that have been severed] that the mystical urn [Note: A water-jar] washed [Col. 0879C].

Whoever is capable of medicine cannot be skilled unless he diligently investigates the physical principle. No one understands the nature of a created thing as well as the one who fashioned it. Who, then, will be able to preserve the world in health—not to mention its monarchy or the proportion within its first [Col. 0880A] form—unless the potter himself is the fashioner? [Note: He says that there is no physician unless he is a natural philosopher. Again, no one can understand the physical principle of each thing so fully as the one who composed it. Therefore no one can preserve the world in health except the one who formed it].

Even if he acknowledges that the form can be perfected through human agency, the holy one remains within it, and the spirit nevertheless supplies it. If anyone serves him purely forever, all good things that come to pass will proceed from him. But he will quickly flee from crimes if he defiles himself by sharing in them [Note: Pollutes himself]. Then, abandoned in his actions, he will immediately perish with his own people unless he digs himself out from among them and stands as before.

**19.** Accordingly, it is fitting that the one who prepares to possess the Augustan office in name should beware of this. Let him accept what has been brought forward by the common vote, and, having attained it, live in such a way that he does not profane it. In his decisions, let him act according to division and frustrate what is his own [Note: His own. He should not presume to do only what seems good to him, but should rather acquiesce in the authority of earlier teachers and the counsel of honorable men].

Let those who still survive as judges [Note: Judges who are alive], and those who have already gone before, be illustrious; and let him place the *diatheca* [Note: The book of the two Testaments, Old and New] before him as a mirror, so that the crafty merchant [Note: A fraudulent shopkeeper who mixes water with wine; this is also applied to false teachers, who pollute truths with falsehoods and customarily pour out harmful doctrines] cannot dilute it [Col. 0880B].

Therefore let him continually implore the Lord, and, devoted, add that he will not postpone his prayer. It is also the duty of the whole people to fulfill this [Note: Complete it], lest they be led astray [Note: Separated] from him. For, since the chief one struggles to abolish the power of the Testament, he foolishly neglects to seek the help of his patron.

“I am ready to answer without distinction” [Note: I am ready to answer; I delay nothing]. “Pray for yourselves, so that it may be done.” Now I shall answer you in the language of Adam [Note: Does he hint at the prayers of the Hebrew psalms? MAI], so that it may now be done for you, even if you prefer me to begin . . . before the highest majesty of you [Note: Several words are missing. MAI] . . . so that he may wash away my offense with peaceful light, fashion me as one pleasing to you, and accept the prayers that must be poured out; so that no deceiver [Note: Deceiver], however troublesome, may first be able to defile them, mutilate the gaping tongue, or, while it inspires it, cause the polished tongue to stumble; rather, may I deserve to be heard by the pious author of mercy [Col. 0880C].

Trusting in whose help, I shall then begin to utter supplicating words. May your Hebrew [language] confirm them, and, with a single utterance, may it be kindled together and fitted with his final crowns upon the lips.

[Col. 0881]

# THE SECOND TEXT OF THE POLYPTIC

Edited by Giovanni Domenico Mansi in Baluzius’s *Miscellanea sacra*, Lucca edition, p. 560.

## HERE BEGINS THE POLYPTIC CALLED THE PERPENDICULAR

## THE LETTER BEGINS

[Col. 0881A]

To the most reverend Fulano, my very distinguished bishop.

Fulanus, desiring that I should thus be blessed, presses upon me the blessed end of Felicissimus Opilio Silvester, who is dead to some but to me not dead: alive, indeed, yet dead to me; dead, yet alive in me. As we travel the path of this labyrinth, teach me either how, by standing firm, to avoid the abyss, or by what route those who have been lifted up in safety may reach delights. You will see what I feel in this; yet so I am compared with you. Cantabrians, as though to pollen [uncertain]. Behold what I am; restore to me what you are, happily. Amen.

The letter ends.

## THE ARGUMENT BEGINS

The sophists do not explain chaos; I shall pursue the ceaseless buzzing of things throughout the world. This is not leisure shaken by a pious pen, nor will little bones be pounded. Now, wearied, I shall set down the perpendicular. Its voice cannot be silenced by sharpening, nor can Attic speech be swallowed [uncertain]. E. A. J. P.

The argument ends.

## HERE BEGINS THE POLYPTIC CALLED THE PERPENDICULAR

The fragile pomp of this age is weakness, and it is sought; it is a plague, and it is pursued in every way. What smiles at its approach delights while it creeps onward; in its youth there is immense labor; when it swells, it lays men low; and when it withdraws, it is blasphemed, because it commonly makes its clients ignoble, while making those who despise it glorious.

This is not surprising, since up to now it has been a ruin for nearly all who desire it. Yet arrogant men still do not fail, nor does the bitterness of elevating themselves moderate them.

They deceive themselves by presenting themselves as superior to their predecessors, whom prudent judgment accuses of sluggishness. I therefore judge that the fasces of these men, if gradually opened and examined, should be recorded beforehand, since they display rigid members loosened from a garland. Do the chroniclers not falsify this—especially those who thunder out the highest “woe” and all their “enough!”? The troop of those who, walking, have led up a tangled hill does not resound; they follow a straight rubric, although they paint an inextricable sign. They persist, yet neither live as survivors nor rejoice as wretched men.

Nor do I now suppose that it is proper privately to record the faces of their deeds, nor that they should be described as orphans, since at an immature age they now see these things clearly and have often heard them recited by their fathers, and more firmly retain what has been impressed upon them. It is now at hand to assess the members of the aforesaid wickedness according to what diligent care, passing lightly over it, has represented in the style of the hypochondriac [Col. 0882A].

The matter we have begun to unfold rises by a threefold distinction to its summit. Some add an as or, when the ruler names a person explicitly, marks him with clear signs; or when the same voice calls everyone; or when it calls one alone; or when, by the strong right of a parent, it is lawful to enjoy the throne.

Wicked toil—and, when mad battles meet triumphs, they quickly rise savagely against another whom the herald had already proclaimed with profane hands. The conspirators favor what is accursed. What? The rival is utterly emptied, through whose benefit the foremost soldiers are enriched; yet they do not seek an inviolate compact in which the master’s sleep may find sweetness.

Meanwhile it is pleasant to pass the released time more agreeably and to possess what has been acquired, so that both princes may be terrified by hostile quarrels and the powerful may not dare to leap out [Col. 0882B]. Against the soldiers, or to deny anything, nothing remains except that the princes should flourish under so miserable a name that they are not even masters of themselves, but masters only of private property.

Then they diligently ruminate and, with secret care, repay these stratagems to their associates. Therefore they are not wearied of secretly visiting one another, divided among branches, through cautious messengers, who even now do not frivolously announce to the pious the schemes by which the soldiers are first incited, supported by investigation. They also solicit foreign leaders with acts of connivance, heap gifts upon them, and quickly lay down sacrifices.

Why does fortune promise the distant ends of the powerful, not yet torn away, which these intermediaries eagerly seek to taste, even if only briefly? They want their assistance to boil over and subdue the proud with them; or, if the powerful lie idle in torpor, they refuse through their own weapons to rage against them and deny support to the oppressed, for they themselves will rage.

Therefore an example of deceit remains: the tribunes who have suffered these things are struck down at the lowest point, while their soldiers seek the flattering airs of kings. The appointed fortifiers then return home with laden shoulders and will not bear their leaders, their first masters; even in the distribution of benefits they put themselves first, whether resources are scarce or abundant.

They lend freely from what is their own and carry away faithful men at another’s expense. They prefer those through whom they receive benefits, but not those from whom they receive them. If chance separates these men, they will serve until they learn from one another what has been carried from one to the other—things better left unspoken.

They appoint certain men to investigate and instruct themselves. From among these they scatter informants through individual houses like seeds; hence they often reap trifles and often learn beforehand what is useful. From this point the soldiers weaken their first loyalty to their masters and strengthen themselves to preserve a second loyalty to the princes—although that loyalty will soon be lacking.

Then they mark themselves with infamy, undermine their masters, and do not refuse to deny the supreme authority [Col. 0883A]. Thus, enticed by foul desire, they sometimes hope to offer slight relief to the sorrowful if chance delays some danger; however, they bring it upon them from their own resources and, by sharing it, overthrow them.

Therefore the princes add fortifications to what is rough and clear away everything worn down by decay, so that no one may bring anything unknown upon himself. Those who possess powerful defenses they either suppress with hostages or strive to remove. If you happen to entrust your estate to their loyalty so that they may be zealous for you, or if you undertake to impose any title, then, measuring out a legal inscription to their own heirs, they claim for themselves everything useful to all, and do not even distribute a portion among those things which they had formerly prepared.

They build citadels of counsel so that no attack may occur to terrify them, but so that they may quietly return to me what they have devised [Col. 0883B] for anyone. In this they establish burial places and arrange threefold paths [uncertain]. But after they have firmly planted their slipping feet, they set aside the quarrels arranged among the minds of the nobles, and declare themselves associates of both opposing parties. They accuse the captors before their rivals, and their rivals before the unfaithful, alleging that they act perversely for those men as well as for themselves.

They charge the separated ones with such a great crime that the unjust quiver may not be disclosed and that it may not bite anyone indiscriminately who would otherwise be ungrateful. They sing for those summoned and prolong the dissension, calling the sacred things to witness that they should not return together with them to their former state until they themselves lie at the bottom and the judges themselves are not separated, striving . . . . . . . . [lacuna] these twisted cares and whisperings. It will prevail if these things are abandoned and left undone.

They do not cleanse the innocent, whom no judgment troubles. Then Bronchus is pressed by horror, and the urgent voice that supports the decrees escapes through polished magical tricks of exile to the courts, with creaking doors and livid pupils [Col. 0883C]. Here the defender of truth is marked with a savage stigma, so that the prey may be torn apart as quickly as possible.

As when the Pharsalian [or Parthian] men in shaggy cloaks threaten the tragelaphus, Scorpus, advancing in front, catches the airs of death; then, twisting the herds under his leadership, he drives the flock of cattle through the air. Every bowman blames him because they had not all been struck down; and, cursing him alone, he blasphemes and tires himself trying to restrain him. So it is with one who is able to recognize the frauds of leaders if he brings them into the open.

But he orders those of the same voice to conceal themselves beneath flashing forms, and they frequently summon the warlike ones, both among the worn-out and among the exhausted, so that they may dissolve themselves in what has been stored up, while they strive besides to open up the most savage things in abundance from blood . . . . . . . [lacuna] or those whom they destroy.

They provide these men with advancement until—[lacuna]. But enough concerning the loss of others. Among them are also certain men who, while envying the fortune acquired by others, wear them down by trying to nullify it through these deceptions. They display deceptive griefs and declare that the princes who had increased their standing had fixed hardships upon them; they betray them as worthy of exclusion, repel them from vindicating these things, and argue that the matter is strong.

While those men strive to carry this out, they seek rather for methods by which such double-dealers may dictate. If they see that someone has now obtained the means by which they can overthrow leaders, they then seek profit from it. But if they make themselves cautious, they expose their associates and undo their machinery. They first claim that others had called them into these matters, and that they soon fled to the others in order to betray them [Col. 0884A]. They demand that the possessions which rebellious men had held be assigned to them as faithful men, so that the rewards of treachery may remain theirs.

They look for ways to tear away what then gives way, and, once the old supports have been erased, with their ranks submerged and those who possess skill likewise submerged, these men also pay the penalty of their losses. Through their unhappy success they become exiles from advantages and are strengthened by no one. In turn they wail; nor will there be any lack of a title for the crime by which their misery is stirred up, in addition to what the ravenous ambones [uncertain] have revealed—alas, what grief!

Then also the death and ruin of the others are thrown against these men, and the leaders who committed foul deeds throughout accuse them as the fuels of crimes. They are ashamed, but do not attempt to restore those who have been exposed.

Yet these things serve only to stir up hatred. Rumor displays a certain bitter bird [Col. 0884B], which, while chirping as its generative heat grows and soothing with relaxed wings, is assisted by a mate unequal in kind but not in nature. When the bird that has done this senses that it is pregnant, it pursues it, rejoicing to dissolve the endowed entrails of its spouse.

Thus leaders grow fat upon the spoils, gape eagerly that they may rise against one another, lest empty desire be prevented from committing every crime it seeks. While the guards, unreconciled and hating one another, drag things in different directions, neither of the two perceives the one whole, nor can individuals resist. They proceed in bands wherever there is only expectation of what the urn will bring forth.

It is shameful for anyone to hurl the spirit itself through the upper airs, and to remove whatever remains unpleasant to each person while it is being held. The happier man who has already been betrayed, and who would otherwise have remained unburdened, is exposed. Hence some exiles reject kisses and do not fear to frustrate their children [Col. 0884C]. Others indeed strike at their livid entrails with a paschma [uncertain]. There are also sluggish men who watch the knot of the pyramid and the cavern, image, or lacuna [uncertain]. Others remain whose sight is defrauded by tyranny, or whom the severed name of their parent seems to preserve while they are still under age.

From others a part is taken away—the part that, having experience, carries the four senses and restrains another when torn away.

Even so, hatred does not press down what has been lulled to sleep; it pursues whatever remains of the stock. But the frenzied desire, while enjoying the guilty, rages without restraint into the precipice itself, lest what it grants be received as a crime that must be accepted. After the eminent have been overthrown by a shortcut, their mockers are entangled in weariness.

Those who once renounced them with empty faith now seek hands that have been seduced [Col. 0884D], hands that can no longer be endowed with estates or resources—hands that the former masters would previously have entrusted with pleasure, had they preserved their first agreements. And if their origin has produced them noble, may they obey the continuous succession of death [uncertain] and wickedness.

Afterward they compel themselves to go shipwrecked on bare feet and claim to be surrendered men, so that, even unwillingly, they may complete what they had promised after lending and receiving gifts. Who are the judges appointed? Those whom it is neither pleasing to report as tested nor pleasing to inspect as inserted in ancient volumes.

They threaten the lordly signs that have been introduced and arrange laws corrupted by coin, so that the equal balance of justice may weigh no one fairly. They cherish the notion that not all should be informed; he himself will emerge unharmed. And although he excuses the one whom he expels, or the one who retains his fortune, he will succumb, overcome by force or [Col. 0885A] driven out by plots.

Nor does a judgment that persists in the same matter often give the same verdict: now it accuses, soon afterward it swells with praises, and again proclaims the same things, even more profane and worse.

But the founder of the lofty fortress, crowned and leaning upon the throne, is raised up in rich splendor, and feigns that he can deceive the remaining cohort with crude syllogisms. He rejoices if the final day removes some of them, while the fallen man enters and the widows who remain behind them receive no choice—whether to remain as they are or to prepare themselves for a double life—unless they redeem their foolish marriages. Either they purchase them from the undeserving or they raise up needy clients of the king, who do not hesitate to obscure stepchildren or exclude wasteful mothers.

A leader sometimes takes men distinguished by shameful figures into the Lithostratus court for disgraceful uses. Then he compels the other indigenous men who have been advanced to live privately [Col. 0885B], while he casts needy foreigners before chosen golden ones, because he hopes that they will be generous toward him. And if they are merely citizens, he sets aside their mouths through sacred wealth, so that they may instead celebrate services and obey commands in everything.

Let them not boast, “Our native lineage has poured out these great things for us.” For they applaud in astonishment, ignorant of what shines through the robe, and the bordered garment has not taught them. Obsius [uncertain] deceives them, and they customarily prefer the liquor expelled from the cave by heat to Indian and Caucasian gems. While they raise the insignia of the eyelashes [uncertain], they do not know how to fit them together properly.

When the common people consult them, they press down their gnashing and roar out barbarous retinues. They disdain what the laws thunder, and by the coldness of their own bellowing terrify their subjects. At first they rejoice in passing on pomp through unfamiliar successes; but when they begin to inspect the customs of fortune [Col. 0885C], although outwardly they may postpone their cares, the wound is seen beneath the breast.

Thus, after they have surrendered themselves to rest on lofty supports, they receive the *stephadium* under the open sky and frequently attend the gloomy water-clocks, and, if they deceive, measure them. Their minds fluctuate while they investigate unfamiliar things: now they fear stolen wealth, now also the ruin of the prince’s descent, as their predecessors taught when they believed it tranquil.

They regard this as neither pardonable nor excusable in any way, while every form of servitude is shaken off by them as though by unworthy stewards. Nor does the authority of the seat excuse anyone in its own regard; nor does reputation drive away insult from those whom the dignity and blessings of the elders, engraved in catalogues, hold back.

If lineage has given them a blemish, they prepare to cover it [Col. 0885D] and to spring forth only from the dignity they have assumed. This is what they urge upon themselves. But while conscience troubles the minds of degenerate offspring, whom fear binds more tightly, they reconsider the insolent master; they recall predecessors and consuls; they inspect the things they have seized and subdued; and they fear to leave the place from which they ask to be companions . . . [lacuna] it is completed by threat.

While long security carelessly prepares a fall, as the sequence of instruction depicts, they do not illuminate the things they have joined together. They force soldiers who have been introduced into one heap to gather into a single mass, so that no one may seek to resist or be exiled.

Then, with one face, they burst out accusing the ten whom they indulge, and preserve their chaste loyalty if it is permitted to withdraw. If one of them happens to oppose the people with a freckle [uncertain], or mutter against his bonds, they compel him to compensate by silence [Col. 0886A]; or, vexed, they cover him from the light and force him to experience a bitter road and traverse unknown ages.

From this their spirits flow away, when they come to be masters of the fallen king’s transitory goods. Hence they often cultivate cunning by displaying arrogance, and hire themselves out to drink from illogical things, nibaria, and carcassian [uncertain]; they distribute calbi [uncertain] to one another and return Sabæan half-belts loaded with shining bosses.

Again they repeat that they are binding themselves in a new loyalty, each lineage giving nymphs to the other in turn, and they exchange pledges for one another in the shrine . . . [lacuna] a clientship to be preserved, and persist in agreements even under such a black bargain. The others swear by the Lord of spirits and by his urns, most faithful witnesses, hidden in polished [vessels] [uncertain].

Therefore they distinguish nation from homeland, overthrow the poor, and, reckless, do not hate any sacred thing.

[Col. 0886B] It is said that when Autolops begins to cut away the hair of the hedgehog, he entangles himself in death and finally, finally betrays himself by his own voice. So it happens to those who presume to violate sacred things.

Meanwhile punishment does not cease. Although the things they had suffered long ago may be believed erased, or although what they had ordered may not have been obtained, opportunity takes revenge upon them. Moreover, they add threefold fulfillment to the harmful deeds for which they had once pretended to repel the light.

Their spoil is furniture, concerning which the curia again cries out, although no one in the curia mutters. Wealth looks on from afar and does not prophesy a share in these matters for those whom the Neotheric buteones [uncertain] crowd together. While their crowd applauds, you will hear a muttered complaint [uncertain], if you wish to speak with them splendidly about truth now worn out.

O times, which bring no celebrated man forward as judge [Col. 0886C], while rustics persist! I recall Busticeta [uncertain], but not the consuls as inclined [uncertain]—men of the sort who take care to weigh everything according to favorable circumstances, while they drag musical symposia through the city, swollen with melodies, echoed and beaten out by broken strings; from there a singing voice supplies them.

Istria provides dances; cupbearers are constantly watchful, mixing clarified wines with nectar; they serve beer and fermented drink so as to drive away the frugal and loosen drunken bodies. Alas, the impiety of those who betray!

They resound everywhere with wanton laughter and provoke one another by casting licentious stories. Then seductions suggest fornications and incest; and obedient slaves spend the night serving their masters, reveling in these things on every side.

[Col. 0886D] Yet they will not long enjoy these things without provoking the jealousy of someone, since they are equal to the others in rank but surpass them in such great dignity. For labor produces harmony, while dissension produces insolence; and the lesser men, separating themselves, hasten to unite together against the injustice of their superiors and complain that more is owed to them—things which those superiors retain and chastise them for attempting to carry out. These men prevail in their bands, and their strength burns with all its might.

In the others, a more mature judgment flourishes; they excel in wealth and are strengthened by the loftiness of their walls. Nevertheless, they consider it impossible to extinguish what is boiling over unless they establish a prince over it—yet they refuse to establish themselves. At last they enter into a plan to propose some foolish person for themselves, through whom they may accomplish what is advantageous to them: someone who will not dare to question or resist them in anything, and whom they even compel, in vain, to set these matters down under sacred divine authority.

For once he has become prelate, if he remains dull, he will wash away no grief. Indeed, the young men will now boldly add their own disparagement of the ancients. Nor do they accept the lord unless he is separated from them. The eloquent threaten, against the unskilled, to inflict worse things; they harass the lord and demand the promises, so that they may rise against their opponents and instruct them. What will he do? Will he be able to avoid both disasters? Yet even abilities do not support an incompetent man. It remains for him to escape his haters and live privately.

But if at first he reveals himself to be cowardly by his conduct, in which prudence at once shines forth with the favor of the diadem, then, terrified, they secretly take measures to lull their hatred. Again they mutter about bringing themselves together, so that by this compact they may again unweave the master's plague—a plague that can no longer remain hidden from the ruler, whose awareness of it is now plain.

He prepares to abolish these trifles [Col. 0887B] together with the triflers, and they themselves are eager to exclude him from the enlarged throne, as an enemy to them. At first, the preceding circumstances hinder them, for these provide the ruler with information. But if they judge these matters to be fearful, and merely suppose that they themselves are failing in them, then even from a distance they direct their treasures to hire champions for themselves.

Thus they retain increased comforts, and even prepare to advance an outsider and a robust leader, and to bow their necks. Then indeed . . . votes, and first through deputies, if it has not been possible to celebrate an assembly. If these arrangements are delayed for a little while, they will fail unfinished. Meanwhile, will the shaken fury of the present President cease raging, and will he grow sluggish in feeding upon the springs? Will he, moreover, act with greater force to make amends to the perpetrators after their overthrow?

And if they prepare to aid those whom they once often attempted, by repeated greetings, to bring forward, as soon as he perceives this omen of their falling reputation—indeed, they turn aside and report to the ears of the powerful ruler that this pest had been too carefully sought out for them by their own soldiers—no one having been able to persuade their minds, and they infect with affection what fear had erased. By such fictions they await profits at his side, although they are treacherous nobles. Long before, they had sent these men privileges which they had purchased by degenerating; but, as though for widows, the ruler gives them little and moderately reproves them, if only these matters had been disclosed to us earlier in truth and openly, while blindness secretly gave assistance.

He also despises their weakened limbs and mocks their savage hearts.

There are also foreign princes who, when they have heard the laments of the soldiers’ other informers, immediately demand that the deceived men be confirmed, lest at some time they return to the favor of the former ruler; and they soon promise to assist them in the same manner. To their king they then cautiously and swiftly send envoys to reveal what the soldiers had confirmed—but not what they themselves had said—so that he might provide pleasing gifts, cancel what had already been confirmed, and rage against his own men, since they would not be able to endure rest among them.

Even if he should endeavor to heap up rewards for them, he will be able to stir up enemies against their destruction while they are believed to be receiving consolation. Then they weave treaties, with retaliation brought forward if it should prove useful.

Again there are men who, when asked to invade another principality, roar and rage, boast of their hardness, and secretly hasten to attack with weapons the unarmed leader. But after they have crossed beyond his borders and see him surrounded by troops, [Col. 0888A] if they then stand still before the shining host and grow cold in spirit, they seek places of refuge in order to withdraw their step.

Even if they see their own army standing firm, should the ruler from afar arrange to send them peaceful angels burdened with gifts, they argue and complain that they have been deceived; they denounce the consuls who had enlisted them as faithless toward themselves and entangled in fraud. They abandon them, distinguish them with death, and then attempt to bring back their steps unharmed and to carry what they have gained into their own private land.

Rarely does it happen, but there is one who, having been persuaded, attacks the consecrated ruler with bare breast and does not desist until he has obtained either the underworld or the palm of victory—or until, through the disaster of war, he shares power with the other and, content with his portion, joins him in a single treaty, confident that he can subdue what is his own.

[Col. 0888B] What advantage will the soldiers gain who had provoked this man? If, in such danger, the survivor breathes out his last breath, let him expect punishment from them; and if he escapes victorious, let him also compel those same men to this course. He no longer leaves himself an inviolate throne, remembering what had taken place, unless they are deprived of authority.

There are men over whom a prince of a single province presides. Even if he has injured them only slightly, they swell with the smoke of arrogance; and at once they approach the ruler crowned with the fearful triple diadem and urge him to take away what the unequal leader possesses.
