But if they explain themselves, will they be able to have a return to their own homes? And even if they succeed, they will eventually bear what is fitting for them.

The pre-eminent ruler will gather diverse battle-lines of nations into his service, together with diffuse words from men who do not know how to live sparingly but plunder whatever is best; and in sacred places they add matrons as though to a brothel.

When they have perceived that the homeland has been devastated, he is not immediately led away, because it is impossible to keep phalanxes abroad for long; nor is it fitting for so great a leader to live far from his own legion, especially with those whose exiled faith he greatly fears. He returns to his own land, which he rejoices to see again.

If those who had solemnly brought him in should happen to propose escorting him away, let them choose a mournful exile, with perpetual confusion remaining amid the ruin; or rather, let them be left in disgrace.

Meanwhile the leader of the present homeland, inferior in troops, either is deeply exiled or, confined within the strongly fortified walls of the city, laments. But when he learns of the enemy’s departure, he summons the desired day and calls into battle those whom he had marked out, whose loyalty was renowned. He appoints the leading men and arranges to confer upon each the rewards owed to the faithful—joyful things to the right-minded, bitter things to the left.

The greatest punishment and penalty is imposed upon those who had summoned the tyrant, and thereafter comes execution. Nor is the ruler alone hated: they also implant hatred against the armies that had endured the insults. More than that, they likewise attempt to impoverish their lesser dependents, until age gradually destroys the whole matter over the years. And if death should cut these men off beforehand, what remains is that they cannot rejoice either in their declining age or in the future. Therefore the vice does not perish.

Again others rise up and revolve through the same things.

But since there are men who were neither [uncertain: Cyrrati] nor able to reach even a strip of canvas because of the brilliance of wisdom, and for whom nothing exists if two men are carried to the urn and bier, so that they may carry home an unharmed [uncertain: domoictionem] with spoils brought back—these men incite me to challenge myself in this way. You erring mockers, if you should undertake to confuse the sealed things of this age, whether they have been practiced or poured out, things which you promise to despise as worthless, then let sterile nature also leave its gifts behind.

If you are able to fabricate the same condition of the high-born and the servant, for whom one must care among the others, the dry and the [river] Cocytus, what are you taking away from the duties of rulers? Or are you able to obscure the assistance which the Most High himself had gathered in order to support the tottering world?

Do you not acknowledge Malachim, or do you not at all applaud him to whom the chorus of virgins gives the trophy of ten thousand enemies? Do you not rather take this up, rather than the “hundredfold utterance” [Greek/uncertain: haecaton prophoneuma], by which you had recalled the course through hidden steps? Nor do you report the [uncertain: procanum] of the temple of the assembly, which also wiped away abominable things.

And now let them enter the New Testament in the order of Helen’s son, the brave man, with [uncertain: strophic] weapons, who, removing the pancratiast, confirmed the rights of the Christian people.

O great leader Theodosius, with such triumphs! You are not led by this man’s speech—you who, rejecting heresies, scattered barbarian weapons and, destroying temples, decreed that their inscriptions should be erased, so that not even an underground chamber might remain in which some remnant of the sacred demon could lie hidden, but that all things might serve one author.

O man brought forth, do you not reckon that the grandson of this man exists in sublimity—he who, controlling the embers, and again subduing the frosts with fire, conquered lust and fury by doctrine, faithful to charity? He was neither sluggish nor falling into sadness, but thereafter triumphed by supplication before the Eternal, rather than by arms.

What does the hand of the common people accomplish? It too will not stand, [Col. 0889C] when the leaders have been separately exhausted. We easily observe what the first ages signify, and here there is a matter worth setting down.

Men strong in arms and limbs had grown from Adam’s first seeds, and fertile offspring produced abundant crowds, increasing through frequent successes and rarely through decline. But the instructed President failed to teach the unskilled cohorts how they might avoid the danger of the surging water.

That Abrahamic people itself, the people of God, was increased by triumphs while it lived submissively under substitutes. Because it despised this after straying beyond the proper bounds, it is exiled far from the threshold and remains an unprofitable stock [sic].

Nor is this true only of it; something similar remains for every earthborn creature. And are only human beings noted, whose mind—what is most excellent—we confess to be with God?

There are also small and provident birds which flourish in cleverness and to which it is granted to carry perpetual celibacy through the air. They cultivate the Stratilates within themselves and render what is owed to the Stratilates. The other creatures also show him to be safe, if they are lively. If he should die, they too become squalid again. But if he departs from his own, they all abandon their orderly ways; they are reluctant to seek foreign dwelling-places with him.

Indeed, the little people prosper under a diligent Cato as leader, without whom the organized region is emptied.

Cease now from what you have begun and use our senses. It pleases me now to rebuke skillfully the sinners [sic]. O men whom it is enough to scatter with your poured-out [uncertain: emicadia]! To what end? So that you may perhaps become even the companions of the great.

In their retaliation, trifles alone are returned. [Col. 0890A] The poisoner seems to be the greater man while he is oppressed; he coughs and does not endure to express even a single panegyric.

Gluttons—just as a key hangs you up from one meal—then, singing, you take care from afar to pursue even a little morsel, and outwardly to pour out a drink; then, turning round, to prepare a dish; or, if this fails, a small coin for madness, if the booty is removed by departure or if authority is taken away.

Gluttony is not postponed in any way, so long as the overburdened belly drives back the bitter burden.

The brotherhood which you acknowledge among yourselves is wholly rustic, among whom the hoe would now be standing, if it were not for carrying things. But it is lamented that, consuming the wound in the breast, this matter in thin liquid does not cease to exude black bile.

O that the eaves had caught you before the sarcophagus now receives you embalmed! And if Pegasus wishes you to be dragged through these things as far as the funeral banquets, he does not then look at the bier but at pleasant faces, nor does he enlighten the corpse-watchers.

For although it might be powerful for you to stain the face of heaven with waters, it is not powerful to stain the judgment of a man, when, drunk, with gloomy grimaces you threaten to abolish the truth, turning rival faces toward the Valgian women and toward light babbling—as though they were defecating moist [uncertain: aritina].

When they have drawn in fire, let drunkenness burn in those foolish men. I reject those who wink silently; I despise their muttering and count their chatter as worthless.

My tongue is not a petty tongue flowing out into dirges. But if your written bond should stir up an injury against my stylus, it is ready that our pages be led to the [uncertain: sennion].

What my obelus will not mark will deserve . . . . . lest a harmful seal cling to it.

Although even now it is possible to quiet the rumors which you have given to the peoples by babbling—if afterward they should proliferate through any useless devourers, then it will be civilized to guard against them, as had long before been promised.

Can the praetors now inspect the battle-lines of the nightingales, in the sweat, any little flower of the plumb-line, even if there is one? But, in the manner of caterpillars, they seek to gnaw—not because there is flavor in the mouth, but so that, by devouring, they may ruin those whom I, as a gardener standing before the barriers, take care to keep out.

Let them approach the perfume-seller; let them assign the eye-salves and comb the fantasies, so that afterward they may separate the bright from the dark.

I have not endured lethargy and presume to drive away the duties of rulers; but I chastise what must not be attempted. For, as I have already said, it is a serious matter foolishly to climb toward the summit, to strive to subdue a captive homeland, and to cheat another of his throne.

This will be plunder and booty; and if someone refuses it, it is better to lead away and expel the primate than to remove him.

Is it less burdensome for one who is driven from his own threshold and pressed down at that very threshold as a baron than for a rustic of another land, who there gathers together the first men whom he had built up for himself without whose right he might be bitten even slightly by the matter? Or for one who, bound by little chains and abstinences, sees everything overturned, caresses his own matron with kisses, and feels his grandson forcibly corrupt the marriage-bed of his own family, even mocking her suitors after their clientele had been led astray by hope?

It is difficult for anyone to invade a kingdom, if this accusation is made by one who delights in a [uncertain: pilemum]. What will arise from this? Perhaps meanwhile he will die and depart into the abyss. But the man who gapes to prepare the described sorrows for others either does not know Avernus or awaits it without fear.

The very Sower of all things will roll him into judgment, so that he may depart ignobly from this age and undergo the punishment of the future.

Therefore, whoever the Almighty wishes to display as worthy of his predictions, or whoever he seeks to advance alone before the assembly of all the nobles, and whoever his native love delights to raise to this purpose, may rightly ascend an empty throne. But when he stands above others, let him beware that divisions do not grow among the people; rather, let his ascent remove every public mourning, if such exists.

Those who have reached the kingdom under such a sanction may perhaps, by blessing, obtain a happy homeland and a final good day. The others, stripped of their position, will pay the penalty of tyranny, which they prolonged even while holding it.

The Pandects can preserve these fragments for you in the school; and if you wish to turn over its thousand faces, it will not obstruct my writings, but will itself come to the aid of the witnesses, so that the stylus may return to those whom you took care to mark beforehand in the face.

Before the offspring of Jesse had breathed forth, he changed his feet into a staff, until, by the sought-for speech of the seer, he was brought forth in the power of the mystical chrism upon the head.

I recall Hezekiah and Josiah, kings who emerged from the hereditary blood of kings with the favor of the people. Was not his father asleep in the royal seat, whose mother was Helena? While he was acting, Providence wished the son to sit beside him.

And Theodosius was born from the distinguished soldiers of Spain. By the aid of the first man, he made the world safe from the barbarians; and by his indications he had first intended to wash himself for the highest things.

I speak of one who, seeing himself clothed in the purple cloak of imperial power and bearing the diadem placed upon him—by what investigation could he recognize the same man, previously unknown to him and without any witness, when at some time he saw his face?

Soon promoted by the Emperor Gratian, he became his colleague; the vision remained, while pressing wars were meanwhile quieted by him.

And therefore it was fitting that his namesake grandson, equal in merit, should peacefully occupy the throne of his father and grandfather. If, according to this model, royal power has been given to someone, guilt will no longer hold him, if he sits and judges himself sufficient for the name of such majesty—although he should by no means rejoice that he may yet remain secure.

Even auspices, if they exist and are worthy, do not by themselves provide happiness; further growth is required.

Therefore I now wish to set forth the doctrine [Greek: λογῳ ΚυνΝου — “by the word of Kynnus” or “of Cynnus,” uncertain] concerning Saul. Saul was raised from a small family line to protect Israel. At the beginning of his reign he drove out the Philistines and began everywhere to empty the remaining hostile nations through easy triumphs.

[Col. 0891D] But when greed compelled him to gape after forbidden things, his smooth limbs soon ceased from battle through torpor. His terrifying mind, not daring to look upon the enemy line, struck itself with its own weapon into fiery punishments.

And the prince Eudoxius had taken King Manasseh from renewed blood. For after God added fifteen years to Hezekiah’s life, Manasseh was born. Succeeding him on the throne, he judged that the things which his father had caused to flourish should meanwhile be extinguished; and the things which he himself produced in his spare time he sanctioned for punishment, attacking Theusebia and restoring the rites and temples of the demon.

Licinius, then, while his colleague was extending himself among the ranks of soldiers, obtained by crafty means such influence over their minds that they pressed forward with their favor to possess foolishly the imperial lot, under which they might chant that they were permitted to remain silent with impunity.

This deceived the diligent Augustus, so that he too might support the man whom he had joined to himself on the throne, not lamenting the marriage of his own sister . . . . . . . . . He had then fortified himself for a while in a rough toga, breathing support for the orthodox and collapsing the worship of idols.

Then he had enlarged the Delphic places and oppressed the tiled structures, and altogether rejected the receivers of the [uncertain: methanica] art. He had restored its followers and the spearmen whom the ancient rulers had drawn to themselves, so that they might handle the treasures with suitable men.

Anna would no longer have burned what had been begun. But his presence, which had been made authoritative throughout the regions, became foolish; moreover, he then added his refusal to the sacred things recently published in bloody antitheses.

If anyone now confessed Jesus, he first sent him to the executioners and thereafter to the [uncertain: lanistae].

[Col. 0892B] Soon he gave everyone over to Bacchus and likewise to Cynthius, together with their accomplices, up to the waist [uncertain].

Moreover, he then raised a sword against Prince Constantine, from whom he had received the kingdom, and he also touched the glory of his kindred. But immediately, when these things had been reported to him, he resisted and removed him from divine favor, and even confirmed the rights after cleansing them.

A worthy appearance scarcely puts forth shoots, or perhaps never does so by birth. Nor does what is expected emerge indiscriminately and reach perfection; rather, it gradually falls away in evil from an excellent stock. Hence comes the crime of rushing toward scepters, as the matters mentioned above thunder.

But even a merely equal consecration will not make anyone great unless he also displays an honorable dignity, being imbued with good character, so far as he can climb into the eternal [Col. 0892C] kingdom.

All these phylacteries are owed to the redemptions of Christ. Let each person preserve a modest way of life according to his own measure. Let him put aside ambition beyond his station; let him be one who rejects it, and not a companion to whom the benefits are enough—benefits which his ancestors had justly left to him, which hereditary generosity supplies under the compulsion of unstained service, which exacted rustic labor pours forth from its own right, and which the appointed art properly brings forward.

And if his superiors diligently delegate offices, let him fulfill them not by displaying pomp here, but by lasting service. If they bring profit, let him repay equal praise and service to the Eternal. Even if he suffers a lapse, let him not, being without fault, cease to implore the same one, nor blaspheme in poverty, ignorant by what judgment he has been struck.

Can unexpected reversals not follow? For if the [uncertain: Caenodoxus] gapes after [lacuna] he will be able to present before himself this man cast down with [uncertain: erinis] and repeatedly thrust back.

Behold! But why, lavishly, like an emphatic herald, do I strive to explain the ordered departure of the departing age, whose diseases no eloquent gloss can endure to conjecture?

Yet it once languished worse, while the physician, lying depressed in mud and repeating dirges, was wasting away, his health already exhausted. A chief physician also stood over him, destroying him with poisonous bites.

But meanwhile he who had smeared him, looking back, extended a hand and came to the wounded man’s aid. He snatched him from the mouth of that same one, whom he also avoided and bit; then, restoring what had been loosened, he made the weakened world stand firm.

For his salvation, what must be avoided and what must be used became known alike. Because he transgressed this and shared in harmful things, while refusing what was salutary, he is seen to relapse so often.

But the craftsman himself, the physician and author of salvation, offers healing to the ungrateful. Let us now earnestly pray that, though moved by fury after the antidotes so often expended and the [uncertain: lixopiritae] likewise stretched out, he may not withdraw his hand or press the surgery; but that he may prescribe the ointments, pour them in from the highest powers, and anoint with them, driving back the wasting disease.

Then, when the delayed fullness of surgery has come, may he find in these matters something small that he can burn or cut away, lest that which has been consecrated to Christ's bridal chamber lament the [uncertain: praesetemina] which it washed in mystical [uncertain: inna-siterna].

No one can be so capable as to be skilled in medicine unless he carefully examines physical reasoning—and no one should understand this as a fiction, as though the one who fashioned it had been deceived.

Who, then, will be able to preserve the world in safety? I do not speak of a monarch, or of a portion within it, unless he himself is the potter of its first formation. And even if what is accomplished through a human formula is openly confessed, the gracious Spirit remains in the thing which he administers; if one serves him purely forever, from him will come all things that become prosperous.

From it he will swiftly flee because of sins, if it has shared in them. What is thus abandoned will immediately perish with its deeds unless it frees itself from them and stands as before.

Therefore it is fitting that whoever prepares to possess the name of Augustus should beware of this judgment and receive what has been imposed upon the common assembly. In this way also let him live after attaining the dignity, so that he does not violate it.

In this matter let him conduct himself according to divine nods, and frustrate his own will, since illustrious arbiters exist—those who still survive and those who have already gone before. Thus let him place a testament as a mirror before himself, which the clever, fraudulent tavern-keeper does not polish while mixing water with wine.

This also applies to false teachers, who, contaminating true things with falsehoods, are accustomed to pour out harmful doctrines. They seek to handle the sacred Scriptures not according to the truth of the matter or the definition of the authors, but by their own invention, so that they may more powerfully win favor for themselves and thereby the support of the people.

Therefore let the devoted man continually implore the Lord and not add delay to delay. It is also necessary that the whole people strive to complete this, lest they be led astray by him, since the foolish man who neglects to ask for the help of his patron struggles to destroy the force of the principal testament.

I stand before you without distinction. Pray now; I shall answer you [Col. 0894B] in the language of Adam, so that it may be done. And if you prefer to have me begin . . . . . . . from the highest majesty, so that he may wash away my guilt with his peaceful light, and may make himself pleased with me and accept the prayers to be poured out—prayers which neither an importunate lawless man may profane nor a gaping tongue mutilate, under the inspiration of that power which does not allow my heart to wander elsewhere—I say plainly, may I deserve to be heard by the pious author of piety.

Trusting in this help, I shall then arise to pour forth suppliant words, which your Hebrew antiphon may confirm in a single utterance, and to whose final words the [uncertain: chronis] may be fitted.

[Col. 0893]

## THE TESTAMENT OF ATTO

[Note: [Col. 0893D] In his preface, Burontius recites the donation made by Atto to the canons of Vercelli. He then presents a brief testament written at Milan in the year 948, by which Atto bequeaths part of his possessions to the Milanese clergy; but Burontius makes no mention of the greater testament issued at the Milanese synod three years earlier, which we present here. MAI.]

(From Mai, *New Collection of Ancient Writers*, vol. VI, from a Vatican manuscript.)

[Col. 0893C] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, to whom be glory through everlasting ages of ages. Amen.

In the reign of the most devout kings, our lords Hugh and Lothair: in the twentieth year of the reign of our lord Hugh and the fifteenth of our lord Lothair; while the venerable father and lord, the most holy Pope Marinus of the universal Church of God, was pontiff in his third year; on the third indiction, on the Ides of May; when a synod had been constituted by the venerable father, our lord Olderic, archbishop of the holy Milanese Church, in the basilica of the most glorious pontiff and confessor, Saint Ambrose, before his holy body; with our lord Hugh, legate sent by the aforesaid kings, and the venerable father, our lord Roger, bishop of Perugia, legate of the most holy lord pope, standing present.

At that synod were the venerable father, the lord archbishop of the holy Milanese Church, and the venerable bishops of Vercelli, Pavia, Novara, Brescia, Lodi, Bergamo, Tortona, Cremona, Asti, Chur, Turin, Ivrea, Aosta, Alba, Acqui, Savona, Genoa, Albenga, [Col. 0894C] Ventimiglia, Piacenza, Parma, Modena, and many other bishops, abbots, priests, and clerics, together with Count Guido and many illustrious nobles of the kingdom.

When the liturgy had been completed, before the synod was dissolved, Lord Atto, bishop of the holy Church of Vercelli, rose and reverently requested permission to speak. When it had been granted, the archbishop had him sit down; then he spoke:

“Venerable fathers and illustrious men, since God said in the holy Gospel, ‘Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them,’ we ought not to doubt that God is in the midst of us.

“Therefore, since I have reached a good old age, and God has admonished us, saying, ‘Be ready, because you do not know the day or the hour when the Lord will come,’ for this reason, if you wish to please me, I would like to arrange my possessions before God and before you, for the salvation of my soul, of my parents, and of all the faithful departed, so that after my death I may have people who will entreat God for my soul, that it may be released from sins.”

[Col. 0895A] When they had heard this, everyone said: “Let whatever the venerable Lord Atto wishes be done.” And he began to speak as follows:

“In the name of Jesus Christ, I, Atto, humble bishop of the holy Church of Vercelli, considering the words of the Lord to be unfailing—namely, ‘Lay up treasures for yourselves in heaven,’ and ‘Give to the poor, for you will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life’—therefore I, the aforesaid Bishop Atto, wish, judge, and by this my judgment decree, together with Hugh the marquis and Brucard the count, my advocates, that everything which I shall decree remain inviolate for all time.

“First, immediately after my death, I judge and bequeath my palace at Stazzona, with its orchard, woodland, and appurtenances in their entirety, to you, venerable father and lord, lord archbishop of Milan, and to those who after you shall govern the Milanese Church as bishops, so that it may remain forever, without diminution, in the power of the archbishops of Milan. In return, I ask them to celebrate sacred rites once a year for the repose of my soul.

“Likewise, I bequeath and assign to the Church of Saint Eusebius, or to its bishopric, of which I am, unworthily, bishop, four estates belonging to me in the valley of Aosta, and two others at Verdezzo—all with their buildings, lands, and rights belonging to me, the aforesaid Bishop Atto, together with their male and female servants and dependents, in their entirety.

“Those who preside over the aforesaid Church after me shall, by right of usufruct alone, throughout all their days, do with their produce whatever they wish, but without alienating the estate. If they alienate anything, all the aforesaid property shall pass into the power of the holy Church of Ivrea. All my successors shall be bound to celebrate a sacred rite once a month, so that God may have mercy on my soul for the faults committed in the administration of the Church entrusted to me.

“Likewise, I judge and bequeath to the canons of the aforesaid holy Church the royal estate with its small court, which belong to me, the aforesaid Bishop Atto, together with their buildings, lands, rights, living and dead property, in their entirety. From their revenues they shall take a common meal on Palm Sunday; the remainder shall be divided among them in equal portions on the octave of Pentecost. On that day they shall celebrate an anniversary for all the bishops of that holy Church of Vercelli.

“I forbid them all alienation; and if they alienate anything, all the property shall pass into the power of the Church of Turin.

“Likewise, I wish that immediately after my death, in honor of the twelve apostles, twelve of my servants, the aforesaid Bishop Atto’s, shall be freed, so that they may be free, together with their wives and children and all their possessions, just as I now, for that future time, manumit and set them free.

“Likewise, I judge and bequeath to my kinsman Lord Aldeman, archpriest of the holy Milanese Church, and to the cardinal priests and decanal priests, and to the clergy of the said Church, both those who now exist and those who shall exist in the future, the four valleys belonging to me, the aforesaid Bishop Atto, which are called Bellania, Leventina, Biasca, and Intrassca, with all their chapels, houses, and lands, whatever their kind, together with their servants and male and female dependents, in their entirety.

“They shall remain forever in the power of the clergy of the said holy Milanese Church, of which I was an unworthy archdeacon.

“Their revenues shall be divided as follows: the archpriest shall receive as much as two cardinal priests; the cardinal priests, together with the first of the decanal priests, shall each receive as much as two decanal priests; and the cardinal deacons and subdeacons shall receive as much as one decanal priest.

“The portion belonging to the cardinal priests shall be divided by the archpriest; that belonging to the cardinal deacons and subdeacons shall be divided by the archdeacon; and the portion belonging to the decanal priests shall be divided by their first priest for his household.

“All these provisions are made on condition that, forever, on the first Monday of the greater Lent, the aforesaid archpriest, the cardinal priests, the first priest, and the decanal priests who shall be in office at the time come with litanies and crosses to this basilica, where, before the bodies of Saints Ambrose, Protasius, and Gervasius, they shall celebrate a sacred rite for the souls of myself, of the good-memory Lord King Desiderius, of Duke Ermenulf his father, and of Asprand and Eberard, his brother and my great-grandfather, and of the aforesaid Bishop Atto, his son, and his other sons.

[Note: [Col. 0895D] Let us note Atto’s royal origin, unknown to Burontius, who fancifully imagines that Atto—whom he recognizes as the sole Atto—was brought to Vercelli from a distant people.]

“On the following Monday the same shall be done before the body of Saint Satyrus, for the repose of my soul and of the good-memory Count Guido, who was my great-grandfather, and of Atto, also called Anscarius, who was marquis, his son; they are buried in the same church.

“Again, the same shall be done on the third following Monday, as above, and there, before the body of Saint Marcellina the virgin, a sacred rite shall be celebrated for the souls of myself and of the good-memory Aldiger, [Note: [Col. 0895D] In another charter of the year 1027, preserved in the same archive of Saint Maurice Major at Milan, a copy of which also exists in the aforesaid Vatican manuscript, these words are read: ‘We grant our churches or chapels which, and so forth, were consecrated to our holy martyrs Nazarius and Celsus and endowed by the religious man Atto, bishop of Vercelli, son of Lord Algerius.’] otherwise Ermenulf, my father, and of his brothers who rest in the same church.

“On the first day, when leaving that church, they shall enter the church of Saint Nabor; on the second they shall go to the basilica of the Three Kings; and on the third they shall proceed to the church of Saint George, at the place called ‘at the palace.’ There they shall perform the *Kyrie* and prayers for the welfare of this city [Col. 0896D] and of all who dwell in it; and finally they shall say a prayer for all the dead.

“Whoever is absent from these three litanies shall receive absolutely nothing, unless he is ill; even then, he shall be bound to perform the same service on another day.

“Likewise, I judge and bequeath to the venerable Lord Rupald, abbot of the monastery near this same basilica, and to his monastery, my estate at Deliciano, with its chapel, houses, lands, and rights, and the servants belonging to me, the aforesaid Bishop Atto, in their entirety.

[Col. 0897A] “This is nevertheless on condition that, while the cardinal priests and decanal priests mentioned above are in the church of Saint Ambrose, the abbot himself and his monks go with their litanies to the church of Saint Mary Major, situated within the city of Milan, at the place called ‘inside the vineyard,’ and there celebrate sacred rites for my soul and for those of my good-memory mother, Lady Maria, and my sister, Lady Imilda, who are buried there.

“On the following day they shall do the same for the souls of my good-memory grandmother, Countess Felinda, and her daughters; and on the third day likewise for the souls of my great-grandmother Rodelinda and of all my dead.

“If this is not done, all the aforesaid bequests shall belong to Lady Bertrada, abbess of the said monastery of Saint Mary Major.

“Likewise, I judge and bequeath to the said venerable Lady Abbess Bertrada, my aunt, [Col. 0897B] together with her nuns and her monastery, five *mansi* of land belonging to me, the aforesaid Bishop Atto, in the estate of Cerdato, with their buildings, servants, dependents, and their families of both sexes, in their entirety, so that they may serve God more conveniently and may remember once a month to pray that my soul be released from sins.

“And all these things I, the aforesaid Bishop Atto, judge and establish on the condition that all those mentioned above—the cardinal priests, decanal priests, abbot, monks, abbess, and nuns, and their successors or female successors—whether together or separately, wholly or in part, may not in any way alienate or seize the said valleys, estates, farms, lands, servants, dependents, or male and female serfs.

“For my firm will is that all the aforesaid things remain forever for divine worship and for the repose of all my dead.

“Therefore I reverently ask you, venerable father and lord archbishop, and all who are present in this holy synod, to place excommunication and anathema upon all who violate this my judgment, wholly or in part.”

Upon hearing this, the lord archbishop and the entire synod, on behalf of God and all the saints, anathematized anyone who, by any device whatsoever, violated this judgment of the venerable father, Lord Atto, bishop of the holy Vercelli Church; and whoever did so would share the lot of Judas the traitor and Simon Magus in eternal Gehenna, together with Satan and his demons. And they all said: “Let it be done, let it be done, let it be done.”

[Col. 0897D] When this had been done, Bishop Atto himself said: “Hear, all you venerable Fathers. Here I have arranged what, in accordance with my conscience, I was able to judge and arrange. As for my remaining possessions, which now appear to belong to me, I judge and bequeath them to my nearest relatives, so that they may do with them whatever they wish, according to the disposition of their elders and as Lombard law provides. Likewise I ask the holy venerable father, the pope, and the most merciful lords, the kings, to deign to confirm this judgment of mine by their letters.”

When these things had been heard, Lord Count Hugh and Lord Bishop Rogerius, the aforesaid envoys, invoking the authority of the lords [Col. 0898A] kings and of the lord pope, ratified all these provisions and promised to have them confirmed. When this had been completed, the same Lord Atto, bishop, together with Hugh the margrave and Count Brucard, his advocates, said: “This is my free will and my final judgment. So may God help me. Amen.” Done in the basilica of Saint Ambrose, pontiff and confessor, where his holy body rests.

+ I, Rogerius, humble bishop, legate and envoy of the most holy father, the venerable Pope Marinus, have approved, confirmed, and subscribed this judgment.

I, Count Hugh, legate and envoy of the most pious lords Hugh and Lothair, kings, have approved and confirmed this judgment and subscribed it with my own hand.

[Col. 0898B] + I, Olricus [Note: [Col. 0897] Above, Oldericus.], archbishop of the holy Milanese Church, have approved and confirmed all the foregoing, at which I was present, and have subscribed with my own hand.

+ I, Atto, unworthy bishop of the sacred Vercelli Church, have subscribed this judgment of mine with my own hand for its confirmation.

+ I, Lincfredus, bishop of Pavia, have approved and confirmed it.

+ Notinghus, bishop of Brescia, have subscribed.

+ Gezzo, bishop of the holy Tortona Church, have subscribed with my own hand.

+ I, Bruningus, bishop of Asti, have subscribed.

+ I, Riculfus, bishop of Turin, have approved and subscribed.

+ Griffo, bishop of Augusta, has subscribed.

[Col. 0898C] + I, Adalgisius, bishop of the holy Acqui Church, have subscribed.

+ Mildo, bishop of the Ventimiglia Church, has confirmed.

+ I, Sigifredus, bishop of Parma, have subscribed.

+ Joannes, bishop of Massa, has confirmed.

+ I, Aldemanus, archpriest of the holy Milanese Church, have approved it and placed my hands in confirmation.

+ Daipertus, bishop of the holy Cremona Church, has confirmed it with his own hand.

+ I, Baldo, bishop of Chur, have subscribed.

+ Asmundus, bishop of Ivrea, have confirmed it with my own hand.

+ I, Daibertus, bishop of Alba, have subscribed.

[Col. 0898D] + Ingulfus, bishop of Albenga, has confirmed.

+ I, Boso, bishop of Piacenza, have subscribed.

+ I, Vuido, bishop of Modena, have approved and subscribed.

+ Lotherius, bishop of the Marian Church, has subscribed.

+ I, Hupaldus, humble abbot, have approved and subscribed.

The marks ** [Note: [Col. 0897] I have supplied the asterisks; in the manuscript there are straight and transverse strokes, in the manner of a grating.] of the hands of Hugh the margrave and Brucard the count, the advocates of the aforesaid venerable father, Lord Bishop Atto, who approved this judgment [Col. 0899A] and placed their hands in confirmation.

The marks of the hands of Aripert, Oldericus, Joannes, Asprand, Burlo, and Canon, witnesses, and of very many other persons who were summoned for this purpose (so the manuscript reads).

I, Vualpertus, humble archdeacon and chancellor of the holy Milanese Church and of this sacred synod, at the command of the above-mentioned Fathers, wrote, delivered, and subscribed this judgment of the venerable father, Lord Atto, bishop of Vercelli.

I, Lambertus, notary of the sacred palace and envoy of the most pious lords Hugh and Lothair, kings, together with the aforementioned lord archdeacon, delivered [Col. 0899B] and subscribed it.

I, Petrus, called Rabbus, notary of the lord Emperor Henry, have carefully collated with the original itself the aforesaid judgment of Lord Atto, bishop of Vercelli, pronounced by him in the Milanese synod and subscribed, as copied above faithfully by the below-named notary Bogerius Bonafides from the original of the aforesaid judgment. That original appears to have been secured by three seals: the first was that of the lords kings, the second bore Saints Peter and Paul, and the third Saint Ambrose, but was almost consumed by age. The original itself was for the most part decayed, so that it could scarcely and only with difficulty be read. I did this at the request of the venerable Lord Ambrose, called de Vicomercato, abbot of the monastery of Saint Ambrose, where his holy body rests; also at the urging of Lady Columba, abbess of the Greater Monastery of Milan; and by command of Lord Joannes, called de Rusca, honorable podestà of the city and commune of Milan, in the presence of the said Bonafides, T. Senago, Jo. Coalia, J. Canova, and A. Lomatio, notaries, and Thomas called Crassus and Rufinus Corbo, legal experts, and Ossa de Ossis, Petrus called Bellabucca, Comasinus de Cremis, Joannes Marcellinus, and Vidone the viscount, witnesses. Since I found it to agree, except for letters being more or fewer to some extent, I subscribed with my own hand.

I, Tebaldus, called de Sunago, notary, have subscribed this transcript because I found it faithful.

[Col. 0900B] I, Joannes, called Coalia, notary of the sacred palace, was present at the aforesaid transcript, and because I found it to agree as above, I subscribed it by order.

I, Joannes, called de Canova, imperial notary, have faithfully compared this transcript and, because I found it consistent with the original, have subscribed it.

I, Anselarus, called de Lamatio, notary, examined this transcript with the notaries mentioned above, and because I found it to agree, have subscribed it.

# APPENDIX TO ATTO

[Col. 0899]

## Fragment of Ancient Prayers, in the Form of Litanies, in Honor of Saint Eusebius

*(From the codex of Otto.)*

[Col. 0899C] … Eusebius was made, and [was] greatest in the Christian law. Hear us.

… He received all [men] to himself as sacred, and, having been made bishop, was sent to Vercelli. Hear us, etc.

… Since it was a heresiarchal city, it had harshly spurned its orthodox shepherd. Hear us, etc.

In the Church of Saint Mary they shut themselves in, lest the Catholic teacher enter among them. Hear us, etc.

Charus, but by God, broke the bars and bolts with the sign of the cross and entered the doors. Hear us, etc.

… Preaching consubstantially from light, he faithfully instructed many. Hear us, etc.

But soon the crafty tyrant Constantius decrees a synod in the metropolitan city. Hear us, etc.

… To write a lesser [formula], in which [one] rashly assails the Son of the Father, [he orders] the Catholics. Hear us, etc.

… The bishop [comes] to meet [them] and lingers at the bank of the river with the wave … of Sicidae [reading uncertain]. Hear us, etc.

[Col. 0900C] The boat, which was on the opposite bank, [came] to him alone, because he had commanded [it]. Hear us, etc.

Thus, having acted swiftly, he goes to Milan to contend with the tyrant. Hear us, etc.

… He did not yield to persuasions; then, bound, he is consigned to exile. Hear us, etc.

… But after the tyrant died, the shepherd returned to his own folds. Hear us, etc.

… He found [men] avid for the Arian doctrine, so that the Catholic now lived with only a few. Hear us, etc.

But the troop rushes upon the pontiff; they gave death to one preaching life. Hear us, etc.

… Thus he then rendered up his holy soul; this place of burial remains renowned. Hear us, etc.

… It resounds and is powerful in miracles; there the sorrowful and the sick are raised up. Hear us, etc.

… Likewise to entreat him that he intercede for us with the Lord. Hear us, etc.

[Col. 0899]

## Names of the Parishes of the Diocese of Saint Eusebius

*(Codex Vaticanus 4322, at the end of Atto’s letter to Waldon.)*

[Col. 0899C] + Prodobio, Cozzo, Martyri, Mediolano, Saint Evasii, Rusciniano, or Cassiani, Castello Turris, [Col. 0900C] Montiglo Pini, Duperia, Monte Calano.

Balzola, Tridino, Cornetae, Medae, Palaciolo, [Col. 0901A] Palazzo, Fennerno Salucra, Ciciliano, Scevoli …

Saint Agathae, Saint Secundi, Saint Peregrini, Bugella, [Col. 0902A] Cossatae, Diffellenga, Badalanco.

Bulgari, Blandendae, Albano, Sente, Radi … Nivola.

[Col. 0901]

# A Dissertation on the Attos

By an erudite man of the eighteenth century.

*(In Mai, New Collection of Ancient Writers from a Vatican Codex.)*

[Col. 0901B] I. Since there are many things that could easily lead even prudent and exceptionally acute men into error, nothing does so more especially than the repetition of the same name among several people. To provide some remedy for this problem, certain writers composed investigations, dissertations, discussions, or something similar concerning men who bore the same names. In this field, the celebrated works include those lists of the most learned Johann Albert Fabricius, especially in his Greek Library, and likewise the dissertations of the learned Leo Allatius on the Simons and the Pselli. Would that he had either brought to completion or published the other works of this kind that he had prepared! [Note: [Col. 0901D] I shall publish from a codex known to me outside the Vatican Library three unpublished dissertations of Leo Allatius, on the Nicetases, the Philos, and the Theodores. A. Maius.] This is what we now eagerly await from a man of similar learning and from the same homeland [Note: [Col. 0901D] I think the author means N. Vernatiam, a Greek-language writer from his homeland in the Vatican Library, to whom many of Allatius’s writings had passed. A. Maius.]. Since I have undertaken to publish the capitularies of various Attos, I have resolved, even if I cannot equal their excellence, at least to imitate their purpose and write a dissertation on several Attos, so that some light may be added to the monuments being published.

II. First, something must be said about the name itself, since it is commonly given in many different forms. For “Hatto, Haddo, Hetto, Hayto, Haydo, Haitho, Otto” are the same name, as the Johann Albert Fabricius whom I have just mentioned observed [Note: [Col. 0901D] *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, s.v. Hatto.], and elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0901D] Ibid., s.v. Ahytho.] he also added other pronunciations of the same name: “Ahytho, Haito, Heito, Haido, Hatto,” and likewise [Note: [Col. 0901D] Ibid., s.v. Adto.] “Adto, Atto.” Papebrochius [Note: [Col. 0901D] On 22 May, vol. V, p. 194, Antwerp edition.], speaking of Saint Atto, formerly abbot of Vallombrosa, warns that older writers call him “Attus, Actus, Actius,” while, “according to the Latin usage of his own time,” others call him, in the form of the Italian vernacular, “Atto” or “Attho.” I wish he had said that the form of the vernacular instead produced the name “Azzo,” since this name is famous among Italians, so much so that, in the single Este family, Muratori [Note: [Col. 0901D] *Estense Antiquities*, vols. I–II.] counted nine princes so called, some of whom were also called Azzolinus. Perhaps “Aszo,” which is read in an old charter preserved by Edmund Martene [Note: [Col. 0901D] Vol. I of the *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, p. 5.], is not a different name.

That Attus or Atto is the same as Azzo, and also as Actis, Actius, and so forth, was observed by the Muratori whom I have just cited [Col. 0901D] in connection with a charter of Azzo, bishop of Pisa, from the year 1017 [Note: [Col. 0902D] *Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, vol. III, col. 1073.]. In his discussion of Margrave Alberto d’Este he says: “He was also called by another name, or surname, Azzo, Ato, Azo, Atho, [Col. 0902B] Aczo, Acto”; and later [Note: [Col. 0902D] Chapter 21, p. 197.] concerning Countess Matilda’s great-grandfather Adalbert or Alberto: “He was also called by a second name, Attone, which is the same as Azzone and Azzo.” Nevertheless [Note: [Col. 0902D] Dissertation XII, vol. 3, col. 728.] he denies, against Leibniz, that Adelbert and Azzone were the same name [Note: [Col. 0902D] See the same author’s *Annals*, under the year 365.].

The very celebrated authors of the *Camaldolese Annals*, however, point out [Note: [Col. 0902D] Under year 109.] that in later ages the names Azzo and Arnald were used interchangeably, as were Cono and Conrad. What Papebrochius added is entirely true: this multiplicity of forms arose from the diversity of languages and from the different pronunciation of one language among different peoples, and the same thing happened with other names. For example, the interchange of *tt* and *dd*, which can be observed here, is also found in other names, as Muratori observed elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0902D] *Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, vol. 3, col. 1073.]. Add, from Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0902D] Ibid., dissertation 33, s.v. addizzare.], another form, “Heido,” and from Francesco Zacharia, in the catalogue of the abbots of Vallombrosa, “Acto” [Note: [Col. 0902D] *Anecdota of the Middle Ages*, p. 176.]. I do not know whether the name “Hatta,” borne by a monk of Blandinium mentioned by [Col. 0902C] Gandavus and by an abbot of Nobiliacum mentioned by Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0902D] *Acta Sanctorum Benedictinorum*, under year 672, no. 20, and *Acta Sanctorum*, century II, part 2, p. 985, and century III, part 1, p. 472.], is likewise the same as Hatto. The same is true of Hetti, of whom there will be discussion below.

III. This difference in the writing or pronunciation of the same name is useful, so that we may use it as a kind of indication or argument for distinguishing different men. For example, Marcus Hansizius, author of *Sacred Germany* [Note: [Col. 0902D] Vol. I, p. 153.], to prove that Atto, bishop of Padua, was different from Atto of Freising, writes: “For the Freisinger is not called Hatto in the Freising records, but Atto.” I am also surprised that the learned and highly experienced examiner of manuscript codices, Lucas D’Achery [Note: [Col. 0902D] In the preface to vol. VI of the *Spicilegium*.], after saying of Ahyto of Basel—whom he himself calls Ahytone—“who is called by others Hatto, Heito, Haido,” should shortly afterward write in the Chronicle of Saint Gall: “Hatto, a corrupt form of the name, is used in place of Haito or Heito.” For the ancients use these names with equal authority.

Moreover, it is easy for those who do not pay attention to err regarding the same Atto of Freising, because the name is pronounced differently in different copies of one manuscript of Anastasius. In the *Life of Leo III* we read: “And after some days, having sent faithful men who had come with him for pontifical service, namely Haldivald and Arno, most reverend archbishops, and Cunibert, Bernhard, Hatto, and Jesse, most reverend and most holy bishops,” etc. Thus the first edition of Anastasius by Velser, as well as the editions of Fabrot [Note: [Col. 0903C] p. 125.], Blanchini [Note: [Col. 0903C] Vol. I, p. 281.], and Muratori [Note: [Col. 0903C] Vol. III, part 1, p. 199.]. But in Vignoli’s edition [Note: [Col. 0903D] No. 20, vol. II, p. 251.] the reading is “Cunipert, Bernard, Otto, and Jesse”; and he cites other manuscript codices in which the reading is “Otto and Jesse.”

The same matter was handled even more incorrectly by the distinguished Cointius, who judged this Atto to have been the bishop of Padua, although in that year, 799, he was not yet a bishop. He was in fact Atto of Freising, as Pagi correctly established [Note: [Col. 0903D] Under the year 799, no. 5.], as did Hansizius, etc. [Note: [Col. 0903D] Vol. I of *Sacred Germany*, p. 152.]. It will therefore not be without benefit to review at least the more celebrated Attos.

IV. I pass over two martyrs: Atto the deacon, concerning whom the Bollandists write in the *Acts of the Saints* [Note: [Col. 0903D] Under 27 April, vol. III, p. 488.], and Atto the Alexandrian martyr, concerning whom the same Bollandists likewise write [Note: [Col. 0903D] Under 10 July, vol. III, p. 33.]. This name seems first to occur around the fourth century. But their acts are uncertain. Certainly, in later centuries it became much more frequent among secular and ecclesiastical men.

Among the former, the most famous is that Atto, son of the duke Atticus, who founded the monastery of Atto, named after him, concerning whom Mabillon writes [Note: [Col. 0903D] *Acta Sanctorum Benedictinorum*, under the year 667, no. 61.]. The same Mabillon tells of Atto, viscount of Odo, duke of Toulouse [Note: [Col. 0903D] Ibid., under the year 840, no. 26.]. A later one was another Atto, viscount, in an old charter preserved by Martene [Note: [Col. 0903D] Vol. I of the *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, p. 149.]; likewise another Atto in the same author [Note: [Col. 0903D] Ibid., p. 335.], the father of Bernard, viscount of Béziers. Count Atto, who fought against the Saracens at Taranto in 991, is named in the Chronicle of Cava.

But none of these bears on our purpose, and there are so many noble laymen named Atto that several of them sometimes occur in a single monument. We shall therefore concern ourselves only with ecclesiastical men. To make this easier, we append here a list of those whom we have found to be more celebrated, beginning with the eighth century. Before the times of the Goths and Lombards it is difficult to find anyone so named. The name Atto could therefore appear to be of barbarian origin, especially since its first syllable occurs in several other names of those peoples; they say that *ti* in the barbarian language designates habitation, but I do not like playing with words.

V. 740. Atto, abbot of Saint Vincent on the Volturno, successor of Tato, according to Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0903D] In the *Acta Sanctorum Benedictinorum*, under the year 740, no. 52.]. It is established from the same annals of Mabillon and others that Stephen II sent him as legate to Aistulf.

754. Hatto, bishop of Strasbourg, is named in a letter of Pope Zacharias in the *Life of Saint Boniface* apud Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0903D] Century IV, part 2, p. 63.]; others call him Heddo.

760. Before the year 761, when Rodulf, bishop of Vercelli, took part in the Roman council under Paul I, Ughellus places Atto I, bishop of Vercelli, on the authority of Cortinellus [Note: [Col. 0903D] In the Vercelli bishops, vol. IV of *Sacred Italy*, no. 26.]. The distinguished editor of Atto of Vercelli’s works, however, testifies that no monuments of him survive. I consider this Atto fictitious. [Mai.]

769. Atto, abbot of Bauzanum, to whom Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, when returning from Rome, granted a large tract of land “for the building of the monastery and its service,” as Tassilo himself says in his charter apud Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0903D] In the *Annals*, under the year 769, no. 1.]. Mabillon carefully investigates whether he was the same as the bishop of Freising [Note: [Col. 0903D] Ibid., under the year 783, no. 41.].

772. Atto, abbot, took part in the council at Dingolfing, according to ancient monuments collected by Velser [Note: [Col. 0903D] In Baronius, under the year 722.].

784. Atto, bishop of Regensburg, according to the Regensburg annals [Note: [Col. 0903D] In Mabillon, vol. IV of the *Anecdota*.].

787. Atto the deacon. Pope Hadrian mentions among Charlemagne’s envoys to Benevento “Atto, a religious deacon,” who, fleeing inside the church of Salerno out of fear of him, held on to the altar of that church [Note: [Col. 0903D] From letters 90 and 91 of Charlemagne, cols. 92 and 83.].

799. Atto, one of the bishops sent by Charlemagne who dealt with the assailants of Leo [Col. 0904B] III [Note: [Col. 0904C] From Anastasius, in Baronius, under this year, no. 8.]. He was the bishop of Freising, concerning whom Hansizius writes [Note: [Col. 0904D] Under “Bishops”;], but most fully in the history of Freising [Note: [Col. 0904D] Part 1, Lalisberg, in Arnpeck, p. 84.]. Carolus Meichelbeck [discusses him]; Hitto succeeded him. In the poem on the bishops of Freising, in Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0904D] Vol. IV of the *Analecta*, p. 526.], this Hatto is listed as the fifth bishop of Freising.

810. Hatto the monk, concerning whom the catalogue of the abbots of Fulda says [Note: [Col. 0904D] In Baronius.]: “Ratgarius … sent Harbanus and Hatto to Tours, to Albinus the master, for the sake of learning the liberal arts.”

811. Atto, bishop of Basel, who served as legate by order of Charlemagne to the emperor Nicephorus [Note: [Col. 0904D] *Acta Pithoeana*, and Baronius, under the year 812, nos. 12 and 14.]. He was bishop of Basel and abbot of Reichenau. We shall discuss him later.

Hatto, bishop of Augsburg, is mentioned in the Saxon Chronicle [Note: [Col. 0904D] See Mabillon.].

817. Hatto, bishop of Passau, died this year [Note: [Col. 0904D] Hansizius, *Sacred Germany*, vol. II, p. 122.]. He had received the episcopate in 806 [Note: [Col. 0904D] The same author, vol. I, p. 152.].

[Col. 0904C] 818. Atto, bishop of Cremona, is said to have been appointed this year in succession to Walfred [Note: [Col. 0904D] In Zacharias, on the bishops of Cremona, p. 62.]. The same man is named in 842 in a placitum preserved by Muratori [Note: [Col. 0904D] Dissertation 31, vol. II of *Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, p. 977.].

821. Hetto of Trier [Note: [Col. 0904D] Hardouin’s collection, vol. IV, col. 1237.] took part in the council at Thionville. He is also mentioned in a fragment on the bishops of Trier [Note: [Col. 0904D] Mabillon, century III of the Benedictines, part 2, p. 613.], where he is called Hetti. His letters to Frotarius, bishop of Toul, are extant [Note: [Col. 0904D] Vol. VII of Labbe’s councils, col. 1865.].

830. Ato, bishop of Saintes, in a charter apud Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0904D] Century IV of the Benedictines, part 1, p. 431.], where Louis the Pious calls him “his kinsman.”

833. Atto, bishop of Nantes, subscribed the assembly at Worms in the year 833 in a charter apud the same Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0904D] Ibid., p. 578; vol. IV of Hardouin’s collection, col. 1373.].

[Col. 0905A] 840. Before this year, in which Saint Adelgisius is said to have flourished, Atto ruled the Church of Novara [Note: [Col. 0905C] Ughellus, on the bishops of Novara, no. 31.].

856. Atto of Fulda, called Bonosus, abbot, died this year [Note: [Col. 0905C] Mabillon, under this year, no. 5.]. Lupus of Ferrières’ Letter 86 to him survives.

859. Atto of Verdun took part in the council of Toul [Note: [Col. 0905C] Hardouin’s collection, vol. V, col. 490.], and in the following year examined the articles of peace between the Frankish kings, which Atto the layman confirmed [Note: [Col. 0905C] Baronius, under the year 860, no. 14.]. In 862 he was sent as legate to Rome [Note: [Col. 0905C] The same, under that year, no. 23.].

He is the man concerning whom the question was raised “that he had been dedicated by regular oblation in the monastery of Saint Germanus of Auxerre and, departing from it contrary to ecclesiastical rules, had attained the episcopal order,” as the Synod of Toul, assembled at Savonnières in this year, relates. He occupied the see from 859 to 870. Mabillon published his epitaph [Note: [Col. 0905C] *Analecta*, vol. II.] and discusses him at length in his annals [Note: [Col. 0905C] Under this year, no. 567.]. The discovery and translation of his body are related in the *Life of Blessed Richard, abbot* [Note: [Col. 0905D] Benedictine century IV, p. 522, 541.].

876. Atto, bishop of Ivrea [Note: [Col. 0905D] Hardouin’s collection, vol. VI, col. 159.].

[Col. 0905B] 877. Azzio of Reggio subscribed the council of Ravenna as follows: “Azzio, bishop of Reggio, have subscribed” [Note: [Col. 0905D] The same, vol. IV, col. 192.]. Ughellus must therefore be corrected, since he says that Azio—whom he calls by that name—became bishop of Reggio Emilia in succession to Aaron in the year 890. In a charter of King Berengar apud the same Ughellus, in 898, he is called “Azzo, venerable prelate of the holy Church of Reggio.” Adelard, who succeeded him long afterward, names him in a placitum preserved by Muratori [Note: [Col. 0905D] *Middle-Age Records*, dissertation 62, col. 203, vol. V.], in the year 944.

890. Hatto, abbot of Reichenau, succeeded Archbishop Sunzo of Mainz. Mabillon describes his abilities [Note: [Col. 0905D] *Acta Sanctorum Benedictinorum*, under the year 890, no. 57.] and his death [Note: [Col. 0905D] Ibid., under the year 912, no. 71.]; Baronius likewise treats him from Regino [Note: [Col. 0905D] Under the year 891, no. 8.]. He is found subscribed to the Council of Tribur [Note: [Col. 0905D] Hardouin’s collection, vol. V, col. 436.] and to the institution of the archbishopric of Magdeburg at the Council of Ravenna [Note: [Col. 0905D] Ibid., col. 654.]. There is also extant a letter of his and of his suffragans to John IX [Note: [Col. 0905D] Ibid., col. 481.].

903. Azo, deacon of the holy Church of Ravenna [Col. 0905C] and abbot-provost of Saint Vitalis [Note: [Col. 0905D] In a charter apud Muratori, vol. III, col. 143.].

912. Ahyto, archbishop of Milan, in an old charter apud Muratori [Note: [Col. 0905D] Dissertation 72, *Middle-Age Records*, vol. VI, p. 193.].

927. In the foundation charter of the Cluniac monastery made by Count William, one finds subscribed “Atto the sinner, bishop,” although his see is not stated [Note: [Col. 0905D] In Mabillon, Benedictine century V, p. 80.].

933. Azzo, bishop of Como, with whom Ratherius was detained in exile, as Mabillon relates [Note: [Col. 0905D] *Acta Sanctorum*, under this year, no. 40.].

935. Atto of Vercelli is named this year in a placitum apud [Col. 0906A] Muratori [Note: [Col. 0905D] Dissertation 31, vol. II of *Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, p. 5.], and in another placitum of the year 942 [Note: [Col. 0906C] Ibid., p. 942.]. Likewise in another of the year 948 [Note: [Col. 0906C] Dissertation 66, vol. V, p. 559.]. Ughellus discusses him [Note: [Col. 0906C] On the bishops of Vercelli, no. 44.]. See Burontius, editor of his works, 1768.

943. Azzo, notary of the Holy Roman Church, in a charter apud Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0906C] *Acta Sanctorum Benedictinorum*, under this year, no. 56.].

964. Atto, bishop of Asolo, concerning whom Mabillon writes [Note: [Col. 0906C] Ibid., under this year, no. 86.].

967. Atto, bishop of Senigallia, took part in the Roman council [Note: [Col. 0906C] Mansi, vol. I, supplement, col. 1155.].

Azzo, abbot of the Aventine monastery at Rome [Note: [Col. 0906C] The distinguished P. Galletti, *Gab.*, p. 49.].

968. Atto, abbot of Fulda, sent ahead by Otto to Rome in 962 [Note: [Col. 0906D] Baronius, under the year 961, no. 1.], subscribed his charter for the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0906D] Hardouin’s collection, vol. VI, part 1, col. 626.]. Later, as archbishop of Mainz, he subscribed the Council of Ravenna and subjected certain places under his authority to Magdeburg: “I, Hatto, archbishop of the holy Church of Mainz, have confirmed and subscribed with my own hand” [Note: [Col. 0906D] Mansi, vol. I, supplement, col. 1157.]. He had become abbot of Fulda in 956 [Note: [Col. 0906D] Mabillon, under this year, no. 97.] and archbishop of Mainz in 968; he died the following year, “with a reputation not entirely favorable,” says Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0906D] Under the year 968.], “because of the inventions of later writers, who maliciously mocked his very illustrious name.”

970. Atto, bishop of Todi, in Ughellus [Note: [Col. 0906D] On the bishops of Todi, no. 19.], who in this year firmly resisted Otto the emperor’s legate, lest he carry the body of Saint Fortunatus, bishop, away to Gaul.

972. Atto, abbot of Saint Basolus [Note: [Col. 0906D] Hardouin’s collection, vol. VI, col. 690.], subscribed the decree of Adalbero, archbishop of Reims.

Atto the recluse, mentioned in the *Life of Saint Ulrich*, to whom, when dying, he gave part of his clothing [Note: [Col. 0906D] Mabillon, in the *Acta Sanctorum Benedictinorum*, under this year, no. 81.].

976. Atto, bishop of Brescia [Note: [Col. 0906D] Ughellus, from Fayno.].

989. Atto, abbot of the monastery of Ticinum in the Golden Heaven, mentioned in a placitum apud Muratori [Note: [Col. 0906D] *Middle-Age Records*, vol. VI, p. 349.].

996. Azzo, bishop of Ostia and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, is named among those who subscribed the charter of Gregory V, issued at Rome on 27 May in the first year of his pontificate, for the monks of the monastery of Amiata against Ariald, or Esvald, [Col. 0906C] bishop of Chiusi.

Atto, bishop of Senigallia, in an old charter apud Muratori [Note: [Col. 0906D] In the Este records.].

1000. Azolinus, bishop of Laon, to whom a letter of Sylvester II is extant [Note: [Col. 0906D] Hardouin’s collection, vol. VI, col. 759.]; in other sources, Ascelinus.

1010. Atto, abbot of Saint Victor of Chiusi of the Camaldolese Order, in an old charter [Note: [Col. 0906D] In the Camaldolese annals, p. 196; see also ibid., p. 225.].

1012. Azo, co-bishop of Arezzo [Note: [Col. 0906D] See the Camaldolese annals, under this year, p. 344.].

1014. Atto, first bishop of Bobbio [Note: [Col. 0906D] Ughellus, vol. IV.], [Col. 0907A] mentioned in the privilege of Emperor Conrad for the Church of Bobbio.

1015. Azzo, bishop of Città di Castello, took part in the Synod of Aquileia [Note: [Col. 0907C] Mansi, supplement, vol. I, col. 1232.].

1017. Azzo, bishop of Pisa, is mentioned in a charter apud Muratori [Note: [Col. 0907C] *Middle-Age Records*, vol. III, col. 1073.]. He is also mentioned in a charter of Clement III from the year 1188 [Note: [Col. 0907C] See the Camaldolese records, under the year 1002, no. 1, and in the appendix, vol. IV, no. 97.].

1026. Acto II, abbot of Saint Victor of Chiusi [Note: [Col. 0907C] From an old charter, in the appendix to the Camaldolese records, [Col. 0907D] vol. I, p. 277.].

1028. Atho or Azo, monk of Vallombrosa, distinguished for holiness [Note: [Col. 0907D] Vol. II of the Camaldolese records, under this year.].

1032. Azo, another monk, concerning whom Peter Damian writes [Note: [Col. 0907D] *Life of Saint Romuald*, chapter 72.].

1037. Acto, bishop of Florence, whose several charters Ughellus preserves [Note: [Col. 0907D] On the Florentine bishops, no. 23.], either for his canons, who lived in common, or for the monastery of Saint Miniatus. In this year he subscribed the Roman council [Note: [Col. 0907D] Hardouin’s collection, vol. VI, col. 916.].

Atto, bishop of Centumcellae, took part in the same [Col. 0907B] Roman council [Note: [Col. 0907D] Ibid.].

1039. Azzo, abbot of Farfa [Note: [Col. 0907D] Galletti, *Gab.*, p. 141.].

1049. Actius, bishop of Fermo, whose exchange of properties with Adelbertus Arduinus in this year is reported by Ughellus. This seems to be Azzo, who is mentioned in an old charter preserved by the authors of the Camaldolese Annals [Note: [Col. 0907D] Appendix, vol. IV, no. 84.].

1050. Atto, bishop of Camerino.

Atto, bishop of the Marsi.

Atto, bishop of Foligno [alternative: Fulginensis], together with Atto of Centumcellae, subscribed the Roman council under Leo IX [Note: [Col. 0907D] Mansi, supplement, vol. I, col. 1293, and Mabillon, Benedictine century V, p. 895.].

1056. Actus or Acto, to whom Nicholas II writes [Note: [Col. 0907D] In Ughellus, on the bishops of Chieti, no. 13.]: “Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Acto, bishop of the holy Church of Aternum.” His account “of the Passion of the Image of Christ the Lord, which took place in the city of Aternum in the year 1062” is extant. Ughellus published it [Note: [Col. 0907D] Ughellus, at the cited place.]. The cleric Mazzucchellus also writes about this bishop.

1058. Azo, bishop of Arezzo, consecrated the Camaldolese church [Note: [Col. 0907C] *Brief Record*, in the appendix, vol. II of the Camaldolese records, no. 89; see the Camaldolese records under this year.].

1059. The Milanese assembly was subscribed by Atto the priest, Atto the deacon, and Atto the subdeacon [Note: [Col. 0907D] Mansi, supplement, vol. I, col. 1328.]. At the Roman council under Nicholas II, Atto, bishop of Novara, and Atto, bishop of Foligno, subscribed [Note: [Col. 0907D] Hardouin’s collection, vol. VI, col. 1067.].

The name of Atto, bishop of Rieti, is also found. But since “Girardus, bishop of Rieti” is found subscribed there as well, this Atto is doubtful to Ughellus [Note: [Col. 0907D] On the bishops of Rieti, no. 16.]. An ancient Vatican codex makes the doubt still greater, for the man who took part in this synod is called the second bishop of Rieti; and a Secondus is mentioned in a donation made to the Church of Rieti. Atto, bishop of Rieti, is found subscribed together with Atto of Novara at the Roman council under Gregory VII in 1081. I therefore suspect that these two Roman councils have been confused and that the subscriptions were transferred from one to the other.

1061. Atto, bishop of Bergamo, was elected archbishop of Milan this year [Note: [Col. 0907D] Ughellus, vol. IV, on the bishops of Bergamo.].

1063. Azo, priest, monk, and abbot of the monastery of Saint Reparata of the Camaldolese Order [Note: [Col. 0907D] Thus he subscribes a charter. Appendix, vol. III of the Camaldolese records, [Col. 0908C] no. 105.].

1067. Atto, or Panzo, bishop of Adria, who completed the cathedral church of Milan, died in 1078 [Note: [Col. 0908C] Ughellus, on the bishops of Adria.].

1070. Atto the deacon took part in the synod of Volterra [Note: [Col. 0908C] Mansi, supplement, vol. I, col. 1374.].

1071. Atto, archbishop of Milan, who, during the great disturbance of that Church, had been intruded by Emperor Henry after the death of Archbishop Guido, while Gothofred was canonically elected through the efforts of Erlambald, defender of the Church, and his election was approved by the Roman Pontiff. Since, however, he never received episcopal ordination, he is not included in the catalogue of the archbishops of Milan by Papebrochius [Note: [Col. 0908C] In his discussion of the Milanese bishops, vol. VII of the *Acta Mai*.].

1075. Atto, bishop of Lucera, took part in the Council of Benevento and subscribed it: “I, Azzo, bishop of Lucera” [Note: [Col. 0908D] Hardouin’s collection, vol. VI, col. 1554.].

1078. Atto, cardinal of Milan, apud Martene [Note: [Col. 0908D] Vol. IV of the *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, col. 103.].

1079. Azo the monk, famous in the monuments of the distinguished Father and abbot Galletti [Note: [Col. 0908D] *Vetera*, p. 20, and *Gab.*, p. 24, under the year 1077.].

1081. Atto, made cardinal by Alexander II, concerning whom Ciacconius writes [Note: [Col. 0908D] Vol. I, col. 841.]. (This is the man whose capitulary, or brief summary of canons, I have now brought to light. Mai.)

Atto, bishop of Novara, and Atto, bishop of Rieti, took part in the Roman council [Note: [Col. 0908D] In Martene, at the cited place.].

1088. Azo, abbot of Saint Flora of Arezzo [Note: [Col. 0908D] In an old charter, vol. III of the Camaldolese records, p. 44.].

1090. Azo, archpriest of Florence [Note: [Col. 0908D] In an old charter, ibid., no. 68, p. 99.].

1092. Azzo, formerly subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, made cardinal deacon [Col. 0908C] under Urban II [Note: [Col. 0908D] Ciacconius.].

1102. Atto of Monte Burranzone, witness to a donation made by Matilda to the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0908D] Baronius, under this year, no. 21.].

1103. Azzo of Acqui [Note: [Col. 0908D] Harduin, *Collection*, vol. VI, part II, col. 1872.] attended the Roman council [Note: [Col. 0908D] From Landulf, in his chronicle.]. He is also found in a legal proceeding of the year 1125 in Muratori [Note: [Col. 0908D] Vol. V, *Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, dissertation LXX, col. 1027.].

1115. Atto of Arles wrote a letter in this year, which Martennius reports [Note: [Col. 0908D] *Ample Collection*, vol. I, col. 634.].

1116. Azo, archbishop of Torres [Note: [Col. 0908D] In an old document in the *Camaldolese Annals*, under this year, no. 21.].

1117. Blessed Azo, Camaldolese monk [Note: [Col. 0908D] Brocchi, *Description of the Mugello*, p. 67, and *Camaldolese Annals*, under this year.].

1119. Atto, archpriest of Saint Mary in Via Lata, subscribes to the election of Callistus II:

> “I, Atto, archpriest of Saint Mary in Via Lata, together with all the clergy of the same church, approve and confirm it” [Note: [Col. 0909C] Mansi, *Supplement*, vol. II, col. 347.].

1119. Atto of Viviers attended the Council of Reims [Note: [Col. 0909C] In Harduin’s *Collection*, vol. VI, part II, near the beginning, [Col. 0909D] col. 1980.].

1120. Atto, bishop of Arles, attended the Council of Toulouse [Note: [Col. 0909D] Mansi, *Supplement*, vol. II, col. 342.], from which Callistus II sent a letter to Pontius, abbot of Aniane, against him and the monks of La Chaise-Dieu. He subscribed to the Council of Vienne in the year 1124 [Note: [Col. 0909D] Martennius, *Treasury*, vol. IV, col. 130.]:

> “I, Atho, archbishop of Arles, approve and subscribe.”

Martennius also publishes a letter of this same man to G. Ademarus [Note: [Col. 0909D] *Ample Collection*, vol. I, col. 634.].

1120. Atto, archdeacon of Piacenza, was elected archbishop of Pisa and died in the year 1122 [Note: [Col. 0909D] From the chronicle in Muratori, vol. VI of the *Historians*, col. 110.].

1123. Azolinus of Augsburg subscribed to the council at which Emperor Henry restored the right of investiture [Note: [Col. 0909D] Harduin, *Collection*, vol. VI, part II, p. 1115.].

1125. Atto, bishop of Pistoia, formerly abbot of Vallombrosa, is renowned as the author of the *Life of Saint John Gualbert*, which Mabillon published [Note: [Col. 0909D] *Sixth Century*, part II, p. 266.], as did the Bollandists [Note: [Col. 0909D] Under 12 July, vol. III, p. 365.]. He is even more renowned for the holiness of his life; therefore Papebrochius treats him at length in the *Acts of the Saints* [Col. 0909B] [Note: [Col. 0909D] Under 22 May, vol. V, p. 194.]. In Zacharias’s list of the abbots of Vallombrosa [Note: [Col. 0909D] *Medieval Anecdotes*, p. 176.] he is counted eighth. Ughelli makes him the twentieth bishop of Pistoia [Note: [Col. 0909D] Ughelli, on the bishops of Pistoia, vol. III, p. 294.] and reports a diploma of Innocent II addressed to him.

1128. Azzo, Camaldolese abbot of Saints Justus and Clement of Volterra [Note: [Col. 0909D] In an old charter, appendix to vol. III of the *Camaldolese Annals*, no. 218.].

1129. Atto of Troyes [Note: [Col. 0909D] Harduin, *Collection*, vol. VI, part II, p. 1148.] attended the Council of Paris. He is mentioned in a bull of Innocent II from the year 1142 [Note: [Col. 0909D] Martennius, vol. III of the *Treasury*, col. 1229.].

1120. Actus, or Azzo, provost of the collegiate church of Saint Antoninus at Piacenza, was appointed by Innocent II cardinal of Saint Anastasia [Note: [Col. 0909D] Ciacconius.] in December of the year 1130 or 1133. He is found subscribing to a diploma of Innocent II from the year 1137 [Note: [Col. 0909D] Appendix to the *Camaldolese Annals*, no. 236.].

1135. Azzo, priest and cardinal of Saint Anastasia under Innocent II [Note: [Col. 0909D] Ciacconius.].

1139. Azo, archbishop of Tyre [Note: [Col. 0910C] In a diploma, vol. III, appendix to the *Camaldolese Annals*, no. 247.].

Azo, Camaldolese prior [Note: [Col. 0910C] Ibid.].

[Col. 0909C] 1143. Actius, or Atus—also called Saint Atto the Second—bishop of Florence, whose letter to Oprandus, abbot of Saint Salvianus, survives [Note: [Col. 0910D] In Ughelli, on the bishops of Florence.]. He wrote it for the benefit of that monastery and its monks, saying that he had experienced their charity during his own need, when he was burdened by the expenses “which he had incurred by often going to Rome and returning in order to recover his ecclesiastical office.” From this they infer that he had been entangled in censures and was compelled to go to Rome in order to free himself from them.

1149. Azo of Camaldoli, abbot of Saint Mary at Florence [Note: [Col. 0910D] *Camaldolese Annals*, under this year, no. 42.].

1174. Atto, abbot of Saint Saviour of Sexto, is named in the judgment of the Pisan judges in the dispute between him and Ubald, archbishop of Pisa [Note: [Col. 0910D] *Pisan Archival Extracts*, in Muratori, vol. III of the *Antiquities*, col. 1173.].

1174. Atto, archpriest of Saint Flavian, bishop of the Church of Aprutium, or Teramo, who transferred the body of Saint Bernard to a more suitable place [Note: [Col. 0910D] Ughelli, on the bishops of Aprutium.].

1193. Atto, bishop of the same Church, successor after Guido to Atto, who is mentioned in a privilege granted by Emperor Henry VI to the Church of Ascoli. He is also mentioned in a donation by the same Henry to Berard, archdeacon of Ascoli, later archbishop of Messina [Note: [Col. 0910D] In Ughelli.].

1197. Atto, bishop of Camerino [Note: [Col. 0910D] Ughelli, on the bishops of Camerino. See the *Camaldolese Annals* under the year 1059, vol. II, p. 215, and under this year, vol. IV, p. 16.].

We do not go beyond the twelfth century, since evidently no further ecclesiastical men bearing this name appear who are known to have written capitularies; and it was solely for their sake that we undertook to list the others. Nevertheless, this name began to be so common, especially in the twelfth century, that it passed into the surname of a noble Pisan family, whose heads were called “of the house of Azzo”; old records concerning them survive [Note: [Col. 0910D] See the *Camaldolese Annals* under the year 1186.]. We shall now speak of the Attos who are most relevant to our purpose and who were authors of capitularies.

[Col. 0910B] **VI.** We begin with Hayto of Basel. Several works are attributed to him, but above all the *Capitulary*, which Lucas Dacherius calls “his most noble offspring” [Note: [Col. 0910D] In the preface to vol. VI of the *Spicilegium*] and was the first to publish. When Emericus Bigotius, returning to Paris from Rome, had given him information about this work, Dacherius requested and obtained from Joannes Bona—later cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, then abbot general of the Fulda monks—a copy made from the Barberini manuscript. When publishing it, Dacherius added [Note: [Col. 0910D] Preface] that it also existed in the Vatican manuscripts 1146, 1147, and 1148. It is also found in our Holstenius manuscript, under the same title reproduced by Dacherius. From there it was transferred into the collections of the councils by Labbe [Note: [Col. 0910D] Vol. VII, col. 1522.], Harduin [Note: [Col. 0910D] Vol. IV, col. 1241.], and others.

Labbe testifies that it cannot be dated later than the year 822. Mabillon assigned it to the year 816 [Note: [Col. 0910D] Under this year, no. 42.], quoting several chapters as a specimen. Hayto died in the year 836. But according to Hermannus Contractus, a monk of Reichenau, he had returned to the monastery of Reichenau thirteen years earlier [Note: [Col. 0910D] Under this year, no. 55.], with the administration of the monastery previously entrusted to his disciple Erlebaldo—that is, in the year 822 or 823. Labbe therefore established the matter correctly, for the precise year in which he issued it cannot be determined with certainty.

It seems that he was already a bishop in 811, when he was sent to the East, since he is called a bishop. Thus the anonymous authors published by Pithoeus [Note: [Col. 0910D] Among the *Writers of the Twelfth Century*]:

> “811. The emperor sent his envoys to Constantinople: Haydon, bishop of Basel; Buggo, count of Tours; and Aio the Lombard of Aquileia, to confirm peace with Nicephorus.”

Mabillon is praised for his treatment of this embassy [Note: [Col. 0910D] Under the year 811, no. 87.], in which he demonstrates its successful outcome, contrary to what the monk of Saint Gall had written—although the latter calls Hatto a man most outstanding in mind and body.

This is the embassy concerning which Hatto wrote the *Hodoeporicum*, which has not yet seen the light of day [Col. 0911A]. Concerning it and another work, the anonymous writer of Melk, published by Pez, says [Note: [Col. 0911D] At the end of the library]:

> “Hetto, a venerable priest of the monastery of Reichenau in the time of Louis, describes in prose the remarkable vision of a certain monk of Reichenau named Wetti, which he saw after being led out of his body and after being brought back died three days later. Later, having become bishop of Basel, he was sent to Constantinople with Counts Buggo and Aio, and described his *Hodoeporicum*.”

Hermannus likewise writes concerning this work under the year 824:

> “Wetti, a monk of Reichenau, was led out of his body and brought back after three days, and then died. Bishop Heito wrote his visions in prose, and Walafrid in heroic verse.”

The vision of Wetti, described by our Hetto, was published together with the visions of Saint Mechtild, Hildegard, and others at Paris in 1513, printed by Henri Estienne; it was also published together with Walafrid Strabo’s description in hexameter verse by Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0911D] *Fourth Century of the Benedictines*, part I, p. 263.], together with a letter of Baluze. But Mabillon’s judgment concerning it and similar matters, in his historical authors, is especially worth reading [Note: [Col. 0911D] Under the year 824, no. 67.].

Hetto of Basel died in the year 836, as the aforementioned Mabillon established [Note: [Col. 0911D] Under this year, no. 55.], and Pagi [Note: [Col. 0911D] Under this year, no. 14.] on the basis of the authorities of Weingarten, Reichenau, and Saint Gall.

Herto enjoyed great favor with Charlemagne. Therefore, among the bishops whom we read as having subscribed Charlemagne’s testament, we find Hetto, bishop of Basel and likewise abbot of Reichenau. He acquired this favor through his own virtues.
