At the age of five he had come to the monastery of Insel, or Reichenau—for it is called by both names—in which, according to Walafrid [Note: [Col. 0911D] In the poem on Wetti’s vision], he shone like a golden star, especially under the abbots John, Peter, and Waldo.

When his reputation reached Charlemagne’s ears, he was summoned by him to the palace and, against his will, promoted to the bishopric of Basel. Afterward, having left it, he returned to his monastery, as we have said. He is praised in the *Life of Saint Meinrad the Hermit* [Note: [Col. 0911D] In Mabillon, *Fourth Benedictine Century*, part II, p. 65.]:

> “At that time there was in the island itself an abbot named Hatto, a man shining greatly in learning, good works, and nobility of character. He also became bishop of the Church of Basel; but when he rejected the affairs of the active life and transferred himself to the beauty of the contemplative life,” etc.

Dacherius collected passages concerning him from ancient writers [Note: [Col. 0911D] In the preface], and he is frequently mentioned in Benedictine authors. I add only that this seems to be the *Capitulary* which, in Legipontius’s catalogue of manuscripts at Reichenau [Note: [Col. 0911D] *Literary History of the Benedictine Order*, part I, p. 576.], is listed under Hatto’s name as “Regulations for the priests of his diocese.”

**VII.** The *Capitulary* of another Atto is contained in our Holstenius manuscript, namely that of Vercelli [Note: [Col. 0911D] Concerning Atto of Vercelli and his works, see Natalis Alexander, *Ninth and Tenth Centuries*, chapter 3, article 36.]. It contains one hundred chapters under this title:

> “Here begin the chapters of canons excerpted from various councils, decretals, statutes, and letters suitable for civil jurisdiction, collected in the time of the lord Atto, bishop.”

Dacherius published these chapters [Note: [Col. 0911D] Vol. VII of the *Spicilegium*, at the beginning] under another title, namely:

> “The *Capitulary* of Atto II, bishop of Vercelli.”

As Dacherius relates in his preface [Col. 0911D], Joannes Bona sent them to him from a Vatican manuscript in the year 1664. But since the Vatican manuscript had been badly damaged by the passage of time [Col. 0912A], he could not obtain a copy of the Vercelli manuscript for purposes of correction.

Recently, however, the distinguished Carlo Burontius del Signore reproduced the Vercelli manuscript in his edition of Atto’s works, publishing this same *Capitulary* under Dacherius’s title in the year 1768. The chapters are as they are in our manuscript and likewise in the edition mentioned [Note: [Col. 0911D] Vol. II, p. 267.] and in Dacherius.

It is astonishing, however, that the first two chapters—

> “1. Admonition of a bishop to priests concerning how they should act toward their subjects. ‘I beseech you, most beloved brothers, to labor with the most vigilant care for the advancement and correction of the congregations entrusted to you,’ etc.  
> 2. Retraction by the same man, and an exhortation concerning order and the distinction of duties, and a good life. ‘You ought truly to know,’ etc.”

—were published by Baronius [Note: [Col. 0912D] Under the year 835, no. 5.] under the name of Theodulf of Orléans, together with other chapters of Theodulf, although they differ entirely from Atto’s chapters.

Joannes Busaeus published the same material from Baronius together with the letters of Hincmar [Note: [Col. 0912D] Mainz, 1602, quarto]; it was subsequently incorporated into Labbe’s [Note: [Col. 0912D] Vol. VII, col. 1137.], Harduin’s [Note: [Col. 0912D] Vol. IV, col. 913.], and other collections of councils. This confirms the opinion of learned men that these materials had been selected from various writers for the use of the churches, and that all had been assigned the name of one more distinguished author.

Since Dacherius had published other works of this Atto—namely, a little book *On Ecclesiastical Pressures* and letters containing frequent lacunae because of a defect in the Vatican manuscript—the Vercelli editor reproduced the same works in a more complete form. In addition, he published a Commentary which he attributed to this Atto on all the Epistles of Paul.

Yet, as he himself relates, he could find neither the two later parts of the treatise *On Ecclesiastical Pressures* in complete form, by which the deficiencies in Dacherius could be supplied, nor another work of Atto’s which he called the *Polypticum* and *Perpendiculum* [Note: [Col. 0912D] Mansi published the second edition of the *Perpendiculum*; I published the first, as I said in its proper place, MAI.], by which harmful things ought to be refuted and honorable things established.

The distinguished Mazzucchelli [Note: [Col. 0912D] Vol. I, p. 1221.] notes that Piccinello [Note: [Col. 0912D] In the *Athenaeum*] attributes another work to Atto against the lustful, gluttons, and gamblers; but he also observes that Rossotto attributes a similar work to Atto Avogadro, likewise bishop of Vercelli.

[Col. 0912C] **VIII.** Atto II is so called in Dacherius’s title because, according to Ughelli, another bishop preceded him in the same Church of Vercelli; Rossotto held the same view [Note: [Col. 0912D] In his catalogue of writers]:

> “But only the memory of one,” writes the Vercelli editor [Note: [Col. 0912D] In the preface], “remains among us, celebrated for Atto’s writings and deeds; concerning any other who either preceded him by years or followed him, we have nothing in the records.”

The remaining details concerning this Atto are obscure, as the same learned man demonstrates. Nevertheless, he suspects that Atto came to Vercelli from Lombardy, and firmly asserts that he attained the episcopate in the year 924 and succeeded Ragembertus. Dacherius, therefore, following Ughelli, departed from the truth when he assigned the year 945 to the beginning of his episcopal office.

This is clearly refuted by the legal proceeding held at Pavia by King Hugh, reported by Muratori [Note: [Col. 0912D] *Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, dissertation 31], where Atto, bishop, attended in the year 935 together with Ratherius, bishop of Verona.

His virtues, and the extent to which he supported his people in the most disastrous times, are demonstrated by del Signore, who published a diploma in which Atto most generously transferred his estates and possessions to relieve the needy [Col. 0912D] [Col. 0913A]. He himself subscribed to this diploma, dated 945, as follows:

> “I, Atto, bishop by the grace of God, have subscribed to what I myself made.”

He was also himself the recipient—that is, his church was—of river channels with islands, banks, and so forth from Kings Hugh and Lothair, according to another diploma quoted by the same author.

That Atto was still alive in the year 948 is inferred from a diploma preserved by Muratori [Note: [Col. 0913D] *Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, dissertation 65], issued in that year and bearing his subscription. It is not known in what year he died. We know only that in 964 his successor Ingon was already bishop.

I add that there survives a letter to Atto by Ambrose, a priest of Milan—who, according to the distinguished Saxius [Note: [Col. 0913D] Vol. I of the *Medieval Library*, col. 44], flourished around the year 850—published in Dacherius’s *Spicilegium*. Atto had consulted him concerning the marriage of persons who had contracted spiritual kinship through baptism; he had also consulted the same Atto concerning certain canons of the Eastern Fathers.

The capitularies of both Attos of whom I have spoken, the one of Basel and the one of Vercelli, had long since been published [Col. 0913B]. Since the differences between our manuscript and the printed editions are very slight, I did not think it worth the effort to publish them again.

**IX.** The third is Atto, whose *Capitulary*, not yet published, is preserved in the Holstenius manuscript under this title:

> “The *Capitulary* of Atto, cardinal priest.”

It is not easy to say who this Atto was, since the title tells us nothing else about him. There are five men of this name—for, as we have said, Atto, Hatto, and Azzo have the same value—who are listed as cardinals by those who collect their deeds or names. This does not concern the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church now under discussion: “Azo, canon and cardinal,” who is mentioned in the records collected by the distinguished Father Abbot Galletti of Gubbio, a town of Latium [Note: [Col. 0913D] P. 97.], was one of those who, although they were canons of certain churches, were called “cardinal canons.” Leo IX granted seven of these to the Church of Besançon in the year 1051 [Note: [Col. 0913D] In the constitution published by Chifflet]:

> “They were ordained to that altar and celebrated Mass there wearing the dalmatic, mitre, sandals, and gloves; one of them, the dean of that place, also used a ring at the solemn celebration of Mass.”

Hence the writer of the history of the foundation of the archbishopric of Magdeburg, published by Meibomius, reports that this right was granted to the archbishop of that Church:

> “that he might have fellowship with the cardinal bishops of the Roman see; and, in addition, might ordain twelve cardinal priests, seven cardinal deacons, and sixteen cardinal subdeacons according to the custom of the Holy Roman Church. Serving daily at the principal altar, except during fasting, they would wear dalmatics, and on feast days sandals.”

Among the true and proper cardinals of the Roman Church relevant here, the first is Azzo, who lived under Gregory V and, in the first year of that pontificate—that is, in the year 996 of the common era—subscribed in Rome to a diploma of that pontiff, issued on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, on behalf of the monks of the monastery of Amiata against Arialdus, or Esualdus, bishop of Chiusi [Note: [Col. 0913D] Ciacconius, vol. I, p. 750.]. The diploma is found in Ughelli [Note: [Col. 0913D] On the bishops of Chiusi, vol. III, col. 618.]:

> “Azo, bishop of the holy Church of Ostia.”

The very distinguished authors of the *Camaldolese Annals* [Note: [Col. 0913D] Under the year 106, no. 8.] note that Ughelli omitted this Azzo from the bishops of Ostia, although he ought not to have omitted him.

> “They themselves produce a diploma of Benedict VIII [Note: [Col. 0913D] Appendix, vol. I, no. 92.] for the abbey of Burgo, dated in the year 1013 through the hands of Azzo, bishop of the holy Church of Ostia and librarian of the holy apostolic see.”

The second is Atto, whose title was unknown to Ciacconius [Note: [Col. 0913D] Vol. I, p. 841.] and Panvinius [Note: [Col. 0913D] P. 68.]. He said that Atto had been created by Alexander II, and reports that he was a most vigorous champion against the schismatics of Gregory VII; he is uncertain, however, whether Atto was bishop of Palestrina. Palatius also mentioned him [Note: [Col. 0913D] Vol. I, *Catalogue of Cardinals*, col. 81.].

The third is Azzo, formerly subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, made cardinal deacon by Urban II. Ciacconius says [Note: [Col. 0913D] Vol. I, p. 895.] that he subscribed diplomas on behalf of the monastery of Monte Cassino and the Church of Salerno. According to Palatius [Note: [Col. 0913D] Vol. I, p. 119.], he attended the Council of Vastalla, celebrated by Paschal II.

The fourth is Actus, or Azzo, provost of the collegiate church of Saint Antoninus at Piacenza, appointed by Innocent II cardinal of Saint Anastasia [Col. 0914B] in December of the year 1130 or 1133. After the cathedral church of Ferrara, dedicated to Saint Gregory, had been consecrated, he died under the same Innocent. Concerning his death, the pope wrote to the canons of Saint Antoninus at Piacenza [Note: [Col. 0913D] Ciacconius, vol. I, p. 986, and the *Camaldolese Annals*, vol. III, under the year 1136.]:

> “As for the death of our dearest son Azzo, your provost and cardinal priest, we grieve all the more deeply because we loved his person all the more; and at his death greater services have been taken away from the holy Roman Church and from us.”

The fifth is Azo, cardinal priest of Saint Anastasia. Jacobillus makes him a man of Todi from the family of the Acti, basing this on a weak argument from the name [Note: [Col. 0914D] In the *Umbrian Annals*]. He is found subscribing to a diploma of Innocent II, dated 19 June 1135, addressed to Peter, provost of Bergamo, in Ughelli [Note: [Col. 0914D] On the bishops of Bergamo, vol. IV, col. 455.]:

> “I, Azo, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia.”

**X.** Let us now see whether any of these men was the author of our *Capitulary*. It is clear that none of the last three can have been its author: the last man mentioned held the title of Saint Anastasia, while the other two were deacons [Col. 0914C]; whereas our Atto was a priest of the title of Saint Mark.

It may therefore be asked whether he was one of the first two, or someone else hitherto unknown to us. An old record preserved by Martennius conveniently resolves the question [Note: [Col. 0914D] This record, published by Martennius, also occurs at the end of the Vatican manuscript. From it we published the *Capitulary of Atto the Cardinal*, with the excellent readings by which the shameful errors of Martennius’s edition are corrected: *alimonia* for *alimenta*, *corbona* for *corbana*, *Heliodorus* for *Eliodorus*, *portuensis* for *portunensis*, *S. Chrysogoni* for *Chrysogonius*, *Conon* for *Cono*, *Atto* for *Ato*, *Sabae* for *Sabbae*, *Mauritius* for [illegible]. MAI.].

In this record, when Gregory VII, in the ninth year of his pontificate—that is, 1081—had gathered bishops, cardinals, abbots, and archpriests to determine whether the goods of churches could be pledged to raise money for resistance against Wibert, archbishop of Ravenna, who was attempting to invade the Roman see, it was decreed that sacred church property should in no way be expended in secular warfare, except for feeding the poor, for the sacred use of divine things, and for the redemption of captives.

Among the others, “Atto, cardinal of Saint Mark,” subscribed to this decree [Note: [Col. 0914D] *Ample Collection*, vol. VII, col. 16.]. He was therefore alive in the year 1081 and was the second of those whom I mentioned.

I think that I can also determine his homeland from another old record preserved by the same Martennius [Note: [Col. 0914D] Vol. IV of the *Anecdotal Treasury*, col. 103], bearing this title:

> “The oath of Berengarius of Tours, made at Rome in the Lateran church concerning the Eucharist in the time of Pope Gregory VII.”

It is a fragment of a Roman council [Col. 0915A] held in the year 1078, at which Berengarius renounced and repudiated an error that he had previously committed and later renewed, and made satisfaction to the pope—if we accept what is said here. The record adds:

> “Those agreeing with me among those who were with the pope were the bishop of Porto, the bishop of Sutri, the bishop of Terracina, the cardinals Atto of Milan, the monk of Tudela, a cardinal of the Roman Church named Deusdedit, Peter the chancellor, etc.”

For if we consider the chronology, these details seem to fit, and it is not credible that two cardinal Attos existed at the same time.

**XI.** It has been disputed whether this Atto the cardinal was bishop of Palestrina. Panvinius asserted that he was; Ughelli omitted him. But Julius Ambrosius Lucentius [Note: [Col. 0915D] In *The Bishops of Palestrina*, no. 22, col. 168, Roman edition of 1704, and in the second edition of Ughelli, vol. I, col. 196.] wrote:

> “Atto, cardinal priest created by Alexander II, steadfast with Gregory VII in defending his rights against the schismatics, is included by Panvinius among the bishops of Palestrina and omitted by Ughelli, who perhaps had no knowledge of him; Oldoinus hesitates and does not decide. Since we have no mention of another bishop of Palestrina after Uberto until the year 1092, I do not know why we should not defer to so great a man, who declares Atto, formerly a cardinal priest, to have been bishop of Palestrina, especially since our Ughelli does not contradict him.”

Leonardus Cecconius seems to agree with Lucentius in his *History of Palestrina* [Note: [Col. 0916D] Book IV, chapter 2, no. 15, p. 239.], placing this Atto after Uberto, bishop of Palestrina; by the year 1092, Berardus, or Bernardus, had already succeeded Uberto.

I therefore believe that during his episcopate Atto gave this *Capitulary* to the priests of Palestrina, calling himself a cardinal of Saint Mark either because the title was not customarily omitted at that time, or because that earlier designation was retained as a form of address.

ANNO DOMINI 964. ADALGER, BISHOP OF AN UNCERTAIN SEE, PERHAPS AUGSBURG, OF THE ORDER OF SAINT BENEDICT.

[Col. 0915]

ADMONITION TO NONSUINDA, A RECLUSE, OR BOOK ON THE CULTIVATION OF THE VIRTUES.

(In Pez, *Newest Treasury of Anecdotes*, vol. II, part I.) (C,G)*

[Col. 0915B] Not unmindful of your pious request, O dearest mother, I have endeavoured to write to you as you asked. For I know the ardour of your mind for the divine Scriptures; I know that you possess zeal for reading and for fulfilling what you read. I therefore remember your tears and all your earnestness, which I have often observed in you while speaking with you concerning the progress of your soul. Consequently, I have not thought it burdensome to fulfil what your charity has endeavoured to suggest to me: so that you too may, by this very admonition, advance step by step in love toward God, and I may deserve to become a sharer in your reward.

I know indeed that the person who saves himself, with the Lord's help alone, is blessed in no small degree; but I know that far more blessed is the one who hastens to draw others with himself into the heavenly kingdom. Therefore I exhort your exceptional [Col. 0915C] love to read this admonition repeatedly, commit it to memory, and carry it out in deed, so that, by showing what is good to others, you may save both yourself and others, and may deserve to receive a happy reward from your immortal Bridegroom for your own progress and that of others.

Consider carefully, lest you do anything by which you displease your heavenly Bridegroom; for he himself, if you persevere well as you have begun, will grant you, with the other saints, unheard-of gladness and unseen joy. The Apostle Paul affirms this when he says: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9). Hasten, therefore, to that joy, to that gladness in which many saints rest. Consider, beloved of God, how great is the happiness of beholding the face of God without end, joining the choirs of the holy angels, rejoicing without end with the multitude of holy people; and strive to draw near to this daily by the steps of the virtues. In order that you may proceed by a straight path to those things which I have mentioned, and may be able to arrive there more quickly, I have written this [Col. 0916C] admonition for your blessedness, through which I desire to admonish you not concerning one virtue only, but concerning many virtues. I call this discourse an *admonition* in the singular because, although the virtues are many and the exhortations innumerable, they nevertheless belong to one way, one path, and lead a human being to one happiness.

CHAPTER I.—On charity.

Since, then, I desire to admonish you concerning very many virtues, I first exhort you with the Apostle Paul to endeavour above all things to possess the virtue of charity. For just as bread is better than all foods, so charity surpasses all virtues; and just as a table without bread is made poor, so no virtue profits without charity. Without true charity, neither tears, nor vigils, nor nakedness, nor chastity, nor almsgiving, nor martyrdom can save a person. Our Lord and Redeemer commends it to us especially: “This,” he says, “I command you, that you love one another” (John 15:17). And again: “By this they will know [Col. 0917B] that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). Praising it, the Apostle John says: “Whoever abides in charity abides in God, and God in him” (1 John 4:15). Preferring it to all virtues, the excellent preacher says: “If I distribute all my possessions to feed the poor, and if I deliver up my body so that I burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3). He then adds: “Charity is patient; it is kind” (ibid., 4): patient in enduring adversities, kind in conferring benefits. Therefore, if charity is patient and kind, strive most faithfully among all things patiently to endure adversities, and carefully to love the very things that you endure.

CHAPTER II.—On humility.

[Col. 0917C] It is certainly fitting to believe that charity never reigns in a person without humility and obedience. If you have true charity, you will immediately be humble and obedient. For humility is an outstanding virtue: it makes heavenly beings out of earthly people; by it the devil is overcome, and by it his snares are avoided. Thus blessed Antony said to Abbot Poemen: “I saw all the snares of the enemy stretched out on the way, and, groaning, I said: ‘Who, do you suppose, will pass through these snares?’ And I heard a voice saying: ‘Humility.’” But blessed Antony, I think, did not see and hear this for himself alone, but also for us, who are sinners and foolish and far removed from his merits: so that, reading and fulfilling these things in deed, we may be able to avoid the devil's snares, who for this purpose seeks how to deceive us.

Therefore the life of the monk Mark also shows how great a virtue humility is. They say that even in youth he was very gentle, humble, and wise; and, because of such virtues, they say that he was so beloved by God that, when he approached the Lord's body, an angel administered the sacraments to him. From this miracle we ought to consider what a great gift humility is, by which a still mortal human being is made so beloved and so acceptable to God.

Abbot Daniel also recounts a miracle through which the virtue of humility is made clear. “There was,” he says, “in Babylon the daughter of a certain leading man there, possessed by a demon. Her father loved a certain monk, who said to him: ‘No one can cure your daughter except certain solitaries whom I know. And if you go to them, they will not consent to do this because of humility. But we shall do this: when they come bringing for sale the wares they make, say that you wish to buy what they sell; and when they enter the house to receive the price, we shall tell them to pray for her, and I believe that your daughter will be healed.’ Going out into the street, they found a monk sitting to sell his baskets; they took him with them into their house, that he might receive the price for the baskets. When that monk had entered the house, the girl who was tormented by the demon came and struck that monk on the cheek. But he turned to her the other cheek, according to the divine precept. Then the demon, being tormented, began to cry out: ‘O, the force of the commandments [Col. 0918B] of Jesus Christ drives me out from here!’ And immediately the girl was cleansed. When the elders came, they told them what had happened; and they glorified God and said that the habitual pride of the devil falls before the humility of the commandments of Jesus Christ.”

Let us too, O most holy mother, consider the humility of this most blessed monk, and take care to imitate it as far as we can. If, therefore, one person's humility cast out a demon, we must undoubtedly believe firmly that our humility will not allow the devil to reign in our hearts. We truly have humility when we consider ourselves inferior to everyone, render reverence to everyone, and humbly endure, for the love of God, all adversities which others inflict upon us. Of this virtue the Lord says in the Gospel: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11). From this verse we must also learn that pride is contrary to humility. Therefore, if we wish to be truly humble, let us flee pride: for pride is cast down, humility is raised up. The prince of the apostles invites us to this virtue, saying: “Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in the time of tribulation” (1 Pet. 5:6). This saying makes most plainly clear to us that if, while we live here, we take care to humble ourselves, mercy will exalt us in the heavenly kingdom at the time of tribulation or recompense—that is, on the day of the Lord's judgment. I have already said above that charity, humility, and obedience cannot be separated from one another.

CHAPTER III.—On obedience.

[Col. 0918D]

Since what has been said thus far concerns charity and humility, it remains for you to attend diligently to the nature of the virtue of obedience. Because of disobedience, the first man was expelled from paradise. Therefore, if you wish to ascend there, strive to be obedient.

To help you recognize how great this virtue is, I shall recall a miracle for you. A certain man living in the world, who had three sons, renounced the world and came to a monastery, leaving his sons in the city. After he had spent three years in the monastery, his thoughts began frequently to bring his sons to his memory, and he was greatly saddened on their account; yet he had not told the abbot that he had sons. Seeing him sad, the abbot said to him: “What is the matter? Why are you sad?” He told him that he had three sons in the city and wished to bring them to his monastery. The abbot then ordered him to bring them.

When he reached the city, he discovered that two of them had already died and that only one remained. Taking him, he brought him to the monastery; but when he sought the abbot, he did not find him there. He asked the brothers where the abbot was, and they said that he had gone to the bakery. So he took his son, whom he had brought, and went to the bakery. When the abbot saw him approaching, he greeted him, took the child he had brought into his arms, embraced and kissed him, and said to the father: “Do you love him?” He replied: “Yes.” Again he said to him: “Tell me now: do you love him?” And he replied: “Yes.”

Then the abbot said: “Take him, therefore, if you love him, and throw him into the furnace while it is burning.” His father took him and cast him into the blazing furnace. Immediately the furnace became like dew. Through this obedience he gained glory, just as the patriarch Abraham did.

I urge you, therefore, to commit this miracle to memory and always to keep the virtue of obedience before your eyes. For just as at that time the obedience of that monk extinguished the fire of the furnace, so now, if you are obedient, that same virtue will extinguish in your heart the fire of vices. And if the fire of vices has been extinguished in you here, you will by no means descend after death into eternal fire, but rather into heavenly glory that endures without end.

Therefore love obedience; cherish obedience, because it is a great virtue. To understand its greatness still more clearly, read the following miracle frequently. The brothers used to say that one of the Fathers had narrated that he had seen three orders in heaven. The first was composed of sick people who gave thanks to God; the second was composed of those who practiced hospitality and diligently ministered to them; the third was composed of those who, for God’s sake, submitted themselves in obedience to spiritual fathers.

The order of the obedient appeared to have a golden chain, and it possessed far greater glory than the others. I said to the one who showed me all these things: “How does this order, which is the first, possess greater glory than the others?” He answered me that those who practice hospitality do so according to their own will; likewise, those who withdraw into the desert have departed from the world by their own decision. But the one who has devoted himself to obedience, casting aside all his own wills, depends upon God and upon the command of his spiritual father; for this reason he possesses greater glory.

Therefore, mother, obedience performed for God’s sake is good. Attend, then, mother, to some trace of this virtue. Obedience is the salvation of all the faithful; obedience is the mother of all virtues; obedience is the discoverer of the kingdom of heaven; obedience, opening the heavens, raises the human being from the earth; obedience is the companion of the angels; obedience is the food of all the saints. For through it they were cleansed, and through it they attained perfection.

**CHAPTER IV — On continence and its varieties**

[Col. 0920A]

But now it is time, after the teaching concerning the three virtues, for you to attend watchfully to the greatness of the virtue of continence, and to recognize that continence is required not only in food and drink, but also in speech, sleep, clothing, and innumerable other matters.

I therefore admonish your devotion not to seek dainty foods, nor to wish to eat before the proper hour, nor to say in your heart: “Look, other people do this or that.” Know for certain that the more each person labors in God’s service in this life, the greater reward he will receive from the Lord after death.

So that the virtue of continence may not seem so burdensome, I shall insert here a miracle which I read in the *Tripartite History*.

Dorotheus, by birth a Theban, took care to live in the following manner: every day he gathered stones from the sea, and each year he built a dwelling, giving those dwellings to people who had none. At night he made baskets in order to provide them with food. His food consisted of six ounces of bread, one small bundle of greens, and water for drinking.

Living in this way from his youth, he did not weaken even in old age. He was never seen sleeping in a bed, stretching out his feet for rest, or sleeping at will, lest, while working, nature should at some point overpower him and close his eyes. Thus he often fell asleep while eating, and the food slipped from his mouth. Once, overcome by sleep, he fell into dung and went to sleep. When he awoke, he was saddened and said quietly: “If an angel had advised me to sleep, he would not have advised me further”—perhaps referring either to sleep itself or to the demon who was trying to obstruct his good works.

Someone said to this laboring man: “Why are you destroying your body in this way?” He replied: “Because it is killing me.”

I have written this continence of the most holy monk for you so that the virtue itself might not seem burdensome to you, and so that you might recognize how far we stand from certain ancient or modern Fathers. Your blessedness has now heard that Dorotheus built a cell every year and gave it to others; you have also heard that he did not lie in bed and lived on bread, water, and herbs. I do not say this so that you may do as much, but so that you may humble yourself and at the same time understand how great an abstinence our Fathers practiced. Nor should you seek delicate foods, especially since it is written in the aforementioned book concerning the monk Moses that for many years he ate nothing but bread and performed much labor.

For six years he prayed throughout the entire night standing, neither bending his knees nor voluntarily closing his eyes in sleep. Moreover, throughout the night he visited the monks’ cells and filled each one’s jars with water, even when the water flowed far away—ten, twenty, or thirty stades distant. Although he disciplined his body in this way, he nevertheless did not lose his former health.

Read these miracles continually, most holy mother, and with God’s help strive through them to advance in abstinence. Let us not be ready to desire everything. Let us recall the continence of the blessed abbot Zeno.

Abbot Zeno was once walking in Palestine. When he became tired, he sat down to eat beside a cucumber garden. His mind then urged him, saying: “Take a cucumber for yourself and eat it.” Rebuking his thought, he said to himself: “Thieves go to torments. Test yourself in this matter, then, to see whether you can endure torments.” He rose and sat in the heat of the sun for five days, saying: “If I cannot endure the heat of the sun, shall I be able to endure the eternal fire?” And he said to his mind: “If you cannot bear torments, do not steal a cucumber and eat it.”

The words of so great a man therefore admonish us to consider how far we are from his way of life. Let us consequently recognize that we are sinners and weak in comparison with holy men, so that, despising ourselves in view of their merits, we may through the Lord’s merciful kindness be able to share in their company.

**CHAPTER V — On continence of the eyes**

That continence is required not only in food but also in sight is clearly indicated by the following miracle. When Pior left his father’s house for the philosophical life, he promised that he would never again see any of his relatives. After fifty years, however, when his sister learned that he was alive and living in the desert, she did not cease pressing until she could see him.

When the bishop of that place saw that, because of this, the sister—now very old—was distressed, he wrote to the superiors of the desert that they should send Pior. Since it is impious to despise the commands of his elders, he obeyed them, took someone with him, and came to his homeland.

When he approached the door of his former house and announced his arrival, he said to his sister as she came, with his eyes closed: “Here I am, Pior; satisfy yourself with seeing me as much as you wish.” Then she, having given thanks, praised God. After praying, he returned to the desert, where he dug for water and found it bitter; he used it until the last day of his life. After his death no one was able to live there.

I believe that, through his prayer, he had made it sweet for his own use, just as elsewhere he had merited, by prayer, that water should flow where none existed. For when Moses and his monks were once digging a well and found no vein of water, and when the depth no longer permitted them to dig farther, Pior arrived at midday. After praying, he descended into the pit, and when he had struck the earth three times, water immediately flowed forth. When he departed after praying, they asked him at least to taste the water. He replied: “I was directed here for this purpose, and what I came for has been accomplished.”

For this reason, most holy mother, I have written these things about the monk Pior to you, so that you might know perfectly that continence is also necessary in sight. You have now heard how cautious this holy monk was: he was neither disobedient to the commands of the elders who ordered him to go to his sister, nor did he look upon her when she saw him, lest he appear to act against his vow.

Therefore I urge your holiness to strive to imitate him. Do not concern yourself with seeing your relatives or friends whom you left in the world, lest concern for them diminish your prayer and your tears, and, like Lot’s wife, you become a pillar of salt by looking back. Recall, then, that Gospel verse: “No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke IX, 62).

**CHAPTER VI — On continence in speech**

I also urge you to be continent in speech, so that you may continually sing with the Psalmist: “I said, ‘I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue’; I have set a guard over my mouth” (Psalm XXXVIII, 2).

Do not therefore speak evil of others. Remember how much Mary suffered in the desert when she slandered Moses, the servant of God and her brother. For the history relates that, because of this fault, she was marked with leprosy and remained outside the camp for seven days; afterward, through the prayer of her brother Moses, she was cleansed of her leprosy.

Far be it from us to curse or slander our neighbor with the tongue by which we bless the Lord. Therefore every slanderer will certainly be rooted out from the company of the saints. So that we may not be rooted out from the company of the saints, let us guard our tongue from slander. Let us not slander the neighbor whom we are commanded to love as ourselves.

Nor is it enough merely to refrain from slander; we must also refrain from idle words, because the Gospel cries out: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account on the day of judgment” (Matthew XII, 36). Idle speech is speech that contributes to the profit neither of the one who speaks it nor of the one who hears it.

Do not therefore utter words that provoke laughter or loud merriment, but rather words that contribute to compunction, tears, and the profit of the soul. Let your speech always be seasoned with salt.

The *Tripartite History* relates that Ammon was bishop of the Tabennisiotes and Theon the superior of many monks. Both were workers of extraordinary deeds and filled with divine prudence and prophecy. Theon is said to have been learned in Egyptian, Greek, and Latin studies and to have maintained silence for thirty years. Moreover, no one ever saw him angry, swearing, lying, or uttering any vain, harsh, or feeble speech.

In their time there was also the monk Elias, living in the desert and nearly one hundred and ten years old. Previously, however, he had lived alone in solitude for almost seventy years, and he reached this age by fasting, maintaining much silence, and conducting himself manfully.

I urge you to read these miracles frequently, so that you may know how cautious you ought to be in speaking. You have now heard—and, as I think, committed to memory—that the highly learned monk Theon maintained silence for thirty years. Since it is neither possible nor always desirable for us to remain silent, I therefore urge you to make it your practice at least always to be silent from the evil of slander.

So that the virtue of silence may please you, hear also what Zacharias answered when questioned about it. Abbot Pastor said that Moses asked the brother Zacharias: “What do you see?” He replied: “Nothing is better than silence, father.” And I said: “It is true, son; be silent.”

At the hour of his death, Abbot Isidore, sitting, looked up toward heaven and said: “Rejoice, son Zacharias, for the gates of the kingdom of heaven have been opened to you.”

You see, most holy mother, that the gates of heaven were opened to Zacharias because of the great virtue of silence. So that they may also be opened to you, love to be silent; cherish silence. For I have read of a certain servant of God that, in order to learn silence, he carried a stone in his mouth for many years.

I admonish you, indeed I admonish you again, to guard your tongue, slander no one, curse no one, and utter no words that provoke laughter. Consider how short this life is and how wretched it is in comparison with eternal life. By considering these things, restraining your tongue, and imitating the conduct of those whose deeds have been mentioned above, you will undoubtedly attain their company and their glory.

Because I wish to impress silence deeply upon your mind, and because many good works perish through the vice of the tongue, I shall add one more brief saying about silence. Evagrius came, during his journey in the monastic life, to a certain old man and said to him: “Tell me, abba, a word by which I may be saved.”

The old man said to him: “If you wish to be saved, when you go to someone, do not speak before he addresses a question to you.” Evagrius was moved to compunction by this saying, did penance in the old man’s presence, and satisfied him by saying: “Believe me, I have read many books, and I have never found such instruction.” He departed greatly advanced.

These words clearly demonstrate, most holy mother, that blessed is the soul that possesses the virtue of perfect silence. Love this virtue, possess this gift, preserve this pearl. Silence must therefore be loved, because through it humility is nourished, tears are glorified, and, finally, many evils are avoided.

**CHAPTER VII — On continence in clothing**

Finally, let your blessedness know, most holy mother, that continence in clothing is very necessary. There are also many who think that the desire for expensive garments is not a sin. But if it were not a sin, the Lord would never have praised John for the roughness of his clothing. For he said to the crowds: “What did you go out into the desert to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses” (Luke VII, 25).

John is therefore denied to have been dressed in soft clothing, because those who wear soft clothing serve an earthly king more than a heavenly one. John, the first monk of the New Testament, is read to have been clothed in camel’s hair.

If he who was sanctified in his mother’s womb, and therefore became greatly beloved and cherished; he who was a true prophet, and more than a prophet, was clothed in camel’s hair, how much more ought we, who are sinners and weak, to be content with humble clothing?

For, as the blessed Pope Gregory says, no one seeks expensive clothing except for empty glory. We are sinners, and therefore we ought not to seek expensive clothing. Rather, we ought to seek adornments of the mind than of the body. The adornments of the mind are charity, faith, humility, goodness, and kindness. With these virtues the mind is adorned so that it may live with God forever.

The flesh, however, even if it is covered with expensive garments, even if it is adorned with gold and silver, is nothing other than flesh, dust, mud, and dung. Therefore do not concern yourself greatly with clothing. We must discipline the body, not continually seek baths or decorated garments, because if we pamper our body, we nourish our enemy. A human being can never have a greater enemy than the body: the body draws the mind toward sin, and for that reason the servant of God must keep it subjected.

**CHAPTER VIII — On abstinence**

[Col. 0924B]

The body must indeed be afflicted through abstinence, vigil, and various practices, but in such a way that it is always able to perform its duty and its obedience. The body must always be chastised and afflicted so that it does not draw the soul toward evil deeds and may always be fit to accomplish what is good.

For the person who so mortifies the body that he is unable even to perform a good work still does not know the virtue of discretion. To teach you how to afflict the body while also exercising moderation, I shall relate something from the life of the holy Fathers.

It was said of a certain Father that, while he was still living in the world and had a wife, he later converted and was tempted by Satan concerning her. He himself related this to the Fathers. When they heard that he was diligent and could do more than had been assigned to him, they imposed greater burdens upon him, so that his body became weakened and he could not rise.

By God’s providence, a certain traveler arrived and passed by his cell, wondering why no one had come out to meet him. He returned and knocked, saying: “Perhaps the brother who lives here has fallen ill.” After he had knocked three times, he entered and found him extremely weak. He said to him: “What is wrong, father?”

The man answered him: “I come from the secular life, and now my enemy is troubling me concerning my wife. I told the Fathers, and they imposed various burdens upon me. When I tried to fulfill their commands, I collapsed, yet the goad continues to grow.”

When the old man heard this, he was saddened and said: “The Fathers and great men have indeed imposed good burdens upon you, burdens by which you are weighed down. But if you are willing to listen to me, a small man, you will soon find rest. Take a little food at the proper time, recover your strength, perform a little work of God, and cast your thought upon God, since you cannot overcome this assault by your own labors.

“Our body is like a garment. If you treat it with discretion, it will endure; but if you do not conduct everything with discretion, it will not endure.”

When he had heard him, the man did so, and within a few days his goad withdrew.

I wished to write this summary in this section because the practices about which I admonished you above—silence, nakedness, abstinence, and chastisement of the body—must be undertaken with discretion. Discretion is a great virtue, because through it evils are avoided and good things preserved.

A good work, therefore, if done without discretion, quickly perishes. For discretion is the mother of all virtues. Therefore, mother, I urge your devotion to do everything with discretion, so that you may fall neither to the right nor to the left.

You also have the following concerning this virtue of discretion in the life of the holy Fathers. Abbot Antony said that there are some who keep their bodies in abstinence, but because they lacked discretion, they became far from God.

A certain man came upon them while hunting wild animals in the forest. He saw Abbot Antony rejoicing with the brothers, and this displeased him. Wishing to show him that one must sometimes accommodate oneself to the brothers, the old man said to him: “Put an arrow in your bow, draw it, and shoot.” He did so. The abbot said to him: “Draw again.” He drew. Again he said to him: “Draw farther.”

The hunter said to him: “If I draw beyond measure, the bow will break.” Abbot Antony said to him: “So it is in the work of God. If we stretch the brothers beyond measure, they quickly fail. It is therefore beneficial to relax their intensity for even an hour’s moment.”

When the hunter heard this, he was moved to compunction and departed greatly advanced by the old man’s saying; the brothers, strengthened, returned to their places.

My greatest concern in writing this to you, most religious mother, was that you should guard yourself unharmed from both dangers: namely, that you should not place care of the body before the service of God, and, on the other hand, that, in order to fulfill the service of God, you should not neglect to provide the body with what it needs.

I do not cease admonishing your devotion, although your good zeal is known to me. Even now I admonish you to keep continence and the virtue of discretion in second place in your memory.

**CHAPTER IX — On compunction**

Since compunction is necessary in every work, this virtue too must be commended, so that compunction may be joined to mortification. For I think that true mortification cannot be possessed by anyone without compunction.

Therefore I urge your charity, mother, to do whatever you do—whether you maintain silence, practice abstinence, love nakedness, or seek secret vigils—for the love of God and with tears. If tears do not come, let salutary compunction be present in you; only be sure to act with the discretion mentioned above, so that others may not be scandalized by you, but rather edified.

Let us therefore be moved to compunction in all our work, so that with the Psalmist we may say to the Lord: “We offer you sacrifices rich in marrow.” A holocaust is called something wholly burned. The one who offers a holocaust to the Lord is the person who gives himself entirely to the Lord; this applies especially to the monastic order.

The marrow of the holocaust signifies compunction. A holocaust without marrow is a good work without compunction. We offer a holocaust rich in marrow when we accomplish a good work with compunction. The Psalmist elsewhere calls this marrow “fat”: “May your sacrifice be made fat” (Psalm XIX, 4).

Compunction is indeed a great virtue. Concerning it, the life of the Fathers records the following: A brother asked another old man: “Father, what shall we do?” The old man said to him: “We must always weep.”

Once an old man happened to die and afterward return to himself. We asked him: “What did you see, abba?” Weeping, he told us: “There I heard a voice without ceasing, saying: ‘Woe to me, woe to me!’” So must we also always speak.

We can very appropriately understand from this why it is fitting for us always to weep: namely, so that after departing this life we may not enter into eternal mourning. It is useful advice to lament here for a time, because this life is short, fleeting, wretched, and quickly passing; the other life has no limit and will never end. And just as the saints will rejoice without end with the angels in heaven, so sinners will be tormented without end with the devil in hell.

If we cannot find tears immediately, whenever we wish, let us not lose heart in prayer; let us persist in our petitions, because the Lord can easily give us tears. Many wish to have tears, but do not find them immediately when they desire them.

Thus it is written in the life of the holy Fathers: A certain brother asked an old man: “My soul desires to have tears, as I hear of old men who weep, but tears do not come to me, and my soul is troubled.” The old man said to him: “The children of Israel entered the promised land after forty years. If you reach it, you will fear no more any war. God wishes the soul to be afflicted in this way, so that it may always desire to enter that land.”

It was also said of the blessed Arsenius that throughout his life, while sitting at his manual work, he kept a cloth before him because tears frequently fell from his eyes.

Hearing these things, dearest mother, let us consider how much we ought to prepare ourselves for lamentation. If those men, so holy and just and in every respect doing the will of God, mortified themselves in this way, how much more ought we, who are sinners, to weep and mourn?

We ought to consider the day of our death and the day of judgment. We ought also to consider what sort of examination will take place there. Let us hear what the blessed Ammon answered a brother who questioned him.

A brother asked Abbot Ammon: “Tell me something true.” The old man said to him: “Go and make your thought like that of criminals who are in prison. They ask where the judge is and when he will come, and while waiting they lament their punishments.”

So too a monk must always be anxious concerning death and rebuke his soul, saying: “Woe to me, woe to me! How shall I stand before the tribunal of Christ, and how shall I render an account of my deeds to him?”

If you meditate in this way continually, you will be able to be saved and to possess compunction. And you, faithful mother, hearing these things, do as this servant of God urges. Think about the punishments of hell: the worm will not die, the fire will not be extinguished, mourning will never cease, and punishment will never end. If you always think about these things, you will be saved.

Always recall, therefore, what Abbot Elias said: “I fear three things: first, when my soul is about to leave my body; second, when I am about to meet God; third, when the sentence is to be pronounced against me.”

And you, mother, meditate upon all these things; think upon them and consider them carefully, so that you may escape the snares of hell and deserve to ascend to the kingdoms of heaven.

Here we must mourn, because it is written: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew V, 5). He certainly does not speak of every kind of mourning, since there are many who mourn the death of their parents or friends, or because they cannot obtain the earthly things they desire; such people are not blessed for their mourning.

Only those who lament their own sins and the sins of others are blessed mourners, as Samuel lamented Saul, and Paul lamented those who had not repented of their fornication and impurity.

In this life we lament our sins and those of our own people, because it was said to those who mourn: “Your mourning will be turned into joy” (John XVI, 20). Let us sow now in mourning, so that then we may reap in joy with those of whom the Psalmist says: “Going, they went and wept, casting their seed; but coming, they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Psalm CXXV, 6).

You see, therefore, how blessed mourning is proclaimed in the holy Scriptures. Hear also what is written concerning it in the life of the holy Fathers.

Once the old men from Mount Nitria sent word to Abbot Macarius the Elder in Scetis, asking him to come to them; otherwise, he should know that the whole multitude would come to him, because they desired to see him before he departed to the Lord.

When he came to the mountain, the whole multitude of brothers gathered around him. The old men asked him to speak a word to the brothers. Weeping, he said: “Let us weep, brothers, and let our eyes pour forth tears before we depart from here, where our tears burn our bodies.”

They all wept, prostrate on the ground, saying: “Father, pray for us.”

Abbot Silvanus was once sitting with the brothers when he fell into an ecstasy of mind and fell on his face. Later he rose, weeping. The brothers asked him: “What is wrong, father?” He remained silent and wept. When they pressed him, he said: “I was carried away to the judgment, and I saw many from our habit going to torments, and many secular people going to the kingdom.”

The old man mourned and thereafter did not wish to leave his cell. If he was asked to go out, he covered his face with his hood, saying: “Why is it necessary to see this temporal light, in which nothing useful exists?”

It is therefore clear, I think, to your prudence how great is the virtue of compunction, through which sins are erased and virtues acquired. I do not want your mind to be alienated from this virtue, which dwells in the breast of perfected people. Through it many have pleased the Lord; through it the devil is conquered; through it vices are overcome.

True tears bring about the things that have been mentioned. The person has true tears who does not commit what he ought to lament. This is also to weep wisely: one weeps wisely who, while lamenting the evil he has committed, does not commit again what he would then have to lament again.

For Isidore says that the unrepentant person is wretched who continues to do what he ought to repent of.

**CHAPTER X — A salutary admonition**

[Col. 0928A]

After mourning, your blessedness must carefully take heed that what you lament with the desire of amendment may not delight you again at the devil’s urging.

Every penitent who, while lamenting, commits again what he laments is like a dog returning to its vomit, and a penitent returning to sin. For many shed tears without ceasing and do not cease to sin.

Therefore, mother, I urge your charity not to wish to repeat what you lament. Know that the person who commits again what he laments is like one who washes a brick: the more he washes it, the more mud he makes.

Isaiah urges us, saying: “Wash yourselves; be clean; remove the evil of your thoughts from my eyes” (Isaiah I, 16). A person is washed but is not clean if he laments a sin and repeats it. Whoever, by lamenting the evil he has done, does not again commit what he would have to lament is washed and made clean.

Concerning the soul that laments its evils and repeats them, it is written in the prophet: “Because you have become utterly vile by repeating your ways” (Jeremiah II, 36).

I do not write these things to you because I suspect such behavior of you, but so that you may know fully and clearly what compunction ought to be.

**CHAPTER XI — On the nature of prayer**
[Col. 0928C]

And since the power of compunction has now been made clear to you, it remains that the manner of praying be disclosed. When Christ was asked by his disciples to teach them to pray, he said: “When you stand to pray, do not speak at great length, but say: ‘Our Father, who art in heaven’” (Mark 11:25), and so forth. Prayer ought to be brief, unless perhaps it is extended through an outpouring of divine grace.

Concerning the blessed Arsenius, however, I have read the following in the *Life of the Fathers*, which I shall now relate. They said of him that, as the Sabbath evening gave way to the light of Sunday, he would leave the sun behind him with his hands extended toward heaven, until the sun rose on Sunday morning and illuminated his face; and so he would remain. Let your charity therefore see, O most holy mother, how strong this man was in the practice of prayer, since he prayed from evening until morning with his hands extended. I have not written this to you so that you might attempt to do the same, but so that you may strive to possess, at the regular hours, the devotion and earnestness that he maintained throughout the night, or even throughout the entire period; and so stand in prayer that your mind may agree with your voice.

[Col. 0928D]

Let your devotion hear one more account of the manner of praying. Abbot Dulos, who was a disciple of Abbot Besarion, related the following: “I once came into the cell of my abbot and found him standing in prayer, with his hands extended toward heaven. He continued doing this without interruption for four days. Afterward he called me and said, ‘Follow me.’ We went out into the desert, and when I became thirsty I said, ‘Abbot, I am thirsty.’ He then took a leather bag, went away from me about a stone’s throw, and after praying brought it back full of water. We immediately went into the city and came to Abbot John. Then, sitting down, we began to speak about the vision he had seen.”

[Col. 0929A]

They also said of Abbot Sisoes that he would not quickly lower his hands; when he stood in prayer, his mind was carried away into higher things. But if it happened that some of the brothers were praying with him, he hastened to lower his hands, lest his mind be carried away and he die.

Another old man also said that continual prayer quickly corrects the mind. One of the Fathers said: “Just as it is impossible for someone to see his face in troubled water, so the soul that has not been cleansed of alien thoughts cannot contemplate God.”

You have also heard that, when Abbot Sisoes did not quickly release his hands, he was carried away into contemplation. Why, then, was he suddenly carried away into contemplation? Without doubt, because he was being mortified.

[Col. 0929B]

Let your devotion also hear, I ask, what zeal the blessed Paul the monk had for prayer, as is recorded in ecclesiastical history. Paul was from Libya in Scythia and had no fewer than five hundred monks. He did no work and received nothing; he prayed only. As though a certain tribute had been imposed upon him, he rendered three hundred prayers to God each day. And lest he omit even one, he set out three hundred stones: with each prayer he took a stone and put it into his bosom. When the stones were used up, he knew that the prayers had been completed.

We therefore ought to humble ourselves greatly, since we are far removed from the merits of those who have been mentioned above, and are not as ready as they were to pray.

[Col. 0929C]

Prayer joined to compunction is a great power. I also want you to pay careful attention to this: Jesus Christ our Savior, when he wished to pray, went up onto a mountain. Jesus therefore went up onto a mountain to pray so that you too might climb the mountain by praying. For not everyone who prays ascends the mountain. The person who seeks in prayer the death of his enemy, or the things of this world so that he may be more honored in this world, certainly does not ascend the mountain by praying. But the person who, in prayer, entreats the Lord for the healing of his own soul or for the sins of others undoubtedly ascends the mountain to pray.

[Col. 0929D]

See that you read these things attentively, O woman dedicated to God, so that you may proceed in an orderly manner from mortification to compunction, and, possessing compunction, may learn the manner of praying.

CAP. XII.—On the Struggle against the Vices.

And since you have been clearly instructed concerning certain virtues, it remains that you consider in your mind how great is the struggle of the vices against the virtues. The contest between vices and virtues is also a great one. You will then be able to conquer all vices by resisting them with divine assistance, if you set virtues against individual vices. For the struggle of the vices against the virtues usually contributes to a person’s progress, because through that contest the mind is stirred up and cleansed of the vice of pride.

[Col. 0930A]

Virtues must likewise be applied against individual vices: against lust, purity of heart must be applied; against anger, patience; against fear, confidence; against lukewarmness, zeal. Against evil sadness, spiritual joy must be employed; against listlessness, courage must be assumed; against avarice, generosity; against pride, humility must be set forth. Against hatred, the virtue of charity must be assumed.

The Apostle Paul also speaks of this struggle: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to one another, so that you may not do whatever you wish” (Gal. 5:17). And you, dedicated to God, by reading these things and committing them to memory, strive to fight manfully against the snares of the wicked enemy.

[Col. 0930B]

If sleepiness weighs upon you, strive to overcome it by loving wakefulness, because sleepiness is destroyed by wakefulness. If the use of baths delights you, let the blessed James, the brother of the Lord, come to your mind. He was the first after the apostles to govern the Church of Jerusalem. Josephus relates of him that he never ate meat, never used a bath, and was never clothed in linen garments; nor did he anoint his head with oil, according to the custom of his people.

If luxuries come to you as a delight, set before your eyes John the Baptist, who was sanctified in his mother’s womb, and of whom the Lord Jesus said that among those born of women none greater had arisen. The holy Gospel also relates of him that he ate wild honey and locusts.

[Col. 0930C]

If you cannot forgive, as you wish, someone who sins against you, slanders you, curses you, or harms you in any way, let there come to your mind how much and what kind of suffering Christ endured for you. For you he became human, mortal, corruptible, and subject to suffering—he who was immortal and incapable of suffering. For you he took flesh from the Virgin, in which he would suffer and die. For you he was scourged, struck with blows, smeared with spittle, crowned with thorns, and finally crucified. Christ endured all these things for you in order to free you from the power of the devil.

While hanging on the cross for you, what did he say? “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). He who was killed without sin prayed for his enemies, while you, if you suffer some annoyance from someone, cannot forgive completely from your heart.

[Col. 0930D]

I believe that if we wish to consider carefully the things I have said, you will easily be able to forgive from your whole heart all who sin against you. By meditating on these things and examining them in your mind, you will be able to overcome anger, love everyone, and fulfill God’s command: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. 5:44).

If the desire to wander comes upon you, remember that you are already dead, that you are crucified. A crucified person never desires to wander, because he thinks of nothing except his own death. You too are already dead to this world. Take care that you do not come back to life for it, nor it for you; rather say with the Apostle Paul: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). By thinking on these things, you will be able to overcome wandering.

[Col. 0931A]

Hear what the Apostle himself teaches concerning the struggle of the vices against the virtues: “If you put to death the deeds of the flesh,” he says, “you will live” (Rom. 8:13). Therefore, if you wish to live, put all vices to death through the virtues. Through charity, put hatred to death; through joy, kill sadness; through peace, extinguish discord; through patience, put impatience to death; through goodness, kill malice; through gentleness, extinguish savagery; through self-restraint, put intemperance to death; through chastity, kill unchastity. If you take care to put the deeds of the flesh to death in this way, you will undoubtedly enjoy everlasting joy with the angels.

CAP. XIII.—An Admonition concerning the Divine Page.

[Col. 0931B]

There is no need to linger long over these matters, because I am sending your charity into the broadest field of the divine Scriptures, so that you may diligently seek there whatever you see to be lacking here. Therefore I ask your devotion always to increase in you its zeal for reading; for the more assiduous anyone is in the divine Scriptures, the greater understanding he receives from them, just as the more land is cultivated, the more abundantly it bears fruit.

For although a person may have a slow understanding, he can nevertheless learn something from the mysteries of the Scriptures if he is constant in reading. “To the one who has, it will be given, and from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away” (Matt. 13:12). That is: to the one who has zeal for reading, the ability to understand will also be given; but from the one who has no zeal for reading, even what he seems to have—that is, the natural ability to understand what is good—will be taken away because of his laziness.

[Col. 0931C]

And just as the person who is slow to understand will receive glory because of his good intention, so the person who neglects the talent given to him will be condemned. Therefore I admonish your charity to have zeal for reading, because all progress proceeds from reading. What we do not know, we learn through reading.

Isidore says that through prayers we are cleansed, and through readings we are instructed. Both are good, if possible; but if it is not possible, it is better to pray than to read. Whoever wishes always to be with God ought frequently to pray and frequently to read. For when we pray, we speak with God; but when we read, God speaks with us.

[Col. 0931D]

If these things are so, O woman dedicated to God, you must have zeal for prayer and reading. Reading supplies knowledge of God; reading drives away the darkness of ignorance; reading confers knowledge upon a person. Through zeal for reading, love of God and of all the virtues is nourished. Through reading you can learn what punishment, what mourning, and what penalty await evil, unjust, and impious people. Through reading you can learn what blessedness, what glory, and what charity are promised to holy and chosen people.

Through reading you can learn what the good and the evil will hear on the day of judgment. To the evil the Lord will say: “Go into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41); but to the good he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

[Col. 0932A]

We learn all these things through reading. Reading reveals how you ought to endure prosperity and adversity. Therefore something must here be added concerning the examples of the Fathers, who strove patiently to endure infirmities and every adversity for the love of Christ, so that your charity, by reading this and committing it to memory, may strive with all your strength to imitate it.

CAP. XIV.—An Admonition concerning Patiently Enduring Adversity and Loving Infirmity.

I therefore urge you that, if infirmity or some other adversity befalls you, and you wish to know perfectly how you ought to endure tribulations and all infirmities, devote yourself to reading. For there you will find written: “Those whom the Lord loves, he reproves and chastises” (Rev. 3:19). Therefore, mother, love to be reproved and chastised by him.

[Col. 0932B]

Whatever infirmity comes, receive it with a grateful spirit. I wish to relate to you one account from the *Tripartite History*, which I also want you to read and commit to memory.

There was an elder named Benjamin, held in great esteem and endowed with a gift of God by which, without medicine, he healed the sick by the touch of his hand or through prayer with oil. It is said that he fell into the disease of dropsy, and that his body swelled so greatly that he could not be carried out through the doors of the cell in which he lived unless the doors, together with the boards placed before them, were removed.

During the time of his illness, therefore, for nearly eight months before his death, he sat in a very spacious cell and continued solemnly to care for the sick. He did not take it hard that this did not benefit his own illness; rather, he also comforted those who sat with him and begged them to pray for his soul and not to concern themselves with his body. “For,” he said, “even when I was healthy, it profited me nothing.”

[Col. 0932C]

Strive to imitate this Benjamin, O most holy mother, in all your infirmities, and always strive to give thanks to the Lord.

Let your devotion also hear about the blessed monk Stephen and how he strove to conduct himself. Stephen lived near the Ocean Sea, leading a perfect life and maintaining complete dedication. He was a highly esteemed monk for about sixty years and was very well known to Antony the Great. He was exceedingly gentle and wise, pleasant and useful in speech; he consoled sorrowful minds and restored them to cheerfulness, although necessary tribulation preceded him. He was the same in his own sufferings.

[Col. 0932D]

Finally, when he contracted an incurable illness and the physicians cut away his putrefying limbs, he nevertheless worked with his hands, plaiting palm leaves, and persuaded those present not to grieve or think about matters of this kind, but only about a good end. “All the things God has made,” he said, “are useful. I know that sufferings of this kind have come upon me because of my sins, and it is better to pay the penalties here than to endure everlasting punishments after death.”

Strive also to speak in the same way when infirmity or some other adversity befalls you. We ought also to consider most carefully that, if those who were holy and just gave thanks to the Lord for infirmity, how much more ought we, who are sinners, to love infirmities and tribulations—especially since the Apostle says that “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21).

[Col. 0933A]

If, then, the kingdom of God is entered through many tribulations, tribulations must be loved with thanksgiving, and infirmities must be endured by us, so that we may deserve to become heirs of the heavenly kingdom. For the sinner who does not deserve to be scourged in this world will be tortured in hell.

It is therefore desirable for us, O most holy mother, that while we live this life we should willingly endure tribulations and infirmities for the love of Christ and for the remission of our sins.

Your devotion ought to know in what ways God scourges a person. For I have read that God scourges a person in five ways.

First, he scourges by way of testing. Thus Job and Tobias were scourged; they were scourged so that they might be tested and made manifest to others as examples worthy of imitation, so that, recognizing their patience, we might strive to imitate them.

[Col. 0933B]

Second, God scourges people so that they do not exalt themselves in pride or place their confidence in security. This especially concerns the saints, as the blessed Apostle Paul says of himself: “And lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me” (2 Cor. 12:7). After he recognized that this scourging was beneficial to him, he said: “Therefore I will gladly glory in my infirmities, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me” (ibid., 9).

Third, God scourges a person because of sin, as in the case of the paralytic, to whom he said: “Your sins are forgiven you” (Matt. 9:2). Then he said: “Take up your bed and go to your house” (ibid., 6). By the fact that he forgave his sins and then healed him of his infirmity, it is most clearly demonstrated that the infirmity had come upon him because of sin.

[Col. 0933C]

Fourth, God scourges a person so that his power or the merit of his works may be demonstrated. Thus, concerning the man born blind, the Lord himself said in the Gospel: “Neither this man sinned nor his parents, that he should be born blind, but so that the Son of God might be glorified through him” (John 9:3). By these words he clearly shows that the man had been born blind so that he might be enlightened by God, and thereby the power of the divinity might be manifested.

Fifth, God scourges people so that here they may begin to suffer the torment that afterward they will suffer without end. This applies only to the wicked, as in the case of Antiochus and Herod, who began here to suffer what afterward they were to suffer in hell. Concerning them it is written: “Crush them with a double crushing” (Jer. 17:18), that is, in the present and in the future.

[Col. 0933D]

In these five ways God scourges a person. The reason it is unknown how each individual is scourged by these means is that every scourged person may fear and amend himself, weeping for what he has done, so that the scourging may contribute to his progress.

Your blessedness must therefore be admonished to learn by heart these five ways in which the Lord scourges a person, so that in every infirmity or tribulation you may always have them before the eyes of your mind. By meditating on these things, you will endure the Lord’s scourging with a grateful spirit.

We must firmly believe that no sin is left without punishment: either each person erases his sin here through repentance, or the Lord mercifully purifies it through his scourging, or it is expiated after death in purgatorial fire. But if a person’s sin has not been erased by these means, after this life he will descend into eternal fire.

[Col. 0934A]

You must by no means despair of your salvation, nor say with those who despair: “My evils are many, and my sins are countless.” Know with certainty that no one can sin so much as the Lord is able to forgive—provided that the sinner repents and strives to turn to him.

And since the subject of hoping for the forgiveness of sins has arisen, I wish to bring to your mind the deed of the Emperor Theodosius, so that your mind may be lifted toward hoping for the forgiveness of sins, and your heart may be moved to pour forth a stream of tears.

[Col. 0934B]

Why should any sinner despair of forgiveness if he turns to the Lord with his whole heart, when the emperor mentioned above, after killing seven thousand people, was able within a few days to obtain forgiveness by lamenting and acknowledging himself guilty?

So that your holiness may know most clearly how these things happened—why he killed seven thousand people, on what occasion he acknowledged himself guilty, how he humbled himself, and how he obtained forgiveness—the words of the *Tripartite History* must here be inserted in their proper order. Through them, with the Lord’s help, you will be able to make progress in many virtues: first, in hoping for the forgiveness of sins, since, though guilty of the blood of so many people, he easily obtained forgiveness; then in humility, since, although he was emperor, through the preaching of the blessed Ambrose he humbled himself so greatly that he recognized himself to be lower than all sinners; and then in tears, since when he entered the church he watered its pavement with his tears.

[Col. 0934C]

I therefore wish your charity not to be unaware that no one can extinguish all vices in himself at once. For when someone has escaped the passion of lust, he falls into avarice; when he has avoided avarice, the pit of envy is prepared for him; and if he has overcome envy, the enemy immediately sets the vice of anger and many other snares, through which he may capture the unwary.

It is therefore not easy for human beings to avoid all the snares of the enemy. But a mind awakened by divine consolation and assisted by divine protection will destroy all the schemes and devices of the ancient enemy.

CAP. XV.—On Hoping for the Forgiveness of Sins, Although the Torments of Punishments Are Countless; and on the Penance Imposed upon the Emperor Theodosius by Saint Ambrose, Here Introduced as an Example.

[Col. 0934D]

The Emperor Theodosius was subject to the passion of anger, but he mingled immense cruelty with a just anger. It is necessary to relate this for the sake of your humility—that is, so that you may profit from reading about him in the virtues mentioned above.

The city of Thessalonica is large and populous. When a revolt had arisen there, certain of its judges were stoned and dragged about. At this Theodosius became indignant and did not restrain the weakness of his anger; [Col. 0935A]

instead, he ordered unjust swords to be unsheathed against everyone and the innocent to be killed together with the guilty. It is said that seven thousand people were killed—not after a trial, but as though all had been cut down in a harvest.

Ambrose heard of this disaster, full of terrible lamentation. When the emperor had come to Milan and wished to enter the holy church according to custom, the blessed Ambrose met him outside at the doors and prevented him from entering the temple with these words:

“Do you not know, O emperor, how great is the magnitude of the slaughter you have committed? Even after the cause of such great fury, does your mind not recognize the burden of its presumption? But if perhaps the power of imperial office prevents recognition of the sin, it is nevertheless fitting that reason should overcome power. You must consider human nature, its mortality and dissolution, and the dust of your ancestors, from which we were made and to which we shall be reduced.

[Col. 0935B]

“Do not, trusting in the purple bloom, imagine that you may ignore the weaknesses of your fellow human beings. One must not trust in purple, but rather consider the equality of human condition. You are a prince, O emperor, but only of fellow servants; for there is one king, God and Creator of all.

“With what eyes, then, will you look upon the Lord’s temple? With what feet will you tread his holy pavement? How will you extend hands from which unjust blood still drips? How will you receive the holy body of the Lord with such hands? With what presumption will you offer to your mouth the cup of the Lord’s precious blood, while so much blood has been unjustly shed through the fury of your words?

[Col. 0935C]

“Withdraw, therefore, withdraw, lest by a second sin you attempt to increase your former wickedness. Accept the bond with which the Lord of all has now bound you; for it is the medicine of the greatest healing.”

[Col. 0935D]

The emperor obeyed these words—for he had been nourished by divine instruction and clearly knew what belonged to priests and what belonged to kings—and, groaning and weeping, returned to the imperial palace.

When eight months had passed continuously, the nativity of our Savior was approaching. The emperor, sitting in the palace amid continual lamentation, shed unceasing tears.
