Rufinus, who at that time was master and enjoyed exceptional confidence with the emperor, entered and, seeing him prostrate in mourning, approached to ask the cause of his tears.

But the emperor, groaning most bitterly and pouring forth abundant tears, said: “You play, Rufinus, and do not feel my sufferings; but I lament and mourn my calamity. The temples of God are open to servants and beggars, and they enter freely to entreat their own Lord; but for me there is no entrance to him. Moreover, heaven itself is closed to me.” As he spoke these words one by one, he interrupted them with sobs.

Rufinus said: “If it pleases you, I will hasten to the bishop and persuade him by my entreaties to release the bond with which he has bound you.”

The emperor replied: “You will not persuade Ambrose. I know that his decree is just, and he will not respect imperial power so as to transgress the divine law.”

When Rufinus continued at length and promised that Ambrose could be persuaded, the emperor ordered him to go quickly. After a short while he himself followed, trusting Rufinus’s promises.

[Col. 0936A]

But as soon as the remarkable Ambrose saw Rufinus, he said: “You have imitated the shamelessness of dogs, O Rufinus. Though responsible for such a great slaughter, you wipe the shame from your brow and are neither embarrassed nor afraid to bark against the divine image.”

When Rufinus pleaded and said that the emperor was coming, Ambrose, inflamed by heavenly zeal, said: “I declare, Rufinus, that I myself will prevent him from entering the church. If he turns the imperial power into tyranny, I will gladly accept death.”

Rufinus heard these and many other words and reported the bishop’s resolve to the emperor, advising him not to leave the palace. But when the emperor learned of this while already in the middle of the street, he said: “I will proceed and receive the just insults upon my face.”

[Col. 0936B]

When he reached the sacred doors, he did not presume to enter the holy church. Instead, he went to the bishop and, finding him seated in the upper gallery, begged him to release his bonds.

Ambrose said that his presence was cruel and that Theodosius was raging against God and trampling upon his laws.

The emperor replied: “I do not rebel against ecclesiastical decrees, nor do I wickedly attempt to enter the sacred doors. Rather, I ask you to release my bonds and strive to implore the Lord’s mercy for me. Do not command that the door be closed to me, which our Lord has opened to all who do penance.”

Then the bishop said: “What penance have you shown after such great iniquities? With what remedies have you healed incurable wounds and injuries?”

The emperor replied: “It is your task both to teach and to prepare the medicines; it is mine to receive what is offered.”

[Col. 0936C]

Then Saint Ambrose said: “Because you committed your judgment in anger, and the sentence was produced not by reason but rather by rage, write a law that annuls the decrees of fury, so that for thirty days a sentence of death may remain only in writing and await the judgment of reason. After those days have passed, when anger has ceased, let reason judge the case and settle before itself what it has recognized according to the truth. During these days it will be determined whether the sentence you have pronounced is just or unjust. If it is just, let it stand; but if unjust, let it be destroyed. Thirty days will be sufficient for this examination.”

The emperor accepted this admonition gladly and, confident that it was excellent, immediately ordered the law to be written anew and confirmed the document with his own hand. When this had been done, Ambrose released his bond.

[Col. 0936D]

This law is observed to the present day. It was composed in the following terms: if the emperor condemned anyone to death, that person was to be kept unharmed for thirty days. Those whom the king’s anger had judged too severely were to have their sentence suspended, so that, during the thirty-day period, when anger had subsided, it might be determined whether the sentence was just or unjust; and whatever was proved just was to be carried out.

Thus the most sacred emperor was permitted to enter the doors. He did not stand to entreat the Lord, nor did he bend his knees; rather, he lay prostrate on the pavement and cried out in David’s words: “My soul has clung to the pavement; give me life,” and so forth (Ps. 118:25). [Col. 0937A]

Tearing his hair with his hands, striking his forehead, and sprinkling the pavement with drops of tears, he begged to obtain forgiveness.

When the time approached at which he was accustomed to offer the gift at the altar, he rose and entered. After he had made the offering as usual and stood within the railings, Ambrose again did not consent but instructed him concerning the distinction of places. First he asked what he was waiting for. When the emperor said that he was awaiting the instructions of the sacred ministers, Ambrose sent word through the archdeacon:

“O emperor, the inner places are assigned only to priests; others are neither permitted to enter nor to touch them. Go out, therefore, and share this waiting with the others. Purple makes emperors, not priests.”

[Col. 0937B]

Then the most faithful emperor accepted this instruction also with a grateful spirit and sent back word: “I did not remain within the railings through presumption, but I knew that this custom existed in the city of Constantinople. I therefore give thanks for such a remedy.”

Thus the bishop and the emperor shone with such great and admirable virtue. I am accustomed to admire the work of both: the confidence of the one and the obedience of the other—that is, the confidence of the priest and the obedience of the king; the fervor of the one’s zeal and the purity of the other’s faith.

An extraordinary deed has now been related, one that can stir you, O most holy mother, to guard many virtues. For this holy contention between Theodosius, the most Christian ruler, and Ambrose, the most blessed bishop, urges a person to hope for the forgiveness of sins. This is above all why I have taken care to write this holy contest to you.

[Col. 0937C]

It also urges you to pursue charity, humility, and obedience—the virtues that at the beginning of this admonition I took care to commend to your devotion. Concerning the virtues of which I admonished you at the beginning of this exhortation, I admonish you concerning the same at the end, so that you may attain the good you have begun with a persevering conclusion.

[Col. 0938A]

It also urges a hard and stony heart to pour forth tears and stimulates the fervor of zeal. I beg your devotion to read frequently this deed, this most holy penance of the most devout ruler, and the zeal of the most holy bishop, because great spiritual progress lies hidden in it.

If, therefore, you are able to carry out in practice what I have written to your holiness, most prudent mother—that is, if you entirely drive all vices away from yourself and wish to preserve the good things related in this admonition—know that you do not accomplish this by your own strength, but through the one who inspires and assists you, who says in the Gospel: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

Indeed, we are not even able to think anything good unless he works in us and gives it, from whom every good proceeds.

Hear also attentively what the Lord says through the prophet Jeremiah concerning this matter: “Let not the wise man glory in his power, and let not the strong man glory in his strength, and let not the rich man glory in his riches; but let the one who glories glory in this: that he knows, understands, and recognizes me” (Jer. 9:23).

[Col. 0938B]

Through these words pride will be carried away like smoke, because wisdom, strength, and all riches are reckoned as nothing. The only true glory is to know and understand that he is the Lord who performs mercy, judgment, and our righteousness.

From this passage the Apostle Paul also took what he wrote to the Corinthians: “Brothers, let the one who glories glory in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10:17).

Where are those who say that a person is governed by his own free choice? Where are those who say that we can initiate good from ourselves? We must by no means believe this, because we are unable even to think, much less to accomplish, anything unless the Lord himself grants it.

[Col. 0938C]

Therefore, if by the abundance of the Lord’s grace you perform a good work and accomplish what I have written to your blessedness, do not attribute it to your own strength or merits, but to him who works in you both the willing and the accomplishing according to his good will. To him belong honor, power, and dominion throughout endless ages of ages. Amen.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 965. SAINT BRUNO, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE.

[Col. 0937]

HISTORICAL NOTICE ON SAINT BRUNO.

(From Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini*.)

Bruno, son of Henry the Fowler and brother of the Emperor Otto the Great, was archbishop of Cologne from the year of Christ 953 to 965. Some attribute to him commentaries on the Pentateuch, such as those extant in print under the names of Bruno of Würzburg and Bruno of Asti, of whom I have already spoken. Sixtus of Siena, however, in Book IV of the *Bibliotheca sancta*, p. 270, testifies that in the Dominican Library at Bologna there exists a manuscript commentary by this Bruno on the four Gospels; in this commentary Bruno testifies that, after the Pentateuch of Moses, he elucidated the four Gospels so as to join the new to the old.

[Col. 0937]

THE LIFE OF SAINT BRUNO, BY RUOTGER, A CLERIC OF COLOGNE.

(From Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. IV, p. 252.)

The life of Bruno, an outstanding man who in character and deeds came very close to the greatness of his brother Otto, was commissioned by Folcmar, also called Poppo—Bruno’s friend and successor in the see of Cologne—to Ruotger, a cleric of Cologne and the deceased’s principal intimate and companion. [Col. 0939] [Note: Folcmar and Poppo are the same name; cf. [Col. 0939]. On Ruotger, see the preface and ch. 13: “the senate of this holy clergy.” Leibniz conjectured that he was master of the schools; the words of ch. 47 do not necessarily establish that he belonged to the community of St. Pantaleon. Ch. 4: “as we learned from him himself, often turning this over in his mind”; chs. 29, 30, and 37: “we saw in battle”; ch. 43: “as Bishop Wicfrid himself testifies.” He also appears to have been among the archbishop’s “retainers,” companions on the French journey.]

Ruotger, a man worthy of such friends, skilled in Roman letters [Note: For example, he knew Terence, ch. 39] and Greek, sound in judgment [Note: Cf., for example, what he says about Frederick, archbishop of Mainz, in ch. 16, and about Duke Henry and his adversaries in ch. 17], and especially well acquainted with matters to be committed to writing, discharged the task without delay and presented Folcmar with an excellent book, written with distinction, as Sigebert observes, though on account of its brevity it must sometimes be read with especially attentive consideration.

The work was completed in 966 or 967, within two years after Bruno’s death and shortly before Widukind’s Saxon history and Hrotsvit’s panegyric, whose praises of Bruno agree with Ruotger’s. [Note: Bruno died on 11 October 965; Folcmar died on 18 July 967. Widukind nevertheless did not use Ruotger’s book, though he praises Bruno in the same spirit, II.36; cf. I.31. For Hrotsvit, see v. 53 ff.; cf. also below, the *Life of John of Gorze*, ch. 116.] It deserves particular confidence and must be counted among the foremost sources of its age; from the moment it appeared, it was highly esteemed by learned men.

Thus Abbot Folcuin followed our author almost word for word in his *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*. Thietmar, celebrating Bruno as outstanding in every kind of divine and human excellence [Note: II.15], says that he was prevented from saying more about the innumerable noble deeds of so great a man because he had written a book about his noble way of life.

At the same time the author of the *Life of Queen Matilda* [Note: Ch. 9] and, a century later, Sigebert [Note: *Life of Theodoric*, ch. 1, *SS. ecclesiastici*, col. 130; chronicle for the years 953–965] copied our work. Hermannus Contractus [Note: At the year 965; nevertheless, he does not seem to have possessed the book], Giles of Orval, a monk [Note: *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège*, ch. 34], and Trithemius knew it. That the author, commended to the memory of the people of Cologne by such titles, did not remain unknown there is shown by another *Life of Bruno*, written in the fourteenth century, which readers will easily recognize as relying chiefly upon Ruotger.

We have prepared our edition after the earlier work of Surius, Leibniz, and Byeus, using three manuscripts—namely, all those that have ever become known.

1. Manuscript of the ducal library of Wolfenbüttel, on parchment, eleventh century, in folio, catalogued among the Augustei as 76, 14. It is generally written in gatherings in a very small hand and contains, on sixty-three pages, several works of great historical importance: Sigebert’s *Life of Theodoric I, Bishop of Metz*; on folios 5–18, the *Lives of Goeric, Clodulf, Adelberon II, Abbot Romaric, the confessor Amatus, Abbot Adelphus,* and *Mansuetus, Bishop of Toul*, by Adzo. These are clearly derived from an older book, just as are the corresponding texts in the royal Paris manuscript no. 5294, written by Betto. Then, on folios 18–24, it contains the *Life of Grodegang, Bishop of Metz*; on folios 25–30, it formerly contained a fragment of Alpert’s books *On the Diversity of Times* and *On the Deeds of the Bishops of Metz*, now preserved in the royal library at Hanover; on folios 31–36, writings of Avitus, Severus, Evodius, and Paulus concerning Saint Stephen; on folio 36, Bede’s letter to Eadfrid concerning the *Life of Cuthbert*; on folio 38, the *Miracles of Saint Wigbert*; and on folio 40, Lucian’s letter concerning Saint Stephen.

Beginning with folio 43, it contains Ruotger’s *Life of Bruno*, a sermon for the feast of Saint Pantaleon, Stephen’s sermon for the feast of Saint Maurinus, the translation of Saint Maurinus, and a sermon of Saint Augustine. On folios 49–63 are the *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège* by Hariger and Anselm. Part of folio 63, folio 64, and other portions of the manuscript are blank.

After the scribes to whom this substantial book is owed, a corrector worked on it, making many alterations throughout and supplying in the margins and on attached slips what had been wrongly omitted. It may be conjectured that this corrector was Sigebert of Gembloux, though comparison with his autograph chronicle will confirm or disprove this. Certainly, the fact that this manuscript was in Sigebert’s hands seems to be confirmed by the works of Sigebert that it contains. Among these, the *Life of Bruno* presents a text such as Ruotger must have written, apart from only a few errors.

[Note: In the same volume there is another manuscript, whose leaves are already numbered 65–156, but it is entirely different from ours: it is on paper and was written only in the fifteenth century. Hence, through an obvious error, the whole book is assigned to the fifteenth century in Ebert’s catalogue of the Wolfenbüttel manuscripts, *Archiv* VI, 5.]

Leibniz had already used it before us in *SS. Brunswicenses* I, 273 ff.; but, misled by Surius’s edition, he produced a less good and less reliable text.

2. Manuscript of the royal library of Brussels, formerly belonging to Saint Pantaleon of Cologne, now catalogued under numbers 329–341, on parchment, in folio, fifteenth century. I examined it in 1826 [Note: *Archiv* VII, 407], and our Bethmann has already put it to use. It was printed by Surius [Note: *Acta Sanctorum* V, p. 701].

It contains the *Life and Miracles of Saint Pantaleon*; the *Life and Translation of Saint Maurinus* by Stephen; the *Life and Translation of Saint Albinus*; the *Life of Queen Matilda*; the testament of the church of Saint Cecilia; a notice concerning the construction of the monastery of Saint Pantaleon; the shorter *Life of Saint Bruno*; Ruotger’s *Life of Saint Bruno*; and sermons of Augustine and Bede. Ruotger’s work includes inserted histories of the translations of Saints Evergisius and Patroclus.

The other *Life*, much of which is drawn from Ruotger’s book, nevertheless deserves to be printed because of the material it owes to other sources now hidden from us. Bethmann copied it and divided it into chapters.

3. Manuscript of the royal library of Brussels, no. 7460, formerly of the Vallicelliana, containing the *Lives of the Saints for the Months of October and November*. It is a very large parchment folio, written in two columns in the thirteenth century. Byeus followed it, using the editions of Surius and Leibniz, in the *Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists, October, vol. IV, pp. 698–790, and accompanied it with a preface and commentary. Bethmann rediscovered it in 1839 and put it to use for our purposes. Its text, with many words omitted and others added, departs from the genuine text.

[Note: Concerning other manuscripts said to contain Ruotger’s work, we add the following: the manuscript of the royal library of Brussels, no. 982, on paper, in folio, from the end of the fifteenth century, contains only excerpts from Ruotger’s book, preserving almost always the same wording, and was therefore neglected by Bethmann. The manuscript of the ducal library of Wolfenbüttel among the Helmstedt manuscripts, no. 353, on paper, in folio, fifteenth century; the manuscript of the University of Leipzig, no. 594; and the royal manuscript of Munich among the Tegernsee manuscripts, no. 897, on parchment, thirteenth century, have no connection whatever with Ruotger’s work.]

We have adopted the division into chapters found in manuscript 3, which differs slightly from Leibniz’s, and have occasionally corrected it wherever the sense seemed to require this. Manuscript 1 has longer chapters, but because several numbers are omitted it could not serve as a guide on this point.

## HERE BEGINS THE PREFACE TO THE LIFE [Note: Manuscripts 1 and 2 read “Here begins the life.”] OF LORD BRUNO, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE

[Col. 0941]

To the most blessed Folcmar, archbishop, in the grace of Christ and most perfect in every splendor of wisdom [Note: Manuscript 1 corrects “grace” to “wisdom”], Ruotger [Note: Manuscript 2: *Rotgherus*; manuscript 3: *Rogerus*], the least of his servants, sends the everlasting glory of true brightness.

The reverence due to your holiness has placed upon my head a heavy burden indeed, but one exceedingly sweet and pleasing in proportion to my small ability: namely, that I should describe, with whatever power of expression I possess, the life of the remarkable and magnificent Archbishop Bruno. Virtue bestowed praise upon him, but the office of my pen could not fulfill it as he deserved. Yet, however I might speak of him [Note: Manuscripts 2 and 3 read “however I might speak of him”], it was delightful, because you commanded me to do so. From the beginning he was so disposed that he did not consider himself born more for his own sake than for ours and for the commonwealth.

He accomplished an exceedingly great number of things, almost without limit, worthy of eternal remembrance; but let no reader expect that I, or anyone else, should set them all forth. If someone promised to undertake this faithfully and truthfully [Note: Manuscript 3 reads “promises”], he would have to mark each of the years he lived after passing beyond childhood [Note: Manuscripts 1, 2, and 3 read *praegressus* rather than *praetergressus*] in a separate and sufficiently spacious volume.

I therefore judge that many people, far and wide, will devote themselves to this labor, so that his deeds may be transmitted, partly by writing and partly by recollection, even to those who will come after us. For he did not conduct his affairs in one province or in one kingdom; through the exchange of his benevolence, labor, and zeal, he sought the salvation of all whom he could reach.

[Col. 0942A] There are many who can carry this out elegantly and wisely. [Note: Manuscript 3 has *solis*, corrected to *scolis*; *discipulis* is absent.] Even if no others of this kind could be found, in his disciples alone every form of learning and eloquence still flourishes, while his memory remains fresh, in so many regions of the world that they would be capable not merely of recounting the greatest distinctions of his deeds but also of embellishing them.

How many bishops among the pupils of so great a man do we know, and how many men highly distinguished in every discipline of ecclesiastical life, who knew him more intimately and could have displayed his life more perfectly in illustrious memorials! But who am I, most excellent lords, that I should have dared to oppose your wishes?

Therefore I have done what I could, as I could [Note: Manuscripts 2 and 3 omit *quomodo potui*, “as I could,” though it was later corrected], relying not upon knowledge but retaining whatever confidence I possess in obedience. Although it seemed less possible for me to accomplish what I had undertaken, I nevertheless resolved always to honor and embrace the dignity of your command, so that, forgetting my inability, I might be wholly eyes and mind in your hands.

Therefore I beseech your lavishly flowing piety [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *largistuae*] that whatever is lacking in this work of mine in the pomp and ornament of expression may be supplied in your ears by the recommendation of him whom, in accordance with the merit of his virtue, you loved so sweetly. May almighty God deign to preserve your blessedness, for our salvation, safe and prosperous for a very long time. [Note: Manuscript 1 has the abbreviated form *colum*; manuscripts 2 and 3 add after *dignetur*: “The prologue ends.”]

## HERE BEGINS THE LIFE OF LORD BRUNO, ARCHBISHOP [Note: Manuscript 3 adds “of Cologne.”]

[Col. 0941]

### 1

It is surely a mark of wisdom to know from where the gift one has received comes [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “receives”], lest one think that it exists from oneself and for oneself, or that it comes indeed from God but is owed to oneself. For if we ask what is owed to us, we find nothing except punishment.

But God’s mercy anticipated us with grace, so that he might have people to whom he could return grace for grace. Even this would already be something owed, because God willed it, not because man deserved it. For what do you have, says the Apostle, that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it? (1 Cor. 4:7.)

Therefore, by the ineffable providence of God’s goodness, it has been granted to his elect both that they should be enriched freely with abundant gifts of grace and that they should nevertheless in some manner merit through grace the very thing with which they are endowed—one in this way, another in that, each according to the operation in him of the one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each as he wills (1 Cor. 12:11).

To the Only-Begotten God gives the Spirit without measure. For in him, as the Apostle says, “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2:9). He distributes it among his members according to the will proper to each, giving them all things abundantly for enjoyment—namely, himself—so that God may be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28).

This unequal splendor and diverse generosity of gifts is now an astonishing problem [Note: Manuscript 2 spells it *ammirabilis*]; one day it will be the honorable beauty and adornment of the Lord’s house, concerning which it is said to God: “Holy is your temple, wondrous in equity” (Ps. 64:5–6).

### 2

It has recently been discovered by many, and sufficiently understood by the more prudent, in Bruno, the venerable Archbishop of Cologne, of blessed memory, what one man may accomplish for another, or how one may excel another [Note: Manuscript 3 omits “or excel”]. Most of his sayings and deeds those who knew him more intimately could not admire enough [Note: Manuscripts 2 and 3 read *pleraque* for *plerique*; manuscript 1 reads *quid* for *qui*.]

For in that one man there were things very unlike one another: nobility of birth; dignity of office; such elevation of knowledge, which usually causes people to swell with pride, that nothing seemed above it [Note: Manuscript 3 omits this phrase]; but humility of spirit and bearing, so far as could be discerned by the more discerning, such that you would think nothing could be beneath them.

For [Note: Manuscript 1 begins with *Nam*; manuscripts 2 and 3 omit it] they were spread upon the middle ground of charity. Everything that could contribute to pride smiled upon him, but he had always most diligently driven it away from himself with the watchful hand of discretion [Note: Manuscript 3 reads “from the one who is always watchful”]. Thus he presented one thing to human eyes and another to the witness of hearts.

We believe that many could be salutarily instructed by the example of his way of life, if we briefly retrace it from childhood. For in it the ordinary and humble have something by which they may grow strong, while the proud and wealthy have something at which they may stand aghast.

His ancestors’ ancestors, down to the memory of mankind, had all been of the highest nobility; no unknown person appears in their lineage, and no degenerate person is easily found [Note: Manuscript 3 reads “unrecorded”; manuscript 2 omits “easily found” but later supplies it]. Yet, apart from the excellence of emperors and kings, he surpassed them all utterly in the grace of his features, the glory of his arts, and every kind of mental accomplishment.

He was born in the year 925, when his father, King Henry [Note: Manuscript 1 has *hienricus*; manuscript 3, *henricus*], the glorious ruler, having subdued the savagery of the barbarians [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *per dogmata* for *perdomita*] and also suppressed the danger of internal disaster, was rebuilding what had been destroyed with great zeal and was at last governing his willing people, by the restraints of justice, in the safest and most desirable peace [Note: Manuscript 3 omits “and most desirable”].

Thus the time of his birth already seemed to display in advance the marks of his future good will. For since he had always most eagerly desired everything that was good [Note: Manuscript 3 omits this clause], he sought the gift of peace, which he knew would benefit all good things, with particular care, as a kind of nourishment and adornment of the other virtues [Note: Manuscript 1 writes “of the rest” with an added letter].

Virtues ought to be nourished and strengthened in a time of tranquility, so that, whenever disturbance arises, they may not cease to keep a person firm in the strength of his condition.

### 3

It would take too long to explain how the king just mentioned, the father of this great man of whom we are speaking, reached that serenity of such welcome peace, since he had found the whole extent of his kingdom shaken and cruelly tormented both by the continual incursions of neighboring peoples and by the gravest dissensions among citizens and even among relatives [Note: Manuscript 3 begins a new chapter here].

On one side the savage Danish people, powerful by land and sea, bristled threateningly; on the other, the hundredfold fury of the Slavs roared like barbarians. Nor was the cruelty of the Hungarians absent: crossing the borders of the Moravians, which not long before impious license had usurped for them, it devastated far and wide many provinces of his kingdom with sword and fire.

The days would fail before the material for narrating this evil did [Note: The editor’s text has *narrandi*; the edition reads *narranti*. Manuscript 3 reads *deficiet*, “will fail.”] Beyond the Rhine, toward the west, everything rebelled against us; indeed, the princes of the kingdom, still august [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *ita*; the editions read *augusti*], were raging almost irreparably against their own vitals. No one except a man endowed with exceptional virtue and singular ability could either cut away or heal all these troubles [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *narrare*, “to relate,” instead of *sanare*, “to heal”].

But after some little time [Note: Manuscripts 2 and 3 read *aliquantum*], such fear seized the foreigners through divine grace that nothing had ever been more frightening to them; and such love bound together those at home that nothing had ever appeared more united in any powerful kingdom.

### 4

At that time, in 929, the noble offspring of kings, about four years old, was sent to Utrecht to be instructed in the liberal studies by the venerable Bishop Balderic [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *imbuendo* for *imbuenda*], who is still alive [Note: He died in 976].

There, as he progressed in a disciplined manner [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *disciplinaliter*], as befitted a boy of good disposition, with keen intelligence, the hated tyranny of the Northmen [Note: Manuscript 3 has the spelling *Normannorum*] somewhat cooled, as though because of such a hostage [Note: Manuscript 3 omits *quasi*, “as though”]. On this occasion the churches and other buildings, scarcely anything of which had remained from their ruins, were restored [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *exstiterant*, “had survived”].

Thus he spent no portion of his life without benefiting God’s holy Church. Through him, although he was still unaware of it, the Christian people, already freed from its enemies, rejoiced in the praises of God.

Then, after he had learned the first rudiments of grammar, he began to read the poet Prudentius under a teacher’s instruction, as we learned from Bruno himself, who often turned this over in his mind to the glory of almighty God. Since Prudentius is both Catholic in faith and purpose, outstanding in eloquence and truth, and most elegant in the variety of his meters and books [Note: Manuscript 3 omits this phrase], he soon pleased the palate of Bruno’s heart with such sweetness that Bruno drank in not only knowledge of the external words but also the innermost marrow of their meaning, and, so to speak, their most limpid nectar, with an eagerness greater than can be expressed.

Afterward, there was no branch of liberal study in all Greek or Latin eloquence that could escape the vitality of his intellect. Nor, as often happens, did either an abundance of wealth, the constant clamor of surrounding crowds, or any distaste stealing in from elsewhere ever turn his mind away from this noble leisure. His constant meditation and tireless devotion to continuous practice bore witness to the purity of his heart, since every such inclination had by then passed wholly into habit, as it is written: “From his practices a boy is understood, whether his works are clean and upright” (Prov. 20:11).

To this was added that, just as he did not allow the ardor of his spirit to be extinguished by the laziness and frivolity of others or corrupted by excessive and empty conversations, so he could not endure at all that the books in which he studied, or any books he had before his eyes, should be carelessly torn, creased, or handled in any way with insufficient care. He considered nothing belonging to him negligible, because, as Solomon says, “He who neglects small things will gradually fall” (Ecclesiasticus 19:1). [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *decidet*, “will fall,” in the future tense.]

### 5

After his father, having founded and thoroughly pacified the empire, departed from human affairs, his son Otto, the elder, strengthened by the Lord’s blessing and anointed with the oil of gladness, began to reign in 936 with the great goodwill and agreement of the princes, in the 188th lustrum and the 63rd cycle of the indictions from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. [Note: That is, within the years 935–940 and 930–945.]

He was a man upon whom the Spirit of God bestowed the singular gift of truth and faith. If I promised to narrate his virtues, I would be taking too much upon myself [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *supserim*; manuscript 3, *presumpserim*, “I would have presumed too much”], and I would scarcely be tolerable. For his praise and glory exceed whatever Cicero himself might have promised in eloquence.

This man honorably and fittingly summoned his brother Bruno, dedicated to God and still a young man, from the schools to the palace—a place suited to so bright a mirror, in which whatever was deformed throughout almost the whole world might appear more clearly in contrast with him. For everything from all his territories that seemed to amount to anything flowed there toward him.

Likewise, all those oppressed by any kind of false accusation sought this one refuge. There an exemplar of wisdom, piety, and justice stood forth beyond human memory. Those who had shortly before seemed at home to themselves the most learned returned from there marked with shame and began again the rudiments of the arts, as though saying, “Now I have begun.” Whoever had no soundness in the left side of his breast withdrew thereafter in embarrassment from this lofty tribunal. [The wording is corrupt; the image appears to concern moral or intellectual deficiency.]

The Lord filled that vessel of his with the spirit of wisdom and understanding. It was not enough for him to gather into the treasury of his heart what he already possessed openly [Note: Manuscript 3 has *sufficit*, “it suffices,” and omits *in*, “into”]; he also brought in foreign riddles, and whatever he perceived to be philosophical and most remote from earthly senses, he gathered from every source.

He himself unfolded the seven liberal arts, long since forgotten. Whatever historians, orators, poets, and philosophers proclaimed as new and great, he examined most diligently with teachers of every language; and wherever the teacher excelled in speed of intellect, there he displayed himself as a pupil in humility.

### 6

Often, when the most learned Greeks and Latins were disputing about the heights of philosophy or the subtlety of any discipline flourishing within it, he himself sat among them as a learned interpreter and satisfied the disputants, to the applause of all [Note: Manuscripts 1 and 2 read *quod* for *quo*]—which he loved less than anything.

For he did not apply an unjust test in that balance, nor did he seek himself outside it; he counted the testimony of his conscience as glory for himself [Note: Manuscript 3 reads: “Nor did he seek glory outside himself, but considered the testimony of his conscience sufficient.”]

The greatest king of the world, who was incapable of being deceived in such matters, frequently observed this. He had strengthened his outward kingdom by the power of courage and counsel and had clothed its inward aspect with such splendor. God himself is believed to have observed these things [Note: Manuscript 3 reads “the creator”], he whose mercy preserves whatever gift he bestows. For who would restrain arrogance at so great and incomparable a height, unless he himself in his goodness provided his protection?

### 7

When certain people asked Israel the Scot [Note: Perhaps the same man whom Flodoard mentions as present at the synod of Verdun in 947, in his *Annals*, as “Israel the Breton”] about Bruno’s character—Israel was the teacher under whose instruction this most illustrious man of whom we speak testified that he had made very great progress—he replied, as we ourselves heard those people carefully turning the matter over and treating his answer almost as an oracle, that Bruno was above all a holy man [Note: Manuscript 3 omits this phrase].

This was a sufficiently praiseworthy and judicious testimony by a teacher concerning his pupil. The Greeks, whom Bruno likewise used as teachers, were amazed at such grace. They carried home to their fellow citizens problems worthy of him—those whose reputed practice had once been either always to hear something new or to discover it (Acts 17:21).

### 8

In the meantime, a thousand times each day, he was compelled to act as advocate for the unfortunate, give counsel to the afflicted, and bring aid to the wretched [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *patrocinali* for *patrocinari*]. He administered all these duties in such a way that he seemed to have become a refuge for every needy person.

Thus, when he was at leisure, scarcely anyone seemed more occupied with business; and when he was occupied with business, he never ceased from leisure. He was intensely devoted to nocturnal study and extraordinarily acute in dictating whatever was most honorable.

He polished and ennobled Latin eloquence [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *laicalem* for *Latialem*] not only in himself, where he excelled, but also in many others [Note: Manuscript 2 reads *scilicet*; manuscript 3 repeatedly misread the abbreviation *scl.*]. He did this neither with arrogance but with both domestic charm and urbane dignity.

After meals, when others—and, as we are told, even people of higher rank—usually relaxed somewhat, he devoted himself more attentively to reading and meditation [Note: Manuscript 1 spells *uaccabat*].

He did not sell the morning twilight at any price, nor did he then entrust himself in any way to sleep when it solicited him. As for the vulgar and theatrical pieces which, spoken by various characters in comedies and tragedies, make certain people shake with endless laughter, he always read them seriously [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *serie*, “seriously”]. He regarded their subject matter as very slight but their authority in the composition of words as very great.

He made use of traveling schools, being at rest not in body but in mind [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *quietis*, “of rest”]. Wherever the royal tents or camps were moved, he carried his library with him like the ark of the Lord [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *aquam*, “water”], bringing with him both the reason for his studies and their instrument: the reason in divine books, the instrument in pagan books. He was like a learned householder who knows how to bring forth from his treasury new things and old (Matt. 13:52).

Nor was there any room for idleness even on the journey. In the crowd he was, as few are, almost alone. He would converse with anyone about something useful, or meditate upon that very matter in every person [Note: Manuscript 2 omits *id ipsum*, “that very matter,” though it was later corrected].

### 9

When it was time for the divine office, he kept his mind intent, commending himself to the Lord in brief but pure prayer. He satisfied those with whom he lived [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *quibuscum* for *his quibus*] by his manner and gesture while at times attending mentally to something else. Otherwise he could not have been so genuinely popular or persuaded so many to better things.

Whatever any priest of the Lord or perfect man was undertaking at that time as a great religious endeavor, he relied upon Bruno as though upon a single companion. No one thought his own authority sufficiently forceful unless he knew that Bruno, like a reserve force [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *succentarium*], was supporting him in the divine battle.

The servant of God made no small progress in the undertaking. He regarded popular rumors as nothing and foresaw not only what lay at his feet but also many things in the future.

Thus, when he saw excessive familiarity in conversation between his brother, who bore the surname of his father, and Cuono, who had been admitted into royal kinship [Note: “By relationship to the king”], especially during the time of Mass, he is said to have declared with prophetic spirit: “Into what bitterness of enmity will these badly formed intimacies dissolve at this fearful time!” The outcome of events soon confirmed his words.

### 10

His first administration was entrusted to him, while still a young man, in certain monasteries [Note: He was already abbot in 947; see Flodoard for that year]. In them he compelled those living there, partly willingly and partly by force, to adopt the regular life, with a suitable ecclesiastical testimony, knowing that good things are bestowed even upon the unwilling.

After a short time, with the generosity of the king’s approval, he restored those places dedicated to God to their former privileges and immunities. From then on he reserved no benefit for himself or his own by right, except whatever the fathers of the monasteries voluntarily offered for the sake of charity.

Among these places is Lorsch, a site made noble by the munificence of kings, which still preserves in memory of so great a man both the privilege of freedom [Note: In 956 it received back the right of free election; see the continuation of Regino] and the memorials of religion.

Then, as he advanced from virtue to virtue with giant strides, so to speak, and wherever he placed his foot always made progress in the Lord’s will, a sudden storm of dissension arose in the Church in 953. I believe that Jesus was asleep in the breasts of those who were keeping watch before the house of the Lord [Note: Manuscript 2 reads *illum*, “him”]. Certain companions of Satan, swollen with the spirit of envy, attempted to extinguish the emperor himself, through whom salvation existed among the people, the light, namely, of the world.

Why was this so, except that their evil works might not be exposed? [Note: Manuscript 3 omits *non*.] For, as the evangelical Truth bears witness, “Everyone who does evil hates the light” (John 3:20).

When, through God’s mercy, this plan conceived in the serpent’s hiss had been frustrated, they spread the poison of their wickedness through the whole interior of his kingdom. Although everywhere it threatened both the silence of the laws and the destruction of the people through killings and plunder, nowhere did it rage more fiercely than in the western regions [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *aestuabant*, “they raged”].

There, princes accustomed to violence and robbery, and peoples eager for revolution, all intent upon civil disasters, preferred to grow rich through the misery of others.

### 11

Then Wicfrid [Note: Manuscript 2 spells the name *wiikfridus*], pastor of the holy Church of Cologne, who had long been very weak but had nevertheless remained sufficiently faithful to the royal majesty and to his homeland, at last left his weary limbs of earth and was joined to the heavenly spirits.

The people, deprived of a pastor, attempted nothing uncertain or changeable amid the confusion; instead, following the counsel of the nobles and of the whole clergy, they chose for themselves, as their one and only desired consolation, Lord Bruno, a magnificent and highly approved man.

Mature in character although young in body, he was humble and gentle amid the greatest splendor of nobility. In the sublimity of the wisdom he had acquired, he had trained his mind not to think more highly than one ought to think but to think with sober judgment (Rom. 12:3). Amid royal abundance he was sparing toward himself and rich toward his friends.

In that first election Bishop Godefrid stood out above the others [Note: Cornelius Byeus conjectures that he was bishop of Speyer; but what role could the bishop of Speyer have had in the diocese of Cologne unless one assumes that he had been appointed as the royal legate for the election?]. But if anyone surpassed another in the vote, it would be difficult to determine who [Note: Manuscripts 2 and 3 omit the clause].

They were carried along in uncertainty between hope and fear for this one reason: measuring the dignity of the office and the glory of the man, they feared that the position they were preparing for him would be unworthy of such greatness. And indeed, if anywhere in the whole kingdom there were a more exalted place, or one more splendid for its clergy, people, churches, and every form of ceremony, it would have been thought by everyone who knew him to be more worthy of receiving such a pastor [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *praeceptui*, “of instruction,” rather than *receptui*, “of reception”].

### 12

When all therefore were united and were of one mind in Christ, they were still looking upon the body of his predecessor, of good memory, unburied and laid out before their eyes according to the custom of the place.

From the most holy senate four eminent men and an equal number of laymen were chosen, all highly educated, to carry all these matters to the palace. After revealing the unanimous election and lamenting their abandonment, they were to demand the aforesaid consolation for the desolate people.

Why say more? Thanks be to God, the royal authority [Note: At that time it was more properly royal than imperial] was pleased to provide for both the time and the place in such a way that it hastily sent the visitor whom they had requested with such steadfastness to guard the abandoned flock.

At last he was sent from the camps of the earthly empire into the tents of the heavenly King, to fight against spiritual wickedness, bearing before him the practices and exercises of virtue, the weapons of faith [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *referens*, “bearing back”; the manuscript itself corrected the reading in an erasure].

In him his new companions soon saw both what pleased them and what frightened them. For he showed himself exceedingly approachable and gentle, and although his diligence allowed nothing in the performance of duties to escape him, he nevertheless asked with the greatest care, from every source, what he ought to do and upon which customs he ought to rely.

His gravity was seasoned with courtesy. Thus, to the crowd that gathered around him, he appeared moderately cheerful [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *modice*, “moderately,” in an adverbial form] and in every respect remarkable.

### 13.

He came to the most sacred see, prepared for this pious administrator by the almighty Lord before the ages and presented at that very time. An immense gathering of the people took place, and infinite trembling among the populace; the city exulted with unprecedented joys. The clergy assembled from the monasteries, a multitude of nuns gathered, and every class and both sexes came together for the rejoicing in greater numbers than usual. On that day of such solemnity, the joyful Church weaned her offspring—until then suckled at her maternal breasts, but now grown up in Christ’s grace—and established herself spiritually as a mother who would afterward give birth, with the sweetest affection, to little sons in whom Christ might be formed (958).

The bishops who were present in large numbers, together with the senate of this holy clergy, had the man chosen by God and by human beings seated upon the pontifical chair. With everyone acclaiming in a voice of rejoicing and salvation, they all raised praise to God with a shout; and, with organs, cymbals, and every other sign of joy, they resounded as loudly as each could.

[Note: [Col. 0949] Witness 2 reads *cathenis* (“chains”), but this is corrected. Witness 3 has *qua quis ei* in place of the printed *quo quisque poterat* (“as much as each was able”).]

### 14.

From then on, all his attention and every effort of his was directed either to the protection or to the adornment of holy Mother Church. She had to be protected externally and adorned internally; protected in secular matters and adorned in spiritual ones.

[Note: [Col. 0949] Witness 3 reads *muniendo scilicet ext. ornando int.* (“namely, protecting externally and adorning internally”); the words *in saecularibus* and *in spiritualibus* are absent in the manuscript.]

Above all, he loved the beauty of the house of the Lord and the place where his glory dwells (Ps. 25:8). He showed with great discernment in many ways that he burned with this desire.

[Note: [Col. 0949] Witnesses 2 and 3 read *specialiter* (“especially”) for *perspicaciter* (“with discernment”).] It is unnecessary to touch upon it here in writing, since the memory of his illustrious deeds is still fresh, and among his people no one who loves faith and truth will cease to speak of him. Nevertheless, as we proposed, some of these matters must not be concealed in the silence of writing, for the example and instruction of very many writers.

It is impossible to unfold the deeds of so great a man through the daily advances of his virtues, or adequately to raise his great merits with praises worthy of his actions—merits which, far and wide, like a most prudent bee, he had gathered by doing good and supporting the poverty of the oppressed, so that he might be the good fragrance of Christ. For some this was life, but for others death. Those who, inflamed by the zeal of bitterness and ignorant of the liberal arts, attempted by slander and cursing to pervert pursuits utterly unlike their own—pursuits which they could neither alter nor knew how to honor—brought upon themselves death and perpetual woe, in accordance with the prophet’s threat:

> “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness!” (Isa. 5:20)

> “But whoever follows me,” says the Lord, “does not walk in darkness” (John 8:12).

[Note: [Col. 0949] In witness 2, the abbreviation or words *dicit Dominus* (“the Lord says”) are absent. Witness 1 has *arcium* for *artium* (“arts”); witness 3 has *deest* (“is absent”).]

This man certainly does not judge before the proper time, nor does he readily condemn anyone according to his own opinion. It is therefore the purpose of the good to displease the worst; hence they measure their lives not by the vanity of popular talk but by the truth of conscience.

### 15.

Before this man, learned in the law of the Lord, ascended the pontifical platform, the seditious citizens of our commonwealth—whom the spirit of Satan had inflamed to rise against the Lord’s anointed—had some hope of gaining possession of Cologne. They therefore supposed that they could either bind the magnanimous people of the Lotharian kingdom to themselves by a treaty of peace, or terrify them through repeated attacks of war, taking advantage of the location.

[Note: [Col. 0949] Witness 2 reads *Coloniam* (“Cologne”) rather than *Colonia*. Witness 3 has *arbitrantur* (“they suppose”) rather than *arbitrabantur* (“they supposed”).]

But after this son of peace, the ever-watchful guardian of God’s churches, entered the city, it cannot be said with what grief those enemies of peace in that kingdom were afflicted, or with what despair they were overwhelmed regarding the completion of their undertaking. Hence came blasphemies, curses, shameful insults, and inventions of impiety of many kinds. Truly, “iniquity lied to itself”: since they knew that the shepherd could neither be corrupted nor seduced in any way, they therefore tried, if such a fraud could succeed, to turn the flock away from his love by these displays of lies.

[Note: [Col. 0949] L reads *inimica* (“the hostile [iniquity]”) rather than *mentita* (“lied”). Witness 3 reads *quem* (“whom”) rather than *quia* (“because”).]

Learned and eminent men know how to incur envy, but they do not wish to possess it.

### 16.

At that time Mainz, a distinguished and wealthy city, was besieged by the emperor and his army. It was filled with enemies and plotters against the kingdom; and where the sincerity of religion had usually flourished, there the greatest cesspool of dissension had gathered.

There was varied talk among the nobles and the populace alike concerning the archbishop of the place. Some raised his innocence to heaven and praised his virtues; they said that he especially condemned the things being done everywhere, and particularly in those regions, wrongly amid the civil conflict. They claimed that he abhorred the factions and therefore withdrew from their midst, caring little to whom the city was open or to whom the soldiers gave obedience.

Such, for the most part, was the opinion of those who, bound together by an impious conspiracy, boasted that in everything they relied upon his constant assistance and counsel. They defended their cause on this sole ground: that the cause could not possibly be blameworthy if such a man was willing to associate with it.

Others—and nearly all those whose hearts divine grace had inspired—revered the authority ordained by God, followed the emperor with complete devotion, and regarded him as protector of resources, avenger of crimes, and bestower of honors.

Even those who were concerned with their household property, wives, and children, or for whom peace and personal safety had somehow become dear, judged this man’s merits quite differently.

For the present, let us leave these matters to God’s judgment and return from this digression to our subject.

### 17. (953)

The emperor therefore invited the new guardian and designated bishop of the city of Agrippina to a new council, having tested what he was capable of in mind and speech before this responsibility had been imposed upon him. There the favor of those assenting was divided on either side, and it was almost uncertain whom one ought rightly to trust.

This was heard more frequently—even from those serving in the royal camp: they praised the courage of the opposing party and preferred, in the same people, the innocence of their cause, saying that they had been compelled, and most unwillingly, to undertake this labor. Since no one, not even among the enemies, was found so insane as to blaspheme royal majesty, they attributed all the guilt and malice of the cruelty that had begun to his brother Henry, duke and illustrious margrave of Bavaria, a man feared by barbarians and all the peoples of those regions, even by the Greeks.

In truth, the better a person was, and the more ready to preserve faith toward the emperor and his kingdom, the more hated they held him to be.

[Note: [Col. 0951] Witnesses 2 and 3 have *Agrippine* for *Agripinae* (“of Agrippina”); witness 3 has *in* for *inter* (“among”). An editorial note paraphrases the point: “Thus they hated Henry because he was useful and faithful to the king.”]

Bruno, the glorious bishop desired by God’s people, voluntarily and willingly cast himself into the hatred directed against that impious and perjured faction of brigands. He gave no one an opportunity, by a divided heart or deceitful lips, either to conceal what he wished or to pretend what he did not wish. Thus he neither resolved to deceive another nor consented to be deceived by another.

Nevertheless, he first tested the hard hearts of the rebels, to see whether they could in any way be cured by the remedies of his life-giving persuasion and teaching. He delayed the final treatment with the cautery until, in pious solicitude, he had more carefully tested what this unbridled audacity promised him.

[Note: [Col. 0951] Witness 3 falsely begins a new chapter with *odivit* (“he hated”); the editor, aware of the error, placed it in the margin. Witness 3 omits *ab alio* (“by another”). Witness 3 also omits *dura* (“hard”) in *dura tentavit corda* (“he tested the hard hearts”). Witness 2 reads *quod* rather than *quid* (“what”).]

### 18.

The emperor’s son Liudulfus was a leader in that conspiracy, a young man uniquely illustrious and remarkable. If he had not believed his seducers, and had wished to be an heir rather than a traitor, he would have been capable not only of preserving but also of adorning the monuments of victory belonging to his fatherland. But because he hastened to become rich and did not deserve to obey his father’s counsel, what happened to him was in accordance with Solomon’s truthful saying: “An inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning will, in the end, lack blessing” (Prov. 20:21).

[Note: [Col. 0951] The name appears as *liodulfus* in witness 1 and *ludolfus* in witness 2. Witness 1 has the correction *confirmanda* (“to be strengthened”) in place of *conservanda* (“to be preserved”). Witness 3 reads *E. uero p.* for *Egregius ergo ut*, and witness 1 has *conteptu* for *contemptu* (“contempt”). Witness 3 omits *tui* (“your”) after *genitoris* (“father”), has *contristare* for *contristari* (“to grieve”), and omits *cum amicis* (“with friends”).]

Thus the outstanding and, as we have said, already designated future priest of the Lord, full of counsel and grieving over his brother’s contempt and his nephew’s destruction, received him under a pledge secured by hostages when he came to the camp with beastlike intent. He had him brought out of the crowd and addressed him privately:

> “You do not know, most illustrious of all the young men whom the earth has borne, how much good you will do for yourself and your people if you admit the words of my admonition into the secret places of your heart. You are the greatest concern of your most glorious father and our glory; what hope do you leave us if you remove yourself from our prayers?
>
> “Do you not regard the venerable gray hair of your pious father, whom it is not expedient for you to grieve or to injure? Do you not remember his paternal devotion toward you from your earliest childhood? Believe me: you offend God when you despise your father. There is no excuse for you. Whatever new undertaking you devise against this kingdom without his consent bears upon his injury.
>
> “You discuss your cause with your enemies, whereas you ought to do so with your friends. They seek in you not you, but what belongs to themselves; they care little for your safety; they measure everything by words, not by the truth of things. This is not wisdom.
>
> “See, I beg you, where they are leading you, lest they seduce you. You were the joy and crown of your father, the hope and delight of the whole kingdom; how have you been changed into bitterness? Stop at last being Absalom, so that you may be Solomon. Consider who exalted you so greatly, who bound all the princes of this kingdom to you by the sworn loyalty of their oaths. Why did he do this? Was it so that you might prove ungrateful? Was it so that you might learn to be a traitor? They are truly mad who wish to deceive you in this way. Fear your father’s daily sobs, dread his frequent groans, shudder at his tears.
>
> “He would bear with less distress the seizure of his entire kingdom by enemies than the fact that you, for whom he preserves the kingdom, have been seduced—alas!—by poisonous flatteries, though your innocent heart is his. The bosom of paternal devotion lies open; there is no deceit in it. Your pious father grieves that his son has been snatched from him by the wickedness of corrupt men; he will rejoice at your return.
>
> “If he is somewhat angrier with your seducers, he will quickly grow calm when he has received you, his delight, and he will judge that this was done not through crime but through error, when he realizes that you have been restored to him—you whom he loved even more than himself!”

[Note: [Col. 0951] Witness 3 adds *tectum* (“roof” or “shelter”) after *cogita* (“consider”). The text reads *fecit* (“he did”); L has *fecisti* (“you did”). Witness 3 omits *deest* (“is absent”) in one place. Witness 3 reads *tua* (“your things”) rather than *sua* (“their things”). Witness 3 adds *Non istud est sapere* (“This is not wisdom”) but omits *ne forte* (“lest perhaps”).]

### 19.

With these words and others like them, Lord Bruno, a good man skilled in speaking, concluded his appeal, being deeply concerned for the salvation of the most excellent young man. But the other, as though Erinnys had stirred his mind to the wickedness he had undertaken, would not allow his heart’s ear to attend to such admonitions; he approached them only with his external hearing, lest he appear too insolent.

For he considered it more honorable to seem innocent of the misery of this dissension than actually to be so. Anxiety and fear were stirred in his youthful mind by his most elegant companions, who, had they not been infected with the contagion of that impious conspiracy, could have been ornaments and a source of delight to imperial dignity. Surely such a desirable and strong-handed man, such an outstanding offspring, deserved to be escorted by such a procession and to glory in this chosen excellence of young men.

Above all, there was in his mind a certain stimulus: Cuono, previously a most courageous leader but then the boldest of brigands. There was also the glory of wealth and power, as they themselves boasted; but in truth there was sterile labor in place of tranquility and constant anxious care in place of security. They made the man who, so to speak, had everything in his hands, by his efforts to possess more, accomplish in every way that he possessed nothing.

Meanwhile, they strove by every means, by deception no less than by force; they rested neither by day nor by night; they made their opponents suspicious of one another; they left nothing unattempted and considered nothing too costly, provided they could obtain possession, by whatever ingenuity, of the greatest and wealthiest cities within the kingdom. From there, they supposed, they could easily rule throughout all the borders of the kingdom.

And so that nothing might be done entirely without fraud, they dealt secretly with Arnold, an especially energetic man who at that time had been entrusted with supreme authority in the land of the Bavarians. By endless promises and by recalling the old hatred, they induced him first to renounce his allegiance to Duke Henry, then the distinguished city of Regensburg, and finally that whole kingdom, through perjury.

[Note: [Col. 0953] Witnesses 1 and 2 read *erinis* for *Erinnis* (“Erinys”); all three read *acceptum* for *coeptum* (“undertaken”); witness 2 has *tabe* for *tabo* (“contagion”); witnesses 2 and 3 add an uncertain abbreviated reading after *possent*; witness 3 has *ut neque* for *neque*, *adversarios interdum* for *adversarios inter se*, and *impetraturos* (“to obtain”) for *imperaturos* (“to rule”).

[Note: [Col. 0953D] “Count palatine, to whom Henry had entrusted Bavaria.” See *Life of Ulrich*, chapter 10. Witness 2 reads *secretas* (“secret things”) rather than *secretius* (“more secretly”). Witness 3 supplies *Regensburg* in the margin.]

Such strength did envy and hatred claim for themselves among them. At the same time they urged on the Hungarians, the ancient plague of their homeland, to invade the kingdom divided against itself, supposing that in this way the anxiety weighing upon them could either be entirely removed or at least diminished.

### 20.

[Note: [Col. 0953] Witness 1 reads *imputa* for *ut puta* (“as though”); witness 3 has *et* and omits *castris* (“camp”) in the phrase concerning departure from the camp.]

Moved by this matter, so sudden and unexpected, and grieving more for their misery than for his own loss, the emperor at last abandoned the siege of Mainz after accepting the agreement that was offered. He arranged to depart hastily from the camp toward the east with those whom he had found faithful, in order to attend to the affairs of those regions. He sent his brother Bruno westward as guardian and administrator—or, to speak more precisely, as archduke—in so perilous a time. He gave him these instructions:

> “I cannot tell you, dearest brother, how much I rejoice that we have always thought alike and that our desires have never differed in any matter. This is what consoles me most amid my bitter circumstances: to see that, by the grace of Almighty God, royal priesthood has been added to our imperial authority.
>
> “In you both priestly religion and royal courage are powerful, so that you know how to give each person his due, which is justice, and are able to resist either the terror or the fraud of our adversaries, which belongs to courage and justice.
>
> “Nor, as I have long understood, is the mother of the liberal arts—and philosophy, the true virtue—absent from you; she has trained you to this modesty and greatness of spirit. I know, my brother, I know that no one will persuade your prudence that it is irrelevant to you how much the wicked exult in the ruin of the good, no matter with what verbal show of honesty they conceal what they intend.
>
> “Perhaps they will say that these matters must be settled by wars, that they do not concern you, and that they do not suit the dignity of your office. You see how many the deceitful boastfulness of such words has led astray in this metropolis, and how many it has incited to the frenzy of civil disaster. If its bishop wished to withdraw from dissension, as he pretends, and from the danger of wars, so that he might live in religious leisure, he would certainly have returned to us and to our commonwealth, rather than to the enemies, what we had bestowed upon him through royal munificence.
>
> “I call them enemies, as nearly everyone regards them: wicked brigands among the citizens, traitors to their homeland, devastators of the kingdom, and deserters from military service. They wished to kill me myself, I believe, with their sacrilegious hands, or to have me perish by whatever most bitter form of death; they have taken my son from me and strive to deprive my brother of the kingdom, his children, his very dear wife, and finally life itself.
>
> “You alone are at last my solid, faithful, and steadfast consolation. From your earliest age you have advanced so far in good deeds that doing good and surveying everything with the greatest diligence have now, through habit, become part of your nature. If, while you are safe, I may enjoy you happily and wholly, as my mind always desires, my longing demands, and my spirit implores, then dignity, glory, and honor will be present. We have protection enough and more than enough; let us not fail ourselves!
>
> “This above all must be carefully guarded. You are my witness—yes, you—that with what care and benevolence I fostered, protected, and embraced these men whom I now endure as so cruel, though I would still most willingly heal them if they were willing to spare themselves. Ah, with what unreasonable haste they rush toward destruction and turn my innocently raised offspring toward every crime! Thus it is exceedingly difficult for those who, through ambition, prefer not to be good but to be seen as good, to exercise restraint in positions of power.
>
> “You know, dearest brother—something I recall with grief—that those whom I had more generously supported, whom I had loved as my closest allies in many circumstances, and whom I had regarded as most closely joined to me, were often harsher and more faithless toward me. This was grievous to endure, a double misery. But what presses upon me outweighs the earlier evils: the one whom I fathered has been snatched from me and has learned to lie in wait for paternal devotion.
>
> “Strive, therefore, man devoted to God—not merely as before, but now above all. Strive, I beg you, by that counsel in which you are especially skilled, so that according to place and time you may either dissuade them from arms or restrain them by whatever means you can. Though absent from you in body, wherever I may be I shall rejoice in you and give thanks for your foresight and moderation. May I be pleased to reckon as mine whatever you do, and may you likewise be pleased with whatever I do.
>
> “I wish and earnestly desire that the sum of our hopes and our delight may be this: not only before God but also before human beings, that we provide one another with the good things that are, and, if possible, maintain peace with everyone.”

Then, after they had fallen into one another’s arms, they parted from each other with tears: the emperor turning eastward and his brother westward.

[Note: [Col. 0953] Witness 2 adds *rebus* (“circumstances”) after *acerbis* (“bitter”). Witness 3 omits *quantos seduxit* (“how many it led astray”); the marginal identification of the metropolitan’s bishop is “Frederick of Mainz.” Witness 1 has *arcium* for *artium* (“arts”) and *uirtutum* (“virtues”) for *uirtutem* (“virtue”). Leibniz prefers *constantiae* (“steadfastness”) to *fortitudinis* or *justitiae* in the phrase concerning resistance to adversaries. Witnesses 1 and 2 read *vellent* (“they would wish”) rather than *velent* (“they conceal”). Witness 3 supplies the fuller phrase *r. v. m. d.*, “traitors to their homeland, devastators of the kingdom, deserters from military service.” Witness 2 has *fratrum* (“brothers”) and witness 3 *fratre* (“brother”) in place of *fratrem*. Witness 3 reads *artibus* (“arts”) rather than *actibus* (“deeds”). Witnesses 1 and 2 read *veniret* (“would come”) rather than *venerit* (“has come”). Witness 3 has *magnis* (“great”) rather than *magis* (“more”). Witness 3 reads *existimavi* (“I judged”) rather than *aestimavi* (“I regarded”). Witness 3 has *perpessum* (“suffered”) rather than *perpessu* (“to be endured”). Witness 3 reads *identidem* (“repeatedly”) rather than *itidem* (“likewise”).]

### 21.

He soon hastened to the palace at Aachen.

[Editorial note: On the date of the election and ordination, compare the Ballerini edition of Ratherius’ works, p. LXXVII. Ratherius was elected and consecrated on the very day on which Bruno was elected and consecrated; Robert, archbishop of Trier; Balderic, bishop of Utrecht; Hildebold, bishop of Minden; Drogo, bishop of Osnabrück; Berengar, bishop of Verdun; and Fulbert, bishop of Cambrai were also present.

Ratherius relates the matter as follows in *Phrenesis*, chapter 1:

> “Driven from the episcopate of Verona in Italy, where he had been ordained, and having sought the assistance of the most glorious King Otto, although no opportunity for restoration had preceded him, and although the most pious king himself was striving to secure it, when the opportunity was granted through the intervention and accomplishment of his brother Bruno, the archbishop, after he had been sought out at the palace called Aachen in the presence of that same king—not only by those more especially concerned, but also by bishops, abbots, counts, and the leading men of the entire kingdom—on the fourth feria of the solemn fast of the seventh month, he was again elected on the following Sunday by the people of the Church of Liège. He was appointed and solemnly enthroned in that same Church by seven fellow bishops, two of whom were archbishops and the rest bishops: namely Bruno, Robert, Balderic, Hildebold, Drogo, Berengar, and Fulbert. This occurred with the assent of the decrees and with the agreement and example of certain of the ancients to whom the same thing had happened, amid the greatest favor of the entire people who were present.
>
> “Afterward, through the ingenuity and accomplishment of the aforementioned Balderic, and through the public force of Counts Regener and Ruodolf—whose nephew, and also Balderic’s brother’s son, was a certain boy of the same name, so that it may not be difficult to conjecture what had happened, and so that the neglect of the quality of the persons may be evident in every respect—because the king’s brother was afraid that the counts mentioned might defect from the king to Conrad, who was then acting against him, and become hostile to him; or, as his defenders assert more truthfully, because the archbishop, as he had desired, could find no helper among the bishop’s friends or soldiers, he was expelled. At Mainz he enjoyed, most abundantly, the exceedingly generous kindness of Archbishop William, the king’s son.
>
> “Having been given leisure, he took care to set down in books the events that had taken place around him, laboring to ensure that their character should not remain hidden even from the curious of his own time. When those two particular enemies of his, Robert and Balderic, heard this, they said that he was insane.”

[Editorial note: The phrase *plebis vel ejusmodi vocabulum deest* means, “the word *plebs* or a similar term is absent.”]

There he met the princes of the kingdom concerned in the matter, instructed them in many and various ways, and urged above all that they should not trust the seducers or their empty promises, should not fear their threats, and should prefer no pledges to their loyalty toward the royal majesty and toward himself. He promised that, before the time and at the time, he would always be ready—even at the risk of his own life, should this be necessary—to restore the Church’s violated peace.

Having done this, he came joyfully to Cologne; the time of ordination was awaited, and the saving joy of anointing. When this had been done, the people’s joy was renewed, and, arrayed in the robe of gladness, the priest of the Lord and Saviour shone forth before all who had assembled. Thereafter precious nard gave forth its fragrance; in the midst of the Church he opened his mouth (Exod. 28:35). In accordance with the legal ordinance, the sound of one entering the house of the Lord God was heard; he became an example and instruction unto salvation for all who obeyed him.

What he did, how he taught, and in what manner he devoted himself for the peace of God’s Churches are wonderful in the doing and difficult in the telling. For the daily works of this man so surpassed the notable achievements of his predecessors that all he had done—whether in enlarging or restoring churches, in transferring relics and bodies of saints into his diocese, in constructing private or public buildings, or in ordering the affairs of the household and family of God’s holy Church—seemed almost incomparable with the works of others.

For, as he understood beyond all his teachers, so he directed the keenness of his heart, the sharpness of his intellect, and the strength of his spirit toward greater works of wisdom and virtue. Concerning religion first and the worship of God—what the Greeks call *theosebeian* (θεοσέβειαν), “reverence for God”—following, according to the wisdom given him, canonical and apostolic authority, he established that the multitude belonging to his venerable see in its various congregations should be of one heart and one soul; that superfluity of clothing, inequality of conduct, and whatever else of this kind seemed effeminate or unseemly in his Church should be most carefully cut away by true and spiritual circumcision, which is the beginning of wisdom; and that all concerned should live with the greatest diligence, according to the rule prescribed for them, intent upon the divine ministries, and should in no way regard anything else as the ground of their salvation.

[Note: [Col. 0955] Witness 3 reads *palatium* (“palace”) rather than *palatii* (“of the palace”). Witness 3 reads *terrerent* (“they should terrify”) rather than *timerent* (“they should fear”). Witness 3 reads *autem* (“however”) rather than *ante* (“before”); the manuscript omits *se* (“himself”). Witness 2 has *vel* (“or”) rather than *ut* (“so that”). Witness 1 reads *actum*, corrected to *actu* (“in the doing”). Witnesses 2 and 3 read *in privatis* (“in private [buildings]”) for *in privatis vel publicis* (“in private or public [buildings]”). Witness 2 reads *operam* (“work”) rather than *opera* (“works”). Witness L has *superos* (“those above”) rather than *super omnes* (“beyond all”). Witness 1 reads *dilexit* (“he loved”) rather than *direxit* (“he directed”). Witness 1 has *theofebian* rather than *theosebian*. Witness 1 reads *diversi* (“different”) rather than *diversis* (“various”); witness 3 omits *hoc modo* (“in this manner”); witness 3 has *mysteriis* (“mysteries”) rather than *ministeriis* (“ministries”). L reads *diligentissime* (“most diligently”) rather than *intentissime* (“most intently”).]

### 22.

He frequently discussed these and similar matters with the venerable fathers and the elders of his clergy, and earnestly admonished them to keep watch with him over the Lord’s flock. Because the fault of the times pressed upon him, so that he could confer with them less often than he wished, he burned with even greater solicitude when absent than when present, fervent in spirit and serving the Lord.

Without were fightings, within fears. He fought against the rage of wolves desiring to lay waste God’s Church; he feared for the simplicity of the Lord’s sheep, as the Apostle says: “I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by his craftiness, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity which is in Christ Jesus” (2 Cor. 11:3).

Thus, with a breast trained against every adversity, he was most steadfast; nor did such a spirit waver in prosperity. By circumstances and frequent exercises alike he taught all subject to him to be diligent in preserving the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. By that singular agility of mind he seemed almost to have surpassed the general maxim that, when the mind is divided among many things, it becomes less effective in each.

Therefore, compelled by imperial authority, he undertook, as has been said, the administration of the kingdom’s affairs among the Lotharians. Although he assigned to every prince and magistrate his own burden and enjoined on each the work suited to him, there was nevertheless nothing that he did not himself attend to, foreseeing with the greatest quickness of counsel what was advantageous for all.

[Note: [Col. 0957] Witness 1 reads *fruens* (“enjoying”) rather than *fervens* (“fervent”); witnesses 2 and 3 read *foris* (“outside”) rather than *foras* (“without”). Witness 3 omits *cogente* (“compelling”). Witnesses 2 and 3 have *Lotharicos* (“Lotharian”) rather than *apud Lotharios* (“among the Lotharians”). Witness 3 omits the phrase concerning the distribution of burdens and assignments of suitable tasks.]

### 23.

Perhaps some, ignorant of the divine dispensation, ask why a bishop administered public affairs and the dangers of war when he had undertaken the care of souls alone. The thing itself readily answers them, if they have any sound judgment, when they see the great and, especially in those regions, unprecedented good of peace spread far and wide through this guardian and teacher of the faithful people—lest in this matter they stumble any longer as though in darkness, where the presence of light is absent.

Nor was such governance of this world new, or previously unfamiliar to the rulers of God’s holy Church; examples are ready to hand for anyone who seeks them.

[Note: [Col. 0957] Witness 3 reads *hujusmodi* (“of this kind”) for *hujus mundi* (“of this world”), and *si quesierit* (“if he seeks”) rather than *si quis requisierit* (“if anyone should seek”). Witness 2 adds *hic* (“here”). It also inserts the following gloss: “Let no one therefore call him blameworthy on this matter, since we read that holy Samuel and many other priests were likewise judges, and that we read that the prophet Daniel condemned two priests to death.” This gloss is partly drawn from Widukind I.31 and was inserted into the text by witness 2 in its usual manner.]

But, hastening to other matters, we leave to each man’s own judgment what he may say about this pious man, knowing that no one is of sound mind who attempts to obscure a most evident good with any reproach of slander. For everything that he did was honorable and beneficial to our commonwealth.

Yet he did not set this end upon his deeds, that they should fly abroad only by winning favor through human mouths; rather, he lived and ordered his works before human beings so that he was a terror to the worst and an honor to the good. By these things it became plainly known to all that in the episcopate he had desired a good work, for which even his envious rivals could not easily blame him—unless it should redound still more to his praise that he displeased such people.
