Held fast, therefore, in this wonderful work, the ever-watchful laborer of the highest householder and supreme bishop, bearing in his hands a burning lamp—that is, the example of good work—led the willing and drew the unwilling toward the things of God.

[Note: [Col. 0957] Witness 1 reads *offendit* (“he stumbles”) and witness 2 *offendunt* (“they stumble”) rather than *offendant* (“they may stumble”). Witness 1 has *uelle*, corrected to *utile* (“useful”); witness 2 also reads *velle*.]

### 24. (954)

But amid these things the ancient plague of the human race did not cease to scatter far and wide the poison of its envy against the works of the pious teacher, now germinating in good hope. For when at last the people of the Lotharian kingdom, scarcely induced by the manifold exhortation of this great man, began to try the charms of peace, wholly unfamiliar to them, and for the most part refused, to their own destruction, to give assent to those who promised themselves security only through civil discord, the savage nation of the Hungarians—barbarity such as our land had never felt—enticed by perverse citizens, crossed most of Germany’s provinces and poured itself over the whole of Gaul, where the noble people of the Franks had long since settled, intending to lay everything waste with sword and fire.

In this campaign Cuono, formerly an outstanding duke, served with his followers—whether in order by this foul cruelty to satisfy his hatred, conceived against Bruno, the man of God, certainly most gentle toward the good, or to help whomsoever he could in so great a danger, is uncertain; but the former account was more widely circulated.

For even before this, because his strength had failed him, he had deceitfully attempted every harsh measure against Bruno: he tried to seize the very wealthy city of Metz by stratagem, made himself suspect to Cologne itself and to the other fortifications of the kingdom, hurled reproaches, and poured out threats. For some time afterward he persisted in the same ferocity in which he had long been.

He left nothing unattempted by which he thought that he could dissolve the compact made among our people through the wisdom of their teacher. A short time before he had been a man of the greatest power and the greatest fortune, but he did not know how he ought to use prosperity. Since, after abusing these things, he lost them, he raged against the good with excessive impatience; yet, by God’s ordering, he was always repulsed from his wicked designs, so that he deeply repented of having undertaken so great a crime with such levity.

[Note: [Col. 0957] Witness 1 reads *exhortatione* (“exhortation”) rather than *exercitatione* (“exercise”); witness 3 has *hujus exercitatione* (“this man’s exercise”) and marks *indoctus* (“unlearned”). Witness 3 omits the phrase *praebere respueret* (“refused to give assent”). Witness 3 reads *Germaniae et plerisque* (“of Germany and most of”) rather than *transitis Germaniae plerisque* (“having crossed most of Germany”). Witness 1 has *pius* (“pious”) rather than *prius* (“formerly”). Witness 2 reads *aliquantum* (“somewhat”) rather than *aliquantulum* (“a little”). Witness 1 has *sevit* (“he raged”) rather than *saevit*; witness 2 reads *inspexit* (“looked upon”) and witness 3 *infelix* (“unhappy”) in place of *inflexit* (“bent”).]

### 25.

In all things, however, the merciful and compassionate Lord spared his priest and the pious guardian of his people, and so ordered everything that grave dangers were often calmed without war and without human destruction. Amid such things he himself, undaunted and intent upon his duties, would either read or discuss the greatest matters, as though unaware of pressing anxieties.

At Trier and in Alsace this became known to nations and peoples: with what constancy and serenity of mind he reproved the unstable and reckless movements of his adversaries, when he showed that those who boasted of being most valiant in matters belonging to others were so weak in their own. Indeed, those whom no battle and no hardship had ever bent, the piety of this man made unwarlike and timid.

He was to be feared for counsel and a multitude of good men, not for cruelty; and no enemy kept such keen watch for destruction as he did for salvation. He was moved least of all by reputation and the judgment of the crowd; he exercised his own judgment, and in whatever he found right he sought to please not himself but God.

Thus—to comprehend much in few words and omit more—an indefatigable soldier of the Lord within and without, at home and in warfare, he contended, more by the strength of his spirit than of his body, against the pestilent and restless, and often at the peril even of his own life, until the fame of his name, wherever it reached, calmed wars, established peace, strengthened zeal in every good art, and enlarged the grace of holy religion and saving tranquillity.

[Note: [Col. 0959] Witness 1 reads *pacis* (“of peace”) for *paucis* (“in few words”).]

Ratherius eodem die quo Bruno electus et consecratus est, praesentibus praeterea Rotberto Trevirensi archiepiscopo, Balderico Ultrajectino, Hildebaldo Mimigardevordensi, Druogone Osnabrugensi, Berengario Virdunensi, Folberto Cameracensi episcopis. Ratherius in Phrenesi haec ita narrat (c. I.): «Pulsus episcopio Veronensi Italiae, [Col. 0955D] ordinatus ubi fuerat, cum ad gloriosissimi regis se contulisset Ottonis auxilium, copiaque restitutionis praecessisset nulla, ipso quoque piissimo rege conante, data optione, interventu fratris ejus Brunonis archipraesulis atque patratu, postquam electus coram eodem ad Aquas quod dicitur Grani palatium, non solum ab his quorum intererat specialius, sed et ab episcopis, abbatibus, comitibus, totiusque regni primoribus quarta solemnis jejunii septimi mensis feria fuerat expetitus: rursum sequenti Dominica ab eodem, hoc est Leodicensis Ecclesiae populo electus, septem a coepiscopis, duo quorum fuerant archipraesules, caeteri praesules, praelibato scilicet Brunone, Rodberto, Baldrico, Hildibaldo, Druogone, Berengario, atque Folberto, conniventia decretorum, consensu atque exemplis nonnullorum, quibus et id contigerat, antiquorum, summo totius quae [Col. 0956C] aderat [ [Col. 0955D] Plebis vel ejusmodi vocabulum deest.] favore, destinatus eidem atque solemniter inthronizatus Ecclesiae; cumque postea ingenio jam fati Baldrici, patratuque, qui eum super ambonem Ecclesiae Coloniensis spectanti cuncto specialius collaudaverat populo, Rodberti Trevirorum archiepiscopi, vi publica comitum Regeneri atque Ruoduolti---nepos ipsorum, qui et filius fratris exstiterat Baldrici, talia ut quid contigerint ne difficile sit conjectari ejusdem nominis [Col. 0956D] puer quidam ut institueretur---et ut per omnia materies personarum acceptione pateat neglecta, timiditate jam dicti regis germani---ne scilicet jam fati comites a rege ad Conradum, qui tunc contra ipsum agebat, deficerent sibique cum eo inimicarentur, vel, quod verius ipsius asserunt defensores, resistendo, quia nullum habere potuit idem archiepiscopus, ut inhiaverat, ex episcopi amicis vel militibus adjutorem---fuisset expulsus, Moguntiaeque benignitate archiepiscopi Willihelmi filii regis munificentissima copiosissime frueretur: data otii occasione, curavit, quae circa eum acta fuerant, in libros digerere, qualitas elaborans ne vel curiosis lateret sui temporis. Utique hoc audientes duo illi ejus specialius inimici, Rodbertus videlicet et Baldricus, dixerunt eum phreneticum esse.» — The long editorial note compares the Ballerini edition, lists the bishops present at Ratherius’s and Bruno’s elections and consecrations, and quotes Ratherius’s *Phrenesis* on his election, enthronement, expulsion, refuge at Mainz, and enemies Robert and Balderic; all names, offices, column breaks, and the embedded lacuna are retained verbatim in the source note.

[Col. 0959D] **26.** Since, therefore, this humble Christ-loving man (*philochristus*) [Note: [Col. 0959] *phylochristus* in 1.] and ardent emulator of the better spiritual gifts, the servant of the Lord Bruno, ought, in accordance with the dignity of his see, to be distinguished also by the privilege of the Roman see and apostolic blessing, and to be united with those who preserve the sound doctrine handed down by the blessed apostle Peter [Note: [Col. 0959] That is, “they preserved,” or “they have to, or ought to, preserve.”], in the integrity of catholic faith, in true confession, and in the inviolable truth of preaching, he sent his synodal letter through Hadamar, venerable abbot of the monastery of Fulda, to Agapitus, the pope of extraordinary holiness. In it he made known what spirit was his, and that he was a shepherd chosen from among the sheep and sent by the Lord. There he was called the harmonious fellow-citizen of the apostles, the prince [Note: [Col. 0959] Perhaps *princeps apostolorum*, “prince of the apostles,” should be read.] and propagator of the Lord’s commandments.

The legate returned from there with great gladness of heart and brought to the pious shepherd, to whom by God’s grace the oil of joy had previously been granted, according to the prophet, instead of mourning [Note: [Col. 0959] *tui* corrected for *luctu* in 1.], the pallium of praise instead of the spirit of sorrow. For the Spirit of God divinely inspired the steadfast man, intent more upon the magnificent power of this sacrament [Note: [Col. 0959] *sacrae menti*, “to the sacred mind,” in L.; *virtutis* in 3.] than upon the things performed visibly, to lift his heart into hope through—or [Note: [Col. 0959] “or,” in 3.]—spiritual joy, so that he would not be saddened by the labor he perceived to be impending. “The heart knows the bitterness of its own soul, and no stranger will share in its joy” (Prov. XIV, 10). These are the words of Wisdom.

**27.** The legate, then, as we have begun to say, returning from Rome, hastened to carry the good news to Cologne, bearing the sacred vestment sent by the universal pontiff, presenting the Lord’s sweet yoke and light burden, as well as the humble ministry administered under it, of which the Lord’s words testify when he says: “He who is greatest among you shall be your minister” (Mark X, [Col. 0960C] 43). At the same time he brought relics from the actual body of the holy martyr Pantaleon and a privilege bestowed by the authority of apostolic majesty. By this privilege the priest of the Lord was permitted, contrary to custom, to put on the same pallium whenever he wished [Note: [Col. 0959] *quoties* in 1; *interdum*, “sometimes.”]; and, since all that was requested had been granted, he was admitted, because of the greatness of his virtue and wisdom, to a share in that work and almost to a seat beside such dignity [Note: [Col. 0959] The reading is uncertain in 1 (*ip*).].

The joyful city hurried out to meet him, and a crowd came running from every direction with acclamations. They gathered in the suburb near the ancient place where the church of that precious martyr stood, still neglected and close to ruin. There the welcome burdens were deposited, and afterward each was placed in its proper location.

**28.** [Note: [Col. 0959] Here, at this point, the division into three chapters is indicated for the first time by the sign § and the number III in 1.]

The festive gathering at that place—festive then, but shortly afterward, alas, turned into a funeral gathering—prompts me to linger here for a while. There that venerable vestment [Note: [Col. 0959] *amictus*; 3 has *amicus*, “friend.”] was received for the first time and there for the last time: once with joyful song, once with mournful song. For the body of the religious and God-worthy priest, which was to be buried there, did not lose the insignia of his office, although, as we believe, his soul carried them away spiritually [Col. 0961A] and therefore happily [Note: [Col. 0961] *in Deo*, “in God,” in L.].

By the hidden counsel of almighty God it was provided that this place should, on this first occasion, be made illustrious for declaring the merits of his holy martyr [Note: [Col. 0961] omitted in 3.], and should become such a place that this peaceful and wonderfully humble man would above all choose, under the protection of that same devout martyr, to await lifeless the day of the dread judgment and the glory of the future resurrection.

Not long afterward, in that same place—so to speak, in a more secluded spot [Note: [Col. 0961] The words “not long afterward, in that same place, in a more secluded spot” are absent in 3.] and one more remote from the nuisance of urban unrest—he established brothers, vigilant and attentive in divine praise, to serve the Lord under the discipline of the monastic rule. Over them he placed an abbot named Christian, namely, a *foronomus* of his own profession, and a man thoroughly learned in the law of the Lord, as this order required.

To him, once he had been ordained, he wrote this brief admonition from the western regions:

> Take care to be what you are called. Do not degenerate from your *gentilitas*. Strive earnestly for this: let it not, as before, become antiquated; but press on from virtue to virtue!

**29.** He was never so detained by the business of civic affairs—to which he was drawn not by personal desire but by the needs of the people—that, with his mind so vigorous in every matter, he did not remain active, especially intent upon religion and reading, in whose pursuit he seemed to be dying. By his example and frequent admonition he inflamed almost everyone whom he had before his eyes to undertake this work.

But he was deeply distressed by those who did not love it in this way. Although they were otherwise his intimates, he removed them from the private and friendly place of grief where he was accustomed to disclose himself to himself more freely and therefore more carefully. The heart of the steadfast man was utterly weary of royal luxury and of the customary enticements of games and pleasures offered to the powerful, especially at that time. Thus, whenever he was somehow compelled to give his own people what he ought not to have given them, he usually wiped away this small excess with a more abundant flood of tears.

He feared the present life, even when it was pleasant, and he had learned it through bitterness. As for the life free from every anxiety and weakness, there is no doubt that he thought about it above all things, since he discussed it so clearly and so often, both with his intimates and before the people entrusted to him. [Note: [Col. 0961] *quid*, “what,” in 1.]

**30.** Though he was young and surrounded by every kind of pomp, I dare to say that he wished to depart, if only he might be with Christ. Hence came his constant tears, almost continual sighs, secret prayers, and sobs that resounded more loudly even in his bed, as those who could conceal this from him less easily testify, even when he wished to remain hidden.

How often did he set the day of death before the eyes of his heart! How often did he burst forth in words concerning what he had conceived in his heart! How often did we hear him, with vehement groaning, prefer what he hoped would come, though not without grave trembling: that he might safely escape the raging shipwreck of this world by God’s mercy alone and at last stand upon the shore of inward security!

He was thought somehow to be about to escape, so as to flee, as though from death, everything that charmed him amid the delights of this world. Many witnesses of his manner of life remain; whenever they perceived him in private, with a contrite heart and humbled spirit, they could marvel at him more than imitate him.

For although he was generally a man of the people, he lived almost as a solitary. Strange to say, among the most cheerful banqueters he himself often abstained. He repeatedly avoided the soft and delicate clothing in which he had been raised and brought to manhood, even in the houses of kings. Among his purple-clad ministers and soldiers, glittering with gold, he himself put on a cheap tunic and rustic sheepskins.

He strongly despised the pleasures of the bed. In the baths, he was scarcely ever washed among those who bathed and sought the brightness of their skin; this is all the more remarkable because from his very cradle he had been brought up amid such cleanliness and royal pomp. [Note: [Col. 0961] *multocies* in 1 here.] He did these things, according to time and place, sometimes openly and sometimes more secretly, both to evade human praise and nevertheless to provide his subjects with an example by doing them. Many advance more through examples than through words.

Among the gentle and humble no one was humbler; against the wicked and the haughty no one was more forceful. Both native and foreigner feared this man—the terror of those who could not be bound by kindness. In a proper and most fitting order, everyone to whom the fame of his greatness reached first became accustomed to fear him and afterward to love him.

**31.** He gathered from every direction the bodies and relics of saints and every kind of memorial, in order to increase their patronage for his people and to spread the glory of the Lord through many peoples far and near by this renown. He prepared places and ministries [Note: [Col. 0961] *monasteria omnia*, “all the monasteries,” in 2 and 3.] for them with abundant expense and provision. More could be said about each of these, if the promised brevity allowed it.

These things are signs of an unconquered faith, by which he sought not what was his own [Note: [Col. 0961] “because they are not his own,” in 3.], but what belonged to Jesus Christ. Everyone knows with what diligence, fervor, and joy he brought the staff and chain of Saint Peter to Cologne—the former from Metz, the latter from Rome. In his honor he wondrously enlarged his most honored church, making what was beautiful most beautiful.

The renowned and illustrious martyrs Patroclus, Eliphius [Note: [Col. 0961] *Elisius* in 1.], Privatus, and Gregory—whose deeds are magnificent, whose merits glorious, and whose protection secure—as well as the precious relics of Christopher and Saint Pantaleon, as has already been said, to whom he more especially entrusted himself as patrons, he drew from various places with marvelous ceremony to the most holy seat of his Church, as though they were most welcome jewels and sweetest pledges.

What happened through the administration of this pious provider concerning the translation of the blessed Evergislus, the third archbishop of that see, is known to many. After he had been placed in the church of the blessed virgin Cecilia with hymns and the celebration of divine praise, the religious people venerate and honor him so greatly that you might think they were reciprocating daily services to one present through his abundant gifts.

[Col. 0963A] [Note: [Col. 0963] In place of the words “known to many … reciprocating,” 2 gives the *Translations of Saints Evergislus and Patroclus*, continuing as follows: “we did not think [it] should be suppressed. Concerning the translation of Saint Evergislus [lacuna] he knows it to have been fulfilled in himself.” With Leibniz, we have placed this work after the end of this *Life*, since it did not proceed from Ruotger but was composed in imitation of his narrative. But the following prevents us from supposing it older than Ruotger and inserted by him into his work: although the author has already spoken briefly above about Patroclus, in this translation the discourse returns to him again, omitting the remaining saints; this is too inept for us to attribute it to Ruotger. Moreover, the words “the metropolitan city [lacuna] extended” and “is venerated even to the present day” clearly could not have been written at that very time, but only later.]

**32.** The other delights and gifts of salvation that he bestowed upon the sons of his Church in so brief a time cannot be weighed or estimated. He gathered them with religious affection and devotion from almost every region and boundary of the world, as though anticipating what was to come: that, in view of the brevity of his days, he might establish enduring gifts for the flock entrusted to him. Yet he took particular care to ensure that those from whom they were taken would feel desire, while those to whom they were brought would experience increased joy; so that both groups, summoned by the good fragrance of Christ that is in the martyrs—or rather, which the martyrs themselves are—though stirred by different emotions, might more eagerly seek what they had neglected, and might perpetually venerate what they rejoiced had been transferred to them.

For whoever does not know how to love the good he possesses, if it is taken away from him, may perhaps learn to love the good of which he is deprived; and, while it is absent, he will possess it more fruitfully in memory than he possessed it uselessly in its presence. In this way that evangelical saying was fulfilled: “To everyone who has, more shall be given, and he shall abound; but from him who does not have, even what he has shall be taken away” (Matt. XXV, 29). [Note: [Col. 0963] *quis* in 3.]

**33.** Meanwhile, in many places throughout the parishes of his bishopric, this faithful and prudent servant of the Lord zealously raised from their foundations churches, monasteries, and other buildings suited to the service of the Lord God and the honor of his saints; he enlarged some that had previously been founded with distinction, and repaired others that had long lain in ruins.

In each of these he arranged, through the prudent skill of his mind, for men who would serve almighty God under the rule of canonical life; and, lest anything should be lacking to them according to their manner of life, he provided generously by careful administration. The memorials of this work and most salutary devotion endure, firmly established in the places where these things were done [Note: [Col. 0963] *monumenta aere perenniora*, “memorials more enduring than bronze,” in 3.], so that they will never permit the memory of so great a man to be obscured by any age, but will preserve it for the praise and glory of Jesus Christ.

He spread the same work among foreign nations and throughout the kingdom entrusted to his care: partly by example, partly by his own work, partly through the differing qualities of persons and frequent admonition. For he did not permit any of his people either to be occupied uselessly or to grow sluggish in idle leisure. He used to declare that “the lazy beast must be kept away from the feeding troughs,” and, according to the Apostle: “Let him who does not work not eat” (II Thess. III, 10).

All the good things that he did, taught, and loved cannot be recorded individually. There will always be such an abundance of material for those who undertake this task [Note: [Col. 0963] *materieri* in 1.] that they will certainly grow weary before completing what they have begun.

Now, concerning his preaching of the word of God, the subtlety of his disputations, and the sincerity of the Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0963] “and the sublimity,” in 3; omitted in 2 and 3 after *disputationum*.], we can marvel at what and how great he was, but we cannot define it. He poured forth so abundantly, in sound discourse, the teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ and the doctrine that accords with piety, that no one who hears this and understands it rightly will doubt that he was full of the wisdom of God through which all things were made.

And so that this keen investigator of the things belonging to Jesus Christ might leave nothing unattempted that could serve divine worship, whenever he found, either within the enclosures of his sheepfolds or outside them, men who desired a solitary life in order to fight the devil with singular courage, he received them with every mark of reverence, fortified them with the charitable consolation of his exhortation, and enclosed them in various monastic and ecclesiastical cells—some singly, others in pairs—with suitable ecclesiastical testimony and the religious service appropriate to the situation [Note: [Col. 0963] “the testimony of God and the Church,” in 3.]. Yet no access was open among them except by speech and sight.

Through the most faithful stewards of his administration he carefully supplied them with expenses and whatever seemed necessary to human weakness. Especially on the feasts of the apostles, whenever they occurred during the year, he visited each of them individually with suitable gifts. Thus, in accordance with the clear standard of apostolic teaching, he prudently took care to do what is good “not only before God but also before human beings” (Rom. XII, 17) [Note: [Col. 0963] “before everyone,” in 3.], so that people of every disposition or condition, if they sought God, might either be approved among his disciples or be instructed by them.

**34.** Concerning the servants of God who had devoted themselves to divine religion in the monastery of Saint Mary, and concerning the canons transferred to the church of the holy apostle Andrew [Note: [Col. 0963D] “Which belonged to the monastery of Saint Mary.”], as well as any other matters of this kind, he certainly left no small difficulty—but only for those whose mental vision is not sufficiently strong to discern clearly his sincere intention in his various works [Note: [Col. 0964D] Namely, “he left only such a difficulty.”].

If they would observe that it is not people who are chosen by God because of a place, but the place that is chosen by God because of people; and that obedience is pleasing to God more than sacrifice, they might perhaps understand that sheep ought to hear the shepherd’s voice, and that what they follow through obedience will be more valid and acceptable to God than what they follow through their own will. “Where there is zeal and contention,” says the apostle James, “there is instability and every evil work” (James III, 16). [Note: [Col. 0965] *est*, “there is,” added in 3.]

Similarly, when he expelled certain wicked plunderers of their homeland and fellow citizens from the kingdom, where they had refused to live peacefully and quietly, and compelled them to go into exile as a plague upon good people, he undoubtedly acted for their benefit, although they did not know it. For the longer a wicked man persists, the heavier and longer punishment he prepares for himself.

When would the good ever be at peace if no one resisted the fury of the wicked? Surely God spared those to whom, in his great patience and goodness, he allowed them to hear while absent what they would never have wished to see while present concerning the peace and condition of their homeland—happy if, at least in exile, they came to know their own blessings and desired the homeland from which they could not be expelled, where all the peacemakers are blessed, because they are called sons of God.

Such, then, by the grace of almighty God, was this man: neither hatred nor envy in any way stirred him to persecute those who were such, nor did hardness or cruelty restrain him from pitying or sparing the wretched. Rather, like an attentive shepherd and true leader of the people of God, he sought the salvation and advantage of all in every undertaking. Those whom he himself led and taught in the way of God he defended vigorously, lest they should be seduced by the perverse and led into error.

He was so far from savagery that even for those to whom he necessarily inflicted something bitter according to the character of their deeds, he himself often wept bitterly. Thus he was accustomed to rejoice with those who rejoiced and to weep with those who wept. For the one who said this also commanded that a certain man be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit might be saved on the day of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0965] *posset*, “might be able,” in 3.].

**35.** (955) Since now the final day and inescapable time were near, when almighty God, showing mercy to the earth and avenging the blood of his people, would repay the enemies of his servants with vengeance, the savage pride of the Hungarian people [Note: [Col. 0965] *etenim*, “for indeed,” in 3.] became excessive beyond measure and wholly intolerable, seduced, I believe, by the success of the previous year [Note: [Col. 0965] *successum*, “success,” in 3.]. For, as it has been most truthfully said, “Before ruin the heart is exalted” (Prov. XVI, 18). There all who worked iniquity fell [Note: [Col. 0965] *operantur*, “work,” in 1 and 2; omitted in 1.].

The peace of the Church, newly established in the royal assembly [Note: [Col. 0965] I have corrected this to *placito*, with Folcuin’s support; the manuscripts have *palatio*.] held at Arnstadt [Note: [Col. 0965] Arnstadt in Thuringia; compare the *Annals of Augsburg*, year 954.], anticipated this impending crisis, and had already been confirmed to a considerable extent through the wisdom of our emperor and his brothers. And indeed it became known among tribes and languages that “God is not the God of dissension but of peace” (I Cor. XIV, 33); at the beginning of this undertaking he wrought such salvation for his people [Note: [Col. 0965] *tanquam*, “as though,” in 3 and Folcuin].

The emperor’s spirit was stirred within him, because he had no time to assemble an army; yet he placed his trust through Christ in God, who is able to save with few as well as with many (I Kings XIV, 6). Cuono was there, no longer a duke but a soldier, with his whole heart, as it was thought, turned toward the peace that shortly before he had savagely attacked. He subdued his limbs with sackcloth and, as is reported, entreated God with groans that, if this were his holy will, after granting victory to our king and his army, he might permit him to be slain by the wicked men with whom he had previously joined himself wrongly, so that he might be freed forever from their company.

On the very vigil of the holy martyr Lawrence, which was then being observed, the emperor ordered a fast, asking God himself, through the martyr’s intercession, to be a refuge for him and his people. The purpose of the work I have undertaken prevents me from expounding the war: begun at the first light of the holy feast and, while evening twilight had scarcely yet come, most successfully concluded through God’s merciful ordering and his fighting for his own; the pitiable death of Cuono after the victory [Note: [Col. 0965] *miserandum*, “to be pitied,” in 2.]; the emperor’s most glorious triumph; the barbarian king himself, dukes, and princes taken captive; and the very numerous trophies throughout the whole breadth of his kingdom, as far as the borders of that people. All these matters await the industry of a work of their own, to the glory and praise of almighty God [Note: [Col. 0965] *expectavit*, “it awaited,” in 3.].

[Col. 0966C] **36.** To return to our subject, from which we have diverged somewhat, let us discuss what the pious archbishop Bruno, ever detesting all wickedness and indefatigable in the execution of justice, did meanwhile.

When he saw that he could not meet his elder brother, the great emperor, on the appointed day with auxiliary forces, and was at the same time concerned that the barbarians, in avoiding the war, might turn aside into Gaul, the province entrusted to his jurisdiction—thinking that he would thus provide for the kingdom and serve the emperor’s wishes more fully—he approached Liudolf, a member of the royal family and his nephew. He soothed his troubled spirit with blandishments sweeter than honey and promised to restore his former position if he would pay closer attention to the things that belonged to him.

After he perceived that the medicinal antidotes of his speeches and exhortations were no longer avoided, as before, by indirect evasions, but were tasted with their customary eagerness and received into the inner chambers of his heart [Note: [Col. 0965] These words are absent in 3.], he immediately invited him pleasantly enough to the venerable place of his bishopric, Bonn, and received him even more pleasantly. He treated him to every pleasure worthy and suitable for them both and most welcome to all who were present, without forgetting his royal dignity.

While they were still together, they received news of what had been accomplished in the military—or rather divine—campaign by divine power. The uncle persisted in consoling his nephew more fully. In a short time, through the inspiration of this counselor, it came to pass that the emperor entrusted all Italy to his son who had been lost and had been found, and, more importantly, firmly bestowed paternal affection upon him.

When he was most pleasing to the people and aspired to the way to Olympus, that wholly unblemished flower and safest strength of the kingdom suddenly departed from this life (957).

His father, the emperor and ever magnificent victor, after receiving consolation following his grief, joined his ancient relationship with his brother through renewed companionship. He came to Cologne and there delighted not so much in fraternal pleasures as in the mutual sight, conversation, and every entirely pleasant intercourse he shared with him.

There too was no lack of a severe judicial censure against wicked and troublesome citizens of the kingdom, nor of the gentle generosity of pious rule toward the good and mild. Careful and vigorous common deliberation was devoted to the condition of the kingdom and to protecting and enlarging its affairs; the greatest prudence ensured that some measures were enacted and others removed with the utmost caution [Note: [Col. 0967] *consilium*, “counsel,” in 2.].

**37.** Meanwhile, with the greatest diligence, the pious shepherd Bruno, defender of the truth and propagator of the Gospel, sought vigorous and industrious men who would each in his own place protect the commonwealth by faithfulness and strength. He took great care that they should lack neither counsel nor resources.

All those among the princes and leading men of the regions, and among the others whose administration concerned the kingdom, who, through his most salutary admonitions, had agreed in full faith to the covenant for the common benefit of all good people, he himself kept among his highest intimates; and he thoroughly reconciled them to the emperor, his brother [Note: [Col. 0967] *consiliabat*, “he counseled,” in 2.], bearing in mind the saying not rashly attributed to a wise man: “When neglected, the good man becomes more sluggish, but the bad man becomes worse.”

He also held in the highest reverence Henry, archbishop of Trier, a man of great merit and supreme integrity, who succeeded the magnificent prelate Ruotbert of Cologne when he died during a serious epidemic while the emperor was also present [Note: [Col. 0967] *Ruotberto* in 2 and 3.]. He likewise honored William, an illustrious and most graciously excellent archimandrite, his nephew and successor of Frederick, bishop of Mainz. Both were outstanding; both were perfectly instructed in the law of the Lord. One was very closely joined to the emperor by kinship, the other by integrity, and both by intimacy.

He frequently brought such men—so illustrious, so certainly wise and religious, and so learned in every good art—into his councils, lest he himself, as human beings do, should at any point stray from the path of truth. We saw them together with him not only providing what was good before God but also before human beings, in reading, counsel, and disputation, but also in the battle line.

For on the western borders of the Lotharingian kingdom there was a kind of untamed barbarism: people who appeared to be offspring of the Church, envying another’s prosperity and no less despising their own salvation, disregarding the allurements of paternal exhortation and scarcely sensing the terror of authority. If they were left to their own jurisdiction, they would seem perverse toward their own people and worst of all toward themselves [Note: [Col. 0967] The words “even those whom he especially honored with the highest reverence” are added in 3.].

He first of all employed the prudent moderation of discernment, so that, according to the character of places and times, in appointing pastors [Note: [Col. 0967] omitted in 3.], and in obedience to the command of our most wise emperor, he might provide for the peace and tranquility of the Lord’s flock. He preferred those above others to whom it was by no means unknown what the shepherd’s office was, what the vice of a hireling was, what acceptance in the ministry entailed [Note: [Col. 0967] *suscepto*, “in the ministry undertaken,” in 2; omitted in 3.], and what ought either to be done or hoped for in a position of compulsion.

Some he appointed so that, like curtains of hyacinth, they might adorn the inner chambers of the Lord’s house; others so that, like haircloth coverings, they might ward off from the outside the violence of storms.

**38.** I wish to recall a certain pious and praiseworthy deed of this pious Father. It is known to have been accomplished at the very beginning of his priesthood, in order to awaken the hope of salvation in the hearts of the oppressed, instead of grief and a spirit of sorrow, although this very act became liable to the accusations of a slanderous tongue because of the poverty of those who rightly divided the matter.

For what does envy not pervert, when it seems that no madness is greater than it? Ratherus, bishop of Verona—a city of Italy—having been expelled from the honor of his own see because of some slight suspicion, as is customary among that people, was, through Bruno’s great effort, formally attached, in accordance with the statutes of the canons, to the vacant see of Liège [Note: [Col. 0967] *Leodicensi*, “of Liège,” in 3.].

This was thought likely to be highly beneficial not only to that Church over which he presided but also to many others around it, because of his abundant learning [Note: [Col. 0967] “abundance of learning,” in 3.] and copious eloquence, by which he appeared to flourish among the wisest.

At the same time, because in those regions, through zeal and contention—from which instability and every evil work usually arise—certain priests of the Lord were also repeatedly scandalizing the ignorant people, often, shamefully, trusting more than was proper in earthly power, the often-mentioned and often-to-be-mentioned lord Bruno, who was already charged with administering the whole kingdom, judged—and rightly—that this man, previously expelled and neglected, could be brought by so great a benefit into the covenant of faith and truth, so that no one could seduce him. He believed that the mouths of those who spoke against him could finally be closed if no occasion for scandal could be found in their bishop [Note: [Col. 0967] omitted in 3.].

But the adverse party prevailed to its own destruction. Whatever had been done for their salvation they considered harmful to themselves. Why say more? An error was committed; violence was used; and there was no cessation until, by expelling him, they had satisfied their cruelty and wickedness.

All hope of his restoration was removed. A most serious conspiracy had been formed, and it seemed impossible to calm it unless he too were entirely removed and Baldric, who was descended from the family of the magnates of that land, were substituted in the same place [Note: [Col. 0969] The relevant words are absent in 1, 2, and 3.].

Countless storms converged from every direction upon this sinkhole; while the Church’s ship struggled with its oarsman, it tossed upon the waves. The helmsman himself could not withstand the force of the storm. He therefore yielded—yielded, not so that he might be conquered by evil, but so that he might conquer evil with good. He yielded to the will of his opponents so that he might slay them with their own sword.

They voluntarily bound themselves by an oath, promising that, if they were permitted to receive the bishop they requested, they would thereafter defend the authority of the Church and imperial right with unconquerable firmness. But, lest anything in such a matter remain incomplete and stir doubts in those curious to investigate other people’s affairs, Bruno accomplished with the emperor, his brother, that the ancient see of the Church of Verona should be restored to Bishop Rather, who had already been deprived of sees twice (961).

**39.** There are many other things, almost innumerable, which in a short account cannot be described—not only what he did with the utmost energy in the affairs of God and for the salvation of the entire people among the Lotharingian people, whom he had wholly undertaken to govern and whom, as can be seen today, he transformed from uncultivated and savage into peaceful and gentle [Note: [Col. 0969] *Lotharicorum*, “of the Lotharian people,” in 2 and 3, and often elsewhere.], but also throughout the entire kingdom of his most glorious emperor.

For he shared completely in the common care with his elder brother, each of whom rightly gloried in the other in the Lord. (962)

Moreover, he wonderfully rescued and exalted Lothair, the son of his sister, descended from an ancient line of kings, when he was being severely oppressed by his cousins. He did not cease until he established him as king in his father’s place and brought under his yoke the sons of Hugh, who were older and more powerful than he, together with all the princes of that kingdom. Thus he provided for everyone, so that under the governance of a single empire all might alike be safe from their enemies and peaceful among themselves.

**40.** A savage disaster threatened that kingdom, and it must not be passed over in silence: the people of the Northmen, among whom none were more practiced in pirate robbery. The people, made accustomed by dissension and civil ruin, had already for the most part become booty for them. Whatever had remained to them they had consumed among themselves through domestic rebellion.

But the provident administration of our ruler, who, because he understood that he was a human being, considered nothing human foreign to himself (Terence, *Heautontimorumenos* I, I, 25), brought it about—I repeat—that all who loved quiet and peace fled to him as to the safest harbor. He also softened the savagery and long-intolerable ferocity of the barbarians themselves. Indeed, at that time their king Harold [Note: [Col. 0969D] Surnamed “Blue-tooth.”], together with a great multitude of his people, submitted his neck to Christ, King of kings, and rejected the vanity of idols.

**41.** The emperor had a son who was still very young, of the most delicate disposition and the most unspoiled charm [Note: [Col. 0969] L. conjectures *voluntatis*, “of will,” instead.], a pledge of peace and the glory of the people. The emperor entrusted him to the archbishops, his uncle and his brother [Note: [Col. 0969D] Namely, Bruno and William of Otto II.], for the protection of the kingdom on this side of the Alps, while he was preparing to depart for Rome and arrange the affairs of all Italy.

Since the boy was destined to become emperor himself, the emperor established him as king, chosen by the unanimous consent of the entire people. Bruno the archbishop, William and Henry, and the other priests of the Lord anointed Otto—his father’s namesake—as king in the palace at Aachen, and the people exulted with the greatest rejoicing, saying: “May the king live forever!”

The brothers were then separated from one another, an invincible pair always equal in strength. As the emperor crossed the Pennine Alps, the pious shepherd and archbishop Bruno remained on this side, admired and desired everywhere with incredible affection. Not long afterward, because he himself could not go in person, he sent his lord and brother auxiliary forces, a substantial body of heavily armed troops [Note: [Col. 0970D] Heavy cavalry, in which ancient Lotharingia still excels today.], from the Lotharingian people.

Godefrid, the duke whom he had raised, commanded them—a wise and religious man, most devoted to peace and most observant of justice, serving the emperor at that time according to his wishes and pleasing to everyone [Note: [Col. 0969] “and pleasing to everyone,” in 2 and 3.]. At that same time he was seized by a fever and died, giving great hope for future peace [Note: [Col. 0970D] He died in 964. *Continuation of Regino*.].

Somewhat secure concerning his innocence, as though he were a witness and confidant of his life, the pious Father Bruno, when the matter of money to be distributed for the remedy of his soul arose, declared that the soul did not greatly need such assistance.

Moreover, his brother anxiously awaited the emperor’s return night and day and joyfully went out to meet him on his return in all his glory. He esteemed his exceptional virtue, dignity, faithfulness, and self-restraint in the undertaking he had accomplished; and together with him he judged that the hope of leisure, the tranquility of minds, the courts and laws, and the authority of the king and princes had been restored in harmony among the people.

He participated in all the emperor’s counsels, since the emperor himself thought of nothing day or night except the welfare of the people, and he excelled among the foremost. In this matter he was a most weighty adviser in establishing the policy, a most faithful companion in procuring it, and a most courageous helper in completing the affairs of the commonwealth.

42. Thus, while the emperor was celebrating the thirtieth year of his reign and his brother the twelfth year of his pontificate, the latter having scarcely passed his fortieth year of age, they celebrated holy Pentecost together at Cologne—a glory greater than which has not been granted to mortals. They were present together amid the sacred rites of the solemn day, along with their august mother, their sister the queen, their nephews and sons who were kings, that entire family beloved by God, and all the senators of the kingdom.

[Note: Col. 0971: *nondum* (“not yet”) in witness 1; *cesari* (“Caesar,” spelled with one *s*) in witness 1.]

[Note: Col. 0971D: One must conclude either that Otto, having returned from Cologne to Ingelheim around 23 May, went back to Cologne a few days later, or—though this is difficult to believe—that Ruotger was mistaken. Certainly the emperor issued charters at Ingelheim on 23 May, at Tribur on 25 May, and at Cologne on 2 and 8 June.]

It is certain that no place had ever flourished with such a gathering, such splendor, or such an assembly of people of every kind, age, and rank.

Thus this faithful and God-pleasing union in every will and work of the most glorious Caesar Augustus and his brother, the supreme and incomparable man Bruno the archbishop; this harmony in administering and successfully conducting everything useful and honorable; this most delightful fellowship in life and in all their duties—cruel death, dreadful death, death alone, I say, severed. And indeed, although nothing seemed more atrocious, nothing could have severed it more innocently.

[Note: Col. 0971: *non* (“not”) in witness 1.]

[Note: Col. 0971: *inter* (“among”) is lacking in witness 3.]

43. Therefore, when the supreme bishop Bruno had left the company of his elder brother as he journeyed eastward—first rushing into his embraces and weeping profusely—and, after giving thanks to God, had seen that everything within the bounds of the kingdom entrusted to him was peaceful and quiet, he admonished all his people once and again—the clergy and the people—about what ought to be done. Soon afterward he went westward to Compiègne, so that there he might recall to concord his nephews, who were divided against one another; establish them in faith and favor; and, with the Lord’s assent, confirm individually the religion of the Church, the honor due to the king, and whatever else belonged to them, as equity required.

[Note: Col. 0971: *populumque* (“and the people”) in witnesses 2 and 3.]

While intent upon this business, he began to grow ill. Thus, detained in the city of Reims by a serious bodily affliction, he was overtaken by illness on the fifth day after it had begun.

[Note: Col. 0971: *deest* (“is lacking”) in witness 3.]

During those days, on the road no less than in his lodging, he was refreshed by constant reading and scarcely any other food. When Bishop Wicfrid of Verdun familiarly asked him—so he himself bears witness—by what severity of illness he was oppressed, he replied that it was not an illness but the dissolution of his body.

[Note: Col. 0971: *ipso* (“himself”) in witness 2.]

[Note: Col. 0972D: “Of Verdun,” an identification supplied by a gloss.]

The bishop of the aforesaid metropolis received him with the greatest dignity and treated him with the utmost humanity. On the feast then being celebrated, that of Saint Remigius, he was somewhat better, so that his attendants and companions hoped for his recovery.

But he summoned the bishops who had come with him, Theodoric of Metz and Wicfrid, and asked them to grant him the opportunity and assistance to make his will.

[Note: Col. 0971: *ut in* (“that in”) in witness 3; *ei exhib.* (“to provide him”) in witness 2.]

When they excused themselves with great sorrow and tears, promising that the desired health would soon return, he resisted them with the strength of mind in which he had always excelled:

“While there is time,” he said, “let this be done; many other things remain for us to do afterward.”

His illness then grew more severe and gained strength. His breath, obstructed in the passage of his throat, already revealed the exhaustion of his vital powers. He summoned a notary and, in the presence of the witnesses mentioned above, dictated his will himself. While he was still living in good hope, he alienated, distributed, and gave to the poor all the possessions he had. Whatever he had accumulated for the arrangement of the external buildings of the churches of God, he divided appropriately according to the wisdom granted to him, after making and confirming his surety and in a manner worthy of his profession.

Anyone who wishes to read this will find it written below. His intellect, polished by purity of heart and constant exercise, which God had rendered refined and splendid by his gift, had not failed him at the end, as is clearly evident from his words.

[Note: Col. 0971: *reddit* (“gave back”) in witnesses 1 and 2; *illud* (“it”) in witness 3.]

44. After this, the poor man of Christ, gathering his strength of mind, again summoned the bishops privately. While they sat beside him and he had made them privy to his inner concerns, he poured forth the following words amid abundant sighs and overflowing tears:

[Note: Col. 0971: *perfudit* (“poured over”) in witness 2, but corrected.]

[Note: Col. 0971: In witness 3, the words from *renum testi et* (“tester of the reins and”) are lacking, and later those from *lucidius innotescat, sed ut ille, qui se parum novit* (“may become more clearly known, but so that he who knows himself little”) are lacking.]

“I seem to see three kinds of confession, by which the human heart reveals itself to the Lord its God, the tester of the reins and searcher of hearts—not so that he, who knows everything, may come to know it more clearly, but so that the one who knows himself poorly may recognize himself more truthfully, and either praise God for good deeds or accuse himself for evil deeds.

“This ought always to be done; for we are commanded to keep watch, lest the thief come and, when we are off our guard, creep in to inflict loss upon us (Matthew 24:42–43).

[Note: Col. 0971: *neque* (“nor”) in witness 2; *veniens* (“coming”) in witness 3, with *que* lacking.]

“But when the Lord knocks at the house through the affliction of illness, the mind must raise itself with whatever strength it can, and rise up with such intention as will enable it to approach its Judge, who is drawing near. With earthly desires lulled to sleep, it must burn with hope for heavenly things; it must not despair of eternal goods, even if it has not deserved them; it must distrust itself and trust in the Lord.

“Behold, beloved brothers: as you see, the door of my breast is being struck; I am being summoned to render an account of my works. If you can do anything, I beg you, bring me aid; extend the hand of your prayer. I am carried uncertainly between hope and fear, and I must strive not to incline too much toward either side. But what strength is mine? I await the remedy of mercy. I am in the hand of my Creator; I await what he wishes to be done with me.

“It is good to confess to the Lord. ‘Confession and magnificence are his work.’ For nothing good can be done except by his working.

“There is also a kind of confession that does not lament sins but nevertheless implores mercy. Of this the Psalmist says in the person of the Lord:

[Note: Col. 0971: *tuam* (“your”) is added after *misericordiam* (“mercy”) in witness 2.] ‘The sacrifice of praise will honor me, and there is the way by which I shall show him my salvation’ (Psalm 49:23).

“This Salvation—that is, the Lord Jesus—I confess with my mouth and believe in my heart that God raised him from the dead.

[Note: Col. 0973: In witness 3, *me et ... suscitavit* (“me and ... raised”) is lacking.]

“In him I acknowledge all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden away. No one can call Jesus Lord except in the Holy Spirit. Before him is all my desire, and my groaning is not hidden from him.

“I said, ‘I will confess my injustices against myself to the Lord’: this is the second kind of confession, lamentation over sins.

“The third is commended by the blessed apostle James: ‘Confess your sins to one another,’ he says, ‘and pray for one another, that you may be saved’ (James 5:16). This I wish to do with you, my lords and brothers; this I earnestly seek. I hope, however, that we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and that he himself is the propitiation for our sins.”

After he had thus poured himself out entirely before the Lord, he requested the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, knowing the power of that sacrament.

[Note: Col. 0973: *virtutem* (“the power”) in witnesses 2 and 3.]

When it had been brought, the man of God showed what he felt in his soul by prostrating his entire body.

[Note: Col. 0973: *toto* (“with his whole”) is lacking in witness 3.]

Refreshed by this life-giving nourishment, he was returned to his little bed stronger in hope. He remained in the same weakness of body and fervor of spirit for no fewer than five days.

45. On the solemn day of the blessed martyrs Gereon and his companions, when the day was already declining, he was suddenly carried away in an ecstasy of mind. He caused great grief among the bishops, dukes, counts, and all who were present, because they thought that the dissolution of his most desired body was immediately at hand.

[Note: Col. 0973: *vertente* (“turning”) in witness 3.]

As was his custom, he soon recovered somewhat and quieted the tumult with his hand. He calmed the tears and groans of those standing around him and called the leading men—and those more worthy of this final address—by name:

[Note: Col. 0973: *ad hoc* (“for this”) in witness 2.]

“Do not,” he said, “do not grieve, brothers, over my lot. By the judgment of divine retribution this condition has been imposed upon all mortals. It is not permitted to refuse what the Almighty has decreed unavoidable. Joyful things soon follow these sad ones. I am going there not with life taken away but changed for the better, where I shall soon see many more and brighter men than I have ever seen here.”

He said no more than this and soon laid his weary limbs back upon his bed. A little later, while daylight was still unbroken, he completed the customary office of evening praise; when deep night had come, he himself completed Compline with the brothers. He commended himself more earnestly to the Lord his God and to the prayers of his saints, as though he were about to depart at once. He fortified his journey with that great viaticum, namely, the holy and unique pledge of our redemption. He marked the bishops, himself, and those who were present with his blessing.

Thus, with attentive mind, he awaited the fearful hour of his dissolution at the command of his Creator.

[Note: Col. 0973: The words “Thus ... he awaited” are lacking in witness 3.]

After midnight had passed, he turned with whatever effort he could toward Bishop Theodoric, his nephew, and said: “My lord, pray!” Then, amid those singing psalms and praying to the Lord, and weeping exceedingly, he breathed out his spirit.

[Note: Col. 0973: *exilavit* (“he breathed out”) in witness 1.]

What could not die in him was returned to the Creator. His lifeless body, as he himself had ordered while alive, was lifted by his tireless companions on the same day—that is, on the fifth day before the Ides of October—and carried in a bier. On the eighth day afterward they reached Cologne, the august metropolis of his see.

[Note: Col. 0973: *nono* (“on the ninth”) in witness 3.]

Some of them still testify under oath, affirming it in an astonishing manner, that throughout that long journey they suffered scarcely any weariness or hardship under so great a burden. Wherever they went, and whatever peoples and lands they encountered, all of them, to use their words, wonderfully esteemed the merits of this man worthy of God—his services to the commonwealth, the emperor, kings, princes, and the whole people—each according to the exceptional ability he possessed.

[Note: Col. 0973: *et* (“and”) is lacking in witnesses 2 and 3.]

46. When such a funeral procession was approaching Cologne, and the excessively grievous report spread throughout all the people of the Lotharingian kingdom, everyone was so overwhelmed—especially the members of that most holy see and Church—as though the departure and death of so great a shepherd were the funeral of the Church itself. For the force and magnitude of grief then grew in proportion to the greatness of the consolation they had previously enjoyed.

[Note: Col. 0973: *deest* (“is lacking”) in witness 3.]

Everyone wept, many until their tears were exhausted. Many, stunned with their limbs stiffened, forgot that they themselves were alive amid the misery of such bereavement.

[Note: Col. 0973: *semetipsis* (“in themselves”) in witnesses 2 and 3.]

Above all others, by mourning and tears, and still more by the inward grief of his heart, he was afflicted who had loved this father of his country more than the rest: Folcmar, a deacon of memorable integrity and diligence, and the prudent and faithful provost and steward of this holy Church. The father himself was accustomed to honor him by that title as his vicar and his closest associate in every matter. At that time the mouths, eyes, and minds of all the desolate were turned toward him alone.

[Note: Col. 0973: *desolatarum* (“of the desolate women”) in witness 1.]

Indeed, by the will and desire of all, he had already been elected—though not yet formally designated—as bishop. The pious father, knowing him, entrusted to him in his absence, by name, the distribution of all his possessions to the needy and to the churches of his bishopric, foreseeing, I believe, his future succession.

47. Near the walls of the city there is a church humble in structure and workmanship, but distinguished by the name of the apostles, in whose honor it is said to have been consecrated. There the lifeless body of their shepherd was clothed with the insignia of the priesthood; access was open to few except bishops and certain priests of the second order.

[Note: Col. 0973: *vallabant* (“they surrounded”) in witness 3.]

Soon afterward it was lifted up, and the clergy and people, repeatedly mingling song and lamentation, carried it to the church of the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, where the venerable see was located. They spent that night sleepless, with great solemnity in vigils and psalmody, their bodies scarcely refreshed.

When morning came, the whole city assembled, together with an innumerable multitude of those who had been terrified by the sudden report and had arrived from various provinces and kingdoms.

[Note: Col. 0975: *de* (“from”) is lacking in witness 3.]

The archbishop of Trier and the bishop of Liège were present.

[Note: Col. 0975D: “Eueraclus,” also “Euercar,” according to a gloss in an eleventh-century manuscript.]

Bishops Theodoric and Wicfrid came forward as witnesses of his final decree and of the message he had sent there to his sons serving God.

[Note: Col. 0975D: “Bishop of Verdun,” according to an eleventh-century gloss.]

His will was read in the venerable presbytery before the altar of the most holy Peter. Those things were also recited which, with a pious and solicitous mind concerning the affairs of God, he had requested and ordered but had not thought necessary to have written down—namely, that throughout that entire year, on every single day, no less than one full pound of denarii should be distributed for the use of the poor.

[Note: Col. 0975: *per singulos dies* (“on each individual day”) is lacking in witness 1; *libra denariorum* (“a pound of denarii”) is lacking in witness 3.]

48. Then, according to the request and desire of his heart, with which he had burned in his final days, the most holy clergy were persuaded to permit his body to be transferred willingly to the monastery of monks which he had not only built at that time outside the city walls in honor of the holy martyrs Pantaleon, Cosmas, Damian, and Quirinus, but which, even up to the present, he continued to build and order by his counsel and foresight.

There, under God’s governance, the notable works of his good will were being carried forward through the merits of the saints, whose relics he had brought there and whose protection he had secured for himself by devout and diligent supplication.

Everyone assented with the greatest readiness to all that he had ordered. Only this was most difficult to persuade them to accept: that his lifeless body should be removed from the highest and most sacred place of his see. They mourned as though they had been deprived of him a second time, yet after long deliberation they did not dare resist even in this his deeply religious will.

The shepherd was led away from his sheep—it cannot be said with what lamentations and cries. He was buried in the church of the blessed martyrs on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November. There, even to this day, it is plainly shown how great he was in the eyes of all good people.

Afterward both good and evil recognized more clearly what kind of man he had been when they lost him. They visit his place of burial; they compete in recounting what he did, what he taught, how he lived, and how he died. At one moment they pray for him; at another they ask that he may deign to pray for them. They do not seek signs; they attend to his life and recall his teaching. In him they promise themselves or their descendants that something great will come.

Finally, all are stirred by his memorials to the praise and glory of God—just as once by the living man, so now by the dead.

[Note: Col. 0975: *deest* (“is lacking”) in witness 3.]

49. The Testament of the Lord and archbishop Bruno, venerable in Christ, happily completed.

[Note: Col. 0975: This heading is lacking in witness 3.]

Bruno, servant of Christ, to his sons serving God at Cologne.

What I have resolved in my mind concerning the things which the divine generosity entrusted to me for distribution, I have decided should be strengthened by your judgment and supported by your testimony, if God does not permit me, being present among you, to communicate these matters personally to you; therefore I have considered it most fitting to send them to you in writing.

[Note: Col. 0975: *ne* (“not”) in witness 1; *nobiscum* (“with us”) in witness 1, against *vobiscum* (“with you”); the understood verb after *scripto ad vos perlato* (“when the writing has been conveyed to you”) is *communicare* (“to communicate”).]

Accordingly, following the decision of our brothers Theodoric and Wicfrid, who themselves are also your members, consider everything carefully and, God willing, carry everything out rightly.

Whatever treasure has been brought into the resources of our church—for whatever there is is kept under the keys of that illustrious man Evizo, treasurer of Saint Peter, except whatever may not yet have been reported by the ministers—so that nothing might appear to have been divided from the Church, let all the golden vessels and whatever is most precious, publicly inspected and carefully accounted for before the lord Popo, provost and steward of our Church, under the testimony of Christ and the Church, before the altar of Saint Peter, be consecrated for perpetual use in the ministry of the holy mother of God Mary and of the blessed apostle Peter in that church.

[Note: Col. 0975: *allati* (“brought in”) in witness 3, against *illati* (“brought into”). *Et quidquid est* (“and whatever there is”) is lacking in witness 3.]

[Note: Col. 0975: *illustris* (“illustrious”) in witness 1; *Poppone* in witnesses 2 and 3, and below; *ecclesiae* (“church”) in witness 1, against *ecclesia* (“church”) in the text.]

[Note: Col. 0975: *mundum* (“clean”) in witness 3, against *nondum* (“not yet”).]

The golden cup, the seal, and the Greek dish which are with us are to be given to Saint Pantaleon. In addition: the candlesticks used daily in our ministry; the silver horse given by the archbishop of Mainz; ten excellent pallia; ten of the finest silver vessels; one hundred pounds for completing the cloister; three hundred for enlarging the church; a broad curtain; three tablecloths; three carpets; the same number of benches or bench-coverings; thirty napkins; and, in addition, whatever of the mares belongs to us, except those found to belong to the church.

[Note: Col. 0975: *scutulam* (“small dish”) in witnesses 2; *pene* (“almost”) in witness 1.]

[Note: Col. 0975: *maguntino* (“Mainz”) in witness 2; *magontio* (“Mainz”) in witness 3.]

I also give the estates which I acquired for our Church: Langalon near the Rhine, Werebetti, Heingelon, Lidron, and Wishem, which the Meuse washes; also the house of our cousin, the bishop of Metz, and the estate of Havingan. Moreover, whatever he holds from the property of our Church, I hand over.

[Note: Col. 0975D: Langalon, below Bonn.]

[Note: Col. 0975: *heingilon* in witness 3.]

[Note: Col. 0976D: Wessem, above Roermond.]

[Note: Col. 0975: *villis* (“estates”) in witnesses 2 and 3.]

Let a third part of the fruits of this year, cultivated for our use, also be given for the use of the monks.

[Note: Col. 0975: *elaboraturum* (“about to be cultivated”) in witness 2.]

Let a gerokomeion—that is, a hospice for the aged—be established in a suitable place, at the abbot’s command, not far from the monastery.

[Note: Col. 0975: *Jerichomium* in witness 3.]

[Note: Col. 0976D: *gerokomeion*, that is, Greek γηροκομεῖον, “hospice for the aged.”]

To it I grant whatever estate is our property, except Leresfelt, situated in Saxony [the reading is uncertain: “up to Leresfelt in Saxony” or “Leresfelt acquired in Saxony”], and whatever Gebhard, formerly provost of Bonn, is known to have possessed near the Moselle.

[Note: Col. 0975: *praeterea* (“in addition”) in witness 3.]

[Note: Col. 0975: The reading *Leresfelt ... usque* is uncertain; perhaps “whatever is situated up to Leresfelt in Saxony,” or “whatever was acquired in Saxony.”]

[Note: Col. 0975: The abbreviated reading *I. p. i. s. u. s.* is added in witness 1 by the hand of a corrector.]

And so that this may be done with the good will of our lord and successor, for the salvation of both of us, let him use Ruothinge, which our labor has increased among the possessions of the Church, as he wishes.

[Note: Col. 0976D: Ruothinge; perhaps Roedingen.]

[Note: Col. 0975: *nostrae* (“of our Church”) in witness 2.]

Let an oratory like the one we are building for the blessed Privatus beside the altar of Saint Martin on the western side of the church be made for the blessed Gregory, the great martyr, who has recently been brought here; there let his most sacred body be deposited. One hundred pounds shall be assigned for its foundation.

[Note: Col. 0975: *construximus* (“we built”) in witness 3, against *construimus* (“we are building”).]

For our brothers at Saint Peter: golden cups, twenty pounds, a curtain, two tablecloths, and two bench-coverings.

At the altar of Saint Gereon: large pitchers, two pallia, and one of the larger carpets; for the brothers, ships (*naves*) and twelve pounds, one tablecloth, and two bench-coverings.

For completing the altar of Saint Severinus: four pounds of gold; for the brothers, eight pounds, two vessels, one tablecloth, and two bench-coverings.

For Saint Cunibert: two small dishes.

For the two holy Ewaldi: three pallia; for the brothers, two vessels, eight pounds, one tablecloth, two bench-coverings, and one carpet.

[Note: Col. 0977: *sancti* (“of the saint”) in witness 1, against *sanctis* (“to the saints”).]

For Saint Andrew: thirty pounds, four pallia, four vessels, and two candlesticks; for the brothers, six pounds.

The blessed martyr Eliphius and Saint Martin the confessor shall receive the same amount; in addition, the estate of Solagon, acquired for our Church by a precarious grant.

[Note: Col. 0977: *precario* (“by a precarious grant”) in witnesses 1 and 2; *precatu* (“by request”) in witness 3.]

At the altar of Saint Mary: two of the finest vessels; for completing the monastery and cloister, one hundred pounds, a curtain, two bench-coverings, and the same number of napkins.

At the altar of Saint Cecilia: three pounds of gold, a curtain, two candlesticks, two vessels, one carpet, and two bench-coverings; for completing the monastery, fifty pounds.

For the community of that monastery: ten pounds and one tablecloth.

For the Holy Virgins: two vessels, two candlesticks, two pallia, a curtain, one carpet, and two bench-coverings; for the holy nuns, ten pounds and one tablecloth.

[Note: Col. 0977: *tapetum* (“carpet”) in witness 2 and below.]

[Note: Col. 0977: *sanctimoniales* (“holy women/nuns”) in witness 3.]

For the altar of the holy martyrs Cassius and Florentius: two pounds of gold, the basins which are with us, two cups, and two pallia; for the brothers, ten pounds.

For Saint Victor and his community, the same amount; for founding the monastery and cloister at Soest, one hundred pounds. For the altar: six vessels, the same number of pallia, one large carpet, two bench-coverings, a cope, and a chasuble from our possessions.

In addition, the estate which Wodilo gave us by our precarious grant; also that which the lord Popo acquired for us at Recklinghausen and Erwitte with sufficient diligence.

[Note: Col. 0977B: Soest; *Richildinchuso* is Recklinghausen.]

[Note: Col. 0978B: *Arvite* is Erwitte.]

[Note: Col. 0977: The third witness marks here the explicit conclusion of the Life of the lord archbishop Bruno; the epitaph is lacking.]

Pour forth prayers from your hearts; send forth tearful voices.

Behold, the father of his country lies buried in stone,

royal offspring, remembered throughout all lands,

Bruno the peaceful, a good and pious man.

The archbishop, to whom Cologne was given as his see,

[Note: Col. 0977: *clara* (“illustrious”) in witnesses 2 and 3.]

was dear to all good people everywhere.

The most living light struck against the gloomy darkness;

the envious tongue is silent; now only true praise is pleasing.

This world was not worthy of so rare a gift;

snatched from this blemish, he now enjoys the Lord.

On the fifth day before the Ides of October, the twelve-year bishop

departed from life; blessed hope was his companion.

[Note: Col. 0977: *duodenus* (“of twelve”) in witnesses 2 and 3.]

[Note: Col. 0977: Witness 2 adds: “Pious Bruno.” Concerning the chasuble you requested from the lord Bruno, you should have no doubt that it was the one which our predecessors Engilbertus and the others had held in the greatest veneration in his name, and which they always used in the solemn commemoration of his death (*obitu* in the manuscript).]

[Col. 0977]

## The Second Life of Bruno

[Note: Col. 0977: From manuscript 3.]

1. After Henry I, the first and most pious king, had been removed from the midst of the living—famous throughout the world for his ineffable clemency and wise administration of the commonwealth, and called the father of his country—his son Otto I, by divine providence, succeeded to his father’s place as the most desired emperor, with the favorable acclamation of the whole court.

[Note: Col. 0977D: Taken from Ruotger, chapter 5.]

[Note: Col. 0977: The manuscript reads: “with the favorable acclamation of the whole court, most eagerly desired.”]

After he had been consecrated king, he appointed his brother Henry duke over the people of Bavaria. Saint Bruno, however, the youngest in age but not least in the honor of his conduct, still lived under the discipline of literary studies and advanced day by day in the service of Christ with a joyful disposition.

When he had advanced in age and wisdom, the king attached him to himself through brotherly affection in the office of archchaplain. Meanwhile, a thousand times each day he was compelled to plead for the unfortunate, advise the afflicted, and bring help to the wretched. He administered all these duties in such a way that he seemed to have become a refuge for all the needy. Nevertheless, every person oppressed by any calumny sought this one asylum. In him an example of wisdom, piety, and justice rose above human memory.

2. At this time Wicfrid governed the Church of Cologne, while Richarius presided over the see of Liège. Through their canonical and spiritual provision, the state of the holy Church flourished. At that time a duke named Kuono held power; because of the solidity of his often-tested loyalty and the multiplicity of his constant service, King Otto had entrusted to him the entire province of Lotharingia.

3. Then Vicfrid, the archbishop of the holy Church of Cologne, worthy of long remembrance, after a long period of great weakness but still sufficiently faithful to the royal majesty and his country, finally left his weary limbs to the earth and was joined to the heavenly spirits.

[Note: Chapters 3 and 4 are taken from Ruotger, chapters 11–13.]

The people, deprived of their shepherd, undertook nothing uncertain or changeable amid their confusion. Following the counsel of the nobles and the entire clergy, they chose for themselves as their one and uniquely desired consolation the lord Bruno, a magnificent and most proven man.

Soon, by divine providence, clergy and people confirmed their common intention in this matter: that the lord Bruno, the king’s brother, should be ordained their bishop, since they had learned through various affairs that his steadfastness was inflexible in every matter of equity and justice.

For he was a magnanimous man, outstanding in prudence and counsel, overflowing with piety, mercy, and charity, a fosterer of concord and peace, so that by the common name he was called “Bruno the peaceful.”

When everyone was in agreement and their wishes converged through God’s providence, after the funeral rites had been honorably celebrated, as was fitting for so venerable a bishop of the see of Cologne, four supreme men and the same number of laymen were unanimously chosen from the most holy senate. All were highly educated. They were to carry all these matters to the palace and, after announcing the unanimity of the election following the lamented vacancy, demand from the emperor the aforesaid consolation for the desolate people.

Why say more? Thanks be to God, it pleased the imperial authority to take account both of the time and of the place and promptly send the visitor requested with such insistence to guard the abandoned flock.

At last he entered from the camp of the earthly empire into the tabernacles of the heavenly King, to fight against spiritual wickedness, carrying before him the practices and exercises of the virtues, the weapons of faith. His new companions soon saw in him both what attracted and what inspired fear. For he showed himself exceedingly approachable and gentle; yet, although nothing escaped his diligence in action, he carefully inquired from every source what he ought to do and upon which customs he should rely. His gravity was tempered with courtesy, and to the crowd that gathered around him he appeared moderately cheerful and in every respect remarkable.

4. He arrived at the most sacred see, prepared for this pious guardian by the almighty Lord before the ages and presented to him at the appointed time.

A great gathering of the people took place, and the common people were seized with immeasurable excitement. The city rejoiced with new joys. The clergy came together from the monasteries; a multitude of nuns assembled; every condition and both sexes gathered for rejoicing in greater numbers than usual.

The bishops who were present in large numbers, together with the senate of this holy clergy, while all cried out in a voice of exultation and salvation, made the man chosen by God and by men sit upon the episcopal throne. Then all together sounded forth praise to God, each crying out as loudly as he could, while organs, cymbals, and every other sign of joy resounded no less.

5. (953) After he had climbed to so great a height of power, his pride did not thereby increase at all. Rather, the holy mind of the bishop inclined itself toward humility, storing in its memory what Scripture admonishes when it says: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclesiasticus 3:20).

His wisdom was ever watchful, and his gentleness exceedingly conciliatory. He kept the serpent’s cunning within the law and did not lose the spirit of the simple dove. He loved the flock entrusted to him and rescued many from error by the staff of discipline. Some he led to better things through the discussions of constant disputation; others he filled with the desire for a holy way of life through the calm maturity of his teaching.

In speech he was gentle, in doctrine humble, a most vigorous destroyer of evil and zealous defender of truth, gracious to the humble and severe toward the proud. Some he received within the fences of the flock and made sheep out of wolves; others he nourished outside the fences. Whatever he taught others, he first fulfilled himself.

6. In that one man there were indeed things highly unlike one another: nobility of birth, dignity of office, and such an elevation of knowledge—which ordinarily causes inflation of pride—that nothing seemed above it, while his spirit and manner were humble.

Henry I, father of this most holy man, king of the Romans and ever Augustus, vigorously governed the empire. After him his son Otto I, brother of this holy man, ruled powerfully. After him came Otto II, Otto III, and Henry, the grandson of Henry the duke of Bavaria, and their other sons and grandsons, who succeeded one another down to the present day.

[Note: Col. 0979: These words seem to indicate that the author lived before the year 1268; compare also chapters 9 and 12.]

His great-great-grandfathers and ancestors, as far back as human memory reaches, were all most noble; no obscure person is found in their line, and no degenerate member is easily discovered.
