Yet, with the excellence of the Augusti and kings left intact, this man surpassed them all in lineage, nobility, and uprightness of character.

He was tall in stature, handsome in face, exceedingly beautiful in appearance, with a broad forehead and high eyebrows. His eyes were large and bright, like a carbuncle. His gaze was fear-inspiring, and his reddish beard was spread generously around his shoulders and chest.

7. Having therefore attained, by God’s ordering, the rank of supreme priest, he desired to be loved rather than feared. He confirmed ecclesiastical laws by canonical authority. From then on, all his intention and all his diligence served either as a defense or an adornment for holy Mother Church: she was to be defended externally and adorned internally; defended in secular matters and adorned in spiritual matters.

Above all, he loved the beauty of the house of the Lord and the place where his glory dwells. He showed in many special ways that he burned with this desire. In everything he also proved himself a strong athlete of God and champion of the Christian faith.

The king, rejoicing at this, observed that the man was growing through the progress of every virtue. He had no doubt that he could find rest with him in spiritual matters, and he dared to share with complete confidence the burdens of royal justice with him. He therefore entrusted him with the administration of all Lotharingia.

[Note: Col. 0981D: See Ruotger, chapter 22, and, concerning chapter 8, Ruotger, chapters 16–20.]

8. Meanwhile, after the lord king’s first wife had died, he had a son by the queen whom he had brought from Italy—a son bearing his own name—and he planned to have him consecrated as his successor by royal blessing.

When his elder son Ludolf learned of this, he, who for a long time had been consumed by desire for this hope, considered the loss irreparable and intolerable, to such an extent that he contemplated bringing danger upon his father’s life or safety.

Accordingly, after Duke Kuono had been corrupted by many kinds of promises, together with certain princes and assembled forces he opened these paths of ambush, so that, after having his captive father’s eyes torn out, he might freely seize the heights of the kingdom.

But when the ambush was immediately detected by divine warning, the king gathered an army and besieged the duke and his son in the city of Mainz. Since they were enclosed by a strong circuit of walls and protected by the powerful conspiracy of the citizens, the king, following the advice of prudent men, judged it better on this occasion to yield the place.

Departing from there, he reached Agrippina-Cologne, where he confirmed the nobles of the kingdom, gathered there unanimously, in their security by an oath of allegiance.

9. Then, after the king had gone to Italy for various necessary reasons, the holy archbishop Bruno came to the palace at Aachen with the bishop of Metz, whom Duke Kuono had expelled from his bishopric after treacherously seizing the city.

[Note: Col. 0981D: Compare Ruotger, chapter 24.]

There the lord abbot Odilo of Stavelot met him. Already worn out by old age and continual illness, he commended himself and all his possessions to Bruno and renewed the complaint which he had postponed in the king’s presence in previous years.

[Note: Col. 0981D: Odilo of Stavelot.]

Moved by this, Emmo—see the *Continuation of Flodoard*, under the year 976—not now secretly but as a public enemy of the abbey, gathered a band of robbers and plundered the Church’s property without mercy or discrimination.

[Note: Col. 0981D: See the *Continuation of Flodoard*, year 976.]

The most pious Saint Bruno could no longer tolerate this injury. He sent a military force, captured the guilty man while he was seeking hiding places in flight, and committed him to extremely severe imprisonment. Then, after receiving the pledge and oath of the bishop of Liège, whose relative Emmo was—namely, that he would never again presume to do anything of the sort—Bruno ordered him to be released from his public fetters.

Not long afterward, he attacked the castle of Longia with a military force, harassed it with a powerful siege, and, after finally capturing it, restored it to the jurisdiction of the Church of Metz, as it remains today.

At the same time, when Duke Kuono had been excluded from the city of Metz—for they had removed a great treasure from it—the holy Bruno gathered an army and pursued him. He drove him from his own borders and thus restored the bishop of Metz, Adalbero, to his place.

[Note: Col. 0982D: Adalbero.]

In this way, after driving the enemies from the borders of his jurisdiction, the venerable bishop brought Ludolf, the king’s son, back into his father’s favor and into concord and friendship with his brother. Through God’s mercy and by the prudence of his pious concern, firm peace was established, and throughout the surrounding regions he perpetually retained the name which, by Christ’s assent, he had acquired before his episcopate: “Bruno the peaceful.”

### 10. The Dignity and See of the Bishop

The pontifical dignity and the see itself were, in those early years, exceedingly humble and almost without distinction. While he bore the name of bishop, he possessed no more reverence, obedience, or honor than any priest or shepherd who, by apostolic indulgence, is endowed through the laying on of hands. Content with nothing more than a bare stole and a single staff, he bound what was to be bound and loosed what was to be loosed. But the jurisdiction of the sword, or of civil affairs—in short, the whole duchy, by which he was elevated to the pontifical rank—we shall endeavor to transmit to posterity, as it has been derived from the commonly circulated edition.

Accordingly, while the glorious Otto was ruling the Roman Empire, his brother was appointed, through Otto’s favor, bishop of the Church of Cologne. He was a man of outstanding character in secular affairs and of extraordinary religious devotion toward God. His life and deeds among us, adorned with the blossoms of many virtues, will delight the inquisitive reader. Indeed, the writer’s pen passed over, for the most part, the man’s remarkable effectiveness without fully treating it, because his fame had already filled the remote corners of the world more swiftly than writing could record it.

During the period of his priesthood, an occasion arose that moved the king with his army toward Italy, where he intended to settle the affairs of the kingdom with the Lombards. He entrusted the administration of Gaul to this brother and bishop, charging him to administer judgment and justice, knowing that under such a patron both Church and people, both citizens and commoners, would be secure.

Saint Bruno, however, undertaking the care of what had been entrusted to him, inspected the churches, villages, castles, and cities; he encouraged each person to carry out what was required; he reconciled those who were at odds with one another; he restored peace; and, once restored, he strengthened it by an oath sworn with the leading men of the provinces.

### 11.

Thus, around the feast of blessed Peter, while the same bishop was at Cologne, he sent an embassy inviting the King of Paris to celebrate the feast. The king, united with him by both blood relationship and affection, did not delay going. He arrived; he was received with fitting and appropriate reverence for the occasion, and was entertained with the greatest possible joy.

Nevertheless, I do not know through what rashness, he had ordered that he should proceed crowned on the holy day. The bishop resisted this, lest, by agreeing to an unusual practice, he expose his brother to offense. It is said that he persuaded the man responsible for the royal crown to contrive matters so that, when he was about to bring it forth on the holy day, he might take advantage of the pressure of the crowd, stumble as though pushed by accident, and, by a feigned mishap, allow the diadem to slip from his head.

So it happened. As the crowd pressed upon him, he fell together with the falling crown, and the feet of the noisy people trampled it.  
[Note: c. reads *allentatur* (“is weakened” or “relaxed”).]

The king could not remain unaware of what had happened. Frustrated in his hope, he proceeded nevertheless, though still wearing a circlet.  
[Note: That is, adorned with a circlet.]

After the rites had been completed, he merely tasted rather than ate the food, refused to recline at table any longer, and, having quickly girded himself, continued on his way. Meanwhile the matter was concealed in silence.

The King of Paris, however, grieving that he had been insulted, devised a similar return for the bishop. Therefore, on the holy day of Saint Dionysius, the apostle of Paris, the king invited the bishop, who was to celebrate solemn Mass with all his clergy, so that he might receive favor in return for favor. The bishop complied. On the holy day, proceeding in pontifical splendor, he found another bishop of that nation standing at the altar.

His learned mind understood that this was vengeance for the old anger. But, since he had already begun the sacred Mass, he turned to another altar and completed the Mass that had been begun, together with his attendants. Without even bidding farewell to the king, and without having eaten, he left the city accompanied by his men, wishing it to become known both to the king and to the city that judgment for the injury inflicted upon him would come upon them.

Without further delay, he returned to his fellow provincials, prepared supplies and necessities, and organized military camps. Then he returned and attacked the king with all his men, drove them back, and expelled them. He consumed and devastated the city with flames, and returned victorious.  
[Note: “enters” in c.]

### 12.

Meanwhile, the jealousy of the Duke of Lorraine, Conrad, was provoked, as though all Gaul had been handed over to a cleric, to the injury of his majesty, and he judged this unbecoming to his nobility. He was not afraid first to violate the agreements of peace; instead, having gathered an army, he began to harass the entire kingdom everywhere with robberies and fires.

What more is there to say? The pious shepherd groaned over the misfortunes of his wounded flock. Now, in the division of his heart, he sought counsel for taking action; with wavering mind he weighed whether it was unjust to yield or whether he ought to fight by engaging on equal terms, because he understood that the authority of the sword had not been entrusted to him in vain.

He therefore consulted the leading men of the provinces, sought and found a solution, and fixed a day. When he engaged the duke, he emerged victorious. After the duke’s army had been thrown into confusion, he reserved the duke himself, captured and placed in chains, for the judgment of his brother, so as not to stain so great a victory with blood.

Thus, when the enemy of peace had been overthrown, peace was restored to the Church.

Not long afterward he joyfully welcomed his brother the emperor, who had completed his Italian business. The emperor could not fail to learn what his brother and bishop had accomplished, how civil, peaceful, and firm a judge and victor he had been. Accordingly, at a solemn council of the princes, it was established by the unanimous decision of all that the sovereignty of the defeated duke should pass perpetually, by use and right, to the bishop of Cologne and his successors; and that, just as bishops were so called, they should also be dukes, and should judge by the sword, whereas previously they had used only a staff.

### 13.

Supported, therefore, by this dignity, Saint Bruno the Peaceful, fosterling of peace and grace, restored peace to people of good will, recalled those who disagreed from their deviant course, and punished the obstinate and hard-hearted, for the terror of others, by various kinds of sentence.

He shook his bride, illustrious Cologne, free from the yoke of servitude; released the restraint of her tribute; and, granting her perpetual liberty, was the first to plant in her the blessing of glory. He gathered into her the relics of the saints collected from every quarter.

He also demolished the bridge extending across the bed of the Rhine, with the most equitable balance of reasoned judgment, because the hands of robbers had defiled it. For on almost every day, farmers from across the Rhine entered Cologne by that bridge for the sake of trade. Since they were scarcely finished with their various business before evening, they would return as the day declined; but on that very bridge they were deprived of their possessions and lives and thrown into the Rhine. The perpetrators of the murders remained concealed, having night as the seal of their crime.

Thereupon Saint Bruno established near the city walls a community of monks, which he made heir to his possessions, ennobling it with a manifold endowment. He began the place by laying its foundations; but, called by a blessed death to the rewards of his good will, he left it unfinished, though he arranged an ample provision of funds for the erection of the building. In it he lies buried and rests. We perceive daily, from the administration of his see, what merit he possesses before God.

### 14. Concerning the Bishop Who Was Expelled and Restored by the Lord Himself to His See

Within Italy, a vigorous man named Ratherus presided over the Church of Verona. In habit he was a monk, an outstanding practitioner of every form of religious observance, and a most eloquent interpreter of the divine Scriptures.

He was canonically elected at the palace of Aachen, when the fast of September was approaching, and was consecrated on the following Sunday by two archbishops: the saint of worthy memory, Bruno of Cologne, and Robert of Trier, together with five fellow bishops. With the consent of the clergy and people, he was enthroned in the aforesaid Church.

Having thus obtained the episcopal chair, he administered the property of the bishopric and ecclesiastical rights with the legitimate rigor of discipline, disregarding the counsels of those who until then, in such matters, had sought not the things of Christ but their own advantages. For although he was otherwise a thoroughly upright man, he was, in keeping with the diversity of human character, a man of unusually forceful spirit and somewhat severe in his replies, out of zeal for justice and equity.

But because, as someone has said, truth produces hatred, this sort of conduct aroused against him the hatred not only of the clergy but also of the citizens. Some of these, closely related by blood to the bishops Robert of Trier and Balderic of Liège, complained of the losses to their profits and, through the bishop’s harshness, stirred those men to hatred and hostility against their lord, declaring him frenzied and unworthy of the honor and title of bishop.

Bishop Ratherus was only moderately moved by these insults. He did not seek external assistance; instead, turning to his book chests, he began composing certain invectives against the bishops Balderic and Robert.

As a result, when the jealousy of his rivals grew inflamed, he was expelled from the episcopal see, not without insult. After his expulsion, he sought the assistance of the glorious King Otto. The king attempted to help him out of consideration for piety, but his adversaries resisted vigorously. Since no opportunity for his restoration arose, it seemed useful for him to take refuge with the kindness of the most devout and holy Archbishop Bruno, his ordainer.

When he came, he was graciously received and honorably treated according to Bruno’s customary manner of kindness. Not long afterward, he was duly restored to his chair. For in the judgment of so great a man, the stubborn conspiracy of all his enemies vanished, and the burden of their accusations fell silent before the steadfast testimony of his defense.

Bruno set forth the entire order of Ratherus’s canonical election and ecclesiastical consecration. Such justice, he argued, ought not to be invalidated by any accusation based on lay testimony; indeed, all the agents of this faction ought greatly to fear the offense of apostolic judgment.

Thus, after the minds of his adversaries had been softened by the antidote of his sweet eloquence, divine mercy so ordered matters that, once all had been pacified in indissoluble harmony, the bishop was restored to his see by those same men with every mark of honor—by the very men who had previously expelled him with unbecoming insult—and he became more improved throughout all the days of his life.

### 15. A Letter of Bishop Ratherus to Bruno

There also survives a letter of that same bishop addressed to Saint Bruno, composed with considerable eloquence.  
[Note: Different from the one that we read in the Works of Ratherus, p. 529.]

In it, calling Bruno his patron, Ratherus declares with immeasurable thanksgiving that, with divine mercy preceding and following him, and with Bruno’s spiritual prudence intervening, he had been transformed into another man; that through the renewal of mind and spirit he had been changed into the effectiveness of a better condition; and that the love of all his people had been cemented into the advancement and increase of his honor.  
[Note: Although the manuscript shows no sign of a lacuna after this, it is nevertheless sufficiently clear that the end of this narrative has been lost. What follows is nothing but a speech about Saint Bruno, lacking its beginning, by some monk of Saint Pantaleon, who perhaps supplied the conclusion of the Life. In the exemplar from which our author copied, several leaves had undoubtedly fallen out; the scribe, not realizing this, wrote the text in this form. Bethmann.]

It appears that something has been lost here.

### The Vision of Abbot Wolberon

For this is the reason why we rejoice in the patronage of so great a man. The times of Frederick, the former archbishop of Cologne, were hateful and hostile to us. He, a violent invader of that sacred community, also oppressed it with many adversities.

For when the abbot of that place had died, he violated their freedom of election, in which they had until then gloried through the indulgence of the apostolic Benedict, and imposed upon them an unknown abbot. He compelled them to obey him by an oath, and afflicted and exiled those who resisted, if not personally, then through the hands of cruel lords.

For the intruded abbot placed many of the brothers of his community whom he had brought with him over the individual obediences, and subjected the entire cloister to them. Under this dissension, it was necessary that the Church should be endangered.

Therefore, seeing the affliction of his people, the Lord, through the merit of Bruno, released Bishop Frederick, the author of this error, from life,  
[Note: In the year 1131.]  
to show that he did not fail his own people; and he caused the intruded abbot to act more gently toward his subjects.

Meanwhile, the exiles were recalled, and the adulterine officials were expelled and sent away. The abbot alone was permitted to remain, and due reverence was shown him; he was troubled by no burden, because they feared God’s judgment in this matter and the disgrace of the world.  
[Note: “was harassed” in c.]

At last the jubilee had arrived on its desired course, and tranquil times followed in serenity, while liberty was granted to the captives and the death of the bishop Frederick, who had died long before, was finally made known.

For one night, after Matins, when the brothers had returned to bed, the custodian of that church, as is customary for custodians, was inspecting the altars and replenishing the lamps. Finally, visiting the tomb of Saint Bruno, he knelt down to pray. Suddenly, his eyes closed, and in spirit he saw the following.

He saw that the aforementioned Bishop Frederick was proceeding with a sorrowful bearing and, with frequent sobs, indicating that he was being harshly treated. The custodian addressed him in spirit as he was and asked the cause of his grief, since the universal Church was unceasingly entreating God on his behalf with many prayers, distributions of alms, and every kind of offering of salutary vows.

He replied:

“True, brother, true are the things you recall. Know that God takes delight in the prayers of the faithful poured out for me. Yet, although I ought to have obtained grace through them, I am gravely hindered by Saint Bruno. He objects that I inflicted many adversities upon this holy community, miserable man that I am; he maintains that satisfaction has not been made to him for these things, nor that I have received what is commensurate with my deserts. For your sake alone, therefore, pardon has until now been denied me.”

The custodian said:

“My lord, if faith must be given to all that you have stated, what are we to presume about such a patron?”

He replied:

“Know that this man possesses great merit before the Most High, and that he is truly the provider and arranger of everything that takes place among you. For he possesses this place and the brothers as a household entrusted to him by God; and, as your advocate, he frequently moves among you, ordering and arranging everything. Since he cares for you, I beg for mercy: let him be moved by your prayers on my behalf!”

Having said no more to him, he disappeared, and the custodian returned to himself.

### Also Concerning the Same Archbishop Bruno

Blessed Bruno is recognized as possessing great merit before God. For whoever suffers from quartan or tertian fever, if he approaches his tomb with devout heart and drinks for three consecutive days from the chalice that had been placed upon his breast in the tomb, will rejoice that, through Bruno’s merits, he has received healing from God.

### Concerning the Miracle That Occurred at His Tomb on the Lord’s Supper

So that the miracle which occurred on the Lord’s Supper should not remain unknown to you, I have resolved to make it known to your charity.

When we had gathered in the morning to pray together, a certain woman came forward with equal devotion in order to pray. For five years she had suffered from an affliction of the hand, so that the tips of her fingers were driven into the middle of her palm. As soon as she prostrated herself at the tomb of Saint Bruno the archbishop, she obtained health with her hand extended. And lest this seem an empty claim, the scars of the contracted fingers plainly prove it.

### Bruno the Peaceful, Friend of the Eternal King

Under your leadership, shepherding, and governance, Cologne rejoices.

With its leader, majesty reigns, and with its leader, honor;

under its leader, welcome peace and a spacious court;

in its leader, cultivated law and abundant wisdom flourish.

With its leader, the great are greater and most of the lesser are lesser;

under its leader, the prudent and the foolish move about,

and rightly he truly knows how to treat each one fittingly.

He treats the humble gently and the timid firmly.

The clergy are honored by him, and the people are helped;

he raises up those filled with wealth and consoles the needy.

He tolerates nothing wicked, but examines the law with equity.

He who does not rest under him knows nothing of delights.

With its leader there are joys of many riches.

And this is rightly so, because, dispensing them graciously,

he does not conceal them, but strives to use them for the benefit of others.

These are the ways by which he acquired his honors,

and through which he wins and attaches more people to himself.

May he remain joyful, not sorrowful, always in these things.  
[Note: At this point the manuscript contains two verses:

“Arboreal flowers signify the honors of the world.

As flowers perish, so the honors of the world perish.”

But it appears that, in the manuscript from which our author copied, they had been added by another hand in an empty space, as often happens in manuscripts. Our scribe, copying everything with the greatest diligence, did not think these verses should be omitted. Bethmann.]

[Col. 0987]

## Bruno’s Diploma

### He Confirms an Exchange Made between Abbot Werinfrid and Count Warner

Bruno, by the grace of God archbishop and son of the holy Church of Cologne, to the servants of God, wishes it to be known both to those present and to those to come that a certain religious abbot of the monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy, named Werinfrid, approached our clemency concerning an exchange which he had made with Count Warner, our faithful man. Since those monasteries were under the protection and defense of our guardianship, he requested that the same exchange be strengthened by our authority.

Because his petition was just, we assented to it and took thought for the advantage of the Church.

For the aforesaid count, our faithful man, possessed near the monastery of Stavelot a certain estate belonging to him, called Baldau. Count Sigifrid was striving intensely, both with us and with our faithful men who were his intercessors, to acquire it. When the abbot heard this and feared the excessive—indeed, interminable—disturbance of the place, he earnestly endeavored to forestall the plan entirely and repeatedly remind our clemency that this should not happen.  
[Note: The ancient fathers avoided above all the society of great magnates and nobles, and therefore especially shunned their neighborhood. Hence they chose dreadful solitudes in which to dwell.]

Accordingly, the aforesaid abbot and the count came together, and Abbot Werinfrid gave to Count Warner, our faithful man, whatever he appeared to possess in the estate called Nohas, in the district of Haspengau, in the county of Tienen: namely, a good estate with its small buildings, mills, waters and watercourses, lands acquired and to be acquired, a great abundance of woodland, a household of both sexes, and everything else belonging to the same place.

And because the monks of the other monastery, namely Malmedy, possessed a certain part of the same estate, the abbot gave to that church, in the district of Condroz, a place called Villa, in the county of Huy: six good manses with a household of both sexes, good woodland, and everything else attached to that estate.

In return, the aforesaid Count Warner, before suitable witnesses, gave whatever he appeared to possess in the aforementioned estate of Baldau: a good estate, though greatly devastated by enemies; good cultivated fields; Cambay; a mill; and a great woodland. For the church of that estate, with a good endowment, privileges, and constitution—that is, land and woodland—had been given to the same monastery in ancient times.

The abbot, with the consent of the monks of both monasteries, and the count, with the consent of his wife, sons, and friends, mutually delivered all these things to one another. Before our highness they confirmed the same exchange. The count sent by suitable witnesses a branch with a clod of earth to the altar of Stavelot and legally completed the transfer with investiture.

And so that this exchange might be held more firmly in future times, at the petition of the same abbot we confirmed it by the writing of our hand.

The sign of Werinfrid, abbot.

The signs of Werinmund, Titger, Norbert, Reginard, and the others.

And of the other monastery: the sign of Odulf, Wisiric, Heilfrid, Rogibald.

The sign of Count Warner, Reginard, Gevard, and Richar, and of many others.

These things were enacted publicly at the palace of Aachen, on the second day before the Kalends of November, during the reign of King Otto, our brother, in the eighteenth year, under Duke Godfrey.

## In the Year of the Lord 965. Leo VIII, Antipope

## Historical Notice

(Cocquelines, *Bullarium*, *Summaries of the Privileges of the Supreme Pontiffs*, enlarged collection.)

At the Roman Synod, after John XII had been deposed from the Holy Roman Church on 6 December 963, Leo VIII, the chief notary, was appointed in his place. When John returned to Rome in the following year, however, after the departure of Emperor Otto, he compelled Leo to flee and abandon the dignity he had usurped.

But when John died on 14 May, the Romans, without the consent or will of Otto, placed Benedict—of whom we shall speak shortly—on the apostolic see. Therefore the emperor went to Rome with Leo. After holding a council, Leo removed the pallium from Benedict, and also the pontifical staff, which he broke. He then invaded the pontifical see again and held it for one year and three months.

## Privileges and Constitutions of Leo VIII, Antipope

### I. Letter of Leo VIII to Rodoald, Patriarch of Aquileia  
*(Year 963.) He sends him the pallium.*

[In Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, V, 44.]

### Leo, Bishop and Servant of the Servants of God, to Our Most Reverend and Most Holy Brother Rodoald, Patriarch of the Holy Church of Aquileia

If shepherds of sheep are content to endure sun and frost day and night in guarding their flocks, and with ever-watchful eyes keep careful watch lest any of them should perish by wandering or be carried away, torn by the bites of wild beasts, with how much labor and care ought we to remain vigilant, who are called shepherds of souls?

Let us attend to our charge, and let us not cease to perform the duty we have undertaken toward the guardianship of the Lord’s sheep, lest on the day of divine judgment the guilt of negligence for our sloth torture us before the supreme Shepherd, since we are now judged more exalted than others by the reverence of our office.

We have sent the pallium to your fraternity, according to custom, for the celebration of the solemnities of Mass. We grant you permission to use it, while the privileges of your Church remain in their present condition, in no other way than you know your predecessors, now departed, to have used it.

Since the honor of this garment must be preserved by the modest vigor of your deeds, we exhort you also to make the adornments of your conduct correspond to it, so that, with God as author, you may rightly be conspicuous in both respects.

Therefore let your life be a rule for your sons. If any strength has been instilled in them, let them be directed by it; in it let them see what they should imitate; by continually contemplating it, let them always progress, so that after God it may be seen to be your doing that they have lived well.

Therefore let your heart be lifted up neither by the prosperous things that flatter temporarily nor cast down by adversity. Whatever may occur, let it be conquered by the virtue of patience.

Let hatred find no place with you, and let undiscriminating favor find none either. Let the wicked experience severity. Let evil suggestion not make the innocent guilty in your eyes. Let favor not excuse the guilty. Do not show yourself lenient toward offenders, lest what you have failed to avenge you permit to be committed. Let there be in you the gentleness of a good shepherd, and let there also be the severe discipline of a judge: one quality to cherish those who live innocently, another to restrain from ferocity those who are restless and savage.

But because sometimes the zeal of rulers, when they wish to be strict avengers of the wicked, turns correction into cruelty, restrain anger by judgment, and let the discipline of equitable custody exalt you, so that neither may wealth persuade the rich man, through his power, to dare anything outside the path of reason in your presence, nor may humility make the poor man despair of his possessions.

Thus, by God’s mercy, you may become such as sacred reading commands when it says: “A bishop must be blameless” (1 Tim. 3:2).

You will be able to use all these things salutarily if you possess charity as your teacher. Whoever follows charity never departs from the right path.

And behold, dearest brother, many other things belong to the priesthood; these are the things of the pallium. If you diligently preserve them, you will have inwardly what you show yourself to have received outwardly.

And so that it may be clear to all Christians with what charity we love you, for love of blessed Mark the Evangelist, our shepherd, the most glorious disciple of Peter, prince of the apostles, who presided over your see, we renew for you by this present privilege the ancient privilege granted by blessed Peter to Saint Hermagoras, successor of blessed Mark the Evangelist, which, because of our sins, was burned by the savagery of the pagans.

We wish and command by apostolic authority that among all the Churches of Italy the see of Aquileia, over which by God’s authority you preside, be regarded as first after the Roman see.

We also grant this for the increase and adornment of your Church: when, by God’s will, you and your successors depart from this light, no one from another Church may be placed over it. Rather, both clergy and laity shall choose from its own bosom one whom they may lawfully establish as their pastor.

God is faithful and will never allow someone to be found in the assembly of the Aquileian Church who could, by the merit of episcopal dignity, rightly be preferred to the others.

May the Holy Trinity surround your fraternity with the protection of its grace and direct us in the way of its fear, so that after the bitterness of this life we may together deserve to reach eternal sweetness.

Given in the most sacred church of the Apostle Peter, on the Ides of December, in the first year of Leo’s pontificate, while Otto was emperor in the second year.

Use discipline in such a way that you punish faults without departing from love for the persons whom you correct. Show yourself merciful to the poor, insofar as virtue permits. Let your defense assist the oppressed; let modest correction oppose those who oppress. Accept no person’s face against justice. Despise no one who seeks what is just.

### II. The Privilege of Pope Leo VIII Concerning Investitures  
*(Year 963, 6 December; 964, January.)*

[In Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, Laws, vol. II, p. 166.]

### Notice

We present the charter, famous since the eleventh century, from folio 192 of Vatican manuscript no. 1984, written at Rome in the eleventh century and the beginning of the twelfth, though corrected with the aid of the imperial Viennese manuscript in the catalogue of canon law, no. 105, folio 13. Gentillotus assigns this latter manuscript to the twelfth century, whereas our copyist assigns it to the thirteenth.

A third copy exists in the same library among the Salzburg manuscripts, no. 323, parchment of the late eleventh or twelfth century, folio 104. A fourth was consulted at Bamberg in a collection of canons of the twelfth or early thirteenth century, marked C. 64, where it appears after the notice concerning Hadrian’s decree and before the constitution of Nicholas II and the Concordat of Worms.

A fifth exists at Cambridge among the manuscripts of Corpus Christi College; a sixth in the library of the city of Bruges in Flanders, where, together with the constitution of Nicholas II concerning the election of the pope, it is placed in a thirteenth-century manuscript beneath Peter of Riga’s work on the whole Bible.

Ivo inserted part of it in the *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 135, and Gratian inserted it in his *Decree*, distinction 63, chapter 23. It appeared in full, but plainly interpolated, from a Florentine manuscript in Theodoric of Niem’s treatise *On the Privileges and Rights of the Empire*, in Schardius’s *Collection of Works on Imperial Jurisdiction*, Basel, 1566, and in Goldast.

We read an account of the event in book 3 of the *Tripartite Collection of Canons* and in Ivo’s *Decree*, book 8, chapter 136.

[Note: We owe to our copyist the text of Ivo in the imperial Viennese manuscript among the Salzburg manuscripts, no. 323, parchment of the late eleventh or twelfth century:

“Pope Leo, having assembled a synod at Rome in the Church of Saint Savior, after the example of blessed Hadrian, bishop of the apostolic see, who granted to the most victorious lord Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards, the dignity of the patriciate, the ordering of the apostolic see, and the investiture of bishops: I also, Leo, servant of the servants of God and bishop, together with all the clergy and people of Rome, establish, confirm, and ratify, and by our apostolic authority grant and bestow upon Lord Otto, first king of the Teutons, and his successors in this kingdom of Italy forever, both the power to choose his successor and the power to appoint the pontiff of the supreme apostolic see.

And therefore, that archbishops and bishops should receive investiture from him, but consecration from the place from which they ought to receive it, except those whom the emperor has granted to the pontiff from among the archbishops.

And that henceforth no one of whatever dignity or religious rank should have the power to elect a patrician or pontiff of the supreme apostolic see, or to ordain any bishop, without the consent of that emperor; yet this must be done without any payment of money.

And that he himself should be patrician and king.

If any bishop should be elected by clergy and people, he shall not be consecrated unless he has been approved and invested by the aforesaid king.

If anyone attempts anything against this apostolic authority, we decree that he shall be subject to excommunication and, unless he repents, punished by irrevocable exile or struck with the ultimate penalties.

The decree ends.”]

The dispute over the authority of the charter is by no means settled by the arguments brought forward thus far. For all the rights here granted to the Teutonic kings—namely, a defined right in the election of the pontiff, the Roman patriciate, and the right of investiture of bishops—are known to have belonged to them from ancient times. Otto had already at that time usurped for himself the right to choose his successor, with the consent of the leading men of Germany.

Nevertheless, the form of the charter certainly raises some suspicion. To say nothing of other matters, one ought to wonder who would ever have written of his predecessor in the papacy, “whose life and conduct we have heard to be sufficiently distinguished”; and the fact that Otto is designated only as king of the Teutons, with the word “emperor” omitted, should cause hesitation. The specification of the time is also lacking.

But since there is no doubt that Otto and Leo renewed the alliance between Empire and Church, faith in the conditions proposed here should not be wholly denied.

### Editorial and Textual Notes

- Section 10: At Col. 0981 the manuscript reads *primus* (“first”) for *primis* (“earliest”); it also reads *hiis* (“these”) where the text has *hujus* (“of this [bishop]”).
- Section 11: The preceding account was long ago copied by Gelenius, *Hierotheca*, p. 59; it is useful in some measure for elucidating Thietmar’s narrative, II.15. It is clear that Bruno did not betray his brother, though no one can readily explain the true course of events. The manuscript c. reads *invitatum* (“having invited”) for *invitavit* (“he invited”).
- Section 12: The Duke of Lorraine is identified in the note as Conrad (*Kuonradi*). Manuscript c. reads *edito* (“given forth”); perhaps *tradita* (“handed over”) is intended.
- Section 13: Manuscript c. reads *pontis* (“of the bridge”) for *pontem* (“the bridge”).
- Section 15: The manuscript reads *amore* (“love”). Although the manuscript shows no visible lacuna after this point, the end of the narrative has plainly been lost; what follows is merely a beginningless discourse on Saint Bruno by a monk of Saint Pantaleon, who may perhaps have supplied the conclusion of the Life. Several leaves had undoubtedly fallen from the exemplar, without the scribe’s noticing it. Bethmann.
- Vision of Abbot Wolberon: The reference is to the time of the earlier Frederick, archbishop of Cologne (from 1099 onward); Frederick II held the see in the middle of the twelfth century. The book itself seems not to extend beyond the middle of the thirteenth century; see above, chapter 12, at the end. Manuscript c. reads *vellitatur* for *vellicatur* (“is troubled”). In the custodian’s question, c. reads *nobisque* (“and for us”) for *nobis quid* (“what [then] for us?”).
- Poem: The manuscript reads *Me* (“me”) rather than *Te* (“you”) in “Under your leadership.”
- Charter notice: The Vatican exemplar was also transcribed in Baronius’s *Annals*, Lucan edition.

### Privilege of Pope Leo VIII
It is fitting for those endowed with apostolic authority to come to the aid of petitioners with kindly compassion [Col. 0993A] and to grant the requests of their minds with eager devotion [Note: “to request for whom,” witness 1; “to be requested,” witness 2]. For from this, above all, a reward is obtained from the Creator of all things [Note: “while,” witness 1], whenever we affirm that the whole clergy and the whole people are in agreement, and that they will undoubtedly have been led to a better condition.

And therefore, because in your humility [Note: “our humility,” witness 1] you justly and reasonably petition our apostolate, humbly asking that, while we gladly carry out [Note: “travel through,” witness 1] the holy synod, convened on our advice [Note: “council,” witnesses 1 and 2], established in the Lateran patriarchate [Note: “Lateran,” witness 2], in the church of Saint Saviour, with many Catholic bishops and abbots, and moreover judges and doctors of law, promulgating how we may remain and live quietly and peacefully; with everyone present [Note: absent in witness 1], and with each of the districts of this blessed city of Rome [Col. 0993B], and from every order, clergy [Note: “clergy,” witness 2] and people, affirming and confirming in every respect that heresy, contention, and every error had been expelled—for error [Note: “excessive error,” witness 2] had been growing excessively in these times—we decree concerning both the Roman Empire and the Apostolic See, concerning the dignity of the patriciate and concerning the investiture [Note: “vestiture,” witness 2] of bishoprics.

Therefore, following the example of blessed Hadrian, bishop of the Apostolic See, whose life and conduct we have heard were sufficiently distinguished [Note: “distinguished,” witness 2], and whom we have recognized as exceedingly reasonable [Note: “reasonably,” witness 1] in his spiritual ordinances [Note: “his” is written twice in witness 1], who [Note: “because,” witness 2] established such a holy synod and [Note: “and, in the presence of all and by their authority,” Theodoric of Niem] granted to the lord Charles, most victorious king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans [Note: “the Roman patriciate and the kingdom of Italy to Charles and his successors,” Theodoric of Niem], the dignity of the patriciate and the appointment of the Apostolic See and of the bishoprics [Note: “and” is absent in witness 1] [Col. 0993C] [Note: “also the investitures of the bishoprics, just as he himself might wish, with discretion and reverence. Therefore we, Leo,” Theodoric of Niem]—we also, Leo, bishop and servant of the servants of God [Note: “bishops,” Theodoric of Niem], likewise [Note: “similarly,” witness 2], together with all the clergy and the entire Roman people of every order [Note: “and of all orders,” witness 2] of this blessed City [Note: “of this city,” witness 1], as appears in the documents themselves, establish, confirm, strengthen, and by our apostolic authority grant and bestow upon the lord Otto [Note: “the lord Otto, the first Teutonic king,” 1984; “the lord Otto, first Augustus, Teutonic king, most provident, our spiritual son in Christ,” Theodoric of Niem], the first Teutonic king, our dearest spiritual son in Christ, and upon his successors in this kingdom of Italy forever, both the power to choose a successor for himself and to appoint the pontiff of the supreme Apostolic See, and consequently [Note: “this also,” witness 2] the archbishops or bishops, provided that they [Note: “only,” Theodoric of Niem] receive investiture from him and receive consecration from whatever quarter it may concern, except those whom the emperor has granted to the pontiff and the archbishops.

Thus, moreover, we assert that henceforth no one, of whatever rank, condition [Note: “condiction,” witness 1], dignity, or religious standing [Note: “or,” witness 2], shall have the power to elect a king or patrician [Note: “prince,” Theodoric of Niem], or the pontiff of the supreme Apostolic See, or any bishop [Note: “bishop, or to ordain,” witness 2]. But to the king of the Roman Empire alone we grant this authority as a mark of reverence [Note: “reverence,” witness 2; “to be revered,” Theodoric of Niem], so that, without any payment, he may arrange all the matters mentioned above [Note: “he may dispose and govern them, as king and Roman patrician,” Theodoric of Niem], and that he himself may be king and patrician.

If someone is elected bishop by the clergy and people, unless he has been approved and invested by the aforesaid king [Note: “above-written,” witness 2], let no one consecrate him [Note: “that is, no one may,” witness 2]. Therefore, if anyone attempts anything against this apostolic authority and tradition, or is found to be a transgressor in any respect, or acts against this [Note: absent in witness 2] our council [Note: “advice,” Theodoric of Niem], let him know that he will fall under the anger of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, of our son the lord Otto and his [Col. 0994B] successors, and of us [Note: “and of all our predecessors and of us,” witness 2]; and, having incurred the bond of anathema, we decree that he shall thereby be subject to the excommunication of the universal Church and of the entire Christian people. Moreover, unless he repent of his evil, let him be punished by irrevocable exile or struck with the ultimate penalties.

But whoever, with pious regard, proves in all things to be a guardian and observer [Note: “guardian and observer,” witness 2] shall deserve to possess the grace of blessing and eternal life with all the saints, without end, forever and ever. Amen. Amen. Amen. [Note: “Amen” occurs only once in witness 2. Theodoric of Niem adds: “The following were present at these proceedings: senators, proconsuls, holders of exarchal offices, district officials, and the Greek, Arab, and Jewish communities, as well as representatives of the principal streets. Moreover, cardinals, archbishops, all the priests and bishops from neighboring cities, processional clergy, notaries, chancellors, and people from every class of the Roman Empire.”]

## III. PRIVILEGE OF LEO VIII FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT PETER OF MONTE MAIORE (A.D. 963–965)

[In Baluze, *Miscellanea*, III, 5.]

[Col. 0994C] Leo, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to Mauringus, religious priest and monk and abbot of the venerable monastery of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, which is situated in the territory of the province and in the place called Montemaggiore, and through you to your successors in that same venerable monastery forever.

If things that accord with pious desires are always to be granted, then surely those which are known to concern the advancement of divine worship must not be entirely refused; they are not only to be requested from benefactors, but undoubtedly demanded by the force of charity. Therefore, because your religious devotion has asked us to confirm for you and your monastery, founded in honor of blessed Peter the apostle, situated on the mountain called Maior, in fulfillment of the vow and out of love for our dearest and most beloved son, the emperor Otto, whose name must be mentioned with the highest reverence, and for Adelaisa, his dearest imperial wife and our dearest spiritual daughter, that we grant the privilege of the Apostolic See—namely, the monastery itself in its entirety, with its churches, lands and woods, farms and homesteads, male and female servants, and the ancient deserted monastery of Horluc with all its adjoining lands and appurtenances; also the estate called Tunneto, with male and female servants, vineyards and lands, with every payment and public obligation, situated in the county of Bedarese; likewise the cell of Saint Honoratus in its entirety, with everything belonging to it, situated in the county of Aix, at the place called Rocca Fraudosa, and in the county of Toulon; the fortress called Septem Furnos with all its appurtenances [Col. 0995B], namely villages, saltworks, fisheries, and the salt pans called Eras, and everything belonging there, situated in the county of Arles; the land of Saint Peter in the fortress of Fossis; the valley called Saint Peter, together with the churches themselves, especially those of Saint Peter, Saint Martin, Saint Julian, Saint Genesius, and Saint Hermes; and, at the bridge, one vessel called Venroso; and in the county of Avignon, in the estate called Casus, eight homesteads and a ruined church, with male and female servants; and in the county of Riez, the estate called Criselgis, with male and female servants; as well as other places which in former times were granted to the same monastery by most Christian people, or which shall henceforth be granted—we confirm all these things by this apostolic privilege to you and your successors [Col. 0995C] forever.

Thus, being established under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, over which by God’s authority we preside, it shall be subject to the jurisdiction of no other church, while the aforesaid monastery shall provide our holy Church with four solidi for lights. But if, because of the length of the journey, or perhaps the danger posed by enemies, or because of discord within the kingdom, you are unable to pay the aforesaid pension each year, it shall be permitted for you, after the third or fourth year, to pay to us and our Church all the pension for the preceding years at one time.

Therefore, favoring your pious requests and by our authority committing to execution what your religious devotion asks, we entirely prohibit any priest of any church from celebrating the solemnity of the Mass within the jurisdiction of the aforesaid monastery by any authority whatsoever, unless he has been invited by the monastery’s abbot. We decree and promulgate by apostolic authority, under threat of the future judgment, that none of our successor pontiffs, nor any other person, great or small—whether duke, margrave, count, gastald, or a man possessing any dignity—may in any way overturn these privileges piously established by our intention. Rather, we define that they shall remain firm, stable, and unshaken; and, under the bond of anathema, they are to be observed for all time unless the offender repents.

Whoever, with pious regard, proves in all things to be the guardian and observer of this document of our privilege, command, and confirmation [Col. 0996A] shall deserve to obtain the grace of blessing from God, the giver of all good things, and to become a participant in eternal life.

Let it therefore be your care to adorn the brothers of the monastery over whom you preside with distinguished conduct and irreproachable life, so that, having preferred to endow those subject to apostolic privileges with unshaken security, he may rather desire and strive for them to be adorned by the daily prayers of discipline with the inviolable gift of heavenly abundance.

Let their life be communal and sincere; let the sincerity of their sober fellowship endure, so that for those to whom the world is dead and buried, the vices may not be aroused by the incentives of contention. For a man is known to labor in vain and without result if he is seen to submit his neck to pride, the mother of vices.

Let humility in God be exalted, because through it the elect have possessed the citadel of heavenly gifts [Col. 0996B]. Let the rule of the traditions delivered by certain holy patrons therefore be before the eyes of mind and body, so that every superior may know how he ought to command his subjects, lest, while harsh things are imposed which do not appear suitable to everyone, the subjects break out into contempt because of the ruler’s lack of discretion.

Let there be moderated vigor; let there be among the brothers an exceptional serenity of solicitude, so that, while all who devote themselves wholly to God serve well in regular obedience in temporal matters, they may attain the eternal joys of the heavenly homeland.

It is enough to have said these things concerning what belongs to care. Above all, however, while we groan for the mercy of our Redeemer, let us await our redemption with the utmost earnestness, awaiting it together with every nation, so that what piety demands may be adequately and confidently fulfilled by the frailty of human condition through the help of its Creator.

[Written by the hand of . . . . . . The remainder is missing.]

## IV. LEO VIII’S CESSION OF THE DONATIONS OF THE ROMAN CHURCH (A.D. 964)

[In Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, Laws, vol. II, p. 168.]

### NOTICE

The constitution published together with the booklet of Theodoric of Niem at the cited place was copied by our copyist from the Caesarean Viennese collection of decretals, marked among the books of canon law as manuscript no. 105, a thirteenth-century manuscript formerly belonging to the monastery of Frankenthal between Speyer and Worms. The charter is most plainly convicted of falsity even by its subscriptions; and it appears to have been composed during the controversy between priesthood and empire under Henry IV or V, as an instrument of defense against the spurious donations attributed to Louis, Otto, and Henry.

The decree of the same Pope Leo.

Leo, servant of the servants of God, bishop, to Otto, our spiritual son in Christ, the august emperor, and to all your successors, the emperors and kings of the kingdom of Italy.

Whatever the lord Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, and also his father Pippin, granted from the royal possessions of this kingdom of Italy to the holy Roman Church of blessed Peter the apostle—whether through documents written by Etherius, his notary, or through oaths, or by donation, or by other means; and whatever came to it through donations from the emperor Justinian and King Aripert—we grant, renounce, and transfer all these things to you, Emperor Otto, and to Adeleida, your wife and partner in the kingdom, and to your successors in this kingdom of Italy, forever, with the holy Gospels and the patronage of many saints, namely, with the cross of the Lord, the sandals of his feet, and the seamless garment [Note: “indestructible,” manuscript], and over the body of blessed Peter, with terrible oaths sworn by the aforesaid pope and his cardinals, with the consent and authority of the entire Roman people, both clergy and laity, from the Roman orders of every district, who were present, approved, and confirmed these things, because of the excessive persecution of the enemies of God and the Church [Col. 0997B], so that almighty God might grant victory to such a king and drive them from the provinces of the Roman Empire.

We wish the donations that we shall specifically name here to be perpetually included among the royal possessions through our apostolic grant. Namely: Surianum [Note: See the revised edition. Adrian the pope obtained this at Borgia, *Brief History of Temporal Dominion*, etc., appendix, pp. 1 ff.]; Mount Bardonis; Luna; the island of Corsica; Reggio; Parma; Mantua; Mount Silicis [Note: “Mount Celete,” Theodoric]; the islands of Venice; the duchy of Ferrara; Gabellum; Comacchio; the duchy of Istria; Dalmatia; the exarchate of Ravenna; Faenza; Cesena; the fortress of Tyberiacus; the fortress of Modigliana; the fortress of Elmiza [Note: “Coniza,” Theodoric]; the fortress of Fanilla; the rock of Appla; and the fortress of Tosianianum [Note: “Tusinianum, the rock of Maurus, Servutealni, the duchy of Rimini,” manuscript and Theodoric]; [Col. 0997C] the fortress of Ceperianum; Thus, you shall have, hold, and possess these things forever [Note: “for the use of your court and armies, to wage war and fight against the aforesaid pagans and against rebels of the Roman Empire. Therefore, by the authority of this document of ours, we confirm and strengthen them in all your descendants, from generation to generation forever,” Theodoric].

For if anyone destroys this authority of ours and is found to have violated it, or acts against it, let him know that he will fall under the anger of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of us and our predecessors. Moreover, unless he repents of his evil, let him be subject as guilty to the Julian law concerning royal authority and the republic, so that those who have attempted anything against the republic or against the majesty of the emperor may suffer the loss of their lives and their property be confiscated.

So be it, so be it.

The following were present at these proceedings [Note: “namely, archbishops and bishops from neighboring regions,” manuscript; “archbishops and bishops, and others from neighboring counties,” Theodoric of Niem]: Eustacius, bishop of Albano [Note: The subscriptions of Theodoric of Niem are as follows: “The archbishop of Cagliari; Bishop Ciconatus; Eustasius, bishop of Albano; Gratiosus, bishop of Palestrina; Benedictus, bishop of Todi; Boardus, bishop of Castro; John, bishop of Perugia; Georgius, bishop of Orte; Valentinus, bishop of Velletri; Andreas, bishop of Mentana; Theodosius, bishop of Mileto; Savianus, bishop of Ferentino; Albertus, bishop of Lucera; Damianus Alanus.
