## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 965. UTHO, BISHOP OF STRASBOURG

[Col. 1001]

### NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LIFE OF SAINT ARBOGAST

(Bollandists, vol. V of June, p. 170.)

Since the art of printing was discovered, very many authors—not only orthodox ones but also heretics—have published the acts of Saint Arbogast, yet in such a way that, generally speaking, the younger they are, the more copiously they present their material. Therefore, so that we might not rashly and without sufficiently reliable authority impose anything in this matter, we have tried, as far as possible, to uncover the earliest sources. Although we were unable to reach authors either contemporary with or nearly contemporary to our saint, we finally came to the one who appears to have been the first to commit these acts to writing, as is clear from the beginning of his work: “They relate the origin of the most holy priest . . .” and so forth.

By these words he clearly indicates, first, how far removed he is from the time of Saint Arbogast, since he calls the material ancient; second, why he omitted what preceded the saint’s episcopate: namely, because antiquity had preserved those matters neither by tradition nor in writing; finally, that he is reporting only certain miracles, not those that he had previously read written somewhere, but those which, passing through the ears of the faithful and being related by later generations, had been poured into his own ears. Thus he presents as the sole witness of his history that pious tradition of the faithful which had endured until his own time.

Let anyone therefore search in vain for a writer of the Life of Saint Arbogast earlier than this one of ours, whoever he ultimately was. Nor should one accept without faith and testimony anything that other authors, certainly later than ours, relate about this holy bishop, whether in greater detail or in contradiction, since the sole foundation of everything known about him is the tradition of earlier people; and in matters of this sort tradition is generally the less suspect the more ancient it is in comparison with the others.

If someone asks me whom, and of what period, I think our author was, I confess that I cannot determine this from any certain indication. Yet if what Guilielmus Eysengreinius reports in his *Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth*, printed at Dillingen in 1565, and what our Possevinus consequently reports in his *Sacred Apparatus*, together with others in their discussions of libraries and writers, is true—if, I say, it is true that the Life of Saint Arbogast was written by Utho, who under this name was the second bishop of Strasbourg [according to Wimpheling, the third], and who governed that church from A.D. 950 to 965, I would dare to affirm that our author cannot be later than the tenth century. He must therefore either be Utho himself, as our Henschenius thinks in his *Dissertation on the Three Dagoberts*, p. 77, or another author earlier than Utho, since he knows of no writer of the acts of Saint Arbogast before himself.

There is also no slight conjecture in favor of Utho. The chronology agrees: if these acts were first written by him in the tenth century, he could properly say that many matters concerning the saint’s life had been effaced by antiquity, since he was writing in the third century after Saint Arbogast. The place also agrees: Utho was bishop of Strasbourg. That our author wrote among the people of Strasbourg may be inferred both from his calling Saint Arbogast “Father” and from the fact that he composed this work there, where the memory of the saint’s miracles and deeds during his episcopate in the Church of Strasbourg was especially vigorous, and where he himself learned them through the reports of later generations.

Finally, if Utho composed any Life of Saint Arbogast, he would undoubtedly have left it in the library of Strasbourg, which he strove so diligently to enrich with books collected from everywhere, as Wimpheling, Eysengrein, and others testify; or at least he would have shared it with his fellow citizens and neighbors, especially religious men and lovers of such studies, who would also have copied it into their codices. Yet we find no other acts of Saint Arbogast transmitted in the manuscripts there than those which we are about to publish. It remains, therefore, for us to judge that this work is Utho’s.

[Col. 1001]

## A BRIEF INQUIRY OF MABILLON ON SAINT ARBOGAST

[Col. 1001C] In the Strasbourg Breviary, Saint Arbogast is said to have been born of illustrious parentage, and therefore of noble parents, and, what is more excellent, to have been born of Christian parents . . . No more is said; and, as it is stated at the beginning of the Life itself . . . it is uncertain . . . From this it follows that nothing certain can be established concerning the time of his birth.

At length, in mature adulthood, he came from Aquitaine into Alsace, as is established by ancient sources . . . But what he first did there was so completely unknown to the tenth-century writer that he passes immediately from his journey to his episcopate, as though, by some divine nod, he had been elevated as soon as he arrived at the islands. Nevertheless, nearly all who wrote afterward understand the matter differently, assigning him a solitary life in Alsace before he occupied the see of Strasbourg.

He must indeed be said to have lived in solitude for a long time before this, if he withdrew there when Deodatus exchanged the bishopric of Nevers for the wildernesses of the Vosges, as is related in the Life of Saint Florentius in Surius under November 7 and in the Life of Saint Deodatus under January 29, where we read:

“Therefore, again and again, to blessed Deodatus, as he was attaining from Christ a hundredfold and eternal life, these men are said, above all others, to have attached themselves as companions in so great a reward: Arbogast and Florentius . . . The former led an eremitical life in the sacred forest which in the German language is called Heiligessorish, and from there was carried off to the episcopate of the city of Strasbourg.”

In his acts it is read that he occupied the chair of the Church of Strasbourg in the time of King Dagobert, by divine command. Since they did not know of a second Dagobert, they referred this to the first; but it must be referred to Dagobert II, who lived around A.D. 680 and no later. For in that year, or at the end of the preceding year, this king was killed.

[Col. 1003]

## ON THE CHURCH OF STRASBOURG

[Col. 1003] The Church of Strasbourg greatly surpasses the other Churches. We have examined its Breviary, printed in A.D. 1489. In it, for July 21, all the antiphons at Matins, Lauds, and Vespers, as well as all the lessons and responsories, are common.

[Col. 1003A] “Rejoice, noble Church, shining with the spiritual elegance of silver, which celebrates the solemn rites vowed to your father Arbogast . . . This special shepherd, our mother Ireland, sent to us . . .”

“Born of illustrious parentage, Arbogast, a native of Ireland, was sent forth like one of the rivers of paradise.”

“As his illness grew worse, foreseeing that his dissolution was approaching, he chose for himself a place of burial outside the gate.”

At the beginning of his work on Saint Arbogast, Jacob Wimpheling pronounces as follows:

[Col. 1004A] “Although I exercised the greatest care in compiling the catalogue of our bishops, I was unable to find writers who agreed in every respect. It seems to matter little in what year each one died, or how many years he presided over this see, provided that in the account of his life, character, and other deeds I do not depart from the truth that I myself have discovered.”

[Col. 1003]

## LIFE OF SAINT ARBOGAST, BISHOP OF STRASBOURG IN FIRST GERMANY, BY UTHO, ALSO BISHOP OF STRASBOURG

[In the Bollandists, June, vol. V, p. 170, from the manuscript of Saint Maximinus of Trier, collated with the manuscript of Wiblingen and with copies formerly published in print.]

### 1

[Col. 1003B] Whether antiquity has effaced the origin or manner of life of the most holy priest of Christ, Arbogast, from childhood up to his advancement to the episcopate, or whether the rarity of written sources has failed to reveal it, the matter is considered uncertain, because writing does not inform us. Yet the distinguishing marks of so great a Father, by which he was renowned in his days, with miracles shining forth, have not been wholly suppressed in silence. They have passed through the ears of the faithful and, being related by later generations, have been poured into our ears.

For they relate that in the time of King Dagobert [Note: We must understand Dagobert II]—when the holy Church was spreading far and wide the doctrine of Catholic teaching, fragrant with its sweetness, and the word of God was prospering everywhere—he came forth from Aquitaine and, by divine command, which later became evident through signs [Note: Both manuscript copies contain “which later became evident through signs” [Col. 1003D], but the printed editions omit it], occupied the chair of the Church of Strasbourg [Col. 1003C], and, having undertaken the burden of governance, ruled it for a long time with fortunate administration.

This blessed priest of Christ became so closely bound to the aforesaid king in friendly intimacy that, when he was summoned into the royal palace, he took pleasure in the king’s conversation, as though he had tasted the sweetness of honey [Note: This comparison is found in both manuscripts and in the Strasbourg Breviary, but not in the supplement to the Lombard history], and made use of his counsel.

## 2.

While both were prospering happily—one as king in his kingdom, the other as bishop in his bishopric—the envy of the enemy of the human race turned this joyful state into its opposite. For one day, when the king’s huntsmen were pursuing a wild boar in the forest as usual [Note: [Col. 1003D] This forest is situated near the place which, whether from an abundance of boars or—more probably—from the unfortunate incident of a boar’s attack, received in common speech the name Ebersheimunster, or “Monastery of the Boar.” It is a small town in the territory of the bishop of Strasbourg, situated on the river Ill, scarcely one German mile north of Schlettstadt; hence the forest itself is called Ebersheimunstermald, as Coccius testifies in *Dagobert*, chapter 15.], the king’s son also, his only child, hastened along with them in the same pursuit [Col. 1004B]. But while the others were wandering with their dogs through pathless places and various winding ways, he, left alone, unexpectedly encountered a solitary [Note: [Col. 1004D] “Solitary,” that is, a boar, as Cangius demonstrates.]. When the horse on which he was riding saw it, it was frightened, turned back from its course, and fled. The boy, wishing to restrain it with the bridle and pulling the rein more tightly toward the other side, alas, fell headlong from the saddle. Still clinging to the rein that he held in his hand, he was dragged along the ground and miserably trampled by the horse’s hooves. His attendants searched for him for a long time; when they found him crushed in this way, they lifted him with the greatest sorrow, placed him on horses, and returned home in a mournful funeral procession. Hence the report arose that he had been struck by a boar [Note: [Col. 1004D] Thus both of our manuscripts read; but the printed editions have removed this remark.].

## 3.

When this news resounded in the king’s palace [Note: [Col. 1004D] The royal residence of Dagobert II was at Kirchem, not far from Molsheim, which the river Bruche watered.], no one can describe how great a gathering of men and women, and how great a lamentation, filled the royal halls, the streets, the fields, and every place where the news was heard [Col. 1004C] [Note: [Col. 1004D] The passage that follows, up to “Meanwhile the boy,” is found in both of our manuscripts, but is absent from the printed Life.]. For not only in the neighboring regions, but in every province where such a disaster was heard of, the greatest grief and astonishment seized everyone. All the chief dignitaries of the kingdom, struck by the same sorrow and rendered powerless by the king’s despair, were themselves in despair, wondering what they should do or in what they could place their hope for the kingdom. For the heir of the kingdom and its entire hope seemed to have been extinguished.

Meanwhile, the boy was placed in bed and the following day was deprived of his present life. As they considered what should be done in such a shock [Col. 1005A], and how they might ease the king’s grief, they finally arrived at the counsel of suggesting that the bishop be summoned to the king. The king received this proposal with the greatest devotion and, immediately sending messengers, asked that the bishop deign to hasten to him with all speed.

## 4.

There was no delay: they carried out the command, approached the bishop, and explained the reason for the invitation amid much mourning. When he heard of the misfortune of his friend, he was wholly shaken in spirit; weeping and groaning greatly, he summoned his retinue and did not delay in hastening there. Meanwhile the king, no less impatient for the bishop’s arrival, went out and, seeing the old man hurrying from a distance, ran to meet him with streaming tears and covered head, surrounded by many companions who were also weeping. As they prepared to greet one another in their customary manner [Col. 1005B], their voices stuck in their throats because of their excessive grief of heart. No one could know how many tears flowed from either side. At last, after a long interval, when they had had their fill of mourning [Note: [Col. 1005D] The passage that follows, up to “How,” is absent from the printed Life; nevertheless, our manuscript copies agree with one another here.], they wiped their eyes and rushed into embraces while their friends greeted them.

The bishop went forward to prayer, and the king followed at a distance with his attendants. The queen too, having learned of the holy man’s arrival, like Martha or Mary on behalf of her brother, her tears pouring forth and sobs shaking her breast, lowered her face in modest shame and fell at the bishop’s knees to plead for her son. He gently raised her with his hand, and, understanding very well what her sobs were imploring, did not ask what she wanted.

## 5.

Finally, fasting, he immediately entered the church and spent the night in prayer, intending to beseech the Lord for the boy [Col. 1005C]. How he prayed, or with what words, is not clear; but what he obtained is not hidden. For when his prayer was finished, at the dawn of the coming day, when the deepest sleep commonly overtakes mortals, he entered slowly to the boy. Having sent away everyone who was keeping vigil over the funeral rites [Note: [Col. 1005D] Thus the manuscripts agree; but in the printed Acts the passage that follows, up to “having sent away everyone,” is absent.], he fell upon his knees and entrusted himself to the protection of blessed Mary, so that she who had given life might obtain life for the boy from her Son [Note: [Col. 1005D] From this point to the beginning of the following section, much is omitted in the printed editions, and some matters are also varied; nevertheless, the manuscript copies agree.]. For otherwise he had not dared to attempt such a thing, unless she had deigned to invoke the Lord on his behalf. What else could he do? Trembling between hope and fear, he awaited the desired aid with urgent prayer.

The merciful Physician did not delay his servant, but, as is customary, bestowed a remedy upon those who thus hope in him. For while he was praying, the boy, as though awakened from a deep sleep, raised his head; he was astonished, uncertain whether he was dreaming or awake. When the saint therefore recognized the fulfillment of his fixed hope in God, he approached joyfully, raised the boy alive, summoned the officials, and ordered them to remove the funeral garments from him and clothe him in the royal garments he had worn before.

## 6.

Those who were present for this service could no longer restrain their cry of joy; it burst forth freely, and they filled the courtyard and the entire royal palace with the loudest shouting. Everyone, roused from sleep, ran here and there, unaware of the cause of so great a sound. The king himself, who was then taking only a little sleep for the first time—for he had lain awake and exceedingly sorrowful throughout the night—was terrified and hurried into the chamber from which such a tumult had arisen. How great a joy beat within his heart is shown by the tears he shed for gladness when he saw reviving the one for whom he himself had desired to die if only he could receive him back.

The mother was summoned and hastened to the feet of so great a man, because her sorrowful heart was comforted by seeing her son alive. All who had gathered to mourn the funeral were likewise filled with joy and hastened to marvel at the boy’s rising [Col. 1006B], each hurrying to go to the others.

## 7.

The king therefore conferred with the queen about how he might reward the bishop, who had bestowed such great benefits upon them, lest he delay the bishop’s return home or cause him to be praised by the eager people. He ordered that gold, silver, and whatever desirable and honorable gifts they could find in the treasuries fit for a king’s offering should be presented with the greatest gratitude, humbly begging the bishop to accept them.

The holy man, however, refused to accept them and said:

“If you desire to offer something to God in thanksgiving, you can enlarge the estate of the church of the blessed Mother of Christ, in order to increase God’s service, since by her merits you have received your son alive. Extend its boundaries, which are narrow for so great a service, by some portion of your kingdom, so that it may be held in usufruct by those who serve the Lord there, if this pleases your royal majesty. For this is a firmer and more lasting means of obtaining blessedness for you, your preceding ancestors, and your future descendants than gold, which delights the eyes when it is seen but grieves the heart when it has been lost.”

## 8.

The king gladly embraced the bishop’s proposal. “Where,” he said, “shall we be able to find a place suitable for serving the Mother of the heavenly King, to whom all things in heaven and on earth belong?”

As he turned these matters over in his mind and cast his thoughts throughout Alsace, wondering whether some place might be found suitable for so great a donation, the town of Rubiacum came to mind [Note: [Col. 1005D] Commonly Rufach; concerning it, see Coccius in *Dagobert*, chapter 21, where he also discusses the parish church dedicated to Saint Arbogast.]. It was exceedingly rich in every resource: pleasant fields, open country, forests, waters, buildings, and inhabitants. It seemed suitable as a dowry for the supreme Queen [Col. 1006D].

The king did not delay. Having at last found what he desired, he immediately summoned the chancellor [Note: [Col. 1006D] “Having immediately summoned the chancellor” is absent from the printed Life, but is found in both of our manuscript copies. Although the word *cancellarius* was scarcely yet in use at that time, it is reasonable to suppose that our author wrote it in order to designate, by a title customary and familiar in his own age, an office that had previously borne another name, now obsolete.]. In the presence of his nobles, who approved so good a plan, he drew up a charter stipulating that Rubiacum, with all its dependencies and adjoining territories belonging to it, including its villages [Col. 1007A], should from that time forward, wholly and integrally, be under the dominion of the holy Church of Strasbourg, which serves Mary, the Mother of God [Note: [Col. 1007B] The cathedral church of Strasbourg was already consecrated to the Mother of God; yet it was not then as magnificent as it is now. See Guillimann, chapter 9, and Morianus in the German-language *Topography of Alsace*, p. 37.], secured by a firm and indissoluble stipulation.

Enriched by this noble gift, the bishop took leave of the king and returned to his own place. After summoning the clergy, the company of soldiers, and the assembly of the people, while all stood by and watched, he placed the accepted charter upon the consecrated altar erected in honor of Saint Mary.

## 9.

Afterward he lived for many years [Note: [Col. 1007B] That is, approximately eight years, as stated in the commentary.], distinguished by holy virtues. Of these, we have judged one miracle, greatly beneficial to the faithful, worthy of being inserted in this work.

It is said that, on the side of the river called the Bruche, which comes down from the Vosges forest [Note: [Col. 1007B] The printed editions have *Bruyscha*; the Wibling manuscript has *Brusen*. In the vernacular it is called Breusch, and in Latin *Bruschius* and *Brucha*. It is a famous river of Alsace which, near Strasbourg, joins the Ill—also called Ell or Elsa—the principal river of Alsace, from which the region takes its name. After the confluence it retains its own name until it empties into the Rhine.], where that river mingles with the river Ill, whose channel runs through Alsace to that point [Col. 1007B], he ordered a small wooden oratory to be built for himself. He would cross the river there in the silence of night, so that he might devote himself more privately to prayer and extend his mind more broadly in divine contemplation.

[Col. 1008A] At times, when he found no boat, he crossed the river on dry feet; after completing his prayer, he returned, walking again upon the water. Thus living a religious life, he cared for people oppressed in various ways, drove demons from possessed bodies, reconciled those who were at odds, and proved a useful governor to each according to the measure of his need.

## 10.

When he sensed that his final day was approaching, he ordered that a burial place be prepared for him on the hill near the city, outside the city, where the church of Saint Michael stands [Note: [Col. 1008B] That hill, with the chapel of Saint Michael upon it, is now within the city walls, as stated in the commentary.], and that he be carried there and buried, imitating Christ the Savior, who chose a tomb for himself outside the gate [Note: [Col. 1008B] The passage that follows is found only in the Trier manuscript.].

After many years, however, he was transferred from there and carried to the monastery of Suburca, where he was honorably buried. There, even now, as those who serve God labor, he bestows many benefits as their patron, amid hymns and praises, with the grace of Christ accompanying him—to whom be honor and glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## In the Year of Our Lord 965. Wibold, Bishop of Cambrai

[Col. 1007]

## Historical Notice

(*Chronicle of Cambrai*, by Balderic. See below the notes of D. Leglay, the latest editor of this Chronicle.)

Wibold, archdeacon of the Church of Noyon, a man sufficiently versed in both secular and ecclesiastical disciplines, was consecrated bishop of Cambrai in the year 965. For the clerics who loved games of chance he ingeniously devised a regulated game, so that, exercising themselves in the schools, they might become accustomed to overcoming vices through charity and might shun secular and quarrelsome gambling. He begins the game in this way:

[Col. 1007]

## [Clerical Game]

I. II. Charity; III. I. I. II. Faith; IIII. I. I. III. Hope; V. I. I. IIII. Justice; VI. I. I. V. Prudence; VII. I. I. VI. Temperance; VIII. I. II. II. Fortitude; V. I. II. III. Peace; VI. I. II. IIII. Chastity; VII. I. II. V. Mercy; VIII. I. II. VI. Obedience; VIIII. I. III. III. Fear; VII. I. III. IIII. Providence; VIII. I. III. V. Discernment; IX. I. III. VI. Perseverance; X. I. IIII. IIII. Goodness; IX. I. IIII. V. Modesty; X. I. IIII. VI. Longanimity; XI. I. V. V. Gentleness; XI. I. V. VI. Kindness; XII. I. VI. VI. Wisdom; XIII. II. II. II. Compunction; VI. II. II. III. Joy; VII. II. II. IIII. Sobriety; VIIII. II. II. V. Delight; IX. II. II. VI. Sweetness; X. II. III. III. Cunning; VIII. II. III. IIII. Simplicity; IX. II. III. V. Hospitality; X. II. III. VI. Thrift; XI. II. IIII. IIII. Patience; X. II. IIII. V. Zeal; XI. II. IIII. VI. Poverty; XII. II. V. V. Mildness; XII. II. V. VI. Virginity; XIII. II. VI. VI. Reverence; XIIII. III. III. III. Piety; VIIII. III. III. IIII. Indulgence; X. III. III. V. Prayer; XI. III. III. VI. Love; XII. III. IIII. IIII. Judgment; XI. III. IIII. V. Vigilance; XII. III. IV. VI. Mortification; XIII. III. V. V. Innocence; XIII. III. V. VI. Contrition; XIIII. III. VI. VI. Confession; XV. IV. IV. IV. Maturity; XII. IV. IV. V. Solicitude; XIII. IV. IV. VI. Constancy; XIV. IV. V. V. Understanding; XIV. IV. V. VI. Sighing; XV. IV. VI. VI. Weeping; XVI. V. V. V. Cheerfulness; XV. V. V. VI. Compassion; XVI. V. VI. VI. Continence; XVII. VI. VI. VI. Humility. XVIII.

“*Cleros* is called *sors* in Latin; hence *cleronomia*, inheritance, and *cleronomus*, heir. Thus clerics are so called because they belong to the lot of the Lord. *Canon* is Greek; in Latin, *regula*, a rule. From it regular canons receive their name. Therefore, since the same canon forbids clerics to be gamblers—for gambling was discovered and wrongly used by the faithless and those lacking hope of good—and since it forbids discord, perjury, and other vices, it is entirely fitting that, abandoning vices, they should each obtain virtues for themselves by lot, with exactness.

“Accordingly, from the same game of chance of which we have spoken, let us compose a clerical game, or, so to speak, a regulated one—not for the sake of mocking anyone, but for the sake of exercise. No one who understands the words of the Gospel, ‘On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets’ (Matthew 22:40), can fail to know that charity holds primacy over all the virtues. Where such profundity resides, it produces from itself a vast and most fruitful offspring of virtues.

“Let us therefore place charity, named together with its many offspring, and assign to each individual one numbers suitable to the lots by such an arrangement that what is contained here cannot be found by examining that, nor what is displayed there be discovered here as permissible [sic]. Beginning from the principal virtue, and proceeding through two and the remaining numbers up to six, with their own threefold revolution and that of the others, let it contain twenty children of the holy Mother and terminate in wisdom.

“After this, beginning with two at compunction, let it contain fifteen virtues of the same series, ending in reverence; then let three, beginning with piety, contain ten acts of confession; likewise, let four, beginning with maturity, contain six forms of weeping; and let five, embracing three beginning with cheerfulness, be closed by continence.

“Let six, the final number, like the first, rejoice in simplicity and possess humility as guardian of the virtues. These joined together make fifty-six. If we examine the matter more carefully, we shall see that this progression of numbers, rising from three to eight, assigns to itself the virtues belonging to each number. The first, the second, the last, and the next-to-last each receive one; the third and the second-from-last receive three. Those within them likewise, from beginning and end toward the four middle numbers, receive respectively three, four, or five virtues, and always express among themselves the twenty-first number.

“Thus three, four, seventeen, and eighteen each measure one virtue: charity, faith, continence, and humility. Five and sixteen measure two: hope and fortitude; weeping and compassion. Six and fifteen measure three: justice, peace, and compunction; confession, sighing, and cheerfulness. Seven and fourteen measure four: prudence, chastity, fear, and joy; reverence, contrition, constancy, and understanding. Eight and thirteen measure five: temperance, mercy, providence, sobriety, and cunning; wisdom, virginity, mortification, innocence, and solicitude. Nine and ten, eleven and twelve, distinguish six each: obedience, discernment, goodness, delight, simplicity, and piety; perseverance, modesty, sweetness, hospitality, patience, and indulgence; longanimity, gentleness, thrift, zeal, prayer, and judgment; kindness, poverty, mildness, love, vigilance, and maturity.

“And, returning to each point: what shall we signify by three, except the name of the Trinity, which sanctifies and returns to the unity of the same beginning? What by four, except the trumpets of the four evangelists? Taken together, these display that most holy sevenfold grace, full of the gifts of the charisms. Seven doubled, with three added, makes seventeen, and with four added, eighteen. Behold how three, eight, and four return into themselves.

“We can also assign ten to the commandment of the Decalogue, which once operated under the Law and now operates under grace, and eight to the eighth age, which has not yet come. But it was more fitting to mention these three here.

“Thus, whoever loves the holy Trinity with intimate affection in the ear of his heart, and desires to preserve it to the end through the sevenfold grace, should seek the charity in which the whole Law is fulfilled; faith, without which it is impossible to please God; continence, so that he may abstain from vices and thereby be able to contain virtues; and humility, without which one who gathers virtues carries them about like dust in the wind. Having acquired them, he should strive to practice them charitably, faithfully, continently, and humbly, so that he may reach their full accumulation.

“We can join the five senses to the number five. When five is multiplied threefold and unity is added, it rises to sixteen. If we discipline these five through physics, logic, and ethics, so that we may always return to the unity of charity, which is God, we shall possess naturally, rationally, and morally the virtues that appear marked by these two numbers.

“Six, whose sixth part is one, its third two, and its half three, is a perfect number because it consists properly of its own parts; perfection of work may therefore be assigned to it. When these numbers are repeated and three is added, they make fifteen. Let us therefore be perfect in works of good action, and let us strive to climb the fifteen steps of the Psalmist, so that we may deserve to behold the holy Trinity in Zion; and, without doubt, we shall not be deprived of the virtues belonging to these numbers.

“Again, seven is present, filled with spiritual grace, and through two it brings forth fourteen. Let us therefore pray to the same Spirit to grant us passage through the practical life to the contemplative life, so that we may deserve to acquire his virtues.

“But since we stated above that the eighth age, to which the title of Psalm 6 refers when it says ‘For the end, for the octave,’ may be assigned to eight, just as ten is indicated below as present, if five are added to this number, they will explain thirteen. The five senses are also rightly subordinated to the eighth life, because, unless their pleasure-seeking appetite is now restrained by the bit and bridle of spiritual discipline, one merits neither this [life] nor those things effected from Abel’s giving of the individual robes until justice is turned into judgment and the saints possess double portions in the land [sense uncertain].

“Now nine, ten, eleven, and twelve remain at the highest level. The first shines consecrated to the nine orders of heavenly beings; the second, to the ten legal words; the third, to the worthy fruits of repentance; the fourth, to the twelve heralds of the New Testament.

“The fifth follows because, as it is written, ‘We all stumble in many ways’ (James 3:2, ‘In many things we offend all’). Whoever, going beyond the ten commandments, stumbles in the eleventh, should, adorned with the splendor of twelve jewels, increase so that the former losses of nine may be repaired; returning through the commandments of ten, let him be covered with the eleven sackcloth garments of the Church, so that one day he may say with the Psalmist: ‘You have turned my mourning into joy for me,’ and the rest (Psalm 29:12).

“Since, then, we have arranged the virtues and numbers in whatever manner we could, let us now determine how they ought to be drawn. Let us take three dice, each having six faces marked with various numbers. Let the greater six, and each of the others, be successively one less, down to the ace; together they make twenty-one. Let us also depict our five vowels—A, E, I, O, U—in their proper order, so that, repeated four times, they equal the same number. In the first, A; in the second, E; in the third, I: beginning with the ace, let each be written continuously in a straight line, and let them end at the same apex, as follows.

“Once these things have been arranged, we wish the numbers to be sought in their proper order through these three dice, as in the game mentioned above, according to what chance dictates.

“We have omitted Y, the sixth vowel and the ‘Achaean’ vowel—not only because we have no need of it in the language we now use and do not fully observe the rules of our native orthographers, but because we are aiming at brevity in the work and at a popular pastime for our own people.

“As for the consonants, since sixteen remain in the alphabet apart from Q, which grammarians call superfluous, we have not counted Q because it can easily be included here through its companion U, without which it loses the force of a letter; and the seventeenth number seemed like an intercalation for completing what we intended. Therefore, just as the vowels are placed in a square, the consonants should be inserted into one triangular pyramid having four surfaces, as follows.

“This pyramid, however, will be governed by the following rule: if even one of its lower consonants is found in the name of the virtue whose vowels have been separated, it shall count for all the others; and what the upper surface of its square displays, this lower surface, that is, its base, shall display.

“Nor is this without reason. For when the body whose parts retain a likeness to the soul is either properly adorned by its natural composition, or diminished in some part and increased by monstrous excess, it seems to possess either a complete spirit or none at all. When the spirit departs, let this lower element return to the place from which it was taken; and let the spirit return to the Lord who gave it (Ecclesiastes 12:7).

“Thus, when the dice and the triangle have been cast together and their individual letters examined, one must immediately return to the margin containing the numbers together with the virtues. When the appropriate distinction has likewise been found in the similarly threefold vowel, we must note the virtue that appears on the side; and, if we can, combine its visible vowels with the vowels, so that we may possess it privately and our fellow players may thereafter be unable to claim the same virtue for themselves in the same game.

“By such contest, playing in turn and circling around, let them divide all the virtues among themselves by lot. If they are not divided between them on equal terms, let those who surpass the others by even one virtue more rejoice that precedence over the rest has fallen to them. This condition must be observed: charity, which is twofold, is to be counted as two virtues if necessary. Because of the eclipse of one letter alone, I and A are to be examined in a second throw after the first; we forbid this to be done in every other case.

“Until the sixth hour of that day, the more eminent players, calling the less eminent their disciples, should urge them to strive to obtain through good morals the virtues that their lot lacks. The inferiors likewise, recognizing themselves as “niati” [sic] of the die, and as though [subject] to superiors [lacuna] pedagogues, must not dare to call them anything other than masters.

“But if it happens that neither can overcome the other, let both, possessing their virtues equally and in mutual relation, always be united by the same charity and rejoice in the name of brothers.

“The same game can perhaps be conducted in another way, more effective and more agreeable to some: after casting only three dice, each player may look not to the force of the elements but to the total sum taken together, and may boast that he possesses however many virtues he finds crowned with that number, as has been described above.

“We set these things before you in this manner, reader, so that, if the style requires anything, you may usefully add it or remove it by correction; but do not introduce anything blasphemous. If you do not wish to praise it, at least do not destroy it.

“If the game becomes worthless or produces weariness in the mind, let the useful arrangement of the numbers and the pleasing inquiry into the virtues at least turn the mind toward it, so that you may exercise yourself in the comparison of numbers and rejoice in the accumulation of virtues. In acquiring them, if you win, you will have no arrogance; if you are defeated, no shame. If you have obtained less, you must be obedient; if more, you must be diligent toward the obedient.

“To all who pursue these virtues in Christ and recall them in deeds and conduct, may there be grace and peace forever. Amen.”

## A dactylic poem in which the author’s name is sought

> Is the author’s name sought through numbers? First they make  
> The first, and second, and eighth, twice ten being taken;  
> Thus the ninth is inserted as the third; the fourth is two;  
> Four and ten make the fifth, and finally the sixth;  
> The eleventh is read there, the seventh twice two, and  
> The final order limits the numbers at three times six.  
> When these are brought together, the sum of contemplation is consecrated,  
> And the ten commandments shine forth, together with the virginity of the soul.  
> Whoever keeps these establishes for himself the joys of heaven.  
> This game urges the clerical company to proceed to the board,  
> So that they may be able to establish the names of the virtues.

[Col. 1013]

## D. Leglay’s Notes on Wibold’s Clerical Game

[Col. 1013A] Wibold, or Wibald, the twenty-sixth bishop of Cambrai, belonged to the family of Levin, which possessed the office of vidame of Cambrai in the eleventh and twelfth centuries and relinquished it around the year 1150, when Fulk of Levin surrendered it to the cathedral chapter. It even appears that this powerful house had well-founded claims to absolute sovereignty, since in 1007, when the emperor Saint Henry gave this county to Bishop Herluin, the vidame was required to renounce whatever rights he might have asserted there. [Col. 1013B]

In any case, Wibold, born at Cambrai around the beginning of the tenth century, was, Balderic says, versed in divine and human letters. Having entered the ecclesiastical state, he became archdeacon of Noyon. The united votes of the people and clergy called him in 965 to the episcopal see of Cambrai and Arras, which had become vacant through the death of Ausbert. The approval of the emperor Otto, who was then in Italy, was obtained without difficulty; but Wibold thought it necessary to go to that monarch in order to receive from him a kind of investiture. He made this journey [Col. 1013C] during the greatest heat of summer. The emperor received him graciously, even granting him sovereignty over the Cambresis and thereby confirming the rights of Wibold’s family.

On his return, the prelate was so exhausted and weakened that, when taking possession of his see and wishing, according to custom, to ring one of the bells of his cathedral, he could not set it in motion. This state of languor ended in death before the year had passed. He was buried in the cathedral church, to which he had left a Gospel text enriched with gold and precious stones, as well as a certain number of books collected during his journey in Italy.

Wibold was the author of an unusual literary monument entitled *Ludus regularis seu clericalis*—“The Regulated or Clerical Game”—which Balderic inserted in his *Chronicle of Cambrai and Arras*, book I, chapter 87. Our prelate devised this amusement to divert his clerics from profane games of chance and to lead them through pleasure toward the practice of virtues. The explanatory text that he attached to his game is scarcely suited to making it intelligible. George Colvener, the editor of Balderic, and Boethius Epo, both professors at the University of Douai, attempted to give a somewhat clearer idea of it; but it must be admitted that their commentary shed little light on the text. [Col. 1013D]

The essential part of the game is a board or chart displaying the names of fifty-six virtues arranged approximately like the figures in the game of the goose. The theological virtues, beginning with charity, occupy the first places; the cardinal virtues follow [Col. 1014A], and so forth. Each virtue is preceded by three numbers, the highest of which never rises above six. After the name of each virtue appears another number giving the total of the three preceding numbers. The die is cast three times, and the player who throws the three numbers corresponding to a particular virtue is obliged to work especially toward acquiring it. [Col. 1014B]

Moreover, in order to concede something to temporal advantages as well, the person to whom chance assigned the more eminent virtues enjoyed a certain superiority over his companions for that day. The game also offered other combinations governed by the letters of the alphabet. One notices in this work that Wibold was imbued with Pythagorean ideas and that, like that Greek philosopher, he attached a mysterious significance to numbers. The game he invented even bears evident relations to *Rithmomachy*, or the philosophical game of Pythagoras, concerning which Claude Boissière published an octavo treatise in 1556. The Greek terms that Wibold deliberately employs in explaining his game give reason to believe that he had some knowledge [Col. 1014C] of Homer’s language, something very rare in the tenth century.

Without pausing over the inextricable maze of this game, we shall limit ourselves here to presenting one of the three tables that Colvener appended to his notes—tables that at least offer a general idea of the manner in which Wibold seems to have intended his clerics to amuse themselves. But before indicating the purpose of this table, let us try to explain the ten verses that conclude the chapter. They constitute a kind of riddle, or rather a logogriph, which M. Peignot might have included in his curious work entitled *Philological Amusements*.

**“Onoma dactilicis actoris quaeritur ipsis / Si numeris?”**—That is: “Would one know, with the aid of numbers, the author’s name?”

**“Primum faciunt, apicemque secundum; / octavumque decem bis ducti”:** Take the twentieth letter of the alphabet, U, or rather V, to form the first, second, and eighth letters [Col. 1014D] of the word sought.

**“sicque novenis / tertius ingeritur”:** Then place the ninth letter, I, in the third position.

**“quartus hinc esse duobus”:** Let the second letter, B, be placed in the fourth position.

**“Quattuor et denis quintus”:** Let the fourteenth letter, O, come next.

**“mox denique sextus, / Undenis legitur”:** Place the letter L in the sixth position.

**“bis binis septimus”:** In the seventh position, place the fourth letter, D.

We have seen above that the letter U occupies the eighth place.

**“Limitat in numeris ter senis ultimus ordo”:** The word is completed by the eighteenth letter, S.

All of this forms the word **Wilboldus**.

**“Queis simul illatis”:** Here Wibold, returning to the numerical mysticism in which he delights, declares that the ten verses which reveal his name form a natural allusion to the ten precepts of the Decalogue and, above all, to the virtue of virginity, whose Latin name, *virginitas*, is in fact composed of ten letters.

> Admonet hic ludus tabulatum pergere clerum,  
> Nomina virtutum condere qui valeant.

“This distich does not form part of the verses that precede it. It is a kind of epilogue by which the author invites the clerics to engage in the game of virtues. The word *tabulatum* is the supine of *tabulare*, which may be interpreted as ‘to play,’ although Ducange does not give it this meaning. If medieval writers were able to use *tablizare* in this sense, there is no reason why *tabulare* should not be admitted.”

The table we have placed here presents Wibold’s game, simplified and reduced, so to speak, to its simplest expression. It is a kind of circular dial, similar to those games seen at country fairs and known as “tire-louets.” In the middle of the dial is a needle or gnomon which, set in motion by the game, stops on the name of a virtue or in an empty interval. Whoever, in a given number of turns, brings up the greatest number of virtues or the most eminent virtue is victorious. In this way of playing, neither dice nor a pyramid is needed, as in the method Wibold and Baldéric’s first annotator described so obscurely. M. Houillon published a verse tale entitled *The Game of Lord Wibold*, octavo, Cambrai, 1832.

AROUND THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 966. WILLIAM, MONK OF CHALON.

[Col. 1017]

**Narrative of William, the monk of that place, who was present, concerning the lightning by which the monastery of Saint Peter of Chalon was struck—that is, the church—under Rudolph, then abbot, on Saturday, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the year of Christ 865.**

(From Chifflet, *History of Tournus*, appendix, from a very ancient manuscript of Saint Lazarus of Autun.)

[Col. 1017A] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 965, in the eighth indiction, on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, with the moon twenty-six days old, on Saturday, after the evening solemnity had been completed and the procession finished in the oratory according to the custom of Saint Benedict, when, after the sound of the bell, we were already washing our hands for supper, the monastery of blessed Peter at Chalon was struck by lightning. The stroke occurred as follows.

While we were singing Vespers, thunder began to be heard from above, as though very far away. When the hour mentioned above had arrived, the sky suddenly thundered with an immense crash; we were all struck down by the tremendous sound, and many of us were thrown prostrate. Three flashes of lightning appeared to fall from heaven, full of fire and exceedingly terrifying. They struck these three parts of our monastery:

[Col. 1017B] the bell tower, which we country people call the *cloccarium*; the great arch of the old wall of Saint Peter, which seems to divide the brothers’ choir from the principal altar; and the ornamental candle standing upright in the very middle of that arch, before the altar.

The following parts of the tower were struck: the likeness of a cock at the top of the finial; the finial itself with all its gilding and ornaments; the roof of the tower; the middle section, that is, at two corners, with its boards, its overlying tiles, and all its nails and fastenings, ornaments, and paintings; and the two corners of the tower walls that stood above the roof of the monastery. All these things were broken, smashed, and pulverized into thousands upon thousands of tiny pieces. They were scattered and dispersed throughout the monastery, across the courtyards, through the street, as far as the bridge [Col. 1017C] by which one enters the city of Chalon, here and there in every direction and place, far and wide, just as the ash of straw is scattered and thrown about when violently snatched up by a whirlwind.

The small columns of the tower below the roof of the monastery, or below the crossbeams, and the other timbers by which they were supported, were cut and shattered, chopped and broken into pieces, as wood is cut [Col. 1018A] for making a fire, and as the finest and tiniest kindling is made for starting one, and as torches are splintered. These too were thrown and scattered throughout the monastery by the two corners of the tower.

As for the great columns, one of which still stands inside the reading stand on which the Gospel is read, it was scored from top to bottom and seemed almost split. In it we found dead coals and extinguished, shattered brands, like split torches: clear enough signs of lightning passing through, penetrating, and scattering all these things. Such was the stroke that struck the bell tower among us on the day indicated above.

The arch was struck in the following manner. [Col. 1018B] The foundation and base of the great marble column on the right side of the monastery, for those looking toward the altar, were shaken and displaced so violently that cracks appeared, looking like separations and openings between them and the rest of the masonry. The fourth corner of the foundation was entirely broken, crushed, and pulverized. The corner of the capital of the same column was likewise broken and thrown some distance away.

The stones of the arch itself were torn from its summit, broken, thrown down, and scattered across the entire pavement, around the altars of Saints Peter and Paul, throughout the choir and in front of it. The largest fragments were a foot in length and breadth and a palm in height; the remaining fragments were reduced to dust. Their size was beyond comprehension and their number innumerable, like sand and dust.

[Col. 1018C] After the stroke had accomplished all this, it moved across to the opposite wall. It did not touch the other marble column of the arch at all, but shook and shattered the wall so violently that it opened a gap and fissure between that wall and the arch. Penetrating the shaken wall, it rushed as far as the tomb of Lord Ardrad, bishop, [Col. 1019A] where it seemed to set a limit to its devastation and wished to come to rest. It struck and displaced the tomb so violently that, at the slightest touch, the loosened stones came apart and fell. Such was the manner of the arch’s being struck.

The ornamental candle too was struck, as has been said. It was not truly a candle, since it had not been made solidly of wax: it was wooden, but covered and fashioned with wax, dyed in various colors, of different sizes and of unlike shapes, and decorated as though with flowers. It was a large wooden pole of considerable height, with four crowns attached around it, separated by equal spaces [according to the maker’s design]. From the middle of each of the four spaces between the crowns extended a rod, resembling a branch. [Col. 1019B] All these parts were wooden, not waxen, though covered with wax and entirely clothed with representations of flowers, as was the whole pole. The candle was struck as follows.

The largest crown, which was near its base, was broken and completely pulverized, together with all its paintings and colors. Likewise, all the flowers on the branches above it were crushed and reduced to fragments. Of the other crowns and branches, and of the entire pole, only as much remained as is shown quite clearly; and one can see with what furious violence all the other despised and cast-off pieces, which appear to have perished in the present destruction of this candle, were scattered. Thus was the striking of the candle completed.

While all the things just described were being destroyed, [Col. 1019C] the entire monastery was filled with smoke of such dense thickness that no sharpness of eye could penetrate it, until the crash and the flashing lightning had ceased. We all thought that we were going to die, and no one dared move from the place where he stood, although he had not fallen; such trembling and fear had come upon everyone.

After the end of the crash and the flashing lightning, we all ran toward the monastery, wishing—though scarcely alive—to see what had happened inside. When we reached the doorway, we did not dare go farther. We saw that everything was filled with smoke, and, seeing nothing else because of the smoke, we cried out to one another that the whole monastery was being devoured by a hidden fire. We sensed an odor and stench of fire such as is usually perceived in ashes left by a great conflagration. [Col. 1019D] For this reason we did not dare advance farther, lest, encountering a fire we could not see, we should be swallowed up by it. We therefore ran back outside and watched the roof of the church, in case we might somehow see a flame revealing itself above.

At this point the father of the monastery, Lord Abbot Rudolph, rushing from his dwelling and boldly passing through the entire danger, ran through the middle of the monastery toward us with the brothers who happened to be with him. We were standing there weeping and mourning the destruction of the place. He cried out and said:

“Run back, brothers, run back into the monastery, and strive with all your strength, laboring to extinguish the fire; at least rescue something from the whole.”

[Col. 1020A] We therefore ran back to the doorway of the monastery with him. He himself began the antiphon:

“An angel stood at the Lord’s tomb, saying to us…”

For we did not know that a place where this antiphon was sung could perish in such danger. After it had been repeated three times, and scarcely brought to an end—for our lips were trembling, and fear had almost entirely drained the strength from our hearts and bodies—we could truly confess of ourselves what we sing as having been written of others older than we:

“Our soul was wasting away amid evils; we were troubled and shaken like a drunkard, and all wisdom was swallowed up.”

Good Lord Jesus, you know that I confess the truth: before you granted us victory, Lord Abbot began this antiphon many times, and none of us was ever able to reach its end. But after this was granted, and [Col. 1020B] after the antiphon had finally been sung three times as stated, the cloud grew thin, the smoke began to disappear, and the dust settled. Until then these three had been carried about together, and their darkness had blinded the whole monastery. As it became thinner, the brothers cried out that perhaps the hidden fire was still lurking above in the beams. They climbed up with all haste and shouted that nothing at all was there. When we heard this, reassured, we all left the church.

Then, while some of us stood and others sat down, the lord abbot spoke as follows:

“We have seen most plainly, brothers, the anger of the Lord upon us and his kindled fury. He is angry with us because of our sins. Therefore let each one of us return to his heart and see there what he is doing or has done. [Col. 1020C] Let us approach his presence in confession. Come, let us repent, adore, fall prostrate, and weep before the Lord who made us. Let us sing to him the seven penitential psalms, and while singing beseech him not to rebuke us in his anger or consume us by chastising us in his fury. Let us invoke his saints to help us. Let us also give thanks, because he has shown his people hard things, given us to drink of the wine of remorse, and has not yet consumed us. Rather, he has given those who fear him a sign, so that we may flee from the face of the bow—that is, from the universal and dreadful judgment—and be delivered, as his beloved.”

With these words he brought his speech to an end. Carrying all this out in deeds, with all of us prostrate before the altar of blessed Mary, ever-virgin, and her companions, each of us returned to and undertook [Col. 1020D] the task on which he had previously been engaged. Yet our spirit, speech, gait, and every movement of our bodies were such as is usual among people scarcely rescued from the danger of death after great labor and exhaustion, who have suffered the greatest losses or bereavements of their loved ones, friends, or possessions. Everything we did was trembling, groaning, mourning, and languishing.

Such was the whole beginning, middle, and end of this danger, and everything noted above that occurred among us. Now I beseech whoever has deigned to read this not to think that it was written by me, the sinner called Wido, without purpose. If he is filled with charity, he has here something from which to rejoice, something from which to fear, and something for which to give thanks. [Col. 1021A] Let him rejoice for us, because we were delivered; let him fear for himself, lest he perish in such things; and let him give thanks to the Lord God, who delivered us and who can rescue him from such dangers and from [Col. 1022A] all others. But whoever lacks charity will neither rejoice for us, nor provide for himself, nor please the Lord God by giving thanks.
